Zhao, Lei, et al. “SpineRegNet: Spine Registration Network for volumetric MR and CT image by the joint estimation of an affine-elastic deformation field. “ Medical Image Analysis 86 (2023): 102786.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.This paper transcends the limitations of traditional SAM, which relies solely on point or box prompts. The proposed method ingeniously integrates high-level clinical semantics and anatomical topological relationships extracted by large language models (LLMs) with traditional atlas shape priors, thereby forming a structurally complete guidance. 2.The method proposed in this paper was validated on dual cross-modality datasets (CT and T1-MRI) against highly comprehensive baselines, covering the latest Transformer, Mamba, and SAM variants, demonstrating its strong generalization capabilities. 3.The ablation studies in this paper are comprehensive in scope. Specifically, the experiments not only independently evaluate the effectiveness of the LoRA fine-tuning and the uncertainty-guided refinement module , but also conduct an in-depth comparison of various prompt fusion strategies, such as concatenation, summation, and the proposed dynamic fusion. Furthermore, this paper performs systematic combinatorial ablation tests on the hierarchical prompting mechanism, including class-level (CLS), relational-level (REL), and shape-level (SHA) prompts , while also exploring the sensitivity of the key hyper-parameter regarding the number of atlases.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The proposed dynamic fusion mechanism in the paper is overly simplistic, relying solely on simple Global Average Pooling (GAP) and Softmax for weight allocation (Equation 4). For highly heterogeneous features (textual semantics vs. spatial topology vs. morphology), such a linear weighting strategy can easily lead to feature homogenization. 2.The paper’s current “Class-Level Prompt” relies on highly templated, hard-coded text (e.g., “This CT image includes…”). Such fixed templates restrict the upper bound of the multimodal model. Directly extracting and utilizing clinical text reports, or leveraging LLM to generate pathological descriptions , would be more effective. 3.The ablation study design still contains a critical gap: the lack of cross-combinatorial validation among the three core contributions. Specifically, the authors should provide a set of progressive ablation experiments (e.g., Baseline vs. Baseline+Prompts vs. Baseline+DynamicTuning vs. Baseline+Prompts+DynamicTuning vs. Full Model) to explicitly quantify the incremental and cumulative contributions of each module within the overall framework.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The issue is significant and the application is clear: The multi-structure segmentation of the spine has practical value for preoperative planning, and the objective of the paper is clear. 2.The method combination is relatively complete: multi-level prompts, dynamic prompt tuning, and uncertainty refinement form a relatively coherent framework. 3.The experimental results are competitive: they outperform the multi-class baselines on both datasets, especially with a significant improvement in the 95HD metric. 4.The ablation experiments basically cover the core modules: the effects of LoRA, uncertainty refinement, prompt fusion methods, multi-level prompts, and the number of atlases have been verified, meeting the basic requirements within the scope of a conference paper.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The authors are encouraged to reduce broad and generic statements such as “uncertainty” and “LLM medical knowledge,” and instead focus the core motivation on the main issue: single-level prompting lacks anatomy-aware hierarchical guidance for spine segmentation. 2.The method details still need to be expressed more precisely. In Eq. (4), the definition of 𝐹𝑖𝑛 is inconsistent: in the preceding text it denotes image features, while in the equation it becomes the concatenation of prompts. It is also unclear whether the dynamic gating depends on image context. Within the limited space, the authors are advised to prioritize clarifying the symbols and data flow, otherwise the method may remain difficult to understand. 3.The practical role of the prompts needs stronger justification. The category prompts and anatomical relation prompts appear to be fixed text. If all samples share the same prompts, their information gain may be limited. The authors are advised to briefly clarify whether the prompts are fixed, whether they are designed separately for CT and MRI, and how their embeddings are aligned with image features. 4.There are concerns regarding the uncertainty module equations. In Eq. (7), the sampling form is written as 𝜇+𝜖𝜎2, whereas it is usually 𝜇+𝜖𝜎. If this is an intentional design, it should be explained. Another issue is that 𝑈𝐺𝑇 is not used in Eq. (8), but it is used in the loss, making the description of the pipeline seem somewhat abrupt. 5.The description of experimental fairness is insufficient. Since many comparison methods are included, the authors are advised to add a sentence clarifying whether all baselines were re-trained under the same data split, input size, and training protocol. For SAM-based methods, it should also be specified whether the same prompt settings were used across all methods. 6.“SPINDER” and “SPIDER” are spelled inconsistently. 7.“AHPR-Net(Our)” is recommended to be changed to “AHPR-Net (Ours)”. 8.In Table 2, the IoU improvement brought by a single prompt is not stable. The authors are advised to briefly explain this in the main text.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We sincerely thank all reviewers for their valuable comments and constructive suggestions. We appreciate the encouraging comments like “The prompt design in this paper is innovative and intuitive” of R1, “This paper transcends the limitations of traditional SAM” of R2, and “The issue is significant, and the application is clear” of R3.[R1] Q1 Computational Cost: We thank the reviewer for raising this important concern regarding computational efficiency. We agree that Monte Carlo (MC) sampling may introduce additional inference overhead compared with deterministic inference. In the future, we will include the runtime analysis. We also appreciate the reviewer’s suggestion regarding acceleration strategies. [R2] Q2 Multi-atlas pre-registration: We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comment regarding the robustness of pre-registration. We would like to clarify that the pre-registration atlas is a coarse anatomical prior to provide high-level topology guidance. The final prediction is still primarily determined by the image-driven segmentation branch. We agree that severe deformities such as scoliosis or fracture may challenge registration-based priors. In the future, we will investigate the impact of complex structures and propose reasonable solutions. [R2,R3]Q3 Cross-combinatorial ablation study: We thank the reviewer for this important suggestion. We agree that progressive cross-combinational ablation studies would better demonstrate the individual and cumulative contributions of each component. In the future, we will add additional ablation experiments. [R3]Q4 Writing issues: In our final revision, we will carefully revise the paper and correct the issues with spelling inconsistencies, repeated abbreviation definitions, and standardize the mathematical notation.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): This paper proposes AHPR-Net, a SAM-based framework for spine segmentation that integrates hierarchical multi-level prompts, including categorical semantics (via CLIP), anatomical relations (via an LLM), and multi-atlas shape priors, alongside dynamic prompt fusion and uncertainty-guided refinement. Reviewers agree that the paper addresses a clinically relevant and technically challenging problem, and that the integration of multi-level cues within a unified framework represents a meaningful advance over conventional SAM prompting strategies (R1–R3). The reported performance across both CT and MRI datasets is strong, and the breadth of comparisons is generally viewed as comprehensive (R2, R3). A key strength highlighted across reviews is the effective combination of heterogeneous information sources. In particular, the use of LLM-derived anatomical relationships and atlas-based priors to complement visual features is seen as a promising cross-modal direction (R1, R2), while the dynamic prompt tuning mechanism is considered more principled than simple feature concatenation. The uncertainty-guided refinement module is also viewed positively for improving boundary quality (R1, R3), and the ablation studies are broadly adequate in assessing individual components such as prompt types and fusion strategies (R2, R3). However, several concerns remain. The design of certain components appears relatively simple or insufficiently justified—for instance, the GAP + softmax-based fusion may be too limited for heterogeneous features (R2), and the actual contribution of prompts is unclear if they rely on fixed templates (R2, R3). There are also issues with methodological clarity, including inconsistent notation and unclear formulations (R3), as well as gaps in experimental reporting, such as missing progressive ablations and limited discussion of fairness across baselines (R2, R3). Practical considerations, including computational overhead from Monte Carlo sampling and robustness of atlas registration in pathological cases, are also underexplored (R1). Most of these concerns are likely to be addressable prior to the camera-ready version. Overall, the work is viewed positively by all three reviewers, and I recommend provisional acceptance.

title: ALFA: Biplanar X-Ray Reconstruction via Anatomy-Latent Field Adaptation
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.Methodological novelty: Decoupling anatomical priors from imaging geometry is a principled departure from geometry-coupled black-box mappings, enabling plug-and-play generalization. 2.Clinical relevance: Preserving patient-specific deformities rather than producing “mean-shape” hallucinations addresses a critical limitation for orthodontic and surgical planning. 3.Strong zero-shot demonstration: The three-scenario experimental design (identical, cross-geometry, mixed-condition) convincingly shows geometry-agnostic performance. 4.Robustness validation: Stress tests under scattering, noise, and misalignment (Fig. 5) meaningfully extend beyond clean-data evaluations.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.Resolution-agnostic claim not validated: While INR-based methods are theoretically resolution-agnostic, the paper provides no experiments at different resolutions (e. g. , 64^3, 128^3, 256^3) to empirically support this claim. 2.Missing efficiency metrics: No runtime comparison against baselines, no memory footprint analysis, and no parameter count for ALFA vs. competitors. This is essential for a 3D reconstruction method claiming clinical viability. 3.Lack of ablation studies: Critical design choices are not ablated including latent vector dimension, INR depth/width, number of positional encoding bands, and most critically the number of sampling points for ray rendering, which is not even stated, severely hampering reproducibility. 4.Limited baselines and simulated data only: Only two older baselines (X2CT-GAN, PerX2CT) are compared diffusion-based methods and Swin-X2S are absent. All experiments use simulated X-rays from CT, not real acquisitions.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The proposed framework introduces a clear separation between anatomical prior learning and physical consistency modeling, which enables zero-shot generalization across different acquisition geometries. 2.The use of INR as a frozen anatomical prior is well-motivated, allowing the model to focus on geometry-specific adaptation during inference, which improves robustness to geometric variations. 3.The method demonstrates strong robustness to noise and scattering, which is important for real-world deployment.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.Limited discussion of clinical relevance of geometric variability: While the method emphasizes robustness to varying geometries (e.g., different SIDs), the clinical motivation for such variability is not sufficiently explained. It would be helpful to clarify in which real-world scenarios such variations occur and why zero-shot adaptation is necessary. 2.Potential issue in experimental setup (Section 3, S3 Mixed-Condition Robustness): The authors state that baselines are trained on mixed geometries including parallel-beam with different SIDs (800/1200 mm). However, under parallel-beam geometry, changing SID does not affect the imaging formation, making this setting questionable and potentially unfair or misleading. 3.Loss of high-frequency details compared to baseline: In Fig. 2, ALFA shows improved reconstruction in certain regions (e.g., sagittal view, underbite and deep overbite cases). However, globally the results appear smoother compared to PerX2CT, suggesting a loss of high-frequency details. It would be important for the authors to discuss: oWhy the method appears globally smoother, oWhy certain local regions still benefit despite the overall smoothing effect.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The problem setting is meaningful, as the paper directly targets generalization across imaging geometries rather than only fixed-geometry 2D-to-3D regression. 2.The method is conceptually clean, separating anatomical prior learning from physics-guided test-time adaptation. 3.Under the authors’ experimental setup, ALFA consistently outperforms X2CT-GAN and PerX2CT in S1, S2, and S3, with particularly strong stability in the unseen-geometry S2 setting, suggesting good geometry robustness in simulation.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The paper makes strong claims about clinical feasibility, but the experiments are limited to simulated biplanar X-rays. 2.The evaluation is somewhat narrow, and it is not fully clear how much of the gain comes from the learned prior versus test-time geometry adaptation. 3.The pathology-preservation claim is supported mainly by qualitative results and global metrics, without stronger pathology-specific analysis.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We sincerely thank the reviewers for recognizing ALFA’s conceptually clean framework, zero-shot generalization, and robustness. Below we address your concerns: 1.Imaging Physics & Setup (R2) We agree that changing SID in parallel beams does not affect image formation and apologize for the ambiguous phrasing in Sec 3.2.To clarify: we did NOT vary SID for parallel beams. The S3 dataset simply merges three distinct subsets: (1) pure parallel-beam, (2) cone-beam (SID=800mm), and (3) cone-beam (SID=1200mm). Supervised baselines were trained on this mixed dataset solely to test their robustness to dataset-level geometric variance. No physical laws were violated, and we will explicitly clarify this. 2.Clinical Motivation & Simulated Data (R1, R2, R3) Motivation (R2): In multi-center settings, SIDs vary widely (e.g., 1000-1800mm) due to vendor differences or patient positioning, causing end-to-end models to fail catastrophically. ALFA provides a zero-shot, plug-and-play solution across heterogeneous clinics. Simulated Data (R1, R3): Acquiring paired biplanar X-rays and 3D CTs in identical poses is practically infeasible due to radiation hazards, making high-fidelity DRRs the standard benchmark. Crucially, baselines require paired data, whereas ALFA only needs unpaired CTs to learn the prior, ensuring high scalability to real clinical X-rays. 3.Efficiency & Multi-resolution (R1) ALFA is highly lightweight (only 15.3M parameters). Inference via Test-Time Optimization (TTO) takes ~15s/case, which is a clinically acceptable overhead for pre-operative planning where accuracy is paramount. While we omitted multi-resolution results due to space limits, this is a proven inherent advantage of INR-based methods, which we will detail in future work. 4.Pathology Metrics (R3) We agree that specialized pathological metrics provide deeper quantitative insights. Currently, our PSNR and SSIM metrics capture global similarity and reflect morphological distortions from pathologies. We will incorporate more specialized, in-depth quantitative pathological analyses in our subsequent work. 5.Smoothness vs. Topological Correctness (R2) ALFA appears smoother due to the “spectral bias” of INRs, which prioritizes fitting low-frequency structural topologies over high-frequency noise. End-to-end models (e.g., X2CT-GAN) hallucinate sharp but anatomically incorrect average teeth. ALFA trades high-frequency texture for topological faithfulness, ensuring that critical macro-level deformations (e.g., underbite/overbite) are strictly and anatomically valid. 6.Hyperparameters & Baselines (R1) Hyperparameters: During training, we randomly sample 51,200 points/subject per epoch. For rendering, we sample 1,024 rays/epoch and 128 points/ray to match real resolution. We will conduct detailed ablation experiments on the components and settings of the model in subsequent work. Baselines: Swin-X2S and Diffusion methods target meshes/segmentations or lack open-source paired training scripts for our volumetric setup. ALFA’s core contribution is the decoupled paradigm; future advanced priors (e.g., diffusion) can seamlessly replace INRs within our framework. 7.Source of Gain: Prior vs. TTO (R3) Both are indispensable. Without the learned prior, TTO is a severely ill-posed 2D-to-3D optimization, causing massive ray-aliasing artifacts. Without physics-guided TTO, performance drops drastically on unseen SIDs (matching S2 baseline failures). ALFA’s gain stems from restricting physical TTO strictly within the valid anatomical manifold defined by the prior.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): This paper introduces ALFA, a decoupled framework for biplanar X-ray 3D reconstruction that separates anatomical prior learning from test-time physics-guided adaptation. The paper received overall positive reviews with scores of 4, 3, and 4.Reviewers appreciated the clean methodological design, the focus on geometry generalization, and the strong simulated results, especially under unseen geometry and robustness settings. The main concerns are about simulation-only validation, limited efficiency/ablation analysis, and the need to better justify some experimental choices. Overall, the contribution is technically sound, relevant to MICCAI, and addresses an important reconstruction problem. I thus recommend early acceptance, and encourage the authors to address the reviewers’ concerns in the final version.

title: AMFG: Anatomy-Grounded Multi-finding Guidance for Training-Free Chest X-Ray Generation
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.AMFG guides a frozen diffusion model at inference using only publicly available pretrained models via three complementary signals. It requires no fine‑tuning or adapter training, making it easy to deploy across different base models. 2.AMFG directly addresses poor spatial calibration in CXR diffusion models by constraining cross‑attention to clinically correct regions via segmentation masks. 3.Comprehensive experiments evaluate AMFG’s generation quality through multiple complementary metrics (FID for image quality, mAUROC for finding presence, Dice and MF‑Acc for spatial localization), and demonstrate downstream clinical utility via classifier augmentation, collectively proving that AMFG improves both finding consistency and anatomical correctness.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.In latent diffusion models, x typically denotes the image, and z=enc(x) the VAE-compressed latent, with the diffusion process operating on z. While Fig. 1 and Eq. (6) use this convention correctly, Section 3.1 contains errors: it incorrectly mixes the predicted clean image x0 and zt through reversed diffusion formula​. Additionally, Section 3.2 and 3.3 use dec(x0), which is redundant since x0 should already be in pixel space. These inconsistencies may confuse readers and should be corrected. 2.Fig. 2 compares generated CXRs across methods, but no highlights (e. g. , arrows, bounding boxes, or overlaid masks) indicate where findings are correctly or incorrectly located. And it does not indicate what the baseline method is. Adding such annotations would better support the claimed advantages of AMFG.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The core insight is compelling and clearly articulated: faithful multi-finding CXR generation requires not just ensuring findings are present, but controlling where they appear and how they interact spatially. This is a real limitation of existing methods that the paper addresses head-on. The training-free design is a genuine practical advantage. By operating entirely at inference time on a frozen model, AMFG is portable across base models, which is a significant benefit over methods like XReal that require retraining adapters for each new model. This makes the approach broadly applicable. The three-component guidance framework (what/where/how) is elegant and well-motivated. Each component has a clear purpose, and the ablation study (Table 2) convincingly shows the contribution of each, with the anatomical grounding loss (L_attn) being the dominant driver. This is a clean and interpretable result. The evaluation is thoughtful. The authors introduce anatomical correctness metrics (Dice, MF-Acc) that go beyond standard FID/mAUROC, and they validate these metrics with cross-validation using an independent segmentor (PSPNet, r=0.94). The downstream classification experiment (Table 3) is particularly valuable because it connects generation quality to actual clinical utility. The paper is well-written, concise, and clearly structured. The method section is easy to follow, and the figures effectively illustrate both the approach and the results.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The Dice evaluation metric shares the same segmentation model (CheXmask) used during guidance. Although the authors address this with a PSPNet cross-validation (r=0.94), this is a correlation check, not an independence guarantee. A stronger validation would be to evaluate Dice entirely with a segmentor that was never used during generation. The current setup risks inflating Dice scores even if the cross-validation suggests otherwise. The finding-to-anatomy mapping (phi) is fixed and manually defined. The paper only demonstrates mappings for a limited set of findings, such as cardiac findings to heart and pulmonary findings to ipsilateral lung. What about findings that span multiple regions or don’t have a clear anatomical anchor (e.g., support devices, fractures)? The authors mention that such findings are guided by L_cls only, but this means the method effectively falls back to ungrounded guidance for a non-trivial subset of CXR findings. The method is evaluated on a single base model (RoentGen) and a single dataset (MIMIC-CXR). The portability claim is a central selling point, but it remains unvalidated. Demonstrating AMFG on even one additional base model (e.g., a different CXR diffusion model) would substantially strengthen the paper. The downstream classification experiment (Table 3) uses only 1,000 synthetic images for augmentation. It would be informative to see how performance scales with the number of synthetic images, and whether there is a saturation point or diminishing returns. The inference time overhead (1.3x) is reported but not broken down by component. How much of this is from the segmentor, the classifier, and the gradient computation? This matters for practical deployment.
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The methodology’s strength lies in the use of publicly available data and models to prove that a simple idea such as anatomical spatial constrains can improve models for other tasks, such as classification. The explanation of the architecture and used components for the training-free approach is solid and understandable and the experimental campaign includes varied approaches from other authors.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The non-overlap condition of the attention maps of the findings “must not excessively overlap”. This criteria is quite vague and I think it can change depending on the finding, so it needs further explanation. The evaluation metrics of Dice score brings up some doubts about the information leakage that the attention mask in the inference gives to the model, that it’s input later on is used for the classifier and it’s output GradCAM. Although the weights of these two models are not shared.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for their positive and constructive feedback. We clarify the main remaining concerns below. (1) Central contribution and novelty. We agree that individual ingredients such as classifier guidance, attention guidance, and anatomical masks have precedents. AMFG’s contribution is the clinically grounded integration of these ingredients for the what/where/how failure modes in multi-finding CXR generation without additional training. The submitted ablation shows that the classifier guidance improves finding presence but the anatomical grounding guidance drives the localization gain, and Table 3 connects this anatomical correctness to downstream utility, with the largest improvement on rare findings. Thus, the key message is that anatomical grounding, not visual realism or additional training alone, is critical for clinically useful synthetic CXR data. Consistently, AMFG outperforms the trained XReal adapter on anatomical metrics (Dice .458 vs .421; MF-Acc 42.6% vs 38.4%). (2) Dice evaluation and possible leakage. We agree that using CheXmask as the anatomical ROI source in both guidance and Dice evaluation is a limitation. However, the evaluated localization signal is not the guidance loss itself: Dice uses GradCAMs from an independent CheXpert-pretrained evaluation classifier, different from the NIH ChestX-ray14 classifier used for the classifier guidance. The PSPNet cross-validation reported in Sec. 4.2 (r=0.94, p<0.001) supports robustness to the mask source, although it is not a full independence guarantee. Importantly, the downstream classification experiment in Table 3 does not use segmentation masks at evaluation time and still shows AMFG’s largest gain, providing additional evidence that the improvement is not solely an artifact of the shared ROI source. (3) Scope of the finding-anatomy mapping and the overlap regularizer. The mapping is intentionally conservative and transparent. AMFG grounds findings only when a reliable anatomical anchor is available; findings without a single target region are guided by the classifier guidance only, as stated in Sec. 3.3.We therefore do not claim universal anatomical grounding for every CXR label; expanding the mapping via radiology knowledge graphs remains future work. Likewise, the overlap regularizer is not a hard clinical assumption that pathologies cannot co-exist or overlap in the image. It is a soft attention-space regularizer that discourages multiple finding tokens from collapsing onto the same region. The ablation also shows that the anatomical grounding guidance is the primary driver, while the finding interaction guidance provides a smaller refinement. We will clarify this wording in the camera-ready. (4) Empirical scope and presentation fixes. We agree that empirical validation currently uses one base model and one dataset, as acknowledged in Sec. 5.Our portability claim refers to AMFG being weight-preserving, requiring no base-model or adapter training, and using standard LDM interfaces, rather than completed empirical validation across CXR diffusion backbones; cross-architecture empirical validation remains future work. Systematic scaling of synthetic augmentation and per-component overhead profiling are also valuable follow-up directions. In the camera-ready, we will correct latent/image notation, running header, Figure 2 caption wording, and typographical issues. These are presentation and clarification fixes only and do not change the method, datasets, experimental protocol, evaluation protocol, or reported results.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): all reviewers agree the experiments are well thought and effective, the paper is clearly written. The remaining concerns can be addressed in rebuttal or camera-ready before acceptance

title: An Artifact-Based Agent Framework for Adaptive and Reproducible Medical Image Processing
reviewer_1_strengths: S1.The authors aim at addressing a real issue related to the clinical translation of imaging techniques; in particular the authors have conducted research and implemented pipelines on actual PACS derived data and know that there is a large difference between the benchmarks of controlled environments and the clinical dataset, which include format differences, nested archives, planning/localizer images, inconsistent naming and missing metadata. The majority of work presented at MICCAI focuses primarily on the architecture of the model; however, this paper is focused on the infrastructure level, where most of the practical failures actually occur. S2.The decision to separate the semantic design (LLM-based, probabilistic) of a system from its deterministic execution (workflow engine) is an intentional and principled approach to achieving both a degree of flexibility as well as scientific repeatability in the final application of the system. The artifact contract is the interface between the two levels of the system architecture and is a very clever method of abstraction, since it is (a) representing the state of the artifact that can be queried, (b) gathering provenance data about the artifact that can be used for auditing purposes and (c) constraining the LLM reasoning to only the structured fields of data associated with the artifact rather than the raw filenames from which the artifact was created. This will help to alleviate a true risk with the use of LLM-driven pipeline tools. S3.The decision to run fully on-premise using Ollama with a DeepSeek-R1 14B system presents a significant engineering commitment that illustrates recognition of the impact of regulatory restrictions (HIPAA/GDPR/institutional agreements) applicable to clinical imaging research/data. This is crucial to be able to use the results derived using the constructed system in other clinical areas and differentiates the work from cloud-dependent agentic systems. S4.The ablation that removed access to the artifact registry (Section 3, Table 2) provides a direct quantitative measure of the value of the artifact contract. By demonstrating that filtering query accuracy drops from 90-95% down to 10-15% when the artifact contract is removed, the authors prove the observed accuracy is a function of structured grounding rather than solely LLM capabilities. The ablation design allows for the isolation of the contribution of structured grounding when producing the observed accuracy levels. S5.The three cohorts include research CT (NLST), clinical CT (LungCaTrial) with significant heterogeneity, and research MRI (BrainICU) with moderate heterogeneity. There are 9 different workflows, covering distinct analytical goals such as data curation, segmentation, risk estimation, and harmonization. This wide range of goals supports the framework nature of the paper, while also creating an opportunity for authors to fall into a common pitfall of evaluating only one curated dataset. S6.The authors have committed to making the code and report available using Snakemake for deterministic execution, which is also a well-established and auditable tool in bioinformatics. There is 100% DAG equivalence across repeated executions under all circumstances.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: W1.Only one existing workflow adaptation tool was compared in the study. Reference works such as Snakemake and NextFlow were mentioned; however, there were no time comparisons or calibration of performance against any of these systems (including your domain expert’s manual workflow assembly) or a “proof of correct operation” using the comparison with any of these systems or as a baseline. Findings from developing correct workflows indicate that the authors should have compared their own algorithm and tooling against a small but viable source of aggregated evidence including i) traditional manual scripting in Snakemake, ii) a conventional LLM, not using an artifact contract, and not using raw file listings, and iii) a basis for comparing against a BIDS formatted Pipeline Manager, would have provided substantial evidence to establish that the Artifact Contract architecture provides the greatest benefit to the user or workflows. W2.A small sample of semantic query brands for testing the audience of the model for providing statistics. Evaluating only 20 questions per category across these datasets provides a small sample size, and lacking a description of an independent generation protocol raises concerns of confirmation bias. The authors need to establish the method used for creating the question set to show their independence and defend against confirmation bias, as the system to establish the benchmarks and created the questions were written by the authors, thus leading to the possibility of the authors subconsciously designing the questions to enable the system to correctly answer all questions, thereby providing support for the authors of the system. At a minimum, the authors of the paper must include a sufficient description of the question generation protocol to establish its independence from bias and ideally include questions authored by an independent party (a collaborating clinician or radiologist). W3.Insufficient timing, latency, and cost analyses will hinder any framework paper that possesses dynamism being able to count any definite human labor saved; without knowing how long it takes to build a workflow in the framework compared with an expert manually, what the agent latency (LLM inference time) will be, and how many tokens are required for each query, we cannot determine whether the framework provides any real increase in operational efficiency or simply a better-structured abstraction of an essentially identical performance. W4.The true ground for determining adaptability metrics consists of a single domain expert’s opinion. Each of the metrics used (Initial Rule Match (IRM), Plan Iteration (PL), and Final Output (FO)) will be made against an “expert provided ground truth. “ The professional profile, years of experience, and institutional independence of the expert are not delineated, nor is there a measure of inter-rater reliability. Multiple valid ways exist to build a medical imaging workflow (i. e. , several valid strategies will exist to enclose intensity normalization, all may work in their respective applications). Since a single-domain-expert ground truth may lead to confusion, two or more experts’ agreement would greatly increase confidence in those metrics. W5.The scalability of the rule library within this evaluation is never stated. The total number of rules within each of the analytical goals as shown in figure A/C; each will contain 11 – 20 rules for this project; there will likely be a few dozen overall; an actual clinical workflow may run in the hundreds of rules across many modalities, and retrieval/planning over a large rule library is known to degrade agent performance due to context window constraints and selection ambiguity. The paper does not discuss how the framework scales, whether the rule library would be modularized or hierarchically indexed, or how performance degrades as the rule count grows. W6.The assertion that the method is reproducible is factually correct, but somewhat exaggerated. 100% Database Access (DAG) equivalence across multiple executions is anticipated when Snakemake is given control of the execution and replicability. The fact that an agent can repeatedly create the same configuration C when the same inputs are supplied is the true novel contribution of this procedure; the agent achieves this by being programmed with a defined Non-Fuzzy Metric (NFM) and defined inputs. Therefore, the LLM’s output is based on its sampling temperature and prompt consistency and is not based on Snakemake. To clarify the above statement, it is worth noting that the DAG equivalence of results is dependent on the probabilistic planning behavior, in which all planning is predetermined. The authors do not specify the decoding temperature for DeepSeek-R1 (e. g. , T=0.0 for greedy decoding), leaving the source of the agent’s deterministic output generation ambiguous. W7.Limited variations in LLM. The document only contains references to two different local LLMs, both 14 billion LLMs: DeepSeek-R1 and Qwen. If smaller local LLMs (7 billion) or larger local LLMs (70 billion, proprietary versions of GPT-4/Claude) were to undergo testing, or if an acknowledgment of the trade-off between localized privacy and capability was indicated, this would be beneficial for clinical facilities in the selection of their infrastructure. W8.The density of the information contained in Figure 2 (system overview) is difficult to read, as it contains a complete user layer, agent layer, execution layer, rule library, memory type, skill set, and an example configuration type all within the same diagram, therefore, at the time of first review, the reader is unable to systematically read the diagram. The diagram could easily be split into two (one depicting the ‘architectural depiction’ and the other depicting the ‘workflow action type’) to provide a clearer understanding. Similarly, the example dialog in Table 1 uses “[omit to save space]” several times, which reduces the transparency of the interaction loop. W9.There is a lack of discussion of agent-side failure modes other than missing metadata. Section 3 (Adaptability) discusses that most failures result from missing or flawed DICOM metadata. This is useful knowledge, but the submission also should discuss agent-side failure modes such as hallucinating nonsensical rules, selecting conflicting rules, or failing to terminate planning. All of these failure modes can easily occur in a real-world deployment of the framework; therefore, mechanisms to address how the proposed generally-constrained design can manage them would be worthwhile to include. W10.The submission does not propose any methodological innovation for image analysis. It’s a framework/systems paper, not a new algorithm/model for a specific medical imaging application. Therefore, this may present some discomfort to reviewers in an MIC-oriented venue; however, this is actually a positive in terms of the Clinical Translation track. Authors should make it clear in the rebuttal that the intention of this submission is to be part of the Clinical Translation track, not a pure methodology track.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The use of AI agents to address “technical” clinical heterogeneity (e.g., heterogeneous data organizations) is very thoughtful Thorough problem formulation, unusual for a software tool contribution. Open-source, local execution stack including Ollama and snakemake. Broad evaluation including reproducibility, adaptability, semantic query and ablation.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Reproducibility experiments do not test DAG stability across multiple LLMs or LLM versions (e.g., DeepSeek versions) Limited discussion of related work.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: Novelty Use of Artifacts: Unlike many workflow managers that focus solely on the final output, this framework prioritizes the paper trail of intermediate results, making the entire processing pipeline transparent and queryable. It is interesting how it keeps the agents from unfounded generation The authors use ablation studies to highlight how it improves performance Formal Rigor: The authors provide a clear mathematical formulation of the framework, which adds theoretical weight to the proposed architecture. Adaptable Framework: A core strength of the framework is its ability to create workflow configurations dynamically based on specific analytical objectives and by using a modular rule library in response to user commands, heterogeneous datasets without manual reconfiguration.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Architectural Ambiguity: While the high-level theory is sound, the specific interactions between the workflow components (ex: the Knowledge, Semantic Querying, Workflow Planning Agent, Workflow Assembling Agent, and Snakemake) are underspecified. Snakemake appears to be the foundation of the framework, but how it functions or the reason for its selection is not specified. The paper lacks discussion of relevant neuroimaging workflow tools such as Nipoppy, Neurobagel or the BIDS app ecosystem, and provides no justification for the selection of Snakemake over other executors (e.g., Nextflow). Very vague language is used. In Section 2.2 Adaptation via Workflow Assembly, it is unclear what the “planning component” is or how the “inspection skill” evaluates new datasets or how a feasible goal is established. Is DeepSeek used for all the mentioned agents? Was there fine-tuning/training involved? This isn’t specified and little description is given for agents other than the Semantic Querying Agent. Deterministic Paradox: There is a fundamental tension between the deterministic claim and the use of LLMs (DeepSeek/Qwen) for semantic querying and planning. The authors do not sufficiently address how the LLM is configured to control non-determinism or whether LLM hallucinations or non-deterministic sampling could compromise the contract. While the presence of artifacts and rules are supposed to ground the LLMs in truth, it is not clear how that prevents hallucinations or a loss of reproducibility with introduction of subtle variations possibly from different computational environments Incomplete Implementation Details: Crucial information regarding computational requirements is missing and the handling of competing tools (e.g., different brain segmentation algorithms/pipelines) is missing. It is unclear how a user defines the underlying toolsets within the configuration. In brain MRI processing, multiple tools can perform the same task. It is unclear whether the framework restricts or supports specific tools, and at what level users are expected to specify them. It is also not specified whether the system relies on pre-written Snakemake wrappers or generates them dynamically. These details are not addressed in the paper. Due to the framework’s use of several LLMs and GPUs for the experiments, it would be helpful to specify what computational resources a potential user might need (GPU, memory, etc.) Nitpick: DeepSeek has been banned or is heavily regulated by some institutions. If the user isn’t legally allowed to use this model at work, is there a workaround? Minor comment: In the experiments, 2 out of the 3 datasets are not cited, so it is unclear if it is possible to obtain them in order to replicate the paper. Moreover, besides describing them as moderate/high heterogeneity, it is unclear of their composition or file layout.
reviewer_3_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We sincerely thank all three reviewers for their comments and the AC’s recommendation of early acceptance. We are especially grateful for the consistent recognition of the artifact contract, the semantic/deterministic separation, and the clinical-translation focus. This response clarifies major points raised by the AC & reviewers. 1.Determinism and stability across LLMs. Meta-Reviewer, R1 (W6), R2, R3 We appreciate this point and would like to clarify our framing. Snakemake provides DAG-level determinism once a configuration C is fixed. For a fixed C assembled by the agent, it is automatically stored as an artifact and can be re-executed to produce the exact output. This is verified in Tables 1 & 2.Independent user interaction with the agent may produce different configuration C, however, it will always check pre-existing configuration artifact. We will clarify our definition of reproducibility in the camera-ready version. 2.Related work: BIDS, Nipoppy, Neurobagel. Meta-Reviewer, R1, R3 Thank you for the suggestion. We would like to clarify that BIDS, Nipoppy, and Neurobagel are complementary standards/tools rather than alternative agent architectures, i.e., each can be registered as a rule (or set of rules) and incorporated in our modular library S (e.g., a BIDS-conversion rule, a Neurobagel-query rule). Our major contribution lies in the semantic agent layer and artifact contract that sit above such tools, i.e., prompting with users to decide which tools to use in which dataset. We will add a related-work paragraph making the complementary relationship between our work and these existing tools more explicit. 3.Report timing. Meta-Reviewer, R1 (W3) This is a very valuable comment. Due to the page limit, we will include discuss this in the Discussion; more thorough time analysis will be included in our journal extension. 4.Other comments from R1 We sincerely thank R1 for the careful reading and valuable comments on strengths and weaknesses. Several points were already in the paper but can be stated more visibly, and we will tighten them in the camera-ready: stating decoding temperature explicitly (W6); positioning the paper as Clinical Translation (W10); elaborate on Figure 2 and Table 1 dialog (W8); and briefly noting agent-side failure modes and guardrails imposed by the contract (W9). The remaining comments (additional baselines, larger independently-authored query sets, rule-library scaling, broader LLM-size sweeps; W1, W2, W5, W7) are excellent directions, and we will include them in future work due to page limit. 5.Other comments from R2 We thank R2 for the positive evaluation. The cross-LLM reproducibility and related-work are addressed above, will be reflected in the camera-ready version. 6.Other comments from R3 We sincerely thank R3 and gently clarify a few points. We will incorporate clarifications in the camera-ready. 6a) DeepSeek-R1 the open-source model and the DeepSeek App are two different things: the former is a set of model weights and architecture released publicly, while the latter is a cloud-based service (e.g., ChatGPT). In our paper, we download the weights and run inference entirely on our local GPU (Sec. 2.2). Conceptually, it is not fundamentally different from downloading a pretrained nnU-Net and running inference locally. 6b) No fine-tuning was performed on any LLM, as such fine tuning is beyond clinical computational capabilities. The framework operates by prompting & artifact-contract grounding as inference mode, consistent with the single-A6000 footprint reported in the paper. 6c) Competing tools (e.g., alternative brain-segmentation pipelines) are each registered as a separate rule in S; the agent selects among them based on goal, artifact state, and user preference upon request. We again thank the meta reviewer and all reviewers; the feedback will help us improve this and our future work.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): The paper presents a novel AI Agent with semantic planning layers on top of a deterministic medical image processing workflow engine (Snakemake) to address the issues of adapting research workflows to clinical practice, where data heterogeneity and privacy constraints limit this transition. The paper reads easily and is well-organized. The problem formulation is clear and particularly remarkable for a software tool paper. In addition, the proposed framework has been designed to address clinical constraints: open-source models and local execution to meet privacy requirements. The authors provided a deep and broad evaluation of their framework across 3 datasets, including a real-world clinical dataset, along with relevant ablations. Overall, this paper presents a strong contribution that targets an unmet need in research-to-clinics transitions. I recommend its provisional acceptance, but would still like to suggest the authors address a few concerns raised by reviewers: R1 and R3 pointed out a lack of clarity in model presentation, with only minor justifications of implementation parameters, model choices, etc. Please add a bit more detail about these. For more insights on clinical usability, provide a few metrics on computation time, assembly time vs. workflow complexity, to better highlight the benefit of the proposed framework for clinical practice. All reviewers were concerned about the non-deterministic nature of the workflow. While the authors claim that adding this semantic planning layer on top of an LLM leads to determinism and reproducible results, they should also discuss stability across multiple LLMs or versions, and how the introduction of subtle variations, possibly from different computational environments, would affect reproducibility. The paper lacks discussion about how the proposed framework compares (theoretically) to relevant neuroimaging workflow tools such as Nipoppy, Neurobagel, or the BIDS app ecosystem. I strongly advise the authors to include a statement on related work and a literature review. In any case, as stated by R1, I believe this paper falls in the scope of “Clinical translation” rather than “MIC”. Since the aforementioned comments would be critical for a method paper, its positioning as a clinical translation paper encourages me to recommend acceptance.

title: Anatomically Accurate 3D Vessel Generation via 3-Phase Chebyshev Curve Diffusion
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.Novel representing vessel centerlines as Chebyshev polynomial coefficients is an elegant choice. Chebyshev polynomials achieve minimax-optimal approximation on [−1,1], providing clear theoretical advantages over B-splines (knot-placement dependency) and Fourier bases (Gibbs phenomena at open endpoints). The K=48 expansion achieves 0.003–0.020 mm reconstruction error, far below the ~0.3 mm voxel resolution, demonstrating the compact efficiency of this representation. 2.It is very interesting for polar decomposition and three-phase diffusion. Decomposing Cartesian coefficient pairs (c_n,k, c_b,k) into magnitude r_k and angle θ_k enables diffusion in domain-appropriate spaces. The ablation study convincingly validates this design (removing polar decomposition degrades curvature Wasserstein by 11×). The decision to sample θ_k≥1 from von Mises distributions is data-driven (Pearson correlation <0.04), reflecting careful analysis of the data distribution 3.It presented the comprehensive and convincing evaluation of the method. The evaluation spans tree-level (CD), edge-level (Wasserstein distances for curvature, tortuosity, radius, tapering), physiological constraints (Murray law compliance), and statistical coverage (Bounds compliance). The improvement of Murray’s law compliance to 35–37% is particularly noteworthy for physiological plausibility. The ablation study clearly isolates each component’s contribution.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.For the presentation of topology, it is limited to tree structures. The method is constrained to binary tree topology by the Stage 1 RVAE, unable to handle loop structures (e. g. , circle of Willis) or more complex vascular networks. This severely limits generalizability. Discrete diffusion models [18,17] mentioned in related work already handle arbitrary network topologies, representing a notable regression. The authors should discuss specific technical challenges for extending to general graph topologies in more detail. 2.It somewhat unfairness of baseline comparisons. VesselGPT [8] was originally designed for cerebral vasculature, not coronary arteries, and supports only unconditional generation. Although the authors adapted it, cross-domain transfer may not represent VesselGPT’s true capabilities. VesselGPT supports only unconditional generation while this method and PartVessel use GT topology as conditioning, making qualitative comparison (Fig. 3) inherently unfair. The authors should provide more details about the adaptation and discuss its limitations. Moreover, with only two baselines (one being the foundation framework), the comparison lacks breadth. A comparison with diffusion in B-spline coefficient space, for instance, would more convincingly demonstrate the advantage of the Chebyshev representation. 3.With Stage training, the authors acknowledge a significant gap in mean bifurcation count for LCA (3.2 vs. GT 4.8), which directly affects tree-level CD and overall generation quality. However, the Stage 1 modifications are limited to auxiliary heads; the topology generation itself is not improved. Since Stage 1 topology constrains Stage 2 inputs, this upstream bottleneck may systematically limit overall quality and deserves deeper analysis. We would like to see the detail discussion about it in the revised version 4.The motivation emphasizes the value of generated vessels for segmentation training or endovascular robot simulation. While the experimental section validates no downstream applications. There is no demonstration that generated vessels improve segmentation via data augmentation, nor any evaluation of generated sample suitability in simulation environments. This leaves the practical clinical value without direct evidence. 5.Experiments are conducted only on ImageCAS coronary arteries (LCA and RCA). Given the relatively regular structure of coronary arteries (mainly binary trees), performance on more complex vascular structures such as cerebral and pulmonary vessels remains unknown. Cross-anatomical generalization is not validated.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The 3-phase Chebyshev curve diffusion and temperature-calibration mechanisms improve vessel generation, enhancing curve smoothness and mm-scale size consistency.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The use of public datasets demonstrates the performance of the proposed method in specific cases. The validation could be strengthened by further testing on synthetic data that represents extreme or challenging scenarios.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: Strengths: 1.Diffusing in Chebyshev coefficient space is genuinely new for vascular generation. Chebyshev polynomials achieve minimax-optimal approximation, giving 0.003–0.020mm reconstruction error against a 0.3mm voxel resolution using just 48 coefficients per edge. 2.Smoothness is guaranteed by the representation itself. This directly shows in results: curvature variance of 21.5 vs PartVessel’s 107.2, which nearly matches ground truth (23.9). 3.For actual medical use (surgical simulation, segmentation training), having real physical dimensions is important. Compared methods can’t be evaluated in mm at all. This method achieves within 5% error on length and 3% on radius. Using Murray’s law compliance as a metric goes beyond geometric evaluation. The improvement is substantial: 0% (PartVessel), 17% (VesselGPT), 37% (theirs), suggesting the continuous radius representation produces genuinely more physiologically plausible vessels. 5.Every component of the pipeline is individually tested, including hint nodes, polar decomposition, phase decomposition, and temperature calibration. 6.Observing that higher-order angles have near-zero correlation with conditioning (Pearson < 0.04) and sampling them from von Mises distributions rather than a diffusion model is an efficient, empirically grounded architectural choice.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Weaknesses: 1.Stage 1 (key graph generation) is unchanged and is a clear bottleneck. The paper acknowledges that Stage 1 under-generates bifurcations for LCA (mean 3.2 vs ground truth 4.8). This directly hurts CD on LCA, which the paper attributes to Stage 1 rather than curve quality. Since Stage 1 determines the overall topology of the vessel tree, leaving it unimproved limits the clinical utility of the full pipeline regardless of how good Stage 2 is. 2.Murray’s law compliance is low in absolute terms. 35-37% means roughly two out of three bifurcations violate a known physiological law. The paper frames this as a win over baselines, which it is, but the absolute number is weak for any downstream clinical application. The paper does not discuss why compliance is still so low or how it could be improved. 3.The ScaleHead is a simple and expected engineering addition. Predicting a single scalar scale factor from the root hidden state is a straightforward MLP regression task. The more interesting question is whether the scale factor could be made a direct part of the latent space or sampled from a learned distribution rather than point-estimated, which would give control over tree size at inference. As implemented, ScaleHead always predicts the same deterministic scale for a given z, limiting size diversity in generated trees. This is a limitation worth discussing that the paper does not address. 4.The VesselGPT comparison is questionable. VesselGPT was designed for cerebral vasculature and is evaluated here on the coronary arteries out of domain. Despite this disadvantage, VesselGPT outperforms the proposed method on tapering (LCA) and radius (RCA). This raises questions about how competitive the proposed method would be against VesselGPT on its intended domain and weakens the validity of the comparison overall. 5.Single dataset and single anatomy. The method is evaluated exclusively on the ImageCAS coronary artery dataset with 855/861 samples. There is no evaluation on other vessel types such as cerebral, hepatic, or pulmonary vasculature, which have different geometric and topological properties. It is unclear whether the Chebyshev representation and the 3-phase decomposition generalise beyond coronary arteries. 6.K=48 coefficients is not justified beyond reconstruction error. The paper sets K=48 based on achieving low reconstruction error but provides no analysis of the tradeoff between K and generation quality. A smaller K would mean a lower-dimensional diffusion space, potentially easier to learn. It is possible that a much smaller K would achieve similar generation quality while being simpler, but this is never investigated. 7.The paper builds heavily on PartVessel but provides only a brief and difficult to follow description of it, making the paper hard to understand without referring to the original PartVessel work. A more complete description of PartVessel would make the paper more self-contained.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and AC. To our knowledge, vessel-centerline diffusion in Chebyshev coefficient space (Section 1) is novel; polar decomposition is validated by ablation (Table 2: 11× curvature degradation when removed). All quantities derive from existing data (no new training/generation). 1.VesselGPT comparison [R1, R3]. VesselGPT (MICCAI 2025), originally evaluated on cerebral vasculature, is autoregressive; we adapt it to ImageCAS coronary arteries and, since VesselGPT supports only unconditional generation, evaluate 1,000 samples (Section 4). Across 14 cells (Table 1), ours obtains the best in 11—curvature and tortuosity Wasserstein best on both arteries; Murray’s compliance (35–37%) surpasses PartVessel (0%) and VesselGPT (15–17%). VesselGPT leads on tapering (LCA) and radius (RCA), aligned with its B-spline cross-section parameterization (Section 2); our 3-phase design trades local radius fidelity for global geometry. CD: RCA best (Ours 59.0 / PartVessel 72.8 / VesselGPT 119.9), LCA close to PartVessel (Ours 59.1 / 57.0 / 99.0); the LCA gap is from Stage-1 bifurcation undercount, not curve quality. 2.Stage-1 bifurcation undercount [R1, R3]. Stage-1 extends PartVessel’s RVAE to additionally predict degree-2 hint nodes (intermediate trajectory waypoints, Section 3.3), used to condition Stage-2’s curve generation. Removing hint nodes degrades curvature Wasserstein by 11× (Table 2). Per-tree node count rises 11.45→23.87 (LCA, +12.42) and 7.21→16.79 (RCA, +9.58); hint nodes contribute +12.42 (LCA, all) and +9.33 (RCA, ~97% of the increase). Under the same RVAE capacity, this larger prediction target likely reduces bifurcation accuracy; a diffusion-based Stage-1 is a future direction. 3.Murray’s law and GT reference [R1, R3]. Following R1, we computed GT compliance on ImageCAS: strict (±20%) = 16.6%/15.9% (LCA/RCA); loose (±50%) = 53.1%/62.4%. Held-out 163 is consistent (16.6%/17.1%). GT mean of (Σr_child³)/r_parent³ is 1.46/1.40 vs ideal 1.0—reflecting that GT radii are skeleton-derived from standard centerline-extraction preprocessing (not direct mm measurements), inherited equally by all methods. Under this preprocessing-bounded reference, our 35–37% (2.2× GT, uniformly best) represents substantial movement toward physiological plausibility; closure to ideal Murray would require advances in centerline-radius estimation itself. 4.Diversity quantification [R1]. Manifold coverage on LCA (fraction of GT 6D-feature k-means clusters reached): Ours 0.70 vs PartVessel 0.50.Raw diversity (coefficient of variation of per-edge curvature/radius/length): +14% (LCA), +59% (RCA) over PartVessel. 5.ScaleHead determinism [R3]. ScaleHead is deterministic for fixed z. By design, Stage-2 operates in normalized coordinate space (Section 3.1); mm-scale recovery is architecturally confined to Stage-1’s root latent z, not an arbitrary choice. Tree-level scale diversity arises from different z; length/radius match GT within 5%/3% (Section 4.1). Decoupling scale from z would require two-stage redesign (future direction). 6.K=48 and B-spline baseline [R3, R1]. K=48 reconstruction error (0.003–0.020 mm) is well below voxel resolution (~0.3 mm, Section 3.3). Smaller K (e.g., K=24) also yields sub-voxel reconstruction; we chose K=48 since the model handles it stably with extra precision margin (K tunable to dataset/compute). We considered B-spline coefficient diffusion: per-curve adaptive knots would add a Stage-1 prediction target—and given the Stage-1 trade-off from hint nodes (Topic 2), would likely worsen bifurcation accuracy; fixed shared knots compound a hyperparameter with K. Chebyshev avoids both via an orthogonal global basis (Section 2). Limitations. Loop-topology via graph diffusion (Section 5), downstream applications, cross-anatomy validation, and synthetic stress testing are future directions. A short Chebyshev intro and PartVessel-summary clarification fit within camera-ready limits.

title: Anatomy-Aware Hierarchical Multiple Instance Learning for Interpretable COPD Diagnosis and Phenotype Analysis
reviewer_1_strengths: Clinically grounded anatomical prior: The integration of lung lobe anatomy as a spatial prior is clinically well motivated, making the model’s reasoning more consistent with radiological practice. Clear and coherent technical presentation: The manuscript is well structured, and the method section is clearly written, making the overall model architecture easy to understand. The accompanying figures are clearly plotted for the proposed hierarchical MIL framework. Meaningful interpretability insights: The lobe level analysis adds practical interpretability by linking model attention to clinically meaningful lung regions, offering a clearer understanding of how the framework arrives at its COPD severity predictions.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Limited encoder generalization: Relying exclusively on ResNet18 prevents a fair assessment of how well the proposed MIL framework generalizes across different feature extractors. The absence of comparisons with stronger or CT specific pretrained encoders (e. g. , DenseNet121, CT-CLIP) makes it unclear whether the reported improvements are a fundamental benefit of the hierarchical framework or merely an artifact of the specific interaction with a relatively shallow ResNet18. Unclear derivation of lobe fraction vectors: The formulation of the lobe fraction vectors is insufficiently described; it remains ambiguous whether these fractions are derived from slice level area ratios. Lack of transparency in benchmarking: The inclusion of a “Hierarchical MIL” baseline in the result table did not have clear citation or detailed description.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1) Excellent clinical interpretability: This is the most significant highlight of the paper. Traditional MIL models lack anatomical constraints and operate as “black boxes.” This work cleverly utilizes anatomical priors (lobe-fraction vectors) and a gated attention mechanism to translate attention weights into clinically readable lobe-level contribution profiles. This greatly enhances the trustworthiness and transparency of the model in real-world medical scenarios. 2) Clinically aligned task modeling: Introducing an all-threshold ordinal regression head to predict the GOLD severity stage is highly logical. It aligns much better with the objective clinical reality of continuous disease progression compared to standard unordered multi-class classification. 3) Solid cross-cohort validation: Evaluated on a large-scale internal dataset (PanCan) and an independent external cohort (ECLIPSE) comprising over 4,000 scans, the model demonstrates highly consistent spatial phenotype shifts (disease contribution shifting from upper to middle/lower lobes with increasing severity). This proves the method’s strong generalization capability and biological plausibility.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1) Marginal performance improvement: While the model excels in interpretability, its improvements in core quantitative metrics (e.g., binary AUC, severity staging QWK) are very marginal compared to existing baselines like TransMIL (as shown in Table 1). It is difficult to fully justify the algorithmic superiority of the proposed framework based purely on predictive performance. 2) No code availability: The authors do not provide a link to open-source code or promise to release it. For a MICCAI-level paper proposing a novel MIL framework, the lack of code severely limits the reproducibility of the research. 3) Lack of robustness analysis for upstream segmentation errors: The framework heavily relies on pre-trained lobe segmentation masks. In advanced COPD patients (GOLD 3-4), severe emphysema often leads to blurred lung boundaries and a high risk of segmentation failure. The paper does not discuss the robustness or error propagation to downstream anatomical attention distributions when the upstream segmentation is inaccurate. 4) Insufficient ablation study: The main text lacks detailed ablation analyses to decouple the contributions of individual modules. For instance, what is the specific performance gain of the auxiliary ordinal loss on the primary binary classification task? How much does performance degrade if predicting directly without lobe-guided hierarchical aggregation? The absence of these experiments weakens the methodological necessity of the proposed architectural design.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The paper addresses a clinically relevant problem and the overall motivation is clear. The proposed framework is well organized, and incorporating lung lobe information into MIL is a reasonable and intuitive design choice. Another positive aspect is the inclusion of external validation, which makes the experimental study more convincing.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The current experimental section is still not fully sufficient to support the claimed contribution. First, the paper lacks several key ablation studies, so it remains unclear which component is actually driving the gain. Second, the interpretability claim is mainly based on attention scores, but stronger supporting evidence is still needed; for example, more direct visual analysis or case-level qualitative comparisons would make this part much more convincing. Third, the baseline comparison is not strong enough, as several recent MIL methods are missing, such as RRT and MambaMIL. Finally, although the method is competitive, the improvement over strong baselines is relatively limited, and some reported standard deviations are not small, yet there is no further stability analysis to show the robustness of the method.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank all reviewers for their constructive and thoughtful feedback. We address each point below but are not allowed to provide new results here. [R1, R2, R3] Marginal Quantitative Improvement. We agree the quantitative gains are modest. Our primary contribution is not a large jump in classification performance but the integration of lung anatomy into MIL to enable anatomically grounded interpretability and spatial phenotype analysis while maintaining high predictive performance. Notably, AnatoMIL matches a higher-complexity transformer (TransMIL) while adding clinically meaningful lobe-level contribution profiles. [R1, R2, R3] Ablation Study. While an explicit ablation table is not presented, our comparisons demonstrate the incremental benefit of two key design choices: hierarchical aggregation and anatomy-aware lobe priors. The gain from ABMIL to HierarchicalMIL reflects hierarchical pooling, while the gain from HierarchicalMIL to AnatoMIL reflects anatomical guidance. Regarding the ordinal head, its primary objective is not to improve binary AUC, but to model the clinically ordered nature of COPD progression, providing stage-aware supervision aligned with GOLD criteria and encouraging the shared embedding to reflect disease progression. [R1] Encoder Generalization. ResNet-18 was chosen as a lightweight and widely used backbone to evaluate all methods under the identical feature extraction conditions and isolate the effect of the proposed MIL aggregation strategy. Prior work by Tang et al. (Ref. [17]) showed on the same PanCan cohort that deeper ResNet variants (50/101/152) did not yield major improvements in COPD detection, suggesting encoder depth is not the primary performance driver. We agree evaluating CT-specific pretrained encoders would be valuable. [R1] HierarchicalMIL Baseline Clarification. HierarchicalMIL refers to Zhang et al. (MICCAI 2024, Ref. [25]), which introduced hierarchical aggregation for COPD grading. We will add this citation. [R1] Lobe Fraction Vector Derivation. Lobe segmentation is performed on the 3D volume. The vectors used by the MIL model are instance-level lobe fractions, computed for each selected 2D axial slice rather than as a single whole-lung 3D ratio. We will clarify this in the revision. [R2] Segmentation Robustness. This is a valid practical concern, with two mitigating factors already in the framework. First, TotalSegmentator (Ref. [20]) is a state-of-the-art segmentation model trained on large-scale CT datasets with demonstrated robustness across pathologies. Second, we use soft lobe-fraction vectors rather than hard binary slice-to-lobe assignments, making lobe representations less sensitive to imperfect segmentations. We agree explicitly analyzing severe segmentation failures is an important future direction. [R2] Code Availability. We will release the full source code upon acceptance. [R3] Missing Baselines. RRT and MambaMIL were originally developed for histopathology WSIs, where MIL bags contain much longer patch sequences than in our CT data. We expect our small bags of selected axial slices would reduce the relative advantage of long-sequence modeling architectures, but we agree evaluating additional MIL approaches would be worthwhile. [R3] Qualitative Interpretability Evidence. To propose our method, we prioritized cohort-level analyses to reveal systematic and reproducible spatial patterns generalizable across patients and independent datasets. Figure 2 demonstrates consistent lobe-level contribution patterns across GOLD stages in both cohorts, providing population-level evidence for the interpretability of the proposed framework. However, we agree case-level visualizations would complement this analysis and should be part of future work. [R3] Stability Analysis. The proposed method is similarly stable in a 5-fold CV compared to the baselines and produced similar improvements across both datasets, but we agree an explicit stability analysis should be done in extended work.

title: Anatomy-Aware Prediction of Bronchoscopic Accessibility from 3D CT
reviewer_1_strengths: The authors propose an AnatomyAware mixture-of-experts (MoE) model that integrates several specialized modules, including a CT expert for local morphological features, a lobe expert for anatomical priors, and a path geometry expert that encodes the sequential constraints of the bronchial tree.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1、The authors use mask labels in the methodology section. They should discuss whether this may introduce a risk of label leakage. In addition, the paper does not explain how the mask labels are obtained during testing. 2、The method is mainly described in words, with a lack of rigorous mathematical formulation, which makes the overall pipeline somewhat unclear. 3、There are no references from the past three years in the manuscript, which raises concerns regarding the novelty of both the research direction and the proposed method. 4、The figure uses the term “Path Expert,” whereas the main text refers to it as “Path Geometry Expert. ” This inconsistency should be corrected. 5、The manuscript does not clearly describe how the outputs of the expert modules are incorporated into the gating network.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.Most CAD work in bronchoscopy is either segmentation or planning. Predicting whether a procedure will succed from static CT affects patient triage. The paper makes a reasonable case that experts struggle with this decision. 2.The dataset contribution is the strongest. 438 cases from 3 centers with procedure outcome labels is very much valuable. 3.The path expert is the most defensible modelling choice. Converting the approach trajectory into a sequence of geometric features (and feeding it into a BiGRU) is a neat idea. The ablation shows that this module alone adds a +0.04 AUROC on top of CT alone.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The MoE framing is not defended properly. The key comparison is missing (simple concatenation of the three expert features followed by an MLP with no gating). Without this, the adaptive gating contribution cannot be separated from the decomposition itself. 2.The lobe expert adds almost noting alone (0.55 AUROC) and a marginal +0.03 in combination. A simple sanity check (concatenate a one-hot lobe vector to the CT features) is missing. If that matches the lobe expert, embedding + MLP framing is not justified. 3.Multi-center validation is not done despite having 3 centers. Pooled 5-fold CV with patient-level splits is okay, but leave-one-center-out would test whether the model generalizes across sites. 4.The dataset description misses what “success” means operationally. Is it based on the diagnostic yeild from the sample or is it a subjective call or something else? Details like per-center counts, peripheral vs central lesions breakdown, lesion size distributions, etc. can be reported. 5.The human performance comparison is hard to interpret because the aggregation protocol is not described. The metric of AUROC is computed from three probability values (mapped to the 3-level difficulty) and with atmost 3 threshold points vs. a continuous 0-1 model output, AUROC may not reflect the relevant evaluation properly. A reasonable fix is to report sensitivity and specificity at each of the 3 difficulty levels.

reviewer_3_strengths: 1.To the reviewer’s knowledge, this work is the first to formulate the supervised end-to-end bronchoscopy accessibility prediction problem. 2.The fusion of the features from three different modality(Raw CT, Lobe location, airway segmentation) 3.The quantitative performance of the proposed work over the compared state-of-the-arts method has big margin. 4.The curation of the largest dataset for bronchoscopy accessibility prediction from three clinical centers.
