title: Bridging Vision Foundation Model Priors with CLIP for Spatial-aware Few-shot Anomaly Detection in Medical Images
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The paper is well organized, and the proposed method is well motivated. 2.This paper addresses an important limitation of CLIP-based few-shot medical anomaly detection, namely weak spatial grounding despite strong semantic discrimination. 3.The proposed method shows consistent performance gains on three public datasets across multiple shot settings.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.Limited novelty: While the overall framework is reasonable and effective, the novelty of the proposed component appears moderate. The Sliding-Window Aggregation is conceptually close to prior window-based CLIP methods such as [1]. The authors should clarify more clearly what is conceptually novel beyond adapting this idea to the current medical setting. In addition, fusing CLIP and DINO features such as [2] have been popularly proposed recently. Authors should clarify their technical novelty compared to other existing methods. 2.The practical trade-offs are not discussed enough. Since the proposed method relies on overlapping local windows and additional support-memory comparison, more explicit discussion of inference cost, efficiency, and scalability would strengthen the practical significance of the method. [1] Jeong, Jongheon, et al. “WinCLIP: Zero-/Few-shot anomaly classification and segmentation. ” Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition. 2023. [2] Bi, Xiuli, et al. “SSR: Semantic and Spatial Rectification for CLIP-based Weakly Supervised Segmentation. “ Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence. Vol. 40.No. 4.2026.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.Clear problem motivation. The paper identifies a concrete and well-known limitation of CLIP-based anomaly detection — poor spatial grounding — and directly targets it with each proposed component, giving the work a coherent narrative. 2.Strong empirical gains. The improvements are substantial, particularly on LiverCT where Spatial-FAD outperforms the next best method by over 19% Dice across all shot settings, suggesting the approach addresses a genuine bottleneck. 3.Comprehensive evaluation. Experiments span three modalities (CT, OCT, MRI) and four shot settings, providing a thorough empirical picture across diverse clinical scenarios.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.Missing evaluation of DINOv3 as a standalone anomaly detector. The paper leverages DINOv3’s spatially coherent patch representations as a structural prior but never evaluates it directly on the anomaly detection task. Given its boundary-aware local-to-global training, it is non-trivial whether DINOv3 alone is already effective for lesion localization via patch-level matching or affinity-based scoring. Such an evaluation would provide important insight into how well DINOv3 transfers to medical anomaly detection in its own right. 2.Sliding-window aggregation is not applied to competing methods. Sliding-window-based feature extraction has been explored in prior anomaly detection literature [1], yet this connection is not discussed. In this work, SWA is the largest single contributor to performance (+17% Dice), but it is applied only to Spatial-FAD and not to competing CLIP-based methods such as MVFA or MadCLIP. Since SWA is a generally applicable strategy for improving spatial resolution, its exclusive use makes it difficult to determine whether the observed performance gains arise from the full Spatial-FAD design or primarily from this resolution enhancement. Applying SWA to strong baselines would help clarify the contribution of the proposed components. 3.Figure 3(b) and 3(c) are not clearly labeled. The caption does not specify which panel corresponds to normal versus abnormal prototypes. Based on x-axis ranges and implementation details this can be inferred, but should be explicitly stated to avoid ambiguity. 4.Prototype-enhanced support memory is insufficiently justified. The three-score fusion uses a fixed 1/3 average with no learned weighting, assuming equal reliability across signals of clearly different quality. More critically, since MVFA uses only normal support images, the gain from PSM could be attributed entirely to incorporating abnormal examples rather than to the prototype design itself. A controlled ablation against a dense memory bank that also includes abnormal images is needed to isolate the prototype contribution. [1] Dong, Haoyu, et al. “SWSSL: Sliding window-based self-supervised learning for anomaly detection in high-resolution images.” IEEE Transactions on Medical Imaging 42.12 (2023): 3860-3870.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The paper addresses a clear and important limitation of existing CLIP-based few-shot anomaly detection methods, namely strong image-level discrimination but weak spatial localization. The overall method is coherent and well motivated. The VFM prior, sliding-window aggregation, and prototype-based support memory are all aligned with the goal of improving lesion segmentation quality The empirical results are strong, especially in terms of Dice, and the improvements are consistent across three datasets and multiple shot settings. The qualitative results support the quantitative findings, showing clearer boundaries and more accurate localization.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The largest gain in the ablation appears to come from the sliding-window aggregation strategy, whereas the title and framing emphasize bridging VFM priors with CLIP. This makes the attribution of the main contribution somewhat less clear. The paper does not provide enough discussion of the computational and memory overhead introduced by sliding-window inference, which is important for judging both practical value and fairness of comparison. The paper would be strengthened by additional analysis showing why the proposed DINO-based affinity prior is preferable to simpler alternatives for spatial refinement or feature smoothing. The main empirical gain is clearly in segmentation quality, while the AUC improvements are more modest and not uniformly best across all dataset/shot combinations. The claims around classification performance should therefore be phrased somewhat more carefully. The ablation study is only conducted on LiverCT under the 4-shot setting. While informative, broader ablations across additional datasets or shot settings would make the conclusions about component effectiveness more convincing.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We are glad and encouraged that reviewers find our work “well-motivated” (All), “addresses an important limitation” (All), “strong empirical gains” (All), “solid” (R1), “comprehensive evaluation” (R2), and “supportive qualitative results” (R3). All the reviewers expressed positive ratings. Thanks for the constructive comments. Responses to the remaining concerns are as follows. Q1 (R1): Difference from SSR. A1: Our method differs from SSR in two main aspects: (i) the role of DINO and (ii) whether CLIP features are directly enhanced. SSR uses DINO only as a post-hoc auxiliary cue by combining DINO affinity with CLIP affinity to suppress CAM noise, without improving CLIP features themselves. In contrast, we use DINO as a structural prior during feature learning to directly enhance CLIP representations, leading to stronger spatial localization for anomaly detection. Q2 (All): Concerns on sliding-window aggregation (SWA). A2: (1) Despite SWA’s gains, the other two modules (DINO-guided fusion & PSM) constitute the core scientific contribution in this work, aiming at addressing two fundamental problems of few-shot anomaly detection: the lack of fine-grained local structural information for precise spatial localization and inefficient use of limited support data. These modules and SWA are highly complementary, as our core modules build robust and discriminative features that provide the foundation for SWA to further enhance spatial resolution and improve the final localization quality. (2) Notably, even without SWA, adding only the DINO-guided module to the baseline still brings a +15.85% Dice gain, showing that the improvement is not mainly driven by SWA. (3) For fair comparison, we also apply SWA to competing methods. With SWA, MVFA and MadCLIP achieve 48.19 and 50.61 Dice, respectively, still clearly below our 56.33, demonstrating the effectiveness and complementarity of our core modules. Q3 (R1, R3): Efficiency and scalability of our method. A3: (1) For SWA, as stated in our manuscript, we concatenate all cropped sub-images along the batch dimension, obtaining whole-image embeddings in a single forward pass. This utilizes GPU parallelism and incurs only a marginal increase in inference time: < 0.025s on an NVIDIA A40 GPU. (2) For our memory scheme, the main overhead comes from storing the memory bank and computing patch-prototype similarities. Let d be the feature dimension, m^2/n^2 the patch number per image for MVFA/ours, and n_n/n_a the normal/abnormal prototype number in our memory scheme. Under the k-shot setting, memory size comparison: MVFA:kd m^2 vs Ours:(n_n+n_a)d. Similarity FLOPs per image: MVFA:2kd m^4 vs Ours:2d(n_n+n_a)*n^2.With k=4, n_n=50, n_a=4, m=17, n=37 (typical for MVFA and ours), our memory and FLOPs are < 5% and <23% of MVFA, respectively. Also, our design is independent of the shot number k, yielding better scalability. Q4 (R2): More ablation studies on PSM. A4: Although adding abnormal images to a dense memory bank improves Dice from 53.65 to 55.38, it remains below our PSM (56.33) and incurs higher computation (See Q3). This confirms that the gain also benefits from the prototype design rather than merely adding abnormal data. For fusion weights, the fixed average already yields consistent gains, indicating our robustness without complex coefficient tuning. Additional optimization may further improve performance. Q5 (R2): Evaluation of DINOv3 as a standalone anomaly detector. A5: When frozen DINOv3 is used alone for anomaly detection via support–query patch matching, it yields only 12.43% Dice on LiverCT (4-shot). This suggests that, in the medical domain, DINOv3 may not reliably establish cross-image patch correspondences without task-specific adaptation. In contrast, within-image affinities are more reliable and can be effectively exploited by our method to improve spatial localization. Minor concerns like the Fig. 3 caption and careful claim of classification results will be carefully revised.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper proposes a coherent framework for improving spatial localization in CLIP-based few-shot medical anomaly detection and demonstrates consistent empirical gains across multiple datasets and settings. Reviewers agree that the problem is important and the overall approach is well motivated, with strengths in experimental performance and clarity of presentation. At the same time, several substantive concerns are consistently raised across reviews, including the need to better clarify novelty relative to prior CLIP+DINO and sliding-window approaches, more clearly isolate the contribution of individual components (particularly the dominant effect of sliding-window aggregation), provide deeper analysis of key design choices (e.g., DINO priors and prototype design), and discuss computational cost and fairness of comparison . Given these points, the paper is forwarded to rebuttal. Authors are encouraged to address these concerns through careful clarification, additional analysis based on existing results, and improved positioning. In accordance with conference policy, no new major experiments should be introduced; instead, rebuttal should focus on explanation, analysis, and justification. Reviewers are requested to re-evaluate the paper in light of the rebuttal. | The paper proposes a coherent framework for improving spatial localization in CLIP-based few-shot medical anomaly detection by combining vision foundation model priors with CLIP-based anomaly scoring. Reviewers recognized the importance of the problem, the practical relevance of spatial-aware anomaly detection, the generally clear presentation, and the consistent empirical performance across multiple datasets and shot settings. The initial concerns mainly related to attribution of gains, novelty relative to prior CLIP+DINO and sliding-window approaches, the role of the DINO-guided module and prototype memory design, and computational cost. The rebuttal clarified these points in a generally satisfactory manner and helped position the contribution more clearly. While the novelty remains moderate and some analyses could be strengthened in the final version, the paper presents a well-motivated and practically useful contribution. I therefore recommend acceptance. The authors should incorporate the rebuttal clarifications, more carefully discuss the contribution of each component, and explicitly acknowledge remaining limitations in the camera-ready version. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): All three reviewers recommend acceptance post-rebuttal. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The authors have provided solid and comprehensive responses in the rebuttal, satisfactorily clarifying the key technical and methodological queries raised during the review phase. Specifically, the authors have successfully articulated the core innovations of their framework over existing CLIP+DINO baseline. Crucially, they have provided compelling empirical evidence to quantify the independent contributions of individual modules; specifically, the authors demonstrated that incorporating the DINO-guided module into the baseline alone yields a 15.85% improvement in Dice similarity without relying on sliding-window aggregation, effectively proving that the performance gain is inherently driven by their core methodological design rather than the sliding-window mechanism. Furthermore, the deeper analyses regarding the DINO prior, prototype design, computational overhead, and baseline fairness have successfully resolved the remaining technical doubts. By rigorously untangling the driving forces behind the performance gains and justifying the theoretical depth of their foundation model integration, the paper delivers validated, high-impact insights to the community. In light of MICCAI policy that no new results can be added in the rebuttal phase, I have re-evaluated this paper based on its original content. The design works effectively (bringing large performance gains, as evidenced in the original manuscript), is technically sound, and the paper is easy to follow. Therefore, I recommend acceptance.

title: Calibrated Confidence Expression for Radiology Report Generation
reviewer_1_strengths: First, the paper addresses an important and timely problem, since safe deployment of radiology LVLMs requires not only good reports but also reliable uncertainty signals. Second, the proposed formulation is interesting because it moves beyond post-hoc uncertainty estimation and directly trains the model to produce interpretable verbalized confidence alongside the report. Third, the paper studies both report-level and sentence-level confidence, which is clinically meaningful because the latter can support targeted review of specific findings rather than only whole-report triage. Fourth, the experimental evaluation is fairly solid, including calibration metrics, OOD evaluation on IU-Xray, and a small clinician study showing better alignment with expert judgment. Finally, the paper presents consistent empirical gains over several baseline confidence estimation methods while largely preserving report-generation quality.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The main weakness is that the novelty is somewhat incremental rather than fully groundbreaking, because the paper extends existing lines of work on confidence calibration and uncertainty-aware radiology report generation rather than introducing a completely new paradigm. In addition, the clinical evaluation is still relatively limited, as it only involves 50 reports and 3 raters, which is useful but not yet strong enough to fully establish clinical utility. Some methodological choices also need clearer justification, such as the dependence on GREEN / Precision GREEN as the external correctness signal and whether calibration quality transfers robustly beyond that metric. Moreover, the paper focuses on calibration while intentionally not improving report quality itself, which is reasonable, but this also limits the broader practical impact of the method. Overall, these issues prevent me from rating the paper more strongly, but they do not outweigh the paper’s clear motivation, sound design, and promising empirical results.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The proposed idea is intuitive and well aligned with established practices in fully supervised learning, where calibration is explicitly incorporated into the objective function to guide the learning process and enforce reliable confidence estimates. The topic is highly relevant, as vision–language models must accurately express uncertainty to be trustworthy in real-world applications. The experimental evaluation is thorough, and the inclusion of clinical validation further strengthens the empirical assessment.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Overall, I believe the paper would benefit from deeper clarification on some aspects, outlined below. While the authors define the reward function used in their approach, a high-level introduction to GRPO would greatly aid comprehension and help establish common ground for the reader. In Section 2, the authors state that confidence score generation is formulated as a Markov Decision Process. However, this claim is not further explained or elaborated upon. Additionally, the statement that “our RL approach utilizes a continuous reward signal that respects the ordinal nature of confidence” would benefit from an explicit explanation, as its practical implications are not immediately evident. Finally, the paper would be strengthened by a more explicit discussion of how the proposed method differs from the most closely related approaches in the state of the art, which are also used as baselines. Briefly explaining the GREEN metrics would also improve the accessibility and completeness of the presentation.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: Firstly, this paper addresses the challenge of uncalibrated confidence in radiology report generation, where LVLMs often produce overconfident outputs with hallucinations, and proposes a novel RL-based framework that models confidence expression as a policy optimization problem. This approach effectively addresses the gap in multimodal calibration research. Secondly, the framework supports both report-level and sentence-level confidence expression, enabling confidence-guided triage of complete radiology reports and targeted review of uncertain statements to facilitate selective radiologist verification in clinical workflows. Thirdly, the experimental validation is comprehensive and rigorous, covering multiple datasets, various baseline comparisons, and a small-scale clinical evaluation with radiologists, fully demonstrating the method’s calibration effectiveness, generalization ability, and clinical alignment.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Firstly, the paper states that the continuous correctness score s is derived from the GREEN metric but provides no detailed explanation of how GREEN quantifies radiology report quality to generate a continuous value in the range of [0,1], nor does it verify whether the s obtained by this metric can accurately reflect the actual clinical quality of radiology reports. Secondly, the reward scaling factor λ is set to 100 without a systematic parameter sensitivity analysis, and the paper provides no explanation for this specific choice or guidance on adapting λ across different LVLMs or radiology datasets. Thirdly, the clinical evaluation is limited to 50 reports with three raters, and the sample size is too small to draw definitive conclusions about the alignment between ConRad’s confidence scores and clinical judgment.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and the AC for their valuable feedback and for recognizing the clinical motivation and importance of our work (R1,R2,R3) as well as our thorough (R2), rigorous (R3) and fairly solid (R1) experimental evaluation. In the following, we address all comments: Novelty (R1) ConRad introduces confidence estimation for the multimodal setting of radiology reporting by teaching LVLMs an internal understanding of calibrated confidence. Unlike prior work, which is mainly based on sampling, external probes, or report-extracted uncertainty phrasing [24-27,29], ConRad directly trains the LVLM to express calibrated confidence jointly with the generated report on both report and sentence level. Report stability (R1) Our method is intentionally designed to keep the task performance of the trained model unchanged, as this prevents unintended or accidental changes of reporting behavior. We propose ConRad as a post-training method that can perform targeted training of confidence calibration alone. Human evaluation (R1,R3) Our goal here was to provide an initial indication of alignment between model confidence predictions and clinician judgement and help contextualize the main results. This was achieved by considerable effort of 3 expert radiologists who agreed to rate 50 reports on sentence level. We of course agree that a larger number of readers would further strengthen the study. GREEN (R1,R2) We agree that GREEN is only a proxy for clinical correctness. We chose it as it is currently among the most clinically meaningful radiology report metrics. It explicitly targets clinically significant factual errors and was shown to align better with expert evaluation than prior metrics [17]. Additionally, the reward only requires a scalar correctness signal, so the same framework could be optimized against any metric. If it is of interest to the reviewers, we can report calibration of the same GREEN-trained model using alternative correctness metrics. Compared with Verbalize Base, ConRad also clearly reduces ECE when correctness is measured by CheXbert (0.52→0.20) or RadGraph (0.72→0.19), indicating that the learned calibration transfers beyond the training metric. Lambda (R3) The choice of λ was inherited from initial PPO experiments, where it led to faster convergence. However, in GRPO rewards are normalized within each sampled group before computing advantages, so the λ only influences the trade-off between format and task reward, which led to similar convergence in initial experiments. Clarifications (R2) We will add these clarifications to the final manuscript: GRPO is the standard RL algorithm for LLM finetuning. It samples multiple candidate outputs for the same input, normalizes and compares their rewards within this output group, and updates the model to increase the likelihood of the comparatively higher-reward outputs. Confidence ordinality: In SFT, textual confidence tokens are treated as independent labels. In contrast, our reward varies continuously with the distance between predicted confidence and correctness, so near-misses are preferred over large miscalibration. This better reflects that confidence is ordinal, i.e., discrete but meaningfully ordered, rather than categorical. Baselines: Verbalize Supervised mimics GREEN labels token-wise via cross-entropy; Trained Probe predicts correctness from hidden states rather than verbalizing it; Sequence Probability, P(True), and Self-Consistency are post-hoc; Verbalize Base is zero-shot prompting. GREEN is a common report generation metric evaluating a candidate report against the reference report using an LLM as a judge, evaluating the ratio of matched findings and clinically significant errors. Markov Decision Process (MDP): RL is usually formulated as MDP modeling sequential decision processes. For our problem, the confidence-token predictions are the actions, the prompt and report form the state, and the log-score provides the per-rollout reward.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper addresses the critical issue of overconfidence in Large Vision-Language Models by introducing a reinforcement learning framework for calibrated verbalized confidence. Using the Group Relative Policy Optimization algorithm, the model is trained to express its certainty, either at the report or sentence level, alongside the generated findings. The framework utilizes a logarithmic scoring rule as a reward function, which mathematically incentivizes the model to align its stated confidence with the actual clinical correctness of the report (as measured by the GREEN metric), ensuring that the expressed certainty is a reliable indicator for radiologist verification. While the paper presents significant contributions, its recommendation for acceptance is contingent upon the authors clarifying the following points during the rebuttal phase: 1.Reviewers noted that the work extends existing uncertainty-aware paradigms rather than introducing a fundamentally new one. Specifically, since the method intentionally focuses on calibration without seeking to improve the underlying report quality (BLEU/CIDEr), its broader clinical impact is somewhat constrained compared to models that improve both accuracy and reliability. 2.The human evaluation is limited to only 50 reports and 3 raters. This sample size is statistically insufficient to definitively conclude that the model’s “verbalized confidence” aligns with expert clinical judgment or to establish widespread clinical utility. 3.The framework’s “correctness signal” relies entirely on the GREEN (or Precision GREEN) metric. Reviewers pointed out a lack of justification for why GREEN is an appropriate proxy for clinical truth in this RL loop, nor is there evidence that the calibration remains robust if evaluated against different factual correctness benchmarks (e.g., RadGraph or CheXbert). 4.A significant reward scaling factor (lambda = 100) is used without a sensitivity analysis or systematic justification. It remains unclear how this parameter should be adapted for different LVLMs or datasets, which raises concerns about the framework’s generalizability and the stability of the RL training. 5.Include a high-level summary of the GRPO algorithm and why it was chosen over other RL methods (like PPO) for this specific calibration task. | The authors have addressed the reviewers’ comments well. Two reviewers acknowledged the significance of the work. Therefore acceptance of the paper is concluded. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): the reviewers agree the paper is clinically motivated, but share concerns that the authors need to better justify and validate the correctness signal used for calibration due to GREEN being an automated proxy. The authors addressed the issue well by human evaulation (3 radiologists, 50 repors), as well as showing calibration improvements transfer beyond GREEN to CheXbert and RadGraph metrics. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper is accepted, as the reviewers agree that it addresses an important safety problem in radiology report generation by improving uncertainty estimation and confidence calibration for VLMs. Although the novelty is somewhat incremental and the clinical validation remains limited, the method shows consistent gains in clinically interpretable calibration. The remaining issues mainly concern clarity and presentation, which can be addressed in the final revision.

title: Can Agents Distinguish Visually Hard-to-Separate Diseases in a Zero-Shot Setting? A Pilot Study
reviewer_1_strengths: The authors address a clinically meaningful and under-investigated task: zero-shot discrimination of visually confusable diseases. They propose a simple yet effective CARE framework that requires no additional training or fine-tuning. Extensive benchmarking and well-designed ablation experiments are conducted on two representative medical imaging tasks, demonstrating clear performance gains over baseline methods. The framework also helps reduce unsupported visual claims, providing interpretable and verifiable diagnostic reasoning.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The novelty of the proposed CARE framework is limited, as it mainly adopts prompt engineering and lacks conceptual and methodological innovation. 2.The task difficulty is overstated. Some disease samples can be visually distinguished by simple features such as color in Mel vs APN Fig1(a). 3.The baseline selection is inappropriate and unfair, mixing models with large performance gaps and different capabilities. Gemini3 > GLM> Qwen3 4.The multi-agent system is not a genuine agent architecture but only uses the same MLLM with different role‑specific prompts, and the agent concept is overstated. 5.The experimental setting is oversimplified and clinically unrealistic, with strict binary classification and no clinical context. 6.The overall performance is still insufficient for clinical use, and the generalization ability is not fully verified.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The paper’s focus on visually hard-to-separate disease pairs with different management implications is well motivated. 2.For methods, the role split between two specialist agents and an image-grounded judge is intuitive, and the qualitative examples help illustrate what the adjudication step is doing. 3.The empirical section is reasonably solid for a pilot study. The paper evaluates two modalities, compares against several single-agent baselines, and includes compute-matched ablations.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The evaluation setting is controlled, which is reasonable for a pilot study, but it is still somewhat artificial. The XOR formulation simplifies the task and does not reflect real co-occurrence, especially for edema and pneumonia. The paper acknowledges this limitation, but it still weakens the clinical interpretation of the results. 2.The idea is promising, but the current “among the first” wording feels a bit too broad. I think the paper would benefit from a clearer discussion of nearby work on medical agentic reasoning and robustness, especially recent work such as ‘PASS’ (AAAI-26 oral) [1], which studies interpretable and adaptive chest X-ray reasoning through probabilistic agentic workflows, and the MICCAI’25 paper ‘Knowing or Guessing’ [2]. These works do not invalidate the paper’s exact setting, but they do make the novelty boundary look narrower than currently stated. A more precise claim around training-free, zero-shot, image-only contrastive adjudication for visually confounded differential diagnosis would read as stronger and more credible. 3.Reproducibility is fair but not yet strong. The overall framework is understandable, but for a prompting-based method I would still like clearer reporting of prompts, inference settings, and some of the curation details. 4.The chest X-ray result is encouraging, but not fully convincing yet. CARE improves over Gemini-3-Flash, but still remains below Gemini-3-Pro on that task, so the practical benefit of the additional multi-agent overhead is not yet fully clear. [1] Feng et al., PASS: Probabilistic Agentic Supernet Sampling for Interpretable and Adaptive Chest X-Ray Reasoning, AAAI 2026 Oral. [2] Jiang et al., Knowing or Guessing? Robust Medical Visual Question Answering via Joint Consistency and Contrastive Learning, MICCAI 2025.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The CARE system introduces a structured disagreement mechanism that effectively mimics the diagnostic process of human experts. Unlike standard self-reflection or majority-voting methods, CARE forces agents into mutually exclusive roles (one arguing for Disease A, another for Disease B), which successfully surfaces inconsistencies and reduces overconfident “hallucinated” claims. The study specifically focuses on two clinically significant proxy tasks: melanoma vs. atypical nevus and pulmonary edema vs. pneumonia. These pairs represent a “hard-to-separate” frontier where visual features are highly overlapped, making them an ideal and rigorous testbed for evaluating the reasoning limits of multimodal LLMs. The method is entirely prompt-based and requires no task-specific fine-tuning or additional annotated data. This makes the framework highly scalable and applicable to other medical imaging domains where high-quality labeled data for training might be scarce.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The authors note the exclusion of congenital and recurrent nevi because these subtypes are “often very difficult without clinical context”. However, as the paper’s title explicitly asks if agents can distinguish “visually hard-to-separate” diseases, manually removing the most challenging cases effectively defines a “simplified difficulty.” The authors should clarify if this exclusion intentionally shielded the zero-shot agents from the most difficult edge cases and whether the 11-percentage-point gain would significantly diminish if these cases were included. To mitigate class imbalance, atypical nevi were subsampled to match the melanoma count (from 399 original cases to 257). The authors must clarify the specific methodology used for this subsampling (e.g., was it purely random?). Given the “visually confounded” nature of the task, it is critical to discuss whether this selection process introduced any bias or altered the prevalence of hard-to-distinguish cases compared to the original distribution. The study employs a forced exclusive-or (XOR) setting for diagnosis. In real-world clinical practice, conditions like pulmonary edema and pneumonia frequently co-occur. By forcing a binary choice, the evaluation may artificially inflate accuracy and mask potential conflicts or “hallucinations” the model might encounter when dealing with comorbidities. The authors should discuss whether the Judge Agent should be granted the option of “both” or “neither” to better reflect clinical truth. While “Blind-CARE” and “Self-Check” variants were tested , the current results do not fully isolate whether the performance gain stems from “contrastive reasoning” or simply the inherent capabilities of a superior judge. A more direct baseline (e.g. a single Gemini-3-Flash model performing a direct diagnosis without any debate assistance) should be emphasized for comparison. If the marginal gain of CARE over a standard single-call model is small, the added computational cost of a three-agent architecture may not be justified. The qualitative analysis focuses on successful error corrections by the Judge Agent. To provide a balanced view of the system’s limitations, the authors should present cases where “reverse interference” occurred: situations where the two disease-specific agents provided such “persuasive” yet incorrect arguments that they successfully misled the judge.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank all reviewers for constructive comments and for recognizing the forward-looking nature of this study. We address main concerns below: 1.Limited novelty (R1). CARE is not merely a prompt design, but a methodology of explicitly constructing disagreement. By doing this in a binary diagnosis setting, the system can comprehensively consider both sides before making a final decision. Importantly, it doesn’t require post-training or fine-tuning, with acceptable inference overhead. 2.Below-clinical performance (R1,R2). This study is not meant to claim clinical readiness, but to expose this important yet unsolved problem to the community. We have highlighted this point in Sec 3.2 and Sec 4. 3.Overstated task difficulty and agent concept (R1). We disagree with R1’s claim that melanoma (MEL) and atypical nevus (ANV) can be distinguished “simply by color.” In dermoscopic imaging, color is well known to be an unreliable and highly variable feature due to camera white balance, illumination temperature, etc. MEL vs. ANV remains challenging [15], and reducing it to color greatly oversimplifies the task. Moreover, we have clearly defined “agent” as “systems that can receive observations and perform goal-directed actions” based on [2]. Agent does not necessitate tool-use and RAG, it is the observation-action that really matters. 4.Baseline choice (R1, R3). We believe R1 has misinterpreted Table 1.The models listed there are not direct baselines for CARE, but rather as a benchmark survey to evaluate how current MLLM-based agents perform in this setting. For both R1 and R3, the actual comparison validating CARE is between Gemini-3-Flash (Baseline) and Gemini-3-Flash (CARE), where the underlying MLLM remains identical and only the inference framework changes. Therefore, the reported gains are not derived from comparing against weaker models, but from controlled comparisons under the same backbone model. 5.Oversimplified setting (R1/R2/R3). (1) absence of clinical context. Currently no publicly dataset provides paired imaging and clinical context. Therefore, as stated in the Discussion, our experiments should be viewed as imaging-only proxy tasks. Note that MLLM-based agents can naturally incorporate additional clinical context as textual input, allowing seamless extension to richer multimodal settings. (2) Simplified binary edema vs. pneumonia formulation. This pilot study is to establish that distinguishing visually confounded diseases remains unsolved for MLLM-based agents. As agents already struggle under this binary setting, more realistic non-exclusive formulations would likely be even more challenging. It doesn’t undermine our conclusion. 6.Practical benefit (R2). CARE is designed as a plug-and-play framework rather than a model-specific architecture. Applying CARE to Qwen3-VL-32B improved MEL vs. ANV F1 by 3.8 percentage points and increased the Youden index from 0.347 to 0.426.In principle, CARE could also be applied to Gemini-3-Pro. However, Gemini-3-Pro is limited to 250 API calls per day. An entire CARE inference would require 8 days for dermoscopy and 26 days for chest X-ray evaluation. Due to these constraints, we treated Gemini-3-Pro as a single-agent upper-bound reference rather than another CARE backbone. 7.Related work (R2). We thank R2 for pointing out these works and will cite them. Our work differs from these studies in focus. PASS investigates agents with tool-use mechanisms, while “Knowing or Guessing” proposes training recipes. In contrast, CARE focuses on training-free inference-time contrastive adjudication. 8.Data curation (R3). For ANV, we performed controlled subgroup-aware random sampling. We also apologize for the ambiguity in the manuscript regarding congenital and recurrent nevi. These subtypes were excluded because they are often considered theoretically indistinguishable from melanoma based on dermoscopy alone. The exclusion was to improve rigor rather than simplify the benchmark.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): After reviewing this manuscript together with the reviewers’ evaluations, I note that the paper received mixed but generally constructive feedback. The reviewers recognize the clinical relevance of distinguishing visually confounded diseases in a zero-shot setting, as well as the potential value of the CARE framework for contrastive adjudication and reducing unsupported claims. At the same time, several important concerns remain, including limited methodological novelty, possible overstatement of the multi-agent formulation, simplified binary/XOR experimental settings, baseline fairness, and insufficient evidence of clinical realism and generalization. Based on my assessment, these issues would benefit from clarification and targeted response by the authors. I therefore recommend that the paper proceed to the rebuttal phase for further consideration. | The paper is recommended for acceptance based on its solid contribution as a timely pilot study and the thoroughness of the post-rebuttal clarifications. The authors successfully addressed initial concerns regarding baseline fairness and task framing. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): the reviewers acknowledges the method is clinical meaningful, timely, with well established empirical gains. the authors addresses the points raised by reviewers well; baseline comparison, the novelty boundary, data curation, and the intended scope as an imaging-only pilot. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper proposes CARE, a training-free three-agent framework for zero-shot differentiation of visually confounded disease pairs. The setting is meaningful and underexplored, and the core idea of constructing explicit disagreement for contrastive adjudication is well motivated. After rebuttal, both Reviewer #2 and Reviewer #3 are satisfied and explicitly recommend acceptance. The main criticisms raised by Reviewer #1 concern limited novelty, baseline fairness, oversimplified experimental settings, and below-clinical performance. The authors have provided substantive responses: they clarified that CARE is a methodology of constructing disagreement rather than mere prompt engineering, which is a valid conceptual contribution; they explained that the baseline comparison is conducted under identical backbone models, thus the gains are fairly attributed; they acknowledged the simplified binary setting and the imaging-only nature as limitations of this pilot study, while noting that the framework can naturally incorporate clinical context in future work; and they were transparent that the current performance is not clinical-ready but aims to expose an unsolved problem to the community. The clarification on the definition of agent is also reasonable. The remaining concerns, including the binary task formulation and the absence of clinical context, are acknowledged as limitations and are acceptable for a pilot study that opens a new direction. I recommend accept. For the camera-ready version, the authors should: (1) clearly state the limitations regarding binary classification and imaging-only evaluation in the abstract and conclusion; (2) provide the exact definition of agent adopted in this work early in the manuscript; (3) ensure full reproducibility details, including prompts and inference configurations, are documented; and (4) incorporate the newly cited related work as promised in the rebuttal.

title: Can Experts Adapt Without Training? On Test-Time Modality Generalization in MVLMs
reviewer_1_strengths: 1- MoBE requires no gradient updates, no backpropagation, no source data access, and no modality labels at test time. This is a practically important property — it makes the method deployable in clinical settings where computational resources are limited and labeled data is unavailable. 2- Replacing fixed top-k selection with relative entropy thresholding removes the need to manually tune k per dataset. Figure 3b demonstrates that fixed top-k is sensitive to k — too many experts hurts performance — while dynamic-k automatically matches the best fixed-k performance across modalities. This is a practically meaningful contribution for deployment in diverse clinical settings. 3- The ablation experiments presented in Figure 3a clearly demonstrate the contribution of each component of the method. It is important to see that each component has meaningful contribution. 4- The method is evaluated across three distinct benchmark types (seen modalities, unseen modalities, and heterogeneous datasets) and two backbone families (BiomedCLIP and PubmedCLIP). The consistency of gains across all settings demonstrate the potential of the proposed method.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1- The paper never includes an experiment where the ground truth modality label is used to directly route to the correct expert. For seen modalities in Table 1 this is trivially available — ChestMNIST is X-ray, so simply using the X-ray expert directly would give a natural upper bound. Without this comparison it is impossible to know how much performance is lost due to routing errors, whether EBA adaptation improves over the correct expert alone, or whether dynamic-k routing successfully recovers modality-correct behavior. This is the single most important missing experiment in the paper. 2- The paper is clearly written but it may still be difficult to reproduce the results based on the description in the paper. The details such as the MLP expert architecture, training hyperparameters, the confidence thresholds, the blending parameter \lambda and the entropy gap threshold \tau are all unreported or underspecified to fully reproduce the results. Furthermore, no source code is provided nor is there any promise to release it upon acceptance. Taken together, these omissions make it effectively impossible for other researchers to independently verify or build upon the reported results.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The proposed framework is attractive from a deployment perspective because it is optimization-free at test time. Instead of relying on backpropagation, it combines entropy-based dynamic expert selection with Bayesian online adaptation. 2.The paper explains its method design through the specialization–generalization tradeoff in MoE settings, providing an intuitive framework for why dynamic expert selection is needed. 3.The experimental evaluation includes unseen modalities and heterogeneous medical datasets, which allows the paper to assess the generalization ability of the method from multiple perspectives.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The authors investigate how medical vision-language models can perform test-time adaptation. They propose a fully optimization-free framework that performs dynamic expert selection and adaptation at test time. By augmenting a static MVLM with test-time routing and online statistics, the method improves performance over current state-of-the-art test-time adaptation (TTA) methods on seen, unseen, and heterogeneous medical benchmarks. However, the work still has the following limitations: (1). The authors’ method is built upon five modality-specialized experts, which are derived from MLP branches fine-tuned on ROCOV2 after partitioning the data by modality. While this design is reasonable in itself, it also means that, compared with single-model baselines, the method introduces additional modality-specialized structure and parameters. The current experiments are still insufficient to fully disentangle whether the observed improvements come primarily from the test-time adaptation mechanism itself, or to a significant extent from the added expert structure and modality-specific priors. (2). The method involves several key hyperparameters and design choices, such as the threshold for dynamic-k routing, the confidence thresholds in EBA, the fusion coefficient, and the way the test stream order is defined. Test-time adaptation methods are typically quite sensitive to sample order, threshold settings, and initialization strategy. (3). There is an inconsistency between Table 3 and the main text regarding the average accuracy on the heterogeneous benchmark. (4). Although the authors emphasize that the method does not require backpropagation, the multiple expert forward passes themselves still impose a nontrivial deployment overhead. (5). Are some classical CTTA methods developed for conventional models, such as CoTTA, also effective for medical VLMs?
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The shift from gradient-based test-time adaptation (like TENT or MoME) to a Bayesian, memory-based updating mechanism is highly original and practical. By updating statistical variables (prototypes and priors) rather than network weights, the method avoids catastrophic forgetting and significantly reduces the computational overhead typically associated with continuous learning at test time. 2.The dynamic-$k$ routing with inverse-entropy weighting is a highly elegant solution to the MoE routing problem. Using a relative gap threshold ($\tau$) rather than a hard cutoff ensures that the model can dynamically fall back on multiple experts when uncertainty is high, or rely on a single expert when confidence is absolute.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The framework’s success relies heavily on the semantic foundation provided by the 5 pre-trained ROCOv2 modality experts (CT, MRI, X-ray, Ultrasound, Angiogram). As seen in the BloodMNIST (microscopy) results, when a target modality is entirely disjoint from the source experts’ knowledge base, the entropy-based routing loses discriminability, and performance gains are marginal.
reviewer_3_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for their constructive feedback. We are encouraged that Reviewer_1 valued MoBE’s training-free deployment, dynamic-k routing, clear ablations, and consistent gains; Reviewer_2 highlighted the optimization-free design, intuitive specialization-generalization motivation, and broad seen/unseen/heterogeneous evaluation; and Reviewer_4 recognized the originality and practicality of Bayesian memory adaptation with dynamic-k routing. We address the concerns below and will incorporate the clarifications, and will release our GitHub codebase with camera-ready submission. Reviewer_1– 1.1 [Routing with Ground Truth Labels]: We thank the reviewer for this important suggestion. Fig. 1(b) compares expert routing using self-entropy versus cross-entropy. The latter uses ground-truth labels and therefore serves as an oracle comparison. Although this is a compact figure, it shows that self-entropy-based routing can be a practical alternative when labels are unavailable at inference. We agree that an additional modality-wise ablation comparing oracle versus self-entropy routing would be valuable; however, due to space constraints and the inclusion of several other ablations, we summarized this comparison through Fig. 1(b). 1.2 [Reproducibility]: We agree that some implementation details should be stated more explicitly. Sec. 3.1 already specifies the backbone, frozen encoders, (E=5) ROCOv2-derived experts, modality partitioning, preprocessing, batch size, GPU, and evaluation metric. We will add the missing values for the MLP architecture, tau, theta_1, theta_2, and stream ordering in a few additional lines in the camera-ready version. The algorithm itself is defined by Eqs. (1)-(5). Overall, we will release the code publicly with camera-ready submission. Reviewer_2– 2.1 [Component-wise effect]: We agree that MoBE benefits from both modality-specialized experts and test-time adaptation. Fig. 3(a) disentangles these effects by comparing frozen BiomedCLIP, fixed top-(k) MoE, dynamic-(k), EBA, and full MoBE. This ablation shows that expert structure helps, dynamic routing improves expert selection, and EBA adds further gains through online posterior refinement. 2.2 [Reproducibility]: We will clarify the selected hyperparameter values and test-stream ordering to make the method reproducible. We will also release the code. 2.3 [Typo]: Correct. The heterogeneous benchmark average is 46.49%, as reported in Table 3.The main text value 46.69% is a typo and will be corrected to 46.49%. This does not change the conclusion that MoBE achieves the best average performance. 2.4 [Additional forward passes]: We agree. MoBE avoids backpropagation but still requires multiple expert forward passes. Table 5 already reports this trade-off: MoBE is slower than frozen BiomedCLIP but faster than optimization-based MoME while achieving higher accuracy. We will state this limitation explicitly in the paper. 2.5 [CoTTA baseline]: We compare against representative TTA/VLM adaptation baselines, including TENT, EATA, TPT, WATT, TDA, CoOp/CoCoOp, and MoME. CoTTA is designed for teacher-student updates and augmentation consistency in conventional classifiers, which does not directly match our frozen zero-shot MVLM setting. Reviewer_4– 4.1 [Available experts’ dependency]: We agree. MoBE relies on the semantic coverage of the available expert bank. BloodMNIST illustrates this limitation: microscopy is weakly covered by the five ROCOv2 experts, making entropy less discriminative and reducing gains. This defines the operating regime of MoBE rather than contradicting the method: routing and EBA are most effective when the expert bank partially covers the test modality. A sentence around this will be added in the main paper, that future work should expand expert coverage or add fallback/rejection mechanisms for poorly covered modalities.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): The reviewers provided scores of accept, weak accept, and weak reject. The main reason for the weak reject, according to the justification section, is that the authors do not share the code. This issue was also raised by Reviewer 1.However, MICCAI guidelines do not require code release for acceptance. Although I encourage the authors to share the code, this should not be considered an acceptance criterion. All reviewers are generally positive about the work, including the methodology, broad experimentation, clinical feasibility, efficiency, and performance gains. The remaining concerns are minor and can be addressed with small changes in the final version of the manuscript. Therefore, I recommend acceptance and encourage the authors to incorporate the reviewers’ comments into the final version.

title: CancerVerse: A Fully Open Longitudinal and Multimodal Dataset for Multicancer Screening
reviewer_1_strengths: Addressing a Critical Dataset Gap: Most existing public CT datasets (e. g. , KiTS, LiTS, PanTS) are single-organ and single time-point, typically capturing tumors at confirmed (often later) stages. CancerVerse advances the field by providing longitudinal data and voxel-wise annotations for 13 cancer types, including nine types that previously lacked public CT datasets with voxel-wise annotations. Clinically Realistic Evaluation Design: By formulating evaluation around fixed false positives per scan (FROC analysis) rather than standard ROC curves, the benchmark better reflects real clinical constraints in screening settings, where false positives are costly. Multimodal Integration: The dataset incorporates radiology reports, pathology, and clinical variables—features that are rare in public datasets. The use of report-based supervision is a practical design choice that may improve scalability. Commitment to Open Science: Releasing the dataset under a CC BY-NC 4.0 license, along with standardized formats and trained segmentation backbones, will provide a valuable resource for the MICCAI community.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Missing Data Dynamics: While the authors acknowledge incomplete multimodal data availability, the paper lacks detailed missingness statistics. Providing availability percentages for clinical variables and laboratory tests across the 9,316 patients would help assess the dataset’s practical usability. Scope of Longitudinal Modeling: The dataset’s longitudinal structure is a key strength. While the current work evaluates detection at different time points, extending the benchmark to temporal forecasting tasks—such as disease progression modeling or future cancer prediction—would better demonstrate its full potential. Limited Methodological Novelty: The modeling framework combines established techniques, including temporal aggregation and report-based supervision. As such, the primary contribution lies in dataset curation and benchmarking. The authors may consider emphasizing this more clearly rather than positioning the work as an algorithmic innovation. Modality Limitations: The dataset is primarily CT-based. Future extensions could incorporate additional imaging modalities (e. g. , MRI or PET) to support more comprehensive multiparametric screening.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The dataset itself is a substantial contribution. Its scale, longitudinal structure, multimodal alignment, and voxel-wise annotations make it highly compelling and help fill an important gap in public resources for screening-oriented medical AI. 2.The paper also provides a comprehensive benchmark that clearly demonstrates the value of longitudinal and multimodal data for multicancer screening. 3.The validation is thorough and convincing. In particular, the inclusion of a verified healthy cohort and external datasets strengthens the credibility and practical relevance of the findings. 4.The paper is generally well written and well organized, with clear motivation and polished presentation.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The handling of heterogeneous data is insufficiently described. For instance, different patients have varying numbers of CT scans, but the manuscript does not clearly explain how such variable-length longitudinal data are processed. In addition, the feature extraction pipeline for non-imaging data (e.g., reports, pathology, and clinical variables) remains unclear. 2.Benign cases are particularly important in cancer screening, as they are essential for a realistic evaluation of false positives and specificity. It would therefore be helpful for the paper to discuss their composition and role in the paper. 3.Some aspects of the evaluation protocol are unclear. First, it is not clear whether the sensitivity reported in Table 1 is calculated at the patient level or the lesion level. Second, the definition of negative samples for specificity and FP/case evaluation is ambiguous. Are these metrics computed only on the verified healthy cohort, or are patients with other cancer types also treated as negative samples when evaluating a specific cancer type?
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The dataset is of unprecedented size, especially considering the accompanying information in the form of segmentation masks, radiology reports, other health related data and its longitudinal nature. The dataset includes annotations for 13 cancer types, some of which are rare to non-existent in available public datasets. The authors benchmark different widely adopted segmentation models on their proposed dataset, showing superior performance of a longitudinal model with multimodal information over all the baseline methods.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: While the proposed dataset is interesting there are several issues I have with this paper: Dataset Construction: As the dataset is the main contribution of this paper, I would have liked to see more details on the generation of voxel-wise tumor masks, which is a very time-consuming task for this large of a dataset. Many recent large scale datasets and collections struggle with exactly that actually struggle with annotation quality even for easier target structures like organs (e.g. https://huggingface.co/datasets/mrmrx/CADS-dataset, https://github.com/MrGiovanni/AbdomenAtlas). Consequentially, I would have liked to see more details on quality assurance and control and the annotation procedure in general. Evaluation: The authors train segmentation models on the dataset, however, their main evaluation focuses on sensitivity and specificity, disregarding the main objective of segmentation. Dice is only shown as a mean over all structures in Fig. 3, however, it would be more helpful to see this per structure. Additionally, it seems like a case is counted as a true positive, if there is any prediction in the image, which might be heavily misleading. Accordingly, the metrics sensitivity at 0.25/0.5 FP/scan don’t really make sense in this setting, as this mixes up instance wise and case wise measurements and is not what is classically reported as FROC in detection metrics. Interrater evaluation: The comparison against interrater performance should be reported on the same split of the test set. Fig. 3 currently reports this against the performance on the full test set, which could be heavily misleading due to different distributions and frequencies of the tumor classes. Baseline Models: While the comparison against a large suit of baseline models is appreciated, it is not really sensible for the ULS family of models, which are not developed for fully automatic segmentation but always assume a lesion at the center of the patch. This also raises a question regarding the validity of the results as this should usually result in a significantly higher sensitivity due to this bias of always predicting something. Overstated claims: The authors claim that they provide the first publicly available annotations for 9 of the 13 tumor types. While this is true for most of the tumor classes, some of these are actually covered by other datasets already, e.g. esophagus and uterus in AbdomenAtlas 2.0 (https://github.com/BodyMaps/AbdomenAtlas2.0).
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and meta-reviewer. R1 and R3 recommend acceptance. R4 calls CancerVerse “of unprecedented size… 13 cancer types, some rare to non-existent in public datasets… superior performance over all baselines.” The meta-reviewer calls it “an important contribution to the MICCAI community.” R1: Q1-Missing Data Dynamics. Availability across 9,316 patients: reports 100%, pathology 58%, clinical variables 64%. We will add this to the camera-ready. Q2-Scope of Longitudinal Modeling. Agreed. We hope the release of CancerVerse can encourage more exploration from our community. Q3-Limited Methodological Novelty. Our paper presents a dataset-and-benchmark contribution; no “novel method” is claimed. The longitudinal-and-multimodal model tested in this paper combines two existing models (longitudinal model, Rokuss, MICCAI’24; multimodal model, Bassi, MICCAI’25). Q4-Modality Limitations. Agreed. Additional imaging modalities (e.g., MRI) are planned for future versions. R3: Q1-Handling of heterogeneous data. Variable-length CTs are processed by a shared nnU-Net encoder followed by a temporal-difference layer (Rokuss’24). Single-scan patients fall back to the image-only. Reports are encoded by Llama-3-70B with tumor-attribute auxiliary labels (Bassi’25). Clinical variables are encoded by an MLP. Modalities are fused via cross-attention. Q2-Benign cases. Composition: 77% with no cancer and other disease, 23% with only benign lesions (e.g., IPMN). Role: computing specificity and FP/scan. Q3-Evaluation protocol. Sensitivity in Tab. 1 is lesion-level. Negatives are both the verified healthy cohort (>1 year follow-up) and patients with other cancer types. R4: Q1-Dataset Construction. R4 cites annotation-quality issues in CADS and AbdomenAtlas, but both are organ datasets that heavily used AI-assisted annotation pipelines, acknowledged by their papers. CancerVerse is fundamentally different. We manually annotate voxel-wise tumor masks across 13 cancer types. No AI-generated masks. Every lesion was drawn by at least one human expert. 28 expert annotators. More than 13 months of work. Quality assurance: a representative multicancer subset was annotated independently by three experts to verify consistency (Sec. 3.1). Q2-Evaluation. (i) We will add per-cancer Dice to the camera-ready (liv/kid/pan/col/spl/bla/gal/adr/eso/sto/duo/ute/pros = 67/64/48/41/52/45/46/55/49/38/39/63/57). In cancer screening, sensitivity and specificity matter most; precise contouring is downstream. (ii) This is a misunderstanding. We use instance-wise evaluation for both positive and negative patients, precisely following the classical definition of FROC. That means one case can have more than one false positive instance. Q3-Interrater evaluation. This is an excellent point. We have now reported a mean Dice of 50.8% on the same split. We will update Fig. 3 accordingly. Q4-Baseline Models. ULS models have a known limitation: they require the lesion at the center of the patch (Grauw, MedIA’25). We evaluate using a sliding window on whole CT volumes (the realistic screening setting), where the lesion is usually not at the window center, which is why ULS sensitivity in Tab. 1 is low. We report every baseline at its operating point on the ROC curve (nearest to top-left) for fair comparison. We will add this analysis to the camera-ready. Q5-Overstated claim. We revise “9 novel cancer types” to “7” and cite AbdomenAtlas 2.0. To our knowledge, among publicly released whole-volume abdominal CT datasets, CancerVerse is one of only two exceeding 20,000 first-time-released CT scans (alongside Merlin, n=25,494; Nature’26). It is the only public dataset combining voxel-wise tumor annotations across 13 cancer types with longitudinal trajectories, paired radiology and pathology reports, clinical variables, and a verified healthy follow-up cohort. The full dataset will be released on 09/01 if accepted, ahead of MICCAI’26.We respectfully ask for reconsideration.

title: CardioGS: Deformation-Driven 4D Gaussian Splatting with Self-supervised Cardiac Clock Learning for Rotational DSA Reconstruction
reviewer_1_strengths: The paper addresses a challenging and clinically relevant imaging scenario of rotational DSA, operating under sparse-view acquisition conditions. The proposed method demonstrates improvements over baselines. In addition, the inclusion of ablation studies helps clarify the contribution. Finally, the public release of the code is a strong positive aspect.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The framework combines multiple sophisticated components, which makes the overall method difficult to interpret. Most of mathematical formulations would benefit from additional intuition to improve accessibility. For example, the curriculum design with the parameter beta seems heuristic, and its impact is not evaluated. Furthermore, several limitations could be more explicitly discussed: for example, since the deformation model depends on the learned cardiac clock, inaccuracies in ClockNet negatively affect geometry reconstruction.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The paper is well written and concise. The architecture figure is particularly informative, making the overall approach clear and easy to understand. 2.The idea of splitting time conditioning into two separate factors, cardiac motion and contrast agent transport, rather than using a single temporal input, is both novel and well-motivated. The experimental results indicate that this design choice leads to noticeable improvements in 3D reconstruction quality. More broadly, the findings suggest that modeling different sources of temporal inconsistency separately is beneficial not only for reconstruction performance but also for improving model interpretability. 3.The proposed approach appears adaptable to other 3D reconstruction tasks, such as lung imaging, suggesting broad applicability.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.Regarding the cardiac clock, while the rationale for avoiding direct modeling of the modular phase is well explained, it is not entirely clear why the model predicts heart rate (frequency) instead of directly estimating the final conditioning u(tau). Additional clarification on this design choice would strengthen the methodological justification. 2.The discussion of limitations and future work could be expanded. A slightly more detailed analysis would help readers better understand the broader implications of the proposed approach and its potential impact on the field. The authors adopt a control-node-based approach to manipulate 3.Gaussian geometries. It would be valuable to understand whether this design choice is driven purely by computational efficiency or also by domain-specific considerations related to vessel structures. Additionally, it raises the question of whether directly manipulating Gaussian parameters could further improve reconstruction quality, even at the cost of increased computational complexity.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: Major Strengths: 1.Monotonic cardiac clock controls the continuous positional encoding and provides cycle consistency regularization. Instead of using raw timestamp conditioning alone, the model learns a monotonic reparameterization of time through an instantaneous frequency integrated by Gauss–Legendre quadrature. 2.Well discussed theory and components needed for the moving pieces of this work. 3.The deformation module is not an unconstrained per-point warp. It is a sparse control-node graph with KNN-RBF interpolation, plus cycle-consistency regularization. That is a good compromise between flexibility and stability.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Major Weakness: 1.Even though the field is queried in canonical space, the 4D hash grid still allows, (i) temporal variation that mimics motion and (ii) especially along projection rays. This is apparent when I looked at the shared repository. 2.ClockNet enforces monotonicity (this is good), but there is a high chance it will learn neal-linear mapping from the data due to KNN based graph formation.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We sincerely thank the reviewers and meta-reviewer for constructive comments that help improve the manuscript’s clarity and rigor. Reference reliability [Meta,R3]. Ref. 13 has an erroneous/incomplete entry due to a verification oversight. It served only as broad DSA background, not to support any method assumption, loss term, comparison, or conclusion. We apologize; it will be corrected or removed, and references re-checked for accuracy and relevance. Projection ambiguity [Meta,R3]. We agree projection-only supervision cannot guarantee unique disentanglement of appearance, deformation, and temporal dynamics. Similar projections may arise from true displacement or opacity changes that alter apparent vessel location and perceived motion along projection rays. CardioGS does not prove uniqueness; its separated opacity-at-τ and clock-conditioned geometry pathways make the ambiguity more constrained, improving conditioning relative to generic time-conditioned fields. Opacity is queried at canonical undeformed Gaussian positions and acquisition time τ, so it cannot directly move centers/covariances. Geometry uses a spatially coherent, clock-conditioned sparse control-node graph with cycle consistency. We will use “reduces ambiguity” or “improves conditioning,” not “restores identifiability.” Method design and reliability [R2,R3,R1]. [R2: frequency vs. u(τ)] The learned frequency is the positive cardiac-clock progression rate; integrating gives cumulative progress w(τ)=∫_0^τ f_θ(s)ds, so u(τ) is monotonic while allowing nonuniform progression. With a smooth unwrapped clock rather than a wrapped phase, cycle consistency needs the scale of one cardiac cycle in normalized u-space. The integral gives C=w(1); after normalization, one cycle corresponds to Δu=1/(C+ε). Direct u(τ) regression is possible, but would need extra monotonicity constraints and a separate cycle-scale estimate. [R3: near-linear clock] A clock close to acquisition time is valid when cardiac progression is regular. ClockNet does not force nonlinearity; it is adaptive, near-linear for regular motion and nonlinear when progression is irregular. Graph topology/RBF weights are built from canonical 3D positions, while node transforms are time-conditioned; thus KNN formation enforces spatial coherence, not temporal linearity. [R2/R1: deformation prior, beta, clock sensitivity] The graph is not merely computational; it encodes coherent vessel motion. CardioGS remains per-Gaussian, but shared control nodes/KNN-RBF couple deformations, avoiding isolated local geometry explanations under sparse projections; node-number ablation and the graph gain support this expressiveness-regularization trade-off. Beta is a stability curriculum: start with reliable acquisition-time conditioning, then introduce learned-clock conditioning. It was set by stability tuning; fuller hyperparameter study remains future work. If clock prediction is inaccurate, geometry may degrade, especially with irregular motion/poor projections. Yet even in the hardest 15-view case, experiments show no systematic degradation. Data scope and metric/visual gap [R4]. [R4: private data] Evaluation is on one private in-vivo porcine rotational cardiac DSA dataset; we acknowledge this limitation. To our knowledge, no comparable public cardiac benchmark provides dynamic projections, calibrated geometry, and dense-view 3D reference. Once new public/internal in-vivo DSA data become available, we will expand evaluation for fair comparison. [R4: metrics vs. visualization] R2-Gaussian is t-independent; 4DRGS models time-dependent rendering. For quality metrics, R2-Gaussian outperforms 4DRGS only on CD/HD at 15 views; its lower GauN is expected for a static model. Its worse PSNR/SSIM and visualization indicate weaker temporal rendering. CD/HD after ICP favor phase-averaged 3D alignment under extreme sparsity, whereas visualization and PSNR/SSIM reflect dynamic 2D synthesis; this is not a contradiction to dynamic modeling.

title: CARE: Clinically Aligned Retrieval Evidence for Consistent Radiology Report Generation
reviewer_1_strengths: 1) Elegant Theoretical Motivation: The paper identifies a fundamental bottleneck in end-to-end RAG optimization—the destabilization of the retrieval space. Adapting the momentum update mechanism (inspired by contrastive learning paradigms like MoCo) to manage cross-modal retrieval queues is a technically sound and elegant solution. 2) Exceptional Zero-Shot Domain Adaptation: The framework exhibits remarkable out-of-domain generalization. On the unseen MIMIC-CXR benchmark, simply populating the external memory queue with target-domain text (without any image or label fine-tuning) nearly doubled the clinical entity extraction performance (RG-F1), highlighting its flexibility for real-world deployment. 3) Effective Mitigation of Mode Collapse: The N-gram diversity analysis effectively proves that CARE successfully breaks the “shortcut learning” loop. By anchoring generation to stabilized retrieved evidence, the model avoids regurgitating rigid, repetitive templates (e. g. , defaulting to “clear lungs”), resulting in richer and more clinically detailed reports.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1) Frozen LLM Limits Deep Adaptation: The framework freezes the core LLM parameters during training to save compute, optimizing only the query encoder and projection layers. While efficient, this approach may bottleneck the model’s ability to deeply internalize complex, institution-specific reasoning logic or highly specialized syntactic styles for longer reports. 2) Unverified Robustness to Noisy Retrievals: The system assumes the retrieval queue will return highly relevant and accurate evidence. However, real-world Electronic Health Records (EHR) are notoriously noisy. The paper lacks an ablation study or stress test demonstrating the generator’s robustness and self-correction capability when forced to condition on erroneous or contradictory retrieved reports. 3) Absence of Human Expert Evaluation: Although the automated clinical metrics (e. g. , RadGraph F1) show significant improvement, these metrics cannot fully capture clinical fluency, coherence, and clinical utility. The lack of qualitative assessment by expert radiologists slightly weakens the clinical impact claims.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: Well-Motivated Retrieval Design (MoCo-style for Multimodal RAG) Adapts momentum encoder + memory queue (from contrastive learning) to both multimodal retrieval and report generation. Clinically Meaningful Alignment Objective Introduces disease-aware alignment loss and enforces diagnostic consistency between input image and retrieved reports. Improves Generalization Demonstrates training-free adaptation to unseen dataset (MIMIC-CXR) with nearly 2× improvement in entity extraction (RG-F1).
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Method is well-engineered but lacks strong conceptual novelty. Core components are known: MoCo-style momentum encoder RAG, contrastive learning, label alignment. Still Relies on Retrieval Quality (Upper Bound Issue), no mechanism to verify or filter incorrect retrieved evidence. No Fine-Grained Alignment: Alignment happens at report level (retrieval) not at entity-level grounding or region-level correspondence.
