reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for their highly constructive feedback and recognition of CARE’s theoretical motivation. Our work resolves systems-level retrieval instability to enable robust, training-free cross-domain adaptation for practical clinical deployment. Primary concerns are addressed below. Q1: (R1, R2) Robustness to noisy retrieved evidence. Although CheXbert pseudo-labels are standard in prior work, CARE mitigates their rigidity through soft retrieval-guided conditioning rather than hard retrieval supervision. Retrieved candidates receive adaptive soft weights (α) based on continuous visual-textual similarity, naturally suppressing noisy or incompatible evidence during alignment. Generation is jointly conditioned on visual features and weighted retrieval evidence, while supervision still comes from the ground-truth report, reducing over-reliance on noisy retrievals. We will note the lack of adversarial stress-testing as a limitation. Q2: (R3) Concerns regarding slightly lower RG-F1 and CliQ0 performance. We agree that RG-F1 and CliQ0 are important clinically grounded metrics. However, these global overlap metrics may not fully capture sensitivity to less frequent pathological findings. Because normal cases dominate the training distribution, standard SFT models often converge toward repetitive “normal” templates, maintaining strong report-level scores while underdetecting abnormalities. This behavior is evident in LLaVA-Rad (SFT), which achieves high RG-F1 (38.0) but lower pathology-sensitive performance (5Mi/5Ma-F1: 34.4/23.2), and is even more severe in LLaVA-Med (1.0/0.3). In contrast, CARE stabilizes retrieval grounding and consistently improves abnormality sensitivity across both backbones (35.1/26.9 and 20.4/15.4). Our diversity analysis is intended as complementary evidence that CARE mitigates repetitive template collapse rather than memorizing dominant normal patterns. We will clarify this distinction more explicitly in the revised paper. Q3: (R3) Missing comparison to MIMIC-CXR-fine-tuned version. We would like to clarify that while supervised models naturally achieve higher MIMIC-CXR scores, CARE targets a fundamentally different setting: training-free cross-domain adaptation. In clinical environments, institutions often lack the computational resources or annotated data required for repeated retraining. Under this zero-shot constraint, adapting the retrieval memory via CARE demonstrates significant effectiveness, improving RG-F1 from 7.0 to 13.0 without any target-domain training. We will clarify this in the revised paper. Q4: (R2) Conceptual novelty. While the core components (e.g., MoCo) are established, our novelty is functional rather than strictly architectural: resolving an underexplored systems-level instability in multimodal RAG. Beyond expanding the negative pool, CARE leverages the momentum queue to maintain a temporally stable retrieval space. Prior systems assume a static space; updated queries drift from stale queue keys, destabilizing LLM retrieval supervision. CARE stabilizes this process, ensuring reliable supervision under distribution shifts. We will clarify this stabilization perspective more explicitly in the revised manuscript. Q5: (R1) Frozen LLM. We froze the LLM to isolate our retrieval stabilization module and maintain a minimal training footprint. This bottlenecks internalizing institution-specific syntactic styles; integrating PEFT (e.g., LoRA) will be outlined as a next step. Q6: (R3) Missing definition of “CheXbert F1 score”. We apologize for the missing definition of “CheXbert F1 score”, which we refer as 5Mi-F1 and 5Ma-F1 metrics in tables 1 and 2.We will clarify this in the dataset and evaluation metrics section. Other comments: We will improve figures qualities with more enlarged labels and clearer format (R3). We will also rephrase “hallucination” to “factual inconsistency” for a more precise expression (R3). Our code will be released upon acceptance (R1, R2).
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper addresses the instability of retrieval-augmented generation in radiology. Existing RAG frameworks often suffer from “representation drift,” where updated query encoders diverge from static historical keys in the retrieval database. CARE introduces a momentum-based retrieval supervision mechanism to maintain a stable representation space. This is paired with a disease-aware alignment objective to ensure that retrieved reports provide a consistent diagnostic prior for the language model decoder. While the paper presents good contributions, its recommendation for acceptance is contingent upon the authors clarifying the following points during the rebuttal phase: 1.A significant concern is the model’s reliance on the quality of retrieved evidence. Reviewers noted that the framework lacks a mechanism to filter or “self-correct” when the retrieval queue returns erroneous, noisy, or contradictory reports from the EHR. 2.While the paper highlights improvements in linguistic metrics, reviewers pointed out that the model underperforms in categories most relevant to clinical utility, such as RadGraph F1 and RadCliQ. The reviewer argued that lexical diversity or N-gram improvements cannot outweigh the impact of superior clinical accuracy, making the authors’ claims regarding clinical utility questionable. 3.The framework is seen as well-engineered but conceptually incremental. It relies on established components like MoCo-style momentum encoders and standard contrastive learning. Furthermore, alignment occurs only at the report level. The model lacks entity-level grounding or region-to-text correspondence, which limits its ability to pinpoint specific visual findings. | The authors have addressed the reviewers’ comments well. Two reviewers acknowledged significance of the work. Therefore acceptance of the paper is concluded. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): The scores are still mixed after the rebuttal. Although CARE is well motivated, I recommend rejection. The contribution is incremental, adapting known momentum-queue and contrastive ideas to RAG, while lacking entity- or region-level grounding and robust filtering of noisy retrieved evidence. Most importantly, the method underperforms on key clinical utility metrics such as RG-F1 and CliQ0, and the rebuttal does not convincingly establish practical clinical value or meaningful progress toward deployment.

title: CARE: Confidence-Aware Reasoning for Reliable Medical VQA
reviewer_1_strengths: The paper addresses a clinically meaningful problem that is more specific than simply improving Med-VQA accuracy. Focusing on whether model confidence tracks diagnostic correctness is important for triage, escalation, and safe downstream use, and this is a well-motivated target for medical reasoning models. The proposed training recipe is simple and practically implementable. CAR is integrated directly into GRPO without introducing a separate uncertainty head or a complicated auxiliary model, which makes the method easy to understand and potentially easy to adopt in related medical MLLM pipelines. The empirical results are strong and consistent on the reported benchmarks. In Table 1, CARE is the only method reported to rank first across accuracy, ECE, and hallucination rate on all three datasets, which suggests that the method is not merely trading calibration for accuracy or vice versa. The training-stage analysis is useful. The separation of Training-Free, SFT, RL, and SFT+RL provides a more informative picture than a single end-point comparison, and the open-ended versus closed-ended discussion offers practical insight into when structured CoT initialization appears most helpful.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The central contribution of CAR is not cleanly isolated by the current ablations. Table 2 varies training stages, but there is no same-backbone comparison between RL with a standard accuracy/form reward and RL with CAR. The evaluation metrics could be removed to set aside more room for ablation studies.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: Strengths 1.The paper studies confidence miscalibration in medical VQA. This is an important and practical problem for clinical deployment. 2.The pipeline is clear and well structured. The combination of CoT data synthesis, SFT initialization, and RL optimization is easy to follow. 3.The experiments cover multiple datasets. The evaluation includes accuracy, calibration, and hallucination metrics. Results are consistently strong across benchmarks. 4.The overall presentation is good and easy to follow
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Weaknesses Method 1.The paper defines confidence as the average token probability of the generated output. This definition is explicit, but is it a valid proxy for answer-level confidence? It seems closer to generation likelihood than epistemic uncertainty. How sensitive is this measure to output length or decoding settings such as temperature? 2.The method may lack sufficient insight. Several recent works [1,2,3] have explored confidence-aware or confidence-driven optimization. What is the key methodological difference between CAR and these approaches? 3.The reward design may not guarantee true calibration. It encourages higher confidence scores derived from token-level probabilities on correct outputs and penalizes them on incorrect ones. But does this ensure alignment with empirical accuracy, or only reshape token-level likelihood? Experiments 1.The hallucination metric relies on a VLM judge (Lingshu-32B), but the inference setup is unclear. How are temperature, prompting, and evaluation consistency controlled? 2.The contribution of the proposed reward is not isolated. In Table 2, the ablation only compares training stages, without isolating CAR. It may be helpful to include comparisons with RL without CAR to better understand its impact. 3.It may also be important to report statistical significance. In Table 1, results on small datasets such as VQA-RAD are presented without variance. How stable are these improvements across different runs? [1] Gu, Bowen, et al. “Probabilistic medical predictions of large language models.” npj Digital Medicine 7.1 (2024): 367.[2] Li, Pengyi, et al. “Confidence is all you need: Few-shot rl fine-tuning of language models.” arXiv preprint arXiv:2506.06395 (2025). [3] Prabhudesai, Mihir, et al. “Maximizing confidence alone improves reasoning.” arXiv preprint arXiv:2505.22660 (2025).
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The research problem addressed in this paper, calibrating the output confidence of MLLMs, is both practical and significant. Well-calibrated confidence scores can serve as a critical indicator for clinicians, enabling them to better assess the reliability of model outputs and make more informed decisions.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The connection between the two proposed contributions needs to be clarified. Specifically, it remains unclear how the constructed CoT data benefits the confidence-calibrative RL training, or conversely, how the proposed RL reward leverages the constructed CoT data to achieve better calibration. Further elaboration on the interplay between these two components would help readers understand how they jointly strengthen the overall framework. 2.The novelty of the proposed CoT curation process warrants further clarification. Several existing methods already construct CoT data from visual content, questions, and final conclusions [1], making the distinction of the proposed approach less apparent. Including a discussion of related multi-modal medical CoT construction methods (e.g., [1][2]) would provide important context and help readers better appreciate the specific contributions of this work. 3.The rationale behind the confidence calibration reward requires more justification. The reward is computed by averaging the confidence scores across all output tokens; however, not all tokens are equally informative with respect to the final conclusion — for instance, tokens such as or punctuation marks carry little semantic relevance. Whether the inclusion of such tokens distorts the reward signal is not discussed. Additionally, the claim that "a white-box signal derived from the model's own output distribution can be directly tied to diagnostic correctness within the reward function" lacks sufficient supporting evidence and should be substantiated more rigorously. 4.Additional experiments are needed to more convincingly support the paper’s claims. The rationale for benchmarking compact-scale models (≤3B parameters) against the trained 7B model should be clarified, as this comparison may not be entirely fair. More importantly, ablative studies that individually quantify the contributions of the proposed CoT construction and the new reward to overall performance improvement are necessary. The current ablation focuses on different training schemes, which does not directly validate the two core contributions. Furthermore, the confidence shift shown in Figure 3 is somewhat expected given that the reward directly supervises this behavior. A more informative analysis would present the confidence shift conditioned separately on correct and incorrect conclusions, which would provide stronger evidence that the model genuinely learns to re-calibrate its confidence during the reasoning process rather than simply responding to the reward signal. [1] Niu, Shuai, et al. “Multimodal clinical reasoning through knowledge-augmented rationale generation.” arXiv preprint arXiv:2411.07611 (2024). [2] Sun, Haoran, et al. “Chiron-o1: Igniting multimodal large language models towards generalizable medical reasoning via mentor-intern collaborative search.” arXiv preprint arXiv:2506.16962 (2025).
reviewer_3_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the AC and reviewers for recognizing the clinical relevance, clear story, and comprehensive evaluation of CARE. The major concerns are whether CoT/CAR contributions are isolated, confidence validity, and how CARE differs from related work. We address them below. Ablation for CoT and CAR (R1Q1/R1Q2/R2Q5/R4Q4). We conducted an ablation study under different GRPO settings on SLAKE: Setting / ACC / ECE / HR Base GRPO: 71.25 / 25.92 / 16.37 with CoT: 77.94 / 18.89 / 14.88 with CAR: 82.47 / 14.83 / 12.38 CARE: 87.30 / 11.50 / 7.01 This confirms their complementarity: CoT strengthens reasoning initialization, while CAR improves calibration beyond standard GRPO. Validity of confidence proxy (R2Q1/R4Q3/R2Q3). Prior work defines calibration as confidence-performance alignment [1]. Accordingly, we use ECE to directly evaluate whether our answer-level confidence proxy aligns with actual accuracy. The consistent ECE reductions in Table 1 and our new ablation support the validity of this proxy, showing that CAR improves confidence-accuracy alignment rather than merely increasing likelihood. Differentiation from confidence-driven works (R2Q2). Mentioned rencent work ask the model to report confidence, or reward high confidence alone. Instead, CAR use confidence in GRPO as a correctness-conditioned calibration term. Does CAR really recalibrate? (R2Q3/R4Q4). We further added conditioned confidence analysis on VQA-RAD. reviewer_1_strengths: The paper’s main strength lies in the effective combination of existing state-of-the-art components — including the diffusion pre-training approach from [1], squeeze-excitation modules from [2], and the Cross-Modality Heterogeneous Graph Fusion (CMHGF) from [3] — into a coherent and functional framework that achieves good overall performance. reviewer_1_weaknesses: The paper has two major weaknesses. First, the state-of-the-art comparison is misleading: the baselines reported are vanilla implementations (e. g. , basic nnUNet), whereas published methods in the literature substantially outperform the values reported — for instance, the best participants in the AutoPET challenge achieved mean Dice scores between 0.74 and 0.79 [1], compared to the authors’ result of 0.63; similarly for HECKTOR, SE-nnUNet [2] reports a Dice of 0.75, which exceeds the vanilla nnUNet value of 0.68 reported in the paper but is beaten by the authors’ result of 0.78. Second, the results lack any measure of statistical variability, making it impossible to assess whether the observed differences are statistically significant. On the minor side, the computational cost is not discussed despite the ablation study showing that the PET-only variant achieves 96% of the best Dice score with only about half the parameters (57%). Several methodological details are also missing: for MA-MIP, the number of projections and the angular step size are not specified; and for Dual-SE, neither the meaning of “dual” nor the role of “global” in the Global Average Pooling is clarified. reviewer_2_strengths: The paper’s main strengths are that it presents a well-motivated and coherent method rather than a loosely assembled architecture, with novelty centered on PET-guided asymmetric graph fusion that uses metabolically salient PET regions to selectively pull complementary boundary information from CT. This is interesting because it reflects the distinct clinical roles of the two modalities better than standard symmetric fusion or simple concatenation. The use of a frozen diffusion-pretrained backbone with lightweight adapters is also a strong aspect, since it offers a practical way to exploit self-supervised priors under limited annotation and multi-center variation. In addition, the MA-MIP 2.5D representation is a smart efficiency choice that preserves global volumetric context without full 3D cost. These ideas are supported by broad evaluation across three public datasets, comparisons with strong baselines, and targeted ablation studies that validate the contribution of the pretraining, adapters, fusion design, and timestep choice.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The main weaknesses of the paper are that several of its core ideas appear more integrative than fundamentally new: the diffusion backbone is based on standard DDPM pretraining, the asymmetric graph fusion is explicitly built on prior heterogeneous multimodal fusion work, and the MA-MIP strategy is close to prior projection-based PET segmentation methods already cited by the paper itself. In addition, while the application is clinically relevant, the evidence for clinical feasibility is still limited to retrospective benchmark results with standard segmentation metrics, without reader studies, workflow impact, or treatment-planning evaluation. The experimental section is solid but does not fully probe robustness to issues such as scanner variation, missing modalities, lesion type, or low-data regimes, and the efficiency claims are not directly quantified with runtime or memory comparisons. Finally, although the method performs strongly overall, it is not uniformly best on every metric, and the paper does not fully disentangle how much of the gain comes specifically from diffusion priors versus pretraining or architectural design more broadly.

This is a clear improvement over naive concatenation, which is explicitly criticized in the paper. 3.Strong multi-dataset validation (important for MICCAI): Evaluation on three datasets with different characteristics is a major strength. The paper is largely a combination of existing ideas: 1.Diffusion priors for representation learning already explored (e.g., diffusion-based pretraining in medical imaging). 2.Graph-based fusion and asymmetric fusion already exist (e.g., AAHN, CMHGF). 3.MIP-based 2.5D modeling previously proposed. author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and meta-reviewer for their comments. We address the key concerns below. [Fair SOTA comparison, R1-Q1] The difference between our absolute scores and some published values mainly reflects dataset/protocol differences, not weak baselines. For HECKTOR, we used the expanded HECKTOR 2025 dataset (Ref. 14), which is larger and more heterogeneous than the 2022 version (from 854 to ~1,200 cases and from 9 to 11 centers); therefore, DSC values are not directly comparable. For AutoPET, standard DSC is sensitive to the 50.6% negative cases, and top entries often used dataset-specific post-processing, such as removing small connected components. To evaluate intrinsic representation ability, we did not use such post-hoc optimization and reported standard DSC, HD95, and Recall on positive cases. Under the official post-hoc oDSC protocol, CDFP-Net reaches 0.8488.[Variance and significance, R1-Q2] All metrics are averaged over five independent runs. Wilcoxon signed-rank tests show significant improvements across datasets (all p<0.05; e.g., p=0.017 on HECKTOR), supporting the robustness of the gains. [Computational cost, R1-Q3/R2-Q3/R3-Q3] CDFP-Net requires 133.14 GFLOPs, with 268.17 ms average single-sample inference time. Although PET-only is lighter, the full model improves HECKTOR DSC from 75.31% to 78.44% and reduces HD95 from 12.16 mm to 8.26 mm, showing a meaningful boundary/accuracy gain relative to the added cost. [Method details, R1-Q3/R2-Q3/R3-Q6] MA-MIP uses a 5° step, producing 72 projections per volume. To avoid confusion with the dual-stream backbone, “Dual-SE” is better described as two-stage SE, since it is deployed at the input and bottleneck stages. GAP recalibrates channels using global macro-context rather than local intensity spikes. PET and CT diffusion encoders are pre-trained separately on unlabeled modality-specific data. All datasets are split at the patient level into pre-training, fine-tuning, and test sets using a 7:2:1 ratio, with sliding-window cropping applied to all MA-MIP projections. [Contribution and novelty, R2-Q1/R3-Q1] We agree that CDFP-Net builds on diffusion pre-training, projection-based modeling, and graph fusion. Its contribution is a PET-CT-specific system aligned with three bottlenecks: limited annotation, high 3D cost, and PET-CT physical heterogeneity. The frozen diffusion backbone transfers self-supervised generative priors with lightweight adapters, while the modality-asymmetric dynamic graph mechanism uses metabolically salient PET regions as anchors to query CT boundary cues. This preserves modality heterogeneity and enables PET-guided, structure-assisted refinement beyond simple concatenation or symmetric fusion. [Clinical scope, R2-Q2/R3-Q5] We agree that the current evidence is retrospective and does not establish deployment readiness. Our claims should be interpreted as retrospective performance warranting further validation, not direct clinical feasibility. Future work will include prospective validation, reader studies, workflow assessment, and treatment-planning endpoint evaluation. [Baselines and positioning, R3-Q2] Our baselines include recent PET-CT fusion and medical SSL methods, including CIPA, AAHN, and MedCoSS, plus representative 3D segmentation models. We acknowledge that diffusion-based segmentation and foundation-model comparisons would further strengthen positioning and will explore them in future work. [References, R3-Q8] Available preprints have been updated to peer-reviewed versions where possible. Ref. 14 remains an arXiv citation because it is the required reference for the unpublished HECKTOR 2025 dataset. [Fusion logic, R1-Q4] We appreciate this important point. In the Q=CT ablation, the residual target was not changed to the CT bottleneck, which may understate the reverse-guidance setting. We will add supplemental experiments with CT-target residual addition to test the PET-guided, CT-assisted fusion hypothesis.

title: CDPM-Align: Multi-Scale Guidance-Aligned Diffusion Pretraining for Robust Few-Shot Anatomical Landmark Detection
reviewer_1_strengths: The paper introduces a novel technical mechanism that uses classifier-free guidance signals as structural descriptors, ensuring robustness to anatomical heterogeneity where standard SSL methods often fail. The framework demonstrates high data efficiency, matching the performance of of large model using a targeted in-domain corpus of 988 images. This approach is backed by rigorous multi-metric validation across three benchmarks. Ultimately, the results confirm that the model maintains clinical precision and stability in 10-shot and 25-shot scenarios.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The proposed method is currently restricted to 2D X-ray images, leaving its performance and the scalability of the multi-scale alignment loss unproven for 3D volumetric data such as CT or MRI. Furthermore, the framework relies on heuristic hyperparameter selection; the alignment weights and diffusion timesteps are determined empirically without a formal theoretical derivation. From a resource perspective, the alignment phase introduces a 1.3x computational overhead due to the requirement of four forward passes per iteration, which may pose a barrier for hardware-constrained environments. Finally, the evaluation lacks a direct head-to-head comparison with emerging medical foundation models, instead relying on externally reported figures rather than standardized few-shot benchmarks.

reviewer_2_strengths: 1.Novel multi-scale guidance alignment loss The authors introduce a multi-scale guidance alignment loss that enforces directional consistency of the classifier-free guidance signal (Delta h) across independently sampled diffusion steps. This design is well-motivated and demonstrates measurable improvements over baseline methods in the experimental results. 2.Clinically motivated evaluation setting The work focuses on challenging low-data settings (10 shot and 25 shot landmark detection), which are highly relevant to real-world clinical scenarios where annotations are scarce. This strengthens the practical significance of the study. 3.Computation-aware design The proposed strategy activates the multi-scale alignment loss only during a later training phase (10% of total iterations). This is a thoughtful design choice that significantly reduces computational overhead (from 4× to 1.3×) while maintaining strong performance gains. (Sec. 2.2)
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.Details for baseline initialization and training protocol In Section 3.1, the setup for the baseline models is not sufficiently clear, leading to potential architectural confusion. Specifically, it is unclear if the authors: (a) Constructed a U-Net using a pre-trained ResNet-101 encoder (e.g. DINO) and then performed the Stage 1 generative pre-training (diffusion) for the baseline, or; (b) Simply utilized the pre-trained ResNet-101 encoder (e.g., DINO) to pre-train the pooled corpus and attached a randomly initialized decoder only at the beginning of the Stage 2 downstream task. The manuscript would be significantly strengthened if this initialization protocol was explicitly clarified. 2.Baseline fairness If the (b) from the point 1 is true, the proposed CDPM-align model possesses a significant structural advantage by starting the 10-shot task with a fully pre-trained decoder, whereas the baselines would be forced to learn dense upsampling from scratch. This is supported by the fact that all self-supervised ResNet-101 baselines (DINO, MoCo v3, SimCLRv2) in Tables 1-3 consistently underperform compared to ResNet-101 (ImageNet). On the same task (while different dataset), prior work Di Via et al [8] has shown self-supervised ResNet-101 encoders (DINO, MoCo v3, SimCLRv2) outperform ImageNet-supervised ResNet-101.Yet in this paper, the opposite pattern appears. A possible explanation is that the baselines are disadvantaged by the decoder initialization protocol. I suggest clarifying the baseline model construction and re-assess the fairness of the evaluation. 3.Uncertainty quantification claims Although the proposed method adopts the Expected Radial Error (ERE) as a measure of uncertainty, the uncertainty analysis remains insufficient. In particular, given the authors’ claim that a lower ERE indicates better uncertainty quantification, a more thorough analysis and discussion of this relationship would be expected. 4.(Minor) Readability of figures and tables While the experimental evaluation is comprehensive, all figures and tables are difficult to read due to small font sizes, particularly in printed format. author_feedback: We thank all reviewers for the encouraging feedback. We are glad the guidance alignment mechanism is recognised as novel and well-motivated (R2, R3, R4), and that the few-shot evaluation (R3, R4) and experimental evidence (R2, R4) are appreciated. We address the remaining concerns below, following the submitted paper’s reference numbering. Camera ready includes the link to our GitHub repository, where we release the code as open-source. Baseline initialisation and fairness (R3-1, R3-2). The SSL baselines use a UNet with a pretrained ResNet-101 encoder and a randomly initialised decoder; the ImageNet baseline uses the same architecture. CDPM/CDPM-align pretrains the full UNet via diffusion, replacing only the output head downstream. SSL vs. ImageNet is architecturally matched (both share random decoders), so SSL underperformance points to encoder representation quality rather than decoder disadvantage. The discrepancy with [8], where SSL outperformed ImageNet, stems from two differences: (i) here, SSL is pretrained on the pooled multidomain corpus (chest + cephalo + hand) rather than a single-domain setting (as done in [8]), with discriminative objectives collapsing on heterogeneous data; (ii) this work adopts contour-hugging heatmaps [19] instead of Gaussian ones as in [8], a more representation-sensitive setting. Unlike SSL, the generative paradigm pretrains the entire UNet by construction; the ablation in Table 4 (lambda=0 vs. lambda=5) isolates the alignment contribution within the same architecture. Novelty and design choices (R4-1, R4-2, R2). We appreciate R4’s recognition that the paper is ”well-motivated, methodologically sound, and supported by strong experimental evidence”. The novelty lies in repurposing the classifier-free guidance signal ∆h as a structural descriptor for representation learning. To our knowledge, no prior work has enforced cross-timestep directional consistency on ∆h for dense prediction. Table 4 confirms that alignment alone improves MRE by 24% on Shenzhen 10-shot. Cosine similarity is magnitude-invariant, suited for ∆h whose norm varies across timesteps while its direction encodes structural information. The range [T/4, 3T/4] targets the regime where ∆h is most class-discriminative, avoiding both near-clean and noise-dominated timesteps. Multiscale extraction follows established UNet feature hierarchy practice [1]. Uncertainty quantification (R3-3). Uncertainty quantification is clinically relevant (highlighted as a strenght by R4). Under this perspective, we exploited uncertainty estimation as an evaluation metric for different pre-training strategies. Accordingly, we relied on ERE as a quantitative measure of uncertaintly, as validated originally in [19], which introduced the metric and showed its correlation with MRE under contour-hugging heatmaps. ERE measures the expected distance between the predicted landmark and a heatmap sample, capturing spatial concentration. Crucially, ERE is informative only when heatmaps allow freeform distributions, as in [19]; Gaussian targets with fixed shape make ERE a trivial function of bandwidth. CDPM-align achieves ERE at most equal to MRE across all 6 conditions, with sub-millimetre ERE at 25-shot on ISBI2015 and DHA (25-34% improvement over [8]). 2D limitation and overhead (R2). We agree that 3D extension is important future work (Sec. 4); the alignment mechanism is dimensionality-agnostic. The 1.3x overhead, which R3 acknowledges as a ”thoughtful design choice”, adds 20 min on A100.Regarding medical foundation models, we incorporated a concurrent work [11] in our paper and benchmarked our few-shot results against the fully supervised results reported in its tables, obtaining comparable performance and supporting the robustness of our guidance-alignment signal in generative pretraining.

author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for the constructive feedback. We address key concerns below. (1) Novelty: The primary contribution is not a new segmentation architecture or ordinal loss, but a clinically motivated reformulation with tolerance-aware evaluation and inter-expert contextualization. R1’s concern that loss substitution is incremental is valid: EMD, CORAL, and MSE are established tools. However, we are constrained since clinical settings generate discrete CVM stages which is an established common practice. Furthermore, no prior CVM work has applied any continuous formulation (Table 1, ‘Continuous?’ column, all ‘No’). We pair this with a clinically-grounded evaluation framework (Tol-1/Tol-2, inter-expert agreement) that exposes what exact-match accuracy conceals: adjacent-stage errors dominate and match clinician variability patterns. The proposed framework bridges the lack of metrics to assess the continuous modeling of CVM staging. (2) Benchmarking: No public benchmark exists, each prior method uses a private dataset, different annotation setup, and often a collapsed staging scheme (some reduce six stages to three, inflating accuracy), making cross-paper quantitative comparison hard. Specifically: Zhang et al. (CDSNet) and Zhang F. et al. use hand-wrist and 3D CT modalities incompatible with our 2D LC setting; Li et al. (PSC-CVM) requires object-detection masks and contour keypoints; Wang et al. (PCVMNet), Atici et al. (TRIPOD), and Balaha et al. depend on landmarks, age features, or handcrafted markers absent from our dataset. We will extend Table 1 with R1’s cited methods to make ORACLE’s positioning explicit. Further, Refs. 3–6 report clinician variability without automated models and serve as motivating evidence, not competing baselines. (3) Clinically superior (R2, R3, MR): We accept this phrasing is too strong and will revise it to ‘clinically better-aligned.’ Clinical reporting will remain categorical, but the underlying biological process is continuous, empirically reflected in expert disagreement concentrating at adjacent stages (Refs. 3–6; inter-senior κ = 0.74 in our study). A model trained with ordinal loss penalises distant-stage errors more heavily, whereas cross-entropy treats a 1-stage and a 3-stage error identically. Performance evidence supports the alignment claim: CORAL outperforms CE by +3.5% accuracy, with model–expert κ matching inter-senior κ. Prospective clinical trials remain future work, as we acknowledge. (4) R3 ethics query: Code was shared with reviewers; we will share the dataset via CMT upon request. (5) Minor Comments: We will (i) restructure the Introduction to highlight the three-gap motivation; (ii) add missing citations (U-Net++, ResNet-152, EfficientNet-B5, ConvNeXt-Base, AdamW); (iii) fix the grammatical error in 4.3 and align the EfficientNet-B5 description across 4.2 and Fig. 1; (iv) replace ‘clinically superior’ throughout. On R3’s technical questions: EMD computes squared ℓ₂ distance between predicted and target CDFs over K−1 cumulative bins, penalising larger ordinal gaps quadratically; CORAL outputs K−1 binary thresholds predicting stage > k, with class probabilities from consecutive sigmoid differences; the background segmentation class reduces false positives: only classes 1–3 feed downstream classification. Tol-k = |predicted − ground truth| ≤ k; “100% expert verification” means all 569 masks were reviewed and corrected by two senior orthodontists; “unannotated” means stage-labelled without pixel-level masks; the ±1 threshold was confirmed through clinician consultation; morphology is learned from pixel-level supervision with no handcrafted features. Learnt segmentation weights: Lovász 43.1%, FocalBoundary 28.6%, Tversky 27.1%. The final manuscript will present the first CVM framework grounded in continuous modeling, expert-verified annotation, and inter-expert-calibrated evaluation.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper proposes the ORACLE framework, which reformulates cervical vertebral maturation (CVM) staging as an ordinal/continuous learning problem, integrating vertebral segmentation with alternative loss formulations (e.g., EMD, CORAL, regression) and evaluating performance using tolerance-based metrics and inter-expert agreement. Reviewers generally agree that the problem is clinically relevant and that moving beyond strict categorical classification toward ordinal modeling is conceptually meaningful and better aligned with the gradual nature of skeletal development (R1,R2). The inclusion of tolerance-based evaluation and comparison with expert variability is also viewed as a strength that improves clinical relevance (R1,R2,R3). However, there are several notable concerns. A primary issue raised by multiple reviewers is the limited methodological novelty. The framework relies heavily on established components (U-Net++ for segmentation), with the main variation being different loss formulations, which are seen as incremental rather than fundamentally novel (R1,R2,R3). In addition, the experimental section lacks important comparisons to prior CVM-specific methods, making it difficult to contextualise the performance gains against the current state of the art (R1, R3). Clarity and positioning are also recurring weaknesses. The introduction and overall framing do not clearly distinguish the paper’s contributions from existing ordinal learning approaches (R2), and several methodological details (e.g., loss definitions, parameterisation, and metric formulations) are insufficiently explained (R3). There are also missing citations for standard architectures and minor inconsistencies in the description of the pipeline (R1). Furthermore, the claim that continuous modelling is “clinically superior” is not fully substantiated with direct evidence, and would benefit from a more careful and nuanced justification (R2, R3). Overall, while the paper addresses an important problem and proposes a reasonable reformulation with clinically motivated evaluation, the technical contribution is viewed as incremental and the experimental validation and clarity need strengthening. Based on the balance of reviews (R1: Weak Reject; R2: Weak Accept; R3: Accept), I would recommend a rebuttal. | The final review recommendations are two Accepts and one Reject. However, both R1 and R3 highlighted several important weaknesses that should be addressed. In particular, the main concern centres on the paper’s continuous formulation, where the classification problem is reframed using a regression loss. R1 questioned the novelty of this idea, noting that prior works had already explored continuous representations. Similarly, R3 was unconvinced by the claim of better clinical alignment, arguing that the method models biological growth rather than reflecting the actual categorical clinical workflow, while also raising concerns about benchmarking and clarity of the clinical evaluation process. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Author have addressed several of the issues in the rebuttal, and even though the contributions seems incremental, it tackles a relevant clinical problem, the concept is sound and the evaluation is well conceptualized. With improvements in clarity and stronger positioning, the work could be a useful contribution. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): the methodological contribution is incremental—combining established components without a novel technical insight. The claim of “clinical superiority” is not substantiated, and the manuscript’s framing and detail need strengthening. These fundamental gaps outweigh the clinically relevant motivation and the strength of tolerance-based evaluation. Deviation from reviewers’ recommendation: While the reviews were mixed (Weak Reject, Weak Accept, Accept (switched to nagative after rebuttal)), I am inclined to reject it in its current form

title: CheXanatomy: Anatomy–Aware Vision–Language Modeling for Chest Radiographs
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The proposed framework is technically coherent, with a clear integration of CT-derived supervision, tokenized anatomical prediction, and parameter-efficient adaptation of a pretrained VLM. 2.The experimental study is reasonably comprehensive, including in-distribution, out-of-distribution, and low-data transfer settings, as well as ablations on model scale, input resolution, and vision encoder fine-tuning.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The methodological novelty is limited, as the paper mainly integrates existing ideas for a new anatomy-aware VLM setting. 2.The segmentation comparison is limited, with evaluation mainly against a U-Net baseline rather than a broader set of strong CXR segmentation methods. 3.The paper relies heavily on synthetic CT-derived supervision, but does not directly assess the quality of the synthetic data or projected labels. 4.Some important methodological details remain unclear, particularly the VQ-VAE used for mask tokenization, which weakens reproducibility. 5.The presentation could be improved for better clarity and overall coherence. For example, the related work section should summarize the limitations of existing methods more explicitly and connect them more clearly to the contribution of this paper.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The paper has a clear and coherent central idea and the formulation is easy to follow - Figure 1 explains the full pipeline well. 2.The work makes good use of scalable synthetic supervision. Generating synthetic chest radiographs from CT volumes and projecting segmentation labels is a practical way to avoid the lack of dense CXR annotations, and the scale is meaningful. 3.The out-of-distribution results are encouraging and visually convincing. In Figure 2, the best 10B/448 model is roughly comparable to U-Net on Dice/IoU on real CXRs while showing clearly better Hausdorff distance and Fourier descriptor distance. Figure 3 supports this qualitatively: the VLM outputs look smoother and more anatomically stable, with fewer jagged boundaries and fewer small irregular false-positive regions than the U-Net baseline. 4.The few-shot transfer experiment is strong and relevant. Figure 4 shows that anatomy-pretrained models outperform non-pretrained baselines most clearly in the very low-data regime (0-3% of RadVLM training data), which supports the claim that anatomy supervision provides a useful spatial prior and improves sample efficiency for downstream localization tasks. 5.The paper includes useful ablations on model size, input resolution, and vision-encoder fine-tuning. These experiments help the reader understand where the gains are coming from, and the finding that higher resolution helps more than vision-encoder fine-tuning is informative for future work in this direction.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The real-world validation is narrow compared with the scope of the claim. The model is trained on 80 anatomical targets, but real-data evaluation is limited to lungs and heart on CheXmask and ribs on VinDr-RibCXR. This leaves it unclear whether the claimed anatomy-aware representation really extends to the broader 80-class setting, especially for small, thin, or heavily overlapping structures. The paper would be stronger with per-structure results and broader real-data validation. 2.The paper sometimes overstates what has been demonstrated about “anatomy-aware medical VLMs.” The experiments show segmentation and improved low-data grounding, but they do not show that the anatomy supervision improves actual multimodal radiology tasks such as report generation, grounded reporting, or clinically meaningful phrase grounding. The paper would benefit from a more careful positioning of what is and is not validated here. 3.The reporting could be more rigorous. Figure 2 is promising, but the paper does not provide statistical testing, confidence intervals, or per-class breakdowns, and the bottom-row plot combines two different real datasets with different structures and annotation styles. That makes the claim of improved robustness harder to interpret precisely. 4.There are also a few presentation issues that should be fixed in revision: Figure 1 uses “Paligemma” instead of “PaliGemma”; the figure shows “Gemma 2 (2B / 9B)” while the text mainly discusses 3B/10B models; there is inconsistent notation for image size (“224 x224”, “224x224”, “448 × 448”); and the sentence around “bounding box IoU Fig. 4” is missing punctuation. These are minor, but polishing them would improve clarity.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The paper has a very interesting objective: “distilling” the total segmentator into 2D synthetic X-rays, without using more traditional segmentation methods on the MIC literature. The authors demonstrate “it works!”, even if results are not very impressive yet, its a first step and can bring interesting discussions on architectural direction on the field. Of highlight is the analysis of data fraction in results being favorable to the autoregressive VLM training. Writing is very streamlined and easy to follow, going directly to the point. The synthethic data generated on this work could be of value to the community (together with the promised code) but there is no mention of public sharing of the generated x-rays and masks.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Although the idea is very interesting and demonstrated to work, results are not very impressive, especially considering the more than 10-year-old basic UNet baseline. Comparisons with other methods (representative of other architectural strategies) are necessary such as nnUNet and MEDSam. Especially concerning is the very high result variance displayed by the boxplots.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for their constructive feedback. Since several comments recur across reviews, we group responses thematically. We will revise our manuscript accordingly including correction of formatting issues and legends(R2.4). Contribution/scope. The central contribution of CheXanatomy is formulating projected CXR anatomy as native autoregressive VLM generation, where dense, multi-label, overlapping anatomical masks are predicted through next-token generation without an external segmentation module(R1.1). This differs from referred-object VLM segmentation, which handles a single object per query rather than dense, overlapping multi-label structures. CheXanatomy is not designed to set segmentation SOTA or replace specialized segmentation models; we will clarify this in the revision(R1.2,R2.2,R3.1). Baselines. We considered alternatives, including adapted nnU-Net with multi-channel outputs, since nnU-Net is not natively designed for large-scale overlapping masks(R1.2,R3.1). In preliminary evaluation, this was suboptimal for our highly overlapping multi-label task(R1.2,R3.1). We therefore used a specialized multi-channel U-Net, which matched the task and provided a strong baseline(R1.2,R3.1). MedSAM is an interactive bounding box-promptable model that differs fundamentally from autoregressive multi-label dense generation from a text query, and is therefore not directly comparable(R3.1). We will expand the discussion of alternatives (e.g., U-Net++) and clarify that the goal is not exhaustive benchmarking but evaluating token-space anatomy supervision against a task-matched multi-channel baseline(R1.2,R3.1). Synthetic-label validity. We will clarify that experienced radiologists reviewed TotalSegmentator outputs, DRR plausibility, mask alignment, overt segmentation failures, and ambiguities from overlapping projected structures(R1.3). We will add representative overlays and clarify the review process(R1.3). Real-world validation. We evaluated publicly available CXR datasets we identified that provide anatomical dense masks relevant to our targets (CheXmask and RibCXR)(R2.1). This covers both compact organs and overlapping structures, but remains narrower than the 80-class synthetic setting because such fine-grained real CXR anatomy datasets are very limited(R2.1). We will state this limitation and clarify that CheXmask labels are automatically generated pseudo-labels rather than purely manual ground truth(R2.1,R2.3). RadVLM and claim scope. The RadVLM experiments provide complementary evidence for spatial transfer beyond the segmentation labels(R2.2). However, bounding-box localization is not dense segmentation(R2.2). We will present RadVLM as evidence for improved low-data spatial transfer, not validation of all 80 segmentation classes(R2.1,R2.2). We will also scope claims about anatomy-aware VLMs more carefully: the experiments show improved segmentation robustness and low-data localization transfer, not improved report generation or grounded reporting(R2.2). Reproducibility. We will release the CheXanatomy codebase with the camera-ready version, including prompts, configs, scripts, and data splits(R1.4,R3.3). This includes the pipeline to recreate synthetic data from the publicly available CT-RATE data(R3.3). The VQ-VAE tokenizer is publicly available as part of PaliGemma and will be integrated into our released code; we will also report mask reconstruction details and metrics(R1.4). Reporting and variance. We will separate CheXmask and RibCXR results to avoid combining datasets with different structures and styles(R2.3). We will also add per-structure breakdowns, confidence intervals, and statistical comparisons where appropriate(R2.1,R2.3). This will clarify that the observed aggregate variance primarily reflects systematic differences in segmentation accuracy across anatomical targets (e.g. heart is easier to segment than ribs), rather than high within-structure variability or instability of outputs(R3.2).
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): The paper presents an interesting and coherent direction for injecting anatomical supervision into pretrained vision-language models using CT-derived synthetic chest radiographs and token-space autoregressive segmentation. However, the current evaluation is not yet strong enough to support acceptance. The segmentation comparison is limited mainly to a basic U-Net baseline, while stronger and more representative CXR segmentation baselines such as nnU-Net, U-Net++, DeepLab, or other CT-projection-supervision methods are missing. In addition, the reliability of the synthetic supervision pipeline is not sufficiently validated: the paper does not directly assess DRR image quality, projected-mask accuracy, TotalSegmentator error propagation, or conflicts from overlapping anatomical structures. Key VQ-VAE details and reconstruction metrics are also missing, which weakens reproducibility. The reported results show high variance, but no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals are provided. Finally, the nature of CheXmask labels should be clarified, since they are not purely manual ground truth, and the authors should specify whether synthetic CXRs, projected masks, VQ-VAE components, prompts, configs, scripts, and data splits will be released. | The post-rebuttal opinions are mixed but lean positive, with two reviewers recommending acceptance and one reviewer maintaining rejection. The negative reviewer remains concerned that the paper does not sufficiently justify why token-space autoregressive generation is preferable to conventional segmentation methods for dense, multi-label, overlapping anatomical masks. However, the other two reviewers state that their main concerns were addressed, including clearer scope definition and explanation of result variance. Overall, the work presents an interesting and discussion-worthy direction for anatomy-aware adaptation of VLMs to CXR segmentation using CT-derived synthetic supervision. Remaining limitations regarding stronger segmentation baselines, synthetic-label validation, VQ-VAE details, statistical analysis, and claim scope should be clearly addressed in the final version. The authors should provide the full open-source implementation to improve the reproducibility. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper proposes a coherent approach for injecting CT-derived anatomical supervision into chest radiograph vision-language models via autoregressive token-space generation of dense, multi-label, overlapping anatomical masks. Initial concerns focused on limited segmentation baselines, synthetic-label validity, high variance, and incomplete reproducibility details. Two reviewers who initially recommended weak reject moved to accept, and the authors clarified the scope: the work is not intended to establish segmentation SOTA, but to explore anatomy-aware supervision for VLMs. The rebuttal also clarifies synthetic-label review, the pseudo-label nature of CheXmask, release plans, and a more careful presentation of real-world validation and variance. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Reviewers 2 and 3 support acceptance after rebuttal. Although Reviewer 1 remains concerned that the autoregressive formulation is not sufficiently justified over conventional segmentation approaches, I view the contribution as sufficiently novel and discussion-worthy for acceptance.

title: CIPHER: Causal Intervention Pathways for Healthcare Equity and Robustness
reviewer_1_strengths: The paper formulates medical image generation in a causal framework, explicitly separating disease and sensitive attributes as intervenable variables while keeping patient-specific structure fixed. This allows controlled counterfactual data generation without modifying the model or training objective. The four-path design decomposes data generation into generation (from noise) and instance-level editing (from real images), with separate control over disease and sensitive attributes.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The baselines are insufficient. Standard augmentation baselines (e. g. , MixUp, CutMix, and recent augmentation methods in the CXR domain [1]) are missing, making it hard to judge the advantage of the proposed method. Also, P1–P4 function more as ablations than true baselines. [1] Prakash, Eva, et al. “Evaluating and Improving the Effectiveness of Synthetic Chest X-Rays for Medical Image Analysis. “ Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF International Conference on Computer Vision. 2025. Since the method relies on conditioning with metadata tokens and synthetic data generation, it is unclear whether the improvements come from the proposed framework or simply from stronger data augmentation. The explanation of the four paths is somewhat repetitive, while the experimental analysis is relatively limited in comparison. (Also, why is Section 2 titled “Analysis”?) Additional qualitative analysis (e. g. , before and after Path 3 and 4 editing) would help better understand the behavior of the method, especially since changes in sensitive attributes (e. g. , age) in CXR images can be subtle and not clearly observable.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The paper is well written and easy to follow. 2.The proposed unified causal model, which captures how sensitive attributes influence the image generation process, is valuable for many real-world applications. The four pathways through which bias can arise, as well as the corresponding intervention strategies to mitigate it, are clearly explained. 3.Experiments across two imaging modalities, CXR and dermoscopy, and under both in-distribution and out-of-distribution settings demonstrate the effectiveness and generalizability of the proposed method.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.It is unclear how the method handles multiple sensitive attributes: are they mitigated jointly or one by one? This matters because one-at-a-time debiasing can be problematic in the presence of causal dependence among attributes. In particular, if D is a collider between sensitive attributes (for example S1 -> D <- S2) then conditioning on D while mitigating bias for S1 can induce a spurious association with S2, potentially creating additional or residual bias. The same can happen with C as a collider between sensitive attributes. The paper would benefit from clarifying this point. 2.From the results, both Path 1 and Path 2 show cases in which fairness underperforms the conventional baseline, RandAugment. Is there an explanation for this behavior? 3.In the description of Path 2, the authors state that they “systematically vary S to reshape subgroup composition.” It is unclear what “systematically varying” means in practice. Does this simply refer to balancing S? 4.The results are presented with error bars, but it is unclear how these were generated. Were they obtained through cross-validation or repeated runs?
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: Novel formulation: the causal framework presented in this work offers a paradigm for mitigating bias in medical image classifiers using synthetic data. Traditionally, previous works, such as Moroianu, S.L. et al. (2025), train image generation models with controls for both disease and demographic (sensitive) attributes, and generate balanced synthetic datasets (i.e., equal proportions of sensitive attributes) that are then used to train downstream image classifiers. However, by more carefully considering the data generation process and its relationship to different types of bias, the proposed framework, CIPHER, offers a novel approach to generating synthetic images to combat bias. Evaluation on multiple domains: the experiments in the paper apply the proposed framework to 3 datasets corresponding to 2 different applications: CheXpert Plus and MIMIC-CXR for chest xrays disease classification, and MILK10K for dermoscopy disease classification. Validating CIPHER across different domains helps elucidate the generalizability of the proposed framework. References: [1] Moroianu, Stefania L., et al. “Improving Performance, Robustness, and Fairness of Radiographic AI Models with Finely-Controllable Synthetic Data.” arXiv preprint arXiv:2508.16783 (2025).
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Unclear methodology and experimental protocol: In general, Sec 3.Methodology and Sec 4.2.Ablation Experiments are difficult to follow and have many missing details. This makes it difficult to appreciate the benefits of CIPHER relative to related work, such as that of Moroianu, S.L. et al. (2025). The authors should make it clearer how the different pathways relate to the strategies employed in prior work, or whether each pathway is a unique contribution. I summarize some key points that are unclear or missing below: Data generation for different pathways: it was really difficult to follow what intervening on a pathway means practically for downstream image classifier training. Can authors please clarify how input conditions were sampled to generate the synthetic dataset for each pathway i.e., how are the conditions c_s and c_d sampled for Path 1 and Path 2? Are sensitive attributes combined together or studied separately? Does intervening simply imply creating a balanced synthetic dataset? CIPHER: What exactly is the “CIPHER” method in relation to the four proposed pathways? Is the final synthetic dataset an equal combination of images from each of the four pathways? Image classifier training details: How are the image classifiers (DenseNet-121) trained, i.e., what were the optimizers, losses, batch sizes, learning rates, etc.? What do different runs entail to generate the error bars? References: [1] Moroianu, Stefania L., et al. “Improving Performance, Robustness, and Fairness of Radiographic AI Models with Finely-Controllable Synthetic Data.” arXiv preprint arXiv:2508.16783 (2025).
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and AC for their thoughtful feedback. Reviewers acknowledge that our causal analysis for fairness is intriguing, valuable, and novel (R1–3), clearly demonstrated (R2), that CIPHER is versatile and effective (R1–2), and that evaluations across three datasets are thorough (R2–3). As highlighted by R3, our paper offers a fresh and carefully crafted perspective on mitigating bias in medical classifiers, which we believe will be of broad interest to the MICCAI community. Below, we address reviewer concerns regarding baselines, technical contributions, and experimental protocols. 1.R1 on baselines. Prior work has shown that synthesis-based methods consistently outperform simple baselines (“Generative models improve fairness of medical classifiers under distribution shifts”); accordingly, we focus our comparisons on synthesis-based methods. For completeness, we additionally report results for MixUp, CutMix, JTT (Just Train Twice), and SELF (Selected Last-layer Finetuning), confirming our findings (order: CIPHER / MixUp / CutMix / JTT / SELF). CXR-ID: age gap 0.068/0.077/0.079/0.083/0.085; race gap 0.027/0.031/0.033/0.034/0.037.CXR-OOD: age gap 0.068/0.085/0.081/0.089/0.094; race gap 0.036/0.058/0.062/0.049/0.055.Dermoscopy: age gap 0.104/0.162/0.109/0.116/0.106; gender gap 0.020/0.032/0.028/0.041/0.032; skin-tone gap 0.046/0.118/0.095/0.125/0.115.We further emphasize that CIPHER differs fundamentally from existing synthesis-based methods such as Prakash et al., which rely on label-conditioned generation, equivalent to the P1 variant in our ablations. We compare thoroughly against P1 and demonstrate superior performance, supporting our claims regarding the importance of causal structure. 2.R3 on method contributions. In causal theory, an intervention severs the dependency from causes to the intervened variable. Our analysis identifies four pathways through which the sensitive attribute S influences the observed outcome Y, and we show that each can be blocked by learning the appropriate joint distribution and causal structure. For example, our first generative model intervenes on P1 (Fig. 2) by synthesizing disease (D)-conditioned images; training a classifier on these images causes it to disregard within-disease variation, so predictions on Y are no longer affected by manifestation bias. This effect is difficult to achieve by hand-crafted means but is learned implicitly from data (Table 1: both smaller and larger chest cavities would be correctly predicted as “Pneumothorax”). The remaining pathways can be understood analogously by referring to Sec. 2.Because the causal graph in Fig. 1 has not been previously discussed in this context, existing methods heuristically exploit synthesis-based augmentation via a single mechanism and lack a complete causal view (e.g. Moroianu et al. conflate P1 and P2). CIPHER addresses all pathways, and our ablations consistently confirm its advantages. 3.R1 on the effectiveness of causality over strong data augmentation. The benefit of data augmentation depends jointly on the quantity and quality of synthesized samples. We carefully control for both (see Sec. 4.1) by augmenting with an equal number of synthesized samples generated by the same pretrained model across all methods. The observed reduction in subgroup gaps by CIPHER under this fixed data budget directly demonstrates the effectiveness of the causal structure, not merely the augmentation volume. 4.R2 on handling multiple sensitive attributes. The current framework mitigates one sensitive attribute at a time. Extending the SCM to support joint interventions over multiple attributes is a natural and straightforward extension, which we plan to include. 5.R1 on qualitative edits. We will provide additional visualizations via supplementary online content. 6.R2–3 on implementation details. Error bars denote standard deviations over five independent runs. Code, data, and pretrained models will be made publicly available.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This manuscript has received mixed reviews, with major concerns centered on insufficient baselines (e.g., missing standard augmentation methods like MixUp/CutMix and fairness baselines), unclear experimental methodology, and difficulty isolating whether improvements come from the causal framework or simply stronger data augmentation. During the rebuttal period, the authors are required to address these limitations. | The paper presents a novel causal framework for fairness in medical imaging, formalizing bias pathways through a structural causal model with four distinct intervention strategies. Reviewers acknowledge the strong formulation, clear exposition, and validation across multiple modalities (CXR and dermoscopy). While Reviewer #1 raises baseline concerns, Reviewer #2 and #3 find the work valuable and methodologically sound. The rebuttal sufficiently addresses reproducibility and clarifies the causal contribution. Recommendation: Accept. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): All the reviewers agree that the proposed method has technical merits. The main concern of R1 is isolating the effects of data augmentation, which could be potentially addressed in the revised manuscript. Though additional results have been included in the rebuttal, these results have been ignored in this evaluation and the decision is primarily based on the technical contributions of this work. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): I agree with R1 that there are a few technical issues that worth further discussion and validation, but it seems there is a consensus that the proposed method is generally innovative and thought provoking. I believe this paper might stimulate a meaningful and vibrant discussion at MICCAI.

title: ClinCoT: Clinical-Aware Visual Chain-of-Thought for Medical Vision Language Models
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.ClinCoT is well clinically motivated. The hypothesis-driven region proposal mechanism is mimics how radiologists’ reason and form potential differential diagnoses. By examining localized regions rather than processing entire images uniformly, ClinCoT can generate multiple hypothesis driven answers, giving the framework strong conceptual grounding. 2.Consensus weighted scoring (Eq. 4) using two independent Med-LLM evaluators allows for the penalization of disagreement, while leveraging pair construction allows for an optimized forward reasoning trajectory that grounds the model in its preferred track. Critically, the explicit construction of both a dispreferred and a preferred reasoning chain forces the model to learn discriminative boundaries between clinically valid and invalid reasoning trajectories. This dual-chain design anchors the model’s intermediate reasoning steps to localized pathological evidence, producing a more grounded and stable reasoning trajectory particularly beneficial for VQA answer generation. 3.ClinCoT leverages iterative learning to address distributional shift. The iterative preference data regeneration scheme is a principled adaptation of online DPO to the medical domain, preventing stale preference data from degrading alignment as the model’s policy evolves.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.Comparing ClinCoT and MMedPO, we see mixed VQA. ClinCoT underperforms MMedPO on VQA-RAD open-ended recall (33.15 vs. 36.36 without SFT), which the authors attribute to instability in intermediate reasoning for short-form answers. However, no concrete ablation or analysis is provided to validate this hypothesis or to clarify under what conditions region-conditioned CoT is reliably beneficial or fails. 2.The computational cost is not discussed in the manuscript. The pipeline involves multiple Med-LLM evaluator calls per training sample across m=4 iterative rounds, which is likely computationally expensive. No wall-clock time, compute cost, or efficiency comparison against baselines is provided. Depending on clinical inference time, this approach would not be ideal for live-patient / radiologist interaction but could be optimized for overnight data review and patient summaries for day-staffs.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The proposed study addresses an important limitation of current Medical Vision-Language Models (Med-VLMs). Many existing methods remain predominantly text-centric and do not explicitly model how localized visual evidence shapes intermediate reasoning. In contrast, the proposed hypotheses-driven visual reasoning framework is clinically well-motivated. 2.The proposed margin-aware DPO leverages differences in preference scores, which may more accurately capture the unequal contributions of various regions to the final decision for finer discrimination between preference pairs. 3.The proposed automatic data generation pipeline is scalable and clinically meaningful, as it leverages intermediate reasoning conditioned on localized contexts derived from the clinically grounded preference pairs. 4.The authors evaluate ClinCoT on three benchmarks: two medical visual-question answering (VQA) datasets (VQA-RAD and SLAKE) and one report generation dataset (IU-Xray). They compared ClinCoT against seven baselines, including standard DPO and its variants: DPO, self-rewarding, STLLaVA-Med, POVID, SIMA, FiSAO, and MMedPO.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The authors note that most existing CoT approaches are text-centric. However, the study does not include a direct performance comparison with a text-centric CoT baseline. 2.In Section 2.1, the authors mention that disease-conditioned region hypotheses are obtained using a clinically aware visual tool. This suggests that the proposed method heavily depends on the quality of the disease-conditioned activation maps. However, the study does not validate the anatomical or clinical accuracy of the extracted regions. 3.In Section 2.1, two Med-LLM evaluators are employed in the consensus-weighted scoring strategy to assess the quality of all generated responses. However, using two Med-LLM evaluators may raise practical concerns, including high computational costs, reproducibility, and potential evaluator bias. Additionally, the study does not address how closely these evaluators’ performances correlate with those of medical professionals or experts. 4.Including a qualitative review of the reasoning chains by radiologists to evaluate whether the generated chains follow clinically appropriate inference paths would strengthen the study. 5.In Section 3.2, the results indicate that ClinCoT underperforms compared to MMedPO on the VQA-RAD dataset in the non-supervised fine-tuning (SFT) setting. This suggests that the advantages of CoT-based reasoning may depend on the specific task characteristics and training configurations. It would be valuable to discuss this observation more explicitly.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: It highlights the limitations of existing CoT approaches, which place too much emphasis on text and neglect visual cues. This direction aligns well with the actual logic of radiological diagnosis.
