title: Clinically-Grounded Hierarchical Classification for Consistent Chest X-ray Interpretation
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The method is well-designed and innovative. The authors propose the CHASE framework, which effectively models radiologists’ clinical “coarse-to-fine” reading workflow as a hierarchical classification system, aligning closely with real-world diagnostic reasoning. Notably, the Hierarchy-Violation Penalty (HVP) loss function employs an asymmetric design that permits the model to make coarse-grained predictions (e. g. , abnormality at an anatomical region level) before committing to fine-grained pathological labels, reflecting a deep understanding of clinical decision-making. 2.The experimental design is rigorous and well-controlled. All baseline methods share the same EVA-X backbone, effectively eliminating confounding factors due to differences in feature representation capacity. Furthermore, the authors conduct systematic ablation studies—including careful tuning of hyperparameters α and β—to clearly demonstrate the contribution of each component to overall performance. 3.Experiments are conducted on a large-scale dataset and demonstrate competitive results. CHASE achieves or approaches the performance of level-specific single-stage oracles across the three hierarchies. It also shows significant improvements in hierarchical probabilistic consistency, and attention visualizations confirm its strong alignment with anatomical structures, boosting interpretability. 4.The work is highly reproducible. The authors provide an anonymous code repository and include detailed descriptions of training protocols, hyperparameter settings, and implementation specifics, laying a solid foundation for future research and validation.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The flowchart lacks clear visual logic and appears slightly blurry. 2.Validation is performed only on the single MIMIC-CXR dataset. 3.The paper does not discuss the limitations of the proposed method.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: (a) Superior Probabilistic Consistency: CHASE significantly improves hierarchy consistency, achieving a probabilistic consistency, outperforming both flat and hierarchical baselines like H-CAST. (b) Anatomically Grounded Interpretability: Level-wise attention maps confirm that the model’s reasoning follows a logical spatial progression: coarse-level heads focus on broad systems, while leaf-level heads isolate specific localized abnormalities.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: (a) Baseline Selection: While the authors compare against H-CAST and Hier-ViT, the comparison could be strengthened by including more recent CXR-specific hierarchical models or anatomy-aware approaches mentioned in the introduction. (b) Insufficient Comparison with Modern Foundation Models and VLMs:Although the authors use EVA-X as a shared backbone to ensure a fair comparison , the evaluation lacks a direct performance benchmark against state-of-the-art (SOTA) Vision Foundation Models (e.g., Ark, EXA-X, RAD-DINO) or Vision-Language Models (VLMs) specifically fine-tuned for chest X-ray tasks (e.g., Med-CLIP, BioViL, or newer multimodal architectures).Without these comparisons, it remains unclear whether the proposed hierarchical constraints offer significant advantages over the implicit multi-task or reasoning capabilities inherent in large-scale pre-trained medical VLMs. (c) Lack of External Validation: Performance is reported exclusively on the MIMIC-CXR/Chest ImaGenome dataset. Validation on a distinct external cohort is necessary to prove the robustness of the hierarchical constraints across different clinical settings and imaging protocols. (d) Selection of Supervision Depths. The authors attach level-specific heads to Blocks 6, 9, and 12, claiming these represent the lower, middle, and final thirds of the backbone to ensure “well-separated supervisory signals”. However, there is no empirical evidence (e.g., an ablation study on different block combinations) provided to justify why these specific layers are optimal for the Top, Mid, and Leaf levels.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The problem formulation bears clear clinical motivation. Instead of simply treating chest radiograph analysis as flat multi-label classification, this paper highlights the hierarchical relationship of region–subregion–pathological finding. Such a design aligns well with real clinical reading workflows and effectively addresses the common granularity inconsistency problem existing in automated chest X-ray diagnosis systems. The proposed method is comprehensively designed with clear logic. CHASE integrates multi-layer BCE loss, global KL alignment, and hierarchy-violation penalty, where each component serves a distinct purpose. This joint design guarantees discriminative ability at all hierarchical levels, enforces cross-layer distribution consistency, and explicitly suppresses parent–child hierarchical contradictions. Even readers outside this specialized research domain can easily follow the technical motivation and overall pipeline of the proposed framework. The experiments are conducted at a large scale with standardized settings. All experiments adopt publicly available large-scale chest X-ray datasets. Moreover, all compared models share the identical EVA-X backbone, which eliminates performance gains brought by backbone replacement and ensures fair comparisons. The evaluation considers not only classification accuracy but also hierarchical consistency. The paper reports AUC and ACC across different hierarchical levels and further introduces dedicated consistency metrics. This provides direct quantitative evidence to verify whether the proposed method fundamentally alleviates the core issue of hierarchical prediction conflicts. The manuscript is well-organized and clearly written. Strong coherence is maintained among Figure 1, Table 1 and the methodology section. The correlations among the hierarchical taxonomy, loss functions and overall training objectives are explicitly illustrated and easy to understand.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: From a methodological perspective, the innovation leans more toward structural integration; the sense of a major methodological breakthrough is not particularly strong. Some aspects of the design still appear somewhat heuristic, such as the selection of where the heads are attached at different levels. The paper does a good job of proving improvements in consistency, but how these improvements translate into greater clinical utility could be further illustrated through more error case studies. I am not an expert in this specific sub-field; therefore, I have limited confidence in judging whether the taxonomy itself is optimal or if it covers the most critical clinical hierarchies.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank all reviewers and the meta-reviewer for their constructive feedback. R1/R3 highlighted the clinical relevance, rigorous ablations, reproducibility, and hierarchy-consistency improvements of CHASE, while R2 raised concerns regarding baselines, architectural justification, and generalization. Per MICCAI 2026 guidelines, we do not report new experimental results and focus on clarifying the submitted evidence. We address the major points below. 1.Additional baselines (R2) CHASE is a hierarchy-consistency framework, not a SOTA representation model. Our controlled protocol evaluates Flat-ViT, Hier-ViT, H-CAST, and CHASE under the same backbone and unified 54-label space, directly testing whether explicit hierarchical supervision improves anatomically coherent Top-Mid-Leaf predictions. Prior hierarchical and anatomy-aware CXR methods are related but not directly comparable: CXR hierarchical classifiers typically use limited pathology-centered labels without our Region-Subregion-Finding structure, and anatomy-aware detection models do not define outputs over our 54-label hierarchy. Re-formulating them under our taxonomy and 197 valid anatomical paths would be a prerequisite; otherwise, comparisons conflate different output spaces and evaluation targets. Table 3 provides direct evidence: removing KL and HVP reduces probabilistic consistency from 74.26 to 64.89, showing that cross-level coherence is not obtained by joint multi-label training alone. In the final version, we will discuss RAD-DINO-v2 and Ark+ as complementary backbone-strength references, distinct from CHASE’s hierarchy-consistency contribution. For VLMs such as BioViL, applying our consistency metrics would require prompt design, text-to-label mapping, and hierarchy-path decoding; we will discuss structured VLM evaluation as future work. 2.Architectural design choices and novelty (R2, R3) We appreciate R3’s comment that the novelty is closer to structural integration than to a single isolated algorithmic component. This reflects our intended contribution: to our knowledge, CHASE is the first single-stage CXR framework to explicitly enforce probabilistic consistency across a dense Top-Mid-Leaf anatomical hierarchy within a shared ViT backbone. This unified design requires separating supervision across hierarchy levels rather than relying on a single late representation for all predictions. Blocks 6, 9, and 12 were selected to balance discrimination and inter-level separation: earlier settings such as [1,2,12] favored consistency but weakened discrimination, while later settings such as [5,11,12] showed the opposite trend. Blocks [6,9,12] provided the best trade-off. We will clarify this rationale in Sec. 2.2. 3.External validation and limitations (R1, R2, R3) We acknowledge single-source evaluation as a limitation. Chest ImaGenome remains, to our knowledge, the only public CXR dataset providing dense cross-level anatomical linkages required for rigorous Top-Mid-Leaf consistency evaluation. Datasets such as CheXpert lack the Region-Subregion-Finding structure and support only partial leaf-level transferability assessment. We will expand the Limitations section to cover dataset constraints, taxonomy adaptability, and broader validation opportunities. 4.Clinical utility (R3) The asymmetric HVP targets the clinically critical error of activating fine-grained findings without parent-region support, reflecting how radiologists form broad anatomical suspicion before specific diagnoses. A representative flat-baseline failure is a broken hierarchy path, e.g., predicting lung and lung opacity along “lung → left upper → opacity” while assigning insufficient probability to the intermediate “left upper” node. Figure 2 supports CHASE’s intended behavior through attention maps progressing from broad regions to localized findings. We will use such examples to strengthen the clinical discussion. We believe these clarifications address the reviewers’ concerns.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper received three good quality reviews with two accept and one reject rating. The final score will be depended on the rebuttal quality and details. The paper proposes a clinically motivated hierarchical chest X-ray classification framework that models region–subregion–finding relationships and improves hierarchical probabilistic consistency while maintaining competitive predictive performance and interpretable anatomy-aligned attention. Reviewers generally found the formulation clear, reproducible, and well supported by ablations, but noted that the contribution is more of a thoughtful structural integration than a major methodological breakthrough. The authors should address the lack of external validation beyond MIMIC-CXR/Chest ImaGenome, add stronger comparisons to recent CXR-specific hierarchical/anatomy-aware models and modern medical foundation/VLM baselines, justify the heuristic choice of supervision layers, improve the flowchart/figures, and include a clearer limitations and clinical-utility discussion with error-case analysis. | From a comprehensive overall review of this paper for its positives and negatives, this paper is clearly a well developed work that should be accepted by MICCAI. All reviewers and the primary AC would agree that the proposed CHASE framework is logically designed, interpretable, and sufficiently innovative. Its hierarchical classification strategy follows the clinical coarse-to-fine reading workflow, and the loss design is logical, solid and consistent with real clinical decision-making. The experimental setup is rigorous with fair baselines and thorough ablation studies. Only one dataset was used for evaluation but this may not be a big issue. Some of the negative issues will be fixed in the future version as discussed in the rebuttal. “The method achieves competitive performance on a large-scale dataset, while significantly improving hierarchical probabilistic consistency and interpretability. In addition, the paper provides public code with detailed configurations, ensuring strong reproducibility.” Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper probes the architecture of ViT to extract hierarchical information that would have been otherwise straightforward to capture in CNN architectures. The experiments are showing that extracting this information helps keep the model anatomically consistent in its predictions. The rebuttal addresses most of the concerns. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper presents a clinically grounded hierarchical classification framework for chest X-ray interpretation. Reviewers also praised the clear formulation, rigorous ablation studies, strong reproducibility, and the anatomically interpretable attention maps. In rebuttal, the authors clarified that their contribution is a hierarchy-consistency framework rather than a representation learning benchmark, provided empirical reasoning for the block-level head placement, and acknowledged the dataset limitations along with plans to expand the discussion of clinical utility and error cases. Two of the three reviewers ultimately support acceptance, and the rebuttal satisfactorily addressed the main weaknesses. Meta-review #4 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): CHASE presents a clinically grounded hierarchical classification framework that meaningfully improves probabilistic consistency across anatomical region–subregion–finding levels while maintaining competitive predictive performance. The method’s strength lies not in a single algorithmic breakthrough but in the thoughtful structural integration of clinical reasoning into a single-stage ViT, i.e., a contribution that reviewers acknowledged as well-designed, reproducible, and well-supported by ablations. The rebuttal effectively clarifies scope boundaries: CHASE is a consistency framework, not a representation leader, and comparisons to VLMs or anatomy-aware detectors would require non-trivial output-space reformulation. Remaining concerns, including single-dataset validation (MIMIC-CXR/Chest ImaGenome) and absence of direct benchmarks against modern medical foundation models (e.g., RAD-DINO, BioViL), are legitimate but not fatal. The authors appropriately acknowledge these as limitations and future work. Given the practical constraints of public datasets offering dense hierarchical annotations, the paper meets the bar for acceptance. I recommend acceptance, with encouragement to pursue external validation and VLM comparisons in future extensions.

title: Co-MoCo: Collaborative Learning Enabled Motion Compensation for Weight-Bearing CBCT
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The core innovation of this paper is the introduction of a collaborative motion compensation framework that unites image-domain priors with physical consistency in an end-to-end differentiable pipeline. 2.Comprehensive experiments and evaluation: The authors did not stop at simulated data; they tested the method on a real-world WB-CBCT system with human volunteers.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.While the paper presents a real-world validation on human volunteers and porcine hind limbs , the evaluation is purely qualitative. 2.The proposed Co-MoCo framework relies on an iterative optimization pipeline (Stage II) that updates motion parameters over 100 iterations using a differentiable cone-beam backprojector and a neural network. However, the authors do not report the memory footprint or the time required to reconstruct a single 3D volume on their NVIDIA RTX 4090 setup 3.In Section 2.2, the authors describe the Motion-Aware Dual-Decoder Network (MADN) and state that it takes a motion intensity map ($\sigma_{jit}$) as input. They note that this map is “derived from a pre-trained discriminator that quantifies the severity of motion”. The paper omits the architectural details, training methodology, and data sources used for this “pre-trained discriminator. “
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: (1) The topic is highly practical and addresses a current clinical pain point. The paper focuses on motion artifacts in weight-bearing CBCT, which is a clinically relevant problem in orthopedic and musculoskeletal rehabilitation scenarios. The introduction clearly explains the clinical value of WB-CBCT for weight-bearing imaging of the knee, foot/ankle, and lower extremities, as well as its susceptibility to involuntary patient motion due to the relatively long scanning time. Therefore, the work is well motivated and has a clear application background. (2) The method is well designed and demonstrates a meaningful degree of innovation, with a clear collaborative relationship between its components. The paper attempts to let image restoration and motion parameter estimation mutually reinforce each other within a unified framework, which is more valuable than using restoration-only or motion-estimation-only strategies. In particular, under severe motion, single-module methods are clearly limited, whereas the joint framework is still able to maintain high image quality, suggesting that the proposed design brings real synergistic benefits. (3) The quantitative experiments are comprehensive. The study includes both mild-motion and severe-motion settings and compares the proposed method against multiple image restoration and motion compensation approaches, making the results readable and convincing. (4) The real-data examples enhance the credibility of the method. In addition to simulation experiments, the authors also validate the framework on a real WB-CBCT system using human volunteer data and porcine hind-limb data. Although this part is still mainly qualitative, it nevertheless shows that the method is not limited to a purely simulated environment and has a certain degree of practical feasibility. (5) The proposed method not only achieves better numerical results than the competing methods, but also shows more intuitive improvements in residual blur reduction, streak artifact suppression, and preservation of high-frequency details. For motion artifact correction tasks, metric improvements alone are sometimes insufficient to demonstrate practical value, and the visual improvements shown in this paper make the conclusions more convincing.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: (1) The real-data validation remains largely qualitative and lacks further quantitative analysis. Although the human volunteer and porcine hind-limb results strengthen the practical relevance of the paper, this part currently relies mainly on visual inspection and lacks a more systematic quantitative evaluation. As such, the generalization ability and stability of the method in real clinical scenarios have not yet been fully established. (2) The assumption on the motion model is somewhat idealized. The paper mainly models patient motion as a 6-DoF rigid trajectory. While this assumption may be reasonable for some motion patterns in lower-limb WB-CBCT, in real scenarios, especially when soft tissue or local limb posture changes are more pronounced, more complex local non-rigid deformations may still occur. The paper does not yet discuss the applicability boundary of this assumption in sufficient depth, and therefore the robustness of the method under more complex motion patterns remains to be demonstrated. (3) The discussion of runtime efficiency and deployment cost is insufficient. The manuscript does not explicitly report the inference time or optimization time per case. Given that the proposed framework may require iterative optimization of motion parameters within a differentiable reconstruction loop, runtime and computational cost will be important considerations for future clinical deployment. The current version is somewhat limited in this respect. (4) Some baselines perform relatively poorly under severe motion, but the paper does not further analyze the reasons for this. Several image-domain baselines show substantial performance degradation in the severe-motion setting, yet the manuscript does not discuss why these baseline results are poor. This weakens the completeness of the comparative study to some extent.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The paper innovatively couples an image-domain generative prior with a physical forward model, solving the motion-corrupted inverse problem by iteratively optimizing 6-DoF rigid motion parameters to overcome the over-smoothing limitations of pure image-domain methods. 2.The paper introduces Optimal Transport Conditional Flow Matching (OT-CFM) to train a dual-decoder network (MADN), which serves as a high-quality, artifact-free manifold regularization constraint for the subsequent joint optimization of physical parameters. 3.The paper demonstrates the clinical feasibility and effectiveness of the proposed framework through comprehensive validation on both simulated motion datasets and real-world clinical scans.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The motivation for selecting Optimal Transport Conditional Flow Matching (OT-CFM) as the artifact-free prior, rather than other generative models, is insufficiently justified. Additionally, the authors need to clarify whether the identical flow matching setup is applied across different motion parameters, and rigorously explain how a completely frozen MADN can consistently guarantee reliable prior guidance during the iterative optimization process. 2.The strategy of alternating optimization between image domains and motion parameters has been extensively explored in previous literature. The authors should properly cite these prior works and explicitly discuss the methodological differences and specific advantages of the proposed framework over existing alternating optimization schemes. 3.To convincingly demonstrate its effectiveness, the experimental section must include a quantitative comparison with at least one state-of-the-art baseline method that jointly optimizes image and motion parameters. 4.The authors are strongly encouraged to open-source their codebase and release the real-world clinical dataset to facilitate reproducibility and benefit related research within the medical imaging community. 5.The manuscript lacks structural cohesion in the methodology section. The logical flow and transitions between Sections 2.1, 2.2, and 2.3 are somewhat disjointed and require further elaboration to present a unified narrative. 6.The paper omits critical computational efficiency metrics. The authors should report and compare the network parameter counts and running times against the baseline methods to verify the real-time clinical feasibility of the proposed pipeline.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank AC for the insightful summary. We thank R2 and R3 for accepting our paper as “tackles a highly relevant and challenging problem”, “addresses a clinically meaningful and practically valuable problem”, and thank R4 for appreciating our work as “strong clinical feasibility and innovative design”. Below, we provide point-by-point responses. AC-Q1&R2-Q1&R3-Q1: Lack of quantitative analysis on real data Acquiring GT in WB-CBCT scans is hard due to inevitable patient motion, though motion-tracking devices [1] could provide reliable references in future work. To provide a quantitative analysis on real data, we report results on the porcine case in Fig. 4.Our approach achieves lower MSE (6691.25 vs. 7412.84/8688.25/10147.37), higher SSIM (0.8411 vs. 0.8132/0.7881/0.7171), and higher PSNR (35.49 vs. 34.55/33.08/31.44) than Thies’s, Uformer, and FDK. [1] Maier J, et al. Inertial measurements for motion compensation in weight-bearing cone-beam CT of the knee. AC-Q2&R2-Q2&R3-Q3&R4-Q6: Lack of computational cost information Our method, run for 100 iterations with 40 control points on an NVIDIA RTX 4090 (projection size 400×1024×1536; volume 80×512×512/80×256×256), requires 9055/2256 sec and 14.0/12.9 GB GPU memory, while Thies’s [25] takes 8840/2203 sec and 15.3/13.7 GB GPU memory. AC-Q3&R2-Q4&R3-Q2: Validity of the 6-DOF assumption The 6-DOF rigid motion assumption is widely adopted for bone-dominant motion. However, lower-limb motion can be influenced by joint articulation and soft-tissue deformation. On real data, performing separate optimizations for thigh, knee, and leg can mitigate this issue, as shown in Fig. 4.Above limitations and potential of non-rigid modeling will be discussed in revision. AC-Q4&R4-Q1: Intuition behind artifact-free prior 1)OT-CFM enables stable and continuous trajectory learning by leveraging few-step transport estimation, providing faster inference than diffusion-based models. As shown in Tables 1 and 2, it also outperforms competing NN methods. 2) The MADN maintains a unified flow framework and uses varying degrees of motion information through a pre-trained discriminator, thereby performs effectively across different motion intensities. Additional ablation studies were omitted due to constraints. AC-Q5&R3-Q4: Concerns about baseline comparisons Under severe motion, image quality is highly degraded. Purely image-domain NN provides multiple plausible solutions for a single voxel, leading to excessive blurring. The proposed framework utilizes real projections and scan geometry as strong physical constraints through a differentiable P-Matrix back-projector, thus iteratively narrowing solution space toward a physically consistent state. R2-Q4&R3-Q4&R4-Q4: Concerns about reproducibility We promise to release code once acceptance. Clinical datasets cannot be shared due to hospital privacy. R2-Q3: Lack of implementation details of pre-trained discriminator Motion maps are generated by a lightweight U-Net trained on simulated motion dataset (vary degrees of motion) to provide motion intensity information for the MADN. More details will be found in our released code. R4-Q2&Q3: Discussion and comparison with existing alternating optimization schemes Previous alternating schemes primarily rely on costly, view-constrained forward-projector, suboptimal regularizers such as TV and VIF and on scarce high-quality CAD (on head data). In contrast, we utilize a differentiable P-Matrix back-projector to enable strong physical constraints and high-quality OT-CFM guidance. As noted in Table 1, we have included a comparison with the state-of-the-art alternating optimization scheme by Thies [25]. More comprehensive comparisons will be conducted in future work. R4-Q5: Lack of structural cohesion in methodology Our methodology is organized as: Problem Formulation (Sec. 2.1), Prior Generation (Sec. 2.2), Physical Modeling (Sec. 2.3), Overall Architecture (Sec. 2.4). We will improve structural coherence in revision.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The authors proposed Co-MoCo, a collaborative motion compensation framework that integrates image-domain priors with physical consistency through an end-to-end differentiable pipeline. Stage 1 contains a Motion-Aware Dual-Decoder Network (MADN) trained via Optimal Transport Conditional Flow Matching (OT-CFM) to generate an artifact-free prior. In Stage 2 this prior is integrated into a correction loop to iteratively refine 6-DoF rigid motion trajectories. Reviewers all gave weak acceptance/borderline scores. The motivation behind image-domain priors with physical consistency is widely acknowledged, and the experiments are comprehensive with real-patient data. However, it’s noted that common concerns include (1) qualitative evaluation on real-patient data, which might be reasonable since there is no motion GT, but the authors might need to further discuss this and include potential future directions with motion-tracking devices to get GT; (2) lacking computational cost information since there are iterative optimization loops; (3) the validity of the 6-DOF motion trajectory assumption; (4) the intuition behind artifact-free prior selection and (5) concerns regarding baseline comparisons. The authors are encouraged to address these concerns and provide other missing details as required by the reviewers. | Thank the authors for providing this detailed response. Most of the concerns were sufficiently addressed, including real data quantitative analysis and runtime report. The authors are encouraged to discuss the potential of non-rigid motion modeling in the camera-ready version. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): After rebuttal, the paper leans toward acceptance. The reviewers agreed that the problem is clinically important and that the proposed Co-MoCo framework offers an interesting integration of learned image priors with physics-based motion correction for WB-CBCT. The rebuttal addressed several major concerns by providing runtime and memory estimates, clarification of the 6-DOF assumption, additional details on the motion-intensity discriminator, and discussion of prior alternating-optimization methods. Two reviewers were satisfied by the rebuttal and now recommend accept. Reviewer 2 maintains a reject recommendation, citing limited real-data validation, long runtime, and the remaining limitations of the rigid-motion model. These are valid concerns and should be acknowledged, particularly the high computational cost and limited quantitative real-data evidence. However, given the novelty and clinical relevance of the framework, the improved clarification after rebuttal, and the overall positive reviewer balance, I recommend acceptance. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The authors have responded to most of the reviewers’ comments. While one reviewer still has concerns about the evaluation and feasibility of clinical deployment, I think the authors should expand their discussion on the limitations in the final version.

title: Concept-Guided Noisy Negative Suppression for Zero-Shot Classification and Grounding of Chest X-Ray Findings
reviewer_1_strengths: The paper addresses a real limitation of contrastive learning in medical vision-language models by identifying and mitigating noisy negatives across patients, introducing a concept-level formulation that better reflects semantic consistency. The proposed framework is coherent and enables more accurate supervision and improved alignment by combining a structured ontology, cross-patient pair relabeling, and a concept-aware contrastive loss. The experimental results show consistent improvements over strong baselines across tasks, supporting the effectiveness of the approach. The paper is well written and clearly structured, making the method easy to follow.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The method critically depends on LLM-based extraction of structured concepts from radiology reports, which is used to relabel training pairs and guide supervision. However, the paper provides no quantitative or clinical validation of this ontology. Since datasets such as MIMIC-CXR do not provide ground-truth structured annotations of this form, it remains unclear how accurate or reliable these extracted labels are, and errors in this stage could propagate to the learning objective. The ontology is defined by a fixed set of 41 target entities (as specified in the extraction prompt), but the paper does not explain how this concept set was constructed. It is unclear whether these concepts are manually curated, derived from existing clinical ontologies, or adapted from prior work (e. g. , [A]). Could the authors clarify the selection process for these 41 concepts and discuss how sensitive the method is to this choice? While the ablation study shows that the full system improves performance, it does not clearly disentangle the contributions of ontology-based text representation and noisy-negative suppression, making it unclear which component is primarily responsible for the observed gains. In particular, the ablation evaluates components built on top of the ontology, but does not assess the design, coverage, or impact of the ontology itself. [A] Peng, Yifan, et al. “Automatic recognition of abdominal lymph nodes from clinical text. “ Proceedings of the 3rd Clinical Natural Language Processing Workshop. 2020.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.the authors identify the critical issue of noisy negatives in contrastive learning for chest X-ray vision-language alignment. By proposing a concept-guided suppression framework, they effectively reduce semantic ambiguity and improve the reliability of zero-shot classification and grounding tasks. 2.the authors construct a hierarchical clinical concept ontology and integrate it into a multi-step relabeling strategy. This design enables fine-grained reasoning over findings and attributes, leading to more precise alignment and strong performance gains across multiple datasets.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Major Weaknesses: 1.The rationale behind the design of the 41 predefined concepts is not clearly explained. In Section 2.2, “N is the number of sampled texts per image” are unclear. it is not specified whether the text is sampled directly from the original reports or from an external source. In addition, the definition of M_{i,j} is ambiguous. The meaning of this variable and the reason why its shape is (NB) \times B are not sufficiently justified. It is unclear why the formulation is not simply N \times B. Furthermore, the interpretation of the entries in M_{i,j} is confusing. In particular, the choice of assigning M_{i,j}=1 to represent a “No–No” correspondence, rather than a “Yes–Yes” match, is counterintuitive and requires further explanation. 2.In the concept-aware NCE loss, the use of an arbitrary number of positive pairs has already been explored in prior works such as [1] and [2]. The authors are encouraged to briefly discuss the differences and connections between their approach and these existing methods, in order to better highlight the novelty and contribution of the proposed formulation. [1] Stablerep: Synthetic images from text-to-image models make strong visual representation learners, NeurIPS, 2024. [2] Enhanced Contrastive Learning with Multi-view Longitudinal Data for Chest X-ray Report Generation, CVPR, 2025. 3.To the best of my knowledge, the Open-I dataset only provides image–report pairs and does not include explicit classification labels. It is therefore unclear how zero-shot classification is conducted on this dataset. Minor Weaknesses: 1.In Section 2.1, the statement that “each [sample] is sampled with a 50% probability during training” is unclear in relation to the official data split of the MIMIC-CXR dataset.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.Identifies and addresses a critical limitation of standard contrastive learning in medical imaging – the noisy negatives problem where cross-patient pairs with similar findings are incorrectly treated as negatives – and proposes a principled concept-based suppression framework. 2.Introduces a novel hierarchical concept ontology paired with a three-step cross-patient relabeling strategy, which preserves both linguistic diversity and prompt consistency while enabling fine-grained discrimination of findings. 3.Demonstrates strong empirical gains over state-of-the-art methods across multiple zero-shot grounding (word, phrase, sentence levels) and five zero-shot classification datasets, with ablation studies confirming the contribution of each component.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.Reliance on a predefined and fixed set of 41 clinical concepts – The hierarchical ontology is limited to these concepts, which may not cover all possible findings or generalize to other diseases or imaging modalities without manual re-construction. 2.Potential scalability and computational overhead – The framework involves LLM-based ontology construction, a lightweight LM for hard negative mining, and a concept-aware attention mechanism, which adds complexity and training cost compared to simpler contrastive baselines.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and meta-reviewer for the positive assessment and constructive suggestions. We would like to clarify several points here: 1.The 41 concepts are predefined chest X-ray finding phrases, which help identify semantically consistent, contradictory, and ambiguous cross-patient pairs. Their selection is based on previous chest X-ray datasets and discussions with radiologists. 2.Extracting structured information from chest X-ray reports during training is a common practice in prior work, such as CARZero and RadZero. Although this step may introduce noise, it has been shown to perform better than using raw reports or the original auto-extracted labels in MIMIC-CXR. 3.Sampled texts refer to the texts sampled from the selected concepts, as well as the texts generated by counterfactual prompting. The shape (N·B) * B indicates that the contrastive learning is conducted with N·B texts and B images in a batch. 4.Regarding the Open-I dataset, we follow the labels used in the CARZero codebase for our zero-shot classification experiments. 5.LLM extraction is an offline preprocessing step, and the lightweight NLI model is only used for pending “Yes-Yes” pairs during training; inference does not require these extra modules. 6.Prior work, such as MedCLIP, partially mitigates the issue of false negatives by leveraging finding labels, but it still overlooks the rich and subtle information in radiology reports. title: Conditional Diffusion Prompting for Ambiguous Medical Image Segmentation
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.While diffusion models and conditional diffusion models have been widely used and studied, the motivations behind the use of diffusion prompting and conditioning the prompt-space denoising on image embeddings make sense. The paper innovatively applied them to the ambiguous medical image segmentation task. 2.The paper is well organized and presented clearly. 3.Extensive experiments have been conducted and results demonstrates its effectiveness.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The Fig. 1 should be further improved as ‘DP’ and ‘CDP’ is not annotated in the figure. Such annotations help the reader better match the figure and description. 2.Providing source code is recommended for ensure reproducibility as the space for description of implementation is limited. 3.The compared approaches are outdated: Prob UNet(2018), PHiSeg (2019, which is actually mentioned but not compared), SSN (2020), CAR (2021), Mose (2022).
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The paper focuses on learning a distribution of plausible masks rather than producing a single deterministic output. This is a meaningful problem formulation for clinical settings with substantial inter-expert variability. 2.The paper moves uncertainty modeling from output mask space to dense prompt embedding space. Conditioning prompt-space diffusion on stochastic image embeddings is also an intuitive way to connect prompt uncertainty with image ambiguity.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The proposed method involves a relatively long and complex pipeline, which makes the main technical contribution somewhat unclear. The final performance gain may come from several interacting components, including the semantic mask prompt generator, prompt-space diffusion, stochastic image latent modeling, or their combination, but the paper does not fully disentangle their individual contributions. As a result, it is difficult to identify a clean methodological focus and clearly understand what the primary source of improvement is. 2.While the idea of performing diffusion in dense prompt embedding space is interesting, the paper does not sufficiently explain why prompt space is a more appropriate or necessary modeling space than mask space or latent mask space. 3.The method requires DDIM sampling with 100 reverse steps, and 16 samples are generated per test image to evaluate the segmentation distribution. From a deployment perspective, the performance gain may not clearly justify this inference overhead, so the paper would benefit from additional efficiency analysis, such as per-image sampling time, memory consumption, and the trade-off between performance and sampling cost. 4.The experimental comparison lacks more analysis against closely related classes of methods. For example, compared with traditional latent-variable AMIS methods, it remains unclear whether the observed gains mainly come from the use of a promptable decoder or from the proposed diffusion prompting mechanism itself. A more structured comparison across methodological categories would make the empirical claims more convincing.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.This paper introduces diffusion in dense prompt embedding space, offering a structured alternative to mask-space modeling or random prompt perturbations for varied medical imaging tasks. 2.CDP conditions prompt diffusion on stochastic image latents, ensuring generated segmentations are both diverse and aligned with image ambiguity, addressing a key limitation of prior SAM-based methods. 3.Achieves competitive GED, HM-IoU and Dmax on multiple benchmarks (LIDC, ISIC, Prostate, Pancreatic-lesion), demonstrating improved distribution matching and fidelity. Ablation studies show consistent gains from DP and CDP components, and sensitivity analyses indicate robustness to hyperparameters and sampling count.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The paper does not clearly establish why diffusion in prompt space is superior to mask-space diffusion or other latent modeling approaches. There should at least be some discussion around that if not experimental validation. 2.This relies on a frozen mask generator and SAM-style encoder, which may propagate biases or limit adaptability if the initial prompt distribution is suboptimal. What should be the necessary steps for that ? Is that a major issue? Expanding on this, while GED and Dmax are reported, the work lacks explicit quantitative analysis of mode diversity or collapse. The authors mention this qualitatively in Section 4.2 and while Dmax shows the best-case scenario, it doesn’t prove diversity. The paper would greatly benefit from an analysis using metrics such as Self-Similarity or Bhattacharyya Distance, making clear how distinct the generated samples truly are in a quantitative sense. 3.Diffusion-based sampling introduces significant inference overhead, but the paper does not provide runtime or FLOPs comparisons with baselines. 4.Several important implementation details required for reproducibility for example, specific architecture of the lightweight denoiser, the noise schedule parameters for the diffusion process and the dimensionality of the latent variables and many other hyperparameters as well as design choices are missing from the “Implementation Details” section.

author_feedback: We sincerely thank the AC and reviewers for the constructive comments and address the raised concerns below. 1.Comparisons (R1, R2) We agree that more recent and structurally related methods should be better covered. In the manuscript, we include comparisons with both traditional latent-variable AMIS methods (Table 1) and A-SAM [2] (NeurIPS 2024), a recent promptable AMIS baseline. On LIDC, our method reduces GED by 9.8% and improves HM-IoU from 0.768 to 0.839 (+9.2%) compared with A-SAM, indicating that the improvement is not simply due to adopting a promptable decoder. We further compare with ATFM [27] (AAAI 2026), a more recent flow-matching-based mask-space generative method, where our method still achieves superior HM-IoU performance (0.839 vs. 0.667), and improves best-match Dice by approximately 3.0%. Finally, both A-SAM and ATFM have previously demonstrated advantages over PHiSeg (2019). We will also include PHiSeg in the revision for a more comprehensive comparison. 2.Why Diffusion in Prompt Space (R2, R3) Prompt space is particularly suitable for SAM-style decoders because it serves as the decoder’s native control variable, unlike mask-space modeling performed after decoding. Modeling this space preserves the promptable decoder prior while allowing stochastic sampling. Previous work, such as A-SAM [2], explicitly models prompt-space ambiguity and demonstrates superior performance. Building on this, our method further replaces Gaussian prompt sampling with diffusion denoising in dense prompt space, conditioned on stochastic image embeddings, such that prompt uncertainty is aligned with underlying image ambiguity. 3.Inference Overhead and Efficiency Analysis (R2, R3) We thank the reviewer for the valuable suggestion. We provide the runtime, memory, sampling-cost trade-off, and FLOPs comparison with A-SAM. Our method uses higher computation than A-SAM, with 49.54 vs. 22.66 GFLOPs/sample. However, this overhead is tunable: the 100-step DDIM setting is our upper-bound setting for stronger distribution modeling. Reducing it to 10 steps lowers the runtime from 3.464s to 0.721s with 16 samples/image, while peak memory remains about 9.42 GB; with 100 steps, the runtime scales from 0.220s for 1 sample to 3.464s for 16 samples. Together with Table 3, these results show a clear cost-quality trade-off: fewer DDIM steps or samples substantially reduce latency, while the full setting provides stronger distribution modeling when higher fidelity is desired. We will include these efficiency analyses and discussions in the revision. 4.Reproducibility and Source Code (R1, R3) We will specify the key settings (e.g., ViT-B SAM, LoRA rank 4, 256-d latent variables) and release the code and models upon acceptance to ensure reproducibility. 5.Fig. 1 Annotation (R1) We thank the reviewer for the suggestion. We will explicitly annotate “DP” and “CDP” in Fig. 1 to match the description. 6.Ablation Clarity (R2) We apologize for the insufficient clarity of the ablation analysis in the current manuscript. In Table 2, we disentangle the contributions of each major component, including the semantic mask prompt generator (denoted as “Base”, 0.7823 HM-IoU), prompt-space diffusion (denoted as “DP”, 0.8363 HM-IoU), and stochastic image latent modeling (denoted as “CDP”, 0.8493 HM-IoU). These results show that the primary performance improvement does not originate from the prompt generator alone, but mainly from the proposed diffusion prompting framework. To further improve clarity, we will revise the manuscript to more explicitly emphasize the role and contribution of each component. 7.Diversity Analysis (R3) We provide Self-Similarity and Bhattacharyya Distance on LIDC to quantify mode diversity/collapse beyond GED and Dmax. Compared with the baseline, CDP reduces Self-Similarity from 0.469 to 0.387 and increases Bhattacharyya Distance from 1.301 to 1.525, indicating lower sample similarity and larger distributional separation.

title: Conformal 3D Lesion Segmentation with Balanced Risk Control
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The authors claim that their methodology is the first to adapt SCP to binary segmentation settings. 2.The topic of conformal prediction for segmentation is timely and would be of great interest to the uncertainty quantification (UQ) community within MICCAI. 3.The proposed methodology is applied post model development, which is important for clinical settings as UQ is unfortunately often an afterthought. 4.The methodology provides a FNR guarantee, which is especially important in tasks like lesion segmentation. Importantly, empirical results demonstrated that the guarantee did not substantially deteriorate the FPR. 5.The manuscript is well written and formulated: (1) large assortment of experiments: 6 datasets, 5 models; (2) claims a release of code; (3) appropriately grounds the methodology in a clinical context in the introduction; (4) contains a figure that effectively functions as a graphical abstract; (5) multiple figures demonstrate the variability of the results, instead of just rely on point estimates of performance; and (6) an ablation study is performed on calibration dataset size.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The manuscript would benefit from a stronger connection to the existing literature on conformal prediction for medical image segmentation. For example, the introduction does not adequately situate the work within recent developments. 2.The proposed prediction compactness (PC) metric is difficult to interpret and appears to be largely redundant with standard measures such as FPR or precision. Under a fixed FNR constraint, PC effectively reduces to a normalized measure of predicted mask size, which does not provide additional insight beyond existing metrics and may obscure clinically relevant aspects of segmentation quality. 3.The vast majority of the results were only presented for one dataset. For example, the results of the comparison with heuristic thresholding, the evaluation of how the FPR was affected, the PC results, and the ablation study on calibration dataset size were only presented for KiTS21.While I understand the space is limited, this makes the reader question whether the results extend to new modalities/segmentation tasks. 4.Lack of comparison with other threshold-selection methods. The work basically demonstrates that a SCP-selected decision threshold improves FNR while not completely compromising FPR over a heuristic threshold of 0.5 on the KiTS dataset. Comparing against other threshold-selection methodologies, or discussing why comparison is not feasible, would strengthen the manuscript. 5.The methodology is mostly evaluated in terms of FNR/FPRs. As changing the decision threshold changes the predictive segmentation mask, it would have been informative to also use metrics that measure segmentation performance (such as DSC, HD, etc. )
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: Novel methodological contribution: CLS is the first work to provide statistical guarantees for FNR control in segmentation through conformal prediction. The formulation of FNR-specific and FPR-specific loss functions as nonconformity scores is technically sound and innovative. The derivation of the critical threshold ti as the solution to a constrained optimization problem (minimizing FPR while bounding FNR) elegantly adapts conformal prediction theory to the segmentation domain. Strong theoretical foundation: Theorem 1 provides rigorous statistical guarantees for FNR control, with a clear proof establishing that the calibrated threshold ensures Pr(L_FNR_test(ˆt) ≤ ε) ≥ 1−α. The exchangeability assumption is appropriate and standard for conformal prediction methods. Comprehensive experimental validation: The evaluation spans six diverse 3D medical segmentation datasets (KiTS21, LiTS, NIH-LN ABD, LIDC-IDRI, MDSC-Colon, MDSC-Pancreas) and five state-of-the-art backbone architectures (Med3D, nnUNet, UNETR, Swin-UNETR, SAM-Med3D). This breadth demonstrates generalizability across anatomical regions and model designs. Clinically motivated problem formulation: The paper effectively identifies and articulates a critical real-world problem—uncontrolled FNR in lesion segmentation leading to missed diagnoses. The distinction between voxel-level FNR (V-FNR) and presence-level FNR (P-FNR) is particularly relevant clinically, as complete lesion misses (P-FNR) are especially dangerous. Novel evaluation metric: The introduction of Prediction Compactness (PC) as a metric for spatial efficiency under risk constraints provides a practical tool for comparing uncertainty-aware segmentation models. This addresses an important gap in how to evaluate segmentation quality when operating under formal risk guarantees. Robustness analysis: The experiments examining different calibration-test split ratios (Figure 5b) demonstrate that CLS maintains statistical validity even with limited calibration data (10%), which is crucial for practical deployment scenarios.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Limited comparison with relevant baselines: While the paper compares CLS against fixed thresholding (t=0.5), it lacks comparison with other uncertainty calibration or threshold adaptation methods commonly used in medical image segmentation. Specifically, there is no comparison with: Temperature scaling or Platt scaling for calibration Other risk-control methods such as those based on Bayesian neural networks or ensemble uncertainty Recent conformal prediction variants for segmentation (e.g., [1] Angelopoulos et al. on image classification uncertainty sets, or segmentation-specific conformal methods if they exist) Insufficient ablation studies: The paper does not investigate: The effect of different ε values on the same dataset with fixed α The interaction between model calibration quality and CLS performance—poorly calibrated models may require larger calibration sets Computational overhead of the calibration procedure compared to standard inference Missing clinical utility validation: While the paper claims clinical relevance, there is no validation with clinical readers or assessment of how the predicted compactness (PC) or risk levels (α) correlate with actual clinical decision-making. The clinical significance of the FNR reductions shown in Table 1 is asserted but not demonstrated through clinical outcomes or reader studies. Assumption limitations not fully discussed: The exchangeability assumption may be violated in real clinical deployment due to: Domain shift between calibration and test data (different scanners, protocols, patient populations) Temporal drift in data distribution The paper briefly acknowledges this but does not provide empirical validation of robustness to such violations, which is critical for safety-critical clinical applications. Incomplete discussion of failure modes: Figure 3 shows occasional ECR violations below the theoretical bound 1−α. The paper attributes this to “finite-sample variability,” but does not quantify: The frequency or severity of these violations Whether certain datasets or models are more prone to violations Practical consequences when the guarantee fails Limited exploration of the ε-α trade-off space: The experiments primarily use ε=0.2, α=0.2 or ε=0.4, α=0.2.A more systematic exploration of how these hyperparameters interact and their practical selection guidance would strengthen the work.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: (1) Clinically meaningful objective. The paper focuses on controlling false negatives in lesion segmentation, which is an important safety-related failure mode in medical imaging. This is a better-motivated target than relying on a default threshold such as 0.5, especially in sparse-lesion settings where missed lesions can be clinically consequential. (2) Simple and practical post-hoc formulation. The method is conceptually simple: given a pretrained segmentation network, it calibrates a decision threshold using held-out data, without requiring retraining. This makes it potentially easy to deploy on top of existing systems. (3) Clear theoretical motivation. The paper gives a concise conformal-style argument under exchangeability and derives a threshold from calibration-case critical values. The theoretical framing is easy to follow and aligned with the broader conformal prediction literature. (4) Broad empirical coverage. The evaluation spans six 3D lesion segmentation datasets and five architectures, which is stronger than a single-dataset proof of concept and suggests the method is not backbone-specific. (5) Useful calibration perspective. The paper highlights that standard thresholding can lead to very poor FNR behavior in lesion segmentation and that post-hoc risk calibration can materially change that trade-off. This is a worthwhile perspective for safety-aware segmentation deployment.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: (1) The novelty is not fully convincing relative to prior conformal segmentation work. The paper claims to be, to the best of the authors’ knowledge, the first post-processing approach to provide FNR guarantees in segmentation, but this seems too strong. Prior work has already adapted conformal prediction to image segmentation and explicitly addressed the false-negative / coverage side of the problem through prediction sets, including binary segmentation settings and biomedical segmentation settings, e.g., [1–3]. (2) The experimental baseline is too weak for a methodological paper. Most of the empirical comparison is against standard heuristic thresholding (for example, 0.5), which is useful as a sanity check but not sufficient to establish SoTA novelty. Given the existing literature on conformal segmentation, the paper should compare directly against representative prior conformal approaches rather than only against fixed-threshold inference, e.g., [1–3]. (3) The paper’s contribution appears closer to a task-specific adaptation of existing conformal ideas than to a fundamentally new methodological framework. The main idea is to calibrate a segmentation threshold on a held-out set so that false negative risk is controlled with high probability. That is a sensible and practical idea, but the manuscript does not clearly articulate why this adaptation is substantially different from prior segmentation-oriented conformal formulations based on score thresholding, prediction sets, or inner/outer confidence regions, e.g., [1–3]. (4) The empirical evaluation is reasonably broad in terms of datasets and backbones, but it is narrow in terms of metrics and comparisons. The paper focuses mainly on ECR, voxel-level FNR/FPR, and prediction compactness, while standard segmentation metrics such as Dice, lesion-wise sensitivity, or boundary-aware metrics are not emphasized enough. For a MICCAI audience, it is important to understand whether the proposed risk control comes at an acceptable cost in overall segmentation quality. (5) The proposed “prediction compactness” metric is not yet fully justified as a meaningful new benchmark. It is intuitively related to prediction size and false-positive behavior, but the paper does not clearly establish why it should be preferred over, or interpreted differently from, more standard notions of mask size, over-segmentation, or set size that are already discussed in prior conformal segmentation literature, e.g., [1–3]. (6) Some claims are stronger than the evidence presented. For example, the paper states that the method consistently enforces the desired control, but the manuscript also notes that empirical compliance can occasionally fall slightly below the nominal lower bound in practice. This does not invalidate the method, but the wording should be more careful and the practical limitations should be discussed more explicitly. (7) The related work section is underdeveloped for a methodological submission. In particular, the paper would benefit from a more careful discussion of prior segmentation-specific conformal methods and from a clearer explanation of what is genuinely new here: the risk definition, the threshold construction, the target guarantee, or the empirical application. At present, the positioning overstates novelty and understates prior SoTA, e.g., [1–3]. Refs [1] Mossina, L., and Friedrich, C. “Conformal Semantic Image Segmentation: Post-hoc Quantification of Predictive Uncertainty.” In Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition Workshops (CVPR Workshops), 2024. [2] Mossina, L., and Friedrich, C. “Conformal Prediction for Image Segmentation Using Morphological Prediction Sets.” In Medical Image Computing and Computer Assisted Intervention (MICCAI), 2025. [3] Davenport, S. “Conformal Confidence Sets for Biomedical Image Segmentation.” arXiv preprint arXiv:2410.03406, 2024.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for their thoughtful comments. We are encouraged by their recognition of the clinical importance of controlling false negatives, the relevance of post-hoc calibration, and the empirical breadth across datasets and backbones. We will revise the manuscript to better clarify the positioning, guarantee, and scope of CLS. Clarifying the contribution. To R1/R2/R3.We do not claim that CLS is the first use of conformal prediction for segmentation. Its specific contribution is to address a clinically motivated risk objective not directly targeted by standard thresholding or many existing conformal segmentation formulations: controlling the probability that the per-case voxel-level FNR exceeds a user-specified tolerance. CLS calibrates a single post-processing threshold so that the deployed output remains a standard binary mask while satisfying a finite-sample marginal conformal guarantee under exchangeability. This is distinct from methods that construct voxel-wise prediction sets, uncertainty regions, or morphology-based conformal masks. We will revise the abstract, introduction, and contribution list accordingly. Relation to heuristic and validation-based thresholding. To R1/R2/R3.We include the fixed-0.5 comparison because it is a common operational choice that directly reveals the key clinical failure mode: sparse lesions may receive low predicted probabilities, causing high V-FNR and complete misses. CLS does not merely lower the threshold; it replaces an uncontrolled heuristic with a statistically calibrated rule. A validation-tuned threshold may reduce empirical FNR on a held-out set but does not provide the same finite-sample marginal guarantee for unseen exchangeable cases. We will discuss this distinction alongside validation-based thresholding and recent conformal segmentation methods in the related work. Clarifying the guarantee. To R1/R2.The theorem provides a marginal per-test-case guarantee: for an exchangeable test example, the probability that its voxel-level FNR-specific loss exceeds the tolerance is at most \alpha. It is not a deterministic guarantee that every finite test split must show empirical compliance above 1-\alpha. Split-level fluctuations below the nominal 1-\alpha line in Fig. 3 therefore do not contradict the conformal statement; they reflect finite-sample variability of empirical compliance estimates. We will revise the theorem explanation, ECR discussion, and figure caption to eliminate this ambiguity. Prediction compactness. To R1/R2/R3.PC is not intended to replace standard metrics such as Dice, sensitivity, HD95, or NSD. Its role is narrower: once FNR tolerance is controlled, PC summarizes the spatial expansion required to achieve that control, serving as an auxiliary footprint measure for comparing backbone conservatism under FNR-controlled calibration. We will reposition it as an auxiliary metric to be interpreted alongside V-FNR, P-FNR, and V-FPR. Clinical scope and assumptions. To R1/R2.Our claim is methodological: CLS provides a post-hoc mechanism to control missed-lesion risk under the standard exchangeability assumption. We agree that reader studies and outcome-based validation are needed before clinical deployment. We will explicitly note that scanner/protocol shifts, temporal drift, and cross-institutional deployment may weaken exchangeability, and that future work should incorporate domain-shift detection or site-specific recalibration. Finally, we will correct all noted presentation issues, including typos, fixed-threshold notation, the quantile explanation, P-FNR notation, calibration/test split description, and figure readability. Overall, CLS offers a practical, statistically grounded way to convert existing 3D lesion segmentation models into risk-aware systems that explicitly prioritize reducing missed lesions while preserving a standard binary-mask output.
