title: Counterfactual Anatomy-Guided Spatial-Temporal Decoding for Annotation-Free Hallucination Mitigation in Medical VLMs
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.Valid Methodological Insight: The authors correctly observe that ground-truth (GT) bounding boxes in medical datasets are often too coarse, and suppressing them removes too much visual context, weakening the contrastive signal during decoding. The push for compact masks is well-motivated. 2.Impressive Closed-ended Performance: The method shows substantial improvements in factual grounding, notably increasing closed-ended accuracy on the SLAKE dataset from 61.42 to 81.49 for Phi-3.5V-Med. 3.Plug-and-Play Design: Operating entirely at inference time without requiring model retraining is highly desirable for deploying large medical foundation models.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.Ignored Computational Catastrophe: The paper severely glosses over the inference latency. For every single question, the system must: 1) Run MedSAM3; 2) Generate a draft answer via greedy decoding; 3) Perform two occlusion forward passes (blur and mean) for up to $K=16$ candidate regions to calculate the causal effect. This means running the VLM over 33 times just to select a region before the final decoding even begins. This computational overhead makes the method completely impractical for real-world clinical use, yet the authors provide zero latency/FLOPs analysis. 2.Misleading “Annotation-Free” Claim: The framework is not truly zero-shot or annotation-free; it merely outsources the annotation dependency to MedSAM3.If MedSAM3 has poor zero-shot performance on a specific sub-modality (e. g. , a rare ultrasound view), the candidate proposals will fail, causing the entire pipeline to collapse. 3.Heavy Reliance on Heuristics and Hyperparameters: The method introduces an excessive number of hyperparameters: mask area penalty ($\lambda$), variance penalty ($\mu$), guidance scale ($\gamma$), inside/outside ROI weights ($\alpha$, $\beta$), and temporal weights ($w_m$, $w_p$). Relying on empirical “grid search” to tune these limits the claimed “plug-and-play” generalization.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1) The motivation is well-introduced. Hallucination is a common research topic and training-free make the model more generalizable. 2) The proposed method is logically sound. It smartly combines existing methods’ segmentation ability to enable annotation-free settings. 3) The experiments are persuasive. The effectiveness of the proposed method has been validated on three commonly-used medical VLM on both MIMIC and SLAKE datasets.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1) The evaluation is limited to visual question answering task, while free-text report generation should also be a crucial ability of medical VLMs. 2) The proposed method can cause significant delay on response time. It would be great if author/s can acknowledge this and report the inference time before and after adding the proposed mechanisms. 3) It lacks failure case analysis.
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.Hallucination mitigation in medical VLMs is an important problem, and decoding-time approaches are attractive due to their plug-and-play nature. 2.CAST removes the dependency on ground-truth ROI annotations by leveraging automatic region discovery, which improves practical applicability. 3.The method shows strong gains in closed-ended accuracy across multiple models and datasets.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The paper claims that compact masks provide a cleaner contrastive signal than coarse masks, but does not provide direct experimental evidence to support this claim. 2.CAST relies on segmentation-based anatomical regions. However, for questions involving global properties (e.g., imaging modality or general conditions), it is unclear how the method would operate effectively. 3.The paper argues that compact regions are preferable, but this may not always hold. Preserving some surrounding context could be beneficial for diagnosis, as the contrast between lesion and background is often important. 4.The intuition that “the prior step’s distribution encodes language momentum” is not clearly justified. It remains unclear why subtracting the previous-step logits leads to better grounding, and how this mechanism interacts with spatial contrast during decoding. 5.While CAST performs strongly on closed-ended questions, its performance on open-ended questions is often inferior to existing methods (as shown in Table 1), which raises concerns about the general effectiveness of the method.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank all reviewers. R1(well-motivated, substantial improvements), R3 (recommended Accept); R4 (improves practical applicability). We hope our responses address the concerns and justify updating the remaining ratings to Accept. Inference latency: Wall-clock per question on Phi-3.5V-Med/SLAKE is: Baseline 3.13s, OPERA 3.15s (1.00×), VCD 3.48s (1.11×), ARCD 3.58s (1.14×), DoLA 6.64s (2.12×), CAST 6.68s (2.13×). CAST overhead matches DoLA. MedSAM3 proposals are precomputed once/image and read from disk; online MedSAM3 would add only ~0.13s/question. ROI scoring uses teacher-forced likelihood over a short draft (T_score=32), not full autoregressive generation; each occlusion pass takes ~256 ms, below a ~3s generation. K candidates can run in parallel for further gains. Annotation-free and MedSAM3 dependence: Annotation-free means no per-dataset segmentation labels at inference, as in CLIP or SAM pipelines. CAST handles MedSAM3 failure by design: MedSAM3 only proposes candidates, while Stage 2 selects via Δℓ_mean−λ·area+μ·consistency. Semantically wrong proposals receive near-zero causal signal in both perturbation modes and cannot enter the top K=16 rankings. The area-prior fallback in Sec.3.3 covers the residual 1.3% of images with fewer than three valid proposals. CAST relies on causal discriminability, not anatomical exactness, as compact auto masks with about 7% coverage consistently outperform coarse GT boxes with about 39% coverage. Hyperparameters: The same defaults (γ=1.5, α=0.01, β=3.0, λ=μ=0.1, wm=1.0, wp=0.5, K=16) are reused across all three Med-VLMs and both datasets, without per-cell tuning. γ follows the standard CFG range; α,β follow ARCD; wm:wp=2:1 is one fixed ratio. Fig. 2 confirms stability: removing λ lowers overall by 3.4%; single-occlusion variants drop 3.3–4.0%; spatial-only and temporal-only drop to 53.66% and 53.91% vs. full 59.25%. Compactness/context/temporal contrast: We don‘t claim compact masks are always preferable. We claim overly large masks weaken ROI-guided CFG as suppressing them removes too much information from the unconditional branch. Fig.2 is an ablation holding the VLM and decoder fixed and varying only mask source. The mask compactness analysis (Sec.3.2) shows GT coverage >40% noticeably reduces closed accuracy, and GT slightly reduces accuracy versus NULL decoding. Sec.3.1 explains: as area(m)→1, log p_c−log p_u collapses to a global correction, eliminating localized contrastive signal. CAST keeps context: the conditional branch always sees the full image, while the unconditional branch suppresses ROI tokens (α=0.01) and upweights surrounding tokens (β=3.0), amplifying lesion-versus-background contrast. Compactness describes the contrastive signal, not the model input. Formally, ℓ_CFG(t−1) approximates prior-token logit bias; subtracting wp·ℓ_CFG(t−1) penalizes tokens already favored before the latest visual re-anchoring, implementing step-wise debiased decoding aligned with Anti-LM and contrastive decoding. Ablating wp=0 reduces SLAKE closed accuracy, confirming its role. Open-ended analysis: The open/closed gap largely reflects SLAKE/MIMIC open-ended scoring rather than poorer decoding. It uses token recall against very short references (avg. ≈1.7 tokens), so lexical mismatch is penalized despite semantic correctness: color questions with GT Black/Gray get 0 when VLMs answer descriptively, and abnormality questions (≈18% of open queries) with rigid GTs such as Pneumonia or Lung Cancer reject synonyms like pulmonary infection. These errors stem from the base VLM’s lexical surface form and are mostly invariant to token-level contrastive decoding. CAST’s contribution is to suppress hallucinated affirmations on diagnostically loaded queries, captured by closed-ended evaluation; it yields consistent gains there (+13.7 on SLAKE) while staying neutral on open-ended. We view this as the desired safety trade-off in medical VQA, where confident false claims pose the main clinical risk.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper is well motivated in addressing hallucinations in medical VLMs and received mixed reviews. To better demonstrate its contributions, the authors should further analyze inference efficiency and include failure case studies. More details can be found in the reviewers’ comments. | The author provides detailed feedback, and the rebuttal has addressed most of the concerns raised by the reviewers. Although one reviewer hasn’t sent the feedback, the other two are happy with the rebuttal. The contribution is acceptable for MICCAI. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper addresses the important issue of hallucination mitigation in Medical Vision-Language Models (VLMs) by proposing an inference-time, annotation-free spatial-temporal decoding framework. Initially, reviewers expressed concerns regarding the computational overhead, the true “annotation-free” nature of the method, the reliance on numerous hyperparameters, and the weaker performance on open-ended questions. The authors’ rebuttal effectively addressed these critical points. They provided a detailed latency analysis showing that the overhead matches existing baselines like DoLA and that the MedSAM3 proposals can be precomputed. They clarified how the method robustly handles poor region proposals and demonstrated the stability of their hyperparameter choices across different models and datasets without per-cell tuning. Furthermore, they adequately explained that the open-ended performance gap is largely an artifact of the rigid lexical scoring metrics rather than a flaw in the decoding strategy itself. As the rebuttal resolved the primary computational and methodological concerns—leading one skeptical reviewer to upgrade their recommendation to Accept—the paper is recommended for inclusion. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): CAST is a strong inference-time contribution. It removes the need for ground-truth ROI annotations by selecting compact counterfactual anatomy masks and then applying spatial-temporal contrastive decoding. But the method depends on a capable medical segmentation model and multiple forward/occlusion passes, so the practical latency and failure modes under poor segmentation need more attention in their future work.

title: Counterfactual Stress-Testing for Fixing Lung Cancer Segmentation Models
reviewer_1_strengths: This paper addresses an important and clinically meaningful robustness problem in lung tumor segmentation tasks. It operates beyond average test-set performance and generic augmentation, and instead asks which specific tumor phenotypes can lead to segmentation failure. The paper proposes a practical way to intervene on interpretable tumor-specific radiomics factors, generate corresponding counterfactual image-mask pairs, and visualize how segmentation performance changes across controlled phenotype shifts. This is visualized well in the shown images as well. This approach is further compared against strong augmentations and generative models. The experimental section is very brief and thoroughly explanative for a 9 page paper.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: There are only two points this reviewer would like to point out: 1.The counterfactual interventions are defined mainly through tumor-intrinsic radiomics descriptors extracted from the tumor segmented regions themselves. Small question: what are the statistics of the segmentations? is the approach viable across the entire corpus of tumor sizes or is it susceptible to big/small clear/unclear tumors? The current framing makes the interventions interpretable, but it also narrows the stress-testing space. Failure modes driven by tumor-context interactions may not be fully captured by the current set of intervention variables, which rely on the the radiomics features that capture the tumor characteristics itself but not of the composite scan (which is imperative to a proper nnU-Net segmentation). 2.The framework depends on pseudo-label masks from the generator, so generator bias may propagate into both stress testing and repair. This is partly similar to recent self-supervised learning frameworks that leak their position bias into the learning. Not so important, but this reviewer also found the presentation of the flow-based generator and OT machinery somewhat dense relative to the main paper contribution, and some of the causal or identifiability language may be stronger than necessary in practice. A significant portion of the time was spent on analyzing and drawing the paper flow graphs on OT and flow matching than the overall holistic approach at hand.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The paper presents extensive analysis of the generated counterfactual examples including their effect on downstream segmentation, their fidelity wrt. an in-house validation set and the evolution of segmentation performance over intervention deciles. The idea of leveraging hard counterfactual example is a popular way of enhancing downstream segmentation performance and the authors’ implementaton is of novelty. The paper is generally well-written and easy to understand.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: – The result of this paper is only tested on one dataset (NSCLC Radiogenomics), while there exists more datasets on lung cancer segmentation in general (MSD-Lung, etc). The author should provide reasons why they choose not to test their method on them. Also, the results are only evaluated on dice, evaluating them with other widely used metrics such as HD95 can be better. While complementing segmentation dataset with counterfactual samples is of significance intuitively, there exists a line of work that does tumor inpainting that also boosts downstream tumor segmentation performance, some even utilize textual prompts to be of more versatility (LesionDiffusion, GuideGen, DiffTumor, FreeTumor, etc). Discussing the differences or comparing with them can make the proposed counterfactual method more convincing.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The motivation is clinically relevant. The paper correctly points out that current robustness work measures sensitivity to corruptions like noise or motion, but rarely isolates which tumour attributes drive failure. Framing robustness as sensitivity to interpretable radiomic attributes is a reasonable response to this gap. Individual-level CRCs are a distinctive angle. Most prior robustness analyses operate at the cohort level. Asking, within a single patient, how the prediction would change if the tumour were larger or more spherical is a different kind of question, and one that could be useful for deployment auditing. The ablation study demonstrates the importance of the fine-tuning sample selection strategy. Comparing CF-hard to CF-rand with the same number of added samples makes it clear that the gain comes from targeting failure regimes rather than from more training data. The experimental setup uses an in-house cohort for generator training and two public NSCLC datasets for segmentation training and independent testing, which is a reasonable and diverse data arrangement.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The SCM assumption that an intervention on one parent changes only that parent is not met in practice. Markovian abduction–intervention–prediction requires the parents to be mutually independent and independent of U. Table 1’s non-target drift (0.11 to 0.26 z-score, highest for fractal dimension) is direct evidence that, on this data, interventions on one parent move the others. Section 4.3 acknowledges this but does not resolve it. Without clean target isolation, the framework sits closer to conditional regeneration than to a causal intervention. 2.The identity-preservation claim is never empirically validated. The whole framework relies on abduction recovering a non-tumour latent so that intervening on r leaves the surrounding anatomy intact. Table 1 only measures radiomic drift inside the tumour mask, which says nothing about what happens outside it. Basic checks are absent: background SSIM or difference maps, cycle consistency of abduction then regeneration, or cross-patient swap tests. Without these, CRC drops at extreme deciles cannot be separated from unintended background drift. 3.The chosen parents do not represent the failure modes the intro emphasises. The introduction frames the problem around small lesions, poorly defined boundaries, GGO, and adjacent anatomy with similar attenuation. Of the six parents, only volume directly targets small lesions. Fractal dimension captures geometric complexity but not partial-volume or GGO-induced fuzziness, mean HU partially reflects GGO but not its spatial pattern, and attenuation similarity with adjacent tissue (a contrast property rather than a tumour-internal one) is not covered at all. 4.Dice is the sole evaluation metric despite the paper’s own warning. The opening notes that mean Dice can hide brittle behaviour, yet CRC construction, hard-sample selection at τ = 0.7, and the final test-set comparison all use Dice alone. HD95 or surface Dice would directly probe the boundary-complexity failures the method claims to address, and could plausibly change which counterfactuals get labelled hard. 5.Figure 4’s method comparison is reported for only one feature, and that feature is the most favourable to the narrative. The left and middle panels show baseline-only CRCs for wavelet entropy and volume; only the right panel compares all methods, and only under fractal-dimension intervention. Fractal dimension is the feature where the baseline collapses most sharply in Table 2 and where generator image fidelity is lowest among shape-related parents (ρ = 0.85, drift = 0.26). Its extracted value also depends on the exact mask used, which makes it particularly hard to separate true segmentation brittleness from generator-mask artefacts at extreme deciles. A method-comparison grid across all six features, or test-set Dice stratified by quintile, would be needed to show the gain generalises. 6.The dataset description is internally inconsistent and does not match the cited sources. Reference [1] (Aerts et al.) is NSCLC-Radiomics (Lung1, 422 subjects with manual GTV), and [2] (Bakr et al., Sci. Data 5:180202, 2018) is NSCLC-Radiogenomics (211 subjects, masks released for only 144). Section 4.1 assigns the names in reverse. Even after correcting the swap, the 207-case test split does not align with 144 available Radiogenomics masks, and the provenance of the test masks is not stated. Table 1 and Figure 4 also report results on an “in-house validation set” that is never defined: the 100 public validation cases from Section 4.1, a slice of the 1,472 generator-training crops, or a third cohort. Since the headline rests on a test-set Dice improvement, these need to be stated precisely.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: 1.Identity preservation and SCM framing [R1, R4]. The SCM/abduction angle is central to the method. Our goal is not to generate another plausible tumour, but to answer an individual-level counterfactual question: what would this same case look like if one radiomic parent were changed? This requires abduction–intervention–prediction: without this step, generative augmentation changes both tumour phenotype and patient-specific anatomy. This is motivated by the identifiability theory in [1], which shows that, under dynamic-OT/flow-matching assumptions, the monotonic transport map supports unique abduction for high-dimensional counterfactual prediction. Thus, the Markovian SCM formulation is important because it separates patient-specific exogenous variation from the intervened radiomic parent and makes the CRC an individual-level counterfactual robustness curve rather than an unconditional synthesis curve. This is precisely the property needed for clinically meaningful stress testing of the same patient. We agree that our implementation is approximate. The non-target drift in Table 1 reflects finite-sample/finite-capacity error rather than perfect parent isolation. In particular, minibatch OT with a batch size of only 100 due to memory requirements cannot exactly recover the population dynamic-OT coupling required, so leakage between correlated radiomic features is expected and will be explained in the paper. We also agree that identity preservation should be checked outside the tumour. We have now computed background preservation on the overlapping non-tumour region after removing both factual and counterfactual masks: background MSE is 0.03 ± 0.01 and SSIM is 0.89.These new results support the claim that the patient-specific context is largely preserved. 2.Radiomics scope [R2, R4]. We agree that the current parents are tumour-intrinsic and do not capture all context-driven failures. We will state this limitation and add validation-set ranges showing that CRCs span the tumour distribution in the validation set: volume 46–129 cm³, sphericity 0.33–0.80, fractal dimension 2.38–2.78, mean HU −20 to 118, HU SD 35–199, and wavelet entropy 2.1–6.9.Table 2 already shows failures across multiple parents/quintiles. Fig. 4 shows one method-comparison CRC for illustration. Generalisation is assessed on the independent test set in Table 3, where CF-hard outperforms all baselines. 3.Boundary metrics [R2, R4]: Dice was used for CRCs and τ=0.7 mining because it is the standard nnU-Net selection metric and gives a stable failure criterion across parents. We now add HD95: baseline 8.7±5.5 mm, BigAug 7.2±4.6, GAN-Aug 7.5±4.8, Rad-OS 8.1±5.1, CF-rand 6.9±4.7, and CF-hard 5.6±3.8.Thus, CF-hard improves boundary accuracy as well as overlap. We will also explore HD95/ASD-based mining as future work. 4.Pseudo-labels, related work and minor errors [R1, R2, R4]. We agree pseudo-label bias is possible; we do not treat generator masks as perfect, and support them with fidelity, drift, and added background-preservation checks. Since CF-hard and CF-rand use the same generator, pseudo-labels, and sample budget, the gain isolates CRC-guided failure selection. MSD-Lung is valuable future validation. We do not use LesionDiffusion, GuideGen, DiffTumor, and FreeTumor as direct baselines as we already control for augmentation benefit with BigAug and GAN-Aug under the same sample budget but will include them in our related work. Our distinct contribution compared to these methods is to diagnosing and repairing named radiomic failure regimes. We will correct the swapped NSCLC-Radiomics/Radiogenomics citations, state cohort provenance, exclusions, splits, and mask sources, and define the in-house validation set. We will also fix the A100 typo, relabel Fig. 4’s y-axis as Dice, and improve figure placement. [1] Ribeiro, F.D.S., Santhirasekaram, A., Glocker, B.: Counterfactual identifiability via dynamic optimal transport. arXiv preprint arXiv:2510.08294 (2025)
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): A counterfactual stress testing framework to identify the failure modes in tumor segmentation is presented, which then is used to improve segmentation performance. The counterfactual generation using the 3D flow matching with minibatch coupling and radiomic features conditioning is seen as novel. The paper is well-written and experimental evaluation are reasonable to establish downstream utility. Concerns were raised regarding certain claims including identity preservation as well as several minor concerns that should be addressed carefully in the rebuttal. | The authors addressed most of the reviewers’ concerns and the updated results satisfied reviewers’ concerns. However, as pointed out by reviewer 2, please acknowledge the limitations and position the work clearly taking in to account its limitations and what it can address. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper targets a sharp angle in lung cancer segmentation through counterfactual stress testing and is sufficiently validated. Essentially, it asks: for the same patient, and also at the population level, which tumor attributes (among selected radiomic features) would cause the segmentation model to fail? An additional practical outcome is that the generated failure-mode samples can be used to augment training and improve the original segmentation network. The remaining concerns are: (1) identity preservation is a key component and is partially validated, but changing one radiomic feature may also affect other features, which needs further exploration; (2) the generated masks may introduce additional pseudo-label errors; (3) validation on additional datasets with broader comparisons would further strengthen the paper. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): All reviewers agree that the paper has merits on how it presents an interpretable robustness check allowing to identify difficult tumors. The rebuttal touches on most concerns, and two out of three reviewers believe their points have been sufficiently addressed.

title: CPR: Chained Perceptual Refinement for Coarse-to-Fine Medical Image Classification
reviewer_1_strengths: This paper (1) innovatively reconstructs the classification of high-resolution medical images as a sequential decision-making process from global to local. The strategy network simultaneously predicts the center coordinates and spatial range of the refined region, achieving dynamic scale contraction, which is closer to the gradual focus diagnosis process of clinical doctors than the fixed size and unconstrained block sampling in existing methods. (2)The state transition mechanism accumulates evidence in a residual manner without increasing input resolution. (3) At the same time, a reduction in computational complexity was achieved with the same accuracy, and the experimental setup was clear.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: (1) Insufficient explanation of the novelty differences between existing adaptive computing and multi-scale methods; (2) The key stability indicators during reinforcement learning training were not reported, and the potential impact of high variance in policy gradient estimation in medical image small sample high noise scenarios was not discussed. (3) Qualitative or quantitative analysis of failed cases was not provided. For medical applications, it is crucial to understand when a model may incorrectly focus on non lesion areas or excessively contract, resulting in loss of contextual information.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The paper addresses a highly practical problem: how to preserve fine-grained diagnostic information in medical images without performing dense, high-resolution inference. 2.The proposed stepwise refinement approach from global to local is intuitive and reasonable. Furthermore, the predicted location and scale are more suitable for medical images with significant resolution differences than fixed-size cropping. 3.Experiments cover five public datasets, multiple medical imaging modalities, and various backbone networks, providing more convincing validation than single-dataset validation. 4.The paper reports not only accuracy but also memory usage and GFLOPs, consistent with the method’s core efficiency claims. 5.Qualitative visualization and scale-controlled ablation experiments provide strong support for the method’s behavior.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.Regarding methodological novelty, the authors need to more clearly define the differences between this paper and existing adaptive vision/coarse-to-fine methods. The current work shares a clear conceptual connection with existing methods such as Adaptive NN, OverLock, and PAMIL in the core idea of “global overview followed by local region focus” or “dynamically driven region selection.” Therefore, based solely on the current manuscript, I cannot fully determine the key innovations of CPR and its irreplaceability compared to these works. 2.Ablation experiments are still incomplete. There is a lack of comparison with simpler alternatives, such as fixed coarse-to-fine scheduling, non-reinforcement learning pruning strategies, and deterministic attention mechanisms. Therefore, the necessity of PPO and the chained design cannot be fully confirmed at present. 3.There are some inconsistencies in the wording. For example, the abstract emphasizes predicting the crop center, while the method section defines (x_t, y_t) as the top-left coordinate; the descriptions of the state variables z_t and H_t are also inconsistent. Wang, Yulin, et al. “Emulating human-like adaptive vision for efficient and flexible machine visual perception.” Nature Machine Intelligence (2025): 1-19. Lou, Meng, and Yizhou Yu. “Overlock: An overview-first-look-closely-next convnet with context-mixing dynamic kernels.” Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition. 2025. Zheng, Tingting, Kui Jiang, and Hongxun Yao. “Dynamic policy-driven adaptive multi-instance learning for whole slide image classification.” Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF conference on computer vision and pattern recognition. 2024.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The proposed method is supported by a thorough evaluation across five diverse datasets. The results consistently demonstrate that the framework achieves superior classification performance while maintaining significantly lower computational and memory overhead compared to traditional high-resolution processing techniques.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The core concept of utilizing iterative local crops to extract fine-grained information is well-established in the literature, yet the manuscript lacks a comprehensive discussion of, and comparison with, relevant prior art. While the authors compare their work to AdaptiveNN, they overlook several foundational and contemporary models with similar architectural parallels: RA-CNN [a]: This model similarly employs a recurrent, iterative approach to propose variable-sized crops with intermediate supervision. SSPS/M2Former [b]: Recent work that also utilizes variable-sized patches for fine-grained recognition. Feature Accumulation Strategies: The proposed formulation closely resembles a recurrent network with a linear gate. Similar strategies using LSTMs for feature refinement have been proposed by Shroff et al. [c], and alternative aggregation methods, such as positional aggregation in TNet [d], already exist. Therefore, the authors should contextualize their contribution relative to these and other similar methods and ideally provide quantitative comparisons to justify the necessity of the new formulation. Evaluating against only one specialized model (AdaptiveNN) is insufficient for a paper claiming a superior “low-cost” approach. The authors should include standard iterative or hard-attention baselines to substantiate their claims of achieving a better accuracy-to-cost trade-off. To validate the efficacy of the policy network, the ablation study should include a configuration where crop boxes are randomly sampled rather than predicted. This is a critical baseline to demonstrate that the learned policy network is identifying salient regions and that the performance gains are not merely a byproduct of processing higher-resolution patches, regardless of their location.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We use W to denote Weakness and R to denote Reviewer. (Joint Reply: R1-W1, R2-W1) Novelty and relation to adaptive/coarse-to-fine methods. We thank the reviewers for raising this point. CPR differs from prior adaptive, hard-attention, and coarse-to-fine methods in three key aspects: (1) it predicts both crop location and scale, rather than using fixed-size crops, predefined multi-scale inputs, or only location proposals; (2) it performs chained perceptual refinement, where each step updates a residual perceptual state instead of independently aggregating local crops; and (3) it targets high-resolution medical classification with fixed backbone input size and bounded memory. Compared with AdaptiveNN, CPR adds adaptive scale refinement; compared with OverLock, CPR revisits the original high-resolution image via adaptive crop-and-refine actions rather than context-mixing kernels; compared with PAMIL, CPR addresses image-level classification rather than WSI MIL. (R1-W2) Stability, variance, and statistical reliability. We repeated CPR with three random seeds on COVID and BUSI datasets. CPR obtains 98.64 ± 0.17% on COVID and 95.16 ± 0.30% on BUSI, consistently outperforming the compared baselines. The small standard deviations indicate that CPR is robust across different runs, suggesting that the policy-gradient-based learning component does not introduce noticeable performance instability. (R1-W3) Failure cases, clinical reliability, and limitations. We thank the reviewer for this important suggestion. Our qualitative inspection identifies two main failure modes. First, CPR may over-contract the crop when lesions are subtle, diffuse, or spread over a large region, which can lead to the loss of useful contextual information. Second, when visually salient non-lesion structures are present, the policy may attend to irrelevant regions and accumulate misleading evidence. These observations suggest that CPR is most effective when discriminative evidence is spatially localized, while diffuse, ambiguous, or weakly contrasted lesion patterns remain challenging. We will add this failure-case analysis to the revised manuscript. (R2-W1) Novelty. Please see R1-W1. (R2-W2) Ablation completeness. To address the reviewer’s concern, we include additional ablation baselines on the BUSI dataset using the ViT-S model: Random Crop, Fixed Coarse-to-Fine, Deterministic Attention, and No-Chain CPR. These variants achieve 93.29%, 93.61%, 94.25%, and 94.25%, respectively, while the full CPR achieves the best performance of 94.89%. These results further validate the effectiveness of CPR. (R2-W3) inconsistencies in wording. We will thoroughly check the manuscript revise the inconsistent wording to ensure clarity and consistency in the revised version. (R3-W1) Similar Architectural Baselines. We thank the reviewer for this helpful suggestion. To address this concern, we additionally compare CPR with four related architectural baselines: (1) RA-CNN, (2) M2Former, (3) Focus Longer to See Better, and (4) TNet. On BUSI, these methods achieve 88.82%, 93.61%, 90.10%, and 94.25%, respectively, while CPR achieves the best performance of 94.89%. On COVID, they achieve 98.25%, 95.71%, 95.59%, and 98.37%, respectively, while CPR further improves the performance to 98.67%. These results demonstrate that CPR consistently outperforms these baselines, further validating the effectiveness of our proposed method. (R3-W2) Policy network ablation. We thank the reviewer for this insightful suggestion. To address this concern, we report two additional baselines on the BUSI dataset using the ViT-S model: CPR with Random Crop and CPR with Deterministic Attention. These baselines achieve 93.29% and 94.25%, respectively, while the full CPR achieves 94.89%. These results indicate that the learned policy network provides more effective region selection than random cropping or deterministic attention, thereby contributing to the overall performance improvement.

The authors are suggest to address these limitations in the rebuttal phase. | After rebuttal, all reviewers decide to accept the paper, the author successfully adderss the problems , and I recommend the acceptance of the paper. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper addresses an important and practical problem in high-resolution medical image classification, aiming to improve the balance between diagnostic performance and computational efficiency. The initial reviews raised concerns about novelty, comparison with related adaptive/coarse-to-fine methods, and the completeness of ablation studies. The authors’ rebuttal provides reasonable clarification addressing these main concerns. Importantly, the reviewer opinions converged toward acceptance after the rebuttal, indicating agreement that the major concerns were sufficiently addressed. While the method remains somewhat incremental and some implementation details could still be improved, the overall empirical results across multiple datasets are positive. I therefore recommend acceptance. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): After considering the reviews and rebuttal discussion, I recommend acceptance. The paper addresses an important and practical challenge in medical imaging: preserving fine-grained diagnostic information in high-resolution images under limited computational budgets. The proposed coarse-to-fine refinement framework is well motivated and demonstrates a strong balance between accuracy, memory efficiency, and computational cost across multiple datasets, modalities, and backbone architectures. In particular, the chained refinement mechanism and adaptive scale-aware region selection provide a clinically meaningful alternative to fixed-resolution or fixed-crop strategies. While some concerns regarding novelty relative to prior adaptive vision and coarse-to-fine methods were initially raised, the rebuttal satisfactorily clarified the distinctions from related work and strengthened the empirical support through additional analyses, ablations, and discussions of stability and failure cases. Overall, the paper presents a technically sound and practically valuable contribution with sufficiently broad experimental validation for acceptance at MICCAI.

title: CRIMSON: A Clinically-Grounded LLM-Based Metric for Generative Radiology Report Evaluation
reviewer_1_strengths: The paper addresses a clinically well-motivated problem and targets an important limitation of existing radiology report evaluation metrics. A major strength is that the paper recognizes that different reporting errors can have very different clinical consequences. Missing a life-threatening abnormality should not be treated the same as omitting a benign or age-related finding. The paper further argues that the importance of a finding may depend on patient age and indication, making the incorporation of patient context into report evaluation both clinically meaningful and practically relevant. The method shows meaningful novelty in its unified formulation of clinical significance weighting, fine-grained attribute-level error modeling, and context-aware evaluation. CRIMSON not only distinguishes false findings and missing findings, but also models multiple attribute-level discrepancies in matched findings, such as location, severity, measurement, and certainty. At the same time, it introduces clinically motivated significance weighting and allows this significance assessment to depend on patient context. Compared with metrics based mainly on surface similarity or coarse error counting, this unified framework is more aligned with real clinical reasoning. The treatment of normal findings is a valuable design choice that reflects an understanding of variation in clinical reporting practice. The paper excludes normal findings from the main evaluation on the grounds that reporting of normal findings varies substantially across radiologists, and including them may introduce noise unrelated to true report quality. This is a thoughtful design decision that helps the metric focus more on clinically meaningful content rather than stylistic or template-driven variation.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: One limitation of the paper is that the proposed method is fundamentally an evaluation framework driven by a strong closed-source LLM, with GPT-5.2 explicitly used as the backbone throughout the pipeline. This design choice is not inherently problematic, and prompt design can reasonably be considered part of the methodological contribution. However, it also means that the observed performance may depend, at least in part, on the capability of the chosen judge model. For this reason, comparison against other LLM-based radiology evaluation methods is important. The paper does include at least one clearly LLM-based baseline, namely GREEN, so the gains cannot simply be attributed to the use of an LLM alone; however, the comparison with other closely related LLM-based evaluators is still somewhat limited. More importantly, if the authors intend CRIMSON to be viewed as a more general and reusable evaluation framework, rather than a specific GPT-5.2 + prompting pipeline, it would be helpful to include additional analysis of robustness, such as consistency across different backbone models or at least run-to-run variance. Integration of patient context: Incorporating patient-specific factors such as age and clinical indication into evaluation is a novel and important contribution, better reflecting real-world radiologic reasoning and improving the clinical validity of the metric. Fine-grained and interpretable error modeling: The proposed taxonomy of false findings, missing findings, and attribute-level errors (with partial credit) provides a transparent and interpretable evaluation framework that can be useful for both benchmarking and model debugging. Strong clinical validation: The method is evaluated against radiologist-annotated error counts and preferences, showing strong correlation and improved alignment compared to prior metrics. The inclusion of multiple expert radiologists strengthens the credibility of the results. Introduction of clinically relevant benchmarks: The proposed RadJudge and RadPref benchmarks provide valuable testbeds for future research and highlight clinically meaningful evaluation scenarios beyond standard metrics. Practical deployment considerations: The fine-tuned MedGemmaCRIMSON model enables privacy-preserving, local evaluation, which is highly relevant for real-world clinical adoption where data-sharing constraints are critical.

Extending CRIMSON to other imaging modalities (e.g., CT, MRI) would likely require substantial redesign of the taxonomy and clinical weighting scheme. While the MedGemmaCRIMSON model enables local deployment, it is trained to approximate GPT-5.2 outputs. It therefore remains unclear how much of the performance gain is attributable to the proposed scoring framework versus the strength of the underlying LLM evaluator. This makes it difficult to assess which design choices are most responsible for the observed performance gains. Potential benchmark bias: The RadJudge benchmark is constructed around clinically nuanced scenarios aligned with the design principles of CRIMSON. While useful, this may partially favor the proposed method and does not fully substitute for independent external validation. Subjectivity of clinical weighting: The severity weights and error categorization are based on expert-defined guidelines. Incorporating patient age and indication into severity assignment — such that aortic calcification in a 25-year-old is weighted differently from the same finding in a 75-year-old — is clinically correct and appears to be a meaningful and relatively underexplored addition to existing evaluation metrics. author_feedback: Thank you for the review. We acknowledge the comments regarding the lack of external validation. We currently do not have access to datasets collected at different institutions or from diverse patient populations, which limits our ability to perform such evaluations at this stage. We, however, highlight that we have a large internal data cohort captured using different scanners, providing strong evaluation, and as part of future work, aim to evaluate it on multisituational datasets We also agree that the dataset is subject to selection bias, which we explicitly acknowledge in the limitations section. Constructing a fully unbiased dataset would require angiograms from asymptomatic individuals. However, acquiring such data is inherently challenging, as it would involve exposing healthy patients to an invasive angiographic procedure without a clinical indication. Regarding the comments on evaluating different severity thresholds, Table 1 and Figure 3 present both the data distribution and model performance across multiple thresholds. While we do not explicitly adopt the threshold defined by the American College of Cardiology guidelines, the evaluated thresholds closely align with those recommendations. Lastly, the novelty of our work does not stem from the contrastive pretraining methodology itself, but rather from the adaptation of the CLIP framework to paired angiography and ECG data. Specifically, our contribution lies in extending a multi-view encoder architecture for contrastive learning by introducing separate CLS and CLIP tokens, enabling effective alignment between angiography and ECG modalities within the contrastive framework.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): This submission presents a clinically relevant and technically sound study on transferring angiography-derived information to ECG representations for severe coronary stenosis classification. The main strengths are the clear clinical motivation, the new angiography-ECG cross-modal pretraining setting, the reasonably large internal paired cohort, and the comparative experimental validation. After checking the manuscript, the core contribution is supported: the proposed StenCE framework improves ECG-based severe stenosis classification, with the strongest result reported for the most severe threshold, and the paper also includes baseline comparisons, multi-threshold evaluation, and an ablation supporting the main design choices. The decisive concerns are the absence of external validation, the selected angiography-referred population that introduces acknowledged selection bias, and the fact that performance declines substantially for less severe stenosis levels. These are real limitations. However, some reviewer criticisms are only partially supported. After checking the manuscript, the concern that evaluation focuses only on the most severe cases is overstated because the paper already evaluates several stenosis thresholds and discusses the resulting drop in performance. Similarly, the criticism that the contribution is too limited methodologically to merit consideration gives insufficient weight to the new modality pairing, the comparative evidence, and the ablation study. Accordingly, I assign limited weight to those criticisms in the overall assessment.

reviewer_3_strengths: 1.Pragmatic clinical insight: Instead of solely relying on algorithmic solutions to address the low soft-tissue contrast in CBCT, this study innovatively introduces clinical physical aids—a mouth opener and impression tray—to reshape the imaging boundaries. This front-end approach to improving data quality demonstrates practical thinking and strong clinical awareness. 2.Novel task formulation: The unconstrained 3D voxel segmentation problem is elegantly reformulated as a scalar field regression task constrained by geometric priors derived from the tooth surface mesh. Through CSR, the method extracts features along the tooth-surface normal direction corresponding to the “bone–gingiva–air” transition, effectively reducing background anatomical noise. This formulation offers theoretical advantages in handling adherent soft-tissue edges. 3.Empirical validation: Experiments show that the proposed approach achieves a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.38 mm without requiring auxiliary intraoral scan (IOS) data for registration. This has the potential to simplify clinical periodontal assessment workflows and reduce cumulative errors from multi-modal registration.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The method’s strong reliance on upstream geometric priors renders it potentially sensitive to error propagation. Both the CSR and BGR modules are fully dependent on the accuracy of the tooth surface meshes extracted by nnU-Net. However, in real-world CBCT clinical data, metal artifacts—such as those from crowns or implants—can lead to failed tooth segmentation or severely distorted surface meshes. The manuscript lacks an analysis of how such upstream mesh extraction errors may impact the robustness of downstream gingival predictions. 2.The manuscript compares the BGR network, which leverages point cloud and surface normal features, with conventional 3D CNNs (e.g., 3D U-Net, DeepLabV3+) that operate directly on raw CBCT voxels. While this comparison demonstrates that “surface-constrained” approaches outperform “unconstrained voxel classification,” it does not sufficiently establish the inherent advantage of the Gaussian regression (BGR) itself. To make the evaluation more rigorous, I suggest the authors to include a baseline model that also operates on the tooth surface manifold—e.g., a PointNet++ or graph neural network performing direct binary classification on the point cloud. 3.Although the physical scanning protocol effectively enhances image contrast, the manuscript does not discuss its applicability boundaries in extreme clinical scenarios. For instance, in patients with severe gag reflex, limited mouth opening, or partial tooth loss, the placement of the physical tools may be constrained, which could limit the generalizability of the proposed method. 4.The introduction quickly jumps to the limitations of voxel-based CNNs but overlooks a deeper discussion of the methodological context. Additionally, visualizations of the continuous Gaussian confidence fields predicted along the tooth surfaces could be included. Providing these visualizations would greatly enhance the interpretability of the method and increase readers’ confidence in its effectiveness. [1] Wang C, He Z, Chen L, et al. Cham: Springer Nature Switzerland, 2025: 268-277.[2] Zhou, Z., Chen, Y., He, A., Que, X., Wang, K., Yao, R., & Li, T. (2024). author_feedback: We thank the Meta-AE and reviewers for recognizing the clinical motivation, the protocol and method co-design, and the consistent gains over voxe-based methods. We address the major concerns below. (1) Protocol scope and isolation of algorithmic gain [Meta reviewer, R1.1, R2.1]. The protocol is a prerequisite that makes CBCT gingival margin imaging tractable. In routine CBCT, buccal and lingual soft tissues adhere to the arch with nearly identical intensity to gingiva, leaving the margin invisible even to experienced clinicians, and no algorithm can recover information that is not encoded. Our lip retractor and impression tray protocol introduces this air interface as a simple chair side add on to the existing CBCT workflow, using routine clinical aids with no scanner modification. All comparison methods in Table 1 use the same CBCT data acquired under this protocol and the same patient level five fold split. The gains over nnU-Net (0.38 vs 0.50 mm MAE, 56.2% vs 34.6% IoU@0.3mm) therefore reflect the algorithmic contribution rather than any acquisition advantage. (2) Baseline comparisons [Meta reviewer, R2.3, R4.2]. We appreciate the suggestion of stronger voxel baselines. Our method still outperforms recent architectures. SwinUNETR yields 0.48 ± 0.16 mm MAE and 37.1 ± 17.6% IoU@0.3mm, and 3D UXNet yields 0.46 ± 0.15 mm MAE and 38.8 ± 17.4% IoU@0.3mm. These will be added to Table 1.R4.2 also requested a surface manifold baseline. This is already present in Table 2 as “w/o Cross surface (K=1)”, which uses the same PointMLP encoder on the same tooth point cloud with coordinates and normals only, i.e. direct surface classification. Its IoU is 35.7% vs 56.2% for the full model, isolating CSR. “w/o Gaussian Band” reaches 53.2%, isolating BGR. (3) Reporting, ethics, and reproducibility [R1.2, R2.2, R2.4, R4.4, R4.5]. The five fold cross validation is patient level with no patient overlap, on 28 patients and 684 teeth spanning gingivitis to Stage IV periodontitis. The study was approved under SH9H-2026-T98-1, with anonymized data and informed consent. We will state the split protocol, IRB approval, and anonymization explicitly. We will expand the Introduction and Related Work to cover tooth, gingiva, and alveolar bone segmentation together with surface, mesh, and graph based learning, including the suggested ITMatch and NKUT references. We will also report training and evaluation details for the upstream nnU-Net tooth instance segmentation that precedes Marching Cubes and Laplacian smoothing, and provide a per fold MAE and IoU breakdown. (4) Clinical boundaries, robustness, and interpretability [R1.3, R4.1, R4.3, R4.5]. For multi rooted teeth the gingival margin lies at the CEJ on the crown above the furcation, so root multiplicity does not affect surface normals in the sampled −0.3 to 1.7 mm band. Molars achieve 0.39 mm MAE and 55.6% IoU, consistent with single rooted teeth. On error propagation, we excluded target teeth with full crowns or in tooth implants while retaining minor restorations. On this cohort the upstream nnU-Net reaches 96% Dice on teeth, sufficient to support stable downstream prediction. Stratified evaluation on severe metal artifact cases is left as future work. The protocol uses standard intraoral aids and is well tolerated, though severe gag reflex, restricted mouth opening, or extensive tooth loss can constrain placement, and we will state these boundaries in the Discussion. For interpretability we will add figures showing the 1D intensity profiles from the three anatomical regions and the predicted Gaussian confidence field rendered on the tooth surface. We believe these clarifications and additions address the central concerns and respectfully hope the reviewers will consider raising their recommendation

author_feedback: We sincerely thank the reviewers and AC for their careful reviews and insightful comments. We clarify several main issues below. To R1 & R3 Result: All results are averaged over 3 runs; Mean±SD will be added if space permits. Preliminary tests (p<0.05, SD≤1.0%) confirm significance. To R1 Technical Clarification: (1) Uncertainty: The co-evolution module initializes via Teacher and SAM discrepancies and runs only 1 iteration to prevent redundant overhead; XOR localizes conflicts solely for resampling and never computes the loss. Gradients flow through the continuous W(x,y), perfectly preserving uncertainty. (2) Circular Dependency: M_final is refined independently by SAM, measures consensus with external knowledge, breaks the confirmation loop. (3) Static gScoreCAM suffices since macroscopic anatomy is constant; SAM and the subsequent processes handle dynamic refinements. (4) Loss Complementarity: L_con aligns global representations, while L_unlabel enforces local boundary precision—strictly complementary. Sec. 3.3 shows identical hyperparameter across three datasets ensures robustness, making dataset-specific tuning unnecessary. Clinical Deployability: BiomedCLIP and SAM operate strictly during training (peak 16GB, V100). Inference only uses a lightweight U-Net, taking <17ms and ~1.82GB at 256*256 ensuring scalable deployment. Baselines & Efficacy: With limited space, Table 1 selectively reports four SOTAs (CVPR/TMI 2025) and four reproduced classics. CSGE consistently dominates across 5 ratios. At 1% labels (ΔDSC>4.9%), it effectively reduces annotation requirement from 10% to 1%. 2D Data & Agnosticism: We focused on 2D binary segmentation as a rigorous testbed, leveraging its status as a top-tier SSL benchmark. Sec. 3.2 validates our architecture-agnostic. Replacing SAM with MedSAM/SAM3 yields cross-dataset gains (+3.2%DSC, +2.8%IoU), or integrating nnU-Net adds a 5.02% boost. This high modularity makes future 3D/multi-class extension straightforward. To R2 Resampling: While initial prompts provide global localization, resampled points target XOR conflict regions to resolve ambiguities and refine boundaries where Teacher and SAM disagree. Distance d: d(x,y) is the Euclidean distance to E_SAM boundary. Small d prioritizes SAM’s geometric precision, large d trusts teacher semantics for regional consistency. Upper-bound: Fully supervised results will be included. To R3 Metrics, Ratios & Contributions: Standard Semi-SL metrics DSC and mIoU globally capture our bottlenecks: semantic incompleteness (misalignment), false positives (bias), and blurred boundaries (boundary loss). We will detail this mapping in the revision. Multi-ratio evaluations (1%-30%) demonstrate our framework’s robustness, specifically its ability to surpass SOTA at the 1% label, where traditional Semi-SL often fails. Ablation & Results: Due to space limits, Sec 3.3 highlights key components ablations. We will clarify how multiple components form unified modules: As the concurrent work SEMISAM-O1 (MedIA 2026) confirms, single foundation models face ceilings due to lacking constraints, our semantic-geometric integration is theoretically and empirically essential (+SAM/BiomedCLIP, DSC+5.1%). XOR mitigates normal region misclassification (+Conflict Iterative, DSC+3.6%); spatial trust maximally preserves boundary information (+Spatial Trust Map, DSC+1.6%). Manuscript Structure: The revised Abstract/Introduction in camera ready will specify tasks/datasets and introduce the text modality earlier to explain how BiomedCLIP’s macroscopic guidance prevents early bias from SAM. Metric impacts and contributions will be unified. Figures & Formatting: Captions will clarify framework links (Fig. 1) and EMA flow (Fig. 2), and add row labels (Fig. 3). “Co-evolution” is defined as SAM’s iterative geometric refinement of student predictions. Terminology is standardized to “Semi-SL”, with all symbols and acronyms defined at first occurrence alongside thorough proofreading.

title: CSWinUNETR: Segmentation of Thin Anatomical Structures in Medical Images
reviewer_1_strengths: The paper has several notable strengths. First, it addresses an important and challenging problem, namely the segmentation of thin and tortuous anatomical structures, where preserving fine branches and structural continuity is particularly difficult. Second, the method is technically well motivated: while the individual ingredients are not entirely new on their own, the paper combines cross-shaped attention, multi-scale detail enhancement, and a sparse-control snake-style convolution in a coherent way that is well aligned with the target problem. In particular, the sparse-control formulation is an interesting refinement aimed at improving stability when modeling curvilinear trajectories. Third, the evaluation is relatively comprehensive, covering four heterogeneous datasets across both 2D and 3D settings, with quantitative, qualitative, and ablation results that make the empirical case reasonably convincing.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The methodological novelty appears moderate rather than substantial. 1.The proposed method combines several design elements that are already established in prior work at the component level. In particular, the use of cross-shaped stripe attention is closely related to CSWin Transformer: A General Vision Transformer Backbone with Cross-Shaped Windows (2022), while the cyclic shift mechanism follows the design idea popularized by Swin Transformer: Hierarchical Vision Transformer Using Shifted Windows (2021). In addition, the use of snake-style dynamic convolution for curvilinear structure modeling is strongly related to Dynamic Snake Convolution Based on Topological Geometric Constraints for Tubular Structure Segmentation (2023). Moreover, CSWin-UNet: Transformer UNet with Cross-Shaped Windows for Medical Image Segmentation (2025) has already adapted CSWin-style attention to medical image segmentation. Therefore, the main contribution of the present paper seems to lie more in the integration and task-specific refinement of existing ideas than in a fundamentally new segmentation formulation. 2.The efficiency and deployment trade-offs are not characterized in sufficient detail. Although the paper reports parameter counts, it does not provide a more complete efficiency analysis, such as FLOPs, inference speed, or memory usage. This omission is particularly relevant because the method targets both 2D and 3D medical image segmentation and combines attention-based modeling with dynamic curvilinear aggregation, both of which may introduce nontrivial computational overhead. A more thorough efficiency analysis would make the practical utility of the method easier to assess.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The SDSConv module is an interesting refinement of prior dynamic snake/deformable operators. Integrating CSWin attention with a Swin-style cyclic shift is a simple but effective architecture. 2.Evaluation spans four benchmarks across different modalities and dimensions, improving generality. 3.Comparisons with many baselines, including strong backbones (nnUNetv2, UNETR, SwinUNETR/v2), thin-structure-oriented methods (DSCNet, CS²-Net, ER-Net), and nnUNet variants (clDice, cbDice, skeleton-recall).
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The method section needs more detail. Specifically, the 3D version of SDSConv is not clear. The text mentions two axes (x and y), but 3D images have three (x, y, and z). Please explain how the model handles the third axis in practice. 2.The introduction does not clearly explain the difference or the motivation for your method compared to baselines like CSWin-UNet. Even though you used them as baselines, it is not clear what makes your specific design unique.

reviewer_3_strengths: The experiments in this paper are relatively thorough, but the novelty is insufficient.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The novelty of this paper is limited, as the proposed method largely assembles existing research, such as references [5], [7], [19], and [22], without introducing substantial new ideas. Moreover, the experimental results show that, despite a significant increase in the number of model parameters compared to other methods, the proposed approach does not achieve a particularly notable improvement in performance metrics.
