title: Decoupled Single-Mask Annotation Noise Detection via Cross-Sectional Patch Self-consistency
reviewer_1_strengths: The work uses cross-sectional image patches and masks as a reference for comparison, which is a very intuitive and interesting idea. Provides an interpretable and training-free algorithm. Explains the results with qualitative examples, even for failed cases.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Major: 1.The method was evaluated only on the ImageCAS dataset, limiting its generalizability to out-of-distribution datasets. 2.Even though the paper evaluates the method with and without quality weighting, it does not compare with other similar methods for its performance against existing noisy mask localisation methods, eg: Dong et al. , Deep Self-Cleansing for Medical Image Segmentation with Noisy Labels 3.The use of MSE to compare image patches is not intuitive here, as structural comparison is more important, why not SSIM? Minor: 1.The computation cost of patch comparisons could have been studied. 2.Figure 1 lacks some clarity. The masks for the yellow and brown patches appear at different positions compared to their corresponding image patches. 3.The first paragraph under the Methodology section describes the Multi-rater consistency equation and provides the citation [15]. However, the cited work does not describe this equation. 4.The word “curvenetwork” in the first paragraph of the introduction is missing a hyphen or space after “curve”. 5.The paper does not state the value of “K” used, preventing the reader from recreating the results.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The paper addresses a practically important and underexplored problem, namely annotation noise detection in the single-mask setting, which is common in vascular CT datasets. The core idea is intuitive and well-grounded, leveraging anatomical recurrence to define a self-consistency criterion that is easy to interpret. The method is decoupled from model training, which is a strong advantage over training-based noise handling approaches and allows explicit auditing of annotations. The use of cross-sectional patch extraction with Bishop frames is technically sound and ensures stable geometric representation. The framework provides interpretable outputs, where each detected noisy region is supported by explicit patch-pair evidence. The analysis reveals systematic annotation biases (e.g., higher errors in oblique vessels), which is insightful and adds value beyond performance improvement. The method demonstrates practical utility, as quality-weighted training improves boundary-sensitive metrics, indicating that detected noise is meaningful.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The overall performance improvement is modest, particularly in standard metrics such as Dice, which raises questions about practical impact. The evaluation is limited to a single dataset, making it unclear how well the method generalizes to other anatomies or imaging modalities. The approach relies on accurate centreline extraction, but the sensitivity of the method to errors in this step is not discussed. The similarity metric (MSE) used for patch retrieval is relatively simple and fails in cases involving rotation or intensity variation, as shown in the failure analysis. The method focuses on noise detection rather than correction, which limits its direct applicability in automated pipelines. Some assumptions, such as cross-sectional recurrence across subjects, may not hold equally well in more heterogeneous datasets.
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The proposed framework addresses the single-mask annotation issue without requiring additional annotations or a large computational burden. 2.The proposed method fully exploits the geometric characteristics of vessels and their self-consistency to detect segmentation noise. 3.The proposed method is well aligned with the problem setting, and the solution is also highly interpretable.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The current work seems to lack comparisons with existing methods for addressing single-mask annotation noise. However, since the reviewer is not an expert in this specific area, it is unclear whether similar work already exists.
reviewer_3_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and AC for the constructive feedback and thoughtful assessment of our work. We especially appreciate the recognition of the paper as a decoupled and interpretable framework for annotation noise auditing in the practical single-mask setting. We address the major concerns below. ## Comparative analysis We agree that comparisons with existing noisy-label methods provide useful context. However, our framework addresses a fundamentally different objective from existing single-mask noisy-label learning methods. Existing methods are primarily training-coupled robust learning frameworks whose objective is to improve segmentation robustness on a presumed “clean” evaluation set. Potential annotation noise is inferred indirectly from optimization dynamics (e.g., sample loss, prediction disagreement, feature divergence, pseudo-label refinement). As a result, it is often ambiguous whether a flagged region corresponds to a mislabeled annotation or simply a hard sample during optimization. In contrast, our framework is fully decoupled from network training and instead formulates annotation inconsistency as violations of anatomical cross-sectional self-consistency directly from the image-mask pair itself. The framework therefore evaluates the consistency of the annotation itself rather than model behavior during optimization. This difference also changes how the output is consumed. Existing methods mainly identify potential noisy labels for exclusion/replacement within the training loop, whereas our framework provides explicit evidence for human QA: a suspicious patch together with multiple image-near-identical patches exhibiting consistent masks. Accordingly, our framework provides two key relative advantages in the practical single-mask setting: (i) interpretability/auditability: every flagged region is directly associated with explicit image-near-identical patch evidence that can be inspected by a human QA reviewer; (ii) annotation-centric quality control: the framework directly evaluates consistency of the annotation itself, enabling dataset quality auditing rather than only improving downstream training robustness. Our goal is therefore not primarily to develop another training-time denoising strategy, but to identify a criterion that correct annotations themselves should satisfy. We will clarify this distinction and add comparative discussion with existing SMND methods in the revised manuscript. Per MICCAI rebuttal policy, we cannot include new experimental comparisons during rebuttal. ## MSE vs. SSIM and centerline sensitivity SSIM is difficult to scale to our setting (~10^6 patches and ~10^12 pairwise comparisons). MSE was chosen primarily for computational feasibility and compatibility with scalable vector retrieval. Its limitations (e.g., rotation/window-level sensitivity) are already explicitly analyzed in the failure cases (Fig. 6). Similarly, centerline/Bishop-frame errors mainly reduce retrieval recall rather than precision. Our design prioritizes precision (ensuring detected noise is truly suspicious and auditable), while recall can potentially be improved by denser sampling over rotation/shift spaces at increased computational cost. We will further clarify this discussion in the revised manuscript. ## Reproducibility clarifications We will clarify the implementation details requested in the meta-review, including: K=100 (chosen as a trade-off between variance estimation stability and bin locality), clarification of the image/mask manifold illustration in Fig.1, and attribution/clarification of Eq.1 (“segmentations obtained repeatedly from the same image” in [15]). Minor typo/formatting issues will also be corrected in the revised manuscript. ## Statistical uncertainty reporting We will revise the presentation of the existing quantitative results to include statistical uncertainty measures (e.g., confidence intervals / mean±std) for clearer interpretation of the reported gains.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper presents an elegant and interpretable “decoupled” framework for detecting annotation noise in medical imaging when only a single rater’s mask is available. By leveraging the anatomical recurrence of cross-sectional vascular patches to identify inconsistencies, the work addresses a practical challenge with an approach that requires no training overhead. While reviewers generally lean toward acceptance, the primary concerns center on a lack of comparative rigor, specifically the absence of established baselines for noisy label detection. Furthermore, the submission requires additional technical clarity regarding hyperparameter selection and the sensitivity of the method to preprocessing steps like centerline extraction. Rebuttal Instructions: The authors must provide a comparative analysis against at least one established baseline for noisy label detection in a single-mask setting to demonstrate a clear relative advantage. To ensure reproducibility, the authors are required to provide missing hyperparameter values (specifically “K”), clarify discrepancies in Figure 1, and address the citation for the multi-rater consistency equation. Additionally, the rebuttal should justify the choice of MSE over structural metrics like SSIM for patch similarity and include a discussion on the framework’s sensitivity to errors in the centerline extraction process. Finally, authors should provide statistical uncertainty measures, such as confidence intervals, to confirm that the reported performance gains are meaningful. | Decoupled Single-Mask Annotation Noise Detection presents a highly practical, training-free framework that effectively addresses single-rater label inconsistencies by exploiting the geometric and cross-sectional recurrence of tubular vascular structures. The authors successfully addressed initial concerns regarding comparative baseline rigor and hyperparameter sensitivity by clarifying that the framework acts as a decoupled, interpretable auditing tool for human quality assurance rather than a standard training-coupled optimization pipeline. A unanimous post-rebuttal consensus to accept (Scores: 3 $\rightarrow$ 4, 5, 5) and concrete commitments to incorporate critical hyperparameter definitions ($K=100$) and statistical uncertainty measures, this work offers a valuable and reproducible contribution to dataset curation in medical imaging. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper proposes a simple yet effective method for identifying noisy regions within CT vessel annotations by measuring the consistency between appearance changes and mask shape changes across adjacent frames. The approach is well-motivated, and the authors further demonstrate that explicitly accounting for the identified noisy annotations during training yields measurable improvements in downstream segmentation performance. The reviewers converged on a positive recommendation, and I concur with this consensus in supporting acceptance. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper presents a practical and interpretable framework for annotation noise detection in the single-mask setting. Reviewers highlighted the decoupled design and anatomical motivation as strengths, while concerns focused on comparisons and reproducibility details. The rebuttal addressed most of these points. Based on the reviewer feedback and rebuttal, the paper is above the acceptance threshold.

title: DEER: A Foundation Model with Dual-Branch CT-Enhanced Embeddings for Thoracoabdominal Radiographs
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The idea of leveraging CT localizers as a previously overlooked data source is novel and clinically well-motivated. Localizers are routinely acquired during CT scanning but rarely utilized for model training. Pairing them with diagnostically rich CT reports to enhance DR representations is a creative use of existing clinical data. 2.The scope of evaluation is broad, covering 10 downstream tasks across multiple anatomical regions (chest, abdomen, pelvis, spine) and diverse pathologies (pulmonary diseases, congenital heart diseases, COVID-19, fractures, developmental dysplasia, spondylolisthesis). The paper addresses the underexplored area of abdominal DR interpretation, which has practical clinical value. Most existing DR foundation models focus exclusively on chest X-rays. 4.The paper is generally well-written and the figures (especially Fig. 1) effectively communicate the overall framework and data composition.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The dual-branch design is essentially standard CLIP contrastive learning with two separate CLS tokens and projection heads sharing a ViT backbone. The contribution is primarily data-driven (scale and data source) rather than method-driven. 2.The ablation in Fig. 3e only compares “with vs. without localizer,” but adding localizers also adds 1 million extra training samples. 3.Since DR and CT localizer images are not paired (they come from different patients and examinations), the transfer of CT diagnostic knowledge to DR representations relies entirely on implicit sharing through the backbone weights. However, no analysis is provided to verify that this transfer actually occurs. The authors could provide: (a) probing experiments testing whether DR-branch features can predict CT-report entities, (b) attention map comparisons across branches, or (c) feature similarity analysis between the two branches. Without such evidence, the “CT-enhanced” claim remains unsubstantiated. 4.All 10 tasks are classification tasks. For a foundation model built on a CLIP framework, the absence of zero-shot classification and linear probing experiments is a significant gap. These are the standard protocols for evaluating the quality of pretrained representations and would more directly reflect the benefit of pretraining than fine-tuning, which can mask representation quality differences.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The manuscript leverages CT localizers as a bridge to incorporate the richer information contained in 3D CT reports into the training process, thereby facilitating the understanding of 2D digital radiography images. The resulting dataset constructed under this paradigm is valuable in both modality diversity and scale. 2.A shared encoder is used for DR and CT localizer images, coupled with separate projectors to refine their respective representations, constitutes a reasonable and meaningful dual-branch design. 3.The downstream experiments and evaluation protocols are comprehensive. 4.The manuscript is well-written and generally easy to follow.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The motivation of the manuscript appears to stem from two aspects: (1) the underexplored potential of CT localizers, and (2) the neglect of abdominal DR. In addition, the authors state in the abstract that “Developing an effective DR foundation model with strong disease discrimination through self-supervised learning remains a significant challenge.” While these claims are reasonable, they would benefit from a more detailed discussion and stronger grounding in related work. In particular, it would be helpful to specify which existing models have adopted what types of pretraining strategies, as well as the modality and scale of the datasets used, so that these high-level assertions can be better contextualized and more convincingly supported. 2.The experimental implementation details require more thorough description. For instance, it is unclear whether all models are evaluated under a unified experimental setting or with their individually optimized configurations (e.g., input image resolution), and which datasets lack predefined train–test splits and therefore require cross-validation. 3.The statistical significance analysis presented in this work requires further clarification. For example, how the comparison pairs for the t-test are defined and selected. 4.It can be observed that some downstream tasks exhibit relatively large standard deviations (e.g., COVIDGR and PelviXNet), which in turn lead to higher p-values in the t-test. The underlying reasons for this phenomenon should be further analyzed and explained. 5.Section 3.5 can be regarded as an ablation study evaluating the effect of incorporating LOC into the pretraining process. However, the experimental setup requires more detailed description. In particular, a more rigorous design would control for the scale of pretraining data to ensure that the observed performance gains arise from the additional modality rather than simply from increased data scale. In addition, as I understand that the y-axis in Fig. 3(e) represents percentages, which should be explicitly labeled or clarified to avoid potential confusion.
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The problem setting is important and clinically meaningful. The paper goes beyond chest-only radiograph foundation models and expands the scope to thoracoabdominal radiographs, with additional transfer evaluation on pelvic and spinal tasks. 2.The use of CT localizers as a bridge is an interesting idea. Leveraging CT localizers and CT reports to enhance DR representations is a novel and intuitively motivated design choice. 3.The scale of pretraining and the breadth of evaluation are strong. The model is pretrained on 2.1 million image-report pairs and evaluated across 10 downstream tasks covering chest, abdomen, pelvis, and lumbar spine. 4.The empirical results are strong. DEER shows competitive or superior performance across multiple datasets, and the paper presents consistent gains from image-report pretraining and additional LOC incorporation.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The source of the performance gain is not sufficiently disentangled. Although the paper emphasizes the architectural advantages of DEER, the proposed method also benefits from substantially larger-scale data and strong pretrained initialization, making it unclear how much of the improvement is truly attributable to the CT-enhanced dual-branch design itself. As a result, the current results do not fully isolate the methodological contribution of the proposed framework. 2.The paper does not fully establish whether LOC and DR are sufficiently distinct to justify separate branch-specific modeling. Since both are fundamentally 2D projection-based radiographic images, it remains unclear whether the observed gains from incorporating LOC reflect true modality complementarity or are instead driven by confounding factors such as increased data scale, richer CT-report supervision, or broader anatomical coverage. 3.A further concern is the potential misalignment between CT localizers and CT reports. Because CT localizers are typically acquired before the actual CT scan for scan planning and field-of-view determination, the final CT coverage may differ from that of the localizer. Consequently, some findings described in the CT report may correspond to regions that are only partially covered, or not visible at all, in the localizer image, which could weaken the assumption that localizers provide well-aligned supervision for report-guided representation learning.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We sincerely thank the reviewers for their valuable suggestions and for recognizing the novelty of using LOC and the clinical significance toward thoracoabdominal DR. The final version will be revised accordingly and will include the following information. Q(R1): Contribution is data-driven rather than method-driven. A: LOC are visually similar to DR while naturally paired with CT reports, yet they have been largely overlooked in prior research. Our novelty and methodological contribution are identifying LOC as an effective bridge for enhancing DR learning, which may provide useful insights for future foundation model development. Q(R1, R2, R3): In Fig. 3e, is the improvement brought by LOC due to additional 1M data samples, broader anatomical coverage, or the modality itself? A: During this work, we conduct exploratory experiments. We did not observe consistent improvements in DR tasks when adding modalities other than LOC. Specifically, we sampled 1M non-DR image-text pairs from MedTrinity-25M, including modalities such as CT and MR across anatomical regions like chest and abdomen. When adding these additional 1M samples to the DR training data, performance decreases (CHD-CXR -0.5%, PelviXNet -0.9%, compared to DEER). On BUU-LSPINE, it decreases -12.4% from DEER, even substantially worse than training without additional data. In contrast, using LOC and CT reports led to improvements, suggesting that the gain mainly comes from LOC and CT reports rather than simply from increasing the data scale. LOC can serve as an additional modality, further boosting DR foundation models beyond large-scale DR datasets. Q(R1): Zero-shot and linear-probing. A: We did not include zero-shot evaluation because most of the compared methods are not directly applicable in a zero-shot setting. Since baseline models are not pretrained on abdominal data, we focus on the fine-tuning setting to ensure a fair comparison under MICCAI’s page limit. In fact, as a CLIP framework, DEER has advantages under linear-probing (CHD-CXR +1.4%, PelviXNet +0.6%, over the best baseline). Q(R3): Justify separate branch-specific modeling. A: Even though both DR and LOC are 2D projection images, LOC has a lower dose and poorer image quality compared to DR (Fig. 1), resulting in a domain gap. Before full evaluation, we conducted ablation studies on a subset of the data. The results show that directly mixing DR and LOC for joint training without a dual-branch design leads to degraded performance (CHD-CXR -0.5%, PelviXNet -1.2%). Q(R3): Pretrained initialization. A: Using pretrained initialization is a standard practice. RAD-DINO & MedGemma are both initialized from large-scale pretrained DINOv2 & Gemma. DEER still outperforms. Q(R3): LOC and CT reports may not align well. A: LOC are used for CT scan planning, and in most cases their coverage is broader than the final CT, thereby encompassing anatomy described in the CT report. Even providing only weak supervision, our novelty is introducing largely overlooked LOC into DR model training and boosting performance, as in “Q(R1, R2, R3)”. Q(R1): Further evidence for knowledge transfer from CT to DR. A: We appreciate this insightful suggestion. While DEER potentially enables predicting CT report entities, evaluating this would require a DR-CT paired dataset, which is very rare and beyond the scope of this work. Due to page limits, data source limits, and restrictions on supplementary material, we focus the main paper on primary results and key insights. In the future we will explore CT entity prediction (Sec 4), and detailed feature-level analyses. Q(R2): Implementation details. A: We use each model’s native pretraining resolution and apply unified settings for fine-tuning. The t-test is performed across runs of different models. For datasets without an official test split, we adopt 5-fold cross-validation and report the mean and std across folds (Sec 3.1). The relatively large std is due to inter-fold variability.

title: DentMamba: An Anatomy-Aware Global-Local Hybrid Network for Large-Scale Multi-class Dental Disease Detection
reviewer_1_strengths: ①Good balance between accuracy and efficiency: DentMamba achieves 84.6 AP on the clinical dataset and 74.6 AP on OralXrays-9 with only 17M parameters, significantly outperforming many Transformer-based methods and demonstrating a stronger accuracy-efficiency trade-off. ②Strong performance on small object detection: Thanks to the Anatomamba Block and DSAHL design, the model achieves 52.1% on small lesion detection, outperforming existing methods by 5.9 percentage points, validating the effectiveness of anatomical priors in detecting tiny lesions.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: ①The paper adopts a Mamba architecture, but the experimental section does not include comparisons with any other Mamba-based detection models. This makes it difficult to know whether the performance gains come from the Mamba architecture itself or from the anatomy-aware modules and loss function design. ②The framework relies on a first-stage tooth localization step to crop ROIs, but does not discuss how localization errors propagate to the second-stage detector. If the localization stage misses or misaligns a tooth, the subsequent detection will simply fail. The paper lacks a quantitative analysis of how sensitive the overall framework is to this coupling.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: Overall, I think the strengths of the paper are mainly in its task relevance and empirical performance. The problem is clinically meaningful, the method is built in a task-aware way, and the reported results are enough to make the paper competitive. 1) The task is clinically meaningful: dental disease detection on panoramic X-rays is both useful and realistic, naturally involving small lesions, strong class imbalance, large scale variation, and complex background. 2) The use of anatomical prior is interesting. The AnatoMamba module uses a 5×3 anisotropic convolution to better match the vertical structure of teeth and roots, which is a reasonable design choice for dental images. 3) The paper has a clear focus on small-lesion detection. The DSAHL loss combines NWD and GIoU in a scale-adaptive way, which is relevant because small lesion detection is one of the hardest parts of this task. 4) The reported results are strong. The paper reports 84.6 AP / 52.1 APS on the private clinical dataset and 74.6 AP / 24.5 APS on OralXrays-9.On the public benchmark, these numbers are competitive with recent methods, especially on APS. 5) The model is relatively efficient, with only 17M parameters, while several strong baselines such as Co-DINO and MOQAM are much larger.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: My main concerns are about fairness and transparency. title: Detecting Clinical Hallucinations in LVLMs via Counterfactual Visual Grounding Uncertainty
reviewer_1_strengths: **Clear, intuitive idea. ** Grounding a contralateral/mutually-exclusive counterpart as a consistency check is a simple and compelling framing. **Model-agnostic by construction. ** The verifier is decoupled from the audited LVLM, so the method is applicable to closed-source models. **Interpretability. ** Returns bounding-box evidence alongside a decision, which is clinically useful. **Strong MRI results. ** On MRI, the method dominates baselines on both HDR and precision across all four LVLMs. **Ablation supports the CF branch. ** MCS AUC drops from 0.88 to 0.36 without CF; IoU reweighting gives an additional small gain (AUC 0.86 → 0.88 for MCS). **Efficiency. ** A 2B verifier is competitive against a 13B FaithScore pipeline.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: **Prior Art could be disciussed more. ** [2503.20504] UniVRSE: Unified Vision-conditioned Response Semantic Entropy for Hallucination Detection in Medical Vision-Language Models is cited, but at a bit strange point, and not discussed, even though this method could also be described as similarly counterfactual (distorting image and evaluating prediction changes). **Construct validity: test set and method share the same inductive bias. ** Test hallucinations are “induced via mutually exclusive counterfactual labels” — the same substitution principle the CF branch is designed to detect. Established benchmarks (POPE, Med-HallMark, MedHEval) construct hallucinations via mechanisms independent of any specific detector. The present construction likely inflates results, particularly on MRI where laterality is salient, and does not test detection of other hallucination categories (fabrication, omission, severity, measurement, confabulated priors). **MCS-only AUC of 0.3572 is below-random and diagnostic. ** Below-random AUC typically signals score-direction inversion or anti-correlation between score and label, not a “weak” detector. Under sign flip, AUC = 0.6428 (a reasonable standalone signal). The authors should report the sign-flipped AUC and per-category breakdowns; as presented, the ablation may be overstated. **Incomplete metrics. ** Only HDR (recall) and precision are reported in Tab. 1.POPE, MedHallBench, etc. all report F1, which makes it easier to compare approaches along a single metric. **Writing. ** Abstract: “Code and datasets will be accessed. “ Section 3.2 contains a fragment: “our visual-aware ver and the counterfactual-driven Therefore…”. Fig. 4 sub-panel labels (a)/(b) appear inconsistent with the caption and Sec. 3.4 text.

reviewer_3_strengths: This paper proposes a novel method for identifying clinical hallucinations via counterfactual entity perturbation, which has the potential to inspire further research in this area and to support future translation into clinical practice.The presented methodology uses the alignment of responses with visual regions, which improves the transferability to the clinical setting by enhancing interpretability. In addition, this novel methodological research approach opens the door for new ways of tackling misdiagnosis and therefore more robust and reliable AI in clinical practice, as results have been shown to be above state-of-the-art methodologies. The main highlight is the plug-and-play and vision-traceable methodology that also enables uncertainty estimation by means of counterfactual entity perturbation, which is a very interesting leveraging of a technique for probing and improving model behavior that has proven relevant in sensitive domains like clinical AI/ML.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Counterfactual entity perturbation is a useful approach for detecting hallucinations, but it also comes with several limitations. One of the main concerns is the realism of the generated perturbations, which may not always correspond to clinically plausible variations, especially in complex imaging scenarios where maintaining anatomical consistency is challenging. As a result, some counterfactual examples may fall outside the data distribution, making the model’s responses difficult to interpret. In addition, it is not clear whether the method establishes true causal relationships, as it can overlook dependencies between features and thus simplify underlying clinical factors. Its effectiveness can also depend heavily on how the perturbations are designed, which requires careful consideration and domain expertise. Furthermore, generating and evaluating counterfactuals can be computationally intensive, and there is a risk of interpreting changes in model predictions as clinically meaningful when they may instead reflect artifacts of the model. Including a dedicated discussion of these limitations would help provide a more balanced view of the approach and encourage further work in this area.

author_feedback: We sincerely thank reviewers for constructive feedback: R1 finds the core idea “interesting, clear and intuitive”, and praises its “clinical interpretability” and “efficiency (2B vs. 13B)”; R2 considers it a “well-motivated reasonable approach” and will raise the score if more details are clarified; R3 rates Strong Accept (6/6): “…a plug-and-play and vision-traceable method…can have an impact by opening the door to future research in this area while exhibiting potential for its transferability to the clinic.” Responses below. 1.UniVRSE could be discussed more (R1Q1) 1) Thanks for highlighting the UniVRSE arXiv preprint. Our citation [Ref. 9] specifically supports taxonomy in Sec. 1 and Fig. 1, which was informed by its peer-reviewed MICCAI 2025 version available at our submission time. So, the citation is correct. 2) In the revised version, we will add a discussion of UniVRSE. It introduces an image-distortion-based semantic uncertainty algorithm (aligns with Fig. 1(b)) that is effective for Chest X-ray report generation and VQA. In contrast, we provide direct visual evidence for interpretability (Fig. 1(c)). 2.Whether the test set shares the same inductive bias as the detector (R1Q2) 1) Test set comes from a static perturbation across four model families (Sec. 3.1), while the detector applies counterfactual reasoning for dynamic consistency verification, independent of our method. Thus, no shared inductive bias exists. 2) Benchmarks like POPE (noted by R1) evaluate LVLM hallucinations while we evaluate detection methods. Given this fundamental difference, their direct relevance to our work is limited. 3.Other hallucination types (R1Q2) To maintain focus, this work concentrates on “text-image consistency” (see Abs). R1 noted other categories (e.g., severity, omission), but they varied fundamentally in detection logic (e.g. omitting regular and normal findings is clinically routine rather than hallucinatory), warranting dedicated future study. 4.Missing F1 and issue about MCS-only AUC (R1Q3, R1Q4) 1) F1: We can directly calculate F1 from Recall and Precision in Tab. 1.2) AUC: We thank the reviewer for the score-direction insight. MCS-only (w/o CF), sign-flipped AUC=0.6428, is a reasonable signal; with CF, AUC rises to 0.8811 (+0.2383), confirming CF’s necessity (Fig. 3(b)). 5.Details on verifier training and domain-gap robustness (R2Q1) 1) Training: LoRA fine-tuning on Qwen3-VL-2B for visual grounding, AdamW (lr=1e-4, wd=1e-4), CosineLR (3% warmup), bs=16 with 8-step grad accumulation, 5 epochs, 2×A100, 33,266 samples from IMIS-Bench. 2) Domain-gap: Our core contribution is designing a plug-and-play method applicable to arbitrary LVLMs (Sec. 2.1), where addressing the domain gap is beyond our main focus. However, we still mitigate it by training the verifier on IMIS-Bench (Sec. 3.1), a collection of 80 datasets. This broad coverage largely reduces the domain gap. 6.Concerns about counterfactual details and Eq.4 (R2Q2) Eq. 4 retrieves a counterfactual perturbation of e (from Eq. 1-2) from knowledge base K. The non-overlap guarantee is built into K’s construction: we apply a strict spatial exclusion rule that discards any entity whose bounding box could overlap with others on identical MRI/CT slices, which was independently verified by radiologist to ensure clinical validity. 7.Causality and cost (R3) 1) Causality and future directions: Thanks for highlighting these important considerations regarding realism and causal validity. We fully agree that addressing confounding effects and modeling complex clinical dependencies are critical. Encouragingly, some directions align with the future work outlined in our Conclusion, specifically the extension to complex spatial relationships and temporal sequences. 2) Cost: Our 2B verifier is more efficient than Faithscore (13B)(Tab. 1), so the consumption of a CF branch is acceptable. 8.Writing (R1Q5) We thank the reviewer. All will be corrected in the revised version.

title: Deterministic Hallucination Detection in Medical VQA via Confidence-Evidence Bayesian Gain
reviewer_1_strengths: The paper’s major strengths are its computational efficiency (only 3 forward passes vs. 20+ generations for baselines).
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The formula σ⋅(1+E) of CEBaG is a heuristic design and lacks strict probabilistic or information-theoretic basis. Section 2.2 claims that this is “posterior uncertainty weighted by visual information gain”, but the multiplication combination method has no theoretical derivation support. Why not use addition or a more complex function form? The ablation experiments show (Table 3), the simple σ alone can achieve 67.0% AUC, while the complete CEBaG only improves to 67.9%, indicating that the gain mainly comes from the variance term, and the multiplicative effect of the evidence term is negligible. 2.The fatal limitation of “white box” requirements. On page 8 of the paper, it is acknowledged that “the limitation lies in its reliance on access to model log-probabilities, restricting usage to white-box models”. This is a significant drawback in the actual clinical environment. Many commercial medical AI systems (such as Google’s Med-PaLM M series) only provide API access and do not expose token probabilities. 3.The experimental setups actually only involved 3 small-scale datasets (VQA-RAD had only 451 samples, and PathVQA had 1000 samples). This sample size is insufficient for statistical significance testing (the paper did not report confidence intervals or significance tests), and the paper lacks cross-language and cross-modal (such as dermatology, endoscopy) validations. 4.The paper did not conduct a thorough analysis of the failure scenarios of CEBaG. From Table 1, on the SLAKE dataset of MedGemma-1.5, CEBaG (with an AUC of 57.5%) was even lower than the random level (assuming 50% as the baseline), almost on par with SE (57.7%). The authors did not explain why the method completely failed under this specific setting, which is crucial for understanding the boundaries of the method. 5.The two answers in Fig. 1 show a significant difference in quality. The grounded example involves specific anatomical localization (“right temporal lobe”). The hallucinated example is merely a simple existence judgment (“spleen is present”). This suggests that the method may be effective only for detailed descriptive answers, but has insufficient ability to distinguish between short yes/no answers (which are very common in clinical VQA). However, the paper does not discuss the impact of answer length or type on the performance. 6.The caption of Fig. 1 (b) is Incomplete and only the upper part is revealed. For the answer in Fig. 1 (b), after “yes” there is a comma, but in the horizontal axis, a period is shown. 7.Figure 1(b) shows a “textbook-like” grounded answer (G = 38.5) and a “textbook-like” hallucination (G = 1.6). This extreme case comparison is misleading. In fact, according to the ablation experiments in Table 3, the AUC of “E only” is only 59.0%, which is much lower than 67.0% of “σ only”, indicating that the G values of a large number of samples are in a blurry area (intermediate values), rather than this idealized polarization. In the lower right corner of Fig. 1, there is an “asterisk” indicating that it typically represents “AI-generated” in academic publication standards. The use of AI-generated charts in medical AI papers is ironic: a paper claiming to be able to detect AI hallucinations may have its own charts that are themselves the result of AI hallucinations.
reviewer_1_rating: (1) Strong Reject — must be rejected due to major flaws
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The computation of evidence gain by evaluating the difference between the posterior and prior using Bayes’ rule is an interesting approach. Simplifying the evidence gain as the mutual information between the response and the image is both intuitive and reasonable. 2.The entire process of obtaining the CEBaG score requires only three forward passes, without the need for additional model training or external knowledge as guidance, making it extremely efficient for hallucination detection. 3.The comprehensive experiments conducted across four base models, three benchmarks, and four comparison methods provide strong and convincing validation of the proposed CEBaG’s performance.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.Since CEBaG detects hallucinations from two perspectives: response uncertainty and visual evidence. A more detailed discussion, along with case studies, is needed to explore the contributions and interplay of these two components. For instance, under what circumstances does uncertainty in the response play a critical role, and in which cases does visual evidence become dominant? 2.CEBaG_λλ in Section 3.3 is not sufficiently explained in the methodology section. Adding a scalar weight to the method results in significant performance gains, which raises the question of whether more adaptive designs could further improve performance, rather than adhering to a strictly hyperparameter-free approach. 3.Since CEBaG requires three forward passes, it is unclear whether sampling parameters, such as the sampling policy (e.g., Top-k/p) or temperature, could influence the final results in hallucination detection. Evaluating the sensitivity of the method to these parameters would enhance the study’s robustness. 4.According to the ablation study in Table 3, response uncertainty appears to have a much larger impact on performance than per-token evidence gains. The authors should provide a more detailed discussion on these findings and elaborate on the implications of this observation. Minor comments: The image quality of Fig. 1 needs improvement. The bottom-right portion of Fig. 1 is incomplete and should be revised to display all content clearly.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The method requires no training. The method is less computationally demanding than existing ones.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.I have two concerns regarding Eqn. (1). 1a) “This formulation can be interpreted as posterior uncertainty weighted by visual information gain.” How does the formulation handle cases with low σ but high positive G? 1b) Following the question above, the relative contribution between σ and E is indeed an important factor (hyper-parameter) to consider. Otherwise, cases with low σ but high positive G would be incorrectly identified as hallucinations. By the way, what is the magnitude comparison between these two variables? 2.Table 1: Although the proposed method can only be applied to open-source models, it is still important and necessary to compare against cutting-edge proprietary models. 3.”Furthermore, our method maintained stable detection performance across GREEN thresholds between 0.4 and 0.8, …” This claim is not supported by any evidence. 4.Table 2: There are no direct efficiency metrics, e.g., FLOPS, latency, or memory use, reported. 5.Table 3: What hyper-parameter(s) are swept over in CEBaGλ? 6.In Introduction: “The resulting score, σ · (1 + |G|/L), is parameter-free, …” The formulation is introduced later. It is confusing to place it here without any explanation. Similarly, G is used before it is introduced in Section 2.1. 7.The metrics AUC and AUG are not explained. 8.Fig. 1(b): How is the per-token evidence gain, for each token, computed?
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and AC, and address all the points below. Meta/R1.1/R3.1: The formulation is derived to be minimal, principled, and hyperparameter-free. (i) σ is the standard token-level predictive variance widely used in LM uncertainty estimation. (ii) Sec. 2.1 derives G from Bayes’ rule as the pointwise mutual information between response r and image x_v conditional on x_q, and E=|G|/L is its length-normalized magnitude. Both are independently grounded. (iii) The multiplicative combination is a deliberate design satisfying three requirements: f(0,E)=0 (a confident answer with high visual sensitivity is non-hallucinated, per R3 Q1a), monotonicity in both arguments, and freedom from per-dataset normalization. σ (1+E) is the simplest function meeting all three. Additive σ+α E (R1.1) violates f(0,E)=0, requires tuning α, and flags confident image-grounded answers as hallucinations. The parameter-free score is therefore principled, not arbitrary. Meta/R1.1/R2.4: Per Table 3, CEBaG beats σ-only in 10/16 settings, with gains up to +4.7 in the long-answer dominated datasets. The E term is specifically helpful in longer answers with a small number of image-sensitive tokens (e.g. cases with linguistically sound but hallucinated observations, which would otherwise hide the uncertainty of important tokens behind confident grammatical tokens). The +0.9 average understates E’s contribution by dilution with the majority short-answer questions (VQA-RAD closed, SLAKE). R1.4: This is a model-dataset property, not a CEBaG-specific failure: AvgProb=57.4, SE=57.7, VASE=59.5, RadFlag=57.2, CEBaG=57.5 - all five methods within 2.5 AUC. MedGemma-1.5 produces uniformly confident outputs on SLAKE, compressing the σ signal all uncertainty methods rely on. CEBaG remains best in 13/16 settings overall. R1.5/1.6/1.7: Fig. 1, though based on real measurements (MedGemma/VQA-RAD idx=317, 405), is purely a schematic to help readers understand the concept of evidence gain. The empirical claims rest entirely on Tables 1-3 over 16 settings, not on this figure. The figure was stylized with assistance from a generative AI tool. We will replace it with a non-stylized version, fix the caption, and move it to Sec. 1 (also per R3). R1.2/R3.2: We use “white-box” deliberately instead of “open-source”, meaning access to the log-probabilities. (1) Many frontier labs’ completions APIs (incl. OpenAI) support logprobs, so CEBaG is applicable in principle to commercial models, albeit with several API calls instead of the 3-forward-pass. (2) For medical VQA specifically, local hosting is the dominant deployment pattern under HIPAA/GDPR. The discontinuation of Med-PaLM M by Google in favor of open models such as MedGemma and MedGemma-1.5 further affirms this. (3) This is not a limitation only for CEBaG. All compared methods, including the state-of-the-art VASE (MICCAI 2025), share the same limitation. R1.3: We strictly followed the VASE evaluation protocol for fair, direct comparison. The total N=2512 across three benchmarks matches prior MICCAI work on this task. This is an evaluation only work (no training), and therefore significance testing is well powered. The current datasets span different modalities such as general radiology (VQA-RAD) and pathology (PathVQA). R3.1a/b: The multiplication specifically accounts for cases with low sigma but high positive G, by using the evidence gain to amplify the token-level uncertainty. In our settings, sigma is typically ~0.45+/-0.19 and E is typically ~0.71+/-0.73. R2.2/R3.5: CEBaG_λ uses min-max-normalized E and sweeps a single scalar weight lambda in [-1.5,+1.5], selecting the λ that maximizes AUC per (model,dataset). λ is the only hyperparameter, reported as an upper bound, not the proposed method. R2.3/R3.4/R3.6-7: Scoring is teacher-forced/deterministic (Top-k/p N/A). CEBaG≈1.5x one generation vs. SE/VASE’s added 7B encoder. AUC/AUG and G will be defined explicitly in Sec. 3.
