However, significant concerns remain regarding the theoretical foundation of the proposed formulation, particularly the heuristic combination of uncertainty and evidence terms, as well as the limited empirical validation supporting the contribution of the evidence component. Authors need to carefully read the reviews and address the points, especially for R1. | The paper presents an efficient training-free method, but key concerns remain after rebuttal. R1 kept rejection, though R2/R3 are positive with the rebuttal. This is not an easy decision and the AI-assisted figure issue should be handled cautiously, but it further raises concerns about presentation reliability. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Reviewers have acknowledged the merits of the paper: relevance of problem, neat problem formulation, and efficient computation, while raised concerns on limited type of hallucinations that it can address (global MIRAGE and token prob std), the use of GenAI to generate figures/charts, and unstable performance (sometimes counterproductive) of E. In the camera-ready, the authors must 1.clearly narrow down the scope of the type of halluciantion it addresses and avoid selling it as a generic hallucination identification approach; 2.re-draw the figures and qualitative examples that reflect the authentic nature of the work as accurate as possible without the use of GenAI; 3.be more transparent about the parameter searching approach of the lambda and more clearly admit the stability limitations of their vanilla approach. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper proposes an efficient, training-free hallucination detection method for medical VQA. The hallucination problem is timely, and the method is practical because it avoids stochastic sampling and external models in the loop. The main concern comes from R1: the formulation is somewhat questionable, and the contribution of the evidence term is modest. Although this concern remains valid, the rebuttal provides a reasonable justification for the design, and CEBaG did outperform the variance-only baseline in most AUC settings. The formulation could be further investigated, and the paper provides a good opportunity for such discussion. The paper could also be strengthened by adding clinical validation on a subset, rather than relying solely on GREEN-generated labels. The method is only validated on open-source models, which I think is minor limitation. Overall, the method is efficient and sufficiently validated for acceptance.

title: Diagnose Like a Doctor: Misdiagnosis-Aware Structured Memory for Continual Learning of Medical Vision-Language Models
reviewer_1_strengths: 1:Clinically motivated formulation. The proposed Pitfall Graph explicitly models disease mimics and exclusion criteria, introducing “negative diagnostic knowledge” into the learning process. This is well aligned with real clinical reasoning, where errors often arise from confusion between visually similar conditions rather than missing knowledge. 2: Technically non-trivial integration. The framework combines graph-guided query generation, retrieval from a large-scale multimodal database, visual-semantic reranking, and dual-model distillation within a continual learning setup. This goes beyond standard replay or RAG pipelines and provides a coherent mechanism to shape decision boundaries during sequential updates. 3: Strong reported empirical performance. The method shows consistent improvements over recent continual VLM baselines across 11 datasets, with gains in ACC/AUC and less negative BWT, particularly under challenging random task order settings.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1: The paper’s mechanistic conclusion is not fully isolated by the experiments. The motivation for the method is that modeling mimics and exclusion criteria may improve fine-grained discrimination beyond conventional positive-only retrieval. This is an interesting idea, and the proposed Pitfall Graph is a meaningful way to encode such information. However, the experiments do not include a direct comparison to a standard RAG/retrieval-only variant using the same external database and training setup. The closest ablation (w/o HPG) removes the graph component but still keeps retrieval, reranking, and distillation, so it does not cleanly isolate how much benefit specifically comes from the misdiagnosis-aware structure. Therefore, while the overall method performs well, the paper does not yet provide sufficiently controlled evidence for the stronger conclusion that the gains are specifically driven by modeling mimics/exclusion criteria rather than by the broader retrieval-and-distillation framework. 2: Potential confounding from large external memory. The method relies on a large-scale external multimodal database (Open-PMC-18M). Competing baselines do not appear to have access to an equivalent memory source, making it difficult to disentangle whether improvements stem from the proposed formulation or simply from additional data and retrieval capacity. 3: Evaluation setting is weaker than the clinical claims suggest. The experiments are conducted under a task-incremental learning setting with known task boundaries, which is substantially easier than class-incremental or task-agnostic scenarios. Despite the “diagnose like a doctor” framing, evaluation remains limited to benchmark classification without clinical validation, reader studies, or deployment-oriented analysis. 4: Reproducibility is limited. The manuscript does not provide sufficient implementation details to reproduce the method reliably, and no code repository is provided at the time of submission.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: Highly Novel Formulation: The construction of the Hierarchical Pitfall Graph is an excellent, intuitive contribution. Standard retrieval models focus on reinforcing positive semantic matches, overlooking hard negatives. Explicitly encoding diagnostic logic to teach the model what a disease is not directly mirrors human clinical cognitive workflows. Extensive and Robust Evaluation: The experimental design is exceptionally thorough, testing the method across 11 datasets spanning 9 imaging modalities (including CT, MRI, Ultrasound, Histopathology, etc.). Strong Empirical Results: The proposed method achieves state-of-the-art accuracy, significantly outperforming recent baselines like GIFT, ZSCL, and CoOp in both modality-wise and random order setups. For example, in the challenging random order setting, it achieves 71.68% Accuracy and 88.79% AUC. Scalable Rehearsal Strategy: Bypassing traditional, limited-capacity static rehearsal buffers by dynamically querying a large-scale multimodal database (Open-PMC-18M) represents a strong step forward for large-scale medical CL.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Computational Overhead: The framework relies on continuously querying an 18-million sample database and performing Visual-Semantic Reranking during training. The paper lacks a detailed discussion on the computational complexity, training time, and memory overhead introduced by this dense retrieval step. Graph Construction Noise: The HPG relies on unstructured clinical evidence mined from PubMed. The paper does not thoroughly discuss the potential noise, hallucinations, or error-propagation risks involved in mining these exclusionary edges at scale. Reliance on Proprietary Models for Main Experiments: While the authors thoughtfully provide an ablation study using open-source models (like Qwen-3-32B and DeepSeek-V3) , the primary experimental backbone relies on the proprietary GPT-4 model. This can restrict immediate reproducibility.
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The paper offers an interesting perspective by framing database case retrieval around the way experienced clinicians make diagnoses, namely through careful exclusion of potential mimics. 2.The experimental evaluation includes comparisons against recent continual-learning baselines for medical VLMs.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.Method motivation and experimental fairness. I am not fully convinced by the use of an external medical knowledge database in the VLM-CL setting. Conceptually, this seems closer to a retrieval- or replay-based strategy, since it assumes that similar and known exemplars are available in the database. In a more clinically realistic continual-learning scenario, both models and human experts would need to learn unseen knowledge rather than rely on retrieval from a predefined database. This also raises a fairness concern in the experiments, since baselines such as LwF, iCaRL, and MoE-CL do not appear to have access to a comparable external knowledge source or replay mechanism, which may partly explain the performance gap. 2.Missing dataset-task information. In Section 3.1, a clearer definition of the task associated with each dataset would make the experimental protocol easier to understand. 3.Unclear terminology around knowledge replay. Some terms related to the retrieval mechanism are not clearly defined. In Dense Retrieval and Visual-Semantic Reranking, the phrase “dynamically retrieve historical exemplars” is not entirely clear. The paper would benefit from a more explicit distinction between this knowledge replay stream and standard rehearsal replay in continual learning. In particular, it should clarify that no old-task samples are explicitly stored and replayed, and that the method instead relies solely on retrieval from an external multimodal database. Similar ambiguity also appears in the use of “historical exemplars” in the Introduction and Fig. 2, and “historical concepts” in the Dual-Model Logit Distillation section.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and meta-reviewer for their constructive comments. We address the main concerns: HPG contribution/novelty, retrieval fairness, evaluation scope/task definition, overhead/noise, and reproducibility. 1) HPG contribution and novelty (R1/R3). We agree that isolating the source of improvement is important. The submitted Table 2 ablation provides relevant evidence: “w/o HPG” keeps the same external database, retrieval, visual-semantic reranking, and dual-model distillation, while removing only the HPG-guided mimic/exclusion structure. Its consistent degradation under both task orders indicates that HPG contributes beyond generic retrieval/distillation. A positive-only RAG baseline is useful future work, but the submitted ablation already tests whether the misdiagnosis-aware structure adds value beyond the remaining pipeline. The novelty is not simply RAG/replay, but encoding negative diagnostic knowledge, i.e., mimics and exclusion criteria, into retrieval topology, so retrieved knowledge emphasizes discriminative boundaries rather than only positive disease definitions. 2) External memory, fairness, and replay terminology (R1/R3). We compare with representative CL and continual VLM baselines under the same task-incremental protocol. Our goal is retrieval-augmented CL, not memory-free CL. Open-PMC-18M is used as an offline non-parametric biomedical image-text memory, not as supervised storage of old target-task samples or target-dataset labels. No previous target-task samples are saved or replayed. Thus, our “knowledge replay stream” is not standard rehearsal replay: “historical exemplars” are image-text pairs retrieved from Open-PMC-18M, and “historical concepts” are teacher responses on these retrieved exemplars for distillation. These samples serve as semantic/visual anchors, not additional labeled training data. Since external retrieval is part of our framework, the key fairness evidence is the retrieval-preserving HPG ablation: with the same memory and pipeline, removing the graph still weakens performance, indicating gains beyond external data. We clarify this terminology here and will use it consistently if accepted. 3) Evaluation scope, task definition, and clinical claims (R1/R3). The paper follows the task-incremental formulation in Sec. 2.1, where tasks arrive sequentially with task-specific label spaces. In Sec. 3.1, the task unit is the dataset rather than an individual class: each of the 11 datasets defines one sequential diagnostic classification task with its own label space, covering multiple modalities and organs. We agree that class-incremental/task-agnostic CL is more challenging, and benchmark classification does not establish clinical deployment readiness. “Diagnose like a doctor” is a design motivation: using mimics and exclusion criteria to reduce fine-grained confusion. We do not claim clinical validation, reader-study performance, or deployment readiness. 4) Overhead and graph noise (R2). Retrieval does not require repeatedly training on all 18M samples. The database is indexed offline; dense retrieval selects a small candidate set, and VSR reranks only these retrieved candidates. Thus, the added cost mainly comes from top-k retrieval/reranking, not full-database optimization. For graph noise, HPG combines UMLS/MeSH with PubMed evidence. Noisy edges affect retrieval prompts rather than labels, and VSR further reduces their impact by filtering visually inconsistent candidates. The w/o HPG ablation and Fig. 5 show that HPG remains useful despite possible noise. 5) Reproducibility and proprietary models (R1/R2). We acknowledge that no code repository was provided at submission. Still, Sec. 3.1 reports the backbone, LLM, hardware, hyperparameters, iterations, and dataset/task sources. Table 2 includes open-source LLM/backbone variants, mitigating concerns about dependence on GPT-4.If accepted, we will release code and settings.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): For the rebuttal, the authors should analyze the contribution of the proposed misdiagnosis-aware structure, clarify the novelty, and provide enough details for reproducibility and fairness of experiments. | The paper addresses continual learning for medical VLMs by introducing a misdiagnosis-aware memory structure that models disease mimics and exclusion criteria. Although concerns remain about reliance on external retrieval memory and task-incremental evaluation, the rebuttal clarified that the HPG ablation preserves the same retrieval pipeline while removing only the misdiagnosis-aware structure, supporting its added value. Overall, the work is technically relevant and sufficiently justified for acceptance. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper addresses an important continual medical VLM learning problem and proposes a clinically meaningful misdiagnosis-aware structured memory via mimics and exclusion criteria. Although concerns remain about external retrieval memory and the task-incremental setting, the rebuttal reasonably clarifies that the HPG ablation preserves the same memory/retrieval pipeline and isolates the contribution of the misdiagnosis-aware structure. Overall, the empirical breadth and post-rebuttal reviewer balance support acceptance. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): After rebuttal, the overall reviewer opinions are mixed but lean positive. Reviewer #1 supports acceptance after the authors clarified that the “w/o HPG” ablation keeps the same external database, retrieval, reranking, and distillation components while removing only the HPG structure, partially isolating the contribution of the proposed misdiagnosis-aware graph. Reviewer #2 strongly supports acceptance, emphasizing the novelty of modeling mimics and exclusion criteria and the broad evaluation across 11 medical datasets. Reviewer #3 remains negative, mainly due to concerns about the necessity and fairness of external memory/retrieval and the realism of the task-incremental setting with task identity available at inference. Overall, the paper remains borderline, but the rebuttal sufficiently addresses the central contribution concern for a majority of reviewers. I therefore recommend acceptance, with the expectation that the final version clearly discusses the limitations regarding external-memory fairness, task-incremental evaluation, computational cost, and reproducibility/code release.

title: Diagnosing 3D Volumes from Camera Video: A Semantic-Robust Framework Without Direct DICOM Access
reviewer_1_strengths: I uses a standard imaging data set and uses an interesting and well though through mix of different encoders, transformers, and task-aware algorithmic experts. It is very well written and employs a good methodology and experimental validation.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Ultrasound 2D imaging moving along an (for example) arterial structure with the images continuously displayed could be a great application with an HDMI output directly fed into a recorder. The limitation to the CT dataset and a short discussion of other areas of application are the main limitations.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The paper is in general well written, and solves a problem: how to make camera captured data usable in a clinical context without direct dicom access, when this data is 3D. The experimental set-up is appropriate and covers a wide range of scenarios. The results suggest that their proposed approach can solve the problem
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The main issue with this paper is that the comparison to the baselines is unfair. The video stream is fed to the competing methods (CT-Net, CT-Clip) as they are (trained on volumes), while their proposed method is fine-tuned to captured videos. Obviously the other methods are going to fail catastrophically; what would be interesting is to fine-tune the competing methods to take the videos as input (without any of the new ideas proposed in this paper) and then see what is the benefit of the proposed method. Without this, it is impossible to understand if the proposed method works for all the clever architectural choices in the preprocessor, or simply because it is fine-tuned to the data as it will be acquired. For instance, how would the proposed method perform if the actual dicoms were fed to it? most likely would also fail catastrophically! The results are lacking depth: only average values are provided. some estimate of the dispersion is required, eg. variance, or even better confidence intervals. This would connect with some kind of statistical test on the significance of the numbers provided.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The core research question is original and practically motivated. Removing the dependency on DICOM access and PACS infrastructure could genuinely broaden AI deployment in resource-limited clinical settings. The zero-shot Pleural Effusion result, where video AUC matches clean DICOM at 0.88 without any video fine-tuning, is the paper’s most compelling finding and provides real scientific insight about how low-frequency pathologies are encoded in semantic features. The ablation study shows that inter-slice modeling via the Transformer block is the most critical architectural component.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.ScreenCAD’s performances largely hinges on MedDINOv3.This is shown by the performance of ABMIL and Task Token compared to baselines. While ABMIL, replacing MedDINOv3 embeddings by Attention-Based MIL [9], perform worst than baselines, Task Token’s are better than baselines. The current evidence suggests ScreenCAD works because MedDINOv3 works. 2.Baseline comparison is structurally unfair. CT-Net and CT-CLIP are 3D DICOM architectures with no video-handling capability whatsoever. Their zero-shot video collapse is expected and uninformative. On clean DICOM and fine-tuned video settings, these baselines are competitive with or superior to ScreenCAD in several metrics, which the paper underemphasizes. A fair comparison requires either equipping baselines with the same SVL preprocessing and MIL aggregation, or including video-native models such as VideoMAE as proper competitors. 3.Evaluation is too narrow. While the video data collection setting is dataset-agnostic and the title claims “3D volumetric diagnosis” broadly, all results come from one dataset (CT-RATE) and two tasks. The baseline scores on CT-RATE are partially already reported in the original CT-RATE paper, limiting the independent experimental contribution. The title claims broad volumetric diagnosis but no MRI or PET modality is tested, and no additional CT pathologies are explored. 4.The setting is less realistic than presented, and the data collection agent is unevaluated. Camera capture of 2D radiographs is practical because a single photograph suffices. Recording a clinician scrolling through hundreds of CT slices is a fundamentally different and more operationally demanding scenario. The authors acknowledge the controlled setup (single camera, single monitor, single viewer, ±15° angle range) but do not test generalization beyond it. More importantly, all training and test videos are generated by an automated agent described as following a “human-like browsing pattern.” Since this agent defines the entire data distribution, its scrolling statistics should be characterized quantitatively and validated against real human browsing behavior. Currently, the model may be learning to exploit the agent’s specific scrolling rhythm rather than generalizing to real clinical use.
reviewer_3_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: Thanks for the valuable comments. We appreciate the recognition of our work and have addressed each of the reviewers’ concerns as follows. 1.Task Scope, Applications, and Generalization (R1, R4): We agree that ultrasound video is promising. HDMI capture removes degradation, while our work studies the complementary question of whether diagnosis remains reliable after severe ``analog-to-digital’’ camera degradation. Camera capture also avoids HDMI/PACS integration, which is useful in resource-limited settings. We will clarify this trade-off and discuss ultrasound, broader modalities, datasets, devices, viewers, and workflows as future validation. CT-RATE with Medical Material and Pleural Effusion is intended as a first reproducible testbed for this new task. 2.Baseline Protocol and Fairness (R2, R4): We will revise the manuscript to explicitly describe how video inputs are adapted for all baselines. All methods are evaluated after the same SVL preprocessing, so they receive the same localized medical viewport sequence. The remaining difference comes from each architecture’s intrinsic input constraints: CT-Net and CT-CLIP require fixed-size 3D tensors. For video inputs, we resize the SVL-extracted sequence to 420x420x402 for CT-Net. For CT-CLIP, since many videos contain more frames than its fixed depth, we first temporally sample frames to preserve coverage across the browsing trajectory, and then center-crop or pad the sampled volume to 480x480x240 following its original protocol. ScreenCAD’s variable-length MIL aggregation is not an extra preprocessing advantage, but a core architectural requirement for screen-recorded browsing videos, whose lengths vary due to scrolling speed, pauses, and reversals. We also fine-tuned CT-Net/CT-CLIP on captured videos; despite this, on Pleural Effusion Video FT they reach 0.71–0.73 AUC, while ScreenCAD reaches 0.90.3.MedDINOv3 Dependency and Architectural Contribution (R4): We agree that MedDINOv3 is an important component of ScreenCAD. Our point is that the backbone alone is insufficient. Table 1/2 compare ABMIL and Task Token under the same MedDINOv3 backbone, and Table 3 further ablates the aggregation components. For example, on Medical Material under Video ZS, replacing our Task-Token aggregator with standard ABMIL drops AUC from 0.72 to 0.58.This suggests that MedDINOv3 provides a strong clean-domain representation, while the proposed inter-slice and task-aware aggregation design provides additional robustness for low-quality screen-captured inputs. 4.Clean Performance, Metrics, and Statistical Analysis (R2, R4): We acknowledge that CT-Net/CT-CLIP are competitive on native DICOM inputs and may be slightly better on some secondary metrics in the Clean setting, which is expected because they are designed for native 3D DICOM CT volumes. Importantly, ScreenCAD remains competitive on Clean DICOMs while showing substantially stronger robustness in Video ZS and Video FT settings, which is the central focus of this work. We will avoid overstatement, clearly mark AUC as the primary metric due to class imbalance, report 95\% confidence intervals for key metrics, and perform statistical significance tests to examine whether observed differences are significant. 5.Realism, privacy, and clinical use (R2, R4): Our acquisition uses a controlled browsing agent with stochastic scrolling speed, occasional pauses, and limited reversals to generate screen-recorded videos with variable temporal patterns. We do not claim that this fully matches real clinician browsing; rather, it is a first controlled testbed for studying whether diagnostic information survives camera capture. We will clarify this limitation and note clinician-recorded videos, diverse devices/viewers, and broader acquisition settings as future validation. SVL reduces privacy risk by cropping peripheral UI/environmental regions, but screen-recorded medical data still require appropriate privacy protection and regulatory compliance.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): All reviewers agreed that the idea behind the paper is sound and highly innovative (and I agree), yet that does not necessarily guarantee acceptance. The authors are encouraged to address the following issues raised by the reviewers and explain how they can be remedied in the frame of the rebuttal process. 1) Unfair comparison between ScreenCAD and baselines (R2, W1; R4, W2) has to be addressed –> this is highly critical 2) Results need more details in terms of display to be able to better assess their quality (R2, W2) 3) Agentic component is not evaluated and details are missing for agent scrolling screen (R4, W4) 4) Explanation on why CT only was evaluated (R1, W2; R4, W3) Note: Rx = reviewer x Wx = weakness x | As previously mentioned, the paper is certainly innovative. Within the rebuttal, I could see that the most critical aspects (baseline comparison fairness) is not necessarily terrible. This aligns with reviewers 1 and 2.The remaining issues are also properly discussed and I really hope the authors are not lazy and really implement in the camera-ready version what they promised. Luckily for the authors, reviewer 4 did not justify the rejection such that based on my own evaluation and the one of the other two reviewers I give it a GO. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper addresses an original and clinically relevant question: whether camera-captured scrolling videos of volumetric CT retain sufficient information for AI diagnosis when direct DICOM/PACS access is unavailable. Reviewers recognized the novelty, motivation, and potential clinical utility. The rebuttal substantially clarifies the main concern about baseline fairness by explaining that all methods used the same SVL-preprocessed video inputs and that CT-Net/CT-CLIP were also fine-tuned on captured videos. It also explains the role of MedDINOv3 versus the proposed task-token aggregation. Some limitations remain, especially the CT-only evaluation and controlled browsing-agent setup. Overall, based on the reviewer discussion, I recommend acceptance. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Two reviewers recommend acceptance after a successful rebuttal that addressed the primary concern centred around fairness of baseline methods. I agree that this paper formulates and investigates an interesting question (clinical value of video-recordings of high quality volumetric DICOM data). Even though investigating this question for other modalities than CT would be interesting, this paper is a solid first step with an innovative experimental setup.

title: Diagnostic Evidence-Based Prototype Learning via Dirichlet Process for Multimodal Bone Tumor Subtyping
reviewer_1_strengths: The clinical motivation is highly valuable and clearly defined. The paper targets the real clinical pain points in bone tumor imaging diagnosis where MRI is frequently unavailable and inter-modal feature overlap causes conflicts. The problem definition closely aligns with practical medical scenarios. The method demonstrates strong novelty and interpretability. Rather than relying on simple deterministic fusion or feature concatenation, the paper innovatively introduces the Dirichlet Process into multimodal fusion. By dynamically quantifying evidence reliability to arbitrate conflicts, it enhances model robustness while providing interpretability for diagnostic decisions. When handling missing modalities, the DP-guided “asymmetric distillation” is adopted to prevent clinically dangerous phenomena from occurring.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Insufficient experimental generalizability and prominent class imbalance issues. All 4,443 test cases come from a single clinical center. Although the total sample size is large, no multi-center external independent cohort validation has been conducted, nor has comparison and validation been performed on public datasets. The model’s generalization ability under different equipment, scanning protocols, and data distribution discrepancies cannot be adequately demonstrated, raising concerns about clinical practicability and transferability. Incomplete ablation study with key validations missing. The paper only conducts a simple analysis on the number of prototypes K, without performing hyperparameter sensitivity validation. This includes the dropout probability, the rationale and stability of the four balancing coefficients λ in the loss function, all of which remain unexplained, directly affecting the reproducibility of the method.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The paper targets an important and clinically relevant problem: primary bone tumor grading and histotype subtyping from incomplete CT/MRI data, which is well motivated in the introduction and abstract. 2.The method is reasonably novel in how it combines prototype learning with DP-style evidential arbitration and selective modality dropping, rather than using standard deterministic fusion alone. 3.The comparative evaluation is fairly comprehensive, covering multiple metrics including AUROC, ACC, Macro-F1, and BACC, and the manuscript additionally reports 95% confidence intervals and p-values against the best competing baseline, which strengthens confidence in the reported performance gains. 4.The construction of a relatively large in-house bone tumor dataset is itself a meaningful contribution for this task, and the scale of data collection and curation reflects substantial practical effort that deserves recognition.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.Reproducibility is relatively limited. Although the paper states that code is available, the study relies on a private in-house dataset, and the manuscript does not provide sufficiently detailed information on preprocessing, input construction, and other implementation details needed for faithful reproduction. If the dataset is not publicly released, this becomes a more substantial limitation for the community. 2.The paper strongly emphasizes uncertainty, reliability, and conflict resolution, but the evaluation is almost entirely classification-centric. I did not find dedicated uncertainty/calibration metrics or failure analysis showing that the evidential scores are actually better calibrated in practice. No direct evidence found in the manuscript. 3.The missing-modality story is promising but not fully stress-tested. The dataset contains many CT-only cases and fewer paired CT-MRI cases, while the distillation module is applied only to naturally paired samples; I did not find a detailed stratified analysis by missingness pattern or severity beyond the overall benchmark tables and ablation summary. 4.The paper argues that prior methods rely on deterministic feature aggregation and provide limited interpretable diagnostic evidence, and positions DPDEP as a more evidence-aware and clinically meaningful alternative. However, the manuscript does not provide direct comparative visualization or interpretability analysis against baseline methods to substantiate this claim. While Fig. 3 offers a qualitative view of prototype assignments within the proposed model, it does not demonstrate that DPDEP yields more interpretable diagnostic evidence than prior approaches. This leaves one of the paper’ s central claimed advantages insufficiently validated.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1 The paper studies a clinically relevant problem in a realistic setting. 2 The proposed formulation is technically interesting. A key strength is the attempt to combine modality-specific prototype learning with an evidential fusion mechanism, rather than relying on standard deterministic multimodal fusion. In particular, the paper frames multimodal fusion as prototype-level evidence arbitration, which is an interesting perspective and gives the method a clearer conceptual identity than a conventional fusion network. 3 The paper includes a practically motivated design for missing-modality training. The asymmetric evidential distillation component is a reasonable and application-relevant design choice, as it explicitly aims to transfer joint CT–MRI reasoning to incomplete-input settings. This is a meaningful attempt to preserve multimodal benefits when one modality is absent at inference time.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.It seems that the role of the DP is not sufficiently justified. It does not convincingly show why DP is necessary beyond acting as a more complex sparsity-inducing prototype weighting mechanism. In particular, it remains unclear whether the gains come from the DP formulation itself or, from adaptive weighting over prototype evidence, since simpler non-DP alternatives are not compared. 2.The main evaluation setting in Section 3.2 is not clearly specified. Table 2 reports the headline comparison, but it is unclear whether these results are obtained on naturally incomplete cases, synthetically degraded inputs, paired CT-MRI samples, CT-only samples, or some mixture of these settings. Since robustness to missing modalities is a central claim of the paper, this ambiguity makes it difficult to interpret what the reported gains actually reflect. 3.The main uncertainty/reliability claim is not directly evaluated. The paper only reports standard classification metrics such as AUROC, ACC, Macro-F1, and BACC. It appears that no results on reliability are provided. 4 The experimental comparison is not sufficiently up-to-date to support the “SOTA” claim. While the included baselines are relevant, the paper does not compare recent work on incomplete/missing-modality multimodal medical diagnosis. In particular, recent MICCAI 2025 methods such as Robust Incomplete-Modality Alignment for Ophthalmic Disease Grading and Diagnosis via Labeled Optimal Transport and MM-DINOv2 address closely related issues of diagnosis/classification under incomplete or missing medical imaging modalities, yet are not discussed or compared. The paper would benefit from clarifying why such recent methods were excluded. 5.The method appears largely generic rather than specifically designed for primary bone tumors. Although the clinical application is PBT subtyping, the methodological components are mostly generic missing-modality multimodal learning modules. The manuscript does not clearly show what part of the method is truly tailored to bone tumor diagnosis, rather than transferable to a broader multimodal classification setting. 6.Sensitivity analysis on λ_kd, λ_dp-dist, λ_div, and λ_dp is missing. The paper only analyzes the effect of the prototype number K.
reviewer_3_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We appreciate the favorable comments on the clinical importance of PBT diagnosis(R1,R2,R3), our novel DP-based evidential design(R1,R2,R3), and the comprehensive evaluation(R2). We address the main concerns below with additional analyses and clarifications. Q1: Reproducibility/Generalizability(R1,R2) For reproducibility, we will release synthetic/demo raw data and runnable code for preprocessing, input construction, feature extraction, mask generation, training, and evaluation, with splits/settings/hyperparameters in configs. Class imbalance is addressed by class-weighted CE and Macro-F1/BACC. Generalizability is supported by the 2010–2025 cohort with multiple scanners/protocols and frozen 3D foundation features. We also add a preliminary 188-case external-center malignancy validation, where DPDEP remains best under cross-center shift, supporting transferability while broader multi-center validation remains future work. Q2: Hyperparameter sensitivity(R1,R3) We add sensitivity analyses for p_drop, λ_kd, λ_dp-dist, λ_div, and λ_dp. Performance remains stable around the reported settings. Lower p_ drop weakens missing-modality robustness, while overly high p_drop hurts complete-modality reasoning. Too-small loss weights underuse distillation/regularization, whereas too-large weights over-constrain the student/prototype allocation. The values in Sec.3.1 are best or near-best across metrics. Q3: Interpretability comparison(R2) DPDEP provides built-in evidence decomposition via activated CT/MRI prototypes and modality reliability/conflict before fusion, unlike deterministic fusion baselines. We further add a model-agnostic evidence retrieval analysis: each method retrieves top-k nearest training cases from its final embedding, and we compare macro-averaged same-label C@1/C@5(top-k purity) and mAP. DPDEP scores best, showing more diagnosis-consistent evidence. Q4: Reliability evaluation(R2,R3) DPDEP estimates reliability from marginal prototype evidence and down-weights lower-reliability evidence under CT/MRI conflict. We added uncertainty-based failure detection and calibration analysis. For DPDEP, uncertainty is derived from DP-based modality reliability/arbitration scores; for baselines, we use softmax confidence. DPDEP achieves higher error-detection AUROC(0.87 vs. 0.83) and lower ECE(0.032 vs. 0.044), showing better failure identification and calibration than deterministic fusion baselines. Q5: Missing-modality setting(R2,R3) The main evaluation(Tab.2–3) follows real clinical missingness, where 69.6% cases are MRI-missing. To further stress-test robustness, we randomly masked MRI in 10%, 25%, and 40% of naturally paired test cases and computed the relative drop from the paired full-modality setting. DPDEP remains best at all rates and shows the smallest drop, indicating robustness beyond the observed missing pattern. Q6: DP necessity(R3) DP turns prototype matching into sparse evidence estimation and reliability-aware CT/MRI arbitration. In ablation, DPL already serves as an adaptive weighted prototype baseline; adding DPEF brings clear gains, with further improvement after DPAED. Thus DP contributes beyond generic prototype weighting by inducing sparse evidence allocation and conflict-aware evidential fusion. R1/R2 also recognized this DP-specific design as innovative/reasonably novel. Q7: Recent baselines(R3) RIMA targets 2D fundus/OCT ophthalmic diagnosis and MM-DINOv2 focuses on foundation-model adaptation with modality masking, so neither is directly comparable to our 3D CT/MRI PBT setting without adaptation. We adapted both using the same frozen 3D features, DPDEP still outperforms them across metrics. Q8: PBT specificity of DPDEP(R3) DPDEP addresses a PBT-relevant problem(R2) and is well motivated by bone tumor imaging diagnosis(R1). DPEF arbitrates complementary/conflicting CT/MRI evidence used in PBT diagnosis, while DPAED targets real MRI-missing PBT cases without hallucinating missing-modal evidence.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): A further rebuttal is required for the reviewers to reach a consensus. | The paper addresses an important clinical challenge in multimodal primary bone tumor diagnosis and presents a novel evidence arbitration framework based on Dirichlet Process modeling. The work is supported by a large-scale clinical dataset and comprehensive experiments demonstrating strong empirical performance. While one reviewer remains unconvinced regarding the necessity of the DP formulation and the completeness of baseline comparisons, the majority of reviewers found these concerns sufficiently addressed in the rebuttal and agreed that the method provides a meaningful contribution. Given the strong experimental evidence and clinical relevance, I recommend acceptance. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): The rebuttal fails to substantiate the necessity of the proposed DP design, provide validation of reliability claims, or ensure sufficiently SOTA baselines, leaving the core contributions insufficiently supported. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper represents a strong and clinically meaningful contribution with clear potential impact. The work addresses an important real-world problem in multimodal bone tumor diagnosis, particularly under missing-modality and conflicting cross-modal evidence settings, and introduces a technically interesting Dirichlet Process-based evidence arbitration framework that balances predictive performance, interpretability, and clinical safety. The experimental validation is comprehensive, involving a relatively large clinical cohort with strong performance across a challenging nine-class classification task, supported by ablation studies and statistical analysis. While some limitations remain regarding external validation, calibration evaluation, and implementation details, the reviewers agreed these are addressable issues that do not diminish the core novelty and practical significance of the work.

title: DiCoP-SAM: Disagreement-Band Guided Corrective Prompting for Collaborative Semi-Supervised Medical Image Segmentation
reviewer_1_strengths: The core idea of using disagreement between models in a semi-supervised setting to generate corrective signals is intuitive and well-motivated. The proposed two-stage framework is technically sound and well-structured. Stage-I (TriGate-CPS) is a sensible extension of cross pseudo-supervision that explicitly models uncertainty to improve pseudo-label quality. Stage-II (DiCoP) presents a clever, GT-free mechanism to translate model disagreement into actionable, corrective prompts for SAM, which is a key contribution.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The overall framework is a sophisticated combination of existing ideas: cross pseudo-supervision (CPS), knowledge distillation, and prompt-based finetuning of SAM. While the integration is novel, the core building blocks are not. For example, using model disagreement or uncertainty to guide learning is a known concept in active learning and co-training. 2.The point generation strategy in DiCoP (Section 2.2) relies on several manually set hyperparameters. How were these values chosen? The paper mentions these values in Section 3 but does not provide a sensitivity analysis. This is a significant weakness. 3.The claim of being “GT-free” for prompt generation is slightly misleading. While the point prompts for unlabeled data are indeed generated without GT, the entire system is trained on a labeled set where GT is used to supervise the foreground, background, and uncertainty. 4.The computational overhead of the proposed two-stage training process is not discussed. The framework involves running two CNN branches, fusing their outputs, running SAM with generated prompts, and performing distillation. This seems computationally expensive compared to standard SSL methods. A discussion of training time, memory usage, and inference speed would be valuable for assessing the practical applicability of the method. 5.The description of the loss function for the uncertainty gate is vague. On page 4, it states it uses BCE with a “soft high-risk target derived from the GT boundary band. “ The exact formulation of this soft target is not provided, which hinders reproducibility. 6.The paper mentions applying “entropy-guided patch-level CutMix” in the late training stage. This seems like an important detail for achieving the reported performance, yet it is mentioned only briefly and not included in the main formulation or ablation studies.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.Reasonable method design. The authors propose a novel integration of SAM within a semi-supervised segmentation framework through a two-stage training scheme. title: Diff-SABR: Diffusion-Based Symmetry-Aware Reconstruction of Alveolar Bone Defects from CBCT
reviewer_1_strengths: The paper introduces a mathematical model of bone resorption using a hyperbolic paraboloid, which enables realistic simulation of complex, asymmetric multi-site bone defects and provides a principled alternative to simple masking techniques. The method effectively incorporates anatomical priors by leveraging the jawbone’s natural bilateral symmetry. AlignNet is used to correct pose-induced misalignments before applying the symmetry prior in the diffusion model, ensuring structurally consistent reconstructions. Ablation studies demonstrate the contribution of each component, showing that combining weak supervision with alignment improves the clinical DSC from 0.04 ± 0.06 to 0.82 ± 0.04, highlighting the effectiveness of the proposed strategy.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: In Figure 2(b), the input to AlignNet is the mask (fixed mask and moving mask), whereas in Figure 2(c) within the Diff-SABR module, AlignNet’s input becomes the defect CBCT and the symmetry CBCT. This inconsistency raises a concern: Was AlignNet trained on masks? If so, directly applying it to CBCT volumes may affect its performance or reliability. Please clarify this mismatch. The clinical dataset comprises 43 cases, with merely 10 cases reserved for testing. This relatively small sample size may not fully capture the extensive structural variability of alveolar bone defects present across the broader patient population. The approach relies on aligning the defect region with contralateral healthy bone, but the manuscript does not discuss how midline-crossing or bilateral defects are handled. The authors should clarify the applicability and limitations of their method in cases with midline-crossing, bilateral, or highly asymmetric defects. The method relies on aligning the defect with the contralateral healthy bone, but the paper does not explain how midline-crossing or bilateral defects are managed. In such cases, a corresponding contralateral patch may be unavailable, which could reduce alignment accuracy and compromise defect reconstruction. The proposed method employs a 3D latent diffusion model, which is potentially memory- and computation-intensive. The paper does not report GPU memory usage or inference time, leaving its practicality and feasibility in clinical scenarios unclear.

author_feedback: We thank reviewers for their constructive comments. [AlignNet & symmetry guidance – R1,R4] We clarify that AlignNet is trained and applied on thresholded bone-only CBCT representations, not raw intensity volumes. In Fig. 2, the “fixed” and “moving” masks denote binarized bone maps extracted from the defect-side and mirrored contralateral CBCT volumes for affine alignment. The estimated affine transform is then applied to the mirrored contralateral CBCT volume before it is used as denoising guidance. Thus, AlignNet does not perform deformable registration or anatomical replacement. It only reduces pose- and morphology-induced mismatch so that the contralateral anatomy provides stable, patient-specific symmetry guidance. [Limited Clinical Data & Simulation Strategy – R1,R2,R4] We acknowledge that paired CBCT scans with ground-truth alveolar reconstruction are inherently difficult to obtain. Our evaluation included maxillary, mandibular, anterior, and posterior defects to cover diverse anatomical locations. This clinical constraint motivated our anatomically informed simulation and weakly supervised framework. The proposed hyperbolic-paraboloid simulation reflects clinically observed asymmetric ridge resorption patterns, including bucco-lingual collapse and vertical loss, rather than arbitrary random masking. Unlike random masking, our simulation preserves clinically plausible morphology and structural continuity, helping reduce the synthetic-to-clinical gap. [Mask definitions & framework clarity – R4] We clarify the mask terminology. The hard mask Mh denotes the simulation-derived ground-truth defect label, whereas the soft mask Ms denotes the clinical pseudo label. The fixed/moving masks in AlignNet are thresholded bone-only CBCT maps used only for affine registration. The ROI cuboid mask Mr is a coarse localization prior for the candidate defect region. The Mask-VAE is used to encode spatial mask representations, allowing Mr to provide structural guidance during denoising. We also acknowledge that the notation in the manuscript could have been clearer, particularly the distinction between masks used for registration, supervision, and localization. [Clinical Pseudo Label Generation – R2,R4] Clinical pseudo labels are generated by measuring the discrepancy between defect-side anatomy and the aligned contralateral reference after symmetry registration. They are represented as signed distance maps, yielding continuous soft masks rather than discrete binary masks. Since dense voxel-wise annotations are unavailable, these labels are used as weak anatomical guidance rather than exact ground truth. [Conditioning design – R4] The three conditioning paths are complementary. Concatenation injects spatial priors, FiLM modulates intermediate features according to anatomical context, and cross-attention models structural correspondence between reconstruction latents and the aligned contralateral anatomy. This design is intended to combine local defect localization with global symmetry guidance. [Baseline Comparison – R1,R2] We compared with 3D U-Net, WGAN-GP, and VQ-based diffusion as representative supervised and generative baselines under the same training protocol. WGAN- and VQ-based models remain relevant references for medical image synthesis and reconstruction. We used 3D U-Net as a controlled supervised baseline for architectural consistency. [Applicability & limitations – R1,R2] Diff-SABR is primarily designed for unilateral defects where reliable contralateral anatomy is available and can serve as patient-specific symmetry guidance. The more complex defect patterns require mechanisms beyond direct symmetry guidance and are an important direction for future work. [Inference Time – R1,R2] Our latent-mask diffusion framework required 1.99 seconds per case with 3.6 GB GPU memory usage using DDIM-50 sampling on a single NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU. [Ethical Approval & IRB – R2] IRB details were omitted only to preserve review anonymity.

title: Differential Privacy Representation Geometry for Medical Image Analysis
reviewer_1_strengths: The paper presents a clear and easy-to-follow structure, with the main strengths being : 1) Useful diagnostic framing. Separating “what the encoder preserves” from “what the task head exploits” under DP is practically valuable. Most DP medical imaging work reports only end-to-end metrics, conflating representational damage with optimization difficulty. The utilization gap gives practitioners an actionable signal: if it’s large, the remedy is better head optimization rather than relaxing privacy. 2) Broad and controlled experimental design. The evaluation covers over 594,000 images across four chest X-ray datasets, three pretrained initializations with distinct properties (supervised, self-supervised, domain-specific), and multiple privacy budgets — all with non-privacy hyperparameters held fixed. This isolates the effect of DP on geometry cleanly and makes the findings more credible than a single-dataset study would. 3) Initialization-aware analysis. The paper shows that DP’s geometric effects are strongly initialization-dependent — spectral dimension increases under stronger privacy for ImageNet but decreases for DINOv3, displacement patterns differ across priors. This challenges the simplistic narrative that DP uniformly collapses features, and is directly relevant to foundation model selection for privacy-constrained medical imaging.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: For Δ and d_eff, the framework only issues deployment warnings (e. g. , “large Δ may hurt transfer”, “low d_eff may limit adaptation”) without offering or testing remediation. This is acceptable given their nature. For G, however, the paper explicitly suggests concrete fixes, freezing the encoder, retraining the head, or adjusting clipping for head parameters, but none of these are validated. Since G is presented as the central and most actionable contribution, at least one experiment showing that a suggested intervention actually closes the gap (under preserved privacy) would substantially strengthen the paper. As it stands, the most actionable claim remains conjecture.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: By effective dimension as a spectral summary to detect anisotropy shifts under DP is a well-motivated geometric lens rarely applied in medical imaging privacy studies. Correlation analyses across datasets and initializations provide a structured view of how geometry and utilization relate to end-to-end utility. The findings highlight concrete levers for practice and inform privacy model selection.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: My biggest concern is that the main mechanistic claim of this paper is not sufficiently validated. The observed post-DP separability may simply be a consequence of overparameterization and strong pretrained priors, rather than evidence that DP primarily harms utilization rather than representation quality. Since all experiments use a large ConvNeXt-Small backbone with strong initialization, the paper does not rule out model capacity itself as the source of the reported effect. The privacy guarantee is only weakly justified. The choice of \delta is not sufficiently motivated for a medical setting and does not appear particularly conservative relative to dataset size (should be much less than 1/N). The DP setup is under-specified. Key DP-SGD details, including the actual clipping norm, noise multipliers, and training duration, are missing, making the privacy-utility tradeoff hard to assess or reproduce.
reviewer_2_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: Novelty: the proposed framework offers interesting diagnostic insights beyond standard privacy vs utility trade-offs. Motivation: the method is well-motivated. Experiments: the authors provide a thorough experimental validation that spans various datasets and initialization strategies.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Inconsistency: there appears to be a significant discrepancy between the numerical reporting in Section 4 and the visualizations in Figure 2.For instance, the text reports a +17.0 pneumonia gap for ImageNet at \epsilon=1.0, yet the corresponding y-axis in the figure does not exceed 12.Similar mismatches occur throughout the section. I ask the authors to clarify whether these are indeed inconsistent or if I am misinterpreting the plot. Metric choice: the authors quantify representation displacement using an isotropic measure (average Euclidean distance from initialization). However, given the paper’s later emphasis on anisotropic reshaping, this metric may be suboptimal. Have the authors explored covariance-aware alternatives, such as the Mahalanobis distance? Extreme cases: in the ImageNet branch, the largest displacement is observed at \epsilon=\infty rather than under DP constraints. I would welcome the authors’ intuition on this. Specifically, could the different augmentation strategies employed for DP versus non-DP training be a confounding factor? Generalizability: while the DP-RGMI framework is conceptually model- and dataset-agnostic, the current empirical validation is restricted to a single backbone family and image modality. This limited scope somewhat weakens the claim of broad applicability. Minor: The caption labels in the original template (Fig. X, Table Y) are typically bolded. This formatting may have been overridden by a LaTeX package. The literature more commonly uses “DINOv3” rather than “DinoV3.”
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank reviewers (R1,R2,R4) and AC. Minor points (“DINOv3”, captions, scope wording) will be revised. [R2 (main): Capacity/strong-prior confound for utilization gap G] The three initializations span the standard taxonomy: ImageNet (supervised non-medical), DinoV3 (self-supervised non-medical), MIMIC-CXR (supervised in-domain). Existing results rule out both alternatives: (i) Same ConvNeXt-Small, three priors, three different G at strongest privacy (MIMIC=3.4, DinoV3=6.1, ImageNet=8.0; Tab.1). If capacity drove G, gaps would be uniform. (ii) The “stronger prior” prediction is INVERTED: MIMIC (strongest, in-domain prior) yields SMALLEST G; ImageNet (weakest) yields LARGEST. Stronger priors REDUCE G, opposite to R2’s hypothesis. (iii) G(inf)~=0 for ALL priors. The gap arises ONLY under DP while capacity/prior are constant across runs, isolating DP-SGD optimization. (iv) Pattern replicates on three datasets (Tab.2: rho= up to -0.98). (v) G is label-structured (Fig.2: pneumonia largest), inconsistent with a generic capacity/prior artifact. The backbone is a methodological requirement: BatchNorm is incompatible with per-sample gradients in DP-SGD; transformers show unstable DP optimization (Sec.3,[13]). Cross-architecture consistency is established in [13,16,18,22]. [R4 (main): Sec.4 vs Fig.2 inconsistency] We sincerely thank R4 for catching this. The numbers in the “Utilization failure is label-structured” paragraph contain transcription typos: values were copied from the wrong rows of our source results table, producing inconsistent numbers in that paragraph alone. Fig.2 is correct, Tab.1 is correct, and the qualitative interpretation is correct (pneumonia largest, MIMIC smallest, label-structured failure across priors). Accurate pneumonia gaps in Fig.2: +10.6 (ImageNet,eps=1.0), +9.6 (MIMIC,eps=0.7), +11.0 (DinoV3,eps=0.7); no finding (ImageNet,eps=1.0) is +5.6.The discrepancy is localized to one paragraph; figure, table, correlation analysis, and conclusions are consistent with the correct values, confirming a clerical mistake. Text will be corrected (presentation amendment, no change to experiments). [R2: DP-SGD specification] delta=6e-6 satisfies delta<1/N_train for all training sets (largest CheXpert: 1/N~7.9e-6), per standard medical DP practice [13,16,18,22]. Per Sec.3, non-privacy hyperparameters are fixed across runs; eps is controlled via sigma using a Renyi accountant; q=128/|D_train|. Clipping and per-eps sigma follow established protocols [13,16,18,22]; eps<10 is the accepted medical DP regime [13]; we probe to eps~1.A per-run sigma/clip/epoch summary will be added. [R1 (main): Validation of G interventions] The linear probe IS a controlled instantiation of “freeze encoder + retrain head”. Probe AUROC > end-to-end AUROC under DP (Tab.1, all priors and datasets) directly demonstrates recoverable structure exists and IS recovered when head optimization is decoupled from joint DP-SGD. Full deployment validation (head-only DP-SGD, modified clipping) is natural follow-up. Sec.5 will be reframed as diagnostic implications rather than prescriptive recipes. [R4: Mahalanobis vs Euclidean Delta] Delta is deliberately Euclidean to keep diagnostics orthogonal. Mahalanobis would whiten by a covariance whose anisotropy d_eff is designed to capture, conflating displacement with spectral structure. [R4: Largest ImageNet Delta at eps=inf] Non-private updates are unconstrained, so larger drift is expected. DP-SGD clips gradients and adds noise, dampening per-step movement. Augmentations are identical across DP and non-DP. [R4: Single backbone] DP-RGMI is model-agnostic by construction (Sec.2); architecture is constrained by DP-SGD compatibility. Cross-architecture consistency is shown in [13,16,18,22]. [Code/data] Code anonymized; public release on acceptance committed in Sec.3. All datasets and initialization weights are public. The 27-config evaluation across 4 datasets and 3 priors supports the DP-RGMI decomposition.

title: Diffusion-Guided Anatomical Position Encoding for Dense Longitudinal CT Correspondence
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The idea of reinterpreting a generative CT diffusion model as a carrier of cross-subject anatomical consistency and distilling its similarity structure (rather than raw features) is insightful and well-executed. 2.Strong quantitative results without task-specific annotations. 3.Table 3 (page 8) clearly isolates the contribution of each component. it confirms the value of diffusion-based supervision beyond standard contrastive learning.
