title: DUCX: Decomposing Unfairness in Tool-Using Chest X-Ray Agents
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.Novel decomposition of fairness for tool-using agents 2.The evaluation spans five driver backbones, two demographic axes (gender and age), and two datasets, including CheXAgentBench and the curated MIMIC-FairnessVQA. The paper does not stop at aggregate accuracy; it reports multiple fairness metrics such as ΔACC, DP, EoD, and FUT, and then drills down into intermediate behavior. 3.Good practical relevance 3.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The paper often uses language suggesting that a stage is “responsible” for disparities, but the analyses are mainly descriptive and correlational. For example, tool-exposure bias conditions on tool usage, but tool usage is itself chosen by the planner and may depend on question type, difficulty, or latent case characteristics. Likewise, transition differences do not show that those transitions caused end-to-end disparities. Without controlled interventions, causal attribution is weak. 2.Because the proposed framework still uses standard group disparity metrics and mostly audits subgroup performance at different internal stages, the conceptual jump from prior fairness auditing is not enormous. The paper should more clearly position itself as process-level auditing for agents, rather than implying a fundamentally new fairness paradigm. 3.MIMIC-FairnessVQA is useful, but the benchmark is partly constructed using LLM-generated six-choice questions from reports, followed by manual verification. That introduces possible concerns: (1) generated questions may reflect LLM stylistic priors rather than authentic clinician questioning, (2) fairness patterns may partly come from the generated-question distribution, (3) answer verification is mentioned, but the paper gives little detail on annotation protocol, inter-rater reliability, or failure cases.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The shift from end-to-end to process-level fairness auditing for agentic system is novel and impactful. Rather than treating the agent as a black box and only measuring disparity on its final prediction, the paper argues that it is both reasonable and practically valuable to step inside the pipeline and attribute disparity to the stage where it originates. This is a well-motivated move as an end-to-end fairness number cannot tell whether a subgroup gap is inherited from a particular tool, introduced by the planner’s tool-selection and routing, or amplified during final response generation, and consequently it gives no actionable guidance about where to intervene. The paper’s stage-wise framing makes each of these pathways explicit and individually diagnosable, which is a genuine conceptual contribution beyond single-decision-function fairness audits. 2.Beyond the general motivation for process-level auditing, the paper’s specific contribution is decomposing process-level disparity into three distinct sources that correspond to the decision points of a tool-using agent, including tool-exposure bias (i.e., does a given tool deliver unequal utility when invoked for different subgroups?), tool-transition bias (i.e., does the planner route different subgroups through systematically different tool chains?), and LLM reasoning bias in the final report (i.e., does response synthesis differ by subgroup in quality, uncertainty expression, or demographic framing?). Proposing and naming this particular three-way decomposition is the novel piece. It gives each stage its own targeted diagnostic and provides the community with a usable vocabulary and a starting template for future agent-fairness work. 3.Comprehensive experimental analysis. The paper evaluates five driver LLMs, spanning open-source LLMs, VLMs, and proprietary systems, under a unified setup on two benchmarks. This breadth enables the authors to distinguish backbone-specific behaviors from stage-level patterns that remain consistent across models, which is a necessary condition for the decomposition findings to generalize beyond a single LLM. End-to-end fairness claims are further supported by non-parametric bootstrapping with reported confidence intervals in Table 1. 4.New demographic-aware benchmark. MIMIC-FairnessVQA, curated with balanced sampling over gender and age-60 threshold with five task focuses per study, partially addresses the scarcity of agent-suitable fairness datasets and may serve as a reusable resource for broader research on demographic fairness in medical visual question answering.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The paper only diagnoses the problem and does not try to fix it. It describes where the unfairness comes from across the three stages, but proposes no method to reduce the disparity, and stage-targeted debiasing is only mentioned as future work in the conclusion. For a MICCAI audience, this leaves the practical impact narrow as readers learn that the agentic pipeline clearly exposes bias, but are not given a way to make the agent fairer. 2.The proposed metrics are tightly tied to MedRAX’s linear ReAct chain and do not cleanly extend to richer agent architectures. The authors justify using MedRAX because decomposition is “well-defined and modular” in a single-agent ReAct pipeline, which is an honest but narrow choice. Specifically, Delta_TTB loses its Markov interpretation in tree-based, DAG-based, or multi-agent pipelines. One can still count tool-to-tool transitions in these settings, but the resulting matrix is no longer a proper Markov transition matrix, because a node can have multiple successors, different sub-agents have their own tool chains, and P(next tool | current tool) is therefore not well-defined. The matrix then becomes a descriptive frequency table rather than a probabilistic routing policy, which weakens the claim that it captures “planning-level disparity”. Delta_TEB also becomes too coarse in multi-agent settings: the “was this tool used” indicator still applies, but when the same tool may be invoked by several sub-agents, Delta_TEB cannot tell which invocation actually caused the downstream error. The title’s broad framing, “Tool-Using Chest X-ray Agents”, therefore over-promises relative to what the three-stage decomposition structurally supports. 3.Tool-exposure bias may be confounded by case-difficulty differences across subgroups. Delta_TEB(A) is measured only on the subset of cases where tool A was invoked, but this subset is not a random sample. The driver LLM decides when to call A, and this decision depends on the image and case context. For example, if the LLM tends to call the segmenter more often on visually harder cases for one subgroup and on easier cases for the other, then the accuracy gap within “segmenter-used” cases will mix two different effects: the segmenter genuinely performing unequally across subgroups, and systematically different kinds of cases being routed to the segmenter for each subgroup. This means the headline 50% gap on CheXAgentBench cannot be read as tool bias alone. The paper reports the exposure rate P(E_A=1 | g), which tells us how often each subgroup triggers the tool but not whether the triggered cases are comparable in difficulty. A stronger analysis would match cases of similar difficulty across subgroups before computing Delta_TEB, or re-weight each case by how likely the driver LLM was to invoke the tool on it, so that cases the LLM preferred to route through the tool do not dominate the comparison. 4.Tool-transition bias is not actually reduced to a quantitative fairness evaluation. Under an ideal fair routing policy, P^(g1) = P^(g2), so Delta_TTB = 0 (the zero matrix). The paper, however, never collapses Delta_TTB into a scalar (e.g., Frobenius norm, entrywise L1, total variation distance, or row-wise KL divergence), so there is no criterion for when a transition matrix is “close enough” to the fair ideal, and no quantity that can be compared across driver LLMs, datasets, or attributes. The only evaluation is visual inspection of red/blue heatmaps (Fig. 3) together with qualitative prose observations (e.g., “female patients are more likely than male patients to proceed directly from the Classifier”). There is also no global significance test (e.g., chi-squared on transition-count contingency tables), which contrasts with the bootstrap rigor applied to end-to-end metrics in Table 1.As a result, “tool-transition bias” functions as a description, not a fairness measurement. 5.Sensitive attributes are limited to two binary axes. Only gender (M/F) and age (>=60 vs <60) are considered. Race/ethnicity is absent, despite being the most studied axis in prior CXR fairness work, and the age threshold is fixed at 60 without a sensitivity analysis. 6.Per-subgroup base rates are never reported, and the appropriateness of DP under genuine prevalence differences is not discussed. Disease prevalence often differs across demographic subgroups in medical imaging (e.g., osteoporosis by sex/age), so a model that accurately reflects such differences can still violate Demographic Parity (Chouldechova 2017[1]). Without P(y=1 | g) per subgroup on either benchmark, a reader cannot tell whether a non-zero DP in Table 1 reflects model bias or biological prevalence. Reporting per-subgroup positive-class rates, which the authors already have, and discussing when DP is informative vs. misleading would make the fairness claims more defensible. 7.Minor notation issue. Eq. 3 reuses the symbol N for the tool-pool size (T = {A_1, …, A_N} and P^(g) in R^(N x N)), which conflicts with N = dataset size defined in Sec. 2.2 (Eq. 1); the Markov matrix dimension should use |T| or a distinct symbol. [1] Chouldechova A. Fair prediction with disparate impact: A study of bias in recidivism prediction instruments[J]. Big data, 2017, 5(2): 153-163.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.Timely and critical problem formulation: The shift from standalone models to agentic systems in medical AI introduces new pathways for bias. By addressing pipeline biases in LLM-powered tool-using agents, this work tackles a highly relevant and previously overlooked issue in clinical AI fairness. 2.Novel decomposition framework: The DUCX framework provides a clear, traceable methodology for attributing unfairness to specific stages of the agent’s execution (exposure, transition, and reasoning). This granular approach is a significant advancement over standard end-to-end fairness metrics (e.g., Equalized Odds), offering actionable insights into where disparities originate. 3.Valuable new benchmark: The curation of MIMIC-FairnessVQA, featuring balanced gender and age attributes alongside standardized multiple-choice questions, provides a much-needed resource for the community to evaluate fairness in medical VQA agents.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.Limited agent architectures: The evaluation is currently restricted to a single agent framework (MedRAX). While MedRAX provides the necessary trajectory observability for the DUCX decomposition, validating the framework on alternative agent architectures (e.g., multi-agent systems or different planning paradigms) would strengthen the claims of generalizability. 2.Scope of demographic attributes: The analysis focuses exclusively on gender and age (binarized at 60 years). Expanding the evaluation to include other critical attributes, such as race, ethnicity, or intersectional subgroups, would provide a more comprehensive picture of the fairness landscape in these systems. 3.Lack of clinical grounding: While the algorithmic disparities are well-documented, the paper lacks an assessment of how these specific biases (e.g., differences in hedging or tool transitions) translate into tangible clinical risks or diagnostic errors in a real-world setting. A qualitative analysis involving clinical experts would add significant value.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank all reviewers for their constructive and positive feedback and address major concerns below. A. Diagnosis without mitigation (R1, R2-W1, R3) DUCX is intentionally scoped as diagnostic, the first process-level fairness audit for tool-using medical agents. We believe rigorous diagnosis must precede principled intervention: without knowing where disparity originates, mitigation risks targeting the wrong stage. Our decomposition directly enables stage-targeted debiasing (e.g., exposure rebalancing, fairness-constrained routing) by providing the map that makes each intervention well-defined. This parallels how FairMedFM established foundation-model fairness benchmarking without proposing debiasing — a contribution valued precisely because it grounded subsequent mitigation work. B. Generalizability beyond MedRAX (R1, R2-W2, R3-W1) MedRAX was chosen for trajectory observability and modularity, prerequisites for meaningful decomposition. MedRAX is not a convenience choice but the necessary first testbed: process-level fairness decomposition requires observable trajectories and modular tool calls. In DAG or multi-agent systems, the same principle extends from Markov transitions to graph-edge or sub-agent transition statistics; this is an extension of bookkeeping, not a limitation of the core audit idea. At the same time, to the best of our knowledge, prior work has not explicitly investigated fairness evaluation and mitigation in agentic medical AI systems. We therefore chose MedRAX, a representative tool-using medical agent, as an appropriate starting point for methodological development at this early stage. The proposed framework is readily extensible, and we plan to broaden the evaluation to additional classes of medical agents in future work. C. Causal attribution and confounding (R1-W1, R2-W3, R2-W4) We note that strict causal attribution in agentic pipelines requires counterfactual trajectories, intervening on the planner’s tool choices while holding all else fixed, a problem that remains open even in the causal inference literature, where identifying causal effects in sequential decision processes with endogenous actions is an active area of research. It is therefore not a standard expectation for a fairness audit paper. That said, our design partially mitigates confounding: conditioning on tool exposure is a stratification strategy that isolates within-tool disparity from routing differences, and reporting per-group exposure rates P(E_A=1|g) makes the non-random routing visible to the reader. We present the 50% conditional gap as a signal warranting targeted investigation, not as proof of tool-level bias in isolation. For Delta_TTB (R2-W4), the matrix is intentionally primary because it identifies which routing edge shifts by subgroup; scalar summaries can complement this presentation but would obscure the actionable source of disparity. D. Limited demographic attributes (R2-W5, R3-W2) We focus on age and gender because they are consistently available across the evaluated agent benchmarks and support balanced, statistically meaningful subgroup analysis. Race, ethnicity and intersectional attributes are important, but using them responsibly requires reliable metadata and sufficient subgroup sizes; otherwise the audit risks unstable or misleading conclusions. E. MIMIC-FairnessVQA curation (R1-W3) Questions were generated using structured templates following the MedRAX-style protocol to reduce stylistic drift. Two annotators independently verified answer correctness against the original reports, and disagreements were resolved by consensus. F. DP under prevalence differences (R2-W6); Notation (R2-W7) We use DP alongside EoD because each captures different fairness desiderata. We will report per-subgroup positive-class rates and discuss when DP is informative vs. misleading under prevalence shifts, per Chouldechova (2017).
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): Consistent positive ratings are provided by reviewers, with high quality, novelty, and relevance acknowledged. The authors are encouraged to address the remaining issues to a reasonable extent in the camera-ready version.

title: Dynamic Sub-domain Modeling for Robust Medical Image Segmentation
reviewer_1_strengths: Strengths – Framing intra domain heterogeneity as a latent mixture is underexplored in medical image segmentation. – The ability to determine K from data with bounded growth, merging, and pruning is a good technical advance over standard MoE approaches. It avoids the need for prior knowledge about the number of sub domains. – The strict constraint of no test-time gradient updates is clinically important for deployment. – 20 datasets across 6+ imaging modalities under a unified 2D protocol, with worst case sub domain Dice and Boundary F1 alongside standard metrics is comprehensive – All four main components dynamic vs. fixed-K discovery, hypernetwork vs. static adapters, uncertainty tempered vs standard routing, ROI vs global only descriptor are individually ablated and shown to contribute to the design choices. – The UMAP visualization and uncertainty and routing analysis in Fig 2 and 3 provide genuine insight into what the model has learned going.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Weaknesses – Fig. 2(b) appears uniformly positive across all 20 datasets and all 13 baselines, with no losses shown. The authors must provide per dataset breakdowns and appropriate statistical significance testing for example Wilcoxon signed rank. – For datasets lacking metadata, sub domains are constructed by clustering training image descriptors. Since the same descriptor network contributes to both sub domain definition and model behavior, this risks circular evaluation of robustness. – The paper explicitly claims to report runtime and peak GPU memory, but these figures are absent from all tables and figures. – UMAP visualization is underspecified. Fig. 2(a) shows only Dataset A and Dataset B without identifying which of the 20 datasets these correspond to. – The paper does not discuss scenarios where the framework may underperform
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.Well-motivated problem framing. The paper points out a common but under-addressed failure mode, even within one dataset, shifts from scanner/protocol/patient morphology can create a mixture of sub-distributions that a single model averages over. 2.The proposed architecture is technically sound. For example, modulating the routing temperature based on expert disagreement is a clever mechanism to prevent overconfident predictions on ambiguous boundary cases. 3.The evaluation includes 20 distinct public datasets spanning multiple modalities (MRI, CT, Ultrasound, Endoscopy, Dermoscopy, etc.). providing evidence of the method’s generalizability.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.In Section 4 (Settings), the authors state: “runtime and peak GPU memory are reported.” However, this data is completely missing from the provided text. 2.Since the network relies on automatic prompts to generate local descriptors, the paper lacks details on how robust the system is to poor-quality automatic prompts. If the initial prompt generation fails or is highly inaccurate, does the sub-domain descriptor “r” collapse, leading to incorrect expert routing? An ablation or discussion on prompt sensitivity would strengthen the paper. 3.Considering the substantial heterogeneity across the 20 datasets, particularly in modality and degree of intra-domain variation, it is important to clarify whether the key hyperparameters τ, ρ, and α were kept fixed across all datasets or tuned separately for each one. If a single hyperparameter setting works well across 20 highly diverse datasets, that would be a major strength and should be explicitly highlighted. If, instead, these parameters were tuned per dataset, the paper should clearly describe the tuning protocol and discuss the associated overhead when transferring the method to a new dataset, especially relative to methods such as SAM2/MedSAM2 that do not appear to require this level of dataset-specific tuning. 4.The notation around the temperature scaling is currently under-specified. the paper does not clearly define either T_0 or the subscript r in T_r. 5.A key concern is how the method behaves when a genuinely new sub-domain appears at test time. Because the prototypes are fixed during inference, the model can only reweight known experts and cannot explicitly instantiate a new prototype for an unseen mode. 6.Figure 2(a) does not convincingly support the paper’s core claim of meaningful sub-domain discovery. While Dataset A shows some clustered structure, Dataset B appears largely as a homogeneous blob with no clear sub-domain separation. Thus, it remains unclear whether the reported gains come from explicit sub-domain modeling or simply from the increased capacity introduced by the hypernetwork, multiple experts, and routing mechanism. The current results and ablations do not sufficiently disentangle semantic expert specialization from a generic MoE/ensemble effect.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: Conceptual novelty and perspective: The work reframes intra-domain variability (scanner, protocol, anatomy differences) as meaningful structure rather than noise, dynamically assigning specialized experts to discovered sub-domains and improving boundary delineation (e.g., Boundary F1). Dynamic, nonparametric sub-domain discovery: Nonparametric prototypes allow the number of sub-domains to grow as new modes appear during training, avoiding the need to predefine sub-domain counts and enhancing adaptability. Inference-time practicality: The framework is fully gradient free at test time, relying on the learned prototypes and routing mechanism without parameter updates, which is attractive for stable and efficient clinical deployment. Broad and convincing validation: The method is evaluated on 20 datasets across multiple imaging modalities and consistently outperforms strong baselines such as nnU Net 2D, SegMamba, and MedSAM2+APG, with supporting analyses (e.g., UMAP) to illustrate generalization. Robust performance under domain shifts: The dynamic combination of experts yields high Dice (87.9) and competitive HD95 (11.8) across heterogeneous domains, including previously unseen distributions.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Limited architectural/detail transparency: Key components such as the prototype memory bank, the structure of expert models, and the mechanism by which experts expand remain under-specified, which hinders reproducibility and makes it hard to reimplement the method faithfully. Sensitivity to thresholding and noise: Prototype creation hinges on a threshold parameter τ; despite pruning/merging, real world noisy clinical data may require careful tuning, weakening claims of full automation. Dependence on SAM-based descriptor space: Sub-domain descriptors are derived from a frozen SAM encoder, so if this backbone fails to capture highly specialized medical textures, sub-domain discovery and expert specialization may be suboptimal. Lack of explicit 3D modeling: The approach operates slice wise in 2D and does not explicitly enforce inter-slice or volumetric consistency, which is important for many 3D medical segmentation tasks. Incomplete statistical analysis: While mean values and 95% confidence intervals are reported, there are no formal significance tests (e.g., paired t tests or Wilcoxon tests), so the strength of claims over baselines is not rigorously quantified.

title: E-MRL: Cross-View Aligned Evidence-Driven Multimodal Reinforcement Learning for Reliable 3D Tumor Analysis
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.This paper investigates the critical issues of visual hallucination and lack of visual grounding in medical vision-language models for 3D tumor analysis and clinical applications. 2.The framework design is clear and intuitive. The proposed diagnosis–localization–verification pipeline is easy to understand and aligns well with the workflow of radiologists, improving interpretability compared to purely end-to-end text generation models. 3.The method strengthens visual grounding by requiring the model to predict a key evidence slice and verify it through a local re-query process, thereby linking textual predictions to visual evidence. 4.The combination of tumor existence, fine-grained attribute supervision, and cross-view consistency provides richer training signals than standard text-based objectives. 5.The consistency between the global report and local slice-level evidence offers a reasonable way to reduce hallucination and improve reliability. 6.The method is compared with multiple strong baselines and demonstrates consistent improvements in both diagnostic accuracy and attribute-level reliability.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.Why is reinforcement learning used? What is the necessity of applying RL in this task? 2.What are the main contributions of the proposed method for this task? 3.Are there no prior works addressing this task? 4.What is the difference between using reinforcement learning and supervised fine-tuning (SFT) for this task? 5.What are the GPU requirements and training time for this method? 6.Does the method overly rely on LLM-based evaluation for reward design? 7.How does reinforcement learning mitigate hallucinations?
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The paper aims to address an important failure mode of medical VLMs: generating correct-sounding reports based on language priors rather than actual visual evidence. The analogy to radiologist workflow is reasonable. The cross-view consistency alignment is also intuitive and reasonable.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The SFT process lacks sufficient explanation. As shown in Tables 1 and 2, the most substantial performance gains appear to stem from the SFT stage. However, neither the training corpus nor its construction process is clearly described in the paper. A more detailed explanation of these components is necessary to evaluate the validity and reproducibility of the proposed approach. 2.The use of the “3D” concept in this paper warrants further clarification. Although the model takes CT scans as input by treating them as video sequences, this type of input arguably constitutes a 2D+1D representation, as the information is derived solely from the axial view. The authors should clarify whether this truly qualifies as 3D processing and address this distinction more explicitly. 3.Several existing works have similarly employed lesion localization methods to enhance MLLMs’ lesion-grounded reasoning and diagnostic capabilities [1][2]. The paper would benefit from a more thorough discussion of how the proposed method differs from and compares to these CT-grounded reasoning models, in order to better contextualize the contributions and provide a more comprehensive analysis. [1] Wu, Linshan, Jiaxin Zhuang, and Hao Chen. “Glance and Focus Reinforcement for Pan-cancer Screening.” arXiv preprint arXiv:2601.19103 (2026). [2] Li, Yifan, et al. “MedReason-R1: Learning to Reason for CT Diagnosis with Reinforcement Learning and Local Zoom.” arXiv preprint arXiv:2510.19626 (2025).
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The paper tackles an important and clinically relevant problem: visually grounded 3D CT tumor report generation. A key strength is the evidence-driven design, where the model is required to generate both a global report and a key evidence slice, followed by local slice re-query for verification. This provides a more interpretable and visually grounded alternative to standard text-only report optimization. The multi-granularity reward, combining tumor existence, lesion attributes, and cross-view/local evidence consistency, is well aligned with clinically meaningful reporting requirements. The evaluation is also relatively comprehensive, covering commercial VLMs, 2D and 3D medical VLMs, RadGPT, SFT baselines, reward ablations, and both diagnostic and visual-grounding metrics.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.Limited algorithmic novelty. The MDP framing and GRPO-style process optimization are not fundamentally new; autoregressive VLM generation can already be cast as an MDP, and prior work has explored GRPO/process supervision and medical VLM RL. The more specific contribution is an application-driven combination of key-slice localization, local re-query, and reward design, rather than a new RL framework. The paper itself cites related medical VLM/RL or grounding works such as MedVLM-R1, Med3D-R1, VALOR, and MedMO. 2.Evaluation has potential circularity and judge-dependence. Fine-grained rewards and metrics rely on Qwen-235B judging size, location, and enhancement. In addition, the authors state that Table 2 uses RadGPT-generated fine-grained reports as references, which weakens the clinical validity of the attribute and grounding evaluation. 3.The RL gain over SFT is moderate, and baseline fairness is unclear. The largest improvement comes from SFT: average B-Acc increases from 53.55% to 83.57%, while E-MRL further improves it to 87.93%. Thus, the specific contribution of the proposed RL component is smaller than the overall headline gain. It is also unclear whether commercial and 2D VLM baselines receive comparable 3D visual inputs. 4.Reproducibility and presentation issues. Important details are missing, including GRPO group size, update steps, KL/clipping hyperparameters, judge prompts, key-slice parsing failures, and 3D volume preprocessing. The writing and formatting also need polishing, with grammar issues, inconsistent quotation marks/fonts, and typos.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for the constructive feedback. We respectly respond as follows. @R1-Q2, R4-Q1 Main contribution. We clarify that our key innovation is not a general policy optimization algorithm, but a diagnosis-localization-verification reasoning framework for CT tumor report generation. The model first performs a global diagnosis on the full CT and predicts a key slice for local reasoning. And we introduce a novel cross-view consistency reward to encourage reliable evidence localization. Accordingly, the main contributions are: (1) extend one-shot report generation to two-stage reasoning. (2) enforce global-local consistency via key-slice re-query. (3) shift the optimization target from text to evidence-grounded correctness, mitigating hallucination. @R2-Q1, R4-Q3, R1-Q1457 The distinct roles and implementation details of SFT and RL. Our results show that general-purpose models(e.g. Qwen, commercial models), perform poorly on tumor tasks, making SFT necessary for domain-specific initialization and explaining the gain from 53.55 to 83.57.However, SFT mainly fits the text distribution and lacks interpretability and reliability. Our evidence-based RL improves lesion-attribute correctness and evidence-grounding, which are more clinically relevant to radiologists. On attribute VQA(Tab 2), our E-MRL improves over SFT from 57.49 to 67.53(+17.5%). In implementation, we built ~9.2K single-organ SFT samples from AbdomenAtlas3.0 with mask-derived key-slice supervision. For RL, we select about 2K hard cases with incorrect attribute predictions for targeted optimization. title: EA-LDM: Explicit Alignment Latent Diffusion Model for Patient-Specific CT Reconstruction from Bi-planar X-Rays
reviewer_1_strengths: This paper focuses on the registration of intraoperative X-ray images with preoperative CT by leveraging CT reconstruction from only two biplanar X-ray views (anteroposterior and lateral). The proposed method incorporates patient-specific modeling and optimization, enabling it to account for inter-patient variability as well as temporal anatomical changes that may occur between preoperative imaging and surgery. These features enhance its suitability for real-world clinical applications. The approach has been extensively validated on standard datasets and demonstrates competitive performance when compared with existing state-of-the-art methods in the literature.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The paper remains overly generalized, and does not adequately address how the proposed framework can be adapted or customized to different anatomical regions. While the methodology is presented as broadly applicable, there is limited discussion on anatomy-specific constraints, variations, or the need for specialized modeling strategies. Although the RADCURE dataset (focused on oropharyngeal anatomy) is used for evaluation, the paper does not clearly explain how the algorithm is trained or tailored for this specific anatomical domain. In particular, it is unclear whether the model incorporates anatomy-aware priors or whether it relies purely on generic feature learning. Furthermore, the use of pretrained CT-based weights for processing X-ray inputs raises concerns. Given the inherent domain gap between CT volumes and X-ray projections, such pretrained representations may not yield meaningful latent features for accurate 2D-to-3D reconstruction. A more detailed justification or domain adaptation strategy is needed. A central challenge that is insufficiently addressed is the reconstruction of a 3D volume from only two biplanar X-ray images (AP and lateral). This is a highly ill-posed problem, and the paper does not convincingly demonstrate how the proposed method overcomes the associated ambiguities. Additionally, the availability of preoperative CT scans suggests that the problem could instead be formulated as a 2D–3D registration task. In such a scenario, intraoperative X-rays could be registered to the preoperative CT, allowing surgical planning to proceed directly on the CT data without requiring full 3D reconstruction. The paper does not provide a clear comparison or justification for choosing reconstruction over registration. In this context, the motivation for employing EA-LDM for 3D reconstruction needs to be more explicitly articulated. Specifically, the advantages of this approach should be clearly contrasted against conventional 2D–3D registration methods in terms of accuracy, robustness, computational efficiency, and clinical utility.

author_feedback: We thank all reviewers for their insightful comments. Adaptation to Specific Anatomical Structures [R1-1/2] EA-LDM is not limited to a specific anatomy, but a general framework for CT reconstruction. Through Patient-Specific Optimization (PSO) on the patient’s own pCT, the model learns detailed anatomical priors and enables adaptation to temporal anatomical changes. Moreover, region-specific loss can further boost performance. Its robustness has been validated on complex head and neck data. Domain Gap Problem [R1-3] We clarify that the Alignment Network (AN, Fig. 2) is designed for X-rays, so CT pretrained weights are not directly applied. We agree that a domain gap does exist. However, a shared latent semantic representation has been validated for reconstruction [1] since both rely on kV X-rays and similar attenuation. We thank Reviewer 1 for pointing out a promising future research direction regarding the domain gap. Ill-posed Nature [R1-4] For the ill-posed nature, we emphasize that exact reconstruction is unattainable; our goal is to approximate the ground truth by leveraging priors, e.g., patient-specific priors from pCT. Experiment results showed our method achieved best performance by exploiting these priors. Why not Registration or Limited-angle CT [R1-5, R3-4] Adaptive Radiotherapy (ART) requires updated 3D tissue density for dose optimization. 2D-3D registration is insufficient as it estimates only position. Limited-angle CT takes 10–30s to acquire 30–100 projections, causing image degradation from organ motion (e.g., peristalsis) and higher radiation. Clinical Application [R1-6, R3-1/2] Radiotherapy is a cancer treatment using radiation to destroy tumors, delivered over multiple fractions across several weeks. In the standard ART workflow, a planning CT (pCT) is first acquired, on which the clinical target and radiation dose are determined. At each fraction, CBCT is acquired from the onboard kV system for patient setup and plan optimization (e.g., dose optimization) before treatment, which is time-consuming, high-dose, and increases complication risks. Therefore, our application directly utilizes the bi-planar X-ray mode of the same kV system to reconstruct CT volumes, offering a faster, lower-dose substitute for CBCT. Moreover, as the anatomy constantly changes over the treatment weeks, it is important to reconstruct CT at each fraction rather than relying on the pCT. About the Evaluation [R1-7, R2-2/4] NeRF-based comparison. We clarify that INRR3CT is NeRF-based, which we quantitatively outperform quantitatively (e.g. +2.1 dB PSNR) and qualitatively. Therefore, evaluation with DRRs remains standard in this field [1,2]. meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper proposes EA-LDM, an explicit-alignment latent diffusion model for patient-specific CT reconstruction from bi-planar X-rays. The reviewers recognized the potential clinical relevance of reconstructing or aligning patient-specific 3D anatomy from sparse intraoperative X-ray views, as well as the technical contributions of explicit alignment networks and patient-specific optimization. Some reviewers also considered the paper well structured, with useful ablation studies and competitive quantitative results against recent reconstruction baselines. However, the reviews also identified several important concerns. The clinical motivation and problem formulation are not fully clear, especially why full 3D reconstruction from two X-rays is preferable to conventional 2D–3D registration when preoperative CT is available. Reviewers also raised concerns about the ill-posed nature of reconstructing 3D CT from only AP/lateral X-rays, the lack of validation on real biplanar X-ray images, and unclear adaptation to specific anatomical regions. The use of pretrained CT-based latent representations for X-ray inputs also requires stronger justification given the domain gap. There are additional reproducibility concerns, including undefined hyperparameters, unclear variables in figures, and missing details about cohort sizes and loss weighting. Given the relatively positive scores from two reviewers and the overall quality of the submission, I recommend giving the authors a rebuttal opportunity. The authors should carefully address the reviewers’ concerns during rebuttal. | Despite highly polarized post-rebuttal feedback (Accept, Accept, Reject), the authors’ rebuttal successfully dismantled the negative consensus by resolving core clinical and technical misunderstandings. First, they justified the reconstruction task over traditional 2D-3D registration by explaining that active radiation dose optimization strictly requires updated 3D tissue density volumes rather than mere spatial alignment. Second, they established true clinical utility, showing that pairing instantaneous bi-planar X-rays with historical pCTs accurately captures ongoing temporal anatomical variations (e.g., tumor regression) while entirely bypassing the high radiation dose and minute-long gantry rotations mandated by onboard CBCT or limited-angle scans. Third, they clarified that multi-view rendering baselines were not ignored, as the heavily outperformed baseline INRR3CT is itself a NeRF-based architecture. Backed by a 92-patient clinical cohort demonstrating superior numerical (PSNR/SSIM), visual, and downstream segmentation fidelity, this well-grounded framework satisfies publication standards and is recommended for acceptance. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Authors have adequately addressed comments. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): The clinical scenario targeted by this work remains somewhat controversial. In addition, many technical details and design choices are not clearly explained, and the overall organization of the manuscript needs substantial improvement. Given the considerable amount of revision required, I do not believe the paper is suitable for publication in its current form.

The present study introduces a quadrant formulation to simultaneously handle both. The method performs quadrant-wise, bidirectional optimization, which allows it to selectively reinforce reliable predictions while actively suppressing error-prone ones. The inclusion of a dynamic memory bank further stabilizes this process. This is a novel formulation and the results are promising.

author_feedback: We thank all reviewers. For bounds/sensitivity/repeatability, we had already run these checks. They did not affect the main conclusion, but were omitted due to the page limit. Since rebuttal rules bar new experimental results, we report no new numbers here. If accepted, we will add bounds, q/N sensitivity, and repeatability metrics in the revision, while clarifying design choices below. Q: High-risk quadrant (R2) A: R2 suggested that low-entropy & low-consistency samples may look risky because they resemble confident but unstable predictions. It is intuitive, but ECFR defines high-risk differently: the quadrant with the largest proportion/number of incorrect predictions. This is supported by the zero-shot preliminary study, not intuition alone. In Fig.1(b), samples were split by median entropy and median consistency for comparable quadrant statistics. LCHE had the lowest accuracy and the densest wrong predictions, while LCLE did not. Thus ECFR names LCHE the high-risk zone. We will clarify this definition and the preliminary study. Q: Metric definitions, λ, and thresholds (R1&R2) A: We agree that metric definitions were too compressed due to space. T_w and T_s denote weak and strong stochastic transformations of the same test image. We will define them clearly. In Eq.(2), λ=±1 is not a loss-weight hyperparameter. It only controls direction: +1 minimizes the entropy/JS term, while -1 makes minimizing the signed objective equivalent to maximizing that term. This gives the two opposite flows in Fig.2.For Eq.(3), as stated in Sec.2.3(pp.5-6), thresholds are online FIFO-bank quantiles: τ_H=Q(B_H,q) is the q-quantile of recent entropy values, and τ_D=Q(B_D,q) is the q-quantile of recent JS divergence values. In Sec.3.1, q is 0.5 for ECFR-0.5 or an accuracy prior for ECFR-Acc. Q: Selection and stability of q (R1&R2) A: ECFR-Acc is designed for a prior-informed setting with an overall target-domain reliability estimate from deployment logs, validation records, or a small audit cohort. Since public benchmarks lack such logs, our experiments used zero-shot accuracy as its substitute to set q. This does not use sample labels during online adaptation. It only maps an overall accuracy to the routing quantile. ECFR can do this because its thresholds are adjustable: ECFR-0.5 is the no-prior version and already outperforms other baselines in Table 1, while ECFR-Acc shows how ECFR can use an available reliability prior that most TTA baselines cannot exploit. Our q-sensitivity check supports stable performance near the accuracy range. Prior-free adaptive q selection is future work. Q: Bounds, N sensitivity, and repeatability (R1&R2) A: For bounds, Table 1 reports zero-shot, which is the no-adaptation lower bound. We also checked the label-using upper-bound setting where the model is fully trained on target data. It provides ceiling context but is not a fair comparator to unsupervised online TTA. For the FIFO memory bank, N-sensitivity shows low sensitivity across a broad range, so N=128 is not fragile. For repeatability, different-seed streams show variation much smaller than the Table 1 gaps. These checks support, rather than alter, the submitted conclusion. If accepted, we will add the corresponding metrics to the revision. Q: Rationale, p restoration, and citation issues (R2&R3) A: We agree that “theoretical motivation” is too strong and mainly empirical/heuristic. We will rename it “heuristic motivation” and soften the claims. For stochastic restoration, the exact sentence appears once, but the idea is restated once in Sec.3.1.We will remove this redundancy. p controls reset frequency toward source weights: larger p limits drift/forgetting but weakens target adaptation, while smaller p adapts more freely but raises forgetting risk. For citation, we will replace the mismatched reference with Ahmad et al., Quant. Imaging Med. Surg. 16(4):321 (2026), a review on real-world shift/robustness in CXR foundation models.

title: ECLIPSE: EHR-Constrained Localized Inference for Pan-Tumor Segmentation
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The problem formulation is clear and clinically meaningful. Instead of vaguely claiming that EHR information may help segmentation, the paper identifies a more specific issue: image-only coarse spatial hypotheses may be clinically implausible, and structured descriptors such as subregion, lesion count, and tumor size can serve as feasibility constraints during hypothesis generation. 2.The proposed pipeline is logically coherent. The method follows a clear sequence of coarse visual localization, clinically constrained hypothesis selection, and prompt-based refinement. This is much more convincing than a loosely assembled multimodal design. 3.The role of structured clinical information is better motivated than in many prior multimodal segmentation papers. Here, EHR descriptors are assigned explicit functional roles in spatial inference, rather than being simply concatenated as additional features. 4.The empirical gains appear substantial across datasets, suggesting that the overall framework is effective and that structured clinical priors may indeed improve pan-tumor segmentation performance.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The main concern relates to pseudo EHR descriptors in experiments. For public datasets without available EHR, the authors generate pseudo descriptors from the ground-truth masks is understandable given the scarcity of public datasets with structured EHR. However, it remains important to clarify whether the private Colon-FD cohort uses real EHR-derived descriptors or similarly generated pseudo descriptors. And it would also be helpful to explain how the pseudo descriptors are generated from the ground-truth masks for the public datasets. If Colon-FD indeed uses real structured clinical information, then this concern is largely alleviated and the paper would have a much stronger clinical grounding. 2.Several implementation details are not sufficiently specified. In particular, the definition of the parameter α in box generation is unclear, the role of “FC” in the framework figure is not explicitly explained, and in formula 11 may contain a notation inconsistency or requires clarification. These issues do not appear to undermine the overall method, but they reduce clarity and reproducibility. Manuscript only states that a combined Dice and BCE loss is applied, without clearly defining the exact formulation, weighting, or whether both stages follow the same supervision scheme. 3.The ablation section could also be clearer. In Table 2, the exact configuration of the “Baseline” is not clearly defined. In addition, since CCHG is the core methodological contribution and consists of multiple feasibility constraints, the paper would be strengthened by including internal ablations within CCHG. This is a relatively minor issue compared with the main methodological concern above, but it would still help readers better understand what is being ablated.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The method demonstrates consistent and clinically meaningful improvements over four established baselines across all seven tumor types The ablation study clearly demonstrates the necessity of the CCHG module The integration of EHR descriptors as soft spatial constraints is a clinically motivated and novel approach
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Major: The evaluation relies exclusively on DSC. The dataset composition is insufficiently described. Are some tumor types severely underrepresented? No limitations section is present. Minor: Figure 1 requires significant magnification to read and Figure 2 lacks numbers and descriptions that are only introduced later in the text The CCHG module is introduced and described multiple times throughout the paper unnecessarily. The DSC gains are ranging from 3.88% to 8.91%, but the authors do not discuss the clinical relevance of these margins or cite supporting literature. Runtime is not reported, which is relevant for clinical deployment assessment The bibliography does not conform to MICCAI formatting guidelines.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The most appealing aspect of the paper is its attempt to connect clinical reporting logic with spatial segmentation. Many recent universal or prompt-based medical segmentation methods still rely on generic image prompts, while this work asks a more clinically grounded question: if radiologists already record lesion count, approximate size, and anatomical subregion, can these descriptors narrow the spatial search space for tumor segmentation? This is a meaningful perspective, especially for pan-tumor segmentation where purely image-driven models may produce diffuse or anatomically implausible responses. Another strength is that the proposed CCHG module has an intuitive role in the pipeline. The module does not merely concatenate EHR features with image features; instead, it operationalizes clinical descriptors as constraints on where and how many lesions should be proposed. This makes the method easier to understand than many black-box multimodal fusion strategies. The improvement from the baseline to baseline+CCHG is also large, suggesting that the constraint mechanism is doing something substantial rather than serving as a cosmetic component. The paper also makes a reasonable effort to evaluate generalization across different tumor sites. The inclusion of an unseen adrenal tumor dataset and a private Colon-FD cohort gives the work more clinical breadth than a single-organ study. The qualitative results are consistent with the stated motivation: ECLIPSE appears to reduce anatomically implausible spillover and produce more localized tumor masks than several universal segmentation baselines. This supports the broader claim that structured clinical priors can help suppress false positives in heterogeneous pan-tumor scenarios.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The chosen baselines are mostly universal or prompt-based segmentation models, but the paper does not compare with strong CT tumor segmentation pipelines trained or adapted for the same organs, such as nnU-Net-style organ-specific or tumor-specific baselines. This matters because the proposed method receives highly informative clinical constraints, whereas some baselines may receive only point or text prompts. The comparison, therefore, mixes two questions: whether ECLIPSE is a better segmentation model, and whether extra localization information helps segmentation. A fairer evaluation would include strong 3D CT tumor baselines, organ-specific expert models, and a setting where the same EHR-derived boxes or constraints are provided to competing promptable models. The formulation of the tumor-type prompt and class input is underspecified. The method assumes a tumor-type prompt, but the paper does not clearly define where this prompt comes from at inference time, whether it is extracted from EHR, manually selected, or assumed to be known. This is not a small implementation detail, because in pan-tumor CT segmentation, the model must know whether it is searching for a liver tumor, a kidney tumor, a lung tumor, an adrenal tumor, or multiple possible lesions. If the class is externally provided, the task becomes segmentation of known clinical findings rather than open pan-tumor detection. If the class is not externally provided, the paper needs to explain how the organ or tumor type is inferred. Relatedly, the current CCHG descriptor E = (r, n, d) appears too simplistic for realistic multifocal and multi-organ disease. A patient may have lesions in different organs, with different diameters and different anatomical subregions. The paper evaluates a “mixed tumor” dataset, but it is not clear whether it handles a single CT volume containing simultaneous heterogeneous tumor types, such as liver and kidney tumors in the same scan. The current description suggests a single tumor-type prompt, a single subregion descriptor, and a single longest-diameter parameter for box expansion. This may not generalize to multi-lesion cases where each lesion has its own organ, size, and location descriptor. The evaluation is also too narrow. Reporting only DSC does not sufficiently characterize tumor segmentation performance. Tumor segmentation is highly sensitive to small lesions, lesion-level detection, false positives outside plausible organs, and boundary accuracy. Metrics such as HD95, NSD, lesion-wise recall/precision, false-positive volume, count consistency, and small-lesion stratified performance would provide a much clearer picture. This is particularly important here because the method explicitly claims improvements in localization, count consistency, and anatomically constrained prediction, but the evaluation does not directly measure these properties.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the AC and reviewers for their constructive feedback and for recognizing the clinical motivation (R2, R3, R5), methodological novelty (R2, R3, R5), and potential practical value (R3, R5) of our work. Below, we address the reviewers’ comments point by point. 1) Pseudo-EHR descriptors and Colon-FD clinical grounding (R2-Q1, R5): ECLIPSE targets EHR-constrained pan-tumor segmentation of suspected clinical findings. Colon-FD uses real clinical EHR, where tumor type, lesion count, maximal diameter, and coarse anatomical location are extracted from clinical records. For public datasets without released EHR, pseudo descriptors only simulate such clinical EHR information: lesion count is obtained by connected-component analysis, maximal diameter by the largest physical lesion extent, and anatomical subregion by the overlap with predefined organ subregions. 2) Baselines and fair comparisons (R5-Q1): For strong CT tumor baselines, we selected recent SOTA universal/prompt-based models because they are most relevant to ECLIPSE and have been benchmarked against nnU-Net-style pipelines in several prior studies, such as Universal Model or MA-SAM. Unlike point prompts that directly mark tumor locations, ECLIPSE infers feasible tumor regions from clinically available EHR descriptors without manually specified tumor points. Due to page limits and rebuttal policy, we will clarify this choice and provide more detailed comparisons in an extended version. 3) Tumor-type prompt and multi-organ disease (R5-Q2/Q3): The tumor-type prompt is obtained from the EHR, where tumor type and subregion have already been preliminarily identified, as described in Sec. Introduction and Fig. 1(b). Importantly, MSWAL is a public mixed-tumor dataset, with many scans containing multiple tumor types or lesions from different organs. For such cases, ECLIPSE processes each tumor finding separately with its own prompt and EHR descriptor, and then merges the masks. The MSWAL results support this strategy. 4) Evaluation beyond DSC (R3-Q1, R5-Q4): We agree that additional metrics may provide complementary perspectives. In the submitted manuscript, we used DSC as the primary metric because it is widely adopted in tumor segmentation benchmarks and enables consistent comparison across all baselines and datasets. The qualitative results in Fig. 3 provide complementary visual evidence. Following the rebuttal policy, we do not introduce new metrics here. A more comprehensive evaluation will be provided in the journal version. 5) Implementation details (R1-Q2): We clarify that α is a safety-margin coefficient for expanding the EHR-reported tumor size d into a loose segmentation box. “FC” denotes a Fully Connected layer, and S in Eq. 11 is the spatial response map from Eq. 5.The training loss is Dice+BCE with 1:1 weighting for both stages. 6) Ablation study (R2-Q3): The “Baseline” in Table 2 denotes the model before CCHG, namely the ViT and CLIP encoders with multimodal fusion followed by the decoder, as described in Sec. 2.1 and Fig. 2.CCHG further introduces three feasibility constraints: anatomical subregion for regional coherence, lesion count for cardinality consistency, and tumor size for scale plausibility. As these complementary constraints are methodological necessities for generating clinically plausible tumor masks, we omitted internal ablations due to page limits; but we will clarify the baseline configuration and the role of each CCHG component. 7) Dataset, limitations, and presentation (R3-Q2/Q3): The dataset composition is summarized in Fig. 1 with corresponding references; we did not include an additional dataset table due to page limits. reviewer_3_strengths: 1.Novelty: The proposed solution is well suited to the application domain. The authors incorporate deformation field statistics into the conformal prediction (CP) framework, addressing a gap that, to my knowledge, has not been explored in existing methods. The manner of incorporation is also meaningful rather than superficial. In particular, the choice of nonconformity score, based on the absolute error of the volume scaling factor, is domain-specific and differs from standard residual- or quantile-based approaches. This design is supported by a clear rationale, namely that multiplicative errors in the deformation propagate multiplicatively to the scalar target. 2.Rigorous Analysis: The authors provide a comprehensive evaluation by analyzing both coverage and interval size across global, regional, and label-wise volumetry. In addition, they examine the regression model to provide interpretability, with results that support the usefulness of deformation field statistics in datasets where ConVOLT shows improved performance. The paper also offers a reasonable explanation for the comparatively weaker performance on the NLST dataset when using the Demons registration method.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.Formulation: The proposed method relies on an intermediate regressor to predict the volume scaling factor from deformation field statistics, and then applies conformal prediction to the residuals of this regressor. It is not clear why this two-step approach is necessary. An alternative formulation could directly condition the conformal prediction procedure on the deformation-derived features. For example, by using quantile regression with these features to predict intervals for the volumes. This would eliminate the need for the intermediate regression step. The authors could clarify why the current design provides advantages over a more direct conditioning approach. 2.Data Split: The data split (10/15/5) for ThoraxCBCT raises concerns as it results in a test set of only 5 samples. This makes it difficult to draw reliable conclusions about coverage and interval efficiency. With 5 samples, coverage can only be evaluated in increments of 20%, and this is reflected in a relatively large standard deviation of coverage (0.14), indicating high variability. Additionally, the calibration sets is unusually large relative to the dataset size (0.4/0.4/0.2, 10/15/5), raising questions about why such a large calibration set is needed and whether the method requires it to achieve stable coverage. 3.Baselines: The authors mention CQR (conditional quantile regression) as a baseline but cite Conformalized Quantile Regression. Can the authors clarify whether Conformalized Quantile Regression was actually used? Additionally, it is unclear what features were used for CQR — the only indication provided is that “residual volumetric variability is largely explained by volume magnitude itself.” 4.Ablation: Which features are considered localized and which are global? Additionally, can the authors explain the reduction in prediction interval size for VoxelMorph on ThoraxCBCT?

author_feedback: We sincerely thank the reviewers and AC for the constructive feedback. We are glad that reviewers found our work novel and well evaluated (R2, R3). We focus on the top concerns. Applicability/timeliness (R1,M): We respectfully clarify that registration/template-based volumetry remains relevant despite modern direct segmentation. ConVOLT targets settings where registration remains central: atlas-defined anatomical consistency and atlas/template deployment (OASIS), and longitudinal/respiratory analyses requiring dense correspondence or regional volume change (ThoraxCBCT, NLST). Such settings remain actively studied in volumetric deformable registration (e.g., VoxelMorph/TransMorph/HyperMorph/SynthMorph, Learn2Reg). Moreover, ConVOLT is not restricted to classical “non-ML” registration: we evaluate using VoxelMorph, a learning-based registration method. R1’s point about multi-atlas and hybrid deep-registration methods is therefore complementary rather than disqualifying — any pipeline that estimates deformation fields exposes the geometric quantities that ConVOLT leverages for efficient volumetric UQ. For direct segmenters, an analogous extension would use logits, embeddings, feature maps, or probabilities. Sample size for ThoraxCBCT (R3,M): We agree ThoraxCBCT is small. With 5 test cases, split-level coverage is coarse and variable; under a simple binomial approximation with marginal coverage near 0.9, test noise alone gives sqrt(0.9*0.1/5)=0.13, close to the observed SD=0.14.We included it because it is a clinically relevant low-sample registration benchmark from Learn2Reg. The 15-case calibration split was chosen because split CP at alpha=0.1 estimates an upper conformal quantile; fewer calibration cases would make this more discrete/conservative. This applies to all split-CP methods, not only to ConVOLT. ConVOLT features (R1-R3,M): We clarify that ConVOLT features are listed in the “Experimental Protocol” with notation from the problem setup. ConVOLT features were chosen a priori to summarize quantities expected to reflect registration difficulty: Jacobian statistics for expansion/contraction, Jacobian quantiles and folding fractions for extreme local volume changes, displacement and grad log-J/divergence/curl summaries for deformation magnitude and spatial irregularity, and fixed-warped similarity residuals for residual mismatch. Global experiments compute features over the full mask; regional/label experiments compute the same feature types restricted to the region/boundary. ConVOLT versus CQR (R3,M): We agree that CQR conditioned on deformation features is a reasonable alternative, but it lacks ConVOLT’s structural constraints. Mapping a conformal interval in beta-space back to volume preserves non-negativity and scales interval width with the predicted volume. It separates point correction from uncertainty calibration: one ridge regressor estimates an interpretable multiplicative correction, while split CP supplies the finite-sample-valid radius. It also reduces the estimation burden in small-data and label-wise settings by using a single regressor rather than two conditional quantile regressors per target. Finally, coefficients directly indicate deformation features associated with multiplicative volumetric bias, whereas CQR has separate lower- and upper-quantile models whose effects on interval size are less transparent. Baselines (R3,M): SCP uses no conditioning features; LCP conditions on |Yhat^0| using local calibration; CQR is conformalized quantile regression and conditions on baseline volume/change. These output-space baselines intentionally do not use registration internals, because the central comparison is whether deformation-aware calibration improves over black-box/output-space calibration. Minor clarifications (R1,R2): We used closed-form ridge regression with an unpenalized intercept and fixed lambda=1e-2.We used NCC similarity, a standard VoxelMorph-style objective.

title: Efficient Flow Matching for Sparse-View CT Reconstruction
reviewer_1_strengths: This is a novel and well-motivated approach that could become an important direction for flow-matching-based CT reconstruction, especially in the case of large volumes where computational cost is critical. The idea of reusing the velocity field is simple yet effective, and the empirical observation that consecutive velocities are similar is convincing. The method has strong practical relevance and the experimental results support the claimed efficiency gains.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: It seems to me that there is a problem in the proof. The current proof is based on an update of the form x_{k+1} = DC(x_k - Delta t v_tk (x_tk)) and xhat_{k+1} = DC(x_k - Delta t v_tk0 (x_tk0)) with DC kappa-non-expansive. However, the update defined in (6) and (7) is x_{k+1} = x’_k+1 + DC(x_tk - tk v_tk(x_tk)) with x’_k+1 = x_k - Delta t v_tk (x_tk). With this model, the error |delta_k+1| is bounded by (kappa + 1) |delta_k| + (tk*kappa + Delta t) | v_tk - v_tk0 |. With this upper bound, I find that |delta_k0+M| is O(Delta t) and not O(Delta t^2). The authors should carefully re-examine the proof and modify the statement if necessary. Minor There is a notation clash between xhat_0 (the expected non-noisy image E(x0 | x1)) and xhat_k (the alternative algorithm). The Euler scheme in the single step error part corresponds to the image-to-noise ODE, while the rest of the paper considers sampling from noise to image. This should be clarified.

reviewer_2_weaknesses: I particularly like the paper’s proposed strategy for reducing NFEs, as it is both intuitive and well motivated. reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The motivation of accelerating CT reconstruction is convincing and potentially useful for clinical practice. 2.The authors attempted to provide theoretical guarantees for their proposed method, which is essential for its reliable use and often neglected in the field.

author_feedback: We thank all reviewers for their positive assessment (novelty, motivation, practical relevance) and constructive feedback. We address the concerns below. Issues in proof(R1R3) We carefully re-examined the proof and agree there was a discrepancy between the theoretical formulation and the actual update rule. The previous proof modeled the DC step on the current state, while the actual algorithm applies DC to the estimated clean image. We revised the proof by: 1)unifying notation (x̃) for the reuse trajectory, 2)consistently using the reverse noise-to-image ODE, and 3)explicitly modeling DC on the estimated clean image. The single-step bound remains O(Δt²), matching Euler local truncation error, while the accumulated deviation over one reuse block becomes O(M²Δt), rather than O(M²Δt²). We corrected the proposition and adjusted the claims accordingly. The complete proof will be released in the public repository. DC operation(R2R3) We use conjugate gradient [Fletcher 1964] as the DC operation because it efficiently solves the least-squares problem (AᵀA+γI)x=x̂₀+Aᵀy. Compared with directly injecting L1/L2 gradients into the generative process, the decoupled optimization is less sensitive to delicate guidance-step tuning since DC refinement is separated from generative transport dynamics. Choice of baselines/lack of CT-specific methods(R2) Our goal is not to outperform every recent CT-specific diffusion variant, but to investigate whether flow matching can serve as an efficient alternative to diffusion-based solvers. We therefore selected representative baselines covering different DC strategies: DPS (posterior sampling), MCG (manifold guidance), PGDM (pseudo-inverse guidance), and DDS (decoupled CG refinement). Recent benchmark (DM4CT, ICLR2026) suggests many diffusion-based CT methods (including more recent ones) achieve comparable reconstruction quality while differing substantially in computational cost. Motivated by this, our focus is introducing flow matching for sparse-view CT reconstruction and improving efficiency through velocity reuse, rather than incremental PSNR gains over every recent diffusion variant. We agree that adding more recent CT-specific baselines would further strengthen the evaluation and will clarify this limitation in updated version. Perceptual metrics LPIPS(R2) We computed LPIPS and will include it in the revised version. Although ADMM-TV achieves slightly higher PSNR/SSIM than FMCT on AAPM 40-view reconstruction, its LPIPS is substantially worse (ADMM 0.272 vs FMCT 0.101/EFMCT 0.129), indicating weaker perceptual detail preservation. Reuse strategy for diffusion/Poisson noise(R2) Due to the stochastic SDE nature of diffusion models, we empirically observe that score reuse is less stable for diffusion than for flow matching, often requiring more iterations and producing worse reconstructions. Under noisy measurements, DC corrections become less stable and interrupt reuse steps more frequently, although the strategy remains effective under moderate noise levels. We will include this in the discussion. Training details and fairness(R2) The diffusion and flow models use identical architectures, datasets, optimizers, and training settings. The primary difference is the learning target: diffusion learns score, while flow matching learns the velocity field. We will add training details into the paper. Velocity similarity drop near final steps(R2) We empirically observe that final sampling stages perform the most detailed refinement, leading to larger velocity deviations and lower cosine similarity. Accordingly, our initial implementation disables reuse in the final stages(flow_recon.py, line 88). Geometry choice(R2) We use parallel-beam geometry to provide a controlled setting isolating reconstruction methodology from geometry-specific acquisition factors. Nevertheless, (E)FMCT remains geometry-agnostic. Preliminary fan-beam experiments show similar trends in reconstruction quality and acceleration.

reviewer_3_strengths: The paper addresses an important and underexplored problem in medical image analysis: class-incremental learning in settings where new disease or cell categories may be introduced over time without full retraining. This is clinically relevant because medical datasets are often expanded gradually, and models need to preserve prior knowledge while learning new categories. A major strength is the clear methodological motivation. The authors identify a mismatch between standard random projection and the geometry of medical image features. Random projection treats all feature directions equally, whereas medical image features may have an anisotropic spectrum in which only some directions are highly discriminative. The proposed eigen-directed projection is a reasonable and technically interesting way to exploit this structure. The experimental evaluation is broad. The paper compares 14 class-incremental learning methods across 4 medical datasets, which makes the empirical contribution useful even beyond the proposed method itself. The finding that analytic classifier-based methods outperform several recent CLIP-based, prompt-based, and LoRA-based methods in this setting is valuable and worth reporting. The ablation study is also a strength. The results suggest that eigen-directed projection and random projection provide complementary benefits. In particular, the ablation showing that EDP alone improves performance over the baseline, and that adding RP further improves performance, supports the claim that the two components are not redundant. The ChestX results are particularly notable. EDRP appears to substantially outperform several competitors on this difficult benchmark, with relatively low variance. This suggests potential robustness in a challenging medical imaging setting where many methods perform poorly. The method is computationally attractive because it is training-free and uses analytic classifier learning. This makes it potentially practical for medical imaging scenarios where repeated retraining may be expensive or difficult.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: A key weakness is that some implementation details are underspecified. The feature buffer is central to the proposed method, but the paper does not clearly explain how it is constructed, how many samples it stores, whether it remains fixed or grows as new tasks arrive, and how memory scales with the number of tasks. Since the paper claims memory efficiency, this point needs to be clarified. If the buffer grows with the number of tasks, the memory advantage over RanPAC or related methods may be less convincing in longer class-incremental sequences. The ChestX comparison table appears incomplete. Table 2 includes RanPAC, InfLoRA, PROOF, and joint training, but it does not include some of the closest competitors from Table 1, such as SLDA and LoRanPAC. Since the ChestX results are one of the strongest empirical claims in the paper, the comparison should include the most relevant competing methods, or the authors should explain why they were omitted. The dual-view mapping algorithm needs more detail. The authors do not clearly specify how the projection dimension is split between the random projection branch and the eigen-directed branch. This is important for reproducibility and for understanding how sensitive the method is to this design choice. The paper would benefit from a clearer analysis of forgetting over time. A plot showing accuracy after each new task is introduced would help readers understand whether the method preserves old knowledge better than competitors, rather than only improving final or average accuracy. The experiments appear to rely on a ViT-B/16 backbone. The anisotropic spectrum argument is plausible for ViT features, but it may not generalize to CNN-based encoders or other pretrained feature extractors. Testing the method with an additional backbone, or explicitly acknowledging this as a limitation, would strengthen the paper. There are also minor presentation issues. Figure 5 could be improved by making the class mean markers more visible. There are small writing issues, including the typo “dirven” on page 5.Some explanatory sentences, such as the statement about discriminative cues lying outside the dominant subspace, should be rewritten for clarity.

author_feedback: We sincerely thank all reviewers. We’re glad to receive three posititve scores of 5/4/4.We carefully address concerns below and code will be released in revision. Q1: Modest extension of RanPAC (R1). A1: We respectfully clarify that EDRP is not a drop-in replacement. Our work follows a complete pipeline: (1)benchmarking that reveals classifier-based methods unexpectedly outperform alternatives in medical CIL; (2)margin-theoretic analysis showing separability is bottlenecked by the weakest projection directions; (3)diagnosing the mismatch between isotropic projection and anisotropic medical spectra; (4)a dual-view design where each component contributes non-redundantly, with a memory reduction. Q2: More backbones (R1, R3). A2: We first want to kindly clarify that our framework is backbone-agnostic, and the benefit of eigen-directed projection is orthogonal to backbone choice, since Fig. 2b is a general property of ViT embeddings regardless of pretraining data. We have conducted the evaluation on medical-domain backbones on Skin8, EDRP consistently outperforms RanPAC and LoRanPAC (e.g., +2.56% and +2.30% Last Acc on BioMed, +1.51% and +1.75% Last Acc on UniMed). Q3: Non-shuffled setting on MedMNIST-Sub (R1). A3: The shuffling protocol we initially designed was intended to simulate a complicated multidisciplinary consultation scenario. In the non-shuffled configuration, our EDRP still maintains its advantage over both RanPAC and LoRanPAC (e.g., +1.08% and +14.98% Acc), further indicating the generality of our method. Q4: Low performance of most methods on ChestX (R2). A4: Prior work Star-Prompt reports joint training with only 48.92% Acc on ChestX, consistent with our Table 2.The reason for such low performance lies in intrinsic dataset difficulty. Even so, our EDRP still achieves the highest accuracy. Q5: Buffer scalability (R2, R3). A5: Unlike prior medical CIL methods that store raw images for replay (e.g., ACL), our feature buffer stores only compact ViT embeddings (768-dim per sample), which is approximately 196 times more compact than a single image (224×224×3). This efficiency allows us to buffer 80% of per-class samples’ embeddings for more accurate eigenspace estimation. Although RanPAC’ buffer size does not change with the number of tasks, it needs to store a full M²-dimensional covariance matrix (e.g., M=10^4), which ovbiously exceeds our total storage as shown in Table 5.Q6: Missing forgetting metrics (R2, R3). A6: EDRP achieves a BWT of −12.50% vs. RanPAC’s −13.84% on Skin8, indicating less forgetting. We will include forgetting metrics in revision. Thanks. Q7: Incomplete comparison on ChestX (R3). A7: In our original experiments, EDRP consistently outperformed SLDA by +11.62%, RanPAC by +17.47%, and LoRanPAC by +3.70%. However, SLDA and LoRanPAC were omitted from Table 2 as they were unstable across seeds and showed no obvious advantage. We’ll clarify in revision. Thanks. Q8: Projection dimension split (R3). A8: M is evenly split: M_f = M_a = M/2; we’ll clarify this point in revision. Q9: Algorithm classification in Fig.1 (R4). A9: Thanks for carefully reading our work. The Classifier-based category refers to methods keeping the backbone frozen with only classifier updates. While these methods do use pre-trained ViTs, they differ from the Pre-trained ViT-based category, which adapts the backbone via prompts/LoRA. We will clarify this distinction. Q10: Buffer contents and privacy (R4). A10: The buffer stores compact ViT embeddings that cannot be inverted to reconstruct original images, offering privacy advantages. Q11: Shuffling and first-session adaptation (FSA) (R4). A11: Category shuffling means we randomly reorder the 36 classes from MedMNIST’s four sub-datasets across tasks. The FSA strategy, originally proposed in RanPAC, applies a lightweight adapter on task 1 before freezing the backbone to improve downstream feature quality. Q12: Presentation issues (R3, R4). A12: We’ll fix all these minor issues. Thanks.
