reviewer_3_strengths: The technical contributions are noteworthy: B-CosASAP effectively provides artifact-free explanations and improved localization without compromising predictive performance. Furthermore, B-CosBP addresses the common issue of aliasing-prone downsampling by incorporating spatial blurring, resulting in superior explanation quality and localization accuracy. The authors have validated the efficiency and robustness of their proposed approaches through empirical experiments using two widely recognized public datasets, RSNA and VinBigData (VinBigXray).
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.Insufficient Presentation of Empirical Results While the authors claim that the proposed approach outperforms existing attribution methods, it is difficult to be fully convinced of its efficiency based on the current manuscript. In the experiments section, various metrics (Accuracy, AUROC, Recall, EPG micro Precision/Recall) are presented in Figure 3.However, relying solely on a performance comparison chart is insufficient for a rigorous technical evaluation. Notably, several lines in the plots overlap, making it impossible to distinguish the specific performance of each method. To improve clarity and facilitate a detailed comparison, the authors should provide a comprehensive table including the exact numerical values and statistical summaries rather than relying on cluttered figures. 2.Lack of Statistical Rigor The manuscript currently lacks the necessary statistical analysis to support its claims. Although I acknowledge the page constraints of a conference paper, reporting minimal statistical significance—such as p-values, Cohen’s d, or E-values—is essential to demonstrate that the observed improvements are statistically meaningful. Without these measures, the “efficiency” of the proposed framework remains speculative. 3.Inadequate Localization Validation In Figure 1, the authors present only a single IoU result as a qualitative example. Providing a single case is not acceptable as representative evidence for the performance across the entire dataset. A more extensive quantitative evaluation of IoU (or similar localization metrics) across the full test set is required to validate the model’s interpretability and localization capabilities.

meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper addresses an important topic: improving the faithfulness and visual quality of explanations in inherently interpretable B-cos networks for chest X-ray diagnosis. Reviewers appreciated the motivation, the use of anti-aliasing strategies to reduce grid artifacts, and the potential relevance for interpretable medical AI. However, the reviews raise important concerns. The main issues are the unclear trade-off between artifact reduction and diagnostic performance, insufficient quantitative reporting, lack of statistical analysis, and limited localization validation. Reviewers also noted that the current figures make it difficult to assess the true magnitude of the gains. I recommend inviting the paper for rebuttal. The authors should address: 1- Clarify the performance–interpretability trade-off. 2- Strengthen localization validation beyond single examples. 3- Better justify which model is preferable for deployment. | In the rebuttal, the authors substantially clarified the main concerns raised in the initial reviews. In particular, they provided full quantitative tables, additional localization metrics beyond isolated examples, and statistical analysis over repeated runs. These clarifications make the performance-interpretability trade-off much clearer. The rebuttal shows that the proposed variants improve localization quality, including mIoU, while maintaining competitive predictive performance, even if no single variant dominates across every metric and dataset. The explanation of when B-cos_ASAP is preferable versus when B-cos_BP is preferable is also reasonable and improves the practical interpretation of the results. The paper still has some limitations. The gains are not uniformly large across all settings, and the final paper should present results in tables rather than crowded plots, with a clearer discussion of deployment preferences and trade-offs. However, the main concerns about insufficient quantitative reporting, limited localization validation, and lack of statistical support were addressed convincingly in the rebuttal, and all reviewers moved to acceptance. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper is one of the few works on visualization anti-aliasing offering better explainability on anomaly detection in chest X-ray imaging. All reviewers appear convinced with the rebuttal and have recommended acceptance. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): All three reviewers now propose to accept the paper, as they indicate that all concerns have been properly addressed. Clear-cut case.

title: Fast Few-Shot Embolization Simulations in Ischemic Stroke Using Equivariant Neural Fields
reviewer_1_strengths: The authors used an SE(3)-equivariant representation to train a model to predict the Lagragian motion of the clot. To the reviewer’s knowledge, adaption of this method to simulate clot motion has not been reported before. Clot motion in the vessel undergoes complex forces including hemodynamics, vessel wall friction, and its intrinsic deformation, especially at bifurcations or going from large lumens to small lumens. Traditional FEM methods, such as the Abaqus model used in this manuscript, are well known to be time-consuming and can suffer from numerical instability. The method proposed, although assuming a rigid body motion of the clot, can serve as a potentially useful tool for future clot motion studies.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1) oversimplified boundary conditions. The authors assume a constant pressure of 0.002 MPa. This is not commonly seen in the literature; researchers typically use inlet-outlet pressure difference (such as Mirakhorli, F. , Vahidi, B. , Pazouki, M. et al. A Fluid-Structure Interaction Analysis of Blood Clot Motion in a Branch of Pulmonary Arteries. Cardiovasc Eng Tech 14, 79–91 (2023). ), or flow rate boundary conditions as these numbers can be easily measured and verified in the clinical field. Justification of this setting is needed. In addition, friction was also neglected in this study. 2) insufficient validation. Given the aforementioned oversimplification of the physics, the proposed Abaqus models can not be treated as “ground truth”. Validation against phantom experiments should be provided. In addition, human vascular anatomy, especially the neurovasculature, notably has extreme variability in tortuosity. A 10-case test set is statistically insufficient to claim generalizability or robustness of the proposed method. 3) lack of elaboration on collision dynamics. The authors noted that baseline models suffered from “clipping”, they did not provide a rigorous mathematical proof or a loss-term analysis of how their model prevents this. 4) minimum contribution to clinical practice. First, in real-world stoke cases, clots usually formed in other places (heart or carotid) without prior knowledge on its actual location, size and shape since the patients are often without any symptoms. Therefore, it’s unrealistic to apply modeling to “predict” the embolization process. Second, knowing how the clot embolized does no help or has no effect on changing the stoke management workflow. Clinicians use angiography to pinpoint the embolized clot and conduct thrombectomy. That is the gold standard, and no clinicians will seek help from any models to “find” the embolized clot. The reviewer recommends reading the latest clinical guideline (2026 Guideline for the Early Management of Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke: A Guideline From the American Heart Association/American Stroke Association).

author_feedback: We thank all the reviewers for their time and feedback. Clinical relevance (R1): We agree that embolization simulation in isolation has limited direct clinical utility. We note that our goal is not to predict or localize the clot for diagnosis per se, which we agree is the role of angiography. Rather, accurate embolization is a necessary component of full in-silico thrombectomy treatment models, establishing initial conditions for clot retrieval simulation and patient-specific digital twins. We acknowledge this motivation is present in the introduction but not made sufficiently explicit. The paper is an early proof of concept wherethe core contribution is an efficient neural surrogate capturing embolization dynamics from limited training data, as a first stepping stone toward fast, full treatment simulation. Deployment in a clinical context would require rigorous validation studies, probably including more realistic boundary conditions, and phantom experiments, well beyond the scope of this paper. We will make this framing more explicit in the introduction. Simulation setup (R1): The constant pressure boundary condition was chosen to match prior computational thrombectomy studies. We agree this is a simplification and will acknowledge it more explicitly. Clot-vessel friction is modeled through the contact and material formulation of the clot and vessel. Test set size (R1): Each of the 10 test trajectories contains 195 timesteps, yielding approximately 1950 per-step evaluations (measured by the per-step error). While these states are not fully independent as they come from sequential trajectories, they are also not fully dependent either for the model, as the model receives no temporal context and processes each state in isolation. The 10 test cases cover distinct patient-specific geometries, and the out-of-domain evaluation demonstrates generalization to qualitatively different tubular shapes. Combined with the five-fold cross-validation on the development set, we believe this forms a sufficient basis for assessing model performance and see generalization behaviour to unseen vessel geometries. Collision dynamics (R1): We do not apply physics-informed losses or hard constraints to prevent clipping, and make no formal claims about collision prevention. We empirically observe an absence of the severe instabilities seen in the baselines, such as large-scale clipping through the vessel wall and clot fragmentation. Code/dataset release (R1-2-3): Code will be released upon acceptance and a link will be provided in the manuscript. We will investigate options for data sharing. Pressure field independence (R2): Since blood pressure is constant, the flow field is precomputed on the empty vessel and does not update as the clot moves, consistent with current thrombectomy simulation models. RoPE and SO(3) equivariance (R3): RoPE does not break equivariance. Node positions are lifted to all group elements ‘g in G’ alongside features, so relative positions are consistently rotated across all group frames. ‘phi_q’ and ‘phi_c’ (R3): These are indeed learnable equivariant linear layers. GATr (R3): We chose platonic transformers as equivariance is induced via weight-sharing across group elements without modifying the computation graph of a regular performer model, preserving the efficient kernelized attention formulation. But GATr would have definitely been an interesting baseline as well. Single clot parameter set (R2): Agreed, varying clot mechanical properties is an important next step. ‘Implicit neural representation’ (R3): The decoder queries arbitrary spatial locations at inference time, allowing for full-resolution inference from a subsampled latent state. We agree the terminology is potentially confusing as this property is also referred to as the neural field property in the literature. We thank all the reviewers for their comments and feedback on typos, figures, and annotations.

title: FDRAS: Failure Diagnosis and Repair for Airway Segmentation
reviewer_1_strengths: The explicit decoupling of failure localization from correction is the central methodological distinction from prior work. Existing methods either stop at error detection without correction (quality-control methods) or perform correction without prior explicit localization (PTR, UTR, ATRNet). FDRAS places supervised error prediction as a distinct, interpretable stage, giving the refinement network conditioned access to spatially localized failure information rather than operating from global features alone. The complementary error representation covers the two main failure modes in airway segmentation under domain shift. The SDF error map is dense and continuous, capturing geometric boundary discrepancies throughout the volume. The tree error map is sparse and binary, localizing branch-level connectivity failures. Together they form a structured representation of structural failure that neither metric alone would capture. The evaluation setup is appropriately strict. Training is on ATM; evaluation is zero-shot on two external datasets with different population characteristics (AirRC: pulmonary nodules; AeroPath: airway pathologies). Testing across two backbones with different architectures and performance levels tests the backbone-agnostic claim under realistic conditions. The ablation in Table 2 isolates both critical design choices (cross-attention conditioning and error-map conditioning). Removing cross-attention produces the largest structural degradation (TD drop >7 pp on both datasets); removing error conditioning produces a large DSC drop on AirRC (–7.7 pp). Both components are shown to be necessary. The ex-vivo validation tests a severe distribution shift. The backbone is a 3D U-Net trained on separate private ex-vivo data. The acquisition context shifts from in-vivo CT to ex-vivo CT. FDRAS receives no additional training, yet the predicted SDF error map highlights geometric inconsistencies at distal branches, and the refinement restores branch continuity toward the nodule region. As a single case it is only qualitative evidence, but under conditions where failure would be easy to justify.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: With TfeNet on AeroPath, FDRAS reduces DSC by 3.5 pp (87.2 vs 83.7) and precision by 6.6 pp (85.4 vs 78.8). The paper attributes the precision drop to distal branch recovery, not spurious over-segmentation. But a simultaneous DSC drop contradicts this: if the added segments were anatomically correct branches, DSC would be stable or improve. TfeNet already achieves 90.5% TD and 87.4% BD on AeroPath before refinement, suggesting the backbone performs well on this pathological set. FDRAS may be diagnosing structural failures that are not present and introducing incorrect corrections. No per-case analysis or stratification is provided to explain this behavior. The training configuration for the TfeNet experiments is not stated. The methods section describes FDRAS as trained on nnUNet-generated initial segmentations. If FDRAS was retrained with TfeNet as the source backbone, this must be stated, as it would mean backbone-agnostic operation requires retraining per backbone, a different claim than backbone-agnostic inference. The diagnosis network is the paper’s most novel component, yet no evaluation of error map prediction quality is provided. The SDF and tree error maps during training are derived from GT. The diagnosis network must learn to predict these from (M, I) at inference without GT. No comparison between predicted and GT-derived error maps is shown. The ablation demonstrates that removing error conditioning hurts performance (Table 2, w/o EM), but this does not confirm the predicted maps accurately localize failures. The corrective benefit may arise from the conditioning mechanism or from generic spatial features of (M, I) rather than from precise error localization. No confidence intervals or significance tests are reported for either dataset. This could be particularly useful in the case of AeroPath, which contains only 27 cases. The ablation evaluates error-map conditioning as a whole (w/o EM) but does not separate SDF-only from tree-only configurations. The two maps capture distinct failure modes. Knowing their individual contributions would validate the two-map design and guide future work.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The paper addresses a clinically relevant and practically important problem. In airway segmentation, structural continuity and distal branch completeness are often more important than voxel-wise overlap alone, particularly for applications such as bronchoscopy navigation and lesion targeting. Framing the problem as post-hoc refinement under domain shift is therefore well motivated. The central idea of decoupling error localisation from correction is appealing and reasonably original in this setting. The manuscript makes a convincing case that existing approaches tend either to diagnose failures without repairing them, or to repair masks without explicitly modelling the underlying errors. Introducing an intermediate error-representation layer is a sensible and useful contribution. The structural error representation is also well designed. Combining a dense SDF discrepancy field with a sparse tree-connectivity map aligns well with the failure modes described in the introduction, namely both boundary errors and disconnected distal branches. This is a stronger formulation than relying on connectivity cues alone. Training on ATM and testing zero-shot on two external datasets is appropriate for the paper’s domain-shift claims, and the use of two different backbones supports the claim that the framework is not tied to a single upstream segmenter. The reported gains on structural metrics appear meaningful, and the ablation results support the contribution of both explicit error conditioning and cross-attention. Overall, the paper is clearly written and easy to follow.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The main weakness is that the empirical validation remains somewhat narrow relative to the broader framing around deployment reliability. Although the zero-shot evaluation is valuable, the experiments are confined to airway segmentation alone. As a result, the paper is convincing as a task-specific airway refinement study, but somewhat less so as a more general reliability-layer contribution. A further limitation is that the diagnosis stage, which is conceptually central to the method, is not evaluated in sufficient depth on its own. The paper supervises training using ground-truth discrepancy maps, including the skeleton-derived tree error map, but provides limited analysis of how accurately these maps are predicted at inference or how diagnosis quality relates to final repair quality. Stronger standalone evaluation of this stage would materially strengthen the paper. Some of the performance trade-offs also warrant more cautious discussion. In Table 1, precision drops noticeably in some settings, particularly with TfeNet on AeroPath. The authors suggest this reflects recovery of distal branches rather than implausible over-segmentation, which is plausible, but the support provided is largely qualitative. A clearer discussion of when such added branches are beneficial versus potentially false positive would improve the paper. Finally, the ex-vivo validation is interesting but remains qualitative, which limits the strength of any conclusions drawn from it. The paper would also benefit from more explicit analysis of failure cases and limits, particularly since the conclusion notes that severely collapsed segmentations cannot be fully recovered. For a post-hoc repair framework, understanding where the method stops helping is central to its practical value.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: Improving reliability of airway segmentation using a diagnostic method that also repairs errors in distal branches/discontinuities, instead of another segmentation framework is a useful contribution in this work. Many airway segmentation methods need refinement steps to obtain fully useful airway networks. Decoupling the errors into boundary discrepancies (measured using signed distance function (SDF)) and branch connectivity using skeleton analysis, is an interesting way to improve the reliability of airway segmentation quality. Strong zero shot performance is reported in Table 1, and thorough evaluations (including ablations) are reported. Additional validation on ex-vivo human lung specimen is a valuable contribution that is seldom seen in airway segmentation works. I hope the authors will make this specimen data available along with the code.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Method is not described in detail. For example, the authors say “feature embeddings extracted by lightweight 3D convolutional blocks” or “employ a spatially reduced cross-attention operator”. The specific choice for these modules is not defined anywhere. So, would any “lightweight 3D convolution” block work? And the specific value for the reduction factor s is not mentioned. The initial segmentations analysed are shown using two backbone networks (nnUnet and TFeNet). Why are the refinement approaches, including FDRAS unable to improve nnUnet to the level of TFeNet? Is this because there are large gaps in performance already with the backbones (about 12 pp DSC)? This points to the limitations of refinement approaches as they are heavily dependent on the initial segmentation. What is the prescribed approach then to obtain useful segmentations? The qualitative comparison shown in Fig 2 is not actually showing a problem with distal airways. The zoom inset is for the main bronchi, and I am quite surprised that already the input segmentation has the “hole” which is not rectified by other methods. Why is this so challenging? Perhaps focusing on loss of connectivity in smaller airways might make this qualitative example more compelling. Justification for chosen hyperparameters (five lambda terms). How were these parameters chosen? And how sensitive is the performance of the method to these choices? Also, curious to see many of these parameters are simply set to 1? Is it fixed across different datasets?
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the AC and reviewers for their feedback and address the main concerns: TfeNet-AeroPath trade-off, diagnosis, backbone, and protocol clarity. 1.TfeNet-AeroPath Regression and Precision Drop (AC, R1 & R2) We agree that the TfeNet-AeroPath results require careful interpretation. Reorganizing the existing case-level outputs (without new experiments, per MICCAI rules) shows that FDRAS consistently improves branch-level metrics: TD rises in 25/27 cases and BD in 19/27, while Dice improves in roughly half of the cases. Voxel-wise DSC and precision may decrease slightly relative to the ground truth, as FDRAS occasionally alters voxels outside annotated branches. While this enhances distal connectivity, these modifications are not explicitly validated and are noted as a limitation and a potential direction for future research. Branch-level gains indicate that FDRAS effectively restores distal structures without introducing grossly implausible anatomy. If permitted, we will include this per-case summary with relevant statistical reporting in the supplement. 2.Diagnosis-Stage Evaluation (AC, R1 & R2) In the submitted manuscript, diagnosis is evaluated through its functional role in repair: it is supervised with GT-derived SDF and skeleton/tree error targets, and removing error-map conditioning reduces DSC by 7.7 pp on AirRC and 6.5 pp on AeroPath. This supports the usefulness of predicted error maps for repair, but we agree it is not a complete standalone diagnosis benchmark. If permitted, we will add map-level diagnosis assessment from the existing predictions and GT-derived targets in the supplement, along with SDF-only/tree-only ablations. 3.Dependence on Initial Segmentation Quality (AC & R3) The gap between nnUNet and TFeNet arises from initial segmentation quality: FDRAS improves structural completeness but cannot create branches entirely missing in the initial mask. Nevertheless, applying FDRAS to nnUNet narrows the gap with TFeNet: DSC on AirRC differences decreases from 12.6 pp to 4.1 pp, while TD/BD differences also decrease, indicating meaningful structural recovery. On AeroPath, similar trends are observed. By targeting errors without full re-segmentation, FDRAS can improve the structural completeness of the backbones evaluated. We will clarify this in the Conclusion and present FDRAS as a bounded, topology-aware reliability layer for targeted correction, designed to enhance existing segmentations rather than replace them. 4.Backbone Protocol and Implementation Clarity (R1 & R3) R1 asked about backbone handling: the same FDRAS checkpoint trained on ATM with frozen nnUNet predictions was used for all nnUNet and TFeNet evaluations; no TFeNet-specific retraining was performed. R3 asked for architectural details: lightweight 3D blocks use two 3×3×3 convolutions with instance normalization and ReLU, with up-sampling via ConvTranspose3d and skip connections. Cross-attention uses spatial reduction s=4 with residual addition. Loss weights were set to default values to avoid scenario-specific tuning. These details clarify model design and hyperparameters. Code and weights will be released upon acceptance; architectural details will be added to Methods, and sensitivity analysis noted as future work. 5.Ex-Vivo Validation and Qualitative Claims (R1, R2 & R3) R3 asked why standard methods fail and whether Fig. 2 shows distal airway failure. We will revise the figure/caption to highlight a clearer distal case. The zoom inset shows a “hole” in the main bronchi not corrected by other methods, which assume common in-vivo shapes and do not model structural errors, limiting recovery of ex-vivo cases. We agree the validation is qualitative: FDRAS can operate on extreme cases, while main evidence remains zero-shot evaluation on AirRC and AeroPath. We thank the AC and reviewers again and will revise the manuscript accordingly.

Why are the refinement approaches, including FDRAS unable to improve nnUnet to the level of TFeNet? Is this because there are large gaps in performance already with the backbones (about 12 pp DSC)? This points to the limitations of refinement approaches as they are heavily dependent on the initial segmentation.” Hence, rebuttal is required for this paper. | After the rebuttal, all reviewers keep their initial positive score, although one reviewer’s concern is partially addressed (regarding the improvement on initial segmentation). Recommend acceptance of this work. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): All three reviewers recommend acceptance after rebuttal. Reviewers generally agreed that the diagnosis-conditioned repair framework is well motivated, clinically relevant, and demonstrates consistent improvements in structural airway metrics under domain shift. The rebuttal successfully clarified the TfeNet-AeroPath trade-off, the backbone-agnostic evaluation protocol, and the intended role of FDRAS as a topology-aware reliability layer rather than a full re-segmentation method. title: Federated Medical Image Segmentation under Modality Heterogeneity via Specialized Adapters
reviewer_1_strengths: The targeted problem is timely, and the overall presentation of the method is smooth. They propose a modality-agnostic approach that enables organ segmentation under modality heterogeneity, which can arise in many practical real-world situations.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: There are unclear points mainly in the implementation and evaluations. These points are as follows: 1- The proposed method is only evaluated on liver segmentation, as it can be considered a relatively simple task where training a smaller model than SAM on limited data can still provide reasonable performance. Evaluating the method on more challenging tasks is needed. 2- In this work, the SAM decoder as well as the shared and modality-specific adapters are trained, which can result in a very long training time compared to nnUNet and this is not reflected here. Also, selecting 25 percent of the slices per 3D case at each epoch and running the training for 25 rounds might lead to convergence for liver segmentation, would that still be the case for more challenging tasks? 3- There are enough publicly available CT and MRI datasets available, why isn’t the model tested on real-world client data distributions? Details on the clients’ data distribution in each modality, as well as the number and modality distribution of the test sets, are lacking. Is the metric averaged on both modalities? 4- In Protocol 3, where clients are fully modality-disjoint, how does FednnUNet handle federated aggregation among all clients? Are federated models trained specifically for each modality? There are some details missing in the implementation.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The paper addresses federated medical image segmentation under modality heterogeneity, including fully modality-disjoint settings. It proposes a framework that separates modality-specific and shared representations using specialized and shared adapters within a SAM-based model. The aggregation is adapted to this setting through modality-restricted aggregation for specialized adapters and modality-balanced aggregation for shared components, which aims to reduce cross-modality interference. A prototype alignment loss is introduced to encourage consistent shared representations across clients. The evaluation covers multiple datasets and heterogeneity protocols, including challenging fully disjoint scenarios, and includes ablation studies to assess the contribution of each component, as well as qualitative and representation analyses supporting the design choices
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The paper has several limitations. The proposed use of adapters within a SAM-based architecture builds directly on prior work such as MSA (Medical SAM Adapter) and related adapter-based fine-tuning approaches, and the idea of separating shared and specialized components is conceptually similar to existing personalized federated learning methods that partition parameters into global and local parts. As such, the architectural contribution appears to be an extension of existing designs rather than a fundamentally new formulation. The aggregation strategies, including modality-restricted and modality-balanced aggregation, are intuitive but resemble grouped or weighted aggregation schemes commonly used in federated learning, and the novelty relative to prior approaches is not fully clarified. The prototype alignment mechanism is also related to prior work on prototype-based or representation alignment methods (e.g., prototypical networks and FL approaches using class or feature prototypes), and its contribution beyond existing alignment techniques is somewhat incremental. In terms of evaluation, experiments are limited to liver segmentation datasets, which may restrict the generality of the conclusions to other organs, tasks, or imaging settings. Although multiple datasets are used, they are combined into a specific benchmark, and it is unclear how the method performs in more diverse or real-world multi-institution scenarios. Finally, while an out-of-distribution experiment is included, it is relatively limited (few rounds of fine-tuning), and does not fully demonstrate robustness to unseen modalities or larger domain shifts.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: This seems to be the first work on multimodal FL with SAM. The highlights are modality-specific/shared adapter design and the use of proximal regularization to align the shared adapters.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The main weakness is in the evaluation. The authors did not include baseline aggregation strategies specifically designed to cope with multimodality/data heterogeneity, such as: [1] K. Borazjani, N. Khosravan, L. Ying and S. Hosseinalipour, “Multi-Modal Federated Learning for Cancer Staging Over Non-IID Datasets With Unbalanced Modalities,” in IEEE Transactions on Medical Imaging, vol. 44, no. 1, pp. 556-573, Jan. 2025, doi: 10.1109/TMI.2024.3450855.[2] Fan Qi, Shuai Li; Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR), 2024, pp. 12312-12321 and more classical ones such as FedProx, etc. Instead, the only comparison is to FedAvg.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: 1.Evaluation Scope and Generalizability (R1-Q1, R1-Q2, R1-Q3, R2, META-Q2): We appreciate the reviewers’ suggestion to evaluate more challenging tasks. We selected liver segmentation because it offers one of the most diverse collections of publicly available, multi-institutional, multimodal datasets (six datasets spanning four CT and two MRI sources) that reflect real-world client data distributions. The collapse of FednnU-Net (AFA) to 61.07% Dice and FedMSA to 83.01% Dice under Protocol 3 (Table 1) demonstrates that the benchmark is non-trivial for modality-heterogeneous FL. To further assess generalizability, as shown in Fig. 5, we evaluated FedMoSA on BraTS for brain tumor segmentation across T2 and FLAIR under a fully modality-disjoint setting. FedMoSA achieved 88.76 Dice with only five fine-tuning rounds (META-Q2), suggesting the federated optimization is not anatomy-specific and addressing R1-Q3 on convergence. Evaluating additional organs remains a valuable future direction. 2.On the Novelty (R2, META-Q1): While some components of our design are known in the literature, our primary contribution is their principled combination for modality-disjoint federated learning (FL), a setting in which cross-modality aggregation can cause measurable performance collapse. For example, FedMSA, which uses the same SAM backbone but lacks modality-specialized adapters, drops to 72.24% IoU under Protocol 3, while FedMoSA achieves 84.85% (+12.6 IoU). This improvement disappears under Protocol 1, where heterogeneity is minimal, confirming that the observed gain is specific to modality-disjoint conditions. Furthermore, prototype-based alignment at the shared adapter feature level has not been explored in prior FL work; this approach reduces inter-client variance by 15x (9.8e-7 vs. MSA’s 1.5e-5, Fig. 4c). Our modality-balanced weighting strategy jointly accounts for both dataset size and modality diversity, a combination not present in previous FL aggregation methods. Finally, ablation studies in Fig. 4a and 4b demonstrate that replacing either aggregation strategy with FedAvg consistently degrades performance. 3.Missing Baselines (R3, META-Q3): We thank the reviewers for these references. Borazjani et al. focus on multi-modal fusion for cancer staging, combining multiple distinct data types per patient. In contrast, our setting uses only medical images, each with a single modality (CT or MRI), and clients are fully modality-disjoint. The model must generalize across modalities without access to paired data, making direct comparison infeasible. Qi & Li’s hypergraph framework assumes a public multi-modal dataset on the server, which violates our privacy constraints. FedProx, a regularization method, does not address modality-specific aggregation but will be included as an additional baseline in the revision. 4.Implementation Details (R1-Q2, R1-Q3, R1-Q4, META-Q3): Training cost (R1-Q2): Only lightweight adapters (bottleneck dim 48) and the decoder are updated and communicated each round, reducing per-round communication to 35.96 MB for two modalities. This represents an 87.3% reduction compared to the 378 MB full model (Table 2). Data distribution (R1-Q3): Section 3 details the six datasets, 80:10:10 patient-level splits, and three protocol configurations. The global test set consists of equal, non-overlapping samples from all clients. FednnU-Net under Protocol 3 (R1-Q4): FFE aggregates all parameters via FedAvg without modality awareness, while AFA aggregates only structurally identical components. Local metrics are reported per client, and global metrics reflect joint CT and MRI performance. 5.Known Modality Assumption (R2): We appreciate the reviewer’s concern. In clinical practice, modality labels are available and routinely used. Our assumption of known modality matches real-world conditions. Studying dynamic routing for unseen modalities is a valuable future direction, as we note in our conclusion.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper proposes a SAM-based efficient federated segmentation framework for modality-heterogeneous medical data. The topic is relevant and practical, as modality heterogeneity is a common challenge in real-world federated medical imaging settings. Based on the reviewers’ comments and my own assessment, I recommend that this paper proceed to the rebuttal stage. The authors should address several key issues: first, the method appears relatively simple, with aggregation weights mainly determined by modality availability and sample size, while local prototype learning is a common strategy for improving federated consistency; the authors should clarify the distinctiveness and advantages of their design. Second, the method should be evaluated on more challenging organ segmentation datasets to better demonstrate its robustness and generalizability. Third, the experimental details should be expanded, and recent works on federated domain shift or heterogeneity mitigation should be included for comparison to ensure a fair and up-to-date assessment. | The paper addresses an important and practical problem in federated medical image segmentation, namely modality heterogeneity across clients, including fully modality-disjoint settings. The proposed FedMoSA framework is well motivated: separating shared and modality-specific adapters within a SAM-based model, together with modality-aware aggregation and prototype alignment, provides a coherent solution to reduce harmful cross-modality interference. The initial reviews raised valid concerns about the moderate novelty of the components, the evaluation being centered mainly on liver segmentation, and the lack of comparisons with more specialized heterogeneity-aware FL baselines. The rebuttal addresses these concerns reasonably well. In particular, the authors clarify the distinction from standard adapter-based SAM and generic prototype alignment, provide evidence that the gains are most pronounced under modality-disjoint settings, add a BraTS-based evaluation to support generalizability beyond liver segmentation, and explain why some proposed baselines are not directly comparable under their privacy and modality assumptions. The additional implementation details on patient-level splits, communication cost, and protocol design also make the experimental setting clearer. Some limitations remain, especially the moderate methodological novelty and the need for broader validation across more organs and unseen modalities. Still, the problem setting is timely, the benchmark is non-trivial, the method is technically sound, and the empirical improvements under severe modality heterogeneity are convincing. I therefore support acceptance, with the expectation that the final version includes the clarified baseline discussion and additional experimental details from the rebuttal. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): After reviewing the authors’ rebuttal and the post-rebuttal recommendations from reviewers, I recommend Accept. The rebuttal effectively addresses the key concerns. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper proposes FedMoSA, a SAM-based federated learning framework for medical image segmentation under modality heterogeneity. Based on the reviewers’ feedback, the authors’ rebuttal addresses the main concerns, and I recommend accepting this manuscript.

title: Fine-Grained Cerebrovascular Parsing in DSA via Structurally-Grounded Semantic Disentanglement
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The transition from binary vessel segmentation to fine-grained anatomical parsing is meaningful for downstream clinical analysis. 2.The idea of combining a global vessel prior with class-wise predictions via consistency constraints is intuitive and well-motivated. 3.The method shows consistent gains over baseline models, and the ablation studies provide some support for each component.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The paper claims “semantic disentanglement”, and Fig. 2 suggests feature-level separation (“redundant vs diverse features”). However, the orthogonality loss is applied on output probability maps A_i rather than intermediate feature representations. 2.The paper does not clearly describe how the final segmentation is produced: The framework concatenates M_{prior} and A_i, but the fusion mechanism is not specified It is unclear how conflicts between branches are resolved The role of P_{ens} is limited to loss computation and not used in inference 3.The paper describes the model as “MoE-driven”, but: There is no gating or routing mechanism The model simply concatenates features from multiple branches 4.Although the method targets fine-grained parsing, the merging of CA and VA into a single category in quantitative evaluation, along with the lack of clear visualization of VA in qualitative results, raises concerns about the model’s ability to distinguish anatomically similar but distinct structures. 5.The role of SAM is not fully justified. It is unclear whether it contributes meaningful anatomical reasoning or simply acts as a pretrained backbone. The necessity of certain design choices (e. g. , dual decoders for SAM features, final concatenation with M_{prior}) is not sufficiently validated. 7.The clarity of the framework diagram (Fig. 2) could be further improved, as several intermediate steps are either omitted or not fully consistent with the textual description. Missing intermediate operations: The transition from intermediate features (e. g. , F_1 \in \mathbb{R}^{32\times H \times W}) to the final probability map M_{prior} is not explicitly illustrated. According to the formulation, M_{prior} is obtained via a sigmoid activation, but this step is not clearly depicted in the diagram. Ambiguity in feature representation: The text distinguishes between local features (CNN) and global features (SAM-based). However, this distinction is not clearly reflected in the diagram, where multiple branches (e. g. , F_2, F_3, F_4) are presented without explicitly indicating how “local” versus “global” information is encoded or preserved. 8.The definition of the baseline in Table 2 and Table 3 is not entirely clear. It appears that the baseline is obtained by removing certain components from the full model rather than using a standard architecture, but the exact configuration is not explicitly described.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The manuscript is well-written, and the figures and tables are clear and easy to interpret. The research topic is highly valuable and clinically meaningful. The experimental evaluation is thorough and comprehensive.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.As a study focused on the vessel parsing task, the proposed method relies heavily on high-quality, pixel-level annotations of DSA images. The practical application value and clinical impact of this work would be significantly strengthened if the authors could conduct cross-dataset testing to explicitly demonstrate the model’s generalization ability across different data sources. 2.The design of the Orthogonal Semantic Disentanglement (OSD) module relies on the assumption that the representations from different segmentation heads are orthogonal and uncorrelated. However, in reality, distinct anatomical vascular structures maintain inherent correlations and physical connectivity (e.g., CA connects directly with the PCA and MCA). Therefore, forcing these anatomical structures to be strictly orthogonal in the feature space seems somewhat counterintuitive and potentially unreasonable. The authors should justify this design choice or discuss its potential limitations regarding physically connected vessels.
