reviewer_3_strengths: The paper proposes a dual-stream expert synergy module and a self-consistent structural grounding mechanism to address the challenges of complex vascular topology and vessel overlap. The experimental evaluation is relatively comprehensive, and the comparisons and analyses are clearly presented.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The motivation for using SAM as one branch is unclear. The authors state only that it is for global encoding, but this capability could also be achieved with ViT. 2.The authors design Lcons to enforce anatomical correctness. However, it is unclear why Mprior is not directly used as a multiplicative mask to suppress irrelevant regions. 3.The claim that DgCNN serves as a global encoder lacks sufficient justification. The experiments in Figure 5 do not clearly demonstrate its global modeling capability. 4.The hyperparameter analysis in Figure 4 appears to be conducted on the test set, which violates standard experimental protocols. 5.The performance of Swin-UNet in the comparison is unexpectedly low, and the authors do not provide a corresponding explanation.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for their constructive feedback. Our work’s clinical value (R1/R2), SCSG/OSD effectiveness (R2/R4), and thorough experiments (R1/R2/R4) were recognized. Our responses are as follows: 1.Disentanglement & Orthogonality (R1, R2) Prediction-Level Disentanglement: L_ortho is applied to output probability maps A_i, not intermediate features, to supervise each head’s response uniqueness. Penalizing redundant co-activation forces preceding layers to learn discriminative features that resolve projective ambiguities. The Fig. 2 label will be corrected to “redundant vs. diverse predictions.” Physical Connectivity: OSD’s orthogonality constraint operates on the prediction probability space, not the anatomical feature space, so it does not deny physical connectivity between vessels. It penalizes “all heads producing identical patterns across the entire image,” not co-activation at junction points, compatible with connected vessels. L_cons ensures the union of vessel categories covers the full binary mask, preventing the vascular tree from being torn apart. 2.Architectural & Inference Clarity (R1, R4) Inference Mechanism: The final prediction is produced by concatenating the outputs from N parallel segmentation heads with M_prior along the channel dimension, yielding the final multi-channel output. The max probability class is selected per pixel. P_ens are training-only topological anchors that enforce global consistency via L_cons. Soft Grounding vs. Multiplicative Masking: Hard masking with M_prior risks error propagation; if the prior misses a low-contrast vessel, it is permanently deleted. L_cons provides a soft structural constraint that preserves gradient flow, allowing anatomical branches to recover uncertain regions. 3.Multi-Expert Synergy & SAM (R1, R4) SAM provides segmentation-aware priors (boundaries, connectivity) from its SA-1B mask pretraining, unlike ViT which lacks such structural priors. The CNN branch captures local textures; LoRA-tuned SAM captures long-range dependencies for fragmented vessels. Table 3 validates this: D^{CNN}_l gives 77.35% Dice, adding D^{Tr}_g reaches 77.62%, and D^{CNN}_g achieves 78.51% (clDice: 51.62% → 53.70%). D^{CNN}_g is “global” as it decodes SAM-derived global features. Decoders for SAM features: As shown in Table 3, adding D^{Tr}_g focuses on long-range topological continuity, while adding D^{CNN}_g refines spatial alignment. Removing either leads to a drop in clDice or Dice. 4.Terminology of MoE (R1) We acknowledge the lack of a routing mechanism. We will refine “MoE-driven” to “Multi-Expert Synergy,” integrating heterogeneous features (CNN for local, SAM for global) rather than sparse conditional computation. 5.CA/VA Categorization (R1) CA and VA are distinct categories in our architecture. Their merged reporting in Table 1 was a space-saving measure; both achieve individual Dice of 0.9324 (CA) and 0.9579 (VA). We will report disaggregated metrics and VA-specific visualizations in the revision. 6.Baseline and Experimental Protocol (R1 & R4) Table 2 baseline, without SCSG or OSD, i.e., all auxiliary losses (orthogonality and consistency) are removed, uses a single segmentation head. Table 3 baseline removes all three decoders, relying only on the topmost local CNN decoder. Swin-UNet Performance: Low performance stems from overfitting on the small dataset (175 images) and insufficient long-tail modeling. Pure Transformers lack CNN inductive biases. Protocol: Fig. 4 reflects grid-search on the training set; the test set was only used for testing and reporting. 7.Performance on other datasets (R2) Cross-dataset validation is valuable, but our task requires pixel-level annotations for multiple anatomical vessel categories in DSA. No public DSA dataset currently provides a compatible label space. Evaluating on binary vessel datasets would not assess the proposed anatomical parsing task. We will release our code and dataset to benefit the community.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper addresses an important and clinically relevant problem moving DSA analysis from binary vessel segmentation to fine-grained cerebrovascular parsing. However, the current evidence leaves several issues unresolved: the final inference/fusion procedure is unclear, the “MoE” and SAM/global-encoder claims need stronger justification, the OSD design should be reconciled with anatomical connectivity and with the fact that orthogonality is applied to probability maps rather than features, and several experimental details require clarification. | The rebuttal addresses a meaningful portion of these concerns. Overall, I recommend acceptance. The topic is clinically important, the proposed framework appears to improve over the evaluated baselines, and two reviewers found the rebuttal sufficient to support acceptance. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Based on the outcome of the rebuttal process, two reviewers assigned an “Accept” rating, while one reviewer assigned a “Reject” rating. Although the paper still suffers from issues such as exaggerated claims and insufficient supporting evidence (R1), the study itself possesses “significant practical application value” (R2). Furthermore, the rebuttal successfully clarified certain doubts regarding the design rationale (R3), and the manuscript is clearly written (R2). Consequently, the overall consensus is positive, and the inclination is to “Accept” this paper. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): Authors only partially addressed the reviewers concerns about overstated disentanglement, unclear inference/fusion, insufficient SAM-specific validation, and incomplete fine-grained evaluation. Please, refer to Reviewers’ post-rebuttal comments for more details.

title: FlowReg: Reconstruction-Guided Flow Matching for Universal Spinal CT/X-Ray Registration
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.Leveraging 3D reconstruction as a spatial prior for 2D/3D registration is a reasonable and potentially effective direction to mitigate the ill-posed nature of projection-based matching. 2.The framework is designed to support multiple vertebrae within a single model, which is relevant for practical clinical workflows. 3.The integration of reconstruction and registration into a single training framework is well-motivated and may provide regularization benefits.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.In section of “Riemannian Flow Matching Registration”, the formulation appears inconsistent. While the paper claims to operate on SE(3), the actual method performs linear interpolation directly in se(3) without clearly mapping back to the manifold. This suggests a potential misunderstanding of the distinction between SE(3) and its Lie algebra. 2.The method mixes Euclidean optimization in se(3) with a geodesic constraint in SE(3) without a consistent formulation. Since the trajectory is defined via linear interpolation in R^6 rather than geodesics on SE(3), the claimed Riemannian formulation is not technically valid, and the added geodesic loss appears to be temporary rather than principled. 3.The DAFF module performs feature difference, element-wise product, concatenation, and MLP-based fusion (Sec. 2), which are standard operations without clear novelty or theoretical justification. Additionally, flow matching for pose estimation has been explored in prior work (as also cited in [12,19]), making the methodological contribution incremental. 3.The paper claims that flow matching “fundamentally resolves” issues such as local minima and convergence (Sec. 1), but does not provide theoretical analysis or controlled experiments isolating these effects. Similarly, the claim that DAFF “reconciles cross-modal disparities” is not directly validated beyond overall performance improvements. 4.Although the framework outputs multiple vertebrae poses, it does not explicitly model inter-vertebral constraints or relative motion. The dataset includes only 11 three-level samples (Sec. 3.1), which is insufficient to demonstrate robustness under realistic multi-vertebra motion scenarios. And there is a lack of clear experimental results regarding multi-vertebral registration. 5.The model is pre-trained on 37,950 synthetic samples generated from 253 CT scans (Sec. 3.1) and then fine-tuned on the real dataset (Sec. 3.2). However, the paper does not clarify whether subject-level splits are enforced, raising potential data leakage concerns. Furthermore, fine-tuning on the target dataset weakens claims of generalization to unseen data. 6.The real dataset contains only 62 samples (30 single-, 21 two-, 11 three-level cases) (Sec. 3.1), yet five-fold cross-validation is applied (Sec. 3.2). Given the small sample size and imbalance, this evaluation protocol may not provide reliable estimates of performance. 7.The ablation study (Table 2) combines multiple factors such as DAFF and sim-to-real training (D2), making it difficult to attribute improvements to individual components. For example, improvements from (2) to (3) may stem from domain adaptation rather than the DAFF module itself. 8.The ground-truth poses are obtained via C-arm cone-beam acquisition (Sec. 3.1), but the relationship between the preoperative CT and intraoperative imaging is not clearly specified. In particular, it is unclear whether there exists any significant inter-vertebral motion between the preoperative CT and intraoperative scans. If the vertebrae remain largely rigid, the task may reduce to a near global rigid alignment rather than true multi-vertebra registration. Furthermore, potential spatial inconsistencies between preoperative CT and CBCT (e. g. , differences in patient positioning, deformation, or calibration) are not discussed. This raises concerns about the accuracy and consistency of the supervision signal, and whether the provided “ground-truth” poses are reliable for evaluating fine-grained multi-vertebra registration performance.
reviewer_1_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The application of the Riemannian Flow Matching method to the SE(3) 2D/3D registration is novel. The learning objective is targeted at the key ill-posed registration pose field and mapped from the data-driven manner. This idea is brilliant and from the qualitative presentation (Fig.1), the FlowReg loss field is much more smooth than the other methods. 2.The other two contributions, the DAFF module and the reconstruction branch also presented superior performance to the overall pipeline success and the reconstruction quality from its ablation study. Plus, the framework handles the multiple vertebral motion, up to three vertebrae. This is a significant contribution in a unified end-to-end learning paradigm by enforcing the correspondence learning from the cross-domain feature fusion and the reconstruction overlay check. 3.The presentation and the writing of this manuscript are clear. The experiments are designed with great rigour, and the results presented are solid.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The CT resolution is limited to 64 voxel per dimension. Given a reasonable volumetric physical dimension of 300 mm, the voxel size is about 5 mm / voxel, which is very coarse. It would be interesting if the manuscript can discuss how this work can generalize to 3D or 2D domain with higher resolution. 2.This method is specifically demonstrated on N <= 3 vertebrae. The authors should clarify if the cropped vertebrae are always at the same level or they are a mix of multiple levels, and how this framework can generalize to or recognize mismatched 3D volume and 2D images. 3.Robustness to image artifacts or other objects. In real clinical scenario, the image quality can be impacted by various factors, such as additional surgical instruments (cables, K-wires, screws) in the scene, it would be interesting to know how the DAFF module can generalize to impaired images. 4.It’s worth noting that the real testing results are performed on an in-house, limited number of samples (<100 samples). This small evaluation subset posts the clinical validation quality at risk.
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: One major strength is that the paper is well written and it’s evaluation is done cleanly, also the ablations are done well. Another major strength is the usage of Riemannian Flows during the registration, it makes sense to formulate the registration of the different vertebrae as a flow problem, which is empirically validated when looking at the results. Furthermore this technique is very fast with only using 0.42s.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The following minor weaknesses need to be addressed: give some details about the population of the real world dataset the method was tested on i.e. age, gender etc. the details about semantic segmentation and localization of the vertebrae on the real x-rays should be given a bit more context and given some more results as it’s one of the fundaments for the method to work, as it’s not obvious that they work as well as reported on the real dataset this paper is using. in the introduction one could give some more references to feature-based and contour-based approaches as these also have shown to be promising for 2d-3d registration.
reviewer_3_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We sincerely thank all reviewers and the Area Chair for their valuable time, constructive comments, and positive assessment of our work. 1.SE(3)/se(3) formulation and wording [Meta, R1W1-R1W3]: We agree that our wording may have conflated the parameterization space with the supervision space. Following standard RFM practice [12], we parameterize conditional paths in se(3), where linear interpolation defines a tractable vector field for stable pose learning; we do not claim this path is an exact SE(3) geodesic. Predicted velocities/poses are mapped back to SE(3) via the exponential map before rendering, warping, and geodesic-loss computation. Thus, RFM learns pose evolution in se(3), while the geodesic loss enforces SE(3) manifold consistency. We will rephrase “Riemannian flow on SE(3)” as “RFM with se(3) parameterization and SE(3) geodesic supervision,” and soften “fundamentally resolves” to an empirical claim, e.g., “substantially mitigates.” 2.DAFF design rationale [R1W3, R2W3]: DAFF uses standard operations, but is tailored to X-ray/DRR fusion: difference maps capture artifacts/misalignment and Hadamard maps capture shared anatomy. Table 2 rows (2)-(3),(6)-(7) share D2, isolating DAFF gains. Severe occlusions remain a limitation. 3.Inter-vertebral motion and data split [Meta, R1W4, R2W4]: FlowReg does not treat multiple vertebrae as a single rigid body; it predicts semantically indexed vertebra-specific 6-DoF poses. To compensate for limited real multi-vertebra data, synthetic samples from 253 public CTs include local inter-vertebral perturbations following [21] (rotations x±12°, y±6°, z±2°; translations ±2 mm), approximating lateral bending, axial rotation, and flexion/extension. RFM jointly learns pose velocities and implicitly captures inter-pose correlations; explicit biomechanical constraints remain future work. Patient-level splitting was enforced in synthetic pre-training and real-data five-fold validation; public CTs and private clinical data are independent, avoiding real-subject exposure. Each clinical case is evaluated once. 4.GT pose and evaluation details [Meta, R1W8]: Preoperative CT is acquired supine, while intraoperative X-ray/CBCT is acquired prone. This posture change can cause spinal curvature changes and inter-vertebral motion, so the task is not near-global rigid registration. The intraoperative GT pose was established by a hybrid protocol combining optical tracking and manual refinement: reference frames on the C-arm detector and patient ROI were synchronously captured by an NDI Polaris tracker to estimate the initial CT-to-X-ray relationship. Intraoperative C-arm CBCT was used as the surgical 3D reference, and vertebra-by-vertebra CT-to-CBCT registration yielded vertebra-specific transforms to mitigate supine/prone deformation. mTRE averages Euclidean distances between six CT landmarks transformed by GT and predicted poses: the centers of both pedicles and the four outermost vertebral-body corners. Residual errors from skin-motion artifacts and calibration uncertainty may remain, and will be discussed as a limitation. 5.CT spatial resolution and artifact robustness [Meta, R2-W1, R2-W3]: The 64^3 volume is not the original CT resolution or a 300-mm whole-spine volume. VerSe’20 CTs have voxel spacing from 0.19×0.19×0.40 to 1.67×1.67×5.00 mm^3, with median matrix size 512×512×292.Our private CTs are 512×512×401 with 0.3×0.3×0.625 mm^3 spacing. CTs are resampled to a unified physical coordinate system; each vertebra is localized/segmented, cropped with margin, and resized to 64^3 as a vertebra-level spatial prior. Higher-resolution variants can use coarse-to-fine refinement. For artifacts, CLAHE and local masks suppress background; DAFF models DRR/X-ray differences and shared responses, while the 3D reconstruction branch provides a geometric prior, making the model less sensitive to projection noise than render-and-compare methods. Severe tool/implant occlusions remain a limitation.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper addresses 2d/3d registration for X-ray/CT, proposing a network with a 3D reconstruction branch that informs pose estimation. Strong evaluation demonstrates the advantage of the results. There are potential issues with the presentation of mathematical details (se(3) vs SE(3)) and overly strong claims (fundamentally resolving issues of local minima), but these are minor issues which can be addressed in the rebuttal. R1 raised further concerns inter-vertebral motion. The authors should clarify whether their method treats multiple vertebrae as a single rigid body or if it accounts for inter-vertebral motion. Concerns about subject-level data leakage should be addressed. The real dataset size is sufficient for CAI. Further discussion of CT spatial resolution, evaluation details, and robustness to image artifacts is warranted. Given the strengths of the paper, I look forward to the rebuttal and the response to the concerns raised. | While R1 maintains some concerns regarding mathematical details and evaluation robustness, these are not fundamental issues that would prevent acceptance, and the overall strength of the paper significantly outweighs these observed weaknesses. In light of the strong support from R2 and R3, I recommend acceptance of this paper. I will address R1’s remaining concerns here, as I do not consider them to be critical issues that would prevent acceptance: 1.Mathematical formulation: R1’s concerns about the mathematical formulation of the problem can be addressed in the CR. While some claims were softened in the rebuttal because a fundamental theoretical guarantee is out of scope, the method still represents a significant advancement in the field with strong empirical results. Because the question of “true Riemannian/geodesic flow” is not fundamental to the contribution of the paper, I do not consider this a critical issue that would prevent acceptance. 2.DAFF effect isolation: While more substantial ablations would further isolate the effect of DAFF within the complete FlowReg framework, other reviewers have not identified this as a critical issue, stating “the studies are performed with great rigor and solid results” (R2) and specifically mentions the strong ablations (R3). 3.Evaluation: The rebuttal has clarified questions about patient-level splitting during cross-evaluation. While rebuttal does not explicitly address the question of fine-tuning on the real data test set, and this would be a critical flaw if it were the case, I believe it is reasonable to assume that fine-tuning was on each training set during cross-validation, ensuring patient-level separation between training and test sets. The authors should clarify this point in the CR, but I do not consider this a critical issue that would prevent acceptance. If there was fine-tuning on the test set, I strongly recommend the authors to withdraw the paper based on flawed evaluation. However, I do not have evidence that this is the case, and I would give the authors the benefit of the doubt on this point. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): A few issues remain unresolved after rebuttal: 1) Strictly not a Riemannian parametrisation for optimisation. While it’s true that the wording of “we formulate the registration … on the SE(3) manifold, …” needs to be clarified to make it explicit that riemannian constraints are enforced via loss rather than explicit parametrisation - this seems a small adjustment that is fairly acceptable to fix in the final version - and it doesn’t take away from the main results and contributions of the paper 2) Ablations appear reasonable to me 3) Cross-validation also appears sound and clear to me. A model is pre-trained on VERSE’20 and then fine-tuning is performed in cross-validation on a proprietary dataset. Main issue is that dataset is small (mitigated by cross validation) and that results are not fully reproducible due to use of proprietary data (which goes beyond the rebuttal discussion). I am therefore leaning towards accepting the paper, while urging the authors to clarify the optimisation framework and in which sense riemannian consraints are applied. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): I will align with the accept decisions for this work. Although some points were not fully addressed during the rebuttal process, the response space was limited and the authors appropriately focused on the major concerns raised by the reviewers. In addition, two reviewers were strongly in favor of acceptance, further supporting the overall positive assessment of the paper.

title: Frequency-Aware Post-Training Quantization for Medical Image Denoising
reviewer_1_strengths: The paper identifies a concrete and well-motivated failure mode of existing PTQ for medical denoising, namely the mismatch between spatial-domain calibration and frequency-selective degradation under ultra-low precision. The method is technically coherent: the SWT-based diagnosis directly motivates the wavelet-guided refinement objective, rather than appearing as an unrelated add-on. The evaluation is reasonably broad for this problem setting, covering two medical imaging scenarios and three representative denoising backbones, with results at 2/4/8 bits. The empirical gains are strong, including up to 5.54 dB PSNR improvement over baselines and up to 8× model compression, and the ablation study shows that the second-stage wavelet refinement contributes substantial additional gains. The paper also considers deployment, including ONNX Runtime export and an anonymized project link, which is a practical strength.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The novelty is meaningful but somewhat incremental. The paper builds on established PTQ baselines such as BRECQ, PTQ4SR, and 2DQuant, while also drawing on wavelet/subband ideas that have already appeared in low-dose CT restoration literature. In that sense, the main novelty lies more in the task-specific integration of frequency-aware refinement into PTQ for medical denoising than in a fundamentally new quantization principle. Several important design choices are empirical, especially the band weights used in the wavelet-guided loss. The paper would be stronger with a sensitivity analysis for these weights and for the calibration-set size, since both may affect the stability and practical applicability of the method. The deployment claim is not fully supported quantitatively. The text states that there is no additional latency overhead compared with FP32, but the deployment table reports model size and compression ratio rather than actual runtime, throughput, or memory measurements. This makes it difficult to assess the real deployment benefit beyond storage reduction. The evaluation focuses mainly on image fidelity metrics such as PSNR/SSIM and qualitative examples. Given the medical setting, it would be more convincing to include a stronger task-oriented or reader-oriented analysis showing that diagnostically relevant structures are indeed better preserved after quantization. The paper would benefit from a clearer comparison or discussion against stronger deployment-oriented alternatives, such as quantization-aware training or mixed-precision strategies. This would help clarify when the proposed PTQ approach is preferable in practice. The quality of Fig. 1 should be improved. In the right panel, the stacked image examples contain visible artifacts that look like residual watermark-like patterns or incompletely edited/generated image content. This raises concerns about figure preparation and visual reliability. The authors should replace or clean these images and ensure that all visual materials are properly anonymized, traceable, and publication-ready.
reviewer_1_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The core contribution of this paper lies in performing optimization for Post-Training Quantization in the frequency domain, rather than directly in the image domain, by leveraging wavelet transform.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The limitations of this paper are as follows: 1.The core contribution appears to lie in transforming the input image during the optimization stage and performing loss computation in the transformed domain. This modification seems relatively simple, with limited implementation difficulty and workload. 2.The relationship between Stage 1 and Stage 2 is not clearly explained. In particular, the paper does not provide sufficient analysis on why the Tensor-Level Coarse Calibration can offer a stable initialization. 3.The authors claim that quantization in the spatial domain leads to the loss of high-frequency information. However, from the qualitative results, the compared methods seem to mainly suffer from reduced denoising capability rather than poor edge preservation, while the proposed method introduces some degree of edge blurring. The authors should provide further explanation for this observation.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The proposed solution is simple yet meaningful: incorporating frequency-domain awareness via wavelet decomposition and reweighting reconstruction errors. The two-stage design is logical and integrates naturally with existing PTQ pipelines. The proposed method achieves substantial improvements over prior work, including gains of up to ~5.5 dB PSNR in fluoroscopy and consistent advantages across architectures. Notably, the approach remains robust in extremely low-bit settings (e.g., 2-bit), where most PTQ methods degrade significantly. This is a strong empirical validation of the core idea.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The frequency weighting scheme (e.g., λ coefficients for subbands) appears empirically chosen. The paper would benefit from either a principled derivation or a more thorough sensitivity analysis to demonstrate robustness to these hyperparameters. Experiments are confined to medical image denoising. While the motivation is domain-specific, it remains unclear whether the proposed method generalizes to other restoration tasks (e.g., super-resolution, deblurring) or even to non-medical image domains.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: [R1: references/visual reliability] We verified the bibliography against original publication records and will correct the metadata errors flagged by R1: Strategies for reducing radiation dose in CT author list; CTformer year/volume/author list; Restormer author list; SwinIR venue (ICCV Workshop, not CVPR); and Ref.22 title/SPIE volume/page mismatch. We will also fix capitalization, missing pages, and inaccurate entries across the reference list. These are metadata errors, not unsupported citations. Fig.1 was manually prepared from actual saved experimental outputs, not AI-generated, watermarked, or synthetic content. [R1/meta: deployment/clinical claims] Table 2 reports only model size and compression; it does not support latency, throughput, or memory claims. We will remove “without incurring additional latency overhead compared to FP32” and limit the deployment claim to ONNX-exported model-size compression: 3.88–4.00x for INT8 and 7.47–8.00x for INT4.We will also remove reader-level or diagnostic claims not supported by PSNR/SSIM. “Diagnostically critical structures” will be revised to reconstruction-fidelity/frequency-distortion wording. [R1/R3: empirical weights/calibration size] The subband weights lambda_LL=0.2, lambda_HF=0.3, lambda_HH=0.5 were fixed across datasets/backbones to reflect the HH-dominant distortion in Fig.2; they were not tuned per test set and are not claimed to be optimal. We will add a compact robustness analysis for representative weights and calibration-set sizes. The claim will be robustness within reasonable settings, not a principled optimum. [R2: Stage 1/Stage 2 relation] Stage 1 and Stage 2 optimize the same clipping-bound parameters Φ. Stage 1 provides a stable initialization under ultra-low-bit quantization by reconstructing quantized weights and activations to better align with the FP32 distributions before output-level refinement. Starting from this initialization Φ(0), Stage 2 refines Φ using the SWT-based output loss to correct the remaining frequency-selective distortion. Thus, Stage 1 stabilizes local quantization, while Stage 2 focuses on reducing output-level subband distortion. This design is supported by the ablation study, where Stage1+2 consistently outperforms Stage1 alone across all backbones and datasets, and Fig.5 shows reduced standardized HH error. [R2: high-frequency/edge wording] High-frequency degradation should not be interpreted solely as edge disappearance. In our setting, quantization-induced high-frequency distortion may appear as residual noise amplification, texture corruption, or attenuation of fine structures depending on the backbone architecture and bit-width. We will replace “preserves fine structural details with comparatively reduced distortion” with wording that more precisely describes reduced high-frequency quantization distortion. This also addresses the reviewer’s observation that the visual degradation may reflect reduced denoising capability rather than only edge loss. [R1/R2/R3: novelty and alternatives] The contribution is not SWT itself, but identifying frequency-selective failure of spatial PTQ for medical denoising and turning it into a two-stage, architecture-agnostic PTQ objective. QAT and mixed precision target different regimes. QAT requires retraining and usually full training data; our setting freezes the pretrained denoiser and uses only calibration samples. Mixed precision can improve fidelity but introduces layer-wise bit allocation and hardware/policy complexity; we intentionally test the stricter uniform W/A low-bit setting to isolate frequency-aware PTQ. [Scope/MICCAI positioning] We will position the method as medical image denoising PTQ, not general restoration or clinical validation. We will add MICCAI-relevant related work on low-dose imaging, medical restoration, efficient deployment, and state extension to other restoration tasks and reader/task-level evaluation as future work.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): This paper presents a technically sound and empirically well-supported methodological contribution on post-training quantization for medical image denoising. The strengths of the submission are clear. The paper identifies a plausible failure mode of standard spatial-domain PTQ under ultra-low precision, namely disproportionate degradation of high-frequency components, and translates that observation into a coherent two-stage frequency-aware refinement strategy. The experimental validation is broad for the claimed scope, covering two medical denoising settings, three backbone families, multiple PTQ baselines, and 2/4/8-bit quantization. The reported gains at 2-bit and 4-bit are substantial, and the ablation provides evidence that the second stage contributes meaningfully beyond the initial tensor-level calibration. The main concerns are more limited in scope. The band-weighting scheme is empirically chosen without a robustness study, the deployment discussion overstates what is actually shown because latency is claimed without runtime measurements, and the evaluation remains focused on reconstruction fidelity rather than task- or reader-level medical assessment. In addition, the bibliography contains several metadata inaccuracies that should be corrected, and the MICCAI-specific positioning could be stronger. After checking the manuscript, however, some reviewer concerns carry limited weight: the comment that the relationship between Stage 1 and Stage 2 is unclear is only partially supported because the manuscript explicitly defines Stage 1 as the initialization for Stage 2 and reports their respective contributions in the ablation, while the concern about suspicious artifacts in Fig. 1 is not substantiated by the submitted figure. Accordingly, I assign limited weight to those criticisms in the overall assessment.

title: From Baseline to Future CT: Large-Scale Diffusion Pretraining for Single-Scan IPF Progression Prediction
reviewer_1_strengths: The pretraining strategy is the most clearly supported contribution. The decision to learn a thoracic prior from a large-scale screening dataset, where repeat imaging is available and acquisition variability is broad, and then adapt to a data-limited disease cohort, is a reasonable approach to a real bottleneck. The Scratch ablation, which retains the screening-pretrained autoencoder and diffusion backbone but trains the ControlNet exclusively on IPF data, degrades consistently across all reported metrics on both the internal and external test sets. The primary comparison is statistically significant after Holm correction on both sets, which makes the benefit of longitudinal pretraining the most credibly established result in the paper. The evaluation design is a further strength. The paper reports both an internal test set and a fully held-out external site, giving at least a preliminary view of behavior under site shift. Statistical testing uses paired one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Holm correction, which is appropriate given the directional hypothesis and the multiple metrics being tested. The AE ceiling (deterministic reconstruction of the ground-truth follow-up through the frozen autoencoder) contextualizes the headroom remaining in the progression modelling component: the ceiling is at 0.981 SSIM versus the proposed model at 0.947, indicating that the compression step itself is not the bottleneck. Supplementing pixel-level metrics with a perceptual distance based on an open-source thoracic CT foundation model encoder is also appropriate. For IPF, where the clinically relevant features are local and spatially subtle, perceptual alignment in an encoded feature space is a more meaningful quality measure than global SSIM alone.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The evaluation is restricted to image fidelity metrics, with no assessment of clinical utility. SSIM, MSE, PSNR, and ViT feature distance measure how closely a synthesized scan resembles a ground-truth follow-up, but they do not address whether the predicted progression is clinically informative. For IPF, the clinically relevant question is whether the model can predict the trajectory of functional decline with any accuracy. The paper acknowledges the absence of expert-annotation-free voxel-level progression measures as an active area of research, but that acknowledgment does not substitute for a downstream evaluation, even a surrogate one. Without some correlation between synthesized image changes and functional endpoints, the clinical value of the approach remains asserted rather than demonstrated. The external test set contains 17 pairs. This is too small to draw reliable conclusions about generalization under site shift. The results show the same metric ordering as internal testing, which is encouraging, but with this sample size the standard deviations dominate and the evaluation cannot support strong generalization claims. The paper itself flags this as a limitation, but it is worth noting that “transfer feasibility” is the most that can be responsibly claimed, not stability across sites. The comparison with prior work is narrow. The most directly comparable published method for single-scan IPF follow-up synthesis is Jiang et al. (2025) [6], published in Medical Image Analysis. The paper excludes it on the grounds that it uses text-based lung-function conditioning and 2.5D slice-based synthesis, which differ from the proposed setting. The exclusion is not unreasonable on technical grounds, but the clinical task is identical, and the paper would benefit from a more explicit discussion of what the input difference implies for the comparison. As it stands, the only comparison methods are an in-house latent U-Net and latent cVAE, both matched to the same latent resolution, which is a weaker competitive baseline than the published literature. No ethics statement appears in the paper. The study uses multi-center patient imaging data collected across several countries. IRB approval or equivalent ethics review is not mentioned anywhere in the text. This is likely a consequence of anonymization requirements, but it should be added to the camera-ready version.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The assumption that generative pre-training can enhance longitudinal prediction performance is compelling. 2.Given that PSNR, SSIM, and MSE have inherent limitations in evaluating generative models, the inclusion of ViT distance and Airway error is a significant addition. 3.The study benefits significantly from a substantial pre-training dataset and rigorous external validation, which enhance the generalizability of the proposed model.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.Lack of Evidence for Patch-wise Training Benefits The rationale behind using patch-wise training to preserve details is not sufficiently justified. The authors did not provide comparative results between whole-image training and patch-size ablations. Since other architectures like U-Net and CVAE can also be implemented in a patch-wise manner but may not show similar detail preservation, the authors should clarify if whole-image experiments were conducted for comparison. 2.Insufficient Qualitative Evidence and Performance Issues The qualitative evaluation is limited, with only two results provided. It is difficult to assess a generative model’s performance based on such a small sample. Specifically:In Fig. 2A, the Ground Truth (GT) at t=1 shows honeycombing patterns, which the proposed model fails to predict accurately.In Fig. 2B, the GT at t=2 exhibits ground-glass opacities, yet the model does not reflect these features well.Additionally, the authors should provide results for the ‘from-scratch’ training setup to demonstrate the actual gain from pre-training. 3.Limited Ablation of Baseline Models The ablation study is relatively weak. Given the recent advancements in generative modeling, why did the authors limit their comparison to only two models (U-Net and CVAE)? A broader range of diffusion-based baselines should be considered. 4.Missing Experimental Details The manuscript lacks essential experimental details such as batch size, learning rate, GPU specifications, and Hounsfield Unit (HU) windowing used in pre-processing. Furthermore, the absence of source code makes the figures and results difficult to reproduce.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: (i) Authors attempt to addresses a genuine and difficult clinical problem, predicting IPF progression from a single baseline CT. Furthermore, their methodoly attempt to do this by decoupling strategy (large-scale thoracic pretraining followed by limited-data IPF adaptation) is well-motivated and addresses a real bottleneck in longitudinal disease modelling. (ii) Operating in a 256³ latent space rather than 2.5D slice-based synthesis better captures volumetric fibrotic structures (traction bronchiectasis, honeycombing) that are clinically meaningful in IPF. The patch-based autoencoding with overlap-average stitching is a practical and technically sound solution for making high-resolution 3D synthesis tractable. (iii) The paper includes internal and external held-out cohort evaluation (site-shift), a systematic ablation study isolating the contribution of longitudinal pretraining (Proposed vs. Scratch), and appropriate statistical testing (paired one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Holm correction). The AE ceiling also provides a useful upper bound for contextualizing the progression modelling gap. (iv) Training the ControlNet adaptor from scratch on cohort-scale IPF data alone is insufficient for stable high-capacity 3D diffusion modelling. This is consistently demonstrated across all metrics on both the internal and external test sets (all Holm-corrected p < 0.001 internally; p < 0.05 externally).
reviewer_3_weaknesses: (i) Reported metrics (SSIM, MSE, PSNR, ViT feature distance, airway volume error) are generic image fidelity measurements. There is no radiologist assessment of whether the synthesized progression patterns (e.g., extent of honeycombing, ground-glass opacity change, reticulation) are clinically plausible or directionally accurate relative to ground truth. This limits the ability to assess whether the model is learning meaningful IPF-specific progression rather than generic texture fidelity. [Minor] (ii) The external cohort comprises only 17 baseline–follow-up pairs. While the site-shift result is encouraging, this sample size does not provide sufficient statistical power to draw robust conclusions about deployment generalization. The authors acknowledge this, but it remains a meaningful limitation for a key claim of the paper. [Minor] (iii) Jiang et al. [6] is the most directly comparable single-scan IPF progression prediction method. The authors cite differences in input assumptions and generation regime to justify omitting a quantitative comparison, but at minimum a qualitative comparison or discussion of performance relative to reported numbers in [6] would substantially strengthen the experimental positioning. (iv) Key details necessary to reproduce the work are absent. For example, the depth and width of the 3D U-Net denoiser and ControlNet, the number of training steps/epochs for each stage, and the optimizer choice and learning rate schedule. Furthermore, the value of m (number of latent samples averaged at inference for stabilization) is missing. [Major] (v) The results tables report aggregate means and standard deviations across all test pairs without stratifying by disease severity or progression phenotype (e.g., stable vs. rapidly progressive IPF trajectories, baseline fibrosis extent, FVC decline category). Without this information, it is unclear whether the reported performance is driven primarily by stable IPF cases, where the follow-up scan closely resembles the baseline, or whether the model generalizes to the more clinically challenging rapidly progressive phenotype. This is particularly relevant for the external cohort, where patient demographics and disease stage distributions relative to the internal cohort are unreported. Stratified results or at minimum a table of cohort characteristics (age, sex, baseline FVC % predicted, median follow-up interval) would allow readers to contextualize the clinical scope and potential bias of the reported metrics
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the Reviewers and Chairs. Clinical scope/metrics (R2-R4). We agree that radiologist scoring and downstream endpoints are important for assessing clinical utility. This is a methodological study of longitudinal CT synthesis: generated follow-up CT is evaluated against observed follow-up in-lung, structurally and in thoracic feature space. We do not claim deployment-level utility. The Discussion confirms our focus on in-lung similarity rather than an IPF-specific endpoint, for which annotation-free CT-based standards remain underdeveloped. CT foundation-model distance and airway error assess thoracic feature alignment and airway structure, complementing SSIM/MSE/PSNR. Progression vs generic generation (R3). R3 questioned whether gains reflect progression modelling or generic high-fidelity generation typical of diffusion. Proposed vs Scratch ablation isolates this: both use the same screening-pretrained autoencoder (AE) and diffusion (LDM) backbone, differing only in ControlNet (CN) longitudinal pretraining; thus latent image quality and diffusion capacity are controlled. Scratch degrades across all metrics, including airway error (Tables 1-2), while Proposed significantly improves pre-specified fidelity/perceptual metrics. This suggests gains arise from a transferable longitudinal adaptor, not merely a high-capacity diffusion backbone. Patch-wise design (R3). We agree that patch/full-volume ablations would characterise this design. However, the main isolated claim is longitudinal pretraining, not universal superiority of patch-wise training. Patch-wise autoencoding and overlap-average stitching make 256^3 synthesis tractable while preserving a 64^3 latent grid. Direct 256^3 AE training at comparable capacity exceeded A6000 memory, while reducing capacity would confound comparison; stronger compression attenuated high-frequency detail in senior board-certified radiologist review. The high AE ceiling in Tables 1-2 indicates that the representation preserves follow-up detail, so the remaining gap is progression modelling rather than decoding. All comparison models use the same latent representation. Qualitative evidence (R3,R4). We agree that Fig. 2 cannot exhaustively establish clinical plausibility. The cases are illustrative, and evidence rests primarily on aggregate paired evaluation across all test pairs. In these examples, senior thoracic radiologist review identified local fibrotic progression patterns, including traction bronchiectasis in zoomed regions, which were absent or over-smoothed in baseline outputs. Predicting exact emergence/extent of subtle patterns from one scan remains challenging; definitive assessment requires clinical endpoint validation. Prior work (R2,R4). Jiang et al. is the closest clinical-task prior, but direct comparison is not straightforward because inputs, datasets, and generation regimes differ. Jiang et al. use OSIC data, lung-function-test guidance via CLIP text encoding, and 2.5D slice generation; our framework uses baseline CT, time horizon, and covariates for full-volume 3D synthesis in a 64^3 latent space. Reported numbers are not directly comparable. Without identical conditioning, data, and implementation, comparison would conflate formulation with performance. We therefore used baselines with identical inputs/conditioning (latent U-Net/cVAE), providing a controlled evaluation. Reproducibility/cohort/ethics (R2-R4). Scans were clipped to [-1200,800]; AdamW; initial LRs AE/LDM/CN/IPF-finetune=1e-4/3e-5/6e-5/4e-6; effective-batch =6/16/4/4; epochs=120/100/50/30.AE channels=(64,128,256); LDM/CN channels=(128,256,512), 2 ResBlocks, condition channels=5. Diffusion used T=1000, DDIM=300, m=5 on Nvidia A6000.Configs/code will be released upon acceptance. Scans were de-identified and used under relevant data-governance/ethics approvals. Details were omitted for anonymisation. The external cohort is modest, supporting transfer feasibility, not deployment generalisation.

title: From Exams to Trajectories: Neural Controlled Differential Equations for Longitudinal Mammography Vision-Language Pretraining
reviewer_1_strengths: The problem solves a difficult problem and reports improvements to an important application. The idea of using continuous-time encoder is new in this setting. There is an ablation study on the different components (Table 3)
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The paper is impossible to read when printed. I suspect it violates guidelines by making font sizes too small in tables. As a further example, Fig 2(a) is very hard to see even in the pdf when zoomed-up and the different models are hard to compare. The intuition behind the continuous-time advantage is not well described/motivated. The source data is inherently at discrete time events so the natural choice is to model it as such. Right now this is disregarded due to “heuristic”. The new approach is in my opinion also heuristic. Then, on the other hand, there is nothing wrong with heuristics! However, one would like to understand why it works better and what priors it brings. Given that there is not any new technical novelty, the evaluation becomes more important. First, it is not clear whether the numbers come from previous work or if it is re-implemented. Then, I have tried to compare to previous work, for instance, Mirai [32], which the authors claim to follow, but the experiments in the present paper do not seem to be conducted in the same manner even though it is using the same data. Training and test sets are not described.

reviewer_2_strengths: The paper is well written and structured The proposed multimodal framework effectively combines mammographic images with masked text reports for risk prediction The design of the auxiliary losses has clinical relevance (asymmetry aware loss) The experimental evaluation is comprehensive, including comparisons with multiple baselines across several metrics (e.g., WMAE, Brier score, c index, and time dependent AUCs) The ablation study is comprehensive and offers insights into the contribution of each component The reported results are promising and competitive compared with existing methods

reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The paper clearly identifies two important gaps: discrete-time modeling limitations for irregular screening intervals and lack of temporal grounding in vision-language mammography models. 2.The TVQA objective is an interesting contribution: It allows temporal reasoning in language and provides a more structured supervision signal. 3.There is a complete experimental validation that includes multiple datasets, diverse tasks, ablations and robustness analysis to irregular sampling. 4.There is a use of clinically relevant evaluation metrics like the use of Risk Prediction’s Brier Score, C-index, and long-horizon AUC.

This limitation is acknowledged but not deeply analyzed. 2.There is little discussion of efficiency, training cost or inference speed, which is important for clinical adoption. 3.The robustness analysis is a strong point, but could include more realistic missing-data scenarios. How does Dynamo perform with real radiology reports instead of pseudo-reports? 4.Can the authors provide qualitative examples demonstrating temporal reasoning (e.g., report changes over time)? reviewer_3_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for the feedback and will add clarifications. We are glad they appreciate the difficulty and importance of the problem(R1,R3), the novelty of leveraging a continuous-time encoder(R1), our clinical relevant losses(R2), and comprehensive empirical studies(R1,R2,R3). *Intuition behind continuous-time advantage (R1) While exams are discrete, the underlying disease evolution is continuous and sampled at irregular intervals. Our approach explicitly captures this by integrating a latent state over real elapsed time, imposing a smooth-in-time prior that improves robustness to irregular sampling and missing visits, versus discrete models with ad-hoc positional encoding. Empirically, replacing NCDE with a Transformer degrades i.e. C-index from 82.79 to 75.38 (Table 3), and NCDE is markedly more stable under visit-dropout/irregular regimes (Fig. 2b). We will improve this description. *Novelty (R1) Clinically, disease progresses continuously while exams are irregular, and interpretation combines stable phenotypes with subtle, view-specific asymmetries. We encode these priors by introducing the first exam-level Neural CDE for longitudinal mammography, using coarse (phenotype) and fine (asymmetry/view-local) streams, augmented with trajectory‑conditioned TVQA and explicit asymmetry regularization. *Evaluation and dataset distribution (R1,R2) To ensure a fair comparison, we adopt a common protocol instead of reusing prior numbers. All baselines are trained and/or evaluated on the same EMBED/CSAW-CC patient wise 70/10/20 train/val/test splits as Dynamo. Multiple follow up visits are available for approx. 64% (EMBED) and 75% (CSAW-CC) of patients. Differences from published Mirai style results can arise from cohort construction, horizons, and preprocessing. Mirai and AsymmMirai were directly evaluated using public final checkpoints. CLIP, DINOv2, Random-ViT, ALBEF, MedGemma, and Mammo-CLIP used public pretrained encoders, with downstream heads/finetuning on patient wise splits. OncoNet, VMRA-MaR, and MaMA were retrained as public final checkpoints matching the task were unavailable. *Computational aspects (R2,R3) The final model has 121M parameters. Training used PyTorch FP16 DDP on 8 NVIDIA H200 GPUs for 30 epochs, batch size 256, requiring 132 GPU+CPU hours. Inference on 115,810 test samples required 0.3 h, or 0.0024 h per 1000 instances. We will add the computational aspects in the revision. *Synthetic reports (R3) We follow prior work in synthesizing reports, due to the lack of available datasets. However, we agree that we could further elaborate the potential challenges with this approach and will do so in the future work section. *Qualitative examples of report changes (R3) Fig.1 contains a concrete TVQA instance: the model is asked to recover a masked dynamic term describing a BI-RADS category change at a 1 year follow up, with candidate terms encoding opposite temporal directions. The prediction is conditioned on the NCDE state z_i, which summarizes the patient history up to exam i. We will revise Fig. 1 to highlight this example more clearly. *Sensitivity to irregular sampling (R3) While we can see a noticeable drop when comparing the performance for the patients with the most regular screening intervals to the most irregular ones (Fig. 2b), this drop is considerably smaller for the proposed method compared to the common transformer-based approach. NCDE natively treats missing exams as longer integration intervals, which stabilizes performance in extremely sparse settings. *Formal statistical comparison (R2) This is a fair comment and formal statistical comparisons were not reported due to the considerable computation requirements of these models. *Typos, presentation, visually dense (R1,R2) Thank you for pointing out the typos. The choice of summarizing the CSAW-CC results in a figure was motivated by space constraints. We understand that this was sub-optimal and will revise it in the final version.

title: From Sparsity to Geometry: Spatial Modeling for 3D Reconstruction from Biplanar Bone X-rays
reviewer_1_strengths: The idea is novel and motivated by an empirical observation of x-rays with sparse contents The spatial modeling approach is intuitive and achieved by sampling multiple points along the 3D ray The idea was validated using fermur bone x-ray dataset with significant performance gain achieved
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Effectiveness of the spatial modeling techniques was only verified in x-rays with sparse contents, not in more general setting such as lung x-rays. Not much details were provided for implementation
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.Clear motivation and well-defined hypothesis The paper isolates a specific factor: spatial/geometric modeling and studies its role in reconstruction quality under varying input sparsity. This is a focused and well-motivated research question. 2.Controlled experimental design (architectural side) The comparison between explicit, canonical, and implicit modeling under the same backbone and training protocol is methodologically sound and allows attribution of performance differences to spatial assumptions rather than confounding factors. 3.Insight on sparsity vs geometry The observation that explicit geometry matters more in low-information regimes (e.g., femur) than in dense settings (e.g., chest) is interesting and potentially valuable for the community.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.Unclear and potentially flawed evaluation protocol: The most serious concern is the evaluation setup, which is both unclear and potentially misleading: The model is trained and evaluated entirely on projections simulated from CT volumes. The loss is defined only in projection space (2D), with no direct supervision on 3D geometry Evaluation is performed on “held-out AP/LAT projections generated from the corresponding CT volumes” However, the paper does not clearly specify: how these “held-out” projections differ from the input AP/LAT views. Whether they correspond to different camera parameters, perturbations, or simply re-renderings under identical geometry. This creates a fundamental ambiguity: It is unclear whether the model is evaluated on truly unseen projections or simply on projections generated under the same synthetic setup and geometry as the inputs. This raises a concerns about evaluation circularity. If held-out AP/LAT projections are not meaningfully different from the conditioning inputs, the task risks becoming partially redundant. 2.No direct evaluation of 3D reconstruction quality All metrics (SSIM, PSNR, LPIPS) are computed in projection space (2D), however, the method is framed as a 3D reconstruction approach, but it is not validated in 3D. 3.Synthetic-only setup Both training and testing rely entirely on synthetic projections from CT. No validation on: real radiographs, mismatched geometry or noisy acquisition conditions. 4.Dataset limitations Femur dataset is very small (34 volumes) Results on LIDC show only marginal gains, suggesting limited impact in realistic dense scenarios
reviewer_2_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The paper presents a systematic definition of the proposed method. Based on the images and quantitative results, the proposed method indeed seems to improve specifically the sparser datasets. There is a small additional experiment with different dataset ratios.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The two evaluation datasets are relatively small. The source code is not public and will not be published, or at least this is not mentioned in the submission.
reviewer_3_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank all reviewers for their helpful, thoughtful feedback. Our responses are as below: Q1 Verification of spatial modeling effectiveness (R1) A1: We also validated on LIDC chest/lung data, representing dense anatomy. While LIDC lacks the same controlled ablation as femur, the compared methods cover explicit (ExpGS), canonical (DIF-Gaussian, PerX2CT), and implicit (DiT, X2CT-GAN) paradigms, providing complementary evidence in dense anatomy. Q2 Implementation details and reproducibility (R1, R3) A2: Implementation details: ResNet-50 encoder; 8-layer Transformer (8 heads, d=512); N=64 depth samples; 256^2 resolution; Adam (lr=1e-4, batch=4). Supervision: 72 views/CT, 4 sampled views/iteration. Code will be released upon acceptance. Q3 Evaluation protocol, held-out projections, and potential circularity (R2) A3: We apologize for the imprecise wording. We confirm that Table 1 reports metrics averaged over all 72 rendered views per test CT, not just AP/LAT. The actual protocol: 72 DRRs per CT (5° intervals); AP/LAT are inputs; 4 random views sampled as supervision during training; at evaluation, the predicted Gaussian field is rendered to all 72 views and compared to ground truth. Thus, the task is AP/LAT –> 3D representation –> multiview rendering, not 2D-to-2D copying. To clarify, the 72-view evaluation spans the full angular orbit; two re-rendered views at the AP/LAT angles are kept to ensure full orbit coverage, and the reported metrics are dominated by novel-view renderings (70/72). Here, “held-out” refers to unseen test CT volumes (e.g. 8 testing CTs in Femur, and 100 LIDC test cases), where AP/LAT views are given as inputs and the predicted 3D field is rendered around the orbit. We will correct the misleading phrase “held-out AP/LAT projections” in the manuscript. Q4 Projection-space loss and no direct 3D supervision (R2) A4: Although CT volumes are available for DRR generation in this controlled study, our training objective intentionally follows projection-supervised 3DGS/NeRF-style reconstruction rather than voxel regression. We agree direct 3D evaluation would further strengthen the claim. Q5 3D quality evaluation (R2) A5: We acknowledge the lack of direct 3D metrics is a limitation. Our focus is a geometry-consistent multi-view Gaussian representation; rendered-view metrics (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS) are commonly used for 3DGS-based medical reconstruction (3DGR-CAR by Fu et al. 2024; Gaussian Pancakes by Bonilla et al. 2024). Direct voxel-level evaluation requires converting 3DGS into voxels with a standardized protocol, which may introduce extra variables. We will clarify this limitation and evaluation scope. Q6 Synthetic-only setup (R2) A6: We acknowledge that synthetic projections cannot prove generalization to real clinical X-rays. We use CT-derived projections as a controlled setting to compare spatial modeling under known geometry, consistent views, and clear supervision. This setting is admittedly idealized, but avoids ethical (dosage) and physical challenges, and is commonly used in recent related methodological works, such as VolumeNeRF (MICCAI 2024) and DCT-Net (MICCAI 2025). Thus, our experiments are controlled projection-supervised validation, not clinical-deployment validation; real X-ray generalization, geometry mismatch, noise, and domain adaptation remain future work. Q7 Small femur dataset and marginal gains on LIDC (R2, R3) A7: We agree that the Femur set is relatively small (n=34), reflecting the scarcity of long-bone CT data. Our LIDC scale ablation (Fig. 4) shows that even at 5% training data (45 cases, comparable to Femur scale), all methods remain stable, confirming that the conclusion is driven by spatial modeling rather than data scale. Marginal LIDC gains are expected: explicit geometry benefits sparse inputs (femur) more than dense anatomy (chest), consistent with the main findings of our work.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper presents a novel and well-motivated approach to incorporating explicit geometric constraints for biplanar 3D reconstruction, with promising results, particularly in sparse settings. While reviewers appreciate the methodological clarity and controlled experimental design, there are notable concerns regarding the evaluation protocol (e.g., reliance on synthetic data and projection-space metrics), limited validation of true 3D reconstruction quality, and reproducibility details. Given the mixed assessments, I invite the authors to provide a rebuttal addressing these issues, particularly clarifying the evaluation setup and strengthening evidence for 3D reconstruction performance. | The authors have addressed the reviewers’ comments. Discussion on the evaluation should be expanded, especially regarding why 3D evaluation was not conducted. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The decision is to accept the paper. The authors propose an effective method incorporating explicit geometric constraints for biplanar 3D reconstruction which performs particularly well in sparse anatomical settings. During the rebuttal phase they successfully clarified critical misunderstandings regarding the evaluation protocol by explaining that the performance metrics reflect novel view renderings across a full orbit. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): I recommend acceptance. The paper presents a focused and well-motivated study of explicit spatial modeling for 3D reconstruction from biplanar X-rays, with particular benefit in sparse anatomical settings. The core idea is intuitive, technically clear, and supported by controlled comparisons between explicit, canonical, and implicit spatial modeling strategies. The rebuttal substantially addressed the main concern about the evaluation protocol. In particular, the authors clarified that AP/LAT views are used as conditioning inputs, while the predicted 3D Gaussian representation is evaluated through rendering over a 72-view orbit on unseen test CT volumes. title: FSE-Reg: Enhancing 3D Deformable Registration with Frozen Large-Scale Pre-trained Segmentation Encoders
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The overall framework and motivation of the proposed method are described in a clear and accessible manner, and the importance of the method as well as its key contributions are generally well explained. 2.In conventional segmentation-assisted deformable registration approaches, output-level cues such as masks or pseudo-labels may be directly affected by registration errors or be vulnerable to domain shift. In this regard, it is interesting that the present work addresses this issue from the perspective of multi-scale feature-level similarity constraints, and proposes a structure that progressively refines the registration field at the feature-representation level rather than directly transferring output-level cues. 3.Compared with joint segmentation-registration learning-based deformable registration methods, which often suffer from high computational cost and complex multi-stage training procedures, this paper presents a comparatively efficient learning pipeline by employing a frozen 3D backbone and introducing decoder designs such as the DPI-Fuse module. 4.The experiments are designed in a sufficiently diverse manner to support the validity of the proposed framework, and the overall performance improvements achieved by the method make the paper reasonably convincing.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.Although the proposed framework provides detailed analyses and meaningful results, the claim of meaningful generalization without fine-tuning on unseen datasets could be better supported by additional experiments with a wider variety of 3D backbones. Such analyses would provide stronger evidence for the authors’ claim. 2.The main novelty of the paper appears to lie in the overall framework design, and among its components, the DPI-Fuse module seems to be one of the key novel elements. However, based on the ablation study, the contribution of DPI-Fuse to performance improvement does not appear sufficiently prominent, which leaves some room for doubt regarding the independent effectiveness of this module. 3.Although the overall results are well presented, Fig. 2 is less effective in illustrating registration quality. The small image size and boxed regions make local differences difficult to compare, and a more direct comparison with the fixed images would improve the qualitative presentation.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The proposed framework is cleanly structured: the frozen encoder provides stable multi-scale anatomical features, while the trainable decoder performs deformation estimation on top. The DPI-Fuse module, although lightweight, is a reasonable interaction design that explicitly models both mismatch and agreement cues between fixed and moving features, which is intuitive and well integrated into coarse-to-fine flow refinement. 2.The experimental results are convincing and represent the strongest aspect of the paper. FSE-Reg consistently outperforms competitive baselines across multiple datasets, with particularly clear gains on external datasets (AMOS and DIR-QA) without fine-tuning. 3.The paper includes extensive comparisons across multiple backbones, multiple datasets, qualitative visualizations, early-stage convergence analysis, and ablation studies. The ablation experiments clearly demonstrate the contribution of each component.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The paper emphasizes that only a lightweight deformation decoder is trained on top of the frozen encoder, but the actual computational complexity is not clearly quantified. The paper does not report decoder parameter counts, total trainable parameters, FLOPs, runtime, or memory usage compared with baseline registration methods. Including such analysis would better substantiate the claimed efficiency advantage. 2.Although DPI-Fuse is shown to be effective in the ablation study, its evaluation is limited to removal-based comparisons. The paper does not compare DPI-Fuse against stronger alternative interaction mechanisms such as correlation-based fusion, attention-based fusion, or simpler competitive baselines like concat-only fusion. As a result, it is difficult to determine whether the proposed fusion design is uniquely advantageous. 3.While the framework is technically sound and practically effective, the main contributions are largely based on integrating existing ideas in a well-engineered manner rather than introducing a fundamentally new registration paradigm. The paper’s value lies more in strong empirical validation than in conceptual novelty.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: There are quite a few interesting ideas/results in this work. 1.The authors demonstrate in Fig. 3 that by using a frozen encoder, there is less parameter to train, which results in faster convergence during training. The faster convergence can also be attributed to the fact that using a frozen pre-trained encoder disentangles representation learning (encoder) from learning deformation fields (decoder). Therefore, the decoder only need to focus on predicting deformation fields from already information-rich features. 2.The idea that one can use a pre-trained 3D segmentation encoder as the encoder for the registration network is quite interesting and the motivation is for this idea is strong. The pre-trained 3D segmentation encoder is trained on a segmentation task, and is thus able to extract richer features with anatomy-related information, which is potentially helpful for image registration task. Furthermore, the authors argue that doing so also allow them to perform what they call feature-space anatomical consistency. 3.The motivation for DPI-Fuse makes sense and results in improvement in performance. Specifically, the authors claim that difference captures mismatch and product captures agreement, both of which are important for image registration task.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The novelty of the work is somewhat limited. 1.The idea of using an pre-trained and frozen feature extractor (contribution 1) instead of relying on intensity information is not new. A somewhat related but old idea was introduced in HAMMER by Shen D, et al., IEEE TMI, 2002 (https://doi.org/10.1109/tmi.2002.803111). There was no pre-trained networks back then but the idea is similar, i.e., relying on higher dimensional features instead of intensity information alone. 2.As far as I know, not a lot of work explore deep supervision in the context of image registration. However, the idea of enforcing consistency in the feature-space is still somewhat standard and simple. This essentially boils down to introducing an additional loss term that computes dissimilarity between warped and fixed feature maps at different resolutions. The clarity of the paper can be greatly improved. 1.At the end of section 1, the authors introduce DPI-Fuse and claim that it is used for “explicit difference/product interactions”. However, it is unclear at this point what difference/product interaction mean and how this interaction is potentially helpful for image registration. 2.Section 2.2 is quite verbose. The entire section can be summarized as follows. Intensity-based dissimilarity is ambiguous while feature-based dissimilarity is more informative. Therefore, an additional loss term based on cosine-similarity is included that quantifies dissimilarity between warped and fixed feature maps at different resolution levels. Consider making this section more concise. 3.The line right after equation (1). What does (\cdot)(p) mean? This notation is not standard and is hard for the readers to understand. 4.In Section 2.3, the “difference term” makes sense. However, it is unclear why the “product term” quantifies agreement.
