title: Geometry-Aware Point-to-Voxel Fusion via Gaussian Splatting for Intracranial Aneurysm Segmentation
reviewer_1_strengths: Combining geometric and intensity features will address the limitations of each in aneurysm segmentation. Also, the fact that the geometric features are not learned may provide an interpretable way to assess their impact on the model.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The ablation may have provided a way to assess geometric features in more detail, for instance, by making some changes or alterations to the cloud points.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The paper contributes to bridging the gap between medical imaging and general 3D computer vision by applying 3D feature extraction and Gaussian splatting in a way that enables DL architectures to leverage vessel information in a principled way, which itself is critical for aneurysm detection. I believe this is a very clever way to integrate vessel information. The proposed gating mechanism, while simple, has a positive impact and highlights the need to modulate geometric information for effective aneurysm detection. The authors propose using a nnDetection model to generate candidate ROIs, simplifying the computational cost of running the model on entire scans. With more training data, this could lead to close-to-perfect filtering of relevant areas. The architecture achieves a very high recall with few to no false positives, albeit this has serious caveats that I will discuss in the weaknesses section.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: There is limited clarity about how the vessel segmentation labels were obtained. The authors claim “Vessel masks are predicted solely from CTA volumes without accessing aneurysm annotations.”, which implies the authors labelled the training data not only for aneurysm detection but for vessel segmentation too. While the authors claim that they also trained the segmentation model using 5-fold cross validation, it is not clear whether the folds were a 1:1 match (ideally, each model should use vessel segmentations from a segmentation model that only had seen the exact same training data, without any access to the evaluation data for that fold). This raises concerns about data leakage as there is a non-zero chance that the areas where aneurysms occur have morphological differences present in the vessel segmentations that the downstream model could leverage to predict the existence of an aneurysm. Furthermore, there is no indication about what extent of the brain vasculature is covered in these annotations. The authors should clarify on this point. The need to train a new vessel segmentation model on newly annotated data seems questionable considering there are several publicly available models dating as far back as 2023 that can segment vessels, ranging from just the Circle of Willis to almost the entire arterial network. Likewise, datasets such as TopCoW, TopBrain, and VesselVerse could have been used to train a segmentation network. In all fairness, this is not a weakness per se, but using existing data or models could have helped solve the critical concerns listed above. The evaluation does not provide insight on whether the proposed method generalizes well outside of the training data, which per the authors’ own claims only contains aneurysms from a few arterial regions. The authors describe using five-fold cross-validation on a single data set with no held-out data. Essentially, this means that the models are evaluated in-domain. As of today, there exist over 400 CTA evaluation scans with dense aneurysm annotations from datasets such as the Large IA Dataset (https://zenodo.org/records/6801398) or CMHA (https://springernature.figshare.com/articles/dataset/CMHA_Intracranial_Aneurysm_CTA_Image_3D_Model_Dataset_with_Clinical_Morphological_Hemodynamic_Data/26965450), plus the RSNA dataset with over 800 aneurysms annotated as coordinates. The Large IA Dataset also contains a sizeable training partition with over 1,000 scans. Even if the authors were compute-limited, they could have used a subset of the available training and evaluation data to better evaluate their approach. I’m sharing these links in hopes you can use them to resubmit the paper if it’s rejected, but please take into account that no new results can be reported in the rebuttal. No evaluation is provided to ablate the impact of the candidate ROIs. While this is a clever way to save compute, a sliding window approach could have been implemented to have a better idea of how this model would perform in a real life scenario, particularly since results are reported based on an oracle fallback for the aneurysms where the ROI detection model failed. Likewise, there is no ablation for the use of the vessel segmentation masks as-is without Gaussian splatting, meaning there is no way to tell if the contribution comes from the features or the vasculature itself. There are no comparisons with respect to methods in the literature that use vessel information to enhance aneurysm detection and the only two baselines are fairly simple methods that use only voxel information.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The paper addresses a clearly motivated problem: small aneurysms often resemble normal vascular bends, making intensity-only segmentation difficult. 2.The use of Gaussian splatting as a fixed-kernel point-to-voxel projection is effective, as it enables smoother and more natural embedding of geometric features than simple nearest-neighbor assignment. 3.The overall design is coherent and well motivated, with geometric feature extraction, point-to-voxel projection, and gated fusion combined in a consistent manner.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.Although the use of Gaussian splatting for modality fusion is a reasonable and technically sound design choice, the underlying idea of using point-cloud geometry as a prior is already quite common, which limits the overall methodological novelty. 2.The range of comparative baselines is limited. Since the paper emphasizes geometry-aware fusion, comparisons with more geometry-aware or vascular-structure-aware methods would strengthen the claims. In particular, because SwinUNETR is included as part of the ablation study, the comparison in Table 2 is effectively reduced to nnU-Net, which makes the empirical scope appear rather narrow.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank R1–R3, who affirm both the methodological (“strong methodological contribution,” “clever vessel integration”) and clinical (“coherent and well motivated”) value of our work. We address each concern below. (1) R2 — Fold alignment and absence of leakage. No data leakage. We used one fixed patient-level 5-fold split for both vessel segmentation and IA segmentation. In each fold, both models train only on the training cases and are evaluated only on the held-out cases. Vessel masks for held-out cases come from the vessel model trained only on the training cases. No held-out case enters vessel-model training, validation, hyperparameter tuning, model selection, or IA-segmentation training. Vessel labels are binary lumen annotations with no aneurysm masks. Therefore, any morphology in the predicted vessel mask is inferred from the held-out CTA itself, not memorised from training exposure. We agree §3.2 was not explicit enough and will revise accordingly. (2) R2&R3 — What Gaussian splatting adds over direct vessel masks. A binary mask encodes only vessel location, not the surface properties (curvature, density, normals) driving discrimination (Fig. 3b: aneurysm/vessel ratios 1.23–1.27×). Our 10-D descriptors are splatted onto the voxel grid via differentiable, sub-voxel-continuous projection—smoother than nearest-neighbour voxelization, and more directly aligned with fixed geometric descriptors than generic learnable rendering [11]. (3) R2 — External validation. Public IA resources each differ in access/modality/annotation/task: Large IA is access-restricted, CMHA has CTA + 3D models but no voxel-wise IA masks, RSNA has coordinates only, CADA uses 3DRA not CTA (closed), and IntraA is hemodynamic. Our 266-lesion multi-vendor cohort, dual-expert annotation, 5-fold CV + 95% CIs supports an in-domain study. External validation is future work. (4) R2&R3 — Vessel-aware baselines. Our method is not comparable to end-to-end vessel-aware pipelines bundled with skull stripping/TTA/component filtering and partially non-public preprocessing. We will release code, preprocessing, and hyperparameters. In Table 3, the “w/o Gating” variant is itself a vessel-aware geometric variant: being vessel-derived, the 10 descriptors inherently mix vessel-location information with surface geometry (curvature, density, normals). It already beats the Baseline (Recall 75.0→84.6, FPs halved), though this inherent mix is necessarily noisy across channels. We agree mask-as-channel is the cleanest ablation for disentangling descriptor content from vasculature presence. That said, simply re-weighting these geometric feature channels yields a substantial leap (DSC 0.591→0.770; DGRF learns heterogeneous weights—Fig. 3c: Density 13.8%, NV 13.0%, Curvature 12.1% vs ~7–9%), supporting that surface geometric content contributes beyond vessel-awareness alone. We will add this control in the camera-ready if permitted. (5) R2 — Why train a new vessel model? With matched folds (see (1)), our in-house vessel model introduces no leakage. We prioritized internal rigour for this submission, and external vessel models are future work. Meanwhile, our framework already tolerates moderate-quality vessel masks (Dice 77.35%). (6) R2 — Oracle fallback. All methods receive identical ROI inputs under the same 5-fold protocol. 84.6% come from the detector, with oracle covering the remaining detector misses. The evaluation is therefore fair for matched-patch segmentation comparison. (7) R3 — Novelty. We acknowledge that using point-cloud geometry as a prior is not new in itself. Our key novelty lies in modality alignment: to our knowledge, we are the first to re-project sparse point-cloud surface features back into the dense CTA voxel grid via Gaussian splatting and jointly train this voxel-aligned geometric stream with the voxel backbone for IA segmentation. (8) R1 — CTA + GFE design guide. CTA = Computed Tomography Angiography. Per-channel GFE formulas accompany our code.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper fuses point cloud geometric features with voxel features via Gaussian splatting and dual-gated residual fusion for intracranial aneurysm segmentation. The approach makes sense and the non-learned geometric features are a nice touch for interpretability. R1 was positive and recommended an oral, while R2 and R3 provided more detailed technical critiques. R2 raised what I consider the central issue: the vessel segmentation model was trained on the same dataset as the aneurysm detection model, and it is not clear whether the cross-validation folds were aligned between the two. If not, morphological cues in the vessel segmentations could leak information about aneurysm presence, which would undermine the results. This may have a reasonable explanation that the authors simply did not describe clearly enough, so I want to give them the opportunity to address it. R2 also noted that some results rely on oracle fallback where the ROI detector failed, which makes reported performance hard to interpret at face value. R2 and R3 both noted that baselines are too narrow, with no vessel-aware aneurysm detection methods compared and Table 2 effectively reducing to nnU-Net alone. For the rebuttal, please try to address all reviewers’ concerns, epecially the following four: 1.confirm that vessel segmentation folds exactly match detection folds with no data overlap; 2.justify the absence of vessel-based detection baselines; 3.discuss why available external datasets were not used; 4.clarify what Gaussian splatting adds over using vessel masks directly. Point 1 is the one that matters most for my final recommendation. | This is a borderline accept and I agree with all reviewers’ comments on the original submission. The round one review turned on one question above all others: whether the vessel-segmentation model and the aneurysm model shared cross-validation folds, since a leak there would have made the reported gains meaningless. The rebuttal settles it. The authors use a single patient-level 5-fold split for both stages, train each fold’s vessel model only on that fold’s training patients, and note that the vessel labels are binary lumen masks carrying no aneurysm information, so there is no aneurysm signal to memorize. R2, who is Very confident and who had raised this exact concern at a Weak Reject, accepted the explanation and moved to Accept. R1 had already recommended acceptance independent of rebuttal. MICCAI rebuttal rules do not allow the authors to add new experiments, but R3’s concern is correct and clearly more baseline comparisons are needed although partly answered by the existing “w/o Gating” ablation. This is the major issue should be solved in the future work. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): Although the rebuttal somehow addresses the data-leakage concern and clarifies the novelty of voxel re-projection using Gaussian splatting, important concerns remain regarding insufficient comparisons with recent relevant baselines and inadequate external validation, making it difficult to fully assess the strength and impact of the proposed methodology. Therefore, the AC recommends rejection. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Overall, there is consensus that the paper addresses a relevant clinical problem and proposes a technically sound geometry-aware fusion approach for aneurysm segmentation. The main concerns have been adequately clarified in the rebuttal, and I therefore recommend acceptance. At the same time, there remain valid concerns about the limited comparison to vessel-aware baselines, the lack of external validation. I encourage the authors to address these points as much as possible in the camera-ready version. I also strongly encourage the authors to make the code and model weights publicly available for the benefit of the community.

title: GGFI-Net: Genomics-Guided Cross-Modal Imputation for Multimodal Survival Analysis with Missing Modality
reviewer_1_strengths: A major strength of this paper is that it focuses on a very practical issue in multimodal survival modeling: in real clinical datasets, modalities are often fragmented or missing, and the sample size is usually too small to support heavy generative approaches. That is a strong and relevant setup, because many multimodal methods quietly assume paired, complete data, which is often unrealistic in practice. By directly targeting missing-modality survival prediction under data scarcity, the paper addresses a real bottleneck for clinical translation rather than an artificially clean benchmark setting. Its methodological idea is reasonably novel and motivated. Instead of trying to reconstruct full missing CT images with GANs or diffusion models, the authors propose to impute radiological latent features directly from genomics-derived pathway features. This is interesting because it avoids the instability and data hunger of full-image generation and focuses on the level that actually matters for downstream survival prediction: the latent representation. That choice is both technically efficient and conceptually sensible. The paper is also strong in its overall framework coherence. The two main components—LCM and GDSD—fit together logically. First, genomic information is used to estimate missing radiology features. Then, the survival distillation module constrains the downstream multimodal model so those imputed features remain prognostically meaningful. This gives the work a clean conceptual pipeline rather than a pile of unrelated modules. The system diagram on page 3 supports this nicely: the architecture clearly shows how real and imputed image features, genomic inputs, teacher supervision, and multimodal fusion interact. That clarity is a real strength in a methods paper. ￼ Another strong point is the handling of small-sample, incomplete multimodal data. The paper does not simply test its method on a fully paired cohort and stop there. It explicitly designs the experiments around two clinically relevant scenarios: a modality-complete CPTAC-PDA cohort and a modality-deficient TCGA-PAAD cohort. This is a good experimental design choice because it lets the authors show that the method is useful not only when all modalities are present, but also when one modality is absent at inference time. That makes the contribution more practically meaningful than a standard multimodal fusion paper. ￼
reviewer_1_weaknesses: A major weakness is the very limited paired multimodal sample size used to support the core cross-modal mapping. The central idea of the method is to learn a genomics-to-radiomics latent mapping through the LCM, but the paired cohort used for this is only 60 CPTAC-PDA cases. That is a small foundation on which to learn a stable cross-modal relationship, especially given the biological and imaging heterogeneity of pancreatic cancer. Even though the authors try to reduce dimensionality and keep the mapper lightweight, it remains unclear whether such a small paired cohort is sufficient to learn a robust and generalizable genomics-to-imaging correspondence. ￼ Another major weakness is that the paper’s missing-modality evaluation is not a true paired missingness setting across the same population, but rather uses different cohorts for the complete-modality and missing-modality experiments. The CPTAC-PDA cohort contains paired CT and genomics, while the TCGA-PAAD cohort contains genomics only. This means the paper is not simply testing how the model behaves when CT is absent from otherwise comparable cases; instead, it is effectively transferring from one multimodal cohort to a different genomics-only cohort. As a result, the observed performance may reflect not only modality missingness but also cross-cohort differences in patient characteristics, data generation pipelines, and latent distribution shift. That makes the missing-modality claim harder to isolate cleanly. ￼ A related concern is that the paper’s central imputation claim is validated only indirectly through downstream survival performance, rather than through a more direct assessment of whether the imputed radiological features are faithful or biologically meaningful. The LCM is trained to minimize feature reconstruction loss against frozen CT embeddings, and the downstream student model is regularized through distillation, but the paper does not provide much direct evidence that the generated radiological features truly capture imaging-related structure beyond helping a survival model. Another weakness is that the incremental value of the full method is not fully disentangled from the strength of the genomics branch itself. The teacher network is genomics-only, genomics are always complete, and the distilled student is heavily guided by this teacher. In that setting, it becomes somewhat ambiguous how much of the final gain really comes from recovering missing radiological information, versus how much comes from a strong genomics-driven representation plus regularization. The comparison to TeacherNet helps, but because the teacher is such a central part of the framework, the paper does not completely resolve whether the imputed modality contributes unique complementary information or mainly acts as an auxiliary learned expansion of genomic signal. ￼ The evaluation, while reasonably careful, also has some clarity limitations. The paper states that Kaplan–Meier curves and log-rank tests were generated by pooling predicted risk scores across all outer test folds under nested cross-validation, but it does not clearly explain how high-risk and low-risk groups were defined for this pooled analysis. Since Kaplan–Meier stratification requires dichotomization of continuous risk scores, the thresholding strategy should be described explicitly. Without that detail, the KM analysis is harder to interpret and reproduce. ￼ The paper somewhat overstates robustness in real-world clinical settings relative to what is actually shown. The conclusion says the framework provides a practical solution for fragmented and incomplete multimodal data, but the current evidence is still limited to retrospective public datasets and internal cross-validation-style testing. There is no true external validation on an independent missing-modality clinical cohort collected under separate conditions. For a paper that emphasizes clinical feasibility, that gap matters. ￼
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The work targets the practical issue of missing modalities, which is a major barrier in real-world clinical deployment. 2.The proposed methodology is novel and ensures light weight modeling, not using computationally heavy models like GANs.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.No discussion or limitations - There is no explicit acknowledgement of limitations or a dedicated discussion section. 2.Claims of performance superiority need to be toned down - the C-index and iAUC gains are relatively modest, so superiority claims need to be toned down or supported by statistical testing. 3.Blending Ratio (R) - The optimal blending ratio may be dataset dependent. TCGA shows 30% while CPTAC appears closer to 0% based on the plots. It would be helpful to discuss whether a universal ratio exists or if an adaptive strategy is needed. 4.Validation Cohort and Generalizability - There is no dedicated external validation set to ensure generalizability. 5.No comparison with radiology-only models - This comparison is important to check whether multimodal integration truly provides benefit over unimodal imaging models. 6.Many modalities exist, some more readily available than others. Can this method be extended to other modalities? Why were these specific modalities chosen? 7.Statistical testing for model comparison is missing ( eg, paired t-tests or bootstrapped CI etc). This is necessary to ensure that differences in the performance are significant. Minor: Table and Figure captions should be standalone and descriptive Some citations appear out to be of order. Please clarify that the entire framework (including all modules) is retrained within each fold of the 5-fold cross-validation.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The paper addresses a truly significant gap: multimodal models almost always deal with aggregated data, but clinical repositories are regularly disaggregated. The introduction pragmatically justifies framing the solution in terms of feature-level imputation (instead of full-modality synthesis). There is principled biological dimensionality reduction. Reducing >60,000 raw RNA-seq features to a 50-dimensional embedding using GSVA-based MSigDB Hallmark pathway scores is a significant domain-informed decision. It performs specifically chosen PCA compression, is biologically interpretable, and is a design choice uncommon in similar work. Lightweight and overfitting-sensitive design. The architectural sparsity (a frozen 128-dimensional radiological encoder, a small LCM, and a small teacher network) is also suitable to the dataset size (n=60 paired data). Throughout, the authors acknowledge and discuss the small-sample problem, which is refreshingly straightforward. Uncertainty-weighted multi-task loss. A principled and reproducible method of multi-objective optimization is to use learnable log-variance parameters (homoscedastic uncertainty weighting, Kendall et al. 2018) to trade off Cox, distillation, and feature alignment losses. Ablation is a fairly thorough study. The authors purify the fusion mechanism (Table 2) as well as the LCM blending ratio (Fig. 3), which gives a reason for their design decisions. The result that logit-level distillation (LKD) adds value over feature-level alignment (Lfeat) is a potentially intriguing and particular understanding. Real-life assessment of truly disjoint cohorts. A realistic split in deployment involves dividing one cohort into the modality-complete case and another into the missing-modality case, rather than artificially obscuring modalities in a single dataset.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Essentially a small paired dataset (n=60). The LCM and GDSD student networks are only trained on 60 paired cases but with a 5-fold cross-validation. Table 1 does not provide any statistical significance tests of comparisons. The standard deviations of GGPI-Net and DeepSurv are often similar (e.g. C-index of 0.709±0.056 vs. 0.676±0.064 on CPTAC-PDA), so it is not clear whether there are any significant gains. This is the main empirical shortcoming of the paper. Asymmetric comparison for the missing-modality scenario. In TCGA-PAAD, GGPI-Net imputes radiological features, whereas all baselines use only genomics. This is the desired comparison, but it implies that GGFI-Net has a structural advantage (learned cross-modal prior) that is not conditioned. A stricter baseline would be a model that is trained with random noise or zero imputation instead of LCM outputs to only capture the contribution of the mapper and not the regularization effect of the distillation itself. None of the comparisons with existing missing-modality methods. The baselines are only genomics-only survival models. There is no comparison with other missing-modality imputation methods for survival analysis, such as HetMorph, imputMAE (cited as Boyko et al. 2025), or the methods reviewed in Qian et al. (2025). This omission makes it difficult to evaluate whether LCM is preferable to alternative imputation strategies. The cross-modal mapping assumption is not proved. The LCM makes a vehemently biological assumption that there is a learnable genomics-to-radiomics mapping. There is no analysis to determine the extent to which the imputed radiomic features are close to the actual CT-derived features (e.g., a reconstruction quality measure or t-SNE visualization of imputed and real embeddings). This would greatly empower the methodological assertions. Lack of technical information on the LCM architecture. The paper itself does not specify the architecture of the mapper M (number of layers, activation functions, hidden dimensions); it only mentions that it is trained to minimize Lmap. In the absence of this, it is impossible to test and test the “lightweight” claim, and reproducibility is lost. The 30 percent blending ratio is decided empirically but not rigorously cross-validated. Fig. 3 indicates the ratio chosen from experimental results; however, it is unclear whether this ratio was determined using a held-out validation set or the same set used to report results, which would overstate performance. Limited dataset scope. Experiments are confined to pancreatic cancer. Although this is right on the heterogeneity basis, it restricts generalizability assertions. The conclusion claims that GGFI-Net is applicable to real-world clinical environments in general, which is overstated since only a disease is assessed. The analysis of the TCGA-PAAD results should be considered. The change in C-index on TCGA-PAAD (vs. TeacherNet) of 0.645 to 0.679 is reported as the main finding, whereas TeacherNet in Table 2 has 0.625 with the same loss pattern as GGFI-Net, which forms an incongruity in the baseline. There is no explanation of this discrepancy.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: 1.Small paired cohort/generalizability (R1–R3). We agree that larger paired datasets and external validation would strengthen this study. This limitation is mainly due to the scarcity of public pancreatic cancer datasets with paired CT, RNA-seq and survival data. GGFI-Net should be viewed as a proof-of-concept, not a fully validated clinical solution. We will explicitly discuss this limitation and tone down generalizability claims. 2.Performance claims/statistics (R2,R3). Formal statistical testing was not included in the submitted manuscript; therefore, we will not claim statistically proven superiority. The reported mean±SD should be interpreted as empirical performance trends under the nested-CV protocol. We will remove overly strong wording such as “significant superiority”. 3.Blending ratio R (R2,R3). R is not a universal constant. Fig. 3 is a sensitivity analysis rather than evidence for a generally optimal value. R=30% is an empirical setting selected from validation trends, not an independently validated optimum. We will clarify that in manuscript. 4.Baselines, modality choice and SOTA methods (R2,R3). A radiology-only baseline would address a different complete-modality question, which would indeed further broaden the evaluation, whereas our central setting is CT-missing survival prediction. The primary comparison is between genomics-only prediction and genomics-guided CT-representation imputation. CT and RNA-seq were chosen for prognostic relevance and data availability; the framework can extend to other modalities with paired data. Most methods reviewed by Qian et al. target complete modality reconstruction, segmentation/classification or different modality configurations. Related survival-oriented latent-space methods, such as HGCN (Hou et al) and impuTMAE, would require matched modality availability, missingness patterns and survival protocols for fair comparison. We will avoid implying that LCM is generally preferable to existing imputation strategies. 5.Missing-modality setting (R1,R3). The missing-modality evaluation indeed involves transfer between CPTAC-PDA (paired CT/genomics) and TCGA-PAAD (genomics only), introducing potential cohort shift. Our intent was to emulate a clinically realistic scenario in which multimodal data are available only in a subset of patients, while deployment occurs in genomics-only cohorts. We will clarify that our framework addresses both missing-modality learning and cross-cohort transfer, rather than a strictly controlled paired missingness experiment. We thank the idea about zero/noise-imputation controls and embedding-level analyses, which are valuable future validations. 6.Imputed representations and LCM contribution (R1,R3). We agree that direct analysis of imputed representations would strengthen the interpretation. However, LCM is not designed to reconstruct CT images, but to learn CT-embedding-aligned auxiliary representations when CT is unavailable. Its output is constrained by reconstruction loss against frozen CT embeddings, distinguishing it from unconstrained genomic feature expansion. TeacherNet provides partial evidence that the full model is not merely reproducing the genomics-only teacher, although it does not fully disentangle CT-aligned representation learning from distillation regularization. We will avoid claiming faithful recovery of radiological information and describe LCM as CT-embedding-aligned auxiliary representation learning. 7.Reproducibility (R2, R3). We will add the details about LCM architecture to the manuscript. Code will also be released upon acceptance. 8.Other clarifications. (R1) For KM analysis, groups are split by median predicted risk. (R2) The captions and citations order will be reorganized. Except for the autoencoder trained on MSD, the imputation module and GDSD are retrained within each fold. (R3) The TeacherNet inconsistency is a typographical error; the correct value is in Table 1, and Table 2 will be corrected.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): An clinically motivated framework for imputing features from genomic pathway scores. Concerns focuse on the experiment, including small dataset, no strong missing-modality baselines, and evaluation of imputed features. | Although there are some flaws in the experiments, the novelty and motivation of the proposed method were recognized by all reviewers. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This work addresses multimodal pancreatic cancer survival prediction under missing-modality constraints by directly imputing radiological latent features from biologically grounded genomic pathway maps. While the paired training dataset is inevitably constrained by the real-world scarcity of multi-omic clinical repositories, the framework’s architecture is optimized for small-sample conditions without relying on data-hungry image generation models. The authors have delivered a transparent rebuttal, agreeing to reframe their manuscript to reflect empirical trends appropriately, providing essential implementation metrics, and correcting baseline notation. As a highly translational proof-of-concept targeting an unavoidable clinical missingness bottleneck, the paper possesses sufficient technical and conceptual merit to justify acceptance. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): This paper addresses an important and clinically relevant problem of multimodal survival prediction under missing-modality settings. Reviewers appreciated the practical motivation and the novel idea of learning CT-aligned representations from genomic features. However, after considering the reviews and rebuttal, I remain concerned about the strength of the empirical evidence supporting the proposed framework. The key cross-modal mapping is learned from a very limited paired cohort, and several important validations remain absent, including comparisons with existing missing-modality approaches, direct analysis of the imputed representations, and control experiments to disentangle the contribution of the mapper from the distillation framework. In addition, the reported performance gains are relatively modest and are not supported by formal statistical significance testing. While the work is an interesting proof-of-concept, I do not find the current experimental validation sufficient to support acceptance.

title: Glasses: Adapter-Enhanced DINOv3 with Boundary-Aware Multi-Scale Representations for Medical Image Segmentation
reviewer_1_strengths: The main strengths of this study are as follows:(1) It proposes a multi-scale deformable attention adapter designed for fine-tuning DINOv3 features. (2) It adopts a UNet-like architecture with two encoders and one decoder to jointly learn and fuse global and local features.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The key weaknesses of this paper are as follows:(1) The performance improvements over baseline methods are marginal. (2) Validating the method only on two public datasets is insufficient, especially since these datasets focus on relatively straightforward segmentation tasks (abdominal organs and skin lesions). (3) The input–output flow in Figure 2 is unclear and confusing. (4) The overall novelty and technical insight of the proposed method are limited. (5) The framework name “Glasses” bears no clear connection to the proposed methodology. (6) No qualitative visualizations are provided to illustrate how the proposed adapter functions or improves structural feature representation.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The model combines the robust global context of a largely frozen DINOv3 backbone with a dedicated convolutional stream to capture both high-level meaning and fine-grained anatomical details. The Multi-Scale Deformable Attention Adapter allows the model to learn medical-specific spatial features without retraining the entire Transformer, preserving powerful pre-trained representations while reducing computational overhead. By using an Edge-Aware Convolutional Encoder with nested supervision, the framework explicitly prioritizes contour accuracy to improve the model’s performance.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: While freezing DINOv3 preserves semantic stability, it may prevent the model from fully adapting its core feature extraction ability to the unique stylistic and domain-specific characteristics of medical images.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The paper precisely targets the current pain point of Vision Transformers (ViTs) in medical image segmentation: strong global semantics but weak local boundaries. The logic of using a parallel adapter for aligning semantics to structures and an independent edge encoder for explicit structural modeling is very clear, effectively forming a complementary dual-stream architecture. 2.Utilizing Deformable Attention for the sampling and residual updating of frozen features is an elegant approach to feature interaction. Furthermore, the nested boundary supervision mechanism projects features of different depths into a unified boundary space via progressive alignment operators. This design is theoretically rigorous and effectively avoids feature conflicts during multi-scale prediction. 3.Glasses achieves SOTA performance on two classic and challenging public datasets, Synapse and ISIC 2018.Particularly on the Synapse dataset, it not only reaches a mean Dice coefficient of 83.52%, but more importantly, the Hausdorff Distance (HD) is significantly reduced to 12.28 mm, directly demonstrating the model’s superiority in precise boundary prediction. 4.The ablation experiments detailed in Table 3 solidly prove the independent value and necessity of core components, including the Multi-Scale Deformable Adapter, the parallel CNN branch, and the nested boundary supervision strategy.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.This paper lacks an analysis discussing the model’s sensitivity to hyperparameters. For example, the weights in the semantic loss function, alpha and beta. 2.While the proposed framework leverages DINOv3 as its backbone , the comparative experiments fail to include other state-of-the-art segmentation methods that also utilize the pre-trained DINOv3 model. 3.The experimental section lacks comparisons with methodologies that employ related pre-trained vision models (e.g., other ViT variants, SAM, or equivalent foundation models) coupled with fine-tuning strategies. 4.Although the proposed Glasses framework achieves state-of-the-art overall mean Dice and Hausdorff Distance on the Synapse dataset , the quantitative results in Table 1 reveal that it does not attain the highest scores across all individual organ categories.The manuscript currently lacks a critical discussion explaining this phenomenon.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We sincerely thank all reviewers for their detailed and constructive feedback. Here are responses to their suggestions and concerns. R1Q1: Improvements over Baselines Thank you for your comment. While the Dice improvements over strong baselines are moderate, Glasses consistently improves both segmentation accuracy and boundary quality across two different medical segmentation tasks. On Synapse, it achieves the lowest HD (12.28 mm), reflecting improved boundary localization and anatomical continuity. On ISIC 2018, it also shows competitive performances. R1Q2: Validation on Two Datasets Synapse and ISIC 2018 cover distinct medical segmentation scenarios with different modalities, anatomical structures, and boundary characteristics. The consistent improvements across both datasets suggest that the framework generalizes beyond dataset-specific settings. R1Q3 & Q6: Clarity of Figure 2 and Adapter Visualization Thank you for pointing this out. In Fig. 2, lightweight convolutional structural priors serve as queries, while DINOv3 tokens provide semantic key-value representations for cross-scale interaction. Through deformable sampling and residual iterative updating, the adapter transforms single-scale tokens into structure-aware multi-scale representations. We also agree that qualitative visualization can help illustrate the adapter’s effect. In the final version, we will improve the feature-flow illustration and corresponding description. R1Q4: Novelty and Technical Insight Glasses is not a simple CNN-Transformer fusion. Its novelty lies in structure-aware adaptation for largely frozen DINOv3 and explicit boundary-aware structural modeling. The Multi-Scale Deformable Attention Adapter performs deformable sampling and residual semantic updating between lightweight structural priors and DINOv3 tokens, transforming single-scale tokens into hierarchical structure-aware representations without modifying the frozen backbone. In addition, the nested boundary supervision projects multi-scale structural features from the parallel convolutional encoder into a unified boundary representation space, improving cross-scale edge consistency. R1Q5: Framework Name “Glasses” is intended as a metaphor for enhanced structural perception and boundary awareness in medical image segmentation. We will clarify this in the final version. R2Q1: Frozen DINOv3 Adaptation In our framework, we perform selective fine-tuning only on the higher-level DINOv3 layers, complemented by the proposed structure-aware adapter, which interacts with lightweight structural priors to progressively adapt the pre-trained DINOv3 features to medical segmentation tasks. This allows the backbone to retain robust global semantics while becoming task-adaptive, improving structural modeling on limited datasets. R3Q1: Hyperparameter Sensitivity Thank you for your valuable suggestion. The weighting parameters balance the contributions of cross-entropy and Dice terms. Due to space limitations, the ablation study on the weighting parameters was not included. A more comprehensive sensitivity study remains future work. R3Q2 & Q3: Comparison with DINOv3-/Foundation-Model-Based Methods Our primary goal is to evaluate whether the proposed strategy can enhance largely frozen foundation Transformer representations for medical image segmentation. We agree that broader comparisons with other DINOv3-based or foundation-model-based segmentation methods could provide further insights, and we plan to investigate in future work. R3Q4: Organ-Wise Performance Differences Glasses does not achieve the highest Dice score for every individual organ category. This is largely due to the inherent characteristics of the Synapse dataset, where annotations and contrast vary. Our framework is designed to enhance overall structural consistency and boundary accuracy. Even when the per-organ Dice is not the highest, Glasses improves the overall mean Dice and significantly reduces Hausdorff Distance.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): This paper presents Glasses, a structure-enhanced DINOv3 adaptation framework for medical image segmentation. Overall, the work addresses an important and practical problem in medical image segmentation: how to leverage strong pre-trained semantic representations while complementing them with local structural and boundary-aware modeling. All three reviewers considered the topic relevant, the methodological design reasonably clear, and the experimental results on public benchmarks such as Synapse and ISIC competitive. The proposed structure-enhanced DINOv3 adaptation framework is well aligned with the medical image segmentation task, and the overall empirical results are competitive. The main concerns raised by the reviewers appear to be addressable in the final version through additional discussion, clearer illustration of the framework, more qualitative analysis, and expanded experimental interpretation. Therefore, this paper is recommended for early acceptance.

title: GLeVE: Graph-Guided Lesion Grounding with Proposal Verification in 3D CT
reviewer_1_strengths: The paper addresses an important and well-defined problem of lesion-level grounding, which is more clinically meaningful than phrase-level alignment. The idea of modeling each lesion as a structured semantic unit using graph reasoning is intuitive and useful. The method is well designed with a clear pipeline and shows consistent improvements over strong baselines, including in low-supervision settings. Experiments are solid and support the contributions.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The overall novelty is somewhat limited, as the method mainly combines existing components (graph reasoning, proposal verification, coarse-to-fine refinement) rather than introducing a fundamentally new formulation. 2.The pipeline is quite complex and involves multiple modules (LLM parsing, graph transformer, proposal generation, verification, octree refinement), which may limit scalability and real-world deployment. 3.The region-level verification strategy is not fully justified; it is unclear why verifying candidates at the region level is optimal compared to voxel-level or hybrid strategies, and no theoretical or empirical comparison is provided. 4.The method relies on several hyperparameters (e. g. , λ weights in the loss, temperature τ), but there is limited discussion on how these are selected or how sensitive the model is to these choices. 5.The optimization strategy and training stability are not well analyzed, especially given the combination of weak and strong supervision losses, which could affect convergence behavior. 6.The approach depends on accurate report parsing and structured extraction, making it potentially sensitive to noise or variability in real clinical reports. 7.Evaluation is limited to a single dataset, and the generalization of the method to other datasets, organs, or imaging modalities is not demonstrated.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The paper tackles a very important problem related to grounding findings from radiology reports. The ideas proposed, including Lesion Semantic Modeling and Querying, Anatomy-Prior Lesion Proposal and Verification and octree refinement of predicted masks are relatively novel and interesting The results are strong and reporting of results is comprehensive
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The paper’s result are limited to one dataset that only contains tumor leions. Other datasets like ReXGroundingCT (https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.22030) which covers more diverse lesion types could be used. Moreover, I think mixing grounding of organs and grounding of findings in the same evaluation introduces inflated results. Grounding of organs is a much easier task, and arguably one in which grounding is not useful, because the set of possible organs is very small. Gounding findings is much harder as findings can in multiple different places on the scan, and have varying characteristics (size, shape, etc) The paper took me a lot of time to read mainly because of how it is written, especially the choice of mathematical symbols. I think a lot of the equation and symbols should be re-written to be more consistent across the paper and with literature. Many variables (like ϕ in equation 2 or Ψ in the QueryBank or C in R^C) are not explained/defined. Even if something seems obvious, please try to define all variables. Also, why is ψ used for MLP? These are non-standard definitions that create confusion.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The authors present an interesting combination of frameworks to leverage each for a optimized grounding radiology reporting. They use a mix of composite semantics, organ segmentation and an octree-based autoregressive refinement, which provides an increased performance compared to state-of-the-art appraoches. These methods collectively enhance model understanding and precision in complex tasks – which can be beneficial for clinical reporting. For instance, graph-structured representation learning captures the information from descriptions in reports, allowing the model to reason about interactions between observed patterns in the scan. Additionally, they interestingly leveraged geometry-aware anatomical embeddings, informed by priors, to provide domain knowledge crucial in clinical settings for optimal and localized diagnosis. The multi-candidate verification and autoregressive refinement strategies also provide this method with a built-in quality-check-like mechanism and a key-to-key alignment between reports and imaging.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Limitations of the present work should be further discussed. For instance, graphs have been known to misunderstand structure whilst using priors can bias the results by over-assumptions on the data. Furthermore, refinement can further exarcebate the mistake-to-success ratio by polishing the mistakes dragged from previous steps instead of correcting them. It should be discussed whether the octree approach for small lesions could yield wrong results if the data is noisy or when reconstruction kernels are diverse – which is very frequent in clinical imaging. Latency is not discussed and raises the question about the computational cost of the present architecture. For clinical feasibility this could be a major concern.
reviewer_3_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal

title: Good Enough? An Investigation on the Impact of Label Quality in Large-Scale Medical Datasets
reviewer_1_strengths: First, it addresses a highly relevant and practical problem in medical imaging: the trade-off between annotation quality and scalability. Given that large datasets such as DAP-Atlas or AbdomenAtlas require thousands of hours of expert effort, the paper tackles an important question—whether such costly refinement is necessary—making the work highly impactful for both dataset construction and model development. Second, the paper proposes a novel and well-designed experimental framework to study label quality. Instead of relying on synthetic noise (as commonly done in prior works using perturbations or morphological operations), it generates realistic pseudo-label noise using a diverse set of models (nnU-Net, TotalSegmentator, STU-Net variants, MedSAM). This setup closely mimics modern dataset curation pipelines and avoids unrealistic assumptions about noise distributions, which is a clear methodological improvement over prior studies
reviewer_1_weaknesses: First, the study relies entirely on pseudo-labels generated by models as a proxy for annotation noise, which may not fully capture real-world annotation errors. Although this is more realistic than synthetic perturbations, it still differs from genuine human annotation variability. As a result, the conclusions may not fully generalize to real clinical annotation settings. Second, the experimental setup, while controlled, is somewhat limited in model diversity. The study fixes a single segmentation architecture (DynUNet / nnU-Net style training) to isolate data effects. While this improves internal validity, it raises concerns about external validity: it is unclear whether the conclusions hold for other architectures, especially newer foundation models or transformer-based segmentation approaches.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: Extensive and diverse 3D datasets: The study is grounded in a robust experimental framework, utilizing a wide array of large-scale 3D medical segmentation datasets that accurately reflect the complexities of clinical volumetric imaging across various anatomical regions. Comprehensive simulation of label noise: A significant merit of the work is the inclusion of diverse label-generation models, such as nnU-Net, MedSAM, and the STU-Net family. By leveraging these varied architectures to produce a spectrum of pseudo-label qualities, the authors successfully simulate real-world annotation noise and its impact on model training. Clear and coherent presentation: The manuscript is well-structured and the results are presented with a high degree of transparency. The figures and tables are clearly plotted, making the core findings regarding the relationship between pre-training and fine-tuning easy to understand at a glance.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Lack of self-supervised learning baselines: A critical methodological gap is the absence of comparisons with self-supervised learning (SSL) paradigms (e.g., DINO). Without an SSL baseline, it remains unclear whether the pre-training gains stem from the “noisy labels” or simply from the model’s exposure to a larger data volume. Undefined boundary of label noise: While the study shows pre-training is robust to label quality (Dice 70-90%), it fails to explore the “break-down point” of this robustness. It remains unknown whether a noise threshold exists or if even completely randomly generated masks would yield similar results, which leaves the actual necessity of using “pseudo-labels” for pre-training unproven. Technical error in visualization: There is a noticeable technical oversight in Figure 3.c, where the bar representing the STU-Net Large results for the AbdomenAtlas dataset is missing. It is unclear whether this is a plotting error or if the performance value is lower than the visible y-axis limit.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1 The paper addresses an interesting and practically relevant problem, and the use of model-generated pseudo labels to mimic modern dataset construction pipelines is a meaningful and moderately novel experimental setting. 2 The overall logic of the paper is clear, and the experimental setup is described in sufficient detail, supporting reproducibility. 3 The experiments are fairly comprehensive, covering seven pseudo-label generation models and four base datasets, with additional evaluation on one extra model and two extra datasets. 4 The empirical analysis is relatively thorough, and the figures and tables are well organized and easy to follow.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1 I remain unconvinced by the second conclusion in 3.1.The reported performance trend is obtained by fitting a quadratic polynomial to only seven discrete data points, yet several actual nnUNet points deviate noticeably from the fitted curve. From the figure, the performance of Orig does not appear to exceed nnUNet and even drops substantially in some cases. Therefore, the statement “As the dataset quality approaches 100, the performance curves begin to plateau” does not seem to be fully supported by the raw plotted results, and may be overly influenced by the fitted trend rather than directly supported by the discrete experimental observations. 2 In 2.2, the second finding states that “nnUNet outperforms on most datasets, achieving Dice scores from 82.8% to 95.2%.” However, I could not find any value corresponding to “82.8” in the table. This indicates that there is an issue in either the main text or the table, and the reported numbers should be carefully checked and made consistent.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank all reviewers for their constructive feedback and their general positive assessment. We address the main concerns below. Pseudo-labels as a noise proxy (R1). Our pseudo-label setup is intentionally faithful to current large-scale practice, where datasets [8, 20, 27] are themselves constructed from model-generated masks with sparse expert verification, rather than via the synthetic perturbations used in prior work [1, 3, 24]. We acknowledge that for smaller, manually annotated cohorts, inter-rater variability may be the more realistic noise source. For this study, we deliberately keep the noise model consistent across our four datasets, which span 100 to 5,200 cases, to enable a controlled comparison of how the same noise type interacts with dataset scale. Architectural diversity (R1). With well over 100 full 3D segmentation training runs already required to span our 8 label variants, 4 base datasets, and 2 fine-tuning targets, adding an architecture family scales this beyond our available hardware resources. We deliberately fixed DynUnet to isolate the data effect; DynUnet/nnU-Net remains the most consistently competitive 3D backbone in the recent literature, so we believe studying this architecture is the most beneficial to the community. Extending the architecture selection is a natural and interesting follow-up. SSL baselines and breakdown point (R2). We restricted ourselves to supervised pre-training to avoid a task shift between pre-training and fine-tuning, and because Li et al. [13] (ICLR 2024) report supervised pre-training to be much more sample-efficient than SSL on 3D medical data, so the question for us became how important data quality is under the more efficient supervised pre-training regime. Regarding the breakdown point: MedSAM on AbdomenAtlas reaches only 39.4% Dice and 24.8% Surface Dice (Table 1), well below any plausible expert-curation threshold, yet models pretrained on it still play in the same league with models pretrained on higher quality datasets (Fig.3c). This datapoint already probes the low-quality regime, though a fully randomized-mask control would push it further, and we agree it is an interesting follow-up. Missing STU-Net Large bar in Fig. 3c (R2). This is not a plotting oversight: STU-Net Large pre-training on AbdomenAtlas did not converge under our fixed, deterministic training schedule. We will mark this explicitly in the camera-ready version and thank R2 for catching it. Plateau claim and quadratic fit (R3). R3 is right that the 2nd-degree fit smooths the discrete observations. The intended claim that marginal gains shrink at high label quality is most clearly carried by AbdomenAtlas (Fig. 2, right), where the four STU-Net variants span ~4 Dice points in label quality but yield largely overlapping model performance and even perform similarly to the model trained on the original labels. 82.8% inconsistency (R3). Correct: 82.8% is a leftover from BTCV experiments that were removed for spatial reasons from the final manuscript; the actual lower bound in Table 1 is now 83.7% (Word). We thank R3 for catching this and will fix it.

title: Graph Neural Networks for Morphometric Characterization of the Aortic Valve
reviewer_1_strengths: The authors address a relevant clinical problem. The idea of the consideration of the spatial relations between relevant landmarks via graph representations is well motivated. The approach is well described.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The paper seems to be work-in-progress. There are several mistakes (e. g. surgerical, landmarks of the aortic,. . . ) in the text and references, which do not support the statements in the text ([7]). There is no assessment of the of inter- or intraobserver variability of the reference annotations or an ablation study.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The problem is clinically relevant. Accurate aortic valve measurements are important for surgical planning, and automating robust measurement from detected landmarks addresses a real clinical need. 2.The graph-based representation is well-motivated and clearly formalized. Defining edges via similarity of landmark subsets is an intuitive and principled way to encode anatomical dependencies between measurements. 3.The GNN architecture — from row-wise MLP embedding, through mean-pooled context, GCN message passing, context re-injection via residual MLP, to softmax-weighted candidate selection — is described in detail with clear notation and equations. The design choice to select among anatomically plausible candidates rather than directly regressing measurements is a sensible inductive bias. 4.The evaluation covers a comprehensive set of 29 measurements (18 linear, 11 angular), and results show consistent improvement over the baseline.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.Reference [6] is cited in the context of deriving measurements from landmarks, but it is a general anatomy review that describes aortic root structure — it does not define a measurement protocol. The 29 evaluated measurements remain undefined: which landmark subsets are used and what geometric operations are applied for each measurement are not specified in the paper or in the cited reference. 2.The geometric descriptor for larger set of landmarks is described with “e.g.” and “etc.”, leaving the exact feature set and dimensionality D unspecified. Since the descriptor is the foundational input to the entire pipeline, the complete feature list should be explicitly stated. 3.The baseline comparison is insufficient to isolate the GNN’s contribution. The baseline uses a single Center-of-Mass point per landmark, while the proposed method uses a GNN-weighted average over K=1000 candidate combinations. The observed improvement could arise from three distinct sources: (a) the inherent robustness of ensembling over multiple candidates, (b) the GNN’s learned weighting, or (c) diversity among candidate points. Without an ablation comparing uniform (equal-weight) averaging over the same K=1000 combinations against the GNN-weighted result, the reader cannot determine how much of the improvement is attributable to the GNN architecture versus the trivial benefit of multi-candidate averaging. 4.No training loss function is specified anywhere in the paper. The architecture is described in full detail, but the optimization objective — what the GNN is trained to minimize — is absent. This raises several unanswered questions: whether MSE or MAE is used, how losses across linear (mm-scale) and angular (degree-scale) measurements are balanced, whether any regularization is applied to the softmax weights, and what serves as the ground truth reference for supervision. 5.The ground truth was provided by “an experienced cardiovascular surgeon” but no inter-observer variability analysis is reported. For clinical measurements, a single annotator’s measurements are insufficient to establish a reliable reference standard. Without inter-observer analysis, it is unclear whether the GNN’s improvement is within the noise floor of human measurement variability. 6.The authors acknowledge dependence on landmark detection accuracy as a limitation but provide no quantification. No landmark localization error is reported, and no sensitivity analysis examines how upstream detection noise affects downstream measurements. Without this, it is impossible to assess whether the GNN is learning genuinely optimal geometric weighting or compensating for detection noise.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: Although the proposed methodology has been applied in other domains for extracting anatomical measurements, to the best of our knowledge, it has not previously been used to derive measurements related to the aortic valve. Additionally, the method has been trained and evaluated using three different cohorts from two independent institutions, which supports its robustness and generalizability.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The main limitation of the proposed approach, as acknowledged by the authors, is that it functions primarily as a refinement tool. Consequently, if the initial landmark detection results are highly inaccurate, the method cannot effectively correct them. Nevertheless, in practical terms, current landmark detection techniques are generally robust, and in cases of failure, it is reasonable to assume that inconsistent results would be readily identified by a specialist. Furthermore, the non-public nature of the datasets used in this study limits the ability to fully assess the generalizability and external validity of the proposed method.
reviewer_3_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and meta-reviewer for providing valuable feedback. Several comments are pointing to new/additional experimental results, which are however not allowed in the rebuttal. Nevertheless, we indicate on our framework performance that will be considered in our eventual future work. We therefore focused on the following comments: Measurement details (MR, R#2, R#6): The evaluated morphometric measurements are computed from anatomically defined landmark subsets using deterministic geometric operations. Depending on the measurement, these operations include Euclidean distances, angles between vectors or plane normals, centroid-based angular calculations, and ellipse fitting using SVD and Powell optimization. We will provide a list of landmark-to-measurement assignment for each morphometric measurement in Table 1. Geometric descriptors, loss function and compactness (MR, R#2, R#6): Candidate descriptors consist of: 1) Euclidean distances between landmarks, 2) angular relationships encoded as cosine similarities, 3) PCA descriptors using the two largest eigenvalues, and 4) compactness as the mean distance of participating landmarks to their centroid (describes spatial dispersion and overall scale of landmark configuration, complementing pairwise distances with a rotation-invariant global descriptor). The model is trained using a standard MSE regression objective applied jointly across all predicted measurements (with no weighting of linear and angular measurements, auxiliary losses or softmax regularization terms). Ablation study (MR, R#1, R#2, R#6): We differentiated the contribution of graph-based weighting from candidate-based averaging, and evaluated a uniform averaging baseline using the same candidate sets and the same number of candidate combinations, but without GNN. Compared to CoM, the reduction in MAE was the greatest for GNN, whereas uniform averaging achieved smaller improvements, indicating that the observed gains are not solely explained by ensemble averaging, but additionally benefit from GNN. We acknowledge this experimental suggestion, and will consider it in our future work. Observer variability (MR, R#1, R#2): In terms of normalized MAE, the proposed GNN achieved an error of 2.5±0.9% for linear and 9.6±10.2% for angular measurements. For a subset of 25 cases, the inter-observer variability was 3.0±1.6% and 15.4±15.8%, while the intra-observer variability was 1.6±1.0% and 8.4±9.5%, respectively, confirming that the proposed framework operates within the inter-observer variability. Note that no new experiments were performed, as these results were already available but not reported. Noise (MR, R#5): We evaluated the effect of perturbations applied to candidate landmark coordinates using different Gaussian noise levels, and GNN showed substantially greater robustness compared to the CoM baseline. The relative advantage of GNN over CoM increased with noise, indicating that graph-based aggregation improves robustness by leveraging anatomical contextual information. We acknowledge this experimental suggestion, and will consider it in our future work. Landmark localization (R#1, R#2, R#6): This was performed by nnU-Net with the default configuration and automatic hyperparameter selection. The only task-specific modification was ground truth mask generation (spherical landmark-centered regions with a radius of 3.6 mm). Based on the predicted heatmaps, the landmark localization error was below 0.95 mm for 99.4% of landmarks (only two exceeded 3.6 mm). Note that no new experiments were performed, as these results were already available but not reported. Code and Data (All): We are evaluating the possibility of publicly releasing the source code. For data, we will allow sharing upon reasonable request. Ethical approval for data acquisition and usage exist and will be reported. Text/referencing errors (MR, R#2, R#6): Thank you, we will correct the typos and referencing errors.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): While reviewers agreed that the paper addresses a clinically relevant problem with a well-motivated, detailed graph-based GNN architecture and validation across multiple cohorts, they also raised serious concerns about the paper’s methodological clarity, evaluation rigor, and reproducibility: First, critical methodological details are missing, including undefined aortic valve measurements, unspecified geometric descriptors, and no stated training loss function, hindering reproducibility. Second, the evaluation is insufficient—baseline comparisons fail to isolate the GNN’s contribution, there is no inter-observer variability analysis for ground truth annotations, and no quantification of how landmark detection errors affect downstream measurements. Third, the paper contains text/referencing errors and uses non-public datasets, limiting external validity and trustworthiness. Since the reviews are mixed, we would like to invite the authors to provide a rebuttal. In addition to clarify other concerns, please try to address the following points during rebuttal: provide more details about the aortic valve measurements and their landmark subsets, specify the full geometric descriptor set and training loss function; conduct an ablation to isolate the GNN’s contribution (vs. multi-candidate averaging), report inter-observer variability for annotations, and quantify how landmark detection noise impacts measurements; correct text/referencing errors and provide details to enhance external validity (e.g., dataset access or more cohort details). | Reviewers agreed that the paper addresses a clinically relevant problem with a well-motivated graph-based approach for refining aortic valve measurements, and that the method is comprehensively evaluated across multiple institutions, demonstrating potential robustness and generalizability. However, they also raised serious concerns about the paper’s technical completeness and scientific rigor: (1)​critical methodological details were missing or underspecified, including the measurement protocol linking landmarks to clinical metrics, the complete geometric descriptor set, and the training loss function; (2) the contribution of the GNN was not convincingly isolated, as the improvement could stem from multi-candidate ensembling rather than learned relational modeling, and no ablation with uniform averaging was provided; and (3)​the reliability of the reference standard was unclear, with no inter-observer variability analysis, no quantification of landmark localization accuracy, and limited discussion of clinical interpretability and robustness. The rebuttal has successfully addressed most concerns by supplying the missing specifications, reporting inter-observer variability and landmark detection performance, and clarifying the loss formulation and descriptor design. Since the review scores are all positive after rebuttal, I recommend accepting this manuscript. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Though with some limited novelty and short in ablation study, in general it is a quite interesting and novel study Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper presents a clinically relevant and well motivated method for refining aortic valve morphometric measurements using graph-based modeling of landmark dependencies. The rebuttal addressed several important concerns, including measurement definitions, descriptor details, loss function, observer variability, landmark localization performance, and ethical approval. While the ablation analysis and external generalization remain limited, the contribution is sufficiently novel and the reported results support acceptance.

title: GU-SAM2: A Semi-supervised Medical Image Segmentation Framework via Gated Feature Fusion of MIM-Pretrained U-Net and SAM 2
reviewer_1_strengths: This paper adapts SAM2 to the medical segmentation scenario by leveraging two-stage training, with the first stage pre-training a U-Net using unlabeled data and the second stage fusing the features of the pre-trained U-Net with those of SAM2. Gated Feature Fusion Module (GFFM) introduce both spatial/pixel-wise and channel-wise weighting schemes, with the idea of highlighting the target organ and suppressing the background. This design looks reasonable and is effective. GU-SAM2 achieves the state-of-the-art performance on several segmentation datasets and generally is robust to label-scarce settings, e. g. , with only 1-3 labeled samples. This label-efficient learning is important for the clinical setting where the labels are expensive to obtain.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Whether the proposed method is more efficient or not? How many extra parameters and FLOPs are introduced by the GU-SAM2 when compared with SAM2? author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and meta-reviewer for the constructive comments. We first clarify the positioning of GU-SAM2.It is better positioned as a label-decoupled adaptation framework for transferring natural-image/video foundation models to medical imaging. We used the term “semi-supervised” because the overall pipeline uses unlabeled and labeled data in separate stages, and the two data sources can have different scale. Conceptually, GU-SAM2 is closer to PEFT methods such as Adapter or LoRA, but differs in that it first learns medical-domain priors through self-supervised MIM, reducing the dependence on labeled data during adaptation. We agree that “semi-supervised” may not fully match its conventional definition and may imply comparison with pseudo-label- or consistency-based methods. We will therefore revise the wording and position GU-SAM2 more accurately as self-supervised medical-prior learning followed by supervised adaptation. We acknowledge that the claim of resolving tracking bias is mainly supported by visual and case-level evidence rather than dedicated temporal-consistency metrics. This is a limitation. The claim is motivated by two recurring SAM2 failures: missing newly appearing connected components of the same organ, and over-tracking similar background regions after the target disappears. GU-SAM2 alleviates these patterns through medical-prior injection. We will state this claim more cautiously as evidence from observed failure modes and visual analysis, not as a fully quantified temporal-consistency validation. Regarding efficiency, the additional U-Net encoder and four GFFM modules introduce about 13.09M parameters. For a 512×512 input, they require about 56.14 GMACs, corresponding to 112.27 GFLOPs when one multiply-add is counted as two FLOPs. For experimental fairness, all experiments use strict five-fold cross-validation, and results are averaged over folds. MIM pre-training uses only training-fold images with labels discarded; test images are never used for training. Baselines follow their original papers or official implementations. Regarding fairness between prompt-based and non-prompt-based methods: due to GPU memory limits and limited video-sequence diversity, training uses short 2-4 frame clips, so fully relying on long-range memory may accumulate errors. This setting follows each model family’s native usage while keeping prompt density much lower than slice-wise 2D SAM prompting. We will also clarify implementation details. “Small/Hard” does not mean organ size equals difficulty; it refers to targets with small foreground, ambiguous boundaries, complex shapes, or low contrast. Such structures are more prone to under-segmentation, mis-segmentation, or missed detection in automatic models, while spatial prompts reduce this risk. We will clarify this category. For MIM, each image is resized to 512×512 and replicated to three channels. Up to 5 random rectangular masks are generated, each about 1/6 to 1/3 of the image size, and masked regions are replaced by random noise to encourage contextual, textural, and anatomical reconstruction. For loss design, we tried Dice+CE and Dice+Focal, but they did not improve performance and were sometimes less stable for small targets and low-label settings. We therefore used Dice loss, which directly matches the evaluation metric and handles foreground-background imbalance. Finally, we agree that Random U-Net and Add are not the strongest baselines. Table 4 is intended to verify effectiveness, not optimality. Random U-Net tests whether uninformative external features harm SAM2 and whether GFFM suppresses them; Add tests whether direct injection is sufficient. Results show that MIM-U-Net provides useful medical priors and GFFM is more robust than direct addition. MIM is also consistent with SAM2’s Hiera/MAE-MIM pre-training paradigm, while GFFM is lightweight, suitable for small-batch and low-label settings, and less prone to overfitting than cross-attention.

However, reviewers raised concerns regarding the lack of quantitative metrics for tracking consistency, the absence of comparisons with state-of-the-art semi-supervised methods, and the insufficient justification for the added computational overhead and the choice of SAM 2 over medical foundation models.
