title: Hallucination Detection and Correction in Medical VLMs via Counter-Evidence Verification
reviewer_1_strengths: 1- Novel counterfactual intervention mechanism : The idea of masking visual evidence regions and re-querying the VLM to test the causal dependency of claims on visual input is genuinely creative and conceptually appealing. Unlike purely similarity-based or uncertainty-based approaches (RadFlag, SE), CoEV provides a causal lens on hallucination testing whether removing visual evidence changes the model’s output. This goes beyond correlation to probe actual visual grounding. 2- Interpretable four-quadrant diagnostic taxonomy : The Q1-Q4 mapping along the factual correctness x visual grounding axes (Eq. 6) is a valuable conceptual contribution. It distinguishes between language-driven bias (Q2), visual misinterpretation (Q3), and total failure (Q4), which is clinically meaningful. Clinicians can understand why a claim was flagged, not just that it was flagged a significant advantage for trust and adoption. 3- Unified detection and correction framework : Unlike detection-only methods, CoEV provides actionable correction for both closed-ended Med-VQA (via verification, Eq. 7) and open-ended report generation (via sentence-level refinement, Eq. 8). The correction results are compelling, particularly the +27.16% accuracy gain for Qwen2-3B on MIMIC-VQA (Table 3). 4- Comprehensive experimental evaluation : The paper evaluates across 4 datasets spanning two task types (MRG and VQA), 4 VLM backbones of varying scales and training paradigms (general-purpose: InternVL3-2B, Qwen2-3B; medical-tuned: Lingshu-7B, LLaVA-Med), with multiple complementary metrics. This breadth provides solid evidence of generalizability across architectures. 5- Training-free, plug-and-play design : CoEV requires no fine-tuning or additional labeled data, making it practically deployable as a post-hoc layer on any existing VLM pipeline. This is a major practical advantage for clinical adoption. 6- Well-structured ablation study : Table 4 cleanly demonstrates that both diagnostic axes (textual and visual) contribute complementary signal, with the combined model achieving the best F1-Score (0.6112). The progressive improvement pattern is convincing.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1- Simplistic masking strategy may introduce artifacts : The Evidence Intervention Module (Eq. 4) masks regions with black pixels. This is a crude intervention that could introduce distribution shift: VLMs may react to the unnatural black patch itself (as an out-of-distribution artifact) rather than to the genuine absence of visual evidence. More principled interventions (e. g. , inpainting with plausible tissue textures, Gaussian blurring, or learned perturbations) should be discussed. The authors should at minimum analyze whether the black mask itself triggers false behavioral changes in the VLM, potentially inflating the false positive rate for hallucination detection. 2- Under-specified claim persistence function : The function phi(c_i, T’_i) in Eq. 5, which determines whether a claim persists in the re-generated output after masking, is critically under-defined. Is this exact string matching? Semantic similarity? CheXbert re-extraction? This is the linchpin of the entire CECE module, and different implementations would yield vastly different results. Without this specification, the method cannot be reproduced. 3- Self-correction circularity concern : The correction mechanism (Eq. 8) relies on the same VLM that generated the hallucination to rewrite the flagged sentence. If the VLM has a systematic bias (e. g. , always reporting cardiomegaly), re-prompting it with “corrected” evidence may not overcome this bias. The paper does not discuss when self-correction fails or analyze the correction failure modes. A control experiment using a different VLM for correction would strengthen the claim. 4- Insufficient statistical rigor : No confidence intervals, standard deviations, or significance tests are reported for any result across Tables 1-4.Given that the method involves stochastic components (VLM generation variability, grounding model uncertainty), the reported improvements may not be statistically meaningful. For instance, the gains on IU-Xray for LLaVA-Med detection (Table 1) are modest, and without uncertainty estimates, it is impossible to assess reliability. 5- Ablation study limited to a single dataset : Table 4 presents ablation results only on MIMIC-CXR. The relative contribution of textual vs. visual axes may differ on datasets with different characteristics (e. g. , VQA-RAD with shorter answers vs. MIMIC-CXR with full reports). Extending the ablation to at least one VQA dataset would strengthen the analysis. 6- Ground-truth dependency on GREEN model : The entire evaluation relies on the GREEN model [18] to generate hallucination ground-truth labels. GREEN’s own accuracy and potential systematic biases are not discussed. If GREEN shares biases with the VLMs being evaluated, the ground-truth labels may systematically undercount or overcount certain hallucination types. No validation against human radiologist annotations is provided. 7- Limited to chest X-ray domain : All four evaluation datasets involve chest radiography. The method’s reliance on CheXbert (chest X-ray specific) and Maira-2 (radiology grounding) raises questions about generalizability to other modalities (CT, MRI, pathology, dermatology). The paper does not discuss what adaptations would be needed. 8- Computational overhead not reported : CoEV requires running the VLM at least twice per claim (original + masked), plus CheXbert extraction and Maira-2 grounding for each claim. For a report with multiple claims, this could multiply inference cost significantly. No runtime analysis or GPU memory requirements are provided.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: (1) Novel and intuitive formulation of claim-level counterfactual verification The paper introduces a simple yet effective idea: verifying each claim by masking its associated visual evidence and observing whether the claim persists. Compared to prior global perturbation approaches, this localized, per-claim intervention better captures causal dependence between visual input and generated text. (2) Interpretable diagnostic framework The proposed four-quadrant taxonomy (factuality × grounding) provides a clear and clinically meaningful decomposition of hallucination types, enabling fine-grained analysis rather than binary detection. This improves interpretability and aligns well with clinical needs. (3) Training-free and model-agnostic design The method operates at inference time without retraining the base VLM, making it practical for real-world deployment where retraining large medical models is often infeasible. (4) Strong empirical coverage The evaluation spans multiple datasets, tasks, and model types (general and medical VLMs), demonstrating robustness and general applicability. Improvements in detection metrics (AUC) and downstream performance are generally consistent. (5) Practical correction mechanisms Beyond detection, the framework supports post-hoc correction (verification and rewriting), which is valuable for clinical workflows where actionable outputs are required.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: (1) Key components are under-specified, affecting reproducibility Several critical modules are not described in sufficient detail, including claim extraction, evidence localization, factuality assessment, and persistence estimation. In particular, the paper suggests that evidence regions are localized by a “radiology expert,” which is not scalable in practice. If an external grounding model is used instead, this introduces hidden dependencies that weaken the claim of being training-free and may lead to error propagation. Clear disclosure of these components is necessary for reproducibility. (2) Potential evaluator–label leakage and circularity The use of the same or closely related tools for both label construction and factuality evaluation raises concerns about evaluation bias and circular reasoning. This setup may inflate the reported performance improvements and should be carefully justified or mitigated. (3) Limitations of masking-based counterfactuals The masking strategy may introduce distribution shifts or artifacts, and may not adequately handle cases where visual evidence is global, diffuse, or distributed across multiple regions (e.g., cardiomegaly or interstitial patterns). The paper does not provide a sensitivity analysis on mask size, shape, or alternative masking strategies (such as blur or inpainting), making it unclear how robust the method is. (4) Lack of computational efficiency analysis The approach requires multiple additional model inferences for each claim, which could result in significant computational overhead. The paper does not report runtime or scalability, especially for long reports containing many claims, making it difficult to assess practical feasibility. (5) Limited statistical rigor The paper does not report confidence intervals, statistical significance tests, or variability across runs. Some reported improvements are unusually large and would benefit from stronger statistical validation. (6) Incomplete comparison with related work The method is closely related to prior work on visual counterfactual testing and verification, but these connections are not sufficiently discussed. Additional comparisons with relevant approaches would help better position the contribution and clarify its advantages.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We sincerely thank the reviewers for their constructive feedback and recognition of CoEV as a novel, training-free framework for medical hallucination detection and correction. Reviewer #1’s comments reference “GLoVe” and “global-local verification,” which are unrelated to our submission; therefore, we do not provide a response to Reviewer#1.We provide point-to-point responses to the other comments, which will be integrated into the final version of the paper. [Q] Key Components (R#2, R#3). [A] To ensure reproducibility, we clarify the implementation details as follows: (1) Claim Extraction: CheXbert as the semantic parser P(·) extracts positive disease labels (Cpos) from text. (2) Evidence Localization: The pretrained radiology grounding model MAIRA-2 generates bounding boxes using images and disease descriptions as input. (3) Persistence Estimation (ϕ): ϕ(c_i, T’i) is implemented by feeding the report T’i into the semantic parser P(·) to verify if the claim (c_i) persists as a positive finding despite the absence of visual evidence. (4) Factuality Assessment: factual correctness is determined based on CheXbert disease labels extracted from the generated report and the reference report. claims are considered factual if their labels are semantically consistent. [Q] Intervention Strategy & Artifacts (R#2, R#3). [A] (1) Masking Strategy: Black-pixel masking ensures rigorous “information zeroing”, which ensures visual evidence is genuinely inaccessible. We leave the exploration of alternative interventions for future work and add a corresponding discussion in the limitations section. (2) As illustrated in Fig. 2 in our paper, masking Region A primarily suppresses Claim A while leaving unrelated findings largely unaffected. This localized behavioral change suggests that the VLM response is mainly influenced by evidence removal rather than by a global OOD artifact effect. [Q] Statistical Rigor (R#2, R#3). [A] We acknowledge this omission. We have conducted repeated-run analysis and statistical significance testing, and the improvements over the strongest baselines remain statistically significant across datasets (p < 0.05). Furthermore, the consistent gains across 4 datasets and 4 VLM backbones suggest the improvements are robust rather than due to random variance. [Q] Computational Efficiency (R#2). [A] CoEV is a training-free, plug-and-play solution, avoiding the high costs of fine-tuning. CoEV averages 3.47s per image (vs. 1.78s for VASE) on a NVIDIA L20 (48GB). Given the clinical importance of hallucination detection, we believe this additional latency is a reasonable trade-off for improved reliability and interpretability. [Q] Clarification on Circularity (R#2). [A] We clarify that the correction mechanism is model-agnostic and does not rely on the original VLM. In our implementation, Qwen is used as the correction model, taking only textual evidence and flagged claims as input without reusing the original image. [Q] Generalizability Beyond Chest X-ray (R#2). [A] CoEV is currently developed and evaluated on chest X-ray data. It is modality-agnostic in principle, relying on claim-level counterfactual verification rather than chest X-ray-specific modeling. Extending CoEV to other modalities is part of our future work and would require adapting parsing and grounding modules to modality-specific tools. [Q] Evaluator-Label Independence (R#3). [A] We clarify that CoEV uses CheXbert for factuality assessment, while hallucination ground-truth labels are constructed using GREEN. Although these are different tools, some domain bias may still exist, which will be discussed in the revised manuscript. [Q] Comparison with related works (R#3). [A] Unlike VCD/SID’s global perturbations, we use evidence-guided local counterfactual interventions to explicitly test visual grounding. We will incorporate a more detailed discussion of these methodological distinctions in our updated manuscript.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): [Note from PCs: review submitted by Reviewer #1 has now been removed from the system] I recommend inviting a rebuttal. I note that Reviewer #1 appears to have reviewed a different paper, as the review repeatedly refers to “GLoVe” and global-local verification rather than the submitted CoEV counter-evidence verification method. I therefore do not rely on Reviewer #1’s assessment in forming this recommendation. Based on the substantive reviews from Reviewers #2 and #3, the paper addresses an important clinical safety problem: detecting and correcting hallucinated claims in medical VLM outputs. The proposed claim-level counter-evidence verification strategy is promising, since masking visual evidence and re-querying the VLM provides an intuitive way to test whether a generated clinical statement is visually grounded. The four-quadrant diagnostic map and the extension from detection to correction are also useful and interpretable. However, several issues need clarification before a final decision. The rebuttal should specify key components, especially claim extraction, evidence localization, factuality scoring, and the claim-persistence function after masking. The authors should also address whether black-pixel masking introduces artifacts, discuss possible circularity in label construction and factuality evaluation, report statistical significance or confidence intervals, and provide runtime analysis. A convincing rebuttal on these points would substantially strengthen confidence in the contribution. | I recommend acceptance. Reviewer #1’s review has been removed and was not considered in the final assessment. Based on the substantive reviews from Reviewers #2 and #3, the paper presents a promising and clinically relevant framework for hallucination detection and correction in medical VLMs. The main contribution, claim-level counter-evidence verification by masking visual evidence and checking whether the claim persists, is intuitive, novel, and practically meaningful. The four-quadrant diagnostic map also provides useful interpretability, and the evaluation covers multiple datasets, tasks, and VLM backbones. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Most of the clarity issues raised by the reviewers have been addressed in the rebuttal. The problem is timely, and the baselines are up to date. The authors should commit to releasing the data splits upon acceptance for reproducibility. Based on the content of this paper itself, I consider it sufficient for acceptance. However, my major concern remains the concurrent submission “GloVe”. The two papers do share a common motivation: detecting hallucinations in medical VLMs by checking whether generated claims are supported by visual evidence. The tasks also overlap, including report generation and medical VQA. The baselines and datasets overlap a lot as well (MIMIC-CXR). The methods are not identical for sure, CoEV uses visual region masking as a counter-evidence intervention, while GLoVe combines global semantic assessment with local grounding verification. But there is still methodological overlap, as both rely on the same claim extraction and visual grounding/localization. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): I recommend acceptance. The paper proposes CoEV, a training free framework that detects and corrects hallucinations in medical VLMs through claim level counterfactual visual masking, organized via an interpretable four quadrant taxonomy of factuality and visual grounding. Both reviewers scored the paper 4 and recognized its conceptual novelty, clinical relevance, and broad evaluation across four datasets and four VLM backbones. The rebuttal concretely resolves the major concerns by specifying the previously under defined components (CheXbert for claim extraction and persistence, MAIRA-2 for grounding, CheXbert based factuality scoring), clarifying that correction uses Qwen rather than the original VLM, decoupling ground truth labels (GREEN) from factuality scoring (CheXbert), and reporting significance testing at p < 0.05 along with runtime numbers (3.47s vs 1.78s for VASE).

title: Harmless Copyright Protection for CT Dataset
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.It improves security by using prediction accuracy for verification instead of causing the model to make dangerous mistakes 2.It embeds the watermark in the raw measurement data, making the protection much harder to detect and remove compared to traditional image-level methods. 3.It uses a learnable mask that successfully proves data ownership without ruining the visual quality of the reconstructed medical images.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The experiments are conducted on a very small subset of the COVID-19 Low-Dose CT dataset, using only 15 COVID and 15 normal cases for training, and 5 of each for testing. Furthermore, it appears to treat the data as 2D slices rather than continuous 3D volumes. This limited scale fails to demonstrate clinical feasibility or prove that the learnable mask can maintain both visual fidelity and verification accuracy across massive, highly diverse, real-world 3D medical datasets. 2.The methodology relies solely on standard Filtered Back-Projection (FBP) to reconstruct the images from the watermarked measurement data. In modern clinical practice, advanced Iterative Reconstruction (IR) or Deep Learning-based Reconstruction (DLR) techniques are heavily used for noise reduction. These non-linear, aggressive denoising algorithms could easily filter out or distort the subtle measurement-domain watermark (LMHBW), potentially breaking the downstream prediction-accuracy verification entirely.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.A key strength of the paper is the novelty of its loss design: it combines multiple loss terms to preserve reconstruction quality, ensure that the watermark remains verifiable, and maintain high predictive accuracy on watermarked samples. 2.Another strength is that the paper defines the problem very clearly. The introduction is well written and accessible even to readers outside the specific field, and the topic itself is timely and important, with broad relevance to researchers and practitioners concerned with AI privacy and data protection.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.A major weakness of the paper is the choice of baselines. The compared methods are from 2019 and 2022, which are relatively old for a rapidly evolving field. Although the paper cites the more recent work by Sun et al. (2025) on EntropyMark, it neither includes a direct comparison with that method nor explains why such a comparison was omitted. This makes it harder to assess the true novelty and competitiveness of the proposed approach against the current state of the art. 2.There is also some ambiguity in the presentation of the results. For example, in Table 1, it is unclear what backbone model is being used and what watermarking ratio is assumed. In Table 2, only the proposed method is evaluated across different architectures, whereas it would be more informative to include the same architectural comparison for the baselines as well. That would allow for a fairer and more complete evaluation. 3.In addition, the paper lacks clarity in several technical details and contains a few minor writing issues. For instance, in Equation 5, (m_c) is not defined, and the abbreviation “FBP” appears before its full form is introduced. Some model details are also missing, such as which version of CLIP was used, whether it was pretrained on medical data, and which ResNet variant was adopted. The absence of citations for these architectures further reduces clarity.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The central idea is novel, with contributions that are twofold. First, the watermark is implemented as a learnable mask inserted in the measurement domain rather than the image domain, which makes it more difficult for an adversary to replicate through adversarial watermarking. Second, the authors introduce three custom loss functions that jointly ensure images are reconstructed without loss of fidelity while preserving the effectiveness of copyright protection.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Major Comments The authors refer to CLIP as the pre-trained model but do not clarify whether they employ the original CLIP model or a custom variant pre-trained on domain-specific data. Since the features generated by CLIP are highly dependent on the pre-training data, this ambiguity raises concerns regarding the validity of the feature consistency loss. An ablation study is strongly needed, particularly given the use of three distinct loss functions. Although page constraints may limit the scope, a thorough ablation study would provide empirical evidence that each of the three losses contributes meaningfully to the overall performance. The introduction of the learnable mask is described in vague terms, and additional details would strengthen the presentation. A brief background on the measurement domain, along with some intuition regarding what the data represents in this domain, would provide valuable context for the reader. An important open question is the practical adoption of measurement-domain watermarking in physical devices such as CT scanners. While the proposed approach is novel, its feasibility for real-world deployment warrants further discussion. Minor Comments The abstract would benefit from including specific numerical results rather than the current general statement that “experimental results demonstrate that the proposed threat model enables effective watermark verification while remaining harmless.” There is a typo on Page 2, paragraph 2: “embeddedinto” should be corrected. The acronym “FBP” is used prior to its formal introduction (Page 5, following Equation 1). The organization of Section 2.2 could be improved. The authors introduce two objectives but, rather than proceeding directly to the loss functions, first describe a masking strategy before returning to the loss formulation. Restructuring this section would enhance readability. The authors should justify the selection of SSIM as the image-fidelity loss metric. A citation to prior work establishing SSIM as a standard choice for this purpose would be sufficient. Figure 3 would benefit from explicit annotations to clearly highlight the issues present in the images.

author_feedback: We sincerely thank reviewers for their valuable comments and recognition of our work as “compelling”, “novel” and “a strong contribution to MICCAI”. title: HeartVolMesh: Cardiac Volumetric Mesh Reconstruction via Covariance-Guided Graph Deformation
reviewer_1_strengths: Promoting deterministic vertices to anisotropic Gaussian kernels via covariance-guided graph deformation is a clever and logical adaptation for handling the spatially varying uncertainties inherent in medical imaging. The manuscript is well-written, and the visual presentation (e. g. , the pipeline schematic and performance radar plots) is of high quality. Furthermore, validation on a large cohort of 900 patients demonstrates the robustness and clinical applicability of the proposed pipeline.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The proposed two-stage framework, particularly the template-driven volumetric warping pipeline, shows great potential for standardizing cardiac digital twin generation. However, the specific implementation details of the non-rigid registration and the high-quality tetrahedral templates are crucial for reproducibility. It is strongly recommended that the authors open-source their codebase, pre-trained models, and the standard tetrahedral templates upon publication. Releasing these assets will significantly benefit the research community, allowing peers to readily adopt this pipeline for downstream FEM/CFD simulations and further advance the field.

reviewer_2_strengths: Introduction of covariance based loss for graph deformation improves accuracy of the surface. The integration of several deformation fields into one global deformation field that is applied to deform the volumetric mesh template leads to anatomical plausible results while still using information of the different cardiac structures.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: No evaluation on external/public dataset Performed test for statistical significance is not described e.g. what is the reference method? Are multiple tests performed and is it adjusted for multiple testing? Inaccuracy in Fig. 1 the initial template is most probably deformed by features from the latent space while the last graph deformation is performed using features from the highest resolution conv stage. Also the input data goes into the second stage of the CNN encoder
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: S1 Innovative Representation: Promoting mesh vertices from points to anisotropic Gaussian kernels is a way to handle the spatially varying uncertainty and thin-wall ambiguities inherent in cardiac CTA imaging. S2 Consistency & Correspondence: The template-driven warping approach successfully enforces cross-case correspondence, which is a significant advantage for population-level analyses and standardized downstream simulations. S3 Comprehensive Validation: The paper provides robust quantitative evaluation across a large number of anatomical structures (24 parts), demonstrating that the framework scales well beyond simple ventricular models.

For instance, it is not clear at all the benefit of adding a covariance matrix per node. The notion of covariance and how this helps to better reconstruct the mesh should be explained. W2 Algorithm complexity : While the surface reconstruction is end-to-end, the volumetric warping step (especially with multiple structure-specific deformation fields) seems to introduce a multi-stage process at inference. The paper could clarify the total runtime more explicitly. reviewer_3_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for their valuable feedback. We focus on the main concerns below. Meta/R1/R2/R3 Reproducibility. We have prepared project homepage and github repo with two-stage code, configs, evaluation scripts, 24-part tetrahedral templates, and inference weight. No links are included to preserve anonymity and follow rebuttal rules; the release link will be added after acceptance. Meta/R3W1 Method motivation. Our first contribution is covariance-guided graph deformation. Downstream simulation failure often arise from geometric error at anatomical junctions and thin-wall regions. Per-vertex covariance models spatially varying uncertainty and direction-dependent tolerance caused by partial volume, thin walls, and junction ambiguity, consistent with Reviewer1-S1.Ablations support this: LVMyo CD improves from 4.5/5.8 to 3.6 and RVMyo CD from 3.9/4.5 to 3.1.Our second contribution is volume-to-surface registration for volumetric meshing. In silico trials require volumetric meshes as inputs for EP/CFD/FEM solvers, while almost all image-to-mesh methods output only surfaces; heuristic tetrahedralization can lose cross-case/cross-phase correspondence and case-dependent connectivity. We use learned surface geometry to drive a dense deformation field that warps tetrahedral templates while preserving connectivity and vertex indices. The field can be sampled on compatible LV+aorta or whole-heart templates with different densities/elements, the method is not tied to one fixed template. R2W1 External validation. The submitted evaluation already uses a large multi-centre cohort from multiple sources: 900 patients and 4004 NIfTI images, with a patient-level split to avoid leakage, R1 also recognized this large-scale validation. Public validation on ImageCAS/MMWHS will be important future work. R2W2 Statistics. We used paired two-sided t-tests comparing Ours3p6 with each baseline/ablation on the same cases. Multiple tests were unadjusted, p<0.05 is descriptive, not family-wise corrected. R2W3 Figures. The reviewer is correct: early deformation uses low-resolution/deeper features for global alignment, while final deformation uses higher-resolution/shallower features for local refinement. The arrows were simplified to avoid line crossings; this drawing error will be corrected. R3W2 Complexity/runtime. In our implementation, each case produces 24-parts volumetric meshes with about 1M total vertices in <90 s on one NVIDIA A100 GPU. Stage 1 reconstructs the whole-heart covariance-guided surface mesh in one parallel network inference, not by per-part inference. Stage 2 performs structure-wise registration/warping sequentially; the learning stage is shared, while registration remains modular and parallelizable. R3W3 Implementation details. After per-structure registration, LA/LVMyo/RA/RV/Aorta surface displacements are merged into one sparse set. Each grid node is assigned by nearest-neighbor KD-tree to build a 200^3 field, followed by Gaussian blur (sigma=5), cubic upsampling to 300^3, and another blur (sigma=10). Volume vertices are warped by cubic interpolation. CPD alpha/beta/lambda/max-iter=0.01/70/1/200; aorta uses ICP plus partial TPS. Full code will be released if accepted. R3W4 Hyperparameters. Key settings are specified: 128^3 patches, beta=0.5, regularization weights 0.1, and 300^3 final field. The implementation further uses 3000 surface samples, covariance jitter 1e-5, and Cholesky floor 1e-3.These were selected by grid search on validation data; the same strategy can be used for other clinical datasets. Submitted ablations cover covariance NLL, field coherence/resolution, and mesh regularization. R3W5 Template dependency. Cause we use deformation field, the method can use templates with different element types, densities, and cardiac structures. The method can capture topology-preserving pathological changes, e.g., myo thickness variation. We acknowledge that topology-changing anatomy cannot be generated.

title: HiEDL: Hierarchical Evidential Deep Learning for Uncertainty-Aware Tumor Segmentation from 3D CT via Boundary Regularization
reviewer_1_strengths: Clear and clinically meaningful problem formulation. The paper targets tumor segmentation in CT, where boundary ambiguity between the tumor and its surrounding organ is a real and clinically relevant challenge. The motivation is well articulated: inaccurate tumor delineation can affect diagnosis, treatment planning, and downstream intervention, and uncertainty is especially important in these safety critical regions. The paper also correctly identifies that flat segmentation formulations do not reflect the anatomical reality that tumors reside within organs. This gives the work a strong application-driven motivation rather than being only a technical variation. Interesting hierarchical reformulation of the segmentation task. A major strength is the explicit modeling of the anatomical containment prior through a hierarchical organ to tumor decomposition. Instead of treating background, organ, and tumor as equally independent semantic classes, the method separates the problem into a superordinate background versus foreground task and a subordinate organ versus tumor task within the foreground. This is an intuitive and clinically meaningful formulation, and it is more anatomically consistent than standard flat segmentation. The hierarchy is not merely descriptive; it is embedded directly into the loss design, which makes it a substantive methodological contribution. Principled integration of evidential uncertainty modeling. The use of evidential deep learning is a strength because it gives the model a direct mechanism for representing predictive uncertainty in ambiguous regions, rather than relying purely on deterministic softmax outputs. In the context of tumor segmentation, where organ tumor interfaces are often low contrast and morphologically variable, this is a well motivated design choice. The paper is also careful to connect this uncertainty modeling to the stated clinical problem of overconfidence in difficult regions, which makes the use of evidential learning feel purposeful rather than simply appended. Well motivated boundary regularization strategy. The paper makes a convincing case that region overlap losses alone may be insufficient to resolve subtle boundary errors. The proposed hierarchical boundary loss based on signed distance functions is therefore a meaningful strength of the paper. It directly targets boundary alignment at both the superordinate and subordinate levels and is integrated coherently with the hierarchical formulation. This is particularly relevant for tumor segmentation, where clinically important errors often occur at the surface rather than in bulk volumetric regions. Strong empirical results on two public datasets. The evaluation on both MSD Pancreas and MSD Liver strengthens the paper considerably. The method outperforms several competitive 3D segmentation baselines, including UNETR, UNETR++, SegResNet, and Swin UNETR, on both Dice and NSD. It is especially positive that the improvements are shown not only in region overlap but also in a boundary-sensitive metric, since that aligns directly with the paper’s central motivation. Using two public datasets also improves the credibility and relevance of the empirical results. Useful ablation study supporting the main design choices. The paper includes component analysis showing that the proposed boundary loss contributes meaningfully to the performance gains, and that region loss alone does not provide the same benefit. This is important because it demonstrates that the improvement is not just due to using a different architecture label, but is connected to the actual hierarchical boundary-aware design. The associated uncertainty map visualizations also help illustrate how the proposed method changes the uncertainty distribution in a way that is consistent with the intended anatomical behavior. Clear presentation and coherent paper organization. The method section is well structured and the figures are helpful, especially the diagrams explaining the hierarchical formulation and the uncertainty maps in the ablation study. The technical narrative is easy to follow from motivation, to method, to evaluation. This clarity makes the contribution easier to assess and strengthens the paper overall. Good balance between methodological contribution and application relevance. The paper is not only an application of a standard segmentation model to a medical dataset, nor is it a purely abstract methodological paper detached from clinical significance. Instead, it combines a clinically meaningful problem, an anatomically informed formulation, uncertainty-aware modeling, and practical evaluation on relevant public datasets. That balance is a notable strength and makes the work more compelling overall.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The methodological novelty is meaningful but still somewhat incremental relative to the prior literature. The paper combines three ingredients that are each individually motivated by prior work: evidential deep learning for uncertainty estimation, hierarchical or anatomically structured segmentation ideas, and boundary loss based on signed distance functions. The paper’s value lies in how these are combined for tumor segmentation, but the submission does not fully clarify what part of the framework is genuinely new beyond this integration. In particular, the evidential formulation builds on prior evidential segmentation work such as Li et al. on region based evidential learning, the boundary loss follows the signed distance formulation of Kervadec et al. , and the idea of hierarchical segmentation guided by anatomical structure is also related to recent hierarchical segmentation frameworks such as SALT. The current presentation would be stronger if it more explicitly positioned the precise technical novelty of HiEDL relative to these existing directions. The uncertainty story is not evaluated as rigorously as the title and framing suggest. A central motivation of the paper is uncertainty aware segmentation, yet the empirical evaluation focuses mainly on Dice and NSD. The uncertainty discussion is supported primarily through qualitative uncertainty maps, but there is no quantitative evaluation of uncertainty quality, calibration, or failure detection behavior. Since the paper explicitly argues that evidential modeling is important for addressing overconfidence in safety critical settings, it would be helpful to assess whether the uncertainty estimates are actually better calibrated or more clinically useful than those of the baselines. Without this, the uncertainty component feels less thoroughly validated than the segmentation accuracy improvements. The baseline and ablation study could be stronger and more complete. The paper compares against several strong segmentation architectures, which is good, but the component analysis is relatively limited. In particular, the ablation table compares a baseline, a baseline with region loss, and the full boundary loss version, but it does not isolate all major ingredients as clearly as it could. For example, it would be useful to separate the effect of the hierarchical formulation itself from the evidential component and from the boundary regularization component. As currently presented, it is somewhat difficult to determine how much of the gain comes from the hierarchy, how much from evidential learning, and how much from the boundary term. A more complete ablation would strengthen the causal interpretation of the results. The clinical significance is plausible, but the paper remains primarily a benchmark style segmentation study rather than a strong clinical translation study. The application is clinically relevant, but the experiments are limited to public retrospective datasets and standard segmentation metrics. There is no evaluation of downstream clinical impact, no robustness analysis across acquisition settings, and no user facing or workflow oriented assessment showing how the uncertainty estimates would actually be used in practice. This does not invalidate the work, but it does mean that the clinical claims should remain modest. The paper is strongest as a method paper with medical motivation rather than as evidence of translational readiness. Some implementation and experimental details that would strengthen reproducibility and interpretation are missing or underemphasized. While the paper provides the main preprocessing, training, and loss settings, some details remain limited. For example, the exact architectural backbone used for HiEDL is not foregrounded as clearly as it could be, and the fairness of the comparison to all baselines would be easier to assess with more detail on whether their training configurations were fully harmonized or reproduced from reference implementations. Additional reporting of variance across runs or confidence intervals would also improve the rigor of the empirical comparison. As presented, the results are promising, but more experimental detail would make the conclusions more robust. The gains, while consistent, are moderate in magnitude, so statistical support would help. The method achieves the best Dice and NSD values on both datasets, which is a clear positive. However, the absolute improvements over the strongest baseline are not very large, especially on the pancreas task. In this setting, reporting standard deviations across runs, significance testing, or more extensive robustness experiments would help determine whether the observed improvements are consistently meaningful rather than being potentially sensitive to training variability. The paper would benefit from clearer discussion of limitations. The current conclusion emphasizes the benefits of the hierarchical formulation and uncertainty aware boundary loss, but there is limited discussion of where the method may still fail, such as extremely small tumors, poorly contrasted lesions, or cases where organ boundaries themselves are uncertain. A more explicit limitations discussion would make the paper more balanced and would help readers understand the practical scope of the contribution.

reviewer_2_strengths: The paper addresses an important and clinically relevant issue: uncertainty-aware tumor segmentation, which is crucial for reliable computer-aided diagnosis. reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.Clarity of baseline and necessity of loss components are unclear. Page 7, Table 2: The definition of “Baseline” is not clearly specified in the text. In addition, Table 2 shows that adding hierarchical region loss alone (Baseline w/ Region loss) leads to obvious performance degradation. The authors should clarify the necessity of retaining this loss term in the final objective function. Since the full HiEDL achieves the best performance while region loss alone is harmful, it is strongly suggested to evaluate a simplified variant that only uses hierarchical boundary loss without region loss. If such a simplified version yields comparable or even better performance, the current four-term loss function in Eq. 12 would raise serious concerns about over-parameterization and redundant design. 2.Inappropriate choice of comparative methods. The paper claims a novel framework for tumor segmentation, yet its core segmentation backbone is still a 3D UNet. However, the comparison in Table 1 mainly focuses on Transformer-based models, while the most fundamental and critical baseline vanilla 3D UNet is missing. This makes the experimental comparison logically inconsistent and difficult to interpret. Up-to-date comparisons are essential to validate the practical advantages of HiEDL under the current technical state of the art. 3.Insufficient experimental support for the claimed contribution. From the results shown in Table 1 on the MSD liver and pancreas tumor segmentation tasks, the performance of HiEDL is considerably lower than that of widely recognized methods such as nnUNet reported in the literature. Although the paper proposes a hierarchical evidential learning framework with uncertainty awareness, the experimental results fail to justify the effectiveness and superiority of the method. The discrepancy between methodological motivation and empirical performance weakens the overall contribution significantly. 4.Eq. 12 involves multiple weighting hyperparameters, yet their specific values are not provided. Moreover, the authors do not analyze how these hyperparameters (especially λ) affect training dynamics and final performance. reviewer_3_strengths: 1Explicitly incorporates a strong anatomical prior (hierarchical containment) that is often ignored in flat classification, leading to more anatomically consistent predictions. 2Combines evidential uncertainty modeling with a dedicated hierarchical boundary regularization (SDF-based), effectively reducing over-confidence at ambiguous organ-tumor interfaces. 3Achieves consistent state-of-the-art results on two challenging MSD benchmarks (Pancreas and Liver), outperforming strong baselines (UNETR, UNETR++, SegResNet, Swin UNETR) in both region-level (Dice) and boundary-level (NSD) metrics. 4Thorough ablation studies and uncertainty map visualizations clearly demonstrate the contribution of the hierarchical formulation and boundary loss. 5Practical focus on safety-critical tumor segmentation with uncertainty awareness.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1The hierarchical decoupling is implemented only at the loss level rather than in the network architecture, limiting its ability to guide feature learning. 2Gains over the strongest baseline (Swin UNETR) are solid but relatively modest (Pancreas: Dice +0.0273, NSD +0.0095; Liver: Dice +0.0324, NSD +0.0459). 3No open-source code, pretrained models, or uncertainty evaluation for clinical decision-making (e.g., failure detection) is mentioned. 4Novelty is incremental: it builds on existing EDL and boundary-loss literature without introducing a fundamentally new network component or training paradigm.
reviewer_3_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the meta-reviewer and all reviewers for their constructive feedback and recognition of HiEDL. [Novelty: R1.1/R3.4] HiEDL is not a re-use of EDL [14], SDF loss [12], and hierarchical labeling. (i) Existing EDL segmentation operates under a flat 3-class Dirichlet, forcing organ/tumor evidence to compete with anatomically irrelevant background; we re-parameterize evidence at two semantic levels via α_sup=(α0, α1+α2) and α_in=(α1, α2) restricted to the foreground (Eqs. 5-6) — to our knowledge the first hierarchical evidence aggregation in dense prediction. (ii) The SDF boundary loss [12] is defined for flat foreground labels; we re-derive it at both levels (Eq. 11) using p1+p2 against ϕ(y_sup), and the foreground-renormalized tumor score r_tum against ϕ(y2) with mask m_fg, aligning surface supervision with the hierarchical structure. (iii) Fig. 4 confirms this is not relabeling: standard EDL spreads tumor uncertainty across extra-organ regions, whereas HiEDL confines it to the organ-tumor interface. [Baseline & validation: R2.2/R2.3] Our backbone is an advanced U-Net variant that inherently outperforms vanilla U-Net, so the vanilla U-Net comparison was omitted. We selected representative 3D segmentation networks spanning CNN- and Transformer-based designs and trained them under the same experiment settings. [Ablation: R1.3/R2.1/R2.2] We acknowledge that the ablation could better disentangle hierarchy, evidential modeling, and boundary regularization. We clarify that the “3D U-Net” label in Fig. 2 denotes a generic 3D backbone, not the ablation baseline. In Table 2, the baseline is the Swin UNETR-based setting without the proposed hierarchical objectives, as reflected by identical Dice/NSD to Swin UNETR in Table 1.The region-only variant is the hierarchical region-based EDL objective, providing volumetric anatomical supervision under the containment structure. Its lower performance does not imply redundancy; rather, region-level EDL alone is insufficient for ambiguous tumor surfaces. The boundary term adds complementary surface-sensitive regularization. This synergy is reflected by gains over baseline: +2.7%/+3.2% Dice and +1%/+4.6% NSD on Pancreas/Liver. [Loss-level design: R3.1] The hierarchy is intentionally loss-level, keeping HiEDL backbone- and pipeline-agnostic; gradients from both objectives propagate through the shared backbone and shape feature learning. [Uncertainty: R1.2/R3.3] The manuscript evaluates Dice and NSD, but not calibration or failure-detection metrics. Our intent is to use evidential uncertainty to support boundary-aware segmentation by highlighting ambiguous organ-tumor interfaces, not to claim a clinical failure-detection system. Fig.4 qualitatively shows this behavior. Calibration/failure analyses will be included in future studies. We plan to release code after review. [Hyperparameters: R2.4] Loss weights are in Sec. 3.1: w_sup=w_in=1, λ_sup=λ_in=0.2, t=20; the ramp prevents strong early boundary supervision while region predictions are unstable. [Cost: R2.5] Although explicit benchmarking of runtime and memory overhead is not the primary focus of this work. HiEDL requires no Monte Carlo sampling, ensembling, or repeated inference; uncertainty is computed from Dirichlet evidence in one forward pass. Added cost mainly comes from voxel-wise operations and training-time losses. Future work will include cost analysis. [Statistics & scope: R1.5/R1.6/R3.2] While the numerical gains may appear incremental, HiEDL demonstrates highly consistent improvements in Dice and NSD across two distinct datasets. Under strictly controlled conditions—sharing identical splits, preprocessing, and training—this consistent ranking firmly validates the robustness of our boundary alignment method.

title: Hierarchical Cautious Optimization for Semi-supervised Medical Image Segmentation
reviewer_1_strengths: The proposed formulations are straightforward, intuitive, and clearly presented, making them easy to follow. The evaluation compares the proposed methods against multiple existing momentum-based optimizers across three different datasets. Extensive experiments are conducted to validate the effectiveness and generalizability of the proposed method.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The principle of HCO is straightforward and somewhat innovative, but its convergence relies on a mild alignment condition. A more in-depth theoretical analysis would be helpful. Relying solely on gradient direction alignment may compromise the diversity of object predictions, particularly when considering the abundance of unlabeled images and the wide variation in object shapes and sizes. Only a single semi-supervised learning framework (i. e. , BCP) is used in this study.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The paper points out a reasonable issue in semi-supervised training: gradients from labeled and unlabeled data are not equally reliable, but standard optimizers treat them the same. This is a valid observation, especially in medical imaging where pseudo-label noise can be significant. 2.The method itself is simple and easy to implement. It works at the optimizer level and does not require changing the model, loss, or training pipeline, which makes it easy to try in practice. The idea is fairly general and can be applied to different optimizers such as SGD and Adam. The additional computational cost is also minimal. 3.The experiments cover multiple datasets and settings, which helps demonstrate that the method is not tied to a specific task or framework.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.the main idea is quite simple and somewhat heuristic. The method essentially relies on an element-wise alignment check between labeled and unlabeled gradients, and it is not entirely clear why this specific design is the most effective choice compared to more principled alternatives (e.g., soft weighting, uncertainty-based filtering, or gradient projection methods). 2.The theoretical analysis is limited. The convergence result depends on an additional alignment assumption, but this assumption is not well justified and seems difficult to guarantee in practice, especially given that the paper itself shows that gradient conflicts are common. 3.The reported improvements, particularly on the fetal MRI dataset, are unusually large for an optimizer-level modification. This raises some concerns about the experimental setup. It would be helpful to see more thorough validation (e.g., more seeds, clearer data splits, or additional benchmarks) to better support these results. 4.The experimental evaluation could be stronger. The paper mainly builds on a small number of SSL baselines and does not include comparisons with more recent or stronger methods. In addition, there is no comparison with existing approaches that explicitly address gradient conflicts, which seems closely related to the proposed idea. 5.Some experimental details are not entirely clear (e.g., consistency of evaluation protocols across datasets, number of runs, and data splitting strategy), which makes it harder to assess the robustness of the results.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.Innovative aspect to improve semi-supervised segmentation. This paper improves the performance of semi-supervised segmentation from the aspect of gradients’ reliability, which is reasonable and often ignored in existing works. 2.The experimental validation is comprehensive. Results on different semi-supervised methods and optimizers demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.Lack of comparisons on SOTA semi-supervised methods. While the authors validate their approach on two existing semi-supervised frameworks (BCP and CMT), both of these baselines were introduced in 2023.To better position the contribution and evaluate its general applicability, it is important to assess whether the proposed method remains effective when integrated with more recent and advanced techniques, such as UniMatch V2 [R1] (TPAMI 2025). Including such comparisons would strengthen the paper’s relevance and demonstrate the robustness of the method in contemporary research contexts. 2.The proposed hierarchical cautious optimization method heavily relies on gradient momentum derived from labeled data. This reliance raises a particular concern in scenarios where labeled data are extremely scarce. Under such conditions, gradients computed from the limited labeled examples may not adequately represent the overall data distribution, whereas gradients from unlabeled data could still convey useful information. Consequently, filtering the gradient directions from unlabeled data might prevent the model from learning from potentially informative signals and could exacerbate overfitting. It would therefore be valuable to include experimental validation under extremely low-label settings, for instance, with only one or two labeled examples per class, to better assess the robustness of the method in data-scarce environments. 3.Unclear explanation of some important details. It’s unclear how the empirical verification is conducted and how Eq. (2) is obtained. 4.Lack of more labeled ratios. Currently, the method is evaluated on only two labeled ratios for one dataset, while other datasets are tested under a single labeling ratio. To more comprehensively assess the robustness and practical applicability of the proposed approach, it would be beneficial to include experiments across a wider range of labeled data ratios. author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for the constructive feedback. We address the main concerns below. 1.Experimental scope and SOTA positioning (R1.3, R2.4, R3.1). We evaluate an optimizer-level effect with a paired design — same pipeline, backbone, split, seed, and schedule; the optimizer is the only variable. We run this across two representative 3D SSL paradigms: BCP and CMT. In response to R1.3, we clarify that HCO was not evaluated only with BCP. For broader context, HCO is competitive with recent 3D medical SSL methods despite changing only the optimizer: on Pancreas-CT, it reaches 83.71 Dice, outperforming BCSI (AAAI’26, 83.24) and matching DuCiSC (TMI’25, 83.71); on LA, it reaches 90.75 Dice, comparable to AD-MT (ECCV’24, 90.55), PMT (ECCV’24, 90.81), and below BCSI (AAAI’26, 91.07). HCO is orthogonal to such architectural advances. UniMatch V2 (R3.1) is not an established 3D medical SSL protocol; we adhere to standard 3D medical setups and will state this explicitly in the revision. 2.Method justification and theory (R1.1–2, R2.1–2, R3.3). Why binary alignment gating? HCO is designed for the asymmetric reliability structure of SSL: labeled gradients come from ground truth, whereas unlabeled gradients come from noisier pseudo-label/consistency signals. The goal is not to balance two equally trusted objectives but to prevent unlabeled signal from reversing the trusted labeled direction. Binary gating is the minimal mechanism that enforces this. Note: only the entry into momentum is binary; the resulting momentum and updates remain continuous-valued, preserving update diversity (R1.2). PCGrad/CAGrad handle gradient conflict symmetrically, while CO applies symmetric alignment-based masking. HCO differs from both by making the labeled signal a privileged reference. We ablate this source-aware hierarchy directly: across our result tables, replacing HCO with CO removes or substantially reduces the performance gains. We will sharpen this in the revision. Theory. Eq. (2) is not a pointwise requirement at every step or coordinate. It follows by substituting HCO’s gated update direction into the standard Adam-style descent inequality; the only HCO-specific assumption is positive alignment of that gated direction in expectation. Fig. 1D supports this assumption by showing positive labeled–unlabeled alignment on average, while the negative tail motivates HCO’s filtering of conflicting unlabeled components. We will revise the text to clarify this distinction and the empirical verification procedure. 3.Fetal gains, low-label, and protocol robustness (R2.3, R2.5, R3.2, R3.4). R2.3 raises concern that fetal gains may reflect a setup or validation issue. Several design aspects argue against this: Paired design. Baseline and HCO use the same code, data, splits, backbone, and schedule; only the optimizer differs, reducing the risk that the gains come from pipeline differences. Headroom. The supervised-only baseline reaches only 51% Dice (lungs), 61% (liver) — far from ceiling, helping explain why an effective optimizer change yields larger absolute gains here than on more saturated benchmarks. 16 independent CMT runs. We train each model from scratch across 4 labeled × 4 unlabeled splits. No HCO tuning. We use CMT default hyperparameters; HCO introduces none. This also addresses R3.2’s low-label concern: scarcity should be interpreted relative to task difficulty, not raw label count. With only five labeled fetal volumes, supervised performance is low (51%/61% Dice), yet HCO gives its largest gains (+24% lungs, +16% liver) — suggesting labeled-driven momentum remains a useful anchor even under severe effective scarcity. More broadly, we follow the published label ratios and protocols of BCP and CMT (R3.4): LA — BCP 4/76 and 8/72 splits with two seeds; Pancreas — BCP 12/50 split; Fetal — the 16 CMT folds above with CMT defaults. We will clarify these details in the revision (R2.5).

title: Hierarchical Memory for Radiology Report Generation with Rich Context
reviewer_1_strengths: The proposed method demonstrates clear motivation and clinical relevance by accurately mirroring the real-world workflow of radiologists, who selectively recall information to identify changes and refine diagnoses rather than processing patient history and similar cases as a flat sequence of text. To achieve this, the paper features a highly targeted architectural design that adeptly adapts the Hierarchical Memory Transformer. Specifically, the strategic choices to retain all segment memories—thereby preventing the loss of vital clinical temporal changes —and to utilize image-conditioned multi-modal soft prompts for filtering retrieval noise are particularly effective for the medical domain. Consequently, the framework yields strong empirical results, achieving state-of-the-art clinical accuracy on the MIMIC-CXR dataset and significantly outperforming prior multi-view and longitudinal baselines.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Methodologically, the core algorithmic contribution is somewhat incremental; although integrating image-conditioned soft prompt tuning for radiology reports is beneficial, the fundamental memory structuring mechanism heavily relies on the existing HMT framework and lacks substantial theoretical innovation. Furthermore, the ablation studies reveal an unusually large, unexplained performance surge when transitioning from a flat concatenation baseline to the HM-RRG framework. Such a significant improvement requires deeper quantitative or qualitative investigations, such as attention visualizations, to definitively prove how the memory structure successfully suppresses noise. Additionally, the paper lacks a much-needed computational overhead analysis. Maintaining complex hierarchical memories and calculating cross-attention inevitably introduces processing burdens, necessitating a clear comparison of inference latency, memory footprint, and FLOPs against the flat baseline. Finally, the study’s reliance on a single primary dataset family limits the demonstration of the model’s generalization capabilities.

reviewer_2_strengths: Selective Memory Recall over Flat Context: By replacing noisy, long-context concatenation with a hierarchical memory structure, the model effectively suppresses irrelevant information and selectively recalls only the most pertinent evidence during decoding. Unified Cross-Patient and Longitudinal Evidence: The framework systematically integrates similar cases from other patients with the current patient’s chronological history, ensuring that both global medical knowledge and specific temporal changes are grounded in the query image. State-of-the-Art Factuality: HM-RRG achieves superior clinical accuracy and the highest factuality metrics on the MIMIC-CXR benchmark, proving its capability to generate reliable, evidence-based radiology reports that align with expert standards.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Limited Reproducibility: The paper lacks critical information required for independent verification. To ensure scientific transparency, the authors should have provided a public repository containing the implementation code and data processing pipelines. Narrow Evaluation Scope: The framework was evaluated on only a single dataset (MIMIC-CXR), which raises significant concerns regarding its generalizability and reliability across different clinical settings, patient demographics, or imaging modalities. Insufficient Model Diversity: The study would be more convincing if it included experiments with a wider variety of state-of-the-art LLMs and VLMs. Evaluating the framework across diverse backbones is necessary to demonstrate that its performance gains are architecturally robust and not dependent on a specific model configuration.

reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1,The paper says it follows Longitudinal-MIMIC, but it also changes the construction of each example by aggregating all available prior studies into a chronological stream, whereas the original setup is more limited. At the same time, Table 1 states that many baseline results are cited from the original publications and MLRG, rather than rerun under the paper’s modified history construction. This weakens the fairness of the headline comparison, because the proposed model is evaluated under a richer input formulation while prior methods are largely compared using previously reported numbers. 2,There is some inconsistency for metric reporting. In the experiment text, the paper says it reports average BLEU, ROUGE-L, and BERTScore for NLG, plus CheXbert and RadGraph for clinical accuracy. author_feedback: We thank all reviewers for their valuable comments. Q1: Dataset/backbone scope (R#1, #2, #3). MIMIC-CXR was chosen because HM-RRG requires paired chest X-rays, reports, and longitudinal histories, and it is the largest public resource for this setting. Closest prior works, MLRG [8] and Diff-RRG [18] from MICCAI 2025, also evaluate only on MIMIC-CXR. We will discuss external validation as a limitation. We used BioMistral-7B with CXR-CLIP to enable comparison with Diff-RRG [18] and isolate hierarchical memory. Q2: Reproducibility details (R#2, #3). The BERTScore issue is a presentation error, and we will correct it. We will clarify Stage-2 optimization: decoder LoRA weights, image projector, memory/summary tokens, and memory-retrieval projections are trainable, while the base decoder and CXR-CLIP vision encoder remain frozen. Stage 2 loads the Stage-1 checkpoint and continues training with hierarchical retrieval enabled. We use one memory vector per retrieved report and one segment memory vector per longitudinal segment. Segment representations use L=128 and j=L/2=64.The cache size equals the number of longitudinal segments. We will release preprocessing, retrieval, training, and evaluation code upon acceptance. Q3: Improvement over flat concatenation (R#1). The ablation shows that richer evidence alone is insufficient: flatly concatenating priors and top-5 retrieved reports degrades performance, suggesting that unordered retrieved reports introduce irrelevant or conflicting findings. HM-RRG compresses retrieved reports into current-image-conditioned memory vectors, processes priors as chronological segment memories, and lets each segment query the unified memory to form a compact evidence prompt. This makes evidence selection explicit rather than leaving it to the decoder over a long noisy sequence. Fig. 2 shows HM-RRG preserving relevant disease-progression information while suppressing irrelevant retrieved-report content. We will expand this case discussion with internal evidence-selection steps. Q4: Computational overhead (R#1). Even though HM-RRG adds memory construction and querying, it greatly reduces decoder memory/computation cost compared with full flat long-context decoding. The flat baseline feeds all retrieved and longitudinal reports as one long sequence, whose self-attention memory grows with length. HM-RRG instead compresses retrieved reports into image-conditioned memory vectors, stores priors as segment memories, and attends over this compact memory set to form an evidence prompt. Thus, the decoder avoids processing the full concatenated evidence. We will discuss this with data in the final version. Q5: Contribution beyond HMT (R#1). HMT is text-only, while HM-RRG adapts hierarchical memory to multimodal RRG which is nontrivial: Retrieved reports are compressed into memory vectors conditioned on the current chest X-ray via projected CXR-CLIP features, not stored as generic text memories. HM-RRG also separates unordered cross-patient retrieval from temporally ordered same-patient priors, targeting the RRG-specific challenge of using rich context to avoid missed findings and filter irrelevant information. Q6: Fairness of comparison (R#3). Existing longitudinal RRG methods use different inputs: MLRG [8] uses multi-view longitudinal information and Diff-RRG [18] models disease progression, but neither uses cross-patient retrieved reports. Modifying them to consume additional data types/sources would require major architectural changes, thus no longer faithful reproductions. Note that these works also directly cite results from earlier baselines when the inputs are different. Q7: Robustness (R#3). We will discuss the fixed retrieval setting as a limitation and expand robustness analysis in future work by varying retrieval K, history length (latest prior vs. multiple/all priors), and retrieval noise to test stability as evidence becomes longer or noisier.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper proposes a hierarchical-memory framework for radiology report generation. It replaces flat sequence concatenation with a structured hierarchical-memory framework integrating cross-patient retrieved reports and within-patient longitudinal history. Experiments on MIMIC-CXR show strong gains on clinical accuracy and NLG metrics over prior work, supported by ablations. The paper is clinically well-motivated and mirrors radiologists’ reasoning over prior studies and similar cases via selective recall of relevant findings and changes rather than uniform processing of all contexts. A key conceptual contribution is the modelling of retrieved reports as a compressed, image-conditioned memory bank and longitudinal priors as a temporal stream. Experimental evidence on MIMIC-CXR demonstrates that structured memory management is a superior alternative to traditional long-context prompts for generating reliable medical reports. However, several concerns should be addressed: 1) A deeper analysis of results (e.g. qualitative examples, failure analysis, attention visualizations) would help explain the unusually large improvement from flat concatenation to HM-RRG observed in ablations. 2) A computational overhead analysis (e.g. latency, memory, FLOPs) is important, as hierarchical memory may be costly relative to a flat baseline. 3) Validation is restricted to the MIMIC-CXR dataset; experiments on external datasets would strengthen the generality of the claims. Evaluating across a broader range of state-of-the-art LLM/VLM backbones would also help demonstrate that gains are robust across architectures. 4) The paper should clarify exactly how each baseline is evaluated and ideally provide controlled reruns under the same setup. 5) Metric reporting should be made consistent (e.g., BERTScore mentioned but not shown; differing metric abbreviations). 6) There are missing implementation details in the paper leading to limited reproducibility. Also, providing a public repository would substantially strengthen verifiability and reproducibility. Given the strong clinical motivation and empirical performance, I recommend inviting the paper for rebuttal and request authors to address the reviewers’ concerns. | This paper addresses an important and clinically meaningful problem in radiology report generation, namely, how to integrate two heterogeneous sources of supporting evidence, cross-patient retrieved reports and within-patient longitudinal history. The proposed hierarchical-memory design is well aligned with this motivation, and reviewers broadly recognize the strength of the clinical intuition and the empirical gains on MIMIC-CXR. After the rebuttal, the reviewer consensus became more positive, with most major concerns addressed. The main remaining concern is comparison fairness, as this point was only partially resolved. I agree this is a legitimate limitation and should be acknowledged explicitly in the final version. That said, the rebuttal addresses the issues most critical to the acceptance decision. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The authors have addressed the reviewers’ comments very well. All reviewers have now agreed on acceptance of the paper. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The authors’ rebuttal successfully addresses the major concerns raised by the three reviewers. All reviewers upgraded their initial scores (from Weak Accept/Weak Reject to Accept) after reading the response. The rebuttal clarifies reproducibility details (Stage‑2 trainable components, segment length, cache size, code release) and corrects the BERTScore presentation error. It provides a convincing explanation for the large improvement over flat concatenation, highlighting how image‑conditioned compression and explicit evidence selection mitigate noise from unordered retrieved reports. Computational overhead is justified by noting that the hierarchical memory reduces decoder self‑attention costs compared to processing full long‑context sequences. The rebuttal also acknowledges external validation as a limitation. title: HiFi-Rep: Leveraging High-Resolution Vision Foundation Models with Tri-Planar Slice Context for CT Report Generation
reviewer_1_strengths: The framework maintains 512 x 512 inputs rather than downsampling to smaller resolutions, which is critical for the clinical detection of subtle lesions, as well as keeping some 3D context by using axial, coronal, and sagittal information. HiFi-Rep establishes a new state-of-the-art on the CT-RATE benchmark with significant scores in BLEU-1 and METEOR metrics. By using training-free features from DINOv3 and a domain-specific LLM, the model reduces the heavy computational burden typically associated with training 3D-native architectures.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The authors designate the HiFi-S2D (Space-to-Depth) module as “lossless,” which is technically accurate for the Pixel Shuffle operation itself. However, this is preceded by inter-slice mean pooling along the depth dimension. Mean pooling is a fundamentally lossy operation that collapses 3D volumetric variance into a single 2D average, effectively erasing the “High-Fidelity” (HiFi) depth information before it ever reaches the S2D module. Authors should discuss this limitation instead of relying on the word “lossless”. 2.The paper uses a frozen DINOv3 (a general-purpose 2D foundation model) while discarding MedGemma’s native MedSigLIP encoder. While 2D foundation models inherit “intelligence” from billions of natural images, they lack domain-specific features for medical imaging. The authors provide no ablation study or direct comparison to prove that DINOv3’s general-purpose features outperform medical-specific encoders (like MedSAM or MedSigLIP) in identifying the subtle textures and low-contrast boundaries unique to CT scans. 3.A critical finding in the ablation study is that the “Axial Only” configuration achieves a 0.520 BLEU-1 score, whereas adding Coronal and Sagittal views (the full Tri-Planar setup) only increases this to 0.532.This marginal 0.012 gain suggests that the LLM may not be effectively performing tri-planar reasoning. Without a qualitative analysis showing specific clinical cases where a diagnosis was only possible due to the multi-axial views, the increased computational complexity of processing three planes remains poorly justified. 4.The use of tri-planar natural language markers does not seem optimal, as the model continues to struggle with localization error. This indicates that while the LLM can identify what a pathology is (lexical accuracy), it lacks the native mathematical 3D understanding to accurately place the pathology in 3D space. The absence of explicit 3D positional encodings or cross-view attention mechanisms leaves the model reliant on inferred reasoning, which is prone to spatial hallucinations. Please discuss potential future works or insights to account for this limitation.

reviewer_2_strengths: First, the method starts with high-resolution CT instead of heavily down sampling the input at preprocessing step, which helps retain fine grained anatomical and pathological details which is specially important for chest CT. Third, the proposed HiFi-S2D aggregation module, by rearranging spatial pixels to channel dimension, allows to solve long sequence bottleneck.

reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.Bypassing 3D-native models in favor of a frozen 2D foundation model (DINOv3) is computationally astute. By exclusively fine-tuning the linear projector and LoRA adapters on the LLM side, the framework remains highly resource-efficient while still processing native 512x512 slices. 2.The HiFi-S2D module is a well-motivated solution to the resolution-efficiency paradox. Leveraging Space-to-Depth rather than destructive downsampling or linear projection ensures that high-frequency diagnostic details necessary for spotting subtle lesions are preserved. 3.The model demonstrates clear superiority over both volumetric and 2D slice-based methods.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The methodology is exclusively validated on a single benchmark (CT-RATE). While it is a large-scale dataset, evaluating the model’s zero-shot or fine-tuned generalization on an external, out-of-distribution dataset (e.g., CTRG[1]) would greatly strengthen the claims of robustness. 2.As noted by the authors in their qualitative analysis, the model still suffers from hallucinations and omissions in non-target regions. While common in LLM-based generators, minimizing these clinical inaccuracies is paramount for real-world deployment. 3.The paper relies entirely on automated NLP metrics (BLEU, ROUGE, METEOR, BERTScore). While BERTScore helps measure semantic equivalence, automated metrics notoriously fall short in assessing true clinical validity. A reader study or evaluation by board-certified radiologists scoring for clinical correctness (e.g., F1-RadGraph or similar clinical efficacy metrics) is missing.
