reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for their valuable feedback and address the main concerns below Novelty/Clinical Impact (R2, R4, R1): We politely push back on remarks about limited novelty by reiterating our two main technical contributions. Firstly, we identify a previously unknown issue with Flow SSNs, limiting direct application to 3D. We resolve this by proposing a time-shifted noise schedule tailored to the loss. The resulting method is not just a baseline but sets a new state-of-the-art in 3D stochastic segmentation. Our proposed solution achieves the strongest performance on two challenging segmentation tasks. Secondly, our L2L-Flow addresses efficiency (up to 14x faster inference) and offers a highly competitive alternative to our voxel-space Flow-SSN, with a controllable efficiency/performance trade-off. Importantly, L2L-Flow is tailored for stochastic segmentation, employing a two-sided interpolant between an image prior and a latent label distribution. This differs from standard latent flows where one side is a fixed noise distribution. L2L-Flow is also more easily applicable to different 3D problems compared to Flow-SSN, as noise schedule tuning is no longer required for strong performance. The efficiency benefits of L2L-Flow enable novel applications such as uncertainty-guided adaptive radiotherapy planning. Efficient contour generation allows real-time updates to treatment plans and reduces the likelihood of inter‑fraction anatomical changes between imaging and treatment delivery. As suggested by R1, we will make the framing of our contributions clearer in the final version. Uncertainty Evaluation (R4): Our quantitative evaluation includes standard metrics such as GED, but also went further by evaluating clinical utility through expert review. This qualitative evaluation revealed key limitations of these metrics, where instances of contours with strong GED performance didn’t show clinically meaningful variation. This was especially true of low-rank SSNs as discussed in Section 4.3.We therefore performed further analysis, adding clinical context to our results (noted as a strength by R1), which is largely missing in other works. Fig. 3 evaluates contour variation of our models in relation to clinically meaningful inter-observer variation (IOV). Alongside GED, this enabled our clinicians to assess the usefulness of predicted contours. Importantly, our proposed flow-based methods exhibited the strongest alignment with expert IOV. Baseline Comparisons (R2): We did not compare to diffusion models as rectified flows are from the same model family, and Flow-SSN was already shown to perform better than CCDM [28]. All baselines were faithful 3D adaptations of their 2D implementations and training procedure to ensure fairness. Baseline efficiency comparisons focused on inference time due to its importance in downstream clinical use. Training efficiency was similar across models. As demonstrated by our time-shifted 3D Flow-SSN, scaling and optimising 2D methods for 3D is non-trivial. We will make the nuance surrounding these technical challenges clearer in the final version. Ablations (R2, R5): In the radiotherapy experiments, 4x downsampling was already sufficient to achieve comparable performance to our time-shifted 3D Flow-SSN. An efficiency ablation study was performed on CURVAS in Section 4.4.Due to the small size of the pancreas, we performed a further experiment at 2x downsampling to quantify the speed vs performance tradeoff, as shown in Fig. 4 & 5.A strength of L2L-Flow is its flexibility at adapting the latent capacity depending on data complexity. Scales such as 8x have potential application, and can be explored in future work. We will make the rationale behind our ablation choices clearer in the final version Architecture Details (R5): We will release the code covering full implementation details with the publication. The implementation for the rectified flow was adapted from the open-source Flow-SSN codebase.

title: Learning Directional Semantic Transitions for Longitudinal Chest X-Ray Analysis
reviewer_1_strengths: The problem that this paper is tackling is clinically important and underexplored. Framing progression as a directional semantic transition is conceptually well motivated. Evaluation is reasonably broad, covering both classification and captioning, with appropriate clinical metrics. It is additionally good practice that overlap with MS-CXR-T is excluded from the pretraining set.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Progression encoder design Figure1 (b) indicates that temporal attention is applied over the reshaped tensor (B-N_I)x3xD, while spatial attention is handled separately over (B-3)xN_IxD. This means cross-time interaction is built around fixed patch indices across visits. For Paired CXRs, where patient positioning, inspiration, and projection can vary, I believe it is a nontrivial assumption. Captioning details The manuscript only states that the learned progression representations are fed into a frozen BioMistral-7B. However it does not explain which visual representation are fed to the LLM, how they are projected into the language model input space, how many visual tokens were used, or what parameters are actually optimized. More implementation details are needed. Irreversible clinical findings Not all findings are reversible. The framework assumes all disease processes are reversible (‘improve’ -> ‘worsen’) but there are cases such as fibrosis, calcification, scarring, and post-surgical changes. A calcified nodule cannot de-calcify. Training the model on clinically impossible transitions conflates irreversibility with directionality and prevents the model from learning to flag impossible trajectories. Irreversible findings should be supervised only through the reconstruction path, where directionality is enforced geometrically rather than through flipped semantic labels. At minimum, this assumption should be acknowledged and discussed as a limitation. End-to-end training The overall objective jointly combines all losses from the start and my intuition is that training all losses simultaneously from the start may make it difficult to learn good progression representations, which is the core contribution since P would be encoding transitions between states that are themselves still being learned. I am curious whether a curriculum approach, establishing stable state representations first before introducing the transition and reconstruction objectives, would improve the quality of the learned progression features.

author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for their constructive comments and for recognizing the clinical importance (R2,3), novelty (R2,3), and comprehensive evaluation (R2,3) of our work. Upon acceptance, we will publicly release the code and model weights to facilitate reproducibility. We clarify concerns below. 1.Progression map and spatial alignment (R2,3,4): We agree that longitudinal CXRs are often not spatially aligned, which motivated the use of semantic transition. Unlike direct subtraction or low-level feature differencing, which can be easily confounded by acquisition variation, ProTrans learns disease progression at the semantic level. Specifically, we use state contrastive alignment to ground prior/current images into corresponding semantic states, and introduce a learnable progression map to explicitly model the shift between them. Similar to CLS token in ViT, this map interacts with prior/current visual maps via the progression encoder and is supervised by report-derived progression descriptions via transition contrastive alignment, encouraging it to capture semantically grounded progression cues. We clarify that the progression encoder first uses temporal attention to capture local cross-time cues, and then uses spatial attention to exchange information globally across all visual tokens. After pretraining, the learned progression map is directly used for downstream tasks. It is an explicit transition representation rather than a soft addition. To further disentangle its role, we will add a targeted ablation that removes the progression map and replaces it with direct prior-current feature fusion. This directly tests whether downstream performance comes from explicit transition learning rather than from generic paired-image fusion. Although ProTrans aims to reduce sensitivity to acquisition variation by learning semantic transitions rather than raw visual differences, we agree that this doesn’t fully mitigate robustness concerns. We will add failure-case analysis and explicit registration as future extensions. 2.Captioning implementation (R2): The learned progression map is projected into the LLM embedding dimension via a trainable linear layer and used as visual prompts for frozen BioMistral. Only the projection layer is optimized during downstream adaptation, isolating the contribution of the learned progression features. We will add more details. 3.Irreversible findings (R2): We agree that flipped semantic labels are inappropriate for irreversible findings. In our work, we didn’t apply reversed semantic supervision when the reversed label is clinically invalid. Our current supervision from Chest ImaGenome mainly includes findings such as edema, pleural effusion, etc., where improved/worsened transitions are clinically valid. Reconstruction further provides a label-free visual constraint. 4.Training strategy and components (R2,3): Good point on curriculum training. Our motivation for joint optimization is that state and transition learning are coupled: if the model is first trained only with state alignment, it may learn good single-study semantic features but ignore progression-relevant cues. Combining transition alignment encourages the state space to support directional disease evolution. Ablation study shows that removing state/transition alignment, reconstruction, or bidirectional modeling degrades performance, with transition alignment causing the largest drop. All components contribute to reliable progression learning. 5.Encoder choice (R2,3): We initialized the visual encoder (ViT-B/16) with CXR-pretrained weights. ProTrans is a backbone-agnostic progression pretraining framework, and can be combined with stronger backbones. 6.Others: q^t is a BxB one-hot alignment matrix, B is the batch size; element indexed by k denoting the k-th sample in the batch (R4). “w/o bidirection” means removing the reversed temporal modeling (R4). We will improve Fig.1 (R3) and abstract, introduction (R4), and add InfoNCE citation (R4).
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper proposes ProTrans, a longitudinal CXR pretraining framework that models disease progression as a directional semantic transition using a learnable progression feature map between paired embeddings, supported by joint state-transition contrastive alignment and bidirectional reconstruction. Reviewers acknowledged that it is a clinically important and underexplored problem, a novel formulation of progression as directional semantic transition, and a broad evaluation covering classification and captioning. Weaknesses are also pointed out: (1) The progression encoder assumes patch‑wise spatial correspondence across visits, which is fragile given variation in patient positioning, inspiration, and acquisition (R2, R3). (2) The complex multi‑loss objective makes the source of improvement unclear; a direct ablation of the progression map itself is missing, and the contribution of the LLM component is not isolated (R3, R4). (3) Empirical gains over Coca‑CXR are not uniform across findings, and the abstract/introduction contains vague jargon (R3, R4). Issues to be discussed in rebuttal: Spatial alignment assumption in the progression encoder under realistic CXR variation. Handling of irreversible clinical findings and their impact on directionality learning. Disentangling the contribution of the progression map via targeted ablation; clarifying whether the map is actively used or a “soft” addition. Missing captioning details (visual tokens, projection, trainable parameters). Justification for not using CXR‑pretrained encoders. | The paper introduces a novel and clinically relevant framework for modeling disease progression as directional semantic transitions in longitudinal chest X-rays. The rebuttal effectively clarified implementation details, encoder choices, and the role of the progression map, addressing the majority of critiques from Reviewers #2 and #3.They clarified that the progression map is an explicit semantic transition representation (not a “soft” addition), explained the captioning interface (projection layer into frozen BioMistral), confirmed CXR-pretrained ViT initialization, and acknowledged that irreversible findings were not subjected to reversed supervision because the Chest ImaGenome labels primarily involve reversible conditions (e.g., edema, effusion). They also proposed a targeted ablation removing the progression map, though this was a promise rather than an existing result. Reviewers #2 and #3 found the rebuttal adequate and changed their scores to accept, while Reviewer #4 remained unconvinced about whether the progression map is actually used and noted that the ablation cannot be added post-submission. Despite these limitations, the problem is underexplored and important, the method is well-motivated, and the evaluation is solid. While the strength outweighs the remaining issues, I believe the paper is above the acceptance threshold. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper proposes ProTrans, a longitudinal chest X-ray pretraining framework that models disease progression as directional semantic transitions between prior and current studies through joint state-transition contrastive alignment and bidirectional reconstruction. The work presents a conceptually interesting formulation for progression modeling, supported by evaluations across both progression classification and captioning tasks with clinically meaningful metrics. The main remaining concerns are that the progression encoder may still be sensitive to spatial misalignment across longitudinal CXRs, the contribution of the learnable progression map is not fully isolated due to the lack of a targeted ablation, and the handling of clinically invalid reversed supervision could be more clearly justified and discussed as a limitation. However, the rebuttal adequately clarified several implementation and design choices and two reviewers maintained positive recommendations after rebuttal. Overall, this work presents a technically reasonable and clinically meaningful formulation for longitudinal progression modeling that appears slightly above the acceptance threshold. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper addresses an important longitudinal CXR progression modeling problem with a novel directional semantic transition framework and solid experimental validation, despite some remaining limitations.

title: Learning Dual Prior Presentation for Opportunistic Screening of Visceral Artery Aneurysms on Non-Contrast CT
reviewer_1_strengths: A major strength is the clinical relevance. Opportunistic screening from routine CT is an important direction in medical imaging, and prior work has highlighted opportunistic CT screening as a meaningful translational use case. The paper also targets a problem where prior AI work appears limited, with at least one notable earlier VAA detection study focusing on CTA, not non-contrast CT, which makes the present setting more challenging and potentially impactful. The key idea of replacing a pure discrete lesion class formulation with two continuous prior spaces is well motivated by the anatomy and radiology of VAAs. The geometric confidence prior matches the notion of gradual dilation, while the reliability prior explicitly models anatomically ambiguous regions that commonly trigger false positives. This is more thoughtful than simply adding another segmentation head, and the page-3 framework diagram makes the design easy to understand. In Table 1, DeepVAA improves over nnUNet, U-Mamba, SegMamba, MedNeXt, SwinUNETR, and UXNet on the reported patient-level F1 and VAA Dice metrics, and the external cohort results suggest that the method retains performance better than several baselines under site shift. The ablation tables on page 7 also support that the two priors contribute differently and complement one another: the geometric branch mainly boosts recall, while the anatomical reliability branch mainly improves precision.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: My biggest concern is the insufficient characterization of the dataset and task difficulty. The paper reports 1000 internal and 100 external cases, but it does not clearly state how many patients actually had VAA, how many aneurysms were present, the lesion size distribution, the breakdown by arterial territory, or the prevalence in the internal and external cohorts. Without those details, it is hard to assess the true screening difficulty and the clinical meaning of the reported metrics. The paper reports the proposed method at multiple thresholds (0.05 to 0.30), while the baselines are shown at a single operating point. This makes the comparison somewhat hard to interpret unless the threshold was fixed a priori on validation data and then frozen for all testing. A stronger presentation would report PR curves, FROC-style analysis, or a clearly pre-specified threshold selection procedure. In addition, the lesion-level true-positive definition only requires at least one voxel of overlap, which is permissive and may overestimate lesion detection quality for tiny lesions. Most comparisons are against generic 3D medical segmentation architectures rather than methods tailored to aneurysm detection or vascular screening. The paper cites prior AI-based VAA detection on CTA, but does not compare conceptually or experimentally to simpler diameter-based, centerline-based, or rule-based vascular abnormality detectors. Since earlier work has already explored automated VAA detection on CTA, a clearer comparison to task-specific alternatives would strengthen the novelty and clinical argument. I am not fully satisfied with the clinical validation framing. The paper uses registered CTA-derived annotations projected onto NCCT, which is practical, but the manuscript would be stronger if it clarified registration quality control, inter-reader agreement, and whether the external cohort was collected with materially different scanners or protocols. In a clinically oriented screening paper, these details matter for judging translational robustness.

reviewer_2_strengths: The separation of dilation‑sensitive features from geometric structure representations introduces a meaningful and well‑motivated architectural innovation. This helps the model emphasise both morphological integrity and pathological dilation patterns, which are clinically relevant in vascular disease. Non‑contrast CT is widely available and commonly used in acute care. Demonstrating improved vascular segmentation without contrast agents enhances potential applicability in real‑world clinical environments. Training on one hospital dataset and testing on another provides evidence of cross‑site generalisation, which is an important step toward clinical robustness.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Although the framework is technically sound, the paper does not address how the dual priors influence the final segmentation or how clinicians can interpret the resulting predictions. Tools such as attention visualisation, relevance maps, or uncertainty estimation would help demonstrate whether the model focuses on clinically meaningful vascular regions. Without these, the transparency of the method remains limited. Although two hospital datasets are used, the external testing cohort is relatively small (100 cases), and the study does not evaluate performance across different CT acquisition parameters, noise levels, and scanner variations. Non‑contrast CT imaging is subject to substantial variability in practice, and without robustness testing it is unclear how well the model generalises to broader populations.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: – The reformulation of VAA detection as a representation learning problem offers a conceptually distinct formulation from conventional binary segmentation approaches, and the dual-prior design is motivated by the specific challenges of the task. – The framework attempts to simultaneously address lesion detection sensitivity and false positive suppression through two complementary priors, which is a reasonable design consideration given the anatomical complexity of the problem. – The inclusion of an external cohort for cross-site validation reflects an intention to assess generalizability beyond the training domain, which is a step toward broader validation.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: – Both GCP and ARP are generated through hand-crafted rules rather than being learned directly from data. This raises a fundamental question about whether the framework truly constitutes “representation learning” as claimed, or whether it is better characterized as rule-based feature injection. Furthermore, the combination of the two priors at inference via simple multiplicative suppression is a relatively rudimentary operation that limits the expressive capacity of the overall framework. – Although the model takes NCT as input, the ground truth labels are derived from CTA. Given that NCT and CTA differ fundamentally in image characteristics, vascular boundaries that are clearly delineated on CTA may not have corresponding visual information on NCT. The authors do not provide any analysis of how registration errors between the two modalities may have affected training, nor do they discuss whether the model may have been trained to detect boundaries that are physically invisible on NCT. This inconsistency appears to be in direct conflict with the premise of opportunistic screening on NCT. – Table 1 demonstrates considerable sensitivity of performance metrics to the choice of threshold tau, yet no objective criterion or automated mechanism for selecting the optimal value is provided. The current approach of selecting tau based on internal cohort performance raises concerns about post-hoc tuning, and it remains unclear whether the chosen threshold would generalize to external sites or different imaging protocols. – The external cohort consists of only 100 cases, and neither the internal nor external cohort reports the number of VAA-positive patients or individual lesions. Given the rarity of VAA, the actual number of positive samples is likely very small, which undermines the statistical reliability of the reported performance metrics. Additionally, the absence of size-stratified analysis makes it impossible to assess whether the model performs robustly across the full spectrum of aneurysm sizes. – While ARP is designed to suppress false positives, false negatives carry greater clinical risk in a screening setting. The observed decline in recall from 78.2% to 77.4% upon addition of ARP, though numerically modest, suggests that some true lesions may have been suppressed in the process. Critically, there is no error analysis characterizing which lesions were missed, whether small, located near bifurcations, or exhibiting atypical morphology, nor any quantitative comparison of prediction maps before and after ARP application. – The paper positions DeepVAA as a tool for opportunistic screening, yet provides no discussion of how it would integrate into actual clinical workflows. With precision ranging from 80% to 86%, approximately 10–20% of model-positive cases would be false positives, each potentially triggering unnecessary follow-up CTA. For a screening tool targeting an asymptomatic population, this false positive burden requires explicit clinical justification. The manuscript does not address what level of false positive rate would be acceptable in practice, nor does it discuss the cost-benefit implications of deploying such a system in routine radiology workflow.

author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for their valuable feedback and for recognizing our work as clinically meaningful (R1) and well motivated (R2). We address the major concerns below: Dataset Setup (R1 R2 R3) Each set (train, valid & external) follows a negative/positive patient ratio of 1:1±0.02. The three sets contain 563, 124 & 81 lesions, respectively (celiac trunk 79%, superior mesenteric 11%, right renal 6%, left renal 4%). The recall increased with lesion size, ranging from 61% (<10 mm), 83% (10-20mm), to 100% (>20 mm); these size groups accounted for 33.8%, 61.8% & 4.4%. The internal cohort has two scanner brands (GE, UIH), and the external cohort has four (+Philips, Siemens). Our high performance strongly demonstrates our cross-center robustness. We acknowledge that the external set is relatively small, but our dataset is already the largest NCT-CTA cohort with fine-grained VAA annotations. We will also further expand our multi-center datasets. Tau selection & FP processing (R1 R3) DeepVAA achieves patient AUROC 0.9306 and lesion PRAUC 0.9266.Threshold 0.3 was predefined on validation data, maximizing the Youden Index (0.8365) at the ROC elbow (Sensitivity 86.5%, FPR 2.9%). Clinically, DeepVAA is a triage tool. Size-based analysis shows 14/16 FPs are <15mm artifacts easily dismissed by radiologists, avoiding unnecessary CTAs. Crucially, high-risk VAAs (>20mm) achieve 100% recall with no FPs. Dual Representation Prior (R2 R3) We have addressed this in the ablation study. In Sec 3.2, the dual priors are effective not only when applied individually, but also when working jointly. We respectfully clarify that GCP and ARP are explicitly implemented as learnable convolutional branches optimized by auxiliary losses. Consequently, the network genuinely learns these anatomical representations, and their multiplication at inference acts as a dynamic, data-driven spatial attention mechanism rather than a primitive rule injection. Registration Quality (R1 R3) Offline CTA was used only to overcome the difficulty of manual annotation on NCT. This cross-modality label transfer is a mature paradigm [PANDA & iAorta; Nat Med 2023, 2025]. Because deployment relies exclusively on NCT, the approach is fully compatible with opportunistic screening. Besides, NCT & CTA were acquired consecutively under strict immobilization, and visceral arteries are largely motion-stable. Visual QC confirmed that DeepVAA does not hallucinate CTA boundaries, but learns objective NCT signs including perivascular fat displacement, contour bulging, and calcifications. Recall Drop with ARP (R3) In the validation set (124 lesions), the slight recall drop was due to one missed 7 mm VAA. Given the substantial reduction in FP, missing a <10 mm VAA could be acceptable, as <10 mm lesions are generally not clinically critical cases. Embed with Clinical Workflow (R2 R3) DeepVAA is designed as a PACS-integrated screening assistant rather than a standalone diagnostic system. It runs in the background on routine CTs, providing patient flags and lesion-level visual overlays as a secondary reader without interrupting standard workflows. For AI-flagged cases, the radiologist remains the final decision-maker, verifying highlighted candidates and recommending CTA only when clinically warranted, enabling practical workflow integration. Compare with Vascular Abnormal Detection (R3) We also tested the centerline-based method that measured cross-sectional diameter and detected VAAs via focal diameter enlargement. It suffered a severe trade-off (70% recall/46% specificity vs 33% recall/78% specificity). In contrast, DeepVAA achieves 86.5% recall and 97.1% specificity. Such rule-based methods depend on rigid geometric priors and are limited by the complex branching anatomy. In contrast, DeepVAA learns continuous 3D anatomical context rather than relying on brittle geometric rules. All suggested changes will be added to the paper. The code and IRB info will be public upon acceptance.

title: Learning from Good Neighbors: Slice-wise Quality-aware CT-to-Diffusion MRI Synthesis
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The framework is clear and reasonably well organized. 2.The ablation studies are useful and support the proposed design choices. 3.The method improves LPIPS, PSNR, and MAE over several baselines.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The evaluation is relatively limited, as the test set includes only 23 patients from a single center, which raises concerns about the robustness and generalizability of the reported results. 2.The clinical utility of the method is not quantitatively validated, as the claimed lesion-related benefits are supported only by qualitative examples rather than dedicated lesion-level or downstream clinical analyses. 3.The quality predictor is trained using LPIPS-based pseudo-labels, which may not reliably reflect true perceptual quality or clinical relevance. 4.Given that the main motivation is to improve anatomical consistency across slices, it may be more appropriate to focus on a genuinely 3D modeling strategy rather than relying primarily on slice-wise processing with neighboring-slice refinement. A more native 3D design could better capture volumetric structure and improve 3D anatomical continuity.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The proposed architecture is novel and well aligned with the underlying imaging characteristics, effectively leveraging the anisotropic nature of 2D acquisitions. The incorporation of LPIPS as a perceptual quality measure is well motivated and provides a mechanism for improved image fidelity and potential quality assessment. The use of cross-slice contextual information is a strong design choice, and the authors provide convincing experimental evidence of its benefit. The use of a relatively large training dataset increases confidence in the robustness of the results.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The paper does not sufficiently address the risk of hallucination in cross-modality synthesis (CT to DWI), where fundamentally different physical properties are being inferred. This raises concerns about clinical applicability, particularly for diagnostic use, and warrants stronger discussion and validation beyond quantitative metrics. The use of affine registration for creating paired training data is potentially problematic given the known geometric distortions in DWI. The impact of misregistration on model performance is not discussed. The choice of DWI as the target modality is not well justified, as it represents a particularly challenging synthesis task compared to more structurally aligned modalities (e.g., T1/T2). Key methodological details are unclear, including whether separate models were trained for different b-values or whether weights were shared or fine-tuned. One figure (3) did not render, making evaluation difficult. The experimental reporting lacks clarity. It is unclear whether reported metrics in tables correspond to test averages, and no information on variability (e.g., range or standard deviation across test patients) is provided. The study is limited to a single centre and lacks sufficient detail on dataset composition (e.g., patient diagnoses, scanner vendors, acquisition field strengths, sequence parameters), raising concerns about generalizability

reviewer_3_strengths: The paper is well-written, easy to read, and well-presented. author_feedback: We sincerely thank the three reviewers [R1, R2, R3] for their caluable time and constructive reviews. Regarding reproducibility, we will release code, model weights, and a test-data subset within IRB constraints. We now address the main concerns by Meta-Reviewer [Meta] priority. 1.Additional DWI details [Meta, R2, R3] Synthesis target [Meta-1, R3]: Our target is trace DWI at b=0 and b=1000 s/mm², the direction-independent images that radiologists read on PACS, rather than direction-resolved 4D DW volumes. In clinical protocols, b=1000 DWI is acquired along multiple directions and combined by the scanner into a trace image, and our dataset uses these clinical trace volumes. Therefore, R3’s per-direction recovery concern does not apply, and DTI or multi-shell modeling lies outside our scope. b-value handling [R2]: As noted in Sec. 1, we train separate LDMs for b=0 and b=1000 since they differ in signal physics. All results in Tables 1–3 follow this design. Why DWI [R2]: Per Sec. 1, our scenario is emergency stroke/hemorrhage triage, where acute ischemic lesions are most reliably visible on DWI. Targeting an easier modality such as T1/T2 would undermine the clinical motivation of our work. 2.Hallucination [Meta, R2] We agree the risk is intrinsic but mitigate it via two mechanisms. The Refiner re-injects the CT condition (Eq. 3–4), anchoring outputs to the patient’s anatomy. The Quality Predictor estimates per-slice reliability (Pearson 0.986) to identify low-confidence outputs, ensuring reliability most synthesis models lack. In Fig. 3, LGN preserves true lesions while avoiding false ones in the non-bleed case. Per Sec. 1, LGN is positioned as a triage aid rather than a diagnostic replacement, with reader studies and lesion-level evaluation noted as future work (Sec. 4) 3.Registration error [Meta, R2] Preprocessing (Sec. 3.1) restricts analysis to skull-stripped intracranial tissue, which is approximately rigid. The b=0 image used for registration is free from diffusion-gradient-induced distortion. Residual misregistration affects all baselines equally, preserving Table 3’s relative comparison. 4.Per-patient variability [Meta, R2] Tables 1–3 are averages over 513 slices from 23 patients. From existing results, per-patient std at b=0 is ≈0.01 (LPIPS), ≈0.005 (MAE); LGN’s improvement is consistent across patients. 5.Novelty [R1, R3] Our contribution is the integration of LDM, neighbors, and cross-attention into a quality-aware refinement framework via slice-level quality estimation, as R3 also noted positively. Table 1 shows that adding quality-filtered neighbors improves LPIPS from 0.066 to 0.061.While 3D modeling [R1] may help volumetric continuity, full-volume 3D diffusion is costly and treats all slices uniformly, whereas our slice-wise design enables selective refinement of difficult slices. 6.Dataset and generalization [R1, R2] Our dataset comprises 398 patients at a university hospital under IRB approval (M 56% / F 44%, mean age ~70, range 26–96), centered on acute ischemic stroke including microbleed cases (Fig. 3). CT was acquired on a GE Discovery CT750 HD and MRI on a Philips Ingenia CX 3T, with DWI as trace b=0 and b=1000 s/mm². Multi-center validation is future work, and our core design (slice-wise quality estimation, neighbor-based refinement) readily extends to such settings. 7.Others Clinical utility [R1]: Lesion-level detection is feasible with our work, and as noted in Sec. 4, we plan to address it in future work with reader studies. LPIPS pseudo-label [R1]: It serves relative ranking rather than absolute scoring, and the Pearson score confirms its stability(Sec.3.2). Fig. 3 [R2]: Fig. 3 renders correctly in PC PDF viewers. We will reduce its file size in the camera-ready for mobile compatibility. If given the opportunity for acceptance, we will incorporate the above clarifications into the camera-ready. We respectfully ask the reviewers to consider this work a meaningful contribution. Thank you.

However, they do not substantially undermine the main contributions of the paper. Therefore, I lean toward acceptance. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The technical core of the paper is solid. The authors successfully cleared up a major misunderstanding regarding diffusion gradient directions by clarifying their use of the Trace image. While Reviewer 1 makes valid points regarding the small evaluation cohort (23 patients) and lack of downstream clinical reader studies, the other reviewers found the 2.5D neighbor-refinement architecture innovative for anisotropic data. I recommend Accept as justified above.

title: Learning Hierarchical Anatomy-Grounded Representation for Cross-Modal Registration
reviewer_1_strengths: The motivation that existing contrastive learning approaches often treat voxels as independent instances and overlook the inherent hierarchical anatomical context is well-founded. Exploring alternative strategies for constructing contrastive learning along this direction is both relevant and promising.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The primary weakness of the paper lies in its lack of clarity, which significantly hinders comprehension of the proposed method. Sections 2.1 and 2.2, in particular, are difficult to follow due to ambiguous notation and insufficient explanation. For example, Section 2.1 introduces notation with subscript I without prior definition. Additionally, the description of the hard-sample mining strategy is unclear. The paper states: “for each fine-level anchor, we first select top-K_p coarse correspondence proposals in view B according to coarse feature similarity. We then collect local 3D windows of size \alpha^3 around these proposals and merge them into a fine-level candidate pool P_{f,i}. ” However, the term “correspondence proposals” is not defined, and the fine-level candidate pool P_{f,i} is not specified. Furthermore, Equation (2) appears to define a contrastive learning objective but uses a reconstructed anchor as the query. The paper does not provide sufficient motivation or interpretation for this design choice. In Equation (3), the term L_{\text{rec}}^f is introduced without definition. The role of L_{\text{mat}} is also unclear. It is not well explained why this term is necessary or what is the geometry-derived matchability labels are used as ground truth. Additional suggestions: Since the experiments are conducted on challenge datasets, it would strengthen the paper to include comparisons with methods from those challenges. The figures are too small, and the color-coded deformation fields are difficult to interpret. It would be more meaningful to visualize the learned representation. Overall, while the idea is promising, the paper would benefit from clearer presentation.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The shift from point-wise contrast to structured, hierarchical reconstruction effectively addresses the ambiguity in cross-modal correspondence. The “dustbin” mechanism for unmatchable regions is a clever addition.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The core technical contribution—replacing contrastive loss with a reconstruction loss—is essentially a form of feature interpolation or smoothing over local neighborhoods. Reconstructing a feature vector f_A as a weighted sum of nearby features f_B (via attention) is mathematically similar to existing non-local means or graph convolution operations already prevalent in registration. There is no direct ablation comparing Point-wise Contrast vs. Proposed Reconstruction under identical architectural settings. Without isolating the loss function change, it is unclear if the gains come from the “reconstruction” logic or simply from the hierarchical coarse-to-fine architecture (which could arguably work with standard contrast too).
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: Reconstruction requires the entire similarity distribution to be correct, not just one feature pair — this is a more demanding and informative training signal than standard point-wise contrastive learning. Soft rejection of unmatchable regions prevents corrupted gradients from augmentation artifacts and FOV mismatches. Geometry-derived labels make this fully self-supervised. 3.Zero-shot transfer to ThoraxCBCT and Whole-Body (CT → 4 MR contrasts) without fine-tuning demonstrates that the representation captures anatomy rather than intensity statistics.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The paper argues point-wise contrastive ignores anatomical context, but 3D ResNet features already encode large receptive fields spanning hundreds of voxels. The real advantage of HAGR is a stronger proxy task, not context-awareness per se. This framing should be corrected. 2.8 paired cases on the primary benchmark, with standard deviation of ±27.50%, limits the statistical reliability of conclusions.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: R1: Clarity/notation. Subscript i denotes a spatial index. In hard-sample mining, a “correspondence proposal” is a candidate location in view B selected by similarity to the anchor in view A. For a fine-level anchor f^A_{f,i}, we map its location to the corresponding coarse-grid and select the top-K_p proposal locations in view B with highest feature similarity. The fine-level candidate pool P_{f,i} is the set of fine-level feature vectors collected from local windows centered around the proposals. L^f_rec is the fine-level instance of the unified loss L^l_rec in Eq. (2). Table 1 includes ConvexAdam, a strong Learn2Reg challenge method. We will revise Secs. 2.1–2.2 to define symbols on first use and improve the figure visualizations. R2: Design rationale. Using the reconstructed anchor in Eq. (2) requires the candidate similarity distribution to recover the anchor, whereas using the original anchor would only impose pairwise discrimination. L_mat is a binary cross-entropy loss supervising the coarse matchability predictor that controls the dustbin. It enables soft rejection of unmatchable anchors, which have no valid correspondence, thereby reducing noisy gradients from non-overlapping regions. Binary labels come from known spatial augmentations, where anchors mapped inside the valid overlap are matchable and the rest unmatchable. R2: Ablation evidence. Table 3’s “Contrastive-Only” is the requested controlled comparison. It uses the same two-level hierarchy, training data, and registration stage, while replacing reconstruction-consistency learning with point-wise contrastive learning. The DSC drop (74.56→64.31) supports the contribution of the reconstruction-based proxy task beyond the hierarchical design. R1/R2: Novelty beyond interpolation/smoothing. The weighted sum is not a forward output like non-local means or graph convolution, but a training-time proxy task. Eq. (1) turns the cross-view candidate similarity distribution into a reconstructed query, and Eq. (2) forces this distribution to recover the anchor. Thus, HAGR supervises the ranking of plausible correspondences and encourages the candidate distribution to be correspondence-consistent, rather than averaging features for propagation or matching a single pair. R3: Point-wise contrastive framing. We agree and will rephrase. The main distinction is not receptive-field size, since 3D encoders encode large context, but the supervision imposed by the proxy task. Reconstruction constrains the cross-view correspondence distribution, whereas point-wise contrast supervises only pairwise similarity. R3: Evaluation scope. The 8 paired Learn2Reg cases limit statistical power; we agree this benchmark must be interpreted cautiously. However, the comparison remains fair since all methods use the same paired cases and protocol. In Table 1, HAGR improves mean DSC over the strongest baseline (71.23→74.56) while reducing HD95 (7.77→4.97), suggesting the gain is not merely a fluctuation. Whole-Body (20 subjects, 4 MR contrasts) and ThoraxCBCT (11 subjects) further support generalization (Table 2). R3: Candidate diversity. Fine-stage proposals form the reconstruction pool, not explicit contrastive negatives. Their role is to provide plausible but hard-to-distinguish candidates for learning discriminability. Ambiguous coarse responses may yield multiple plausible hypotheses, while concentrated responses define local refinement around confident candidates; the α³ windows still contain locally varying anatomy. Diffuse weighting yields a mixed query that fails to match the positive anchor or suppress ambiguous alternatives in Eq. (2), so supervision comes from resolving local ambiguity rather than spatial diversity alone. We will rephrase to avoid implying diversity-guaranteed mining. R1: Reproducibility. Code will be released; all training/evaluation datasets are public except the in-house Whole-Body set. We will specify all hyperparameters and augmentation ranges.

title: Learning Modality-Invariant Structure and Distribution Alignment for Multimodal Medical Image Registration
reviewer_1_strengths: One positive aspect is the attempt to integrate contrastive learning directly into the registration process via the proposed RMCA strategy. By constructing positive pairs based on the predicted deformation field rather than relying on pre-aligned data, the method avoids additional supervision and provides a more task-coupled formulation compared to conventional contrastive approaches. This design is conceptually reasonable and aligns with the goal of learning modality-invariant representations in an unsupervised manner. The SAFE module introduces a frequency-based feature decomposition to emphasize structural information, which is intuitively motivated given that anatomical structures are more consistent across modalities than raw intensities. While the idea itself is not entirely new, incorporating it into a registration framework is a sensible design choice that may help improve feature consistency across modalities.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1）The formulation of the contrastive learning component remains somewhat ambiguous. Could the authors clarify how positive and negative pairs are explicitly constructed in practice (e. g. , voxel-level vs. patch-level, intra- vs. inter-sample negatives)? In particular, how do you mitigate the risk of false negatives arising from anatomically similar regions across different subjects? 2）The RMCA strategy relies on the predicted deformation field to establish correspondence. How sensitive is the method to inaccurate deformation in the early stages of training? Although a ramp-up strategy is introduced, it would be helpful to provide a quantitative or ablation analysis demonstrating its effectiveness in stabilizing contrastive learning. 3）For the SAFE module, have the authors analyzed whether the enhanced high-frequency components indeed correspond to anatomical structures rather than noise or modality-specific artifacts? Additional visualization or frequency-domain analysis could strengthen the justification of this design. 4）The contrastive loss is applied only at the finest resolution level. Could the authors elaborate on this design choice? Have you explored multi-scale contrastive alignment, and if so, how does it affect performance? 5）From a methodological perspective, the current framework treats all other samples in the batch as negatives. Would incorporating more structured sampling strategies (e. g. , spatially-aware negatives or hard-negative mining) further improve the effectiveness of the contrastive alignment?
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The method demonstrates consistently strong empirical performance across all three benchmark datasets, achieving substantial and statistically significant improvements over both unimodal and multimodal baselines. The framework is well‑motivated and conceptually coherent. The paper clearly articulates two central challenges in multimodal registration—capturing modality‑invariant anatomical structures and reducing cross‑modal feature discrepancies—and introduces SAFE and RMCA as complementary components that address these challenges within a unified architecture.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Multimodal registration frameworks typically adopt a dual‑branch encoder to accommodate modality‑specific feature characteristics. Given that MR and CT exhibit distinct high‑frequency responses, is it appropriate to share parameters when computing SE‑based channel attention within the SAFE module? Would modality‑specific SE parameters provide greater flexibility or better capture modality‑dependent structural cues? The contrastive learning component relies on deformation‑guided positive pair construction. However, during early training stages, the predicted displacement field may be inaccurate. How does the contrastive loss ensure that these initially constructed positive pairs are reliable? In principle, even slight spatial misalignment would imply that each voxel could have additional potential positive locations among the 2 B H W D-2 candidates. Furthermore, both ARDMR and the proposed method employ contrastive learning, yet the performance gap between them is substantial. What factors contribute to this discrepancy? Furthermore, it is unclear how this method prevents positive samples from being overwhelmed when the entire volume data is unfolded into batches. Why not borrow from the approach of “modality-independent structural image representation learning for deformable multimodal medical image registration,” which samples only a small number of negative samples to ensure that the gradients of positive sample pairs are not overwhelmed? Under the current formulation, the InfoNCE loss appears ineffective.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: A clear strength of the paper is that the problem setting and methodological motivation are both well aligned with the challenges of multimodal registration. The difficulty of multimodal registration indeed comes from both anatomical correspondence and modality discrepancy, and the paper explicitly attempts to improve the registration process from these two perspectives rather than relying only on a new backbone or a different similarity metric. As a result, the overall narrative of the paper is coherent and the method is conceptually easy to follow. The roles of SAFE and RMCA are also conceptually distinct. SAFE is designed to emphasize structure-relevant information at the deepest level, while RMCA introduces contrastive learning into the deformation estimation loop through registration-guided positive-pair construction. In particular, the idea of dynamically constructing cross-modal positives based on the current registration result is more task-specific than decoupling multimodal representation learning from registration, and RMCA is arguably the more distinctive technical component of the paper. The experimental section is reasonably convincing. The paper does not rely on a single benchmark, but instead evaluates the method on three public datasets covering both abdominal and brain MR-CT registration scenarios. The set of baselines is also relatively comprehensive, including a classical method, generic deep registration models, and several recent multimodal approaches. Most importantly, the reported gains are consistent across datasets, and the proposed method achieves both improved DSC and low folding ratios. This makes the empirical evidence itself fairly persuasive. In addition, the ablation results provide at least some support for the proposed components. SAFE alone leads to consistent improvements, RMCA alone yields larger gains in DSC, and the full model performs best across the three datasets. While this does not fully validate all of the paper’s mechanistic interpretations, it does indicate that both modules contribute positively to the final performance rather than the gains being caused purely by training tricks or chance.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Despite the promising overall results, some methodological aspects remain insufficiently clarified. First, the proposed “frequency enhancement” in SAFE is, in practice, closer to a high-frequency enhancement module based on low/high residual decomposition than to a fully established mechanism for learning modality-invariant structural representations. The paper does not directly demonstrate that SAFE truly learns the kind of modality-invariant structure emphasized in the claims. Moreover, SAFE is only applied at the deepest scale, while finer-scale registration stages still rely on the original encoder features. If the main value of SAFE is to strengthen structural consistency, the paper should better justify why this mechanism is only used at the bottom level rather than applied more systematically across scales. This design choice is not sufficiently validated. RMCA is the more interesting part of the method, but its robustness also deserves further discussion. According to the paper, RMCA constructs positive pairs dynamically using the current deformation field, while negatives are taken from other features within the same mini-batch; at the same time, the reported batch size is only 2.Under such a setting, the number of available negatives is very limited, which means that the contrastive signal may be weak and potentially sensitive to batch composition. Given that the overall dataset sizes are not very large, this raises some concern about how robust the claimed cross-modal alignment effect of RMCA really is. The paper does not provide a batch-size sensitivity analysis, nor does it discuss alternative negative sampling strategies, so the mechanistic conclusion about RMCA should be interpreted with caution. In addition, the implementation details of RMCA remain somewhat ambiguous. The text refers to “spatially aligned feature maps as positive pairs,” whereas the loss is written in a standard sample-level InfoNCE form. It is therefore not entirely clear whether the actual implementation performs contrastive learning on globally aggregated sample-level embeddings or on finer-grained local features. Since this detail directly affects the strength of the contrastive supervision, the positive/negative definitions, and reproducibility, a clearer explanation would strengthen the paper. Although the paper evaluates on three datasets, the test sizes of some datasets are still relatively limited, and some reported standard deviations are fairly large. Therefore, the current experiments more convincingly support the conclusion that the method is empirically effective under the present setup than the stronger mechanistic interpretation that SAFE and RMCA fully realize modality-invariant structural learning and robust multimodal alignment. In other words, the empirical results are convincing, but the evidence for the intermediate mechanism is still weaker than the evidence for the final performance.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We appreciate the reviewers’ insightful suggestions and recognition of our work. 1) Formulation of the contrastive learning component (R1, R2, R3) RMCA is applied at the finest-resolution feature level because these features preserve richer spatial and anatomical details, while the learned alignment naturally propagates through the encoder-decoder architecture. Empirically, multi-scale contrastive alignment provided only marginal improvements. The motivation of RMCA is that moving features warped by the predicted deformation field exhibit substantially higher structural consistency with fixed features. In contrast, unaligned features within a batch contain noticeable structural discrepancies caused by motion and inter-subject anatomical variations, as also reflected by the low initial DSC in Table 1.Accordingly, RMCA constructs positive pairs based on spatial correspondence established by the predicted deformation. Specifically, warped moving features and their corresponding fixed features are treated as positive pairs, while unaligned features are regarded as negatives. All positives and negatives are constructed at the inter-sample level. RMCA computes voxel-wise cosine similarity followed by global averaging to measure pairwise feature similarity in the contrastive loss. Unlike ARDMR, which constructs positive pairs from the same patient, RMCA defines positive pairs through deformation-based spatial correspondence. Therefore, our method remains fully unsupervised and does not require pre-aligned or paired data, improving its generalizability. For clarity and reproducibility, we will release our code and the splits of three public datasets. 2) Robustness of RMCA (R1, R2, R3) We agree that deformation fields may be inaccurate during early training, which is consistent with our preliminary observations. To improve the robustness of RMCA, we employ a Gaussian ramp-up strategy for the contrastive loss. Specifically, the contrastive weight is kept low during the early stages when the predicted deformation remains unstable, thereby reducing the influence of unreliable positive pairs. As registration accuracy progressively improves, the contrastive constraint is gradually strengthened, enabling more stable and reliable feature alignment. 3) Analysis of SAFE (R1, R2, R3) High-frequency (HF) components are widely associated with structural and edge information in both natural and medical images [1-2]. In our preliminary experiments, multimodal images reconstructed using only HF components still preserved highly consistent anatomical structures across modalities, supporting the assumption that HF responses contain modality-invariant structural cues. Similar observations have also been reported in [3]. We acknowledge that HF features may also include modality-specific noise. Thus, SAFE operates on features already refined by RMCA and employs a shared SE channel attention to selectively enhance consistent structural responses while suppressing modality-specific activations. Sharing SE parameters encourages the extraction of modality-invariant features activated consistently across modalities, whereas modality-specific SE parameters may reduce cross-modal consistency. Empirically, our preliminary experiments showed that shared SE parameters achieved better registration performance. SAFE is applied only at the deepest scale because high-level features contain stronger modality-invariant semantic and structural information, making them more suitable for cross-modal enhancement. In contrast, finer-scale stages preserve more modality-specific appearance details, where RMCA is used to reduce cross-modal representation gaps while maintaining local details for accurate deformation estimation. The efficacy of SAFE is further validated by consistent improvements across all three datasets in the ablation studies.
