meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): This paper received mixed recommendations from the reviewers, including two Weak Rejects and one Weak Accept. The paper addresses the challenging problem of multimodal medical image registration and demonstrates consistent performance gains across three public datasets. However, the reviewers identified several substantive concerns, including the ambiguous formulation of the contrastive learning component (R1, R2, R3), questions regarding the robustness of the RMCA strategy (R1, R2, R3), and the lack of analysis in the frequency domain (R1, R2). Overall, the paper shows some merits when comparing to existing methods, and the meta-reviewer therefore recommends that it proceed to rebuttal. The authors are encouraged to focus their response on the major concerns outlined above. | After the rebuttal, this paper received mixed recommendations. Reviewer 2 upgraded the rating from Weak Reject to Accept after the authors clarified the complementarity between frequency-domain structural information and dynamic positive-pair construction, and Reviewer 3 maintained an Accept recommendation. However, despite these positive ratings, the reviews collectively continued to raise overlapping concerns regarding the methodology and the extent of the technical contribution. After revisiting the paper and rebuttal, I find that the experimental evaluation does not include sufficiently strong competitive baselines, and that the core components, SAFE and RMCA, do not appear sufficiently novel when considered as standalone contributions. The paper would be strengthened by including comparisons to ConvexAdam and by providing a more detailed analysis of the learned features. In light of the post-rebuttal discussion and the overall reviewer consensus, I recommend Reject. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This work proposed an image registration approach for multimodal registration. The approach makes use of structure-aware frequency enhancement (SAFE; essentially focusing on high frequency components) and multimodal contrastive alignment (RMCA). The method was tested on three different datasets (two abdominal datasets and one for the brain) and achieves uniformly good results. Reviewers appreciated the overall approach, the extensive evaluation, and its good performance. There were some concerns regarding the SAFE approach (specifically, if focusing on high frequencies indeed is expected to produce modality-invariant representations) and RMCA (specifically, if this contrastive approach suffers from instabilities during training when registration are not accurate at the beginning). The rebuttal addressed these questions and reviews were largely positive after the rebuttal. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): After the rebuttal phase, all reviewer’s opinions appear to lean toward acceptance. I believe this work addresses an important problem in multimodal registration, where contrastive learning shows strong potential but requires careful and dedicated design to be effective. I believe the manuscript would benefit from addressing the technical concerns raised by the reviewers. In particular, further clarification is needed regarding the behavior of the model during the initial stages of training, as well as a more detailed explanation of the SAFE module, especially in terms of how it distinguishes between structural information and noise.

title: Learning Quantitative Calibration of Computed Tomography for Bone Mineral Density Estimation Using Multi-Center Data
reviewer_1_strengths: The proposed method leverages QCT with ground-truth volumetric bone mineral density (vBMD) obtained via phantom-based calibration, ensuring physically meaningful density measurements. The approach is evaluated on a large multi-center dataset, employing a leave-one-center-out validation strategy to rigorously assess generalization across different acquisition settings. The method is compared against several calibration-based baseline approaches, and results demonstrate improved performance, particularly in out-of-distribution (OOD) centers. This indicates that the proposed image-to-image translation framework is effective in mitigating inter-scanner variability and recovering QCT-equivalent BMD from heterogeneous CT inputs.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The image to image translation approach instead of physics based calibration as qCT relies on scanner specific calibration as learning approach approximates BMD but don’t always guarantee clinical correctness The pipeline is based on proximal femur segmentation but getting accurate segmentation masks is not given in the paper and this also could limit applicability to other bone anatomical regions as error in segmentation could propagate to BMD estimation as well. Also comparions with other learning based BMD estimation methods should have been made and also extreme contrast shifts on CT as each center would be using same contrast level CT which again could impact the learning based method performance.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The authors propose a relatively simple approach based on image translation, converting routine CTs to QCTs, extracting the vBMD post-hoc. The baseline comparisons are exhaustive and well-described. They cover the most intuitive alternative ways to compute and regress the vBMD, showing that the baselines mostly mimic the training data regression parameters. I fail to see that more complicated deep learning approaches would perform much differently. Their main strength is the insight that some clinics/machines may exhibit vastly different calibration parameters and the demonstration of their method’s out-of-distribution generalization. The method of evaluation is very relevant, showing the reduced loss of generalizability on patients from clinics with substantially different parameters compared to other methods. Likewise, the paper contains an ablation of some of the most relevant factors that likely impact model performance. The quality of writing is overall good and the thesis is sufficiently motivated.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The paper may suffer slightly from “carrying coals to Newcastle”, doing something that may be complicated and ultimately unnecessary. I would have liked to see discussion of why their method works - they are essentially estimating a linear relationship, which apparently may most easily be done through deep learning-based image-to-image translation… The paper lacks more extensive discussion on the correctness and validity of the ground truth vBMD extracted in this fashion from CTs, and the ultimate utility of their method for using the evaluated vBMDs in a downstream task, e.g. fracture survival analysis or osteoporosis risk. Such analysis would have further increased the impact. As for the method, image-to-image translation is not new, and similar efforts exists to convert between modalities, e.g. CT, MRI, or the similar task of radiotherapy dose estimation from MRI or other complementary modalities. The authors should highlight similarities and deviations from this kind of previous work. Finally, I think that it would still have been relevant to withhold data from the in-distribution to see how well it generalizes from training to test on that set. Results-wise, the performance of their method is solid, but as shown in Fig. 3, there is a systematic underestimation of the ground truth vBMD across all methods, and it would have benefited the paper to address this more explicitly, and to propose overall fixes. Additionally, it is right now not clear exactly how the mean+-std was computed, and the deviations are comparatively large. I would also suggest restructuring the Experiments section with e.g. \paragraph to emphasize the different baseline models. I also suggest displaying results in terms of MAPE (mean absolue percentage error) which is often useful in regression tasks.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The study addresses a significant research question that is not yet fully solved in the previous literature. The study shows that a straightforward and simple U-Net algorithm should be enough to calibrate vBMD in CT images. Nine sites are a strong indicator of the method’s generalizability, even though the study had limitations addressed below. The strength of the proposed method is in estimating out-of-distribution data, where it outperforms baseline methods such as mean calibration from training data. I especially liked figure 1, which gave a good overview with one seek the range of vBMD and the calibration coefficients variation within and between sites. It also illustrates the FOW where calibration was done. Also, the schematic overview in Fig. 2 was clear.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The description of prior calibration techniques and the research gap is limited. Even though this is a conference paper, it would have benefited from a concise summary of the earlier methods and their limitations. Approaches often segment different tissue types to calibrate the mapping from HU to vBMD (e.g. reviewed in https://doi.org/10.1002/jbmr.4917). Using U-NET directly is in some sense straightforward, whereas other approaches have high transparency in deriving the vBMD calibration function. Now these issues are not addressed. Authors did not explain why they cropped the image strictly to femur. Previous literature (e.g. https://doi.org/10.1002/jbmr.4917) has shown that information from different tissue types, such as fat and blood in veins and air around the body can be used in calibration. Intuitively, cropping only to femur may limit the method’s capability to calibrate since it can less use information from different tissues. It also remains to be seen how the calibration functions on other bones than bone, since they are not now covered. Authors did not give information about what CT scanner manufacturers and models were covered in their dataset and whether different sites used CTs from different manufacturers, or different imaging voltages, reconstruction kernels or resolutions. Therefore, it remains unclear how well the spectrum of devices and settings from different manufacturers was covered in the study. It remained unclear why Center9 differed so strongly from other sites. The study would have benefited if the authors had discussed potential reasons for the out of distribution results. Ablation study: It is debatable if one can state that Exp. D did not yield better results than Exp. A but still say Exp. C provided a small improvement, when MAE and ICC of C and D are closer to each other than those of A and D. The study did not include algorithm development, not sure if this is a limitation, though, but the study focused on showing that a simple U-Net should work for vBMD calibration.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for their constructive feedback. Below, we address the main concerns. Q1 (R1, R2, R3) Comparison with existing methods We agree that the relationship between our approach and prior methods for BMD estimation should be discussed more comprehensively. Our approach differs fundamentally by formulating the problem as a spatial I2I translation task that predicts voxel-wise QCT density maps rather than regressing BMD [9] or estimating calibration factors [ 1]. We would like to clarify that the use of a simple U-Net and standard loss functions was intentional, serving as a proof-of-concept to evaluate proposed formulation itself. We will clarify this point more explicitly in the revised paper. [ 1] S. Bartenschlager et al.: Opportunistic Screening With CT: Comparison of Phantomless BMD Calibration Methods. JBMR. (2023) Q2 (R1, R2): Conceptual motivation and theoretical justification Our central hypothesis is that the proposed I2I translation framework learns a scanner normalized representation of physical bone density, whereas direct regression only learns a global statistical shortcut. The task is fundamentally spatial and benefits from dense voxel-wise supervision, which provides vastly richer learning signals than direct regression based on single scalar values. We will clarify this point more clearly in the revised paper. Q3 (R1, R2): Validity of ground truth We apologize for the insufficient information regarding the ground-truth (GT) BMD generation. The GT-BMD was generated following the existing pipeline consisting of CT bone segmentation, phantom segmentation, and BMD calculation [ 2]. We assume the proximal femur (PF) segmentation is readily available before applying our method. We will clarify the details of GT-BMD generation in the revised paper. [ 2] K. Uemura et al.: Development of an open-source measurement system to assess the areal bone mineral density of the proximal femur from clinical CT images. Arch Osteoporos. (2022) Q4: (R1, R2): In-distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) setting We apologize for the lack of clarity regarding the experimental protocol. All nine centers were evaluated using a leave-one-center-out cross-validation strategy. After completing all folds, the test results were grouped into ID and OOD categories based on the calibration-factor distributions. Thus, the results aggregate outcomes across multiple cross-validation experiments. The revised paper will provide a clearer description of this setup. Q5 (R2): systematic underestimation of BMD We agree that the proposed framework still exhibits systematic underestimation of BMD for the OOD dataset, and we will explicitly acknowledge this as a limitation in the revised paper. At the same time, our results demonstrate that BMD regression or calibration estimation approaches are substantially less robust, whereas the proposed method maintains high agreement in the OOD setting. We will further expand this discussion in the revised paper. Q6 (R3): CT acquisition and scanner variability We agree that additional details regarding CT acquisition settings would strengthen the manuscript. The dataset includes scanners from GE and Canon, and Center 9 used a lower-dose acquisition protocol, which may contribute to the observed OOD calibration shift. We will provide additional scanner and acquisition details in the revised paper. Q7 (R3): Use of the proximal femur cropped region Although the input volumes are cropped around the PF region, surrounding anatomical structures and soft tissue remain partially visible and may still provide contextual information to the prediction. The cropping strategy was intended to focus the model on the clinically relevant region while retaining limited contextual cues. We will clarify this design choice more explicitly in the revised paper. Other comments: The revised paper will add MAPE as an additional metric (R2). Our code will be made available upon acceptance (R1, R2, R3).
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper receives mixed reviews. Reviewers raise major concerns of this work, such as limited novelty, dependency on calibration during training, and insufficient comparative evaluation. Rebuttal is invited. | The paper received mixed reviews. Based on all reviewers’ comments and author response, I agree that this paper does not provide technical novelty, however, this work provides a compelling argument for considering simple, direct U-Net–based approaches for phantom-less vBMD calibration. It is also validated using data from 9 centers. Hence, I lean to acceptance of this work. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The novelty of the method is very low (it just uses a U-Net). However, the application is relevant, and the results show that a simple method can yield results that can be used in clinical studies. The tests on 9 different sites and machines strengthen the results. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Important notice: despite a reminder, reviewer 1 failed to submit a post-rebuttal evaluation. The paper presents a methodology which is very nicely evaluated in a multicenter setup to provide a valuable clinical solution. The simplicity of the approach is definitely appealing. Also, assuming the authors provide the promised information and implement the adjustments on the camera-ready paper, the paper would be a very nice paper for the main conference.

title: Learning Role-Conditioned Alignment for Medical Image Referring Segmentation
reviewer_1_strengths: Strong, consistent gains across two public MIRS benchmarks with comprehensive baselines (unimodal and multimodal), including recent state-of-the-art approaches. Overall pipeline, module motivations, and ablation design are clearly communicated with an informative figure and structured method description. Addresses a central limitation in MIRS-lack of token-level, role-aware grounding-leading to improved spatial disambiguation in complex pulmonary infection cases.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The method relies critically on partitioning tokens into roles, but the paper does not describe how this role assignment is performed (rule-based parsing, NER, a learned classifier, or dataset-provided structure?). The BRM uses a Sobel operator to extract edges and modulate features. FEUP already uses a Laplacian high-pass filter for a similar purpose. Both are edge-enhancement mechanisms applied at different stages. The paper doesn’t discuss this overlap or justify why both are needed No analysis of robustness to noisy/incomplete/misaligned text, which is realistic in clinical workflows; performance under partial or erroneous role tokens is unknown. The paper claims the three mechanisms are tailored to their respective roles, but provides no visual or interventional evidence that the attention actually specializes by role. A figure showing role-specific attention maps across several test images, ideally paired with a text-component swap experiment, would substantially strengthen this central claim. The global textual gate (Eq. 3) — global average pooling over text, followed by linear projection, sigmoid, and channel-wise multiplication with visual features — is functionally identical to Squeeze-and-Excitation channel attention [Hu et al. , 2018] or FiLM-style feature-wise modulation [Perez et al. , 2018], simply conditioned on text rather than self-derived features. The paper presents this as a novel “textual gate” without citing or acknowledging this well-established lineage. Minor writing issues. “Alignmnet” typo in the abstract. “the the” duplication on page 5.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.Clear presentation. The paper is fairly easy to follow. The motivation, framework, and experiments are clearly organized, and the qualitative results are aligned with the intended effect of the method, namely cleaner predictions and improved boundary quality. 2.Well-motivated problem formulation. The paper identifies a meaningful limitation of prior MIRS methods, namely that most of them treat the input report as a monolithic global feature and do not explicitly distinguish between different token roles such as lesion semantics, quantity, and anatomical location. This is a sensible observation in the medical setting, where these cues are often naturally structured in clinical descriptions. The proposed RCA framework is reasonably coherent and well aligned with the task setting. 3.Relatively solid ablation study analysis. The paper provides a reasonably informative ablation study by evaluating FEUP, each role-conditioned branch, their fusion, and BRM separately, which makes it easier to understand where the improvement comes from. The results support the central claim that semantic, quantity, and location cues are complementary, with the location branch contributing the largest single gain. In addition, the paper compares different visual and language backbone combinations, which suggests that the proposed design is not entirely tied to one specific encoder pair.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The method is tailored to the current benchmark setting, where referring expressions are relatively structured and naturally decomposable into semantic, quantity, and location cues. Although the paper shows robustness across backbone choices, it does not provide evidence of broader generalization across organs, diseases, datasets, or more diverse report styles. As a result, the external validity of the proposed role-conditioned decomposition remains unclear. 2.The presentation of Figure 1 could be more professional and academically polished. In particular, the use of decorative icon-style elements (e.g., the coin stack and map marker) makes the architecture diagram look somewhat informal and less consistent with the visual style typically expected in computer vision or medical imaging papers, it’s more like a NLP-paper-style figure. If such visual symbols are intentionally retained, their technical meaning should be explicitly explained in the figure caption or main text. 3.A minor weakness is that the experimental comparison is not fully comprehensive. The paper’s “state-of-the-art” claim may be incomplete. Given that both MMI-UNet[1] and MIT-SAM[2] are open-source and highly relevant methods on QaTa-COV19 and MosMedData+, it would strengthen the paper to include direct comparisons with them. The Dice of MIT-SAM is 82.08%, higher than this paper. This would make the empirical evaluation more complete and help better support the claimed state-of-the-art position. [1] Bui, P.N., Le, D.T., Choo, H.: Visual-textual matching attention for lesion segmentation in chest images. In: Linguraru, M.G., Dou, Q., Feragen, A., Giannarou, S., Glocker, B., Lekadir, K., Schnabel, J.A. (eds.) Medical Image Computing and Computer Assisted Intervention – MICCAI 2024.pp. 702–711.Springer Nature Switzerland, Cham (2024) [2] Zhou X, Yan L, Ding R, et al. MIT-SAM: Medical image-text SAM with mutually enhanced heterogeneous features fusion for medical image segmentation[J]. IEEE Journal of Biomedical and Health Informatics, 2025.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The paper introduces the RCA framework, which breaks through the limitations of traditional MIRS mechanisms that treat text as a single global feature. By partitioning the text into three functional subsets and designing distinct interaction mechanisms for each, it achieves a more fine-grained cross-modal feature alignment. 2.A Frequency-Enhanced Upsampling (FEUP) strategy is introduced, which effectively overcomes the problem of high-frequency information loss commonly caused by standard upsampling processes. 3.The Boundary Refinement Module (BRM) is incorporated into the architecture, which effectively leverages edge-aware information to precisely delineate fuzzy boundaries in areas where lesions overlap with healthy tissues. 4.The paper provides a comprehensive comparison with various existing unimodal (e.g., UNet++) and multimodal methods (e.g., LviT). The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed RCA method significantly improves lesion prediction using textual descriptions and effectively addresses spatial ambiguity in X-ray and CT imaging.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The paper lacks technical details regarding text processing. Although it states that the input text is partitioned into three functional subsets, it fails to provide a clear explanation or algorithm for how the raw clinical reports are decomposed and mapped into these specific categories. 2.There is a notable absence of experimental evidence concerning the computational overhead. The Role-Conditioned Block (RCB) introduces three parallel attention mechanisms, yet the paper does not discuss or provide data on whether this increased complexity significantly impacts inference latency, GPU memory footprint, or overall running costs in practical applications.
reviewer_3_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We sincerely thank the reviewers for their time and valuable feedback. The positive responses greatly encourage the medical multimodal research community. We will address the key comments, incorporate necessary revisions, and correct all typos in the camera-ready version.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): This submission proposes RCA, a role-conditioned alignment framework for medical image referring segmentation that decomposes clinical text into lesion semantics, quantity, and anatomical location, and reports strong results on QaTa-COV19 and MosMedData+ with generally clear presentation and useful ablations. The reviewers are broadly positive about the motivation, empirical gains, and role-aware design, supporting a provisional accept recommendation. However, authors are encouraged to address several issues in the rebuttal and final version: most importantly, the paper does not specify how raw text is partitioned into the three roles, the claimed role-specific mechanisms are not directly validated through attention visualizations or intervention/swap experiments, and the state-of-the-art claim may be incomplete without comparisons to relevant recent baselines such as MMI-UNet and MIT-SAM.

title: Learning to Optimize Radiotherapy Plans via Fluence Maps Diffusion Model Generation and LSTM-Based Optimization
reviewer_1_strengths: (1). The paper introduces a novel combination of distilled one-shot diffusion models and recurrent meta-optimizers to navigate the non-convex landscape of radiotherapy planning. (2). The LSTM-based L2PLAN module captures gradient history to learn update dynamics, allowing the optimizer to navigate complex dose landscapes more effectively than traditional fixed-rule optimizers. Experimental results demonstrate that L2PLAN achieves comparable performance to standard planners but with 7x to 20x fewer optimization steps. (3). The system provides a seamless transition from patient CT images to deliverable machine plans without manual intervention, significantly balancing planning speed with clinical flexibility.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: (1). As the student generator G_θ is distilled from a teacher, it may inherit approximation errors. The paper does not quantify if the L2PLAN refinement can fully overcome these manifold errors or if the final plan quality is ultimately capped by the teacher’s fidelity. (2). The meta-optimizer is trained using k_i inner-loop steps. The manuscript provides no sensitivity analysis regarding the choice of k_i. In L2O research, the length of this unrolling horizon is a critical determinant of whether the optimizer learns “short-sighted” updates or achieves long-term stability. (3). The authors use a two-layer LSTM to track gradient history. In current L2O research, there is a shift toward Transformer-based architectures for long-range dependency tracking. The authors should clarify if the LSTM was chosen strictly for its lower computational footprint or if they observed performance plateaus with other architectures. (4). The experimental data is restricted exclusively to single-arc prostate plans with a fixed 30^° collimator and 0^° couch angle. The lack of evaluation across dual-arc/multi-arc configurations, hardware from other manufacturers, or different tumor sites like lung or head and neck suggests the claim of a “universal” method lacks sufficient experimental support. (5). While the REQUITE dataset is sizable, the descriptions of the two private prostate cohorts are brief. The paper lacks detail on the diversity of image protocols or specific preprocessing steps used to normalize CT scanner protocols across different institutions, which is vital for verifying institutional generalizability. (6). The regularization weights are fixed throughout the experiments without sensitivity analysis. Given that these weights balance dose fidelity against plan smoothness, the paper should explain if these were manually adjusted or if they require patient-specific tuning for different clinical objectives. (7). The methodology mentions using a “rule-based LS tool” and a “differentiable dose engine” but provides limited information on the specific software versions or proprietary platforms used for the clinical simulations. Specifying the platform used for the VMAT simulation would significantly enhance the transparency of the clinical translation evaluation. (8). The methodology section is rich in mathematical formulation. To improve accessibility for a broader, cross-disciplinary audience, it would be beneficial to bridge these technical details more explicitly with high-level conceptual summaries throughout the section.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1) Novel and clinically motivated problem formulation. 2) The LSTM-based meta-optimizer addresses a real limitation of existing approaches. Rather than relying on fixed-hyperparameter optimizers that require careful iterative tuning, the learned optimizer adapts its momentum parameters dynamically based on gradient history. 3) The experiments are comprehensive and well-designed. The authors isolate different parts to clearly show the actual gain and loss. Statistical significances are also reported in the paper. 4) The application of the teacher student model to distill heavy diffusion model.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1) Evaluation limited to only one type of cancer treatment. 2) Miss some standard clinical dose evaluation metrics.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The authors adopt the teacher diffusion model to obtain the fluence map in one-shot sampling by directly estimating the clean fluence map from noisy ones, which avoids the high computational cost brought by the iterative denoising process. 2.The authors propose a LSTM-based Learning-to-Optimize VMAT Plans module that learns iterative update dynamics to efficiently refine fluence maps toward prescribed dose objectives without tuned initializations or retraining. 3.Experiments on three prostate cancer clinical and public patient cohorts demonstrate the proposed method improves efficiency, flexibility to changing dose objectives, and plan deliverability.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The Fluence Map Diffusion model appears to be trained only as an unconditional diffusion model in the image domain. How does this ensure consistency between the synthesized fluence maps and the physical parameters of the machine? 2.The synthesis of fluence maps is performed via the one-shot sampling from a normal distribution, which may introduce significant uncertainty in the fluence maps, causing the second-stage optimization to start from a largely biased initial point. How do the authors address this uncertainty? 3.Some reported results seem not reliable enough. For instance, the authors use MAE to evaluate dose coverage in the PTV, which I consider a coarse metric because it is easily affected by extreme values. I recommend that the authors report clinically relevant metrics, such as D99.4.Some experimental details are missing, such as the number of sampling steps used during training of the Fluence Map Diffusion model. 5.There are some formatting oversights. For example, Table 2 contains a large number of blank areas. 6.There is some unclear use of italics in Section 3.5, as well as underlining without clear meaning on page 2.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank AC and Reviewers for their constructive comments. Reviewers recognize our method as “novel” (R1,R2,R4), “clinically motivated”, with “well-designed experiments” (R2) achieving gains in “efficiency, flexibility, and deliverability” (R4). However, they require clarifications about (A) generator fidelity/uncertainty and sampling (R1,R2,R4), (B) L2Plan and LS design and parameters (R1), (C) organs/machine generalization (R1,R2), (D) DVH metrics (R2,R4). (A) We thank the Reviewers for raising this point. FMD mitigates errors starting from distillation by combining L_DMD and L_adv anchoring generated samples to real ones. Table 2 shows the 18-step teacher reaches 15.40 FID, while 1-step FMD with both losses reaches 17.52 FID. This residual influences final plan fidelity but is small enough to be absorbed by L2Plan rather than act as a ceiling; a regime weaker generators fall outside of. In addition, because the LSTM trains on samples from N(0,1) spanning both tail and error cases, it learns to navigate complex landscapes: correcting trajectories from atypical initializations and reducing convergence steps for in-distribution ones. The pre-/post-LS statistical agreement (Table 1, Fig. 2(a)) shows that even possible atypical generations across the test set remain deliverable. Future work will complement this analysis by only sampling error- and boundary-like cases for a more precise quantification under extreme starting conditions. Regarding machine consistency, FMD is unconditional but not unconstrained: it is trained on F_del, the manifold of machine-constrained fluence maps defined by leaf-motion, dose-rate, and gantry-rotation limits. (B) We thank R1 for the constructive comments. k={5,10,20} analysis has been experimented: k=5 was short-sighted, k=20 added memory/time without gains, while k=10 is the stability–efficiency optimum, matching L2O findings on unroll length. We acknowledge that Transformers are promising. However, we chose a 2-layer LSTM for its lightweight structure and per-step latency, critical for efficient planning. Regularization weights were tuned on the validation set and fixed across all test cases (no patient-specific tuning). We also clarify implementation details: LS model is C-based parallel rule-based converting each CP fluence map into MLC apertures and MU with sub-pixel and dosimetric-leaf-gap corrections; the dose engine is a frozen physics-informed DL model trained on an LTBE solver, with spherical-harmonic fluence accumulation and a MedNeXT backbone at 4 mm. (C) We agree validation consists of 3 prostate cohorts single-arc VMAT with fixed geometry and Varian M120 MLC and will revise to avoid overclaims. Future work will validate our model generalizability to multi-/dual-arc plans and complex sites. Preprocessing across all cohorts was limited to organ/OAR/helper-structure segmentation via AI-Rad Companion and an in-house C++ pipeline; plans were then created in Eclipse with the RapidPlan prostate SBRT model on single-arc VMAT with Varian M120 MLC. Training REQUITE CTs and contours were augmented by scaling, small rotations, CPAB non-rigid deformation, and clinically plausible PTV/rectum margin changes, expanding training set to 12,153 plans. (D) We agree that DVH metrics are more clinically interpretable. We will specify them for the Fig. 2(c) cases: trade-off PTV [D95=35.79, D2=40.05, HI=0.16], Rectum [Dmean=4.59], Bladder [Dmean=8.84]; PTV-homogeneity PTV [D95=38.23, D2=39.52, HI=0.03], Rectum [Dmean=8.23], Bladder [Dmean=13.04]; OAR-sparing PTV [D95=30.46, D2=40.26, HI=0.22], Rectum [Dmean=3.60], Bladder [Dmean=4.52]. Full-cohorts DVH would require restructuring Table 1 beyond page limits; representative values will be added to the main text and full analysis to an extended version. We hope we can clarify the concerns and provide a revised manuscript that solves “a real limitation of existing approaches” (R2) while “achieving significant and clinically relevant improvements” (R1).
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): All reviewers agree on the novelty of the approach with a clinically motivated problem formulation. Authors are invited to adresses the issues pointed out in the reviewers reports.

title: Learning to Read Where to Look: Disease-Aware Vision–Language Pretraining for 3D CT
reviewer_1_strengths: The paper targets an important gap in 3D CT vision-language pretraining: most prior research uses only global report-volume alignment, whereas this paper tries to recover finer-grained supervision from the already available report Mining 262k snippet-slice pairs from existing reports is the most interesting part of the paper. Without it it would come across as a “train on more data,” paper. It has a strong empirical story and results that are coherent. The ablations also support the main claims, especially that localization can be added without hurting retrieval/classification much. It is practically interesting that retrieval, disease prompting, and localization are all trained in a shared embedding space instead of bolting on separate heads for each task. That makes the method feel clean and conceptually consistent.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The core advantage may come largely from the internal RefCT dataset size and distribution which, as far as I can tell, will not be released. The new task is interesting, but all localization evidence appears to be on the authors’ own RefCT test set. The classification story is less strong than the retrieval story. The paper claims competitive disease classification, which is fair, but not a clear win. On CT-RATE it matches the best reported AUC rather than surpassing it, and on Rad-ChestCT it is slightly below the best baseline within confidence bounds. The model is also receives much stronger supervision than prior work for this task (although I think Merlin also does something similar with ICD10 codes). It might be good to add a fully supervised baseline for reference.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The paper introduced a novel and well-motivated localization task. The ablation clearly shows that the new loss does not degrade performance. The scale and quality of the dataset represent a real amount of work. The performances of the models are better than every open model available.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Performance gains seem predominantly dataset-driven rather than method-driven. The ablation RefCT only already achieves R@10 26.3, surpassing all published baselines before adding any of the three training novelties. The full model reaches 31.5, but the delta attributable to method vs. data is modest. The paper does not sufficiently address whether a simpler model (e.g., vanilla SigLIP fine-tuning) on the same 98k pairs would perform comparably. SPECTRE is trained on A+B+C (no INSPECT); RadFinder adds INSPECT (D) and initializes from SPECTRE’s weights. This compounding advantage makes the reported delta vs. SPECTRE (18.2→31.5) difficult to interpret. A controlled comparison same data, RadFinder method vs. SPECTRE method is missing. Some key other competitors could have been added, such as fvlm, TotalFM, or Pillar0. The implementation reports an effective batch size of 4096 on a single H100 (96 GB), which necessarily implies gradient accumulation with a small per-step micro-batch. This is not discussed. For SigLIP-style contrastive training, the equivalence between gradient accumulation and a true large batch depends on the implementation of the all-pairs sigmoid loss. The actual number of negatives seen per gradient step, and whether the implementation correctly handles this, should be clarified for reproducibility. The localization loss is a strict null result on all global metrics; it neither helps nor hurts, making the “unified model” claim a reframing of a negative result. Moreover, the prompt loss, while clearly beneficial for disease classification, slightly but consistently degrades retrieval on the Merlin benchmark (R@1find 70.7→69.0, R@1impr 42.2→40.3). This trade-off is not discussed. The prompt-based disease supervision is never compared against a standard classification head trained on the same binary labels. The added complexity of the prompt approach: positive/negative prompt construction, per-class imbalance weighting, multi-prompt averaging at inference, is only justified if it outperforms a simpler linear probe or MLP head on the same encoder. Without this baseline, it is unclear whether the AUC gains in Table 1 stem from the prompt-in-embedding-space design or simply from the additional disease supervision signal, regardless of how it is parameterized.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: Approach incorporating radiologists comments for spotting most relevant slices is nice and pragmatic. The chosen architecture is well structured and explained via Fig. 1. As model strategy processing of 3D volumes is utilized at reduced size of 128x128x32 to allow for resource handling. Here it is questionable, if entire 3D volume processiong for adequate 3D information classification is still the best way to go as redundancy is high and slice information low AND fine grained details might be overseen due to resampling. Thus, recent trends clearly favor full resolution orthogonal slices of selected / chosen quality. But at least in this work slice-level embeddings are incorporated, too RadFinder achieves R@10 = 31.5 on CT RATE, clearly outperforming prior methods such as BrgSA (22.2) and SPECTRE (18.2) under identical evaluation. This is really a very meaningful jump, especially as CT RATE is a difficult benchmark where even marginal improvements can be seen as substantial. RadFinder’s AUC of 83.8 on CT‑RATE and 77.0 on Rad‑ChestCT is essentially tied with the best existing models like MPS‑CT (83.8 / 77.3). Due to that, RadFinder does not significantly advance state of the art in disease classification as the improvements largely come from prompt‑based structured label supervision, a technique already used successfully in 2D VLMs. Compared to high‑resolution slice‑based approaches: Methods like MedVista3D-ViT or BrgSA use full-resolution orthogonal slices and sometimes detailed local features, which naturally benefit classification tasks that depend on small-scale image details. Given that RadFinder processes downsampled 3D volumes (128×128×32 windows), achieving parity with such methods is respectable but not groundbreaking. RadFinder drops the mean absolute error from 67 mm down to 36 mm, nearly a factor of two improvement over the best baseline (SigLIP2 finetuned). So this is by far the most impressive technical achievement of the paper.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: State-of-the-art presented in the introduction is not very easy to read. Besides, for 3D CT processing, all the approaches that incorporate 2D slices or selected axial/coronal/sagittal slices only are not mentioned, thereby forcing a trade-off between capturing fine-grained details and maintaining the global structural anatomical context, cf. Setio et al. 2016 “Pulmonary nodule detection in ct images: False positive reduction using multi-view convolutional networks”. CLIP-style 2D representation as input for 3D models are recent trends, too (Wang et al. 2022 MedCLIP: Contrastive learning from unpaired medical images and text) or (Lee et al. 2024 “Read like a radiologist: Efficient vision-language model for 3d medical imaging interpretation.”) Paper rather hard to read regarding the writing style. Medical reports/diagnosis could be encoded by international standard such as Snomed-CT instead of the utilized simplified technical binary decisions such as “absence of hepatic lesion”. These could then still be formed as encoding for the classification model but would allow for a standardized taxonomy. RadFinder’s potential and superiority is highest in retrieval and localization, but not in disease classification per se, where full-resolution 2D slice models are really competitive.
reviewer_3_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and AC for their thoughtful feedback and address their comments below. “SPECTRE is trained on A+B+C […] A controlled comparison same data, RadFinder method vs. SPECTRE method is missing.” (R2) To clarify, SPECTRE was trained on B+C+D (CT-RATE, Merlin, INSPECT), not A+B+C. A=RefCT is our internal dataset and was never available to SPECTRE. The controlled same-data comparison is therefore already in Table 1, row “Public datasets, no loc.” The method-driven gain is substantial on every metric except MAP@5. “RefCT only already achieves R@10 26.3, surpassing all published baselines before adding any of the three training novelties” (R2) To clarify, the “RefCT dataset” row in Table 1 applies all our training novelties, it just removes the public datasets from the training mix. “core advantage may come largely from the internal RefCT dataset” (R1) “performance gains seem predominantly dataset-driven” (R2) Both contribute. The “Public datasets, no loc.” row in Table 1 isolates the method effect, the “RefCT-only” row isolates the data effect. The full model combines both. “competitors […] fvlm, TotalFM, or Pillar0” (R2) fVLM is in Table 1 (AUC; the authors do not report CT-RATE retrieval). Pillar-0 and TotalFM publish no comparable retrieval or classification numbers on CT-RATE. “The implementation reports an effective batch size of 4096 […] which […] implies gradient accumulation” (R2) The gradient accumulation we use is mathematically equivalent to using a true batch size of 4096: We collect all 4096 embeddings first, then accumulate the gradients with all negatives. “The prompt loss […] slightly but consistently degrades retrieval on the Merlin benchmark […] This trade-off is not discussed.” (R2) The prompt loss degrades Merlin results slightly outside the confidence interval while it lifts CT-RATE AUC by 0.27 points and Rad-ChestCT AUC by 0.14 points, a favorable trade-off. “The prompt-based disease supervision is never compared against a standard classification head trained on the same binary labels. […] Without this baseline, it is unclear whether the AUC gains […] stem from the prompt-in-embedding-space design or simply from the additional disease supervision signal.” (R2) In Table 1, the “Global loss only” row uses the disease prompts during evaluation, but does not use any of the disease supervision. AUC drops sharply on both CT-RATE and Rad-ChestCT, showing the importance of the supervision signal. “The added complexity of the prompt approach […] is only justified if it outperforms a simpler linear probe or MLP head on the same encoder” (R2) A distinct advantage of prompt-based classification over a linear classification head is the potential transferability to new diseases and the possibility to improve the prompts without changing the model. “All localization evidence appears to be on the authors’ own RefCT test set.” (R1) We agree. No public CT snippet-slice benchmark exists. “Medical reports/diagnosis could be encoded by international standard such as Snomed-CT” (R3) Mapping free-text reports properly to an international standard is a complex topic and out of scope for our paper, where we apply an existing method to structure reports.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): The paper introduced RadFinder, a 3D CT vision–language model that augments contrastive pretraining with prompt-based disease supervision and a novel snippet-slice localization objective, mined from 98k report–volume pairs (262k snippet–slice pairs). Reviewers agreed on the strength of the paper, including novel, well-motivated localization task; clever use of radiologist report references; strong retrieval and localization gains; clean shared embedding space; large-scale data curation. though some weaknesses are also shared by the reviewers, including performance appears largely dataset-driven (private data, not released); classification only ties SOTA; localization loss shows null effect on global metrics; clarity issues. Overall, the reviewers (scores 5/4/5) and AC recommend acceptance, citing the innovative localization idea and substantial empirical results despite concerns about dataset bias and incomplete ablations.

title: Learning to Trim: End-to-End Causal Graph Pruning with Dynamic Anatomical Feature Banks for Medical VQA
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The paper addresses an important and clinically relevant problem. Shortcut learning and poor robustness under distribution shift are major limitations of current MedVQA systems. The paper targets this issue directly, which makes the work timely and relevant to the MICCAI community. 2.The proposed framework is coherent and reasonably novel in how it integrates debiasing into training. The combination of a momentum-updated dynamic feature bank and a differentiable trimming mechanism is intuitive and well motivated. A key strength is that the method incorporates debiasing into end-to-end optimization instead of using static adjustment or only test-time adaptation. 3.The experimental evaluation is solid and supports the paper’s main claim. The method is evaluated on multiple MedVQA benchmarks, including the OOD benchmark SLAKE-CP, and shows consistent gains over prior work. The ablation study and qualitative visualizations further strengthen the empirical support.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The causal interpretation is stronger than what is formally justified by the method. While the framework is motivated by causal reasoning, the actual implementation is closer to a confounder-aware feature suppression approach. The paper does not fully justify why the feature bank is a faithful proxy for a latent confounder or under what assumptions the trimming operation corresponds to causal adjustment. 2.The component-level novelty is moderate. Several ingredients of the method, such as momentum-updated prototype/memory-style representations, similarity-based masking, and decorrelation losses, are related to existing ideas. meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): This paper proposes a learnable causal trimming framework for Medical VQA, integrating a dynamic anatomical feature bank with a differentiable feature suppression mechanism to improve robustness under distribution shift. The reviewers agree that the paper tackles an important and clinically relevant problem, and presents a coherent and practically meaningful end-to-end debiasing framework. The method is conceptually appealing, and the experimental results are solid and consistently support the claimed improvements. While modeling the confounder C as dataset-specific priors via the feature bank raises a potential concern of learning dataset-dependent bias that may limit generalization, the improved performance on OOD benchmarks (e.g., SLAKE-CP) partially alleviates this issue. However, validation under more diverse distribution shifts would further strengthen this claim. Meanwhile, the work could also be further strengthened by better justifying the causal interpretation of the framework (particularly the role of the feature bank as a proxy for confounders) and improving the methodological clarity of key components (e.g., region/feature definition and implementation details).

title: Learning What Can Move: Patient-Specific Motion Subspaces from a Single Scan
reviewer_1_strengths: The method predicts a reusable motion subspace rather than specific deformation instances. This regularizes the predicted motion and ensures it belongs to an anatomically plausible motion subspace. The method simplifies real-time motion prediction down to coefficient solving, alleviating computing constraints in real-time applications and reducing risks of overfitting to unrealistic deformations to fit the observations. The use of scalar rather than vector displacement modes brings rotational invariance to network predictions, making the method more robust to non-standard image orientations. The mode prediction + solver optimization enables 3D motion prediction from arbitrary observations, making the method highly flexible in its potential applications.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Conditions acceptance rating: The paper should absolutely discuss the RMSim paper (https://iopscience. iop. org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/acb484/pdf) which is extremely close conceptually. Cited from RMSim: “We present a novel 3D Seq2Seq deep learning respiratory motion simulator (RMSim) that learns from 4D-CT images and predicts future breathing phases given a static CT image. “ This is very closely related and highly relevant as prior work, even if the proposed approached, based on a subspace formulation, is genuinely different. Major: The main strength of the method, the plausibility of predicted deformation, is also an important weakness. The method is dependent on the availability of motion-specific data to train the subspace prediction method: if the motion to be predicted does not exist in the dataset, predictions will fail. This is particularly relevant in interventions where the anatomy is deformed by the action of the clinician, for example due to the manipulation of the anatomy by surgical tools. These types of deformations are very unlikely to be represented in the training data, and due to the formulation of the method, will fail to be accurately predicted. The paper does not evaluate the ability of the method to predict out-of-domain deformations. It claims to decouple “what deformations are plausible (modes, predicted once) from which deformation occurs (coefficients, solved per observation)”. This is a somewhat strong affirmation: the space of plausible deformation is vastly greater than the space of deformations observed in the training data, currently restricted to breathing and potentially cardiac motion 4D CTs. The method was only trained and evaluated on breathing motion prediction from a single dataset. The quality of the validation would have been improved by training on one dataset and evaluating on another, ideally experimentally acquired, to evaluate the robustness of the method to deviations from the breathing patterns observed at train time. It would have been further improved by evaluating its accuracy on other types of motion, such as cardiac motion. Minor: Linearity assumption is unexamined. The method assumes anatomical motion is always well-approximated by a low-dimensional linear subspace. This is a strong assumption that is never discussed or justified. Non-linear motion subspaces are a known alternative (see https://arxiv. org/pdf/2404.17620), and the paper does not address under which conditions linearity breaks down. Choice of K is insufficiently justified. Only K=1 and K=2 modes are evaluated, with no sensitivity analysis on K. It is unclear how to choose K for a new anatomy or motion type. The 2D gradient approximation lacks justification. When only a 2D slice is available, the method substitutes ∇I_fix for ∇I_mov in the Jacobian definition. The validity of this approximation is non-trivial and unexplained. A more natural formulation — restricting the problem to 2D and computing gradients directly in 2D — is not considered or compared against. The solver and network details are in “Experiments and Results”, and should be moved to Methods section. Abstract: “instantiating motion then reduces to estimating a small set of coefficients from various observations via a closed-form solver. “ This is unclear Introduction: Need to explain the benefit of generating a reusable motion subspace rather than deformation instances. Introduction: “We introduce a scalar-mode parameterization that naturally admits a closed-form coefficient solver, together with ModeNorm layer that resolves the signed-scale ambiguity in basis–coefficient decomposition” The signed-scale ambiguity should be briefly introduced before. Methods: The “training” part of Fig. 1 could be made a little clearer by replacing the curved arrow with a straight arrow pointing straight down. As it is, it seems L_reg is somehow related to the solver, which it isn’t. Nevertheless, contributions are novel and the method has great potential to enable anatomically accurate, fast registration from sparse observations
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The strength of the paper lies with its novel application of deriving DVF modes from static anatomy and applying the derived modes for various downstream tasks without requiring required model for each specific task.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The claim that all possible motion can be restricted to a low-dimensional subspace is very questionable. For example, patients with bronchus obstruction on one side of the lung will have drastically different motion from those without such obstructions. This motion difference is unlikely to be distinguishable from a single static image. In my opinion, the quantitative comparison with baseline methods are not sufficient. For example, the base line is only established with 3D to 3D task. What about baseline comparison with other tasks? It is true that the pipeline eliminates the need to retrain for other tasks. However, the ultimate real world clinical goal is to make registration more accurate. From the presented results, the proposed method does not outperform one of the baselines and there is lack of comprehensive information on inference speed. Again, without comprehensive baselines for other downstream tasks, the evaluation of the performance is infeasible.
reviewer_2_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The paper proposes a novel approach to image registration that creatively decouples the estimation of the deformation field from the two images. Instead of relying on pairwise observations alone, they first infer a patient-specific motion subspace from a single static scan, which defines what deformations are anatomically plausible for the subject. This decoupling of deformation plausibility from the registration process itself allows them to model the allowed motion subspace for just one of the images. By pre-defining this constrained subspace, they reduce the problem’s complexity and avoid the need to explore implausible deformations during registration. They then select the appropriate solution from the far fewer remaining degrees of freedom very quickly with the second image. This approach brings big gains in speed as compared to the classical image registration approaches as thousends of parameters would be have to be optimised in classical DIR where as in thie approach only a handful needs to be optimised resulting in a large speed gain.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: What I did not understand is on why is there an arrow in Figure 1 that points from the “Fixed image” to the “2.2 Closed-form solver”. This makes no sense to me as the authors claim to decouple the two images
reviewer_3_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank (meta-)reviewers for constructive feedbacks. 1.R2|(1)“The claim that all possible motion can be restricted to a low-dimensional subspace is very questionable”, obstruction example, (2)”This motion difference is unlikely to be distinguishable from a single static image.” Before addressing R2’s points, we clarify some concepts: motion subspace refers to a set of a_k(x), patient-specific and predicted by the network; a specific motion D(x,t_i)=sum^K_k(a_k(x)*w_k(t_i)). We separate two claims R2 conflates: (1)expressiveness of a low-rank subspace vs. (2)predictability of a patient-specific subspace from a static scan. Expressiveness is not an open question for respiratory DVFs: Li et al. (2011) and follow-ups empirically validated low-dim linear subspaces on 4D-CT. Even higher-DOF regimes (CFD flow fields) use linear subspaces (POD), with larger K. Intuitively, approximating D(x,t) by sum^K_k(a_k(x)*w_k(t)), as K grows, error diminishes. BO is thus not a counter-example to expressiveness. The last sentence conflates “motion” and “motion subspace”. We assume the reviewer refers to whether the network can predict the patient-specific subspace when such variability is rare in training. As long as BO cases exist in training, the network can learn the subspace. We acknowledge this as a training-data diversity limitation rather than model formulation. Details in p2. 2.R1|Training-set dependence and OOD Acknowledged; we will add an explicit limitations sentence. Two conditions considered: (i)Anatomy-conditioned variants present in clinic but rare in current training (e.g., BO in p1): a data-coverage issue rather than model limitation, addressable by curating cohorts with such phenotypes. This is common in supervised learning, not specific to our method, and data curation is a standard solution. (ii)Tool-induced/interventional deformation (R1’s surgical example): outside our scope, which targets physiologically driven motion (respiratory, with cardiac a natural extension). Will state this explicitly. 3.R1|Benchmarks, datasets, baselines Agreed, broader benchmarks (more datasets, regions, clinical validation) would strengthen the work. The page budget was spent framing a new problem: predicting a subspace rather than a deformation. Cross-dataset/anatomy evaluation is planned for journal extension. 4.R2|“no improvement” We target real-time motion recovery: system latency budget (e.g., MR-Linac IGRT) is ~100 ms total, of which we target ≤10 ms for motion recovery, differing from DIR with no apples-to-apples baseline. We use pTVReg as a high-accuracy reference (3–5 min/pair, more dataset-robust than the learning baseline) to bound accuracy sacrificed under ~10 ms. NetADM beats the ResNet-18 baseline (Dice 0.921 vs 0.882) and approaches pTVReg (0.930) at ~24000× speed-up (7.5 ms vs 3–5 min). 6.Others RMSim and Neural Modes: will cite in related work. RMSim implicitly encodes motion via 3D-ConvLSTM Seq2Seq, while we learn a linear subspace enabling closed-form solving from sparse observations at ~10 ms. Neural Modes target on computer graphics applications with elastic equilibrium(material force model), a regime distinct from ours (we model neither tissue mechanics nor excitation). Decoupling and Fig 1 arrow: “Decoupling” is at the representation level: f_θ(I_fix)→modes uses only I_fix; the solver ingests whatever real-time observation is available (3D image, 2D slice, 2D mask, surface points), never I_mov as a network input. 2D gradient: Follows the classical Thirion-demons static-force form (small-warp linearization). The “directly 2D” alternative computes gradients on warped images and discards out-of-plane displacements; preliminary tries showed instability. K: K=2 already approaches pTVReg (diminishing returns). Writing/reproducibility: We will clarify the abstract on coefficient solving, move solver/network details to Methods, enlarge Fig 4 fonts, release code upon institutional approval.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper introduces a novel and clinically meaningful approach for learning patient-specific motion from a single scan, enabling real-time estimation without 4D data, with a creative design such as ModeNorm. Despite its originality and practical potential, the work relies on some questionable assumptions and lacks thorough validation and analysis. With two positive and one negative rating, the AC recommends proceeding to rebuttal before making a final decision. | Although some concerns remain regarding the 2D gradient approximation, the choice of (K), and the need for a more transparent discussion of method-intrinsic versus data-dependent limitations, the core contribution is sound and novel. The paper addresses an important problem, and the experimental results demonstrate clear advantages, particularly in computational speed. Therefore, the AC recommends acceptance. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Authors have adequately addressed reviewers concerns in the rebuttal. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): I thank the authors and the reviewers for this insightful rebuttal. Authors satisfyingly addressed concerns about generalisation to new motion (data curation) and clarification of the positioning of the work with existing literature, and successfully defended their choice of baselines. However, the authors acknowledged a few limitations, namely the lack of sensitivity analysis on K, missing extension to other out-of-domains datasets and organs. Overall, this paper introduces a highly novel registration framework which is highly promising. The experimental section lags a bit behind, but 1) it is still reasonable, and 2) it is counter-balanced by the strong emphasis on methodological aspect. Given the very interesting framework and high novelty, I recommend this paper not only for acceptance but also for oral.

title: LeGend: Lesion-Guided Longitudinal CXR Generation via Gaussian-Biased Causal Attention
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.Clear identification of an attention bias issue The paper identifies a non-trivial issue in autoregressive generation, namely the tendency of attention to focus on peripheral regions rather than lesion-relevant areas. This analysis is interesting and provides useful insights into the behavior of such models. 2.Simple and effective design The proposed Gaussian-biased attention is lightweight and easy to integrate into existing autoregressive frameworks without modifying the backbone. This plug-and-play property makes the method practically appealing.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.I don’t really get the motivation of the task I don’t really get the idea of generating follow-up CXRs from a textual progression description, since the text itself is already a high-level summary of the imaging findings. Mapping it back to an image seems inherently ambiguous and ill-posed, as the same description could correspond to many different plausible images. Moreover, this direction does not align well with the typical clinical workflow (image → report rather than report → image), so the practical usefulness of such generation is unclear. 2.The evaluation is not fully aligned with the main claim The paper emphasizes improving lesion-focused attention through the proposed attention mechanism, but the experimental evaluation does not directly validate this claim. Instead, most results are based on global metrics or downstream classification on the whole image. There is a lack of more targeted analysis (e. g. , region-level or lesion-level evaluation) to verify whether the attention is indeed better aligned with clinically relevant regions, making the validation somewhat indirect. 3.Reliance on potentially noisy VLM-derived ROI The lesion regions are obtained from an external VLM, which inevitably introduces localization errors. Since these predicted coordinates are directly used to guide attention during generation, any inaccuracy may be propagated and even amplified in the synthesized images. This raises concerns about the robustness of the method and whether the improvements are limited by the quality of the external VLM rather than the proposed approach itself.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: Novel technical insight. The corner/edge attention bias seems to be a previously unrecognized phenomenon that is identified and quantified with purpose-built metrics (CAR/EAR/Attn-Overlap). The layer-wise analysis in Fig. 1 and Fig. 4 demonstrates the problem and motivates the proposed solution. Method. GBCA is lightweight, just an additive bias plus a small MLP scalar. It still yields good improvements (FID drops from 35 to 26). The simplicity and transferability to other architectures strengthen the contribution. Ablations. The injection depth study (coarse and fine-grained) and the VLM ablation (Qwen vs. Llama vs. random) are well-designed. The random-coordinate control is a intuitive sanity check. Results. Strong quantitative results. Improvements are consistent across all metrics and substantial, particularly in FID and MS-SSIM.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.Single dataset + no statistical testing. All experiments use ICG-CXR (760 test pairs). The improvements are encouraging but no confidence intervals, significance tests, or multi-run variance is reported. Particularly for AUC and F1 where the differences are modest, how confident are the authors that these gaps reflect genuine improvements rather than noise from a single run? Can the authors comment on the expected variance of their results? 2.VLM dependency underexplored. The method critically relies on VLM-predicted coordinates, yet robustness to prediction quality is only indirectly assessed through the Qwen/Llama comparison. How often does the VLM produce clearly incorrect localizations — wrong side, outside the lung field, hallucinated anatomy? And when it does, does GBCA degrade gracefully or catastrophically? The authors have these predictions already; even a qualitative discussion of failure patterns would help readers assess reliability. 3.Limited clinical evaluation. AUC/F1 from a pretrained classifier is a proxy but the paper uses expressions like “clinical faithfulness” and “clinical fidelity”. In my opinion this sets a higher bar than what the evaluation delivers. How would the authors justify this given no radiologist assessment is included? Do the authors see a path toward validating that the generated images are actually useful in a clinical workflow? 4.Fixed σ with no sensitivity analysis. A single global σ is used for all samples regardless of pathology type. Lung nodules and diffuse effusions have fundamentally different spatial extents. How sensitive is performance to this choice? Would the authors expect the method to work equally well across pathology types, and if so, why? 5.Unclear clinical use case. The paper motivates the task broadly around monitoring disease progression and data completion, but never specifies who would use synthetic follow-ups or how. Is the envisioned application data augmentation for classifier training, clinical decision support, education or something else? The strong downstream classifier results hint at augmentation utility, but this isn’t stated explicitly. Clarifying the intended use case would help readers assess whether the evaluation metrics and the level of clinical validation are appropriate for the claimed application.

reviewer_3_strengths: 1) identification of a systematic peripheral attention bias in AR CXR generation, 2) state‑of‑the‑art performance across FID, CLIP‑T, MS‑SSIM, PSNR, and downstream classification metrics, 3) consistent improvements across both Emu3 and EditAR backbones, supporting generalizability.

reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank all reviewers and group responses by motivation, VLM reliability, evaluation, and implementation. Q1: Task motivation and intended clinical use (R1-W1, R2-W5, Meta). Our task is not text-only report-to-image generation. The model generates a follow-up CXR from a prior CXR and progression text: the prior image provides patient-specific anatomy, while the text specifies disease evolution. The intended use is not direct clinical diagnosis, but controllable longitudinal synthesis for settings with sparse or incomplete follow-up imaging, progression-aware augmentation, robustness testing under clinically meaningful temporal changes, and educational visualization. Q2: Robustness to VLM prediction (R1-W3, R2-W2, R3-W1/W4, Meta). GBCA uses VLM points as a soft Gaussian logit bias, not hard masks or deterministic editing targets. Generation remains conditioned on the reference CXR, progression text, and autoregressive visual context. Table 3 shows gain with both Qwen and Llama coordinates, despite their localization differences, while random coordinates substantially degrade all metrics, ruling out arbitrary spatial regularization. During dataset construction, we checked VLM reliability: in unilateral cases, ~90% had at least one point on the text-consistent side, and clear wrong-side cases were rare. Grad-CAM from our downstream disease classifier showed overlap between VLM points and high-response disease regions in about half of correctly classified cases. Thus, the prior is coarse but disease-relevant rather than arbitrary noise. Q3: GBCA design: fixed σ and injection depth (R2-W4, Meta). The Gaussian prior is a coarse salience prior on the 32×32 token grid, not a lesion mask. We use a broad fixed σ to tolerate coordinate noise and avoid overfitting to lesion size without region-level labels, while s(l) adapts the actual bias strength. Table 2 supports mid-layer injection: L14–16 gives the best trade-off, whereas shallow layers lack stable lesion semantics and late or overly wide injection can disrupt refinement. Q4: Validation about attention improvement (R1-W2) We have included direct attention analysis using Attn-Overlap and CAR/EAR in Fig. 1 and Fig. 4, showing that GBCA shifts attention away from corners/edges and toward the lesion-prior region. Since region-level radiologist labels are unavailable in ICG-CXR, downstream disease classification is used as a proxy for disease-relevant consistency, not as definitive clinical validation. Q5: Statistical reliability and single-run variance (R2-W1) Our conclusions are based on full test-set evaluation rather than selected examples. GBCA consistently improves AUC/F1, substantially outperforms random-coordinate guidance, and remains effective across different VLMs and two AR backbones. Table 1 reports three-seed averages; the observed variance was small (below 0.5% for AUC/F1), supporting the stability of the improvements. Q6: Clinical claims and evaluation scope (R2-W3, R3-W2/W3) We will replace “clinical fidelity” with “classifier-assessed clinical consistency” and clarify that deployment requires radiologist reader studies and prospective evaluation. Evaluation is limited to ICG-CXR, which to our knowledge is the only public benchmark for text-controlled longitudinal CXR synthesis, following prior work ProgEmu (MICCAI2025). ICG-CXR is built from hospital-collected MIMIC-CXR and CheXpertPlus radiographs and captures substantial real-world longitudinal progression variability. Broader external validation remains future work. Q7: Resolution and compute overhead (R3-W5/Meta) GBCA is grid-agnostic: for a denser H×W token grid, VLM coordinates can be remapped and σ scaled with grid size. Higher-resolution tokenization may better capture small lesions. The dominant cost remains base AR attention; GBCA only adds a Gaussian bias to existing logits and no extra generative network. We fine-tuned with LoRA for 6k steps on 2×RTX A6000 GPUs.

The authors should also clarify the motivation and intended clinical use case of the task, since generating follow-up CXRs from textual progression descriptions is seen as ambiguous and not aligned with the typical image-to-report workflow. The fixed Gaussian σ across all pathology types and the choice of injection depth need to be clarified. Finally, scalability to higher-resolution inputs and compute overhead should be briefly discussed. | The paper presents an interesting methodological contribution and is sufficiently evaluated. The rebuttal sufficiently addressed most points. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): The post-rebuttal opinions are mixed. Reviewer #1 maintains rejection, arguing that only the motivation was partially addressed and that the necessity of learning from longitudinal CXR–report pairs remains insufficiently justified. Reviewer #2 recommends acceptance, stating that most concerns were addressed. Reviewer #3 does not provide a visible post-rebuttal decision, but the initial review was weakly positive. Overall, the paper remains borderline but leans slightly positive. However, important limitations remain, including unclear clinical use, reliance on VLM-predicted lesion coordinates, lack of radiologist evaluation, single-dataset validation, and limited evidence that longitudinal generation is necessary beyond direct image comparison.
