title: Lesion-Centric Structured Report Generation for 3D CT with Multimodal Large Language Models via Hierarchical Evidence Tokens
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The paper addresses a meaningful problem in 3D CT, where lesion-relevant evidence is localized and long visual sequences can dilute important cues. 2.The proposed method is clean and well structured. The lesion-guided attention loss and GES target complementary aspects of the problem. 3.The experiments are reasonably complete, including backbone comparisons, lesion-prior settings, ablations, low-data evaluation, external validation on LIDC-IDRI, and intervention analysis on GES. 4.The empirical gains are substantial, especially on the ovarian cohort, and the ablations support the contribution of both proposed components.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The methodological novelty is moderate, as both lesion-aware attention regularization and compact latent/query-based evidence summarization are related to existing ideas, and the main contribution lies in their integration for 3D CT MLLMs. 2.A notable part of the gains may come from the lesion-prior design itself, including MaskZ slice selection and explicit lesion marking, so the incremental value of the hierarchical evidence interface could be discussed more clearly. 3.Some medical dataset and protocol details are still limited, including cohort split details, attribute definitions, handling of inapplicable labels, and LIDC-IDRI benchmark construction. 4.The ovarian cohort is still modest in size for a 12-task imbalanced structured prediction problem, making robustness on rare attributes harder to assess.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.This paper introduces a novel hierarchical interface that combines fine-grained image tokens with a compact “Global Evidence Slots” bottleneck to efficiently summarize long 3D CT sequences for MLLM reasoning. 2.This paper proposes an original lesion-guided attention loss that acts as a training-time regularizer to suppress background noise and focus cross-modal attention on critical diagnostic regions without increasing inference complexity. 3.The experimental results demonstrate significant clinical feasibility by achieving substantial performance gains over general-domain and medical-domain baselines on a real-world imbalanced ovarian tumor cohort and a public lung nodule benchmark.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The performance of the proposed method is highly dependent on the provision of precise 3D lesion masks, which may limit its real-world clinical utility where such manual segmentations are not always available or are subject to inter-observer variability. 2.While the Global Evidence Slots provide significant gains , the concept of using learnable queries and cross-attention to summarize long sequences draws heavily from existing architectures like the Perceiver and Slot Attention, reducing the purely structural novelty of the evidence bottleneck. 3.Although the lesion-guided attention loss does not affect inference speed, calculating this regularization term for every text-to-image token interaction during training could increase computational costs and memory requirements compared to standard fine-tuning.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: Improvement over state of the art: The authors show a clear improvement in the structured report generation over state of the art. Applicability: The adaptations the authors propose could be applied to a wide variety of MLLMs, since they mostly extend the models. The GES could also be transferred to other 3D imaging modalities or VLM architectures and could therefore be relevant to other domains. Evaluation with multiple architectures: The authors evaluate their method on multiple architectures and show improvements in all settings. Ablations: The authors show the improvements through ablation. This includes multiple architectures and two different datasets. With the ablation, they show consistent improvements. Utility for low data settings: The authors show that the GES and lesion-guided attention loss improve the model performance in low-data regimes, which is relevant for many clinical applications.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Segmentation mask guidance limits clinical transferability: The author’s approaches use masking and marking of lesions/nodules and a lesion/nodule guided attention. Those rely on existing segmentations. In their evaluation, the authors use high-quality annotations from the datasets. In cases with fully automated processing of the CT scans, these annotations might be sparse or unavailable, or would be provided by a segmentation model, potentially lowering the quality. The evaluation does not show how the approach performs in such cases, making it less expressive. In the introduction, the authors reference segmentation models as a reason why the masks are available. GES Evaluation after Masking: The GES are only evaluated after applying the lesion mask and, therefore, already filtering a significant amount of background tokens. The evaluation does not allow any conclusions on how well the GES can summarize the evidence in low information density settings. Limited evaluation of the multi-label classifier: Without any adaptations, the multi-label classifier outperforms all backbones except MedM-VL in the ablation of the lesion marking, but it is not included in any of the other ablations. The performance of the classifier makes it questionable whether an MLLM is necessary to generate a structured report from 3D volumes, especially in single-task settings. The complete evaluation is only performed on the private dataset and not on LIDC-IDRI, limiting insights into the transfer of the improvements to other tasks. Reproducibility: The description of the architecture is not detailed enough to reproduce the results without additional details (optimizer, loss weights, decoding strategy, seeds, LoRA settings). Furthermore, neither the code nor one of the training datasets is provided. Dataset contents: The authors train and evaluate their model on one private dataset. While they briefly describe the dataset, details on the collection and annotation process are missing.
reviewer_3_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and meta-reviewer for their constructive comments and for recognizing the promise of our lesion-centric framework for improving the reliability of 3D CT MLLMs. We would like to clarify the following points, especially the mask-practicability concern highlighted in the meta-review. Scope and reliance on lesion masks. We agree that requiring segmentation masks may limit direct deployment if high-quality manual masks are assumed. Our work is positioned in a lesion-prior setting: given a CT volume and a lesion/nodule prior, the goal is to study how such priors can be more effectively used for structured attribute reasoning, rather than to solve detection or segmentation. Importantly, our use of masks does not require high-fidelity boundary segmentation. MaskZ mainly needs to identify lesion-containing slices; explicit marking uses a minimum enclosing circle as a coarse localization cue; and the attention regularizer guides attention toward lesion-relevant regions rather than exact contours. Thus, the required prior is conceptually closer to coarse lesion localization, such as loose/interactive annotations or outputs from automatic segmentation, than to precise manual segmentation. We did not systematically evaluate imperfect or coarse masks in the submitted manuscript, so we will not claim verified robustness. We will instead clarify this scope and explicitly discuss coarse-mask/automatic-mask evaluation as an important future direction in the camera-ready version. Incremental value beyond MaskZ/marking. We also clarify that the reported gains are not solely due to lesion-prior preprocessing. All component analyses are conducted on top of the strongest MaskZ+mark baseline. Under this same setting, attention guidance further improves the baseline, GES yields larger gains, and their combination performs best. Moreover, zeroing or shuffling GES causes marked drops, supporting that the improvement comes from meaningful evidence slots rather than merely adding parameters or sequence length. Novelty of GES and relation to prior query/slot-based methods. We acknowledge that learnable queries and cross-attention pooling are related to Perceiver/Slot Attention-style representations, as cited in the paper. Our contribution is not claiming these primitives as new in isolation, but adapting them into a hierarchical evidence token interface for 3D CT MLLMs: fine-grained image tokens are preserved, while compact Global Evidence Slots are injected into the MLLM sequence and participate in language self-attention for task-dependent evidence routing. This differs from using query tokens only as a visual compression module. Structured report generation formulation. We appreciate the comment that our evaluation focuses on discrete attribute prediction. We will make the terminology clearer: this paper studies structured report generation in the form of standardized attribute-level entries, where each clinical field is queried and generated as a categorical answer. We do not claim to generate full free-form narrative radiology reports. Dataset, protocol, and reproducibility details. We agree that several details can be clearer. In the camera-ready version, we will add concise information on cohort split, annotation/label construction, conditional N.A. labels, LIDC-IDRI construction, number of GES, LoRA settings, loss weight, decoding strategy, optimizer/seeds, and missing backbone references. The private ovarian CT cohort cannot be publicly released due to clinical privacy constraints, but the LIDC-IDRI validation is built from a public dataset and will be described more explicitly. We appreciate the reviewers’ suggestions for additional analyses, including coarse/imperfect masks, GES-number ablations, and broader classifier/MLLM comparisons. Following the rebuttal guidelines, we do not introduce new experimental results here; we will instead improve the clarity of existing results and discuss these directions as future work.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): The proposed method targets at the attention dispersion and data imbalance problem of MLLM applications in report generation. The contributions of 3D image understanding with hierarchical evidence token “routing” appear promising in improving the reliability. However, as all reviewers pointed out, the requirement of segmentation mask might severely limit its practicability. The authors are encouraged to provide analysis (ablation if better, e.g., replacement of segmentation mask with looser, coarse-grained labeling/annotation as in interactive segmentation) and respond to the reviewers’ concerns.

title: Leveraging Pathology Co-occurrence for Test-Time Adaptation in Chest X-Ray Diagnosis
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The paper addresses an important and practical problem. Test-time adaptation for multi-label medical diagnosis is highly relevant, and incorporating disease dependency structure is a meaningful direction for this setting. 2.The proposed method is simple and well motivated. Using pathology co-occurrence as a reliability signal for sample weighting is intuitive, easy to implement, and compatible with standard entropy-based TTA. 3.The experimental section is reasonably complete. The paper compares against several established TTA baselines and includes additional analyses on co-occurrence matrix evolution, sample-weight reliability, and norm ablation.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The empirical gains are relatively limited. Although CoWA is often competitive and frequently ranks first or second, the absolute improvement over strong baselines is generally modest, which weakens the overall impact of the method. Table 1 shows that many of the gains are small. 2.The validation scope is narrow. All experiments are conducted on chest X-ray classification, so it remains unclear whether the proposed idea would generalize to other medical imaging modalities or other multi-label diagnostic tasks. 3.The method relies on dataset-level co-occurrence structure, which may introduce or amplify bias. The paper itself notes that co-occurrence patterns vary across datasets. In practice, such variation may reflect differences in label definitions, patient populations, or institutional case mix rather than stable disease mechanisms. Since CoWA directly estimates and uses these correlations during adaptation, it may reinforce dataset-specific associations rather than clinically robust relationships. This limitation is important and currently under-discussed.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.Good visualizations and well presented results. 2.Interesting analysis in Table2 of the performance of the different L-norms.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.This work seems like an importance sampling (IS) based approach for TTA applications. However, no theoretical connections or formulations were drawn against that. PRIORITIZED EXPERIENCE REPLAY https://arxiv.org/pdf/1511.05952.There are some other things as well like being careful with the distribution of the IS-weights o.w. There are some stability concerns etc, which our paper fixes in a very adhoc way via max(w_min,w_i). Maybe there are some better annealing strategies for this? 2.That leads me to another question: IS helps accelerate the convergence speed, so maybe if the authors showed us the validation curves of the classification performance on the val/test datasets over time, we might see something along the lines that other methods might be coming close to the performance of COWA but taking slightly longer. It will also be interesting to validate that an increase in the convergence speed is indeed in fact happening. 3.No ablation studies: What if we replace max(w_min,w_i) with just w_i? What happens then? a. Some numerical metrics or visualizations of the stability of the gradients (measured perhaps by the var(grad) over time ) vs simple L = H, L = wi*H, L = max(w_min,wi) * H would be helpful. b. The H(.) is the shannon entropy right? 4.Otherwise, marginal improvements over AdaBN and also sometimes AdaBN beats this work. So the results aren’t even showing consistent improvements either.
reviewer_2_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The proposed question is a important yet hardly studied one, which being solved will greatly imporve the generalization ability of existing multi-label prediction models. 2.The method prevents severe performance degradation on vulnerable or low-prevalence disease classes by explicitly suppressing unreliable gradient updates that standard methods would otherwise reinforce. The overall demonstration of methods is clear and easy to follow. 3.Comprehensive evaluations across multiple chest X-ray domain shift scenarios show that CoWA consistently achieves superior or highly competitive diagnostic accuracy compared to established TTA baselines.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.It seems when adapt to the target domain the threshold hyperparameter is fixed. Although the author did ablation studies to show the effectiveness of the chosen threshold, it could be better if the author could make the threshold also adapt to the domain field. 2.When adapt to the domain field, CoWA heavily relies on the model’s initial predictions on the target domain to dynamically estimate the pathology co-occurrence matrix. If an extreme domain shift causes the pre-trained model to produce highly inaccurate initial predictions, the resulting empirical matrix will be flawed. It would be better if author can discuss the possibility of this kind of situation.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and AC for the valuable feedback. [R1w1, R2w4: Performance Gains] Avoiding severe degradation on vulnerable classes is as clinically important as maximizing mean AUROC, where CoWA’s gains concentrate. As Tab.1 shows, on Pt. under NIH→MIMIC, No-Adapt achieves 57.5 yet TENT drops to 49.1 and AdaBN to 48.3, while CoWA preserves 55.7.As R1 noted, CoWA achieves the best or second-best mean AUROC across all shifts and is the only method without a severe drop, whereas baselines exhibit large regressions relative to No-Adapt on multiple shifts (e.g., AdaBN on NIH→CheX, TENT on CheX→NIH, EATA on NIH→VinDr; Tab.1). We attribute this robustness to CoWA’s modeling of dependency-based inconsistencies during adaptation, which AdaBN cannot capture as it only updates BN statistics. [R1w3, R3w2: Robustness and Bias] CoWA’s reliance on target-derived signals raises two concerns: that poor initial predictions could corrupt M (R3w2), and that dataset-specific co-occurrence may reinforce biases rather than reflect stable clinical structure (R1w3). For the first: (i) threshold binarization (Eq. 1) blocks low-confidence activations from entering M; (ii) M accumulates across batches, dampening early-stage noise (Fig. 3). Empirically, NIH→MIMIC already captures this regime (Tab.1): source predictions on rare classes (e.g., Pt.) are unreliable yet CoWA achieves the highest mean AUROC. We agree with R1, and note this is intrinsic to unsupervised TTA: any target-derived signal can reinforce target-domain biases. We will reframe the contribution as exploiting target-domain dependence rather than stable clinical structure. [R2w1: Relation to IS] We thank R2 for the IS perspective, which sharpened our framing. CoWA shares IS’s intuition of upweighting reliable samples, but is better framed as confidence-based instance reweighting [1,2]: IS weights are likelihood ratios that make the objective an unbiased estimator under the target distribution, whereas CoWA weights are not likelihood ratios and Eq. 4 is not constructed for unbiased estimation. Their role is instead to suppress unreliable training signals, with weight magnitude reflecting per-sample reliability (Fig. 4). The functional form in Eq. 3 follows a Gibbs (maximum entropy) solution under an expected cost constraint [3], providing principled grounding rather than an arbitrary choice. [R2w1, R2w3a: Stability] CoWA addresses R2’s stability concern both structurally and empirically. By construction, CoWA weights are bounded in [w_min, 1] (Eq. 3, 4), precluding the heavy-tail and weight-collapse behavior of unbounded IS weights. Empirically, we measured BN-affine gradient L2-norm variance over adaptation on CheX→MIMIC under three losses, where H(·) is the (Shannon) binary entropy per class, summed over pathologies (R2w3b): (A) L=H: 2.38e-5 (B) L=w_i·H: 1.05e-5 (C) L=max(w_min,w_i)·H: 1.02e-5 (A)’s 2.3× higher variance is consistent with TENT’s instability on rare classes (Tab.1). The near-identical variance of (B) and (C) addresses R2w3a: consistency-based reweighting accounts for most of the stabilization, while w_min serves as an early-stage safeguard before M stabilizes (Fig. 3); Fig. 4 further shows the weight distribution lies well above w_min after adaptation. More elaborate annealing strategies are left for future work. [R2w2: Convergence] To test R2’s hypothesis that baselines may approach CoWA with more iterations, we measured AUROC validation curves across adaptation steps. The gap widens rather than narrows: CoWA exceeds TENT at every iteration, and after both methods peak at iter 30, TENT’s post-peak AUROC declines 1.42× faster. [Future Work] (R1w2) As CoWA is modality-agnostic, extending it to other modalities would be a valuable next step. (R3w1) We also agree that a principled adaptive threshold for M estimation is a worthwhile direction. Ref. [1] Kumar et al. NIPS 2010, Self-Paced [2] Ren et al. ICML 2018, Reweight [3] Jaynes, 1957, Info Theory
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper introduces CoWA, a test-time adaptation framework for multi-label chest X-ray diagnosis that uses pathology co-occurrence patterns to weight samples during entropy minimization. While clinically intuitive, reviewers hold divided opinions due to limited performance gains and theoretical gaps. -R2’s concern regarding the marginal empirical improvements, particularly instances where baselines like AdaBN outperform CoWA. -Discuss the risk of the method reinforcing dataset-specific biases rather than capturing stable clinical structures, especially across different populations (R1). -Connect the formulation to Importance Sampling and provide ablation studies for the weight truncation strategy to prove gradient stability (R2). -Explain how the framework handles severe initial prediction errors where the estimated co-occurrence matrix might be fundamentally flawed (R3). | This submission proposes an intuitive test-time adaptation framework that incorporates pathology co-occurrence for multi-label medical classification, initially drawing divided reviews regarding empirical gains and theoretical grounding. In the rebuttal, the authors successfully addressed major concerns by providing concrete evidence of gradient stability, clarifying the instance-reweighting formulation, and pledging to reframe the scope to account for dataset-specific bias. Given that the majority of reviewers (2/3) found the clarifications compelling and favor acceptance, the Area Chair recommends a Weak Accept, contingent upon the authors fully integrating these post-rebuttal revisions into the final manuscript. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): I recommend reject: R2 (Faculty) maintained Reject independent of rebuttal on marginal empirical gains (AdaBN sometimes outperforming CoWA) and unresolved theoretical gaps (importance-sampling connection, weight-truncation stability), and the two soft “4 — would not mind if rejected” votes from R1 (no post-rebuttal update) and R3 do not outweigh a Faculty Reject to a documented performance concern that the rebuttal could not resolve. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): I agree with most reviewers that the paper highlights an important yet currently overlooked problem in test-time adaptation: diseases are co-occurring. Most reviewers find the method novel and the experiments convincing. Although the paper lacks some in-depth performance analysis and ablation studies, it would still spark meaningful discussion at MICCAI.

title: LinGuinE: Longitudinal Guidance Estimation for Volumetric Tumour Segmentation
reviewer_1_strengths: The authors generalize the idea of earlier works like Hering et. al. and LesionLocator, building a plug and play framework, which works with any combination of registration and guided segmentation algorithm to track a tumor through the whole image sequence. By separating the temporal component in the form of simple registration, it enables training on single-timepoint data alone. The authors introduce an initial boosting method, which can make the model more resilient to slight registration errors. The authors use 4 datasets with multiple pathologies, showing the generalizability of the proposed framework. The authors demonstrate the capabilities of LinGuinE using the state-of-the-art in registration and promptable registration methods. The authors show additional improvements in performance by in-distribution finetuning of the promptable segmentation method used in the framework. The authors show the robustness to elapsed time between scans for their LinGuinE framework, compared to the baseline methods.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: As also noted by the authors, ED is suboptimal as a metric, when many lesions don’t have associated predictions. Therefore, it would have been interesting to see something like a detection rate as an additional metric to Dice. Minor: The authors claim that their framework is “the first temporally direction agnostic framework, allowing radiologists to provide prompts at any timepoint, facilitating retrospective analysis”. While this is true by design, e. g. LesionLocator can also be applied per timepoint in a non-autoregressive fashion.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: Proposes an innovative solution to a relevant clinical problem Validates on multiple datasets Compares the performance of multiple backbones and compares the proposed approach to relevant baselines. Achieves state-of-the-art results. Performs relevant ablation studies
reviewer_2_weaknesses: A significant limitation, as noted by the authors, is the potential for disappearing lesions. In a fully automated context, this scenario could lead the model to segment an unrelated structure, resulting in an inaccurate response assessment. However, this issue is a candidate for mitigation in future research.
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The paper addresses a clinically meaningful and underexplored problem. Longitudinal lesion tracking with segmentation is more relevant to treatment monitoring and response assessment than standard single-timepoint semantic segmentation. The proposed workflow is practical. Allowing a radiologist to provide guidance at one timepoint and propagate it across a longitudinal study is a reasonable and potentially useful clinical interaction model. Even though the method is conceptually simple, the results are strong, and the benchmarking itself is a valuable contribution to this task
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The algorithmic novelty is moderate. At its core, the method is a combination of existing ingredients, image registration, propagated prompts, guided segmentation, and optional boosting. The main contribution is therefore more of a practical framework and benchmarking effort than a fundamentally new algorithm. While temporal direction agnosticism is useful in practice, it is partly a natural property of a registration-based prompt propagation pipeline, so I would not view it as a major conceptual novelty. A key practical dependency of the framework is the quality of the underlying registration. If registration is inaccurate, the propagated prompt may fall outside the target lesion or even near a different lesion, which can lead the guided segmentation stage to fail or segment the wrong object. The paper partially acknowledges this issue and introduces boosting as a mitigation, but it does not provide a systematic analysis of failure cases or robustness to registration inaccuracies. Given that real longitudinal scans often involve anatomical changes and imperfect alignment, this deserves more explicit discussion.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank all the reviewers for their feedback and careful consideration of our manuscript. We are grateful for the positive remarks and appreciate the thoughtful criticisms raised. To R1 and R6: We agree that the key value of our contribution lies in the practicality and clinical relevance of the framework, along with the benchmarking efforts and new insights into an under-explored problem, rather than major algorithmic novelty. At the same time, we believe there is novelty in repurposing algorithms trained on single time-point data for longitudinal use, the boosting mechanism, and the plug-and-play nature of LinGuinE, which distinguishes it from prior work. To R6: Regarding reproducibility, we would like to kindly point out that most of our results on UniToChest, 4DCBCT, and APLCT should be reproducible by the community since the data and many algorithms are public. We also pledged to release our code package and our ground truth masks for UniToChest (https://github.com/n-e-garibli/LinGuinE). We had not included links to the assets at the time of review to preserve anonymity. To R6: Regarding the concern on the dependence of our framework on underlying registration quality. We considered this issue during development and explored robustness to out-of-tumour point propagation, including experiments with rigid registration. However, we prioritised including other analyses in the manuscript, such as experiments on time-direction agnosticism, the use of real radiologist prompts, and temporal degradation, because we felt these were both more novel and more clinically relevant. We also hope that the effect of registration quality is partially reflected in Table 1, where performance on the lung cancer datasets improves when LGI is used instead of UGI. More broadly, many modern guided segmentation methods are trained such that exact guidance location is not critical, and some closed-set algorithms can perform well as long as the guidance point is sufficiently close to the target object. In our experience, this means that even relatively simple registration can be effective in the LinGuinE setting, making the choice of segmentation algorithm more important than the choice of registration. Whilst we would like to support that claim empirically, unfortunately our understanding is that editing the manuscript to include additional results is not permitted.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): The reviewers have a clear view on the paper as it provides a low-input solution for tracking lesions over time an area that has a clear clinical benefit. Moreover the presentation of the work and the evaluation and later discussion seem solid and were celebrated by the reviewers. While I am giving the paper a provisional accept following the reviewer’s recommendations, I do think it is more of an integration work with a good evaluation. I strongly recommend the authors to comment on the criticisms of reviewer 6.

title: LLM-Bootstrapped Targeted Finding Guidance for Factual MLLM-based Medical Report Generation
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The paper tackles an important problem in medical report generation, namely factual errors (hallucinations). Introducing clinical findings as an explicit intermediate representation is intuitive and aligns well with real-world clinical workflows, effectively decoupling visual understanding from language generation. 2.The use of LLMs to automatically construct a label taxonomy is a practical and meaningful contribution, addressing the high cost of annotation in medical datasets. 3.The method shows consistent performance improvements across multiple MLLMs and datasets, providing reasonable evidence for its generalizability and effectiveness.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.While the MLLM is prompted with both vision tokens and classification labels, the paper does not provide a comparison with a setup where only prompts (without vision tokens) are used. This makes it difficult to isolate the contribution of visual features to report generation performance. 2.The discussion of related work is somewhat limited. Although the paper covers the general progression from CNN-RNN to Transformer and MLLM-based approaches, it lacks a comprehensive review of closely related work on fact-guided or structured report generation, which is directly relevant to the proposed method. 3.The constructed label set is not sufficiently described in terms of concrete examples and granularity. Without a clear understanding of how concepts are organized (e. g. , handling of similar findings, distinction between general findings and severity levels), it is difficult to assess the clinical validity and appropriateness of the taxonomy. 4.The proposed framework consists of multiple components (label taxonomy construction, multi-label classification, and fact-guided generation), but the current experiments do not sufficiently disentangle their individual contributions. As a result, it is unclear which component is primarily responsible for the observed performance gains. 5.Although comparisons with an oracle (ground-truth labels) are provided, there is limited analysis of the gap between predicted and ground-truth labels. This makes it difficult to identify bottlenecks in the pipeline. Furthermore, the interpretation of evaluation metrics, including clinical efficacy, is not sufficiently explained, making it harder to judge the practical clinical significance of the improvements.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: S1: Clinically well-motivated problem framing. Factual hallucination and finding omission are the primary barriers to clinical deployment of MLLM-based reporting. The cognitive decoupling hypothesis (recognition is not narration) is principled and supported by the literature. S2: Novel automated annotation pipeline. The LLM-bootstrapped taxonomy construction (batch extraction, hierarchical synonym merging, frequency filtering) eliminates the need for manual labelling in new clinical domains. As per my understanding, no prior MRG method uses an LLM to generate the multi-label training supervision from existing reports. This is the paper’s most original contribution. S3: Architecture-agnostic, plug-and-play design. The framework is validated across three architecturally distinct MLLMs (Qwen2.5-VL 7B, MedGemma 4B, LLaVA-Med 7B), consistently improving all three. This breadth strengthens the generalisability claim substantially. S4: Strong diagnostic of baseline failure. The mode-collapse pathology of vanilla MLLMs: Qwen2.5-VL with precision=1.0 and recall=0.0145, LLaVA-Med with all-zero clinical efficacy is clearly and quantitatively demonstrated, making a compelling case for factual grounding. S5: Use of RadFact for clinical efficacy evaluation. Adopting LLM-based entailment scoring rather than n-gram metrics for the TB task is methodologically appropriate and ahead of much of the field in MRG evaluation practice. S6: Oracle ablation (Table 4). The predicted vs. ground-truth label oracle experiment cleanly identifies label quality as the pipeline bottleneck, guiding future research priorities. I also appreciate the authors for providing code in an anonymised format for reproducibility.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: W1: Logical contradiction: long-tail filtering (Stage 1) vs. long-tail optimisation (Stage 2). Frequency-based filtering at θ=15 preemptively removes rare findings from the taxonomy. Logit adjustment in Stage 2 then attempts to re-balance rare labels, but it cannot recover classes that were deleted in Stage 1.The paper simultaneously claims to protect rare labels (Stage 2) and eliminates them as a design choice (Stage 1). I would request the authors to address this logical inconsistency in the pipeline’s stated goals. W2: No clinical efficacy metric for the larger ophthalmology dataset. The ophthalmology dataset is the larger and more complex of the two. Reporting only NLG metrics (BLEU, CIDEr) for a Chinese-language clinical dataset is insufficient. Could the same GPT-5-mini used in Stage 1 for Chinese report annotation could, in principle, be repurposed for a RadFact-style clinical entailment evaluation? The absence of any factual correctness metric for the primary multimodal dataset is an evaluation gap that could be addressed. W3: TB dataset seems small for reliable claims without statistical testing. 561 training / 160 test images. No confidence intervals, no significance tests, no multi-seed variance. At this scale, single-image shifts move accuracy by ~0.6%. Wilcoxon tests or bootstrapped confidence intervals are the minimum expected standard. W4: No sensitivity analysis on key hyperparameters (θ, b, κ, τ). The entire Stage 1 taxonomy depends on θ=15 (yielding 7 labels for TB, 42 for ophthalmology). No experiment varies θ or examines how the downstream clinical efficacy changes with taxonomy size. This is a missing ablation. W5: Classifier error propagation not analysed. Macro-F1 of 0.52 on TB means substantial per-class errors. These are injected into Stage 3 via a declarative, authoritative prompt (“The image shows the following findings…”), giving the MLLM no mechanism to express uncertainty or reject erroneous inputs. The large gap between predicted-label (F1=0.28) and oracle-label (F1=0.44) performance is reported but not decomposed. Requesting the authors to clarify which finding categories are most commonly misclassified, and how do those errors manifest in generated reports. W6: Stage 1 validation sample of n=50 is statistically inadequate. 50 reports represent 2.7% of the ophthalmology training set. Perfect 100/100 coverage and matching accuracy on 50 samples from a 1,854-case dataset with 42 labels, including many rare ones, cannot be reliably extrapolated. Inter-rater agreement (Cohen’s Kappa) between the LLM and a second clinical reviewer is not reported. W7: Please cite the GPTs models used. Once again, I congratulate the authors for their hard work in addressing an important challenge in Medical LLMs.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The paper is well written, clearly structured, and easy to follow. It addresses a well-defined problem and situates itself appropriately within the literature on medical report generation. The proposed decomposition into visual recognition and language generation is well motivated and represents an interesting and potentially impactful contribution. The design choices are generally sound, and the experimental evaluation covers the key components of the framework, providing a reasonably comprehensive assessment of its effectiveness.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: My main concern is the absence of any statistical significance analysis supporting the claim that the proposed method outperforms prior work. Reporting higher metric values alone is not sufficient to establish superiority, especially when improvements are relatively small. This is particularly important for metrics such as BLEU-4, ROUGE-L, CIDEr, and METEOR, where absolute differences (e.g., +0.2) are difficult to interpret in terms of practical significance. I strongly recommend performing a paired bootstrap resampling test to compare the proposed method against baselines. This would allow the authors to: Report confidence intervals for each metric Assess whether improvements are statistically significant Strengthen the claims made in Table 1 Including such analysis would substantially improve the rigor of the evaluation. Then, the paper refers to the LLM-generated label vectors (the Y annotations) as “ground truth.” This terminology is somewhat misleading. Typically, “ground truth” implies human-verified, highly reliable annotations, whereas in this case the labels are automatically generated and therefore inherently noisy. A more appropriate term would be “pseudo-labels” or “weak labels.” This is not merely a terminological issue as it also affects how results should be interpreted. For instance, in Table 4, the oracle model using both labels and images outperforms the one using labels alone. While this result is valid, it raises an important question: would performance further improve if the labels were truly accurate (e.g., expert-annotated)? Clarifying this distinction would lead to a more precise discussion of the results. Also, as this is a machine learning paper, it is important to clearly specify how data is used at each stage of the pipeline. While it appears that all components are trained using only the training split, this is not stated explicitly. The authors should clarify: Which data is used to derive the taxonomy Which data is used to train the classifier Which data is used to fine-tune the multimodal model Making this explicit would help rule out any potential data leakage or bias and improve reproducibility. Finally, the paper would benefit from a brief discussion of some potential limitations of the proposed framework. In particular: The reliance on LLMs both for label generation (Stage 1) and, indirectly, for evaluation (e.g., via RadFact) may introduce a degree of circularity, where the system is partially aligned with the same type of model used for supervision and assessment. The multi-stage nature of the pipeline (label extraction -> classification -> report generation) may lead to error propagation, where inaccuracies in intermediate predictions affect the final output. These aspects do not undermine the validity of the approach, but acknowledging and discussing them would provide a more complete picture of the method and its practical implications.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for recognizing Fact-Flow’s motivation, automated annotation pipeline, and gains across MLLMs/datasets. [R2W1: filtering vs. long-tail optimization] We agree the wording was unclear. Filtering and logit adjustment address different problems. Filtering is a minimum-support/noise-control step: labels in <θ reports are too weak for reliable pseudo-label supervision or stable MLC training. Logit adjustment is applied only within the retained taxonomy to mitigate imbalance among supported labels. We do not recover discarded labels, and will revise “protect rare findings” to “improve retained low-frequency findings.” [R3/R2W3: statistical reliability] We agree CIs, paired bootstrap tests, or multi-seed variance would strengthen evaluation. Since rebuttal rules disallow new results, we will avoid statistical claims and change “significant” to “consistent.” Submitted TB results show clinical-F1 gains for all MLLMs: Qwen2.5-VL 0.0286→0.2831, MedGemma 0.2266→0.3055, and LLaVA-Med 0→0.2016.Ophthalmology results are limited to NLG metrics, where Fact-Flow improves most metrics. [R1Q1: visual tokens] Table 4 includes Label Only (Pred), which uses predicted labels without image tokens. Adding images improves clinical F1 from 0.2115 to 0.2831; with oracle labels, from 0.3750 to 0.4421.Thus, visual evidence and factual prompts are complementary. [R1Q4/R1Q5/R2W5/R3: components, metrics, and error propagation] Because Fact-Flow is a sequential pipeline, removing an upstream stage makes downstream stages undefined. We therefore combine intrinsic validation with end-to-end ablations. Table 5 evaluates Stage-1 taxonomy quality and Stage-2 MLC performance; Table 4 identifies Stage-2 label quality as the main bottleneck: oracle labels raise Image+Label clinical F1 from 0.2831 to 0.4421.We cannot add per-category decomposition in rebuttal, but will clarify failure modes: false positives may induce unsupported findings, false negatives may cause omissions, and coarse labels may reduce laterality/location/severity specificity. The current system has no uncertainty/rejection mechanism for incorrect Stage-2 labels. To clarify the metric interpretation, RadFact precision/recall reflect unsupported generated and omitted reference entities, respectively, and F1 balances both. [R3: pseudo-label terminology] We agree “ground truth” is imprecise. We will rename LLM-generated annotations as “pseudo-labels.” The Table 4 oracle rows are upper bounds within the bootstrapped label space, not expert-verified ground truth. [R2W6/R3: Stage-1 validation and circularity] The n=50 report-level check is a sanity check of report-to-label matching, not proof of noiseless supervision. It is complemented by full-taxonomy ophthalmologist validation: 80% valid/decidable, 15% context-dependent, 5% overly generic, and 0% invalid/pseudo-concepts. We will avoid overclaiming reliability. RadFact does not use our taxonomy and is not a closed loop over our labels, but is still LLM-based, so we also report NLG metrics, and we will discuss this limitation. [R2W2: ophthalmology factual evaluation] We agree a validated clinical-efficacy metric for Chinese ophthalmology reports would strengthen the work. Building a RadFact-style evaluator would require a new evaluator/experiment; we will restrict factual-efficacy claims to TB. [R2W4/R1Q2/R1Q3/R2W7/R3: robustness and reproducibility] b and κ are context-budget parameters, θ controls minimum support, and τ=1 follows logit-adjustment practice; all were fixed before test evaluation. Submitted experiments cover different taxonomy sizes (7 TB vs. 42 ophthalmology labels), but not a full sensitivity study, which we will state as a limitation. We will also add taxonomy examples/design principles, position fact-guided/structured MRG, specify/cite LLMs, and clarify data usage: taxonomy/classifier/MLLM training use only training data; validation is for model selection; test only for final evaluation.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper proposes a three-stage framework designed to improve the factual groundedness of Multimodal Large Language Models in radiology. It utilizes a “bootstrapping” approach where an LLM automatically extracts a structured label taxonomy and pseudo-labels from existing free-text reports, bypassing the need for manual annotation. A dedicated classifier is then trained to predict these findings from images, providing a declarative “factual stream” that prompts the MLLM to generate reports aligned with specific clinical findings. While the paper presents good contributions, its recommendation for acceptance is contingent upon the authors clarifying the following points during the rebuttal phase: 1.The pipeline preemptively filters out rare findings in stage 1, effectively deleting them from the taxonomy. However, Stage 2 later attempts “long-tail optimization” via logit adjustment. As reviewers noted, the model cannot optimize for classes it has already discarded, undermining the claim that the framework protects rare clinical findings. Clarify the contradiction between frequency-based filtering and long-tail optimization. 2.The TB dataset is extremely small (160 test images), and the paper lacks confidence intervals, significance tests (e.g., Wilcoxon or paired bootstrap), or multi-seed variance reporting. Without these, the marginal gains in BLEU or CIDEr scores cannot be distinguished from random noise. 3.The framework is highly susceptible to cascading errors. Since the MLLM is given an authoritative prompt (“The image shows the following findings…”), it has no mechanism to reject or question incorrect labels from the Stage 2 classifier. The significant performance gap between “predicted-label” and “oracle-label” setups highlights this bottleneck, yet the paper lacks a detailed analysis of which finding categories are failing most frequently. Reclassify “ground truth”, and discuss the impact of label noise on the final MLLM output. 4.The “ground truth” labels are actually LLM-generated pseudo-labels. Validating this extraction process on only n=50 samples (less than 3% of the dataset) is statistically inadequate to prove the reliability of a 42-label taxonomy. Furthermore, using LLMs for both supervision (Stage 1) and evaluation (RadFact) introduces a risk of circularity that is not addressed. 5.The paper treats several key hyperparameters as fixed without sensitivity analysis. It is unclear how the size of the taxonomy or the aggressiveness of the logit adjustment impacts clinical efficacy, making it difficult to assess the framework’s robustness across different medical domains. | The authors have addressed the reviewers’ comments well. Two reviewers acknowledged the significance of the work. Therefore acceptance of the paper is concluded. It is strongly recommended to include statistical test results in the final version. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): The paper is proposing using automated ground truth labeling for a finding classifier followed by a language model to generate text containing those findings. The evaluation of such generated text is also through mostly lexically-based metrics suitable for evaluation. While one can understand the benefits of automation in annotation, it cannot be taken seriously unless there is a formal comparison with ground truthed datasets when they do exist. Besides, LLM currently mix multiple findings into single concepts, cannot easily respect laterality and location constraints, etc. so the resulting report produced is likely to mismatch ground truth report on such fine-grained aspects of what is a finding and its description. The BLEU, ROUGe and other lexical scores will continue to score high. Since the Radgraph F1 is low (0.3) this indicates that any clinical significance may still be low by this method.

title: LLM-Steered Clinical Knowledge Discovery for CVD Outcome Modeling
reviewer_1_strengths: Major Strengths 1.The paper shifts the focus from predictive performance to reusable clinical knowledge discovery, aligning well with current demands for interpretability and reliability in medical AI. 2.The proposed method integrates feature subset search, statistical validation (paired probing), reinforcement learning, and graph-based representation into a unified pipeline, demonstrating strong internal logical consistency. 3.Unlike traditional feature importance methods that focus on marginal effects, the work quantifies interaction effects via a difference-in-differences formulation, offering a more expressive and informative representation of feature relationships.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Major Weaknesses 1.Experimental results suggest that the LLM primarily alters the search trajectory without significantly improving the final discovered features. In some cases, it even slows convergence. Moreover, the paper lacks thorough ablation studies (e. g. , different prompts, alternative LLMs, or removal of semantic guidance) to justify its inclusion. 2.The evaluation is restricted to a single dataset (COPDGene), with no cross-dataset or cross-population validation, limiting confidence in the generalizability of the proposed approach. 3.The paper does not include comprehensive comparisons with established feature selection and knowledge discovery methods (e. g. , LASSO, Boruta, SHAP-based selection, or causal discovery approaches), weakening the empirical support for its claimed advantages. 4.Several key design choices are insufficiently motivated, including the use of the Ising model for feature subset modeling, the adoption of REINFORCE instead of more stable alternatives, and the specific design of the LLM agenda and model selection. 5.The method involves extensive subset sampling, K-fold evaluation, and paired probing, leading to substantial computational cost. However, the paper does not provide a detailed analysis of efficiency or scalability. 6.The method section is dense, with heavy notation and limited intuitive explanation. Important components such as the reward design and evidence ledger are not sufficiently clarified, affecting accessibility. 7.There are concerns regarding reference formatting and overall writing redundancy, which detract from the paper’s presentation quality.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: Novel Integration of LLMs in Clinical Discovery. EGL–LLM is the first to use an LLM for semantic steering of feature exploration in CVD modeling. The LLM generates agendas based on real-time evidence (e.g., uncertainty, stability) rather than purely statistical criteria, addressing the “black-box” problem in predictive models. Structured Methodology for Interaction Discovery The Ising-form distribution over feature subsets, combined with counterfactual probing (e.g., comparing subsets with/without a feature), provides a principled way to test marginal and interaction effects. Empirical Validation of Clinical Plausibility Both EGL and EGL–LLM recover clinically plausible dominant factors (e.g., Agatston score, hypercholesterolemia) and interactions (e.g., Agatston score with comorbidities). Negative interactions (sub-additive effects) highlight redundancy in overlapping CAC-related markers, aligning with known clinical mechanisms Efficiency in Interaction Evidence Consolidation EGL–LLM achieves faster convergence of interaction evidence in later iterations, demonstrating the value of semantic steering in prioritizing meaningful neighborhoods.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Limited Generalizability: The framework is evaluated only on the COPDGene cohort (smokers/COPD patients). No analysis is provided for non-COPD populations or other diseases, limiting the applicability of the findings. No comparisons are made to existing feature selection/interaction discovery methods (e.g., SHAP, Bayesian networks), making it unclear whether EGL–LLM offers unique advantages. Ambiguity in Clinical Plausibility: While factors like Agatston score are labeled as “clinically plausible,” the paper lacks references to prior studies or statistical validation of these associations in COPDGene. The LLM’s role in avoiding domain-specific biases is not addressed; there is no evidence that generated agendas align with validated clinical knowledge (e.g., clinician review). Methodological Limitations Fixed Evaluation Budget: The identical budget for EGL and EGL–LLM ensures fair comparison but may not reflect real-world scenarios where resources vary. Reward Function Design: The scalar reward R(S) combines confirmation and acquisition terms, but the weighting of AUC/AuPRC in the metric summary m(.) is not explicitly defined, leaving room for arbitrary tuning. CT Pipeline Sensitivity: The CT-derived biomarkers are processed via a specific pipeline, but no comparison is made to alternative methods, risking overfit to this pipeline. Risk of Missing Data Bias: Clinical variables are filtered by a 70% missingness threshold, but the paper does not address how missing data in the remaining 30% might bias the evidence ledger.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1) Interesting and timely research direction: The paper shifts the focus from pure predictive performance to clinical knowledge discovery, which is highly relevant for medical AI where interpretability and reproducibility are critical, minimizing the black box label associated with AI-driven diagnosis in medicine. 2) Novel integration of LLMs for semantic guidance: The use of an LLM as a control mechanism to guide feature exploration based on clinical semantics is a creative idea. Rather than using LLMs for prediction, the work leverages them to evaluate and steer the discovery of clinically meaningful feature subsets and interactions. 3) Effort toward interpretability and transparency: The concept of an evidence ledger that accumulates marginal and interaction effects provides a more interpretable alternative to black-box models, potentially helping mitigate the black-box nature of standard ML approaches. 4) Methodological coherence: The framework (sampling, probing, evidence accumulation, and control) is logically structured and consistent, even if complex.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1) Limited theoretical grounding of the LLM control component: While the idea of semantic steering is interesting, the role of the LLM remains heuristic. There is no formal objective or theoretical justification explaining why or how the LLM-guided agenda improves convergence or guarantees better discovery of clinically relevant interactions. 2) Insufficient analysis of the LLM contribution: The paper would benefit from deeper analysis or ablation of the LLM component. For example, isolating the effects of agenda shaping versus probe prioritization, or comparing against simpler heuristic strategies, would strengthen the claims. 3) Clarity issues in method description: The paper is conceptually dense and sometimes difficult to follow, especially in the description of the sampling policy, reward formulation, and interaction between EGL and the LLM control plane. Several components (e.g., “semantic agenda”, “control paths”) are introduced at a high level without sufficient intuitive explanation.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for recognizing the novelty of evidence-grounded clinical knowledge discovery. Reviewers raised several related comments regarding the role of LLM, comparison with existing methods, cross-dataset validation, and the justification of key design choices. We therefore provide a unified response organized around these shared themes. 1.Role of LLM. Our proposed Evidence-Grounded Learning (EGL) follows numerical scores and can over-test locally good but clinically redundant regions. LLM in our enhanced EGL-LLM serves as a semantic scheduler to explore clinically meaningful features and consolidate interaction evidence. For example, vanilla EGL may stick to interaction between one strong node (like Agaston score) and others, but LLM can explore edges between other variables. Thus, LLM only suggests what features to test, while EGL still verifies them. As shown in Fig.2a, EGL quickly settles on the main nodes, while EGL-LLM keeps small substitutions around it, which helps avoid repeatedly testing the same locally strong variables and keeps the search open to nearby clinically related alternatives. The wider MDS footprint in Fig.2c shows expanded exploration without reducing edge acquisition (Fig.2b); identical top nodes confirm stable individual-variable effects (Fig.2d). The main difference between EGL and EGL-LLM is in the interaction set (Fig.2e), which is the intended effect: semantic scheduling redirects tests toward different neighborhoods of interaction. 2.Comparison with other methods. We agree that LASSO, Boruta, SHAP-based selection, Bayesian networks, and causal inference methods are important. However, their objectives and outputs are not the same as those of EGL. Feature selection methods mainly return selected or ranked predictive variables, while knowledge discovery methods often estimate model-specific interactions, dependencies, or causal structures. EGL instead evaluates the reproducibility of marginal and pairwise evidence through repeated matched subset comparisons and outputs a stable evidence graph. Thus, a fair comparison would require a unified protocol to translate different outputs into comparable node- and edge-level evidence and to assess stability and biological plausibility consistently. We will clarify this limitation, construct fair baselines and perform a comparative study in the future. 3.Cross-dataset validation. COPDGene is a strong primary testbed rather than a narrow single-site dataset: it is a large multi-site cohort and combines CT-derived cardiac/CAC phenotypes with risk factors, comorbidities, medications, and CVD labels. Its scale, site diversity, and multimodal coverage provide a meaningful setting for evaluating stable evidence discovery. We agree that external validation across multiple cohorts would further strengthen the findings, but such validation requires careful harmonization of imaging pipelines, clinical variables, and outcome definitions. We therefore regard this as an important direction for future work beyond the scope of the current study. 4.Justification of key design choices. The Ising-form distribution models correlated feature subsets in binary states (sampled vs not sampled), allowing candidate variables to be sampled jointly when interactions exist. Gibbs sampling was used as a standard sampler for Ising-type distributions. We used a REINFORCE-style algorithm because the search involves stochastic sampling, making it infeasible to backpropagate gradients through the full sampling–evaluation process. The reward captures two types of evidence: the marginal gain from adding an individual variable and the excess joint gain from adding a pair of variables beyond their separate contributions. Practical hyperparameters, including the missing-rate filter, reward weights, and the magnitude of the LLM-induced bias, were tuned empirically but omitted due to space limits.

title: Localization-Grounded Supervision: Revisiting Vanilla SFT of Large Vision-Language Models for Medical Image Analysis
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The paper addresses an important question for medical LVLM adaptation, namely why vanilla SFT often does not fully translate pretrained capabilities into downstream medical performance. 2.The proposed method is simple and easy to integrate, and the overall motivation is clear. 3.The paper includes qualitative and quantitative analyses, including attention visualization and DePass-VL, to support its central claim about insufficient semantic alignment under vanilla SFT. 4.Experiments cover both 2D diagnosis and 3D report generation, as well as multiple architectures and parameter scales.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The proposed method is conceptually simple, and the methodological novelty is limited. The core idea is to augment the supervision target with localization signals, and extend this to 3D through an additional localization task with multi-task learning. While practical, this is more a supervision design than a substantially new modeling contribution. 2.Some of the reported gains, especially on the 2D diagnosis tasks, are extremely large. For example, the improvement on CrossMoDA2021 is surprisingly large for such a lightweight change, which raises concerns about benchmark difficulty, possible shortcut signals, or whether the vanilla SFT baseline is sufficiently strong. 3.The 2D diagnosis benchmarks are derived from segmentation datasets by treating slices with lesion masks as positive and slices without masks as negative, with a balanced 1:1 setting. This construction is convenient, but it may oversimplify the task and may not fully reflect realistic fine-grained medical diagnosis scenarios. 4.The paper makes broad claims about the limitations of vanilla SFT and attributes them mainly to insufficient semantic alignment. Although the attention analysis and DePass-VL results are suggestive, the current experiments may not be sufficient to support such general conclusions across medical LVLM settings.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The central empirical observation that vanilla SFT on small-lesion medical tasks produces diffuse attention and doesn’t push the LVLM to attend to the lesion, is an interesting and useful finding. Also quantifying it with a region-level attribution score is a nice contribution. The idea of attaching bounding-box outputs to the answer to push grounding during SFT is simple and the kind of thing that’s easy for others to adopt. I like simple interventions, and the paper presents this one cleanly. The scaling robustness in Figure 5 that shows the effect across two architecture families and three model sizes is a good presentation of the paper’s contribution, and the consistency of the gains across scales is a useful piece of evidence. The attention visualization pairs in Figure 2 are informative. The diffuse-vs-concentrated contrast is visually persuasive, and the accompanying DePass-VL contribution ratio in Figure 3 implements what the pictures suggest.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Direct prior art on grounded medical report generation is not cited. MAIRA-2 (Bannur et al., “MAIRA-2: Grounded Radiology Report Generation”, Microsoft Research 2024) does essentially the same thing the paper proposes: train an LVLM to predict bounding boxes interleaved with report text as tokenized outputs, using standard cross-entropy on the combined sequence. No special grounding loss; no regression head; grounding is handled autoregressively. VividMed extends this with anatomical segmentation grounding. RadVLM (Deperrois et al. 2025) similarly includes grounding with bounding-box supervision as an instruction type. MedGround frames the “image–text–box triplet” as the key to closing the cognitive-perceptual gap. None of these are cited. The “localization coordinates as a complementary output format” is not a new idea in medical LVLMs. It has a two-year history. The paper’s contribution needs to be repositioned relative to that literature: is the insight that it works with standard Qwen3-VL/InternVL3.5 out of the box without custom detection heads (that is a reasonable, if narrower, contribution), or is it the attention analysis that motivates the choice? Reframing the work as such would be more novel. The CrossMoDA2021 result is implausibly high. Table 1 reports Qwen3-VL (LGS) at ACC=0.9844 / F1=0.9846 on CrossMoDA2021.CrossMoDA2021 is a cross-modality domain adaptation challenge (ceT1 to hrT2) for vestibular schwannoma and cochlea segmentation; it is not easy. The paper converts it to 2D slice classification by presence of segmentation mask. A jump from 0.5938 (vanilla SFT) to 0.9844 with the same backbone and the only difference being that bounding-box coordinates are now in the output is not a small effect. It’s 40 accuracy points on an allegedly balanced 1:1 positive/negative split. The obvious hypotheses are (i) the test split shares patients with the training split (no patient-level split is mentioned), allowing anatomical shortcut learning; (ii) the test set is small and fortuitously easy; (iii) the slice-level “positive = slice has a mask” task is largely solvable by looking at the anatomy visible in the slice, and the bounding-box supervision effectively teaches the model “output a box whenever the relevant anatomy is on screen.” None of these are ruled out by the text. Please provide: cohort sizes, train/val/test split protocol (especially patient-level), class balance per split, and variances. The LUNA16 benchmark construction is nonstandard and underspecified. LUNA16 is a nodule-detection challenge (888 scans, LIDC-IDRI); the paper converts it to 2D slice classification. Again, no split protocol, no patient-level separation is noted, no dataset size, no discussion of how slice-level labels are derived (a slice can contain a nodule partially or have a nodule a few slices away so how are borderline slices handled?). These details matter because the whole argument rests on Table 1’s numbers. DePass-VL is a thin extension. The paper presents DePass-VL as a “regional contribution analysis framework tailored for LVLMs” and one of its two quantitative contributions. DePass-VL partitions input tokens into three groups (task-relevant image regions, non-relevant image regions, other) and runs the standard DePass decomposition. Given a bounding box, doing this is straightforward as it’s an application of DePass, not a methodological extension of it. I would tone down the “we propose DePass-VL” claim to at most, “we apply DePass to LVLMs under a region-level partition.” The attention analysis conflates two different things. Section 2.1 focuses on self-attention weights from answer tokens to image tokens. But in modern decoder-only LVLMs, the signal that propagates to the output logit is not the attention weight alone rather it’s the attention-weighted value vectors run through downstream MLPs and residual streams. DePass itself exists precisely because attention weights are not faithful attributions. The paper acknowledges this at the start of Section 2.2 (“attention-based analysis captures interactions within MHSA but does not account for other components such as the MLP”), which is correct but then the narrative continues to lean on the attention visualisation in Figure 2 as the primary qualitative evidence, and Section 4.5 re-emphasises it. I would recommend making DePass-VL the main evidence and the attention maps the illustrative companion, not the other way round. Table 1 reports point estimates. Figures 4 and 5 likewise. With the kind of tiny derived datasets being used (slices from LUNA16 / CrossMoDA2021), seed-to-seed variance on VLM SFT can be substantial. Please report at least three seeds and include standard deviations; without them the 4-5 accuracy point gains are not convincingly separated from noise, and the 40-point CrossMoDA jump, while too large to be noise, still wants verification that it isn’t a single-seed artefact. The “RL-based methods don’t replace SFT” claim is over-strong from the evidence. The paper runs GRPO on both datasets with apparently one configuration and reports it underperforming SFT. Fine, but GRPO notoriously needs careful reward design and base-model initialisation. Concluding that “RL-based methods such as GRPO do not currently replace SFT as a practical training paradigm for LVLMs in medical image analysis” from two datapoints with a single hyperparameter setting is not warranted. This can be softened. Vanilla SFT accuracies in Figure 5 look unlike seen in practice. The Qwen3-VL 2B/4B/8B vanilla SFT curves seem to plateau around 0.5 accuracy on a 1:1 balanced LUNA16 slice task i.e. essentially chance. A modern 8B LVLM should be able to memorise or at least noisily fit a small balanced classification task, even with suboptimal prompting. To explain these given numbers in the submission, the paper should explain what’s going wrong (learning-rate issue, answer-format mismatch, prompt-ending whitespace, LLM-head-frozen-vs-not, etc.); if they are seed-selected or early-training snapshots, the figure needs caveats. At face value, the vanilla-SFT baseline looks under-tuned. Qwen3-VL (ref [3]) is trained on a very large multimodal corpus that almost certainly includes LIDC-IDRI and LUNA16 derivatives in some form. The paper acknowledges this concern in Sec4.2 (“potential overlap with pretraining data may bias evaluation”) but the only mitigation is “derive 2D from 3D segmentation data.” That doesn’t actually address the data overlap concern. If the pretraining corpus contained LUNA16 images with or without captions mentioning nodules, slice-level labels derived from the same volumes can still be overlapping. A held-out set, or at minimum a de-identified subset with noise applied, would be more convincing. In the 3D setting (RadGenome-Chest CT / CT-RATE), this concern increases as CT-RATE is heavily circulated in the VLM community. Quantitative comparison to MAIRA-2 or similar grounded-VLM baselines is absent. The 3D report generation numbers on RadGenome-Chest CT (F1 0.263, IoU 0.673) are presented without reference to MAIRA-2, VividMed, RadVLM, or any of the other grounded-VLM papers. These are not all directly comparable (MAIRA-2 is chest X-ray, not 3D CT), but the paper’s main empirical claim is that LGS is the right paradigm for grounded medical VLM training, and that claim is not tested against the closest existing paradigm. Minor citation issues. -Ref [9]: the citation should ideally point to both the challenge and the paper if the authors used the challenge framework.

reviewer_3_strengths: The abstract and introduction dig into the core problem of pretrained models to understand why vanilla SFT fails and authors claim to introduce an interpretability with DePass-VL to understand this better. The idea of incorporating explicit localization signals (LGS) is simple and practically useful - specially for small lesions which they show in Figure 2 The authors attempt to mitigate data leakage concerns which I really like and appreciate. reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The paper lacks essential details about dataset construction. Specifically, the number of samples for training/validation/test splits. In Table 1 - even though the datasets used to derive the images is 3D segmentation dataset - with the metrics reported it seems like authors did a classification task - lesion or no-lesion. Task is not explicitly clarified in the paper. These omissions make it difficult to assess statistical significance, lower bound and reproducibility. 2.Figure 5 reports results for InternVL3.5, but these results are not included in Table 1.A unified presentation would improve clarity and allow easier comparison across models. It would benefit the authors to include these results in Table 1. 3.The comparison with GRPO is underexplained. In particular, the paper does not clearly describe the training setup (reward design, policy definition, hyperparameters, etc). And why use GRPO and not other methods. Overall, comparison with RL is ill-motivated. 4.Contribution of DePass-VL is not justified. To understand the novelty and requirement, it would benefit the paper if there is a description of what is lacking is DePass and how authors resolve it. Moreover, compare how this interpretability contribution helps understanding vanilla SFT better. 5.In case of LGS which is the most significant contribution of the paper, key details are missing from the text on how is it implemented. This include mainly how are localization signals incorporated into training (and loss formulation) 6.Minor comments a. Overall the writing feels a bit disintegrated in the paper. I like the effort put in for the experiments and the idea but I struggled to find key details and map them to the figures. b. Section 4.5 largely reiterates observations already presented in Figures 2 and 3, and thus can be avoided. c. Fig 3(b): x-axis says Vanilla SFT/LGS and I assume pink violin plot is SFT and blobs are LGS. If this is the case, the interpretation ‘value smaller than 1 indicates that LGS enhances the LVLM’s focus on task-relevant regions‘ is also valid for Vanilla SFT.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank all reviewers for their constructive feedback. We are encouraged that the reviewers recognize the importance of revisiting vanilla SFT for medical LVLM adaptation, the practical value of LGS, and the usefulness of our analyses. We address the key concerns below. 1.Novelty and prior grounded medical VLMs (R1&R2) We thank R2 for pointing out related works such as MAIRA-2.We agree that predicting localization coordinates with text has been explored. Our contribution is not claiming coordinate prediction itself as new. Instead, we use localization output as a supervision interface to analyze and improve vanilla SFT for off-the-shelf LVLMs. The key contribution is the combination of simple supervision design, mechanistic analysis of vanilla SFT failure, and extension to 3D medical imaging. We will revise Introduction to clarify this positioning. 2.CrossMoDA result and baseline fairness (R1&R2) Our CrossMoDA experiment is not the original 3D cross-modality segmentation challenge, but a derived 2D slice-level binary lesion-presence classification task. Thus, the high accuracy should not be interpreted as solving the original CrossMoDA task. Comparisons in all experiments are controlled (no patient-level data leakage): vanilla SFT and LGS use the same base model, split, learning rate, batch size, optimizer, epochs, parameter-freezing strategy, and prompt setting. The only intended difference is that LGS adds localization coordinates to the answer target. The substantial improvement over baseline precisely demonstrates the simplicity and effectiveness of LGS. We will add training details in the revised version, and release the split for reproducibility. 3.Dataset construction and benchmark purpose (R1&R2&R3) We agree that dataset construction needs more detail. The 2D benchmarks are controlled fine-grained spatial diagnosis tasks, not full clinical diagnosis simulations. Take LUNA16 as the example, we select CT scans with a single lung nodule, use the middle slice of the nodule mask as the positive sample, and use the adjacent slice just outside the mask boundary as the negative sample. This creates lesion-near negatives and reduces coarse anatomical shortcuts. We will report train/validation sizes, patient/scan-level split, label rules, and more details in the revised version. 4.LGS implementation (R3) LGS does not add a detection head or regression loss. Training still uses standard autoregressive next-token cross-entropy. The only change is the target sequence: vanilla SFT predicts only the answer, while LGS predicts the answer plus textual coordinates, e.g., “Yes, [x_min, y_min, x_max, y_max].” For 3D tasks, report-generation samples are mixed with anatomical localization. We will add target examples and loss formulation in the revised version. 5.DePass-VL and attention analysis (R2&R3) We will revise to clarify that DePass-VL is the first adaptation of DePass to LVLMs with region-level token partitions: task-relevant image regions, non-relevant image regions, and other tokens. As correctly pointed out (R2), attention weights alone are not faithful attributions. Thus, DePass-based contribution analysis will be the main quantitative evidence, while attention maps will be presented as qualitative illustrations in the revised version. 6.Claim scope, GRPO, variance, and presentation (R1&R2&R3) We will moderate claims: insufficient fine-grained semantic alignment is an important factor in fine-grained medical tasks, not a only universal cause. We will also soften the GRPO conclusion and present it only as a preliminary comparison, with added reward and hyperparameter details. If permitted by the rebuttal and revision policy, we will report mean±std for the main results in Tab.1, Fig.4&5.Finally, we will add InternVL3.5 results in Fig.5 to Tab.1, improve Fig.3(b) caption, clarify that the plotted value is the per-sample relative ratio, and shorten the repetitive Section 4.5.

title: LoFi: Location-Aware Fine-Grained Representation Learning for Chest X-Ray
reviewer_1_strengths: The paper merges findings from two papers (SigLip and LoCa) to propose one unified training framework and applies it to radiology. Comparison with previous methods is thorough and results are convincing.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited to the combining of two previously introduced methods and its application to two radiology datasets.
