reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: Multi-objective formulation for fine-grained learning: The paper uses a unified training objective that jointly combines contrastive (sigmoid), captioning, and location-aware captioning losses. The key idea is in integrating grounding (box prediction) and dense captioning into an autoregressive LLM framework, enabling implicit region-level supervision even when bounding box annotations are sparse. Effective use of heterogeneous supervision: The method leverages large-scale radiology reports together with partially available text-box pairs in a principled way. Instead of requiring fully annotated datasets, it uses location-aware captioning objectives to bridge weak (report-level) and strong (box-level) supervision. Comprehensive evaluation across retrieval and grounding: The paper demonstrates consistent improvements over multiple baselines on both retrieval and phrase grounding, including external validation using retrieval-based in-context learning.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty relative to prior location-aware captioning work: While the paper claims a novel “location-aware captioning loss,” the core idea of jointly predicting captions and bounding boxes via an autoregressive framework closely resembles prior work such as LocCa (Wan et al., NeurIPS 2024), which already formulates visual pretraining as a combination of caption generation and location prediction tasks (e.g., grounded captioning and referring expression prediction) . LoFi mainly adapts this paradigm to the medical domain with a lightweight LLM, but does not introduce a fundamentally new learning formulation beyond combining existing objectives. Incremental use of retrieval-based in-context learning (ICL): The integration of retrieval-based ICL for grounding is not novel and follows prior work showing that performance depends heavily on retrieved demonstrations (e.g., Yang et al., 2022 as cited in the paper). The paper does not introduce new retrieval strategies, scoring mechanisms, or new insights, only replaces the encoder with a fine-grained one. Reliance on noisy or weak supervision without sufficient analysis: The model is trained using large-scale silver-standard annotations (e.g., machine-generated text-box pairs from MIMIC-Ext), which are known to contain noise and inconsistencies. However, the paper does not provide a detailed analysis of how annotation quality affects performance, nor does it compare against human-annotated subsets. This is important because prior work has highlighted challenges with spatial annotation quality and inter-observer variability in medical grounding tasks.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for their constructive feedback. We address the major concerns below. Novelty beyond prior work: We respectfully disagree that our work is a straightforward extension of prior work. Notably, prior work leaves two concrete gaps. (G1) Contrastive CXR models, GLoRIA, CARZero [11], and RadIR [28], align local features with text IMPLICITLY via attention-weighted similarity; none consume explicit bbox coordinates even when available (e.g., Chest ImaGenome), thereby upper-bounding their fine-grained signal. We benchmark against CARZero/RadIR, which prior work reports surpass GLoRIA. (G2) LocCa [23] shows that explicit grounding/dense-captioning produces strong location-aware features, but only at web scale: 1B pairs from scratch with unreleased weights, which is infeasible at medical scale (227K reports). Filling G1+G2 jointly is non-trivial: (a) medical captioners are not region-aware; (b) region-aware encoders (e.g., SigLIP2) are not generative; (c) joint contrastive+autoregressive training on 227K data is brittle. LoFi’s four choices each address a specific obstacle: (i) SigLIP2 [21] encoder — the strongest open patch-localized semantic features without billion-scale pretraining; (ii) Gemma3-270M decoder — small enough for 227K without overfitting; (iii) attention pooling (64 tokens) + LoRA — bridging the encoder/LLM with few trainable parameters for medical-scale stability; and (iv) our newly designed loss enables retrieval (absent in LocCa) and injects explicit bbox supervision (absent in GLoRIA/CARZero/RadIR). Fig 4 confirms that each loss contributes across all metrics; §1 will be rewritten to lead with this framing. Empirically, we show that no prior family matches LoFi’s SOTA results on external grounding and retrieval. Evaluation protocol and data splitting (R2): We clarify that, following a foundation-model pretraining protocol, Tables 1–3 report the performance of the pretrained checkpoint from the last training epoch, which is intended for release. For Table 4, we used the official PadChest-GR train/val/test split, ensuring patient-level separation. Although multi-seed reporting could further strengthen the results in Table 4, FT w/ Ours clearly improves over FT w/o Ours (F@0.5: 28 to 33; run-to-run variance was small) and is also comparable to the much larger, private-data-trained MAIRA-2.Therefore, we reported the single-run performance of the fine-tuned checkpoint intended for release. Retrieval-based ICL for bbox prediction (R3): We clarify that retrieval-based ICL serves as an evaluation setting for testing whether the learned fine-grained encoder generalizes to practical chest X-ray grounding scenarios. However, our results provide several insights beyond this evaluation setting. First, to the best of our knowledge, LoFi is the first to demonstrate effective ICL for bbox prediction, whereas prior ICL studies largely focus on VQA. Second, retrieval-based ICL offers a practical solution to key medical challenges in external validation, such as inter-observer variability. Third, we show that fine-grained retrieval is critical for ICL-based grounding and that LoFi-based retrieval improves the quality of retrieved demonstrations. Annotation noise (R3): We agree that tight abnormality-level boxes can suffer from inter-observer variability. However, LoFi is trained with loose anatomical-level boxes (e.g., left lower lung) rather than tight abnormality boxes, making the supervision less ambiguous. Furthermore, MIMIC-Ext [17] shows that its annotations are more reliable than alternatives, and we further used only its highest-quality A++-rated text-box pairs for training. Restricting training to a small human-annotated subset would make region-level supervision much less frequent during training; since LoFi learns from non-box samples via the captioning loss, we expect this setting to behave similarly to our ablation w/o Lg,d. Notation (R2): We will clarify the notation and metric definitions.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper proposes LoFi, a location-aware fine-grained vision–language representation learning framework for chest X-rays, which jointly optimizes sigmoid, report captioning, and location-aware captioning losses, using a lightweight large language model. The learned encoder is used in a retrieval-based in-context learning pipeline, yielding improved retrieval and phrase grounding performance on MIMIC-CXR and PadChest-GR datasets. The paper addresses the timely and relevant problem of fine-grained representation learning and phrase grounding for disease localization and explainability in CXRs. It presents a well-motivated unified training approach that combines global and local objectives in a practical way. Empirical evaluation against multiple baselines on two datasets is generally convincing. However, the following concerns should be addressed: 1) Related work: Insufficient related work discussion of closely related global-local medical VLP methods (e.g., GLoRIA) and prior location-aware captioning work (e.g., LocCa). 2) Novelty: Incremental as primarily demonstrated in combining existing ideas (e.g., SigLIP-style contrastive learning with location-aware captioning/grounded captioning paradigms such as LocCa) and applying them to radiology. 3) Clarity and presentation: Paper parts can be repetitive and difficult to follow, and some metrics and equations require clearer definitions and explanations. 4) Statistical reporting: Significance testing or reporting variance across runs is required. 5) Data splitting/leakage: It is unclear whether results are from a single run and that patient-level separation is enforced across train/val/test splits. 6) Noise in weak supervision: silver-standard text–box pairs may be noisy; the paper would benefit from analysis of annotation quality sensitivity and/or comparison to a higher-quality subset. I invite the paper for rebuttal to address the issues highlighted by the reviewers. | After considering the initial reviews, the authors’ rebuttal, and the reviewers’ post-rebuttal replies, I recommend acceptance. The rebuttal clarified the intended novelty relative to prior work, evaluation protocol, data splitting and annotation noise. While concerns about incremental novelty (compared to GLoRIA) and paper clarity remain valid, the overall evidence is positive and the contribution is practically meaningful. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper addresses phrasal grounding directly within LLM frameworks. Earlier work had bounding box prediction done separately. Since LLMs are not as good at regression tasks, it was interesting to see the method still works. Not all concerns of the meta-reviewer appears to have been addresses. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Despite some limitations regarding clarity and novelty, I believe localization is an important problem in medical vision-language pre-training, and the authors made significant performance gains in this direction.

title: Longitudinal Multi-view Modeling for Breast Cancer Risk Prediction
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.Evaluation spans two large, independent public datasets (EMBED and CSAW-CC) with different populations, vendors, and density-labelling schemes (BI-RADS vs LIBRA tertiles). 2.Statistical discipline is above average: 95% bootstrap CIs with 1000 resamples, a paired non-parametric bootstrap test against the second-best baseline, patient-level splits with MammoRegNet trained on a disjoint cohort to prevent leakage, and realistic ~5% positive rate rather than artificial balancing. 3.Reporting both frozen and fine-tuned LMV-Net variants allows architectural gains to be separated from encoder-adaptation gains. 4.On EMBED, the gains over strong baselines are large and statistically significant. Fine-tuned LMV-Net achieves C-index 81.4 vs 74.7 for the next-best method. The two fine-tuned baselines (VMRA-MaR, OA-BreaCR) are compared under matched encoder conditions. 5.The seven-variant ablation is informative and cleanly isolates several contributions. 6.The density-stratified analysis is a clinically meaningful robustness check
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The novelty claims are overstated against the paper’s own reference list. The abstract describes the work as “the first breast-wise longitudinal multi-view risk prediction framework that explicitly aligns the feature maps of each CC and MLO view across multiple time points”, yet the cited prior work already covers essentially every property in this conjunction. The alignment mechanism itself is explicitly imported from MammoRegNet (cited). The abstract should attribute the alignment to MammoRegNet and remove “the first”. 2.The Dual Stream Attention block, positioned as a novel contribution, is a standard two-stream cross-attention transformer encoder. Its specification is a conventional transformer recipe with well-established precedents. The cross-attention between CC and MLO is also geometrically naive: CC and MLO are non-coplanar projections, but the block treats their feature-map positions as interchangeable tokens with no projection-aware positional encoding. 3.The ablation does not include a single-stream transformer baseline operating on the concatenation of CC and MLO tokens with matched parameter count and layer depth. Variant (iv) (“same view both branches”) removes complementary information entirely and is not an equivalent substitute, because a concatenated-token single-stream transformer has access to both views through self-attention over the joint sequence. Without this row, the contribution of the two-stream design cannot be empirically isolated from extra capacity plus access to the complementary view. 4.The improvements are strongly asymmetric between datasets and this is not discussed. On EMBED the fine-tuned C-index gain is 6.7 points; on CSAW-CC only 1.7 points, and the 5-year gain is 0.7 points and not statistically significant. The single-view ablation costs 10.6 C-index points on EMBED but only 0.9 on CSAW-CC, suggesting the value of multi-view modelling is substantially dataset-dependent. The paper currently presents the gains as uniform; the discussion should report the asymmetry explicitly. 5.ImgFeatAlign, the baseline most conceptually similar to LMV-Net (both use MammoRegNet-derived alignment), is reported only with a frozen encoder. The headline comparison therefore conflates architectural with encoder-adaptation gains. The frozen-vs-frozen comparison permitted by the table shows a 3.6-point C-index gap on EMBED and approximately parity on CSAW-CC. This architectural-only gap should be reported explicitly. 6.Table 1 shows 29 positive breast-level exams at 5 years and 34 at 4 years. Bootstrap CIs on AUC from ~30 positives are wide enough that differences below ~0.05 are not reliably distinguishable from noise. Given the ~5% positive rate, the paper would also benefit from PR-AUC or sensitivity at fixed specificity alongside AUC.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The inclusion of features from both current, aligned prior, and differences is novel. 2.The paper is validated on two public datasets. Both datasets show superior performance of the proposed method comparing to state-of-the-art methods. 3.The documentation is pretty comprehensive with detailed description about the methods and model parameters (e.g., model size).
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.Could it be possible that LMV-Net predicts the risk at middle years (say year 3) to be higher than the risk at later years (say year 5)? It is unclear how the authors handle the first increasing then decreasing risks. Simply summing them up may not be the best solution. 2.In Figure 2, what is the reason that the LMV-Net, tested on mammograms with higher breast density (density category D or high), shows higher C-Index on the EMBED dataset but lower C-Index on the CSAW-CC dataset?
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The ablation study is comprehensive, and the comparisons with competing methods is fair. 2.The method section is relatively well organized, and the attention visualization serves as a helpful interpretability component.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The novelty claim appears incremental, and the authors’ statement that they introduce the first breast-wise longitudinal multi-view risk prediction framework seems somewhat overstated, especially in light of prior work such as VMRA-MaR and related studies. 2.Figure 1 is visually overloaded and is difficult to interpret. 3.The paper presents several components using ‘novel’ terminology, but the actual innovation seems limited. In particular, Dual Stream Attention is already a common design in other domains, such as video modeling.
reviewer_3_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank all reviewers for their constructive feedback. We are glad they appreciate our clinically meaningful and thorough analysis(R1), strong ablations(R1,R3), strong performance across datasets(R2,R3), our design and unified modeling approach(R2), and detailed description, ensuring reproducibility(R2). (R1,R2,R3) Novelty/distinction from prior work We agree that the current phrasing in the abstract can be slightly misleading and will revise it and the introduction to more precisely highlight that the novelty comes from considering the multi-view information within the context of *explicit alignment. Prior approaches are either restricted to single-view modeling (OA-BreaCR, ImgFeatAlign) or support multi-view modeling without explicit longitudinal alignment, instead integrating temporal information implicitly (VMRA-MaR) or not at all (Mirai). In contrast, our method is the first to jointly model multi-view and explicit longitudinal alignment, resulting in substantial performance improvements over these prior approaches. This design is clinically motivated: radiologists interpret CC and MLO jointly when comparing timepoints, as they provide complementary diagnostic information. No prior method reflects this workflow in a longitudinal setting with explicit alignment. *(R1) Dual Stream Attention We agree that a concatenated single-stream transformer could be another interesting baseline. However, note that this baseline would result in a single view-agnostic representation and thus also not completely allow DSA disentanglement, as our provided ablation study (vi) shows that multi-level learning (having losses both on the individual and joint risk prediction) is important. Regarding positional encoding, CC and MLO are non-coplanar with strong patient- and acquisition-dependent deformations, making fixed spatial correspondence ill-defined. We therefore avoid token-wise positional alignment and instead model complementary cross-view interactions. Projection-aware encoding remains future work. *(R1,R2) Asymmetric performances EMBED is more diverse (multi-population, multi-scanner), while CSAW-CC is single-scanner and more homogeneous, explaining larger gains on EMBED due to better generalization. For density, EMBED’s density-D subgroup is smaller, while CSAW-CC densities were derived from LIBRA scores and grouped into equally sized categories. Although EMBED density-D shows higher mean performance, the wider confidence intervals indicate greater uncertainty and variability due to the smaller subgroup size. We will clarify this. *(R1) Finetuning comparisons We first evaluated all methods using frozen encoders to ensure a fair comparison. Here, LMV-Net outperforms ImgFeatAlign on both datasets (+3.6% on EMBED and +3.0% C-index on CSAW). The C-index improvement is statistically significant for both datasets; the missing significance marker for frozen LMV-Net in Table 2 (CSAW) is a typo. We then evaluated fine-tuning both models which improved LMV-Net but not ImgFeatAlign. We agree that it would be beneficial to report this result. *(R2) Cumulative risk prediction LMV-Net uses a cumulative probability layer (Eq. 1) enforcing monotonicity, such that risk is non-decreasing across years by design. *(R1) Early stopping We will reformulate: LMV-Net was trained for up to 30 epochs with early stopping after 15 stagnant epochs. *(R1) Bootstrap resampling and metrics Following prior SOTA work (Refs. 22, 23, 28), we adopt bootstrapping at the exam-pair level and AUC and C-index as the primary metric, ensuring fair comparison. We have now recomputed results using patient-level clustered bootstrap and see only negligible differences; previously significant differences remain significant. The similarity arises as the number of exams per patient is relatively homogeneous (mode: 3–4 exams), limiting the impact on the estimates. We will note additional metrics (PR-AUC, etc.) as future work. *(R3) Fig. 1 We will improve readability of Fig. 1.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Reject Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper addresses a clinically relevant problem and provides a reasonably strong empirical evaluation on two public mammography datasets. The overall evidence suggests that the system is potentially useful, especially given the public-data evaluation, realistic class imbalance, leakage-aware design, and ablation analysis. However, the main weakness is consistent across all reviewers: the novelty and framing are not sufficiently convincing. The claimed “first” contribution and repeated use of “novel” appear stronger than the actual technical advance, since key elements rely on known longitudinal alignment and standard two-stream attention designs. In addition, the empirical gain is not uniform across datasets, and the absence of a matched single-stream transformer baseline leaves the value of the dual-stream design insufficiently isolated. The authors should directly revise or defend the novelty claims, especially the use of “first” and “novel,” and clarify the precise distinction from VMRA-MaR, ImgFeatAlign, MammoRegNet-based alignment, and standard two-stream cross-attention models. They should explain whether a matched single-stream transformer baseline can be added or, if not, why the current ablations are sufficient to isolate the contribution of Dual Stream Attention. They should report or discuss frozen-vs-frozen comparisons against ImgFeatAlign to separate architecture gains from encoder fine-tuning gains. They should explain the asymmetric performance between EMBED and CSAW-CC, including density-stratified differences. They should clarify whether cumulative risk predictions are monotonic across prediction years and how inconsistent year-wise risk outputs are handled. They should also clarify early stopping, bootstrap resampling at patient versus pair level, and consider adding PR-AUC or sensitivity at fixed specificity given the small number of positive cases in some horizons. | Although the core architecture of dual-stream attention is well-documented in existing literature, pioneering its use within longitudinal medical imaging research presents a clear and valuable novelty. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper addresses a clinically relevant problem and presents a well-evaluated framework for longitudinal breast cancer risk prediction using multi-view mammography. Reviewers generally agreed that the empirical evaluation is strong, with two public datasets, realistic class imbalance, leakage-aware experimental design, and comprehensive ablation studies. The main concerns were related to overstated novelty claims and the incremental nature of some components, particularly the use of explicit longitudinal alignment and the Dual Stream Attention design. The rebuttal appropriately clarified the intended contribution, softened the “first” and “novel” framing, and better distinguished the work from prior longitudinal and multi-view approaches. In addition, the authors clarified the frozen-versus-finetuned comparisons, cumulative risk monotonicity, and patient-level bootstrap analysis, which strengthened confidence in the reported empirical gains. While some limitations remain, particularly the absence of a matched single-stream transformer baseline, I believe the paper provides sufficient methodological and empirical contribution for acceptance. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): The rebuttal has not sufficiently addressed the main concerns raised by Reviewer #3, which is also agreed by the AC, that the paper overclaimed its novelty. The rebuttal mentioned that “Prior approaches are either restricted to single-view modeling (OA-BreaCR, ImgFeatAlign) or support multi-view modeling without explicit longitudinal alignment.” However, LoMaR (arXiv 2404.19083, MICCAI 2024) as pointed out by the reviewer indeed took both the multi-view and the longitudinal information into consideration. The explicit temporal alignment was conducted in step 2, using MammoRegNet, which is an existing work. The methodology contribution of the manuscript is hence confusing. Therefore, the paper in its current version does not meet the standard of MICCAI.

title: Lost in the Folds: When Cross-Validation Is Not a Deep Ensemble for Uncertainty Estimation
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.Using CV for UQ is becoming a common practice for medical segmentation models due to 5-fold CV being the default for nnU-Net; as such, this paper will be of great interest within the MICCAI UQ community. 2.The work brings to light the need of related literature to not call a method “deep ensembling” if each model in the ensemble was trained on different data subsets of an original dataset. Again, this is becoming a relatively common practice due to nnU-Net’s use of 5-fold CV. 3.The paper claims that it will release a nnU-Net modification enabling DE training, which would be of great benefit to the community. 4.The paper compares CV- to DE-based UQ on 3 segmentation datasets (all different modalities) across multiple UQ tasks (calibration, failure detection, ambiguity, modeling, domain shift robustness). 5.Public datasets are used, enabling reproducibility. 6.The utilized datasets release individual segmentations for multiple raters, allowing for an ambiguity analysis. 7.The work uses 95% bootstrapped confidence intervals to demonstrate the variability of the results. It also uses hypothesis testing to evaluate the significance of the results. Furthermore, it has a figure to demonstrate the performance on individual datapoints, so the reader doesn’t just have to rely on point estimates.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The manuscript highlights a niche problem in the literature. While this is useful, the novelty is more incremental than what is typically expected for a full methodological or application paper. 2.The manuscript lacks a grounding in clinical context; the introduction, recommendations, considerations are mostly related to a research setting. The introduction should have briefly summarized why segmentation and uncertainty quantification is important for clinical settings. Furthermore, the discussion/conclusion should have discussed what the findings mean for those developing UQ for segmentation models in a clinical setting. For example, I would have liked to have seen the following question considered: is CV-based calibration/failure detection enough for resource limited clinical settings, i. e. settings in which running 25 nnU-Net submodels at inference is infeasible? 3.The manuscript does not fully explore the distribution shift results, thereby potentially misleading the reader in the final conclusions. For the RIGA dataset, CV performed better than DE on the task of failure detection on scans from a held-out institution. Even so, the manuscript’s main failure detection recommendations are to use DE, without mentioning that this recommendation may not generalize to distribution shifts. Furthermore, while I understand that the authors may have chosen to report effect size for OOD data instead of raw metric values for space considerations, it leaves the reader wondering how the models actually did under distribution shift. 4.Lacks important implementation details, such as the train/test split ratio and if these splits were performed patient-wise (if applicable for the specific public datasets). The lack of knowing how many images is in the test set is especially problematic for the GoldAtlas dataset, as its sample size is small (n=19) and 4 were already withheld for OOD testing. The other important missing detail is the type of hypothesis testing used to get the p-value (i. e. a ** sided ** test).
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The paper highlights a subtle but relevant distinction between two methods that may easily be mixed up in practice, provides very interesting findings, and turns them into actionable items. This includes a small but immediately useful contribution to a widely used library. The main definitions and motivation are compelling and clearly stated. The experimental investigation leverages a smart setup with multi-rater datasets and considers three aggregation methods.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The main weakness of the submission in its current state is lack of clarity in the evaluation, which partly undermines confidence in the results. First, the paragraph on “Uncertainty quantification and Evaluation” uses notation that is not explicitly declared. It may be guessed that $c$ refers to a specific class, and possibly $v$ to a voxel. $y_n^ (v)$ might be the segmentation from the $n$-th annotator in voxel $v$, as $y_n^ $ is explained (later!), but then $n$ runs over annotators, while its upper limit $N$ was used for the dataset (with index $i$) at the start of section 3.The way the bins $B_m$ are chosen is not explained, and $v\in B_m$ suggests these bins are voxel sets. The use of the accuracy in a bin that is defined inline is not specified. A short definition for each metric in this paragraph would be very helpful (whereas current eqs. (1) and (2) earlier could be inline). The acronym for the area under the risk curve (AURC) should be given upon first mention. Finally, it would be good to have an explicit statement about how averages at the voxel or image level are taken. Second, the statistical tests and OOD comparison in the caption of table 3 are very scarce in terms of details. In order to perform the paired bootstrap test, are the metrics computed by aggregating the voxels at the sample level, and then aggregating the (bootstrapped) samples? Are the significance tests just comparing the confidence intervals with zero? The different way of reporting ID and OOD results, with raw scores in one case and effect sizes in the other, is definitely a cause for confusion. While I agree that in an ideal world one would want to see both (6 lines per metric), if space is an issue, consistently reporting $\Delta$ (2 lines per metric) or both values (4 lines per metric) would be helpful. By comparison, multiplication by 100 does not need to be highlighted with a full sentence in bold, a percent sign in the header line of the table is sufficient. Additionally, the literature search that resulted in table 1 is not described in depth, which makes it hard to assess how systematic it was. While this is a high-level weakness, it is not crucial to the paper’s message about the confusion between DE and CV, which would hold even with episodic evidence.
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The issues identified are highly accurate, pointing out the integration misuse problems that have long been overlooked in the field. The experimental design is rigorous, with only the integration method varied while all other factors kept consistent, leading to reliable conclusions. The provided usage recommendations are highly valuable for engineering practitioners. The paper is well-structured and presents a relatively comprehensive analysis.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The motivation is not fully elaborated, and it is unclear why nnU-Net must have deep integration and the existing integration methods are insufficient. This manuscript consists entirely of experimental analyses and lacks theoretical derivations, such as the approximation relationship between the two and the uncertainty boundary, which are not mentioned. There is insufficient methodological innovation; it is more like a benchmark test and problem clarification without novel algorithm design.

title: Lost in Volume: The CT-SpatialVQA Benchmark for Evaluating Semantic-Spatial Understanding of 3D Medical Vision–Language Models
reviewer_1_strengths: Valuable benchmark for 3D reasoning: The introduction of a question–answer dataset for 3D CT data is a meaningful contribution, enabling systematic evaluation of semantic and spatial reasoning capabilities in medical vision–language models. Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The benchmark is thoroughly evaluated across multiple (eight) 3D medical VLMs, providing useful insights into the current capabilities and limitations of existing approaches.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Limited differentiation from existing benchmarks: While the proposed dataset is a useful contribution, several related benchmarks (e. g. , [1, 2]) already exist, and it is not clearly demonstrated how the proposed dataset provides additional value or distinct advantages. In particular, prior work such as [1] includes segmentation masks for regions of interest, which offer richer supervision and evaluation capabilities, whereas the proposed dataset does not provide such annotations. This limits its utility for tasks requiring precise spatial grounding. Limited novelty in evaluation protocol: Although the paper presents the evaluation protocol as a key contribution, similar approaches leveraging LLMs to assess generated text have already been explored in prior work (e. g. , [3]). title: LOT-Bridge: A Latent Optimal Transport Bridge Based on Signed Distance Fields for Automatic Skull Defect Reconstruction
reviewer_1_strengths: S1.Results on standard benchmarks are remarkable. S2.Strong theoretical background. The paper casts the skull completion problem as an optimal transport (OT) problem in latent and data space. It then leverages principled solutions, based on previous work like Schrödinger Bridge [14] and Wasserstein Auto-Encoders [22], to solve them. S3.Novelty as a framework. While the solutions to the two OT problems are taken almost as is from previous work, putting the framework together and optimizing jointly the bridge model and the decoder to obtain better results in a completion task has not been done before to the best of my knowledge. Moreover, the use of the existing difference operator to compute an implant loss is also an interesting and application-specific contribution. S4.Thorough ablation study: the paper empirically justifies the proposed training strategy and losses by assessing the performance of the model on SkullFix when these contributions are removed and when they are added to a base model, leaving little doubt on their importance for the reported performance on this dataset. Yet, I would have preferred to see the ablation on the more challenging SkullBreak dataset. S5.Sufficient reproducibility. The paper details all the models used by referencing the original papers introducing them (with the exception of the U-Net architecture, which is stated to be the UNet in [22] for 3D data, which I couldn’t find in the reference) and extensively reports the hyperparameters of the training recipe.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: W1.Limited technical novelty. While, as discussed, the paper builds on principled previous work, two of the three claimed contributions are just the application of those results to the skull completion problem, with no changes. I’d suggest to change the claims to state that the contribution of the paper are the joint training strategy and the use of the difference operator to realize the implant loss. W2.AMB module. The third claimed contribution is the AMB module. It is a residual block with two branches: the top one is basically a 3D Squeeze-and-Excitation block with tanh activation in the end that computes a scalar delta in [-1;1] for each example in the mini-batch; the bottom branch is a convolutional block that computes a weight w in [0;1] for each voxel and each example. Then, the features inside the VQ-VAE decoder are updated as F = F + w * delta . It is claimed that when delta > 0 this is a data-driven erosion, whereas it is a dilation when delta < 0.No justification is provided for this claim. Moreover, since this happens a the feature level inside the decoder, it is not even clear to me what erosion and dilation are meant to perform in feature space. While the ablation shows that the AMB module is beneficial, and the authors claim that this is due to the adaptive morphological operator realized by the module, I suspect that it may more simply be due to the added layers and parameters. Can the authors imagine a controlled experiments where the number of parameters is controlled for? Can they explain how the module performs erosion/dilation in feature space and what is it? If this is not the case, I’d suggest to rename the module and change the narrative around it. W3.An effective baseline [A] based on data augmentation has not been considered in the experimental results. [A]. M Wodzinski, K Kwarciak, M Daniol, D Hemmerling: Improving deep learning-based automatic cranial defect reconstruction by heavy data augmentation: from image registration to latent diffusion models, Computers in Biology and Medicine, 2024 W4.The anonymous link used to share the code does not actually contain the code, but only a few generic scripts. It is basically useless for reproducibility.

title: Low-Rank Velocity Fields as a Structural Prior for Unsupervised 4D Medical Image Interpolation
reviewer_1_strengths: Well-motivated structural prior: Low-rank motion modeling aligns with the low-dimensional, spatially correlated nature of anatomical motion. Theoretical support: Provides analysis linking low-rank parameterization to smoothness energy. Effective multi-scale design: Coarse-to-fine modeling is appropriate and well-integrated. Strong empirical results: Achieves leading structure-oriented metrics under endpoint-only supervision. Clear presentation and ablation studies.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Incremental novelty: Mainly integrates existing ideas (low-rank priors, tensor decomposition, multi-scale motion). Limited clinical validation: No evaluation on downstream or clinically relevant tasks (e. g. , tracking, RT workflows). Intrinsic limitation of interpolation: Endpoint-only setting cannot capture irregular motion or excursions; the low-rank prior further biases toward smooth trajectories, potentially suppressing clinically relevant extremes. Limited evaluation scope: Only standard datasets and metrics are used.

The energy bound in Eq. 8 is loose, which holds for any linear operator and says nothing specific about the relationship between low-rank structure and the type of smoothness encouraged. A more insightful analysis would show, for instance, that the DCT-based parameterization preferentially suppresses high-frequency components of the velocity field, or that the Tucker structure induces a specific spectral decay. 2.The percentage of voxels with negative Jacobian determinant (folding) is the standard measure of deformation plausibility. The paper claims smoother, more physically plausible deformations but never reports this. 3.The chosen ranks follow a decreasing pattern from coarse to fine, which is counterintuitive. One might expect finer scales to need more degrees of freedom to capture local detail. 4.No training time, inference time, or parameter count comparisons are provided. reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The paper addresses a concrete and under-constrained clinical scenario; the setting and motivation are well articulated. 2.The Tucker decomposition is applied systematically within the 3D velocity field context; the multi-scale hierarchy is logically consistent and well implemented. 3.The low-rank prior successfully improves anatomical stability, which is crucial for physically meaningful 4D interpolation. 4.The energy bounding analysis, while simple, contributes interpretability and mathematical clarity to the model behavior. 5.Clear implementation details and consistent reporting across datasets (ACDC, 4D-Lung) support reproducibility.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The core idea—imposing low-rank or band-limited priors on motion fields—has been introduced in earlier works ([Fourier-Net 2023], [Deep-SLR 2020], etc.). The paper’s advancement mainly lies in integrating this prior within endpoint-only unsupervised interpolation, which feels primarily an application-specific adaptation rather than a conceptual leap. 2.Results show numerical improvement, but no diagnostic insights are given into why the method outperforms recent state-of-the-art diffusion or transformer-based interpolation approaches. 3.The paper does not discuss the inherent indeterminacy of endpoint-only interpolation — multiple valid motion trajectories may exist between endpoints. A deterministic velocity field assumes a single plausible path, which limits the model’s uncertainty representation. 4.Evaluation on only ACDC and 4D-Lung provides insufficient evidence of generalization across modalities or organ systems. There is no downstream validation (e.g., segmentation, registration accuracy post-interpolation). 5.Choices such as Tucker ranks, scale weights, and frequency truncation parameters (K=128) appear heuristic. Table 2’s ablation provides insights but lacks principled analysis. 6.Equation (8) and (9) provide an upper bound on smoothness energy. How tight is this bound in practice? Is there quantitative evidence correlating the theoretical bound with empirical smoothness metrics of the velocity fields? 7.Tucker decomposition introduces additional parameterization overhead. How does this compare computationally (in FLOPs and memory) with standard voxel-wise velocity networks? Does multi-scale inference significantly increase latency? 8.The paper uses truncated DCT bases. Why choose DCT over learned bases (e.g., via autoencoder or PCA initialization)? Would learned bases within the Tucker form yield better anatomical alignment? 9.The coarse-to-fine motion composition (Eq. 5) might accumulate integration error across scales. Have the authors assessed numerical stability or diffeomorphism preservation post-composition? 10.Does the low-rank velocity field correspond to interpretable anatomical modes (e.g., cardiac contraction vs. expansion)? If so, can this representation aid clinical understanding beyond interpolation? 11.Modern diffusion-based temporal interpolation (FB-Diff 2025, TMSDF 2025) implicitly models multi-modal motion distributions. How does the proposed deterministic approach relate conceptually—can low-rank parametrization be combined with diffusion sampling for uncertainty-aware interpolation?

author_feedback: We thank reviewers and AC for the comments and for recognizing the motivation, soundness, and empirical strength of our work. We clarify the points. 1.Novelty and relation to prior work (R1, R2, R3): We appreciate the reviewers’ observation that low-rank/band-limited priors have precedents. We view the novelty not as the isolated use of “low rank”, but as where and how the compact prior is imposed. In Fourier-domain registration such as Fourier-Net(AAAI 2023), compactness mainly parameterizes pairwise deformation efficiently; in structured low-rank reconstruction such as Deep-SLR(TMI 2020), the prior acts on image reconstruction; PCA/statistical respiratory models compress motion fields after estimation or from population statistics. These lines do not target endpoint-only interpolation ambiguity. Even within 4D interpolation, frequency-guided generative methods such as FB-Diff use Fourier bases to guide diffusion-based synthesis, while endpoint-only methods often use dense deformation/image prediction. Our formulation is different because the velocity tensor itself is factorized into shared spatial bases and a sample-specific Tucker core, making motion capacity explicit and controllable during endpoint-only training. Thus, the contribution is a structural velocity-field prior for stable interpolation, not a simple transfer of an existing compact representation. 2.Smoothness, folding, and deformation plausibility (AC, R2, R3): We thank the reviewers for pointing out the value of Jacobian-based folding analysis. Negative Jacobian percentage is a useful direct measure and would complement the current evaluation. Our smoothness claim is supported by components already in the paper: the truncated DCT span restricts bases to low-frequency components, the H1 regularizer penalizes velocity magnitude and spatial gradients, and the Tucker low-rank form limits motion-field degrees of freedom. Fig. 3(b) reports Effective Rank as a proxy for motion-field complexity. While not a substitute for folding statistics, it supports the intended effect of the prior: limiting overly flexible voxel-wise motion while retaining capacity for anatomical deformation. 3.Rank schedule, DCT basis, and theory (R2, R3): We appreciate these questions, as they help clarify our design. The decreasing rank schedule is intentional: coarse scales model globally coordinated anatomical motion and receive higher modal capacity, while fine scales serve as constrained residual refinements to reduce high-frequency overfitting. This matches Fig. 3(a,b), where increasing rank helps in low-capacity regimes but gains saturate as motion complexity grows. Eq. 8/9 is an interpretability result showing how bounded factors and cores control velocity energy. The spectral bias comes from the truncated DCT basis, while the Tucker form provides compact sample-dependent coefficients. 4.Computational complexity (R2, R3): We thank the reviewers for raising this practical aspect. Tucker parameterization and multi-scale processing introduce structured operations, but they also replace unrestricted voxel-wise velocity prediction with compact cores and separable spatial bases. The goal is to trade dense motion freedom for a controlled low-dimensional representation better suited to endpoint-only learning. We will clarify this trade-off. 5.Clinical validation, endpoint-only ambiguity, and uncertainty (R1, R3): We appreciate this perspective. The paper is primarily methodological: it studies endpoint-only interpolation and proposes a deterministic structural prior for coherent anatomical motion. We do not claim that a single velocity field represents all possible irregular or multi-modal trajectories. Rather, our objective is stable, structurally consistent interpolation under endpoint supervision. ACDC and 4D-Lung cover two distinct motion regimes and support this claim. Downstream validation and combination with uncertainty modeling are valuable extensions.

title: M3D-QAdapter: 3D Medical VQA with Lesion-Level Finding-Segmentation Alignment and Query-Driven Adaptive Token Reduction

reviewer_2_strengths: 1.This paper is the first to systematically investigate the impact of fine-grained, lesion-level alignment between radiology findings and 3D segmentation masks on Med-VQA performance. Rather than relying on coarse image-report level alignment as all prior works do, M3D-QAgent grounds visual features at the individual lesion level, which demonstrably benefits diagnosis-oriented tasks such as temporal diagnosis and image observation. 2.To address the dual challenges of incomplete annotations and extreme class imbalance in the ReXGroundingCT dataset, the paper proposes Safe Negative Mining — a lightweight yet effective strategy that dynamically excludes likely unannotated lesions from negative loss computation during training. Without requiring any additional annotation effort, this approach simultaneously mitigates label noise and reduces the dominance of trivial negative samples, making it a practically transferable technique beyond this specific work. 3.Unlike prior methods that apply predefined, question-agnostic token reduction, M3D-QAgent introduces a dynamic agentic workflow that first plans the anatomical region of interest based on the input question, then selects a compact and representative set of visual tokens via a novel hybrid geometry-semantics FPS. author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for appreciating our work’s clinical relevance, strong results, and novel designs, and for the constructive comments. We address major concerns below and will incorporate corresponding changes in the final version. Q1.”Agentic” terminology. [R1, R3, AC] We appreciate this question and would like to clarify. Our workflow follows the ReAct paradigm [33]: (i) plan which ROIs to scrutinize based on the input question, (ii) act by invoking external tools (SAT-Nano segmentation → hybrid FPS), and (iii) ground the answer on tool outputs. We use “agentic” to emphasize this dynamic plan–act–tool-use loop — different questions produce entirely different ROI plans, segmentation masks, and token subsets from the same CT, rather than following a predetermined path. We acknowledge that the planner is lightweight (keyword matching, ~98% hit rate), and will clarify this nuance in the revision. Q2.Attribution of gains vs. external tools/data. [R1, AC] Each contribution is isolated in Table 2.(b): +ReX w/o SNM vs w/ SNM: 73.1→74.2 Acc, 44.3→45.7 BLEU — gain comes from SNM design, not extra data alone. (c-iv): SAT + random ROI sampling: 73.1 Acc — SAT alone is insufficient. (c-iii): Hybrid FPS without SAT: 72.5 Acc — still outperforms random sampling (72.1). Additionally, we run external resources without our designs (ReX w/o SNM + SAT w/o FPS): Acc 72.5, BLEU 44.5, BERTScore 94.0, inferior to ours 74.2/45.7/94.2, confirming external tools alone yield limited gains; our designs are responsible for the majority of improvement. Q3.Computational overhead. [R1, R3, AC] Per-question latency is 4.46s vs Photon’s ~3s (on V100-32GB). The overhead comes from SAT-Nano segmentation (~2s), which only runs once per CT volume. Since in practice >15 questions are typically asked per volume (as in 3D-RAD), segmentation can be batched and the amortized cost is ~0.13s/question, reducing effective per-question latency to ~2.6s — lower than Photon. Additionally, organ segmentation is a routine clinical step; leveraging existing outputs would eliminate this overhead entirely. Q4.Single-benchmark. [R1, R3, AC] We validated M3D-QAgent on DeepTumorVQA [Chen et al., arXiv 2025] (built from 9,262 abdominal CT volumes): average Acc 69.0% vs Photon 68.6% in multi-choice tasks. The margin over the strongest baseline is preserved, demonstrating that our framework generalizes beyond the CT-RATE distribution. Q5.Privacy and reliance on external API. [R2, AC] GPT-4.1 is invoked only for ~2% fallback cases, and its sole task is to identify which organ the question refers to — a trivially simple classification receiving only question text, never imaging data or PHI. We verified that a local Qwen-2.5-7B yields >99% agreement with GPT-4.1, with negligible VQA difference (<0.1% Acc), which fully eliminates external API dependency and resolves HIPAA/GDPR concerns. Q6.Multi-region scalability. [R2] When a question spans multiple organs, the planner outputs all relevant targets, SAT segments each independently, and their masks are merged into a unified ROI for subsequent token selection. This is architecturally supported as SAT covers 104 anatomical structures. More sophisticated per-organ token budget allocation is a promising future direction. Q7.SNM threshold δ sensitivity. [R3] We swept δ∈{0.6, 0.8, 0.95}: Acc = 73.8/74.2/74.0, BERTScore = 94.1/94.2/94.2.Performance is stable (Δ≤0.4% Acc); δ=0.8 is a robust default. Q8.Clinical correctness. [R3, AC] LLM-assisted error analysis on 500 sampled open-ended cases: correct 34.1%, approximately correct (less specific or synonymous) 23.1%, localization error 32.1%, missed finding 8.8%, hallucinated 2.0%. Hallucination — the most dangerous error — is only 2.0%, and localization is less harmful than fabricating findings. Combined with SOTA on accuracy-based tasks (Table 1), this validates clinical reliability. Cross-method clinical correctness comparison will be in the revision.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper proposes M3D-QAgent, a 3D medical VQA framework that combines lesion-level finding–segmentation alignment with query-driven token reduction to support efficient and clinically meaningful reasoning on volumetric CT data. The work is well motivated and shows strong empirical performance, with a clear design that leverages fine-grained grounding and query-aware token selection to improve both efficiency and diagnostic relevance. The main concerns relate to limitations in analysis, evaluation, and clarity of the current submission. (1) There is insufficient analysis of where the performance gains come from, particularly in disentangling the contributions of lesion-level supervision, external segmentation, and the proposed components. (2) The novelty and “agentic” nature of the framework require clearer positioning, as the planning module appears closer to a structured or rule-based pipeline rather than a fully agentic reasoning system. (3) The current evaluation relies on metrics such as BLEU, ROUGE, and BERTScore, which primarily capture textual similarity and may not adequately reflect clinical correctness, particularly for medical measurement tasks requiring numerical accuracy. (4) The evidence for generalisation remains limited, as evaluation is primarily conducted on a single CT-based benchmark. (5) Practical deployment aspects, such as computational cost, reliance on external APIs, and scalability, remain to be clarified. | This paper proposes M3D-QAgent, a 3D medical VQA framework for volumetric CT that combines lesion-level grounding and query-aware token reduction to improve reasoning under limited token budgets. My assessment of this work is mixed. On one hand, the paper presents a coherent workflow-level methodological contribution, where lesion-level alignment, ROI planning, and query-aware token reduction are integrated into a technically meaningful framework for efficient 3D Med-VQA. The method demonstrates strong benchmark performance and convincing efficiency gains, and the evaluation generally follows standard protocols in the Medical-VQA literature. On the other hand, some concerns remain, including the somewhat overstated “agentic” framing, limited validation beyond a CT-based benchmark, and evaluation relying primarily on benchmark answer-matching and text-similarity metrics, which provide limited evidence of clinically grounded correctness, particularly for quantitative reasoning or measurement-related questions. Additional rebuttal results are excluded from my assessment due to MICCAI rebuttal policy and left for PC consideration. Overall, I view this paper as very borderline; however, after weighing both sides, my impression is that the workflow-level contribution and empirical evidence in the main submission may slightly outweigh the remaining weaknesses. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): The rebuttal clarifies several technical points, including the ReAct-inspired “agentic” design, the ablation isolating contributions of Safe Negative Mining and hybrid FPS, the stability of the SNM threshold, and the feasibility of replacing GPT-4.1 with a local model to address privacy concerns. Additional experiments on DeepTumorVQA and an error analysis on clinical correctness partially mitigate concerns about single-benchmark evaluation and metric limitations. However, the core issues raised by Reviewer #1 regarding incremental novelty and limited performance gains remain insufficiently resolved. The claimed improvements over strong baselines (e.g., Photon) are modest (e.g., +0.9% accuracy on 3D-RAD, +0.4% on DeepTumorVQA), and the framework’s reliance on external segmentation (SAT-Nano) and fine-grained grounding data (ReXGroundingCT) makes it difficult to attribute the majority of gains to the proposed token reduction or agentic planning alone. The rebuttal’s own ablation (external tools without proposed designs yields 72.5% vs. the full model’s 74.2%) still leaves a narrow margin, and the increased memory (36.4 GB vs. 11.9 GB) and latency (4.46 s vs. Photon’s ~3 s) trade-off is not fully justified for a clinically deployable system. Thus, despite the rebuttal’s efforts, the fundamental concerns remain and deny acceptance. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): I agree with the strength of this paper. The authors provide a strong rebuttal to R3’s comments. However, I agree that “agent” is not a suitable term for the evaluated framework; the authors should change the term in the camera-ready version.

title: MAGEFormer: Learning Metric-Consistent Representations for Anisotropic CT Segmentation
reviewer_1_strengths: This paper addresses a well-motivated and under-explored issue in anisotropic CT segmentation by explicitly modeling the mismatch between physical voxel spacing and the isotropic geometric assumptions of standard volumetric Transformers. The proposed framework is conceptually clean, with the three components targeting metric consistency at complementary stages of the pipeline, which gives the method a clear unifying principle. The experimental section is also solid: the use of a unified evaluation protocol improves the credibility of the comparison, and the reported gains in HD95, small-organ performance, and robustness under increasing anisotropy make the empirical case convincing. Overall, the work is technically sound, practically relevant, and supported by reasonably thorough validation.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The paper repeatedly contrasts the proposed framework with “isotropic preprocessing” in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion, but it is not sufficiently clear what specific preprocessing pipeline this term refers to in practice, or whether this comparison is experimentally controlled. 2.Fig. 3 provides helpful qualitative evidence for the anatomical plausibility of the proposed method, and this part would be even stronger if accompanied by a dedicated anatomy-aware or topology-aware quantitative metric. 3.The ablation in Table 3 clearly shows that all proposed components contribute positively to the final performance. It would nevertheless be helpful to report the computational overhead of the full framework more explicitly, so that readers can better assess the performance-efficiency tradeoff introduced by the geometry-aware design.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The method is conceptually coherent. The proposed components are aligned with the central claim and form a reasonably consistent geometry-aware framework. Besides, the method shows improved HD95 and competitive Dice on BTCV and FLARE22 under a unified protocol, with ablations that generally support the design choices.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The major weakness is the limited experimental positioning against prior anisotropy-aware methods. Although the paper is explicitly motivated by anisotropic CT and argues that metric-consistent internal calibration is preferable to handling anisotropy only through preprocessing or localized heuristics, the experimental comparison is made mainly against generic backbones such as nnU-Net, UNETR, Swin-UNETR, and U-Mamba. However, the paper itself notes that prior work has already explored more direct thickness-aware adaptation, including AlignShift, which is specifically introduced as an explicit architectural solution for anisotropic volumes. A direct comparison with such methods would make the paper’s empirical claims considerably more convincing.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The paper points out that ViTs assume an isotropic grid, whereas CT data are inherently anisotropic; this “metric mismatch” is a practically meaningful problem. 2.MASE, GCA, and GVV operate at the encoding, feature interaction, and inference stages respectively, forming a closed-loop design. 3.The method shows more pronounced improvements on anisotropy-sensitive organs such as the adrenal glands and pancreas, which aligns with the intended design.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The proposed modules are closely related to existing methods (e.g., RoPE, attention bias, and TTA), and lack clear distinctive innovation. Specifically, MASE is similar to extensions of RoPE; GCA resembles relative position bias; and GVV is comparable to test-time augmentation. 2.The paper does not report model parameters, FLOPs, or inference time, making it difficult to assess the practical computational cost. 3.Figure 1 is relatively complex and not very easy to interpret.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers (R1–R3) for recognizing MAGEFormer’s geometry-aware design and consistent boundary-accuracy improvements. Experimental scope and positioning vs. AlignShift (R2). AlignShift is cited in our introduction as a representative anisotropy-aware operator-level design, complementary in scope. It is a TSM-inspired, parameter-free 2D-to-3D operator validated for lesion detection on DeepLesion with 2D-pretrained backbones. MAGEFormer instead asks whether the physical spacing metric should be embedded inside a 3D Transformer’s representation, interaction, and inference. A direct benchmark would entangle the metric-consistency question with three confounding axes: task (detection vs. segmentation), backbone (2D-converted vs. native 3D Transformer), and operator-vs-representation locus. We therefore follow the canonical 3D protocol on BTCV/FLARE 22 with standard 3D baselines (nnU-Net, UNETR, Swin-UNETR, U-Mamba, TransUNet) under identical folds, input crop, training schedule, and metric pipeline. Existing evidence isolates the contribution: As shown in Table 3 (+9.24 Dice / −64.63 mm HD95 vs. same-backbone baseline); and Fig. 2(a) shows the gain widens with anisotropy ratio r (n=80), a trend reproduced under synthetic z-degradation in Fig. 2(b). An operator-level cross-paradigm comparison is left to future work. Paradigm / Novelty (R2, R3). Our contribution is structural, not operator-level: physical spacing is promoted from a preprocessing input to a first-class representation variable propagated across encoding, interaction, and inference. Within this framing, MASE, GCA, and GVV instantiate one substrate (the spacing metric G^(0) and its stage-wise propagation s^(ℓ)) at three loci where anisotropic mismatch enters: intra-scale self-attention, cross-scale skip alignment, and inference-time discretization. The surface resemblance to RoPE, relative bias, and TTA is therefore only operator-level: those mechanisms operate on voxel indices rather than enforce metric consistency across stages. Table 3 confirms this complementarity: each component contributes (MASE −38.07 / GCA −40.94 / GVV −12.26 mm HD95) yet their composition is strictly stronger (MASE+GCA 18.76 mm; full 10.58 mm), with the gap widening in the high-anisotropy regime predicted by the design (Fig. 2a–b). Computational efficiency (R1, R3). MAGEFormer is backbone-preserving; the added parameters reduce to a few head-shared scalars per stage (γ̂^(ℓ), τ̂^(ℓ), r̂_a^(ℓ)), a count negligible relative to the backbone. MASE re-parameterizes the existing rotary phase via voxel spacing with no new weights (Sec. 2.2); GCA reuses windowed cross-attention with a shared metric-derived bias (Eq. 6, Sec. 2.3); GVV is parameter-free (Sec. 2.4). At inference, MAGEFormer with GVV matches flip/rotation TTA with a ~4× speedup (Fig. 2c). Table 3 also exposes a trade-off: MASE+GCA without GVV (single-pass, backbone-equivalent cost) attains 0.8295 / 18.76 mm; enabling GVV refines this to 0.8411 / 10.58 mm when boundary fidelity is prioritized. Other clarifications (R1, R3). By “isotropic preprocessing” we mean the conventional resampling/normalization setting where models operate on voxel-index neighborhoods as if geometrically uniform; this is not a separately tuned baseline, and we will make this explicit. Boundary evidence already combines HD95 with per-organ results on anisotropy-sensitive structures (adrenal glands, pancreas), with robustness (Fig. 2a–b), and with qualitative fragmentation/void cases (Fig. 3); topology-aware metrics are a useful complementary axis. Fig. 1 will be revised to separate architectural flow from geometric motivation.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper focused ona under explored problem with technical innovation. Reviewers has minor concerns that the authors can address. | The AC thinks the paper provides limited insights on medical segmentation tasks, but the paper is of high quality and well written. Reviewers also agreed on the metrics and contribution. Recommend accept. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): As noted by the reviewers, considering the effects of voxel spacing on medical image segmentation is clinically relevant and interesting. The reviewers’ comments are minor and have been adequately addressed in the rebuttal. Therefore, I recommend acceptance. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper proposes MAGEFormer, a geometry-calibrated Transformer framework for anisotropic CT segmentation. It embeds physical voxel spacing as a first-class representation variable through three components: Metric-Adaptive Spatial Embedding (MASE) for spacing-calibrated positional frequencies, Geometry-Constrained Attention (GCA) for suppressing physically implausible feature correlations, and Geometric View Voting (GVV) for inference-time discretization-bias reduction. Evaluated on BTCV and FLARE22 under a unified protocol against CNN and Transformer baselines, the method achieves strong boundary accuracy (10.58 mm HD95 on BTCV, 3.40 mm HD95 on FLARE22) with consistent Dice gains.Reviewers agreed that the metric-mismatch problem is practically meaningful and under-explored, the three components form a coherent closed-loop design across encoding/interaction/inference stages, the empirical gains on anisotropy-sensitive organs (adrenal, pancreas) align with the design intent, and the unified evaluation protocol increases comparison credibility. They raised several concerns: (1) the “isotropic preprocessing” baseline is not clearly defined or experimentally controlled; (2) anisotropy-aware baselines such as AlignShift are not directly compared; (3) computational overhead (parameters, FLOPs, inference time) was not initially reported; (4) the components are surface-similar to RoPE, relative position bias, and TTA, raising novelty concerns; (5) topology-aware or boundary-specific quantitative metrics could strengthen Fig. 3’s anatomical plausibility claims; and (6) Figure 1 is complex and not easy to interpret.After rebuttal, the authors reframed the contribution as structural (promoting physical spacing to a first-class metric variable propagated across stages) rather than operator-level, clarified that AlignShift comparison would entangle multiple confounding axes (task, backbone, locus), explained computational efficiency (negligible added parameters, GVV ~4× faster than flip/rotation TTA), and defined the “isotropic preprocessing” terminology. All three reviewers maintain or raise their recommendations to Accept.

title: MamaDino: Mammography-Aware Multi-view Attentional DINO for 3-Year Breast Cancer Risk Prediction
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.Well-motivated architectural design. The combination of frozen self-supervised DINOv3 features (global semantics) with trainable SE-ResNeXt101 (local texture sensitivity) via cross-attention is principled and well-argued. The rationale that CNN tokens query ViT tokens to integrate globally coherent features into the texture-sensitive stream is architecturally elegant. 2.BilateralMixer is a genuine contribution. The three-step bilateral fusion — symmetric CLS-based transformer encoding, gated asymmetry weighting via |eL−eR|, and symmetric feature composition (asymmetry + concordance) — explicitly encodes the clinical reasoning process of comparing left and right breasts. This is the most novel component and the ablation (0.736 vs. 0.731 for simple concatenation) confirms its value, albeit with modest gains. 3.Rigorous evaluation design. Matched case-control test cohorts (in-distribution and OOD from an unseen site) with DeLong’s 95% CIs demonstrate proper evaluation methodology. The OOD cohort from Oxford with different scanner mix (including GE and Hologic) provides genuine external validation. 4.Comprehensive subgroup analysis. Table 2 stratifies by age, ethnicity, scanner manufacturer, cancer type (DCIS vs. invasive), and tumour grade. This level of subgroup analysis is essential for clinical translation and exceeds what many risk prediction papers provide. 5.Competitive performance at substantially lower resolution. Matching Mirai at ~13x fewer pixels is practically meaningful for computational deployment, memory constraints, and potential privacy-preserving applications where resolution reduction may be desirable. 6.Thorough ablation study. Resolution ablations (224, 320, 512), single-stream ablations (DINO-only, SE-ResNeXt-only), and bilateral fusion ablation (concatenation vs. BilateralMixer) systematically isolate the contribution of each design choice. 7.Honest limitations discussion. The authors transparently note that Mirai was evaluated without retraining (using its released model), UK-only data, under-representation of Siemens and non-White groups, and the inability to fully disentangle resolution vs. architecture effects. This level of honesty is commendable.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.Confidence intervals overlap on all key comparisons. The headline claims of “matching or exceeding Mirai” must be qualified: on the OOD set, MamaDino achieves 0.677 (0.647–0.707) vs. Mirai 0.666 (0.635–0.696). These CIs substantially overlap. On the in-distribution set, MamaDino’s 0.736 (0.710–0.762) vs. Mirai’s 0.713 (0.686–0.740) also overlap. While the point estimates favor MamaDino, statistical significance is not established. The paper should explicitly state this rather than framing results as “slightly outperforming. “ 2.Mirai comparison is not fully controlled. Mirai is run at its native resolution (1664x2048) using the released model, while MamaDino is trained on OPTIMAM data. The authors acknowledge this but it remains a substantial confounder: Mirai was trained on different data (US-based cohort) and uses clinical covariates that were unavailable here. A fairer comparison would retrain Mirai (or at least its CNN backbone) on the same OPTIMAM data at the same resolution. Without this, we cannot determine whether the gains come from architecture, training data advantage, or resolution sensitivity of Mirai’s specific weights. 3.Ablation CIs not reported for baselines. Table 1 reports CIs only for Mirai and full MamaDino. The DINO-only, SE-ResNeXt-only, resolution ablations, and concatenation ablation lack CIs, making it impossible to assess whether these differences are meaningful. The BilateralMixer gain (0.736 vs. 0.731) is very small and could easily be within noise without CI. 4.Limited calibration analysis. For a risk prediction model intended for clinical deployment, discrimination (AUC) alone is insufficient. No calibration analysis (e. g. , expected calibration error, calibration curves) is reported. In risk-adapted screening, the absolute risk probability matters for threshold-based decisions, not just ranking. 5.Case-control sampling limits generalizability. The matched case-control design, while standard for validation studies, does not permit assessment of the model’s calibration or positive predictive value in a screening population. The 1:2 and 1:4 case-control ratios artificially inflate the case prevalence, and the OOD set composition (ethnicity largely unavailable) limits demographic generalizability assessment.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: A major strength of the study is the inclusion of an external validation cohort, which increases confidence that the reported performance is not due to overfitting to the development dataset. The paper reports subgroup analyses across several clinically relevant groups, which is useful for understanding model behavior in different populations and settings. In addition, the study somehow considered several ablation-style comparisons, including DINO only, SE ResNeXt only, different input resolutions, and a different patient-level fusion.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.One major concern is that the paper does not provide a good / resonable motivation for using undersampled mammograms for risk prediction. However, the manuscript repeatedly emphasizes that the proposed model can achieve near SOTA performance despite using lower resolution inputs. I would recommend substantially revising the abstract and introduction to better justify this design choice and to tone down the corresponding claims. From a clinical perspective, higher resolution images are often needed to capture subtle imaging features. This may also help explain why MIRAI appears to perform more consistently in the DCIS subgroup, whereas the proposed method seems somewhat weaker in that setting. 2.In the comparison experiments, the DINO branch uses pretrained frozen weights only. It is not clear why the authors chose not to finetune DINO (the vit) for the breast cancer risk prediction task. The manuscript does not appear to provide a clear justification for this design choice. 3.The manuscript does not clearly describe the distribution of time to cancer in the study population. In addition, the test cohorts are constructed using a matched case-control design, which limits the clinical interpretation of the results. In particular, we don’t know the performance under a realistic screening prevalence setting. Or maybe the models have a higher false positive rate? 4.Although the manuscript provides good subgroup analyses, the overall workload of the experiments is still somewhat limited. The number of comparison methods is relatively small. At least more baselines are always welcome and helpful. For example, in Table 1, confidence intervals and OOD results are only reported for a subset of methods. In contrast, the ablation results are reported less comprehensively, without confidence intervals and without corresponding OOD evaluation. This somewhat reduces the overall quality.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The paper proposes a potentially interesting multi view and bilateral architecture, explicitly modeling contralateral asymmetry, a clinically meaningful inductive bias for mammography based risk prediction. The combination of frozen self supervised DINOv3 features with a trainable CNN encoder reflects a thoughtful attempt to leverage complementary inductive biases (global contextual reasoning vs. local texture sensitivity). The model is trained on a large-scale dataset (OPTIMAM, >53k women) and evaluated both in distribution and out of distribution, which strengthens confidence in generalization. Performance is reported across multiple strata (age, ethnicity, scanner, tumor type and grade), which is a strong and commendable aspect rarely included in similar work. Achieving performance comparable to Mirai at significantly reduced resolution is potentially impactful for scalability and deployment in real world screening settings.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The architectural description lacks clarity. Specifically, the sections “Backbone encoders and cross attention” and “BridgeMixer block”, together with Figures 1a and 1b, should be revised to more clearly illustrate data flow, view specific inputs, parallel processing, and fusion points. The motivation for the cross attention fusion between DINOv3 and SE ResNeXt101 features is not fully justified, and it remains unclear what complementary information each branch uniquely contributes beyond empirical performance. Dataset usage is ambiguous: while 53,883 women are reported for training, the exact composition of training, validation, and test cohorts is unclear. It is not explicitly stated whether in distribution test cases are fully held out from OPTIMAM or included in the reported total, nor how validation data were used. Ethical statment of the additional datasets apart from OPTIMAM are not included. The training strategy is insufficiently described: it is unclear whether the SE ResNeXt101 view specific branches, the DINOv3-SEResNetXt101 cross attention module, and the BridgeMixer remaining blocks are trained jointly end to end or in separate stages. Although the paper claims to assess inductive biases, the experimental design does not include a full resolution comparison analogous to Mirai’s setting, making it difficult to conclude whether inductive bias (rather than resolution reduction alone) drives the results. No interpretability or explanation is provided for the predicted risk scores (e.g., saliency, attention maps, or bilateral importance), which is a notable limitation for a clinical risk prediction model. Relevant prior work, such as AsymMirai and recent surveys on mammography based risk modeling, are not cited, limiting the contextualization and comparison of the contribution.
