author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for the constructive feedback. We group concerns below and point to existing manuscript text where applicable. (I) Resolution (R2,R3). We agree that the abstract/introduction overemphasise low resolution. The 512×512 setting reflects our training compute budget, not a claim that lower resolution is preferable. We do not advocate low-resolution mammography in clinical practice. §4 ¶2 already states this “Lower resolution was … a controlled stress-test of representation and fusion choices, rather than to argue against high-resolution” and the Conclusion echoes the same point, but we agree this framing must move to abstract and introduction. Camera-ready will: (a) frame the contribution as complementary CNN–ViT representations plus explicit bilateral fusion; (b) clarify that 512×512 reflects our compute budget rather than a preference. We also acknowledge R2’s point on DCIS subgroup gap (Tab.2) may be consistent with downsampling attenuating fine-scale signal, and will note this limitation explicitly. (II) MIRAI comparison(R1,R3). As R1 notes, §4 ¶4 (Limitations) addresses this point transparently, but we agree and our camera-ready will point at this more visibly. In applying pretrained MIRAI to unseen cohorts, we follow Yala et al.’s own external-validation paradigm. We see the point of R1 about “matches or slightly exceeds”, and we propose that camera-ready will say “comparable, with overlapping CIs”. To clarify, MIRAI is included as a strong external reference, evaluated with its released model and intended preprocessing. Thus, we do not use MIRAI to argue architectural superiority. The controlled evidence for our design comes from ablations under the same preprocessing and input settings: DINO-only 0.621, SE-ResNeXt-only 0.668, max aggr. 0.727, concat. 0.731, and BilateralMixer 0.736.(III) Ablation gains(R1,R2,R3). The core contribution is the integrated architecture, not any single block. Tab. 1 reports three converging ablations at matched 512×512: DINO-only 0.621→MamaDino 0.736 (+0.115); SE-ResNeXt-only 0.668→MamaDino 0.736 (+0.068); and max aggr.→BilateralMixer: 0.727→0.736 in-distribution and 0.666→0.677 OOD. §4 ¶1 already states that these gains are not attributable to any single component. The +0.005 BilateralMixer-vs-concat gain is small in isolation; its value lies in being one of three stacked architectural changes, not a standalone gain. We will mark this more explicitly. (IV) DINOv3(R2). We agree that fine-tuning is a natural next step. We froze DINOv3 to test it as a self-supervised prior, consistent with our Introduction and recent medical DINOv3 studies using frozen/off-the-shelf encoders [9,13]. Task-specific learning was instead concentrated in SE-ResNeXt, cross-attention, and BilateralMixer. This kept the four-view model tractable under our compute budget and avoided adding a large ViT fine-tuning/hyperparameter-search dimension. We do not claim freezing is optimal; full or parameter-efficient fine-tuning is future work. (V) Data, case-control, calibration(R1,R2,R3). The in-distribution test set is held out and patient-disjoint from train/val.; the OOD cohort is from Oxford, an unseen OPTIMAM site, not an additional dataset. The 3-year target is defined in §2.1 as cancer within three years after baseline screening or screen-detected malignancy at next routine screen. We agree that matched case-control design supports discrimination assessment, but not calibration, PPV, or deployment thresholds under real screening prevalence; §4 already states this limitation. R3: 53,883 women refers to the training cohort, while test cohorts are reported separately in §2.1.(VI) Clarity, citations(R3,R2). Staged training is described in §2.3: Stage1 trains SE-ResNeXt plus cross-attention with DINOv3 frozen; Stage2 freezes the fusion encoder and trains only BilateralMixer. We will reference this earlier, clarify Fig.1 to show view-specific paths and fusion points, and cite AsymMirai and Mendes review.

title: MammoFlow: Multiview Mammogram Synthesis with Anatomically Consistent Flow Matching
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The paper addresses a clinically relevant problem in multiview mammography, where paired CC and MLO views are essential for accurate diagnosis but are often limited in availability for data-driven models. 2.The proposed method incorporates geometric prior knowledge into the generative process. In particular, the use of an alignment module combined with a distribution-level consistency constraint based on EMD provides a meaningful way to enforce cross-view anatomical consistency. 3.The experimental results demonstrate improved image quality and include both quantitative evaluation and expert radiologist assessment, which strengthens the practical relevance of the work. The reported improvement in downstream classification performance further supports the utility of the generated data.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The methodological description lacks clarity in several aspects. While the paper introduces multiple components, the overall training pipeline is not clearly described. In particular, the inputs and outputs during both training and inference stages are not explicitly defined, making it difficult to fully understand how the system operates end-to-end. 2.The presentation of the framework is somewhat fragmented, with individual modules described in isolation. A more structured explanation of the data flow and optimization process would improve readability and reproducibility. 3.Figure 3 is difficult to interpret. In particular, it is unclear what the inputs and corresponding outputs are in the figure, making it hard to follow the intended process. The main text also does not provide sufficient explanation to guide the reader through this figure. 4.The alignment process is based on a 2D affine transformation search, but the physical plausibility of such transformations in the context of breast deformation is not sufficiently discussed. Given the complex deformation between CC and MLO views, more justification or analysis of the alignment strategy would strengthen the method.

author_feedback: We thank reviewers for recognizing our work’s clinical relevance (R1), EMD-guided flow matching value (R2), and physical plausibility (R3). R1W1.Training & inference pipeline: Training input is a pair of raw mammograms and the corresponding text prompt, encoded for L_CRF. The images are also used to compute the alignment for L_EMD on the one-step reconstructed image. Inference takes only Gaussian noise and a prompt to generate novel paired views; no alignment is needed. R1W2.Presentation: We will revise Sec. 2 to clarify the full pipeline: training uses real pairs to compute losses, while inference uses only the trained model with noise and pre-defined prompts. R1W3.Fig. 3: Fig. 3 shows 2 random CC&MLO pairs generated from Gaussian noise with the same prompt per method. Col. 1 shows GT images. Rows 1-2 show synthetic cases. The final row plots the aligned view and AP-axis tissue distribution for case 2.Arrows highlight artifacts. R1W4.2D affine alignment: Affine alignment corrects macroscopic positioning, e.g., acquisition angle. Nonrigid deformation is mitigated by spatial relaxation with 1D Gaussian smoothing (Sec. 2.2). Removing it greatly degrades generation (Tab. 2; FID 53.3 to 74.7). Since EMD targets macro-level optimization, we use efficient affine alignment over complex nonrigid estimation. R2W1.Contribution: We add a novel anatomical regularizer, orthogonal to the base model. Since Mammo-RGB and Vanilla also use SD3.5, improvements in Tab. 1 isolate our method’s direct impact. R2W2.Prior constraints: Prior methods treat views separately[1,6], stack them[7], or translate from a GT reference with oversimplified fixed rotation[12]. We model the physical multiview relation: aligned AP-axis tissue distributions should match because they share a breast volume. EMD gives a direct, differentiable anatomical training signal. R2W3.GT alignment: Pre-computed alignment is a training-only prior used to measure AP-axis consistency on one-step predictions. At inference, no GT labels or alignments are used, as the model has learned the correspondence. R2W4.ΔEMD/ΔJSD: We compute EMD/JSD, denoted as D, between CC and aligned MLO AP-axis distributions, and average over the test set. Metric: ΔD=100×|mean(D_syn)−mean(D_GT)|/mean(D_GT). Lower values mean synthetic pairs better match real image statistics. R2W5.Evaluation alignment: No alignment during inference. We apply affine alignment only when computing EMD/JSD for paired images. All other evaluations use raw synthetic images without alignment. R3W1.Clinical need: MammoFlow augments data-limited, imbalanced training. Cancer cases and reliable synthetic CC/MLO pairs are rare. Since radiologists rely on cross-view correspondence, single-view realism is insufficient; synthesized pairs must be anatomically consistent to be useful(p. 2). R3W2.Relation to SOTA: Single-view synthesis[1,6] lacks CC/MLO consistency. View translation[12] requires a GT reference. Tumor artifacting[R3.2] generates single-view images from existing data and may lead to incorrect anatomy. [7] ignores physical relationships. We instead regularize AP-axis correspondence to synthesize novel images. R3W3.Suggested works: [R3.1] resamples real data rather than synthesizes new data, and [R3.2] injects GT tumors to healthy images. Both operate on existing data and don’t create new paired morphologies. We provide constrained paired synthesis with better diversity, which can be combined with these methods. R3W4.Downstream task: We classify binary breast cancer. Prompts control healthy/cancerous label during generation. We fine-tune MammoFlow only on malignant cases to generate malignant pairs, used only to balance classifier training distribution (Sec. 3.1). R3W5.Strengths & limitations: Synthetic mammograms don’t replace clinical data, but anatomical consistency improves their utility (Tab. 1,3,4). Limitations (memory cost, affine approximation, imperfect preprocessing) are in Sec. 4 and will be expanded.

Everything is integrated into a flow-matching generative model. The reviewers agree that the motivation is sound. The use of geometric priors and EMD to enforce cross-view consistency seems to be novel and physically meaningful. The inclusion of radiologist assessment strengthen the work. At the same time, the reviewers identified multiple issues, that must be addressed in a rebuttal. These include that the training and inference pipeline are insufficiently described. Also the 2D affine alignment model requires further justification given complex breast deformations. The presentation of the method needs to be improved. Additionally, discussion about the clinical need of such synthesized data is required, also in view of other related works, as listed by R#3. | The authors addressed the main issues raised by the reviewers in the rebuttal and all reviewers agree on the acceptance of this work. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper’s contribution lies in integrating Earth Mover’s Distance as a cross-view consistency objective within a flow matching–based framework for multi-view mammogram generation. The formulation is technically sound and well-motivated for the problem setting. The reviewers converged on a positive recommendation, and I concur with this consensus in supporting acceptance. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The reviewers highlight the clinical relevance of the targeted problem, the novel use of EMD-based distribution constraint to enforce cross-view anatomical consistency, and the solid experimental results supported by both quantitative evaluation and radiologist assessment. title: MaRS: Robust Out-of-Distribution Detection via Mahalanobis Residual Scoring
reviewer_1_strengths: The paper addresses an important problem in medical image analysis with an approach that is built logically. The intuition that anisotropies in the (reconstructed) feature manifold may be helpful for OOD detection is very reasonable and nicely exploited. An analysis of the different eigenvalues is presented as evidence of the underlying hypothesis. Results are formulated in terms of AUROC over multiple runs, which is the right direction to assess consistency in this case. Several types of distribution shifts are analyzed in the different datasets, thus helping to understand performance across application scenarios. Claims are formulated appropriately to the study by stating that “MaRS consistently outperforms latent-space and reconstruction-based baselines”, leaving the judgement on the state of the art to future systematic evaluations or community experience.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The selection of datasets used for experiments leaves several open questions and is not fully aligned with the goals stated in the introduction. In fact, despite the mention of OpenMIBOOD, MaRS is benchmarked on MIDOG only, leaving out PhaKIR and OASIS-3 without justification. Instead, the authors choose to report results on two datasets from the MedMNIST+ collection with OOD tasks engineered by separating a label subset. This is also somewhat incomplete, as MedMNIST+ has many more datasets, and is described in a rather confused way towards the end of the “Datasets” paragraph of section 3.1.On the one hand, results on incomplete subsets raise the question of whether they hold for the missing entries. This question persists in the ablation studies which are restricted to one of the three benchmarks and the other two respectively. On the other hand, the stated goal is detecting “changes in patient populations, imaging devices, acquisition protocols, and artefacts”. X-ray results address population and part of MIDOG addresses target scanners, but the rest of MIDOG and dermatoscopy address semantic shifts. 2.While running experiments with three different seeds goes in the right direction, the statistical analysis needs better reporting. For a start, runs are not reported individually (e. g. with median [min, max]). Most critically, the details of the Wilcoxon signed-rank test are not specified. Since 3 metric pairs at the dataset-split level would be insufficient for statistical significance, it seems that the test has been performed at the image or pixel level, but the specification is missing. It would also be helpful to report the type of averaging for the metrics in general. Finally, the comment on Mahalanobis++ being deterministic was insufficient for me to understand how the comparison is performed in that case. 3.The comparison between confidence-based and reconstruction-based methods could be considered unfair, since reconstruction trains small multilayer models while confidence-based methods are limited to a linear head. A small ablation would have been helpful to reduce this confounder. 4.While the authors comment on the stability of the estimation of the covariance matrix in the case of Mahalanobis++ in section 3.3 Backbone size / Results, the justification that follows does not state clearly why the same estimation is expected not to be an issue in the case of MaRS. Because of the many parameters that are being estimated, it would be helpful to relate “high-dimensional variability” and “preserving directions most sensitive to distributional shifts” to quantitative measures.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The paper is well written and easy to follow. The problem of OOD detection in medical imaging is well motivated, and the core argument that the failure of reconstruction-based methods stems from scoring rather than reconstruction quality is presented clearly. 2.Evaluation spans three imaging modalities 3.The paper includes ablation studies on key design choices, which helps isolate the contribution of individual components.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.While the paper reports mean FPR, this aggregation may obscure clinically relevant variability across datasets. In safety-critical medical imaging applications, per-dataset FPR values would allow readers to assess whether the aggregate gains of MaRS reflect consistent improvements or are driven by strong performance on a subset of datasets. Given the importance of FPR in deployment contexts, reporting per-dataset FPR alongside the existing mean would substantially strengthen the empirical evaluation. 2.The performance gain by MaRS over other approaches like Mahalanobis++ and Residual (Table 1) is modest. However, MaRS introduces two sources of additional computational cost: the training and inference overhead of the autoencoder, and the estimation of the full covariance matrix over residuals required for Mahalanobis scoring. It is therefore unclear whether this marginal gain justifies adoption over computationally cheaper alternatives. 3.The authors justify using pre-normalization features for MaRS by arguing that LayerNorm suppresses variance anisotropy, and that preserving this structure benefits Mahalanobis-based scoring. However this argument applies equally to Mahalanobis++ which also relies on a covariance matrix to capture anisotropic structure. Figure 3 shows that Mahalanobis++ performance decreases under pre-normalization, while MaRS improves. If anisotropy preservation were the primary explanatory factor, both methods should benefit from pre-norm features given their shared reliance on covariance estimation. The authors do not account for this asymmetry, leaving their justification incomplete.
reviewer_2_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The paper is mathematically sound and based on simple PCA and Mahalanobis metric concepts The paper is evaluated across multiple datasets
reviewer_3_weaknesses: While the paper does compare with different OOD methods, none of the compared methods are state-of-the-art in the medical domain, which makes it challenging to establish the merit of the proposed method in the context of medical data. For example, the OpenMIBOOD (2025) dataset while mentioned, is not evaluated. It is not clear how part 1 of Figure 1 is related to the proposed approach in the paper. The experimental section in the paper talks about DinoV2 and other unsupervised models. Where does the decoder component come in these cases? The setup should be more clearly defined. There are some minute writing. Unnecessary dashes at the end of words such as “reconstructions” and “residual” are present in the Introduction section. Similar dashes appear at several other places in the paper.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for their thoughtful feedback. We are encouraged that they recognized the importance of OOD detection (R1,R2), the soundness of our formulation (R1,R3), the usefulness of anisotropic residual structure for this task (R1), and the clarity of our work (R1,R2,R3). We also appreciate the positive assessment of extensive evaluation (R1,R2,R3), strong baselines (R1), and ablations on backbone choice and normalization (R1,R2). We address major concerns below. [R2] What is novel beyond standard Mahalanobis scoring? We respectfully clarify that MaRS is not a simple re-use of Mahalanobis scoring. Our work shows that covariance estimation on reconstruction residuals is more informative for OOD detection than on raw embeddings. Specifically, Sec. 3.2 quantitatively demonstrates that after subtracting the learned ID projection, the OOD signal concentrates in anisotropic low-variance residual directions, making Mahalanobis scoring effective. This leads to a label-free method that replaces class-conditional statistics with global ID residual covariance and significantly outperforms the class-dependent Mahalanobis++ (Maha++). [R1,R2] Why does pre-LayerNorm help MaRS but not Maha++? Because MaRS and Maha++ estimate covariance in fundamentally different spaces. Maha++ estimates covariance directly on embeddings, where variance mixes semantic and class variation. In raw embeddings, this anisotropy is not necessarily aligned with OOD-relevant directions. MaRS instead subtracts the learned ID manifold projection and estimates covariance on reconstruction residuals. There, low-variance directions reflect stable ID reconstruction behavior, so deviations along them are informative OOD signals (Fig. 2). LayerNorm suppresses this residual variance structure, explaining why MaRS benefits from pre-normalization whereas Maha++ does not. We thank the reviewers for allowing us to clarify this important distinction. [R1,R3] Could you clarify the dataset choice? Yes, we did not categorically exclude OpenMIBOOD, but limited our evaluation to MIDOG (from OpenMIBOOD) due to access and scope constraints. OASIS-3 is access-restricted and approval was not available in time. PhaKIR focuses on surgical endoscopy, whereas our evaluation targets broad, established 2D imaging modalities where off-the-shelf foundation-model embeddings are commonly utilized. We therefore focused on histopathology, chest X-ray, and dermatoscopy, including diverse distribution shifts. [R1,R2] Are the FPR95 gains consistent, and how was significance tested? MaRS consistently outperforms the strongest unsupervised reference method (Residual), while also improving over Maha++ on several settings. Following Table 1, FPR95 (lower is better) for MaRS/Maha++/Residual is: MIDOG-CS 30/32/35, nearOOD 53/52/57, farOOD 0/0/0, X-Ray 36/40/40, Derma 94/94/95.The Wilcoxon test was computed on the 15 paired aggregate results from 5 dataset splits and 3 runs, yielding p=0.018.We reiterate that MaRS is fully unsupervised and does, in contrast to Maha++, not rely on the availability of class labels. [R2] Does MaRS justify its computational cost over Mahalanobis++? Yes, MaRS is computationally lightweight. AE training is one-time and takes only a few minutes on cached embeddings using our small two-layer MLP encoder-decoder. At inference, MaRS adds only minimal overhead from one embedding-level AE forward pass. It then computes a single Mahalanobis score in residual space using one global ID residual covariance. In contrast, Maha++ computes Mahalanobis distances to all class-specific means using a shared embedding covariance. Thus, MaRS is label-free and avoids class-dependent computation, thereby scaling more favorably as the number of classes increases. [R3] What does decoder mean in Fig. 1? The decoder in Fig. 1 is part of our proposed autoencoder module and reconstructs feature embeddings, not images, as detailed in the caption.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Please prioritize addressing the key issues raised by the reviewers, including justifying the dataset choices and missing benchmarks (e.g., OpenMIBOOD), reporting per-dataset metrics (especially FPR) with clearer statistical details, and clarifying whether the observed gains justify the additional computational cost, including the pre-normalization versus Mahalanobis++ discrepancy. | This paper introduces MaRS, a post-hoc out-of-distribution detection method for medical imaging that operates on reconstruction residuals from a lightweight autoencoder trained on in-distribution representations. The use of Mahalanobis distance in the reconstruction-residual space is a novel and well-motivated contribution, and the method is practically appealing as a lightweight post-hoc approach. While some reviewers raised concerns that the empirical gains are marginal, the authors’ rebuttal provides acceptable clarifications regarding the dataset choices and includes corresponding t-tests to support the statistical validity of the reported improvements. Overall, the rebuttal addresses most of the crucial concerns, and the remaining issues do not appear severe enough to outweigh the paper’s novelty and practical relevance. Therefore, the paper is recommended for acceptance. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): After rebuttal, a single reviewer is in favor of the paper. Even that reviewer finds the rebuttal only partly convincing and sees the paper as being acceptable only by a small margin. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): As stated by reviewer 1, the authors addressed some of the key concerns in the limited space available in the rebuttal. The paper presents a valuable modification to a popular OOD detection method which could be interesting to a big part of the community.

title: Mask-Guided Attention Regulation for Anatomically Consistent Counterfactual CXR Synthesis
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.Well-motivated problem formulation The paper addresses a known issue in diffusion-based medical image editing, namely structural drift during generation, and clearly articulates the challenges of maintaining anatomical consistency while introducing localized pathological changes. 2.Training-free and flexible design A key strength of the method is that it operates entirely at inference time without requiring retraining or additional learnable modules. This makes the approach flexible and potentially easier to apply across datasets or domains compared to methods that rely on task-specific training.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.Unclear applicability to high-resolution medical imaging Chest X-rays are typically high-resolution images (e. g. , 1024×1024 or higher), which are important for detecting subtle pathological patterns. However, the paper does not clearly specify the resolution at which the method operates or evaluate its performance at clinically relevant resolutions. If the method is limited to lower resolutions, it may only capture coarse changes, significantly limiting its clinical usefulness. 2.Limited clinical relevance of the constrained editing setup The method constrains generation within lung regions using segmentation masks. While this may improve quantitative metrics by restricting modifications to a smaller area, most clinically relevant findings in CXR are already concentrated in the lung region. Therefore, preserving or improving non-target regions (outside the lungs) may have limited clinical value, and the reported gains may not fully reflect meaningful improvements for diagnosis. 3.Questionable clinical utility of counterfactual CXR generation The clinical motivation for counterfactual generation in CXR is not sufficiently clarified. While counterfactual analysis is often valuable in complex diseases with multiple interacting factors or unclear mechanisms (e. g. , neurodegenerative disorders), its role in CXR—where many findings are more directly observable—remains unclear. The paper does not convincingly demonstrate what specific clinical questions or workflows this approach would support. 4.Lack of clear clinical application scenario Although the paper claims potential benefits such as data augmentation and interpretability, it does not provide concrete clinical use cases or evaluations (e. g. , reader studies or downstream clinical tasks) to support these claims. As a result, the practical impact of the generated counterfactual images remains uncertain.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.Operating solely at inference time, which provides computational efficiency. 2.The lung masks utilized in this study are automatically segmented based on high image contrast, facilitating the acquisition of large-scale data and ensuring high accuracy without the need for manual annotation by medical specialists. Furthermore, the characteristics of the lungs, which possess stability in position and shape, contribute to the model learning consistent spatial reference points.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.Table 1 shows only marginal performance gains over prior work. The proposed method fails to outperform ‘ProgEmu’ on both LPIPS and FID (bold formatting appears to be incorrectly applied in the table). 2.The paper cites InstructX2X[18] in the introduction ‘Structural instability’. Given that InstructX2X adopts a similar mask-and-prompt-based editing strategy, it is recommend to be included as a baseline in the SOTA comparison of Table 1. 3.In Figure 2, cardiomegaly represents pathological enlargement of the heart, and thus the pathology token’s attention should be concentrated on the cardiac region. However, since Omega is derived from the lung segmentation mask (M_anat), the cardiac region either falls entirely outside the mask or is only indirectly captured at the boundary where the lung and heart overlap. As a result, the cross-attention amplification (Eq. 6) cannot accurately target the cardiac region, and the self-attention gating (Eq. 5) may even suppress information flow toward the heart. It would be worth clarifying which specific design choice accounts for the visually plausible ‘mild cardiomegaly’ result shown in Figure 2. 4.The qualitative results for ‘mild pleural effusion’ and ‘mild cardiomegaly’ in Figure 2, much like Table 1, make it difficult to clearly identify the advantages of the proposed method over prior work. Given that attention modulation is the central methodological contribution targeting localized pathology, it is recommended to include attention map visualizations. (Specifically to verify whether attention is indeed concentrated on the target region and whether leakage into non-editing regions is effectively suppressed.) 5.The first contribution stated in the Introduction claims “~reduce repeated training and maintenance costs under cross-device and cross-domain shifts, improving generality and controllability”. It is unclear which aspect of the proposed method substantiates this claim of improved generalization, and no supporting experiments across different devices or domains appear to be provided.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The paper addresses an important problem in medical counterfactual generation. In chest X-rays, preserving anatomy while editing pathology is genuinely hard, and the paper focuses on exactly this issue. The motivation is clear and relevant. The experimental results are reasonably solid. In Table 1, the method gets the best confidence and CLIP-I and competitive FID/LPIPS relative to the compared baselines, and the qualitative results suggest more localized and stable edits in non-target regions. The method is designed as an inference-time regulation approach, which makes it more appealing than methods that require more domain-specific retraining or additional control modules.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The paper focuses only on chest X-rays and does not really test how broadly the method generalizes beyond this setting. Since a lot of the motivation is about general inference-time controllability, the empirical scope feels somewhat limited. The paper would be stronger with expert evaluation or a more task-specific analysis of whether the generated pathology is actually anatomically and clinically meaningful.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We appreciate reviewers’ comments and grouped the responses below. Reply@R1/R3-Clinical utility: We do not position counterfactual CXR generation as replacing radiological diagnosis, and will clarify this scope in the final version. Its value is to create controlled “what-if” pairs that preserve patient anatomy while selectively changing a target pathology. These pairs support shortcut-bias inspection and audit whether diagnostic AI relies on the intended lesion rather than background, acquisition style, or unrelated anatomy, and can support augmentation for underrepresented findings. Thus, preserving non-target regions is central to counterfactual validity. We agree expert studies would further validate clinical usefulness, while this work focuses on anatomy-consistent and pathology-controllable generation. Reply@R1/R2/R3-Resolution and generality: Our experiments use 512×512 images, as stated in the implementation details. This is a practical setting for latent-diffusion editing and enables fair comparison with diffusion baselines under feasible memory cost. We agree this should not be interpreted as diagnostic-resolution clinical deployment, especially for subtle findings, and will make this limitation clearer in the final version. Also, our “generality” claim refers to regulating attention at inference time without retraining new control branches for each setting, not to an empirically proven cross-device or domain performance gain. The submitted evidence mainly supports inference-time controllability in CXR; high-resolution and broader cross-domain validation remain important future directions. Reply@R2-ROI prior and cardiomegaly: We clarify that M_anat/Ω is not lung-only. Sec. 2.3 states that organ masks include “left/right lung and heart,” and M_ROI is selected or combined from them using anatomical cues in the text. Thus, Ω is not restricted to left/right/bilateral lung: lung or pleura findings use lung ROIs, while cardiomegaly uses the heart/cardiac-silhouette ROI. Ω is not designed to automatically discover lesion locations from the model response; it is an interpretable anatomical prior for constraining where a specified counterfactual edit should occur. For shape-changing findings such as cardiomegaly, the ROI is a soft prior and can include the cardiac boundary/margin rather than a rigid original mask, allowing plausible enlargement of the cardiac silhouette. The model response is still involved through pathology-token cross-attention: Eq. 7 measures how token attention aligns with Ω, and Eq. 9 corrects the latent trajectory according to this concentration rather than blindly forcing pixels to change. If the selected ROI mismatches the target pathology, regulation may be less effective; this is a limitation of ROI-based regulation rather than a contradiction of the method. Reply@R2-Metrics and baselines: We thank R2 for catching a clerical bolding error in Table 1: ProgEmu is better on LPIPS and FID, and the boldface should be corrected; this does not affect the reported values. Our claim is a trade-off among pathology alignment, structural preservation, realism, and inference-time flexibility: our method achieves the best Conf and CLIP-I while remaining competitive on LPIPS/FID without training extra control branches. For counterfactual editing, lower LPIPS/FID may reflect conservative editing or realism, but not necessarily successful target-pathology realization. The ablation also supports this: removing pathology cross-attention reduces Conf/CLIP-I, while removing anatomy regularization reduces SSIM. Attention-map visualization would clarify the mechanism and, if space permits, can be included in the final version. Our baselines cover major paradigms including inpainting, progressive editing, instruction-based generation, and multimodal autoregressive counterfactual generation; InstructX2X trains a local editing model, whereas our method performs training-free inference-time attention regulation.

title: MDPNet: A Multi-Scale Deformable Prototype Network for Accurate and Interpretable Medical Image Classification
reviewer_1_strengths: -The method is evaluated on three different datasets representing diverse data modalities (ECG, OCT, and CT) in terms of classification performance. -An ablation study is provided (again focused on classification performance). -Some qualitative exploration of learned prototypes is included for the ECG case (Figure 3)
reviewer_1_weaknesses: My main concern is that the authors claim interpretability as their primary contribution; however, this aspect is only indirectly evaluated through classification performance. The study would be significantly stronger if it included a quantitative evaluation of the robustness and quality of the explanations. Even more compelling would be an assessment involving clinicians, who are the intended end users of the model. Minor: -There is repetition between the last paragraph of the introduction and the listed key contributions. reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The paper addresses an important problem of combining performance and interpretability in medical imaging and presents a conceptually coherent method that integrates multi-scale features with deformable prototype learning.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The paper has several notable weaknesses. First, the overall novelty is limited, as the method primarily combines existing components such as multi-scale feature extraction, deformable prototypes, and logit adjustment without introducing a fundamentally new idea. Second, the interpretability claims are not convincingly validated; the evaluation relies mainly on qualitative visualizations without quantitative metrics or user studies to demonstrate clinical usefulness. Third, the empirical improvements over strong baselines are relatively modest, especially on public datasets, which weakens the impact of the contribution. In addition, the choice of benchmarks is not particularly strong, with one dataset being saturated (OCT) and another being small and potentially unreliable (COVID-CT), raising concerns about generalizability. Finally, the paper lacks deeper analysis, including limited discussion of failure cases, when the method is most effective, and the computational overhead introduced by the proposed components.

reviewer_3_strengths: 1.Clear motivation. The authors should further clarify why this combination is non-trivial and what benefits it provides beyond a straightforward aggregation of existing components. 2.The evaluation of interpretability is too limited. author_feedback: We sincerely thank the reviewers for their constructive comments. We have revised the manuscript to better clarify the interpretability, novelty, dataset-specific results, efficiency, backbone choice, and prototype settings. Common Q1: Interpretability validation. We agree that interpretability should be supported by both visual and quantitative evidence. In the revision, we added a prototype-removal analysis, where top-ranked matched prototypes are removed or masked during inference to evaluate their contribution to prediction. The performance drop shows that the prototypes are not only visual explanations but also decision-relevant evidence. Moreover, we expanded the clinical discussion. For PVC classification, subtype-specific cues may appear across different ECG leads and local waveform segments. Our prototype matching helps trace predictions back to representative diagnostic patterns, improving case-level interpretability over black-box classifiers. Common Q2: Incremental novelty. Our contribution is not a simple combination of existing modules, but a clinically motivated evidence-matching framework. Medical diagnostic cues are often subtle, distributed, and non-contiguous. In PVC classification, discriminative evidence may appear across multiple ECG leads and waveform segments. Conventional prototype methods usually rely on fixed or local matching, which may be insufficient for such evidence. We therefore integrate multi-scale representation with deformable prototype matching to capture flexible evidence correspondence while preserving prototype-level interpretability. We revised the Introduction and Method sections to clarify this motivation. R1 Q1: Repetition and inconsistent task description. We have checked the manuscript and revised repeated or inconsistent descriptions in the Abstract, Introduction, and Method sections. R3 Q1: Limited baseline gains and dataset representativeness. We agree that gains on OCT and CT are smaller than on PVC due to differences in task difficulty and diagnostic patterns. PVC is a five-class fine-grained task with subtle inter-class differences and distributed cues across ECG leads, where deformable prototype matching is particularly useful. OCT and CT contain more visually salient or localized patterns, leaving less room for improvement over strong baselines. Still, our method achieves competitive results on these datasets while providing additional prototype-level interpretability. We clarified this in the revision. R3 Q2: Failure cases and efficiency. We strengthened the failure-case and efficiency analysis. Two failure types were discussed: weak/incomplete discriminative cues and highly similar classes such as LVOT vs. RVOT. These cases show the remaining difficulty in fine-grained inter-class discrimination. For efficiency, we added parameters, FLOPs, and inference time. The extra cost mainly comes from multi-scale feature extraction and deformable prototype matching. We clarified that our method aims to balance performance, interpretability, and computational cost. R3 Q3: Too many concepts. We reorganized the method by clarifying the roles of multi-scale representation, deformable prototype matching, prototype-based interpretability, and logit adjustment, while removing redundant terminology. R4 Q1: Writing and Fig. 3.We revised the writing and improved Fig. 3 by enlarging key regions, adding clearer labels, and rewriting the caption to better explain the visualization pipeline. R4 Q2: DenseNet choice. DenseNet was selected because it provided better feature reuse and stability than ResNet, and was more suitable than ViT for limited medical data. R4 Q3: Prototype number. We added prototype number sensitivity analysis. Too few prototypes may miss diagnostic variations, while too many introduce redundancy. The final setting balances performance, interpretability, and efficiency. More prototypes were used for PVC due to its more challenging five-class classification task.

title: Measuring What VLMs Don’t Say: Validation Metrics Hide Clinical Terminology Erasure in Radiology Report Generation
reviewer_1_strengths: A major strength of this work is its empirical identification of a genuine and often overlooked evaluation blind spot. The authors astutely point out that models can game traditional metrics like BERTScore by producing safe and generic templates. Furthermore, treating the decoding strategy itself as a primary confounding variable is a very insightful experimental design. The sensitivity analysis clearly illustrates the fundamental trade-off between semantic erasure under deterministic decoding and emergent bias under stochastic sampling, providing a strong empirical foundation for their observational claims.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The primary weakness of the paper is its conceptual and methodological incrementalism. While the identified problem is significant, the proposed solution relies on standard statistical techniques. The CAD framework is essentially a direct application of the log ratio of unigram probabilities with Dirichlet smoothing, which is a well-established method in text analysis. Applying this to generated text is a natural extension rather than a fundamentally new methodology. Secondly, the paper lacks direct clinical validation. It remains unproven whether the reference-aligned demographic association shifts measured by CAD and WAE actually correspond to clinically meaningful diagnostic errors or patient harm. Finally, critical reproducibility details are missing, such as the exact patient and site-level data splits and the specific prompts used for the GPT-4.1 baseline.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The paper is well-motivated. Direct NLP metrics are not clinically representative, and high overlap scores can mask clinically uninformative outputs. This is a valid and important issue in medical report generation. 2.The proposed idea to detect such cases of collapsing through analyzing what the model does not say is interesting and novel. 3.The results are informative and align well with intuitive expectations. They show that deterministic decoding yields high evaluation scores but leads to severe template collapse and loss of clinical terminology, while stochastic decoding improves diversity at the cost of increased bias and instability. This trade-off is consistently demonstrated and can provide useful insights into model behavior for future work.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.Corpus-level analysis only: CAD/WAE operate at the dataset level and do not provide per-sample insight. In contrast to standard metrics (e.g., BERTScore, BLEU), which can be evaluated per sample, the proposed metrics are not directly applicable at the individual report level. This limits their usefulness for analyzing specific model errors or for practical clinical validation. 2.Unclear link to clinical correctness: While the paper reports text-based metrics (e.g., BERTScore, RateScore) as indicators of clinical performance, it does not establish whether CAD/WAE correlate with true diagnostic accuracy or clinical utility. It remains unclear whether improvements in these metrics correspond to better medical outcomes. 3.Overemphasis on inference: The paper attributes the observed effects primarily to decoding strategy. However, similar phenomena (e.g., template collapse or loss of terminology) may also originate from training dynamics, such as data imbalance or reliance on language priors. This aspect is not sufficiently discussed. 4.Minor presentation issue: Figure 2 layout (subfigure labeling) could be improved for clarity.
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We sincerely thank the reviewers for their time and valuable feedback. We are happy to see their unanimous appreciation of our work and their recognition of the importance of addressing failures of current VLM evaluation metrics. Our framework identified a critical evaluation blind spot in radiology report generation (RRG) where reports collapse to a repetitive template, and introduced metrics which go beyond surface-level text similarity and measure vocabulary erasure and newly biased terms. Please note - Reviewer 3’s [R3] review text concerned a completely different paper than ours (as it critiques “TAVR-VLM”, which is unrelated to our work). However, [R3’s] comment on Field #9 (additional comments) does address our paper and sounds quite positive (“insightful analysis”, “compelling and much-needed warning for community”). We sincerely hope this will be taken into consideration. We address criticisms individually - 1.[R1, Meta#1] Incrementality in Solution: R1 correctly notes that our underlying mathematical formulation (log-odds, Dirichlet smoothing) relies on established statistical principles. However, we want to point out that if there exists a simple solution to a problem, it does not seem sound to reject those in favor of more complicated solutions. Our application of tracking vocabulary-level association shifts between human reference and model prediction is indeed new (as [R2] mentioned “interesting and novel”). Our core contribution is a new validation method for RRG, not the statistical formula. Given the increase in RRG studies across all domains, by establishing this methodological baseline, we hope to standardize demographic-association methodology, which is an important aspect of fairness in report generation. 2.[R2, Meta#3] Corpus-level Analysis: We disagree that operating at the corpus level is a limitation. Algorithmic bias, erasure, and template collapse are meant to be measured at the system level, not per-sample: A model cannot be labeled as ‘biased’ or ‘not fair’ based on a single sample. Thus, we recommend using the proposed tools together with standard evaluation metrics (mentioned in Discussion & Conclusion). Our method is intended to be used as a system-level validation method, rather than “real-time or granular error analysis”. 3.[R1, R2, Meta#2] Clinical Validation: The problems we highlight (template collapse, generated reports falsely associating ‘aicd’, ‘pacemaker’ with women, and ‘prostate’ as neutral) are fundamental, and we provide empirical evidence. Identifying the problem at this level does not require expensive, time-consuming clinical trials. We do agree that the mitigation strategies should indeed be validated before use in the clinic. In additional space post-acceptance, we would like to add more qualitative examples showing how CAD-flagged terms directly correspond to self-evident harm (eg, “stenosis” and its CAD-level shift). 4.[R1] Reproducibility: As mentioned in References [1][2] in the abstract, we will provide code, a Python package for the framework, prompts, and model weights post-acceptance. To eliminate ambiguity, we confirm the use of identical prompt templates across all experimental settings. 5.[R2]: Overemphasis on Inference: We agree that training dynamics may also influence the observed phenomenon, and we test it with an imbalanced dataset. We will discuss this further. Thank you for pointing this out. 6.[R2] Minor Presentation Issue: We are happy to improve the labels in Fig 2. The reviewers identified our motivation and recognized the importance of this research in VLM evaluation. We appreciate their praise for our experimental design and analysis of decoding trade-offs. We believe this paper provides a fundamental rethink of validation in report generation. Our auditing tool can help move past the ‘illusion of performance’ and ensure safe and equitable deployment in medical AI. We again thank the reviewers for their appreciation and feedback.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper identifies a research gap in current radiology report generation evaluation: models that achieve high surface-level similarity scores (e.g., BLEU, BERTScore) often suffer from template collapse, where they produce safe, generic text while erasing specific clinical terminology. To quantify this, the authors introduce Clinical Association Displacement and Weighted Association Erasure. These metrics measure demographic-based word association shifts and clinical signal loss, specifically highlighting how deterministic decoding strategies can lead to the erasure of critical diagnostic details across different patient populations. While the paper presents good contributions, its recommendation for acceptance is contingent upon the authors clarifying the following points during the rebuttal phase: 1.Reviewers noted that the core methodology, using log ratios of unigram probabilities with Dirichlet smoothing, is a standard statistical technique in text analysis. While applying these to the specific problem of “terminology erasure” in radiology is useful, it is viewed as an application of existing methods rather than a fundamentally new methodological breakthrough. 2.A primary concern is the missing link between the proposed metrics (CAD/WAE) and actual medical outcomes. It remains unproven whether a high “Association Erasure” score directly correlates with diagnostic errors, patient harm, or decreased clinical utility. Provide evidence or a discussion on how shifts in CAD/WAE correlate with specific diagnostic omissions (e.g., missing a “severe aortic stenosis” finding). 3.Unlike standard metrics like BERTScore, which provide a score for every individual report, CAD and WAE are corpus-level metrics. They provide insights into dataset-wide trends but cannot identify errors in a specific patient’s report. This limitation restricts their use for real-time model auditing or granular error analysis. | The proposed corpus level evaluation additional to other report level measurement is a valuable measure for model evaluation. Reviewer 3’s comments have been updated and considered. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): Unfortunately, I have to recommend reject despite an interesting effort in a modern and popular subject. I noticed that there were two opposite outcomes recommended after the rebuttal round; so, I reviewed the the paper myself (I have relevant expertise). I found the main claim that the common metrics incentivize VLMs to generate templated radiology reports to be supported poorly. The paper never explicitly explains how template bias would actually emerge during the training. Besides, the metrics (BLEU, ROUGE, BERTScore) are largely obsolete in this field, with radiology report evaluation having long moved to domain-specific metrics like RadGraph and RadCliQ (thus, the “gaming” argument was not convincing). I also found the empirical analysis to be somewhat superficial (for example, comparing greedy vs. beam search decoding and using output diversity to validate the proposed metric is obviously not sufficient). Lastly, I also have to agree with the post-rebuttal comments of R1. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper identifies an important evaluation blind spot in radiology report generation: standard metrics fail to penalize template collapse. The proposed CAD and WAE provide a novel vocabulary-level diagnostic framework to quantify this issue. The analysis of decoding strategies reveals a valuable trade-off between semantic erasure and emergent bias. While Reviewer #1 raises concerns about incrementalism, Reviewer #2 and Reviewer #3 finds the work well-motivated and informative. The rebuttal clarifies that CAD/WAE are system-level auditing tools, not per-sample metrics. Recommendation: Accept.

reviewer_1_strengths: Problem motivation is clear and relevant to MICCAI. MEC is a practical, plug-and-play framework that works across multiple RAG baselines, model scales, and benchmarks. New retrieval corpus is strong contribution, enabling reproducible medical RAG research.

author_feedback: We sincerely thank the reviewers and the AC for recognizing this work. Below, we respond to the major concerns: 1.GPT-4o-based corpus construction. (R1, R2, R3) We thank the reviewers for raising this important concern. We would like to clarify that GPT-4o is not used to generate unsupported medical facts or final answers, but to structurally reorganize knowledge from reliable sources into MEC. We used constrained prompts and manually inspected about 5,000 samples after different stages. Since this does not involve open-ended generation of new knowledge, only a few formatting issues appeared, and deviations from original sources were rare. At the early stage of this work, we also tried local Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct and the smaller Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct. MEC built with Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct achieved 0.4417 on MecQA+SR-RAG, which is not substantially different from 0.4489 in Table 1 using GPT-4o-built capsules, suggesting that the gain mainly comes from MEC rather than distillation from a larger model. To ensure construction consistency, we finally decided to use GPT-4o. 2.Traceability, clinical relevance, and ROUGE-L. (R2, R3) We appreciate the reviewers’ thoughtful comments on this issue. However, to better isolate the effect of the MEC structure itself, we evaluate it under controlled benchmark settings. For clinical relevance, MEC supports the recall of traceable medical evidence, e.g., lesion location, polarity, and uncertainty in imaging retrieval. Its traceability is structural and operational: each returned capsule links a compact assertion to a citable evidence snippet, allowing the source evidence supporting the answer to be inspected rather than hidden in redundant long contexts. Table 1, 2 and Fig. 3 show that MEC evidence is easier for the generator to use and more discriminative under the same settings. We agree that ROUGE-L cannot fully measure medical correctness, therefore our conclusion on the effectiveness of MEC does not rely on a single metric, but is jointly supported by controlled comparisons, VQA accuracy, ablation studies, and case analysis. 3.Evidence-source ablation. (R2) We thank the reviewers for this valuable suggestion. In our source-level ablation on Med-FlashCards with DRAGIN, using only Evidence from Medical Texts gives 0.2803; adding Structured Resources improves it to 0.3168; further adding Model Parameters reaches 0.3522.This shows that adding evidence sources can bring consistent gains. Our submitted ablation focuses on MEC fields because our main goal is to verify MEC itself rather than rank knowledge sources; Sec. 3.3 further shows the effectiveness and complementarity of each MEC field. 4.Retrieval pipeline and parametric capsules. (R2, R3) We thank the reviewers for pointing out the need for clarification. MEC is inserted as an evidence representation layer into the open-source baselines in Sec. 3.1, with top-k and other parameters kept consistent. For image retrieval, the same encoder is used within each downstream model setting to ensure a consistent semantic space. Parametric capsules do not let the model freely generate medical knowledge; instead, QA training sets are used as reliable sources to generate answer-aligned evidence, with the question as cue and answer as assertion, making model priors retrievable and constrained while reducing hallucination. 5.Novelty and positioning. (R1, R3) MEC is novel not as a new retriever or decoder, but as a unified organization mechanism for heterogeneous medical evidence. Unlike methods that simply use retrieved data as context, MEC represents different evidence sources through a shared interface, reducing the generator’s implicit alignment burden. Finally, we again sincerely thank the reviewers and the AC for their valuable time and insightful feedback. If this work is fortunate enough to be recognized, we will release the approximately 550K MEC retrieval corpus and construction pipeline as reusable resources for medical RAG.

title: Med-CAP: Counterfactual Evidence and Adaptive Prior Suppression for Robust Medical Visual Question Answering
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The de-biasing effect is remarkable and comprehensive: By adopting the dual-module design of CEM and APS, it simultaneously addresses the core imbalances of Med-VQA, such as the imbalance bias and modality shortcut bias. Compared with single de-biasing methods, the robustness is significantly enhanced, especially in the OOD scenarios that are sensitive to bias. 2.Balances de-biasing and accuracy: Unlike some de-biasing methods that “sacrifice standard accuracy for de-biasing”, Med-CAP maintains the SOTA-level intra-distribution accuracy on standard datasets while enhancing the model’s anti-bias ability. It is more practical. 3.Strong module versatility and easy deployment: Based on the classic UpDn backbone network design, there is no need for large-scale model structure reconstruction. It can flexibly adapt to different Med-VQA models and has good migration and implementation capabilities.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.Counterfactual supervision increases training costs: The CEM module requires constructing two types of counterfactual inputs, “evidence retention” and “evidence discard”, and calculating sufficiency and necessity constraints. Compared to traditional models, the training process is more complex. 2.Limited adaptability: The current results have only been verified on the SLAKE, VQA-RAD and their CP variant datasets. It has not been applied to more diverse types of medical images or more complex clinical question-answering scenarios. Its generalization ability needs further verification. 3.Not adapted to large-scale medical VLM: The current model is based on the traditional UpDn backbone network and has not been extended to a large-scale medical visual language model. It is difficult to fully utilize the semantic understanding ability of large models, and there is room for further performance improvement.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: I find that the Counterfactual Evidence Modeling (CEM) is a good appraoch that promotes visual grounding.Through gradient attribution, the methodenforces sufficiency (keeps evidence from the mutual domain with high GroundTursth confidence) and necessity by dropping evidence with low confidence, via a margin loss. This is a clever causal-inspired extension of prior counterfactual VQA work, and ablations show it boosts Open question accuracy meaningfully(e.g., +3.5% on SLAKE-CP). Adaptive Prior Suppression (APS) calibrates fused logits by subtracting question-only priors and scales priors confidence and evidence strength from CEM. This instance-adaptive debiasing outperforms fixed-subtraction methods like RUBi, especially on OOD biased splits, without hurting closed-ended performance too much - or that i can tell. Overall strengths: I think the dual mechanisms complement each other. CEM provides evidence quantification, and APS uses it for calibration. Strong empirical results across baselines (classical VQA, medical debiasers, VLMs), with qualitative cases showing better attention on relevant regions. The expressed design makes it practical and should be not too difficult to replicate.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1)The CEM builds directly on gradient attribution (e.g., Grad-CAM) and counterfactual VQA (e.g., Niu et al. 2021), while APS extends RUBi-style priors with adaptivity. The fusion is effective but not revolutionary, It seems like the effort is mostly hyperparameter-tuned scaling. 2) Backbone choice: UpDn (2018) is outdated; results beat recent VLMs (e.g., Qwen2.5-VL at 70.86% on SLAKE-CP), but these may be suboptimal prompts/fine-tuning. No comparison to fine-tuned modern medical VLMs (e.g., LLaVA-Med++) limits claims of broad superiority. 3)Gradient attribution limitations: The attribution seems to rely upon gradient alonfor evidence maskng, which is noisyand may miss broader context or suffer from saturation, particularly a concern with ‘real’ clinical datasets. Top-K selection with ϵ-suppression is heuristic-heavy and there are no robustness analysis to attribution failures. Granted, hard to squeeze that into a short-form paper. 4)Evaluation scope: The method works well on SLAKE/VQA-RAD(-CP), but medical VQA has more datasets (e.g., PathVQA, MIMIC-CXR). OOD is distribution-shift via priors, not true clinical shifts (e.g., new pathologies/modalities). THe authors show hyperparameter sensitivity, but use outside of benhcmark sets may not/probably wont’ perform as well.
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: A key strength of the paper is that it explicitly addresses two complementary sources of bias in Medical Visual Question Answering (Med‑VQA): modality shortcut bias and answer prior / data imbalance bias. Treating these failure modes jointly, rather than in isolation, is a practically meaningful design choice given how they often interact in Med‑VQA settings. The proposed framework is technically well motivated and internally coherent. Counterfactual Evidence Modeling (CEM) encourages stronger visual grounding by enforcing sensitivity to evidence‑preserving and evidence‑suppressing representations, while Adaptive Prior Suppression (APS) provides a sample‑adaptive mechanism for reducing the influence of question‑only priors. The coupling between these components via an estimated evidence‑strength signal is a reasonable and interesting way to integrate counterfactual reasoning with prior correction. The paper is also well aligned with the goals of robust and trustworthy medical AI, emphasizing failure modes under bias‑sensitive and out‑of‑distribution settings rather than focusing solely on in‑distribution accuracy. This framing is appropriate for the medical domain, where reliance on spurious correlations can be particularly problematic. Finally, the experimental evaluation is carefully designed. The use of both standard Med‑VQA benchmarks and bias‑sensitive variants allows for a more meaningful assessment of robustness, and the ablation studies help clarify the contributions of the main components of the proposed framework.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The novelty relative to recent Med‑VQA debiasing work is somewhat unclear. Related methods such as DeBCF, CCIS‑MVQA, DeCoCT, CEDO, and Med‑BiasX have already explored counterfactual or causal approaches to reducing language bias in closely related settings, so the paper would benefit from a clearer articulation of what is fundamentally new beyond the specific integration of components. In addition, the empirical gains are relatively modest and reported without variability measures (e.g., standard deviations or confidence intervals), making it difficult to assess statistical robustness. More direct head‑to‑head comparisons with the most relevant recent baselines would further strengthen the empirical claims.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank all reviewers for their constructive feedback. Below, Q refers to the questions in Section 7, and J refers to the justifications in Section 14. Response to Reviewer #1. Q1/J3: Training cost. A: The training time is only 205 seconds on the VQA-RAD dataset with a single A100 40GB GPU. In addition, since Med-CAP introduces no additional inference-time parameters, its extra cost is training-only, and the inference cost remains the same as the original model. Q2: Limited adaptability. A: Following your valuable suggestion, we added more experiments on PathVQA and VQA-Med 2019.Med-CAP improves absolute accuracy by 2.28 points on PathVQA and 2.12 points on VQA-Med 2019, showing robustness on more Med-VQA benchmarks. Q3/J2: Backbone. A: Following your great advice, we added experiments with MedCLIP. As a plug-and-play debiasing module, Med-CAP improves the MedCLIP-based baseline by 2.56 absolute accuracy points on SLAKE and 2.74 points on VQA-RAD, showing that it is not tied to UpDn. J1: Novelty. A: Med-CAP has two main novelties: 1) Med-CAP effectively addresses both visual and textual biases. title: Med3D-R1: Mitigating Narrative Bias and Enhancing Reasoning Consistency in 3D Medical Vision-Language Models
reviewer_1_strengths: 1) The paper is the first to explicitly identify and quantify the structural narrative bias in standardized radiology reports. This is a subtle but significant issue in medical text generation, and the proposed ARW strategy provides a simple yet effective remedy. 2) RAM elegantly regularizes feature drift using a non-trainable anchor, with ablation results confirming its stabilizing effect on cross-modal alignment. 3) The two-stage training paradigm is clearly defined. The quantization of the consistency reward signal demonstrates careful engineering to ensure stable policy updates during GRPO. 4) The use of both radiologist evaluation and LLM-as-a-judge for reasoning quality (Table 2) compensates for the limitations of surface-level metrics (BLEU/ROUGE) in assessing clinical logic.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1) Figure 2(c) shows that 2D medical VLMs utilizing GRPO-based RL still underperform Med3D-R1 (S2). The paper attributes the gain to the 3D model and consistency reward but does not elaborate on why a similar RL strategy fails to yield comparable gains for 2D models. 2) Table 3 shows a sharp decline in CIDEr and BLEU when λ > 1.10, attributed to “overemphasizing abnormalities. “ A qualitative example would strengthen this observation. 3) Table 5 clearly indicates that the consistency reward’s efficacy is contingent on using RM-Mistral-7B, while Qwen/Llama provide suboptimal or harmful supervision.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: One main strength of this paper is that the motivation is quite compelling. The authors identify an interesting form of structural narrative bias in CT reports: normal findings tend to appear earlier while abnormal findings are concentrated later in the report. They further argue that this may bias autoregressive models toward over-predicting normal findings. I think this is a meaningful observation, and it gives the work a clearer clinical motivation. Another strength is that the method is easy to understand. Each component is designed to solve a specific problem: RAM addresses unstable cross-modal alignment, ARW targets report bias, and the consistency reward in the RL stage is used to reduce reasoning hallucination. Because of this, the whole framework feels coherent. The experiments are fairly sufficient. The paper includes comparison with multiple baselines, ablation studies on the proposed modules, and additional analysis such as reward quantization and reward model comparison. These results provide reasonabe support for the effectiveness of the method.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The biggest issue, in my opinion, is that the claim about improving reasoning quality is still not fully convincing. The proposed consistency reward mainly encourages the generated reasoning trace to be more similar to the reference report, but this does not necessarily mean the reasoning itself is truly correct or clinically faithful. In other words, the method may improve the consistency of generated text more than the actual validity of the reasoning process.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The three challenges identified in the paper are quite interesting and are relevant to the current VLM landscape of problems. The individual contributions made to address the three identified challenges are supported by ablation studies. The paper depicts an improvement in performance on CT-RATE and RAD-ChestCT for abnormality diagnosis over existing 3D VLMs.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: a. While the three contributions made in the paper are quite interesting, the paper lacks strong evidence to motivate them. For example. Fig 1.shows the structure followed in the reports. While this is an interesting observation, I’m curious to know if such a structure is followed only in CT-RATE/RAD-ChestCT or all types of radiological reporting done globally? Additionally, is there any merit in adhering to such a structure for a radiologist (but is possibly detrimental to the model)? Highlighting this aspect will motivate this challenge better to show how emerging techniques need to be modified in order to adhere to standard clinical practices. The current manuscript seems to have a disconnect with the clinical nuance for this statement. b. In section 2.1, while the RAM seems like an interesting approach, the conclusion of RAM reducing feature drift and yielding more stable 3D text alignment is not backed by an intuitive explanation on why it would help to do so. While the results depict an improvement, the methodology section needs to hint at strong reasoning on why the proposed method seems viable over other existing alignment techniques. Without this reasoning, it’s hard to understand how the proposed solution seems to be providing superior conceptual novelty over existing methods. c. In section 2.2, the usage of DeepSeek or any other LLM needs to be clearly motivated. If the structure of the reports is fairly standard (Fig 1.), then one can also apply a non-LLM-based technique (such as using regex, etc.) here, as this would not allow the method to get computationally expensive. The reasoning behind why the sentence segmentation step needs to be carried out by another LLM needs to be justified, even briefly so, in the paper. d. In section 2.3, the authors describe that existing RL-based medical VLMs such as those in [13, 17 from the paper] optimize only the final answer, making the intermediate reasoning clinically implausible. Once again, this argument is not supported by strong evidence, such as by showing a few examples of intermediate reasoning chains from [13,17]. The lack of evidence in support of this observation makes it less appealing. e. Continuing on the previous point, the paper does not describe why supervising only the final output corrupts the intermediate reasoning in the first place or cite any existing literature examining this phenomenon. The misalignment between visual and textual features could be one of the possible reasons, but as the method already uses an alignment mechanism, I’m curious to know what could be the possible reason behind this effect. Examining this aspect would make the observation about intermediate reasoning much stronger and thereby support the novelty of the solution. f. I would recommend the authors to cite the works used for comparison in the main results i.e Fig 2.c and the ablations tables, to relate to the main text. g. While Table 2.shows an ablation for Consistency reward, a one-on-one comparison with [13, 17] is needed to show the improvement in intermediate reasoning chains after applying the proposed method, along with the overall improvement. h. In section 3.2, the language model that is used as the decoder needs to be specified. i. As the manuscript does not provide any information of a source code release, it requires detailed specifications of hyper-parameters for reproducibility.
reviewer_3_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank all reviewers and ACs for their valuable feedback. We are encouraged that R1 and R2 recognized the novelty and empirical strength of Med3D-R1, and following the meta-review, we focus on the major concerns regarding clinical motivation, technical justification, and evidence of reasoning improvement. 1.Clinical motivation of structural report bias (R3-a, Meta) R3 questions whether the normal-before-abnormal structure is dataset-specific. We clarify that our empirical claim is limited to the submitted training corpus, where Fig. 1 quantifies a clear positional regularity. More broadly, this pattern is consistent with structured radiology reporting practice, where normal anatomy is often documented systematically before abnormal findings. Similar tendencies are also observable in structured report datasets such as MR-RATE, while our formal quantitative claim remains limited to the submitted corpus. Our point is not to criticize this clinically useful convention, but to show that autoregressive training can turn it into a harmful positional prior. 2.Technical justification of RAM and DeepSeek-based sentence labeling (R3-b/c) RAM addresses the instability of mapping high-variance 3D tokens into the lower-variance language space. The fixed anchor is not semantic evidence, but a stable center of the pretrained text-embedding space. Thus, the projector learns bounded residual deviations rather than an unconstrained full mapping, reducing extreme tokens and feature drift. Table 1 supports this: removing RAM decreases all report metrics and especially semantic scores (BERT_F1/LLM_Score). For DeepSeek-V3, we clarify that it is not used for sentence segmentation. Reports are first split into sentences by rule-based preprocessing. DeepSeek-V3 is only used to label each sentence as normal, abnormal, or uncertain. Regex can split sentences or sections, but is less reliable for negation, uncertainty, and nuanced radiological descriptions. This offline step is used only for training-data construction and adds no inference overhead. 3.Evidence-consistent reasoning improvement (R2, R3-d/e, Meta) R2/R3 note that consistency with reference reports does not guarantee clinically faithful reasoning. We agree and clarify the scope: Med3D-R1 does not claim absolute clinical truth, but aims to improve evidence-consistent reasoning under report-based supervision, encouraging reasoning traces to align with report-supported facts and penalizing unsupported intermediate statements. Thus, Table 2 includes radiologist assessment alongside LLM-as-a-judge evaluation, rather than BLEU/ROUGE. These results support improved clinical faithfulness within the scope of available report supervision. 4.Comparison with prior RL-based VLMs (R3-g) R3 requests a direct reasoning-chain comparison with [13,17]. Fig. 2(c) already provides a one-on-one MVQA comparison with Med-R1 and MedVLM-R1, where Med3D-R1 achieves higher diagnostic accuracy. In addition, Table 2 isolates the effect of the consistency reward within our framework, and radiologist evaluation supports improved clinical faithfulness. These results suggest that evidence-consistency supervision improves reasoning reliability beyond final-answer rewards. 5.Source of gains and reward design (R1) Fig. 2(c) does not attribute gains to RL alone: S1 gives 3D evidence and RAM-stabilized alignment; S2 adds consistency reward. The λ>1.10 drop reflects reduced textual fidelity from abnormal overemphasis. Table 5 suggests discriminative RM-Mistral is more reliable than generative judges for reward scoring. 6.Minor clarifications and reproducibility (R3-f/h/i) We thank R3 for pointing out these missing details. The language decoder is Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, which will be explicitly specified in the final version. We will also add citations for the compared methods used in Fig. 2(c) and the ablation tables. We are committed to releasing the code with implementation details and the trained model upon acceptance.
