author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and meta-reviewer for their careful assessment and recognition of our work’s motivation, training-free/model-agnostic design, and broad evaluation. Below, we address the main concerns. 1.Hyperparameters and robustness. We agree that the manuscript should explicitly state settings. In all Table 1 and 2 experiments, we used γ=0.05 (IAF) and τ=0.9 (Dynamic Information Nucleus Selection), fixed across models/datasets. γ controls IAF’s sensitivity to inter-slice changes, selected via validation-set calibration (standard ML hyperparameter protocol): for each 3D volume, we computed normalized mean L1 differences to the anchor slice, aggregated validation-set scores, and chose γ near the transition point where near-duplicate slices are removed while anatomical/pathological changes are retained. τ=0.9 (performance-first) keeps the smallest top-k tokens with cumulative normalized importance >0.9. These settings were not tuned per test case; we will revise the paper to report them and explain the calibration. 2.Efficiency and FlashAttn compatibility. We agree that the visual-token retention ratio does not translate linearly into end-to-end speedup, since total latency also includes pruning overhead and autoregressive text generation. MedPruner achieves substantial speedup primarily during the LLM next token prediction stage, benefiting from the reduced number of visual tokens. FlashAttn is still used in the main VLM forward pass whenever supported. However, because FlashAttn does not explicitly materialize the full attention matrix, the attention statistics needed for pruning are computed in a separate, lightweight scoring step. After token selection, the compressed visual sequence is passed back to the model, and subsequent attention computation remains FlashAttn-compatible. We will revise the paper to clarify this implementation detail and present efficiency claims more clearly. 3.Novelty and Compression Ratio Problem (R3). We agree that several recent studies have explored visual token reduction for efficient multimodal inference. However, our work differs in both motivation and strategy. Prior work mainly targets 2D/general VLM inputs and often employs LLaVA-style pipelines with predefined pruning ratios. In contrast, we observe that different medical models exhibit distinct attention distributions when processing 3D volumetric information. In particular, MedGemma’s attention weights are highly concentrated on a single or a very small subset of tokens (as noted in Sec. 3.2). By adaptively determining token retention based on each input’s information density, our design specifically addresses 3D medical data heterogeneity, better balancing efficiency and information preservation. We will revise the manuscript to further elaborate on these architectural differences and our specialized design for the 3D medical domain. 4.Clarifications and presentation issues (R4). Q1: The dimension of “importance vector” is 1 x M, where M is the number of tokens in the slice. After aggregating attention across heads, we average the M x M attention matrix along the query-token dimension to obtain an M-dimensional token-importance vector, apply temperature-scaled softmax, sort scores, and keep the smallest top-k set whose cumulative mass exceeds tau. It is worth noting that the representation dimension of each token remains unchanged; MedPruner only changes the number of retained visual tokens. We will revise the manuscript to make this wording precise. Q2: Qwen3-VL-8B was used for report generation but not for VQA because its DeepStack-style visual processing is inefficient when handling many 3D slices, and it is not specifically designed as a medical-domain VQA model. We will clearly state this model selection criterion. Q3-4: We will also align the “Average” column across tables and resolve the notation conflict by reserving K for the key matrix and using a different symbol for the token number.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The reviews are mixed but overall lean positive, with two reviewers supporting acceptance and one reviewer raising concerns about incremental novelty, missing threshold details, and practical compatibility with attention-map implementations. Given the mixed scores and the fact that the main concerns are largely about clarity, reproducibility, and claim calibration rather than a clear invalidation of the results, this paper should proceed to rebuttal/discussion rather than early accept or early reject. The rebuttal should clarify the values and selection of γ and τ, the robustness of the slice-level filtering threshold, the relationship between token reduction and actual inference speed, andcompatibility with efficient attention implementations. | I recommend acceptance. The rebuttal addressed every concern flagged by specifying the fixed hyperparameters γ=0.05 and τ=0.9 across all experiments along with a validation-based calibration procedure, clarifying FlashAttention compatibility through a separate lightweight attention scoring step followed by a compressed sequence passed back to FlashAttn-compatible forward computation, calibrating the efficiency claim by attributing speedup primarily to the LLM decoding stage, and positioning the contribution as input-density-aware pruning targeting the heterogeneous attention distributions of 3D medical VLMs relative to the prior token-pruning literature. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The authors have addressed the reviewers’ comments well. All reviewers have agreed the acceptance of the paper. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The initial reviews were mixed but leaned positive. R2 and R4 supported acceptance, while R3 raised a borderline rejection mainly due to incremental novelty, missing details on gamma and tau, lack of gamma sensitivity analysis, and concerns about compatibility with attention implementations such as FlashAttention. R2 also questioned whether the very low visual-token retention rates translate into proportional end-to-end inference speedup. These concerns were relevant, particularly because the original manuscript did not fully specify the threshold settings and used efficiency language that could be interpreted as stronger than the measured latency gains. The rebuttal improved the assessment by clarifying that gamma=0.05 and tau=0.9 were used consistently across models and datasets, and by explaining the validation-based calibration procedure for gamma. It also clarified that token reduction does not linearly translate into end-to-end speedup because latency includes pruning overhead and autoregressive text generation, and explained how attention statistics can be computed in a separate scoring step while retaining FlashAttention compatibility in the main forward pass. The response also addressed presentation issues raised by R4, including the dimensionality of the importance vector, the Qwen model selection discrepancy across tasks, the average metric column, and notation conflicts. These clarifications do not fully remove all limitations. The method remains partly heuristic, the novelty over recent token-pruning and token-merging methods is moderate, and the robustness of gamma would be stronger with a direct sensitivity analysis. The efficiency claims should also be stated more cautiously in the final version, with clear separation between token retention, LLM-stage speedup, pruning overhead, and end-to-end latency. However, these weaknesses do not invalidate the main empirical findings, and they are mostly issues of reproducibility detail, claim calibration, and presentation rather than fundamental flaws in the method or evaluation.

title: MedTri: Structured Medical Report Normalization for Enhanced Vision–Language Pretraining
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The paper tackles a real and important preprocessing problem in medical VLP: radiology reports are long, stylistically heterogeneous, and often contain image-irrelevant content. 2.The proposed system achieves substantially lower computational cost than alternatives. 3.The framework is developed and evaluated across multiple modalities (both X-ray and CT) using large-scale, standard datasets, demonstrating a commendable engineering effort.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.Insufficient novelty. The triplet-based report decomposition is highly reminiscent of MedKLIP (ICCV 2023, Wu et al. ), which decomposes reports into {entity, position, exist} triplets. It also includes an “entity translation” module that queries a medical knowledge base to expand disease entities into detailed visual descriptions — this is functionally very similar to MedTri-K. Without explicit comparison and differentiation, the claimed novelty of the triplet schema and the knowledge expansion module is substantially weakened. The comparison between their method and the related work mentioned is inadequate, which may further influence their novelty positioning. The paper cites MedFiLIP as a related work doing text normalization, yet does not include it as an experimental baseline. MedFiLIP uses GPT-based information extraction to produce fine-grained entities with severity, location, and category — a structure closely resembling the MedTri triplet. CT-GLIP already constructs organ-level image–text pairs and further introduces an abnormality dictionary to strengthen grounded contrastive learning. Relative to these papers, MedTri looks more like a new structured normalization schema plus a lightweight deployment recipe, rather than a fundamentally new paradigm. 2.Limited downstream task diversity. All downstream evaluations are zero-shot multi-label classification. There is no evaluation on retrieval, segmentation, or report generation — tasks that would more convincingly demonstrate the generalizability of the normalization. The discussion section acknowledges this but the limitation significantly narrows the empirical claims. 3.The improvements are modest. The improvements of MedTri over raw reports are relatively small (e. g. , 0.792 vs. 0.781 ACC on MIMIC 100% with SwinT), and no confidence intervals or statistical tests are reported for downstream tasks. It is difficult to assess whether the observed gains are reliably above noise, particularly in the 100% data regime. 4.The paper does not report the train/val split ratio (only mentioning 500 for testing) for the local text normalization model, does not describe how the 20 physicians were selected or inter-rater reliability, and does not discuss potential failure modes of the normalization (e. g. , hallucinated anatomical entities, information loss for rare conditions).
reviewer_1_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The triplet graph designed in this framework accurately captures the basic semantic units for radiological reasoning, which efficiently eliminates irrelevant noise in medical reports that has no connection with medical images. 2.The researchers verified the efficacy of this method on two mainstream imaging modalities (X-ray and CT) as well as multiple public datasets. 3.MedTri achieves promising results under limited labeled data scenarios (1% and 10% data proportion). This is of great practical significance, considering the high cost and scarcity of annotations in medical artificial intelligence research.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.Experimental outcomes show unstable performance of knowledge enhancement (MedTri-K) and counterfactual enhancement (MedTri-C) under different data scales. For instance, MedTri-K brings only trivial performance gains when using the full dataset. 2.This study only conducts evaluations on the classification downstream task. Testing over a broader range of downstream tasks would make the work more comprehensive and solid.
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The proposed [Anatomical Entity: Radiologic Description + Diagnosis Category] triplet schema effectively filters out stylistic noise and clinically irrelevant content while preserving essential morphological and spatial details for pretraining. 2.The structured format enables clever text-level augmentations without altering the core pipeline. Specifically, MedTri-K enriches knowledge for low-data regimes , and MedTri-C generates anatomy-grounded counterfactuals to improve fine-grained multimodal alignment.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The framework relies on a lightweight local model to parse and generate the structured triplets. The paper lacks a robust error analysis (e.g., assessing the rate of hallucinated anatomies or missed negations by BioBart) and fails to evaluate how these inevitable extraction errors propagate and impact the downstream vision-language alignment. 2.Although the study notes that 20 board-certified physicians conducted a double-blind assessment using a 5-point Likert scale, the evaluation lacks crucial statistical transparency. The authors fail to disclose the exact number of samples evaluated by the experts and omit any inter-rater reliability metrics (such as Fleiss’ Kappa or Cohen’s Kappa). Without these fundamental statistical validations, the high clinical scores reported for MedTri lack the necessary robustness and remain unconvincing from a clinical perspective.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank all reviewers and AC for the constructive comments. We appreciate that the reviewers recognized MedTri as “a valuable piece of research” that “greatly enhances vision-language alignment” (R2), and as an “application study” with “high deployability,” “solid empirical results,” and “practical utility for the community” (R3). We are encouraged that R2 and R3 gave weak or strong accept recommendations; R1 concerns appear related to different interpretations of our intended positioning. Below, we clarify these concerns and explain revisions. R1&AC: Contribution We would like to clarify that our intended positioning is: MedTri is an application study rather than a new methodology or paradigm. Our contributions are: 1.We validate text normalization as an independent factor for improving medical VLP. 2.MedTri provides a lightweight, locally deployable implementation. 3.MedTri supports easy modular text-side augmentations without changing the pipeline. We will revise “platform” to “deployable component” to avoid overstating the scope. R1&AC: Compared baseline MedKLIP, MedFILIP, and CT-GLIP are highly relevant; however, they are not direct controlled baselines, because they combine additional VLP-specific designs, e.g. MedFILIP’s semantic similarity matrix and CT-GLIP’ segmentation mask and diagnosis contrastive loss. A full comparison can introduce additional factors, confounding the isolated effect of normalization and precluding a fair comparison. For MedKLIP, its triplets are extracted by RadGraph, which focuses on discrete clinical entities and labels rather than preserving anatomical radiologic descriptions. This is why we included RadGraph as the compared baseline. R1&AC: Performance improvement Our conclusion is based on comparisons across datasets, scales, encoders, and modalities rather than a single setting. Wilcoxon signed-rank tests showed significant improvements of MedTri over raw reports and RadGraph on X-ray (p=0.000231 and 0.000194), and CT (p=0.03125), indicating that the gains are consistent, instead of random variation. These will be added in the revision, while confidence intervals will be added where applicable. R2&AC: MedTri-K and MedTri-C The scale-dependent behavior is expected. MedTri-K is specially designed for low-resource settings, so its full-data gains can be saturated. MedTri-C uses anatomy-ground negatives and becomes more effective when enough samples support fine-grained discrimination. Statistical tests further show that their improvements are significant vs. MedTri, with p=0.00733 and 0.000245, respectively. R1&R3&AC: Evaluation The reports were randomly split into train/val sets at 9:1 ratio. 20 board-certified physicians independently rated 50 randomly selected cases across. ICC was 0.983 for anatomical correctness and 0.990 for image groundedness, while Fleiss’ kappa was 0.656 and 0.634, indicating excellent reliability of averaged scores and agreement among physicians. Cohen’s kappa was not used because it is designed for two raters. These will be added in the revision. R1&R3&AC: Extraction-error In our current study, this is addressed at two levels. 1) Physician evaluation directly assessed anatomical correctness and image groundedness, the two criteria most sensitive to hallucinated entities and information loss. The near-ceiling scores and strong reliability suggest that such errors were not systematic. 2) Models were trained directly on normalized reports, and the consistent gains indicate that residual errors, if present, did not dominate the VLP signal. R1&R2&AC: Downstream task Our current choice of zero-shot classification was intended as a controlled probe of pretrained representation quality while keeping downstream heads and task-specific designs fixed. We therefore evaluate across modalities, datasets, encoders, and data scales. We will state this scope more clearly and discuss broader downstream evaluation as future work.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): MedTri proposes a lightweight text normalization framework that converts free-text radiology reports into structured triplets to improve medical vision-language pretraining (VLP), with optional knowledge expansion and counterfactual augmentation modules. Reviewers acknowledge the practical importance of tackling report heterogeneity, the low computational cost, multi-modality evaluation (X-ray and CT), and the strong performance in low-data regimes. However, the weaknesses are noted. Novelty is questioned, considering the triplet schema closely resembles MedKLIP, and missing baselines (e.g., MedFiLIP, CT-GLIP) weaken the claimed contribution. Downstream evaluation is limited to zero-shot classification only, without diverse tasks. Performance gains over raw reports are modest (e.g., 0.792 vs. 0.781 ACC on MIMIC), and no statistical significance or confidence intervals are reported. Additionally, there is no assessment of how extraction errors propagate to downstream VLP. Issues to be discussed during rebuttal: Limited downstream task diversity (only classification; no retrieval, segmentation, or generation) Insufficient novelty and missing baseline comparisons (MedKLIP, MedFiLIP, CT-GLIP) Lack of statistical significance testing and confidence intervals for reported improvements Physician evaluation lacks inter-rater reliability metrics (Fleiss’ kappa / Cohen’s kappa) and sample size details Unstable performance of MedTri-K and MedTri-C across different data scales | The rebuttal successfully resolves most critical issues. The authors have convincingly repositioned MedTri as an impactful application study that validates text normalization as an independent factor for medical VLP, with lightweight deployability and modular augmentations. The addition of statistical significance tests strengthens confidence in the reported improvements, and the detailed inter‑rater reliability metrics address transparency concerns about physician evaluation. However, two limitations persist. First, downstream evaluation remains confined to zero‑shot classification; the absence of retrieval, segmentation, or generation tasks narrows the demonstration of generalization. The authors acknowledge this as future work, which is acceptable given the paper’s scope. Second, the modest absolute gains in full‑data settings, while statistically significant, raise questions about practical clinical impact, though the low‑data regime improvements are more compelling. Reviewer #1’s novelty concerns are partially mitigated by the clarified positioning, but researchers seeking fundamental methodological advances may still find the contribution incremental. Overall, the practical utility, solid empirical execution across X‑ray and CT, and responsive rebuttal justify acceptance. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): There is 1 Reject and 1 Accept after rebuttal. R3 did not update the final recommendation and was initially positive. Reviewers generally agree that the work addresses a practical problem in medical VLP and demonstrates utility across datasets and modalities. The rebuttal clarified the intended positioning of the work, provided additional details on statistical analysis and physician evaluation, and addressed several concerns regarding the augmentation modules and normalization quality. While concerns about novelty relative to prior structured-report approaches remain, I view the contribution primarily as a useful and well-executed application study. I recommend acceptance.

title: MedTriFlow: Efficient Resolution-Agnostic 3D Medical Image Generation with Implicit Triplane Representation
reviewer_1_strengths: The main strength are: 1.The paper has a clear structure and is easy to follow. 2.The motivation is clear. Existing generative models are typically limited to a fixed resolution, which is a notable limitation that deserves further attention. 3, The proposed methodology appears reasonable overall. The use of a triplane representation is an interesting way to address the aforementioned problem. In particular, training a triplane-based AE and using a flow-matching model for latent-space sampling is a sensible design choice. 4.The introduction of the triplane AE is a technical novel idea.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The main weaknesses are: 1.The experimentation is a bit limited. The authors only investigate a specific number of CBCT projection views or different MRI acceleration scales. This makes it difficult to determine whether the proposed method consistently outperforms competing approaches under different levels of sparsity. In a future version of the paper, presenting an exploration of different number of views and scales would provide a more complete understanding of its robustness and generalization ability. 2.The proposed methodology appears to contain a larger number of parameters than the other compared methods. That might raise concerns about the fairness of the comparison and the model complexity. A discussion about the trade-off between reconstruction performance and parameter efficiency would strengthen the paper. 3.It is not entirely clear how the task-specific input is projected into the triplane latent representation before being provided to the ControlNet. Adding 1-2 additional sentences explaining this transition would help the reader better follow the overall pipeline. Minor weaknesses: 1.The pre-trained U-Net is not cited. 2.There are some missing notations in the section 2.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.This paper is well-motivated since the limitation of fixed-resolution 3D generation is real and important in 3D medical imaging. 2.The authors integrate triplane autoencoder, continuous anatomical field, and latent flow matching to achieve efficient and flexible 3D generation, which is reasonable. 3.The continuous anatomical field design is interesting, which uses an implicit neural representation to decode triplane features into a continuous 3D field and achieve the resolution-agnostic generation claim.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The “resolution-agnostic” generation claim is somewhat overstated. All training volumes are resampled and padded to 256^3.As a result, the model is not trained on native resolutions. That is, not truly resolution-agnostic learning from native-resolution data. It is unclear whether the 1024^3 generation is anatomically meaningful. 2.Issues about the ablation studies. The authors are suggested to ablation some key designs to make it easier to assess which designs are essential., e.g., flow matching vs. latent diffusion, and the implicit anatomical field vs. a conventional voxel decoder. 3.About how to verify the generation quality, in addition to the generation and reconstruction metrics, more verification can be performed, e.g., Turing tests, use generated images for downstream classification tasks. 4.In terms of native resolution 3D image generation, has anyone tried the video generation approach? The author could discuss the advantages and disadvantages of these two approaches.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.Resolution-agnostic output: INR-based continuous field decoding enables an arbitrary-resolution volume. 2.Flow matching in compact triplane latent achieves fast inference.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.Novelty is limited. Triplane-based compact reconstruction with diffusion models is not new, and the proposed triplane design does not show a clear structural improvement over prior work (e.g., Blaze3DM). The main contribution appears to be mapping a triplane latent to an INR-based field to enable resolution-agnostic reconstruction. However, arbitrary-resolution reconstruction via INR is conceptually close to LIIF, and related LIIF-style ideas have already been studied in medical imaging (e.g., “MedIL: Generating Arbitrary-Resolution Medical Images with Implicit Latent Spaces”). Overall, the authors should more explicitly differentiate the technical designs of both the triplane and the INR components from prior work and clarify why their integration is non-trivial. 2.While higher resolution can be important for diagnosis and surgical settings, it is not clear that arbitrary continuous resolution is necessary. The paper should clarify the specific use case(s) in which a “resolution-agnostic” capability is essential, rather than supporting only a few fixed resolutions. 3.High-resolution benefit is not quantitatively demonstrated. Fig. 3 shows qualitative outputs, but the paper does not report quantitative metrics at higher resolutions. It remains unclear whether coordinate-query high-resolution outputs outperform simple interpolation or super-resolution baselines. Since resolution-agnostic generation is positioned as a key contribution, the paper should demonstrate that its upsampling results are superior to interpolation. If no clear quality gains are observed, the practical value of “resolution-agnostic” capability should be re-justified. 4.Compute cost at high resolution is unclear. Implicit-field decoding typically requires dense per-voxel queries, which can become expensive as resolution increases. Although the paper notes that voxel-based methods are “compounded by the cubic scaling of computational costs with resolution,” the proposed approach may face a similar issue when generating high-resolution outputs. A fair runtime comparison against interpolation baselines at higher resolutions would strengthen the claim. 5.For downstream tasks, the method uses a coarse reconstruction as a structural condition. I am curious how this conditioning enforces consistency between the output and the observed data, and whether any explicit data-consistency loss is required. For example, is the final output explicitly constrained to match the observed data after applying the corresponding degradation operator? 6.The ablation study mainly varies LPIPS and adversarial losses, showing improved perceptual reconstruction quality. However, these loss terms are widely used and do not constitute the paper’s core contribution; they are better framed as training details rather than key mechanisms. The authors should instead design ablations to validate the effectiveness of the proposed modules, especially the components critical to the “resolution-agnostic” mechanism.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and respond to the main concerns below. Q1.Meaning of resolution-agnostic generation (Meta-reviewer, R2, R3). Downstream 3D medical tasks live on heterogeneous grids. Dental CBCT, whole-body CT, and MR sequences differ in voxel spacing, resolution, and FOV, and reconstruction grids follow scanner geometry rather than the training grid of a generative prior. A model tied to a fixed grid cannot serve these settings without retraining. Our claim is not native-resolution training, but that one latent code can be decoded at the spacing, resolution, and FOV a downstream task requires through a continuous anatomical field. The encoder still operates on a normalized 256³ grid, which we will state in Sec. 2.Extending encoding to ingest variable native spacing and FOV is our next step. Video-generation-style approaches are also relevant; they treat a volume as an ordered slice sequence, whereas we model it as a 3D implicit neural field from compact triplane features. Q2.Quantitative gain and runtime at high resolution (Meta-reviewer, R3). To verify a real gain at 512³, we compared continuous field decoding with upsampling baselines on both tasks. Each baseline runs at 256³ and is upsampled to 512³ by trilinear or tricubic interpolation, or by a task-specific super-resolution model (Dn-Dp for CT, ArSSR for MRI); ours decodes the same latent directly at 512³. Sparse-view CBCT (PSNR/SSIM), ours 25.94/0.7568, trilinear 23.86/0.7348, tricubic 23.34/0.7335, Dn-Dp 25.07/0.7412.Fast MRI, ours 27.46/0.8651, trilinear 24.97/0.8365, tricubic 24.42/0.8307, ArSSR 26.42/0.8487.Continuous field decoding thus surpasses both interpolation and super-resolution baselines. Latent generation is resolution-independent (~1.2 s); decoding scales with queried voxels (1.4 s at 256³, 4.1 s at 512³, 24.3 s at 1024³), so generation stays in compact 2D latent space. Q3.Novelty relative to Blaze3DM, LIIF, MedIL (Meta-reviewer, R3). Our contribution is the joint design rather than triplane or INR alone. Blaze3DM uses per-volume optimized triplane embeddings and does not learn an encoder-based shared latent space for generative modeling. LIIF and MedIL target image-level continuous representation and native resolution autoencoding without an efficient 3D generative prior. We couple a triplane autoencoder, flow matching in the shared 2D triplane latent, and continuous field decoding within one trainable pipeline. Triplane features and the INR decoder are jointly optimized, so the latent stays compressible for flow matching yet expressive for queries off the training grid. Because the embedding is 2D, the backbone scales with standard 2D diffusion scaling laws and avoids the cubic cost of voxel-based 3D generators. We will clarify this distinction. Q4.Robustness and architectural ablation (Meta-reviewer, R1, R2, R3). 20-view CBCT 26.13/0.7514 and 12× MRI 27.09/0.8623 show the framework remains competitive under heavier undersampling. Replacing our continuous field decoder by a voxel decoder drops reconstruction from 30.78/0.9051 to 29.02/0.8818, isolating the decoding design from the perceptual and adversarial losses already reported. Further comparison with latent diffusion would provide additional insight. Q5.Conditioning, complexity, clarity (Meta-reviewer, R1, R3). The task-specific input passes through the trained triplane encoder and is injected into the flow matching network via the ControlNet branch. We frame downstream reconstruction as structure-guided generative reconstruction; the coarse reconstruction supplies anatomical structure and data fidelity is learned from paired data rather than imposed by a final degradation consistency loss. Although our model has more parameters than several baselines, Table 1 reports the fastest inference and strongest PSNR and SSIM, so the capacity is effectively used. The missing U-Net citation and notation issues in Sec. 2 will be corrected.

title: MedTSC-Net: Bridging Semantic and Scale Gaps in Text-Guided Medical Image Segmentation
reviewer_1_strengths: Strengths: MedTSC-Net presents a well-motivated framework addressing real limitations in text-guided medical segmentation. The three proposed modules (VLH, CASA, RFA) are logically cohesive and target distinct failure modes. Results on both datasets are compelling, and the few-shot analysis (87.99% Dice with only 5% data) is particularly convincing for clinical relevance.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Weaknesses: The evaluation is limited to COVID-19 datasets, raising concerns about generalizability to other anatomies or modalities. The architectural complexity introduced by three additional modules lacks thorough computational cost analysis (FLOPs, inference time). Additionally, the VLH alignment depth K=12 and other hyperparameter choices appear empirically set without sensitivity analysis, and the qualitative text-manipulation experiments (Fig. 4) remain anecdotal without quantitative grounding.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.This paper addresses an important problem in medical visual language segmentation: shallow interaction strategies and scale mismatch between pre-trained encoders and task-specific decoders. 2.The proposed Visual-Linguistic Harmonizer introduces early-stage cross-modal alignment, which helps reduce semantic discrepancies between image and text representations. 3.Experimental results demonstrate consistent improvements over baselines across multiple datasets.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The CASA module builds upon standard channel and spatial attention mechanisms, and its contribution is largely incremental rather than conceptually innovative. 2.Lack analysis of computational complexity and inference efficiency. 3.Not provide sufficient analysis of how alignment depth (K in VLH) affects performance.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The author suggests that the use of text can be employed to guide and enhance the effect of image segmentation. 2.The method proposed in the article achieved the best results in both the comparative experiments and the visualizations. 3.The author proposed an appropriate module for the model based on the newly added text guidance.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The author did not specify the source of the texts in the dataset, whether it matches actual clinical practice, and whether there are any unfair comparisons. 2.The text in the dataset used during training has marked the positions and quantities of the divisions, which may lead to unfair comparisons and prevent the direct demonstration of the superiority of the algorithm. 3.The paper fails to adequately demonstrate what unique mechanisms the proposed module approach has added. Currently, it seems more like a combination of improvements to existing modules rather than a clear breakthrough in a new methodology.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: Q1: Methodological Novelty (R1, R2, R3) A2: Though lacking foundational math innovations, our core contribution is a systematic clinical solution addressing three referring segmentation bottlenecks: (1) inadequate multi-modal alignment; (2) over-reliance on local text, ignoring global contexts (e.g., severity); and (3) encoder-decoder capability gaps. By aligning multi-scale visual features with global semantics, we bridge these gaps. Few-shot results confirm robustness under data scarcity, proving real-world utility. Q2: Hyperparameter Sensitivity (R1, R2) A2: We set K as a hyperparameter to flexibly accommodate different pre-trained text encoder scales. During development with our 12-layer BERT, we explored numerous Harmonizer setups (e.g., varying application stages, skip-connections, and K values). The optimal configuration empirically proved to be covering all BERT layers and the final two vision encoder stages, determining our choice of K=12.Q3: Computational Complexity and Inference Efficiency (R1 R2) A3: MedTSC-Net is highly efficient. Compared to Ariadne [11], trainable parameters increase by only 4.7% (+2M) to 45M. Requiring 15.7 GFLOPs/image, it achieves a 45ms average latency on one RTX 3090, satisfying real-time clinical needs. Q4: Generalization Capability (R1) A4: Our primary focus on COVID-19 stems from the current scarcity of high-quality, text-annotated medical segmentation benchmarks. Nevertheless, our evaluation spans two distinct imaging modalities: chest X-rays (QaTa-COV19) and CT slices (MosMedData+). MedTSC-Net consistently improves performance on both, demonstrating its robustness against imaging variations. Furthermore, our framework relies on no organ-specific priors or hand-crafted anatomical rules. Although omitted from the main text due to space limits, we conducted a preliminary lightweight validation on the MoNuSeg pathology dataset (nuclei segmentation). MedTSC-Net achieved an 81.54% Dice score (+0.55% over Ariadne’s 80.99%), clearly validating its strong generalization potential beyond lung infection scenarios. Q5: Quantitative Basis for Text Perturbation Experiments (R1) A5: Omitted for space, our quantitative text perturbation analysis involved removing specific details (severity, quantity, location) or using a generic “lung infection” prompt. The model’s Dice score ranged from 91.89% (optimal) to 88.34% (lower bound). Crucially, even this 88.34% lower bound outperforms pure-vision baselines. This proves that embedding text priors during training does more than just enable cross-modal reasoning; it fundamentally strengthens the visual branch’s own representation learning capability. Q6: Source and Nature of Textual Data (R3) A6: The public datasets we used (QaTa-COV19 and MosMedData+) feature non-arbitrary, authoritative text annotations directly adopted from the pioneering LViT [10]. Ensuring high clinical reliability, these texts were manually annotated and cross-validated by two senior medical experts from UT Southwestern Medical Center. Encompassing infection severity, specific locations, and lesion quantity, this structural design faithfully replicates real-world radiology reports and physician referral notes, perfectly aligning our evaluation with actual clinical practice. Q7: Fairness of Text-Guided Comparisons (R3) A7: We respectfully clarify that utilizing detailed text prompts is the defining formulation of referring segmentation, not “label leakage” compared to traditional blind segmentation. Following standard protocols (LViT [10], Ariadne [11]), all evaluated multimodal baselines received identical image-text pairs. MedTSC-Net achieves SOTA performance under absolute information parity, proving the inherent superiority of our multi-modal interactive architecture rather than an unfair information advantage. Pure-vision methods were included solely to establish a performance lower bound and quantify the benefits of text priors, a standard practice in this field.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Reviewers found MedTSC-Net well motivated, clearly presented, and empirically strong, with consistent gains on QaTa-COV19 and MosMedData+ and compelling few-shot results. However, the overall reviews remain mixed due to concerns about limited generalizability beyond COVID lung data, moderate novelty of the VLH/CASA/RFA components, missing computational cost and hyperparameter sensitivity analysis, and especially the provenance and fairness of the text guidance, which may encode lesion location/count information and affect comparisons. | The rebuttal addressed several concrete concerns. However, across the reviews there is also broad agreement that the method is more incremental than foundational. The final paper should temper claims of broad generalization and clarify the role and clinical nature of the text prompts. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper addresses a relevant problem in text-guided medical image segmentation, namely how to better align visual features with clinical textual descriptions under limited annotation. The proposed MedTSC-Net is well motivated, and its three modules are organized around clear technical goals: early visual-linguistic alignment, text-guided attention, and receptive-field adjustment. The experimental results on QaTa-COV19 and MosMedData+ are consistently strong, and the few-shot results are particularly valuable given the annotation burden in medical imaging. The reviewers raised valid concerns about the moderate novelty of the individual modules, the limited evaluation beyond COVID-related lung data, computational cost, and the fairness of text guidance. The rebuttal addresses these issues to a reasonable extent. In particular, the authors clarify the provenance of the textual annotations, explain that all multimodal baselines use the same image-text pairs, provide efficiency numbers, and add evidence from text perturbation and preliminary non-lung validation. While the method is still more of a careful system-level integration than a fundamentally new formulation, the empirical evidence is strong, the problem setting is clinically meaningful, and two reviewers moved to or maintained acceptance after rebuttal. Overall, I believe the paper makes a solid and useful contribution to text-guided medical segmentation. I would support acceptance, while encouraging the authors to further temper broad generalization claims and include the added efficiency and text-guidance analyses in the final version. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper proposes MedTSC-Net, which is a text-guided medical image segmentation framework addressing semantic and scale mismatches between modalities. Overall, the method is a well-motivated framework with empirical improvements and few-shot performance, although the methodology novelty is moderate. Authors addressed most concerns of R1 and R2, such as computational complexity and some ablation settings. Hence, recommend acceptance of this work.

title: MedVol-R1: Reward-Driven Evidence Grounding for Volumetric Reasoning Segmentation
reviewer_1_strengths: The framework explicitly decouples the language-driven reasoning process from the voxel-level 3D mask generation. Instead of relying on opaque, specialized segmentation tokens that collapse the decision process into an uninterpretable latent space, MedVol-R1 forces the LVLM to output a verifiable “2D evidence anchor”. A frozen MedSAM2 model then propagates this 2D anchor into a full 3D volumetric mask. This design solves the “black box” problem of existing LVLM segmentors. Furthermore, this is the first framework to apply GRPO to the task of VRS. It transitions the field away from pure SFT, which often leads to mere “surface-level pattern mimicry”. And the authors designed a highly tailored, multi-component reward system that evaluates the LVLM’s rollouts from four complementary perspectives.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.Given the two-stage decoupled nature of the pipeline, the framework heavily relies on the LVLM to output a perfectly accurate 2D evidence anchor. If the LVLM reasons incorrectly, such as selecting the wrong key slice or inaccurate 2D boxes, can the frozen MedSAM2 identify, reject, or rectify this error? 2.The cross-slice consistency reward (Rc) evaluates the volumetric coherence strictly within a local axial neighborhood of ±Δ adjacent slices around the predicted key slice. The choice of this hyperparameter Δ is critical: if Δ is too small, it fails to enforce true global 3D consistency; if Δ is too large, MedSAM2’s slice-to-slice propagation might naturally degrade due to anatomical variations, unfairly penalizing the LVLM’s otherwise correct key-slice selection. The manuscript currently lacks an explanation or an ablation study on how Δ was chosen. 3.The experiments evaluate the framework on CT-ORG, AbdomenCT-1K, and KiTS23.While Figure 2 provides specific examples, the author should also clearly list the specific types of organs and lesions that the current method is capable of segmenting across these datasets. Furthermore, I am curious how the fixed anatomical labels were replaced with the “free-form linguistic descriptions” or implicit queries？ 4.Figure 2 only provides qualitative comparisons between the GT, the M3D baseline, and MedVol-R1; the authors should include the visualization results of SAT and BiomedParseV2.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: auditable intermediate step. It aligns very well with the rationale on why they used RL. Ablation is very clean.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: They heavily rely on a single slice. And it is not very clear whether the performance gain came from their technical novelty or just giving MedSAM2 a better prompt.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: (1) Apply GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) to 3D medical volumetric reasoning segmentation, with a four-dimensional complementary reward (format, axial visibility, 2D IoU, cross-slice Dice), enabling structured reasoning without requiring CoT annotations. (2) Formalizes volumetric reasoning segmentation under implicit clinical queries as a distinct task, identifies the inherent limitations of existing “specialized segmentation token” paradigms in terms of interpretability and generalization, and proposes targeted improvements. The novel explicit decoupling of volumetric reasoning from geometric mask extraction effectively addresses the interpretability and generalization bottlenecks of current LVLM-based methods for implicit clinical queries. (3) Sufficiently comprehensive ablation studies, with quantitative validation of both the necessity of cold-start initialization and the contribution of each reward component. The results are self-consistent with the design motivations.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: (1) All experiments were conducted solely on three CT subsets of M3D-Seg. It is recommended to supplement with one or two MRI datasets or real-world clinical free-text queries that have not been paraphrased, in order to further validate cross-modal / real-world generalizability. (2) Source code should be open-sourced.
reviewer_3_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We sincerely thank all reviewers for their constructive comments and for recognizing the novelty of MedVol-R1.Q1(R1&R2): Is the gain from learned evidence grounding or merely from giving MedSAM2 a better prompt? What if the LVLM predicts a wrong anchor? A1: We thank the reviewers for this important question. MedSAM2 is essential but kept frozen, serving only as a low-level mask executor that delineates and propagates masks from a slice/box prompt. It does not understand the free-form VRS query, select the informative axial slice, or localize the query-relevant ROI; these decisions are learned by the LVLM through our evidence-grounding policy. Thus, the gain is not from improving MedSAM2 itself, but from learning to provide a query-conditioned, actionable 2D anchor. We agree that a better prompt is crucial. However, the prompt is not manual or oracle-provided; it is predicted by the LVLM from the volume and query. Therefore, “giving MedSAM2 a better prompt” is precisely the effect of learned evidence grounding. Our ablations keep MedSAM2 fixed and vary the grounding strategy, isolating learned query-conditioned anchoring. If the LVLM predicts a wrong anchor, MedSAM2 will usually propagate from the incorrect evidence, since it cannot semantically reject or correct a wrong prompt. To reduce such failures, we optimize axial visibility, 2D localization, and cross-slice consistency rewards. The explicit anchor also makes errors diagnosable as slice-selection, box-localization, or propagation failures. We will clarify this limitation and discuss future agentic refinement, where the system inspects the initial 3D mask and refines it with MedSAM2’s positive/negative box or point prompts. Q2(R1&R3): What targets are evaluated, and how are fixed labels converted into implicit queries? A2: For AbdomenCT-1K and CT-ORG, we follow M3D-Seg: targets come from original semantic labels, each mapped to multiple ChatGPT-generated descriptions in the M3D-Seg term dictionary. We randomly sample one as the implicit query, e.g., “liver” → “the organ that stores and regulates glycogen.” For KiTS23, we construct reasoning-oriented queries using mask-derived spatial/semantic relations, e.g., a cyst associated with the left kidney can be described as “an abnormal lesion on the left kidney.” We will clarify this protocol and show representative label–query pairs. Q3(R1): Choice of Δ in the cross-slice consistency reward. A3: We agree that Δ is a critical trade-off. We set Δ=5, forming an 11-slice neighborhood around the predicted key slice. Rc provides local rather than global volumetric supervision: too small Δ approaches 2D supervision, while too large Δ may introduce noisy rewards from anatomical variation and propagation errors. We will add the ablation study. Q4(R1): Qualitative comparison with SAT and BiomedParseV2.A4: Due to the page limit, Fig. 2 currently shows GT, M3D, and MedVol-R1.In the revision, we will include SAT and BiomedParseV2 on the same cases and annotate each with the label and sampled query. Q5(R2&R3): Reproducibility and code release. A5: We will release the training/inference code after the anonymity period. Q6(R3): Generalization beyond CT and M3D-Seg-style queries. A6: We agree that cross-modality validation and real clinical free-text queries are important. This work focuses on CT-based VRS because M3D-Seg subsets provide dense 3D annotations, public protocols, and controlled comparison with baselines, allowing us to isolate reward-driven evidence grounding. We will clarify that our claims are limited to CT-based VRS with M3D-Seg-style label-derived implicit queries; MRI/other modalities and uncurated clinical reports will be discussed as future work. Q7(R3): Minor revisions. A7: We will define all abbreviations at first mention, including LVLM, GRPO, and SAM, and clarify that Qwen3-VL-4B balances reasoning ability and computational feasibility for GRPO-based volumetric evidence grounding.

It first trains a LVLM to produce a verifiable 2D evidence anchor, which is then propagated into 3D mask by MedSAM2.All reviewers agree that the framework is conceptually novel and the results are promising, and gives all positive rating. title: MedXEdit-GRPO: Reasoning-Aware Online RL for Counterfactual Medical Image Generation
reviewer_1_strengths: The paper uses GRPO to train a model that performs counterfactual edits on chest X-ray images. Additionally, the authors claim to release the dataset, code, and model weights.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The tuple (P, I_in, I_out) or (P, I_in, I_target) is mentioned in Section 3.1 without a description of what the variables mean. There is only a partial explanation of the variables in Section 3.2. You say you train on 24 GPUs, please also provide the amount of VRAM per GPU to give a better impression of the needed resources. No statistical evaluation is performed. Confidence intervals, e. g. based on bootstrapping, would be helpful to better assess the differences in the results. The word “significantly” is used without showing statistical significance. Perhaps “substantially” or similar would be better, so that the reader does not get a wrong impression (or alternatively, the authors could add a test for statistical significance). In the first sentence of Section 3.1, it says “Inspired by [28,16]”, however these two papers are not mentioned in the Related Work section. It is not described in much detail how the images for the MedXEdit-Score are generated.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.Transitioning to an online RL framework (GRPO) for medical image editing is original. 2.By forcing the reward model to generate a rationale before a scalar score, the authors leverage the VLM’s internal logic, which significantly improves the reliability and interpretability of the reward signal. 3.The authors tackle the entire RLHF pipeline, from the curation of a novel preference dataset to the training of the reward model, and finally the policy optimization.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The entire reward model relies on the distillation of rationales and scores from Gemini-3-Flash. While Gemini is a powerful general-purpose VLM, medical image interpretation (especially subtle counterfactual changes in CXRs) requires deep domain expertise. Although the authors mention a 200-pair verification by radiologists, 200 is a relatively small sample size compared to the 30,000 training samples. The paper lacks a deeper analysis of potential hallucinations, biases, or systematic errors introduced by the Gemini teacher model. 2.Since the generative policy is initialized with UniMedVL, UniMedVL serves as the most critical baseline. The authors should clearly state the improvement compared to this baseline. 3.Table 3 compares MedXEdit-Score against a “Hybrid Reward”. However, a more insightful ablation would isolate the reasoning component during the RL phase. For instance, how does the RL policy perform if trained with a reward model that only outputs scores without the reasoning step?
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: End-to-end design: authors construct a complete, cohesive pipeline encompassing reward data generation, reward modeling, and RL fine-tuning. This full-stack approach makes the system practically applicable and thoroughly realized. Reward modeling: The “reasoning-before-scoring” framework is well-considered. The proposed reward model outperforms generic medical baselines as well as a non-reasoning variant, validating that the evaluator is executing a nontrivial and beneficial reasoning step. Empirical performance: The proposed method achieves state-of-the-art results across multiple key metrics when compared directly to a strong set of established baselines. Clinical relevance: Counterfactual exploration and robustness analysis are meaningful targets in medical imaging. Qualitative results show that the model’s edits are appropriately localized. Furthermore, shifting the field from SFT-oriented approaches toward reward-guided policy alignment represents a valuable progression for the domain.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Overstated novelty: The manuscript frames reinforcement learning as a largely unexplored avenue in this domain, which overlooks adjacent precedents. For example, CXRL utilized policy-gradient RL for chest X-ray generation, and HIVE employed human-feedback reward modeling for general image editing. Given that existing works already map much of the task landscape, the contribution should be framed as a strong domain-specific integration rather than a foundational breakthrough. Reward model bias: Distilling reward data primarily from Gemini-3-Flash and relying on only three source generators introduces a substantial risk. The learned reward model may easily inherit the specific biases, preferences, and blind spots of this narrow set of teachers. Limited dataset contribution: The dataset curation relies heavily on the automated extension of open datasets using AI tools. With only 200 radiologist-verified preference pairs, the dataset lacks the extensive expert curation required to be considered a major standalone contribution, as the current automated methodology is relatively trivial to replicate. Evaluation circularity: Employing MedXEdit-Score as both the reward function for RL and the final “Holistic Score” metric creates a circular evaluation loop. This diminishes the persuasiveness of the reported holistic gains, making the external, independent metrics far more reliable indicators of success. Narrow validation scope: The experiments are exclusively conducted on chest X-rays derived from ICG-CXR. There is no external dataset validation, nor is there evidence demonstrating generalization to other modalities or distinct CXR distributions. Insufficient expert evaluation: While radiologists verified a small subset of preference pairs, the paper lacks a comprehensive expert study evaluating the final edited images. Consequently, claims regarding clinical plausibility and anatomical preservation rely almost entirely on proxy metrics rather than direct clinical judgment. Incremental performance gains: Although the method outperforms strong baselines, the improvements are modest, and the framework does not achieve universal superiority across all evaluated metrics.

title: Merlin Plus: A Large-Scale, Multi-cancer, Image-Mask-Report Dataset
reviewer_1_strengths: Large-scale CT (25,494) dataset with radiologist validated lesion-level masks spanning 9 organs This dataset complements existing tumor datasets with additional organs and more detailed masks compared to previous datasets, eg. ULS. The proposed active learning for segmentation from reports is novel and can be generalized to other applications
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The quality of final refined masks is not discussed. For example, a limited study on reproducibility, and inter-observer variably could assist in gaining confidence about the quality of final masks.
reviewer_1_rating: (6) Strong Accept — must be accepted due to excellence
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.Clinically relevant gap addressed with meaningful scale. The focus on 9 tumor types absent from public segmentation datasets addresses a genuine and important gap. Although there partially exist datasets with some of the annotated lesion subtypes, having ONE comprehensive dataset is a major advancement. 2.Clever use of existing reports to initialize the annotation pipeline. The approach of leveraging existing radiology reports as weak supervision (i.e. starting from R-Super to produce reasonable initial proposals) rather than only requiring fully manual masks from scratch is elegant. 3.Intuitive active learning criterion. The report-confidence score (Dice between the soft model output and the report-refined binary mask) is a cheap and sensible proxy for uncertainty: poor model predictions require large corrections in Step 3, resulting in low Dice and flagging the case for radiologist review. 4.Longitudinal metadata and multi-modal annotations. The inclusion of anonymized CT dates and patient IDs enabling longitudinal tracking, combined with ICD-coded malignancy labels, makes Merlin Plus significantly richer than a standard segmentation benchmark. If the authors’ claims hold and this is indeed novel, this opens doors for temporal modeling and survival analysis that most datasets in this space do not support.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.(Critical) Baseline comparison is insufficient and potentially flawed The only public baseline is ULS23 (de Grauw et al., Medical Image Analysis 2025). ULS is a prompt-based universal lesion segmentation model trained with center-cropped patches, assuming a lesion is ALWAYS present in the patch center. Running it as a fully automatic sliding-window model would introduce a fundamental evaluation mismatch. The paper does not clarify whether the evaluation was prompt-based or automatic. If prompt-based: comparison should include e.g. LesionLocator (Rokuss et al., CVPR 2025), a zero-shot universal tumor segmentation and tracking model or a general-purpose prompt-based segmentation model e.g. MedSAM2 (Ma et al., arXiv 2025). If fully automatic: relevant baselines would include GF-Screen (Wu et al., ICLR 2026), a reinforcement-based pan-cancer segmentation model covering many lesion types, or general-purpose models such as VISTA3D (He et al., CVPR 2025) and SegVol (Du et al., NeurIPS 2024),VoxTell (arXiv 2025) or TotalSegmentator (Wassertal et. al.) for lesions. I acknowledge that running all of these may not be feasible, but at minimum the ULS evaluation mode should be clarified and at least one stronger baseline must be included for proper evaluation. 2.(Critical) Evaluation metrics are insufficient The primary metric in Table 1 is detection F1-score (organ-level, volume-thresholded) with sensitivity and specificity. While detection performance is relevant and consistent with the R-Super protocol, DSC is the standard metric for segmentation and is almost entirely absent from the main results. DSC values are only buried in the table caption for a subset of models (“Average DSC: 17 for MedFormer, 25 for R-Super with masks, 10 for R-Super reports only”) without a proper per-organ breakdown. This raises two concerns: The reported DSC values are very low. Averages of ~17–25 are far below what lesion segmentation methods typically achieve on established benchmarks (e.g., LiTS, KiTS, PanTS: DSC 40–70+). Values in this range warrant explicit discussion: are they driven by small/early-stage lesions, annotation quality, or model underfitting? The paper is silent on this. A dataset paper validated through segmentation models must report segmentation quality. Detection F1 alone does not demonstrate the value of voxel-wise masks, which are the primary contribution. Without per-organ DSC, downstream users cannot meaningfully assess model quality. Finally, no standard deviation is reported anywhere in Table 1, making it difficult to assess result reliability across runs. 3.Authors claim “For per-voxel annotations, we focused on malignant tumors for 9 organs missing masks in public datasets.” however several public datasets actually encompass large parts of these lesion types e.g. “Q. Chen et. al. Scaling Tumor Segmentation: Best Lessons from Real and Synthetic Data”. 4.Figure 1 issues The caption for panel (a) describes an organ-wise distribution reporting “the number of CT scans with lesions and the number of small lesions (< 2 cm)”, but the actual panel (a) appears to show qualitative CT/mask examples of an adrenal lesion, i.e. caption and figure content do not match. Only one number per organ appears in the distribution plot, not the two numbers (# CTs and # small lesions) described in the caption. Panel (b) shows longitudinal time point distribution but is missing a Y-axis, making it impossible to assess what fraction of patients actually have more than one scan. Or how many patients had 3+ examinations. Is this longitudinal data novel or already existent in the original Merlin dataset? 5.(Minor) Pipeline novelty is slightly overstated Steps 1–3 (including sub-steps 3A–3D: report attribute extraction, organ-constrained masking, ball convolution-based tumor localization, and volume-matched binarization) closely follow the R-Super framework (Bassi et al., MICCAI 2025), which is also the primary baseline in the paper. The genuine novelty seems to be the report-confidence score (Step 4) and the active learning loop around it. The authors should clearly delineate what is directly adapted from R-Super vs. what is new, rather than presenting the full pipeline as their contribution. 6.No ablation on the active learning selection criterion The report-confidence score is presented as a key design choice, but there is no experiment showing it actually outperforms alternative selection strategies (e.g., random selection, entropy-based uncertainty). While I am generally convinced of the idea, even a simple annotation efficiency curve would substantially strengthen this claim. 7.Missing annotation statistics Step 5 mentions “e.g., the 50 masks with the lowest score per tumor type” leaving the actual number ambiguous. The total number of active learning cycles is not reported. It is unclear how many masks were radiologist-refined vs. automatically accepted as high-quality. Were in the end all masks at least visually inspected? 8.(clarity and organization) Manuscript appears incomplete Several issues suggest the paper was submitted prematurely: Keywords section still reads “First keyword · Second keyword · Another keyword” Section 2.1 contains an unfilled placeholder: “we create # multi-tumor masks in just 5 months”. Howerver, the total mask count is arguably the most important statistic for a tumor lesion dataset paper and is missing The sentence “R-Super teacher segmentation models to segment tumors” is syntactically broken The paper does not fill the allotted page limit; space could have been used for additional dataset statistics or a qualitative figure
reviewer_2_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: Major Strengths1.This is a genuinely impactful dataset for an under-served clinical problem. The motivation is compelling and accurate: public CT tumor segmentation datasets are dominated by liver, kidney, pancreas, colon, adrenal, and lung tumors, while cancers in the other organs collectively account for roughly half of global cancer mortality. Releasing voxel-wise masks for spleen, adrenal, bladder, gallbladder, esophagus, stomach, duodenum, prostate, and uterus tumors (particularly rare types like esophagus (n=108) and duodenum (n=249)) represents substantial community value. If released as promised, this fills a real gap that cannot be addressed by methodological improvements alone.2.Report-based active learning genuinely solves the cold-start problem. The core insight i.e that traditional active learning fails when no adequate seed model exists for the target tumor types, and that R-Super can bootstrap reasonable initial masks from report supervision alone, is well-motivated and non-obvious. The design choice to couple Ball-Convolution-based tumor localization with report-derived counts and diameters is a clever way to inject weak structural priors that reduce radiologist correction burden. This is a legitimately novel workflow contribution, not just “LLM + active learning.”3.The report-confidence score is a principled triage mechanism. Using the Dice between the soft (pre-refinement) mask and the report-refined mask as a proxy for “how much did the refinement have to do” is a sensible signal for flagging unreliable cases. Low Dice implies that the model’s confidence was misaligned with the report description, which is precisely the condition under which radiologist review adds the most value. The intuition that refinement magnitude correlates with unreliability is well-argued.4.Comprehensive multimodal integration. Beyond masks, the dataset ties together CT, radiology reports, ICD-9/ICD-10 codes (2.9M+ assigned codes, 16,553 unique values), patient demographics, scanner metadata, and longitudinal timestamps. This richness enables research beyond segmentation (longitudinal progression modeling, demographic fairness studies, scanner-invariance analysis) that narrower datasets cannot support.5.Evaluation against both public models and within-dataset baselines. Table 1 compares against ULS (the strongest public multi-tumor baseline), a classification baseline, and R-Super trained on reports alone. The within-dataset comparison (Merlin vs. Merlin Plus) isolates the value of the masks themselves, while the ULS comparison isolates the value versus the state of the public art. Both comparisons are meaningful and the gap (+10% F1 on average) is substantial.6.Small-lesion coverage. Explicit reporting of lesions under 2 cm is important for the early-detection use case the paper motivates. Early-stage tumors are precisely the small-diameter cases that most benefit from mask-level supervision.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Major Weaknesses Four radiologists created/corrected the masks, yet there is no reported measure of inter-rater agreement (Dice, Hausdorff, surface distance), no double-reading subset, and no analysis of which tumor types showed high versus low annotator concordance. For small lesions (<2 cm) across rare tumor types (esophagus n=108, duodenum n=249), inter-rater variability is typically substantial and directly affects downstream model ceiling performance. Without this, the claim of “high-quality segmentations” is an assertion rather than a demonstration. This is a critical omission for a dataset paper. 2.A quantitative validation of the active learning pipeline is missing. The paper claims a 5× speedup (30 min -> 5 min per scan) but provides no data supporting this: no time-motion study, no breakdown by tumor type or lesion size, no comparison against a from-scratch annotation arm on a matched subset, no reporting of how many cases required full redrawing versus minor correction. Similarly, the number of active learning cycles run, the number of masks corrected at each cycle, and the per-cycle performance improvement are absent. For a paper whose second core contribution is the annotation pipeline, these metrics are essential. 3.The Dice scores are surprisingly low and under-discussed. Table 1’s caption reports average Dice of 17 (MedFormer), 25 (R-Super with reports+masks), and 10 (R-Super reports only). A DSC of 25 for a “state-of-the-art” segmentation model trained on “radiologist-validated” masks is remarkably poor and it implies that the masks are either too inconsistent to learn from, the tumors are genuinely too hard (likely in some organs), or both. This deserves substantial discussion and per-organ breakdown, but the number appears only in the caption and is never addressed in the text. A dataset paper claiming segmentation value cannot leave a DSC of 17–25 unexplained. 4.The report-confidence score has an unexamined failure mode. The scoring mechanism (Dice between soft and report-refined mask) flags cases where the refinement did substantial work. But this conflates two distinct failure modes: (a) the soft mask was wrong and the refinement correctly fixed it (flagged as unreliable, appropriately), and (b) the soft mask was right but the refinement mechanically moved it (e.g., due to imprecise organ mask dilation or a tumor slightly outside the reported slice), also flagged as unreliable, but incorrectly. There is no validation that radiologist-flagged masks actually had errors versus cases where the score fired spuriously. Without a precision/recall analysis of the flagging mechanism, we don’t know whether the radiologist time is well-spent. 5.The single-site bias is unaddressed. All CT scans are from Stanford Hospital. Scanner distribution, patient demographics, and imaging protocols are not compared to other healthcare systems. Models trained on Merlin Plus may exhibit substantial performance degradation on data from hospitals with different scanner vendors, contrast protocols, or patient populations. The paper does not evaluate on an external test set, does not report scanner or demographic confounders in performance, and does not discuss this limitation. For a dataset paper intended to serve the community, external validation is a reasonable expectation. 6.There is a methodological ambiguity in Step 3(D) volume matching. The report-derived volume estimation uses “sphere/ellipsoid volume approximations” from 1D diameters, with a 30% agreement tolerance. The choice of sphere vs. ellipsoid is not specified per tumor type, and the 30% threshold is unjustified; tumors are rarely spherical, and report diameters often capture only the long axis. This procedural step materially affects ground-truth quality and warrants more scrutiny. 7.Overlap with concurrent submission is not disclosed in-paper. The companion paper (TR-Distillation, 4063 concurrent submission) shares substantial machinery (R-Super, Ball Convolutions, the same LLM extraction pipeline, the same tumor-type focus). While the program chairs’ note handles the formal disclosure, from a reviewer’s standpoint the two papers read as two angles on the same research program. This paper would benefit from clearer articulation of what is novel in Merlin Plus beyond applying the (previously published) R-Super framework to a new cohort. 8.Ethics, consent, and release mechanism are completely absent. The paper claims Merlin Plus will be “publicly available” but does not describe the data use agreement, IRB approval, de-identification protocol beyond the phrase “anonymized patient IDs,” or the license under which masks will be released. Given that this is a Stanford Hospital dataset with demographic metadata including race, the paper must address these points. Stanford’s Merlin dataset itself has specific access controls that Merlin Plus inherits, and this should be explicit. This is particularly important because Section 2.2 describes ICD code integration from the same patient encounter — additional PHI that needs explicit disclosure of de-identification. 9.”ICD-10 codes identify malignancy” claim is clinically imprecise. ICD-10 codes record encounter-level diagnoses but do not reliably identify whether a specific imaging finding on a specific scan is malignant. A patient may have a historical cancer diagnosis (recorded in ICD-10) but the lesion visible on the current scan may be benign, treated, or unrelated. The paper states malignancy is “cross-checked with reports,” but the cross-checking procedure is not described. Mislabeling of benign lesions as malignant (or vice versa) at scale would materially compromise the dataset. 10.THere are many inconsistencies and errors in the text. The abstract states 25,494 scans; Section 2.3 states 25,528 scans. The keywords are placeholders (“First keyword · Second keyword · Another keyword”). Section 2.1 contains the unfilled token “create # multi-tumor masks.” Reference [13] cites arXiv:2601.22134 with year 2026 — this appears to be a non-existent/future arXiv ID. Footnote 2 refers to “these 8 tumor types” while the main text consistently claims 9 tumor types. These errors in a submission suggest rushed preparation and reduce confidence in the numerical precision throughout. 11.The ULS is a weak comparator that the paper over-attributes meaning to. ULS is a universal lesion segmentation model, it was designed for lesion agnosticism, not organ-specific cancer segmentation. Showing that a model trained on in-distribution tumor-specific data outperforms an out-of-distribution universal lesion model at F1 score is expected. The more meaningful comparison ( against organ-specific segmenters fine-tuned on ULS subsets or on related cohorts ) is not conducted.

title: MIL-PF: Multiple Instance Learning on Precomputed Features for Mammography Classification
reviewer_1_strengths: This paper provides a simple yet effective approach to leverage pretrained foundation models for the downstream task of classifying multiview mammography images. This approach requires little training and only needs image level annotations. The paper provides extensive and solid evidence that the proposed MIL-PF approach often outperforms alternative state of the art approaches. The authors perform several runs for each experiment, provide sufficient ablation studies and validation to give support to their claims. Overall, it offers a simple yet effective approach to train models on downstream tasks while relying on pre-computed features obtained from frozen foundation models. The authors also show that multiple foundation models can be plugged in with similar performances, regardless of being previously trained on this type of data, thereby opening new possibilities based on generic foundation models, ie, models not necessarily trained on mammographies or even medical images).
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The major weakness of the paper is its novelty. On one hand, using frozen foundation models for downstream tasks has been extensively explored in the last few years. The paper’s reference [8] is one such example, which already uses features extracted with a frozen MammoCLIP to perform the classification of mammography images. Another work that compares multiple foundation models for this specific task, including a non-medical DINOv2, is [A], also published in MICCAI 2025.Additionally, there are plenty of other works based on this type of approach for other applications. The proposed MIL framework is also not novel, as the described Perceiver-style cross attention is identical to recent approaches based on prompt learning or context optimization (see, eg [B]). While this paper provides additional evidence that this line of work is relevant and effective, it is not proposing a novel approach. Nonetheless, I conceive that it may be the first to combine the using pre-computed features from foundation models with a cross attention mechanism to aggregate patch level information for a MIL framework. The results are also not always convincing, in the sense that some of the alternative approaches achieve equally good or better results in some of the tests. This is particularly evident in the classification results for VinDr and also for the (weakly supervised) detection metrics, considering the results obtained with [8]. The latter could be indicative that modality-specific encoders can be better at capturing medically relevant features than generic ones. [A] Germani, E. , Selin-Türk, I. , Zeineddine, F. , Mourad, C. , & Albarqouni, S. (2025, September). Bias and generalizability of foundation models across datasets in breast mammography. In International Conference on Medical Image Computing and Computer-Assisted Intervention (pp. 24-34). Cham: Springer Nature Switzerland. [B] Chen, H. , & Martel, A. L. (2025, September). Breast Cancer Detection from Multi-view Screening Mammograms with Visual Prompt Tuning. In Deep Breast Workshop on AI and Imaging for Diagnostic and Treatment Challenges in Breast Care (pp. 91-100). Cham: Springer Nature Switzerland.
