reviewer_2_strengths: The paper demonstrates that general-purpose vision foundation models (e.g., DINOv2, MedSigLIP) can achieve state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance in mammography classification without the need for task-specific fine-tuning of the backbones. This is achieved through global-local dual-stream architecture that effectively balances overall tissue context with fine-grained lesion signals While maintaining a highly efficient and lightweight structure (~40k parameters and 2M FLOPS per forward pass), the framework provides interpretable attention maps. This visual feedback demonstrates strong potential for xAI. Overall, the manuscript is well-written and follows a clear, logical structure that effectively communicates the technical framework and clinical motivations. The method section is theoretically sound, and the experimental setup is robust, characterized by large-scale evaluations and a rigorous validation process.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: While the empirical findings regarding the generalization of foundation models to mammography are valuable, the proposed architecture lacks significant technical novelty. The framework primarily relies on a combination of existing components—specifically, a frozen backbone with a standard Perceiver-style cross-attention mechanism and a late-fusion strategy Despite the competitive classification performance, the model exhibits notably low detection accuracy (mAP) for small lesions, though the authors correctly identify this as a limitation tied to the large input tile sizes and mark it for future work Given the 11% variance in Spec@Sens=0.9, the authors should provide p-values and confidence intervals to establish statistical significance over baselines. Reporting the mean and standard deviation across all 36 runs, rather than only the best-performing validation model, is essential to confirm the framework’s true clinical stability and sensitivity.

reviewer_3_weaknesses: The methodological novelty is very limited, as the approach mainly combines existing components, including frozen foundation encoders, standard MIL formulations. The claimed contribution “We formalize a class of mammography-motivated MIL problems and propose an architecture designed to address them.” is also very weak. author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for the valuable feedback. They note that MIL-PF is simple yet effective [R1], tackles relevant clinical tasks [R3] and demonstrates valuable and extensively evaluated performance [R1, R2]. All found the method highly efficient and clearly presented. [R1, R2, R3] Novelty: We agree that MIL-PF relies on existing parts and, in the paper, we never claim any of the fundamentals (frozen encoders, Perceiver, dual-stream, etc.) as novel. Rather, we demonstrate the mammography benefits of our particular component arrangement (end of Sec. 3.3). Known parts and ~30x less trainable parameters (single encoder forward pass in training) are preferred when constrained clinically or in hardware, and, since we achieve state-of-the-art results this way, we find MIL-PF valuable for MICCAI; especially since no significantly similar mammography setting is present in the literature. Finally, we will adapt the final wording to emphasize these specifics in the light of reviewers’ comments. [R3] Novelty: R3 raises novelty versus cardiac/retinal, but doesn’t point to specific work. Closest analogs we found are Shad et. al (Nature 2026, arXiv:2312.00357) for frozen foundation models, Huang et al. (ISBI 2025, arXiv:2403.06024) for MIL, and MVCINN (Luo et. al., AAAI 2023) for multi-view/attention. Crucially, none combine all, and none target MIL-PF’s regime: ~5k×5k images, variable number of views, sparse ROIs, bag-labels without text reports. [R1] Novelty: We consider [A] (Germani et al.), [B] (Chen & Martel) and [8] valuable, but none comprehensively covers MIL-PF’s goal. [A] focuses on the foundation model biases, not classification, and not important domain architectural specifics like MIL-PF, and, even in this context, the DINOv2’s value is not recognized (as R1 notices), which is an important MIL-PF’s insight, thanks to the large clinical benchmark (EMBED). We respectfully disagree that [B] is identical to Perceiver-style attention used in our paper. In [B], the prompts are injected in the backbone’s internals; MIL-PF’s latent sits entirely outside the encoder, querying over precomputed embeddings - precisely enabling efficiency. We acknowledge similarities with [8], but demonstrate superior classification performance, precomputing importance, simpler architecture and general encoders’ potential over MammoCLIP. [R1] Results not convincing: On the largest (most diverse) dataset, MIL-PF improves AUC by 4% and Spec. by 20% over the strongest baseline, remaining best or almost the best on the other classification tasks, while massively decreasing trainable parameters over the baselines. [R1, R2] p-values: would strengthen the claims. However, MIL-PF’s EMBED gains are large and reproduce well across 2 encoders, 3 datasets, and 3 metrics, while the 36 runs’ val/test near-perfect alignment indicates stability. [R1] Dual-stream ablation: While p-values would be useful, we consider the 36 runs’ increase of >1% in AUC and especially increase of up to 10% in Spec. significant enough for our dual-stream claims. [R1] CLIP: No scaled text-image mammography corpus exists; MammoCLIP relies on templated/synthetic captions as a workaround; requires sacrifice of arbitrary input resolution and native multi-view support, important specifics MIL-PF handles by design. meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper received mixed reviews, including two weak accepts and one reject. The work addresses a practically relevant problem in mammography classification and presents a simple, efficient, and clearly organized framework based on frozen foundation-model features and lightweight MIL aggregation; the positive reviews highlight its empirical strength, including evaluation on multiple mammography benchmarks and evidence that precomputed features from general or medical foundation models can achieve competitive, and in some cases state-of-the-art, performance. However, the main concern is limited methodological novelty, as the framework largely builds on established ideas such as frozen feature extraction, MIL aggregation, and Perceiver-style cross-attention, making its distinction from prior work insufficiently clear. The paper would benefit from stronger positioning against related studies, including MammoCLIP-based feature extraction, foundation-model comparisons in mammography, and visual-prompt or Perceiver-style aggregation methods. Several experimental and methodological details also require clarification, including label definitions, dataset handling, embedding-size choices, detection-analysis settings, and the statistical significance of the reported improvements. Overall, the paper is practically meaningful and empirically promising, but its contribution relative to existing work remains somewhat unclear; therefore, the authors are invited to submit a rebuttal before a final decision is made. | After rebuttal, this paper receives three accept recommendations, including two reviewers who maintained weak acceptance and one reviewer who changed from rejection to acceptance. The AC acknowledges that the paper addresses a clinically important problem in mammography classification and proposes a simple, efficient, and practically attractive MIL framework built on precomputed frozen foundation-model features. The reviewers consistently recognize the paper’s strengths in clear presentation, computational efficiency, use of only image-level labels, and extensive evaluation across multiple mammography benchmarks. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper presents MIL-PF, a simple and efficient framework using frozen foundation-model features with a lightweight MIL head for mammography classification. Reviewers agree that the methodological novelty is limited, as the work combines existing components, but the rebuttal clarified the positioning and practical contribution. The empirical results are strong, especially on large-scale mammography benchmarks, and the framework is computationally attractive with very few trainable parameters. Overall, the paper makes a valuable application-oriented contribution and is recommended for acceptance, provided the final version avoids overclaiming novelty and better situates the work relative to prior methods. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The authors have addressed the concerns regarding novelty, ablation study, and p-values, and discussed related works. All reviewers are convinced to accept this manuscript after the rebuttal.

title: Missingness-Aware Multimodal Learning for Four-Class Adrenal Tumor Classification
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.Missingness-aware fusion mechanism: It explicitly models the missing patterns of clinical data to dynamically adjust the fusion weights of imaging/clinical modalities. Unlike simple missing value imputation or discarding strategies, this design better aligns with the characteristics of real-world clinical data. 2.Prototype regularization method: It optimizes intra-class compactness and inter-class separation in the multimodal feature space, and achieves superior classification performance for rare tumor classes compared with traditional imbalance solutions such as Focal Loss. 3.Clinically feasible design: It accomplishes four-class adrenal tumor classification using non-contrast CT combined with non-hormonal clinical data, avoiding the risks of contrast agents and complex endocrine tests, thus facilitating clinical translation and implementation. 4.Comprehensive experimental validation and reproducibility: The paper conducts sufficient comparative experiments and ablation experiments to comprehensively verify the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed method. It clearly provides detailed experimental settings, implementation details and evaluation metrics, and also offers a valid anonymous code link, ensuring good reproducibility of the experimental results.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.Insufficient Effectiveness in t-SNE Visualization:The t-SNE plots in Fig. 2 fail to intuitively demonstrate the superiority of the prototype regularization loss (Lproto). Visually, the difference in feature clustering and separation performance between Lproto and Focal Loss is not distinct enough, which undermines the clear illustration of Lproto’s value in optimizing intra-class compactness and inter-class separation. 2.Lack of Framework Innovation:The overall design of the framework leans heavily towards engineering-oriented modular integration and hyperparameter tuning. It lacks breakthrough theoretical innovations or novel multimodal fusion paradigms. The originality of the core mechanisms needs to be further strengthened to enhance the academic contribution of the study.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The work targets a realistic clinical setting with missingness and class imbalance. The proposed solution carries clinical significance and potential utility. 2.The method explicitly encodes missing patterns and uses a reliability descriptor to adaptively weight modalities, which provides a more effective alternative to standard imputation or static fusion. 3.Experiments show strong empirical validation.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.While the overall framework is well integrated, most components build on existing ideas. Feature-wise modulation follows prior work such as FiLM (Perez et al., 2018), and multimodal interaction with tabular data has been explored in DAFT (Wolf et al., 2022) and HyperFusion (Duenias et al., 2025). Handling missing modalities via adaptive mechanisms is also related to DrFuse (Yao et al., 2024). As such, the contribution lies more in the combination of these techniques rather than a fundamentally new formulation. 2.The use of prototype-based objectives is inspired by prior work such as ProCo (Du et al., 2024), but the paper provides limited intuition for why this specific formulation is particularly suitable for the multimodal fusion setting. The improvement over alternatives (e.g., focal loss) is shown empirically but lacks deeper theoretical or geometric justification. 3.The study is based on a single-center retrospective cohort, which may introduce selection bias and limit generalizability. There is no external validation or cross-institutional testing.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: Novel missingness-aware fusion mechanism: The paper explicitly models missing clinical data and uses it to guide cross-modal interaction and adaptive weighting. This is interesting because, unlike prior work that relies on imputation or assumes complete inputs, the model conditions fusion on input reliability, making it more robust to real-world clinical settings. Effective handling of class imbalance via prototype regularization: The proposed distribution-aware prototype loss improves intra-class compactness and inter-class separation in the fused embedding space. This goes beyond standard reweighting (e.g., focal loss) and leads to better minority-class performance, which is critical in medical datasets. Clinically relevant evaluation: The work demonstrates effectiveness on a realistic multimodal setup (non-contrast CT + incomplete clinical data) with substantial missingness and imbalance, supported by comprehensive experiments, ablations, and analysis, including improved recall for underrepresented tumor types.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty relative to prior multimodal fusion work: While the paper emphasizes missingness-aware fusion, many components build directly on existing ideas, e.g., FiLM-style modulation (Perez et al., 2018), DAFT (Wolf et al., 2022), and missing-modality handling in DrFuse (Yao et al., 2024). The adaptive weighting via a learned reliability signal is incremental over these works, and the paper does not clearly articulate what fundamentally distinguishes it beyond combining these ideas. Evaluation lacks external validation and generalizability analysis: All experiments are conducted on a single retrospective cohort from one institution. There is no multi-center validation or testing on external datasets, which is critical for clinical deployment. Given known domain shifts in medical imaging, this limits confidence in real-world applicability. Handling of missing data is relatively simple and potentially suboptimal: Missing values are still imputed using basic statistical methods, and missingness is only encoded as a binary indicator. More advanced approaches (e.g., generative modeling, uncertainty-aware imputation, or masked modeling) are not explored, making the approach somewhat limited compared to state-of-the-art missing-data techniques. Clinical utility and comparison to standard workflows are not fully established: Although the paper motivates reducing reliance on hormonal testing and contrast imaging, it does not provide direct comparison with clinical baselines or decision protocols, nor does it evaluate how the model would integrate into practice (e.g., decision curves, cost-benefit analysis, or physician-in-the-loop scenarios). This weakens the claim of practical clinical impact.

title: Mitigating Grade Boundary Conflicts for Disease Severity Grading with Ambiguous Labels
reviewer_1_strengths: The paper presents a practical solution to the label ambiguity problem in medical image grading. The two-module design, consisting of GBH for boundary harmonization and UniProj for ordinal consistency, is logically coherent and well motivated. The experimental evaluation includes multiple baselines spanning proxy label strategies, noise robust methods, and grading specific approaches, with ablation studies confirming the contribution of each component. The t-SNE visualizations provide intuitive evidence of improved feature clustering.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: -Although the paper argues that label-level unimodality is superior to prediction-level ordinal constraints used in SRJT and URL, UniProj still imposes the same unimodality prior, making this distinction insufficiently justified. The performance gain may instead mainly come from GBH rather than the location where unimodality is enforced. An ablation of UniProj alone, GBH alone, and the full HDU framework would be necessary to support this claim. (3) The evaluation lacks cross-architecture generalizability analysis. LIDC-IDRI uses EfficientNet-B0 while Kaggle DR uses ResNet34 as the backbone. It is therefore unclear whether the observed performance gains are robust to backbone choice or specific to the selected architectures. Moreover, using different backbones across the two datasets makes it difficult to disentangle the method’s contribution from architectural differences. Validating HDU with multiple backbones on the same dataset (e. g. , both ResNet and EfficientNet on LIDC-IDRI) would substantially strengthen the claims of generalizability. (4) The paper adopts Early Learning Regularization (ELR) as part of the loss function but does not report the specific values of its key hyperparameters, namely the momentum coefficient β (Equation 6) and the regularization weight λ (Equation 5). Moreover, no sensitivity analysis is provided to examine how performance varies with different choices of these parameters. (5) On Page 3, “Extensive experiments demonstrates” should be “Extensive experiments demonstrate”.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The work is clinically relevant, particularly in scenarios where severity grade labels are ambiguous and inter-rater disagreement is common. 2.The manuscript is well-written along with that solid mathematical foundations are provided. 3.Comprehensive ablation studies have been conducted, effectively evaluating their contributions. 4.The manuscript provided detailed implementation information, demonstrating strong methodological rigor and clarity. 5.The integration of the proposed modules is coherent, and systematically designed. 6.Explanations of the results are also provided through qualitative study.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The Grade Boundaries Harmonization module appears to be closely related to the Prototype-guided Pseudo Labeling Module proposed in [1], which leverages Categorical Prototype Extraction. The manuscript should clearly indicate the differences with those proposed in [1]. 2.The proposed UniProj module [2], which projects calibrated labels onto a unimodal distribution to capture ordinal relationships in grading tasks, appears to overlap conceptually with existing approaches in the literature [2]. The authors should more explicitly highlight what distinguishes this formulation from prior work and justify its novelty. 3.Overall, related work citations could be included to better position the manuscript within existing literature; [1-3] for Prototype-guided Pseudo Labeling mechanisms, label memory bank and concept of projecting labels onto unimodal distribution. 4.Minor comment: The in-text citations in the manuscript should be properly reordered and formatted for consistency. For example, [17,19,18] should be rearranged as [17–19], [12,11] as [11–12], and [10,9,14] as [9,10,14]. References: [1] W. Yang, R. Zhang, J. Chen, L. Wang, and J. Kim, “Prototype-guided pseudo labeling for semi-supervised text classification,” in Proceedings of the 61st Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers), 2023, pp. 16369–16382. Albuquerque, “Unimodal distributions for ordinal regression,” IEEE Transactions on Artificial Intelligence, vol. 6, no. 9, pp. 2498–2509, Sept. 2025, doi: 10.1109/TAI.2025.3549740. [3] N. C. reviewer_3_strengths: The main strengths of this paper are that it addresses a clinically relevant problem, proposes a technically coherent framework tailored to ambiguous ordinal grading, and demonstrates consistent improvements over several baselines on two medical grading benchmarks. The method is clearly presented, and the overall pipeline is reasonably aligned with the ordinal nature of disease severity grading.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The proposed GBH module is essentially a prototype/reference-based label refinement mechanism. Its effectiveness relies on the assumption that the current batch of prototypes provides reliable class references, which may not hold when adjacent grades heavily overlap or when the learned representation is still unstable. Prototype-based methods often suffer from class ambiguity due to distribution differences. Can its effectiveness be proven through generalization tests? 2.I suggest comparing some reference-based ordinal regression methods, such as Geometric order learning for rank estimation and Blind Image Quality Assessment Based on Geometric Order Learning. 3.The ablation was insufficient. I would like to see the individual effects of GBH and UniProj. 4.It is better to show the visualizations of the accuracy of classification for each specific category.

author_feedback: We sincerely thank the reviewers for their valuable comments and recognition of our work. GQ1(R1,R3)-Ablation Study: On LIDC-IDRI, the Soft Label (SL) achieved 65.36%/88.22% (Acc/AUC). SL+UniProj achieved 66.02%/89.27%, validating label-wise ordinal guidance. SL+GBH achieved 67.57%/89.95%, showing the importance of resolving boundary conflicts. SL+GBH+UniProj achieved 72.26%/91.27%, showing their complementary effects. Further adding ELR yielded the HDU, which achieved 74.48%/91.57%. R1Q1-Label-Level Unimodality: Unlike prediction-level unimodality constraints (e.g., URL), UniProj enforces unimodality directly on labels, providing more explicit ordinal supervision. On LIDC-IDRI, label-level UniProj outperformed a prediction-level variant (91.57% vs. 88.15% AUC, 62.22% vs. 57.69% F1, 74.48% vs. 73.18% Acc). R1Q2-Different Backbone: We evaluated HDU on LIDC-IDRI using EfficientNet-B0, ResNet18, and ResNet34.HDU consistently outperformed URL across all backbones, achieving 74.48%/91.57% vs. 73.83%/87.41% (Effi-B0), 75.78%/88.68% vs. 71.48%/87.77% (Res-18), and 73.43%/90.26% vs. 71.09%/81.62% (Res-34) in Acc/AUC, demonstrating robust cross-architecture generalizability. R1Q3-ELR Hyperparameters: The hyperparameters were selected via grid search, with λ = 1.5, β = 0.2.We apologize for missing these and will include the settings and sensitivity analysis in the final version and supplementary. R2Q1-Difference with [Ref1]: We acknowledge that GBH shares the high-level idea of prototype-guided label refinement with [Ref1]. However, [Ref1] focuses on semi-supervised text classification with pseudo-labeling for unlabeled samples, whereas GBH is designed for ambiguous multi-annotator ordinal grading with grade boundary conflicts. Instead of hard pseudo-labeling, GBH performs probabilistic label calibration via prototype-guided harmonization and memory-based refinement. R2Q2-Difference with [Ref2]: We acknowledge the conceptual connection between UniProj and prior unimodal ordinal regression methods such as [Ref2]. Unlike existing prediction-level constraints, UniProj performs label-level unimodal projection for ambiguous multi-annotator grading to jointly model ordinal relationships and harmonize grade boundary conflicts. Results in R1Q1 further show that label-level projection is more effective in our setting. We will include discussions of [Ref1–3] in the final version. R3Q1-GBH: We agree that prototype reliability may be affected by unstable representations and overlapping adjacent grades. Therefore, instead of direct hard pseudo-labeling, GBH adopts a conservative soft calibration strategy. Following the early-learning phenomenon that DNNs first fit clean patterns before memorizing noisy labels, we introduce a warm-up stage so that prototypes are computed from stable representations. Moreover, adjacent-grade overlap is exactly the grade-boundary conflict targeted by GBH. Instead of enforcing hard separation, GBH uses class-stratified prototype similarities to generate soft probabilistic labels that alleviate inconsistent annotations. Consistent gains across different backbones (see R1Q2) further support the robustness of GBH. R3Q2-Compared with Ordinal Regression Methods: We compared HDU with GOL and QCN on LIDC as suggested, achieving 52.34%/74.22% and 51.17%/72.65% (Acc/AUC), both far below HDU (74.48%/91.57%). We found that these methods assume a smooth and relatively uniform ordinal geometry, which suits tasks such as age estimation or IQA. In contrast, disease severity grading often has non-uniform grade intervals, making embedding-level ranking constraints insufficient. Explicit boundary harmonization is more effective. R3Q3-Per-category Analysis: Compared with URL, HDU achieves comparable recall on most grades while improving Grade 1 recall from 86.59% to 88.65% and Grade 5 recall from 63.15% to 78.94%, showing stronger discrimination of non-severe and severe cases. Details will be included in the supplymentary.

title: MM-UNet: Meta Mamba UNet for Volumetric Medical Image Segmentation
reviewer_1_strengths: The paper effectively identifies limitation of SSMs when applied to medical imaging: the difficulty in fitting high-variance intensity data. The proposed Hybrid Module, which places Mamba blocks after dual CNN layers and within a residual structure, is a well-motivated architectural adaptation. This design successfully leverages the local inductive bias of CNNs to provide a more stable feature distribution for Mamba’s global sequence modeling. One of the standout aspects of this work is the extensive ablation study on 3D scan orders. Rather than arbitrarily choosing a scanning path, the authors rigorously evaluated nine different configurations. This thorough investigation provides valuable empirical insights for the community regarding the optimal way to serialize volumetric medical data for SSM-based architectures. The MM-UNet demonstrates consistently strong performance across three major and diverse 3D medical imaging datasets: AMOS22, BTCV, and ACDC. Achieving competitive Dice scores against established heavyweights like nnU-Net and Swin-UNETR highlights the practical potential of the proposed framework in clinical segmentation tasks. The paper provides interesting visualizations of Mamba’s attention maps. By comparing forward and backward scanning patterns, the authors offer a clear visual demonstration of how the bidirectional scanning strategy captures complementary receptive fields. This adds a layer of interpretability to the model, showing how it maintains spatial coherence despite the 1D flattening of 3D volumes. The inclusion of practical inference-time strategies, such as 3D Gaussian weighting to suppress boundary errors, shows a clear focus on clinical feasibility. This attention to detail suggests that the method is designed with real-world medical image characteristics in mind, where boundary precision and spatial consistency are paramount.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The authors explicitly state that an 8-fold Test-Time Augmentation via axis-flipping was employed during inference for MM-UNet. However, it is fundamentally unclear whether the baseline models (especially SwinUNETR, VMUNet, and UMamba) in Tables 1-3 were evaluated under the exact same 8-fold TTA protocol. If the baselines were evaluated without TTA, the marginal performance gains (e. g. , +0.2% over Swin-UNETR on BTCV) are heavily confounded by this inference-time trick rather than the proposed architectural novelty. The authors should provide a fair comparison table without TTA for all methods, or explicitly confirm that all reported baseline results also utilize the exact same TTA strategy. There is a logical paradox between the authors’ architectural claims and their inference strategy. To justify the 8-fold TTA, the authors argue that “This is analogous to applying multiple scan orders in Mamba”. However, this directly contradicts their own findings in the ablation study (Section 2.3), where they demonstrated that extending to multiple scanning pairs (e. g. , 3 pairs or 6 pairs) yields lower Dice scores (0.908 and 0.907, respectively) because “multiple pairs provide no additional benefit and may introduce redundancy”. Furthermore, they explicitly claimed earlier that “a single pair of opposite scan orders is sufficient to represent the input”. The authors argue that SSMs struggle with high-variance data and propose embedding Mamba within a residual block after two CNN layers because “pre-trained feature maps behind CNN layers. . . exhibit lower variance”. This mathematical justification is questionable. If the fundamental limitation of SSMs is strictly the statistical variance of the input features, standard Normalization techniques (e. g. , LayerNorm, InstanceNorm)—which mathematically standardize the features to have unit variance—would entirely resolve this issue without the need for CNNs. In the abstract and contributions, the authors state: “We introduce a bi-directional scan order strategy to mitigate discontinuities. . . “. Presenting this as a novel introduction is inaccurate and overlooks the established consensus in the recent SSM literature. Multi-directional scanning strategies are already a fundamental design choice in visual SSMs to address 1D-to-2D/3D structural disruption.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.Addresses core limitations of Mamba in 3D imaging: Unlike many works that directly apply 2D Mamba to 3D data, this paper takes a more principled approach. It analyzes, from a theoretical perspective, how SSMs struggle with high-variance data (linked to the properties of the HiPPO operator), and addresses this by placing Mamba inside residual connections to stabilize the input. This problem-driven design is both thoughtful and academically meaningful. 2.Thorough architecture and scanning ablations: The paper builds a “meta” framework that includes pure CNN, pure SSM, and hybrid models for systematic comparison. It also evaluates more than ten different 3D scanning strategies (e.g., DHW, WHD, Zigzag, 3D Window Scan), making the final choice of “1D BiScan” well-supported and convincing. 3.Strong performance on challenging 3D clinical datasets: The model achieves excellent results on large-scale and difficult 3D datasets such as AMOS22 (Task 1 & 2) and BTCV. For instance, it reaches 91.5% Dice on AMOS22 Task 1, outperforming nnUNet by 1.7%, demonstrating strong capability in handling complex 3D anatomical structures.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Over-reliance on test-time augmentation (TTA): The paper uses 8× flip-based TTA during inference (as shown in Fig. 4), averaging predictions over eight passes for each 3D patch. While this can boost Dice scores, it also significantly increases inference time. Since no results on inference time or FPS are reported, it’s unclear how much of the performance gain comes from the model itself versus the extra computational cost introduced by repeated inference. The term “Meta” feels somewhat overstated: The model is named “Meta Mamba UNet,” but in practice, it mainly involves manually designed building blocks (e.g., EncMetaBlock, DecMetaBlock) and systematic ablation. While this is a thorough and well-executed study, the use of “Meta”—which often implies meta-learning or neural architecture search—may be somewhat misleading.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: Major Strengths 1.It has a genuinely useful unifying framework. Framing VM-UNet, SwinUMamba, U-Mamba, and nnUNet as specific instantiations of a common meta-architecture is a clarifying contribution. It lets the community reason about where Mamba helps (encoder/bottleneck) versus where it does not (decoder) in a controlled way rather than through cross-paper comparisons that confound architecture with training recipe. 2.It has a principled, mechanistic critique of SSMs for images. The analysis in Section 2.1 and Fig. 2(a), showing that S4 smooths high-variance points due to HiPPO polynomial projection, and that row-transition discontinuities produce nearly-inverse predictions, is the kind of diagnostic evidence that is too rare in vision-Mamba papers. Most prior work asserts that Mamba “captures long-range dependencies” and moves on; this paper actually probes when and why it fails on 2D data. 3.The variance-inside-residual observation is novel and actionable. Fig. 2(b)’s comparison of feature-map variance inside vs. outside residual connections, linked causally to SSM sensitivity to variance, provides a crisp mechanistic justification for placing MetaSSM inside the residual branch. The resulting 0.9% improvement is small but consistent with the stated hypothesis. 4.The ablations are systematic. Table 4’s scan-order ablation (B1–B9) is thorough: it tests not just “does bi-directional help” but also whether more directions help (they don’t), whether unpaired directions hurt (yes), and whether 2D/window/zigzag/inclined alternatives offer advantages (no). The negative results here are informative and strengthen the final design choice. 5.There is strong and diverse empirical evaluation. Four benchmarks (AMOS22 T1, AMOS22 T2, ACDC, BTCV) spanning CT, MRI, abdominal, and cardiac anatomy, with comparisons to nine baselines including three Mamba-based competitors and three transformer-based ones. The AMOS22 results are from the official leaderboard, which mitigates concerns about evaluation cherry-picking. Per-organ Dice is reported rather than only averages. 6.Practically useful negative result. The finding that replacing the decoder with Mamba hurts performance (89.4%) while replacing the encoder/bottleneck helps is a useful guideline for future Mamba-based segmentation architectures and explains, post hoc, why U-Mamba’s design (encoder-side Mamba) works better than VM-UNet’s (everywhere).
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Major Weaknesses 1.The “high-variance” claim is under-quantified and possibly conflated. The central mechanistic storyi.e SSMs struggle with high variance, residual connections reduce variance, therefore put SSMs in residuals, rests on one qualitative figure (Fig. 2b) reporting three variance numbers (0.308 / 0.285 / 0.482) from a single pre-trained model. There is no statistical test, no variation across layers/models/datasets, and no controlled experiment (e.g., injecting variance into a synthetic input and measuring SSM error) to establish the causal link. A 0.285 vs. 0.308 difference is particularly thin to motivate an architectural principle. The paper would be substantially stronger with a formal analysis of SSM error as a function of input variance, or at minimum a correlation plot across many layers. 2.Inference-time 8-flip TTA is not acknowledged as a confound. Fig. 4 describes averaging predictions over 8 flip variants with 3D Gaussian weighting at inference. This is classical test-time augmentation and typically adds 0.3–1.0% Dice on its own. It is unclear whether the baselines (nnUNet, UMamba, SwinUMamba, VMUNet) in Tables 1–3 were evaluated with matched TTA. If not, part of the reported improvement is attributable to inference procedure rather than architecture. This needs to be stated explicitly and ablated. 3.there is no compute/parameter/latency comparison. The paper argues MetaSSM is efficient (“substantially fewer parameters and lower computational cost” than transformer attention) but provides no parameter counts, FLOPs, memory use, or training/inference time for MM-UNet versus baselines. For a method whose central motivation is that SSMs offer linear-time long-sequence modeling, the absence of any efficiency table is a significant omission. Without it, the reader cannot evaluate whether the gains over nnUNet (+1.7% on AMOS T1) come at 1.1× or 3× the cost. 4.Limited novelty at the component level. Each individual ingredient has close antecedents: a)Bi-directional scanning is central to Vision Mamba (Zhu et al., ref [26]) and VMamba (ref [17]); the paper’s “1D BiScan” is essentially the same idea applied to 3D flattening. b)CNNtoMamba hybrid blocks are exactly what U-Mamba (ref [18]) proposes. c)Placing sequence modules inside residual branches is standard practice in ResNet/Transformer literature. The novelty is therefore in the combination and systematic justification (the meta-architecture framing and the variance-based rationale), not in any single new component. This is a legitimate contribution, but the paper overclaims in places (e.g., “first architecture capable of representing existing Mamba-based models”) when it is more accurate to say it provides a useful analysis framework. 5.The authors dont report statistical significance . Gains over the strongest baseline (UMamba) are +1.0% on AMOS T1, +0.8% on AMOS T2, +0.71% on ACDC, +1.8% on BTCV. On BTCV (only 6 validation scans) in particular, the gap could fall within run-to-run variance. No standard deviations, no paired significance tests, no multi-seed results are reported. For a paper claiming SOTA by margins of <1% on several benchmarks, this is a serious gap. 6.Fig. 2(a)’s S4 experiment is an argument about S4, not Mamba. The intrinsic-limitation analysis uses S4 (ref [7]), whereas the deployed MetaSSM uses Mamba (selective SSM, ref [5]). Mamba’s input-dependent Δ, B, C parameters were explicitly introduced to overcome S4’s inability to handle content-dependent variation. The paper does not rerun the variance/discontinuity analysis on Mamba itself, so it is unclear whether the motivating pathology fully applies to the model actually used. This is a non-trivial logical gap in the paper’s central argument. 7.There are clarity issues in Section 2.1 and Fig. 5.The scan-order figure is dense and under-labeled; the mapping between (2a)–(2p) panels and the B1–B9 ablation rows requires substantial cross-referencing. The claim in Fig. 3 that “each attention map effectively captures image patterns across the temporal dimension” is asserted rather than quantified — the figure shows that forward/backward scans have complementary coverage at depth extremes, which is expected by construction of bi-directional scanning, not additional evidence of quality. 8.There are reference and notation issues. Reference [11] appears to point to the 2019 nnUNet arXiv preprint, but the authoritative Nature Methods paper (Isensee et al., 2021) is not cited. Reference [15] (3D UX-Net) is cited in the nnUNet row of Table 1 in a way that is confusing. “SSMs” and “Mamba” are used interchangeably throughout despite being distinct (Mamba is a specific selective SSM). The term “MetaScan” appears in Fig. 5 and Table 4 but is never formally defined in the text. 9.There is ambiguidty in BTCV protocol. The paper states BTCV uses “24 train / 6 val” but reports results against baselines including UNETR and Swin-UNETR that used different splits in their original papers. Without clarification that all methods in Table 2 were re-run under identical splits, the comparison is difficult to interpret. 10.No qualitative failure analysis. Fig. 6 shows cases where MM-UNet outperforms competitors but no cases where it fails. For a clinical translation argument, understanding failure modes (small organs, boundary errors, rare pathology) would strengthen the paper.

Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): While one reviewer expressed enthusiasm about limited novelty, I agree with other two reviewers that the work is rigorous, well-evidenced, and a useful addition to the community’s understanding of how to integrate SSMs into volumetric segmentation pipelines. Thus, I prefer to accept this paper. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): The rebuttal includes additional experiments that were not permitted under the rebuttal guidelines. I believe this creates an unfair review process for other submissions that adhered to the rules and limited their responses accordingly. Independently of this issue, I do not believe the work is technically mature enough for acceptance at MICCAI. From a technical standpoint, several major concerns remain unresolved: 1.Important recent baselines such as MICCAI 2024 SegMamba and NeurIPS 2024 VMamba are missing from the evaluation. 2.Variants of Mamba-UNet architectures have already been introduced in prior work, and the novelty of the proposed method appears limited. The reviewers supporting acceptance seem to have overlooked this point, especially given that the reported performance metrics are extremely close to existing approaches and no statistical significance analysis was provided. 3.The paper does not adequately analyze failure cases or anatomy-specific performance variations. For example, on the BTCV dataset, the proposed method achieves substantially lower Dice performance for gallbladder segmentation compared to the baseline (0.66 vs. 0.79), yet this limitation is neither investigated nor discussed. 4.The reported Dice improvements are very small, and no statistical significance testing was performed in the original submission. The rebuttal also does not provide a convincing explanation regarding the practical importance of these gains. Furthermore, the standard deviations introduced in the rebuttal—which themselves constitute new experimental results—are minimal and suggest the differences may not be meaningful. 5.The parameter analysis presented in the rebuttal also fails to demonstrate a substantial advantage over UMamba. The parameter counts are nearly identical, and the segmentation metrics are similarly close. This again raises the question of what the actual methodological contribution is beyond another incremental combination of Mamba and U-Net style components. In addition, the complexity analysis was only performed on the AMOS22 dataset, limiting the generalizability of the claims. 6.Regarding test-time augmentation (TTA), the rebuttal states: “Without TTA, the drop of our method is larger than nnUNet but smaller than UMamba. The added Mamba blocks introduce minimal overhead but consistently improve accuracy.” However, the actual Dice differences between TTA and non-TTA settings are extremely small (approximately 0.002–0.003 across methods). Therefore, describing these gains as “consistently improving accuracy” appears overstated and potentially misleading. 7.The rebuttal further explains that 8-flip TTA is applied only during inference by averaging predictions from flipped inputs. However, it remains unclear why this process has almost no measurable impact on performance. In 3D medical image segmentation, inference from multiple viewpoints typically affects prediction quality, particularly when such augmentations are not fully represented during training. The negligible changes reported here raise questions regarding the implementation details and the interpretation of the TTA analysis.

title: MoCaf-Mamba: Modality Completion and Alignment in Feature Space for Missing-Modality Segmentation
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The three-module design (MCFS, DFA and STM) is well organized, with each component playing a clear role, resulting in an effective and coherent overall framework. 2.The paper provides anonymized open-source code and conducts experiments on three datasets under various missing-modality settings, thereby supporting the reliability and reproducibility of the results.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The cascaded dependency between modality completion and feature alignment is insufficiently justified. While the paper reasonably integrates two key challenges—modality completion and inter-modality misalignment—into a unified framework, the current pipeline performs feature-space modality completion prior to feature alignment. This raises an important question: how can the method ensure that the completed features are sufficiently accurate and stable to support reliable downstream alignment? If the completion quality is suboptimal, the errors may propagate directly to the DFA module and negatively affect the subsequent alignment process. At present, this dependency is not discussed or validated in sufficient depth. 2.The justification for adopting Mamba as the backbone remains insufficient. The current ablation study mainly validates the contribution of the proposed modules. However, since the baseline is already Mamba-based, it does not clearly demonstrate the specific advantage of Mamba over more conventional backbones such as CNNs or Transformers. A direct comparison with non-Mamba backbones would strengthen this point. 3.The paper lacks feature-space visualization and analysis. The current evaluation mainly focuses on segmentation performance and output examples. Since the core contribution lies in feature-space completion and alignment, visualizing feature representations before and after completion/alignment, especially to demonstrate the effect of completion quality on subsequent alignment, would provide more direct evidence for the effectiveness of the proposed mechanism and improve the interpretability of the paper.

author_feedback: We thank the Area Chair and Reviewers for their constructive feedback. We will revise the manuscript to improve method clarity, Fig. 1, related work, visualization, and proofreading. 1.Mamba & non-Mamba backbone comparison (R1W2&R2W1&R3W3): We use Mamba because 3D missing-modality segmentation requires long-range volumetric context with manageable cost. 3D CNNs have limited effective receptive fields, while 3D Transformers require quadratic token complexity. Mamba provides global modeling of large anatomical context to infer missing latent semantics, with linear complexity. We have additionally conducted comparisons with ResNet3D-18 (CNN) and Swin3D (Transformer), which achieved Avg Dice of 0.7155 and 0.7284, respectively, both below MoCaf-Mamba. We will add these results and Params/FLOPs/throughput comparisons. 2.Arbitrary missing modalities & MCFS formulation (R2W2&R3W2/R3W3&R4W1): MoCaf-Mamba can handle any number of missing modalities. Tables 1–3 include all missing subsets; e.g., three modalities are missing for single-modality BraTS inputs. In implementation, all K modality slots are fixed and ordered; unavailable slots are zero-filled, and modality dropout challenge the model with arbitrary patterns. Thus, Φ_fuse receives a fixed-dimensional ordered input and doesn’t need to be permutation-invariant. We will rewrite Eq. (1) with an availability mask and correct the notation. The Style Token is a modality-level prior, while patient-specific information comes from fused spatial features, inter-individual differences are preserved. Unlike placeholder or pixel-level reconstruction methods, MCFS performs supervised feature-space completion conditioned on available modality context. 3.Completion-before-alignment and DFA clarification(R1W1&R2W3&R3W4/W5&R4W2): Completion is placed before alignment because aligning absent/zero features is ill-posed. MCFS first reconstructs segmentation-relevant latent anchors under feature reconstruction loss, after which DFA refines residual geometric discrepancies. We will add t-SNE/feature-map visualizations before/after MCFS and DFA to better show that completion stabilizes representations and DFA reduces mismatch. We will also clarify Eq. (3): DFA does not use one shared field for all modalities. The offset predictor outputs modality-specific 3D fields Δ_i, and each feature F_i is warped by its own bounded field λ · tanh(Δ_i). DFA is applied hierarchically because residual mismatch may occur at different semantic scales, requiring scale-specific correction. Although DFA gives a moderate gain (+0.5 Avg Dice), it improves the thin alignment-sensitive PZ from 65.0 to 65.8. STM Clarity and Complexity (R2Min2&R4W3): E_spatial denotes the output of the local 3D convolutional branch. STM forms K modality tokens plus one hybrid token at each voxel and applies self-attention only along this modality-token dimension, not over spatial voxels. Thus, the attention length is K + 1 (≤5), making the overhead small. We will clarify token construction and report Params/FLOPs/throughput. 5.Performance and Comparisons (R2Min4&R3W5): Under extreme cases, i.e. only one modality is available, MoCaf-Mamba remains competitive; e.g., T1c-only TC on BraTS2023 is 89.5 vs. 89.6 (mmFormer). More importantly, our goal is robustness under arbitrary missing patterns, where MoCaf-Mamba achieves the best average Dice across BraTS2023, Prostate158, and MM-WHS. We will compare with DRIFA-Net when available for 3D missing modality, and otherwise discuss it in related work/limitations Presentation fixes and visualization (R1W3&R2W4/W5/Min1/Min3&R3W1/W4&R4): We will redesign Fig. 1 with clearer arrows/fonts and an illustration of residual inter-modality misalignment; reorganize “Multimodal Fusion and Alignment”; add feature-space visualizations; and fix the undefined F_k, duplicate “Results on BraTS2023”, abstract formatting, and non-English code comments.

reviewer_1_strengths: Applicable to various modalities including dermoscopy, radiology, ultrasound, and colonoscopy within a framework. Comparing with state-of-the-art segmentation methods across multi-modal datasets.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The sensitivity to hyperparameters, which is an important factor in maintaining stable performance in cross-modality and cross-domain segmentation, is not investigated. reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.Inspired by the dynamic focusing mechanism of human vision, a novel network design incorporates two innovative and efficient modules: DFC dynamically adjusts convolutional weights and receptive fields to achieve adaptive feature extraction; IAFd utilizes wavelet transform and cross-layer interactive attention mechanisms to improve decoding and fusion efficiency. 2.Strong domain generalization and modality independence effectively address the critical domain offset problem in clinical medical image segmentation. 3.Comprehensive and rigorous evaluations were conducted on 10 datasets covering 4 imaging modalities. reviewer_3_strengths: 1) The paper addresses an important and practical problem. Domain shift is a major barrier to deploying segmentation models in real clinical settings, and the paper directly targets this issue by evaluating on unseen datasets across multiple modalities. This is a meaningful and clinically relevant problem formulation. 2) The method is reasonably well motivated and architecturally coherent. The paper presents a clear intuition inspired by dynamic visual focusing and translates it into two concrete modules, DFC and IAFD. The framework diagram on page 3 helps explain how adaptive perception and decoder fusion are integrated within the overall network. 3) The empirical evaluation is broad. The experiments cover four imaging modalities and ten datasets, with both seen-domain and unseen-domain testing. This is broader than many medical segmentation papers that focus on only one modality or one dataset pair. The quantitative results in Tables 1 and 2 show consistent gains over several strong baselines. 4) The reported results on unseen datasets are strong. The paper’s most convincing evidence is the improvement under unseen clinical settings, where the gains over prior methods become larger in some cases. This supports the claim that the method is aimed at generalization rather than only in-domain optimization.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1) The methodological novelty is only moderate, especially for DFC. The paper explicitly states that the feature-focusing part of DFC. In other words, an important component of the proposed method is already built on top of CondConv-style dynamic convolution, which reduces the novelty of this module. The paper would be stronger if it more clearly articulated what is fundamentally new beyond extending dynamic kernel weighting and adding scale attention. 2) The paper is not sufficiently differentiated from very closely related prior DG work. The most relevant prior work appears to be MADGNet [22], titled “Modality-agnostic domain generalizable medical image segmentation by multi-frequency in multi-scale attention.” This prior work is extremely close in both problem setting and high-level design language. Although the paper compares against MADGNet in Tables 1 and 2, the method section does not sharply explain what conceptual gap remains after[A], and why SCFNet should be seen as a substantial advance rather than another dynamic/frequency-attention variant. Similarly, the paper itself cites domain and content adaptive convolution based multi-source domain generalization [3], which also suggests that adaptive convolution for medical DG is already an active direction. 3) The evaluation protocol is broad, but the exact training setup is somewhat unclear. It is not fully clear whether the model is trained jointly across modalities, separately per modality, or with some shared protocol across datasets. The paper presents itself as “modality-agnostic,” but the experiments are organized by modality-specific datasets and tasks. This ambiguity makes it hard to judge how strong the claimed modality-agnostic generalization really is. 4) Important ablation studies are missing. Given that the main claim rests on two new modules, I would expect ablations such as: baseline U-Net vs +DFC vs +IAFD vs full model, effect of the feature-focusing and scale-focusing branches separately, effect of the wavelet decomposition in IAFD, computational cost and parameter overhead. These analyses are important for understanding where the performance gain comes from, but they are not presented in the current manuscript. 5) Baseline selection is somewhat mixed for a domain-generalization paper. While the paper compares against several strong segmentation models, many baselines are generic segmentation architectures rather than specialized DG methods. Since the central claim is about domain generalization, stronger comparison to more dedicated DG segmentation methods would make the evidence more convincing. author_feedback: We sincerely thank all Reviewers and the Meta-reviewer for your time and constructive comments. Below, we clarify the issues raised by Reviewers. Novelty and differences from prior DG (Domain generalization) works. (Reviewers 3, Meta-Reviewer1) Thanks for your valuable comments. Compared with CondaConv [4], DFC is not a simple addition of scale attention, but an innovative optimization of the dynamic mechanism for lesion-characteristic domain shifts. The novelty and differences lie in the following 3 aspects: In the dynamic coding stage, DFC introduces spatial-distribution awareness to preserve region-level spatial information. In the dynamic operating range, it not only generates dynamic convolutional weights but also dynamically adjusts the aggregation range. In the dynamic granularity, it extends image-level dynamics to region-level dynamic perception. These designs enable more adaptive and effective feature extraction under domain shifts. Compared with MADGNet [22] and DADC [3], SCFNet handles domain shifts in a different way. MADGNet mainly relies on multi-scale convolutional branches and frequency attention, which apply the same operations to all inputs and thus remain essentially static. Although DADC introduces dynamic feature extraction, its dynamicity is mainly limited to image-level convolutional weight generation based on global pooling. In contrast, SCFNet performs spatial-distribution-guided region-level dynamic perception by dynamically adjusting both weights and aggregation ranges. Together with advantage-information interaction fusion, SCFNet can better handle characteristic shifts across images and among different regions within an image, leading to more accurate and generalizable segmentation. Experimental setting and baseline selection. (Reviewer 3) SCFNet is trained separately for each modality with the corresponding seen data: two merged seen datasets for colonoscopy and one seen dataset for each other modality. The trained model is then tested separately on each seen and unseen dataset of the same modality without additional adaptation, to evaluate segmentation performance and cross-center generalization. Here, “modality-agnostic” means that SCFNet is a unified segmentation framework without requiring modality-specific priors or designs. We will optimize the description in the paper to avoid ambiguity. The baselines were selected by considering both method-level perception characteristics and the task-level need for generalization. We highly appreciate the reviewer’s suggestion to strengthen comparisons with dedicated DG segmentation methods, and will conduct more systematic evaluations in future work. Ablation and efficiency. (Reviewers 2, 3, and 4, Meta-Reviewer1) We apologize that these analyses are not fully presented due to space limitations. During preparation of the paper, we conducted ablation and efficiency analyses on DFC, IAFD, the overall architecture, the balance among parameters, computation consumption and performance, and so on. These analyses demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed modules, architecture, and hyperparameters. We sincerely hope to share them in more detail during the conference discussion. Hyperparameter and cross-domain validation. (Reviewers 1 and 2) We agree that these analyses are important for evaluating stability and applicability. Current experiments focus on intra-modality cross-center generalization, with hyperparameters set based on preliminary analyses. We will conduct sensitivity analysis and explore cross-imaging-domain validation in future work. DFC scaling, distinctiveness, experimental description, and Fig. 2.(Reviewers 1, 2 and 3) We sincerely thank the reviewers for their valuable suggestions regarding the method description, implementation details, and figure readability. We will optimize the descriptions of the scaling implementation of DFC, method distinctiveness, and experimental settings, and adjust the layout of Fig. 2 to improve readability.

reviewer_3_strengths: 1.This paper proposes a hierarchical modeling framework that preserves vessel segment identity. By extracting the vessel centerline and constructing a connected graph, this method decomposes the vessel tree topology into structurally stable linear vessel segments, allowing vessel identity to be anchored to the topological structure rather than to the pixel appearance, which is highly susceptible to changes in multiple viewpoints, cardiac motion, or contrast agents. 2.The study introduces a “segment-aware decision field” and a hierarchical feature aggregation mechanism, which aligns with the actual clinical workflow of cardiologists. Simultaneously, the model strictly groups and hierarchically summarizes multi-view video features according to the physical anatomical structure of the left and right coronary arteries, effectively preventing erroneous entanglement and confusion of features between different anatomical systems. 3.Regarding data utilization and domain resource development: Addressing the long-standing pain points in the field of coronary angiography multi-view video, such as the scarcity and fragmentation of high-quality labeled data, the authors innovatively integrated multiple publicly available datasets. They completed complete vessel segmentation labels for up to 1.2 million images, constructing and committing to open-sourcing this imaging dataset with extremely high clinical translational potential.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The experimental section of this paper only compares the proposed framework with the single baseline model CarS and its variants. If this study claims that its hierarchical aggregation and spatiotemporal processing are superior to traditional “black box” models, it should introduce more representative spatiotemporal video analysis baselines for comparison. For example, models such as CathAI’s automated coronary interpretation could be introduced, with slight modifications to their feature extraction backend to adapt them to the SYNTAX regression task, thus more convincingly demonstrating the superiority of this strategy. 2.When transforming discrete segment-level narrowing assessments into continuous spatial representations, the paper states that the Gaussian form is not optimal. Therefore, comparative experiments with different spatial kernel functions or continuous distribution strategies based on accurate lumen profiles should be added to the experimental section. Otherwise, the design of this core module will lack solid theoretical support and sufficient experimental verification. 3.When non-intersecting blood vessels overlap in a specific two-dimensional viewpoint, the algorithm inevitably generates “pseudo-bidding nodes.” This pseudo-topological structure incorrectly truncates what should be complete blood vessel segments, fundamentally altering the connected graph structure from that viewpoint. Furthermore, the segmentation diagrams shown in Figure 2 from different viewpoints are positioned relatively close together, failing to adequately illustrate the effect. Therefore, it is necessary to clearly explain how the current method identifies and eliminates “pseudo-bidding points,” and supplement this with relevant robustness analysis or ablation experiments, specifically demonstrating how it effectively avoids entanglement of erroneous anatomical features. 4.The mechanism for obtaining the key parameter $s_k$ appears to be a black box, as the paper doesn’t explain in detail how this crucial parameter is derived. If it’s automatically estimated by an algorithm, then specific implementation details and the accuracy of this step must be provided, as it directly determines the quality of the subsequent heatmap generation. 5.The keyframe extraction method is opaque. In Figure 2, the feature information for the entire framework comes from selecting keyframes from the case sequence. In real coronary angiography videos, many frames are invalid due to factors such as incomplete or dissipated contrast agent and angiography deviation caused by heartbeat. The paper does not explain how these frames were selected. It is recommended to supplement the specific algorithmic logic for keyframe selection. 6.The current evaluation is based solely on cross-validation using a mixture of these publicly available datasets. Given that the annotation and completion strategies for these datasets are designed by the researchers themselves, this introduces certain risks. The model must be rigorously validated on an independent external clinical cohort completely uninvolved in the training and label completion pipeline. Otherwise, the model may simply overfit to the self-designed pseudo-label completion logic and may not truly generalize to the complex and ever-changing real-world clinical environment.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We sincerely thank the meta-reviewer and reviewers for their constructive comments. We are encouraged that R1 recognized our segment identity-preserving hierarchical framework, structured annotations, and improved performance, while R2 noted that our pipeline is clinically well motivated and achieves the best reported CardioSyntax performance. We address the main concerns below. R2Q1: The videos provided in the supplementary material show the segmentation results of the complete videos. We did not remove low-quality frames, especially the first few frames where no vessels are visible, because we wanted to present the full video sequence. During training, however, we only used high-quality video clips. R1Q1, R3Q5: We annotated high-quality video segments from all video-frame data of 120 patients. We then trained a binary classifier to distinguish high-quality frames from other frames. The training set contains more than 800 videos from 120 patients. Specifically, we trained a ResNet-34 model for this task. If the paper is accepted, we will release this dataset, the code, and the trained weights. R2Q2: We strongly agree with this concern. However, public datasets currently lack full-pipeline annotations, which is also one of the main challenges in this field. Nevertheless, our method already includes several strategies to reduce error accumulation. These include iterative training of the segmentation model for better mask generation, a more stable frame-level segment tracking algorithm, and avoiding overlap when cropping vessel videos. R2Q3: According to clinical guidelines, the SYNTAX score can indeed be divided into several risk levels. One major reason we used the metrics in the paper is that they reflect prediction reliability while also allowing a fair comparison with CardioSyntax. In future work, we will further promote and explore more suitable evaluation metrics. R3Q1: To the best of our knowledge, CathAI is not a full-pipeline automatic coronary angiography interpretation model. It uses 2D images rather than temporal video data, and its final goal is stenosis detection and severity estimation. In addition, its code, weights, and dataset have not been publicly released, making it difficult to reproduce. Among current works on temporal coronary angiography analysis, a representative example is STQD-Det published in TPAMI, but it also does not release any files that would allow reproduction. R3Q2: What we intended to express is that we do not claim the Gaussian distribution used in our method is the optimal choice. We used it mainly because it provides a continuous representation. This is a good research direction and problem. In future work, we will continue to explore more suitable representation methods. R3Q3: In fact, the purpose of using bifurcation points for vessel segmentation and tracking is to generate stable video crops for each vessel segment. We remove video crops with high overlap. DeepCoro then outputs the stenosis severity for each input video crop. We map the stenosis severity of all cropped videos into heatmaps using Gaussian distributions. The heatmap represents all suspicious stenosis regions in the image. In our view, incorrect bifurcation points do not significantly affect the actual meaning of the heatmap. This is because, regardless of whether a vessel is mistakenly divided into multiple segments, if stenosis exists, it will still be reflected in the heatmap. R3Q4: The extraction process of $s_k$ is not a black box. We follow Algorithm 1 in VesSAM, which performs vessel segments splitting based on the skeleton graph and bifurcation points. R3Q6: We fully agree that external validation is very important. However, to the best of our knowledge, there is currently no other publicly available large-scale multi-view video coronary angiography dataset. This limitation is also one of the key motivations for our research in this field.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper addresses the important problem of automatic SYNTAX scoring for coronary arteries. The approach taken is interpretable breaking down the problem into artery segmentation and stenosis calculations. All reviewers have seen the merit but there are some concerns raised. Authors are invited to submit a strong rebuttal addressing these concerns. | All three reviewers are on board for acceptance for this paper addressing an important problem of SYNTAX scoring. Many aspects of a good paper are present in this one. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): There is consensus among the reviewers that the paper addresses an important clinical problem and proposes a clinically aligned framework. The rebuttal clarified the main concerns. I therefore recommend acceptance. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The initial reviews were generally positive but raised several substantive concerns. R1 supported acceptance and emphasized the clinical alignment, structured annotations, and performance gains, while noting that some experimental details were insufficient for reproducibility. R2 also recommended acceptance but raised concerns about segmentation robustness, error propagation in a multi-stage pipeline, and the lack of clinically risk-stratified metrics. R3 initially recommended weak rejection, mainly due to limited comparison with other spatiotemporal or angiography models, insufficient analysis of the Gaussian decision-field design, possible failure modes caused by vessel overlap or pseudo-bifurcation points, unclear frame selection, and the lack of an independent external clinical cohort. The rebuttal was useful in clarifying several points. It explained that the supplementary videos showed complete sequences, whereas training used selected high-quality clips identified with a ResNet-34 classifier; it also clarified the frame-selection procedure, the origin of the segment parameter through the VesSAM skeleton-graph splitting procedure, and the distinction between the proposed video-based SYNTAX scoring pipeline and CathAI-like stenosis-estimation systems. The rebuttal also explained the rationale for using the reported regression metrics for comparability with CardioSyntax and described measures intended to reduce error accumulation, including iterative segmentation refinement, segment tracking, and overlap removal during vessel cropping. These clarifications were sufficient for R3 to move from weak reject to accept, and R2 maintained an accept recommendation. Some limitations remain. The submitted paper still does not provide an independent external clinical validation cohort, and the absence of risk-class-wise clinical metrics limits assessment of clinical decision impact. The Gaussian form used for the decision field is acknowledged as a practical continuous representation rather than an optimized or fully validated design, and there is limited ablation of alternative kernels or lumen-profile-based spatial representations. The comparison set is also relatively narrow, relying mainly on CarS and variants rather than a broader set of adapted video or angiography baselines. These issues should be considered when interpreting the clinical readiness of the method. Overall, the strengths outweigh the remaining limitations for a MICCAI conference paper.

title: MoSE: Mixture-of-Scale-Experts for Medical Image Restoration
reviewer_1_strengths: (1) The authors conducted extensive testing on highly challenging multimodal benchmarks. Experiments covered not only the public, comprehensive MedIR dataset, which includes CT denoising, MRI super-resolution, and PET synthesis, but also a private high-resolution endoscopic super-resolution (ESR) dataset obtained through clinical collaboration, fully validating the model’s robustness across different imaging mechanisms. (2) While maintaining a high PSNR, the inference time was significantly lower than mainstream methods such as TAT ​​and SwinIR, demonstrating the superiority of sparse activation architectures in real-time clinical processing. (3) A scale-aware load balancing loss was introduced, minimizing the coefficient of variation between importance and load to ensure that experts at different scales are fully utilized during training.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: (1) The design of heterogeneous experts has been extensively explored in the literature of deep learning and MoE. While this paper emphasizes its specificity and progressive receptive field design in medical image degradation and describes its architectural flexibility in handling diverse medical image degradation compared to traditional MoE, it does not adequately discuss or compare existing heterogeneous architectures in the MoE field. (2) The authors propose a new evaluation metric, ATLS, and demonstrate its superiority over other methods in experiments. However, the ATLS metric relies on a general vision-language pre-trained model, Qwen3-VL-Embedding, for feature extraction. Although the authors claim its sensitivity to minute textures, medical images (such as endoscopic microvessels and MRI tissue structures) have highly specialized and unique noise distributions. The authors do not provide any evidence that the model’s embedding similarity is highly correlated with the visual evaluation (MOS) of professional radiologists. (3) The model simultaneously uses shared experts to provide geometric priors and dynamically selected heterogeneous scale experts, which are fused through channel cross-attention (C-XCA). When the local features of the scale expert conflict with the global prior of the shared expert, the authors lack a deep theoretical explanation for whether a simple attention mechanism will lead to the distortion of the anatomical structure.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The motivation for the study is reasonable. Conventional all-in-one models can be computationally inefficient, while homogeneous mixture-of-experts frameworks may not capture the diversity of anatomical structures and degradation patterns. The heterogeneous expert design sounds appropriate. The experimental design includes ablations and the reported results show consistent incremental improvements, across multiple tasks including endoscopic super resolution, MRI super resolution, CT denoising, and PET synthesis. The paper emphasizes both performance and efficiency. It achieves competitive PSNR with reduced inference time and parameter count supports the practical value.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: In Figure 4, highlighting specific regions with arrows and briefly explaining the observed improvements across different methods would improve interpretability. It is unclear whether Figure 5a reports inference time and PSNR jointly across all tasks or if the results are separated by modality. This should be clarified. For Figure 5b, the interpretation “As the number increases, the deviation decreases, and the curves stabilize at around 100 patches. Considering both stability and efficiency, we adopt 100 patches as the default setting.” of patch count in ATLS evaluation appears ambiguous. As far as I understand the ATLS correctly, ATLS is an evaluation metric that the paper proposed to measure the output of the model to the ground truth target for more local, fine details, and patch is randomly sampled from each case to evaluate the similarity. In that frame, I believe the increasing patch number would always increase the reliability of the evaluation. The rationale for selecting a subset of patches instead of evaluating over the full image is not clearly justified. From table 2, three single expert baselines did not achieve the best results compared to the author’s methods. It would be useful to better understand why the combined expert setting outperforms single expert baselines. The OCG module is introduced as a key contribution, but its effect is not clearly visualized. The routing mechanism is described as adaptive, yet there is limited empirical analysis of its behavior. It would be valuable to examine expert utilization patterns, relationships between input characteristics and routing decisions, and whether meaningful specialization emerges across experts.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The introduction of MoSE is novel. 2.The use of multimodal LLM for quality evaluation is novel.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The introduction of different expert E_k is unclear. Do they differ in the number of downsampling stages or in the number of blocks? 2.Does MoSE use top-k gating or top-1 gating? 3.What is the difference between the Scale-Aware Load-Balancing Loss and the standard load-balancing loss?
