author_feedback: We sincerely appreciate the valuable comments on the motivation, efficiency, and strong experimental evaluation of our method. Our feedback is as follows. Q1(R1&R2&R3): Novelty clarification of scale-heterogeneous experts. MoSE is designed for the diverse anatomical texture complexities in medical image restoration. MoSE uses three experts with different downsampling depths for dynamic scale selection, avoiding reliance on a fixed single-scale expert that may over-smooth details or lack context. Unlike natural-image heterogeneous expert methods such as MoCE-IR and AdaptIR, MoSE designs experts according to the scale of anatomical structures in medical images, with the shared expert and OCG providing structural and high-frequency guidance. MoSE outperforms MoCE-IR on MedIR tasks. Q2(R1&R2): Medical validity and patch sampling of ATLS. ATLS uses patch-level rather than full-image comparison because subtle but important differences may be averaged out by large similar background regions in full-image evaluation. We adopt 100 patches as more patches improve reliability but increase computational cost and may reduce sensitivity to local; ATLS empirically stabilizes around 100 patches, with only minor changes at 150/200.To validate its medical relevance, we evaluate 20 paired restoration results where PSNR/SSIM and ATLS give inconsistent rankings. Method names and metric values are hidden; two junior clinicians independently select the image more suitable for diagnosis, and a senior clinician reviews the results. Clinicians tend to prefer images with higher ATLS even when PSNR/SSIM are lower, indicating ATLS better aligns with clinical perception and complements pixel-level. Q3 (R1): Fusion between shared and scale experts. The shared expert and selected scale expert provide complementary information. The scale expert remains the main restoration path, while the shared expert provides auxiliary global basic feature guidance through residual and learnable C-XCA fusion. Since C-XCA mainly performs channel-wise feature reweighting rather than spatial geometric rearrangement, it reduces the risk of distortion. Q4(R2&R3): Expert routing, utilization, and specialization. MoSE uses top-1 gating. On the ESR test set, the router assigns 40%, 33%, and 27% of images to Experts 1–3, showing balanced usage without expert collapse. To verify routing effectiveness, we group images by their router-selected expert and randomly sample 50 images from each group. For each image, we keep the input unchanged and separately perform inference using each non-selected expert. The router-selected expert consistently achieves better PSNR/SSIM than the two non-selected experts, with gains of 0.045–0.612 dB in PSNR and 0.003–0.023 in SSIM. This confirms that MoSE learns meaningful scale-specific specialization. Q5(R2): Figure clarification and visualization. For Fig. 4, we will add arrows to highlight and briefly explain the observed improvements. For Fig. 5a, we clarify that it reports the test results on the Endoscopic SR (ESR) dataset. For OCG, visualization results show that it better preserves micro-vessel contours and mucosal textures in endoscopic images, while producing clearer low-contrast tissue boundaries in MRI/CT images. Q6 (R3): Scale-aware load balancing. In practice, instead of enforcing a uniform distribution as in the standard loss, we weight routing probabilities I_e with a depth-based bias, enabling adaptive routing of images to scale experts according to their frequency characteristics. Q7(R3): Additional Method Comparisons. We add comparisons with the suggested MedIR methods. Restore-RWKV, RAT, DASMamba-MedIR, and DaPT achieve average PSNR/ATLS of 36.02/0.83, 37.57/0.86, 36.15/0.84, and 37.21/0.85 on AMIR, and 31.49/0.72, 32.23/0.77, 31.74/0.74, and 32.01/0.76 on ESR. MoSE performs better (AMIR: 38.21/0.88, ESR: 33.88/0.83). We will incorporate all revisions into the final version, and release our code and ESR dataset.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper proposes a Mixture-of-Scale-Experts framework for medical image restoration with promising empirical performance across multiple modalities. Reviewers appreciate the motivation, efficiency gains, and broad experimental validation. However, there are notable concerns regarding the level of methodological novelty, justification of the proposed ATLS metric, and insufficient analysis of the expert routing mechanism and architectural design choices. Given these mixed evaluations, I invite the authors to provide a rebuttal addressing the concerns on novelty, metric validation, and deeper analysis of the model behavior. | The authors have addressed most of the reviewer comments. In the final version, the authors should down tone the claim of SOTA performance as there is no comparison with task-specific image restoration methods, and should include this as a primary limitation of the experiments. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The authors’ responses effectively address the reviewers’ concerns. I recommend acceptance, while encouraging the authors to consider the reviewers’ suggestions in the final revision. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): After reading the rebuttal, I recommend Accept. The paper proposes a mixture-of-scale expert design for medical image restoration. The method has a concrete structure: the experts use different receptive fields, the router selects a scale-specific branch for each input, and a shared branch is kept in parallel to provide stable geometric context. The experiments cover several restoration settings, including endoscopic super-resolution, MRI super-resolution, CT denoising, and PET synthesis. The reported results show gains in restoration quality while keeping inference cost lower than several transformer-based baselines. My initial concerns were mainly about evidence and presentation. The heterogeneous expert design is related to existing MoE work, so the paper needs to explain what is specific to medical restoration rather than presenting heterogeneity itself as new. The rebuttal clarifies this point and gives a more convincing account of the scale-specialized design. It also addresses the routing mechanism, the scale-aware loss, and the role of the OCG module. These additions make the method easier to judge as a medical restoration model rather than only as a generic MoE variant. Some issues should still be fixed in the final version. ATLS should be presented carefully, since an embedding-based metric is not a substitute for reader studies or clinical visual assessment. The paper should also make the expert routing behavior visible, clarify the patch sampling used by ATLS, and include the missing MedIR comparisons or at least discuss them directly. I do not think these points change the decision, because the core method and the empirical results are sound enough for acceptance.

title: MRSeg3D: A Perturbation-Resilient Model for 3D Medical Reasoning Segmentation
reviewer_1_strengths: The paper’s strengths are its clear problem formulation and targeted design. Instead of treating medical image segmentation just as a standard prompt task, the authors break down consistency into instruction robustness and reasoning-segmentation alignment. This is a very useful perspective for clinical translation. Methodologically, MRSeg3D avoids simply scaling up the language model. The authors noticed that baseline models lose visual evidence as reasoning progresses, so they addressed this directly by re-injecting intermediate visual features. This proves the value of targeted architectural tweaks. Additionally, the experimental evaluation is extensive. Testing on 25 datasets is solid work, and the model clearly outperforms a strong baseline, especially in the most challenging free-text scenarios.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The main weaknesses are the clinical realism of the benchmark and the lack of statistical rigor. The authors describe the Level III test as real-world clinical discourse, but these texts were actually generated by DeepSeek. There is no mention of clinician validation or human quality control. Therefore, the demonstrated robustness really only shows generalization to synthetic prompts, which isn’t the same as clinical readiness. Furthermore, for a paper focused on stability, it lacks multiple-run variance, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests. This makes the performance gains less convincing. Additionally, the data protocols for the 25 datasets are not transparent enough regarding patient-level splits and deduplication. Finally, the mechanistic claim about semantic drift is slightly overstated; it currently reads more like a reasonable hypothesis than a strictly proven mechanism.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The paper addresses a timely and relevant problem: robustness of 3D medical reasoning segmentation under perturbed natural-language instructions. Rather than only reporting performance under a fixed prompting setup, the paper explicitly studies instruction-level fragility and reasoning and segmentation consistency, which is an important perspective for clinically relevant multimodal systems. 1.Benchmark contribution The tiered perturbation benchmark with multiple instruction templates enables a finer-grained robustness analysis as linguistic ambiguity increases, compared with conventional label-style prompting. This evaluation design is a concrete strength because it connects prompt variability to measurable degradation modes. 2.Diagnostic decomposition Separately evaluating reasoning quality vs segmentation fidelity is well motivated and can reveal decoupled failures (e.g., stable language understanding with degraded masks), which strengthens interpretability of multimodal errors. 3.Targeted architectural refinement As a targeted refinement of a strong single-encoder reasoning-segmentation framework. The vision injectors and the Seg-Local projection path are both tied to specific hypothesized failure modes, namely loss of visual grounding during reasoning and imperfect transformation from [SEG] token representations to final masks. This makes the method design more convincing than a purely heuristic module addition.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The degree of novelty is somewhat limited. While the paper is well motivated and the architectural design is coherent, MRSeg3D is best understood as a targeted refinement of strong single-encoder reasoning-segmentation baselines, especially R1Seg-3D, rather than a fundamentally new formulation. In particular, the main changes are the addition of intermediate visual injection during reasoning and a local projection path for segmentation execution. These components are reasonable and potentially effective, but they may still be viewed as incremental extensions on top of prior designs. 2.The central mechanism claim is plausible, but not fully established causally. The authors argue that robustness degradation mainly comes from insufficient visual grounding and semantic drift during reasoning / decoding. While Table 5 and Fig. 6 are consistent with this interpretation, the paper does not include a more explicit mechanism study that separately tests this claim, for example by isolating the effect of visual injection during reasoning versus the effect of the segmentation-side local projection under matched conditions. Therefore, the results support the effectiveness of the proposed design, but they do not fully establish that the claimed mechanism is the primary cause. 3.The perturbation benchmark is useful, but its connection to real clinical language remains limited. The tiered perturbation protocol is a valuable part of the paper and enables more fine-grained robustness analysis. At the same time, it remains a template-based benchmark designed by the authors. Therefore, the results should be interpreted as robustness under the proposed perturbation setting, rather than robustness to the full diversity, ambiguity, and messiness of genuine clinical language in practice. 4.There is a noticeable gap between the training setup and the evaluation scope. The paper states that training uses only instruction templates 1 and 5, while evaluation covers a much broader range of perturbation types. This makes the reported robustness results interesting, but it also raises questions about how much of the gain comes from architectural robustness versus generalization under a particular train/test protocol. More discussion of this point would strengthen the paper. 5.Some implementation and reproducibility details remain relatively high level in the main paper. The paper gives the overall architecture and staged training procedure, but many details that would matter for full reproducibility appear brief in the main text. This is a practical weakness, although it is partially mitigated by the authors’ statement that code and models will be made publicly available. 6.Some claims are framed a bit more strongly than the evidence strictly supports. The experiments support improved robustness and performance under the proposed benchmark, but broader claims about handling realistic clinical discourse should be stated more cautiously, especially since the paper itself acknowledges that pathology-specific and open-ended clinical scenarios remain challenging.

title: MSHF-Net: Multimodal Breast Cancer Molecular Subtype Prediction via Segmentation-Guided Hierarchical Fusion Network
reviewer_1_strengths: This study addresses an important and highly practical clinical problem rather than a purely technical task. Preoperative, non-invasive prediction of breast cancer molecular subtype has clear potential value for treatment planning and clinical decision-making, and it directly responds to a real unmet need in breast cancer management. In this sense, the work is clinically meaningful and well motivated. A notable strength of the paper is that it appears to be among the first attempts in this area to jointly integrate mammography, ultrasound, and clinical information for this specific prediction task. This is especially valuable because multimodal clinical datasets of this kind are difficult to collect, often limited in scale, and highly valuable in practice. From this perspective, the contribution of the paper should not be judged only by technical novelty, but also by its effort to address a genuine clinical pain point using scarce and precious real-world data. Methodologically, the multimodal design is reasonable, and the hierarchical fusion strategy is more structured than simple feature concatenation. The experimental section is also fairly comprehensive, including backbone comparisons, fusion comparisons, modality ablation, and component ablation. Overall, the manuscript is generally well organized and easy to follow.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The main limitation is that the SGA module depends on tumor masks at inference time, yet the paper does not provide an automatic segmentation pipeline or evaluate performance under mask-free, noisy-mask, or automatically generated mask conditions. This reduces the current readiness of the framework for routine clinical deployment. In addition, the fairness of the baseline comparisons is not entirely clear, particularly because the proposed method appears to benefit from additional lesion-mask supervision. Important details regarding the representation and preprocessing of clinical variables are also insufficiently described. These concerns are meaningful, but in my view they do not outweigh the overall value of the study. Given the clinical relevance of the task, the rarity of the multimodal dataset, and the fact that this work represents an early and important attempt in this direction, these issues seem more like limitations to be addressed in revision or future work than reasons for rejection. The authors should clarify how tumor masks are obtained during testing and, ideally, provide either a complete segmentation-to-classification pipeline or experiments examining the model’s sensitivity to mask quality. The manuscript would also benefit from stronger statistical analysis, clearer reporting of baseline training settings, and a more detailed description of the design and preprocessing of clinical features. If possible, the authors should also discuss the practical clinical workflow more explicitly, including how the proposed model might be used in real-world settings and what steps are needed to improve deployment feasibility. External validation would further strengthen the paper, although I understand that such multimodal clinical data are difficult to obtain and that this may be beyond the scope of the current study.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.Clinical Relevance: Predicting molecular subtypes via imaging is a high-impact task that could reduce the need for invasive biopsies. 2.Architectural Design: The dual-branch approach (SGA) is logically sound, as pathology-related features are often localized within small regions of a full mammogram or ultrasound frame. 3.Clear Methodology: The paper provides a detailed technical description of the H-TMF and SGA modules, making the approach theoretically reproducible.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: three main weaknesses: 1.Critical Statistical Inconsistency (Accuracy vs. Sample Size): The authors state in Section 4.1 that the test set consists of 40 samples (N=40). Mathematically, for a sample size of 40, any metric derived from a simple count (Accuracy, Precision, Recall) must be a multiple of 1/40 = 2.5%. However, Table 1 reports values such as 80.5%, 80.2%, and 78.3%. These results are mathematically impossible for a 40-sample cohort unless the authors are reporting the average of multiple cross-validation folds without clearly stating so. This lack of transparency regarding the denominator of the performance metrics raises significant concerns about the technical rigor of the evaluation. 2.Limited Clinical Evidence (Single-Center Validation):The study relies entirely on a single private dataset. In medical imaging, models often overfit to the specific hardware (e.g., GE vs. Siemens machines) or scanning protocols of a single institution. Without External Validation on an independent dataset (e.g., public datasets like CBIS-DDSM or a separate hospital cohort), the generalizability and clinical reliability of MSHF-Net remain unproven. 3.Missing Statistical Significance Analysis:The performance gains (e.g., an improvement from 80.0% to 82.5%) are marginal given the small test size. The authors fail to provide P-values or 95% Confidence Intervals (CI). Without these, it is impossible to determine if the proposed H-TMF module offers a statistically significant improvement or if the gain is due to random variance in the small test set.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: Major Strengths: The manuscript is well-written, and the proposed framework is explained with sufficient technical detail and can be easily extend to different medical application setting beyond the considered task of the paper. The experimentation is comprehensive, featuring an in-depth ablation study that effectively probes the contribution of each individual component within the framework. The authors provide a wide comparison against state-of-the-art methods, as well as early, late, and attention-based fusion strategies. The model achieves strong results (82% Accuracy and 85% AUC) on a difficult task, particularly as it relies solely on non-invasive radiomic features and clinical characteristics
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Major Weaknesses: The paper does not sufficiently elaborate on the rationale behind the specific hierarchical integration design. It is unclear why cross-attention was not applied uniformly across all stages—from the dual MG views to the clinical data integration. There is a lack of discussion regarding why dynamic integration was utilized for the MG views but not extended to the integration of US and MG. While results include standard deviation, the manuscript does not specify if these represent a K-fold cross-validation or repetitions over multiple random seeds, which is critical for assessing reproducibility. While the performance gains of MSHF-Net over the state-of-the-art appear notable, the manuscript does not provide statistical significance tests (Paired t-test, Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test) to confirm that these improvements are consistent and mathematically significant.

author_feedback: We thank all reviewers for their support of our paper, including its “clinically valuable questions” (R1&2&3), “targeted method design” (R1&2&3), “comprehensive experiments” (R1&3), and “clear overall writing” (R1&3). Below, we address two general concerns, then respond to each reviewer. G1: Experimental Protocols and Statistical Analyses (R1&2&3) We performed three repetitions of five-fold cross-validation (using three different random seeds), where four subsets were used for training and one subset for evaluation in each run, with the evaluation subset rotated across folds. All results are reported as the mean and 95% confidence interval half-width for each metric. Details will be added to the revision. G2: Lack of Statistical Significance Tests (R2&3) We have provided the P-values for the optimal and suboptimal models based on AUC in the anonymous code link. This was omitted from the manuscript due to space constraints but will be added in the revision. R1Q1: Mask-Related Issue In Sec 3.1, lesion masks were annotated by two experienced breast radiologists to ensure high-quality supervision. During evaluation, annotated masks were also used as input. This work is not a comprehensive segmentation-classification system; instead, it investigates if concentrating on lesion patches with high-quality masks enhances molecular subtyping. R1Q2: Clinical Features Sec 2.2 outlines the clinical modalities, with implementation details in the anonymous code link. We use five clinical features: age, maximal tumor diameter, menopausal state, tumor location, and breast fiber type. The first two are z-score normalized; the others are one-hot encoded. R1Q3: Comparison Fairness In Sec 3.1, all experiments used the identical deployment parameters. And each experiment used identical lesion masks for ROI cropping, restricting inputs to lesion regions. Additionally, MSHF-Net’s SGA module uses the mask to generate spatial weight maps, ensuring fair comparison. R2Q1: Experimental Data We sincerely apologize for the lack of clarity in experimental results. In Sec 3.1, we mentioned that the test dataset had only 40 samples. However, in subsequent experiments, we performed three repetitions of five-fold cross-validation by partitioning the dataset into training and evaluation subsets. Statistical analysis was conducted using these three repetitions of five-fold cross-validation together with 95% confidence intervals. Accordingly, each reported metric was calculated based on the evaluation results obtained from four folds containing 80 samples and one fold containing 81 samples. Therefore, the results reported in our tables are reasonable and statistically reliable. We will further clarify the description in Sec 3.1 in the revision. R2Q2: Single-center Dataset Given that the input modalities for this work include mammography (CC and MLO) images, ultrasound images, corresponding mammography and ultrasound masks, and clinical information, it is quite challenging to obtain such comprehensive multimodal data. However, the model’s generalization ability has been validated to some extent through five-fold cross-validation and the 95% confidence intervals obtained from statistical analyses based on existing datasets. R3Q1: Hierarchical Fusion Hierarchical fusion models different levels of multimodal integration. Table 3 shows it outperforms uniform attention fusion, as it better adapts to modality heterogeneity and avoids dominance by a single modality. In contrast, uniform fusion may suffer from suboptimal feature representation due to distribution and semantic gaps, reducing multimodal complementarity. R3Q2: Dynamic Integration Fusion strategies are adapted based on modality relationships. Dynamic weighting models the view consistency between CC and MLO, which share anatomy but differ in projection. For heterogeneous modalities such as MG and US, Cross-Attention better captures inter-modal interactions and enhances pathology-relevant complementarity.

title: Multi-agent Test-Time Adaptation for Robust Medical Image-to-Image Translation
reviewer_1_strengths: The framework is modular and predictor-agnostic, and the experiments on both GAN-based and flow-matching-based predictors support that claim to some extent. The ablation study is useful in showing that monitoring, actuator selection, and sample selection all contribute to the final behavior. The paper goes beyond a single benchmark and evaluates on both MRI translation and CT denoising, which is a meaningful strength.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The serious issue is the calibration protocol for the selection threshold tau in the CT experiments. The paper states that tau is determined from the full available test set and then reused during evaluation on the abdominal and chest test sets. This means the evaluation data are used to define the adaptation policy itself. That is not a valid test-time protocol and materially compromises the reported CT results. Threshold calibration must be performed on a validation split or on source-domain held-out data only. Reconstruction error is used as a proxy for distribution shift and as the basis for deciding whether adaptation is beneficial. That is plausible, but the paper does not directly evaluate whether this signal predicts adaptation benefit.
reviewer_1_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: A key strength is the sample specific adaptation policy. Existing test time adaptation baselines often adapt every sample, whereas this method adapts only selected cases and still reports improvements in PSNR and SSIM. That is a practically meaningful idea under heterogeneous domain shift. The experimental section is reasonably broad. The paper includes MRI and CT tasks, several external datasets, and ablation studies examining the roles of monitoring, adaptation, and selection.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The method assumes that test time domain shift can be corrected by channel wise feature remapping while preserving spatial structure. This is plausible for mild feature mismatch, but the paper does not provide enough information on how much the mismatch is allowed for their method to work. For samples selected for adaptation, the method evaluates many actuator configurations and performs multiple adaptation iterations for each one. It is unclear whether there is any early stopping rule, or whether all iterations are always executed once a configuration has been chosen. The inference cost also appears potentially substantial. Even if only a subset of test samples is adapted, evaluating many actuator subsets with repeated optimization steps may still introduce considerable overhead. The paper would be stronger with a clearer analysis of runtime relative to simpler test time adaptation baselines.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1)The paper introduces a clear decomposition into monitoring, selection, adaptation, and prediction agents, which provides a structured and interpretable framework. 2)The method adapts only a subset of intermediate representations via actuator modules, which is more efficient and potentially more stable than full-model adaptation. 3) The use of reconstruction errors across multiple representation levels enables label-free detection of distribution shift, making the approach practical for real-world medical settings.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1) The use of random search over actuator subsets is computationally expensive and lacks guarantees, raising concerns about scalability and optimality, especially as the number of feature levels increases. 2) The framework requires multiple forward passes and adaptation steps per test sample, which may limit applicability in time-sensitive or large-scale medical imaging scenarios. 3) Reconstruction error may not always correlate with harmful domain shift, potentially leading to unnecessary or suboptimal adaptations; stronger justification or validation is needed.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and meta-reviewer for their feedback. R1, CT threshold calibration: The manuscript sentence was incorrectly worded. The threshold tau is computed from the full source-domain Mayo abdominal training set, not from the CT test sets. Since the CT Predictor Agent is trained on Mayo abdominal scans, this is the natural reference for the upper tail of the in-distribution reconstruction error. Tau is fixed before evaluating the abdominal and chest test cohorts, and the same fixed threshold is then applied to both CT test sets. No evaluation sample is used to define the adaptation policy. The reported results were obtained under this protocol. The dynamic strategies, sigma2 and sigma3, are initialized from this reference and update tau online during inference. We will correct the manuscript accordingly. R1/R2/R4, Monitoring signal validity: Distribution shift is quantified through reconstruction errors produced by the Monitoring Agent, whose observers are trained on source-domain representations and frozen at test time. Higher output-level error indicates deviation from the source-domain distribution. This signal is a label-free, unsupervised shift score, not a deterministic predictor of adaptation gain. The evaluated shifts are not simulated perturbations, but arise from real distribution differences: cross-cohort, population, and pathology-driven shifts in MRI, as reported in Tab. 1, and anatomical-domain shifts in CT. Fig. 3 validates the monitoring-selection mechanism: among selected samples, the GAN-based Predictor Agent exceeds 80% win rate in 3/4 metric-task settings, reaching 98.6% in CT denoising. For the flow-matching Predictor Agent, PSNR improvements remain prevalent; SSIM shows more balanced win/loss in MRI, consistent with the stronger baseline and smaller improvement margin. These results indicate that the policy tends to trigger adaptation when beneficial. Sensitivity to synthetic shift severity is future work; here, we focus on real external-cohort and anatomical shifts. R2, Applicability of feature-level adaptation: The 1x1 actuators perform channel-wise feature remapping while preserving spatial structure. They address shifts in intensity, contrast, and representation statistics. The evaluated MRI and CT shifts go beyond mild mismatch while preserving the spatial correspondence required by the translation task. More extreme shifts requiring spatial transformations or large structural changes would require more expressive adaptation mechanisms, which could be explored within the proposed MAS framework. R2/R4, Computational cost, early stopping, and sensitivity to K/n: During TTA, the Predictor and Monitoring Agents remain frozen; only selected actuators are updated, limiting trainable parameters and instability risk. Adaptation is not applied to all samples. When the reconstruction error does not exceed tau, the sample follows the standard Predictor Agent inference path, with no actuator search or optimization. For selected samples, n is the number of intermediate representation levels exposed by the Predictor Agent and associated with candidate actuators. The Selection Agent samples K=50 actuator subsets uniformly at random; active actuators vary across subsets and are not fixed a priori. Fixing K bounds the search and avoids exhaustive enumeration of all actuator combinations. Each candidate subset is reset and optimized for at most T=10 iterations, with early stopping when the monitoring loss no longer improves. K=50 balances actuator-space exploration and test-time cost. Tab. 2 illustrates this selective design: sigma2 and sigma3 adapt fewer than 10% of MRI samples in all settings, compared to 100% for both competitors. This limits average test-time overhead for large-scale inference. R1/R2/R4, Reproducibility: We will better detail actuator sampling, early stopping, and frozen/trainable components in the revised manuscript, and release training, inference, and TTA code upon acceptance.

title: Multi-regional CT Radiomics Fusion to Quantify Pathology-Derived Pollutant Burden in Lung Cancer
reviewer_1_strengths: -The proposed framework was trained with an in-house cohort and tested with an external trial dataset, which tries to demonstrate its generalizability. -Based on the fact that classification models from six different regions were integrated, it allows to capture different patterns which correlate with biological understanding, for instance, diffuse parenchymal patterns and localized tumor-host interactions.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: -Based on the fact that region segmentations used to extract features were done manually, which could introduce inter-observer variability and be labor-intensive. It does not affect the performance presented in the manuscript, it could represent a limitation to be implemented in a real-world clinical workflow. -A good point for model training is that the cohort for that purpose was balanced in terms of the classes, however it is not the same for the external cohort, and it can be noted with the shift in precision-recall metrics. -This comment could be taken as contradictory with one of the strengths, but although I recognize the effort of the authors to use two different cohorts (different institutions, public/private, acquisition parameters), there is a notable drop performance between training and testing (from AUC of 0.733 in training to AUC of 0.609 in the external NLST dataset).
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.Interesting question: the problem of determining a CT based lung pollutant index seems very interesting and potentially impactful to me. 2.Good methodological design and rigor: the paper is methodologically sound and the experiments are well designed (much more rigorous than typical conference papers). The design choices are well justified and also stress tested (for example, the sensitivity of results to choice of thresholds). The external validation is also performed quite rigorously – the same numeric LPI cutoff is used as the threshold for the binary labeling. Pretty comprehensive ablation studies and subgroup analyses have also been performed. I commend the authors for a well designed study. 3.The organization and writing are clear.

Since the study uses radiomics features which can be quite sensitive to changes in reconstruction kernels, the authors need to mention/specify how/which series were chosen for analysis. This worries me a bit, since radiomics features often tend to not generalize well due to these factors, and the current AUC values are quite low as it is. 2.Manual segmentations seem to have been used in the analysis. However, that is not really scalable. reviewer_3_strengths: (1) Building on previous research, this study defined a Lung Pollutant Index (LPI) based on information derived from pathological slice images. The proposed index may serve as a novel risk factor for the health management of pulmonary pollution status in general populations, especially among non-smokers. (2) Constructing a non-invasive CT-based model to estimate the LPI represents a feasible and population-friendly solution with great public health significance. (3) The validation and evaluation of this study were conducted on both internal datasets and publicly available datasets.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: (1) The LPI metric has not been formally published and is currently under peer review. Therefore, the validity of this indicator requires further rigorous evaluation. (2) The stratification criteria for the high‑LPI and low‑LPI groups lack sufficient justification. It remains unclear whether the current grouping threshold possesses genuine clinical significance or merely represents an empirical cutoff optimized for favorable model performance; solid supporting evidence is absent. (3) The reported AUC values are still relatively moderate and suboptimal. (4) A unified LPI threshold was adopted to dichotomize both the internal private dataset and the public dataset into high‑ and low‑LPI subgroups. Nevertheless, the public dataset exhibits a substantially higher proportion of high‑LPI samples. This raises concerns regarding the rationality of such a unified cutoff: heterogeneity in pathological slide information across different patient cohorts may compromise the computational stability and generalizability of the LPI calculation.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and meta-reviewers for their constructive comments. We address the major concerns below. 1.Manual segmentation and scalability. We agree that manual segmentation may introduce inter-observer variability and limit scalability. In this proof-of-concept study, manual delineation was used to ensure anatomically accurate region definitions for pathology-anchored model development. However, the proposed CT-LPI framework is not intrinsically dependent on manual segmentation and can be coupled with automated or semi-automated lung, tumor, and peritumoral segmentation methods. We also note that the main finding is based on consistent multi-region trends rather than a single boundary-sensitive ROI, which may reduce dependence on any one manual contour. 2.External performance and domain shift. We agree that the external NLST AUC is moderate and lower than the internal AUC. We interpret this result as proof-of-concept rather than evidence of a deployment-ready clinical model. This is a challenging task because CT-LPI aims to predict subtle tissue-level pollutant burden from routine CT, rather than a visually obvious disease phenotype. The NLST cohort also differs from the internal cohort in case mix, disease stage, acquisition protocol, scanner settings, and reconstruction kernel. Despite this stringent external setting, the model remained above chance in NLST, supporting the presence of partially transferable pollutant-associated CT signal. 3.NLST series selection and reconstruction kernels. We thank the reviewers for emphasizing reconstruction-kernel heterogeneity. For NLST, we selected the CT reconstruction series referenced by the tumor segmentation and excluded cases in which tumor and lung masks referenced different series. The selected NLST series had heterogeneous kernels, whereas the internal cohort used LUNG kernels. Thus, sharp-equivalent lung kernels represented only a subset of NLST. We agree that this likely contributed to the external performance drop. We will clarify the series-selection procedure and reconstruction-kernel limitation. 4.LPI definition, dichotomization, and threshold transfer. LPI is not an arbitrary label; it is derived from quantification of anthracotic carbon pigment deposition in lung tissue and therefore provides a tissue-level measure of pollutant-associated burden. Our goal was not to establish LPI as a finalized clinical biomarker, but to test whether CT contains imaging features predictive of tissue-resident pollutant burden. We formulated the task as classification because LPI values are small and occupy a narrow range, where precise continuous prediction may be unstable in the current cohort size. The high/low cutoff was pre-specified as the 60th percentile in the internal cohort, corresponding to LPI ≈ 0.001, to provide sufficient representation of the high-LPI subgroup while avoiding extreme tail grouping; it was not optimized for model performance. The same numeric cutoff was applied to NLST to avoid re-optimizing the threshold on the external set. We agree that the higher high-LPI proportion in NLST may reflect both true cohort differences and pathology-side heterogeneity, including slide availability, tissue sampling, staining, and scanning.

The evaluation is strengthened by the inclusion of both an internal cohort and an independent external validation using the NLST dataset. title: Multi-stage NeRF for Efficient 3D Coronary Artery Reconstruction from Two Narrow-Angle Angiographic Projections
reviewer_1_strengths: The paper reads very well. Clear and concise, but also precise technical detail where needed. Elegant figures. Overall top presentation. The clinical motivation for a method which uses narrow-angle angiographic projects is solid, and the technical contributions are a direct response to this. All contributions are validated with experiments, and the improvement in performance trend when acquisition is changed from orthogonal planes is good evidence that the method fits its purpose. The ray aligned regularisation loss to reduce ambiguity in the gradients is a super interesting idea and drives most of the performance gains. The improvement in efficiency as a result of the multi-stage training is significant.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: One of the key arguments of the work is that it is solving a problem in XA which is more aligned to real world clinical settings. However, the authors do not use real XA data. Rather they use 2D X-ray projections generated from 3D CCTA volumes. I understand there is a large overlap in the physics and acquisition of CCTA and XA, and the authors try to reproduce X-ray acquisition protocols, but there are also dissimilarities such as the appearance of contrast and tissue textures, different motion artifacts, calibration error. Will the losses and regularisations proposed be equally effective on real XA images as they are on CCTA-derived X-ray images? This is not evidenced. Perhaps I am missing something here but 0.99 dice similarity on both ImageCAS and ASOCA seems to good to be true? The dice similarity for SOTA segmentation methods on these datasets is ~0.85 dice. Perhaps this is due to the strong ~6x downsampling on the ground truths to 80x80x80? This is extremely coarse - I dont think its possible to resolve a 50% stenosis at this resolution. The authors should report the dice by upsampling their predictions rather than downscaling the ground truth. The qualitative results reveal that the predicted reconstructions are very low quality. I am skeptical whether these are good enough to be clinically useful either to analyse stenosis or other downstream tasks. For example none of the predictions have anatomically plausible surfaces and contain many topological errors. At 80x80x80 resolution, I don’t think any clinically relevant biomarkers can be extracted. It begs the questions: what can this method actually be used for?
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.Addresses clinically relevant constraints neglected by previous NeRF-style approaches. 2.Multi-stage spatial focusing effectively mitigates gradient dilution and improves optimization stability. 3.Ray-aligned constraint is physically meaningful and directly tackles projection ambiguity—a consistently overlooked issue. 4.Bimodal penalty improves early vessel-background separation, accelerating convergence. 5.Implementation based on multi-resolution hash encoding (InstantNGP) ensures high computational efficiency while keeping self-supervised learning feasible per case. 6.Experimental results are comprehensive across datasets; quantitative gains under narrow-angle conditions are significant.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The method reconstructs static geometry; however, coronary angiography images are affected by motion. How robust is NeCA++ under minor temporal misalignment between the two projections? Could motion compensation or temporal regularization be added later? 2.How sensitive is reconstruction quality to the binarization threshold and morphological dilation used to define the active region? 3.Is there any quantitative validation that stage‑1 localization does not miss thin branches or small distal arteries? 4.The λ values (7.5 for $L_{ray}$, 2 for $L_{bin}$) are fixed “experimentally.” Was any grid search or sensitivity study performed? Do these values generalize across datasets and angular settings? 5.How were the number of levels $L$ and feature dimensions per level chosen? Did the authors evaluate if adaptive activation (rather than sequential activation) could further accelerate convergence? 6.Only three baselines are compared. Are there recent NeRF acceleration techniques (e.g., mip‑NeRF 360, KiloNeRF, tensor field NeRF) or other sparse‑view 3D reconstruction approaches that could serve as stronger baselines? 7.The results are purely quantitative. Would subjective assessment by clinicians (e.g., vessel continuity or stenosis identification accuracy) corroborate the improved geometry fidelity? 8.The method still assumes known projection matrices $P_1$, $P_2$. In real practice these may be noisy or partially uncalibrated—how tolerant is NeCA++ to such calibration errors? 9.Does the learned structure exploit prior coronary shapes implicitly? Could the approach reconstruct other vascular regions (e.g., cerebral or peripheral) without major modification?
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The article addresses a clinically relevant and highly ill-posed problem reconstructing 3D coronary structures from two narrow-angle projections and proposes a structured solution. The multi-stage coarse-to-fine optimisation with active-region restriction is well-motivated and improves both efficiency and stability. The ray-aligned constraint and bimodal density regularisation explicitly target projection ambiguity and vessel-background separation. The method demonstrates strong robustness across decreasing angular separations, outperforming baselines under realistic settings, while also achieving significant computational efficiency.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The article does not provide a theoretical analysis of the fundamental ambiguity of reconstructing 3D structure from two narrow-angle projections, leaving identifiability unclear. All experiments rely on synthetic projections without validation on real clinical data, which limits their practical credibility. The reconstruction resolution (80x80x80) is relatively low for medical applications, and scalability to higher resolutions is not discussed. Additionally, the method performs per-case optimisation rather than learning a generalisable mapping, and the proposed regularisation terms remain heuristic without deeper theoretical justification.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We wholeheartedly thank the Area Chair and the three Reviewers for their constructive suggestions. We will carefully revise the manuscript accordingly and include the code link. Low-resolution reconstruction [AC, R1, R4]: The high Dice scores are indeed influenced by downsampling. Following Reviewer’s suggestion, we evaluated by upsampling the generated reconstructions to 256^3, achieving Dice scores of 0.71 and 0.78 on the ImageCAS and ASOCA datasets and outperforming the best competing approach by 30% and 27%, respectively. We completely agree that upsampling the reconstruction does not preserve smaller anatomical details. We will discuss this limitation and explore more efficient representations, such as point clouds, in our future work. Parameter selection and sensitivity [AC, R2 (Q2 - Q5)]: We did sensitivity analysis on the binarization threshold, morphological dilation, loss weights, and hash levels. A threshold of 70% of the maximum grey value attained the best performance, while varying it by ±10% caused only minor changes in Dice (2.1%). Cube dilation sizes of 0, 3, and 6 voxels produced nearly identical metrics, suggesting that binarization also captures thin and distal arteries. For possible discontinuity in segmentation, we retained dilation. Varying λ_ray from 6.5 to 8.5 and λ_bin from 1 to 3 altered Dice by <2.3%. We tested 12-18 hash levels and found that increasing beyond 16 improved Dice by <0.001.These parameters were selected experimentally on validation set and applied consistently across datasets and angular settings. Generalization to Clinical X-ray Angiography (XRA) [AC, R1, R4, R2 (Q1)]: Use of 2D projections from real CCTA data enabled quantitative evaluation of the proposed reconstruction losses and regularizations whilst isolating the impact of motion artifacts. The challenges addressed in this work arise from acquisition geometry and vascular anatomy, which also exist in clinical XRA. So, the proposed framework can be applicable to clinical XRA following a motion correction step [1]. Performance under uncalibrated XRA and other vascular regions (e.g., cerebral or peripheral) [R2 (Q8, Q9), R4]: Due to its self-supervised learning framework, NeCA++ performs patient-specific deformation modelling rather than learning a generalizable mapping, making it largely modality-insensitive. Additionally, ray regularization and multi-view consistency constraints improve robustness to calibration perturbations. The method can also be extended to other vascular regions with minimal modification. LCx reconstruction [R1]: We acknowledge that we used both left (including LCx) and right coronary trees rather than single branches. Lack of comparison with recent NeRF (e.g., mip-NeRF 360, KiloNeRF) [R2 (Q6)]: These methods are designed for natural scenes and rely on photometric consistency assumptions that do not hold for angiography. Subjective assessment by clinicians [R2 (Q7)]: Clinical assessment is valuable, and we plan to conduct an inter-observer study in future work. Theoretical ambiguity of reconstructing 3D structures from two narrow-angle projections [R4]: The theoretical ambiguity has been previously analysed [1], which is now explicitly cited and discussed in the revised manuscript. Justification of regularization term [R4]: Section 2.3 discusses that L_ray promotes continuous vascular structures while suppressing outliers through gradient constraints, and L_bin encourages binary occupancy through a quadratic formulation. Diagnostic value of CCTA for CAD [R1]: We agree and will revise the Introduction accordingly. XRA calibration [R1]: We agree that XRA calibration is a necessary step due to noise in the acquisition parameters. We will revise the Introduction accordingly. Comparison with DeepCA [23] [R1]: Our self-supervised NeCA++ requires only 2D projections for 3D reconstruction, whereas supervised methods such as DeepCA rely on paired 3D and 2D XRA images for training.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper proposes a method for 3D reconstruction of the coronary artery from 2 narrow-angle x-ray projections, relying on implicit reconstruction (NeRF) techniques. The method is tested on synthetic and real data, where 2D X-Ray projections are simulated from 3D CCTA volumes. All reviewers agree that the paper is generally well presented, well motivated, and proposes a sound solution for a relevant problem. title: Multimodal Large Language Model-Driven Self-Verification Reasoning for Interpretable Diagnosis of Diffuse Cystic Lung Diseases
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.Novel integration of global and local reasoning for volumetric CT analysis The paper introduces a hybrid diagnostic formulation that combines global summarisation of 3D CT data with localised slice-level verification. By first constructing a compact global representation and then refining decisions using selected slices, the method achieves a balance between holistic understanding and fine-grained evidence analysis, resulting in both efficiency and clinical meaningfulness. 2.The proposed model works in steps instead of making a single decision by introducing a feedback-driven inference mechanism. The novelty lies in treating diagnosis as a dynamic reasoning process rather than a static prediction task, which is particularly interesting because it closely mirrors how clinicians refine decisions based on evidence. 3.The framework provides explicit intermediate outputs, including which slices it used as evidence, how its decision changed over time and a confidence score. This is a strong contribution because interpretability is often a bottleneck in deploying AI systems in healthcare. Unlike black-box models, this approach enables traceability and interpretability, improving clinical trust and facilitating human-AI collaboration. 4.The proposed global summarisation mechanism allows the model to process hundreds of CT slices without exceeding computational limits. This is an effective and practical solution to a common challenge in volumetric imaging. 5.The model performs better than existing deep learning methods. The paper also includes ablation studies by demonstrating performance degradation when removing either the global context or the reasoning loop, supporting the design choices.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The study is conducted on a relatively small cohort (~217 cases), with an uneven distribution across disease categories. This introduces two key limitations: the risk of overfitting and bias toward dominant classes, and results may not generalise well to new data. The system uses existing large models (like Gemini-3-Pro) without training them specifically for this task. As a result, the reasoning process is guided by prompts rather than learned policies, and slice selection and verification may be suboptimal or inconsistent. The paper focuses primarily on aggregate performance metrics, with insufficient investigation into failure cases and potential systematic biases. The paper does not provide inference time comparisons, resource requirements, or scalability analysis to assess practical feasibility in clinical workflows. The paper does not sufficiently analyse the trade-off between compression and diagnostic fidelity, which is critical in medical imaging tasks. While the method is compared against standard deep learning approaches and relatively old 3D CNN models. It requires comparing with state-of-the-art 3D CNN/Transformer models, or recent hybrid global-local architectures.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The paper tackles a clinically important and challenging rare-disease diagnosis problem with clear practical relevance. The proposed framework is novel and well motivated, as it mirrors the radiologist workflow of combining global distribution assessment with local feature verification. The paper offers a solution to the context-length limitation of MLLMs for volumetric CT through GSP, while MSVR improves interpretability and reasoning transparency. The experiments are comprehensive, which support the value of the proposed design.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The strongest results rely on proprietary MLLM backbones, which may reduce reproducibility. The dataset size remains modest, especially for a 4-class rare-disease setting, so broader validation would strengthen the claims. The framework depends on accurate upstream segmentation and structured preprocessing, which may complicate deployment.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: S1.Well-motivated clinical problem with a cognitively aligned framework design. The clinical challenge of DCLDs differential diagnosis is clearly articulated: rare disease with limited data, overlapping cystic phenotypes requiring both global spatial reasoning and local morphological analysis. The two-stage GSP→MSVR pipeline elegantly mirrors the radiologist’s cognitive pathway of “first assess overall spatial distribution, then locally verify key morphological features” [Gupta et al., ERJ 2015, Ref. 5 in paper]. This clinical grounding is a notable strength over generic MLLM prompting approaches. S2.Novel and effective GSP representation. The idea of compressing 3D cyst distribution into a single surface-rendered image with a slice-index navigation axis is creative and pragmatic. The ablation study strongly supports its value: removing GSP causes a dramatic accuracy drop of 32.7 percentage points (82.5% → 49.8%). Additionally, the finding that ConvNeXt-S trained on 3D renderings (76.4%) outperforms all standard 3D volumetric models (≤65.0%) independently validates the discriminative power of this representation, even outside the MLLM framework. S3.Self-verification mechanism with demonstrated hallucination correction. The MSVR closed-loop design—where the model actively retrieves evidence to confirm or refute its current hypothesis—draws on established reasoning paradigms (CoT [Ref. 20], Reflexion [Ref. 23], ReAct [Ref. 24]) but applies them in a medically meaningful way. The qualitative example in Fig. 4 is compelling: standard Gemini-3-Pro produces a hallucinated BHD diagnosis biased by clinical metadata priors, while the proposed framework retrieves axial slices revealing morphological evidence inconsistent with BHD and correctly revises the diagnosis to LAM. S4.Comprehensive experimental design. The evaluation includes: (i) multi-center validation (internal + external cohorts); (ii) systematic comparison against 6 supervised baselines and 2 medical MLLMs; (iii) parameter sensitivity analysis for slice budget M and max iterations T; (iv) a well-structured ablation study isolating the contribution of each component. The cross-center generalization gap is notably smaller for the proposed method than for supervised baselines, suggesting robustness.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: W1.Dataset Size Still Modest Although the dataset is collected from multiple centers, its overall size remains relatively limited, comprising 217 cases in total, with only 80 cases in the external cohort and just 23 PLCH cases among the four subtypes. Such small subgroup sizes may introduce substantial variance and limit the statistical reliability of the reported results. Moreover, the manuscript does not provide confidence intervals or statistical significance analyses, making it difficult to assess the robustness and stability of the performance improvements. W2.Lack of Direct Comparison with Radiologists The study does not include a direct comparison with radiologists or pulmonologists. Without benchmarking against human expert performance, the claim of “physician-level reasoning” is not sufficiently supported. W3.Hallucination Reduction Not Quantitatively Measured The manuscript claims mitigation of hallucinations but provides: No formal hallucination metric No error-type breakdown No calibration analysis Quantitative evaluation (e.g., confidence calibration curves or error taxonomy) would strengthen this claim.

author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and AC for their constructive comments. We group concerns into four themes: dataset size, reliability, and generalization; clinical feasibility and reproducibility; baseline strength; and method clarification with failure patterns. Dataset size, statistical reliability, and generalization (AC, R1-W1, R2-W2, R3-W1). We agree that cohort size and imbalance are important limitations. DCLDs are rare, and collecting confirmed multi-center cases with pixel-level cyst annotations is challenging. To our knowledge, our cohort is among the largest available multi-center datasets for this DCLD differential diagnosis task. Evaluation is not limited to internal validation: Center B is an independent external cohort, and the submitted results show meaningful cross-center performance. The submitted external-center and per-subtype analyses help contextualize reliability under this rare-disease sample size. Per-class analysis (Fig. 3(a) already reports the corresponding results) shows the model is not simply biased toward large classes; PLCH still obtains an F1 of 69.6%, indicating retained discriminative performance even on the minority subtype. Clinical feasibility and reproducibility (AC, R1-W4, R2-W1, R2-W3, R3). The preprocessing stage is externally validated in the submitted manuscript, supporting the reliability of the upstream segmentation module. The segmentation model can be deployed on a single RTX 4090 GPU, and deployment profiling indicates that the full pipeline is practical for non-emergency DCLD decision support. The system has also been deployed in an anonymized hospital setting and received positive feedback. For reproducibility beyond commercial APIs, the pipeline is modular and can be executed with local open-source MLLM backbones; therefore, commercial MLLMs are high-capability backbones rather than the only executable form. All closed-source models were accessed through OpenRouter, and the detailed model identifiers, inference settings, prompts, preprocessing pipeline, and code are provided in the anonymized repository. Baseline strength (R1-W6). We understand the concern about the strength of baseline comparisons. We also examined modern supervised architectures, including a Swin Transformer-based encoder and M3T, but they did not outperform the traditional 3D CNN baselines in this rare-disease small-sample setting. This suggests that the core bottleneck is the lack of disease-specific training data rather than the architecture itself. This further supports the rationale of our training-free MLLM reasoning framework: rather than relying solely on fitting a supervised classifier from limited rare-disease data, the proposed framework explicitly combines global lesion distribution with local evidence verification. Method clarification and failure patterns (R1-W2, R1-W3, R1-W5, R3). GSP is not intended to replace the original CT volume. It provides a global distribution map and slice-index navigation, while MSVR returns to original axial slices for fine-grained morphological verification. This directly addresses the compression-fidelity concern: global spatial information is compressed, but local diagnostic details are checked from the source CT slices. The ablations support this design, as removing GSP causes the largest performance drop and removing MSVR also substantially degrades results. Slice selection is guided by carefully designed prompts; in rare diseases, this training-free design helps avoid overfitting, while learning retrieval becomes promising with larger datasets or data-rich transfers. Failure review showed that the main ambiguity lies between BHD and LIP, which is clinically plausible because both may show heterogeneous cyst size and uneven distribution; distinguishing them requires subtle analysis of cyst shape and local relationships. Thus, remaining errors are concentrated in genuinely difficult differential patterns rather than random majority-class collapse.

title: Mutual Distillation of Dual-Foundation Models for Semi-supervised PET/CT Segmentation
reviewer_1_strengths: The paper is well-organized and easy to follow. The research problem of the anatomical-functional mismatch and cross-modal information fusion in semi-supervised segmentation is well-motivated. The mutual distillation framework that synergistically exploits structural and functional foundation models is somewhat innovative. Segmentation experiments contained the proposed MuDuo and several existing semi-supervised methods in three different data configurations. Ablation studies were implemented to validate the effectiveness of multiple components in the proposed MuDuo.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: It is natural that the combination of multiple foundation models yields superior segmentation performance, as demonstated by previous semi-supervised learning studies. However, demonstrating that the combination of structural and functional foundation models leads to a better model, as shown in their experiments, provides valuable insights to the community. Segmentation experiments are conducted solely on an outdated U-Net backbone, leaving it unclear whether the observed improvements would hold for other architectures, such as transformers. The majority of the semi-supervised methods adopted are relatively dated, and only one is derived from the foundation model SAM.

author_feedback: We sincerely thank all reviewers for their constructive comments. We especially appreciate R3’s concerns on novelty, reproducibility, hyper-parameter justification, and validation scope. We agree that several key designs should be clarified and will revise the manuscript accordingly. Regarding novelty, MuDuo should not be positioned as a new generic SSL paradigm. Its precise contribution is a PET/CT-specific dual-teacher semi-supervised framework for organ segmentation. Rather than simply combining two foundation models, MuDuo queries modality-specialized teachers in complementary ways: SAM-Med3D uses CT-side mask prompts to exploit anatomical priors, while SegAnyPET uses PET-side point prompts to exploit metabolic uptake priors. Their outputs are selected by cross-modal IoU consensus and fused as pseudo labels for consistency learning. We will delimit this contribution and avoid over-generalized claims. We apologize for the unclear description of the prompt generator. In our implementation, it is a lightweight U-Net trained on the labeled subset with organ annotations before the semi-supervised stage. During mutual distillation, the prompt generator, SAM-Med3D, and SegAnyPET are frozen, and only the student model is optimized. For CT, it produces class probability maps as mask prompts for SAM-Med3D. For PET, it produces coarse logits; each predicted organ region is smoothed, and the top-K foreground locations are sampled as point prompts for SegAnyPET. We will add details on its supervision, freezing strategy, and calling order. Regarding hyper-parameters, MuDuo does not rely on a manually tuned absolute IoU threshold. The fixed tau=0.5 is only an ablation baseline. Our final strategy is adaptive top-50% IoU filtering, where CT/PET predictions are ranked by cross-modal agreement and only the most reliable half is retained. This is more robust to organ size and case difficulty. Table 2 supports this design: adaptive top-50% improves Dice and reduces HD95 over both no filtering and fixed tau=0.5.K=3 is motivated by heterogeneous PET uptake, where one point may cover only the high-uptake core. Table 2 also shows that multi-point prompting improves both Dice and HD95 over K=1. Regarding validation, we agree that broader evaluation would further strengthen the work. Still, the manuscript includes 5/10/20 low-label settings, PET-only and PET/CT baselines, four metrics, qualitative comparisons, and ablations on teacher configuration, IoU filtering, and prompting. We will clarify that these ablations verify structural-functional complementarity, improved pseudo-label reliability, and better PET-teacher guidance. We will also state the evidence scope: the experiments are based on an organ-annotated AutoPET subset and a 3D U-Net student. Although MuDuo is conceptually compatible with other backbones, we will not claim empirical generalization beyond the reported experiments. We thank R2 for the comments on title, task description, data split, and absolute Dice. We will revise the title and task description to focus on PET/CT organ segmentation rather than the original AutoPET lesion segmentation task. We will clarify that methods are compared under the same protocol within each label setting, and avoid implying identical test sets across 5/10/20 settings if this is not the case. We will also discuss why the absolute Dice is modest: whole-body PET organ segmentation is challenging due to low PET resolution, blurred boundaries, heterogeneous uptake, uneven organ visibility, and PET/CT spatial mismatch. Thus, our main evidence lies in consistent relative improvements and boundary-metric gains under low-label regimes. Finally, we accept R1’s concern regarding backbone and baseline scope. We will moderate the related claims: MuDuo shows that cross-modal foundation-model consensus improves semi-supervised PET/CT organ segmentation under the current U-Net student setting, but we will not overstate gains across all architectures.
