title: MVDA-Net: Multi-View Dual-Alignment Network for 3D Carotid Artery Segmentation
reviewer_1_strengths: The paper proposes MVDA-Net for 3D carotid artery segmentation in CTA, addressing challenges such as discontinuous lesions and severe foreground scarcity. It introduces three complementary modules: SAOP for multi-view contextual modeling, HIAR for boundary refinement via inverted attention, and SFA for spatial–semantic feature alignment. The method is evaluated on a newly curated clinical dataset and multiple public benchmarks, achieving state-of-the-art performance.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The use of multi-view pooling and axis projection for handling foreground–background imbalance and capturing global context is not new, as similar ideas appear in prior works (e. g. , APAUNet, LW-CTrans). Likewise, attention mechanisms for boundary refinement have already been explored (e. g. , BMANet), reducing the originality of the proposed design. 2.It is not clearly specified how feature maps (e. g. , F_i and F_(i+1)) are defined and selected. In particular, the indexing iis not justified, and the distinction between low-level and high-level features remains ambiguous. 3.There is a task–evaluation mismatch. Although the modules (SAOP, HIAR, SFA) are claimed to be designed for carotid artery segmentation, it is unclear how well they generalize to other organs or lesions. Moreover, the evaluation on datasets such as MSD Lung, MSD Spleen, and BraTS is not fully aligned with the primary task of 3D carotid artery segmentation stated in the paper.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The paper is well-organized and follows a logical structure that enhances technical readability. The authors provide a comprehensive overview of the MVDA-Net architecture, effectively utilizing clear diagrams to illustrate the system workflow and individual module configurations. Each primary component, including the SAOPFormer, HIAR, and SFA, is clearly defined with its own dedicated subsection and mathematical formulation, ensuring the proposed framework is easy to follow. A notable strength of this work is the explicit alignment between identified challenges in 3D carotid arterial segmentation and the proposed solutions. The authors specifically design the Spatially-Aware Orthogonal Projection (SAOP) module to address discontinuous lesion distribution and extreme foreground scarcity. Simultaneously, the Hierarchical Inverted Attention Refinement (HIAR) and Synergistic Feature Alignment (SFA) modules are purposefully engineered to overcome low-contrast boundary delineation and insufficient spatial-semantic complementarity, respectively. -The model is evaluated by validating the MVDA-Net across a diverse range of datasets. Beyond testing on a specialized in-house carotid artery dataset, the authors perform extensive experiments on three distinct public benchmarks: MSD Lung, MSD Spleen, and BraTS. Achieving the highest performance across these various anatomical structures and imaging modalities (CT and MRI) provides evidence of the model’s robustness and generalization capabilities.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Although the paper emphasizes boundary refinement via the HIAR module, the evaluation relies solely on the Dice score. To adequately validate the claimed improvements in boundary precision, surface-based metrics such as Hausdorff Distance (HD95) should be included. While 5-fold cross-validation is mentioned for the in-house dataset, the experimental setup for the three public benchmarks is unclear. The absence of standard deviations (std), confidence intervals, and p-values makes it difficult to assess whether the performance gains over baselines are statistically significant. There is a lack of clarity in Equations (4) and (5) relative to the architecture shown in Figure 3b. The mathematical formulation of the SFA module is not sufficiently detailed to ensure reproducibility, which is particularly concerning given that the source code is not provided. The reported input size of 192×192×32 for the MSD Lung dataset appears unusually shallow for the Z-axis. The authors should verify this configuration, as such a significant reduction in spatial resolution could lead to substantial information loss. The assertion that this is the “first model specifically designed for 3D carotid arterial segmentation in CTA” is an overclaim. Previous studies have already addressed this specific clinical task. Huang, X., Wang, J., & Li, Z. (2023). 3D carotid artery segmentation using shape-constrained active contours. Computers in Biology and Medicine, 153, 106530. Xie, H., Gu, H., Li, M., Zhu, L., Wang, T., Li, Z., & Wu, H. (2025). Carotid artery segmentation in computed tomography angiography (CTA) using multi-scale deep supervision with Swin-UNet and advanced data augmentation. Quantitative imaging in medicine and surgery, 15(4), 3161–3175. Therefore, the authors should revise their positioning relative to these existing works.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: A key strength of this paper is the introduction of the MVDA-Net architecture, which addresses specific challenges in carotid artery segmentation using three innovative modules: SAOP, HIAR, and SFA. The SAOP module enhances small target representation and addresses foreground scarcity by incorporating multi-view projections across anatomical planes. The HIAR module refines boundary delineation by propagating attention from deep to shallow features, improving the delineation of vessel walls and calcifications. The SFA module efficiently aligns encoder-decoder features, improving spatial-semantic complementarity, which is crucial for accurate segmentation of complex vascular structures. The method is thoroughly validated using both an in-house carotid artery dataset and public benchmark datasets, demonstrating its state-of-the-art performance. The experiments highlight MVDA-Net’s superiority in segmentation accuracy, particularly for challenging structures like vessel walls and calcifications. Carotid artery segmentation is critical for the diagnosis and treatment of atherosclerotic vascular diseases, and the model’s potential to improve segmentation accuracy could have significant implications in clinical decision-making.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The paper presents a strong methodology for carotid artery segmentation, but there are several areas that could be further strengthened or clarified. 1.While the method is validated on three public datasets (Lung, Spleen, and BraTS), the segmentation tasks on these datasets differ significantly from the task of carotid artery segmentation in terms of morphology, texture, and pathological features. The excellent performance on non-vascular organs and tumors demonstrates the model’s strong feature learning ability, but it does not directly prove the model’s effectiveness in addressing carotid artery-specific challenges, such as the subtle double-edge boundaries of the vessel wall or irregular calcification contours. The results on these non-vascular datasets do not fully validate the model’s ability to handle the unique complexities associated with carotid artery segmentation. 2.The paper primarily uses Dice as the performance evaluation metric, which, while commonly used in segmentation tasks, is not comprehensive enough to assess boundary precision. For a task like carotid artery segmentation, where boundary accuracy is crucial, additional metrics such as Hausdorff distance, average surface distance, or other boundary-specific metrics would provide a more thorough evaluation of the model’s performance. These metrics would particularly help validate the effectiveness of the HIAR module in boundary refinement. 3.The ablation study in Table 2 shows the performance improvements from combining different modules. However, the paper does not delve deeply into the impact of specific design choices within each module. 4.The paper does not mention important efficiency metrics such as model parameter count, FLOPs, training/inference time, or memory usage. These metrics are critical for assessing the feasibility of deploying MVDA-Net in clinical settings, where resource constraints may play a significant role. A discussion on these aspects would help determine whether the model is suitable for real-time clinical applications or large-scale clinical deployment.
reviewer_3_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We appreciate the comments and respond below. Reviewer#1 Q1: Originality of the proposed design. Our method specifically targets key challenges in carotid artery CTA segmentation: discontinuous lesion distribution, extreme foreground scarcity, inadequate capture of low-contrast subtle double-edge boundaries of the vessel wall, and irregular calcification contours. Different from APAUNet and LW-CTrans, our SAOP addresses the challenge of discontinuous lesions through spatial-aware feature recalibration, improving the spatial distinguishability of multiple lesion regions. Different from BMANet, our HIAR applies an inverted attention mechanism to deep encoder features to suppress high-confidence region responses, guiding shallow features to focus on uncertain regions such as boundaries. To further enhance shallow feature representation, we design 3D SimAM to selectively enhance fine-grained details while suppressing redundancy. Q2: Unclear definition of feature maps. In HIAR, F_i and F_(i+1) (1≤i≤4) denote feature maps from adjacent encoder stages. F_i from a shallower stage provides richer spatial details (low-level), while F_(i+1) from a deeper stage provides stronger semantic information (high-level). These definitions will be clarified in the revised manuscript. Q3: Task-evaluation mismatch and cross-dataset validation. Except for our self-constructed dataset, no publicly available carotid artery test set provides dense voxel-wise annotations. We further tested on the MSD Lung, MSD Spleen, and BraTS datasets due to their shared challenges with carotid artery segmentation, including extremely low foreground proportions (0.04%, 0.47%, and 1.16%, respectively) and irregular boundaries. Evaluation on these datasets validates the generalization of our method under similarly challenging segmentation scenarios. Reviewer#2 Q1: Lack of boundary-specific evaluation metrics. In the HIAR ablation study on CA, the model with HIAR yielded a better HD95 compared to the baseline. This confirms the effectiveness of HIAR in boundary refinement. Due to page limits, these results will be released with the code upon acceptance. Q2: Experimental setup and statistical significance analysis. For MSD Lung and BraTS, we followed the official splits of UNETR++ and nnFormer, respectively. These details will be added in the revised manuscript. Statistical significance analysis will be released with the code upon acceptance. Q3: Unclear descriptions in Eq.(4)-(5) and SFA. We will clarify Eq.(4)-(5) and SFA with detailed symbols and interactions in the revised manuscript and release the code upon acceptance. Q4: Input size for MSD Lung dataset. For MSD Lung, we adopt the same nnUNet-based preprocessing and patch planning strategy as UNETR++. The 192×192×32 is the training patch size; nnUNet’s sampling strategy (33% foreground-centered, 67% random) is applied, ensuring no information loss. Q5: Overclaim regarding first 3D carotid artery model. We acknowledge the overclaim and will remove the “first” claim and clarify our positioning relative to prior works. Existing studies only focus on anatomical carotid segmentation, whereas our work targets multi-structure segmentation of vessel wall, lumen, and calcification in carotid CTA. Reviewer#3 Q1: Please refer to our response to R1Q3.Q2: Please refer to our response to R2Q1.Q3: Ablation analysis. As shown in Tab.3, ablation on SAOPBlock verifies the effectiveness of adaptive fusion weights. For SFA, the difference-based branch models spatial complementarity, while the summation-based branch balances semantic information. Ablating them individually and jointly confirms that their combination is superior, validating the necessity of both. Due to page limits, detailed results will be released with the code upon acceptance. Q4: Computational efficiency. On CA, our method achieves 50.02M parameters, 357.69 GFLOPs, 16.82 GB memory, and 0.068 s inference time, with comparable computational efficiency to baselines.

Reviewers appreciated the clear organization of the paper, the generally well-structured method presentation, and the extensive empirical evaluation on both an in-house carotid dataset and multiple public benchmarks. The clinical relevance of carotid artery segmentation was also recognized, and the reported performance is promising. At the same time, the reviewers raised several important concerns that require clarification. A central issue is the degree of methodological novelty, as some of the core design elements appear related to existing multi-view context modeling, attention-based refinement, and feature alignment approaches. The authors should better position the contribution relative to prior work and moderate claims such as being the first model specifically designed for 3D carotid artery segmentation. Reviewers also noted that some technical details remain unclear, particularly the definition of intermediate feature maps and the mathematical formulation of the SFA module, which affects reproducibility. On the experimental side, the current evaluation does not fully support all claims. In particular, boundary refinement is emphasized, but only Dice is reported; additional boundary-sensitive metrics such as HD95 or ASD would be important. Reviewers also asked for clearer reporting of the experimental setup on the public datasets, inclusion of uncertainty or significance analysis, and discussion of efficiency metrics. Finally, while the public benchmark results are useful, their connection to the carotid-specific challenges of the target task should be more carefully justified. Overall, the paper addresses an important application and shows promising results, but the current reviews indicate that several issues regarding novelty, reproducibility, and evaluation remain unresolved. I encourage the authors to use the rebuttal to clarify these points. | This paper presents MVDA-Net for 3D carotid artery segmentation in CTA, combining slice-aware, hierarchical, and boundary-oriented modules. The application is clinically relevant, the technical design is clearly motivated, and the empirical results are consistently strong across multiple datasets. After rebuttal, two reviewers (R2 and R3) are clearly positive, noting that the authors addressed the main concerns on overclaims, reproducibility, and evaluation details. R1 remains cautious about novelty and the justification of feature-level choices, but these reservations do not override the overall technical soundness and demonstrated practical value. The work is recognized as incremental rather than breakthrough, yet the integrated design delivers solid gains validated by thorough ablation and cross-dataset experiments. I recommend accept. For the camera-ready version, the authors must: (1) include boundary-sensitive metrics (HD95 or ASD) to substantiate the boundary refinement claims; (2) provide a clear justification for the selection of adjacent encoder feature levels and the operational definition of low-level vs. high-level features; and (3) moderate all remaining overclaims, particularly regarding novelty and task-specificity, in line with the rebuttal commitments. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper proposes MVDA-Net, a U-shaped architecture for 3D carotid artery segmentation in CTA imaging, built from three modules (SAOP, HIAR, and SFA) targeting global context, boundary refinement, and encoder-decoder feature alignment. The majority opinion is positive, though all three reviewers flag limited methodological novelty: the core ideas stay close to well-established strategies, and the contribution is largely one of combining existing components. R1 remains the most critical, noting that the rebuttal did not adequately justify the design choices or clarify operational definitions. R2 and R3 lean toward acceptance, with R2 reversing an initial negative assessment based on the rebuttal. All acknowledge that the method is technically sound and shows consistent gains across a private dataset and three public benchmarks, with an ablation supporting each module. On balance, the concerns over limited methodological novelty and the somewhat composite nature of the architecture do not outweigh the consistent results and the clinical value of the application. Assuming the authors sufficiently address the requested revisions—R1’s concerns on methodological ambiguity, removal of overstated claims, and stronger statistical and evaluation rigor—I lean toward acceptance. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): The reviewers have a consensus on the potential merit and good quality. But in terms of a large volume of medical image segmentation model papers, this paper only justified one task with an existing method with modification. The good quality of this paper still maintains its competitiveness.

title: NASD-Diff: A Noise-Assisted Structural Difference Diffusion Model for CT Angiography Generation from NCCT
reviewer_1_strengths: The paper addresses a clinically meaningful problem and presents a method whose core design is well aligned with that problem formulation. The overall story is coherent from Abstract to Experiments: the paper identifies the limitation of globally noise-driven diffusion for NCCT-to-CTA synthesis, proposes a structural-difference-aware degradation process, and then validates the design with both baseline comparisons and ablations. The experimental section is reasonably comprehensive for internal benchmarking, including multiple strong baselines, full-metric comparison, component ablation, and analysis of the noise coefficient. The visual results and ablation trends are also consistent with the claimed role of NASD in improving vascular clarity and texture fidelity.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The evidence for clinical utility is still limited. The evaluation is based on a single carotid dataset with 10 test patients and mainly generic image-quality metrics, without reader study, downstream vascular analysis, or external validation. 2.The core novelty is concentrated in the NASD degradation idea; CSCEM, GPRM, and perceptual refinement feel more incremental, and listing “experimental validation” as a contribution weakens the novelty framing. 3.The method section leaves several implementation choices underexplained, especially the optimization/training behavior of GPRM, the exact conditioning/prediction interface of the decoupled branches, and the practical role of cross-slice inputs in a still largely 2D pipeline. 4.The claims are somewhat stronger than the evidence. Statements about “clinical potential” and “clinically acceptable limits” are not yet fully supported by the current experimental protocol. 5.For a vascular synthesis task, the evaluation lacks anatomy-aware or vessel-specific fidelity measures, which makes it difficult to judge whether the observed metric gains translate into better vascular depiction in a clinically meaningful sense.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: ajor Strengths Clinically important problem. A software-based strategy to directly generate CT Angiography (CTA) from Non-Contrast CT (NCCT) scans without contrast agent injection could reduce the risk for patients with iodine allergy, renal insufficiency, or multiple myeloma, aligning with MICCAI’s clinical translation priorities. Noise-assisted structural difference modeling strategy. The changes in vascular structure caused by contrast agent between NCCT and CTA were explicitly captured. Combining this strategy in the forward propagation process of the diffusion model improved the generation of vascular structure and overall texture details. Decoupling structural difference prediction and noise prediction. Optimizing vascular structure and texture details improves the structural accuracy and detail clarity of the generated CTA images. Open-source commitment. If the collected carotid artery dataset containing 492 patients and the related code from the paper could be open-sourced, it would be of great significance to the community. Clean degradation ablation. The results of ablation experiments a and b in Table 2 clearly demonstrate that each contribution proposed by the authors contributes to the overall CTA image generation.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Most issues below are reporting gaps, not technical errors, and can be addressed in the rebuttal without new experiments. W1.A complete description of perceptual loss [Major]. In the Training and Sampling section, the authors propose using Llpips to perceive similarity from deep features, measuring the visual consistency between the generated CTA image and the real CTA image. It’s important to clarify here whether this involves overlaying the number of image channels to match the natural image, or if some other operation is performed. W2.Implementation Details [Major]. The authors do not explicitly specify in the Implementation Details whether data augmentation strategies were employed to enhance the model’s robustness and generalization capability. W3.Diffusion model coefficients [Major]. The full text does not explicitly explain the details of the diffusion model correlation coefficients used in the entire framework, including but not limited to: the number of forward and backward samples, the sampling method, etc. W4.Model parameters and running efficiency [Major]. The discussion of model parameters and computational efficiency remains insufficient. In particular, sampling time—an inherent bottleneck in diffusion-based models—is not adequately analyzed. Furthermore, the report lacks a comprehensive comparison of runtime performance with competing methods, leaving the efficiency advantages or trade-offs of the proposed approach unclear. W5.The formula details are insufficient [Moderate]. In formula 3, || ||2 represents the L2 norm or the square term, which needs to be clarified.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.A key strength is the noise-assisted structural difference degradation operator, which reformulates the forward process using the NCCT–CTA structural difference instead of relying only on global random noise. This is interesting because it explicitly targets the vascular enhancement changes that are central to NCCT-to-CTA generation. 2.The reverse model is reasonably well designed for the problem. The Decoupled Structural-Texture Network (DeST-Net) separates structural-difference prediction from noise prediction, while the cross-slice conditional embedding module leverages adjacent-slice context and the refinement module improves perceptual quality. These components are task-motivated rather than generic additions. 3.Empirical study is fairly comprehensive.The paper compares against a broad set of GAN-, translation-, and diffusion-based baselines, reports multiple distortion and perceptual metrics, and includes both component ablations and a study of the noise control coefficient λ. The study is based on paired NCCT–CTA data from 492 patients, with explicit training/validation/test splits and registered image pairs, which strengthens the practical relevance of the experiments.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The forward operator relies on m = x_CTA − x_NCCT computed from registered pairs; m will absorb misregistration and non-vascular differences, potentially biasing the learned “structural difference” away from pure vascular enhancement. 2.The use of LPIPS is clear at a high level, but the manuscript does not specify which pretrained feature backbone is used to compute the perceptual loss. 3.Although the task is clinically motivated, the evaluation is restricted to image-quality metrics and qualitative visual comparisons on a single paired carotid dataset. Stronger claims such as “clinically acceptable limits” and broader “clinical potential” are therefore somewhat ahead of the evidence currently presented, since no reader study or downstream vascular-assessment analysis is included.

title: NEARL: Interacted Query Adaptation with Orthogonal Regularization for Medical Vision-Language Understanding
reviewer_1_strengths: 1) The comparison with the CLIP backbone in terms of parameter count is interesting and suggests that NEARL achieves competitive inference throughput with limited parameter overhead. While this points toward potential resource efficiency, additional discussion on real-world deployment constraints would further strengthen the claim of clinical applicability. 2) The proposed adapter module appears to mitigate interference during incremental learning, as indicated by the ablation results. The design rationale is plausible, and the observed improvements in cross-modal interaction are encouraging. However, a deeper analysis of why orthogonality helps, via feature-space visualization or gradient dynamics, would provide more convincing mechanistic insight. 3) The evaluation spans multiple diseases and imaging modalities, which is a notable strength. Performance gains over prior methods are consistently reported, suggesting reasonable generalization. That said, dataset-specific performance variations and potential biases are not thoroughly examined; addressing these would improve confidence in the method’s robustness across heterogeneous clinical settings.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1） The baseline methods used in the comparative experiments are relatively outdated. It is recommended to include comparisons with more recent state-of-the-art approaches to better demonstrate the competitiveness of the proposed method. Alternatively, if incorporating newer baselines is not feasible, please provide a thorough discussion explaining why certain recent methods underperform compared to the classical baselines in this specific setting, thereby strengthening the validity and rigor of the experimental evaluation.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.NEARL introduces a bidirectional framework that fully leverages the duality of vision-language models, improving alignment between visual and textual features, which addresses the limitations of prior unidirectional approaches. 2.The OCA module decouples truly novel knowledge from incremental updates using orthogonal regularization, preventing interference with pre-trained features and enabling focused acquisition of new domain-specific information. 3.NEARL achieves superior performance across multiple medical imaging modalities.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.Questionable Motivation: While NEARL introduces USEformer and OCA to improve medical vision-language alignment, the overall novelty and practical significance are limited. The framework primarily relies on adapting a frozen CLIP model pretrained on natural image-text pairs with lightweight modules. Given the availability of numerous general-purpose and domain-specific medical foundation models, it is unclear why starting from a frozen natural-image CLIP is preferable to leveraging these pretrained medical models, which may already encode relevant medical visual-language representations. 2.Limited Evaluation Scope: Although NEARL is evaluated across three imaging modalities, experiments are limited to only three datasets, raising concerns about the generalizability to broader medical imaging datasets. Additional evaluation on more datasets could strengthen the evidence. 3.Unclear Task Definition: It is not explicitly stated whether the reported results correspond to zero-shot or other evaluation settings. Expanding the experiment to include multiple evaluation settings (e.g., few-shot, retrieval) would clarify the model’s applicability and robustness. 4.Visualization Comparisons: In Figure 2, the visualizations should be compared against representative bidirectional/unidirectional modality interaction baselines to better illustrate the contribution of the proposed modules to cross-modal alignment. 5.Parameter and Efficiency Analysis: While the authors claim that NEARL introduces only 1.46M additional parameters and achieves fast inference, it is unclear how this compares quantitatively to other baselines. More detailed analysis of parameter efficiency and runtime gains relative to existing methods is needed to support the claimed advantages.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: One major strength is the novel bidirectional cross-modal interaction design, which differs from existing prompt learning or unidirectional modality adaptation methods that only optimize one modality or pass information in a single direction; USEformer builds real two-way communication between image and text branches, which better exploits the dual structure of CLIP and alleviates modality misalignment in the medical domain, making the cross-modal alignment more thorough and suitable for medical vision-language tasks. Another strength is the orthogonal regularization mechanism in OCA, which uses a simple yet effective Gram-Schmidt process to strictly separate adaptive features from pre-trained features, avoiding interference with the original generalization ability of CLIP and making the domain adaptation more focused and stable, and this orthogonal design is computationally efficient compared with other orthogonalization methods like Householder transformation, fitting clinical real-time needs. The paper also shows strong evaluation completeness: it tests NEARL on three distinct medical datasets with different imaging modalities and disease types, compares with a wide range of state-of-the-art methods including prompt learning, unidirectional adaptation, and even unimodal medical models, and achieves clear performance gains, such as a 2.3% relative accuracy increase on the pneumonia dataset. Additionally, the framework is highly parameter-efficient with only 1.46M extra parameters, delivers fast inference speed (500 fps on RTX 3090) and low memory overhead, which demonstrates practical clinical feasibility for real-time diagnostic screening. Comprehensive ablation studies and visual feature analysis further verify the effectiveness of each core module and explain the limitations of prior unimodal adaptation strategies, making the work solid and convincing.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The main weakness is that the core ideas of cross-modal interaction via learnable queries and adapter-based fine-tuning with regularization are not completely new in the vision-language field. Learnable query tokens for cross-modal fusion have been explored in many prior VLM adaptation works such as MaPLe and CoCoOp, and orthogonal regularization has also been used in some parameter-efficient adaptation methods to reduce feature conflict, so the overall paradigm of combining query-based interaction and orthogonal adapter follows existing technical routines without a radically new methodological foundation. Also, the experiments are limited to standard medical image classification tasks on three public datasets, without testing on more challenging medical vision-language tasks like image captioning, visual question answering, or lesion segmentation, which limits the demonstration of the framework’s generalization to broader medical VL understanding scenarios. Furthermore, the paper does not provide in-depth analysis on the sensitivity of key hyperparameters such as the number of query tokens, query dimension, and the number of USEformer layers, and there is no comparison with other recent orthogonal or bidirectional adaptation methods specifically designed for medical VLMs, making the novelty and superiority of the design less distinctive in the medical domain literature.
reviewer_3_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank all reviewers for their comments. R1-Real-world constraints: NEARL is deployment-friendly with low inference memory (~1 GB) and exceptional data efficiency (only ~4k images for pneumonia adaptation). R1-Evidence of orthogonality: Prior works (e.g., Cogswell et al., ICLR 2016) suggest that reducing feature redundancy improves generalization. If adapter updates are not orthogonal to frozen features, they introduce overlap and conflict. Baselines show nontrivial angles (>5°), while OCA enforces near-perfect orthogonality (90° ± 0.02°), enabling non-redundant adaptation and generalization. R1-Performance variations: Improvement margins vary across datasets due to differences in imaging modality, disease characteristics, and task difficulty. For instance, the visual overlap between normal and pathological patterns in X-rays makes adaptation inherently harder. Despite this, NEARL consistently delivers positive gains, highlighting its robustness. R1- Baseline recency: When tested against recent methods, e.g., HiCroPL (ICCV 2025) and Spotlighter (EMNLP 2025), NEARL consistently performs best, achieving 94.7% v.s. 89.7% and 82.9%, respectively, further demonstrating its effectiveness. R2-Backbone choice: NEARL is backbone-agnostic and plug-and-play. We adopt natural-domain CLIP because prior medical adaptation works (e.g., ViP) use the same backbone for fair comparison. With a medical backbone (PubMedCLIP), NEARL reaches 94.0%, up from 62.5% (zero-shot), and surpasses baselines e.g., FATE (86.8%) and MaPLe (92.3%). R2-Evaluation scope: Our evaluation spans three widely used medical imaging modalities: X-ray, OCT, and MRI. On ISIC dermoscopy dataset, NEARL achieves 89.1% acc, outperforming previous methods e.g., FATE (84.5%) and MaPLe (85.8%), further supporting its effectiveness across diverse datasets. R2-Unclear task definition: Our experiments follow the standard PEFT setting used in prior medical adaptation works (e.g., ViP, XCoOp): all methods are tuned on the full training split with a frozen backbone, rather than zero-/few-shot evaluation, ensuring fair comparison. Few-shot or retrieval-based evaluation is beyond our current scope and left for future study. Thanks! R2-Visualization comparisons: Most baselines freeze the image encoder. While methods like MaPLe introduce trainable tokens, it does not enforce compatibility with the frozen space. T-SNE shows MaPLe features exhibit weaker separability. Due to the text-only rebuttal format, we cannot include visualization here. R2-Parameter/efficiency comparison: Existing methods use 8.19K–26.11M parameters at 470–540 fps. NEARL uses 1.46M parameters at a comparable 500 fps, yet achieves the best overall performance. R3-Differences from recent general and medical adaptation methods: First, NEARL uses learnable vectors as compact cross-modal queries, rather than prompt-based adaptation methods as in CoCoOp, MaPLe, or HiCroPL, enabling layer-wise retrieval of complementary information from the opposite modality. Second, the orthogonality constraint in NEARL is imposed directly in feature space, rather than in weight or gradient space as in O-LoRA and BOFA, thereby effectively reducing feature redundancy and improving representation generalization. Third, unlike bidirectional methods like BiPVL-Seg that merely rely on self-/cross-attention interaction, NEARL performs lightweight CLIP adaptation with compact queries, lightweight adapters, and explicit feature-space decoupling. R3-Limited to classification: We focus on medical image classification because it is the standard evaluation setting adopted by prior medical CLIP-based methods, e.g., ViP and XCoOp, enabling a fair comparison. Since NEARL is task-agnostic, we will explore it on other tasks in future work. Thanks! R3-Ablation: Sensitivity analysis on key hyperparameters shows minor performance changes across settings, generally within 2%, indicating that NEARL is robust and not highly sensitive to hyperparameter choices.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The principal concerns the authors must address in rebuttal are: Motivation for using a frozen natural-image CLIP rather than existing medical foundation models (MedCLIP, BiomedCLIP, PubMedCLIP) as the backbone (R2). This is the most consequential critique and directly affects the claimed contribution. Novelty positioning relative to learnable-query (MaPLe, CoCoOp) and orthogonal-adapter prior work (R3); the combination is reasonable but the delta needs sharper articulation. Baseline recency — comparisons skew toward older methods (R1); authors should justify selection or add recent medical VLM adapters. Evaluation scope and task setting — only three datasets, and zero-shot vs. few-shot vs. fine-tuned protocol is ambiguous (R2). Clarification is essential for interpreting the gains. Quantitative parameter/efficiency comparison against baselines, not just absolute numbers (R2). Mechanistic evidence for orthogonality — feature-space or gradient-level analysis would substantiate the design claim (R1). | All of the 3 reviewers agreed to accept this paper after rebuttal. title: NeuroSymb-MRG: Differentiable Abductive Reasoning with Active Uncertainty Minimization for Radiology Report Generation
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.This paper tackles several common limitations of existing methods, including visual-linguistic biases, factual inconsistency, and the lack of explicit multi-hop reasoning, and proposes a unified framework centered on neuro-symbolic reasoning. The problem is meaningful and well motivated in the context of clinical report generation. 2.The most notable strength of the paper is its attempt to move beyond the conventional end-to-end paradigm for radiology report generation by introducing an explicit neuro-symbolic reasoning stage. Through the pipeline of “clinical concept prediction -> rule composition -> clause generation”,the paper incorporates a structured reasoning process into report generation. 3.Another task-specific highlight is the active uncertainty minimization mechanism based on rule-level uncertainty. This design combines uncertainty estimation with clinician-in-the-loop refinement, which is well aligned with the practical needs of medical generation tasks. 4.The paper also provides relatively comprehensive component-level ablation studies. In particular, the authors analyze the roles of core modules such as the differentiable logic layer, rule-guided decoder, active uncertainty minimization, retrieval, and verifier.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The core claims of the paper are improved factual consistency and clinically grounded generation. However, the main experiments still rely primarily on surface-level text overlap metrics such as BLEU, ROUGE-L, and METEOR, while lacking more direct evidence from factual consistency metrics, clinical correctness evaluation, or expert human assessment. As a result, the current experimental results are still insufficient to fully support the paper’s central claims, especially stronger claims such as reducing contradictions and improving clinical grounding. 2.The paper integrates many components into a single system, including the visual backbone, concept predictor, differentiable logic, rule-guided decoding, retrieval augmentation, LLM refinement, verifier, knowledge agent, and active uncertainty minimization. While this makes the framework comprehensive, the methodological storyline remains somewhat unfocused, and it is difficult to quickly identify what the paper’s single most important methodological contribution is. At its current stage, the work reads more like a carefully designed pipeline than a sharply focused method paper. The novelty boundary and contribution hierarchy would benefit from further clarification. 3.The specific mechanism of multi-agent orchestration is still not sufficiently clear. Although the paper introduces multiple specialized agents and presents a conflict resolution mechanism based on confidence aggregation, it does not adequately explain the input/output of each agent, their invocation order, or how they actually interact throughout the reasoning and report generation process. Based on the current methodological description, this part appears closer to coordination and packaging of multiple functional modules than to a strict agent-based learning framework. It is therefore difficult to judge whether multi-agent orchestration constitutes a core algorithmic contribution or mainly serves as a high-level system organization strategy. 4.The connection between active uncertainty minimization and promptbook refinement still requires further clarification. The abstract, contribution summary, and framework figure state that rule-level uncertainty can drive clinician-in-the-loop adjudication and promptbook refinement. However, the paper mainly elaborates on the definitions of uncertainty estimation and active sampling, while providing only limited explanation of the representation of the promptbook, how it is updated, and how it concretely operates in Module 2.Therefore, this part currently reads more like an appealing high-level design idea, while its operational details and actual contribution still need to be made more specific.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The main strengths include: the application of differential abductive reasoning in radiology report generation. a sophisticated framework to combine the above with uncertainty minimisation a comprehensive set of experiments which show consistent improvements from the proposed model
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The main weakness is the use of evaluation metrics. For radiology report evaluations, it is well known that Rouge/METEOR scores are limited as they do not deal with semantics and contexts (eg negations) well. It would be important to see the use of other more clinically relevant scores like RATE score, GREEN or similar.
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: Combining differentiable logic with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and active learning is a really fresh take on report generation. It directly addresses the “black box” nature of current LLM-based approaches, which is a huge barrier to clinical adoption. By forcing the model to route its decisions through explicit, soft logical rules before generating text, the system provides a clear audit trail for why a specific sentence was generated. The model achieves very competitive scores on both MIMIC-CXR and IU X-ray, outperforming several recent and strong baselines like MRG-LLM.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The paper relies entirely on standard NLP metrics (BLEU, ROUGE, METEOR). In the medical domain, these metrics are notoriously misleading. A generated report that says “There is a pneumothorax” and a ground truth that says “There is no pneumothorax” will have a very high BLEU score, but a catastrophic clinical error. You really need to include clinical efficacy metrics like CheXbert (F1-score for clinical observations) or RadGraph to prove the logic layer is actually improving factual correctness. 2.In the introduction and the ablations (Table 3), you mention a “learned feedback simulator to accelerate clinician-in-the-loop refinement.” However, looking through Section 3, I can’t find a clear explanation of how this simulator actually works. How is the clinician’s feedback simulated during the training loop? What data is it trained on? This needs a dedicated paragraph. 3.How are the diagnostic rules (the soft trees mentioned in Section 3.5) initialized? Do clinicians have to manually define the skeleton of these rules for every possible disease beforehand, or does the network learn the tree structures entirely from scratch? If it’s manual, I worry about how scalable this is to hundreds of rare findings. 4.Running 5 Monte Carlo dropout passes for active sampling during training sounds quite computationally heavy. It would be helpful to include a brief discussion on the training time/memory overhead compared to a standard end-to-end baseline.
reviewer_3_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: N/A
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): The core problem addressed is the lack of interpretability and factual reliability in automated medical report generation. Current “black-box” models often hallucinate or fail to follow logical clinical reasoning. The proposed NeuroSymb-MRG framework attempts to solve this by forcing the model to follow structured, logical steps before producing text. The reviewers agree that the shift from end-to-end learning to a neuro-symbolic approach (logic-based reasoning) is a significant and “fresh” contribution. It creates a clearer audit trail for clinical decisions. While the framework includes an “uncertainty” mechanism meant for clinician interaction, the actual utility is questioned because the evaluation relies on word-matching rather than clinical accuracy. The paper presents a strong, technically sound framework that is highly relevant to the MICCAI community. However, the disconnect between the “factual consistency” claims and the “text-matching” evaluation must be addressed.

title: NoiBox: Safeguard Frontier via Reverse Adversarial Diffusion for Noisy-Box-Supervised 3D Tumor Segmentation
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The method proposed in this paper avoids the cost of dense voxel-level annotation, making it possible to train models using large-scale single-box annotation data. 2.Utilizing the RAD module to handle uncertainty bands represents a novel perspective. The adversarial mechanism, where foreground evidence diffuses outwardly and background evidence diffuses inwardly, ingeniously replaces traditional pseudo-label self-training, effectively mitigating the lack of global consistency in patch-based training.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The experimental section only selected two datasets, making it difficult to verify the generalization of the method proposed in the paper. It is suggested to conduct experiments using additional datasets such as LIDC-IDRI and KiTS19, as in Reference 16.Meanwhile, the analysis of the experimental part is relatively simple and lacks reasonable explanations. 2.Figure 1 introduces the pipeline of the proposed method, but the process is difficult to understand. It is recommended to provide a detailed introduction in the method section. 3.The meanings of some formula variables and symbols in the article are not explained, such as formulas (3), (5), (7), and (8). Additionally, there is a lack of logical explanation and analysis for why formula (8) is expressed in the form of CspCse multiplication. 4.In Fig. 4, we can find that background evidence propagates inward, and can not find foreground evidence propagates outward. It is recommended to select instances where only part of the foreground is covered within the bounding box.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: great concise summary of prior work in box-supervised segmentation great figure 1 - explains the two portions clearly Compared against a good number of other methods in the box segmentation space figure 3 is a good visualization of the process
reviewer_2_weaknesses: I’m not sure that the evaluation on public datasets is necessarily a major contribution. The contribution is the methodology, and it’s great that you are using public data for evaluation but it is also expected that to support a contribution, one would evaluate it. Thorough comparisons were indeed made to other 3D box-supervised methods, but there are a lot of other 3D segmentation methods out there that are reporting / trying to achieve the same goal of tumor segmentation. Did you compare it at all to one of the point prompt based methods like Vista3D ? They are not box-supervised but have similar goals of getting fast low annotation segmentations. There is limited discussion in terms of impact / how it compares across the domain of tumor segmentation as a whole and no mention or discussion of limitations Smaller comments: In the introduction, the first time you use “safeguard frontier” it would be great to explain what you mean by that. It is a term used repeatedly throughout the work, so it would be good to be clear on what exactly you mean by that.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: Strong clinical motivation. Bounding box annotation is genuinely fast and scalable, and the paper’s focus on noisy boxes reflects real clinical practice. Conceptually elegant and well-motivated. The core idea of letting foreground and background evidence compete and meet at a natural boundary, rather than imposing hard constraints from a noisy box, is intuitive and well-grounded. It directly addresses the confirmation bias problem of pseudo-label self-training methods. Their soft frontier target is a principled way to avoid premature label commitment near uncertain regions. Works across different backbones. Demonstrating consistent performance gains across two different 3D backbones (SwinUNETR and UNETR) is a meaningful strength. It suggests the method is not tailored to a specific architecture and can be adopted broadly. Good ablations. The ablation in Table 2 clearly isolates the contribution of each component, and the qualitative visualization in Figure 3 effectively illustrates how the frontier evolves and tightens over training epochs.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Questionable generalizability of the affinity-based boundary mechanism. The affinity graph implicitly assumes tumor boundaries coincide with regions of high feature dissimilarity. This holds for the compact, circumscribed tumors in MSD-Lung and MSD-Pancreas, but is a meaningful limitation for infiltrative tumors (e.g., glioblastoma, peritoneal carcinomatosis) that spread gradually across tissue boundaries. The paper neither discusses this limitation nor evaluates on datasets with more infiltrative morphologies. Clarity of presentation. The ideas are communicated almost entirely through dense formalism. Key intuitions, particularly what the Dirichlet minimization computes and why it produces 0.5 at the frontier, are absent from the main text. A single intuitive paragraph per key equation would substantially improve readability without sacrificing rigor. Figure 1 is dense and hard to parse on first reading.
reviewer_3_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: 1.Generalization and experimental analysis. (R#1) We have conducted additional experiments on LIDC-IDRI. Across two methods, our method improves the average Dice by 2.39 over the second-best baseline and reduces HD95 by 0.17, showing generalization beyond original datasets. title: Non-linear INR-Based Motion Modeling for 4D Radiotherapy
reviewer_1_strengths: Although INRs have been used for respiratory motion modelling before, this has been for CBCT and MRI (I think), and as far as I am aware they have not been used to build motion models from 4DCT before. The INR framework proposed here seems very sensible and well suited to modelling breathing motion from 4DCT, where the motion is parameterised by a small number (in this case 2) of surrogate signal. The method achieves good results on the DIR-LABs datasets, with better results than the comparison methods, and good TRE values compared to other methods in the literature.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: In my opinion the major weakness of this paper is that it is not addressing the real problems with trying to model and compensate for breathing motion in RT. The authors are correct that simple linear models will not be able to capture non-linear surrogate-motion relationships (although I disagree that this means they cannot represent spatially varying hysteresis and tissue deformation, and the linear models do vary spatially, and so can represent both of these), and the results presented in the paper show that the proposed method is indeed more accurate than the simple linear model they evaluated. However, the reason that motion models built from 4DCT are not used clinically is not because the simple linear models are not accurate enough – it is that the 4DCT itself does not provide a good estimate of the motion that actually occurs during treatment. There are a number of reasons for this: 4DCT assumes reproducible motion so it cannot capture breath-to-breath variability in the motion, and such motion causes artefacts in the 4DCT; there can also be day-to-day variations in the motion, so even if the 4DCT captures the motion well on the day it is acquired, it may not represent the motion on another day; 4DCT and surrogate based motion models also rely on having surrogate signals that have a strong and consistent relationship with the motion, and can be acquired both during imaging and treatment, which in practice can be difficult to obtain. This is why many works on modelling breathing motion for RT in recent years have focussed on how to build models that can account for breath-to-breath variations (e. g. by using unsorted 4DCT as in ref 8), can account for day-to-day variations (e. g. by building models from CBCT projections, or MR data for the MR-Linac), or can account for imperfect surrogate signals (e. g. ref 8). Related to the previous comment, although the propose method achieves good results on the DIR-LABs datasets that it is evaluated on, this does not really give any indication of how accurate it would be in clinical practice. That is, evaluating the models on the same data they are fitted to just measures how well the model can be made to fit the data, it doesn’t evaluate how well it can predict unseen data, which is ultimately what it needs to do – although the results do show that it can fit the data better than the other models (which is a good start!).

reviewer_2_strengths: The paper is extremely well written and presented with exceptionally clear concept figures, tables and result visualisations. The method is novel and nicely integrates the benefits of continuous INR fitting to “hyper”linear surrogate regression, in addition some minor adjustment (anisotropic frequency scaling and The DIRlab validation results clearly demonstrate the high accuracy in terms of TRE making this a very practical new tool for clinical adoption in radiotherapy The authors clearly describe the implementation and promise to release source code for reproducibility

reviewer_2_rating: (6) Strong Accept — must be accepted due to excellence
reviewer_3_strengths: The main strength of this work is the parametrization of the INR with surrogate respiratory signals, which allows for a compact representation of the full respiratory cycle using a low-dimensional, time-varying signal. Further, using appropriate frequency scaling parameters, smooth time-varying deformation transitions within the respiratory cycle can be obtained. In addition, the text is very well written and clear overall, with nice illustrations accompanying the methodological descriptions and results.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The main weakness is the relatively limited comparison to other works in the state-of-the-art. The authors do compare the performance of their proposed framework against a classical method for 4D motion compensation based on surrogate signals (along some ablation variants), but no comparison is given against top performant methods on the DIR-Lab dataset, defeating the purpose of using such publicly available dataset. This is naturally not possible for the full respiratory cycle, but comparing TREs at the two extreme configurations against DIR-Lab public results could already provide information on the proposed framework’s registration accuracy. An additional problem is the fact that the surrogate signal is artificially generated from the image itself. Although understandable given that such data is lacking from the DIR-Lab dataset, there is no guarantee that this corresponds to a real, measurable surrogate signal. I would have expected some sort of robustness analysis by evaluating how noise in the surrogate signal can affect overall registration performance. An additional consideration: it is a bit surprising that the regularization term enforces a spatial jacobian of 1 (volume preserving deformation), since respiratory motion is mostly driven by large volume changes. I believe a physically inspired regularization term would be more appropriate [A]. [A] Z.
