title: OPGAgent: An Agent for Auditable Dental Panoramic X-ray Interpretation
reviewer_1_strengths: A: The proposed tool OPGAgent is inspired by agentic AI tools like MedAgent, DentalGPT, OralGPT etc. and tries to improve the agentic AI collaboration for OPG understanding specifically. The analysis is done in multiple scales: a global image level, quadrant level and individual tooth level. A collection of models (example: MaskDino, Dino, Medsam, Yolo) is used for analyzing different components of OPG image. Then the expert zoo of several large foundational models DentalGPT, OralGPT and GPT-5.2 act on the annotations provided by the analysis tools. The consensus is gauged by a few aligned predictions (two or three). B: The report format is made structured. C: Experiments show improved results on most of the anomaly types in multiple regions.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The type of analysis done by OPGAgent is very similar to existing tools. How it differs from other tools is not made very evident in the paper. The methodological novelty is quite limited. Access to all foundational models used in the OPGAgent tool is quite limited due to the paid nature of these foundational tools. This severely limits benchmarking of the OPGAgent tool against other similar types of tools. Details of which type of anomalies are looked for by the models are missing. For example: details of which detection tools are used for various pathological models are not clear from the paper. The set of tasks handled by utility tools is also not very clear. Some examples are given in section 3.2 but a complete list of tasks is not provided. What opinions are collected from expert zoos? How do these opinions look in terms of output form? How are they processed by the consensus subagents? These details are also missing. Disagreement handling is also not very clear. Is it deterministic and found by a set of rules? If so, what are these rules? Or is it based on parsing and understanding the conflicts? If natural language understanding of conflicts is done, how is it done? Is the triplet form of report done for all compared tools? If not, how are the precision, recall, FP values for all tools computed? What is the nature of memory? How are the different analyses stored in memory? What is the structure of the storage for each level: global, quadrant and tooth level? Though the premise of the tool is laudable, the tool appears very cryptic as described in the paper. Many details are not clear. I am also not sure if such tool building without much methodological advances is a good fit for the conference.
reviewer_1_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The paper is well written and flows nicely. Motivation and processes are clear. 2.The approach is on the cutting edge of current research and development landscape. 3.In places the author(s) go beyond “just and LLM output” like the deterministic reporting with the parser. 4.The variety of the tools ranging from other DL methods to more simple and mathematical utilities are well defined and utilized. 5.Clearly applicable to existing data, easily verifiable results (ignoring the reproducibilty concer) / auditable
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Evaluation: The ablation (table 3) and the main quantitative comparison (table 1) use the same dataset. However, in table 1 the authors report on 4 fronts [E.M. (Exact Match), Det. (Presence), Loc. (Location), Cls. (Grade/Type), FP (False Positives/Case)] while in table 3 they only report on the first front. At the very least the authors should explain why that is. There are no statistical analyses for any of the presented results such as confidence intervals or statistical testing for significance. The coefficients of the score table are not explained anywhere on why they are chosen. Implementation details: I am missing explanation and the implementation details of the tools in the toolbox. Many of the findings depend on these tools yet there is very little individual detailed explanation on these tools. Cost of using the proposed model: The authors do not mention anything about the cost of using the online models, how many tokens/queries are used. There is no information regarding any of the actual usage of online models. How long an analysis takes is similarly not mentioned. There is no discussion of any kind in the paper.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: Architectural Novelty: The shift from single-pass VLMs to a multi-tool agentic workflow successfully balances high-level reasoning with task-specific precision. Hallucination Mitigation: The use of a Consensus Subagent and anatomical constraints to verify findings provides a robust mechanism for clinical auditability. Rigorous Evaluation: The OPG-Bench protocol offers a more clinically relevant evaluation than traditional VQA by using structured (Location, Field, Value) triples.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Planner Dependency: The system relies heavily on the GPT-5.2 planner, which may limit deployment in privacy-sensitive or resource-constrained clinical environments that require local hosting. author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and the AC for their constructive feedback and for acknowledging OPGAgent’s multi-scale Agent design, the structured (Location, Field, Value) triplets, and its performance improvements across multiple regions and dental diseases. We would like to clarify the following points to address the reviewers major concerns. [R1, Meta] Novel Contributions Compared to Prior Work (1) Unlike VLMs that just rely on single-pass outputs, OPGAgent achieves more accurate and auditable results via specialized dental tools – outperforming SOTA VLMs(+6.9%) on OPG-Bench, and beyond the runner-up (+3.5%) on the external benchmark MMOral-OPG VQA. (2) OPGAgent is the first Agent framework dedicated to OPG diagnosis and analysis. To meet the clinical demands for auditable and interpretable results, we explicitly link findings to FDI tooth anchors and utilize tool-assisted consensus verification, producing reports that are suitable for clinical use. Furthermore, our results highlight the limitations of general medical Agent frameworks on OPG tasks: using the same planner, tools, prompts, and a shared Parser Agent, OPGAgent achieves a +21.9% performance improvement over MedAgent-Pro (Table 1). (3) The current VQA paradigm focuses only on individual questions and cannot assess overall performance. We provide a more comprehensive approach: OPG-Bench, a novel evaluation paradigm based on these triplets, providing more evaluation dimensions than VQA on completeness, localization, and classification. [R1, R2, R3, Meta] Detailed Tool Design and Reproducibility Planner: (R1) The Planner follows a Global -> Quadrant -> Tooth structure (detailed in §2.2) to generate the report. (R2) Each case processes roughly 8.5k input tokens and 5k output tokens, takes 1-3 minutes, and costs approximately $0.06.To further demonstrate reproducibility (R2) and address R3’s concern regarding planner dependency, we attempted to replace the planner with an open source model(Qwen3.6-27B), the results show only a 4.5 pts Score drop on OPG-Bench. Tools requiring weights or code: (R1, R2) YOLOv9 [23] trained on DENTEX [8] is used for quadrant/tooth detection. MedSAM [17] is used for tooth segmentation. We leverage the open-source MaskDINO/DINO models released by OralGPT-Omni [10] to detect features diseases (caries, periapical/apical findings, fillings, and impacted teeth). An IoU tool links diseases, teeth, and FDI numbers on the schema to establish consensus, additionally, the mandibular canal and maxillary sinus are paired with the Tooth Mask to identify extraction risks. Consensus Subagent: (R1) When a conflict arises, the subagent first checks for validity against anatomical constraints. The ROI is then routed to the respective Experts for verification. If the conflict persists, Majority Voting is used to make the final determination(detailed in §2.4). Code and model weights will be released upon acceptance as we promised in the submission. [R2, Meta] Statistical Analysis Table 3 uses the same Exact-Match metric as Table 1, we previously thought this was sufficient, so we omitted the Det./Loc./Cls. columns due to space limitations. Per R2’s suggestion, we will include these additional metrics in Table 3 of the final version. The Score assigns weights 50% to Exact-Match because it strictly aligns with every label in the ground truth, while detection, localization, and classification are weighted 20%, 20%, 10% to further reflect lesion detection, anatomical grounding and disease classification capabilities. Paired bootstrap (B=1000, n=1006): all 9 methods σ ≤ 0.0084 (OPGAgent 0.0080). OPGAgent’s 95% CI [48.21, 51.36] is non-overlapping with the strongest baseline Gemini-3-Pro [41.47, 44.56], 8/8 pairs p < 0.001 (Holm-corrected). [Final Version] In the final version, we will include the Qwen3.6-27B on OPG-Bench, add Det./Loc./Cls. to Table 3 per R2’s suggestion, statistical analysis align MeSH keywords, enable LaTeX links, and fix the §2.1 typo.

title: OPS: One-Shot Point Prompted Semantics-Aware Learning for Medical Image Registration
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The proposed approach introduces semantic awareness by leveraging extremely sparse annotations (one point per organ) on a single reference slice. This is particularly interesting because it significantly reduces annotation cost while still enabling the model to capture anatomically meaningful correspondences, effectively bridging the gap between unsupervised and weakly-supervised registration. 2.Use of a pre-trained foundation model (DINOv3) to propagate sparse point prompts into dense semantic similarity maps across the dataset. This effectively leverages the semantic clustering capability of foundation models for registration, avoiding the need for dense supervision.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The proposed method relies on extremely sparse point prompts (one point per organ) to construct semantic priors. Could the authors clarify the strategy for selecting these points (e. g. , anatomical center, boundary, or random selection)? In addition, how sensitive is the method to the spatial location and number of selected points? While a basic robustness analysis is provided, a more systematic evaluation (e. g. , varying point locations or using multiple points per structure) would help better understand the stability and generalizability of the proposed approach. 2.The method assumes that semantic anchors extracted from a single reference slice can generalize across the entire dataset. Could the authors provide further analysis or visualization to demonstrate how well these anchors transfer across subjects with anatomical variability? 3.Additional visualization of the generated semantic similarity maps would help to better assess their quality and interpretability, particularly in challenging cases.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The paper addresses a clearly motivated problem, namely the semantic blindness of conventional unsupervised registration methods that rely only on global image similarity. 2.The proposed one-shot prompting setup is practically appealing, as it attempts to introduce semantic priors with very limited manual annotation cost. 3.The overall framework is coherent and well organized. The generation of semantic similarity maps and their integration through semantic feature embedding and semantics-aware loss optimization form a consistent pipeline. 4.The empirical results are reasonably strong. The method improves both DSC and HD95 over the compared backbones, and the ablation study supports the contribution of each component.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The workflow is practically appealing, but the technical novelty is somewhat less convincing than the framing suggests. In particular, the method does not introduce a fundamentally new registration formulation; rather, it builds a dataset-wide semantic prior from sparse prompts using frozen DINOv3 features, and then incorporates this prior through relatively standard feature embedding and loss re-weighting steps. As a result, the main novelty seems to lie more in the prompt-to-prior workflow than in a clearly new registration mechanism.1 2.This concern is also reflected in the ablation study. On the abdominal dataset, adding SFE alone improves DSC only from 58.52 to 59.39, whereas SLO alone raises it to 65.42, which is already close to the full model at 66.54.A similar pattern is observed on the hippocampus dataset. This suggests that much of the gain may come from semantic loss weighting itself, while the additional benefit of the prompt-derived feature embedding is comparatively modest.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The paper introduces a highly efficient data usage strategy, generating dense semantic priors for an entire dataset from just one point per organ on a single reference slice. This drastically reduces annotation costs compared to traditional weakly-supervised methods requiring full 3D masks, enabling semantic-aware registration on vast unlabeled clinical datasets.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The core reliance on DINOv3 feature similarity assumes consistent feature distributions across images. This breaks down in multi-modal registration (e.g., CT-to-MRI), where intensity and texture differences cause the same organ to have vastly different feature embeddings. The method lacks a mechanism for modality-invariant alignment, severely limiting its clinical scope. In mono-modal settings, the advantage over existing pseudo-labeling strategies (e.g., using pre-trained segmentation models like nnU-Net to generate coarse masks without any user input) is unclear. The complexity of integrating a massive foundation model may not justify the marginal gain over simply running an off-the-shelf segmenter to get richer spatial priors.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for their constructive feedback and for recognizing that our method enables more targeted and interpretable semantic guidance with minimal annotation cost. [R2] Clarification on Technical Novelty: We thank the reviewer for acknowledging the practicality of our workflow. While we do not introduce a new registration architecture, our novelty lies in establishing a point prompted semantics-aware learning that advances unsupervised registration learning at minimal annotation cost. This is done by using extremely sparse point prompts to derive feature similarity maps, and then integrate these maps into the registration learning process via a dual mechanism comprising SFE and SLO. Leveraging the strong generalization capability of DINOv3, our method improves performance on unsupervised registration, which is a clear advantage, and the experimental results substantiate its efficacy. Moreover, our method is plug-and-play and offers users explicit controllability over the registration learning process: by simply altering the point prompts, clinicians can dynamically modulate the network’s attention toward specific anatomical targets during training, thereby enabling customized registration. [R2] Ablation Study on SFE and SLO: The ablation results in Table 2 are consistent with our design, and the two components are complementary to each other. SLO directly reshapes the supervision signal, explicitly forcing the optimizer at the training stage to focus on aligning semantically relevant regions, thereby contributing more substantially to performance gains. SFE injects semantic awareness into feature representations at both training and inference stages. This explains why SFE continues to enhance registration performance even beyond SLO. [R3] Advantage Over Fully Supervised Pseudo-labeling: We would like to clarify the difference between OPS and pseudo-labeling schemes. OPS targets unsupervised registration learning, where the segmentation annotations required by model nnU-Net is hard to obtain and OPS needs only a one-shot interaction. Second, segmentation models are strictly constrained by the organ categories and image domains seen during training, often failing on unseen domains or structures. In contrast, OPS builds on DINOv3’s general-purpose visual representations, requires no organ-specific or modality-specific pre-training. [R1] Prompt Selection Strategy: For each target organ, we randomly pick a single point prompt within the organ, without requiring precise localization. Table 3 quantitatively demonstrates robust performance under varying random point locations. While multi-point prompting is a good idea, it would enable additional annotation cost, which may be not optimal in a clinical environment. [R3] Adaptation to Multi-modal Registration: In fact, OPS naturally accommodates cross-modal scenarios. For example, in CT-MRI registration, only one point prompt targeting the same anatomical structure needs to be provided on each of the CT and MRI reference slices. The CT anchor is then propagated exclusively within CT dataset, while the MRI anchor is propagated exclusively within MRI dataset, thereby generating semantic similarity maps for the same anatomical structure in CT and MRI data to ensure compatibility with OPS. [R1] Cross-subject Robustness and Additional Visualization: The cross-subject generalization is quantitatively validated by our existing experiments. Substantial anatomical variability (organ size, shape, position) exists among the 54 abdominal and 260 hippocampus subjects in the datasets. Supported by DINOv3’s strong cross-image semantic consistency, anchors propagate stably across subjects via feature similarity, producing reliable similarity maps under large anatomical variation. In the upper-right corner of Fig. 2, we provide examples of similarity maps, where it can be observed that similarity maps from different samples capture consistent organ-level semantic information.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper received mixed recommendations from the reviewers, including one Weak Reject and two Weak Accepts. The paper addresses deformable registration using point prompts and a pre-trained vision foundation model, and demonstrates promising results on two datasets. At the same time, the reviewers identified several substantive concerns, including an unclear point selection strategy (R1), unconvincing support for the claimed semantic anchors and the reliance on DINOv3 feature similarity (R1, R3), limited qualitative results (R1), the incremental nature of the methodological contribution (R2), marginal gains from the prompt-derived feature embeddings (R2), and an unclear advantage over a nnU-Net-plus-registration pipeline (R3). Overall, the paper shows merit in its methodology and in its use of vision foundation models for image registration, and the meta-reviewer therefore recommends that it proceed to rebuttal. The authors are encouraged to focus their response on the major concerns outlined above. | The paper proposes a method that combines DINOv3-based semantic clustering with a single-slice, single-point prompting scheme to construct a dataset-wide dense semantic similarity map, which is subsequently integrated into an unsupervised registration framework through SFE and SLO. Following the rebuttal, all reviewers expressed overall positive assessments. In particular, Reviewer 2 explicitly recognized that the practicality of the annotation-efficient workflow itself represents a meaningful contribution and accordingly revised the recommendation to Accept; Reviewer 3 also upgraded the rating to Accept. While the lack of a comparison with nnU-Net remains a minor weakness, it does not substantially undermine the core technical contribution or the empirical validity of the paper. Based on the post-rebuttal discussion and the overall reviewer consensus, I recommend Accept. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper proposes to use sparse point prompts to create feature similarity maps using Dinov3 and to incorporate those maps in an unsupervised registration algorithm. After rebuttal, all reviewers agree that the method is technically sound and that the main concerns have been addressed in the rebuttal. There are some remaining concerns about the experimental design and analysis, but the strengths of the paper outweigh its weakness. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Following the rebuttal phase, two of the three reviewers issued a final decision of “Accept,” while the third reviewer did not respond. However, this reviewer’s initial score was “Weak Accept.” Consequently, the overall assessment of the paper is positive (Accept), and it is therefore recommended for acceptance.

title: Optimal Steps for Fast Diffeomorphic Shape Registration
reviewer_1_strengths: The paper addresses a highly practical problem: fast, robust, topology-preserving shape registration without requiring large training datasets. This is very relevant to clinical shape modeling workflows, especially for anatomical surfaces where volumetric deep-learning registration may be memory-intensive or require substantial training data. The method is technically motivated. It combines ideas from non-rigid ICP, coherent point drift, and LDDMM . The regularization step is described clearly, including the kernel normalization, local loss matrices, conjugate-gradient formulation, and preconditioning. The empirical results are strong. On the VerSe vertebra experiments, the method achieves better Chamfer distance and HD95 than both VoxelMorph and Deformetrica while being around 40× faster than Deformetrica.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The baseline comparison is limited. VoxelMorph is a volumetric learning-based method and may not be the strongest competitor for surface/point-cloud registration. Deformetrica is a relevant diffeomorphic baseline, but the paper would be stronger with comparisons against CPD, robust optimal transport point-cloud registration, functional maps, non-rigid ICP variants, and recent neural or geometric surface-registration methods. The paper claims strict topological consistency, but the evidence is not fully sufficient. LDDMM-style shooting can define diffeomorphic flows in continuous settings, but the implementation is on sampled point clouds/meshes, and the paper does not provide a formal proof or a direct measurement of self-intersections, triangle inversions, or Jacobian positivity. The reported log-Jacobian variance is useful but does not by itself establish topology preservation. There is a slight inconsistency in the presentation: the abstract says the method works “without landmarks, pre-alignment, or supervision,” yet the method section includes a RANSAC-ICP affine pre-alignment and anisotropic bounding-box scaling. This is not necessarily a problem, but the claim should be revised. The experiments are largely focused on vertebrae. Vertebrae are challenging and clinically relevant, but additional anatomical structures with different topology and partial-overlap conditions would strengthen the generality claim. The authors acknowledge partial overlap as future work, which is important because many clinical surfaces are truncated or contain segmentation defects. The computational complexity remains quadratic due to kernel matrix-vector products. The paper reports good runtimes for 10k and 40k points, but it is unclear how the method scales to hundreds of thousands of points or to dense multi-organ atlases.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: Excellent speed up compared to the state of the art and slightly better accuracy Elegant algorithm, robust No neural networks, a big plus for robustness and efficiency.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: None
reviewer_2_rating: (6) Strong Accept — must be accepted due to excellence
reviewer_3_strengths: The most notable strength of the paper is its demonstrated combination of high registration accuracy and computational speed, which is particularly valuable in clinical settings where data is scarce, annotation is expensive, and precision is critical. Unlike deep learning methods that require large training datasets, rarely available in medical imaging, this learning-free approach sidesteps that requirement entirely while still matching the speed advantages typically associated with learned methods. Beyond raw performance, the paper makes a compelling case that thoughtfully assembling well-established techniques from the shape optimisation literature, such as normalized kernel matrix from diffusion operators and the LDDMM-like diffeomorphic shooting, an close the speed gap with learned methods without sacrificing rigour or interpretability. The paper is also well-written and the method is easy to follow, which makes it straightforward to understand and build upon.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The most significant weakness of the paper is its reliance on spatial pre-alignment, which surfaces in two places: the affine initialisation that depends on extrinsic FPFH features, and the exclusive use of 3D coordinates in the two finest scales of the multiscale scheme. This raises concerns about the method’s sensitivity to the initial alignment and scale of the input shapes, even when anisotropic normalisation is applied. An ablation study removing the pre-alignment step would have strengthened the paper considerably, as it would clarify how much of the registration performance is attributable to the core method versus the initialisation. Related to this, the reliance on 3D coordinates as features implicitly assumes that the source and target shapes share similar topology — an assumption that does not always hold in clinical practice. A straightforward counterexample is a vascular tree where one branch is absent in the source but present in the target. The authors do acknowledge partial overlaps as a limitation, but given how frequently topological mismatches arise in anatomical shape analysis, this deserves more explicit treatment. Finally, a more minor but noteworthy issue concerns the atlas estimation experiment: since the constructed atlas inherits the topology of the chosen template, the result is inherently biased by that choice. This is not discussed in the paper and would be worth at least acknowledging in the limitations section.
reviewer_3_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We want to thank the reviewers and AC for their reviews. We address the main points below, the camera-ready will reflect these clarifications. Topology preservation (R1). Our shooting Eq. (8) is the LDDMM Hamiltonian flow of Beg-Miller-Trouvé-Younes [4]. With our exponential kernel k(x,y) = exp(-||x−y||/r), the function k(·, q_i) is globally Lipschitz on R^3 with constant 1/r, so the velocity field v_t(x) = Σ_i k(x, q_i(t)) p_i(t) is Lipschitz uniformly in t ∈ [0,1]. By Cauchy-Lipschitz, the flow ODE has unique solutions and φ_t : R^3 → R^3 is a topology-preserving homeomorphism. The kernel normalization Eq. (4) plays an essential role: the spectrum of the normalized kernel matrix is bounded in [0,1] (Kessler-Magnet-Feydy [18, Thm 4.4]), so the kinetic energy is controlled, ||v||² = p^⊤K p ≤ ||p||². At the discrete level, our adaptive Euler step constrains dt so that ||q_i(t+dt) − q_i(t)|| ≤ ℓ, where ℓ is the local sampling length: each step is too small to invert a triangle. Pre-alignment (R1). The RANSAC-ICP + anisotropic bounding-box scaling is fully automatic and requires no landmarks, supervision, or template-specific tuning, which is what the abstract claims. It is standard procedure in image registration and LDDMM literature where the data can come from different scanners and be aligned differently. This step is applied identically to every baseline. Deformetrica gives very poor results without it. We will modify the abstract wording regarding this aspect. Baselines (R1, Meta). VoxelMorph is the canonical learning-based reference for medical image registration and Deformetrica is the canonical LDDMM reference. A primary objective of our paper is to demonstrate the massive computational speedup our method offers over classical LDDMM approaches. As shown in our experiments, our approach achieves approximately a 40x speedup over Deformetrica. Furthermore, it accomplishes this while delivering strictly better surface alignment metrics (Chamfer and Hausdorff distances) and preserving better topological integrity, as evidenced by a lower log-Jacobian variance. Comparisons with CPD, robust OT, and non-rigid ICP variants are highly relevant and are intended for extensions of this work. Anatomical scope (R1, R3). The paper already evaluates two topologically distinct and complex families: 757 vertebrae and 54 lung vascular trees. We are currently partnering with clinicians on ongoing experiments on different datasets to extend the applications of our work. FPFH and 3D-coordinate matching (R3). The coarse scales (r_1, r_2) use 3D coordinates and FPFH features for robust long-range matching, and the fine scales (r_3, r_4) turn off FPFH and keep 3D coordinates only because by that stage the source already lies within the local convergence basin of the target. This is a multiscale schedule, not a structural assumption of similar topology. Partial overlap (R1, R3). We identified this limitation in the relevant section of the article and are currently working on it. Atlas template bias (R3). We will add this to the limitations. Quadratic complexity (R1). The O(N^2) bottleneck is the kernel mat-vec inside CG and the Hamiltonian shooting. FGT-like schemes and the Giga-scale Kernel Matrix-Vector Multiplication on GPU of Hu et al. are potential lines of inquiry but lack well maintained GPU implementations to date. Novelty (Meta). A ~40x speedup over Deformetrica at strictly better CD/HD95 is the main claim of our paper. The enabling ingredients are, to our knowledge, new in point-based LDDMM: (i) a Gauss-Newton formulation on a normalized kernel, instead of the quasi-Newton iteration of Deformetrica [5], (ii) the analytic 3x3 Block-Jacobi preconditioner Eq. (7), with closed-form eigenvectors, (iii) CG early termination at tolerance r/10.Combined, these reduce the inner CG loop from 20-30 iterations to 1-5.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): The three reviewers accepted the paper with ratings ranging from Strong Accept to Weak Accept. The confidence from two of the accept reviewers is “Confident but not absolutely certain (3) “ while the Weak Accept reviewer is “Very Confident (4)”. While the reviewers are overall very positive, I have some reservations regarding the level of methodological novelty. The proposed approach appears to combine previously published components rather than introducing fundamentally new techniques. In addition, the empirical comparison, particularly against VoxelMorph, may not be entirely appropriate due to the need to convert point sets into segmentations, which may result into the shown low accuracy. That said, reviewers highlight the solid experimental validation and competitive performance with respect to state-of-the-art methods such as Deformetrica, and find the contribution valuable for the community. I lean towards acceptance, considering the overall positive evaluations and the soundness of the approach, although I agree more with Rv1 comments and Rv3 concerns. I would suggest the authors to improve the camera ready reflecting in the manuscript responses to the main comments provided in this review.

title: OrthoFlow: Decoupled Landmark Prediction and Image Synthesis for Orthodontic Treatment Outcome Visualization
reviewer_1_strengths: This paper addresses a clinically important problem of predicting post treatment facial profiles, which has strong practical relevance for treatment planning and patient communication in orthodontics. A key strength lies in reformulating landmark prediction from a conventional regression task into a flow-matching-based generative process, enabling progressive refinement while preserving structural consistency. The proposed two stage framework that decouples geometry and appearance is well designed, as it improves interpretability and stability by clearly separating structural prediction from image synthesis. Furthermore, the integration of graph-based modeling and Transformer architecture allows the model to effectively capture both local and global relationships among landmarks, which is crucial for maintaining anatomical consistency. The use of text treatment plans as conditional input enhances the method with real clinical workflows. Finally, the paper provides both quantitative evaluations and clinical validation by orthodontists, which strengthens the credibility and practical significance of the proposed approach.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: While the paper is generally well structured, several limitations remain. 1.the overall framework follows a commonly used two stage pipeline combined with flow matching, resulting in somewhat limited methodological novelty. In particular, the approach of first predicting structural representations and then synthesizing images has been widely explored in prior generative modeling works, making the contribution closer to an integration and application of existing techniques rather than a fundamentally new method. 2.Although comparisons with diffusion based methods are included, the evaluation against more recent conditional diffusion models appears limited, making it difficult to establish the relative advantages of the proposed approach. Furthermore, while the proposed method shows improvements over existing approaches in Table 1, the performance gains compared to strong baselines such as DiT appear relatively modest. 3.Since the second stage heavily depends on the predicted landmarks from the first stage, the paper does not sufficiently analyze how errors in landmark prediction affect the final image quality. Considering that orthodontic outcomes can be inherently multi-modal, the lack of evaluation on output diversity is another limitation. 4.The evaluation of image synthesis quality primarily relies on FID and clinical assessment, while reconstruction based metrics such as PSNR or SSIM are not reported. Including such metrics would provide a more comprehensive and objective assessment of the fidelity of generated images from noisy inputs. 5.Although Fig. 1 illustrates the use of both KNN and static graphs, the paper lacks sufficient implementation details, such as the number of neighbors k, the coordinate space used for graph construction, how the static graph is defined, and whether the graph is fixed or dynamically updated. These design choices can significantly affect model performance, and clearer descriptions would be necessary to ensure reproducibility.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The paper proposes a novel framework for predicting post-treatment facial profiles from lateral cephalograms. The two-stage design is well motivated by the decomposition of the orthodontic prediction task into two sub-problems: estimating the movement of anatomical structures and synthesizing the resulting appearance. This insight leads to a rational and effective framework that addresses key limitations of existing approaches. 2.The incorporation of treatment plans as textual conditions is a meaningful contribution. The paper leverages a large language model (LLM) to generate treatment plans from electronic medical records (EMRs) and uses them as conditioning inputs. This design enhances the clinical plausibility of the predictions, as post-treatment outcomes should naturally depend on the specific treatment plan. 3.The proposed dual-path residual graph neural network (GNN) architecture is also novel. The static graph encodes anatomical priors, while the dynamic graph captures cross-tissue correlations, enabling more comprehensive modeling of structural relationships.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.In Stage II, the contour map plays a crucial role in image generation. However, the paper does not clearly explain how the predicted landmarks from Stage I are rendered into an anatomical contour map, which is a key component of the overall pipeline. 2.As noted in the paper, device-specific domain shift is a fundamental challenge. Although the contour map is used as structural guidance, this issue does not appear to be adequately addressed, since the training objective in Stage II mainly focuses on pixel-level differences. Furthermore, the paper use the pre-treatment cephalogram as one of the condition in stage 2.I think it’s unreasonable if there exists a domain shift between pre- and post-treatment images
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.Well-motivated decoupling. The two-stage decomposition of orthodontic outcome prediction into geometric landmark prediction and structure-guided image synthesis is intuitive and helps avoid the pixel-level pitfalls of end-to-end image translation on noisy multi-center data.2.Plan-specific prediction via text conditioning. Using BERT-encoded treatment plans with classifier-free guidance to generate extraction vs. non-extraction predictions for the same patient (Fig. 2) is a clinically meaningful capability that goes beyond deterministic baselines.3.Dual-path graph design. Combining a static anatomical graph with a dynamic KNN graph is a reasonable way to inject structural priors into landmark prediction, and the ablation (w/o Graph) shows a measurable effect on soft-tissue accuracy.4.Scale of the dataset and clinical evaluation. The authors assemble a large orthodontic dataset (44,809 cephalograms / 17,622 patients) and conduct a double-blinded evaluation with three orthodontists (ICC 0.82 / 0.79), which is more rigorous than typical image-synthesis evaluations that rely on FID alone.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.Page 5 contains an unresolved BibTeX reference “Qwen [?]”, indicating the manuscript was not properly compiled before submission 2.The paper claims OrthoFlow “achieves the best overall performance” on landmark prediction, but Table 1 shows that the vanilla Flow Matching baseline achieves better S-low (1.69 mm vs. 1.74 mm) than the proposed method. 3.Table 2 reports quantitative comparisons against Pix2PixHD, UGATIT, and cDDPM, but Figure 3 shows qualitative comparisons against Pix2PixHD, CycleGAN, and cDDPM. UGATIT and CycleGAN are not the same method, and this inconsistency makes the visual evaluation unverifiable.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for acknowledging the clinical importance of this work, the decoupling rationale, the value of plan conditioned prediction, and the rigor of our clinical study. Q1.Typos and naming consistency (R4) The Qwen citation and remaining BibTeX errors will be corrected. UGATIT is implemented on the CycleGAN backbone and we cited the two together. The label “CycleGAN” in Fig. 3 in fact refers to the UGATIT model reported in Table 2.We will unify the naming as UGATIT in the text, Table 2 and Fig. 3 so the quantitative and qualitative comparisons align. Q2.Methodological novelty (R1) As R2 notes, OrthoFlow is, to our knowledge, the first learning-based framework for orthodontic outcome visualization on lateral cephalograms. Beyond the two stage decomposition, our contributions include (a) formulating post-treatment landmark prediction as a Flow Matching generative process conditioned on textual treatment plans(Fig. 2), enabling plan-specific outcomes.(b) a new Graph-Transformer hybrid backbone, and (c) contour guided Flow Matching for structure preserving synthesis.We are the first to jointly explore these components for this task. Q3.Performance against strong baselines (Meta-reviewer, R1, R4) Our gains over DiT and vanilla Flow Matching are not modest. On hard tissue (incisor angle), which is clinically decisive for orthodontic planning, OrthoFlow improves accuracy by 9% to 13% (UT 3.90 vs 4.39 and 4.51, LT 3.74 vs 4.12 and 4.16). On the upper soft tissue, the gain is 3.6% to 8.3%. The only metric on which vanilla Flow Matching edges us is S_low (1.74 vs 1.69 mm, under 3%)(R4), well within the inter-rater variability of cephalometric annotation. Aggregated over all metrics OrthoFlow attains the best overall score and balance. Q4.Output diversity (R1) Diversity in our setting is driven by the clinical plan rather than random sampling, which mirrors clinical practice. Fig. 2 already demonstrates plan-controlled diversity for the same patient, producing clinically meaningful changes in the lateral profile. Q5.Domain shift and PSNR or SSIM (R1, R2) Pre- and post-treatment images are acquired on different devices more than 1 year apart, so a device-level domain shift indeed exists(R2). This is exactly why Stage II conditions on the pre-treatment image style and uses the predicted contour as structural guidance, so the synthesized image inherits the input device appearance while expressing the predicted anatomy. For the same reason, PSNR or SSIM against the post-treatment ground truth would conflate prediction error with device-induced appearance shift and would not reflect anatomical fidelity. FID with paired clinical scoring (ICC 0.82 and 0.79, R4) is the more faithful evaluation. Q6.Implementation details (Meta-reviewer, R1, R2) For the Graph Network, k equals 16, the KNN graph is built in the learned high dimensional feature space and updated per layer, while the static graph encodes fixed anatomical adjacency (Sec. 2.1). For the contour map (Sec. 2.2), predicted landmarks are connected via centripetal Catmull Rom splines for skeletal and soft tissue boundaries and rendered with fixed per tooth templates for the dentition. We will expand both descriptions and release the code. Q7.Effect of landmark error on image quality (Meta-reviewer, R1) Cephalometric landmark detection is a well-studied problem and reaches clinically reliable accuracy with existing methods. In our pipeline the mean detection error is 0.91 mm, while orthodontic interventions typically induce displacements above 5 mm. The detection error is therefore an order of magnitude smaller than the treatment signal and well below the line width used in contour rendering, so its influence on synthesis is marginal, which is consistent with the orthodontist scores.

title: OsteoFlow: Lyapunov-Guided Flow Distillation for Predicting Bone Remodeling after Mandibular Reconstruction
reviewer_1_strengths: The problem of long-term remodeling prediction is high-impact and underexplored. The way authors approached it combining normalizing flows and Lyapunov function to stablize the flow seems novel and effective while avoiding training difficulties in GAN and reducing high sampling cost in diffusion models extensive experiments validate the effectiveness of the proposed method with respect to multiple flow-based, diffusion-based and GAN-based pipelines. Ablations also adequately illustrate the contribution of each proposed component
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The synthesized ROIs seem small (or perhaps low-resolution), higher-resolution synthesis may be of more clinical importance The authors do not provide visual comparisons with baseline methods The two-stage teacher and student pipeline, while understandable, seems a little bit overly complicated compared to baselines, which are all single stage models. It is also possible that the performances of other comparisons can be boosted with another stage.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: Clinically meaningful task, with strong motivatioms - predicting graft-host bone remodeling after mandibular reconstruction addresses a real unmet need (nonunion rates up to 37%). Thorough ablation Table 2 with T1-vs-T2 cleanly isolating the Lyapunov formulation, and a backbone ablation (Table 3) controlling for architecture.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Table 1 claims Wilcoxon $p < 0.05$ across runs but with $n = 3$ runs the minimum two-sided signed-rank $p$ is 0.25 suggesting that the test must be per-ROI, but patient-level clustering (344 ROIs from 120 patients) is unaddressed. Headline ~20% bone MAE gain is mid-slab only (12 slices coinciding with the W training loss region). Full-volume bone MAE improves significantly less, abstract should name both figures as the current reporting is self-favoring. $\alpha$ is tested only at the binary level, a finer sweep is needed to show $\alpha = 1$ is optimal, not just that any positive $\alpha$ helps. No clinical outcome evaluation despite motivating the work with nonunion prediction. All metrics are image similarity. A model accurate on the dominant union class but failing on nonunion cases would still win these averages. Perhaps per-outcome-class / severity bone MAE.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.This paper builds on flow-based modeling and is specifically designed for longitudinal remodeling prediction using teacher guidance. 2.The experimental design is well-structured and demonstrates strong performance.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The paper lacks a figure illustrating the overall workflow of the proposed method, which would help improve clarity. 2.The results and discussion should provide more insight into the clinical impact and relevance of the proposed approach.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for their constructive feedback. We are encouraged by the early acceptance and recognition of novelty/effectiveness (R2,R4,R5), clinical relevance (R2,R4), and strong validation/ablations (R2,R4,R5). Below, we clarify the main points raised. Resolution/ROI (R2): We thank R2 for this observation. The data are retrospective clinical CT scans acquired during routine care, not under a controlled research protocol; resolution varied, so ROIs were resampled to 0.5 mm isotropic spacing. The ROI was localized around the resection/graft-host interface, where callus bridging, remodeling, and union/nonunion changes are expected. This reflects the limited-data setting and tests whether remodeling can be estimated from the local region alone. We clarified that HU windowing may make ROIs appear brighter while suppressing metal outliers. Baseline Visuals (R2): We agree that qualitative baseline comparisons would be useful. Due to space limits, Fig. 2 focused on OsteoFlow predictions across union, partial-union, and nonunion patterns, while Table 1 reported quantitative baseline comparisons. Since the appendix is limited to videos, we will include baseline examples in the GitHub repository near the resection/graft-host interface. Complexity (R2): We acknowledge the added training-time structure. This was motivated by limited data, where the SVF teacher provides a stable anatomical prior. The teacher is trained once, frozen during student training, and discarded at inference, so prediction uses only the student. We clarified that this targets low-data learning rather than inference complexity. Statistics (R4): We thank R4 for raising this point. We clarified in the caption of Table 1 that significance was assessed using paired ROI-level test metrics. We also noted potential within-patient dependence from multiple ROIs per patient and identified patient-level or clustered analysis as a future refinement. Reporting (R4): We thank R4 for this comment. The mid-slab result was emphasized because it corresponds to the resection/graft-host interface, where clinically meaningful remodeling and union/nonunion changes are expected. These localized changes can be diluted over the full ROI. To avoid ambiguity, we kept both evaluations and clarified the abstract/results to report both ∼19.8% mid-slab and ∼7.5% full-volume bone MAE reduction relative to cDDPM(∆). α Sensitivity (R4): We agree this is a useful direction. We had already acknowledged this in the submission, noting that α=1 was selected empirically and detailed α sensitivity is reserved for future work due to space limits. Our aim was not to claim theoretical optimality of α=1, but to show the benefit of Lyapunov-guided correction. The ablations bracket this effect: RF-only removes Lyapunov/teacher guidance, while the privileged teacher provides the opposite hard-guidance reference. Clinical Impact (R4,R5): We thank R4 and R5 for emphasizing clinical interpretation. Our goal is image-based remodeling prediction, which is more nuanced than binary union/nonunion classification. Although the dataset is union-dominant, Fig. 2 includes union, partial-union, and nonunion cases showing relevant patterns. We used image and bone-focused metrics to evaluate continuous change at the graft-host interface, but agree clinical outcome analysis is important. We clarified that the model is not intended for direct clinical decision-making and identified per-outcome/severity evaluation as future work. Workflow (R5): We thank R5 for the suggestion. Fig. 1 provided a conceptual overview of preprocessing, ROI extraction, SVF teacher guidance, and Lyapunov-guided distillation. Since our novelty is mainly in the training/distillation method rather than a new architecture, Algorithm 1 presented the workflow step by step. We clarified Fig.1/caption to make the end-to-end process explicit, including Day-5 CT input, teacher-guided training, Year-1 prediction, and teacher removal at inference.

title: OTCHA: Optimal Transport-Driven Confidence-Aware Latent Hub Alignment for Multi-view Medical Image Classification
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.Addresses a realistic and important problem in multi-view medical imaging, particularly handling unregistered views and view-specific noise. 2.Proposes a structured refinement-before-fusion framework with a coherent use of optimal transport for token-level alignment. 3.Introduces token-level partial matching and confidence estimation to filter irrelevant information. 4.Demonstrates consistent performance improvements across multiple datasets.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The novelty is limited, as the method mainly integrates existing elements such as optimal transport, latent hub representations, and confidence-aware weighting into a unified framework, rather than introducing a fundamentally new modeling perspective. 2.The effectiveness of token filtering is not directly validated. Although the paper claims that token-conditional dustbins allow irrelevant tokens to be discarded, it does not provide explicit analysis showing that the filtered tokens indeed correspond to background or artifacts. 3.The interpretability claim is only weakly supported. Fig. 2 provides an illustrative hub assignment map, but there is no quantitative or controlled evidence showing that the learned correspondences consistently reflect true anatomical or pathological matching across views. 4.The current evaluation is restricted to fixed-view settings. The paper itself notes this limitation in the conclusion, so the robustness of the method under missing-view or variable-view scenarios remains unclear.

This motivation is clear and clinically sensible. The method is technically coherent. The OT formulation, geometry-aware cost, dustbin mechanism, confidence derivation, and hub-mediated message passing fit together cleanly as one design rather than feeling like unrelated add-ons. For example, OTCHA reports XFMamba at 0.889 on MURA and 0.906 on CheXpert, whereas the original XFMamba paper reports notably higher AUROC values on these datasets. This discrepancy may be due to differences in preprocessing, splits, backbone variants, or retraining protocol, but the paper does not clearly explain the source of the gap. author_feedback: We thank all reviewers for recognizing OTCHA’s coherence and practical value, and address the main concerns below. (R1, R2) Contribution: OTCHA introduces a pre-fusion reliability modeling perspective for unregistered multi-view medical image classification. Unlike methods that directly aggregate dense view tokens, OTCHA recasts fusion as reliability-guided token participation through a shared latent hub. This reframes unregistered multi-view fusion from dense aggregation to reliability-guided refinement, which our ablations (Tab. 2) confirm are not reducible to any single component. (R3) Baseline comparison: We agree this needs clarification. Tab. 1 reports benchmark results under a unified evaluation protocol: all baselines were retrained with the same patient-level splits, sample construction, label definitions, preprocessing, and 5-run evaluation, using official model implementations where available. Since some patients have multiple studies, we split by patient before sample construction to prevent data leakage among studies from the same patient. The discrepancy from XFMamba’s paper reflects different split/sample-construction protocols. For MURA, we sampled 2 views once per study (11056/1270/1098); XFMamba’s official code uses pair-level sampling, so studies with >2 views yield multiple pairs (35185/3158/3283). For CheXpert, we constructed samples after patient-level splitting (23577/3923/3913); XFMamba uses random sample-level splitting (23559/3926/3928). We will clarify this in revision. (R3) Computational cost: Due to limited space, the computational cost was insufficiently discussed. We measured per-sample latency and peak memory under the paper settings (inference/training). Relative to MV-HFMD (base; 2-view 1.08/3.47ms, 0.96/6.64GB; 4-view 2.30/7.19ms, 1.63/12.93GB), OTCHA requires 1.65/4.75ms, 0.97/6.85GB (2-view) and 3.42/9.22ms, 1.65/13.34GB (4-view), respectively. Thus, our module adds only 0.57-2.03ms in absolute latency and 1-3% peak memory, suggesting limited added overhead. We will revise the efficiency statement. (R3) Modest gain: While absolute gains on MURA/CheXpert are modest, they are statistically significant over XFMamba (Tab. 1), and OTCHA achieves the best AUROC in all settings. Notably, the gain is most pronounced in the challenging 4-view VinDr-Mammo study-level, where OTCHA significantly outperforms MV-HFMD. With the cost analysis above and the ablations in Tab. 2, this indicates a favorable accuracy-complexity trade-off. (R1) Effectiveness of token filtering: On the VinDr-Mammo test set, we analyzed inference-time OT assignments. Each token’s unit mass is split between hubs and a dustbin, so dustbin mass serves as a rejection score. Treating zero-intensity patches as background (11.9% of all 196K tokens), dustbin mass alone detected background at AUROC 0.781, and the top-20% highest-dustbin tokens are 2.37× enriched in background over random. This supports preferentially filtering background/low-information tokens. (R1) Interpretability: We quantitatively evaluated pathological correspondence on VinDr-Mammo cases with lesion bounding boxes in both paired views. For each lesion patch in one view, we ranked paired-view patches by hub-assignment connectivity and computed AUROC using lesion/non-lesion patches as positive/negative. Same-patient pairs achieved 0.642 on average; patient-level shuffled pairs, where no true lesion correspondence exists, yielded to 0.522 (Wilcoxon p<1e-9). This provides supporting evidence for preferential lesion-level cross-view alignment. (R1, AC) Missing/variable-view: We agree this needs clarification. “Fixed-view” refers to the benchmark protocol, not an architectural constraint; OTCHA supports variable-view inputs (Tab. 1). In a controlled missing-view scenario analysis, OTCHA remained functional under partially available views, although performance showed a modest decrease compared with the full 4-view setting; broader missing-view evaluation remains future work.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper addresses a realistic multi-view medical image classification problem and proposes a technically coherent refinement-before-fusion framework based on optimal transport, latent hubs, token-conditional dustbins, and confidence-aware feature refinement. The reviews are close to the acceptance boundary, and the reviewers generally acknowledge the motivation, clarity, and consistent improvements across VinDr-Mammo, MURA, and CheXpert. However, several points need clarification before a final decision, especially the fairness of baseline comparisons, including the lower reported XFMamba results compared with the original paper, and whether all baselines were retrained under the same protocol. The authors should also provide runtime, memory, and inference-cost analysis, since Sinkhorn-based OT may add nontrivial computational overhead beyond parameter count. The rebuttal should further address the modest gains over strong baselines, directly validate token filtering and hub alignment, and discuss robustness under missing-view or variable-view settings. | The rebuttal adequately clarifies the baseline protocol, computational overhead, and the intended contribution of reliability-guided token participation before fusion. Although the method remains moderately incremental and some diagnostic analyses are provided only at rebuttal stage, the consistent post-rebuttal reviewer support and favorable accuracy–complexity trade-off make the paper acceptable as a weak accept. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The authors have provided solid and detailed clarifications in their rebuttal, satisfactorily addressing the core empirical and technical questions raised during the review process. Specifically, the authors have properly justified the discrepancies regarding the reported XFMamba performance. Crucially, they clarified that all baseline models were evaluated under a strictly unified protocol—employing identical patient-level splits, sample construction strategies, label definitions, and preprocessing pipelines, alongside 5-run repeated evaluations—while utilizing official code repositories for all publicly available baselines to guarantee an absolutely unbiased comparison. Furthermore, the authors delivered a thorough quantitative analysis detailing the inference and training latency per single sample as well as the peak memory footprint, effectively mitigating concerns regarding the computational tax imposed by the Sinkhorn-based optimal transport mechanism. Finally, the rebuttal provided strong empirical evidence directly validating the token filtering and hub alignment modules, while demonstrating the framework’s robust adaptability to scenarios involving missing or variable view counts. While the reviewers’ formal ratings remained unchanged post-rebuttal, the AC independently assesses that the authors’ technical explanations and rigorous cross-validation have fully resolved the primary skepticism, successfully elevating the manuscript to the publication threshold. Therefore, the AC recommends the acceptance of this paper. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The rebuttal has addressed the main concerns from the reviewers and all the reviewers are supportive to accept this paper.

title: OTFusion: Optimal Transport-Driven 3D Multi-modal Medical Image Fusion for Enhanced Cross-Modality Representation
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The paper claims to be an “OT-driven” framework, but the implementation reads more like an OT-inspired regularization strategy using Kantorovich potentials. Standard OT formulations typically define marginal constraints, transport costs, and optimization steps clearly, which are missing or vague here. Therefore, the authors should clarify why the proposed method warrants the “OT-driven” designation despite the absence of these core components. Strengths and Summary This paper focuses on the crucial task of 3D multi-modal medical image fusion, accurately identifying that existing methods lack an explicit mechanism for cross-modal distribution alignment. To address this limitation, the authors reformulate the fusion task as a distribution alignment problem inspired by Optimal Transport (OT) and propose an end-to-end framework named OTFusion. The proposed method elegantly employs a Mapping Network to generate the fused representations and a Potential Network to estimate Kantorovich potentials for OT regularization. Furthermore, it incorporates a Cross-Dimensional Interaction Module (CroDIM) to facilitate enhanced cross-modal feature interaction and structural consistency. Overall, the motivation is clear and the architecture is intuitively designed. 2.Since the core contribution relies heavily on the OT concept, the paper should compare with existing OT-based or OT-inspired fusion methods. Adding these comparisons will help prove that the performance gains come specifically from the proposed OT network design, rather than just a general distribution alignment effect. 3.The logical flow in the method section needs improvement. The text mentions Wasserstein-1 (W1), Wasserstein-2 (W2), the potential network, and the final loss function, but their exact relationships remain confusing. Please explicitly explain how these mathematical components connect and contribute to the final optimization objective.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Major Comments: Comment 1: The paper claims to be an “OT-driven” framework, but the implementation reads more like an OT-inspired regularization strategy using Kantorovich potentials. Adding these comparisons will help prove that the performance gains come specifically from the proposed OT network design, rather than just a general distribution alignment effect. Comment 3: The logical flow in the method section needs improvement. reviewer_2_strengths: The most prominent strength of this paper lies in its reformulation of 3D multimodal medical image fusion as a cross-modal distribution alignment problem, interpreted from the perspective of Optimal Transport (OT) theory. Under this view, fusion is no longer treated as merely concatenating, weighting, or attentively mixing features from two modalities; instead, it is modeled as a minimum-cost coupling problem between the source modality distributions and an idealized fused distribution. The paper conducts experiments on two public 3D datasets, SynthRAD and BraTS, and provides a fairly complete body of evidence, including quantitative comparisons, qualitative visualizations, and ablation studies. The baselines cover a range of existing fusion methods, and the evaluation includes multiple metrics, such as QNCIE, QTE, QG, QP, LMI, NCC, and SSIM, making the empirical validation relatively comprehensive. Another notable strength is that the paper focuses on 3D multimodal medical image fusion, rather than the more common and generally easier 2D fusion setting. Since 3D medical volumes pose greater challenges in terms of spatial continuity, cross-slice consistency, and computational complexity, grounding the method in a genuine 3D setting further enhances the technical significance of the work.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The existing ablation studies are sufficient to demonstrate the effectiveness of the full system. author_feedback: We sincerely thank all reviewers for their thorough and insightful comments. Below we address the methodological and presentation concerns raised. Clarification of terminology and implementation: “Collaborative framework” refers to a standard end-to-end multitask framework in this paper. The segmentation branch predicts infarct core and ischemic tissue; the use of “core and penumbra” in Sec. 2.2 was a typo. The map “M” denotes the attention map derived from segmentation outputs for attention gating. In Sec. 2.3, the statement that mismatch is predicted “from segmentation outputs” is inaccurate; as shown in Fig. 1, mismatch is predicted by an MLP from encoder features. In Sec. 3.1, λ2 should be λ3, corresponding to the diffusion loss. These corrections clarify the intended implementation without changing the methodology. For data concern, the dataset is a LVO dataset of 310 retrospective AIS patients, with following detailed inclusion criteria in [1]. Perfusion maps were affine-registered to NCCT space after skull stripping. Intensities were clipped to [0,100] HU for NCCT and [0,30] s for Tmax following [1]. Infarct core and ischemic tissue labels were obtained by standard thresholds (rCBF < 0.3, Tmax > 6s) and clinically reviewed. [1] Cai, Y. et al. CT perfusion map generation from multiphase CTA using a generative adversarial model for acute ischemic stroke. American Journal of Neuroradiology, 46(12), 2535–2544.Fig.1 may have caused confusion. The arrows returning to the DINOv3 encoder indicate gradient propagation during joint optimization rather than recursive execution. The diffusion branch uses segmentation outputs only as conditioning signals, while denoising is performed by an independent diffusion network. The framework follows sequential multitask optimization, and inference requires only NCCT input. For mismatch branch, threshold of 1.8 follows the DEFUSE-3 criterion. The MLP predicts mismatch status from pooled latent features, providing a global structural constraint complementary to pixel-wise supervision, reducing the influence of small lesion fluctuations on ratio estimation and improving robustness in small infarct cases. Although mismatch is clinically volumetric, we adopt a slice-level approximation, where consistently derived 2D annotations serve as region-level supervision. For diffusion branch, it is designed as a physiology-aware auxiliary constraint rather than a Dice-optimization module. Under Tmax supervision, it learns perfusion-related features and generates pseudo-perfusion representations (generative attention map) from NCCT. The modest Dice gain under 1.8 threshold suggests that the segmentation backbone already captures substantial lesion information, while the diffusion branch contributes through representation regularization and physiological interpretability. Although the Dice differences are modest, we note consistent trends across multiple experiments (Table 2, for threshold 0.8 and 2.8, infarct dice gain are 0.016 and 0.009, Ischemic tissue dice gain are 0.010 and 0.008), suggesting the improvements are systematic rather than random. Furthermore, this framework may provide a promising direction in our future work by mismatch-aware regional structural priors within denoising, which may further improve both pseudo-Tmax quality and Dice gain. For fairness, all baselines, 2D or 3D methods, were adapted into the same dual-head 2D setting while preserving their core architectural components, which ensures that performance differences mainly reflect architectural design rather than dimensionality differences. The 2D formulation was adopted due to NCCT characteristics, including anisotropic resolution, ~5 mm slice thickness, limited through-plane continuity, and variable slice counts. Under these conditions, slice-wise 2D modeling is a practical and widely adopted strategy for NCCT lesion analysis. Code will be released upon acceptance.

title: PhyDiCT: Plug-and-Play CT Reconstruction from Sparse X-Rays via Differentiable Rendering and Strong Priors
reviewer_1_strengths: The idea of image reconstruction with a text-guided diffusion prior is interesting and potentially relevant for radiological applications. In particular, incorporating contextual information through text could be useful in settings where side information is available and clinically meaningful. That said, MedSyn, on which the proposed reconstruction framework is based, dates from 2024.Therefore, I would not be surprised if similar ideas have already been implemented and published, and the paper should clarify more explicitly what is genuinely new here relative to prior work.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The framework uses a projection-space LPIPS term in the data fidelity term J. However, LPIPS(x,y) is, to my knowledge, a bounded function of x, and therefore is not coercive, so that \int exp(-J(y,x)) dx = +infty. Therefore, it is mathematically incorrect to formulate the proposed framework as a sampler from a posterior of the form p(x)exp(-J(y,x)). The inclusion of LPIPS should instead be presented as an additional guidance term incorporated into the diffusion sampler. Using LPIPS to guide the reconstruction in a DPS framework seems new to me. However, its usefulness is difficult to assess without the corresponding ablation study, i. e. , reconstruction without LPIPS in J. author_feedback: We thank all reviewers (R1, R2, R3) for their informative feedback and valuable suggestions. We are encouraged by the positive comments acknowledging our contributions in CT reconstruction with a text-guided prior and a physics-based reward function (R1, R2, R3), as well as the solid experimental demonstrations and result discussions (R2, R3). We address the key concerns below: 1) R1 & R2–Out-of-domain (noised) observation & LPIPS incorporation Thank R1 for pointing LPIPS is not coercive, you are correct. We found that observation methods such as DeepDRR produce realistic noise patterns and beam hardening effect, which are not differentiable. Therefore, the discrepancy introduces domain shifts with respect to our rendering method in Eq.4.Thus, LPIPS term is used as an additional regularization of guidance for perceptual consistency to address out-of-domain observation shifts, where the diffusion trajectory is guided partially by the perceptual gradient. We will add the ablation study without LPIPS term, and revise LPIPS incorporation to make the distinction clearer. 2) R1–Novelty of SGS and EC & R2–Novelty Claims & R3–Explanation of EC We do not claim SGS, nor SDEdit, as our contribution. Instead, we claim the following contributions:1) Incorporating a physical 3D-to-2D projection into the reward function with both MSE and LPIPS regularization (Tab. 1, two rendering settings); 2) Training-free lung 3D CT reconstruction from sparse X-ray (from reward function) and a text-guided prior; 3) A post-hoc EC step to remove artifacts (Fig. 2 last 2 columns, Tab. 1 “w/o EC”). We acknowledge the high-level resemblance between our EC step and DAPS (Zhang et al.), in that both involve adding noise. However, the motivation and mechanism differ substantially. 2.1) Motivation: DAPS aims to solve complicated nonlinear inverse problems through posterior exploration and Langevin-style sampling. However, our EC goal is artifact suppression and manifold alignment after posterior guidance. 2.2) Mechanism: DAPS introduces Decoupled Noise Annealing at each timestep together with posterior guidance. However, our EC is a post-hoc artifact-correction stage, where we add noise through the DDPM forward process and apply denoising steps only (Eqs. 1–2), without reward guidance, after the inverse problem has been solved. The goal is to produce visually cleaner reconstructions (Fig. 2 last 2 columns) and aligning with the data manifold closely. We also theoretically proved the manifold alignment (EC drift is within an upper-bound) but did not include it due to page limit. 3) R1–Studying the effect of text We show quantitative results in Tab. 1 under “ours w/o text.” Removing text slightly degrades CLIP-T2I performance (as expected without text guidance), while focusing more on image quality (CLIP-I2I improves). The remaining metrics stay largely on par with main results. 4) R1–Notation & minor clarification We will provide more details of CBCT, and we will modify the notation. We cited DAPS, and we will cite the other two. We refer to our model as plug-and-play because it requires no training on the target dataset. The text guidance is intended as a strong prior. 5) R2–Two optimization steps per iteration The gradient steps can be viewed as proximal steps for sampler. SGS formulated this procedure as posterior sampling. Therefore, the optimization step is posterior sampling, and two steps follow prior methods such as DAPS and PnP-DM (Tab. 1). 6) R3–Trade off CLIP-T2I & Application scenario of full-training methods The lower CLIP-T2I score in Tab. 1 can be explained by the in-domain training of X2CT and Xray2CTPA, where all other methods adopt a prior model (MedSyn) trained on a different dataset, and it is used as a plug-in module without fine-tuning. If sufficient in-domain paired data are available, full-training is preferred. But for good performance across out-of-distribution observations / datasets, posterior sampling methods are preferred.

The method’s robustness to such errors have not been evaluated. 2.In many modern CBCT systems with high frame rates and short exposure times, the fly-scanning-related motion effects can be relatively minor, limiting the development’s clinical utility. 3.The comparison study is somewhat limited. The paper compares PhyRadGS exclusively against reconstruction methods that rely on a strict static pose assumption, namely FDK, TV-regularized ASD-POCS, NAF, SAX-NeRF, and R2-Gaussian. While it successfully proves that PhyRadGS beats static methods on dynamic data, this is somewhat of an unfair fight. Because fly-scanning inherently introduces motion, static baselines are mathematically expected to fail. 2.Lack of in-vivo clinical data validation The real-world evaluation in the paper is entirely restricted to a double-layer sphere phantom scanned on a commercial CBCT system. A sphere phantom represents highly simplified, high-contrast geometry. It completely lacks the intricate, overlapping, and low-contrast high-frequency anatomical structures found in actual human biology (e.g., bone trabeculae, soft tissue boundaries). Without real-world in-vivo patient scans, the robustness of the algorithm in a true clinical environment remains unproven. The authors missed concurrent works such as: 3DGR-CT, X^2 Gaussian. 3.As the authors explicitly acknowledge in their conclusion, the current physical model strictly assumes rigid motion. The framework successfully models the known mechanical kinematics of the scanner (continuous gantry rotation), but it ignores the patient entirely.

author_feedback: We thank all reviewers for their constructive feedback. Lack of In-Vivo Clinical Data (Reviewer1 Comment 4, Reviewer2 Comment 2, Reviewer3 Comment 2) Real dynamic fly-scanning patient data is extremely difficult to obtain due to ethical constraints. To bridge this gap, we are the first to synthesize fly-scanning data using TIGRE on publicly available anatomical volumes (LIDC-IDRI and Open SciVis) that are widely adopted by NAF (Ref. 27), R2-Gaussian (Ref. 26), SAX-NeRF (Ref. 4), and X-Gaussian (Ref. 3), providing a reproducible benchmark for future research. Our commercial CBCT experiment (2048×2048) is among the very few real scans in this field. The controlled phantom cleanly isolates fly-scanning dynamics: direct validation for our forward model. In-vivo data is planned for future work. Static-Only Baselines Fairness (Reviewer1 Comment 3, Reviewer2 Comment 1) Static methods represent current clinical practice: their failure under fly-scanning directly motivates our work. To directly address the fairness concern, we integrated our Spatio-Temporal (ST) module into R2-Gaussian (Ref. 26) (“R2-Gaussian w/ ST,” Table 1): this achieves +2.29 dB PSNR and +0.038 SSIM over static R2-Gaussian, confirming the gain comes from physics modeling. PhyRadGS achieves better quality than “R2-Gaussian w/ ST” while being ~4x faster (~5 min vs. ~19 min), widening further on high-resolution real data (~9 min vs. ~51 min, Table 1). Concurrent Works (Reviewer2 Comment 2) Regarding concurrent works: 3DGR-CT improves rasterization accuracy for cone-beam geometry but remains fully static. X^2-Gaussian targets 4D CT for self-supervised respiratory motion: motion caused by patient not the system. Both these works try to solve fundamentally different problem, which is why they are not included in comparison. Iteration Count Fairness (Reviewer3 Comment 1) As stated in Sec. 3.1, all 3DGS-based methods (R2-Gaussian, PhyRadGS) were trained under identical settings: 20K iterations on a single RTX 4090, with wall-clock time reported. In our reproduction, R2-Gaussian converges by 20K with performance comparable to its original 30K setting (Ref. 26). Speedup between PhyRadGS (~5 min) vs. “R2-Gaussian w/ ST” (~19 min, Table 1) reflects batch rendering efficiency, not fewer iterations. Calibration Error (Reviewer1 Comment 1) Commercial CBCT systems achieve calibration precision below 0.1° angular uncertainty: two orders of magnitude smaller than the 14.4° integration arc per exposure (fly-scanning protocol). Our real phantom experiment on a commercial system empirically confirms robustness: PhyRadGS achieves 37.43 dB PSNR vs. 35.13 dB for PhyRadGS w/o ST (Table 1). Clinical Utility at High Frame Rates (Reviewer1 Comment 2) Rolling shutter distortion is hardware-intrinsic and frame-rate-independent. Motion blur is caused by integration arc per view, which is determined by angular spacing (360°/N_views) but not frame rate or exposure time: for 25 (50) views, each projection spans 14.4° (7.2°). While increasing view count mitigates motion blur, it raises radiation dose: a key clinical trade-off. PhyRadGS achieves 31.23 dB at ST 25 views (static 50 views 31.96 dB), making smaller dose possible. L1 Regularization Ablation (Reviewer3 Comment 3) As stated in Sec. 2.4, L1 density regularization is a standard technique for suppressing floating artifacts in sparse-view reconstruction, analogous to the TV regularization adopted by R2-Gaussian (Ref. 26). Our ablation (Table 2) focuses on our main contribution: novel parameters M and N. Extended loss ablations are acknowledged for future work. Rigid Motion Assumption (Reviewer2 Comment 3) This limitation is explicitly acknowledged in our Conclusion. PhyRadGS models scanner mechanical kinematics, which are inherently rigid. Patient non-rigid motion is an orthogonal problem addressable by combining our forward model with deformation fields (Refs. 23, 24). This extension is planned as future work.
