author_feedback: We sincerely thank all reviewers for their constructive and encouraging feedback. We appreciate the recognition of our novel methodological contributions (R1, R2, R3, and Meta R2), the strength of our empirical results (R1, R2, R3, and Meta R2), and the clarity of our presentation (R1, R2, R3, and Meta R2). All clarifications, additional implementation details, and relevant discussions will be incorporated into the final version. We address each reviewer’s concerns below: Method Details (Meta R2.Q3, R1.Q1, R1.Q2 and R1.Q4): The overall training loss consists of standard per-word cross-entropy loss and RL loss (eq. 3). The RL loss consists of natural language generation (NLG) reward and clinical efficacy (CE) reward (eq. 5). NLG reward combines BLEU-4, METEOR and ROUGE-L (eq. 6), and CE reward is based on precision/recall from CheXbert (eq. 2). In the PRC-AdaLN module (eq. 1, Fig. 1), the scale and biases were generated using separate MLPs. In both training and evaluation, uncertain CheXbert labels were mapped to positive, while negative and blank labels were mapped to negative. CE precision, recall, and F1 were micro-averaged over all 14 labels and test samples. Additional Dataset (Meta R2.Q1, R1.Q5, R3.Q1): We evaluated our method on CheXpert Plus and it achieved better NLP and clinical metrics compared to R2GenCSR [1], which reported the SOTA performance on CheXpert Plus, and MedGemma. We report representative metrics including ROUGE-L as the selected NLG metric, CheXbert F1, and RadGraph F1.Our method achieved 0.225/0.502/0.169, outperforming R2GenCSR (0.220/0.475/0.159) and MedGemma (0.153/0.434/0.144). Confidence Intervals (Meta R2.Q2 and R3.Q2): Confidence intervals and statistical tests were performed using paired bootstrapping with 10,000 repeats on existing MIMIC-CXR results and CheXpert Plus results. The 95% CIs for our method on MIMIC-CXR were [0.331, 0.336] for ROUGE-L, [0.564, 0.579] for CheXbert F1, and [0.237, 0.245] for RadGraph F1.The 95% CIs on CheXpert Plus were [0.224, 0.227], [0.497, 0.507], and [0.167, 0.171] for the three metrics, respectively. Paired bootstrap tests showed statistically significant improvement compared to MLRG, R2GenCSR, and MedGemma on corresponding datasets (p < 0.0001). Additional Metrics (Meta R2.Q4 and R1.Q3): We calculated RadGraph F1 for MIMIC-CXR and our method achieved the best performance (0.240) compared to MLRG (0.227), and MedGemma (0.190), showing consistent clinically relevant improvement with newer metrics. Ablating PRC-AdaLN module (Meta R2.Q5 and R3.Q3): The controllability comes from both the representation-level λ conditioning and reward level λ weighting. Without the representation-level conditioning, there is no way to control the precision/recall during inference without retraining; without the reward level weighting, the representation-level conditioning does not map to any meaningful outcomes. The testing-time controllability was only possible because the same λ was fed to the PRC-AdaLN module and used for reward during training. We also tried injecting λ differently, such as encoding λ and concatenating to image features. However, this strategy provided less controllability than our current design, since varying λ during inference produced no change in the generated reports. Concurrent Works: (Meta R2.Q6, R1.Q6 and R2.Q1): Thanks for the suggestion and we will discuss recent concurrent works CURE [2] and GDPO [3] in the final version. CURE focuses on curriculum-guided anatomy grounding, while our method focuses on inference-time precision-recall controllability via λ-conditioned representation and λ-controlled clinical reward. We will explore integrating GDPO into our framework in future work. Refs: [1] Wang et al., R2GenCSR, IEEE JBHI, 2026.[2] Messina, Pablo, et al. CURE, arXiv preprint arXiv:2601.15408 (2026). [3] Liu et al., GDPO, arXiv:2601.05242, 2026.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper proposes a reinforcement learning framework for chest X-ray radiology report generation that enables explicit, inference-time control of the clinical precision–recall trade-off via a control parameter during inference. Experiments on MIMIC-CXR report improvements over prior methods in standard NLG and CE metrics, supported by ablations. The problem setting is clinically meaningful and inference-time precision–recall controllability is a practical, well-motivated contribution. The paper is reasonably clearly written, and method shows strong empirical performance on MIMIC-CXR. However, several concerns need to be addressed to increase confidence in the claims, including: 1) Evaluation is restricted to a single dataset (MIMIC-CXR), and authors could provide results on at least one additional dataset or compelling evidence of robustness to distribution shifts. 2) Results are reported as single point estimates without confidence intervals, standard deviations, or significance tests. 3) There are missing or unclear methodological details that affect reproducibility and interpretation (e.g., definition of “clinical loss”, PRC-AdaLN implementation, CheXbert uncertainty mapping, metrics averaging). 4) Clinical validation is narrow (no complementary clinical metrics such as RadGraph, and no human evaluation). 5) Missing ablation of PRC-AdaLN leading to unclear impact of PRC-AdaLN vs. reward-level λ weighting. 6) Positioning of paper not clear relative to recent works (e.g. CURE, GDPO). Overall, the core idea (single-model, inference-time control of the clinical precision–recall trade-off) is novel, relevant, and promising, but the current evidence does not yet meet the bar for acceptance. I invite the paper for rebuttal to address the reviewers’ concerns. | The rebuttal addressed several of the reviewers’ points including the implementation details, confidence intervals, positioning with prior work, and additional evaluation metrics. These clarifications improved reviewers’ confidence, leading two reviewers to update their recommendations to Accept. That said, I also share the AC’s concern that new results on additional dataset introduced in rebuttal should not be used as the basis for the final recommendation, and my assessment therefore does not rely on those additional experiments. Overall, the paper presents a meaningful contribution, and the rebuttal sufficiently resolved most of the key concerns raised on the submitted version. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The authors have addressed the reviewers’ comments well. All reviewers acknowledged the significance of the work. Therefore acceptance of the paper is concluded. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): The paper proposes a reinforcement-learning framework for radiology report generation that aims to enable controllable precision–recall trade-off behavior through a conditioning parameter used in both decoder modulation and clinical reward weighting. The work puts forward a clinically meaningful problem and reports strong performance with interpretable precision–recall trends on MIMIC-CXR. While the method demonstrates predictable precision–recall trade-off behavior through λ, the submitted evidence supports steerability of the operating point rather than reliable control of desired precision or recall targets. In addition, the reinforcement-learning objective explicitly optimizes a CheXbert-defined precision–recall target, while the main clinical evaluation also relies on CheXbert-based metrics, making complementary clinical validation beyond the CheXbert label space particularly important. Although rebuttal-only RadGraph results partially alleviate this concern, they are not part of the submitted study and are not considered in the decision. Finally, the submitted evidence is limited to a single dataset, making generalization beyond MIMIC-CXR less clear. Overall, the work presents a clinically meaningful and promising direction. Incorporating and improving the additional validation provided in the rebuttal and clarifying the above issues would substantially strengthen the work and make the study more convincing.

title: Predicting Radiologist Expertise from 3D Gaze Patterns During CT Interpretation
reviewer_1_strengths: Novelty in Dimension: The research significantly extends gaze-based skill assessment from 2D into the 3D dimension, filling a gap where few studies handle both 3D CT and 3D attention maps simultaneously. Innovative Mechanisms: The proposed log-space bias and gaze-weighted pooling represent novel ways to inject gaze information. Algorithmic Synergy: These two modules function at complementary levels (the attention layer and the pooling stage), creating a powerful synergy that markedly improves model performance.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Dataset Limitations: The expert dataset is very small, involving only three participants. This makes it difficult to determine if the model captures general expert patterns or merely the specific habits of those individuals. Lack of Diagnostic Link: The paper lacks validation concerning diagnostic accuracy. Expertise in radiology is ultimately measured by outcomes (e. g. , sensitivity/specificity for detecting nodules), but these metrics are absent. Clinical Weakness: Without linking gaze patterns to actual diagnostic performance, the clinical claims of the paper are weakened.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The way the authors integrate gaze information into the transformer architecture is clean. The log-space attention bias and gaze-weighted output pooling are two complementary mechanisms that inject gaze information at different stages of the model. The ablation study (Table 2) confirms both contribute (AUC 0.91 combined vs. 0.89 or 0.86 individually). 2.The gaze-to-CT coordinate mapping (gaze drift correction, OCR-based metadata extraction, affine alignment, subject-specific Gaussian calibration) is detailed and addresses real practical challenges in working with eye-tracking data in volumetric imaging. This careful design is needed when dealing with gaze data collection for CTs or volumetric data in general. 3.The evaluation is comprehensive. It covers two distinct families of prior work (skill assessment models and scanpath prediction models) with multiple input combinations. While I feel this work could include more transformer-based methods for comparison, because this is the first work in this domain, I think the current table is sufficient as the metrics, for example F1, are relatively high and reliable and sufficient for publication. 4.The backbone comparison (DINOv2 vs. Med3D, SwinUNETR, UniMISS) and the ablation over attention mode and pooling strategy help justify the design decisions. 5.The authors provide a GitHub link for reproducibility, which is positive and welcomed by the community.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The study uses only five radiologists (three experts, two novices) and 40 CT scans, yielding 182 sessions. This raises concerns about generalizability. The expert/novice distinction is binary based on a 7-year threshold, which is a simplification that ignores the spectrum of expertise. With so few readers, the model may be learning radiologist-specific visual habits rather than generalizable expertise patterns. The test set contains only two radiologists (one expert, one novice), so it is unclear whether the model would transfer to unseen readers with different viewing styles. However, I understand that collecting a large number of experts and CTs requires exponential effort, and given that expert classification can be done reliably by machine learning in the literature, I consider this weakness not a major one. 2.The same 40 CT volumes appear across all radiologists. Since the train and test sets are split by radiologist (A, B, D for training; C, E for testing), the model sees the same CT scans during training and testing, just read by different people. The DINOv2 backbone could learn CT-content features that correlate with which radiologists happened to read which cases, rather than purely learning gaze-based expertise signals. The authors do not discuss or control for this. 3.The paper does not clearly establish who would use this system and in what workflow. In other words, who is the intended user of this system? The potential applications (training feedback, CAD system design) are mentioned only briefly in the final paragraph. There is no discussion of what actionable information a binary expert/novice classification provides beyond what simpler gaze statistics (e.g., total dwell time, fixation count, coverage) could offer. For instance, if an expert were to use this system, what would happen next after the model determines that the reader is an expert? A simple example of a use case in the introduction would be greatly helpful for future readers to understand when they would need this system. 4.Table 1 reports single-point metrics on the test set without error bars or confidence intervals. Given the small test set (67 samples), the reported differences between methods may not be statistically significant. The validation AUC is reported with standard deviation for the ablation (Table 2) but not for the main comparison. 5.The paper does not investigate what gaze patterns the model uses to distinguish experts from novices. There is no attention visualization, feature importance analysis, or qualitative case study showing how the model’s predictions relate to known differences in expert vs. novice reading behavior (e.g., systematic scanning vs. scattered fixations). I find this limiting in terms of interpretability and clinical trust. For example, what if the model simply counts the number of fixations and predicts expertise from that alone? A worthwhile experiment would be to replace the proposed attention and pooling modules with a simple input such as the session length or fixation count, to see how much of the performance can be explained by trivial statistics. 6.While the CT scans come from the publicly available LIDC-IDRI dataset, the eye-tracking data collected by the authors is not shared. This limits reproducibility, especially given that the results depend heavily on the specific gaze data collected from these five individuals.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The use of gaze data in 3D medical imaging is underexplored and has strong potential for improving downstream tasks. The paper is well-motivated and helps bridge the gap between handcrafted metrics, which are task- and data-agnostic. Detailed data collection and preprocessing description. Leveraging gaze both as attention across layers (with learnable weights) and for pooling across slices is interesting and simple to implement. The proposed method outperforms baselines. Leverages gaze scanpath prediction models for expertise classification.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1) Novelty: Integrating gaze by reweighting attention requires collapsing across the time dimension to generate a heatmap, which discards temporal information such as the number of refixations that might be informative for expertise classification. 2) Heatmap Preprocessing: The motivation and effect of applying L1 normalization to the pooled heatmap are unclear, especially since softmax is already used. The authors should clarify this design choice. 3) Writing: It is not clear whether the 3D volume is processed slice-by-slice or as a full volume at the beginning of the method section. It would be helpful to briefly mention or introduce that the volume is partially sampled for clarity. 4) Evaluation: Given the relatively small dataset, some form of cross-validation would strengthen the evaluation. In particular, since samples from the same radiologist should not appear in both the training and test sets, it would be informative to evaluate performance across different splits of experts and novices. An ablation study on the number of sampled slices (K) would be valuable to understand its impact on performance. This is especially important if there is a difference between K = 1 and K > 1, as it would inform the utility of using gaze on 3D volumes versus 2D images. How did the authors arrive at K = 8? The effect of using a fixed \alpha should be analyzed, as it might affect performance.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: Dear Reviewers, Area and Program Chairs, We thank you for your overall positive opinion and thoughtful feedback. Below we address the main concerns and present additional analyses on existing data: Data leakage & experimental design: We clarify that no label leakage occurs from shared CT volumes in train/test splits. The target (expertise) is a property of the reader, not the CT. Each CT carries conflicting labels (paired with both expert and novice gaze), forcing the model to learn gaze dynamics conditioned on the image rather than memorize CT features. Confirming this, a DINOv2 model without gaze yields near-random performance (Test AUC=0.5433), proving CT content alone provides no predictive signal. To directly test for CT-content leakage we evaluated within-CT predictions on the test set. For 29 CTs viewed by both reader C (Expert) and E (Novice), we compared the model’s Expert-probability on the two paired sessions. Under the CT-only hypothesis these probabilities must be equal, yielding within-CT AUC=0.5 and both-correct rate=0% by construction. Instead we observe sign agreement of 86.2% (25/29 CTs with prob_C>prob_E; sign-test p=5.2×10^-5, Wilcoxon p=5.1×10^-6), mean prob_C-prob_E=+0.34, and both paired sessions classified correctly for 65.5% of CTs (with no CT misclassified on both sessions). These results are incompatible with CT-content driving the predictions, thus the model must be conditioning on gaze, which is only other per-session input ( test_stats.txt in GitHub repository). Class-stratified bootstrap on test AUC: 0.909, 95% CI [0.83, 0.97], is strictly above chance. Cross-validation & generalizability: Table 2 ablations use 5-fold reader-disjoint CV on the training pool. A full radiologist-holdout splits across all expert/novice combinations requires >70h of additional training of all methods, which is infeasible within the rebuttal period; these evaluation results will be released on GitHub. We agree with the Reviewers that dataset scale is the primary limitation and we are actively collecting more data. For context, previous 3D CT eye-tracking studies relied on only 2 participants (Pham et al., 2025), and we have 5 participants. Diagnostic accuracy: We thank the Reviewers for pointing out the importance of diagnostic analysis. In our work, we followed common practice and defined expertise by years of experience. It is also important to note that our novices have <1 year of experience, so no novice is at the edge of being classified as expert. We analyzed readings to measure diagnostic performance: experts achieved 0.96 sensitivity/0.98 specificity, novices 0.89/0.58.This will be included in the Dataset section in the camera-ready version. Trivial-statistics baseline & interpretability: Per session we computed 21 gaze features: (i) fixation timing: count, total dwell, mean/median/std fixation duration, session duration; (ii) spatial distribution: duration-weighted gaze centroid and spread (x_mean, y_mean, x_std, y_std, dispersion), coverage, entropy; (iii) slice navigation: unique slices visited, slice range, transition count, mean/std inter-frame scroll velocity, revisit ratio; (iv) windowing: unique WL,WW pairs and their change counts. Logistic regression and random forest on reader-disjoint splits yield intra-train 5-fold CV AUC=0.96 but drop to test AUC=0.59 on held-out readers. This rules out the model exploiting trivial statistics and shows handcrafted features fail to generalize across radiologists, while our gaze-conditioned representations transfer. Method-specific concerns: To clarify, L1 normalization turns heatmaps into probability distributions, making the bias term (α * logw) a log-prior and removing per-radiologist scale differences in raw fixation magnitudes. The model input is the full CT volume. K=8 balances volumetric coverage against compute. Reproducibility: We agree with the Reviewers that reproducibility is important. We will release a sample of the dataset upon publication.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): This submission proposes a gaze-informed transformer framework for expertise classification in thoracic CT, integrating radiologists’ fixation patterns into volumetric feature learning via attention biasing and gaze-weighted pooling. Three reviewers (R1, R2, R3) vote for weak accept. The paper is recognized as a novel and promising contribution, particularly in extending gaze-based expertise assessment from 2D to 3D CT settings. However, all reviewers raise important concerns related to dataset scale, evaluation, and clinical grounding. These issues should be carefully addressed in the rebuttal. All reviewers emphasize that the dataset is small (five radiologists, limited CT scans), raising concerns about generalizability. R2 and R3 raise a serious concern about potential leakage due to shared CT volumes across splits. R3 points out some form of cross-validation would strengthen the evaluation.

title: Preoperative Simulation of Personalized Breast Reconstruction via Implant Prior Controllable Diffusion
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The choice of an inpainting LDM is technically sound for this task, as it maintains the integrity of the contralateral breast and non-surgical anatomy while focusing generative capacity on the ROI. 2.The authors correctly identify that implicit conditioning (cross-attention on text/numeric attributes) is insufficient for enforcing strict 3D geometric constraints in medical imaging, justifying the need for explicit spatial control. 3.The use of an external test set from a different hospital helps assess the model’s generalization capabilities across different scanning protocols.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.Limited novelty: The core architecture is essentially a 3D adaptation of ControlNet applied to a 3D LDM inpainting framework. While the application is novel, the methodological components are standard modules in the current generative AI landscape. 2.The comparative experiments are insufficient. The comparative methods are all traditional generative methods from several years ago; it is necessary to include newer methods from the last 2-3 years. In addtion, GLIGEN and T2I-Adapter are 2D models, I am concerned about the fairness of these comparative experiments. 3.You mention excluding cases with “severe implant deformation”. Does this imply the model is only trained on “ideal” outcomes？ 4.In Section 2.4, the intermediate denoised estimation is passed through a frozen VAE decoder and a segmentation network. As LDMs are known to produce noisy intermediate approximations at earlier timesteps, it is questionable how robust the frozen segmentation network is to these out-of-distribution, noisy predictions. The authors do not state if the SwinUNETR was trained with noise augmentation.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: ++ The work addresses a significant gap in surgical planning by moving beyond qualitative visualization toward reliable, patient-specific 3D morphological simulation. The framework allows for the adjustment of height, width, and projection, enabling surgeons to visualize outcomes for implants with varying properties
reviewer_2_weaknesses: While understandable, the paper uses the mask of the implant (I_p) as a part of the model’s input, which may hinder its downstream application, since the accurate geometry of the implant itself is usually hard to get before the surgurical operation. This paper uses Totalsegmentator for ribcage segmentation and MedVAE for LDM autoencoding, so the actual performance of breast reconstruction is also dependent on the pretrained multi-organ model/autoencoder themselves. – Following the above weakness, if the authors opt to use pretrained models for medical priors, why not directly use diffusion networks pretrained on medical data with additional adapters to realize task-specific synthesis. – Current comparisons (GLIGEN, Siimple-Controlnet, T2I-Adapter) are not tested or pretrained on medical data. Also, they were designed as 2D models, it is important that the authors discuss the reasons how they elevate them to 3D CT synthesis as well as why not choose 3D synthesis methods in the medical domain as baselines.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: This paper introduces an approach for controllable postoperative simulation by explicitly integrating a patient-specific 3D implant spatial prior within a latent diffusion framework and enables direct geometric control over surgical outcomes. The use of a canonical implant template library, combined with anatomy-aware alignment, particularly via principal component analysis (PCA) of the ribcage, provides a way to translate discrete implant specifications into a continuous and physiologically plausible spatial representation. The method is closely tailored to the clinical problem through the use of ROI-based inpainting. This mechanism allows realistic modification of only the surgical region while preserving surrounding anatomy, which is crucial in unilateral reconstruction scenarios. The work demonstrates clear clinical utility by enabling simulation of postoperative outcomes under different user-defined implant configurations. It thus offers a practical tool for preoperative planning and surgical decision-making. Finally, the experimental evaluation combines standard image quality metrics with implant-specific geometric measures (such as Dice and IoU), along with qualitative analyses. The inclusion of cross-institutional testing further strengthens the claims regarding the robustness and generalizability of the proposed method
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The paper also presents several important weaknesses. First, the methodological novelty may appear relatively incremental, as the approach largely builds on existing components such as latent diffusion inpainting (e.g., RePaint), spatial conditioning via ControlNet-like architectures, and template-based anatomical priors without introducing a fundamentally new generative paradigm. Prior work has already explored spatially guided medical image synthesis, particularly in the context of controllable diffusion and anatomy-constrained generation. Moreover, although the construction of the implant prior is well motivated, it primarily relies on aggregating aligned segmentations and on PCA-based alignment. This strategy may lead to an oversimplification of the complex biomechanical interactions between the implant and surrounding soft tissues, and does not explicitly model tissue deformation. In this respect, it remains less expressive than physics-based or biomechanical simulation approaches commonly used in surgical planning. Additionally, the clinical applicability of the method remains limited. The approach assumes the availability of preoperative CT scans, which are not systematically acquired in all breast reconstruction workflows. Moreover, it focuses exclusively on implant-based reconstruction and excludes more complex cases, such as those involving severe deformation or displacement. These choices raise concerns regarding robustness in real-world settings and potential selection bias. Furthermore, comparisons are restricted to general-purpose controllable diffusion methods adapted to the medical setting, rather than to specialized surgical simulation tools. Finally, the claim that the method enables exploration beyond manufacturer implant catalogs through continuous scaling is not clinically validated. This raises questions about the anatomical plausibility of the generated results and their relevance within real-world regulatory constraints.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We appreciate R2 for recognizing the clinical value and multi-center validation, R6 for the detailed technical scrutiny that improved our methodological clarity, and R8 for the profound clinical insights that for sure benefit our future work. We address concerns below. 1) Baseline selection R2W2 R6W4: Fairness is ensured: All baselines were elevated to 3D by replacing 2D conv/attention modules with 3D counterparts, sharing the same 3D LDM backbone, training data, and training iterations. Their reasonable performance (Fig. 2, Tables 1-2) supports the correct adaptation. We will release their code as well, and elaborate the adaptation method in the camera-ready version. We chose baselines to cover representative and recent control methods: GLIGEN2023, T2IAdapter2024, SimpleControlnet2025.Medical models like GuideGen, MedSyn, MAISI target different tasks rather than breast reconstruction, causing domain mismatches and thus are not directly comparable. 2) Novelty R2W1 R8W1: We clarify that our novelty is at the system level for an underexplored clinical task: (i) LDM inpainting for simulation; (ii) template library bridging historical postoperative knowledge to preoperative use; (iii) continuous shape control via template editing; (iv) PCA alignment for anatomical plausibility; (v) control branch improves implant geometry accuracy and sharpness. While (i) follows LDM, all components are task-oriented designs. These formulate, to our knowledge, the first open-source framework for patient-specific breast reconstruction simulation, with continuously adjustable implants. 3) Implant mask R6W1: We agree that the postoperative implant is unknown preoperatively, which motivates Sec.2.3.Importantly, I_p is NOT the postoperative implant of the target case but a planned control signal obtained by template retrieval, size/placement adjustment, and PCA anatomy alignment; thus, it is available preoperatively. Deformations: The same type/size implants show similar mild bottom bending due to skin coverage and rib support. We approximate this by averaging historical implants of the same type/size (red/blue overlap in Figs. 2 3 supports this). 4) Model dependency R6W2: While we use large-FoV CTs for body visualization, we thank the reviewer for noting the potential failure. Quantification: Monitoring rib segmentation volume and HU consistency of bone; Mitigation: if it fails, fall back to bone window thresholding, filtering, connectivity based rib estimation within the ROI as an alternative. 5) Use of pretrain R6W3: As baselines: domain mismatch (see 1). As generation backbones: they are pretrained on general CTs with few implants, lacking implant prior. Injecting control may not reuse their knowledge well and overload the control branch for implant generation, causing instability. Therefore, we train the backbone on domain data. 6) Plausibility of deformations R8W2: Targeting the simulation with accurate shape prior, we did not explicitly model biomechanics interaction. We will add it as limitation and explore physics-constrained generation in future work. 7) Clinical use R8W2: CT availability: Chest CT is acquired for mastectomy and reconstruction for anesthesia planning and lung, lymph metastasis assessment. We appreciate the R8’s practical concern and will explore modality transfer to enhance data availability. Clinical validation: Breast simulators are commercial (for augmentation) or photo-based non public models, hindering direct comparison. Prospective validation needs a longer timeline and will be pursued. Additionally: Outlier cases R2W3 R8W2: Our model aims to simulate the intended postoperative breast shape; rare abnormal cases were excluded to avoid ambiguous generation. Noisy prediction R2W4: SwinUNETR receives denoised intermediate approximation (Eq.4), which is close to a clean image, not noisy; so noise augmentation is unnecessary. We sincerely thank reviewers for their constructive comments, and invaluable feedback.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The use of generative methods for predicting surgical outcomes using patient-specific anatomical constraints and possible implants is a sound concept. Nevertheless the reviewers raised important issues that need to be addressed by the authors. It is requested to the authors to explicitly explain how these aspects can be remedied within the rebuttal phase. In concrete the following aspects need to be discussed: 1) Baseline selection: The major issue detected by the reviewer was the unfair comparison to the baselines (R2, W2; R6, W4) - please explain why this is not the case, or how to remedy this. 2) Novelty: Reviewers claim all components are known and the novelty comes from the integration (R2, W1; R8, W1) - please comment on that. 3) Implant mask: Implants are deformable on their own, such that the implant mask cannot be known before surgery (R6, W1) - clarify if that statement is true and if yes, how this impacts predictions. 4) Dependency on pretrained models: Frozen models can produce errors that propagate downstream (R6, W2) - what measures have authors taken to quantify and mitigate this, in the view that TotalSegmentator does not perform well on ribs if CTs have a small FoV. 5) Use of diffusion networks: Diffusion networks pretrained on medical data exist (R6, W3) - explain the rationale of not using them at least as baseline. 6) Plausibility of deformations: The approach does not guarantee realistic biomechanical deformations (R8, W2) - elaborate if evaluation of deformation fields was performed and at least mention this in the limitation section 7) Clinical use: Limitations of an introduction of the method in a clinical setup are not addressed (R8, W2) - discuss them. Notation: Rx stands for reviewer x; Wx stands for weakness x (being x the paragraph of answer 7) | While I do not think that the authors addressed all raised issues, the main criticism (the fairness of comparison with the baselines which would have been a “deal-breaker”) seems to be solved. While the two reviewers giving an “Accept” remain short in justification, the justification of reviewer 6 to reject the paper is not really valid in my view as it misses the point of the approach: other inpainting methods could be replaced in the same architecture and the paper would still be novel. I still hope the authors keep their word an implement the changes they promise in the camera-ready version. I still believe however they should not claim that deformation is “mild”. That is definitely not the case after working >15 in breast cancer. I recommend addressing this as a limitation: “the model will perform fine as long as the implants do not deform much”. Also, the rebuttal answer for 4) is weak… Again here I recommend explicitly mention this limitation and possibly pointing at literature “correcting” total segmentator or alike. The proposed strategy is also OK, but without implementing it, it should at most be considered a potential future work. The issue with 7) is not to be dismissed that easily. I agree with the line of thoughts of the authors (cases where CT is available and potentially using othermodalities), but porting their model to MRI or US is not going to be easy. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The rebuttal is satisfactory Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This work addresses an important surgical planning problem and proposes a controllable 3D generative framework for personalized breast reconstruction simulation using an anatomically aligned implant spatial prior. The explicit implant prior, ROI-based inpainting formulation, and cross-institutional evaluation provide clinically meaningful strengths, and the rebuttal satisfied most concerns for two reviewers. The remaining concerns about incremental novelty, comparison with more recent medical-domain inpainting or controllable diffusion methods, reliance on implant priors, and limited modeling of soft-tissue deformation should be addressed in the final version.

title: PriLoRA: Prior-Conditioned Low-Rank Adapters for Medical Vision Models
reviewer_1_strengths: The paper is well-written and structured. The key concepts are described in enough detail to make them understandable. PriLoRA introduces a light modulator that leverages prior features extracted from the input and then predicts a small set of parameters that specialize the adapter for each block and each sample. Sinusoidal LoRA therefore becomes an input-conditioned adapter that adjusts its non-linear response per block and per sample, while preserving LoRA modularity and parameter efficiency. The paper is well motivated. Instead of using a fixed linear LoRA update, or a fixed-frequency sinusoidal update (SineLoRA), PriLoRA predicts sample- and block-specific modulation parameters from input-derived prior features. This avoids manual frequency selection across tasks and modalities. To avoid adapting for different modalities and tasks, PriLoRA provides an adapter response that depends on the input. The experimental evaluation on four different medical tasks (image generation, segmentation, classification, and CT reconstruction). PriLoRA is shown to improve robustness over standard LoRA and several representative PEFT baselines. PriLoRA only adds a small overhead in terms of trainable parameters and latency.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: - PriLoRA directly extends from variants like SineLoRA. The authors for not provide muckh on related works, so it is difficult to put the novelty of their work into perspective among SOTA adaptation methods. The paper does not isolate the origins and extent of improvements: from the sinusoidal formulation or the input conditioning? - The paper validates experimentally over several tasks, but usually with only one dataset per task, so robustness is not validated over different institutions, scanners, etc. (with distribution shifts). The authors should provide an analysis of computational complexity for their methods versus SOTA methods. - The code is not made available, so the results in this paper may be difficult for a reader to reproduce.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The paper has two main strengths. First, the method is simple and easy to understand. PriLoRA is a clean extension of LoRA/SineLoRA, with an intuitive formulation based on a lightweight modulator that predicts amplitude, frequency scaling, phase, and offset for the sinusoidal update. Second, the empirical evaluation is fairly comprehensive. The method is tested across multiple medical vision tasks, backbones, and modalities, and the paper also includes ablation studies and efficiency analysis in addition to the main quantitative results.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The design of the PriLoRA modulator appears to be highly task-dependent, rather than a single unified and broadly generalizable design. 2.Figure 1(c) still retains omega_0, while the paper claims that PriLoRA avoids manual frequency tuning. In addition, the roles of omega_0 and beta appear potentially overlapping, since beta rescales the sinusoidal argument that already contains omega_0.I would encourage the authors to further clarify the rationale behind this design choice and explain whether omega_0 still needs to be manually selected in practice. 3.The paper states that rank 8 is used for classification, but the numbers reported in Table 1 match the rank-16 results in Table 2 rather than the rank-8 results. The authors should clarify which rank was actually used for the main classification comparison.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The idea of conditioning the effective LoRA rank through the additional introduced parameters in the sinusoidal modulation is new and interesting. 2.The approach achieves competitive performance. 3.The paper is well-written and easy to understand.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The paper lacks evidence to substantiate several motivating claims. For instance, the “Effect of Parameters” paragraph in Sec. 3.1 states that alpha controls the ability of PriLoRA to attenuate or amplify easy and difficult scenarios, beta captures fine-grained variations, gamma avoids saturation for certain modalities and delta allows domain-specific shifts. However, none of these claims have been validated. 2.Analysis of learned alpha, beta, gamma and delta: While ablations show that removing each of these parameters affects performance, the paper does not provide insights into the learned values of the parameters for different tasks.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal

meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): This paper introduces PriLoRA, a prior-conditioned low-rank adaptation method for medical vision models. It extends LoRA/SineLoRA by using input-derived prior features to modulate the sinusoidal low-rank update, aiming to improve expressivity while keeping the adaptation parameter-efficient. The paper received consistent positive reviews, with all three reviewers recommending Weak Accept. Reviewers appreciated the clear motivation, simple formulation, good writing, and broad evaluation across multiple medical imaging tasks, including generation, segmentation, classification, and CT reconstruction. The main concerns are about the limited analysis of the learned modulation parameters, some unclear design choices, and reproducibility details. Overall, I recommend acceptance. The contribution is somewhat incremental relative to LoRA/SineLoRA, but the method is well motivated, technically sound, and evaluated across a reasonably broad set of medical imaging scenarios. The remaining issues can likely be addressed in the final version.

title: Prior-Guided Hierarchical Vector Quantized-VAE for Digital Subtraction Angiography Generation
reviewer_1_strengths: The paper is well written, with a clear structure and a smooth, logical flow. The motivation is effectively presented, and the design is described and explained in a clear and coherent manner. The results provide convincing evidence that the proposed method achieves higher reconstruction accuracy compared to the referenced approaches.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: While the paper is generally well articulated, the clarity of several arguments could be improved. For example, (1) in the Introduction, the limitations of existing methods are presented as factual statements but are not supported by references. These sentences should be revised to clarify whether they reflect established findings or the authors’ own interpretations, and appropriate citations should be added where necessary. (2) Similarly, in the Methods section, the statement “Continuous latent spaces often encode stochastic motion artifacts and high-frequency noise indistinguishably from the vascular signal” should be supported with relevant references. How to justify the use of SSIM and RMAE as quantitative metrics, when the referenced “ground truth” image contain motion artifacts? The authors should perhaps dicuss.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1) The work makes a significant departure from standard single-scale continuous latent representations. By introducing the first hierarchical VQ-VAE specifically for the DSA task, the authors effectively resolve the feature averaging problem common in global compression. This multi-scale approach ensures that high-fidelity details of tiny collateral vessels are preserved, even at high compression ratios that typically cause loss of signal in conventional models. 2) The integration of a multi-scale window-based cross-attention mechanism provides a sophisticated framework for soft subtraction. Unlike traditional rigid subtraction, this localized attention allows the model to remain highly robust to the non-rigid local misalignments and physiological motion that typically degrade the clinical gold standard. This ensures a cleaner vascular reconstruction without the ghosting artifacts common in manual or simple automated methods. 3) An extensive comparative analysis against a wide array of state-of-the-art baselines supports the paper. By evaluating the PH-VQVAE using a diverse set of metrics, including PSNR, SSIM, RMAE, and LPIPS, the authors provide comprehensive quantitative proof that their hierarchical discrete modeling outperforms existing continuous generative approaches in both mathematical accuracy and perceptual realism.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1) Limited Generalizability and Domain Robustness: The study relies exclusively on a single dataset for both training and testing, which fails to account for domain shift. In clinical practice, performance can vary significantly across different X-ray hardware, imaging protocols (e.g., varying kVp or dose levels), and patient populations. Without cross-dataset validation, it remains unclear whether the PH-VQVAE can maintain its accuracy when deployed in diverse clinical environments. 2) Constraints of Discrete Codebook Representation: While the hierarchical discrete codebook effectively filters noise, it introduces a risk of quantization error. Because the model forces the reconstruction to match a finite set of learned patterns, there is a potential clinical risk of pathology smoothing. Rare vascular structures might be incorrectly mapped to “normal” vessel prototypes in the codebook, leading to the loss of critical diagnostic details.
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1) The proposed model is overall a sound design, as the employed strategies, such as cross-attention and vector quantization, have been successfully employed for many medical image analysis areas. The overall methodology and illustration are straightforward to understand. 2) The experiments include an ablation study and a comparative study and are thus relatively comprehensive. The ablation study is detailed and clear, successfully validating the components of the proposed model. The qualitative results are nicely visualized and presented.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1) The positioning of the proposed method is a bit unclear. Although VQVAE can be regarded as a generative model, its usage in this paper is more similar to a discriminative model. In fact, the proposed model is similar to a U-Net with a modified encoder and regularized latents. From this perspective, some of the compared approaches, such as the diffusion model, might not be appropriate for comparison. Besides, AaDSA, one of the state-of-the-art methods, does not use the mask image, not because the authors did not realize its importance, but because the research objective of AaDSA was to achieve subtraction-free DSA generation. However, the proposed model in this paper employs the mask image, leading to a potentially unfair experimental setup and comparison, and weakening the merit of the proposed model. 2) The motivation for the conducted improvements is insufficiently illustrated. For instance, the paper claims that the employed window-based cross-attention can perform a soft subtraction in the feature space. However, cross-attention is a general computational technique for representation learning that is widely used in deep learning. The connection between it and the soft subtraction in the feature space is unclear, and the paper shows no evidence to validate this argument. Besides, the cross-attention involves nothing like subtraction within it. To sum up, the utilization of techniques such as cross-attention and vector quantization is too general and optimized little with respect to the properties of the DSA generation task. 3) Some arguments are vague and a bit exaggerated. For instance, the paper claims, “Continuous latent spaces often encode stochastic motion artifacts and high-frequency noise indistinguishably from the vascular signal” on page 4.This is a very strong claim, and the paper does not give any theoretical or intuitive explanations to support it. In fact, most state-of-the-art research works related to vascular image analysis employ regular continuous latent representations instead of discrete ones. The paper seems to directly associate the performance improvements with some assumed functionalities of the employed techniques, which can hardly be convincing.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for their constructive feedback (R1/R2: 5, R3: 3). We address the major concerns below. 1.More Fair Comparison (R3) We added a comparison with the latest DSA imaging method, VCC-DSA, which was published online in MIA in April after our submission [Ge et al. MIA2026]. VCC-DSA also uses the mask image as an auxiliary input. After careful reproduction, VCC-DSA achieved PSNR 30.26, SSIM 0.899, and LPIPS 0.269, while our method performs better, especially in perceptual quality (LPIPS 0.085 vs. 0.269). For AaDSA, we agree that the input discrepancy should be addressed. In the original manuscript, we had already compared AaDSA with our contrast-only variant, where both methods use only the contrast image. Under this fair setting, our method improves PSNR 27.35 → 28.11, RMAE 2.26 → 2.00, and LPIPS 0.231 → 0.181, with comparable SSIM. We further added a dual-input comparison by upgrading AaDSA with a mask+contrast dual-branch encoder, termed AaDSA-Mask, and comparing it with our dual-branch concatenation baseline without cross-attention. Our model still performs better: SSIM 0.936 vs. 0.926, PSNR 32.33 vs. 31.90, and LPIPS 0.102 vs. 0.115.These results show that the improvement is not simply due to using the mask image, but comes from the proposed task-specific design. 2.Unclear Claims and Motivations (R1&R2&R3) a) Claims on continuous spaces. Our statement was grounded in prior work. Specifically, prior studies have reported that continuous representations can be vulnerable to error accumulation [CVPR 2022], while VQ latent space can prevent input interference, such as noise and artifacts[MICCAI 2024]. We will soften the claims in the revision and add missing citations. b) Task-specific design and quantization risks. Our cross-attention and VQ are not generic plug-ins but are specifically designed for DSA: i. The key challenge of DSA generation is to remove background structures shared by the mask image and contrast image while preserving contrast-enhanced vessels that only appear in the contrast image. Therefore, we separately encode the mask and contrast images, then perform cross-attention between their latent features. This allows the model to suppress shared background structures, e.g., bone and soft tissue, while enhancing contrast-filled vessels. In this sense, the module performs soft subtraction in latent space, avoiding artifacts caused by pixel-wise hard subtraction under mask–contrast misregistration. Thus, the dual-branch encoding with cross-attention is a task-specific design for DSA rather than a generic attention module. The ablation also supports its effectiveness: Concatenation / Ours — SSIM: 0.936 / 0.940, PSNR: 32.33 / 33.07, LPIPS: 0.102 / 0.095. ii. To avoid the fine-detail loss of standard single-scale VQ, we adopt a hierarchical VQ design to mitigate the quantization risks. With tri-scale VQ, coarse levels preserve global topology while finer levels retain vessel details. Thus, VQ is also tailored to DSA’s need for both artifact suppression and fine-vessel fidelity. 3.Generalizability and Dataset Diversity (R1 & R2) Although our data were collected from a single institution, the dataset is clinically diverse. It spans 6 years of acquisition, includes images from GE and Siemens scanners, and covers different artifact severities as well as both Anteroposterior (AP) and Lateral (LAT) projection views. To further assess generalizability, we evaluated the model separately on AP and LAT views. The results were consistent across views: AP / LAT — SSIM: 0.939 / 0.941, PSNR: 33.01 / 33.11, RMAE: 1.18 / 1.17, LPIPS: 0.100 / 0.089.These results indicate that the model maintains robust performance across different projection views. Reference: 1.Gu et al., CVPR 2022, Vector Quantized Diffusion Model for Text-to-Image Synthesis 2.Han et al., MICCAI 2024, Non-Adversarial Learning: Vector-Quantized Common Latent Space for Multi-Sequence MRI 3.Ge et al. MIA 2026, VCC-DSA
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper proposes a prior-guided hierarchical VQ-VAE framework for DSA generation that aims to improve background suppression and vessel preservation. Reviewers agree the method is well designed with strong empirical performance and clear presentation. I suggest that the authors clarify the raised concerns about 1) unclear motivation and positioning, 2) potentially unfair comparisons, and 3) limited validation of key claims. | The reviewers generally agree that the paper is well presented and proposes a sound prior-guided hierarchical VQ-VAE framework for DSA generation. The rebuttal clarifies several concerns regarding the motivation, positioning, and role of the proposed components. Overall, I would recommend acceptance. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper proposes a dual-branch encoder with cross-attention between reference and contrast images, coupled with a hierarchical VQ-VAE, for DSA reconstruction. The reviewers’ majority opinion is positive. R2 is strongly positive, viewing the hierarchical discrete representation as a meaningful departure from single-scale continuous latents and crediting the extensive benchmarking against SOTA baselines. R3 is negative, judging that the method is positioned as generative but functions more like a discriminative U-Net, and that several claims are made without evidence or are overconfident. My view is that the design is well suited to the DSA task and the empirical results are convincing enough to merit acceptance. That said, R3’s concerns are valid and partly echoed by R1, and the authors are strongly encouraged to add the missing citations and to temper or substantiate the soft-subtraction and continuous-latent claims in the final version. Finally, regarding the additional results in the rebuttal, which are in violation of the ‘no new results’ policy, R3 rightfully does not sway their opinion, and the other reviewers are already positive, and thus the rebuttal did not influence my final recommendation. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): There are concerns of adding new experimental results to support arguments which does not comply with the rebuttal guidelines.

title: Probabilistic Multi-rater Segmentation via Style-Aware Boundary Conditioning
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.Clear clinical motivation: Modeling inter-rater variability as structured style is clinically meaningful and better than treating disagreement as noise. 2.Clear problem-solving design: SCP avoids freezing shared features and enables boundary-aware personalization, which is more suitable for fine-grained medical segmentation than existing methods like D-Persona. 3.Novel and effective loss design: DABL explicitly emphasizes regions of inter-rater disagreement, improving alignment between model uncertainty and clinical ambiguity. 4.Lightweight and efficient: SCP introduces only ~0.11M parameters. 5.Comprehensive and rigorous experiments: Validations cover multi-rater segmentation, distribution fitting, diversity, calibration, robustness to label noise, and ablations.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.Lack of causal validation for uncertainty alignment: Although uncertainty correlates with expert disagreement, the paper does not rigorously verify that this alignment is caused by SCP and DABL rather than probabilistic modeling or longer training. 2.Two-stage training is suboptimal: Freezing the probabilistic backbone in Phase II prevents end-to-end optimization and may limit representation alignment. No comparison with joint training is provided. 3.The paper lacks discussion on: cross-modality / cross-organ generalization, performance on extremely ambiguous or small lesions, and comparison with inter-rater human agreement (e. g. , Kappa).
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: A key strength of this work is its conceptual shift in how multi-rater annotations are modeled. Instead of collapsing annotations into a consensus or treating disagreement as label noise, the paper explicitly models variability as a structured, preference-driven phenomenon. This is operationalized through a disentangled representation of shared anatomical content and rater-specific “style,” which is both intuitive and clinically meaningful. This formulation aligns well with how experts actually differ in practice, primarily along boundary interpretation, making the approach more promising to real-world annotation processes The proposed Style-Conditioned Personalization is a notable technical contribution. Unlike prior approaches that rely on separate heads or post-hoc adaptation, SCP conditions intermediate feature representations using rater-specific embeddings. This enables fine-grained, rater-dependent adjustments during decoding, allowing the model to recover subtle boundary variations that would otherwise be lost in a shared representation. Importantly, this is achieved without duplicating the decoder, making the design both expressive and efficient . Another key strength is the Disagreement-Aware Boundary Loss , which focuses supervision on regions where annotators disagree. By constructing a boundary band around disagreement areas, the method emphasizes clinically meaningful uncertainty while maintaining stability in regions of agreement. This aligns the learning objective with the true source of ambiguity in medical segmentation tasks . The integration of probabilistic modeling with personalization is also well executed. The latent space captures distributional ambiguity, while the style mechanism encodes annotator-specific preferences, resulting in diverse yet controlled predictions. Empirically, the method demonstrates consistent improvements across multiple datasets and metrics, including both diversity and per-rater accuracy Finally, the approach remains lightweight, adding minimal computational overhead, and shows strong uncertainty calibration aligned with inter-rater disagreement, which is particularly important for clinical applicability.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The paper provides limited evidence of clinical impact. Experiments are conducted on standard benchmarks without demonstrating how personalized outputs would influence real clinical workflows. Moreover, the reported failure cases suggest a bias toward majority annotations, potentially limiting the model’s ability to capture minority but clinically relevant interpretations. Also, novelty is another concern, since the method mainly builds on existing probabilistic U-Net and multi-rater personalization frameworks, with the main contributions coming from extensions in conditioning and loss design rather than a fundamentally new approach. Some of the detailed comments here: In Eq. (2), the rater-specific modulation is defined as a Gaussian-like excitation. There is no justification that such a distribution adequately captures complex annotator behaviors, which may be multi-modal or spatially varying. For DABL steps, these steps introduce hyperparameters (τ,λ,α) that directly influence optimization but are not systematically analyzed The two-stage optimization in Eq. (7) where the backbone is frozen before training SCP. This may prevent gradients from DABL and personalization from refining earlier feature representations, resulting in suboptimal alignment between shared and rater-specific components
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The paper’s main strengths lie in its principled treatment of inter-rater variability as structured information rather than noise, enabled by a well-designed style-conditioned personalization (SCP) module that captures fine-grained, rater-specific boundary preferences without requiring heavy architectural duplication, making it both effective and parameter-efficient; its novel disagreement-aware boundary loss (DABL), which focuses supervision on clinically meaningful regions of annotator disagreement and improves boundary precision and uncertainty alignment; and its integration within a probabilistic framework that generates diverse yet anatomically consistent segmentations with well-calibrated uncertainty. Additionally, the method demonstrates consistent empirical gains over strong baselines across multiple datasets, while maintaining minimal computational overhead and producing outputs that better reflect real expert variability.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: While the proposed SCP module improves personalization, the method still relies on a two-stage training procedure with partial freezing, which may limit full end-to-end optimization and adaptation of shared features to rater-specific nuances; the approach introduces additional design complexity (e.g., style tokens, FiLM modulation, boundary weighting) without fully isolating which components contribute most, and ablations remain somewhat limited; the evaluation, although strong, is confined to a few benchmarks and lacks deeper analysis of generalization to unseen raters or domains, which is critical for real clinical deployment; the method assumes access to multiple annotations per image during training, restricting applicability in annotation-scarce settings; and finally, while DABL focuses on disagreement regions, it may overemphasize boundaries at the expense of interior consistency, and its hyperparameters (e.g., band width, weighting) require tuning and are not extensively studied.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal

title: ProMoE-FL: Prototype-conditioned Mixture of Experts for Multimodal Federated Learning with Missing Modalities
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.It has strong robustness and can effectively solve the data heterogeneity problem in federated scenarios. ProMoE-FL introduces a client-aware global prototype library, which can capture cross-institutional modal priors and adapt to the data differences of different medical centers. In the heterogeneous scenarios of real clinical settings, its performance is significantly better than that of traditional interpolation methods, and it solves the problem of poor generalization of traditional methods. 2.It does not rely on public data, and is more practical. Unlike existing methods such as CAR-MFL, ProMoE-FL only relies on private data from each client for training, without the need for additional public data. This avoids the problems of scarce public data and restricted privacy in medical scenarios, and better meets the actual needs of clinical federated learning. 3.The feature synthesis quality is high, and key clinical diagnostic information is retained. Through prototype condition constraints and a hybrid expert routing mechanism, the features synthesized by ProMoE-FL are highly consistent with the real features, can retain key clinical structures such as lung lesions, and avoid feature distortion caused by simple interpolation, providing support for diagnostic tasks.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The prototype bank relies heavily on high-quality multimodal client data. If multimodal clients are scarce, poorly annotated, or suffer from modality bias, the quality of the global prototype bank will degrade, which in turn hurts model performance. 2.The MoE structure increases model complexity and communication overhead. Although the expert design avoids parameter redundancy, it is more complex than simple imputation methods and requires extra coordination between experts and the prototype bank during federated training, raising communication costs. 3.The model’s adaptability to extreme missing-modality scenarios is not fully validated. Experiments only cover conventional missing modality settings. In extremely unbalanced cases, the prototype bank may fail to learn reliable cross-modal relations, and the generalization ability remains untested.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and practically important problem in medical federated learning: missing modalities across institutions. This is a realistic setting in clinical practice, where different sites often have incomplete access to images, reports, or other modalities. Methodologically, the paper proposes a coherent combination of prototype-based conditioning and mixture-of-experts routing. The idea of using a client-aware prototype bank to guide feature synthesis is reasonable and well-motivated for heterogeneous federated settings. The use of a shared MoE design is also sensible from a modeling perspective, as it aims to improve flexibility while avoiding separate generators for each modality pair. The experimental section is relatively broad. The paper evaluates the method on four public chest X-ray datasets and includes both homogeneous and heterogeneous federated partitions, which is stronger than a single-dataset or single-split evaluation. The results are generally consistent and show meaningful gains, especially in the heterogeneous setting, which is arguably the most relevant scenario. I also appreciate that the method does not rely on an external public multimodal dataset by default, unlike some prior approaches. This makes the setting more realistic for healthcare. In addition, qualitative analyses of synthesized features and rare pathologies are useful and support the empirical findings.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The main weakness is that the empirical validation is still not up to the standard expected for a top-tier conference. While the reported downstream AUC improvements are promising, the paper provides only limited direct evidence that the synthesized missing-modality features are truly faithful and clinically meaningful. The t-SNE/UMAP visualizations are useful, but they are still indirect. A more rigorous quantitative evaluation of synthesis quality would substantially improve the paper. A second concern is the reporting of results. The paper states that results are averaged over three random seeds, but standard deviations are reported only for the proposed method, not for competing baselines. This makes it difficult to judge the statistical significance and fairness of the comparison. In addition, the evaluation relies almost entirely on macro-AUC. In a medical multi-label setting, it would also be preferable to report other metrics, such as PR-AUC, F1, sensitivity/specificity, or calibration-related measures. A third weakness is that the computational and communication costs are not adequately analyzed. Since the method introduces multiple experts, routing, prototype banks, and extra modules beyond the base federated model, the paper should report parameter counts, training/inference overhead, and server-client communication cost. This is particularly important in federated learning, where communication efficiency is a central consideration. Relatedly, although the paper presents gating visualizations suggesting balanced expert usage, it does not provide an explicit mechanism, regularizer, or stronger quantitative analysis to rule out expert collapse or degenerate routing behavior. The current evidence is suggestive, but not yet fully convincing. The ablation study is also limited. The paper compares MoE against a single PCD in a single heterogeneous setting, which is helpful, but additional ablations would strengthen the claims. For example, it would be useful to isolate the effect of the prototype bank, the accumulation strategy, the number of experts, and the routing design. A major weakness is that the proposed method appears substantially closer to prior feature-imputation approaches than the paper currently acknowledges, particularly “Multimodal Federated Learning With Missing Modalities through Feature Imputation Network”. At a high level, both works follow the same core paradigm: learning cross-modal feature completion from multimodal clients and using the synthesized bottleneck features to support unimodal clients during federated training. In the current submission, the main differences lie in the introduction of a prototype-conditioned mechanism and a mixture-of-experts routing strategy. However, these additions appear to extend rather than fundamentally redefine the original framework. As a result, the contribution may be better characterized as an architectural enhancement of the Feature Imputation Network paradigm rather than a conceptually distinct approach. This impression is further reinforced by the highly similar visual presentation. The overall pipeline figure adopts a closely related graphical style, module arrangement, and narrative decomposition (e.g., a federated system overview, multimodal vs. unimodal client training, and a dedicated feature synthesis block between the encoders and the classifier). Such similarity in both methodology and presentation makes the novelty claim less convincing. The authors should more clearly articulate how their method fundamentally differs from and advances beyond the Feature Imputation Network framework. Finally, the method’s stress testing is not sufficiently comprehensive. The client splits still retain some multimodal clients. An extreme setting in which all or nearly all clients are single-modality would better test the approach’s robustness and limits. This would be especially relevant for the paper’s practical claims. author_feedback: We thank all reviewers for recognizing the clinical relevance(R1-R3), technical soundness(R2), rigorous validation(R1, R2), practical value(R1, R2), novelty(R1) and clarity(R3) of our work. Clarification of Novelty [R2]: Like FeatImp([21]), ProMoE-FL operates in feature space and synthesizes missing-modality features, but is fundamentally distinct in robustness and design. Rather than relying solely on present features, we guide synthesis via a global prototype bank as a federation-wide prior capturing complementary modality information. Client-aware prototypes handle non-IID shifts, mitigating client drift (Tab.1, hetero.). Our MoE architecture dynamically routes transformations per instance, avoiding rigid static mappings. Deviations and More Metrics [R2, R3]: We follow the evaluation setup and AUC metrics of prior works ([21, 22]). We report std. for ProMoE-FL to demonstrate stability across random seeds; notably, our lower bound consistently surpasses the mean of the strongest baseline e.g., in 8:0:2 hetero., our lower bound of 78.16 exceeds FeatImp’s mean of 77.15.Further, our avg std. of 0.78 is lower than FeatImp’s 0.88, showing greater stability. Per reviewer feedback, we will include standard deviations for all baselines upon revision. Communication Overhead [R1-R3]: The only additional parameters are the lightweight prototype bank and routing mechanism, comprising ~0.3% of total parameters. MoE also enables favorable scaling with modality count rather than combinatorial growth. We will clarify this in the final version. Multimodal Reliance & Extreme Missing Modalities [R1, R2]: Our client-aware prototype bank incorporates unimodal client prototypes, mitigating reliance on multimodal clients. Following prior works ([21, 22]), our 8:0:2, 4:4:2, and 0:8:2 configurations leave only 20% of clients multimodal, reflecting realistic extreme settings. Unlike prior works evaluating a single heterogeneous setting, we also stress-test across 9 configurations. Clarity, Hyperparameters & Convergence [R1-R3]: All presentation issues (reference formatting, non-IID definition, capitalization, placement of the “to the best of” statement) will be corrected in the revision. The hyperparameter λ = 0.05 is tuned over {0.01, 0.05, 0.10} and remains robust across all configurations. Convergence was stable across runs, evidenced by consistent validation metrics. Implementation details will be released with source code and replication guidelines upon acceptance. Generalization beyond Chest X-ray [R1]: ProMoE-FL is modality-agnostic by design, formulated for an arbitrary set of modalities. Chest X-ray and radiology reports were chosen for their large-scale heterogeneous datasets suitable to stress-test a federated architecture. MoE Ablations [R2, R3]: The 8:0:2 setting was chosen as the most challenging configuration (Tab.1), making component contributions most distinguishable under stress. Our ablation explicitly isolates contributions of the prototype bank and MoE module. Fig. 2(c) shows balanced expert utilization; experts are not specialized per synthesis direction. Routing behavior analysis remains a valuable future direction. Feature Visualizations [R2]: Downstream AUC is a rigorous measure of synthesis quality as poor synthesis would directly degrade classification performance, strongly supported by our consistent SOTA results. t-SNE/UMAP visualizations provide complementary qualitative evidence. CLIP-based Approaches [R3]: FACMIC and pFedST do not handle missing modalities, making direct comparison methodologically unfair. Our framework is encoder-agnostic and makes no design assumptions specific to image-text pairs. Specific Performance Discrepancy [R3]: The 4:0:6 vs. 6:0:4 trend is consistent across all methods. In homogeneous settings, fewer multimodal clients reduce available cross-modal prior information. Under heterogeneity, multimodal priors may introduce distributional bias during unimodal synthesis, degrading performance.

reviewer_3_strengths: The work is well motivated, as it brings together open-set active learning and federated active learning in a medical imaging setting, where both privacy constraints and data quality issues are highly relevant. In practice, active learning can easily mistake OOD samples for highly informative ones, leading to wasted annotation budget. Addressing this problem is therefore both meaningful and practically important. The proposed method is lightweight, introducing only a small number of additional parameters, while effectively narrowing the performance gap between open-set and closed-set settings. The gains on intermediate metrics are particularly clear, suggesting that the method is effective at improving sample selection quality. The global/local prompt decomposition is also a reasonably novel design in the federated setting. The global prompts are intended to capture shared semantic knowledge across clients, while the local prompts adapt to client-specific OOD characteristics. This design is well aligned with the realistic heterogeneity across hospitals and medical centers, where scanner types, acquisition protocols, and artifact distributions often differ substantially.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: In Sec 2.2, the paper first defines p_c^k(x) and \hat{y}^k(x), stating that “PromptGate filters U^(r)_k into an ID-candicate pool”. Immediately after, it defines p_c^k(x) and \hat{y}^k(x) again and repeats very similar line “PromptGate filters U^(r)_k into an ID-candicate pool(VLM-gated)”. it’s repetitive and confusing. Insufficient analysis of early-round instability: 1.The manuscript notes that query precision (QP) can dip at round 2 after the first CoOp update on a small 128-shot subset, but provides no analysis of how severe or common this is across clients. 2.There is no experiments show whether this early instability could lead to the irreversible loss of informative ID samples that are incorrectly gated out, potentially harming final model performance even though it’s mentioned in Sec 2.2 that“empirically, ID leakage into \epsilon_k^(r) is negligible.”. The description of the gating mechanism is also somewhat unclear. Although the paper refers to a “high-confidence ID candidate pool” and defines p_max(x), the actual formulation only keeps samples whose argmax prediction belongs to an ID class, without using an explicit confidence threshold. It is therefore unclear whether the gate is category-based or confidence-based. Some implementation details should also be clarified, such as whether prompt learning is retrained at each round or updated incrementally, and how the temperature parameter is selected. Finally, although the paper highlights the mixed global+local prompt design, the results suggest that the Local variant is often the strongest or most stable. This raises the question of whether the main benefit comes from local personalization rather than federated global aggregation. More complete statistics and ablations, such as different OOD ratios, initial labeled-set sizes, prompt token numbers, and per-client performance, would strengthen the paper.
