author_feedback: We sincerely thank the AC, R1, R2, and R3.All reviewers find the work “well motivated”, the “experimental design strong and thorough” (R1), “clinical problem and technical solution working well” (R1), and “serves as an acquisition-agnostic, plug-and-play gating module” (R2). [R2, AC] Novelty over FOCoOp, FedOTP, and FedPHA. We are glad this concurrent work validates our global/local prompt decomposition, but all three address closed-set federated classification on fixed labeled datasets. FedOTP uses UOT over patches; FedPHA uses SVD projection; FOCoOp trains OOD pseudo-prompts with post-hoc MCM scoring — none has an acquisition gate, an unlabeled pool, or a mechanism to consume the supervised non-target label OS-FAL provides. PromptGate contributes: (a) the first learnable-prompt VLM gate for OS-FAL (CSC CoOp, global/local decomposition, (K+1)-class cross-entropy); (b) decoupling gate from acquisition rule; (c) converting OS-FAL into approximately closed-set AL across 6 strategies x 2 datasets. Prompts are warm-started and refined each AL round from oracle labels, progressively sharpening the ID/OOD boundary — driven by the AL loop itself, absent from all three papers. We will add them to the related work. [R2, R3, AC] Local outperforms Mixed, is global aggregation necessary? No single configuration dominates universally. Table 1: Local leads on Random, FEAL, and LfOSA on FedISIC; Global leads on OpenPath (86.6 purity, 64.4 BMA) and FEAL purity; FedEMBED follows the same mixed pattern. The right choice depends on OOD variability across clients: when OOD artifacts are similar across sites, global prompts capture a stronger shared prior; when OOD is client-specific (as in FedISIC), local adaptation is more beneficial. We offer all three as dataset-dependent options; global aggregation always preserves privacy-preserving collaboration and distributed annotation cost across institutions that cannot share patient data. [R2] Necessity of filtering on FedEMBED. Two factors explain the small BMA gaps: (1) OOD prevalence is low (4.8-13.2%), so unfiltered AL is already mostly ID by chance; (2) FedEMBED OOD labels are pseudo-labels. The decisive test is FedISIC (50% OOD): PromptGate yields +22% purity and +0-6% BMA across all 6 strategies. In short, PromptGate is safe under low-OOD and substantially helpful under high-OOD, precisely what clinical deployment requires. [R3] Gating mechanism. The gate is category-based over K+1 classes: x is retained iff y-hat^k(x) in {1,…,K}. We avoided an explicit confidence threshold to prevent ambiguity with Entropy-based AL scores; implicit confidence filtering is achieved via the temperature-scaled softmax — we will clarify this in the text. [R3] Early-round instability in FedISIC and ID leakage. The round-2 QP dip has two compounding causes. First, at R=1 the VLM has seen only 128 shots and remains uncertain about OOD; uncertainty-based strategies (Entropy, FEAL, PAL, LfOSA) select ambiguous samples, disproportionately OOD, dragging QP down. This holds for the baseline (Static VLM as well). Second, reported QP values are means across 3 seeds x 6 AL methods, so uncertainty-based methods dominate (Entropy: 11.0%, FEAL: 11.6%, PAL: 14.1%, LfOSA: 15.8%; Random: 61% OpenPath: 97.9%). From R=3 onward, as the VLM accumulates oracle labels, this vanishes, and QP recovers to near-perfect. Samples in epsilon_k^(r) are not permanently removed: they remain in U_k and are re-evaluated each round. On FedISIC, all variants stabilise at ≤ 1.3% leakage, meaning ≥ 98.7% of true-ID samples are correctly retained in the ID pool, replacing the informal “negligible” claim. [R3] Implementation details. Prompts are updated incrementally each round (15 epochs SGD, warm-started). tau_VLM = 0.0117 follows BiomedCLIP convention. Details will be added to Sec. 2.3.[R1, R3] Writing clarity. We will: a) align the abstract open-set phrasing with Sec. 2.1; b) rewrite Sec. 1; c) remove the duplicate definitions in Sec 2.2

title: PromptMedCT: A Training-Free LLM-Guided Framework for Volumetric CT Data Realization with Quantifiable Disease Manifestations and Multi-Tier Annotations

The synthetic-to-real evaluation, although encouraging, remains limited to segmentation performance; additional downstream tasks or broader benchmarks would further strengthen the claims. The reliance on predefined lesion dictionaries and template databases may limit diversity and realism in more complex or rare pathological scenarios.

title: ProSMA-UNet: Decoder Conditioning for Proximal-Sparse Skip Feature Selection
reviewer_1_strengths: 1) The paper addresses a real and important weakness of U-shaped segmentation networks: skip connections are useful for localisation, but they can also leak low-level clutter and bypass semantic filtering. That motivation is sensible, especially in low-contrast medical images, and the paper stays focused on that specific design problem rather than trying to overcomplicate the architecture. 2) I like the technical clarity of the proposed mechanism. The method is easy to follow: construct a compatibility field from encoder and decoder features, enforce sparsity with a proximal l1 step, and then use spatial and channel gating together. Figure 1 communicates the idea well, especially the contrast between standard soft attention and explicit sparse selection with exact zeros. 3) The use of a proximal operator for skip gating is also an interesting design choice. Even if the underlying soft-thresholding idea is mathematically standard, its use here as a skip-filtering mechanism is reasonably novel in this context. The paper’s framing of skip fusion as feature selection rather than merely reweighting is conceptually sound. 4) The empirical results are broadly positive. On the reported 2D datasets, the method is consistently strongest, with gains over prior baselines on BUSI, GlaS, and Kvasir-SEG. On 3D, the improvement on Colon is particularly large, with F1 rising from 53.05 to 63.14 over the strongest listed baseline, while Spleen also improves modestly. The method therefore appears effective across both 2D and 3D settings. 5) The ablation study is simple but useful. It suggests that sparse spatial selection contributes the larger gain, while channel gating adds complementary value. That is at least consistent with the method’s intended design.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1) It is not clear to me if the experimental comparison is fully balanced. On the 2D side, some baseline results are taken directly from prior work rather than reproduced here under a unified training protocol, and UKAN2.0 is missing on GlaS due to memory limits. That weakens the SOTA claim somewhat, because not all methods are being compared on equal footing. The paper also explicitly states that for BUSI and GlaS some baselines are taken from U-KAN under the same protocol, rather than rerun here. 2) The strongest gains occur on the 3D Colon task, but the paper does not provide enough analysis of why the gain is so large there. A nearly 10-point F1 jump over the best baseline is substantial. That could be a genuine strength, but it also demands more scrutiny: was Colon especially sensitive to noisy skip features, were there optimisation differences, or is the baseline set simply too narrow? At the moment the paper reports the number, but does not really explain it. 3) Related to that, the 3D baseline set feels limited. The comparison is against 3D U-Net, U-KAN 3D, and UKAN2.0 3D, but not against stronger contemporary 3D segmentation baselines such as nnU-Net-style pipelines or other established 3D U-Net variants like UNETR or Swin UNETR. Given that the method is a skip-connection modification rather than a wholesale architectural replacement, it would have been more convincing to compare against stronger and more standard 3D medical segmentation baselines. 4) The narrative around ‘explicit noise removal’ is plausible but not yet fully evidenced. Figure 1 is intuitive and the qualitative examples are encouraging, but the paper does not directly measure sparsity levels, feature suppression patterns, or whether harmful skip activations are actually reduced in a meaningful way. In other words, the mechanism is interpretable in theory, but the empirical validation of that interpretation is still limited. 5) Since ProSMA adds multiple components at each skip connection, a complexity analysis in terms of parameter count, FLOPs, memory footprint, or inference time is needed. Otherwise, it remains unclear whether the gains reflect better skip selection or are partly explained by increased parameter count and computational budget.

reviewer_3_strengths: 1.Underexplored problem: Semi-supervised learning for dense regression in 3D medical volumes is a real gap in the literature, most SSL work focuses on classification or segmentation. author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and AC for their comments. We will release the code and provide the public dataset (Cohort B) download link upon acceptance. Below are our responses. A. Method novelty/description. [R2-W1, R3-W4] Related methods. Resp: We thank the reviewers for pointing out CPCL, UPCoL, DyCON, and related uncertainty-estimation methods. These studies mainly rely on discrete category-level signals, e.g., class predictions or probability maps. Our task is continuous voxel-wise regression, where pseudo-targets have no categorical confidence scores. Their uncertainty formulations are therefore not directly applicable as baselines. We will cite these works and clarify differences from ProtoReg. [R2-W2, R3-W3] Difference from DyCON. Resp: ProtoReg differs from DyCON in two key aspects. First, DyCON estimates uncertainty from discrete segmentation probabilities, while ProtoReg models uncertainty from continuous functional values through functional prototypes. This bridges discrete prototype learning and continuous voxel-wise regression, providing reliability signals for pseudo-targets without class probabilities. Second, DyCON performs voxel/pixel-level uncertainty weighting, while DUW-CL computes reliability-weighted consistency at both voxel and anatomically meaningful lung-sub-unit levels. This captures regional functional continuity and suppresses fragmented pseudo-label noise. We will add these clarifications. [R2-W3, R3-W1, W2] Notation and weighting schedule. Resp: We will check all notations and further define β before Eq. (8), clarifying its role in DUW-CL. In DUW-CL, w always gives higher weights to low-entropy predictions, while β controls entropy-weighting strength. As β decays, the gap between low- and high-entropy weights becomes smaller, smoothly expanding training from highly reliable regions to broader consistency refinement. B. Data/preprocessing clarification. [R3-W5, R3-W6, R5-W5] Preprocessing and dataset split. Resp: We will further add preprocessing and split details. Paired volumes were pre-registered and processed using a standardized pipeline [16,17]. Original CT/SPECT sizes are approximately 512×512×200 and 128^3.Only the pre-segmented lung ROI was resampled to 128^3, preserving CT–SPECT spatial correspondence and minimizing task-relevant information loss. Cohorts A/B use separate fixed 80/20 train/test splits; 25% of training is used for validation, and labeled/unlabeled splits are applied only to the remaining training data. Test sets contain 48/20 cases, and results are per-case mean±SD. C. Results/statistics clarification. [R5-W1, A1] Statistical Significance. Resp: We have conducted metric-wise paired statistical tests against UniMatchV2-Reg and will report p-values in the revision. ProtoReg achieves statistically significant improvements (p<0.05) over UniMatchV2-Reg on most metrics under most settings. Under Cohort A 20%, ProtoReg reaches p<0.05 on SSIM, MAE, and FL20.On Cohort B, most metrics also reach p<0.05 under both 100% and 20% settings. [R5-A2, W2] SSL performance on Cohort B. Resp: We will clarify this in the revision. Several SSL baselines underperform Sup-only in Cohort B 100%, likely due to domain shift or pseudo-label noise when full-label supervision is strong. ProtoReg mitigates this through prototype-induced uncertainty and dual-level weighting. [R5-W3, W4, A3] Ablation. Resp: We will clarify the ablation findings. LSV-level weighting achieves statistically significant improvements in MAE, SSIM, and FL20.These metrics better reflect functional-region consistency and clinically relevant spatial fidelity, while Spearman ρ mainly measures global rank correlation and is less sensitive to local structural improvements. Due to page limits, we reported Cohort A 20% ablations, which best reflect the low-label reliability problem. We also conducted 100%-label ablations with consistent component benefits, and will include them with broader Cohort B analyses in an extended version.

author_feedback: We are glad that reviewers find our work to address a “highly relevant clinical challenge” (R3) with an “interesting, meticulously designed, and novel” method (All), “significant improvements” (R2/R3), “convincing results and comprehensive ablations” (R3). We prioritize the major concerns below. Q1 (R2): Evaluation size and baseline fairness. A1: We used the same official CPAISD split (92/10/10 cases) for all baselines and CPAISD is the only target benchmark for NCCT-only hyperacute tissue-window segmentation with CTP-derived core/penumbra labels. Thus the test set is not 10/367: UniToBrain and ISLES are just auxiliary sources for prototype construction/alignment without extra target labels, while target evaluation follows the official 10/112 CPAISD test set. We also note R2 likely meant CPAISD, not AISD. Yet, we agree that stronger validation is useful and have added 5-fold cross-validation on CPAISD: FT-P-ProPhyT obtains 71.03% Avg. Dice vs 21.20/23.60/48.52/67.50 for nnUNet/nnUNet(Syn.)/BEA-Net/SAM-Med2D(FT-P). Q2 (R1/R2): CTP heterogeneity/harmonization and temporal protocol differences. A2: We agree that CTP acquisition/software variability is important. While we do not explicitly model such heterogeneity, ProPhyT does not directly operate on raw 4D CTP temporal curves. Instead, it learns high-level embeddings from processed 3D CTP perfusion maps, where temporal dynamics have been summarized into physiological parameters such as CBF and Tmax, and retrieves similarity-weighted prototype patterns for robustness to cross-site variations. Top-K aggregation further reduces reliance on any single noisy prototype, consistent with our ablations and R3’s positive assessment. Importantly, we evaluate on the independent CPAISD (NCCT-only, not used in prototype construction/alignment), where strong performance suggests good practical generalization of the learned physiological embedding and retrieval pipeline. Q3 (R1/R3): SparK masked reconstruction and role of the CTP encoder. A3: SparK is used as a masked image modeling-based self-supervised learning method, where representations are learned by reconstructing hidden regions from visual context without external labels. During pretraining, SparK includes an encoder and a lightweight decoder; the decoder supplies the reconstruction loss and is discarded afterward. Only the pretrained CTP encoder is retained to define the hemodynamic embedding space and construct the prototype bank. The pretrained NCCT encoder is then aligned to this space for prototype retrieval. We have revised Fig. 2 to show the decoder as a dashed pretraining-only branch. Q4 (R1): ISLES final infarct as proxy core. A4: We agree that follow-up final infarct is not equivalent to baseline ischemic core. Thus, ISLES labels are not used as target ground truth; CPAISD is the only dataset for supervised core/penumbra training and evaluation. In ISLES, the final-infarct mask is used only during NCCT-CTP retrieval learning as a weak outcome-derived lesion prior: representations of lesion-similar cases are pulled closer, while unrelated cases are separated. This makes cross-modal alignment lesion-aware and reduces domination by normal/background similarity, without treating final infarct as an exact core label. We will revise the wording. Q5 (R1/R3): Clarifications on CTP literature, timing, split, τ, baselines, and FT-Auto. A5: We will add Tomasetti et al. and clarify that 4D CTP methods require CTP at inference, while ProPhyT targets NCCT-only missing-perfusion inference. We will correct Fig. 1(c) to overall examination time, not gantry scan duration. The split is correct: 92+10+10=112.We set τ = 0.07.We rename Syn. rows as Pix2Pix+nnU-Net/Swin-UNet with [8]. We have explicitly clarified on Page 7 that detector-derived coarse prompts correspond to our FT-Auto variant, avoiding confusion with the interactive mode. Other minor concerns will be carefully revised. Code will be released to help follow the details.

title: Proxy-CAC: Learning Coronary Calcium Segmentation from Volume-Level Scores
reviewer_1_strengths: Novelty. The authors tackle the problem of segmenting structures from an aggregated measurement (the Agatston score). While generating segmentations from aggregated measurements is a problem tackled in the literature (see [Cano20], below, also in the computation of the Agatston score), the proposed method shows novelty by training on a process non-differentiable score, such as the Agatston. Equations 2-4 are a clever way to make the Agatston discrete value continuous. The approximation of the Agatston score in this work (Eq. 2) is computed in a per-voxel basis. However, in the original score, the computation is in a per lesion basis, as the authors explain in equation 1.It is surprising that with this approximation, the network improves in the phase II. [Cano20] C. Cano-Espinosa, G. González, G. R. Washko, M. Cazorla and R. S. J. Estépar, “Biomarker Localization From Deep Learning Regression Networks,” in IEEE Transactions on Medical Imaging, vol. 39, no. 6, pp. 2121-2132, June 2020, doi: 10.1109/TMI. 2020.2965486.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The authors perform a sequential training, where first a pure segmentation network is trained and then refined with the proposed method. Why to forget the segmentation data after the first step? Wouldn’t it make sense to keep it within the optimization, but evaluating the term of the cost function only on the cases where the data is available? The scans are resampled to 0.3x0.3x3.0 mm. Why such large slice thickness? It is better to show Bland-Altman plots than correlation plots in Fig 2. The comparison of Proxy-CAC against AI-CAC and S2CAC is unfair, as, as the authors acknowledge, testing is done on the Dc dataset, which is out of distribution for the other methods, but not for Proxy-CAC.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.Clinically relevant problem formulation : The paper addresses an important and realistic limitation in medical imaging: the lack of dense annotations in large-scale datasets. Most clinical datasets provide only summary scores (e.g., Agatston score), and leveraging such weak supervision is highly valuable. 2.Scalable use of real-world data : The method is demonstrated on a large dataset (27,700 CT scans), showing the feasibility of scaling beyond small, manually annotated datasets. This is a strong practical contribution. 3.Integration of domain knowledge into learning : The differentiable Agatston approximation incorporates prior clinical knowledge (e.g., HU thresholds and density weighting) into the learning process, which is a meaningful design choice compared to purely data-driven regression approaches. 4.Interpretability-oriented design : Unlike direct regression methods, the proposed framework produces voxel-level outputs, which are potentially useful for clinical verification and interpretability. 5.Generalizable idea : The concept of learning dense predictions from structured clinical endpoints via differentiable proxies could be extended to other medical imaging tasks, making the approach broadly relevant.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.Fundamentally ill-posed problem formulation : Learning voxel-level segmentation from a single scalar Agatston score is inherently underdetermined. Multiple segmentation configurations can produce the same score, meaning the supervision signal does not uniquely constrain the solution. This raises concerns about whether the learned segmentations are anatomically meaningful or simply optimized to match the score. 2.Inaccurate approximation of the Agatston scoring process : The proposed differentiable formulation deviates significantly from the true Agatston definition. The original method operates on connected components (lesions) and uses maximum HU per lesion. The proposed method applies voxel-wise weighting without connectivity constraints. This mismatch may lead to incorrect modeling of lesion structure and reduces clinical fidelity. 3.No quantitative evaluation of segmentation quality : A critical limitation is the absence of standard segmentation metrics (e.g., Dice, IoU). Even though large datasets lack voxel-level labels, the dataset includes ground-truth masks, yet no segmentation performance is reported. This omission significantly weakens the validation of the method. 4.Weak and subjective qualitative evaluation : The qualitative analysis is limited to a small number of examples and relies on informal expert assessment. This is insufficient to support claims of interpretability or clinical reliability. 5.Unclear impact on segmentation vs regression : The reported improvement in Cohen’s kappa may primarily reflect improved score regression rather than better segmentation. Since risk categories are derived from score thresholds, gains in regression accuracy naturally improve classification metrics. 6.Unfair or inconsistent comparison with prior work : The proposed method is evaluated on cropped cardiac ROIs, whereas some baselines are applied to full chest CT scans. This introduces a bias and makes the comparison less reliable. 7.Lack of strong baselines : The comparison is limited to a standard 3D U-Net. More competitive baselines, such as Multi-task learning (segmentation + regression) and direct regression models with auxiliary supervision are not included, making it difficult to assess the true advantage of the method. 8.Limited methodological analysis : Several design choices are not sufficiently justified or analyzed: Use of SMAPE loss instead of standard regression losses Two-phase training with complete removal of segmentation loss in Phase 2 Temperature annealing schedule for the differentiable approximation No ablation or sensitivity analysis is provided. 9.Lack of external validation : The model is evaluated on a single institutional dataset. Generalization to other populations, scanners, or protocols is not demonstrated, limiting clinical applicability. 10.Clinical reliability concerns : The paper acknowledges that segmentation masks may be incomplete or degraded. In clinical settings, incorrect localization of calcifications could reduce trust, even if the overall score is accurate.
reviewer_2_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: This paper is well aligned with an important clinical problem. The central idea is also genuinely interesting: the Agatston score is a clinically meaningful but non-differentiable target, and the authors convert it into a differentiable supervisory signal so that large numbers of scans with only report-level labels can still be used to train an interpretable segmentation model. That is a strong framing for weakly supervised learning in a clinically grounded setting. The two-stage training strategy is also sensible. Dense voxel-level supervision is used first to anchor the anatomy, after which score-level supervision expands learning to a much larger real-world dataset. I also found the reported experimental gains meaningful and the statistical presentation stronger than in many application papers. In particular, the improvement in risk-tier agreement appears substantial, and the inclusion of bootstrap confidence intervals for kappa is appreciated.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: My main reservation is that the paper ultimately makes a segmentation claim, but the main large-scale evaluation is still largely score-based rather than voxel-based. Improved agreement with the Agatston score does not necessarily imply more accurate coronary segmentation. In principle, a model could still match the overall score while placing calcium in imperfect spatial locations. The qualitative examples suggesting fewer non-coronary false positives are useful, but they do not fully close this gap. Second, the comparisons with AI-CAC and S2CAC are difficult to interpret cleanly because the benchmarking conditions are not fully matched. In particular, AI-CAC appears to be run on full-chest gated CT, whereas S2CAC and Proxy-CAC are evaluated on coned-down cardiac field-of-view scans, and the compared methods do not appear to have been retrained under identical data and preprocessing conditions. Therefore, part of the observed performance gap may reflect domain or field-of-view mismatch rather than purely methodological advantage. Third, the differentiable Agatston score remains an approximation of the real scoring procedure. It does not fully reproduce lesion-wise connected-component handling or the original slice-based area computation logic. I do not consider this fatal, but the approximation gap should be acknowledged more explicitly. Fourth, even the paper’s own qualitative analysis suggests that phase II supervision may introduce some lesion under-coverage, which indicates that the segmentation problem is not fully solved. Finally, the presentation of the ground-truth mask description on page 8 is somewhat confusing and should be cleaned up for clarity.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for their feedback and recognition of our study’s value. We address the main concerns here and will modify the manuscript accordingly: We acknowledge the need for quantitative segmentation evaluation and concerns about lesion under-segmentation (R2, R3). While our large-scale dataset (Dc) lacks dense masks, a clinical expert annotated 50 random samples from the test set (10/category). We post-process predicted masks by identifying connected pixels within segmented regions above the clinical 130 HU threshold. We observed an increase in Dice score from 0.69 in Phase I to 0.79 in Phase II (0.55 to 0.61 without postprocessing). This jump demonstrates that scalar supervision provides superior lesion identification. Furthermore, Agatston scores derived from the refined masks achieve a Kappa of 0.83 [95% CI: 0.82, 0.84], proving the reliability of the masks. Regarding concerns on the deviation from standard Agatston computation: In the Differentiable Agatston Score (DAS), we replace each non-differentiable operation in the standard Agatston calculation with a soft approximation, while maintaining mathematical fidelity. Using the masks in the COCA dataset, we compared DAS outputs against Agatston scores and obtained a Pearson correlation of 0.996, indicating high accuracy of our approximation. R2 (7.1) raises a valid point regarding the unconstrained nature of scalar supervision. We clarify that the framework is designed to impose constraints: Phase I provides a good initialization for the segmentation model, preventing it from converging on non-anatomical degenerate solutions. Phase II uses the score to refine the model; the DAS module incorporates clinical priors (130 HU thresholding), limiting the solution space to calcified voxels. R1, R2 question the use of a two-phase training approach rather than a simultaneous multi-task strategy. We use Ds to give the segmentation network a reasonable starting point; our focus is performance on Dc, the multi-center dataset for deployment. Since Ds comes from a different system, keeping the Ds mask loss active in Phase 2 would hurt generalization in Dc. Empirically, Phase 2 results in a small drop in segmentation performance on the Ds test set (Dice 0.74 → 0.69) and a large gain in segmentation performance on the Dc test set (Dice 0.61 → 0.79). This is an expected behavior of successful domain adaptation. We agree that external validation is a vital target for future research, we clarify that our Dc dataset represents a heterogeneous “real-world” cohort. It encompasses multi-site and multi-vendor data from a single hospital system, ensuring robustness against variations in clinical practice. We acknowledge concerns about the fairness when comparing Proxy-CAC with external models (AI-CAC and S2CAC). We will clarify that this comparison was intended to highlight a significant gap: available segmentation models trained on external distributions often underperform on other datasets. Our model provides a solution for fine-tuning a real-world dataset with only scalar labels. R2 suggests adding direct regression and multi-task learning baselines. Direct regression may give competitive accuracy, but it removes the main reason for our design choice: inspection of intermediate lesions. Standard multi-task learning, where a shared encoder feeds separate segmentation and regression heads, has the same problem. In our design, the DAS layer computes the scalar directly from the segmentation, so every score is explained by its mask, and any error in the score can be traced back to a lesion. Regarding specific implementation choices, we standardized resampling to 3.0 mm, as it remains the clinical standard for Agatston quantification. L score (SMAPE derived) was selected as it provides scale-invariance, which is essential for accurate risk stratification. We will clarify unclear design choices and improve presentations in line with the reviewer’s suggestions.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper offers a method for learning of interpretable CAC segmentation from volume level clinical scores. In the rebuttal, please address the concerns from the reviewers comprehensively. | The reviewers unanimously provided positive recommendations, and I agree with their decision. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Authors satisfactorily addressed all reviewers concerns in the rebuttal and all reviewers agree on accepting the manuscript. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): My decision closely aligns with the comments from reviewer #3.In that sense, what I mean is that I find the idea of a differentiable score that can be more or less generalised to other problems for weak supervision is a novel and interesting idea.
