title: Reference-Guided Gradient Balancing Loss for Long-Tailed Multi-label Medical Image Classification
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The paper is well motivated and relatively easy to follow. 2.Leveraging TP/TN predictions within the same batch as dynamic, class-specific anchors is an elegant idea. 3.RGB achieves SoTA on all three benchmarks across different class groups. 4.RGB is a pure loss function replacement, so it should be easy to be used, which is a significant advantage for clinical adoption.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The paper frames its problem as long-tailed multi-label classification, but this characterization is questionable for medical imaging datasets. Long-tailed learning literature [1] typically targets datasets with a very large number of categories where the label frequency follows a heavy-tailed distribution. Medical imaging datasets, however, contain a limited number of disease labels , which is more accurately characterized as a class imbalance problem [2]. The distinction matters because long-tailed methods make implicit assumptions about label cardinality that do not hold here. The authors should either justify the long-tailed framing more rigorously or reposition the problem as class-imbalanced multi-label classification. 2.The paper partitions classes into head/medium/tail groups using dataset-specific prevalence thresholds (10%/1.5% for CXR-14, 10%/2% for CXR-LT, 40%/5% for CheXpert) with no principled justification for these choices. It is unclear whether these thresholds were selected based on data statistics, prior work conventions, or tuned to favor the reported results. 3.Figures should be provided in lossless format. 4.The dynamic weighting parameter $\lambda = 1 - \frac{1}{\log_2(D_k)}$ is undefined when $D_k = 1$ ($\log_2(1) = 0$) and becomes negative when $D_k < 2$, which inverts the exponent sign and reverses the ranking objective. Crucially, this pathological case arises precisely for the rarest disease classes. 5.The paper describes $\lambda$ as a “dynamic gradient weighting hyperparameter,” but $D_k$ is a fixed dataset-level statistic computed before training. $\lambda$ is therefore a static, class-specific constant, not a dynamic quantity. 6.The prediction probability $p$ is defined as $\frac{1}{1+e^{-s_k}}$ using only the class index $k$, yet it is used as $p_i$ in Eq. 2 as if it were sample-dependent. The intended definition should be $p_{i,k} = \frac{1}{1+e^{-s_{i,k}}}$. 7.In the $\neg$TP branch of $\mathcal{L}{\text{ref}}$ (Eq. 4), the term $e^{s{j,k} - s_{l,k}}$ produces a gradient on TN logit $s_{l,k}$ that pushes it upward (relative to FP logits). Simultaneously, the second case of $\mathcal{L}{\text{sup}}$ (Eq. 5) applies $\log(1 + e^{s{l,k}})$ to all TN samples, pushing their logits downward. These two objectives are in direct conflict whenever FP predictions exist but no TP reference is available, which could cause gradient instability or cancel useful learning signal. 1.Zhang, Y. , Kang, B. , Hooi, B. , Yan, S. and Feng, J. , 2023.Deep long-tailed learning: A survey. IEEE transactions on pattern analysis and machine intelligence, 45(9), pp. 10795-10816. 2.Cong, C. , Liu, S. , Rana, P. , Pagnucco, M. , Di Ieva, A. , Berkovsky, S. and Song, Y. , 2024.Adaptive unified contrastive learning with graph-based feature aggregator for imbalanced medical image classification. Expert Systems with Applications, 251, p. 123783.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The paper addresses an important and practical problem. Long-tailed multi-label chest X-ray classification is clinically relevant, and the observation that gradients from abundant negative labels can overwhelm learning for rare diseases is well motivated. The proposed loss is also easy to understand and fairly well structured: the positive enhancement term directly targets rare and hard positives, while the adaptive negative suppression term uses true positives or true negatives as reference anchors to guide correction of false-positive logits. The ablation studies are helpful and show that both components contribute. The TP-or-TN reference design also appears better than using only TP or only TN reference sets.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: My main concern is that the paper’s “state-of-the-art” framing is too strong and not sufficiently contextualized. The experiments show that RGB outperforms the selected loss-function baselines under the authors’ own protocol, but this is not the same as establishing broader state of the art on CXR-LT. The CXR-LT 2024 challenge paper reports that Team A took first place in Task 1 with mAP 0.281, mAUROC 0.847, and mF1 0.289, and it specifically notes that Team A also achieved the best overall performance and strong tail-group performance. This matters because the RGB paper’s reported CXR-LT result, 79.33 mAUC, is numerically below the official challenge-leading CXR-LT 2024 result of about 0.847 mAUROC, even before considering stronger system design choices. While the metric naming and exact protocol are not perfectly identical, the burden is still on the authors to delimit the scope of their claim. As written, the paper gives the impression of broader SOTA than the evidence supports. A related issue is that the paper does not position itself against stronger CXR-LT system-level methods such as CheXFusion, which was the 1st-place solution in the ICCV CVAMD 2023 Shared Task on CXR-LT and reported 0.372 mAP on the MIMIC-CXR test set using multi-view transformer fusion, balancing, and self-training. CheXFusion and the 2024 challenge-winning pipeline are not directly comparable line-by-line to RGB because they use different task years, label sets, and system architectures. However, that is exactly the point: RGB is being evaluated as a loss-only method in a fixed DenseNet121 setup, not as a top-performing CXR-LT system. Therefore, the paper should not claim broad state of the art on CXR-LT without a much more careful qualification. More broadly, the validation scope is somewhat narrow. All experiments are limited to chest X-ray datasets and a single DenseNet121 backbone. There is no evidence that the method transfers to other medical modalities, stronger architectures, or multi-view/study-level settings, which are especially relevant in the CXR-LT literature. The method is also batch-dependent, since the reference-guided correction relies on the presence of TP or TN reference predictions within a batch. The paper provides a fallback when TP is absent, but it does not study sensitivity to batch size or extremely sparse class prevalence, which seems important for the tail classes it aims to help. Finally, the mechanistic support for the “dominant negative gradients” claim remains somewhat limited. The gradient visualization is suggestive, but the paper would be stronger with explicit statistics on gradient magnitudes for head, medium, and tail classes over training, instead of mainly qualitative figures.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: S1.Well-motivated reference mechanism. Using correct predictions (TP/TN) within a batch as class-specific references to guide false positive logit correction (Eq. 4) is a novel and intuitive idea that goes beyond uniform negative suppression in DR [14]. The conditional fallback to TN when no TP exists is a practical design choice validated by Table 3. S2.Consistent SoTA across three large-scale datasets. RGB achieves the highest macro F1 on all three datasets (33.27%, 22.45%, 48.02%) and the highest mAUC on CXR-14 and CheXpert (Table 1). Notably, tail-class macro F1 is the best across all datasets, directly supporting the paper’s claims about long-tailed effectiveness. S3.Thorough ablation and analysis. The ablation study (Table 2) clearly isolates the contributions of L_pe and L_ans, and the reference set comparison (Table 3) justifies the TP-or-TN design. The gradient visualization (Fig. 2a) provides direct evidence that RGB selectively reduces false positive gradients rather than uniformly suppressing all negatives.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: W1.Reliance on noisy within-batch predictions. The reference loss L_ref (Eq. 4) partitions samples into TP/FP/TN sets based on the model’s own predictions (ŷ), which are unreliable during early training and for tail classes with few positive samples. The paper does not discuss how ŷ is thresholded, how the method behaves when predictions are mostly incorrect, or whether a warm-up period is needed. This is a fundamental design concern that deserves analysis (e.g., tracking reference set accuracy over epochs). W2.All three datasets are chest X-rays. While the datasets differ in scale and label count (14/37/13 classes), they share the same imaging modality. Generalizability to other MIA modalities (CT, fundus, dermoscopy, histopathology) that have different positive/negative ratios and label structures remains undemonstrated. The paper’s title and claims are broader than the experimental evidence supports. W3.Edge case in λ (Eq. 2) and missing hyperparameter sensitivity. When D_k = 1, log_2(D_k) = 0 and λ is undefined (division by zero); when D_k = 2, λ = 0, which nullifies L_pe for that class entirely. This is problematic for exactly the rare tail classes the method targets. Additionally, while γ1 and γ2 require per-dataset grid search (3/3 for CXR-14, 2.4/3 for CXR-LT, 1.9/2 for CheXpert), no sensitivity analysis is provided beyond the claim of stability within ±0.1. W4.Overclaimed novelty. Contribution (1) states RGB is “the first multi-label loss specifically designed to address the inherent dominance of negative gradients in MIA,” but ASL [19] explicitly applies asymmetric focusing to suppress negative gradients, and RAL [18] directly addresses positive-negative gradient asymmetry in long-tailed multi-label settings. The claim should be scoped to the reference-guided mechanism specifically.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We sincerely appreciate the reviewers’ valuable comments. The major concerns and our responses are listed below. The source code will be released upon acceptance. λ and γ (R1,R3): We agree that λ is more precisely a class-specific weighting coefficient rather than a dynamic parameter, and we will revise the wording accordingly. While D_k denotes the number of images per class, we verified commonly used multi-label medical image datasets prior to proposing this method, and to the best of our knowledge, D_k ≤ 2 does not occur, including for tail classes. While γ sensitivity analysis was omitted due to space, performance remains robust across a wide range of values. SOTA / Novelty claim (R2,R3): We agree that RGB focuses on loss function design rather than system-level optimization. Our intention is to demonstrate its effectiveness relative to representative multi-label loss functions, not claim overall CXR-LT challenge leadership. Accordingly, we will revise our SOTA statement to a multi-label loss design in the revision. Regarding novelty, we agree that prior methods, such as ASL and RAL, also suppress negative gradients and will remove Contribution (1) to better focus the other three contributions, as the reviewer suggests. Batch-dependent (R2,R3): We agree that RGB is batch-dependent. However, the conditional “TP or TN” design mitigates data-sparse issues by using TN references when TP is absent. Empirically, RGB shows stable gains as batch size increases from 64 to 256 (512 was memory-limited). This analysis was omitted due to space limitations. Strong performance on the highly sparse CXR-LT dataset further suggests robustness in extreme long-tailed settings. Prediction definition (R1,R3): We will clarify the probability p in the revision. The threshold of prediction ŷ_{i,k} is fixed to 0.5 for all experiments, and we will clarify this point in the revision. Problem definition (R1): We value the reviewer’s observation on the category scale. While CXR-LT contains 37 labels, it was specifically designed for long-tailed problems in MIA with a heavy-tailed distribution. This formulation is standard in recent MIA literature, including the CXR-LT MICCAI challenge. Generalizability (R2,R3): We agree that evaluation on different modalities is a valuable future direction. As a loss-level formulation operating solely on logits, RGB is directly compatible with different architectures and MIA modalities without modification. We also evaluated RGB on ResNet50 (to be released with the code) and observed a consistent performance trend. Due to space limitations, the results were not included in the submission. Gradient Conflict (R1): While L_sup suppresses TN logits, L_ref further uses them as relative anchors to guide FP logits to the correct side of the decision boundary via pairwise logit comparison. Thus, TN logits serve as a reference structure rather than being explicitly optimized upward. This synergy is empirically validated by our “TP or TN” strategy, which achieves the best performance across datasets (Tab. 3). Partition (R1): We determine cut points based on the “elbow” point in the descending prevalence distribution. We will clarify this setting in the revision. No correct predictions & warm up (R3): In practice, TN references are inherently abundant because negative samples dominate in sparse medical datasets, making cases with no correct predictions rare. Confidence weighting naturally filters early-training noise, removing the need for a warm-up stage. Trade-off between metrics (R3): L_ans improves ma-F1 by mitigating dominant-negative gradients, while slightly shifting optimization from head-class-dominated mi-F1 in L_clsep. The proposed L_pe solves this and shows our overall design enhances both macro and micro metrics (Table 2), confirming that the two components work complementarily. Figures (R1): We will export the vector image format in the revision.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Reviewers are split: one recommends weak reject and two recommend weak accept. After careful consideration, I recommend sending this paper for rebuttal. The reference-guided mechanism is novel and well-motivated — using TP/TN predictions as class-specific anchors to guide false positive suppression is an elegant idea, and consistent improvements across three chest X-ray benchmarks are encouraging. The ablation studies are thorough and the method is easy to integrate as a pure loss replacement. However, several concerns need to be addressed. The SOTA claim is overstated — RGB is evaluated as a loss-only method under a fixed DenseNet121 setup and does not establish broader state of the art relative to challenge-winning systems on CXR-LT. The method relies on within-batch predictions as references, which are unreliable during early training and for extreme tail classes, yet no stability analysis is provided. A mathematical edge case exists in the λ formulation that breaks for the rarest classes (D_k ≤ 2), which is precisely the setting the method targets. Evaluation is limited to a single modality and backbone, limiting generalizability claims. The authors are asked to clarify the following points in their rebuttal: How the λ edge case is handled for classes with D_k ≤ 2.- The stability of within-batch reference predictions over training, particularly for tail classes. Whether the SOTA claim can be scoped more precisely to loss-function comparisons rather than system-level results. How ŷ is thresholded in the TP/FP/TN partition. | This paper introduces a well-motivated algorithm that addresses a related problem. However, a key concern is the clarity of its claimed contribution, which the authors have agreed to revise during the rebuttal phase. Overall, I believe the paper is worthy of discussion at MICCAI. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper received Accept, Reject, and Weak Accept (no post-rebuttal submitted). The authors’ rebuttal agreed to narrow the SOTA claim to a loss-function comparison and to remove Contribution (1), but the framing still overstates the evidence and the validation of the batch-dependent design is not in the submitted paper. All three reviewers agreed the loss formulation is practically motivated and the gains over selected baselines are real, and the Reject is conditional on the framing reframe the rebuttal commits to. The authors should narrow the SOTA claim, remove Contribution (1), and discuss stronger system-level CXR-LT baselines in related work. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): After rebuttal, the reviewer opinions remain mixed. Reviewer #1 supports acceptance, stating that most concerns were addressed, while Reviewer #2 maintains rejection because the SOTA claim remains over-scoped and important evidence on batch-size behavior, γ sensitivity, and stronger backbones is absent from the submitted manuscript. Reviewer #3 does not provide a visible post-rebuttal final opinion in the provided text, but the initial review was weak accept with concerns about batch-dependent references, λ edge cases, and limited modality/backbone diversity. Overall, the proposed RGB loss is a practical and reasonably novel loss-level contribution with consistent gains over selected loss-function baselines, but it should not be framed as a broadly state-of-the-art CXR-LT system. The final version clearly narrows the claims to loss-function comparison and explicitly discusses the remaining limitations regarding batch dependence, tail-class stability, λ edge cases, single-backbone evaluation, and limited modality generalization. The authors should provide the full open-source implementation to improve the reproducibility.

title: Reformulating Chest X-Ray Report Generation as Fine-Grained Visual Question Answering with Structured Clinical Report Templates
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The problem addressed in this paper is widespread: VLMs tend to generate hallucinations when producing reports. 2.The two-stage strategy employed in this paper is supported by strong theoretical grounding. 3.The approach of this paper is interesting, novel, and reasonable. 4.The experimental results validate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

reviewer_3_strengths: 1.Clinically motivated problem formulation. The paper addresses an important and practical problem in radiology report generation, focusing on improving factual consistency and structured reasoning, which is highly relevant for clinical applications. 2.Structured supervision design. The proposed tree-structured template and decomposition into node-level attributes provide a reasonable way to introduce structured inductive bias into report generation. 3.Comprehensive experiments. The proposed TGST framework shows stable improvements across different models, suggesting some generalizability of the approach.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.Limited methodological novelty. The core components of the framework largely consist of existing techniques, including LLM-based information extraction, structured template construction, VQA reformulation, and standard LoRA fine-tuning. The contribution is mainly a combination of known ideas rather than a fundamentally new learning framework or algorithm. 2.Pipeline-style design. The method is heavily reliant on a multi-stage engineering pipeline. author_feedback: We sincerely thank the reviewers and ACs for their constructive comments and for recognizing the value of our method. GQ1(R1,R2)-Template Design and Generalizability: Our hierarchical clinical template was designed with clinicians based on established radiology reporting principles and common pulmonary findings, rather than dataset-specific heuristics. It is expected to generalize to other CXR datasets (e.g., MIMIC-CXR), although minor vocabulary adaptation may be needed due to reporting differences. While the current version focuses on pulmonary findings, TGST can be extended to other regions by redefining the template nodes. We are extending it to whole-chest structured reporting on larger datasets for a future journal release. GQ2(R2,R3)-Stage II Self-training Bias: We agree that VLM-based template completion may introduce biased or hallucinated pseudo-labels. However, unlike free-text pseudo-report generation, our process is constrained by the structured template and closed-set VQA formulation. Stage-I anchors the template to explicit findings from the original reports, while Stage-II only fills missing attributes within predefined candidate spaces. Logical pruning and null assignment further reduce unsupported completions. Although hallucinations cannot be fully eliminated, the strong empirical improvements suggest that the generated supervision remains sufficiently reliable in practice. We will further incorporate grounding verification and pseudo-label quality control in the journal extension. GQ3(R2,R3)-Limited Validation: We acknowledge that evaluation only on IU-Xray may limit the assessment of large-scale generalizability. We chose IU-Xray as a controlled benchmark to validate TGST in a pulmonary-focused setting. Unlike conventional report generation methods, TGST additionally requires hierarchical template construction, fine-grained attribute definition, and structured VQA supervision, which become substantially more complex in whole-chest and large-scale settings. Nevertheless, the consistent improvements across multiple VLMs provide encouraging evidence for the effectiveness of the proposed framework. We are extending TGST to whole-chest structured reporting and larger-scale datasets for a journal extension. GQ4(R1,R3)-Performance Gain and Supervision Advantage: The performance gains mainly come from reformulating report generation into structured fine-grained VQA, rather than isolated engineering components. Conventional long-text supervision provides sparse and entangled signals, while TGST decomposes report generation into constrained attribute-level objectives, yielding denser supervision and more localized visual-text alignment. We agree that additional ablations would further strengthen the analysis and will include more detailed studies in the journal extension. All experiments use public VLMs/datasets and standard LoRA fine-tuning, and the structured template and code will be released. R1Q1-Baseline Model Dependency: The results do not suggest that TGST depends on a specific backbone, as consistent improvements are observed across all evaluated VLMs. The varying gains mainly reflect differences in medical-domain adaptation and performance ceilings. General-domain VLMs such as InternVL and Qwen benefit more from the structured clinical supervision, while medical-domain models such as HuatuoGPT already possess stronger medical priors, leading to smaller but still significant gains. R3Q1-Clarification of Novelty: Our contribution is not a new algorithm, but a clinically structured training paradigm for chest X-ray report generation. Specifically, we reformulate free-text report generation into template-guided fine-grained VQA with hierarchical clinical decomposition. This restructures sparse long-text supervision into explicit attribute-level clinical reasoning signals, enabling more localized visual-text alignment and improved factual consistency.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): This paper proposes a template-guided structured training framework that reframes report generation as a fine-grained VQA task to reduce hallucinations. Reviewers shared a similar impression of the strengths, including clinically motivated formulation, structured supervision design, and consistent empirical gains across models. Though some weaknesses were also pinpointed by the reviewers, e.g., unclear template generalizability to other organs/datasets; potential bias from VLM self-training in Stage II; experiments only on a small IU-X-ray dataset, all three reviewers lean towards accepting the paper. Overall, reviewers and AC acknowledge its practical value in reducing factual errors, given the clinical relevance. It will be helpful if the author could address the comments in the revision.

title: RefTr: Recurrent Refinement of Confluent Trajectories for 3D Tubular Tree Centerlines
reviewer_1_strengths: The proposed method of obtaining many confluent trajectories, refining and merging them using a self-attention is a novel contribution. This harps back to methods that used multiple hypothesis tracking for airway segmentation [0] (but is not discussed in the paper). The use of successive refinement and merging can improve overall centerline extraction capabilities as demonstrated in the evaluations. Fig 1 is a useful illustration that clearly shows the different components and how they interact in the method. Experimental evaluation is thorough, and the performance of the proposed method is competitive across datasets and metrics compared to the baseline methods. Reporting ablation and efficiency metrics also shows further competitiveness of the method.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: How are the token sets learned? The image encoder provides the image features to the producer, but where do the “learned input token sets” come from? How are they learned? At s=1 already, the tokens are learned which are only further refined by Producer and Refiner blocks. So, the input learned tokens are fixed? The loss objective in Eq. 1 has several weights (alphas). No further discussion on how these were tuned and what the final values are is presented. I am also not sure I understand the different components as they are not described in sufficient detail. TNMS is not described in detail. The authors say duplicate nodes are identified “using a radius-adaprive spatial threshold”. As far as I could check, there are no additional details provided about this method or the related paramters. And TNMS appears to be an important element going by Table 4 ablation. The title says “vascular tree” only whereas the method is validated also for airways in ATM22 dataset [1]. Are the authors sure the centerlines in this dataset are of the vascular tree and not airway tree? Why mention the concurrent submission and provide it as supplementary material? What is EVAR? It is unclear what the specific point the authors are trying to make with this claim. Paper should be self-contained. [0] Selvan et al. “Extracting tree structures in CT data by tracking multiple statistically ranked hypotheses. “ Medical Physics 46.10 (2019): 4431-4440. [1] https://atm22.grand-challenge. org/
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: Relevant and important problem: Accurate and topologically correct centerline extraction is critical for many clinical applications. Technically sound framework: The proposed architecture is coherent and builds on a reasonable design (Transformer-based image-to-graph modeling). Comprehensive experiments: o Multiple datasets (synthetic + real) o Multi-level evaluation (node / branch / graph) o Runtime and parameter comparisons o Ablation study covering key components Efficiency improvements: The model achieves reduced decoder parameters and faster inference, which is practically meaningful.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: (1) Limited novelty and incremental contribution (Major) The proposed method is heavily built upon the authors’ prior work (Trexplorer / Trexplorer Super), and the incremental contribution is relatively small: The “recurrent refinement” mechanism appears to be a natural extension of iterative decoding already present in prior work, rather than a fundamentally new idea. Many-to-one matching is a standard technique (e.g., DETR variants). TNMS is a simple engineering extension (duplicate merging + pruning), with limited algorithmic novelty. The main conceptual addition, “confluent trajectories,” is not sufficiently formalized or justified. Overall, the work reads more as an incremental refinement of an existing framework, with marginal gains relative to Trexplorer Super. (2) Unclear definition and overclaim of “confluent trajectories” (Major) The notion of “confluent trajectories” is central to the paper but: The motivation of this choice is not convincingly explained and its concept is not rigorously defined. The current manuscript lacks: o formal definition o theoretical justification o comparison to alternative representations Moreover, the claim that this representation “explicitly enforces valid topology” is not fully supported: Topology still relies on post-hoc reconstruction (divergence prediction + TNMS). No formal guarantee of topology correctness is provided. This weakens the conceptual contribution. (3) Comparison bias toward authors’ own prior work (Major) The experimental comparison is heavily dominated by the authors’ previous methods (Trexplorer variants), which raises concerns about fairness and completeness. There is insufficient comparison to other categories of methods, including: Topology-aware segmentation approaches (e.g., clDice-based methods: Shit et al., DOI: 10.1109/CVPR46437.2021.01629) CNN-based centerline / tracing methods (e.g., DeepVesselNet: Tetteh et al., 2020, DOI: 10.3389/fnins.2020.592352) → more recent variants or follow-ups should also be considered Skeletonization / topology-preserving learning approaches (Qiu, et.al, DOI:10.1016/j.media.2025.103578 or other recent works on differentiable skeletonization or topology constraints) Recent graph-based or foundation models (e.g., VesselFM, Wittmann, et. al, DOI: arXiv:2411.17386) Given that the paper claims advantages in topology preservation, comparison against topology-preserving losses (e.g., clDice) is particularly important and currently missing. (4) Evaluation inconsistency with prior work (Major) The paper introduces new radius-aware metrics (rAP, rF1, etc.), which were not used in prior Trexplorer publications. This raises concerns: Are results directly comparable to previously reported baselines? Why are legacy metrics not reported alongside the new ones? Could the new metrics favor the proposed method design? Additionally: It is unclear whether the same dataset splits and evaluation protocols are used. The performance metrics reported in this paper for comparison methods are different from previous publications. This limits the ability to fairly assess improvement over prior work. (5) Qualitative comparison inconsistency (Moderate–Major) The qualitative results (Fig. 2) show significantly weaker performance for prior methods compared to their original publications. This raises concerns about: sample selection bias comparability with previously reported visual results It would be more convincing to: show the same cases as prior papers, or include a broader set of representative examples (6) Weak justification for Parse dataset performance (Major) The authors attribute weaker performance on Parse 2022 to missing small branches in ground truth, supported by radiologist review. This explanation is not fully convincing: The method appears worse overall, not only in recall. The claim is not quantitatively validated. If ground truth is indeed flawed: a stronger contribution would be to correct and release improved annotations, rather than relying on anecdotal justification. (7) Clarity issues in method description (Moderate) The training and role of “learned input token sets” are not clearly explained. The divergence prediction mechanism and topology reconstruction pipeline could be clarified. (8) Overlap with concurrent submission (Minor to Moderate) The authors provide a supplementary document that appears to be a separate concurrent MICCAI submission focusing on a clinical application (EVAR), which directly builds upon RefTr. While such parallel submissions are not uncommon, this raises potential concerns: Double counting of novelty Inflation of contribution through splitting method and application The methodological novelty is largely concentrated in the current paper, while the supplementary submission primarily demonstrates application-level extension. This is acceptable but should be considered during meta-review.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The main strength of the paper lies in its reasonably clear methodological motivation. Rather than making only incremental architectural modifications, the work reformulates the reconstruction problem at the level of trajectory generation and recurrent refinement, which gives the method a degree of conceptual novelty. The experimental section is also relatively comprehensive, including multiple public datasets, point-/branch-/graph-level evaluation, efficiency comparisons, and ablation studies. In particular, the reported reduction in decoder parameters and runtime strengthens the practical relevance of the method. Finally, the ablation results broadly support the proposed design choices, especially the roles of recurrent refinement, many-to-one matching, past-memory attention, and TNMS.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.While the high-level concepts are understandable, the construction of the decoder, the organization of tags, and the specific roles of self-memory, cross-memory, and past memory attention are not clearly described, leaving the reader quite confused. 2.Furthermore, some improvements seem to rely on a design loop: intentional over-prediction followed by suppression of duplicates via TNMS. This raises the question: how much of the gain stems from the core generation mechanism itself, and how much from post-processing? 3.There is also insufficient justification for fixing the matching assignment from the first refinement step, as suboptimal early proposals may persist into subsequent refinement stages.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for their thoughtful feedback. Major concerns are addressed below. 1.Novelty (R2) RefTr’s novelty is threefold and acknowledged by R1 and R3: (i) trajectory-level reformulation: Trexplorer Super predicts one node at a time; RefTr jointly predicts and refines entire confluent trajectories; (ii) inference-time ensembling: many-to-one matching produces multiple candidates, merged at the patch level via pairwise divergence positions, boosting recall on small branches; (iii) TNMS: an O(N log N) algorithm removing residual duplicates globally in trees with thousands of nodes in under a second on CPU; no prior algorithm targets this task. Result: 2.4x decoder parameter reduction, faster inference, superior P/R across datasets. 2.Many-to-one vs DETR variants (R2) Group/H/Co-DETR use one-to-many only at training, discarding extras at inference. RefTr keeps and merges redundant predictions at inference, creating an inference-time ensemble, functionally distinct from DETR’s training-only mechanism. 3.Confluent trajectories and topology (R2) Formally defined in Sec. 2 and illustrated in Fig. 1(a). The representation (trajectories + end positions + pairwise divergence positions) defines a valid tree by construction; TNMS only merges duplicate branches. Empirically Betti-0 = Betti-1 = 0 on all datasets (Tab. 2). 4.Core mechanism vs TNMS (R2, R3) Table 4 ablates multiple core components (recurrent refinement, many-to-one matching, past-memory attention, and Producer/Refiner design choices), all with TNMS enabled. Removing any of these significantly degrades performance, establishing the core mechanism, not TNMS, as the source of the gains. Removing TNMS instead leaves recall essentially unchanged but reduces precision, since residual cross-patch duplicates are then counted as FPs. The core mechanism finds structures correctly; TNMS reclaims precision lost to residual duplicates. 5.Baselines (R2) RefTr and the compared baselines are image-to-graph models trained directly on centerline graphs (far cheaper to annotate). clDice, DeepVesselNet, VesselFM, and Qiu et al. are voxel-segmentation methods requiring costly voxel-level labels (as stated in Sec. 1) and address a different problem setting. 6.Metrics and Parse Performance (R2) Same splits and protocols as prior work; only metrics are upgraded. Radius-aware metrics are motivated as more robust across vessel scales. Legacy metrics were computed but omitted for space (e.g., RefTr Legacy Point-wise on ATM: Precision 0.6993, Recall 0.6413, F1 0.6549). On Parse, point-level metrics are better than Trexplorer Super; branch-level is comparable. The Parse GT issue was verified by a radiologist; public re-annotation is beyond scope. Fig. 2 shows challenging cases where prior methods struggle. 7.Architecture clarifications (R1, R3) Learned token sets are fixed trainable embeddings optimized end-to-end, analogous to DETR object queries [2]; image-agnostic until cross-attention. The decoder uses standard Transformer attention (self for inter-trajectory interactions, cross for image features, past-memory for ancestor context from up to 5 prior patches). We tested re-matching every step; reassignment disrupts refinement and destabilizes training. TNMS radius-adaptive threshold τ = max(τ_min, τ_pos * r), with τ_pos=0.3, τ_min=2.0; branches with duplicate fraction >= ρ=0.2 are merged. Loss weights (L1): alpha_pos=4.2, alpha_rad=1.2, alpha_end=0.9, alpha_div=0.3. 8.Other concerns (R1, R2) Surface similarities to MHT exist (multiple candidates, deferred decisions), but MHT prunes hypotheses while RefTr maintains them for ensembling. Title will be updated to “Tubular Tree” to cover airways. The concurrent EVAR paper is a clinical application of RefTr, disclosed per MICCAI transparency rules. We will incorporate the above clarifications and additions in the camera-ready. Full implementation details, legacy metrics and more qualitative examples will follow with the code.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): There are some discrepancies among the three reviewers, consisting of one weak reject and two weak accepts. The paper tackles an important task of 3D vascular centerline extraction, for which a Transformer-based image-to-graph framework is proposed, and evaluated on multiple public datasets with favorable results. Meanwhile, there are a number of aspects of the work that raise concerns. It would be beneficial if the authors provide further input and clarifications in the areas specifically brought out by the reviewers, including but not limited to, elucidating the main contributions, and the detailed description of the ingredients realizing the main tech contributions; improvement of the current presentation, and clarify key terms such as “confluent trajectories”, its motivation, definition and justification; critical evaluations with the SoTA baselines that go beyond own prior efforts; overlapping with the authors’ concurrent submission. | Started with diverse comments and concerns and diverging ratings, the rebuttal is not effective in addressing the major concerns, including but not limited to technical contributions and empirical baselines. Overall it requires significant revision efforts that goes beyond minor nature to get into MICCAI in this round. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The reviewers agreed that the problem is important and that the submitted work is technically coherent. Overall, this paper appears to make a useful and practically relevant contribution, supported by multi-dataset experiments, ablations, and efficiency improvements. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper reconstructs tubular structures by generating many confluent trajectories and refining and merging them via recurrent self-attention.This paper reconstructs tubular structures by generating many confluent trajectories and refining and merging them via recurrent self-attention. The majority recommend acceptance. R1 and R3 both credit the trajectory-level reformulation as a genuine conceptual contribution and find the evaluation thorough—multiple public datasets, point-/branch-/graph-level metrics, efficiency analysis, and supportive ablations—maintaining their positive recommendations after rebuttal. R2 recommends rejection, but its two major points (limited novelty relative to the authors’ prior work, and comparison bias toward it) rest on inferring authorship from unpublished prior work, which violates the double-blind policy and cannot be weighed as a standard critique. R2’s remaining concerns are reasonable but largely concern presentation and should be addressable in the final version. On balance, the methodological contribution is substantive and the evaluation comprehensive enough to merit acceptance. The authors are encouraged to add a formal definition and justification of confluent trajectories and to broaden the discussion of related topology-aware and tracing methods.

title: Reliability-Aware Cross-Prompt Aggregation for Propagation-Based Segmentation of Arbitrary 3D Medical Objects
reviewer_1_strengths: The paper presents the novel idea of fusing the initial prompt with the front prompt for volume-aware segmentation. The use of cycle consistency as a measure of prediction reliability is a particularly elegant contribution. The reported Dice gains appear high in absolute terms, although the results exhibit considerable variability, as evidenced by high standard deviations.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The paper has two major weaknesses. First, the computational cost of the proposed method appears to be substantial (if I understood correctly), as it requires one additional inference to obtain both the initial and front prompt predictions, plus two further inferences for computing cycle consistency; this overhead is not discussed anywhere in the paper. Second, the lack of genuine external validation is a concern: the pretrained PAM model used was trained on the same datasets employed in this study, so no true out-of-distribution evaluation is provided. As a minor observation, the ablation studies reveal that performance is already quite high with the initial prompts alone (96.7% of best performance), while distance-based fusion reaches 99.3%; this raises the question of whether the additional inference steps, and those required by cycle consistency in particular, are truly justified. Finally, the proposed methodology has a somewhat limited novelty with regards to the PAM approach.
reviewer_1_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: Training-free, plug-and-play on top of a frozen PAM — easy to adopt in the foundation-model era. Problem diagnosis is sharp: error accumulation and rigid distance-based refresh are correctly identified, and the two-prompt design directly addresses both. Strong empirical breadth — 10 external datasets across CT, MR, and SRX, six metrics, consistent improvements across the board. Ablation cleanly isolates each component: single-prompt (0.803) → average fusion (0.820) → distance-only (0.825) → confidence-only (0.826) → full (0.831), so every contribution is justified. The reliability metrics are validated empirically — Pearson ≈0.63, Spearman ≈0.69 correlation with true Dice — which is a rare and useful piece of analysis.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: cycle consistency and cross-modal/prompt agreement are well-known ideas from SSL and interactive-segmentation work; the contribution is a careful combination rather than a new mechanism. No runtime or FLOPs analysis, which is critical for a training-free method — cycle consistency requires backward propagation to both prompts at every slice (roughly 3× the vanilla PAM cost). τ = 100 is hand-picked with no sensitivity analysis, yet slice spacing varies substantially across the 10 datasets. Initial-prompt confidence is hard-coded to 1; it is never down-weighted even when propagation moves far from it. Missing baselines: no SAM2, no nnU-Net reference upper bound, and no simple ensembling baseline (e.g., averaging propagation restarts from different initial slices). No statistical significance testing on per-dataset differences; some radar-chart gains may lie within variance. Writing is serviceable but generic; a sharper conceptual argument for why cycle consistency and cross-prompt agreement are complementary (not redundant) would strengthen the paper.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.This paper addresses error accumulation without training, using both global (initial) and local (front) prompts. 2.This paper adaptively weights prompt predictions via two unsupervised metrics: cycle consistency and cross-prompt agreement. 3.Experiments on ten external multi-modal datasets show consistent improvements across six metrics over the SOTA methods.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.This paper requires computing forward passes per slice plus cycle consistency evaluations. This maybe doubles inference time compared to vanilla PAM. The paper does not report inference time or computational cost. 2.The weight τ is fixed. The paper does not present sensitivity analysis for this hyperparameter across different slice spacings or modalities.
reviewer_3_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank all reviewers for their comments and for recognizing the clear motivation, novel/well-suited method and thorough evaluation. We address main concerns below. Q1: Computational cost (R1-R3) We report per-volume inference time on HaN-Seg, which has the most objects (1259) and organs among ten datasets. On one NVIDIA A800-SXM4-80GB GPU, the times are: SegVol 8.08s, MedSAM 8.26s, MedSAM2 9.60s, PAM 2.86s, and Ours 7.11s. Although our method adds inference overhead compared to vanilla PAM, it remains faster than the other methods and improves mean Dice by 4.6% on ten external datasets, showing a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off. Q2: External validation, baselines, and statistics (R1,R2) All ten reported datasets are external and unseen during PAM training. Following original PAM setting, PAM was trained/validated on 34 internal datasets and additionally evaluated on ten external datasets. Our method uses the pretrained PAM weights and reports only external results, demonstrating out-of-distribution generalization. For baselines, MedSAM2 represents the medical extension of SAM2 and is included. We added supervised nnUNet on Adrenal-ACC-Ki67-Seg and ACDC. Dice scores are: nnUNet 0.854/0.929, PAM 0.891/0.860, and Ours 0.908/0.883.Our method remains competitive with nnUNet and can be better when annotations are scarce or targets are complex. For statistics, paired Wilcoxon tests on Dice show that our method significantly improves over PAM on all ten datasets (all per-dataset p<1e−5). To address R1’s concern about whether extra inference steps are justified, we report p-value on the merged ten dataset: Ours vs. initial-prompt only, p=4.41e−92; Ours vs. distance-only, p=5.34e−04, confirming the value of cross-prompt inference and reliability-aware weighting. Q3: Sensitivity to tau and initial-prompt confidence (R2,R3) Because distance weighting uses physical distance (slice interval multiplied by spacing), tau is less sensitive to spacing variations. We further conducted a sensitivity analysis with tau in {50, 100, 200}, and mean Dice is 0.828, 0.831, 0.829, within a narrow 0.003 range, showing robustness. The slight drops at tau=50/200 are expected: smaller tau over-emphasizes the front slice, while larger tau weakens distance discrimination and makes weights closer to uniform. We set initial-prompt confidence to 1 due to its high reliability and lack of reference slice for reliability estimation. Still, when propagation moves away, its distance weight decays, reducing total contribution. Q4: Novelty (R1,R2) Unlike PAM’s single-prompt fixed propagation, we propose cross-prompt aggregation with two novel training-free reliability estimation metrics for adaptive prompt fusion. Cycle Consistency and Cross-Prompt Agreement estimate reliability without labels and guide adaptive fusion of initial/front predictions, suppressing unreliable predictions and reducing error accumulation. Their positive correlations with true slice Dice also suggest value for future segmentation studies. Q5: Other issues of R1 (1) Robustness in challenging cases: ACDC cardiac MRI exhibits large basal-to-apical geometric variations. As shown in Q2, our method significantly improves over PAM on ACDC, showing robustness. (2) Standard deviation in Table 1 is computed across the ten datasets. (3) We will remove radar-chart shading to improve readability. Q6: Other issues of R2 (1) In Table 2, “Average” is equal-weight two-prompt fusion, while “Distance only” uses distance-aware weights without confidence metrics. Thus R2’s simpler baseline (average plus distance weighting) equals our “Distance only” setting, with Dice=0.825.(2) Cycle Consistency and Cross-Prompt Agreement are positively correlated (average Pearson/Spearman=0.6875/0.6810), as both reflect reliability, but are not redundant: the former measures backward self-consistency, while the latter measures two-prompt consensus. Correlation below 1 indicates related but complementary cues.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The work proposes a reliability-aware cross-prompt aggregation method for propagation-based 3D medical image segmentation. The recommendation is mixed among reviewers. The main disagreements are on methodology novelty, empirical evaluation and lack of sufficient evidences and explanations for some claims. Based on my reading, I think that the reviewers raised effective concerns. Please try to fix these concerns in the rebuttal. | This paper received very mixed ratings, one for accept, one for reject and one for weak accept but not read the rebuttal file. I read the paper and rebuttal file, and think that the authors solve the main concerns though some important issues still need to be fixed. But due to the novelty of the method, I tend to accept. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): NashNet introduces an innovative, training-free wrapper that elegantly addresses error compounding in volumetric slice propagation by implementing an unsupervised dual-prompt aggregation architecture. The authors successfully resolved initial concerns surrounding computational overhead and external validation during the rebuttal, demonstrating that their method remains highly competitive with established baselines like MedSAM2 while achieving a 4.6% mean Dice increase across ten completely unseen external datasets. Highly significant statistical verification ($p < 1e-3$) proves the value of its cycle-consistency loop over simpler distance-based baselines, this work represents a robust and clinically viable contribution. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): This submission is a borderline case, where several of the concerns are not fully resolved. After reading the paper, I feel that the novelty of the proposed work is rather incremental, and that several of the proposed modules are not actually required. For instance, as highlighted by one reviewer, the trade-off of including more components (beyond the distance aware scheme) is questionable, as it brings negligible gains compared to the additional computational cost, which may undermine even more the actual contribution. Furthermore, while overall gains seem to improve over the baseline PAM, per-dataset scores are not reported, making it hard to assess whether the proposed PAM extension is indeed a consistently better approach, or it largely outperforms other methods in a small number of datasets, falling behind in the remaining ones. Given these concerns, and that there are not strongly supportive comments from the reviewers (beyond the large number of datasets in the empirical validation), I am inclined towards recommending rejection for this work.

title: ReScan-IA: A Spatially-Adaptive Diffusion Framework for Controllable 3D Intracranial Aneurysm Inpainting
reviewer_1_strengths: This papers solves an important problem of data scarcity and imbalance in intracranial aneurysm analysis. The paper proposes a novel controllable 3D diffusion framework with spatially-adaptive conditioning. The method incorporates anatomical information (vessel masks) ensuring vascular continuity. Experimental results shows strong improvement in segmentation and detection using synthetic data. Strong validation on large multi-center data and external datasets, showing good method generalization.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: It lacks comparison with recent diffusion/GAN-based medical synthesis methods. -Limitations and Clinical Integration are not discussed adequately. Large descriptive blocks make the methodology hard to follow. Add clearer pipeline diagrams. -Statistical comparisons (t-test ) would enhance the proposed work validation. -Please address generalizability of the proposed to different datasets and protocols in the limitations. Patch-based approach may miss global anatomical consistency and shows inconsistent results across datasets.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The paper addresses a clinically relevant problem, namely the limited availability of annotated aneurysm data in CTA, which restricts the performance of deep learning models. A key strength is the integration of controllable generative modeling with anatomical priors. Spatial control signals and vessel information guide synthesis and help ensure anatomically consistent results. The use of the method for data augmentation is well motivated. Improvements in downstream segmentation and detection tasks support its practical value. The use of 3D volumetric modeling is appropriate and avoids the limitations of 2D approaches.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The paper has several weaknesses that reduce clarity and limit the strength of the experimental evaluation. 1.The model architecture is under-specified in the manuscript. Key details such as the number of U-Net levels, channel sizes, normalization layers, and the exact implementation of the 3D SPADE-like modulation are not clearly described. Although code is provided, these details should also be documented in the paper. 2.The training and validation protocol is not clearly described. The paper does not specify the train/validation/test split ratio, whether splitting is performed at the patient level, or how the LargeIA and RSNA Intracranial Aneurysm Detection challenge datasets are combined. This makes it difficult to assess experimental rigor and potential data leakage. 3.The external test sets are insufficiently described. While two independent cohorts (External A and External B) are used, the number of samples in each dataset is not reported. In addition, their source and acquisition characteristics are not described. Without these details, the strength of the cross-dataset generalization claims is difficult to assess. 4.The patch-based training strategy is unclear. The paper does not explain how patches are sampled (random vs. aneurysm-centered), how overlap is handled during inference, or how full volumes are reconstructed. Potential boundary artifacts are not discussed. 5.The ablation study is limited and lacks quantitative comparison. The analysis relies mainly on qualitative results. There is no systematic quantitative evaluation of key components such as vessel prior (v), spatial control (s), or their interaction. 6.Preprocessing choices are not justified. Key parameters such as resolution, intensity clipping are described but not motivated or analyzed for sensitivity. Post-processing steps are also not described.
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: Motivation: The idea of using spatial masks to ensure vascular structure, rather than focusing only on the aneurysm mask, is very neat. Adapting SPADE layers: SPADE layers are designed to condition on segmentation masks. Extending them to 3D and showing superior results (see minor points) suggests an alternative to pure concatenation and expensive cross-attention-based conditioning.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Ambiguity: A few points in the paper are unclear. For instance, the authors mention that they use the multi-class Circle of Willis labels to get the vascular structure. However, it appears that the multi-class labels are not used; it is simply a binary segmentation mask. Experimental Setup: The experiments are not clear to me. For instance, in the segmentation-only case (2), 25 locations were sampled for each of the 10 patients. The locations should be sampled only from the existing patients (i.e, the 10 patients), else it is an unfair comparison. I am not sure if that was the case. Further, the 250 synthetic samples seem to work better than the 250 real samples. So, the synthetic samples are “more diverse” than the real samples. This makes the last experiment completely uninutitive to me. If you can get so much out of just 10 real samples, then the same experiment should be repeated for the 250 samples, and you would get even better results. Why stick with the 250 synthetics generated from 10 samples? How are the cases with multiple aneurysms handled? The RSNA Intracranial Aneurysm Detection challenge shows that patients can have multiple aneurysms. In such a scenario, do the authors always select all the aneurysms or only a subset?
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for recognizing the strengths of our work and for the early acceptance decision. We would like to address a few points raised by the reviewers briefly. Experimental setup, patient-level split, and leakage prevention. We will revise the manuscript to clarify the patient-level split and the relationship between ReScan-IA training, synthetic generation, downstream training, and external evaluation datasets. The ReScan-IA training set consisted of 1223 subjects, including 287 from the RSNA dataset and 936 from the LargeIA dataset. An additional 250 held-out LargeIA subjects formed the internal pool for downstream aneurysm segmentation experiments. External datasets A and B were not used for either ReScan-IA diffusion training or downstream model training. For downstream segmentation and detection, all real subjects came from the held-out internal downstream experiments training dataset. Synthetic aneurysm templates were sampled only from the ReScan-IA training pool, excluding External A/B. This increased lesion diversity without patient-level leakage. Circle of Willis labels and binary vessel prior. We will revise the wording to clearly distinguish the binary vessel prior from multi-class vessel location control. In our implementation, the diffusion model receives only a binary vessel prior as input-level anatomical conditioning. Multi-class Circle of Willis labels are used only during synthetic sampling to identify the parent vessel, select anatomically corresponding insertion sites, and match aneurysm templates by vessel territory. This was done to improve the anatomical plausibility of introduced synthetic aneurysms.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): despite of a weak reject with reasonable justifications, the reviews are still good enough to support an early accept.

title: Rethinking RAG: Mitigating Text-Driven Hallucinations via Feature-Level Retrieval Integration in Medical LVLMs
reviewer_1_strengths: First, the paper addresses a meaningful and timely problem, namely that conventional medical RAG may unintentionally increase hallucinations by biasing generation toward retrieved text instead of image evidence. Second, the proposed feature-level retrieval integration is technically interesting and reasonably novel in the medical LVLM setting, especially when combined with the attention grounding loss and the negation-aware filtering module. Third, the method is supported by a fairly comprehensive evaluation across three benchmarks spanning both radiology and ophthalmology, where it consistently outperforms the base model and several strong RAG baselines such as FactMM-RAG, RULE, and MMed-RAG. Fourth, the ablation study is useful and shows that both the grounding loss and negation-aware retrieval contribute substantially to performance. Finally, the attention-ratio analysis is a particularly strong aspect of the paper because it provides mechanistic evidence that the method indeed increases reliance on visual tokens rather than only improving final metrics.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The main weakness is that the novelty is moderate rather than fully groundbreaking, since the work still builds on the broader medical RAG, while the cross-attention style fusion is also conceptually related to prior multimodal architectures. In particular, the negation-aware retrieval module is effective but somewhat heuristic, and simple sign inversion of embeddings, and the paper does not compare this against stronger learned semantic contradiction modeling. A second weakness is that the evaluation still relies mainly on VQA metrics and ROUGE/METEOR, without a stronger clinical factuality analysis or expert reader study to directly verify hallucination reduction in practice. In addition, the VQA benchmark is constructed from GPT-4-generated yes/no pairs, which introduces an additional synthetic layer and may not fully reflect real clinical questioning settings. Overall, these limitations keep the paper at a weak accept level for me rather than a clear accept, but the idea is still promising and the empirical evidence is solid enough to merit positive consideration.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The proposed method is generally well-motivated and properly validated. Instead of directly appending the retrieved reference pairs as raw images/texts, the paper fused them into the original query image token using a properly designed cross-attention mechanism before entering the LLM. The experimental results in Table 4 further support the argument, where the proposed method indeed aligns the LLM’s attention to the image tokens. 2.The idea of using the gated fusion mechanism and grounding loss is quite elegant and intuitive. The gated fusion mechanism ensures that the fused features are combined with the raw ViT feature adaptively and ensures the worst-case performance. And the grounding loss aligns the local correlation between the query patches and reference images with their semantical similarity. 3.The evaluation in the paper is very detailed and robust. It not only demonstrates a uniform performance improvement on three different datasets with two different modalities but also provides a thorough ablation that analyzes the contribution of each building component.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.One of the reviewer’s major concerns is the design of negation-aware retrieval. Using negation detection to avoid contradictory retrieved pairs is intuitively convincing. Directly negating the feature embedding is not that straightforward. “Mass presented” and “Mass not presented” are not opposite in terms of high-dimensional geometry. Additionally, naive negation detection may also confuse cases like “Mass presented” and “Mass free”, where both are affirmative sentences but their meaning are completely different. 2.The complexity of the proposed method is quite concerning, given its marginal performance improvements. The proposed method introduces multiple new hyperparameters like $alpha$ and $K$. However, the sensitivity with respect to these hyperparameters is not properly evaluated in the paper (limited by the paper length). On the other hand, the performance improvements in Table 1 compared with the baselines are not very significant as well. Most of the improvements are only ~1.5% to the second-best method. 3.The base model used here is relatively outdated. The paper uses LLaVA-Med-1.5 as the base model, but this is a model that was released 3 years ago, and there are more robust base models like Lingshu, MedGemma, and HuatuoGPT-V. It would be more helpful to evaluate the proposed method on more recent baselines.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The authors clearly identify a fundamental structural limitation in existing text-prompt RAG approaches, language bias and shortcut copying, and address it through a principled feature-level integration. The attention ratio analysis provides convincing empirical support for this motivation. The proposed method achieves SOTA results across all benchmarks. This suggests the framework generalizes well across imaging modalities. Addressing CLIP’s insensitivity to negated clinical findings is a clinically meaningful and underexplored contribution. The embedding polarity-flip is an elegant and lightweight solution, and the qualitative example effectively illustrates its practical impact in filtering diagnostically contradictory cases. Each proposed component is individually validated, and the results demonstrate that all components contribute meaningfully, with the grounding loss and negation-aware retrieval showing the largest individual impact.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Relying solely on NLP metrics (ROUGE-L, METEOR) is inadequate for medical report generation. These metrics measure lexical overlap rather than clinical accuracy. Incorporating clinical efficacy metrics would more convincingly demonstrate the medical validity of generated reports. Currently, you can’t conclude from the report generation table. Restricting VQA evaluation to binary yes/no questions risks inflating performance gains due to class imbalance or decision boundary biases. More fine-grained question types (e.g., open-ended, multiple-choice) would provide a more rigorous and clinically meaningful assessment of the method’s diagnostic reasoning capability. All experiments are conducted solely on LLaVA-Med. Given that different VLMs exhibit varying sensitivities to additional context, evaluating on at least one additional backbone would strengthen the generalizability claims of the framework. Table 3 does not specify which dataset the ablation results correspond to, making it difficult to contextualize the reported numbers. Limited architectural novelty: using cross-attention for multimodal feature fusion is a well-established paradigm. In recent multimodal RAG literature (e.g., read Abootorabi et al., Ask in Any Modality, 2025), cross-attention-based fusion has been widely adopted. The contribution is therefore more of a careful domain adaptation than a fundamentally novel architecture, though the specific design choices are well-suited to the medical setting. A qualitative visualization of attention patterns, both with and without the loss, is necessary to assess whether the model is attending to semantically meaningful regions.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We sincerely appreciate the reviewers for their constructive comments, and appreciate the opportunity to clarify several points raised in the reviews. (R1) Negation-aware retrieval is heuristic, just a sign inversion of embeddings: Sign inversion in cosine-similarity space was chosen as a deliberate lightweight and training-free design, broadly compatible with any CLIP-based retriever and free of additional supervision. A fully learned semantic-contradiction model could in principle capture finer cases such as “mass present” vs. “mass free”, but would introduce training overhead and dataset-specific supervision. Combined with the symmetric sentence-level matching (Eq. 1) and the consistency score (Eq. 2), our filtering helps filter clinically contradictory cases in practice, as shown in Fig. 2 (left) and the +5.36pp Acc contribution in Table 3.(R1, R3) Reliance on lexical metrics and binary VQA: These protocols were adopted to align exactly with the medical-RAG baselines we compare against (RULE, MMed-RAG, FactMM-RAG), which all use the same metrics and yes/no VQA, so a controlled comparison required following the same setup. To complement these protocols, we additionally report the attention-decomposition analysis (Table 4), which provides mechanistic evidence that our gains stem from increased visual grounding rather than text copying. Incorporating clinical-efficacy metrics and open-ended VQA would offer complementary evidence in subsequent studies. (R2) Why does the proposed method give a much higher visual-token attention score, even though the input token length is the same as raw LLaVA-Med: The input token sequence to the LLM (system prompt + visual tokens + question) is indeed identical to the raw LLaVA-Med-1.5, so the increase in Vision ratio is not due to changes in token composition. Rather, retrieved evidence is injected into the ViT hidden states via gated cross-attention before the projection, so the visual tokens entering the LLM carry higher task-relevant signal density while their length remains unchanged. As the LLM finds more diagnostically useful information within the visual segment, attention shifts toward it, as shown in Table 4 where the Vision ratio rises from 0.06 to 0.27 on MIMIC-CXR. In contrast, text-prompt RAG appends retrieved evidence as post-vision text tokens, which inflate Post-Vision and further suppress the Vision ratio below the base model. (R2, R3) Experiments are limited to a single and outdated backbone (LLaVA-Med-1.5): The choice of LLaVA-Med-1.5 was intentional, since all medical-RAG baselines we compare against (FactMM-RAG, RULE, MMed-RAG) use the same backbone, which is necessary to isolate the contribution of our retrieval-integration design. Extending the framework to more recent Med-LVLM backbones is a meaningful direction for follow-up work. (R3) Section 2.3 clarity, Table 3 dataset, and table readability: We appreciate these suggestions and agree that these aspects could be presented more clearly. For reference, the Table 3 ablation results are on MIMIC-CXR (the Full model row matches the corresponding row in Table 1).
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): All three reviewers independently assigned a score of 4, showing clear consensus. The paper addresses a well-motivated problem—language shortcuts in text-prompt RAG for medical VLMs—and proposes a coherent feature-level integration via gated cross-attention, a negation-aware retrieval strategy, and a correspondence-based grounding loss. Empirical results are consistent across three benchmarks and two modalities, and the attention-ratio analysis provides mechanistic support for the core claim. Common concerns across reviews include reliance on lexical metrics (ROUGE/METEOR) without clinical efficacy measures, binary-only VQA evaluation, and experiments limited to a single and outdated backbone LLaVA-Med. Authors should address these issues in the camera-ready version.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Anatomical Guidance for Text-to-CT Generation
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The method addresses a clinically relevant gap: synthesising CT volumes from reports without relying on segmentation masks at inference. Retrieving a semantically similar case and using its mask approximates anatomical structure while preserving the flexibility of text conditioning. 2.The approach leverages a pretrained latent diffusion model and adds a ControlNet branch to inject the proxy mask through zero‑initialised residual connections, so only the control branch is trained. This preserves the existing generative capabilities, simplifies optimisation and makes the system modular. Experiments report image fidelity using two‑dimensional and three‑dimensional FID, clinical consistency via a pretrained CT‑Net classifier, and spatial controllability via Dice and HD95 after segmenting generated volumes. Baselines include multi‑stage pipelines (GenerateCT, MedSyn), diffusion‑based report models (Text‑to‑CT, Report2CT), a mask‑conditioned upper bound (MAISI) and ablations on retrieval quality. An ablation comparing nearest, farthest and random retrieval demonstrates that semantically aligned proxies improve FID, classification AUC and Dice scores, whereas poor retrieval degrades performance. Statistical tests (paired Wilcoxon) are reported. 4.The paper clearly formulates the problem, retrieval mechanism and ControlNet integration with equations and describes training and inference procedures. Dataset splits, preprocessing and hyper‑parameters are provided, and code release upon acceptance is promised.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The proposed method uses known components: a three‑dimensional vision‑language encoder, nearest‑neighbour retrieval and ControlNet conditioning and applies them to CT generation. MAISI already uses ControlNet with segmentation masks; here the mask is replaced by a retrieved proxy. The contribution is therefore incremental and primarily combines existing tools rather than introducing a fundamentally new generative mechanism. 2.The method relies on retrieving a single nearest neighbour based on report embeddings. There is no quantitative analysis of how often the retrieved mask matches the target anatomy. Failure modes where the nearest neighbour is anatomically dissimilar for example, different pathology or organ size are not examined. Using multiple neighbours or alternative retrieval strategies is not explored. Experiments are conducted only on the CT‑RATE dataset using automated metrics. Clinical consistency is measured via CT‑Net classification on real CTs, which tests recognisability rather than whether the generated image reflects the described pathology. Moreover, spatial controllability compares generated masks to the retrieved proxy rather than ground‑truth anatomy, thus high Dice scores may reflect copying the proxy rather than generating correct anatomy. FID is known to correlate poorly with clinical plausibility. There is no external validation by radiologists, no pathology‑specific breakdown, and no tests on other body regions or report styles. 4.The paper compares to several baselines but does not discuss or evaluate alternative controllable text‑to‑CT strategies, such as models guided by pseudo‑masks, landmarks or multiple proxies. Retrieval‑based generative models outside medical imaging are not cited. A comparison against a simpler structural prior without retrieval would help isolate the contribution of the retrieval step.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1) Well-motivated problem: addresses the gap between semantic-only and structure-driven generation. 2) Interesting use of retrieval to approximate anatomical priors without requiring annotations at inference. 3) Technically sound integration with latent diffusion + ControlNet. 4) Multi-axis evaluation (FID, CT-Net, Dice/HD95). 5) Ablation on retrieval strategies (nearest/random/farthest) is useful.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1) Lack of validation of the core retrieval assumption: The method critically depends on retrieving a “semantically related clinical case using a 3D vision-language encoder” (Abstract, p.1), yet there is no rigorous quantitative or qualitative validation that the retrieved cases are indeed semantically or anatomically aligned with the input reports. The paper does not provide retrieval metrics (e.g., recall@k, similarity distributions) or qualitative retrieval examples beyond limited illustration (Fig. 2, p.8). 2) Unclear training and domain alignment of the vision-language encoder: On page 3, the authors state that “text conditioning is implemented through embeddings extracted from a vision-language model based on the CLIP paradigm [24], extended with a 3D image encoder.” However, it is unclear whether this encoder is sufficiently pretrained or fine-tuned on radiology-specific data(in this case CT). Without strong modality-specific alignment, the reliability of semantic retrieval from radiology reports is questionable. 3) No radiologist or expert evaluation: Despite operating in a clinically sensitive domain, the paper lacks any expert (radiologist) validation. This is particularly important given that the method assumes that retrieved reports and their associated anatomy are clinically meaningful proxies. 4) Assumption that radiology reports fully represent image content is not validated: The approach assumes that the input report provides a sufficiently complete and accurate semantic description of the underlying CT volume. However, radiology reports are often incomplete, variable, and focused on salient findings rather than full anatomical description. The paper does not analyze how this limitation affects retrieval or generation. 5) Evaluation of spatial controllability is proxy-based: Dice and HD95 are computed against retrieved masks rather than ground truth (p.7), which may overestimate anatomical correctness and does not confirm true alignment with the intended anatomy. 6) Moderate methodological novelty: The framework is primarily a combination of existing components (retrieval + latent diffusion + ControlNet), with limited fundamentally new modeling contributions.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The clinical motivation is strong. Text-only CT synthesis often produces spatially inconsistent outputs, and requiring a ground-truth segmentation mask at inference is unrealistic in most deployment settings. Framing anatomy as a “retrievable proxy” is a natural and promising solution to this tension. 2.The retrieval quality ablation is clean and directly supports the paper’s central message. It cleanly isolates the contribution of semantic alignment from the structural conditioning mechanism itself.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The framework is quite incremental over Text-to-CT [22]. The proposed method essentially adds a ControlNet branch to that prior model, with the mask sourced from retrieval rather than ground truth. This is fine, but the framing overstates the architectural novelty. 2.The paper positions MAISI as an upper bound that “assumes access to ground-truth annotations at inference time,” but this is not fully accurate. MAISI itself supports inference with TotalSegmentator-predicted masks rather than ground-truth masks, the same tool used here to generate training proxies.
