Comparing FID between systems with different training distributions is problematic and is not acknowledged anywhere. MAISI was trained on ~10K multi-site CT volumes from diverse datasets; this system and all text-conditioned baselines train on CT-RATE (~27K chest CTs).
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank all reviewers and the AC for the constructive feedback. [R1,R2,R3] Retrieval Validation: We clarify that our ablation was designed to validate the core retrieval assumption. Comparing RAG-Nearest, Random, and Farthest under identical generative conditions directly isolates retrieval quality: the monotonic, statistically significant degradation from Nearest→Random→Farthest across all evaluation axes (paired Wilcoxon p<0.05) is direct empirical evidence that semantic similarity correlates with anatomically and clinically meaningful proxies. Regarding explicit retrieval metrics: our system uses the 3D encoder of [22], the following numbers are from that paper, not new results from our experiments. [22] evaluates the encoder retrieval on CT-RATE achieving Re@5=0.041, Re@10=0.072, Re@50=0.229, Re@100=0.368 and MAP@1=0.987, MAP@5=0.848.MAP@K is the most informative metric for our task: the proxy does not need to replicate the target anatomy, but to provide a structurally coherent scaffold aligned with the report pathological content. MAP@1 confirms the nearest neighbor shares the same pathological class in nearly all cases. [R1,R2,R3] Novelty: No prior work addresses annotation-free anatomical conditioning for text-to-CT generation. We agree the individual components are not new in isolation, and that architecturally we build on [22], a deliberate choice, as it ranks as SOTA on the VLM3D Challenge [12], the MICCAI benchmark for this task. Our core contribution is identifying and addressing a systematic limitation of text-to-CT methods: radiology reports are inherently underspecified with respect to spatial structure, and this limitation propagates directly into anatomically inconsistent outputs, with consequences in real deployment scenarios (Morrison et al., “A Human-centered approach to identifying promises, risks & challenges of text-to-image generative AI in radiology”, AIES 2025). We propose retrieval-augmented anatomical proxy conditioning to counter this flaw, achieving statistically significant improvements across all three evaluation axes. [R1,R2] Spatial Controllability: Dice and HD95 are intentionally computed against the retrieved proxy, measuring the model’s ability to follow the provided scaffold, which is the relevant capability in our setting. Evaluating against the GT would be misleading, as the report does not describe individual anatomy. In addition, a model trivially copying the proxy would score high here but degrade on AUC (Table 2); RAG-Nearest achieves both the highest Dice and highest AUC, confirming the two axes are complementary and that structural guidance does not come at the cost of semantic quality. [R2] Encoder Domain Alignment: We apologise for the ambiguity. The encoder used for retrieval is pre-trained on CT-RATE, not a generic CLIP encoder. This will be stated explicitly in the final version. [R3] MAISI Comparison: R3 correctly notes that MAISI supports predicted masks at inference, however the key distinction is not the mask source, but whose mask is used: MAISI conditions on the target volume’s own mask, giving it direct structural access to the case being synthesized, making it an oracle upper bound. Our method requires no mask at inference; the proxy is obtained purely via retrieval from the input report. MAISI has no mechanism to obtain a structural proxy from a report alone, nor can it leverage the report for conditioning. MAISI’s oracle status will be stated more explicitly in the final version. [R3] FID comparability: All methods were retrained on CT-RATE following official repositories, ensuring uniform training distribution, shape, and preprocessing. This was necessary since FID is a distributional metric sensitive to data shape and CT-Net would otherwise operate on heterogeneous inputs. This will be further acknowledged in the final version. [R1,R2] Radiologist Evaluation: We acknowledge the absence of a reader study as a limitation and consider it a priority for future work
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): This is borderline. One weak accept and two weak rejects, but all three reviewers agree the problem is important and that the retrieval-based anatomical proxy is a sensible idea. The main issue is that the core retrieval assumption is not validated strongly enough. Multiple reviewers point out that the whole method depends on retrieving anatomically and semantically meaningful neighbours, yet the paper does not provide enough direct evidence that this actually happens. This is the most important point for rebuttal. There are also concerns that the contribution is more incremental than the paper claims, essentially adding retrieval-based proxy conditioning to an existing text-to-CT and ControlNet setup. In addition, Reviewer 3 raises a specific concern that the positioning against MAISI may be overstated, since MAISI can also operate with predicted masks rather than true masks at inference. The evaluation is generally solid, but several parts remain indirect. Spatial controllability is measured against the retrieved proxy rather than true anatomy, and there is no expert validation or deeper analysis of retrieval failures and pathology-specific behaviour. The authors should focus on validating retrieval quality more directly, clarifying the training and domain alignment of the vision-language encoder, moderating or justifying the novelty claims, and addressing the fairness of the MAISI comparison. If these points are answered convincingly, the paper could still move into the accept range. | The central claim depends on the retrieved proxy being anatomically and semantically meaningful for the input report, but the submitted paper does not provide sufficient direct validation of retrieval quality. The rebuttal clarifies that some retrieval metrics come from prior work rather than the present experiments. The nearest, random, and farthest ablation is useful, but it remains indirect evidence: it shows that better embedding similarity improves generation metrics, not that the retrieved masks are anatomically appropriate for the intended target case. The method is incremental over an existing text-to-CT model and ControlNet-style conditioning. Spatial controllability is evaluated against the retrieved proxy rather than true anatomy, so it primarily measures adherence to the proxy, not anatomical correctness. There is no expert validation, no pathology-specific failure analysis, and the MAISI comparison still requires careful qualification as an oracle or upper-bound comparison. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The rebuttal successfully addresses the core concerns: the retrieval ablation and encoder clarification confirm that semantic retrieval yields anatomically meaningful proxies, satisfying Reviewers #1 and #2.Reviewer #3’s novelty and MAISI comparison concerns are acknowledged but do not undermine the practical contribution of annotation-free anatomical conditioning. The paper is a solid, well-motivated methodological refinement with clear clinical relevance, though future work should include radiologist validation and direct retrieval metrics. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper was reviewed by three experts in the field. The initial recommendations were one Weak Accept and two Weak Rejects. After the rebuttal, reviewers updated their recommendations to Accept. Based on the authors’ rebuttal and the reviewers’ post-rebuttal feedback, I believe the authors have adequately addressed the key concerns, including retrieval validation, novelty, and comparison with MAISI. Therefore, the paper is recommended for acceptance to MICCAI 2026.The authors are encouraged to incorporate the necessary changes discussed during the rebuttal process into the final camera-ready version.

title: Right Answer, Wrong Evidence: Revealing Visual Confabulation in Multi-Image Medical VLMs with the Evidence Attribution Score
reviewer_1_strengths: 1) It addresses an important and clinically relevant problem. The paper goes beyond standard answer accuracy and asks whether a model used the appropriate visual evidence, which is especially important for longitudinal or multi-image medical reasoning tasks. This is a meaningful gap in current evaluation practice. 2) The proposed protocol is practical and model-agnostic. A notable strength is that the method only requires input-output access. That makes it applicable not only to open-source models, but also to closed-source APIs where gradients, attention maps, or internal representations are unavailable. This gives the work clear practical relevance for real-world auditing. 3) The most interesting novelty is the combination of behavioral and self-reported evidence. The mathematically novel part of EAS itself is limited, but the paper’s more original idea is to compare what the model behaviorally depends on (via ablation) against what it says it used (via repeated evidence prompts) at the image level in a multi-image medical setting. That combination is interesting because it targets a failure mode that is difficult to observe through accuracy alone. 4) The empirical results are nontrivial and potentially important. The paper reports high rates of low-EAS behavior even among correct answers, weak correspondence between answer accuracy and EAS, and a strong chain-of-thought effect for open-source models. Even if one is not fully convinced by the metric, these findings are interesting and could motivate follow-up work. 5) The evaluation is broader than a single-point metric report. The authors do not stop at reporting EAS; they also include evidence-swap, perturbation-fragility, and Shapley-based analyses. These do not fully resolve all concerns, but they do show an effort to validate the method more carefully than many explainability papers.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1) The theoretical novelty of the Evidence Alignment Score (EAS) is relatively constrained. Mathematically, EAS is defined as the Jaccard overlap between the Behaviorally Estimated evidence Set (BES) and the Conceptually self-reported evidence Set (CES). In this regard, the primary contribution lies in the operationalization of the BES/CES pipeline rather than the introduction of a fundamentally new metric. This work situates itself within the existing body of literature on faithfulness, hallucinations, and attribution, sharing commonalities with frameworks such as CHAIR (2018), POPE (2023), and FaithScore (2023), as well as classic explainability methods like Grad-CAM and SHAP. 2) EAS does not directly evaluate whether the model utilized clinically appropriate evidence. The metric exclusively quantifies the agreement between two model-derived proxies: behavioral estimation and self-reported attribution. Consequently, a model could rely on a spurious or non-clinical image feature and subsequently report that same image, resulting in a high EAS despite fundamentally flawed reasoning. Without ground-truth annotations for relevant images or clinician-led adjudication, the paper fails to establish a definitive link between high EAS and the use of clinically correct evidence. 3) The BES serves as a somewhat coarse proxy for evidence utilization. By relying on a single-image leave-one-out ablation—counting only those images whose removal alters the discrete final answer—the BES may overlook sub-threshold effects, distributed evidence, or synergistic dependencies between multiple images. This limitation is particularly critical in multi-image medical reasoning, where diagnostic evidence is often encoded across several frames rather than localized within a single, indispensable image. 4) The CES is heuristic-driven and highly sensitive to explanation styles. The determination of CES depends on repeated prompting and a 2-of-3 majority rule, both of which are heuristic in nature. A model’s reporting behavior, prompt sensitivity, or specific instruction-following style may influence the CES more than its actual visual attribution. For instance, a verbose model might be unfairly penalized by the Jaccard denominator, while a more concise model could receive a disproportionately high score. 5) The interpretation of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) results requires further validation. The authors posit that CoT gains indicate enhanced visual engagement in open-source models. While plausible, this conclusion is not uniquely established; since CES is itself derived from prompts, the observed improvements might reflect changes in explicit reporting behavior rather than a fundamental shift in the model’s internal visual reasoning processes. 6) Cross-model comparisons lack a strict ``apples-to-apples’’ foundation. Mean EAS is calculated only for correctly answered questions, meaning different models are evaluated on disparate subsets of the benchmark. This approach introduces potential item-selection bias. A matched analysis, restricted to a common set of questions answered correctly by all compared models, would provide a more rigorous basis for cross-model conclusions. 7) The selection of specific thresholds lacks robust justification. The 2/3 majority rule for CES and the reliability threshold ($\tau=0.3$) appear largely heuristic. Although the manuscript suggests that conclusions remain qualitatively consistent across various thresholds, it lacks a strong clinical or task-specific calibration to demonstrate that these values correspond to meaningful levels of diagnostic reliability. 8) The scope of external validation and benchmark analysis is limited. The study relies on 200 questions from a single benchmark and lacks clinician-labeled evidence for relevance, a text-only baseline, or a thorough analysis of benchmark bias. Given the paper’s emphasis on “text priors,” it remains unclear to what extent low-EAS behavior stems from model-specific confabulation versus inherent answerability from the question text or other dataset artifacts.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The core idea is timely and valuable. Many people are now discussing how VLMs can give correct answers for the wrong reasons, especially in medicine where justification matters. Defining visual confabulation clearly and separating it from regular hallucination is helpful. 2.The EAS formulation is straightforward yet insightful. Using leave-one-out ablation for behavioral dependence is model-agnostic and works for both open- and closed-source models, which is practical. The three causal validations (evidence swap, perturbation fragility, and Shapley agreement) give decent support that EAS tracks real grounding rather than just correlation. 3.The chain-of-thought finding is striking and potentially useful: it suggests open-source models have latent visual capabilities that default prompting fails to engage. This behavioral divide between model families is something accuracy metrics completely miss. The paper is clearly written, the figures are helpful, and the discussion on limitations is honest.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The main limitation is the small evaluation scale. The authors use only 200 questions from MedFrameQA, even though the full benchmark has over 2,800 pairs. While they argue that the computational cost (thousands of forward passes) makes larger tests difficult, 200 examples feel thin when drawing broad conclusions about systematic differences between all open-source and closed-source models, or about confabulation rates in general. More questions, or at least a clearer justification for why this subset is representative, would strengthen the claims. 2.Another concern is the Claimed Evidence Set (CES). Asking the model three times “which images are important” and taking a 2/3 majority is a reasonable heuristic, but it still relies on the model’s own verbal reporting. It may not reliably reflect what the model actually attends to during inference. The authors could have strengthened this by comparing CES against internal signals (e.g., attention weights or activation patterns in open-source models) or by benchmarking EAS against other grounding metrics from prior work on VLM faithfulness. Without such cross-validation, it is harder to be fully convinced that low EAS always means true visual confabulation rather than limitations in how CES is elicited. 3.The paper could also discuss more explicitly how well leave-one-out captures distributed or redundant visual information across images, even though they provide Shapley results as support.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The empirical effort is substantial. The paper evaluates several model families, compares open- and closed-source systems, studies the effect of image count, and includes additional validation experiments beyond the main metric. 2.The chain-of-thought result is interesting. The observation that CoT substantially increases EAS in open-source models while leaving closed-source models largely unchanged is potentially useful for future work on inference-time safeguards and model auditing. 3.The paper addresses an important and practically relevant problem. In medical multi-image settings, answer accuracy alone is not sufficient if the model does not rely on the appropriate visual evidence. This is a worthwhile evaluation question for clinically motivated AI systems.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.My primary concern is not that the paper applies ideas to medical imaging. That is entirely reasonable for MICCAI. My concern is that the paper presents the broader methodological idea as more novel than it is, while failing to properly acknowledge closely related prior work from ML/CV/xAI and VQA faithfulness. In particular, the paper does not cite (or talk about) important works on models being right for the wrong reasons, shortcut learning, faithful explanations, and faithful/plausible grounding, including Right for the Right Reasons [R1], Unmasking Clever Hans Predictors [R2], ERASER [R3], Taking a HINT [R4], and Measuring Faithful and Plausible Visual Grounding in VQA [R5]. These are not peripheral citations. They are directly relevant to the paper’s central framing. As a result, the paper’s contribution is not positioned accurately enough relative to prior work. The contribution would be much more convincing if framed as an application and adaptation of these ideas to the setting of multi-image medical VLMs, rather than as if the broader conceptual gap were largely unaddressed. In its current form, the paper risks presenting a community’s existing ideas as if they were substantially new in this manuscript. 2.There are also several critical citation errors or misuses, which weaken the credibility of the technical framing: (a) The paper gives the wrong arXiv identifier for MedVH; the cited identifier does not match the MedVH paper [R6]. (b) The paper states that its threshold choice is analogous to slight-to-fair agreement in Cohen’s kappa, but cites Pearl’s Causality for this claim. That is not an appropriate citation for a kappa-interpretation statement. If the paper wants to use that language, it should cite a standard agreement-interpretation reference such as [R7]. reviewer_3_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the Reviewers and ACs for recognizing our clinical relevance, practical protocol, and impactful CoT findings. Major concerns are addressed below. 1) Novelty & Literature (Reviewers 1 & 3): Our main contribution is the BES/CES framework and the resulting Evidence Attribution Score (EAS), which together provide a practical black-box auditing protocol for testing whether multi-image medical VLMs arrive at correct answers for the right visual reasons when gradient access is unavailable. We thank Reviewer 3 for highlighting relevant prior work. While [R1] and [R3] rely on gradient access or token-level rationales, and [R4]-[R5] focus on single-image VQA grounding, our setting is annotation-free and uses image-level evidence across multiple medical images. We agree that [R1]-[R5] provide important conceptual foundations and will cite and discuss them in the Introduction and Related Work. We will also correct the MedVH citation [R6] and replace the Pearl citation with Landis & Koch (1977) [R7] in the camera-ready version. 2) Evaluation Scale (Reviewers 1 & 2): Due to computational cost, we sampled a balanced subset of 200 MedFrameQA questions (50 each for 2-5 images). Unlike standard VQA benchmarking, each EAS evaluation requires repeated CES prompting alongside leave-one-out causal ablations across all images. Evaluating the full benchmark across 8 models requires >200,000 forward passes and ~700,000 API calls/prompts, making exhaustive auditing prohibitive. Our stratified subset (Sec 4) yielded tight 95% bootstrap CIs (width 0.06-0.12) and achieved p<0.001 for all primary findings, providing sufficient statistical precision. 3) Clinical Ground Truth & BES Limitations (Reviewers 1 & 2): EAS is a behavioral proxy, not a clinician-adjudicated ground-truth metric (Sec 6). While high EAS does not guarantee clinical correctness, low EAS on a correct answer conservatively signals potential confabulation and text-prior reliance. Reviewer 1 asks if low EAS reflects benchmark-level text answerability. If low EAS were purely a dataset artifact, we would expect similar BES=∅ rates across models. Instead, substantial model-specific variation (e.g., open-source vs. closed-source) supports that EAS captures genuine visual dependence differences. While leave-one-out ablation may miss synergistic dependencies, our Shapley analysis demonstrated moderate-to-strong agreement (0.393) with LOO BES, supporting LOO as a computationally feasible lower bound. 4) CES Heuristics & Verbosity Bias (Reviewers 1 & 2): The EAS threshold (τ) is a tunable hyperparameter. While findings are robust across τ∈[0.1,0.5], we intentionally set a lenient baseline (τ=0.3) to avoid artificially inflating failure rates from redundant slices. Under even higher evaluated thresholds (e.g., τ=0.7), confabulation predictably soars to 70-90%. Yet, our low baseline still exposes very high rates of confabulation. During pilots, 5 and 7 CES prompts yielded no major shift in decisions. Since 3 prompts already cost 48k queries, scaling further wastes compute without improving results. Jaccard sets contain discrete image IDs (e.g., {Img1, Img3}), not text tokens. A verbose model claiming Img1 in a paragraph has a CES size of 1, identical to a concise model. 5) CoT Gains & Cross-Model Comparisons (Reviewer 1): The strongest evidence that CoT changes visual behavior, not just explanation style, is that BES itself changes. BES is measured entirely through ablation and does not depend on explanation text. Under default prompting, open-source models frequently exhibit text-prior dependency (BES=∅). Under CoT, these cases drop substantially across models, meaning image removal changes the answer more often. This supports the interpretation that CoT increases genuine visual dependence rather than merely changing reporting style. Finally, on the strict intersection of correctly answered questions across all models, rankings and conclusions remain consistent with the main text.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): As both the merits (relevance, model-agnostic design, interesting empirical findings) and limitations (failure to acknowledge/compare existing works in the general ML domain, lack of justification for key experimental design choices) stand out, as mentioned by reviewers, the authors are invited to submit a rebuttal. | The paper received mixed reactions after the rebuttal. Reviewers agree on the relevance of the question and the reasonable clarification regarding the sample size, while having remaining concerns over the over-simplified approach (the overlap between leave-one-out results and self-reported importance) when positioned against the more complex inconsistency/hallucination detection contexts. Taking the reviews, responses, and follow-up comments together, it is reasonable to say that the proposed approach (more like for behavioral consistency under simplified settings) does not fully support the claimed contributions toward addressing the complex mirage + hallucination problem. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Personally I like this paper. It makes a highly important conceptual contribution, separates “getting the answer right” from “using the right evidence,” which is directly relevant for clinical trust. The finding that 40–79% of correct answers are confabulated is striking. I recommend the acceptance of this work. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper is accepted as a borderline but meaningful contribution. The reviewers generally agreed that the work addresses an important and underexplored problem in evaluating evidence grounding and visual confabulation in multimodal medical AI, particularly for closed-source multi-image VLMs. The rebuttal successfully addressed several major concerns, including additional analyses on CoT impact, statistical clarification for the small dataset setting, and improved transparency regarding the evaluation protocol. At the same time, some limitations remain. In particular, the current EAS/BES/CES metrics should be framed more carefully as heuristic proxies for evidence alignment rather than direct measures of clinical validity, and the paper should avoid overstating causal or clinical conclusions. The final version should also incorporate the missing explainability and faithfulness-related citations raised during review and further clarify the limitations of the proposed evaluation framework. Despite these remaining concerns, the benchmark and auditing protocol provide a practical and novel evaluation perspective that is likely to be valuable for the community.

title: Robust automatic brain vessel segmentation in 3D CTA scans using dynamic 4D-CTA data
reviewer_1_strengths: Effective use of dynamic 4D-CTA for annotation efficiency: The paper proposes a practical and well-motivated pipeline that leverages temporal contrast dynamics to separate arteries and veins. By reusing annotations across multiple phases, the approach reduces manual labeling effort, which is a major bottleneck in vascular segmentation tasks. Data-centric contribution with multi-phase diversity: The introduction of the DynaVessel dataset, containing multi-phase CTA volumes with artery and vein labels, is valuable. In particular, the inclusion of multiple contrast phases per patient provides richer supervision and exposes models to a broader range of intensity variations, which is often missing in existing CTA datasets. Improved robustness to contrast variability: The experimental results demonstrate that training on multi-phase data improves robustness across different contrast phases. The analysis of performance across phases (e. g. , Fig. 4–5) provides useful insight into how contrast timing affects segmentation quality. Clear and interpretable preprocessing pipeline: The artery/vein separation method based on registration and intensity comparison is simple, interpretable, and grounded in physiological contrast differences, making it easy to understand and potentially reproduce. Use of standard and well-established backbone (nnU-Net): By building on nnU-Net, the paper isolates the contribution of the data and preprocessing pipeline rather than architectural changes, which strengthens the claim that performance gains are driven by improved data quality and diversity.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: The paper does not introduce a new segmentation model or learning framework, but instead relies on a standard nnU-Net backbone. The main contribution lies in the data curation and preprocessing pipeline. Limited validation of annotation quality: The ground truth is generated via a semi-automatic pipeline (iCafe + thresholding) and validated by a single neuroradiologist. There is no assessment of inter-observer variability or annotation uncertainty. Given the difficulty of artery–vein separation and distal vessel labeling, the reliability of the annotations is not sufficiently established. Evaluation limitations and metric choice: The paper emphasizes a modified Dice coefficient (mDC) that measures sensitivity but does not penalize false positives. This is non-standard and may bias results toward higher scores. Standard Dice, precision-recall analysis, or statistical significance testing are not sufficiently reported, making it harder to fully assess performance improvements. Limited evidence for generalization across scanners and sites: All data appears to be acquired from a single scanner and institution. Despite claims of robustness to real-world variability, there is no evaluation on multi-center or multi-scanner datasets, which limits confidence in clinical applicability.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The provided dataset is very relevant for the community and unique; to my knowledge, no other dynamic CTA datasets are available. Authors show that models derived from such dataset outperform vasculature segmentation when compared to prior datasets.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Novelty: While the dataset + protocol is definitely a contribution in the field, the derivation of a vasculature segmentation model is limited and weakly evaluated. Authors make use of an nnUnet model -as were used in prior works in diverse tastes, e.g. TopCow/TopBrain- with limited baseline comparisons and ablations. Beyond the dataset, it is not clear what is the ‘methodological contribution’ of this work. Labels: While authors could have obtained a timepoint-specific vessel mask for each CTA timepoint in a series; instead, a single arterial / vein mask is annotated from the Peak arterial/venous phases. Given that the dataset is the main novelty in this work, this represents a limitation, since no single timepoint enhances the whole brain vasculature so that it the labels can be considered as a ground-truth for all the timepoints in the series. Such differences are even strengthened in some pathologies (e.g. stroke), where delayed bolus arrival to the ipsilateral brain hemisphere creates larger bolus arrival delays. The work is not easy to read. Please check below my comments about it.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: -Novel and valuable dataset: The most significant contribution lies in the construction of a relatively large 4D-CTA dataset for brain vessel segmentation, which is rare in this domain. The use of dynamic CTA allows efficient annotation reuse across phases and provides rich temporal contrast information. -Clear empirical benefit of data scale: The experiments convincingly show that increasing the amount and diversity of training data leads to improved artery and vein segmentation performance, including better topology-related metrics.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: -Restricted impact on the broader community: Although code and models are promised to be released, the dataset itself does not appear to be publicly distributable. This limits the potential impact of the work on the broader research community and its reuse in follow-up studies. -Limited methodological novelty: While the dataset itself is novel, the technical approach is not. The segmentation models and training strategy rely entirely on established deep learning frameworks (e.g., nnU-Net) and standard loss functions. No new network architecture, learning strategy, or theory is introduced.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for their insightful feedback, which will significantly improve our manuscript: Generalization (R1): To clarify, DynaVessel (DV) comes from one hospital using a Canon-Toshiba scanner, and we evaluate the model on O.O.D. datasets from 2 countries in another continent (Europe): 1) a subset of ISLES, 2) TopCoW (+derived datasets), which was acquired with a Siemens scanner. Covering more scanners/hospitals would be ideal, but the fact a model trained on N=29 patients with multi-phase CTA can achieve SOTA performance on O.O.D. data suggests strong generalization Data availability/Anonymization (R2,R3): Due to changing federal government and institutional mandates, our institutional IRB, compliance and data security administrators have instituted stricter oversight procedures for data sharing, which we have been working through for the last 3 months. We preclude reidentification by removing patient information from DICOM headers and removing facial bones/soft tissue from all scans (no skull stripping). We’re optimistic this will satisfy our new compliance responsibilities and allow us to release DV before the paper is published Methodological novelty (R1,R2,R3): while we don’t propose a new architecture/loss function, DV is the largest CTA dataset for brain vessel segmentation and the first to use Dynamic 4D-CTA to simplify & scale up the annotation process. We appreciate R1’s encouragement to position our contribution as data-centric and will increase the emphasis on this in the revised version Limited ablations (R2): we did dataset-level ablations: Figs. 4 & 5 show ablations of the impact of contrast at inference (tested on all phases) and the impact of training on a single image per patient (at peak vein/peak arterial contrast). We hope these results will address R2’s concerns about ablations Metrics (R1): R1 is right: mDC can be “gamed” by over-segmenting a scan. However, the adHD metric will severely penalize cases where the boundaries of the predictions are far from the targets, as it sums minimum distances from each GT-surface point to the nearest predicted surface point. Our annotations cover more vessels than existing datasets, so traditional metrics wouldn’t convey the impact of our approach on the O.O.D. data. Still, we present extra metrics for binary vessel segmentation with the DV model on 3 datasets: Metric DVtest VVerse TopBrain Dice 0.64 0.20 0.30 Precision 0.55 0.12 0.18 Recall 0.79 0.65 0.90 Qualitative analysis reveals that FNs are infrequent while FPs mostly comprise very distal/scalp vessels (Fig 7c) and bright background objects that can be removed with a brain mask. In addition, we will add statistical significance tests comparing the DV model to all baselines in the revised version Data quality assurance (R1,R2):The 16cm detector used for the Dynamic-4D-CTA protocol means the patient experiences little motion during the 60 second data acquisition, minimizing inter-phase patient motion. We also use intra-patient rigid registration (validated by a radiologist) between the peak arterial phase and other phases to ensure all images are properly aligned (Sec 2.2). We’ll detail the radiologist’s quality verification procedure for vessel annotations and discuss the limitations due to the lack of inter-rater agreement metrics in the camera ready Single-phase annotations (R2): Dynamic-4D-CTA acquires data for all vascular phases, allowing retrospective selection of optimal peak phases per patient. We ensure all relevant vasculature parts are highlighted in the peak phases by including only healthy patients with symmetric vascular trees and no occlusions. Evaluation on cases from TopCoW (e.g., ct_001) that have partly occluded or non-opacified arteries confirmed that DV nnUNet segmentation accuracy is robust to such artifacts and pathologies Clarity (R3):We will improve clarity and accuracy in the abstract (incl. task relevance), the description of iCafe, and variable definitions

Authors promise to open-source this dataset, which will be valuable for the MICCAI community. I recommend acceptance.

title: Robust Mitigation of Age-Dependent Confounding Effects via Sample-Difficulty Decorrelation
reviewer_1_strengths: The age-related bias problem is widespread, important, and not yet extensively analyzed or solved. A strong solution to this problem would be very attractive. The proposed mitigation method is well-motivated, thoroughly developed, and - to my knowledge - rather innovative and quite distinct from any other bias mitigation approaches that I know of. One particularity concerns the fact that the bias attribute (age) is really treated in a continuous fashion here, whereas most other approaches inherently rely on categorical bias variables. There is very little work on bias mitigation w. r. t. continuous attributes yet. The baseline methods are well-chosen and quite comprehensive; the experiments are well-designed, metrics carefully and sensibly chosen, and the new method indeed outperforms all of the competitor methods quite substantially on all relevant dimensions. The manuscript is well-written and the figures are well-designed.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: While there is not much prior work on bias mitigation for continuous attributes, there is some, and this is currently not referenced or discussed. A few examples that I know of: https://proceedings. mlr. press/v97/mary19a/mary19a. pdf https://link. springer. com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-030-86520-7_46 https://openreview. net/pdf?id=YigKlMJwjye https://dl. acm. org/doi/abs/10.1109/TPAMI. 2025.3538915 Including one or several of these methods as additional baselines would further strengthen the manuscript, since these are really the most appropriate baselines. (I will be honest - I have not worked with these myself and do not know how tricky they are to get to work. )
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The paper has a well-established experiments section that (while limited to two datasets) explores different distributions and compares to different existing methods. The motivation for the contribution is well motivated.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Minor Points and Questions 1.Abstract claim on distribution shift. The abstract states that the observed effects “may worsen” under train-test distribution shifts. We would suggest more precise language: the effects do not worsen per se, but rather become more dominant across the data. We ask the authors to revise this characterization accordingly. 2.Motivation for using the gradient as a dynamics metric. In the binary cross-entropy setting, the gradient correlates directly with prediction error, which is itself the quantity of practical interest. It is unclear what additional value the gradient-based framing provides over simply using prediction error. We ask the authors to clarify the motivation for this choice. 3.Warm-up period. The paper does not sufficiently motivate the introduction of a warm-up period. We ask the authors to provide a principled justification or ablation demonstrating its necessity. 4.Age Coverage Modulation and label sensitivity. Since beta is computed with respect to the label, it would be natural for the Age Coverage Modulation to also be defined with respect to the labels present in the minibatch. As currently formulated, the score lacks the label sensitivity needed to be fully expressive. We ask the authors to address this discrepancy. 5.Notational clarity. The paper would benefit from explicitly stating beta = Cov/Var as a standalone equation, which would significantly aid reader intuition. Additionally, the inconsistent switching between subscripts y_i and y is a source of confusion and should be harmonized throughout. 6.Missing evaluation of slope steepness. The experimental section lacks an analysis of the steepness of the calibration slopes. Both MIMIC and CheXpert exhibit approximately similar slopes even under distribution shift, and this should be evaluated and discussed. 7.Terminology: prediction error vs. sample difficulty. The paper at times conflates current prediction error with sample difficulty. These are distinct concepts in the established literature. We strongly encourage the authors to adopt more precise language: what is being measured is the model’s current prediction error on a given sample, not an intrinsic notion of sample difficulty. Major Points 1.Circular dependence in the estimation of beta. The estimates of beta rely on weights w_i, which in turn depend on the residuals, which themselves depend on beta. This circular dependence makes it difficult to understand how the regularizer is computed in practice. We ask the authors to provide a clear, step-by-step description of the computation, ideally specifying at which point in training each quantity is evaluated and whether any fixed-point iteration or approximation is involved. 2.Relationship to Zafar et al. (2017). In essence, the proposed regularizer enforces equalized losses across different age groups. While the paper does not make this connection explicit, the method can be understood as a direct, normalized extension of the fairness constraints introduced by Zafar et al. (2017, arXiv:1507.05259). We consider this a significant omission and ask the authors to discuss this relationship and clearly delineate their methodological contribution relative to this prior work. 3.Limitation to the linear setting. The paper does not adequately address the fact that the proposed method is designed for and limited to the linear case. This is a substantially weaker setting than that addressed by methods capable of correcting non-linear trends, such as Baharlouei et al. (2024, arXiv:2312.03259). We ask the authors to clarify in which specific settings their method offers advantages over existing approaches, and to provide an honest discussion of where and why it falls short in the non-linear regime. 4.Insufficient discussion of limitations. The current discussion of the method’s limitations is cursory. A thorough treatment should address, at minimum, the restriction to linear settings, sensitivity to hyperparameters such as the warm-up period, and the assumptions underlying the coverage modulation. We ask the authors to expand this section substantially.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: Firstly, this paper targets the critical challenge of age-dependent confounding in medical image classification, and proposes a robust decorrelation framework that models the label-conditioned linear correlation between age and sample difficulty. This approach effectively addresses a key limitation of existing methods that enforce age invariance. Secondly, the framework incorporates robust and adaptive components, including the Huber regression-based trend affinity weights enhance resilience to clinical variability and annotation noise, and the Age Coverage Score effectively downweights decorrelation updates when age coverage is limited, improving robustness under age imbalance and train-test age distribution shifts. Thirdly, experiments cover multiple age distribution shift intensities, two distinct radiology datasets, and comparisons with state-of-the-art baselines, providing clear evidence of the method’s superiority in balancing fairness and diagnostic accuracy.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Firstly, the paper uses a one-epoch warm-up phase to estimate trend affinity weights, and immediately fixes these weights after the warm-up phase without any updates during subsequent training. Is this design reasonable? Because as the model learns, the age-difficulty trend may change, which could make the initial weights outdated. Secondly, the adoption of the median absolute deviation (MAD) as the robust scale estimator δ_{y_i} for trend affinity weight calculation is not substantiated by comparative experiments. The paper fails to evaluate alternative robust estimators to verify whether MAD is optimally suited for handling outlier samples in diverse medical image classification. Thirdly, the regularization coefficient λ in Formula (8) is set to 1.2 without a parameter sensitivity analysis, and the paper provides no guidance on adapting this hyperparameter across different clinical datasets.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank R1,2,3 for the useful reviews & for recognizing the critical need to mitigate age confounding effects under distribution shift. [R2] Prior works: Zafar et al. impose a covariance constraint between sensitive attribute and signed decision-boundary distance as a proxy for decision-boundary unfairness. Our goal differs: continuous-age EOdds under train-test age shift. Age can be clinically informative; thus we mitigate dominant age-error trends learned as spurious correlations, not all age effects- avoiding loss of useful age information. In our method, the covariance/variance form is not an explicit fairness constraint; it arises naturally when estimating label-specific age-error slopes beta_hat_y for g_i = |p_i - y_i|. Keeping beta_hat_y near zero maintains flat label-specific error trends across age, improving EOdds robustness when train-test age distributions differ. Huber affinity & age coverage stabilize estimation. We will discuss this distinction. [R2] Gradient/error formulation: We will clarify g_i as the logit-gradient magnitude[R1]. For BCE (sigmoid), g_i = |dL_BCE/dlogit| , so g_i = |p_i - y_i| in [0,1]. Estimated post-warm-up, before memorization or gradient shrinkage dominates [Arpit et al., ICML 2017], g_i is a bounded proxy for model-perceived difficulty. Further, we prefer this over p_i since p_i is not label-conditioned. Raw BCE loss is excluded as it is unbounded. [R2,3] Design choices - coverage, beta, warm-up: We will clarify our method step-by-step. After warm-up, label-conditioned Huber regression estimates trend affinity weights w_i on the full training set; these weights are then fixed. During training, only g_i evolves, and beta_hat_y is a standard WOLS estimate of g_i against fixed w_i & z_i; no fixed-point iteration is used. Fixing w_i is motivated by the fact that early-epoch gradients best reflect each sample’s alignment with the dominant age-difficulty trend before memorization and gradient shrinkage dominate [Arpit et al., ICML 2017]; before warm-up, g_i reflects random initialization, making trend estimation unreliable. One epoch is a viable intervention point: with ~40k training samples a single epoch spans many iterations - enough to yield a stable signal - while still preceding spurious age-shortcut memorization. We acknowledge that warmup epoch =1 is a hyperparameter and will note a sensitivity study. Updating w_i during training would introduce circular co-dependence between trend affinity weights and beta, risking optimization instability. Coverage modulation is already label-conditioned via C_y in Eq. 8; we will make this more clear. [R2,3] Linearity, generalization & limitations: We agree the method targets the dominant first-order linear age-error trends and not all age effects based on empirical observations (Fig. 1). We flatten the dominant main age-shortcut mode without enforcing distributional/feature invariance [Baharlouei et al.], since nonlinear or higher-order age effects may encode clinically meaningful morphology/prevalence signals (introduction). The framework is most effective for cohorts with monotonic age-prevalence trends, e.g., adult cohorts where chronic disease prevalence often increases with age. A zero-slope target also supports robustness under train-test age shift, since it is independent of the sampled age distribution. Nonlinear residual trends remain outside current scope; spline/kernel extensions are natural future work when such modes dominate. -MAD was used as a standard robust scale estimator for Huber residual weighting, not as uniquely optimal; IQR/SD alternatives will be noted as future work. We will expand the limitation section to cover these points. Lambda selection: Lambda controls the fairness-accuracy trade-off and was selected by validation grid search maximizing the validation ratio of DeltaSep10 reduction to AUC drop relative to ERM. These details will be added All remaining minor discussion points will be addressed.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper addresses the important problem of age-dependent confounding in medical image classification. The reviewers generally recognized the paper’s strong motivation, methodological innovation, and coherent experimental evaluation. The paper’s significance in continuous-attribute bias mitigation would be better highlighted if the authors address the reviewers’ concerns, including strengthening the positioning relative to prior work, justifying the gradient-based formulation, clarifying key design choices, providing component motivation and sensitivity analyses, and discussing the method’s limitations and generalizability. | The rebuttal appears to have addressed the reviewers’ concerns directly and helped clarified the distinction between this method and existing continuous-attribute bias mitigation approaches. The combination of significance, technical focus, and a constructive rebuttal justifies acceptance. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The rebuttal addresses most of the concerns. One reviewer still raises a valid concern about the regularization parameter and the need to better analyze its effect. However, the other reviewers recommend acceptance, and the authors clarify several important points, including the computation of beta, the relation to prior work, and the linear scope of the method. I recommend acceptance. In addition to the other modifications mentioned in the rebuttal, the authors should revise the final version to clearly narrow the method’s scope to dominant first-order linear age-error trends. They should also include or strengthen the analysis of the effect of delta, and better explain how the proposed regularized objective differs from and interacts with the original learning objective. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): I would like to raise a point regarding the authors’ claim that “the model over-relies on age as a predictive shortcut.” The evidence presented in the paper does not fully support this statement. What the experiments demonstrate is that age has a measurable impact on prediction error. However, this does not necessarily imply that the model is using age as a shortcut in the causal or algorithmic sense. The distinction is important and should be clarified more carefully in the manuscript. That said, I still find the proposed approach interesting and potentially valuable, as it addresses an important and timely problem: mitigating age-related bias while preserving age-related information that may be informative for the prediction task. This is a challenging problem that has received increasing attention in the neuroimaging and medical AI communities. While the authors do not fully demonstrate that their method achieves this objective, the proposed framework is nevertheless promising. In particular, the behavior of the method appears to depend strongly on the choice of the threshold parameter (\gamma). Depending on its value, the approach may either remove too much age-related information or fail to remove enough of the age effect. A more detailed analysis of this trade-off would strengthen the paper considerably. In addition, a more comprehensive comparison with established age-correction and harmonization approaches, such as W-score normalization and ComBat-based methods, would have been valuable. These methods represent important baselines for the problem under consideration and would help position the contribution more clearly with respect to the existing literature. Nevertheless, despite these concerns, two of the three reviewers support acceptance, and I concur with their overall assessment. The paper tackles a relevant problem and proposes an interesting direction that may stimulate further work in this area. I strongly encourage the authors to address, in the final version, the majority of the points raised by Reviewer 2, which are largely requests for clarification rather than fundamental methodological objections. Doing so would significantly improve the clarity and positioning of the manuscript.

title: Robust Tooth Segmentation Under Orthodontic CBCT: A Metal Artifact-Aware Approach
reviewer_1_strengths: It addresses a real prominent problem of Orthodontic CBCT with metal artifacts important for treatment planning. It uses a novel segmentation loss function that combines a Dice loss and the distance map loss. Collected 20 clinical 3D CBCT scans acquired from patients wearing orthodontic appliances.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The manuscript briefly lists contributions, but comparison against state-of-the-art deep learning segmentation networks (e. g. , nnU-Net, TransUNet, SAM-based approaches) is missing. Statistical comparisons (t-test ) would enhance the proposed work validation. Limitations and Clinical Integration are not discussed adequately. Incorporating layer-wise visualization and feature map analysis could further enhance the interpretability and understanding of the model’s internal representations, thereby improving the overall quality of the work. Use of very small private dataset limits methods validation.
reviewer_1_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The paper innovatively transforms metal artifacts from interference noise into localization cues, optimizes detection boxes through intensity-weighted centroid differences, and utilizes distance map regression to suppress boundary artifacts, forming a rigorous closed-loop solution for strong noise environments. Experimental results strongly demonstrate the robustness of the algorithm in segmenting blurred areas on the surface of teeth.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The dataset is still insufficient in scale and lacks indicators related to inference speed. There remains some doubt regarding the stability and universality of the hypothesis regarding metal artifacts.
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.Clinically relevant problem setting. Orthodontic CBCT with metal artifacts from brackets and wires is a common yet underexplored scenario in tooth segmentation research. Most prior work assumes artifact-free or mildly corrupted scans, so explicitly targeting this setting addresses a practical clinical need. 2.Conceptually appealing two-stage artifact handling. The idea of treating metal artifacts differently across the two stages — exploiting their high-intensity signal for detection while suppressing their influence during segmentation — is a well-motivated design philosophy, even if the individual components are technically simple. 3.Tooth-group-wise analysis. Table 2 provides a breakdown across anterior, premolar, and molar groups, which is informative for understanding how metal artifact severity (relative to tooth size) affects segmentation quality across different tooth types.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.Limited technical novelty. The distance map regression (Sec 2.3) is a well-known auxiliary task for boundary-aware segmentation, and the authors’ own baseline [3] already applies Chamfer distance maps to tooth segmentation. The intensity-weighted center-of-mass loss (Sec 2.2) reduces the entire intensity distribution to a single first-order statistic, which is blind to higher-order distributional differences (e.g., symmetric artifacts yield similar centroids despite substantially different distributions). No analysis is provided on why this coarse summary suffices, nor any comparison with richer alternatives (e.g., higher-order moments, KL divergence). The overall pipeline (VOI cropping → heatmap detection → U-Net) also follows prior work without architectural modification. 2.Outdated baselines and missing comparison with strong public methods. All compared methods (ToothNet, CGDNet, PATRCNN) date from 2019–2020.nnU-Net, a standard baseline in medical image segmentation, is not compared despite being straightforward to apply. More recent work such as ToothSeg (van Nistelrooij et al., JBHI 2026), which also performs CBCT tooth instance segmentation with publicly available code, is neither discussed nor compared.
reviewer_3_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and meta-reviewer for their constructive comments. We are grateful that the clinical relevance of this problem and the practical value of our artifact-aware design were recognized. [On Novelty — R1, R3] Our contribution is an application-oriented formulation in the widely used two-stage detection–segmentation instance segmentation paradigm, adapted to orthodontic CBCT with attached appliances. Rather than proposing a generic denoising module or new backbone, we redesign a two-stage pipeline to be artifact-aware. In detection, high-intensity artifact patterns are exploited as localization cues through the intensity-weighted center-of-mass discrepancy; in segmentation, residual artifact influence is suppressed via normalized distance-map regression. This asymmetric treatment of metal artifacts across stages constitutes our core design contribution. [On Baseline Comparisons — R1, R3] Our comparisons were scoped to tooth-level CBCT instance segmentation pipelines that provide detection and instance-level outputs, namely ToothNet, CGDNet, and PATRCNN. Generic frameworks such as nnU-Net, TransUNet, or SAM-based methods are valuable references; however, applying them to this task requires extra steps for instance separation and tooth numbering, making direct comparison less straightforward. We also acknowledge ToothSeg (van Nistelrooij et al., JBHI 2026) as a strong recent work; however, its dual-branch design combines independent semantic and instance segmentation with self-correction, rather than a detect-then-segment pipeline, making direct one-to-one comparison less straightforward. We will clarify the rationale and scope of our baseline selection in the camera-ready version. [On Dataset Scale — R1, R2, R3] We acknowledge the limited number of clinical volumes. However, collecting CBCT scans from orthodontic patients with in-situ brackets and wires, together with accurate tooth-level segmentation labels, is costly and labor-intensive. Orthodontic CBCT with attached appliances and severe metal artifacts remains underexplored, and large-scale standardized datasets for this scenario are not readily available. Our dataset includes 20 CBCT volumes, 40 jaws, and 520 tooth instances, enabling evaluation across tooth groups and artifact-affected regions. To reduce evaluation bias, we used 5-fold cross-validation and reported mean and standard deviation. Broader validation across diverse datasets, scanners, and acquisition conditions remains important future work. [On HU Normalization and ResNet Description — R3] The preprocessing pipeline was insufficiently described in our manuscript. In practice, HU clipping/windowing was performed during preprocessing, followed by [0,1] normalization for stable and efficient model training. We also agree that omitting upper HU clipping in detection could help preserve the intensity range of metal signals. Although not explored in the current work, we regard it as a valuable insight and promising future direction. Additionally, the ResNet component refers to the tooth-number classification module after detection, not the main segmentation network. To avoid confusion, we will describe the preprocessing procedure and ResNet component in the camera-ready version, and further clarify the implementation through code release. [On Identical Detection Scores in Ablation — R3] Identical detection metrics (AP50, OIR, mIoU) in the MAM-only and MAM+DM rows are expected, as DM is applied only in segmentation and does not affect detection outputs. We will add a clarifying note to the table caption. [On Ethics — R1] All CBCT data were fully anonymized before analysis, and no personally identifiable information was retained. We will include an explicit data anonymization and handling statement. We sincerely appreciate all reviewers’ helpful comments and will incorporate them to improve the clarity and quality of the final manuscript.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): This paper addresses the clinically significant problem of metal artifact degradation in orthodontic CBCT tooth segmentation. The authors propose a Metal Artifact-Aware Module (MAAM) designed to handle severe streaking and beam-hardening artifacts caused by brackets, wires, and other orthodontic appliances. The work is evaluated on a challenging and clinically relevant problem with significant practical implications. Key Strengths Justifying Acceptance: First, the clinical impact is substantial and well-documented. Metal artifacts are prevalent in routine orthodontic CBCT imaging, and accurate segmentation despite these artifacts directly enables better treatment planning. Reviewer 2 (score: 5, Accept) emphasized that the practical impact is “substantial given the prevalence of metal artifacts in routine orthodontic CBCT imaging.” This clinical relevance is unambiguous. Second, the empirical results are compelling. The paper demonstrates significant improvements in segmentation accuracy on cases with severe metal artifacts compared to baseline methods. Reviewer 2 was “impressed by the empirical results,” noting the clear superiority of the proposed approach on the most challenging cases. Third, the evaluation methodology is sound. The paper compares against appropriate baselines and provides both quantitative metrics and qualitative examples demonstrating the method’s effectiveness. The reviewers did not identify any concerns about experimental rigor or reproducibility. Addressing the Novelty Concern: Reviewer 1 raised concerns about novelty, arguing the approach is a combination of existing denoising and segmentation techniques. However, this criticism applies to many accepted MICCAI papers that apply established methods to new clinical problems. The value of this work lies not in inventing new denoising mechanisms but in the effective integration of these techniques for a specific, important clinical application. The practical success demonstrated through strong empirical results justifies acceptance on clinical translation grounds. MICCAI Acceptance Criteria Alignment: This paper aligns with MICCAI’s interest in clinical translation of methodology. The problem is well-motivated, the approach is technically sound, and the results demonstrate clear clinical utility. The method demonstrates that with appropriate artifact-aware design, existing segmentation networks can be effectively applied to challenging clinical scenarios previously considered difficult. Conclusion: Given the strong clinical motivation, compelling empirical results from Reviewer 2, and clear practical utility, this paper meets the bar for acceptance at MICCAI 2026.The clinical significance and successful experimental validation outweigh the incremental novelty concern, which is mitigated by the thoughtful integration of established techniques for a challenging clinical application.

title: RT-Super: Learning Tumor Segmentation from Longitudinal Images and Reports
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The paper addresses a highly relevant and practical problem: most hospitals have abundant reports and serial imaging but very limited voxel-wise tumor masks. The proposed training/inference asymmetry is therefore well motivated clinically: rich context is used only at training time, while inference remains feasible from a single scan. 2.The paper presents strong internal empirical results. In Table 1, the full TR-Distillation model achieves the best overall detection F1 among methods trained on the authors’ dataset and clearly outperforms the public baselines reported in the paper. The ablation labeled “non-longitudinal” also suggests that the longitudinal/multi-phase training signal contributes measurably beyond report supervision alone. 3.The work has clear translational value because it targets tumor types for which public segmentation resources are scarce, and it explicitly studies both the no-mask and few-mask regimes. That makes the contribution more meaningful than a purely incremental accuracy improvement on an already saturated benchmark.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The main novelty is somewhat integrative rather than foundational. Report-based supervision for segmentation is already present in R-Super [2], report/image representation learning is already explored through CLIP-style and vision-language approaches [7,18], the student backbone is MedFormer [11], dynamic kernel selection is explicitly inspired by Dynamic Convolution [10], and registration is built on UniGradIcon [20]. The paper’s real novelty is the combination of these ideas with longitudinal/multi-phase information, which is meaningful, but the manuscript occasionally presents the advance more broadly than the evidence supports. 2.The ablation study is not deep enough to isolate where the gains actually come from. The paper shows a non-longitudinal ablation, but it does not disentangle the impact of: report-aware kernel generation, inter-image cross-attention, consistency loss, LLM-extracted attributes, and the use of pathology information. Without such decomposition, it is difficult to judge which proposed component is essential and which is incidental. 3.The evaluation section lacks critical detail, especially for segmentation. The manuscript reports Dice scores, but the description of the test set emphasizes detection labels from reports/pathology and does not clearly explain how the segmentation ground truth on the test cohort was obtained, how many test masks exist, who annotated them, or whether there was any quality control or inter-rater assessment. This is an important omission for a segmentation paper. 4.The paper is also limited by single-system internal validation. All training and testing data come from the same hospital system/state, so the claims of robustness and broad clinical applicability remain unproven. Given that reporting style, scanner protocols, contrast timing, and follow-up practices can vary substantially across institutions, an external validation set would materially strengthen the work. 5.Some of the public-model comparisons are not fully apples-to-apples. For example, Merlin and MedGemma are used through report generation for tumor detection rather than through a segmentation setting aligned with the proposed task. These comparisons are still interesting, but they are less convincing than the same-data comparisons against R-Super, segmentation, CLIP, and related baselines.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.Clinically grounded motivation and problem formulation. The observation that radiologists routinely consult longitudinal scans, multi-phase images, and prior reports when delineating tumors is compelling. The paper translates this clinical workflow into a principled teacher-student framework where the teacher mimics the radiologist’s information-rich setting and the student mimics the information-poor setting at first diagnosis. The focus on esophagus, spleen, and uterus tumors—which currently lack public segmentation masks—addresses a genuine gap in the field. 2.Novel and technically interesting architecture. The report-aware transformer that dynamically generates convolutional kernels is a creative design. Specifically, the use of a learnable bank of M = 16 candidate 3×3×3 kernels combined via softmax-weighted mixture (Sec. 2.1, page 5) avoids the computational cost of directly generating large kernels, while still allowing report-conditioned feature refinement. The self-distillation design—where the student is physically embedded within the teacher—is efficient and avoids maintaining two separate networks. 3.Comprehensive comparison against public models. The evaluation includes public foundation models (MedGemma, Merlin) and a dedicated lesion segmentation model (ULS), in addition to multiple training paradigms (CLIP, multi-task learning, Models Genesis, Report Supervision, standard supervised segmentation). The +49% average F1-score improvement over the best public model (Table 1) is substantial.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.Vague and ambiguous dataset description. The dataset description in Section 3 is insufficiently precise for a methodological paper and raises several unresolved questions. The text states: “5,000 CT scans paired radiology reports and pathology reports, including esophagus, spleen and uterus tumors, 100 longitudinal CT scans.” It is unclear whether the 100 longitudinal CT scans are a subset of the 5,000 or an additional set, yielding 5,100 total scans. Similarly, the paper mentions “100 multi-phase scans” on page 2 but does not clarify their relationship to the 5,000.The two training variants are described as: TR-Distillation† using 5,000 image–report pairs, and TR-Distillation using 5,000 image–report pairs plus 100 image-mask pairs. But how exactly are the 100 longitudinal scans incorporated during training? Are they always included in both variants? How many of the 5,000 scans contain tumors versus being non-tumor controls? What is the per-organ breakdown of the training set? Without these details, it is difficult to assess the experimental setup or reproduce the work. 2.Unclear and potentially unfair baseline training settings. Closely related to the vague dataset description, the training conditions for baseline methods are not clearly specified, making it difficult to assess whether comparisons are fair. Table 1 marks each method’s use of “longi.” (longitudinal), “report,” and “mask” columns, but the actual number of training samples used by each baseline is never stated explicitly. For instance, it appears from context that methods marked with “report” and “mask” (e.g., R-Super, CLIP, Multi-task learning) may use reports and 100 masks, but do they all have access to the same 5,000 image–report pairs? Methods like Models Genesis and the supervised segmentation baseline appear to use only 100 masks without reports—but do they also train on the remaining ~4,900 unlabeled images in any capacity (e.g., self-supervised pre-training)? The classification baseline is marked only with “report” but its training procedure is barely described. Without explicit, per-baseline specification of how many images, reports, and masks each method uses, the reader cannot determine whether performance differences are attributable to the proposed architecture or to differences in data volume and supervision type. This is especially concerning because TR-Distillation leverages 5,000 reports plus longitudinal data plus multi-phase data—potentially a much richer supervisory signal than what baselines receive. The authors should provide a clear table specifying the exact training data (number of images, reports, masks, longitudinal pairs) used by each method. 3.Dice scores reported only in the table caption, not in the body text. The table caption for Table 1 reports Dice scores: “TR-Distillation: 35 average; 37 spleen; 68 esophagus; 71 uterus. TR-Distillation†: 17 average; 7 spleen; 27 esophagus; 25 uterus. R-Super (best baseline): 30 average, 36 spleen, 21 esophagus, 34 uterus.” However, these Dice scores do not appear anywhere in the body text of Section 3 or elsewhere in the paper. They are also absent from Table 1 itself, which only shows sensitivity (Se), specificity (Sp), and F1-score columns. This is problematic for several reasons. Dice is the standard metric for segmentation quality, and yet it is relegated to a caption with no discussion, no statistical analysis, and no comparison against all baselines. The Dice values themselves are notably low (e.g., 35 average for TR-Distillation, 7 spleen Dice for TR-Distillation†), which warrants discussion. Are these values computed only on true-positive cases? Over all cases including non-tumor controls? The omission of Dice from both the main table and the body text is a significant gap for a segmentation paper. 4.Insufficient ablation study. The paper presents a single ablation that removes longitudinal/multi-phase training entirely (Table 1, bottom row). For an architecture with at least five novel or adapted components—(i) the Consistency Loss, (ii) report cross-attention, (iii) inter-image cross-attention, (iv) dynamic kernel generation via the soft MoE bank, and (v) soft vs. hard distillation targets—a single ablation is inadequate. Without isolating each component, we cannot determine whether the Consistency Loss actually helps, whether the dynamic kernel bank outperforms standard convolutions, or whether soft distillation targets contribute meaningfully. A systematic ablation table (removing one component at a time) is standard for multi-component methodological papers and is essential here. W5.Teacher performance is never reported. The entire framework rests on the premise that the teacher, with access to reports and longitudinal data, produces high-quality pseudo-masks that effectively train the student. Yet the teacher’s segmentation performance is never evaluated anywhere in the paper. This is a significant omission for two reasons: (1) it is impossible to assess the quality of the pseudo-masks that drive learning, and (2) the “distillation gap” (teacher performance minus student performance) remains unknown. If the teacher’s masks are poor, the student cannot be expected to learn well; if the teacher significantly outperforms the student, there may be room for improvement in the distillation mechanism. Reporting teacher Dice scores alongside student scores is essential for validating the core mechanism.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The paper is clearly motivated by real clinical practice. It designs experiments that demonstrate the value of leveraging additional data sources that are often more readily available than clean segmentation masks or classification labels. This is valuable for guiding data curation strategies, as the proposed setting better reflects real clinical conditions, including longitudinal imaging, radiology reports, and pathology reports at the patient level. 2.The paper provides clear explanations at each step and is transparent about its core technical components, such as the loss functions used, how ground-truth labels are handled when available, and the use of MedFormer as the backbone. The technical details are also well motivated, including what information is extracted from existing reports and how it is incorporated into the model.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The overall Dice scores remain relatively low (ranging from 30–70 in Table 1), which raises concerns about practical performance. In addition, the presentation is somewhat unclear, as the Dice metric is only described in the table caption rather than being explicitly labeled within the table itself. 2.The segmentation baselines and comparisons appear limited. The evaluation includes only three methods, two of which are based on TR-Distillation, resulting in a lack of diversity in comparison. It would strengthen the paper to include more established baselines, such as MedFormer and nnU-Net trained with the full set of 100 labeled samples.
