reviewer_3_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the AC and reviewers for recognizing the relevance of longitudinal tumor synthesis and geometry-aware tumor trajectory modeling. We address key concerns. AC: Clinical relevance of AUC 0.772.As clinical context, the model AUC exceeds the clinical tumor volume-change based AUC of 0.70.The goal of this work was to develop OxFlow to create a patient-specific interpolated image sequence of tumor geometry changes between fixed-time images, rather than to assess clinical utility. Downstream task shows that using the interpolated sequences in training benefits outcome prediction. AC: FM stochasticity. For given endpoint masks and alpha for a patient, OT provides a patient-specific deterministic geometric path of tumor evolution with appearance-level variations resulting from FM stochasticity. Generating multi-seed synthetic datasets and robustness to mask input variations are future work. R2/R4/R5: Trajectory realism, “ideal progression,” and real scans. We agree tumor evolution is irregular and heterogeneous, and our use of this phrase to describe smooth geometric interpolation without oscillatory effects (Tab.1/Fig.3) was confusing. We will rename “ideal progression” as “geometric reference trajectory.” The OT trajectory provides a geometrically consistent conditioning path between tumor masks from two scan times for intermediate CT synthesis. It is not intended to capture the full biological dynamics of tumors. Direct comparison to real intermediate scans requires aligning the interpolation step with scan timing; otherwise temporal mismatch and synthesis error are conflated. With such alignment, the OT-derived path could serve as a patient-specific geometric reference for analyzing response deviations. R2: Baselines/related work. We agree broader comparisons are valuable and will add the cited works. Unlike our approach, these methods largely follow a whole-image generation paradigm, where lesion/tumor evolution is implicit in image-level/latent dynamics. By modeling shape evolution in mask space before CT synthesis, OxFlow separates geometry from appearance and enables patient-specific interpolation from endpoint masks without learning implicit dynamics from large longitudinal datasets. R3/R5: Modest Dice gain in Tab.2.Dice is measured only when nnU-Net yields valid tumor segmentations, so it excludes failed cases. Tab.2 shows OxFlow has the lowest failure rate among variants. R3/R5: Downstream setup/CV leakage. The classifier is trained directly on CT slices after performing patient-level data splits, eliminating chance of CV leakage. For each training patient, real tumor slices and OxFlow-synthesized intermediate slices are appended into the same patient bag with the original durable-response label. Validation/test bags contain only real CT slices from held-out patients. The fold split is performed before adding synthetic data; synthetic slices are loaded only for training patient IDs. Interpolation pairs are formed only within the same patient and slice position, so no held-out patient contributes synthetic samples to classifier training. R5: Inference background. At inference, x_bg is constructed from the smaller-tumor endpoint scan using the same masked-background operation as training, minimizing residual tumor appearance and avoiding leakage from the larger observed tumor. R5: Novelty. Our contribution is the geometry-first decomposition: explicitly using OT to model tumor-shape evolution in mask space and conditioning CT synthesis on this trajectory, rather than leaving tumor evolution implicit in image-level generation. R3/R5: Generalization and 2.5D. This work demonstrates feasibility on a real longitudinal CT cohort. External cohorts and other tumor types are future work. We adopted 2.5D given cohort size and training stability; while adjacent-slice context and OT support cross-slice consistency in principle, a full 3D OxFlow extension is ongoing. R2/R4: Reproducibility. We will make the codebase public.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The presented work proposes an interpolation scheme of longitudinal tumor progression data, based on optimal transport interpolation and a generative model based on flow matching. It finds that on a downstream binary classification task regarding progresion free survival after 6 months, there is benefit in using the interpolated lung tumors for this task, compared with other augmentation and synthetization techniques. Reviewer reports are discordant. Whereas there is some positive mentioning about the difficulty and relevance of the tackled problem, there are many concerns regarding the methodological innovation, details of the downstream classification task, modest improvements using the method over baselines, and a need for densely annotated longitudinal ground truth data. I would add to these weaknesses that it is not clear if the absolute performance of the downstream classification task is actually clinically relevant (AUC 77% still seems to be a modest predictor of progression free survival, a prediction which is highly relevant to patients). Moreover, it is not clear if in the flow matching component, several repetitions of the interpolated tumors would lead to differently created interpolations, and if that would have an effect on the downstream classification task. I follow the overall assessment of reviewers, which is inbetween acceptance and rejectance, and due to the in principle relevant and interesting problem area, which might spark discussion at the conference, I invite the authors to prepare a rebuttal for the work, which should structure the mentioned weaknesses according to their importance and clarify/address them. | Reviewers are still very much on the borderline for this paper. Given the rebuttal, I think a number of issues have been clarified, and none that would preclude acceptance remain. Due to the interesting longitudinal application scenario, which might spark some discussion at the conference, I tend to accept this paper. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): I think that the idea is interesting. Although some weaknesses still remain, I thought that authors have provided a good discussion on this early-stage but interesting research, and have provided some convincing responses to specific critiques. I strongly encourage authors to include better clarifications and revisions as suggested by reviewers to strengthen the final version. I would argue for accept. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): After considering the rebuttal and updated reviews, I recommend rejection. Although the paper presents an interesting idea, the core progression assumption remains insufficiently justified, and the experimental validation is relatively limited. In particular, the current evidence does not adequately demonstrate that the proposed geometric trajectory reflects real tumor progression. Therefore, I do not think the paper meets the acceptance threshold.

title: Spherical Clinical Embedding with Adaptive Multi-expert Fusion for AAA Rupture Classification
reviewer_1_strengths: The spherical clinical embedding treating missingness as a structured signal rather than noise is well-motivated and practically valuable for retrospective clinical data. The confidence-driven adaptive router is a principled approach to case-specific fusion, and the robustness experiments under progressively increasing missing rates are rigorous and clinically realistic. Evaluation on OASIS-1 alongside the private AAA dataset provides reasonable evidence of domain-agnostic generalizability.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: No analysis is provided of whether the learned routing weights vary meaningfully across patients or collapse to near-uniform distributions during training. The missing modality simulation protocol is underspecified: it is unclear whether modality branches are zeroed out or dropped entirely, and how baseline methods are adapted to handle missing inputs, which affects the validity of the robustness comparison.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.Multi-modal integration framework with many bells and whistles 2.Generally well written
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Weaknesses: 1.The motivation is not clear: the authors state that physiological models for AAA rupture prediction are “highly dependent on segmentation, meshing, and material modeling assumptions, making them less scalable for practical clinical use.” But the presented method too depends upon segmentations being available. There are also implicit assumptions about CT acquisitions (radiomics fails without these assumptions). The primary contribution seems instead to be a method for multi-modal integration, but it is not really framed that way. 2.Inappropriate experiments: Most of the paper (including the introduction and methods) is framed around AAA rupture prediction, but one of the main experiments is on the OASIS dataset and the label used is a binary dementia label! This has no relation to the AAA task. 3.Inadequate details: Many key details are missing: a. For the AAA rupture prediction task, all relevant details are missing: for example, how many patients had a rupture, what was the time horizon for capturing ruptures, presence of interventions, what clinical factors were used, etc. 4.Basic baselines are missing: For example, what is the performance without multi-modal integration? What if only the CT was present, or only clinical factors? What about replacing the adaptive routing and fusion module with simple averaging? Possibly bad evaluation methodology: It seems that there were 4,550 unruptured and 4,627 ruptured AAA images from 95 patients, and that the evaluation was done on a per-slice basis (hard to tell as it is not clarified, and no confidence intervals are provided). However that neglects the fact that adjacent slices from the same patient are highly correlated and as a result, the metrics are likely to be inflated. One has to control for the correlations to get accurate estimates.
reviewer_2_rating: (1) Strong Reject — must be rejected due to major flaws
reviewer_3_strengths: AAA rupture prediction matters, and moving beyond diameter-only heuristics toward multimodal modeling is a valid and important direction. The four-expert decomposition is sensible: handcrafted structure/radiomics for explicit descriptors, ConvNeXt-based semantic image features for learned morphology, a clinical expert for tabular variables under missingness, and a unified expert for higher-order interactions. This is one of the paper’s good aspects: the architecture matches the problem. The paper explicitly feeds the missingness mask into the clinical pathway and the unified expert, which is more principled than naïve imputation alone.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The paper provides a reasonable high-level method description, but several implementation details that materially affect outcomes are missing or unclear: exact train/test splitting unit, how slice-level features are aggregated and how many slices are used per patient, hyperparameters for α and τ, imputation objective weighting, definitions of simulated modality missingness, preprocessing details for clinical variables, and whether segmentation masks are ground truth or auto-generated for all experiments. That is not fatal, but it is not strong reproducibility. 2.Right now, the ablation is too coarse. It shows two modules matter, but does not isolate whether the gain is from routing, from the unified branch, from mask usage, or from simply having more capacity. 3.The paper simulates missing data/modality from 5% to 30%, but does not specify the missingness mechanism in enough detail. Missing completely at random is much easier than clinically structured missingness. For example, sicker patients may have richer labs, and missingness can be highly informative. Since the clinical expert explicitly uses missingness masks, the exact corruption process matters a lot. Without this, the robustness claim is weaker than presented. 4.The related-work positioning around multimodal mixture-of-experts under missing or heterogeneous modalities is currently incomplete. In particular, the authors should discuss Flex-MoE: Modeling Arbitrary Modality Combination via the Flexible Mixture-of-Experts (NeurIPS 2024 Spotlight), which explicitly studies arbitrary modality combinations and missing-modality robustness; FuseMoE: Mixture-of-Experts Transformers for Fleximodal Fusion (NeurIPS 2024), which develops MoE-based fleximodal fusion for irregular/missing multimodal inputs; and Dynamic Modeling of Patients, Modalities and Tasks via Multi-modal Multi-task Mixture of Experts (ICLR 2025), which is especially relevant for author’s design of modality-specific and shared learning. These papers would help better contextualize what is new here versus prior MoE-based multimodal fusion and missingness-aware routing.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We sincerely thank the reviewers and Meta-reviewer for constructive feedback and address the priority issues below. (Meta/R2, evaluation protocol) We clarify that all evaluations are performed strictly at the patient level. Slice features are aggregated through mean pooling into a single patient-level prediction (Section 2), and all slices from the same patient remain in the same fold under 5-fold stratified CV. So, no slice-correlation leakage occurs. Section 3.1 will be reworded to state this explicitly. (R2, segmentation dependency) Our discussion of biomechanical models intended to highlight the complexity of finite-element pipelines, which require precise segmentation, meshing, and material parameter estimation. Our framework instead uses automatically generated masks from published tool only as a soft attention prior and for radiomics extraction. No biomechanical simulation or meshing is performed. Segmentation serves as a lightweight localization prior, not a physics-dependent requirement. The introduction will be revised accordingly. (Meta/R2, OASIS justification) Our intention was not to claim clinical transferability. OASIS was included to evaluate generalizability under a different setting involving MRI and structured clinical variables. Gains on OASIS (Table 2: 0.8808 ACC vs. 0.8485 best baseline; MCC 0.7408 vs. 0.6854) support that the routing and spherical embedding remain effective across heterogeneous modalities and incomplete data. We will make this motivation explicit in the revision. (Meta/R2/R4, reproducibility and clinical details) The 95-patient cohort was collected retrospectively under IRB approval with a waiver of informed consent. Clinical variables cover demographics, comorbidities (hypertension, COPD, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, heart disease), labs (creatinine, BUN, BP), and risk factors (smoking, steroid use, family history, renal impairment, prior CT). Key hyperparameters are temperature 0.5, sphere dimension 64, sphere weight 0.1, contrastive weight 0.1, and imputation weight 0.1.To further support reproducibility, our full source code and training scripts will be released upon acceptance. The revision will add rupture prevalence, intervention status, time horizon, and preprocessing details. (R1/R4, missing-modality simulation) We simulated missing modalities at the patient level under a missing-completely-at-random protocol. Each non-imaging modality was independently dropped with probability between 5% and 30%, while CT inputs were retained. The missingness mask is passed to the clinical and unified experts, and baselines receive the same zero-imputed inputs for fair comparison. Informative missingness is more clinically realistic and will be noted as a limitation. (R1/R4 ablation; R2 basic baselines; R1 routing) The ablations in Tables 3–4 isolate the spherical and unified experts while preserving backbone capacity, so the drops reflect mechanism rather than added capacity. Removing the unified expert collapses cross-modal interaction and quantifies the value of multimodal integration over uni-modal pathways. The learned routing weights vary across patients and do not collapse, consistent with the 86.25% accuracy retained under 30% missing modality. The revision will isolate routing and mask-guided attention and add a per-patient routing-entropy analysis. (R4, related work) We will extend the related work to include Flex-MoE, FuseMoE (NeurIPS 2024), and the multi-task MoE (ICLR 2025). Prior methods focus on generic modality dropout through learned gating, whereas our approach incorporates missingness-aware spherical clinical embedding and confidence-driven routing derived from expert logits. It enabled routing under test-time modality absence without retraining. (R1/R2, statistics and external validation) Cross-fold std will be added in the revision. Tables 1-4 report per-fold means. The 95-patient single-cohort scale and absence of external validation are acknowledged limitations.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): This work proposes, XMoE, a multimodal MoE framework for AAA rupture classification with spherical clinical embedding for handling missing data and confidence-driven adaptive routing. The clinical problem is relevant and the architecture design is sensible. However, the biggest problem pointed out by reviewers is reproducibility. R2 raised issues that need direct answers. First, the evaluation appears to be done on a per-slice basis across 95 patients (roughly 9,000 slices), and if so, the metrics are inflated because adjacent slices from the same patient are highly correlated. The authors need to confirm whether the evaluation unit is patient-level or slice-level. Second, R2 found the OASIS dementia experiment inappropriate since it has no clinical relation to AAA rupture. Third, R2 noted that the paper criticizes physiological models for depending on segmentation, but the proposed method itself requires segmentation, which is contradictory. R4 also flagged that the ablation is too coarse to isolate what drives the improvement (routing, unified branch, mask usage, or just added capacity), and that recent MoE work on missing modalities (Flex-MoE, FuseMoE, NeurIPS 2024; ICLR 2025) is not discussed. For the rebuttal, please pay more attention to the following aspects: 1.clarify whether evaluation is per-patient or per-slice and address the correlation concern; 2.justify the inclusion of the OASIS experiment; 3.discuss the related MoE papers R4 cited; 4.provide the missing clinical details (rupture prevalence, time horizon, intervention status). Reproducibility issue is critical because it affects the validity of all reported numbers. | The issue is solved. R2 pointed out per-slice scoring inflated every number, but the submitted method already mean-pools to patient level with each patient kept in one fold, so it can’t happen. R1 and R4 both confirmed this. However, the real gaps stay open. No significance tests, no standard deviations (R1, R2), single-center 95 patients with no external test (R1, authors concede), and no CT-only, clinical-only, or simple-average baselines (R2). These are either barred new work or pushed to revision, so the core “fusion helps” claim is under-supported. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): While the initial review process highlighted a stark divergence between the panel, the authors’ comprehensive rebuttal successfully defused the major methodological concerns. Crucially, the authors clarified that their evaluation was executed strictly at the patient level via cross-validation, completely refuting the threat of slice-correlation data leakage. They also clarified that their pipeline avoids expensive, unscalable biomechanical meshing, using segmentation solely as a soft prior. Although the single-center nature of the 95-patient cohort and the inclusion of the unrelated OASIS dataset for out-of-domain evaluation remain minor experimental constraints, the model’s performance stability under simulated missingness (up to 30%) provides compelling validation of its architectural robustness. The reviewers are satisfied with the rebuttal, and the paper is recommended for acceptance. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): After considering the reviews and rebuttal, I recommend acceptance. The paper addresses a clinically important AAA rupture classification problem and proposes a missingness-aware multimodal MoE framework with spherical clinical embedding and adaptive expert fusion. The rebuttal clarifies the most critical concern: evaluation is performed at the patient level, with slice features pooled into one patient-level prediction and all slices from the same patient kept within the same fold. This substantially mitigates the concern about slice-level leakage. My acceptance recommendation relies on the rebuttal clarification that the AAA evaluation was performed strictly at the patient level. The final version should explicitly state the patient-level aggregation, fold assignment, clinical cohort details, and cross-fold variability.

title: SSPT: Spiking Serialized Point Transformer for Couinaud Segmentation in 3D Medical Data
reviewer_1_strengths: Novel and well-scoped contribution: it seems to be the first transformer-based SNN for 3D Couinaud point-cloud segmentation. The energy-efficiency narrative is clean and quantitative (45nm CMOS model, per-layer firing rates reported). The PTv3 comparison at equal parameter count is the right experiment. It isolates spiking dynamics from capacity effects. TSD is a well-motivated solution to the spatio-temporal mismatch problem in SNN point processing. The ablation Table 2 Cat. III is convincing. Serialization ablation (Z-order vs. random vs. k-NN) and time-step analysis (T=1/2/3) are informative and support the design choice made.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Dataset labels are undocumented. Neither LiTS nor MSD8 ships with Couinaud annotations. The paper never states where they come from. Preprocessing details for voxel baselines are not given. Table 2 Cat. III contradicts Table 1.The Scanning Wave row reports LiTS ASD=2.24 / MSD8 ASD=2.44, but Table 1 and the abstract report LiTS=2.44 / MSD8=2.24.The columns appear transposed. No statistical testing performed, the tables lack standard deviations. The claim “the binary gating mechanism of LIF neurons serves as a dynamic threshold, prioritizing high-entropy structural regions such as vessel bifurcations” is not verified. No spike-activity visualization is provided, only segmentation outputs are shown. The “Real-time intraoperative” claim in the conclusion is unsupported. No wall-clock latency or neuromorphic hardware deployment is reported. The energy estimate is theoretical. The theoretical energy model (versus actual neuromorphic hardware measurement) and the single-dataset / single-split evaluation for both MSD8 and LiTS are limitations that should be stated more explicitly.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.Introduces a principled spatio-temporal serialization (TSD) of unordered point clouds to create coherent spike trains, addressing the common mismatch between static 3D geometry and SNN temporal dynamics. 2.Designs a spiking self-attention variant (SSA) that uses binary query spikes with localized windows to approach linear complexity while replacing much of QK multiplications with additions, a compelling hardware-aware rethinking of attention for point clouds. 3.Incorporates a spiking conditional positional encoding (SCPE) with parallel sparse 3D convolutions to compensate spatial information loss due to serialization; the end-to-end hierarchical U-Net-like spiking transformer is well-motivated.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Major concerns: 1.The energy analysis is theoretical (45 nm CMOS model) and not hardware-measured; it does not include memory movement costs or GPU/CPU runtime, which can dominate in practice for point-cloud pipelines. 2.SSA still performs floating-point softmax/value aggregation; the overall fraction of operations actually reduced to additions versus multiplications is not fully quantified per layer, making the magnitude of energy savings somewhat assumption-sensitive. 3.The gating granularity and stability of spike generation (per-channel/per-head) and its impact on attention quality are under-specified; no sensitivity analysis for spike threshold or membrane dynamics is provided. 4.The most serious issue is the unclear source of the Couinaud ground truth. LiTS and MSD8 do not provide Couinaud annotations by default, yet the manuscript does not explain how these labels were obtained, generated, or validated. This is not a minor omission but a fundamental problem that undermines the rigor and credibility of the entire study. 5.The evaluation is incomplete and insufficiently convincing. The paper reports only overall metrics, without segment-wise Dice results for each Couinaud region, especially for anatomically challenging segments such as Segment I (caudate lobe). This makes it difficult to judge the actual clinical usefulness of the method. 6.The computation of ASD is unclear and lacks reproducibility. Since the predictions are point-wise, the paper should clearly describe how point labels are converted into surfaces or volumes before boundary distances are measured. Without these details, the reported ASD values are difficult to interpret. 7.The fairness of the comparisons is questionable. Voxel-based methods are evaluated on dense full-resolution volumes, while the proposed method uses sampled point clouds. The energy comparison is therefore not fully fair, and the paper does not provide runtime or peak memory results to support its practical efficiency claims. 8.Important baselines are missing. The manuscript does not compare against recent Couinaud-specific, vessel-guided, or clinically relevant methods. In particular, Couinaud segmentation in CT has already been addressed in mature frameworks such as TotalSegmentator v2, yet no comparison is provided. This makes the practical contribution unclear. 9.The qualitative results do not convincingly support the claimed advantages. Even in the visual examples, the proposed method still shows noticeable boundary offsets and inaccurate delineations. This weakens the claim that point-cloud-based modeling is particularly advantageous for this task. 10.Several table entries appear duplicated or inconsistent (e.g., identical Dice/ASD in ablation for different serialization settings; some text/table typos), which undermines confidence in reported numbers. 11.Data preprocessing and feature composition are under-specified (e.g., what per-point features are used beyond coordinates/intensity? any normalization, augmentation?). 12.Training/validation/test splits, case counts per split, and cross-validation protocols are not reported; reproducibility is limited without code or detailed settings (e.g., window size w, neighborhood/window overlap, spike thresholds). 13.Does not discuss or compare to recent Couinaud-specific methods that incorporate vascular priors or registration-based augmentations. Given the paper’s focus on topology-aware segmentation and boundary precision, omitting these is a notable gap.
reviewer_2_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: Major Strength 1 The paper presents a novel and well-motivated architecture adaptation by elegantly combining the Z-order space-filling curve with the sliding window mechanism (TSD). This design effectively resolves the critical spatiotemporal mismatch between static 3D geometric point clouds and the continuous spike dynamics of spiking neural networks (SNNs). Such a cross-paradigm alignment is non-trivial and represents an original way to bridge discrete geometric representations with event-based, continuous-time computation, making the work technically innovative and conceptually interesting. Major Strength 2 A key strength lies in the extremely high theoretical energy efficiency enabled by the proposed SSA module. The module maintains linear complexity while drastically reducing floating-point operations. Compared with traditional artificial neural networks, the work reports a remarkable 98.1% reduction in theoretical energy consumption, which is outstanding and highly relevant to resource-constrained medical imaging and clinical deployment scenarios. This strong efficiency advantage significantly enhances the practical value of the method.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Major Weakness 1 The paper is primarily motivated by real-time intraoperative surgical planning and ultra-low-power constraints to justify the use of SNNs. However, Couinaud segmentation is clinically a preoperative offline planning task, where energy consumption and millisecond-level latency are generally less critical than absolute segmentation accuracy. This makes the core motivation less convincing. Major Weakness 2 The paper lacks critical details regarding 3D point cloud extraction from raw CT/MRI volumes. The authors state that data are converted to 3D point clouds via windowing/cropping and then sampled to 60,000 points using FPS. However, how the initial point cloud is generated from the 3D volume is completely unclear, whether by intensity thresholding, uniform grid sampling, or another strategy. This missing step is essential for reproducibility, because segmentation performance strongly depends on the initial point distribution, especially when extracting sparse vascular structures. Major Weakness 3 The claimed energy efficiency is based on theoretical calculations under a 45nm CMOS process, which is acceptable for conceptual validation but incomplete for SNN research. Standard evaluation in this field also requires practical runtime metrics independent of custom ASIC hardware. The authors should supplement their results with actual inference speed (ms/volume or FPS) and peak GPU memory usage (MB) on a commodity GPU such as RTX 3090 to complement the theoretical energy claims and enable fairer comparison with existing ANN methods. Major Weakness 4 To ensure full reproducibility of the proposed method, the authors are strongly encouraged to release the source code (including data preprocessing, model implementation, and evaluation scripts). Without accessible code, it is difficult for the community to verify, reproduce, or build upon the presented approach, which limits the impact and transparency of the work.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We sincerely thank the reviewers for recognizing the design of our SSPT model. We will release the full source code, including the model implementation, preprocessing, augmentation, evaluation, and energy-estimation scripts, upon publication. 1.[R1,R2,R3] Preprocessing pipeline from CT to point clouds We follow APVN (TMI 2024) for raw-volume preprocessing: from paired CT/label volumes, we crop and retain the liver regions covered by Couinaud annotations, apply CT windowing and normalization, and convert the retained voxels into point samples with coordinates, intensity, and labels; training uses controlled point sampling and testing uses full-point chunked inference, while voxel baselines directly use the same ROI-constrained normalized volumes. All methods are consistent in terms of data source, anatomical scope, intensity normalization, and spatial preprocessing. We will detail the pipeline in the revision. 2.[R1,R2,R3] Dataset labels For LiTS, we use the Couinaud annotations released by APVN (TMI 2024), for MSD8, we use the Couinaud annotations released by GLC-UNet (MLMI 2019). We will add the reference in the revised manuscript. 3.[R1,R2,R3] Practical efficiency (peak GPU memory and inference speed) We thank the reviewers for noting this issue. Regarding the efficiency comparison, we report measured efficiency on a single RTX 3090 (24 GB). On the MSD8 test set, SSPT achieves 3.79 s/volume and 6.47 GB peak GPU memory, compared with 6.933 s/volume and 5.91 GB for PTv3, and 4.438 s/volume and 6.08 GB for APVN. Peak memory is reported using maximum memory allocated. Thus, SSPTachieves an inference speed 45.3% faster than PTv3 and 14.6% than APVN, while consuming moderately more GPU memory. We will add the measured results to Table 1. 4.[R1,R2] Energy calculation We thank the reviewers for raising the fairness concern. In our experiment, to fairly evaluate the computational cost of point-based and voxel-based representations, we designed point and voxel inputs with equivalent input sizes (point 65,000, voxel (16* 64 *64)). As stated in the manuscript, we estimate the theoretical compute energy of each forward pass. Following widely adopted protocols of SPT (AAAI 2025) and SDT (NeurIPS 2023), we estimate theoretical compute energy under the 45 nm CMOS model, where ANN energy is computed from total MACs, while SNN energy is computed from first-layer MACs plus firing-rate-weighted ACs in subsequent spiking layers. 5.[R1,R3] Clarifying the clinical scope: offline Couinaud segmentation. We agree that Couinaud segmentation should be positioned as an offline preoperative planning task. We will revise any wording that could be interpreted as claiming demonstrated real-time or intraoperative deployment. Thank you for reminding. 6.[R2] ASD computation and reproducibility. Following the evaluation protocol of the APVN (TMI 2024), We map the point-wise predictions back to the NIfTI label volume using the stored voxel-index coordinates, evaluate them only within the annotated foreground mask, and then compute ASD for labels 1–8 with the surface-distance library using the physical spacing from the reference NIfTI header. We will add the details in the revised manuscript. 7.[R2] Evaluation against SOTA baselines and qualitative analysis In the submitted experiments, we selected APVN (TMI 2024), which is currently the state-of-the-art Couinaud segmentation model with publicly available source code and data. 8.[R1,R2] Table typo and inconsistency correction We thank the reviewers for carefully checking the reported results. We will correct all identified table/text inconsistencies in the revised manuscript. 9.[R1,R2] Statistical robustness and reporting completeness In the revised manuscript, we will report results as mean ± standard deviation, and provide segment-wise Dice. We will also extend spike-activity visualization to support the discussion of binary gating behavior.

title: Steer the Sampling, Not the Kernel Grid: Geometry-Guided Sampling Operator for Volumetric Segmentation
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The paper proposes a novel geometry-guided local operator, GeoSample, that directly targets a core weakness of volumetric segmentation: fixed-grid convolution and pooling often blur thin, elongated, and anisotropic structures. Instead of redesigning the whole backbone, the method rethinks the sampling primitive itself by predicting a voxel-wise local 3D rotation frame and adaptive bounded step sizes, then steering structured symmetric sampling along those directions. This is interesting because it introduces explicit local geometric structure into feature extraction in a way that is better matched to boundary-sensitive medical targets. 2.A major strength is the elegant formulation of geometry-aware cues from the sampled features. The paired symmetric samples are converted into compact average, gradient-like, and curvature-like signals using step-size-normalized finite differences. This is more than a simple deformable sampling variant: the formulation has a clear geometric interpretation, explicitly separates even/context and odd/directional-change information, and is designed to make the representation more stable across different local scales. 3.The method is unified and architecturally coherent. GeoSample is not limited to one component of the network, but is formulated as a single operator that can replace both stride-1 feature refinement and stride>1 downsampling. This is a strong design choice because the same geometric principle is applied consistently across scales, rather than only improving one isolated stage of the encoder-decoder pipeline. 4.The paper includes an additional technically meaningful contribution through the rotation-consistent Consensus Field. This module fuses geometric fields from encoder and decoder features at skip connections using quaternion-based rotation fusion and adaptive gating. This is an original and useful idea because it addresses cross-scale geometric mismatch at the level of the local sampling geometry itself, rather than only fusing appearance features. 5.The experimental evaluation is reasonably broad and supports the main motivation of the work. The method is tested on three public 3D datasets spanning three modalities, namely BraTS (MRI), MSD Hepatic Vessel (CT), and TDSC-ABUS (ultrasound). This diversity is a strength because it demonstrates that the method is not tailored to a single imaging setting and appears to generalize across substantially different anatomical targets and image characteristics. 6.The reported empirical gains are particularly convincing on boundary-sensitive metrics, which is well aligned with the claimed motivation. In the operator-level comparison, the proposed method achieves the best overall mean Dice/HD95/ASSD, performs best on BraTS, achieves the best Dice and HD95 on Hepatic Vessel with near-best ASSD, and substantially improves HD95 and ASSD on TDSC-ABUS while keeping Dice competitive. These results are important because they suggest that the operator is especially effective for preserving fine boundary information rather than only improving coarse region overlap. 7.The plug-in validation across multiple backbones increases the practical value of the paper. The authors show that the operator can be integrated into nnU-Net, Swin-UNETR, and MedNeXt without changing their macro-architectures, and that it yields consistent improvements in overlap and boundary metrics. This strengthens the contribution because it suggests the method is a reusable operator-level improvement rather than a one-off architecture-specific trick. 8.Another strong aspect is the efficiency-accuracy tradeoff. In the U-Net setting, the proposed method reduces parameters from 2.3M to 0.8M and FLOPs from 194.8G to 108.9G while still improving segmentation quality. This is noteworthy because geometry-aware or adaptive operators often increase model cost, whereas here the method appears to deliver both better accuracy and lower complexity, which improves its practical attractiveness for real 3D medical segmentation systems.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The methodological novelty appears narrower than the paper’s positioning suggests. Many core ingredients are adjacent to existing directions already discussed in the manuscript, including deformable convolutions (Dai et al. , ICCV 2017; Zhu et al. , CVPR 2019), volumetric deformable variants such as DeformUX-Net (Lee et al. , 2023), sparse deformable sampling in OBELISK-Net (Heinrich et al. , MedIA 2019), spatial transformer based geometric warping (Jaderberg et al. , NeurIPS 2015), and equivariant/steerable 3D models such as Group Equivariant CNNs (Cohen and Welling, ICML 2016), 3D Steerable CNNs (Weiler et al. , NeurIPS 2018), and SE(3)-Transformers (Fuchs et al. , NeurIPS 2020). The main distinction here is the use of a rotation-constrained local frame with symmetric paired sampling and differential-token construction, which is interesting, but the manuscript does not yet make a sufficiently sharp case for why this goes substantially beyond a structured combination of prior ideas. 2.The experimental validation does not fully support the strongest claims about thin-structure preservation, topology, and clinical relevance. The paper repeatedly motivates the method by arguing that small boundary errors can disconnect branches or distort clinically meaningful topology, especially for thin structures such as vessels. However, the evaluation mainly reports Dice, HD95, and ASSD. These metrics are useful, but they do not directly quantify connectivity or topology preservation. Since the paper itself cites topology-preserving segmentation work (Hu et al. , NeurIPS 2019), the absence of topology-aware evaluation is noticeable. For the hepatic vessel task in particular, metrics such as clDice, centerline Dice, connected-component errors, branch recall, or topology error counts would be much more aligned with the paper’s core claims. 3.The comparison is not fully fair from a model-capacity perspective, which weakens the “better and more efficient” conclusion. In the U-Net setting, the proposed model is substantially lighter than the compared baselines (0.8M parameters and 108.9G FLOPs versus 2.3M/194.8G for baseline U-Net, 2.5M/203.3G for DCNv1, 2.6M/209.3G for DCNv2, and 2.7M/384.5G for Dynamic Downsampling). As a result, the current comparison is not capacity-matched. Some of the performance difference may come from a different parameterization or regularization regime rather than purely from the proposed operator itself. Stronger evidence would require parameter-matched or FLOP-matched baselines, or at least a lighter baseline U-Net with similar capacity. 4.The empirical gains are promising but not yet statistically convincing. All methods are evaluated using a fixed-seed 75/10/15 split, and the paper reports only single summary numbers without repeated runs, standard deviations, confidence intervals, or significance testing. This is important because some gains are modest or mixed. For example, on MSD Hepatic Vessel, the proposed method achieves the best Dice and HD95 but not the best ASSD; on TDSC-ABUS, the Dice improvement over the strongest baseline is small and the main gain is in boundary metrics. These results may still be meaningful, but without statistical analysis it is difficult to judge their robustness. For a TMI submission, multi-seed evaluation or significance testing would make the conclusions much more convincing. 5.The plug-in generalization claim is only partially supported. The paper argues that the operator can be plugged into multiple backbones, but the validation is limited to a single dataset, TDSC-ABUS. Moreover, the intervention is not consistent across architectures: in nnU-Net the authors replace all stride-1 and stride>1 blocks, whereas in Swin-UNETR and MedNeXt they replace only downsampling blocks to preserve backbone-specific refinement. Because the integration strategy differs across backbones, the evidence for general backbone-agnostic applicability is weaker than the paper suggests. The results are encouraging, but they do not yet fully establish generality. 6.The ablation study is too limited for a method with several nontrivial design choices. The current ablation only removes the differential terms and the Consensus Field. However, the proposed method also relies on several specific choices, including SO(3) frame prediction, bounded step sizes, symmetric paired sampling, step-size normalization, odd-signal preservation during pooling, and quaternion-based fusion at skip connections. The manuscript does not isolate the contribution of these components. It would be particularly useful to test symmetric versus unconstrained sampling, bounded step sizes versus free offsets, SO(3) frame prediction versus direct vector prediction, and the effect of K and the normalization by rk. Without these experiments, it remains unclear which parts are truly essential. 7.Reproducibility and practical efficiency analysis remain insufficient. Although the paper describes the main operator design and states that the same training pipeline is used across methods, many implementation details remain under-specified, including the loss function, optimizer, learning-rate schedule, training duration, data augmentation, and exact hyperparameter settings such as rmin, rmax, and epsilon. In addition, the conclusion explicitly acknowledges remaining memory and wall-clock overhead from interpolation-based sampling, as well as early-training stability issues. This makes it important to report actual runtime and GPU memory usage, not only FLOPs. At present, the efficiency discussion is incomplete from a practical deployment perspective.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1）The paper presents a relatively unified operator design rather than a simple combination of engineering components. 2）A notable strength is that the proposed method integrates both feature refinement and downsampling within a single framework. 3）The paper addresses a meaningful problem, namely the loss of boundary and geometric information caused by fixed-grid sampling in 3D segmentation. 4）The experimental results are consistently positive across MRI, CT, and ultrasound, suggesting good cross-modality applicability.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1）In all experiments, the number of sampling directions K is fixed to 3, corresponding to a rotated 3D coordinate frame. author_feedback: We thank the AC/reviewers. Related comments are grouped below. [AC1/R1C1/R2C4] Novelty. GeoSample is fundamentally different from deformable aggregation: we sample to measure voxel-wise geometry, while DCN/OBELISK-style methods sample shifted locations to aggregate features. They learn offsets/patterns for mixing; we learn a local SO(3) frame and bounded steps, then encode context, directional change, and curvature-like variation. STN/equivariant methods warp features or enforce transformation rules, whereas GeoSample uses geometry to construct voxel representations before refinement/downsampling. DeformUX changes blocks, recent DCNs refine offset aggregation, and DefMamba focuses on scan/mixing. Thus they share ingredients but not the same 3D refinement/downsampling primitive; DCNv1/v2 are the closest controlled baselines. We will clarify this in Introduction. [AC1] Performance. We agree the Dice margin is modest, so we do not claim a large Dice-only gain. GeoSample improves HD95 25.6→22.8 and ASSD 4.94→4.72, with parameters/FLOPs 2.5M/203.3G→0.8M/108.9G. This matches the goal: compact geometry-aware sampling for stable boundaries. [R2C1/R2C2/R1C2/R1C6/R2C3] K parameter/topology insights/ablation. K=3 is sufficient for the intended local measurement. It forms a complete 3D frame; we do not claim one six-point stencil recovers whole-structure topology. Each voxel measures context, directional change, and curvature-like change along this frame, while branches are represented by dense measurements across layers/scales. Consensus Field is part of the operator, not an external add-on; our ablation targets the two highest-level design choices—local geometry measurement and cross-scale consistency—showing both are needed for reliable skip connections. Topology motivates why boundary errors matter; our evidence supports boundary/local-geometry quality. Topology-specific evaluation is complementary. We will add this to Discussion. [AC2/R1C5/R2C5] Plug-in and integration. Integration is functionally consistent: common insertion points are resolution changes and skip connections. In nnU-Net, stride-1 refinement and stride>1 reduction are standard convolutional operators, so replacing both is direct substitution. In Swin-UNETR/MedNeXt, stride-1 refinement is the defining self-attention or ConvNeXt-style block; replacing it would change the backbone family rather than test plug-in compatibility. We therefore preserve backbone-specific refinement and replace only downsampling, with Consensus Field at skips. Swin-UNETR self-attention blocks are not replaced. For MedNeXt, we used the base block from official repo with base channel 16, yielding 2.7M params. [AC2/R1C3/R1C7] U-Net. The 2.3M U-Net is a compact fixed scaffold. It has four levels with base channel 16.Each encoder level uses one stride-1 3x3x3 refinement operator and one stride-2 3x3x3 reduction operator; the decoder mirrors this layout. All variants replace the same locations under the same configuration. Thus, the comparison controls scaffold, width, split, and training, rather than equalising parameter count. The lower cost reflects structural efficiency: GeoSample improves segmentation quality with fewer learned weights. [R1C4/R1C5/R5C3] Experimental scope. We agree repeated runs, multi-dataset plug-ins, and larger backbones would be interesting. However, our goal was to answer two operator-level questions: (i) whether GeoSample transfers across modalities/anatomies under the same U-Net scaffold, and (ii) whether it can be inserted into other SOTA pipeline/backbones with consistent gains. Future work could include testing its scalability with ResEncL/MedNeXt-L and other larger models. We will include this in Discussion. [R5C1/R5C2/R1C7] Clarity/reproducibility. We will add a forward-pass summary, enlarge Fig. 1, and add missing training details. The submission included an anonymous Git repo with code/reproducible settings; we will make it public upon acceptance.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The reviewers found that the proposed sampling operator is novel and addresses a clinically relevant problem. Experiments were conducted on datasets covering different imaging modalities and anatomical structures. However, the reviewers noted that the paper is difficult to follow due to the number of formulations. In addition, several important experimental details are missing. The authors should clarify (but not limited to) the following points in the rebuttal: 1.What are the key advantages of the proposed sampling operator compared to existing methods, such as Deformable Conv and other recent approaches? Notably, the performance of Deformable Conv v1 is very similar to that of the proposed framework, with the differences in Dice scores less than 1%. 2.More details should be provided for the baseline U-Net, especially the number of conv layers. The reported parameter count of 2.3M appears unusually small for a 3D U-Net model. In addition, more implementation details for MedNeXt should be provided, as pointed out by Reviewer #2. Note that new results, experiments, or data beyond what was provided at the paper’s original submission are not permitted in the rebuttal. | Two out of the three reviewers are satisfied with the rebuttal, and I share their assessment. Therefore, I recommend acceptance. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): The paper has a methodology ambiguity, though 2 reviewers have positive ratings. For example, after reading, it’s still unclear to me what the geometry signal is that is used for sampling. Many jargon statements and claims make the paper hard to understand. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper proposes GeoSample, a geometry-guided local operator for 3D medical image segmentation that replaces fixed-grid convolution and pooling with voxel-wise, rotation-constrained symmetric sampling. Experiments on BraTS, MSD Hepatic Vessel, and TDSC-ABUS show consistent improvements, particularly on boundary metrics, with reduced parameter count (2.3M→0.8M). Reviewers agreed that the operator-level rethinking of sampling is a meaningful and technically interesting contribution, the elegant formulation separates even/context and odd/directional-change information, the unified design across stride-1 and stride>1 is architecturally coherent, the Consensus Field is an original geometry-aware skip-fusion idea, the evaluation across three modalities is broad, the plug-in validation across nnU-Net/Swin-UNETR/MedNeXt is practically useful, and the efficiency-accuracy tradeoff is favorable. They raised several concerns: (1) novelty positioning relative to deformable convolutions, OBELISK-Net, STN, and equivariant models needs sharpening; (2) topology-aware evaluation (clDice, branch recall, connected-component errors) is missing despite the topology motivation; (3) the capacity-matched baseline comparison is not fully isolated, since the proposed model is lighter than baselines; (4) single fixed-seed evaluation without significance testing; (5) plug-in generalization is only on TDSC-ABUS, with different integration strategies across backbones; (6) the ablation does not isolate several non-trivial design choices (SO(3) frame, K, symmetric sampling, normalization); (7) the methods section is mathematically dense and Figure 1 is hard to read; and (8) reproducibility details (hyperparameters, training settings) are under-specified.After rebuttal, the authors clarified GeoSample’s distinction from DCN/OBELISK/STN-style methods (measuring geometry vs. aggregating shifted features), justified the compact U-Net scaffold, explained the backbone-specific integration choices, and committed to improving figure clarity and reproducibility details. Both reviewers maintain or raise their recommendations to Accept. The AC leans toward acceptance.

title: StrokeTimer: Robust Representation Learning for Ischemic Stroke Onset-Time Estimation from Non-Contrast CT
reviewer_1_strengths: The combination of semantic–style disentanglement and the ECMS module is an interesting and novel approach. Not requiring lesion annotations is a strong advantage, as it reduces the need for costly and time-consuming manual labeling. The use of an NCCT dataset from 18 medical centers strengthens the study by demonstrating diversity and potential robustness across different sources. The use of Grad-CAM++ heatmaps for visualizing stroke onset is valuable for interpretability, although the visualizations and their explanations (e. g. , relationships between normal vs. abnormal regions, onset time, and slice selection) could be clearer. The proposed StrokeTimer shows improved performance compared to other SSL methods, although the overall performance remains relatively modest
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Although StrokeTimer improves over other methods in long-tailed classification (both per class and on average), the overall performance remains relatively low, mostly in the 0.5–0.7 range. In Table 2, some methods achieve REC= 1.00 for the <4.5 class but are not highlighted, which raises concerns about result presentation and consistency (please revise this). Overall, the performance gains do not appear strongly significant across all classes. The method is relatively complex due to the use of self-supervised learning, yet the improvement over non-SSL approaches seems limited, which may not fully justify the added complexity. The evaluation is limited to a single dataset; testing on additional datasets in the future (for journal submission, for example) would help assess the robustness and generalizability of StrokeTimer.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: Traditionally, the estimation of stroke onset time has relied primarily on multimodal MRI. The authors have innovatively utilized non-contrast CT (NCCT) to estimate onset time, proposing a novel methodology specifically tailored to the characteristics of the data. This approach holds the potential to enhance the efficiency of stroke diagnosis and assessment while simultaneously reducing examination costs.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The clinical motivation of this work is highly appreciated. Traditionally, stroke onset-time estimation has relied on multi-modality MRI, where infarct characteristics can be better distinguished across different imaging sequences. Moreover, prior studies often depend on lesion ROI-based feature extraction. Given that early ischemic changes on NCCT are typically subtle and difficult to perceive, it would be helpful if the authors could further clarify how the proposed method is able to effectively focus on lesion-related regions without explicit lesion segmentation. Please specify it. 2.In the first component of the method, the authors introduce a Semantic-Style Disentanglement strategy by leveraging frequency-based encoders to extract semantic and style representations. It would be beneficial to further elaborate on how these disentangled representations specifically contribute to the downstream stroke onset-time estimation task. Providing more intuition or empirical evidence could improve the clarity of this design. 3.Furthermore, it would be helpful if the authors could clarify how the learned disentangled representations are transferred to the downstream task. In particular, more details regarding the fine-tuning strategy or integration mechanism would improve reproducibility and understanding. 4.For Fig. 2, it is suggested to plot the infarct regions (e.g., annotated on skull-stripped NCCT images), so that the focus areas of different methods’ heatmaps can be more clearly interpreted and compared. Overall, this is a well-motivated and promising work with strong experimental validation. Addressing the above points would further improve the clarity and impact of the paper.
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: ﻿Estimating stroke onset time from routine NCCT is an important and challenging task, especially when the true onset is unknown. The paper tackles a real‑world bottleneck in acute stroke triage. ﻿ The framework explicitly models both imaging style variability (scanner/center differences) and severe class imbalance (only 72 samples in the 4.5–6 h window). This integrated treatment is a genuine strength. ﻿ The dataset is large (1,686 scans) and multi‑center (18 sites), which is a major step beyond single‑center studies. The ablation studies clearly demonstrate the contribution of each component (disentanglement vs. ECMS). ﻿ Grad‑CAM++ visualizations show that StrokeTimer’s attention maps focus on clinically meaningful regions (gray‑white matter blurring, hypodensity), enhancing trustworthiness.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.Limited novelty in methodological components. The semantic‑style disentanglement via VAE + FiLM and the prototype‑based contrastive loss are well‑established techniques in the medical imaging literature (e.g., Sarhan et al. ECCV 2020 for orthogonal disentanglement; Li et al. ICLR 2021 for prototypical contrastive learning). The ECMS module essentially combines a weighted mean‑shift update with a frequency‑based prior – a heuristic that lacks theoretical justification. ﻿ 2.Insufficient comparison with recent task‑specific methods. The paper only compares against generic long‑tailed classification baselines (Focal Loss, Balanced Softmax, etc.) and self‑supervised methods (SimCLR, MoCo). However, there exist several recent deep learning approaches specifically designed for stroke onset estimation from NCCT (e.g., Marcus et al. npj Digital Medicine 2024; Sun et al. Medical Image Analysis 2024; Vorberg et al. MICCAI Stroke Workshop 2025). The authors should include these task‑specific baselines to demonstrate that StrokeTimer truly advances the state of the art. Without such comparisons, the claim of “first fully automatic benchmark” is overstated. ﻿ 3.Questionable clinical utility of the 4.5–6h window. The intermediate window (4.5–6 h) is clinically ambiguous: guidelines recommend perfusion imaging for patients in this window rather than relying solely on NCCT. The model’s performance on this class is notably lower (AUC 0.54, F1 0.38) and, as shown in Fig. 3, ECMS even degrades it. The paper should discuss whether this window is worth predicting at all, or whether a binary classification (<4.5 h vs. ≥4.5 h) would be more clinically actionable. ﻿ 4.Lack of external validation. Although the dataset is multi‑center, all experiments use a single internal split (training/validation/test) from the same pooled data. No separate external cohort (e.g., from a different geographic region or acquisition protocol) is used to test generalization. The authors should either perform leave‑one‑center‑out cross‑validation or validate on an independent dataset. ﻿ 5.Reproducibility concerns. The preprocessing steps (CT‑BET for skull stripping, resampling to 48×256×256) and the two‑stage training procedure (80 + 70 epochs) are described, but hyperparameters (e.g., λ weights in Eq. 2, δ and γ in ECMS) are only partially reported. The code is promised “upon acceptance” – ideally, a public code repository should be provided at submission to enable reproducibility. ﻿ 6.Writing and presentation. Several minor issues: the abstract mentions “two national cohorts, and ” with missing names; the dataset split uses only 30 validation and 30 test samples, which is extremely small for evaluating a multi‑class model (especially given only 72 samples in the minority class, a test set of 30 may not be statistically stable). The authors should justify the split size or use cross‑validation.

title: Structural Congruence Matters: Biological Pretraining for Vascular Graph Extraction
reviewer_1_strengths: 1: The paper studies a relevant problem. Reducing the need for expert-annotated vascular graphs is an important problem for image-to-graph learning in medical imaging. 2: The main hypothesis is at least clear and testable. The paper explicitly asks whether a biologically aligned source domain (plants) transfers better than road networks for vascular graph extraction, and evaluates this under matched source size in part of Table 1.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1: The methodological novelty is limited. The paper does not introduce a new image-to-graph architecture or learning objective. It largely reuses RelationFormer and the cross-domain / cross-dimensional training framework of Berger et al. , while replacing the pretraining source domain and adding preprocessing choices such as border-aware clipping and degree-2 node retention. This is a relatively small step beyond prior work. 2: The central claim is stronger than the evidence provided. The paper argues that “structural congruence matters more than scale alone,” but the evidence is only a comparison between roads and plants within one inherited framework. This does not establish that structural congruence is the main causal factor, since the reported gains are entangled with representation and preprocessing changes, especially the retention of degree-2 nodes. 3: Important baselines are missing. The experiments compare mainly against no pretraining and road-based pretraining. There is no comparison to stronger medically relevant pretraining strategies, despite the paper explicitly discussing medical foundation models and “purely semantic medical pretraining. ” As written, the evaluation is insufficient to support broad claims about the superiority of the proposed pretraining paradigm. 4: No ablation study. The experimental design is not sufficiently clean to isolate the main contribution of different components.
reviewer_1_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: In my view, this is a truly surprising and inspiring paper. There is a certain sense of beauty in the experimental findings, particularly in how they reveal the deep connections between disparate biological systems.The conceptual innovation here is profound: it demonstrates that biological transport systems provide far superior priors for vascular extraction than human-made infrastructure like road networks. This suggests that nature-made structures—including our own vascular systems—share a latent generative logic with the botanical world. By aligning our models with these shared principles of growth and flow efficiency, the authors have found a way to bridge the gap between scale and structural truth.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Even though I enjoy reading this paper, I would like to respectfully note some weaknesses. The evaluation seems primarily restricted to the RelationFormer architecture. It remains unclear if these biological priors offer similar gains for other image-to-graph frameworks or traditional segmentation-skeletonization pipelines. While grapevines are used effectively, the study only explores one type of botanical data. Testing on other biological networks (e.g., leaf veins or fungal hyphae) would further validate the “structural congruence” hypothesis.
reviewer_2_rating: (6) Strong Accept — must be accepted due to excellence
reviewer_3_strengths: The paper has the following the strengths: The paper discusses a highly novel perspective on the problem formulation of image to graph extraction for vascular networks. The author have provided in depth intuitive explanation, how the structural congruence between human vascular system and the plant transport networks are driven by similar mechanisms(hierarchical branching, flow optimization, and space-filling organization). The authors have experimentally demonstrated that how this structural congruence between source domain used for pretraining and target domain could lead to better results even within limited data regimes under pre-training, fine-tuning and zero-shot transfer setups. The findings of this paper align with broader trends in the medical deep learning community, which suggest that pretraining on high-quality, structurally aligned data is often more effective than pretraining on large-scale datasets from highly different domains. The preprocessing strategies adopted, effectively preserve topological consistency and geometric detail. In particular, border-aware edge clipping avoids boundary artifacts, while degree-2 node retention maintains curvature information critical for accurate modeling. Together, these choices provide more reliable and informative supervision for downstream learning. The authors have provided code, enabling the proposed approach to be readily adopted for developing more accurate and efficient single-stage image-to-graph extraction pipelines, facilitating its application in zero-shot settings for vascular graph extraction.

author_feedback: We sincerely thank the meta-reviewer and all reviewers for their careful evaluation and constructive feedback. We are particularly encouraged that multiple reviewers recognized the relevance of investigating structural congruence for vascular graph extraction and appreciated the controlled experimental design, especially the scale-matched comparisons and sample-efficiency analysis. Our intention in this work was not to introduce a new image-to-graph architecture, but to isolate the role of biologically aligned structural priors under controlled conditions. For this reason, we intentionally retained the RelationFormer/Berger framework, losses, and optimization settings across all experiments. We believe this strengthens the comparison by avoiding confounding architectural modifications. Regarding the concern that structural congruence is entangled with preprocessing, Table 1 explicitly controls for these factors. Roads are evaluated at both 99.2k and 25.9k source samples, and degree-2 retention is ablated for both roads and plants. Thus, roads+2-degree vs. plants+2-degree isolates the effect of source domain under matched graph representation settings. Under these controlled conditions, plant-based pretraining consistently outperforms infrastructure-based pretraining in both 2D and 3D. We also acknowledge the suggestion regarding broader medical pretraining baselines. Existing medical foundation models such as vesselFM target dense segmentation rather than image-to-graph prediction and do not provide graph-level supervision compatible with RelationFormer-style graph extraction. We therefore compare against the most directly relevant prior work, Berger et al.’s road-based structural pretraining framework. We agree that extending the analysis to additional biological transport systems and other graph extraction paradigms beyond RelationFormer would be valuable future work. Due to space constraints and the goal of maintaining a controlled study, we focus this MICCAI submission on the current setting, while considering broader evaluations for a future journal extension. In the camera-ready version, we have further clarified the methodology and improved the figures to make the experimental design and contributions easier to follow. We thank the reviewers again for their insightful comments.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): After careful consideration, I find the core idea – that plant branching networks transfer better than road networks for vascular graph extraction – genuinely novel and thought-provoking. Honestly, I think the paper is good for MICCAI. The paper is well written and the findings are interesting enough to warrant publication. That said, the paper has clear limitations. The methodological contribution is incremental, as the architecture and training framework are largely borrowed from prior work. The experimental evidence does not fully support the claims, with no ablation study to isolate the contribution of structural alignment from preprocessing changes. Missing baselines further weaken the evaluation. However, the conceptual insight is strong enough that I lean toward acceptance rather than rejection. If the authors integrate the comments given by the reviewers, the paper would be significantly stronger.

title: Structure-Adaptive Sparse Diffusion in Voxel Space for 3D Medical Image Enhancement
reviewer_1_strengths: (a)The innovative sparse diffusion framework operates directly in voxel space (avoiding compressed-representation information loss) and adopts x_0-prediction with velocity supervision. It uses only 5 uniformly subsampled timesteps (vs. 1000 in traditional models) to achieve up to 10× training acceleration without sacrificing resolution or anatomical details, solving the high computational cost of existing 3D diffusion methods. (b)The lightweight Structure-aware Trajectory Modulation (STM) module adaptively adjusts denoising behavior via multi-structure encoding and block-wise time embedding modulation. It addresses anatomical heterogeneity of 3D medical volumes, enabling individualized denoising paths for different patches and balancing efficiency with fine detail preservation. (c)The method is evaluated on 4 public datasets (CT, PET, MRI) for denoising and super-resolution, compared with 4 representative 3D diffusion baselines. Quantitative (PSNR, SSIM, etc. ) and qualitative evaluations, plus ablation studies, confirm its state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance and clarify each component’s contribution.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: (a)The idea of using sparse timestep sampling + x0​-prediction for conditional diffusion has been explored in recent works such as Fast Diffusion (Zhen et al. , CVPR 2023), and Skip Diffusion. The paper does not sufficiently highlight the difference from these fast diffusion frameworks; the core sparsity strategy is largely similar. (b)The STM module uses multi-planar projection + affine modulation on time embedding, which is a standard design in medical vision:Multi-planar (axial/coronal/sagittal) encoding has been widely used in 3D medical CNNs and Transformers (e. g. , nnFormer, UNETR++). Modulating time embedding with spatial content is standard in adaptive diffusion and conditional diffusion models. Thus, STM is a practical combination rather than a fundamentally new mechanism. (c)The paper only compares with 3D diffusion models (DDPM, LDM, WDM), but does not compare with recent fast CNN/Transformer methods (e. g. , HFN, UCTransNet) or GAN-based methods optimized for medical enhancement. It is unclear whether diffusion is still necessary for speed vs. performance.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The paper propose a sparse diffusion framework in 3D voxel space that combines x 0 -prediction with velocity supervision and timestep subsampling, achieving up to 10× faster training while improving enhancement quality.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1 The novelty overlaps with existing works. The conditional x₀ prediction using degraded input priors is basically the same idea as CoreDiff[1]; sparse timestep scheduling is essentially few-step diffusion, which DDIM[2] has already explored; velocity supervision is a weighted combination of noise and x₀ prediction, similar to what RDDM has done; STM resembles the adaLN-Zero modulation in DiT[3] combined with multi-scale convolutions. The paper presents these existing techniques as independent contributions but does not sufficiently discuss the relationship and differences with the above works. The novelty is questionable. 2.The nature of sparse diffusion needs clarification. Both training and inference operate on only 5 timesteps, which is essentially no different from directly training a 5-step diffusion model. The paper describes it as “subsampling from a dense schedule”, but lacks theoretical analysis on why uniform sampling is optimal. 3.The data scale is small and statistical reliability is questionable. All four datasets have small sample sizes (50, 88, 60, 120 cases), with only 10-24 cases for testing. For example, LDCT-and-Projection-data contains 299 patients but only 50 are used without explanation. The reported PSNR improvements (~0.5dB) on such small test sets lack statistical tests, and no standard deviations or confidence intervals are reported. I suggest using more available data or providing statistical significance analysis. 4.The selection of comparison methods is not comprehensive enough. First, all four baselines are 3D versions of general diffusion frameworks, lacking comparison with non-diffusion methods (e.g., 3D U-Net, 3D SRGAN), making it hard to judge whether diffusion models are truly necessary for this task. author_feedback: 1.Novelty and relation to prior work (R1&R2). We agree that sparse diffusion, x_0-prediction, and adaptive modulation individually relate to prior work. Our contribution lies in combining these components into an efficient framework for high-resolution 3D image enhancement. Compared with prior acceleration-oriented methods, our framework differs in three aspects: (1) direct operation in 3D voxel space rather than latent-space or 2D settings; (2) sparse training and inference under the same diffusion parameterization, yielding up to 10x training acceleration; and (3) anatomy-adaptive trajectory modulation within the shared sparse schedule. SkipDiff and PD mainly target inference acceleration via skipping/distillation, whereas our sparse schedule is applied directly during training. CoreDiff incorporates modality-specific degradation priors into the forward diffusion process, whereas we retain the standard Gaussian diffusion parameterization and inject anatomical priors through conditional voxel-space denoising without modality-specific re-derivation. We agree that multi-planar encoding and modulation are established ideas, and STM is not intended as a fundamentally new conditioning mechanism. Instead, it adapts denoising trajectories to local anatomical complexity under extremely sparse schedules by modulating time embeddings rather than features alone. Together, these components enable efficient direct 3D voxel-space enhancement with only five diffusion steps. 2.Baselines and comparison scope (R1&R2). We focused on representative 3D diffusion baselines (latent, wavelet, DDPM, DDIM) because the primary contribution of this work is efficient sparse diffusion in voxel space. We agree broader comparisons are valuable and will add CNN/GAN baselines to the revision. Under identical LDCT settings, RED-CNN-3D and WGAN-VGG-3D achieved SSIM values of 0.72 and 0.73, respectively, below both the diffusion baselines (0.74-0.81) and our method (0.82). We will also expand discussion of restoration-specific baselines in the revision. 3.Clarification of the sparse diffusion formulation (R2). Our method performs sparse sampling from the original T=1000 diffusion schedule while retaining the same noise parameterization and timestep embeddings. Our goal is not to design a fundamentally new shallow diffusion process, but to exploit the empirical redundancy of neighboring denoising steps in conditional enhancement tasks with strong anatomical priors. Table 2 shows that sparse schedules consistently outperform dense schedules in our setting, with performance peaking at K=5 in our experiments. Uniform sampling was chosen as a simple prior-free strategy, while learned or non-uniform schedules remain interesting directions for future work. 4.Dataset scale and statistical reliability. (R2&R3). For LDCT-and-Projection-data, only 50 patients belong to the chest subset with consistent reconstruction kernels, while the remaining cases involve different anatomies or acquisition settings. The other datasets were used in full or near-full. Patch-based training with random cropping and augmentation yields approximately 10^4 effective samples, which increases training diversity despite the limited number of patients. We will additionally report mean ± std and paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests (p<0.01) in the revision. 5.Additional clarifications and reproducibility (R3). We will improve figure resolution, fix the typo, add additional implementation details (UNet configuration, optimization settings, patch extraction, runtime, and GPU memory), and release code upon acceptance. Regarding axial projections, axial context is already captured by the volumetric 3D branch, while sagittal/coronal projections provide complementary through-plane structural cues for anisotropic medical volumes. Preliminary experiments showed that removing sagittal/coronal branches reduced PSNR by $0.2$ dB, whereas adding an additional axial branch provided only marginal gains.
