title: SuRe-Flow: Surface-to-CT Synthesis via Retrieval-Augmented Rectified Flow for CT-Free Superficial Radiotherapy
reviewer_1_strengths: Novel solution to ill-posed inverse problem: The retrieval mechanism elegantly addresses the fundamental 1-to-N ambiguity (single surface → multiple valid internal anatomies) that causes mode averaging in standard conditional flow models. The contrastive learning approach (DSC 0.9442 for Top-1 retrieval) effectively anchors generation to anatomically plausible priors. Strong clinical motivation and validation: Targets a genuine unmet need—eliminating unnecessary CT scans and ionizing radiation exposure for superficial radiotherapy patients (keloids, skin cancer). The dosimetric evaluation in Monaco TPS using 3D Gamma Index (2%/2mm) provides clinically relevant validation beyond standard image quality metrics. Large-scale robust evaluation: Training on 20,022 patients from 100+ centers across 16 countries ensures broad anatomical diversity and generalizability. The depth-stratified analysis (0–20mm, 20–50mm, 50–100mm) demonstrates specific efficacy in the critical therapeutic zone. Technical integration: Sophisticated combination of rectified flow (stable generative prior), ControlNet conditioning, and focal frequency loss specifically designed to preserve sharp density gradients required for accurate electron density heterogeneity corrections. Quantitative superiority: Substantial performance gains over baselines (MAE 5.0 HU vs. 30.2 HU for standard RF in Zone 1; 96.7% vs. 89.4% Gamma passing rate), establishing genuine clinical feasibility.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Limited generalizability beyond superficial targets: The method is specifically optimized for 0–20mm depth (electron beam range). The retrieval mechanism and frequency penalty may not translate to deeper anatomical targets or other imaging modalities without fundamental redesign. Database coverage concerns: While the 20,022-patient database is large, performance depends on retrieving sufficiently similar anatomies. Patients with unusual body habitus, pathological deformities, or surgical alterations may retrieve suboptimal priors, though the paper shows robustness via Top-5 neighborhood sampling during training. Missing comparisons: While compared to MAISI-v2 and a 3D GAN, the paper lacks comparison against other recent medical image synthesis approaches (e. g. , score-based diffusion models, VQ-GANs, or other retrieval-augmented generation methods outside medical imaging). Computational overhead: The paper does not discuss inference latency or computational cost associated with the retrieval database queries (FAISS) and ControlNet architecture, which is relevant for real-time clinical workflow integration with optical surface scanners. Clinical validation depth: While dosimetric accuracy is shown, the study does not assess inter-observer contouring variability on synthetic vs. real CTs, or downstream clinical outcomes (tumor control, toxicity), though these are beyond the scope of a methodological paper.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The paper has several strengths. The most obvious one is the clinical motivation. For superficial radiotherapy cases, avoiding CT simulation could reduce unnecessary imaging burden and simplify workflow, so the application itself is meaningful. Another strength is that the method is well aligned with the problem. Surface-to-CT synthesis is highly ambiguous, and the retrieval module is a reasonable way to provide anatomical priors instead of relying only on a generic generative model. The combination with a rectified flow backbone is also interesting and technically relevant. The experimental setup is also solid. The study uses a large dataset and evaluates not only image metrics but also dosimetric Gamma Index results in a treatment planning system. This makes the paper stronger than many synthesis works that only report visual similarity metrics.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The main concern is the realism of the input setting. The paper aims at generating CT from optical surface scans, but the input surface appears to be derived from CT body contours rather than real scanner data. In practice, optical scans may contain noise, missing regions, motion, clothing artifacts, or posture mismatch. Because of this, it remains unclear how well the method would transfer to a real clinical workflow. Another concern is the retrieval component. Since the method relies on retrieving similar prior cases from the same large dataset, it would be helpful to clarify how very close matches were handled. A comparison with a simple retrieval-only baseline would also help show how much of the improvement comes from the generative model beyond the retrieved prior itself. The clinical validation is promising but still somewhat limited. The paper reports Gamma Index results, which is a strong point, but it would help to know more about the treatment setups that were evaluated and whether results are consistent across different body locations. It would also be useful to see how the method performs in more difficult or less common cases. Finally, although the overall design is reasonable, the paper does not discuss practical efficiency such as inference time, hardware requirements, or workflow integration. These aspects would be useful for judging real clinical usability.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The clinical motivation is well-grounded in radiotherapy physics, and the focus on the superficial zone (0–20 mm) makes the problem both tractable and clinically meaningful. The inclusion of end-to-end dosimetric validation in a treatment planning system (3D Gamma 2%/2mm) is a significant strength and demonstrates real clinical relevance beyond image-level metrics. The scale of training and evaluation (20k+ patients across multiple centers and countries) is substantial and supports claims of robustness and generalizability. The ablation study clearly demonstrates the contribution of each module
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The retrieval module is only validated using external body contour similarity and does not demonstrate alignment of internal tissue density, leaving its core purpose insufficiently supported. 2.The impact of retrieval is not rigorously validated — no ablation with random or mismatched priors is provided, making it unclear whether retrieval is actually responsible for the observed gains. 3.The contrastive learning setup is weak, as positive pairs are generated via augmentations of the same sample rather than anatomically similar patients, which does not guarantee meaningful retrieval behavior. 4.Baseline comparison is limited for a paper of this scale, with no inclusion of recent diffusion-based or anatomy-conditioned synthesis methods, weakening the strength of the empirical claims.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: To clarify, we represent the surfaces as voxelized occupancy masks. This allows optical scanner point clouds and CT-derived external contours to share the same downstream model input after voxelization.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): The paper introduces a contrastive surface-based retrieval module that identifies and injects topologically matched anatomical priors during generation. The overall writing is good, and the method is novel. Beyond the reviewers’ comments, the authors should further discuss how the method ensures geometric fidelity for individuals. Although the retrieval method is used to improve it, this may not be able to depict the lesion with large inter-variations. It would also be beneficial to provide more details on clinical tolerance for the realism of the generated CT images.

title: SurfMark3D: Surface-Based Graph Convolution Framework for Distal Femoral Landmark Localisation in Total Knee Arthroplasty
reviewer_1_strengths: The major strengths of the paper are: Rigid formalization of the proposed graph convolutional blocks and loss functions. Comparison of the performance on multiple state-of-the-art and conventional architectures Ablation on the constituent terms of the loss functions and convolution blocks Showing memory/hardware efficiency in the proposed operators and attention blocks.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The major weaknesses are: The paper only tests the framework on cases with KL<=1, which are relatively having smooth surfaces with less complex geometry than higher severity cases. The authors clearly state that the purpose was to ignore the impact of osteophytes; however, it would have been preferable to see the performance of the proposed method on such cases without severe osteophytes. The Results section in Page 8 Clinical Generalizability and Cross-modality section suddenly reports experimental results on different datasets and experiment settings that have not been explained before. It would have been better to adequately report those in a different study or expanded version of the paper. The results in Table 2 in comparison to previous methods is minimal, where it’s almost in submillieter Euclidean error level. Given that all cases are KL<=1, the improvement level may be clinically insignificant, with the major improvement in the computational efficiency side.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The proposed method demonstrates strong clinical relevance for surgical planning in Total Knee Arthroplasty. The learnable Gaussian spreads and the proposed PointSTAR loss effectively address anisotropic ambiguity and are well-motivated for this task. The whole framework is technically reasonable and clear. The use of multiple evaluation metrics provides a comprehensive assessment of performance. The release of a clinically validated dataset with expert annotations is valuable for the community and enhances reproducibility.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Although the proposed workflow address the problem, the improvements over baselines are relatively small, and no statistical significance testing is provided. The framework includes multiple components (LR-AGConv, BRPA, AWing, PointSTAR, uncertainty weighting). Although ablations are provided, it remains unclear which components are essential vs. marginal contributors to performance gains. Some aspects are not clearly described in the paper. For example, it would be helpful to define MEE in the abstract. In addition, SDR is used throughout the paper without any explicit explanation.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: Public benchmark dataset. The release of 550 expert-annotated distal femur meshes with inter/intra-observer variability reporting (1.24±1.05mm and 1.18±0.90mm respectively) fills a genuine gap in orthopedic landmark research, where comparable public datasets are essentially nonexistent. This alone provides lasting value to the community regardless of the proposed method’s merits. Memory-efficient engineering. The low-rank decomposition of AGConv achieves 43.1% training memory reduction (40.4GB→23.0GB) without accuracy degradation, and the full pipeline requires only 1GB VRAM at inference with 1.7s latency. These are practical engineering contributions with applicability beyond this specific task. PointSTAR loss formulation. The decomposition of prediction uncertainty into surface-normal and tangent-plane components is geometrically well-motivated for surface-constrained landmarks. The ablation demonstrates concrete improvements for geometrically ambiguous landmarks such as FLTA (1.64→1.41mm) and FMCD (1.86→1.60mm), and accelerates training convergence from >100 to ~60 epochs.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Absence of volumetric end-to-end baselines. The paper claims advantages over volumetric and multi-view methods [2,14] but provides no direct comparison. Berger et al. [2] demonstrated that nnU-Net operating directly on CT volumes achieves accuracy statistically equivalent to manual annotation for 6 distal femoral landmarks without requiring any upstream segmentation. The paper’s Table 2 compares only point cloud backbones (PointNet++, PointMLP, PTv3), proving superiority within the point cloud paradigm but failing to justify why the point cloud paradigm itself is preferable to established volumetric approaches. This is a fundamental gap in experimental design. Severe clinical population mismatch. The dataset is restricted to KL≤1 (non-osteophytic) subjects, which essentially excludes the actual TKA patient population (predominantly KL 3-4). TKA candidates present with osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis, bone cysts, and varus/valgus deformity that drastically alter surface geometry. The 1.24mm MEE reported on near-normal femora cannot be extrapolated to pathological anatomy, and no analysis is provided on how model performance would degrade with increasing disease severity. This critically undermines the paper’s claim of clinical relevance for TKA planning. Misalignment between task definition and clinical workflow. In actual TKA surgical planning, individual landmark localisation is not the clinical endpoint. Sizing is determined by implant template fitting after cutting plane simulation, where ML width and AP dimension are evaluated simultaneously relative to the implant catalog. Notching assessment emerges directly from anterior resection plane simulation, not from individual landmark coordinates. The paper reports no downstream surgical planning metrics (e.g., implant size selection accuracy, component alignment error, or cutting plane deviation), making it impossible to assess clinical impact. Unquantified error propagation from upstream segmentation. The pipeline requires MRI→segmentation→mesh→FPS before landmark detection begins, yet no analysis of how upstream segmentation errors propagate to landmark accuracy is provided. The Laplacian smoothing (15-25 iterations) applied to meshes further introduces uncharacterised geometric distortion. The claimed “modality-agnostic” advantage is undermined by this dependence on accurate segmentation, which itself is modality-specific.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank reviewers for recognising our dataset (“filling a genuine gap”, R3), architectural contributions “strong clinical relevance” (R2), “rigid formalization” (R1), and “geometrically well-motivated” formulation (R3). Main concerns addressed below. [A] KL<=1 & scope reframing (R3, AC): We adopt R3’s suggestion: this is a general-purpose, modality-agnostic surface landmark framework, with TKA as the primary validated application. Zero-shot transfer to a distinct anatomy (scapula, 1.8+/-1.35 mm) supports this. Selecting KL<=1 is a ground-truth validity requirement, not an arbitrary restriction. The 11 landmarks are distinct morphological features whose definitions break down on osteophytic surfaces, causing annotation ambiguity. Horteur [8] demonstrates that degenerative morphological changes (osteophytes, bone wear) substantially increase both manual and automatic landmarking errors underscoring the difficulty of establishing reliable ground truth on advanced OA surfaces. Grammens [5] and Berger [2] similarly exclude/defer these cases. Clinically, osteophyte handling is a dedicated upstream preprocessing step prior to landmarking and recent works also treat virtual osteophyte removal as a separate module. [B] Volumetric baselines & cross-modality (R1, R3, AC): While we acknowledge the strength of volumetric baselines like nnU-Net, a direct empirical comparison is challenging due to fundamental differences in problem formulation. Our goal (Sec. 1) is modality-agnostic surface processing. Volumetric methods are inherently modality-dependent: Berger’s [2] nnU-Net consumes raw CT volumes, rendering it inapplicable to MRI. Conversely, our framework accepts segmented meshes from any modality: a single surface model covers MRI and CT-derived meshes without retraining, which volumetric methods cannot structurally offer. Furthermore, they report a higher MEE (2-3mm vs our 1.24mm). Our VSD zero-shot result (1.5+/-0.9mm on CT-derived meshes) bridges this gap: our model achieves near-manual accuracy on CT derived meshes (without CT-specific retraining) empirically validating our paradigm. [C] Downstream planning metrics (R3, AC): We agree downstream integration strengthens clinical impact. Accurate localisation is the foundational prerequisite for downstream measurements; implant sizing, alignment, and cutting-plane definitions derive from these coordinates. Downstream integration remains future work (Sec. 4). We will clarify this scope in the camera-ready. [D] Robustness to upstream variation (R3, AC): ShapeMed [4] reports femoral DSC 0.99/ASSD 0.08-0.15mm, establishing expert-level meshes. Our pipeline (segmentation, Laplacian smoothing, FPS downsampling) precedes model input. Our results demonstrate robustness across these stages. Crucially, the VSD [9] cohort (56 CT-derived meshes, including OA-affected) uses an entirely independent upstream pipeline, confirming robustness to simultaneous shifts in modality, upstream pipelines, and smoothing. [E] Statistical evidence & components (R1, R2, R3, AC): As requested, we applied Wilcoxon signed-rank tests to our existing Table 2 predictions. Our framework achieves statistically significant improvements (p<0.05) over the majority of baselines (PTv3, PointNet++, PointMLP, DeltaConv, PTv2/v3 Attn). For the remaining baselines (PAConv, Self Attn) and intra-ablation variants, differences do not reach p<0.05.This is mathematically expected: because all methods are converging near the human inter-observer floor (1.24+/-1.05 mm) where even our base model already operates (1.28+/-0.90 mm) MEE reduction naturally plateaus. Instead, as R3 appreciated, our meaningful improvements lie along orthogonal axes: architectural efficiency, convergence, and hard-landmark robustness. These improvements hold consistently across all metrics, all 11 individual landmarks (Fig. 3), and three independent runs. [F] Abbreviations (R2): MEE and SDR will be explicitly defined in the camera-ready.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): The paper proposes a point‑cloud / surface based graph framework to localise distal femoral landmarks for Total Knee Arthroplasty planning. It works on segmented 3D surface point clouds and predicts landmark heatmaps. A 550‑case expert‑annotated dataset is released as well. The clinical population does not match the target. The dataset includes only KL ≤ 1.This means almost normal anatomy. TKA patients usually have KL 3–4 with osteophytes and deformity. These changes surface geometry a lot. So the reported ~1.2 mm errors on smooth femora may not transfer to real TKA planning. The paper does not test severe cases or discuss how performance changes. Important baselines are missed. It compares mostly the point‑cloud frameworks. It does not compare against strong volumetric end‑to‑end methods (e.g., nnU‑Net on CT volumes) that can localise landmarks without upstream segmentation and meshing. Without this, the paper does not justify why point clouds are better for this task. Reviewers were also commenting a mismatch of th workflow related to clinical endpoints. In practice, surgeons care about implant sizing, alignment, and cutting planes. They do not use landmark coordinates alone as the final output. The paper does not report downstream planning metrics (implant size accuracy, alignment errors, plane deviation). This weakens the clinical impact claim. The pipeline depends on upstream segmentation and mesh processing. Segmentation errors can propagate to landmark errors. The paper does not quantify this. Laplacian smoothing and sampling may also distort geometry, but the paper does not analyse this. Statistical evidence is weak. The paper reports small improvements over baselines, but it does not report statistical significance. Reviewers also noted unclear reporting of abbreviations (e.g., MEE, SDR) and some results appear suddenly with limited explanation. Overall, the paper has good engineering contributions and a valuable dataset release. But the current validation does not support strong clinical claims for TKA planning. The missing volumetric baselines and the KL≤1 restriction are the biggest gaps. | The rebuttal clarifies some points. The statistical testing and dataset release are positive. However, they do not overcome the main concerns. The authors explain that KL≤1 cases were selected for reliable landmark annotation. But it does not solve the clinical mismatch (the paper is framed around TKA planning). It only explains why the dataset is easier and more reliable to annotate. Second, the modality-agnostic claim: the method is only modality-agnostic after segmentation. The full pipeline still requires CT or MRI segmentation before mesh generation. The paper is not sufficiently validated as a TKA planning method. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Majority of reviewers vote for acceptance. There are a number of critical concerns regarding methodology and experimental validation, however, I think these have been addressed reasonably well. The dataset that will be published is acknowledged and a big pro for this work. With a reformulation of the contribution regarding the intention of the work and a noting of the limitation that TKA disease cases are not the target of this initial work, the manuscript could be of interest to the MICCAI community. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The authors have effectively addressed the reviewers’ concerns, particularly those raised in the meta-review. I find the responses convincing, including those regarding the validation choices, volumetric baselines, and statistical significance analyses. Overall, I believe this is a solid paper, and I am inclined to support its acceptance.

title: SurgRFO: Foundation Model Based Compositional Synthesis of Critical Retained Foreign Objects in Intraoperative Chest X-Rays
reviewer_1_strengths: Significance of clinical application. Detecting RFOs is an important clinical problem (https://www. cureus. com/articles/320644-retained-foreign-object-signals-a-dangerous-atmosphere-in-the-operating-room#!/; https://www. sciencedirect. com/science/article/pii/S0039606025003654). While various safeguards have been explored to facilitate the detection of RFOs, RFOs continue to go undetected due to the complexity of the task. Use and release of clinical radiographs with critical RFOs. Due to the rarity of these objects, evaluating on these images and sharing them with the public is a significant contribution. Robust evaluation of synthetic image quality, including a blinded clinician study, quantitative distribution measures, and a downstream classification performance analysis across three classification models. External validation was performed. The code was made publicly available. The first figure is an informative graphical abstract. The proposed framework splits synthesis into two parts (radiograph then RFO) to strengthen the fidelity of the RFOs. The synthetic images improve downstream classification across three classification models
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Lack of downstream performance comparison with other synthetic generation models/augmentation strategies. The work does not compare its downstream detection results against closely related prior methods, such as https://link. springer. com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-032-08009-7_15 that similarly applies synthetic data augmentation for detecting critical RFOs. In addition, the paper does not provide downstream performance comparisons against alternative generative models or augmentation strategies. As a result, it remains unclear whether the observed gains are attributable to the specific generative methodology proposed, or simply to increasing the effective training set size. Would we see similar performance gains with RoentGen? What about if we just injected RFO patterns into otherwise negative images? Substantial overlap with earlier work, limiting novelty. The work does not consider a 2025 MICCAI workshop paper (https://link. springer. com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-032-08009-7_15), which similarly employs synthetic data augmentation to improve downstream critical RFO detection and releases a synthetically generated dataset of chest radiographs with critical RFOs. The submission should have referred to and contextualized this work (i. e. compared model performance), clearly distinguishing the submission’s contributions from this prior work. Especially when making claims such as “no public dataset dedicated to critical RFOs exists” and “the first publicly available dataset dedicated to critical RFOs. ” The two contributions of using synthetic data augmentation to improve downstream critical RFO detection and the release of a chest radiograph dataset of critical RFOs were again repeated in an arXiv preprint (https://arxiv. org/abs/2507.06937v1) that the submission cited as a work with “high-fidelity and diverse X-ray synthesis”. While the preprint cannot limit the novelty of the submission under consideration as it is not published, it should at least be properly contextualized if cited. Conflicting information on the dataset release. The authors state in the manuscript that they are publicly releasing their dataset (no link is provided), but on GitHub, they state that they cannot release the data due to privacy constraints. As this dataset release is arguably one of the greatest contributions of the work, the GitHub message is concerning. Missing dataset details that are important for contextualizing the results and public release. How many patients were there? With a 6:1:3 patient-level split, how many radiographs did that put in the test dataset? What were the class ratios in the test dataset? It is important for the reader to know the number of scans in the test dataset, how many contained critical RFOs, and how many patients those scans were sourced from. In addition, how many radiologists labeled the images? Were multiple perspectives considered during this labeling process? If so, how were disagreements between radiologist labels managed, especially when it comes to bounding boxes? What were the criteria for differentiating between critical and non-critical RFOs? Was it truly only the training images that were preprocessed? Shouldn’t all images go through the same preprocessing pipeline? Was the same training dataset used for the synthesis network and the classification network? If so, for synthesis network training, I assume all the negatives in the training dataset constituted D_bg and the positives D_rfo? How was Stage-1 synthesis evaluated on 5k images when there were only 944+144 in the dataset? What radiographs were the external cohort compared to, as all reported external images had critical RFOs? Downstream detection performance measures were not reported with measures of uncertainty or confidence. Additionally, the authors did not perform a statistical analysis of the downstream performance gains. Both of which reviewers were supposed to look for in the official MICCAI guidelines (https://conferences. miccai. org/2026/en/REVIEWER-GUIDELINES. html). This is especially concerning as the reader does not know how small of a sample size is being tested, nor the class balance of that sample. Having said that, the proposed model has obvious enough performance gains over the baseline.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.Detecting critical RFOs is a safety-critical task where real positive data are rare; focusing on improving sensitivity/robustness is well aligned with clinical needs. 2.The proposed synthetic positives are used to improve multiple mainstream detectors, suggesting good practical utility and ease of adoption in existing clinical/engineering pipelines.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The paper does not clearly state whether the data used to train the synthesis models (Stage 1/Stage 2) come strictly from the Site 1 training split, or whether Site 1 validation/test cases might be used during synthetic data generation. If the synthesis model is trained on test-patient images and then used to generate data for downstream evaluation, this would compromise the fairness of the internal assessment. 2.In the downstream detection experiments (Sec. 3.2), multiple metrics are reported (e.g., mAP, FROC, FNR, FOR, ACC), but their exact definitions and computation protocols in the detection setting are not clearly specified. Moreover, the overall experimental setup and evaluation procedure in this section are not sufficiently clear. 3.The data section states that Site 2 provides “An additional 20 critical RFO-positive cases,” yet the external results include metrics that depend on false positives (e.g., FROC). The authors should clarify whether the Site 2 external test set includes negative samples, and provide its size and class composition. If no negative cases are included, the paper should explain how these metrics are defined and computed for the external evaluation. 4.Table 4 reveals an interesting gap: in (a), clinicians give comparable quality/realism scores to real and synthetic images, yet in (b), they can still distinguish synthetic images with an accuracy of ~75%. Could the authors explain why the images receive similar quality/realism ratings despite being distinguishable?
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.Clinical relevance and problem importance The paper addresses the detection of critical retained foreign objects (RFOs), which are rare but high-risk events in intraoperative settings. This problem is highly relevant to patient safety and remains underexplored due to extreme data scarcity and subtle visual characteristics. The focus on such a clinically meaningful and challenging task significantly strengthens the impact of the work. 2.Well-motivated compositional synthesis framework The proposed two-stage framework separates global background generation from localized object synthesis, which aligns well with the inherent structure of intraoperative radiographs. This design enables better modeling of rare and small objects that are difficult to capture in fully end-to-end generative approaches. The use of conditional Poisson blending further ensures photometric consistency between synthesized objects and background, improving visual coherence . 3.Performance improvements across downstream task models The experimental results show that augmenting training data with synthesized samples leads to consistent improvements across multiple detection architectures, including Faster R-CNN, RetinaNet, and YOLOv8. 4.Inclusion of clinician-centered evaluation The incorporation of a radiologist-driven Turing-style evaluation adds a clinically meaningful validation of the generated images. The comparable quality ratings between synthetic and real images under blinded assessment support the plausibility of the synthesis results and enhance the translational relevance of the study .
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.Limited integration between stages The proposed method adopts a two-stage pipeline in which background generation and object synthesis are trained independently and combined through a post-hoc optimization process. However, this design prevents joint feature learning between the background (normal chest radiographs) and the synthesized objects (RFOs). As a result, the model is unable to capture globally consistent representations, which may limit both visual coherence and scalability of the framework. 2.Limited dataset size and insufficient generalization validation The dataset contains only 144 positive cases, and the external test set is very small (20 cases). While it is understandable that positive cases are inherently scarce, there exists a large amount of publicly available negative data. Incorporating external public datasets, particularly for downstream evaluation and Turing test analysis, would strengthen the conclusions and provide more convincing evidence of generalization. 3.Incomplete baseline comparisons The experimental comparisons are limited to RoentGen and DreamBooth, which do not fully represent the current state of the art. The absence of more recent and competitive baselines makes it difficult to assess the true advantage of the proposed method. Including stronger and more up-to-date generative models would provide a more comprehensive evaluation. 4.Evaluation metrics are not fully aligned with the task characteristics The use of FID and MS-SSIM for evaluating medical X-ray synthesis is debatable, as these metrics do not necessarily reflect clinical fidelity or the realism of localized lesions. The paper itself acknowledges that MS-SSIM is largely dominated by background similarity. More task-specific metrics would provide a more meaningful and clinically relevant evaluation. 5.Limited analysis of downstream task improvements The downstream evaluation aims to demonstrate that incorporating synthetic data improves detection performance. However, the analysis lacks depth. In addition to accuracy, aspects such as stability and robustness should be considered, for example by reporting standard deviations across multiple runs. Furthermore, evaluating performance under reduced base data (data ablation) could provide stronger evidence of the effectiveness of the synthesized data. Relevant related studies have demonstrated such evaluation strategies and could be referenced for comparison. Layer Separation: Towards Adjustable Joint Space Width Images Synthesis (ACM MM 2025) https://doi.org/10.1145/3746027.3755407 Towards Generalizable Tumor Synthesis (CVPR 2024) https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2024/papers/Chen_Towards_Generalizable_Tumor_Synthesis_CVPR_2024_paper.pdf 6.Lack of discussion on X-ray imaging physics X-ray image synthesis differs fundamentally from natural image synthesis, as it is governed by specific imaging physics. The current approach, which relies on a “copy-paste”-style compositional strategy, may not fully respect the physical formation process of X-ray images (e.g., attenuation and projection). A more detailed discussion or justification of how the proposed method aligns with or approximates these physical principles would strengthen the work.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and meta-reviewer for their constructive comments. All reviewers (R1–R3) acknowledged the clinical importance of rare, safety-critical RFO detection. R2, R3 recognized SurgRFO as a meaningful two-stage synthetic augmentation framework, noting its downstream detection gains (R2, R3), robust synthetic image evaluation including clinician assessment (R1, R3), external validation (R1, R2), code release, and planned release of intraoperative RFO dataset (R1, R3). Below, we address the reviewers’ concerns. R1, Meta-R (Relation to prior RFO synthesis work and novelty): We agree that Zhou et al. (MICCAI DEMI 2026) is relevant and should be contextualized. That work releases CT-based physically synthesized RFO images, rather than real intraoperative radiographs with critical RFOs. Its pipeline inserts RFO meshes into relatively clean CT volumes from normal patients and projects them to X-rays, which is valuable but differs from our target setting: cluttered surgical chest radiographs acquired during real intraoperative workflows. SurgRFO is designed around this domain gap. We curate and release, to our knowledge, the first publicly available real de-identified intraoperative surgical chest radiograph dataset dedicated to critical RFO detection with bounding-box annotations, distinguishing it from prior physically synthesized CT-projection datasets. In the revision, we will add this work to the Introduction, clarify this distinction, and include a contextual comparison. R1, Meta-R (Dataset release): We confirm that, upon acceptance, our public release will include de-identified intraoperative RFO radiographs, annotations, and all synthetic SurgRFO images used in the paper. The earlier GitHub statement was imprecise and has been corrected. We also provided example real and synthetic images in the earlier repository to demonstrate the data format and visual quality. R1, R2, Meta-R (Cohort details, preprocessing, and leakage prevention): We will add a dedicated paragraph detailing cohort composition, labeling, and experimental protocols. The Site-1 cohort contains 144 critical RFO-positive cases and 944 RFO-negative cases, with one case per patient. Positive and negative cohorts were split at the patient level using the same 6:1:3 train/validation/test protocol, ensuring no patient overlap. We will report exact positive/negative counts for each split. All synthesis components, including background adaptation, RFO appearance modeling, placement-prior estimation, and blending-parameter selection, used only the training split; validation/test images were never used for synthesis training or tuning. Detectors were trained on the training split, selected using validation data, and evaluated only on held-out internal and external cohorts. All images followed the same preprocessing pipeline. We will also clarify labeling criteria/workflow, detector training details, and hyperparameters; implementation details are available in the earlier released code. R1, R3, Meta-R (Compare with simpler augmentations): We agree that stronger augmentation comparisons are important. Both real-only and SurgRFO-augmented detector training used the same standard data augmentations, including random flipping and intensity normalization. Thus, the reported gains are not due to basic augmentation being applied only to SurgRFO. To further isolate the contribution of the proposed synthesis strategy, we will add a simple RFO copy-paste/injection baseline using the same number of synthetic-positive samples, allowing direct comparison between SurgRFO and increased synthetic sample count alone. We will clarify the full augmentation protocol. R1, R3, Meta-R (Statistical analysis): We agree that uncertainty analysis is important in this rare-event setting. We will add patient-level bootstrap 95% confidence intervals for the primary downstream metrics using fixed held-out test predictions. These intervals will be reported in the main tables.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Paper summary: This paper introduces SurgRFO, a two-stage synthetic augmentation pipeline that generates realistic RFO-positive surgical chest radiographs and shows that these synthesised positives improve downstream object detection performance, including evaluation on an external site. Strengths: This work addresses a clinically important and safety-critical problem. A key strength is the introduction and public release of a rare clinical radiograph dataset containing critical RFO cases, which represents a valuable contribution to the field. The proposed well-motivated compositional synthesis framework, which separates radiograph generation from localized RFO synthesis, is technically sound and improves the fidelity and realism of synthesized objects. This is further supported by robust evaluation of synthetic image quality through blinded clinician assessment, quantitative distribution analysis, and external validation. Importantly, the synthetic data consistently improve downstream detection performance across multiple mainstream architectures (e.g., Faster R-CNN, RetinaNet, YOLOv8), demonstrating strong practical utility, ease of adoption in existing clinical pipelines, and alignment with the clinical need to improve sensitivity and robustness in rare-event detection. Weaknesses: First, the novelty is somewhat weakened by substantial overlap with prior work on synthetic augmentation for critical RFO detection, yet the manuscript does not adequately contextualize or compare against these closely related methods. In addition, the downstream detection gains are not compared against alternative synthetic generation or simpler augmentation strategies, leaving it unclear whether the improvements stem from the proposed method itself or simply from increased training data. The paper also lacks important dataset and experimental details, including cohort composition, labeling protocols, train/test separation for synthesis, preprocessing consistency, and external cohort setup - which raises concerns about reproducibility and evaluation fairness. Furthermore, downstream performance is reported without statistical significance analysis or measures of uncertainty, despite relatively small positive sample sizes, limiting confidence in the robustness of the reported gains. Decision Rationale: The paper has clear strengths, but several substantive concerns remain unresolved, particularly regarding the limitations above. These points appear addressable through author clarification. I therefore recommend Invite for Rebuttal. | Thank you for the constructive rebuttal for addressing the reviewers’ concerns. The discussion improved confidence in both the technical contribution and the clinical relevance of the work. The Reviewers acknowledged that the paper tackles an important clinical problem and proposes an innovative approach for synthetic augmentation in the setting of rare pathologies and objects. This is an interesting contribution for the MICCAI community. One remaining concern is the limited comparison against other contemporary augmentation strategies, which makes it difficult to fully position the proposed method within the broader augmentation literature. While this limitation should be acknowledged more clearly, the current evidence is sufficient to support the paper’s main claims. The planned public release of real-world RFO data is also expected to provide meaningful value to the community. For the camera-ready version, I recommend authors to strengthen discussion of related augmentation approaches and clarify the scope of claims accordingly. I support the acceptance of this paper. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This manuscript presents a method to generate synthetic XRay images with foreign objects to aid in the development of a method to recognise foreign objects XRay images. This addresses a clinically important dataset and the authors will also release this dataset. The reviewers found the method to be technically sound and interesting. The limitations were limited novelty, and no comparison with other augmentation strategies. Although there is some overlap in methodology with prior works, this manuscript is evaluated on real images with foreign objects whereas other methods generated synthetic evaluation image. I am accepting this manuscript because on balance I find the novelty an important step change the other weaknesses (lack of comparison with other data augmentation methods) are counter balanced by the strengths of the work. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The reviewers’ concerns have been successfully addressed in the rebuttal, making the work a solid contribution especially for what concerns methodological applications in MIC.

title: SurvTTA: Order-Aware Test-Time Adaptation for Heterogeneous Domain Shifts in Multi-modal Survival Analysis
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The work addresses the critical issue of domain shifts in multi-center medical deployments. By focusing on TTA without needing source data or target labels, it offers a practical solution for real-world clinical settings where data privacy and accessibility are major constraints. 2.The core insight to leverage the ordinal nature of survival risk (rather than absolute values) is strong. The Topological Consistency module, which maintains both node-wise risks and edge-wise pairwise orderings, is a sophisticated method to preserve the survival structure under distribution shifts. 3.The integration of Decoupled Geometric Alignment (handling modality-specific shifts) and Uncertainty-aware Gradient Correction (resolving optimization conflicts) demonstrates a comprehensive understanding of the instability issues in TTA, making the framework well-suited for complex heterogeneous data.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.Contradiction in Online Setting: Section 3.1 mentions an “online setting” with data discarded post-inference, yet the method runs “3 epochs” with rollback. Suggestion: Clarify how rollback works without stored data. Is a buffer used? This is crucial for reproducibility. 2.The paper only compares against two specific regression TTA methods. Suggestion: Discuss or test against standard UDA/TTA classification methods (e. g. , adversarial learning, TENT) to better justify why existing general methods fail for survival analysis. 3.The ablation study lacks analysis on key hyperparameters and augmentation strength. Suggestion: Add a brief sensitivity analysis, especially regarding 3D rotations, to ensure anatomical integrity isn’t compromised.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The paper addresses a highly relevant and challenging problem: cross-site generalization in multi-modal survival analysis under heterogeneous domain shifts. Unlike standard classification tasks, survival prediction has intrinsic ordinal structure, and the paper explicitly leverages this property. This is a well-grounded and insightful formulation. 2.A key strength is the idea of modeling survival prediction through risk ordering invariance, rather than absolute score matching. The proposed topological consistency formulation (node-wise + edge-wise constraints) provides a principled way to encode ordinal structure in test-time adaptation. This perspective is both novel and well aligned with survival analysis theory, and represents a meaningful contribution beyond existing TTA methods. 3.The experimental section is thorough and convincing. The use of risk ranking (rather than absolute prediction) and evaluation via Kaplan–Meier curves strengthens the clinical relevance of the work.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.Although the paper compares with several TTA methods, the baselines are relatively limited. It would strengthen the paper to include comparisons with: more recent or stronger domain generalization / adaptation methods, or alternative survival-specific adaptation strategies. 2.The framework introduces multiple components (topology, alignment, gradient correction), which may increase computational overhead and optimization complexity. A discussion on efficiency and scalability would be helpful.
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.Clinically well-motivated problem. TTA for survival analysis under heterogeneous multi-modal domain shifts is a genuinely underexplored problem with practical relevance for cross-site deployment. The paper is the first to address this combination. 2.The insight that survival risk ordering (rather than absolute scores) is site-invariant is well-motivated and directly informs the TC module design. Framing this as a topological graph with node- and edge-level consistency losses is technically coherent. 3.The DGA module’s per-modality treatment is a sensible and important design choice given that different imaging modalities (CT vs. PET) exhibit different degrees of domain shift. This is often overlooked in unified TTA approaches. 4.The failure of SSA on HMR and instability of ST variants highlight a real practical gap, and SurvTTA’s robustness across target sites is a meaningful result.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The HECKTOR target sets appear to have on the order of 20–30 patients each based on dataset sizes and splits. No confidence intervals or statistical significance tests are reported for any of the main results 2.The paper compares against only two regression TTA methods (CASP, SSA) and self-training variants. CASP is from sentiment analysis (AAAI 2025) and SSA from ICLR 2025 — neither is designed for survival prediction. Stronger baseline comparison is needed 3.ResNet-18 with cross-attention or Concat-MLP fusion is a fairly shallow source architecture. It is unclear whether performance gains reflect TTA effectiveness or compensating for a weak source model. 4.Table 2(b) shows that +T+G (mean 70.28%) underperforms +G alone (70.46%). This is a notable finding that contradicts the narrative and is dismissed in a single sentence. A thorough analysis of why these objectives conflict and why UGC resolves them is necessary to validate the design. 5.Presenting post-TTA significance (P=0.036) without confidence intervals or sample size . λ1, λ2, τ, c, and γ govern all three modules and their interactions, how is the hyperparameter selection done.

The reviewers have acknowledged the importance of the problem and the soundness and practicality of the solution. title: SymmDiff: Symmetry-Guided Diffusion for Fracture Localization in Pelvic Radiographs
reviewer_1_strengths: The proposed method is novel. The idea of using symmetry-corrected generated images to identify fracture locations is interesting.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: While the proposed method achieves good performance compared with other state-of-the-art generative models, it would be better if the authors also compared it with commonly used detection methods, such as YOLO. Fracture detection may not necessarily require generative models like DDPM for this task. In addition, the paper lacks evaluation metrics for image quality, such as the FID score. It would also be beneficial to include radiologists to assess the quality of the generated images.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The method is clinically relevent and the Symmetry-Diffusion appoarch is innovative. By embedding contralateral consistency directly into the denoising process, the model suppresses asymmetries caused by normal anatomical variation or projection tilt.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.While the pelvis is generally symmetric, true biological asymmetry and variations in patient positioning (tilt/rotation) during X-ray acquisition are common. Although the authors suggest that latent encoding provides robustness to ‘minor projection mismatch’, the paper would benefit from a more detailed analysis or a ‘stress test’ showing how the model performs under significant pelvic tilt or in patients with pre-existing non-fracture asymmetries. 2.A primary concern for any symmetry-guided model is the occurrence of bilateral fractures. If both sides of the pelvis are fractured, the ‘structural prior’ from the contralateral side may itself be abnormal. While the authors mention using identity constraints and population-level atlases as future work, the current manuscript lacks a clear demonstration of how the model fails or adapts when symmetry is violated on both sides simultaneously. 3.The qualitative results show some fractures that appear relatively obvious visually. To better justify the necessity of this complex generative framework, the authors may provide a more focused evaluation on ‘subtle’ or ‘occult’ fractures where standard radiological interpretation often fails. Quantifying performance specifically on these ‘difficult’ cases would more clearly highlight the clinical value of the SymmDiff approach.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The central methodological idea — conditioning each reverse diffusion step on a patient-specific contralateral reference — is novel within the diffusion-based UAD literature. Prior methods either treat denoising as anatomy-agnostic or apply bilateral comparison post-hoc or in discriminative settings. Embedding symmetry into the reverse trajectory dynamics is a genuinely new contribution that is well-motivated by established clinical reading practice for pelvic radiographs. The clinical rationale is strong. The pelvis is one of the clearest anatomical cases for bilateral comparison, and the paper connects this practice to the technical design in a coherent way. The choice of application domain is not arbitrary — it is one where the proposed inductive bias is most naturally justified. The ablation study is thorough and informative. Five ablations each isolate a specific component, and all show consistent degradation. Importantly, the removal of symmetry conditioning causes the largest performance drop, which confirms that the core mechanism is driving the results rather than ancillary design choices. This is the most convincing evidence in the paper. The ROI-constrained reverse diffusion (Eq. 9) is cleanly formulated with a verifiable identity preservation property outside the ROI. This targeted correction strategy is a sensible design choice that reduces the risk of global structural drift during reconstruction, addressing a known failure mode of diffusion-based UAD. The performance gains over the strongest baseline (THOR) are substantial, particularly at the pixel level (AUPRC 36.2 –> 43.9, F1max 37.2 –> 42.7), suggesting the method provides meaningfully better localization rather than marginal improvement.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The comparison set is narrow and limited exclusively to diffusion-based UAD methods. There is no comparison with feature-based anomaly detection approaches such as PatchCore, which is cited (ref [4]) but not benchmarked. More critically, there is no comparison with a simpler symmetry baseline — for instance, left-right subtraction with alignment and thresholding. Without this, it is impossible to disentangle how much of the performance gain comes from the diffusion framework versus the symmetry prior itself. This is a significant omission that weakens the empirical contribution. The evaluation is conducted on a single anonymized dataset from one institution with no external validation. Pelvic radiographs vary considerably across institutions due to equipment, positioning protocols, and patient demographics. The symmetry assumption can degrade under oblique projections, rotated patients, or bilateral pathology. The authors acknowledge cross-site generalization as future work, but the absence of any robustness analysis on these factors limits confidence in the method’s generalizability. There is no stratification of results by fracture severity, location, or type. With 534 abnormal cases, meaningful subgroup analysis is feasible. This matters because the clinical value proposition differs substantially for subtle versus severe fractures — if the aggregate numbers are driven primarily by severe cases that radiologists would not miss, the practical utility is limited. Five qualitative examples do not substitute for systematic analysis. The latent swap claim (Eq. 8) rests on an unstated assumption that the contralateral latent is closer to the true normal latent than the original input within ROI regions. This is plausible for unilateral fractures but could fail for bilateral pathology, symmetric normal variants, or significant projection asymmetry. The paper does not acknowledge or bound this assumption. No confidence intervals, standard deviations, or statistical significance tests are reported for results. Given the dataset size, some estimate of variance would strengthen the claims considerably. The authors do not describe in sufficient detail several architectural components that are critical for reproducibility. Specifically, the type of VAE encoder and the architecture of the U-Net network are not specified, making it challenging to independently reimplement the method even with access to the described training hyperparameters.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and AC for their insightful feedback and for recognizing the novelty of embedding contralateral consistency directly into the diffusion trajectory. Below we address the major concerns raised by the reviewers. Choice of baselines (R1, R3): SymmDiff is designed for unsupervised anomaly Detection (UAD), motivated by the scarcity of fine-grained fracture annotations and the difficulty of predefining fracture morphologies. Supervised detectors such as YOLO require annotated abnormal cases for training and therefore address a different setting from the proposed UAD formulation. We agree that PatchCore [4] is a strong feature-memory method. Our current evaluation focused on reconstruction-based diffusion methods to isolate the contribution of symmetry-guided correction within a comparable paradigm, as PatchCore takes a fundamentally different approach, scoring anomalies against a memory bank of normal patches rather than via reconstruction discrepancy. A thorough cross-paradigm comparison would meaningfully complement our evaluation and is an important direction we plan to pursue. Contribution of symmetry vs. diffusion (R3): We agree that simple left-right difference is an important conceptual baseline. The submitted ablations help isolate this point. The ROI is derived from bilateral discrepancy, but removing ROI-constrained denoising reduces performance (pixel AUROC 83.2 vs. 88.4), indicating that raw symmetry discrepancy alone is insufficient. Conversely, removing symmetry conditioning degrades the model toward an anatomy-agnostic diffusion baseline (79.9 vs. 76.5), showing that the improvement comes from embedding the contralateral prior into the reverse trajectory, not merely from using diffusion. Direct subtraction compares sides; SymmDiff uses the contralateral side to synthesize a pseudo-healthy correction while preserving non-ROI anatomy. Robustness to symmetry violations (R2, R3): Two failure modes were raised: projection tilt and bilateral fractures. The method does not assume perfect pixel-wise symmetry. The use of latent space rather than pixel space abstracts local textures into higher level features, which improves robustness to minor projection tilt and rotation. For bilateral fractures, the ROI gating with identity constraints (Eq. 9) provides a stabilizing bias: regions outside the ROI mask remain unchanged, so when both sides are abnormal the global anatomy is preserved rather than corrupted by a degraded contralateral prior. Population level healthy atlases could serve as a secondary anchor for bilateral fracture cases, which is a key area for future work. Reproducibility (R3): The VAE is the pre-trained perceptual-compression autoencoder from [12], trained with a perceptual loss, patch-based adversarial objective, and KL regularization, with a down sampling factor of 8, we fine-tune it on pelvic radiographs. The denoiser is an attention U-Net with timestep embedding and a squared-cosine-beta noise schedule, with z_sym incorporated via channel-wise concatenation as described in Sec. 3.2.Configuration files and training scripts will be released with the code.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): All three reviewers recommend weak accept. The core idea of embedding contralateral symmetry directly into the reverse diffusion trajectory is clinically well-motivated and technically novel within the diffusion-based UAD literature, and the ablation credibly demonstrates that symmetry conditioning is the primary performance driver. The authors should address in the final version the absence of a simple left-right subtraction baseline and the missing architecture details, which are critical for reproducibility.

title: Synergistic Perception-Reasoning Governance: Grounding Medical MLLMs with Verifiable Anatomical Evidence
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.It proposes a training-free dual-side evidence injection framework to mitigate visual misinterpretation framework. 2.It designs a task-aware dynamic router that dynamically selects modality-specific evidence injection strategies based on task semantics. 3.It conducts comprehensive experiments across 2 tasks and 6 MLLMs to validate the effectiveness of the proposed method.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The paper lacks detailed descriptions of the experimental settings, such as the specific architecture of the task-aware dynamic router. 2.Clinical questions often involve multiple attributes. For example, “whether the left atrium is enlarged” simultaneously involves anatomical localization (C_A) and measurement (C_M). Is such a categorization reasonable? If a question involves multiple categories, which evidence-injection strategy should be used? Furthermore, as shown in Table 1, errors made by the classifier in the dynamic router may lead to performance that is even worse than the original MLLMs. However, the authors do not provide any evaluation of the classifier’s performance. 3.Organizing the bounding boxes into structured descriptions may introduce redundancy. Compared to directly injecting labels and bounding boxes into the prompt, structured descriptions result in a longer context. 4.The author does not address how the accuracy of the mask/bbox affects both text and vision-side. According to the qualitative analysis presented in the paper, vision-side injection directly influences the model’s attention, and inaccurate masks may lead to more hallucinations. However, the authors neither conduct experiments to evaluate mask accuracy nor discuss how it impacts the experimental results.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The paper evaluates on multiple backbones, multiple datasets, and both close-ended and open-ended tasks and shows convincing good results. The results are also visualized well. 2.The framework is well motivated. it intervenes on both sides of the generation process by anchoring the text prompt with ROI descriptors and recalibrating visual activations. 3.The paper is written nicely and it is easy to read.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.My major concern is the lack of clarity about how ROI labels are obtained. But the paper not mentioned that where these bboxes came from during inference time. Since the “training-free” claim will be substantially weakened if the bounding box need the manually annotated or provided by other detection network. b) Missing of the training detailed of question classifier. The Task-aware Router rely on the classifier h(q) but the paper did not mention how to train the question classifier. If the supervised data is need, that will be conflict to the claim of “Training-free” c) The methodological novelty is moderate. As mentioned in paper, there are many prior work such as VCD, DoLa, OPERA, AVISC, DAMRO, PAI, and M3ID has already explored for the inference-time hallucination. reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the Area Chair (AC) for the recommendation and for recognizing that our work is technically rigorous, addresses visual misinterpretation hallucinations in medical MLLMs, makes meaningful contributions beyond prior studies, and provides convincing empirical validation. We also thank R2, R3, and R4 for their feedback. We address the main concerns below. (1) R3&R4 - ROI/bbox source and MedSAM. We apologize for the unclear ROI acquisition description. Our contribution is not a new ROI proposal or detection algorithm, but an evidence-injection mechanism using reliable anatomical ROI evidence to mitigate visual misinterpretation hallucinations without updating MLLM parameters. The framework is not tied to MedSAM; MedSAM is only one medium for acquiring ROI masks, and any reliable ROI source, such as annotations, detectors, segmentation models, or other promptable models, can be incorporated. (2) R2&R4 - Router and training-free claim. The router is not a separately trained classifier. We use a zero-shot LLM-based router with a fixed classification prompt to map each question into four categories. It trains no router parameters and does not update the medical MLLM backbone; thus, the framework remains training-free with respect to the medical MLLM. Routing accuracies were 91.25% for GPT-4o, 95.54% for GPT-5, 89.67% for Qwen3-0.6B, and 93.64% for Qwen3-1.7B. (3) R2 - Multi-attribute questions and routing issues. We acknowledge that clinical questions may involve multiple attributes; e.g., “whether the left atrium is enlarged” involves both localization and measurement. The current router selects the intervention according to the dominant semantic risk; finer multi-label routing is future work. Routing errors may select a suboptimal intervention and partly explain category-level drops. However, the router does not generate the final answer; it only selects the evidence-injection strategy, so errors mainly affect the intervention path rather than directly injecting incorrect answers. (4) R2&R3 - Inaccurate masks/bboxes. ROI evidence does not provide diagnostic conclusions or finding labels. It only provides approximate anatomical location and region extent, indicating “where the model should pay more attention,” rather than “what answer the model should produce.” The final judgment is still made by the MLLM based on the original image, question, and vision-language reasoning. Severely inaccurate ROIs may weaken grounding or introduce misleading visual priors. However, most ROI evidence obtained in our experiments is reasonably accurate; under such conditions, our evidence-injection method is robust and consistently reduces visual misinterpretation hallucinations. (5) R2 - Structured ROI description. The structured ROI description is not simply used to lengthen the prompt. It converts raw coordinates into semantically interpretable anatomical evidence, including anatomical label, spatial location, bbox extent, and relative area. Compared with raw coordinates alone, this representation is better aligned with the MLLM language interface. (6) R4 - Novelty. Prior works have studied inference-time hallucination mitigation from decoding, contrastive decoding, or attention calibration perspectives. Our novelty lies in using ROI-level verifiable anatomical evidence as a grounding anchor to jointly constrain visual perception and textual reasoning in medical MLLMs. Thus, our contribution is coordinated visual-perceptual and text-reasoning guidance for medical visual misinterpretation hallucinations, rather than another generic decoding heuristic. (7) R3 - Scope and reproducibility. We chose radiology tasks because visual misinterpretation hallucinations are clinically important and quantitatively evaluable. In principle, the framework is not limited to radiology, as it only requires reliable anatomical ROI evidence; validation on other modalities remains future work. The code is released on GitHub: https://github.com/Henry991115/SPRG.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): Paper summary: This paper introduces a training-free framework to address visual misinterpretation hallucinations in medical MLLMs. The authors conducted a comprehensive evaluation across 6 MLLMs and 5 datasets, with reported consistent improvement over diverse baselines. Strengths The reviewers identified several strengths, including: The plug-and-play design of the proposed method is a good advantage, which has real deployment value. The reasonable interpretability of the method. Comprehensive evaluation and consistent improvement over diverse prior baselines. Weaknesses: The main concerns raised by reviewers include: My major concern is the lack of clarity about how ROI labels are obtained, and the missing training details of the question classifier. The paper also lacks detailed descriptions of the experimental settings, such as the specific architecture of the task-aware dynamic router. Review Reconciliation: Reviewer opinions are largely consistent regarding the contributions of this work. Decision: After considering the reviews and manuscript, I believe the paper is technically sound, addresses an important problem in addressing visual misinterpretation hallucinations in medical MLLMs, and presents a meaningful contribution beyond existing work. The empirical validation is convincing. I therefore recommend Provisional Accept.

title: SynMamba: Synergizing Visual Mamba with Synthesized Clinical Semantics for Boundary-Aware Segmentation
reviewer_1_strengths: Clear and well-structured presentation: The paper is well-organized and easy to follow. The motivation, method, and experimental pipeline are presented in a logical and coherent manner, making the contributions easy to understand. Dual-branch architecture design: The proposed dual-branch SynMamba effectively combines global context modeling (via Mamba) and local detail extraction (via CNN), which is well-suited for medical image segmentation tasks requiring both structural and boundary precision. Effective multimodal integration via synthetic clinical narratives: The paper introduces a modality synthesis strategy that generates fluent clinical descriptions from masks and images, and couples them with visual features through an interaction bottleneck. This enables effective fusion of text and image modalities, injecting high-level clinical semantics into the visual backbone and improving cross-modal alignment.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Lack of clarity and fairness in baseline comparisons In Section 3.2, the experimental setup for competing methods is not clearly described. It is unclear whether these baselines are (i) trained from scratch on the datasets, (ii) fine-tuned using the proposed text generation framework, or (iii) directly evaluated using pretrained weights. This ambiguity raises concerns about the fairness and validity of the comparisons, especially given that the proposed method explicitly benefits from synthesized textual supervision. Insufficient details on LLM usage and reproducibility concerns Section 2.5 introduces the use of a “large language model (LLM)” for generating clinical narratives, but does not specify which model is used, how it is prompted, or how the rule-based components are designed. The lack of implementation details (e. g. , prompt design, generation constraints) makes the method difficult to reproduce and evaluate. Inconsistency in dataset scale and insufficient explanation The reported dataset sizes significantly differ from those in cited works [3] and [4]. Specifically, the original datasets contain 423 AP/PA images and 349 CT scans respectively, while the paper reports 2,729 and 9,258 samples. The manuscript does not clearly explain how these numbers are obtained (e. g. , slice-level expansion, preprocessing, or aggregation), which affects reproducibility and makes it difficult to assess the validity of the experimental setup. Unclear design and questionable necessity of the text synthesis pipeline The proposed modality synthesis pipeline (structured attributes → clinical narratives → structured attributes via back-parsing) raises concerns regarding both clarity and necessity. In Fig. 1, an Attribute Extractor is introduced, yet its role is not described in the Modality Synthesis section. It is unclear why attributes must first be explicitly extracted instead of being directly inferred by the LLM, and how this component interacts with the text generation process. Furthermore, the “Regenerate” loop shown in Fig. 1 is not explained: it is unclear how many iterations are performed, what stopping criteria are used, and how this affects computational cost and training efficiency. More fundamentally, since the pipeline ultimately maps back to structured attributes, the benefit of introducing an intermediate natural language representation is not fully justified. This design appears potentially redundant, and a more direct attribute-based modeling approach may be simpler, more efficient, and less prone to error propagation.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The paper is well motivated and addresses a clear problem in medical segmentation. 2.The overall framework is reasonably well designed, with a clear combination of dual-branch visual modeling, synthesized semantic guidance, and boundary-aware supervision. 3.The experimental results are generally convincing, with comparisons against a reasonably broad set of baseline methods that overall support the effectiveness of the proposed method. 4.The ablation study is comprehensive and helps clarify the contribution of the main components.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.While the overall framework is effective, some components build on existing ideas in multimodal segmentation and visual-text fusion, so the technical novelty lies more in the way these elements are combined and adapted to the target problem than in a single fundamentally new formulation. 2.The paper does not evaluate the model with real clinical text, making it difficult to assess the practical value of the synthesized text setting. 3.Although VSSM is motivated as an efficient global modeling tool, the paper does not provide an explicit evaluation of efficiency or computational cost.
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The motivation of combining Mamba with lightweight CNN to overcome the limits and shortcomings in existing models by emphasizing both global vision and local details is clear and well-explained. 2.The text-informed design is useful. The gated visual-text interaction injects clinical priors into visual features which helps sharpening boundary and improving precision.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.Several key equations (e.g., semantic gating map, final feature) are presented without sufficient justification and derivation. Please try to illustrate these equations clearly. 2.In Chapter 2.4, the loss weights are set without providing reasons. Are these values set based on experience, or through several attempts during experiment to achieve the best performance? Briefly explain this can improve clarity. 3.In Chapter 2.5, to eliminate hallucinations, the work implements a back-parsing mechanism, which seems too simplistic to ensure fully “elimination”. And the paper mentions “discard any narratives that exhibit factual errors or logical inconsistencies”. Is this process done manually or automatically using any algorithm? What happens next after this removal process? 4.In qualitative analysis, the paper claims that SynMamba demonstrates superior performance across diverse clinical scenarios. However, it seems that the evaluation scope is narrow since two datasets in this work are both COVID-related images. This raises questions about how well the SynMamba apply to other current clinical practice and lesion areas. The generalization ability or possibility is not discussed in this paper. 5.Some vision-language baselines mentioned (e.g., CLIP, ViLT) are not specifically designed for medical segmentation domain, so they are more likely to underperform on such benchmarks. Therefore, comparing against them does not meaningfully demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method over proper segmentation baselines. 6.The paper mentions “hallucination-free”, which is a very deterministic claim. LLM may still generate unreliable text although some elimination methods are applied. Please consider justifying the strong claim and try to quantify back-parsing rejection rates and test robustness under perturbed text conditions.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank all reviewers for their valuable comments and recognition of our dual-branch design, multimodal integration, and comprehensive ablations. We address the comments below and will revise the paper accordingly. 1.Modality Synthesis and Hallucination Elimination (R1, R3) The Attribute Extractor in Fig. 1 is a fully rule-based module that derives anatomical localization, connected component counts, lesion occupancy ratio, and texture profiling directly from the GT mask. The LLM is used solely to verbalize these structured attributes into a natural-language clinical prompt: Qwen3-VL first rewrites the attributes into a clinical description, and is then queried again to score the consistency between the generated description and the original image–attribute pair; if a mismatch is detected, the rewriting is repeated until a faithful description is produced. Compared with raw attributes, natural-language descriptions better activate the semantic space of pretrained text encoders like, Bio_ClinicalBERT, providing richer linguistic priors for visual-text alignment. We further note that this rewriting task is relatively simple for modern VLMs, since both the structured attributes and the source image are explicitly provided, the probability of a regeneration being triggered is intrinsically low. In our experiments, after the verification step, no faulty or inconsistent samples were observed in the final synthesized dataset, confirming that the Generate-Verify loop is effective in eliminating hallucinations in practice. 2.Comparison Experiments (R1, R2, R3) All baselines were trained from scratch on the same datasets under identical splits. To eliminate any risk of text information leakage, we evaluate our model under a dummy-text input (“Medical image with potential lesion”), which contains no lesion-specific information such as location, size, or severity. The consistently strong performance under this setting demonstrates that the synthesized text serves as a training-time semantic distillation signal rather than a test-time shortcut. Regarding generalization: although both datasets are COVID-related, they cover two distinct imaging modalities (CT and X-ray), and our model achieves state-of-the-art results on both, demonstrating cross-modality robustness. Regarding the absence of real clinical text: since our core motivation is to address the scarcity of paired reports, evaluating on synthesized data is the most faithful reflection of our target scenario.
