Regarding baseline selection: beyond general-purpose VL models (CLIP, ViLT), our comparison includes medical domain-specific vision-language methods such as ConVIRT and TGANet, ensuring a fair and comprehensive evaluation. 3.Dataset Scale Discrepancy (R1) The reported dataset scale in our paper is correct; the issue lies in an incorrect citation. Specifically, the COVID-19-CT dataset used in our experiments is derived from three public sources, including COVID-19-CT-Seg, MosMedData, and medicalsegmentation.com/covid19.For the X-ray experiments, the dataset is actually QaTa-COV19-v2 rather than the previously cited version. We apologize for this citation mistake and will correct it accordingly. 4.Efficiency Evaluation (R2) The inference latency is roughly 50 ms per image on a single A100. 5.Novelty (R2) We acknowledge that SynMamba builds on prior work; however, the dual-branch backbone and the modality synthesis framework represent novel contributions not previously explored in medical image segmentation. 6.Clarity and Presentation (R3) We thank R3 for the detailed feedback and will address all raised issues, including equation clarity, loss weight justification, the Fig. 3 discussion, typos, and sentence fluency in the revision.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): This study proposes SynMamba, a dual-branch segmentation framework that synergizes Mamba-based global modeling and CNN local feature extraction with synthesized clinical semantics to achieve boundary-aware medical segmentation on CT and X-ray datasets. All three reviewers commend its coherent architecture design, effective vision-text interaction mechanism, complete ablation studies, and competitive quantitative and qualitative segmentation results.

title: TAIR: Text-Guided Adaptive Prompt Refinement for Coarse-to-Fine all-in-One Medical Image Restoration
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The paper studies a practically relevant problem, since a unified model for multiple restoration tasks is more appealing than maintaining separate models for each modality or degradation type. 2.The overall framework is logically organized, and the combination of textual prompts, coarse-to-fine refinement, and adaptive prompt weighting is reasonably motivated. 3.The experiments cover several tasks and include both single-task and all-in-one settings, which gives the paper a relatively broad empirical scope.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The paper emphasizes text guidance as its core novelty, but the experiments do not convincingly verify whether the textual information itself is truly helpful. Although there are ablations removing textual prompts, there is no deeper analysis showing whether semantically meaningful text is necessary or whether the model is actually using the text in a meaningful way. 2.The claim of state-of-the-art performance seems somewhat too strong. The comparisons are mainly against a limited set of recent methods, and the performance gains over the strongest baselines are often small. It would be more appropriate to describe the method as competitive rather than definitively state of the art. 3.The ablation study is not fully convincing. It mainly reports performance drops after removing components, but does not provide enough insight into why the proposed modules are necessary or whether simpler alternatives could achieve similar effects. This makes the support for the network design less solid.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.Leveraging textual instructions for MedIR is a novel and intuitively strong idea. 2.The idea of iteratively improving the restored result based on coarse and fine text prompts is interesting. 3.The paper is well written and easy to understand
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.Closeness to prior work: [1] proposes a very similar dual-prompting strategy for all-in-one image restoration but is neither discussed nor compared with. Specifically, TAIR’s proposed AMPI module looks very similar to Prompt-to-Prompt and Prompt-to-Feature interaction modules of [1]. The authors need to discuss the differences with [1]. [1] Li, Zilong, et al. “Prompt-in-prompt learning for universal image restoration.” Available at SSRN 6115113 (2023). 2.While the idea of using coarse to fine prompts is interesting, the paper does not investigate the sensitivity to the text prompts provided. For instance, are the prompt used during training diverse enough to accommodate varying text prompts in inference? 3.The paper claims it is the state-of-the-art, but the improvements are very marginal. 4.For out-of-distribution testing, what were the text prompts provided? Are those text instructions very different from the training tasks? If not, can the method work for a task which requires different text instructions than those seen during training? 5.For out-of-distribution testing, the other all-in-one models (AdaIr, AMIR, etc.) were excluded. Is there any particular reason for this? 6.Can the authors provide an additional metric such as LPIPS instead of RMSE? The reviewer feels PSNR and RMSE convey very similar information.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The coarse-to-fine prompting strategy is well motivated. The framework is flexible and applicable to multiple degradation types.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.It is unclear why natural language is needed instead of standard task embeddings (e.g., one-hot or learnable tokens). The benefit of semantic language guidance is not demonstrated. 2.Missing key baselines: random text, shuffled prompts, or learnable embeddings should be included to verify the actual contribution of text. 3.The coarse-to-fine design may introduce error propagation. Incorrect structures in the coarse stage may be amplified in the refinement stage. 4.The framework may aggravate over-smoothing, since the fine stage depends on already smoothed intermediate outputs. 5.The experimental validation is incomplete. Variants without text guidance or with frozen/random encoders are not provided. No out-of-distribution evaluation is conducted, which is important given the variability in medical imaging data.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank all the reviewers (R1, R2, R3, Mata-R). Q1: Actual necessity of text. (R1, R3, Meta-R) A1: We have trained TAIR completely without text (33.92), with learnable embeddings (34.22), random text (34.04), and shuffled prompts (34.01), all inferior to TAIR (34.44). (1) Why natural language over embeddings. First, instruction-level prompts provide guidance that simple learnable tokens cannot represent (Fig. 2, variant C). Second, coarse-to-fine framework requires distinct guidance per phase, while a shared task embedding would collapse this differentiation. Empirical gains over learnable embeddings further confirm. (2) Whether the model uses text meaningfully. Drops with random/shuffled prompts, where text exists but meaningless or mismatched, show the model relies on prompt semantics, not generic conditioning signal. We will strengthen these in final paper. Q2: Missing baselines and variants. (R3, Meta-R) A2: (1) The variants requested (without text, random text, shuffled prompts, learnable embeddings) are in A1, showing model learns meaningful prompt semantics to guide restoration. Variants (A) and (D) in Table 4 show removing textual prompts from either CCP or CFP degrades performance, verifying textual guidance at both stages. (2) Replacing frozen CLIP encoder with randomly initialized encoder drops avg PSNR to 34.09, confirming pretrained semantic benefit. Q3: Marginal gains and additional metric. (R1, R2, Meta-R) A3: (1) We will soften “state-of-the-art” to “competitive”. (2) For marginal-gain concern: First, TAIR ranks best across all tasks, with only 24.4M params vs TAT’s 41.69M, offering better accuracy-efficiency trade-off. Second, on OOD (Table 3), TAIR exceeds TAT by 0.77/0.91 PSNR on PET 20\times and sparse-view CT, which we believe are non-trivial and meaningful for clinical application. (3) LPIPS\downarrow: TAIR (0.082/0.061/0.109 on MRI/CT/PET) better than second-best TAT (0.084/0.063/0.123), confirming perceptual gains. Full results will be in final paper. Q4: Novelty of AMPI relative to PIP [1]. (R2, Meta-R) A4: PIP learns degradation via learnable embeddings; TAIR uses pretrained language semantics, driving distinct designs. First, to restore both global structure and fine details, TAIR decouples task identity from restoration strategy via different textual prompts, enabling phase-specific instructions for coarse-to-fine refinement; whereas PIP does single-step without decoupling. Second, to handle heterogeneous text/visual prompts, AMPI adaptively weights prompts per image via gating, in contrast to PIP’s static cross-attention. We will cite [1] and discuss our uniqueness in final paper. Q5: Sensitivity of text prompts. (R2, Meta-R) A5: Several paraphrased instructions show consistent performance with <0.4% PSNR variation, confirming robustness to rewording. OOD experiments (Table 3) use unseen task-level prompts, showing generalization beyond training vocabulary. Q6: Comparison and Setup in OOD. (R2, R3) A6: Table 3 reports OOD results. We reuse raining prompts, replacing only task-level text (e.g., “sparse-view CT reconstruction” for unseen degradation type). TAIR generalizes well to unseen texts. Other methods are excluded only due to space limit, with TAT included as second-best. TAIR surpasses all. Full results will be in final paper. Q7: Error propagation, over-smoothing, and ablation rationale. (R1, R3) A7: (1) Error is mitigated by L1 supervision on intermediate output, residual from degraded input, and AMPI’s integration, which together prevent sole dependency on intermediate output. Variant (C) shows large drop, confirming that coarse-to-fine preserves structures rather than harms. (2) Over-smoothing is prevented via degradation-free prompt which reinject guidance regarding detail restoration into fine phase. Removing this (variants E) degrades performance. (3) Simpler alternatives (variant F with plain cross-attention; variants in A1) yields inferior results. Analysis will be in final paper.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): While the framework is interesting, reviewers share significant concerns regarding the actual necessity of text guidance over simple embeddings and the technical novelty relative to prior work. The experimental evaluation is currently insufficient, with reviewers noting marginal gains, missing baselines (e.g., random/shuffled prompts), and sensitivity analysis. The authors are encouraged to address these critical gaps in their rebuttal. | The rebuttal has addressed the major concerns raised by reviewers. Finally, the paper receives 2 accept and 1 weak reject. Although R3 has not dealt with the rebuttal, I think the rebuttal has solved his/her major concerns. Thus, I recommend acceptance. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper introduces TAIR, the first text-guided all-in-one medical image restoration (MedIR) framework that simultaneously handles multiple modalities and degradations (MRI super-resolution, CT denoising, and PET synthesis) within a single model. By introducing dual-level textual prompts (task-level and instruction-level) combined with an Adaptive Multi-Prompt Interaction (AMPI) module and a text-driven quality-aware contrastive loss, the architecture provides explicit semantic guidance over a sequential coarse-to-fine trajectory. The paper received split post-rebuttal reviews (two Accepts, one Weak Reject), with reviewers strongly commending its conceptual novelty, clear presentation, and broad cross-modality empirical validation. Minor concerns remain regarding marginal quantitative gains and under-discussed baseline comparisons, but these are effectively cleared by the authors’ commitment to soften their state-of-the-art claims. Ultimately, the framework’s value is heavily justified by its parameter efficiency (24.4M parameters) and its robust zero-shot generalization capabilities on out-of-distribution clinical targets, such as unseen low-dose PET parameters and novel sparse-view CT artifacts. The paper satisfies publication standards and is supported for acceptance as a poster. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): While reviewer#3 did not change the decision after the authors’ response, I think the authors have addressed the comments appropriately. However, the paper should compared to task-specific image restoration DL designs to validate if it is beneficial to do all-in-one.

title: Task-Performance Routing for Multi-teacher Distillation in CT Medical Image Segmentation
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The framework adopts a hierarchical fusion design, which selects the best-performing teacher for hard regions while encouraging complementary fusion in easy regions. 2.Evaluating their performance across multiple datasets prove the generalizability of the model.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.Figure 1 only presents the distinct spatial activation patterns of the two teacher networks, but does not demonstrate the complementary spatial activation patterns learned by the student network. 2.Figure 2 describes that the Routing Module Mechanism requires computing both region-based error and confidence. However, only region-wise cross-entropy errors are introduced in the manuscript, with no mention of confidence. 3.In the Routing Weight Generation section, it is stated that region-wise cross-entropy errors are computed from the final logits and the ground truth. However, the description only explains how to calculate region-wise cross-entropy errors based on the final layer, without mentioning how the l-th layer is processed. 4.The caption of Table 1 states that the unit of Dice is %, yet the Dice value of 0.8545 presented in the table is unreasonably low. Furthermore, it can be observed that the performance improvement of the TPR in multi-organ segmentation is not significant. 5.The proposed method involves an excessive number of hyperparameters, which raises concerns about the robustness of the TPR. 6.The ablation study in Table 4 appears incomplete. 7.Tables 2, 3, and 4 present ablation studies on the MSD-Pancreas dataset, while Figure 3 shows visualization results on the BTCV dataset, leading to inconsistency in content. In addition, there is no comparison with other methods in Figure 3, making it impossible to demonstrate the advantages of the TPR.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The main idea of routing teachers based on region-wise performance is simple, intuitive, and well motivated. 2.The split between hard and easy regions is a reasonable design that helps avoid over-committing to a single teacher in easy areas. 3.The evaluation covers three datasets and two teacher pairs, which provides broad evidence of effectiveness. 4.The ablation study is informative and separates the contributions of global weighting, spatial routing, hierarchical granularity, and loss terms.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The routing relies on ground-truth labels to compute region-wise errors during training. This makes the method less applicable. Although the paper acknowledges this point, it remains an important limitation. 2.The figures in the paper appear blurry, and some text is difficult to read. 3.In the codebase, hard_region_mask seems to be used only for logging, and there is no clear implementation of a separate hard/easy region mechanism. 4.The reported gains are relatively modest in several settings, but the paper does not provide enough information about variance, confidence intervals, or multi-seed stability. This makes it harder to judge the robustness of the improvements. 5.The advantage-based weighting can still assign positive weights to a teacher even when that teacher is worse than the current student in a region. 6.The method is formulated in a way that could extend beyond two teachers, but experiments only consider the case of two teachers. It is therefore unclear how the approach scales when the number of teachers increases, especially for routing stability and balance.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: Elegant Handling of 3D Spatial Heterogeneity: The paper presents a highly intuitive and medically relevant premise—that tissue contrast, boundary ambiguity, and organ morphology vary drastically across a single 3D CT volume. The hierarchical 3D region partitioning aligns with the spatial abstraction levels of modern CNN/Transformer encoders. Parameter-Free Routing Mechanism: Relying on the cross-entropy error to route to the best teacher is a clever, parameter-free solution. This avoids the need for complex, learnable routing networks (like those in Mixture-of-Experts) which are prone to overfitting on the limited data typically available in medical imaging downstream tasks. Use of Strong, Modern Baselines: The authors benchmark their method using contemporary, state-of-the-art medical foundation models (SuPreM, VoCo, CLIP-Driven) and modern architectures (SwinUNETR). This makes the results highly relevant to the current landscape of medical image analysis. Extensive Ablation Studies: The experimental validation is rigorous. The component-wise ablations (Table 2), granularity strategy comparisons (Table 3), and loss component analyses (Table 4) isolate and mathematically prove the contribution of every single design choice in the framework.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Dependence on Ground Truth for Routing: A significant limitation (which the authors briefly acknowledge) is that the routing mechanism fundamentally relies on calculating the prediction error against the ground truth during training. This strictly limits TPR to fully supervised settings, preventing its application in semi-supervised or unsupervised domain adaptation scenarios where MTKD is traditionally highly valuable. Limited Dataset Scale for Foundation Model Distillation: While the teachers are foundation models pre-trained on massive datasets, the downstream evaluation is performed on relatively standard, small-scale datasets (BTCV, MSD-Liver, MSD-Pancreas). Evaluating the distillation framework on a larger, more complex benchmark like AMOS22 or AbdomenCT-1K would make the claims of “superior knowledge fusion” much more robust. High Training Memory Overhead: Forward-passing multiple large models (e.g., two SwinUNETR teachers and one student) simultaneously to compute features and logits requires immense GPU memory. The paper would benefit from a brief discussion on the computational complexity and memory footprint during the training phase, as this limits the batch size and the scalability to N > 2 teachers.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and AC for their constructive feedback and for recognizing TPR’s motivation, parameter-free hierarchical hard/easy routing, multi-dataset evaluation, and inference-free deployment. We address the main concerns below. (1) AC/R1 - Intermediate-layer routing. Sec. 2.2 was unclear on how final-logit errors are used for intermediate layers. TPR computes voxel-wise cross-entropy error maps from the final logits of the student and each frozen teacher, then pools these maps with the stage-specific 3D grid to obtain region-level errors for each encoder stage. Thus, shallow layers use finer grids for local boundary ambiguity, while deeper layers use coarser grids for semantic coherence. We will clarify this output-space error pooling and stage-wise routing in Sec. 2.2 and Fig. 2. (2) AC/R1 - Confidence vs. error. The finalized TPR formulation is error-based and does not use confidence as an additional routing signal. The word “confidence” came from an exploratory draft of Fig. 2 and caused confusion. We will remove this wording and consistently describe the router as task-error-driven routing. (3) AC/R1/R2 - Robustness, ablations, and notation. The submitted manuscript already reports paired t-test significance for the ablation studies in Tables 2-4 (p<0.05), showing that the main routing, granularity, and loss designs contribute consistently. Table 1 also shows that TPR improves over individual teachers, adaptive ensemble, and MTKD baselines across three datasets and two teacher-pair settings, rather than in a single isolated case. We will make this existing evidence clearer in the text. We will also clarify the loss-component ablation in Table 4 and correct the Dice notation in Table 1: values such as 0.8545 are Dice fractions and should be reported as 85.45% or clearly labeled as fractions. (4) R1/R2 - Figure clarity and qualitative comparison. We will improve the resolution and readability of all figures. Fig. 1 is intended as motivation, showing teacher complementarity, while Fig. 3 already includes the student prediction and Student Advantage map. We will revise the captions and cross-reference Fig. 3 more clearly to show how the student benefits from teacher complementarity, and clarify the teacher/student comparisons. (5) AC/R2/R3 - Scope, scalability, and training memory. TPR targets fully supervised downstream distillation: labels are needed only during training to estimate region-wise task errors, and the deployed model is a single student. In semi-supervised or label-scarce settings, unreliable or missing labels would make error-based routing less reliable; we will clarify this limitation and leave label-free or pseudo-label-based routing as future work. Our experiments focus on two teachers and three public CT benchmarks covering multi-organ, liver, and pancreas segmentation; evaluation on larger teacher pools and larger benchmarks such as AMOS/AbdomenCT-1K remains future work. The routing rule itself is not restricted to two teachers: hard-region weights can be computed over all teacher advantages, and easy-region fusion can assign equal weights to all teachers. Regarding cost, teachers are frozen and evaluated under no_grad, so no teacher backward graph is stored; sequential teacher forward can reduce peak memory. TPR has no inference-time overhead. (6) AC/R2 - Code-paper discrepancy. The initially released code package mistakenly contained an earlier testing branch where hard_region_mask was mainly used for monitoring/debugging, causing the impression that the hard/easy mechanism was not implemented. The finalized implementation used for the intended TPR mechanism explicitly uses hard_region_mask to switch routing weights: hard regions use advantage-based softmax routing, while easy regions use uniform complementary fusion, following Eq. (2). We will ensure the code released after acceptance matches this implementation.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Scores are 3/4/4.The two weak accepts emphasize methodological soundness; the weak reject (R1, faculty) is driven by ambiguous exposition and incomplete ablations rather than disagreement with the core idea. The concerns are largely addressable, so the paper is invited for rebuttal. Authors should prioritize (a) clarifying the intermediate-layer routing formulation and the role of confidence vs. error in the routing module, (b) reporting multi-seed variance on the headline numbers, (c) discussing scalability to N>2 teachers and training-time memory footprint, and (d) reconciling the code-vs-paper discrepancy around the hard/easy region mechanism. | Reviewers viewed the paper favorably overall, highlighting Task-Performance Routing (TPR) as a simple, intuitive, and well-motivated multi-teacher distillation framework that exploits the complementary strengths of different medical foundation models through region-wise routing. Strengths included the parameter-free routing mechanism, hierarchical spatial adaptation across feature levels, strong empirical performance on multiple CT segmentation benchmarks, comparisons with modern foundation-model teachers, and comprehensive ablation studies validating key design choices. Initial concerns focused on reliance on ground-truth errors for routing during training, limited evaluation to two-teacher settings, unclear implementation details and presentation issues, modest performance gains in some settings without multi-seed variance analysis, training-memory overhead, and questions regarding scalability and robustness. These concerns led to one Weak Reject and two Weak Accept recommendations before rebuttal. Following the authors’ responses, reviewers agreed that the major methodological and presentation concerns had been sufficiently clarified, resulting in all reviewers supporting acceptance. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): After the rebuttal, all reviewers agreed that the paper should be accepted. The Area Chair supports this consensus and recommends acceptance. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): All reviewers agree to accept the paper. I do agree with R2 about the concerns about result robustness and more ablation results. However, this leads to a greay area in the final decision as I’m not sure whether this may requires additional experiments which against MICCAI’s rebuttal rules. Here I recommend a poster presentation of this work, not oral. The authors should also try to correspond to R2W5 with a few words (no need to be detailed as long as the improvements introduced in this paper are proved to be statistically significant).

title: TAVR-VLM: Risk-Conditioned Causal Grounding for Hallucination-Resistant Report Generation
reviewer_1_strengths: The authors address a clinically critical and under-explored task: trustworthy preoperative report generation for TAVR with reduced diagnostic hallucinations. They propose a novel and structurally interpretable R-CGA framework that enforces a strict top-down causal hierarchy from risk hypothesis to visual grounding to report generation. Comprehensive benchmarking, thorough ablation studies, and parameter sensitivity analysis are conducted on a large-scale multi-modal TAVR dataset, showing consistent and significant performance gains over strong baselines including state-of-the-art open-source and closed-source VLMs. The framework effectively suppresses unsupported clinical claims via explicit causal constraints, offering verifiable, anatomically grounded diagnostic reasoning for high-stakes surgical decision-making.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The reported high CIDEr score is potentially misleading and over-optimistic, as it is strongly inflated by the highly template-based TAVR report structure rather than genuine semantic and clinical superiority. 2.All experiments are limited to a single in-house dataset, and the method’s generalizability is not validated on public medical report generation datasets or external multi-center cohorts. 3.The definition and computation of the hallucination rate rely heavily on model-internal attention masks rather than independent human annotation, making it less objective and difficult to cross-validate. 4.The clinical translation potential is overclaimed. There is no evaluation on out-of-distribution or rare anatomical cases, and no expert user study to validate real-world clinical usability.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: Risk assessment and recommendation for TAVR pre-intervention planning carries significant clinical value. The motivation to align the decision-making reasoning process with cardiologists’ established TAVR workflow is well-grounded and demonstrates clear clinical utility.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The motivation behind this work is commendable; however, the central claim that “hallucination arises as a failure of the top-down causal link between global risk states and local anatomical evidence” requires stronger empirical or theoretical grounding. Given that this assertion serves as the primary design rationale for the proposed framework, the authors should provide more concrete supporting evidence to substantiate this claim before it can be fully accepted as a foundational premise. 2.The role and impact of the causal risk bottleneck warrants further clarification. As described in the paper, the risk score predicted in Stage 1 serves as the cornerstone of the global risk mask, risk-driven visual purification, and the final prediction. This makes the reliability of the risk estimator critical to the overall framework. The authors should provide a more thorough analysis of this component’s behaviour, in particular, what happens when the risk prediction is incorrect. A dedicated error analysis or robustness study examining the downstream effects of risk estimation failures would significantly strengthen the paper’s claims. 3.Several aspects of the methodology section remain insufficiently described. First, the distinctions between the discrete procedural risk levels ({l, m, h}) are not clearly defined. The authors should specify how these levels are operationalized and what criteria govern their boundaries. Second, the reconstruction loss L_rec appears undefined in the main text and should be formally introduced. Third, the process for selecting the subset of token indices corresponding to clinically salient entities when computing the Token-level Mask is unclear. Together, these gaps make the methodological section difficult to follow, and addressing them is essential for reproducibility. 4.The design of the risk estimation module raises two concerns. First, since the entire framework is trained from scratch, there is a risk of a chicken-and-egg problem: if the risk estimator is not yet well-trained in early stages, its errors may propagate and mislead the subsequent generation process, potentially causing compounding performance degradation. The authors should discuss how this instability is mitigated during training. Second, given the availability of numerous strong pretrained models for both CT and echocardiography feature encoding, the motivation for training the feature extractor from scratch is unclear. The authors should justify this choice and, ideally, compare it against fine-tuning pretrained encoders as a baseline. 5.Additional clarification is needed for parts of the experimental section. In the case study, Case A references a “mitral valve procedure” statement from the baseline VLM, but it is not made clear what specifically is problematic about this output. A brief explanation would make the qualitative comparison more informative. Additionally, the authors should indicate whether the proposed benchmark will be publicly released, as this is important for the community to verify and build upon the reported results.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: Clinical Importance: The application for TAVR planning addresses a highly critical and complex, high-stakes surgical domain, which is less explored compared to general radiology tasks. Intuitive Design: The “Risk -> Region -> Word” attention hierarchy is clinically well-motivated, aligning the model’s focus with relevant anatomical regions driven by global risk factors. Heterogeneous Multimodal Integration: The paper makes a solid engineering effort in fusing diverse data types (3D visual, temporal ultrasound clips, and tabular data), which is necessary for comprehensive surgical pathway assessments.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Methodological Comparison Fairness: A primary concern is the disparity between the proposed model and its baseline counterparts. TAVR-VLM utilizes a rich set of multimodal inputs (3D CT, Echo, and Tabular data), whereas several compared baselines are generic 2D VLMs or text generators that were not originally designed for such high-dimensional localized input. It is difficult to determine whether the reported performance margin stems from the inherent innovation of the R-CGA module or simply from the significant advantage of having richer input modalities. Data Transparency: The study relies entirely on a private “M3 TAVR” dataset. The manuscript provides insufficient detail regarding the cohort’s provenance, inclusion criteria, and the specific multi-reader annotation protocols used for establishing ground-truth spatial bounding boxes. Lack of External Validation: Given the high-risk nature of TAVR surgical planning, the complete lack of external or cross-institutional validation makes the claims regarding the model’s “clinical viability” premature. Vague Metric Definitions: Certain safety-critical metrics, such as the “Hallucination Rate,” are described vaguely without clear algorithmic definitions of how a generated entity is adjudicated as a hallucination relative to the three input modalities.
reviewer_3_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We sincerely thank the Area Chairs and Reviewers for recognizing TAVR-VLM’s clinical importance, intuitive design, and strong performance. We address the primary concerns below. 1.Baseline Fairness and Multimodal Inputs (AC, R3) We respectfully clarify that our experimental design already accounts for this. To maintain domain fairness, we explicitly extracted standardized 2D slices for the 2D-centric baselines. More importantly, the superiority of TAVR-VLM stems from the R-CGA module, not just input dimensionality. We empirically prove this in our ablation study (Table 2): when we use the exact same multimodal inputs but remove the causal visual purification (w/o V_act), the hallucination rate spikes from 8.2% to 18.4%. This isolates the architectural contribution, confirming the performance gap is not an artifact of richer data inputs. 2.Empirical Evidence for Causal Link & Objective Validation (AC, R1, R2, R3) Empirical Evidence: The causal link is empirically substantiated in Table 2 and Figure 2a. When the top-down alignment is severed by disabling the causal consistency loss (lambda_causal=0), spatial grounding precision (mIoU) drops to 0.350 and the hallucination rate doubles to 16.1%. This explicitly proves that enforcing the global risk bottleneck prevents the model from exploiting spurious correlations. Objective Validation: Our hallucination and spatial anchoring metrics do not rely solely on internal masks. As detailed in Section 3.1, we evaluate spatial grounding precision (mIoU) against independent, expert-annotated region-of-interests (ROIs) obtained for a subset of 200 patients in the test set. This ensures an objective, human-validated assessment of the model’s anatomical anchoring. 3.Methodological Gaps and Training Stability (AC, R2) Definitions: Due to space constraints, some formalisms were condensed. The discrete risk levels (l, m, h) are operationalized based on standard STS scores and VARC-3 guidelines. L_rec is a standard cross-entropy loss applied to the structured recommendation outputs. Training Stability: R2 correctly notes the risk of early-stage errors propagating. We mitigated this precisely through the Stop-Gradient operator in the causal consistency loss. This asymmetric constraint prevents degenerate solutions where the global mask diffuses to minimize loss. Our ablation confirms that standard backpropagation without Stop-Gradient degrades performance. 4.Dataset Generalizability and Clinical Claims (AC, R1, R3) We agree with R1 that claims of “clinical translation” should be tempered without out-of-distribution external validation; we will revise the manuscript to frame TAVR-VLM as a robust algorithmic proof-of-concept. However, M3TAVR is the largest structurally annotated cohort of its kind (1,482 patients). To ensure internal validity and prevent data leakage, we enforced a strict patient-level stratified split (70/10/20). Because comprehensive 3D+Temporal+Tabular TAVR datasets do not publicly exist, we rely on this rigorous internal validation. We commit to clarifying our cohort inclusion criteria and open-sourcing our core codebase to facilitate community reproducibility. We sincerely appreciate the committee’s rigorous feedback. By clarifying our domain-fair baselines, emphasizing the objective ROI validation, and empirically substantiating the causal link, we hope to have resolved the primary concerns. We believe TAVR-VLM represents a significant, fundamentally interpretable step forward for surgical AI, and we hope these clarifications merit acceptance at MICCAI.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): While reviewers agreed that the paper addresses a clinically critical and under-explored task with a well-motivated, interpretable framework aligned with cardiologists’ workflow, they also raised serious concerns about the paper’s evaluation rigor, methodological clarity, and generalizability: First, experiments are limited to a single private dataset without external or cross-institutional validation, and metric definitions lack objectivity and clarity. Second, methodological comparisons are unfair, as baselines lack the rich multimodal inputs used by the proposed model. Third, key methodological aspects are insufficiently described or justified, including undefined risk levels, unclear training stability for the risk estimator, and unsubstantiated claims about the causal link underlying hallucinations. Since the reviews are mixed, we would like to invite the authors to provide a rebuttal. In addition to clarify other concerns, please try to address the following points during rebuttal: if possible, validate the model’s generalizability with external/multi-center data or public datasets; ensure fair baseline comparisons by adapting baselines to use the same multimodal inputs; clarify methodological gaps and justify key choices; and provide empirical/theoretical evidence for the causal link between risk states and hallucinations, along with objective validation of the hallucination rate. | This is a borderline paper with mixed reviews. Reviewers agreed that the work addresses a clinically critical and underexplored task in TAVR preoperative planning and proposes a structurally interpretable R-CGA framework that aligns well with cardiologists’ workflows. However, they also raised serious concerns about the paper’s soundness and significance: first, the reported metrics such as CIDEr may be inflated due to the template-based nature of TAVR reports, and the definition of hallucination relies heavily on internal model signals rather than independent clinical validation; second, the experimental validation is limited to a single private dataset, with insufficient transparency regarding cohort selection, annotation protocols, and no external or multi-center validation; third, key methodological details remain unclear, including the handling of incorrect risk predictions, the selection of clinically salient tokens, and the fairness of comparisons given the model’s access to richer multimodal inputs than baselines. The rebuttal addressed some concerns, but did not resolved all. After careful deliberation, I lean a bit towards accepting this manuscripts due to its potential clinical values. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): Despite authors’ efforts to address the concerns of all three reviewers, some still remained unaddressed. As Reviewer 2 specifies, when the risk prediction is incorrect, it is still unclear how the system responds. On the other hand, given lack of external validation, the hallucination evaluation lacks objectivity. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Although one reviewer maintained concerns regarding incomplete clarification of risk-prediction failure cases, token-level mask construction, and experimental details, the other reviewers provided very positive assessments and found the rebuttal substantially strengthened the paper. In particular, the authors added convincing ablation evidence isolating the contribution of the proposed module, clarified the use of human expert ground truth for spatial evaluation, agreed to moderate clinical claims, and committed to code release. Given the strong post-rebuttal support from two reviewers and the paper’s value as a useful proof-of-concept, I recommend acceptance, while encouraging the authors to address the remaining clarity issues in the final version.

title: TCCT: Trajectory-Conditioned CBCT Reconstruction for Sinusoidal Non-circular Orbits with a Fourier Neural Operator
reviewer_1_strengths: The central design choice is the right one: redundancy weighting is exactly the trajectory-dependent piece of SV-FBP, and the rest of the pipeline can stay classical. Factoring the problem this way, by keeping the known operator and learning only the component that is genuinely hard to specify analytically, is what makes this paper interesting. Conditioning on trajectory parameters rather than retraining per orbit is a practically useful direction for robotic CBCT. Evaluation on clinically derived test anatomy is a meaningful step up from phantom-only studies. The runtime advantage over ART and the competitive numbers against trajectory-specific differentiable SV-FBP give the method a clear practical argument.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The main weakness is the gap between the title and what is actually shown. Non-circular orbits suggests broad trajectory generalization, but the experiments cover a single sinusoidal family, and the unseen-frequency robustness study samples within the training range. This is interpolation rather than out-of-distribution generalization, and the paper should say so plainly. Training uses only 24 synthetic phantoms with 6 for validation, which is small enough to raise some concern about robustness. Test projections are simulated from clinical CT volumes, so measured robotic CBCT performance is not demonstrated. The Section 3.3 operating threshold is selected on the test set, which makes the sensitivity/specificity point much weaker than the AUC result. The main comparisons are to trajectory-specific differentiable SV-FBP and ART(50), and prior geometry-conditioned reconstruction work is not engaged with as clearly as it could be.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: Practical Problem Definition: Addressing the trajectory variability in robotic CBCT is a practical problem with clinical and technical value. Efficient Hybrid Architecture: The approach of combining an established mathematical foundation (SV-FBP) with an AI module (operator-learning) specifically for dynamic weight calculation is structurally sound. It ensures mathematical stability while leveraging deep learning for complex, variant components. GT-Free Training: Successfully training the model using only a reconstruction-driven objective on simulated data, without requiring explicit ground-truth for redundancy weights, is a commendable achievement.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Lack of Practical Effectiveness (Core reason for rejection): The paper highlights robustness across various sinusoidal trajectories (frequencies 1 through 9) as its main contribution. However, according to Table 1, under highly variable trajectory conditions (frequencies 7, 8, and 9), the proposed method shows a degradation in SSIM compared to existing baseline methods, even if the PSNR is slightly improved over SV-FBP. Since SSIM is a critical metric for evaluating structural image quality, this drop severely undermines the claim that explicitly analyzing and learning trajectory features provides a robust advantage over traditional SV-FBP in complex environments. Unsubstantiated Claims on Efficiency and Generalization: The authors claim that “Unlike differentiable SV-FBP, which requires trajectory-specific training, TCCT generalizes across trajectories without retraining, providing greater flexibility in practical applications.” However, the manuscript lacks concrete quantitative evidence to substantiate these advantages. Lack of Computational Metrics: There is no comparative analysis of computational efficiency, such as training time, inference time, or resource utilization, to demonstrate exactly how much more efficient TCCT is compared to the trajectory-specific SV-FBP baseline. Insufficient Proof of Domain Generalization: The paper does not adequately evaluate the completely novel trajectory domains. Without showing the actual performance drop or robustness when confronted with a different type of trajectory without retraining, the claimed superiority and practical flexibility of the proposed methodology remain unproven and difficult to understand. Questionable Necessity Compared to Modern 3D Reconstruction Techniques: The framework explicitly designs a module to learn trajectory features. However, in scenarios where camera intrinsic and extrinsic parameters are already known, recent methodologies like 3D Gaussian Splatting (GS) can directly utilize these geometric descriptors for highly accurate 3D reconstruction. Without a comparative analysis against these parameter-based rendering approaches, the fundamental necessity of the proposed trajectory-learning module remains questionable. Logical Disconnect in the Abstract: The flow of the abstract is somewhat disjointed. Right after proposing the trajectory-conditioned framework, it abruptly introduces what the Fourier Neural Operator learns. Without reading the main text, the relationship between the overarching TC-SNO framework and the specific Fourier Neural Operator is unclear, which hampers readability. Omission of Critical Experimental Details: Although the task may not strictly be a sparse-view CBCT reconstruction, reconstructing a CBCT volume from projection images inherently depends on the number of views. The paper fails to clearly state how many projection images were used in the experiments, which limits the reproducibility and objective assessment of the proposed method’s performance. Insufficient Baselines: To comprehensively prove the superiority of the proposed method, the experiments must include comparisons not only with traditional FBP-based methods but also with state-of-the-art view-synthesis or GS-based methods that utilize camera parameters (e.g., R2-GS [1], DIF-GS [2]). [1] R. Zha, et al, “R^2-Gaussian: Rectifying Radiative Gaussian Splatting for Tomographic Reconstruction”, NeurIPS, 2024.[2] Y. Lin, et al, “Learning 3D Gaussians for Extremely Sparse-View Cone-Beam CT Reconstruction”, MICCAI, 2025.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: I find this work to be a meaningful methodological extension of prior work. The per-trajectory retraining requirement of DRACO is a genuine practical bottleneck in robotic CBCT, where acquisition trajectories may vary across procedures. Framing redundancy-weight estimation as a trajectory-conditioned operator-learning problem is therefore a natural and well-motivated extension. A particularly non-trivial aspect is that the reconstruction-driven training paradigm established in DRACO remains effective in this setting, even when the redundancy weights are dynamically predicted by TC-SNO rather than optimized as fixed trajectory-specific parameters. I also find the architectural choice to be well motivated. The use of a Fourier Neural Operator is well motivated by the paper’s formulation of the trajectory-to-weight mapping as a function-to-function problem. For the sinusoidal trajectory family considered here, where the acquisition geometry evolves smoothly and periodically, the spectral bias of FNO is a plausible and well-justified inductive bias.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The main weakness is that the scope of the title, abstract, and several claims in the main text exceeds the actual experimental evidence. The paper is framed as addressing general non-circular trajectory CBCT reconstruction, yet all experiments are conducted within a sinusoidal trajectory family parameterized by frequency. The discussion itself acknowledges that the reported results represent interpolation within the training range rather than out-of-distribution generalization, and explicitly leaves more complex trajectories and real-world validation to future work. In this sense, the current framing appears broader than what is directly supported by the experiments. This point is especially important because the direct predecessor of this work, DRACO, evaluated a wider range of orbit types, including circular, sinusoidal, circle-plus-arc, random nearest-neighbor, and real projection data from a stochastic multi-tilt circular orbit. Therefore, I believe the paper would be substantially strengthened by narrowing its framing toward trajectory-conditioned generalization within a sinusoidal orbit family. A second weakness is that the ablation study is not described clearly enough to fully support the paper’s architectural conclusions. In Table 2, the “SV-FBP baseline” is described as being trained across trajectories and converging to a trajectory-agnostic compromise solution, but the manuscript does not specify its exact configuration in enough detail. As a result, it is difficult to determine precisely how trajectories are handled in this baseline, whether any explicit trajectory conditioning is used, and to what extent the observed gain should be attributed to trajectory conditioning itself versus the specific Fourier-based implementation adopted in TC-SNO. Clarifying this point would make the ablation more interpretable and strengthen the paper’s central methodological claim. Beyond the two main weakness discussed above, there is also a minor point that would benefit from clarification. The abstract states that the proposed framework enables future end-to-end “dual-domain optimization” for noise suppression, artifact reduction, and trajectory optimization, yet this term is neither defined nor revisited in the main text. It would therefore be helpful if the authors clarified what the two domains refer to in this context and how this claim connects to the current TCCT framework.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank all reviewers for their constructive feedback. TCCT is a trajectory-conditioned CBCT reconstruction framework for sinusoidal non-circular trajectories. Our main contributions are: (1) one model for a continuously varying sinusoidal orbit family (R1-3); (2) a known-operator design that keeps SV-FBP fixed and learns only redundancy weights, preserving FBP-like efficiency (R1-3); and (3) reconstruction-driven training without ground-truth weights (R2), evaluated on clinical CT-derived simulated CBCT data (R1). Scope beyond the evidence (R1,R3): We agree that the wording should better match the evidence. We’ll narrow the claims to sinusoidal non-circular CBCT orbits. The unseen-frequency study shows interpolation within the training frequency range, not OOD generalization to arbitrary trajectories, as stated in Sec.5.However, to our knowledge, no prior FBP-like pipeline handles variable trajectories without per-orbit retraining, a key bottleneck for applying fast iteration-free inversion formulas in robotic CT. Training phantoms and clinical simulation (R1): The 24 phantoms are not fixed cases: each uses randomly sampled sinusoidal trajectories. Since TCCT learns geometry-to-weight mapping rather than an anatomy prior, the phantoms supervise trajectory-dependent redundancy learning. Real robotic CBCT data were not used: Sec.3 uses clinical CT volumes to simulate CBCT projections under Artis zeego geometry. This evaluates phantom-to-anatomy transfer under controlled simulation. To our knowledge, no public dataset provides real robotic CBCT projections with accurate non-circular trajectory metadata matching our setting. Real validation remains future work. SSIM degradation at high-frequency trajectories (R2): We acknowledge the lower SSIM for some high-frequency orbits. For frequencies 7-9, however, the drop is modest, averaging 0.0088 SSIM, i.e., about 1.0% relative to trajectory-specific SV-FBP. Tab.1 compares one TCCT model against separately trained per-orbit SV-FBP models, a strong per-orbit reference. Our claim is competitive quality without per-orbit retraining, not per-orbit optimality. We’ll state this trade-off more explicitly. Efficiency and computational details (R1,R2): Sec.3 states training used an A40 GPU. We’ll further specify that trajectory-specific SV-FBP requires about 21h per orbit, whereas TCCT trains once for the full sinusoidal family in about 24h, thus Tab.1 needs 9 SV-FBP trainings versus one TCCT training. For inference, Sec.3.2 reports about 2s/volume for TCCT versus 30s/volume for ART(50), both on an RTX 4080S GPU. TCCT is not faster than trajectory-specific SV-FBP per inference. Its efficiency comes from avoiding per-trajectory retraining, which is the intended practical advantage for variable orbits. Tab.2 SV-FBP configuration and GS comparison (R2,R3): We’ll clarify that Tab.2 uses the non-conditioned SV-FBP from Sec.2.2: it receives no trajectory parameters G and learns shared weights across sinusoidal trajectories. We’ll remove “baseline” to avoid confusion with the per-orbit SV-FBP models in Tab.1.TCCT conditions only the SV-FBP redundancy-weight operator while keeping the reconstruction analytic, making trajectory-specific SV-FBP the closest baseline. NeRF/GS methods mainly target sparse-view reconstruction with object-specific/test-time optimization. At our 200-view scale, their objective and computational setting are not comparable. Other experimental and terminology clarifications (R1–R3): Sec.3 already specifies 200 projections. We’ll make this more visible. As stated, code will be released upon acceptance, including phantom generation, trajectory sampling and the simulation pipeline. We’ll describe them more explicitly. We’ll clarify the abstract and “dual-domain optimization” in relation to TCCT. R1’s Sec.3.3 threshold comment may refer to another manuscript: our paper reports only MSE/PSNR/SSIM/Params ablations, with no AUC/sensitivity/specificity, or test-set-selected threshold.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper presents an interesting and technically sound trajectory-conditioned reconstruction framework that addresses a practical limitation of prior SV-FBP-based methods. Reviewers generally appreciate the hybrid known-operator design and the potential to avoid trajectory-specific retraining. However, several important concerns remain, particularly regarding the scope of generalization claims (currently limited to interpolation within a sinusoidal trajectory family), limited experimental validation (synthetic training and simulated projections), insufficient comparison with modern baselines, and some unclear or potentially overstated claims. Additional clarifications on experimental setup, efficiency, and evaluation methodology are also requested. Given these points, the authors are invited to provide a rebuttal addressing the reviewers’ concerns and clarifying the contributions and limitations of the work. | The authors have addressed the reviewer’s comments. Please update those correspondingly in your camera-ready version. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The authors have largely clarified the previously unclear points in their rebuttal, and the reviewers appear satisfied with the responses, with all agreeing on acceptance. The AC therefore recommends acceptance. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The authors clarified the concerns in the rebuttal.

title: TCFD-Net: Temporal-Calibrated Feature Disentanglement Network for Dual-Timepoint CT-Based Immunotherapy Response Prediction in Advanced Non-small Cell Lung Cancer
reviewer_1_strengths: Strengths include: (1) The need to better encode temporal features, particularly when assessing treatment response, is well-motivated, and the general approach seems promising. (2) The inclusion of over 1,100 patients with advanced lung cancer who received immunotherapy across two independent centers. (3) t-SNE visualization provides compelling qualitative support that the proposed approach can disentangle treatment-induced dynamic and static information.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The evaluation was performed on a single split during internal validation and an external validation set. The lack of resampling means that only point estimates are given in Tables 1-3.It is unclear how reliable these estimates are without confidence intervals. The manuscript lacks an explicit discussion of the limitations.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: Novelty: The core idea of explicitly disentangling static and dynamic features is a clever and important contribution to the field. Beyond building predictive models, this approach has immense potential to elucidate biological underpinnings of time-invariant and treatment specific changes through multi-omic correlative analyses (eg. between time varying features and pathomic/genomic measurements). Strong Experimental Results: The performance improvements (AUC and accuracy) over existing methods are substantial and consistent across both internal and external datasets. This highlights the value of the proposed approach. Interpretability: The visualization of feature distributions using t-SNE demonstrates a clear separation of invariant and variant features providing insight into how the network is operating and validating the disentanglement process.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Loss Function Weighting: The paper mentions using loss function weights (λ values) during training but doesn’t elaborate on how these weights were determined. This is a critical aspect of training and the lack of detail makes it difficult to reproduce the exact results or provide an idea of contribution of individual losses. Limited details on implementation: While the paper describes the general architecture, more details on the specific implementation of the 3D encoders, Swin Transformers, and Time-Gating Mechanism (units in the MLP) would be helpful for reproducibility. Clarity on time between CT scans: Typically, immediate post-treatment CTs are acquired every 6-9 weeks post-IO initiation. It would be helpful to include the median and range of time between pre and post-treatment CT scans in the dataset to understand the variance in scan intervals. Potential for overfitting: While demonstrating good external validation, the complexity and number of loss functions used in training increase the risk of overfitting, particularly since the training set was from a single institution and had modest size (534 patients). Was any data augmentation applied? Histology: Please use specific terminologies for if the patients had advanced “small cell” or “non-small cell” lung cancer, or whether the dataset included both histologies. Typo: Effectiveness and Interpretability of TIVDM are presented in Table 2, the text mentions table 1.
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: (1) Significant improvement in external testing performance; (2) Comprehensive method design with closed-loop logical chain.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: (1) Figure 1 lacks aesthetic appeal and clarity in presentation; (2) The formulas and variables in the text fail to specify variable dimensions and domains, hindering formula comprehension; (3) The paper only reports AUC and ACC, which are insufficient for medical prediction tasks. Additional metrics such as SEN, SPE, 95% CI, and Delong test should be included; (4) Reference errors exist, e.g.: “Treatment responses were categorized per RECIST 1.1 criteria, grouping Complete Response (CR) and Partial Response (PR) as Responders, while Stable Disease (SD) and Progressive Disease (PD) were classified as Non-responders [19].” Reference [19] does not adhere to RECIST 1.1 criteria. (5) The clinical modeling is insufficient, lacking detailed definitions of key data parameters. For example: Is the CT input the entire thoracic volume, tumor patches, or ROI crops? Does the tumor require manual segmentation or automatic detection? How should patients with multiple lesions be handled? These issues are not clearly addressed.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank all reviewers’ valuable comments. Here are our responses: Q1 for Meta&R1&3: Lacks SEN, SPE, 95%CI, and Delong test Tables1–3 now report SEN, SPE, 95%CI (1000 bootstrap iteration) for all models. Updated metrics for our model (AUC/ACC/SEN/SPE, with 95%CIs) are as follows. Internal testing: 0.848(0.788–0.904)/0.752(0.680–0.817)/0.742(0.638–0.846)/0.759(0.671–0.849), significantly outperforming TRL and HARM3 (both p<0.01, DeLong test). External testing: 0.828(0.787–0.868)/0.754(0.708–0.797)/0.780(0.719–0.843)/0.735(0.671–0.797), significantly outperforming LC-NICER, M2Fusion, TRL, and HARM3 (all p<0.01, DeLong test). Q2 for R1: Lacks the discussion of limitations Limitations on multimodal integration, lack of prospective validation, and generalizability to other tumor types have been added to the final version. Q3 for Meta&R1: Mechanisms of the TIVDM is unclear Disentanglement in the parallel 3D encoders is driven by asymmetric supervision. Both branches are concatenated and trained via BCE loss to extract response-relevant features. Within this subspace, the upper branch is constrained by a cross-time MSE consistency loss and a batch distance loss to learn time-invariant, response-relevant features while preventing collapse. A subspace orthogonality loss forces the lower branch to capture the response-relevant time-variant signals. Q4 for Meta&R2: Loss function weighting is unclear The weighting coefficients λ1/λ2/λ3/λ4 were determined via grid search to maximize the validation set AUC, yielding 0.4/0.2/0.2/0.2.Q5 for Meta&R2: Limits details of 3D encoders and TGM The 3D encoders are implemented as 3D Swin Transformers, adapted from the 2D Swin by upgrading all spatial operators to their 3D counterparts. The architecture uses an initial embedding dimension of 16 and a depth configuration of [2,2,2,2] (8 Swin Transformer blocks in total) for input volumes of 128×128×128.The TGM is a two-layer MLP with hidden layer W1∈ℝ^(128×1)(128 units) and output layer W2∈ℝ^(256×128) (256 units), matched to the feature channel dimension. Q6 for Meta&R2: Clarity on time between CT scans The median pre- and post-treatment CT intervals at the two centers were 8.4 weeks (range 4.6–29.6) and 8.0 weeks (range 4.6–24.0), aligning with the 6–9 week window typically used for IO response assessment, with deviations reflecting real-world scheduling variability. Q7 for R2: Potential for overfitting and data augmentation Multiple strategies to mitigate overfitting was applied. (i) Data augmentation via TorchIO(random flipping, random Gaussian noise); (ii) Regularization: encoder dropout, weight decay through AdamW, and LR decay during training. Q8 for Meta&R2: Patient histology Our dataset comprises exclusively patients with non-small cell lung cancer, as now clarified in the final version. Q9 for R2: Typo We have made the corrections. Q10 for R3: Figure 1 lacks aesthetic appeal and clarity Figure 1 has been redesigned in the revised manuscript to improve clarity and visual quality, including clearer module labels, more structured model feature flow, simplified data-flow arrows. Q11 for R3: The formulas and variables fail to specify variable dimensions The revised manuscript explicitly specifies dimensions and domains of all key variables and feature representations.
