title: TeDyS: Temporal Dynamics with Spatial Context for Longitudinal Progression Prediction
reviewer_1_strengths: 1) Modeling variations in follow-up in longitudinal imaging datasets is clinically relevant. Modeling in terms of long term and short term residuals with respect to follow-up time from baseline is interesting. 2) The introduction is very well written providing context for including temporal variations in longitudinal imaging based disease progression modelling. 3) Evaluating on 2 different case studies is a strength.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1) The modeling seems similar to a typical LSTM architecture which has been studied quite a bit (example PMID: 38341100). While the authors compare TeDys to LSTM, they haven’t really mentioned LSTM anywhere in the introduction or discussion. It is not very clear how this is unique and different compared to existing methods. 2) Feature encoders are directly used from pre-trained segmentation models. Can the authors compare with other foundation models such as MedSAM or SAMMed3D? Is there any rationale for using nnUnet? 3) Mean pooling of short and long term seems too simplistic. How are the long term and short term dynamics interacting with each other? 4) It is unclear what is the attention based on? Do the authors look at disease specific regions of interest form the scans to track changes? Perhaps more detail about the regions of interest or some qualitative visualizations would have helped understand the disease progression better.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The main novelty is the explicit treatment of long- and short-term dynamics in longitudinal prediction tasks using appropriate techniques. This is achieved by explicitly splitting the long- and short-term dynamics into two different mechanisms: entropic optimal transport for the short-term and a neural ODE block for the long-term dynamics.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The proposed method demonstrates improvements on the private dataset but yields performance comparable to existing baselines on the public dataset. Given the large standard deviations reported, it is unclear if the observed improvements are statistically significant or robust across different cohorts. It is unclear if the 5-fold cross-validation was stratified by progression intervals (the target labels). Given the small sample size and high variance in metrics, a lack of rigorous stratification raises concerns about potential data leakage or spurious findings. The utility of the public dataset for evaluating longitudinal progression is questionable, as most subjects have only two visits. Furthermore, with only 14 conversion cases (~9%), a 5-fold split leaves very few converter samples per fold. There is a risk that the model is performing static disease classification rather than capturing true prognostic trajectories. If this is intended, it should be mentioned as a limitation. The ablation studies suggest that the decomposed STD mechanism does not substantially improve performance over the LTD block. This calls into question the practical necessity of the added architectural complexity.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The paper addresses a clinically important and realistic problem of longitudinal progression prediction under irregular follow-up, with clear relevance to patient management and treatment planning. 2.The proposed framework introduces an explicit and well-motivated decomposition of temporal dynamics into short-term and long-term components, providing a more structured alternative to standard sequence modeling approaches. 3.Experimental validation is solid, including evaluation across two datasets and imaging modalities, with consistent improvements over longitudinal baselines and supporting ablation studies.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.While the overall framework is coherent, many individual components (e.g., query-based modeling, Neural ODEs, optimal transport alignment) build on existing techniques. The contribution is primarily an integration rather than a fundamentally new modeling paradigm. 2.Although ablations are included, the framework remains relatively complex, and further analysis isolating individual components would improve interpretability. 3.The in-house dataset is relatively small, and although a public dataset is included, validation across additional cohorts or institutions would strengthen claims of generalizability.
reviewer_3_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We sincerely thank the reviewers and meta-reviewer for their thoughtful feedback. We address the main concerns below. [R2, R4W3: Dataset and statistical reliability] All experiments used patient-level 5-fold CV, with all longitudinal visits from the same subject kept within the same fold, preventing scan-level leakage. Fold construction considered progression-interval/time-to-progression information to preserve progression-related heterogeneity across folds. We further audited the binary conversion/progression distribution and confirmed that every fold contained positive cases. We will report fold-wise label counts and converter-level confusion matrices in the revision. OASIS2 was included to evaluate whether the trend generalizes to public brain MRI, while its limited converters/visits may contribute to fold-wise variance. Within this evaluation, conversion cases were represented across folds, and TeDyS achieved approximately 71% accuracy on these cases. In the larger ADNI MRI cohort, TeDyS achieved the best numerical performance, improving accuracy (0.7887→0.8098) and AUC (0.8501→0.8606) over the strongest baseline, while better identifying positive cases in the binary task (0.6379→0.7586; McNemar’s mid-p p=0.0287; bootstrap p=0.0274). We will clarify the OASIS2 limitation and discuss larger-cohort validation. [R1W1, R4W1: Difference from LSTM and novelty] Unlike LSTM variants that implicitly accumulate temporal evidence in recurrent hidden and cell states, h_t and c_t, TeDyS explicitly constructs two progression signals before query updating: Delta_STD_t = X_t minus X_tilde_(t-1 to t) for aligned adjacent-visit change, and Delta_LTD_t = X_t minus X_hat_(t given 1) for baseline-referenced long-term deviation. These residual dynamics directly condition the temporal query updates, while the TeDyS gate adaptively balances STD and LTD evidence at each visit. Thus, TeDyS is not a generic recurrent memory model or a simple combination of existing modules, but a progression-specific temporal decomposition framework that separates, aligns, and integrates complementary short- and long-term evidence for longitudinal prediction. [R1W3, R2W4, R2C1C2, R4W2: Necessity of STD/LTD complexity] We agree that LTD dominates overall AUC, while STD targets short sequences where long-term trajectories are weak. In-house, STD outperformed LTD for two-timepoint cases (AUC 0.5872 vs. 0.5370), whereas LTD was stronger for >=3 visits (0.8001 vs. 0.5389), supporting their complementary roles across sequence lengths. Although the AUC gain from adding STD is modest, the full model improves Acc/Recall/F1 over LTD-only, suggesting improved progression sensitivity and short-sequence robustness. Entropic OT is used to align slot tokens across visits before computing STD residuals, since slot ordering is not temporally fixed. Mean pooling only summarizes STD/LTD evidence for the gate, while token-level residuals are fused before query update. The added complexity is modest: STD-only, LTD-only, and STD+LTD use 4.29M, 4.66M, and 5.38M parameters, respectively. We will also add brief qualitative progression visualizations showing that the temporal attention highlights regions with longitudinal changes. [R1W4: Encoder selection] We selected nnUNet as a practical medical-image backbone because its segmentation-oriented features provide organ/lesion-aware spatial representations relevant to disease progression, with manageable computational cost. TeDyS is not restricted to nnUNet, as the same temporal modeling pipeline can be applied to MedSAM, SAMMed3D, or other foundation encoders. Overall, TeDyS models short-term visit-to-visit changes and long-term baseline-anchored trends as complementary temporal evidence for irregular longitudinal imaging. The in-house CT, public MRI, and larger-cohort results support TeDyS as a structured alternative to implicit recurrent temporal aggregation across different modalities, anatomies, and disease settings.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): The paper presents an approach to model longitudinal disease progression by explicitly decomposing temporal dynamics into short-term and long-term components. While the use of Neural ODEs is technically sound, the authors must address significant concerns regarding the method’s unique contribution compared to standard LSTM architectures. Reviewers noted a critical lack of detail concerning the absence of clear stratification in the cross-validation process and the potential for data leakage given the small N. Additionally, the modest performance gains on public datasets, coupled with high standard deviations, raise questions about the statistical significance of the findings. The authors should also justify the necessity of the added architectural complexity, as current ablation studies suggest the short-term dynamics module may not substantially improve performance. Finally (probably not super critical), providing a clear rationale for the chosen feature encoders and qualitative visualizations of the disease-specific regions of interest would greatly strengthen the paper. | Concerns about methodological rationale and advantages over LSTM-based methods are not adequately addressed post-rebuttal. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): While there are some reservations on the novelty, the framework is coherent and the method was evaluated on 2 different case studies, which were highlighted as strong points. Therefore the paper is leaning towards accept. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper presents an interesting methodology for a critical problem relevant to the MICCAI community. Even though the two datasets are relatively small, the experimental setup is well-designed with adequate baselines and clear improvements.

title: Temporal Phase-Difference Guided Spatiotemporal Learning for DSA Vessel Segmentation
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The core motivation is reasonable from both clinical and technical perspectives. The paper correctly points out that, in DSA, vessel visibility is largely driven by the temporal propagation of the contrast agent, while background tissues and bony structures usually remain relatively stable after subtraction. Based on this observation, introducing an explicit phase-difference prior is a domain-motivated design choice rather than a simple generic architectural modification. 2.The overall architecture is clearly organized. The authors decouple temporal dynamics modeling from spatial prior guidance: temporal features are extracted by the TFE blocks and pooled into 2D representations, while MinIP and FPD-MaxIP are introduced as static and dynamic priors, respectively, and fused at later stages. This decoupled design makes the framework more modular and also facilitates analysis of the contribution of each component. 3.The quantitative results are competitive. According to the reported results, the proposed method outperforms the listed baselines on both DIAS and DSCA, achieving the best performance across metrics such as DSC, IoU, AUC, and clDice, while maintaining a moderate model size and computational cost in terms of parameters and FLOPs.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The experimental results are not sufficient to support the claim of “cross-dataset generalization. ” The introduction and contribution statements explicitly mention improved “cross-dataset generalization. ” However, from the experimental section, the authors only conduct standard in-domain training and testing on DIAS and DSCA separately. A truly cross-dataset setup is missing. For example, the authors should train on DIAS and test on DSCA (and ideally vice versa) to properly support this claim. 2.The fairness of the baseline comparison remains insufficiently clarified. The paper does not clearly state whether all baseline methods were retrained under the same preprocessing pipeline, patch size, and data split settings. 3.The discussion of failure cases and clinical applicability is limited. The paper emphasizes improved preservation of thin distal vessels and better background suppression, but it does not include a dedicated analysis of failure cases. For example, under what conditions does FPD-MaxIP fail? Could it amplify noise, motion artifacts, venous contamination, or abnormal contrast propagation patterns? Since this prior relies on a fixed early-to-late phase difference, its robustness to irregular temporal dynamics and variation in acquisition protocols should be discussed more explicitly. For instance, in clinical practice, patients may differ substantially in blood flow velocity, heart rate, and contrast injection rate, meaning that the arrival and washout phases of the contrast agent are not fixed. 4.Typos and formatting issues. a) In the last paragraph of the Introduction, there appears to be hidden Chinese text in the sentence around “We develop … sting methods. ” b) The caption of Fig. 2 contains two items labeled (d).
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.Temporal modeling is crucial for analyzing sequential medical images. This paper introduces the SSM block to capture temporal variations across consecutive frames, tailored specifically for vessel segmentation. And the corresponding experimental results effectively demonstrate its utility. 2.The proposed forward phase-difference prior looks novel. Visual comparisons in Fig. 1 highlight that the FPD-MaxIP provides distinct and complementary information compared to the traditional MinIP prior, reinforcing the segmentation process through improved contrast-induced feature representation. 3.The authors perform extensive experiments, including comparisons with multiple approaches and ablation studies, validating the proposed model design and highlight its advantages.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Method: 1.TFE block: Why is there a reshape operation in every layer of the TFE block (as shown in Fig. 2(a))? The TFE module integrates both SSM-based temporal modeling and temporal attention mechanisms. What are the distinct purposes of these two steps, and why are both necessary? 2.FPD-MaxIP: Does the simultaneous use of MinIP and MaxIP-based difference priors risk introducing conflicting features for the model to learn? When computing the forward phase-difference prior, why is T/2 chosen to distinguish between the early stage and the late stage? Would it be possible to adopt a more adaptive approach to select this parameter? Will using a difference-based method to compute features potentially make the features more sensitive to respiratory motion? Experiments: 1.Considering temporal attention is integrated in the TFE module, is it possible to visualize the attention maps to provide interpretability for the temporal modeling process? 2.Based on table. 1, TemSAM is trained on a subset of the DIAS dataset and achieves strong generalization ability on the DSCA dataset, while the author’s method requires training and testing on the same data distribution within the DSCA dataset, the experimental results show that TemSAM and the author’s method has different advantages across various metrics on both datasets. Can the authors provide a more detailed discussion on the key advantages of the proposed method compared to SAM-based methods. Does the proposed method also exhibit generalization ability?
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The conceptual design of FPD-MaxIP is highly novel. The experimental evaluation is comprehensive and thoroughly validates the proposed method.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.Since FPD-MaxIP is explicitly designed to suppress persistent tissue and bony artifacts, the evaluation metric “Precision” should be introduced in the experiments to better reflect the model’s ability to reduce false positives. 2.The calculation of the AUC metric needs to be double-checked for potential errors. In the original papers of VSS-Net and TemSAM, the reported AUC scores for almost all compared methods are > 0.97.However, in Table 1 of this manuscript, the AUC values for the compared methods are surprisingly < 0.9.Please clarify this discrepancy. 3.Although the ablation study in Table 2 demonstrates that jointly introducing MinIP and FPD-MaxIP yields the best performance, the specific synergistic mechanism between these two priors in the DSA vessel segmentation task requires further explanation. As shown in Fig. 1, FPD-MaxIP effectively suppresses background structures and enhances vessel details; what, then, are the specific limitations or shortcomings of FPD-MaxIP compared to MinIP that necessitate their combination?
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for their constructive comments. We address the major concerns by grouping related comments. To support reproducibility, we will release the code. a. Generalization claim and typos issues (R1). We appreciate the reviewer’s comment regarding the scope of our claim. To avoid overstatement, we clarify that the submitted experiments demonstrate consistent performance on DIAS and DSCA under dataset-specific training/testing, not strict cross-dataset transfer. This does not affect the core contribution, namely FPD-MaxIP and its integration with temporal modeling and projection priors. We will revise “cross-dataset generalization” to “consistent in-domain performance across two DSA benchmarks”. Besides, we will also correct the reported typos and formatting issues. b. AUC interpretation (R4). After checking the submitted evaluation pipeline, we found that AUC was computed from thresholded prediction maps. Thus, it should not be interpreted as standard AUC computed from continuous probability scores, explaining the difference from prior VSS-Net and TemSAM reports. Since our main conclusions rely on Dice, IoU, clDice, and qualitative results, we agree that the current AUC presentation may be misleading. We will recompute AUC from probability scores or remove this column. c1.TFE design and T/2 split (R2). SSM captures long-range contrast propagation over [B,THW,C], while temporal attention predicts weights [B,T,1,1,1] and reweights [B,T,H,W,C] by broadcasting, emphasizing informative phases. Without SSM, temporal dependencies may be weak; without attention, uniform pooling may dilute transient vessel responses. The T/2 split is an empirical setting that provides broad early-late phase contrast in our experiments. Compared with raw MaxIP or local frame differences, FPD-MaxIP better suppresses stable bony or soft-tissue residuals, although severe motion may still introduce residual edges. We will clarify this limitation and explore adaptive phase selection in the future. c2.Complementarity and failure discussion of MinIP and FPD-MaxIP (R1,2,4). MinIP preserves global vessel topology, while FPD-MaxIP suppresses temporally persistent background responses through phase-difference computation. Their combination couples structural support with dynamic contrast enhancement, explaining the gains in Table 2.However, FPD-MaxIP may become less reliable when the fixed early-late split mismatches patient-specific contrast dynamics or acquisition conditions, such as delayed/uneven filling or severe motion. MinIP can partially mitigate this issue by providing stable vessel support and topology cues, reducing local discontinuity. Future work will explore adaptive phase selection to improve robustness. d. False-positive suppression (R4). We agree that Precision is important for false-positive suppression. Although not listed, IoU penalizes false positives in its denominator and shows a consistent trend. Precision can also be derived from DSC and Sen as (DSC×Sen)/(2Sen−DSC) under the same threshold and aggregation setting. These results support FPD-MaxIP’s false-positive suppression ability. We will add Precision if revision is permitted. e. Baseline fairness and TemSAM (R1,2,4). Except for TemSAM, all compared baselines were retrained using the same official splits and protocol, including preprocessing and 64×64 patch training. TemSAM is reported separately as an external SAM-based reference, using results from the original paper due to reproducibility constraints under our matched protocol. Our method leverages DSA-specific phase-difference and projection priors to suppress stable background responses and preserve vessel connectivity, without large foundation models. The results support consistent performance on DIAS and DSCA under dataset-specific training/testing, while strict cross-dataset generalization requires further validation. We will clarify these settings in the revision.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Scores are 3/4/4, with the most confident reviewer (R4, confidence 4) recommending weak accept on the strength of the FPD-MaxIP design and comprehensive evaluation. The weak reject (R1) is driven primarily by the unsupported cross-dataset claim and missing failure-case analysis rather than by disagreement with the core idea. The paper is borderline but the concerns are largely addressable, so the paper is invited for rebuttal. Authors should prioritize (a) a true cross-dataset transfer experiment (e.g., DIAS→DSCA) or a retraction/softening of the generalization claim, (b) reconciling the AUC discrepancy with the original VSS-Net and TemSAM papers, (c) clarifying the SSM-vs-temporal-attention rationale, the T/2 split, and the MinIP/FPD-MaxIP synergy mechanism, (d) reporting Precision and a brief failure-case discussion, and (e) confirming that all baselines were retrained under identical preprocessing and splits. | Reviewers agreed that the FPD-MaxIP prior is conceptually novel and clinically well-motivated, the decoupling of temporal dynamics modeling from spatial prior guidance is a clean architectural choice, and the quantitative results are competitive across two benchmarks. They raised several concerns: (1) the claimed cross-dataset generalization is not supported by actual cross-dataset training/testing experiments; (2) reported AUC values (<0.9) are inconsistent with prior VSS-Net and TemSAM reports (>0.97), suggesting a metric-computation discrepancy; (3) Precision is missing, despite the method’s focus on false-positive suppression; (4) the TFE block design (SSM + temporal attention + reshape operations) is under-justified; (5) the T/2 phase split is empirical, with no adaptive alternative; (6) the synergy between MinIP and FPD-MaxIP needs clearer explanation; (7) failure cases for FPD-MaxIP (motion artifacts, irregular contrast dynamics, patient-specific variation) are not discussed; (8) baseline fairness (matched preprocessing, splits) and TemSAM’s reuse from original paper need clarification; and (9) typos and formatting issues are present.After rebuttal, the concerns were largely resolved or addressed — the authors agreed to soften the cross-dataset claim, acknowledged the AUC issue and committed to recomputing or removing it, clarified TFE design, explained MinIP/FPD-MaxIP complementarity and limitations, and confirmed baseline retraining under matched protocols. All three reviewers raise their recommendations to Accept (one explicitly conditional on including the corrected AUC and Precision metrics in the camera-ready). Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The proposed FPD-MaxIP prior is a clinically motivated and technically meaningful design, as it explicitly captures contrast-induced temporal changes rather than relying only on implicit temporal modeling. Its integration with Mamba-based temporal encoding and MinIP-based structural guidance is also well supported by the ablation studies. The rebuttal satisfactorily addressed the main concerns raised during review, including the scope of the generalization claim, the role of temporal modeling and attention, the complementarity between MinIP and FPD-MaxIP, baseline fairness, and potential failure cases. All post-rebuttal reviewer recommendations are positive, and I agree that the paper is above the acceptance threshold. For the camera-ready version, the authors should carefully revise the manuscript to avoid overstating cross-dataset generalization, correct the AUC computation or remove the misleading AUC column, clarify the baseline training settings, and fix the remaining formatting/typo issues. These revisions will make the contribution and evaluation more precise and convincing. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The author’s response addresses the reviewers’ concerns.

title: Test-Time Adaptation in Optical Coherence Tomography Using Trajectory-Aligned Time-Independent Flow
reviewer_1_strengths: The paper introduces Flow Matching, a cutting-edge generative model, to the test-time adaptation (TTA) task in medical imaging. It provides an inspiring design choice by removing time conditioning to address the discrepancy between real physical noise and theoretical Gaussian noise. The required reference histograms can be pre-extracted and averaged from synthetic trajectories, incurring virtually no additional computational cost during inference.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: (1) The authors explicitly state in the manuscript, “Notably, our experiments demonstrate that this approach performs robustly even without the inclusion of explicit data-fidelity terms”. In medical image reconstruction, this complete abandonment of fidelity constraints on the input anatomy is dangerous. During the subsequent dozens of ODE solving steps, the generative model can easily mistake early, subtle pathological structures for noise and erase them, or “hallucinate” healthy retinal tissues that fit the high-quality distribution but do not actually exist. (2) The core histogram matching and ODE reconstruction heavily rely on a globally fixed target time point hyperparameter, s_target. Although the authors conducted an ablation study in Figure 3, claiming relatively steady performance across different reference time points, this does not mask this flaw. In real clinical scenarios, the base physical noise levels of OCT images acquired from different patients fluctuate drastically. Using a globally uniform constant to align the distribution of all images contradicts the image-specific nature of TTA and fails to dynamically adapt to the true physical state of each scan. (3) The proposed method achieves results comparable to fully supervised methods. However, for the geographic atrophy (GA) segmentation task (Topcon to Spectralis), the supervised upper bound is 77.3 , while this paper’s best performance is only 57.1.A gap of 20 percentage points indicates that the method fails to genuinely resolve the severe domain mismatch. Furthermore, the non-generative TTA baseline methods compared are rather outdated; for instance, TENT is from 2021, and CoTTA is from 2022.The lack of comparison with the latest TTA technologies from the past two years weakens the persuasiveness of their state-of-the-art claims.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The method is clearly motivated, technically coherent, and the design is easy to follow. The experiments are solid: comparisons include TENT, CoTTA, CPDM, DDA, and standard flow matching; results are reported on two tasks and multiple devices; and the ablation supports both proposed components.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The main limitation is novelty: the contribution is more of a strong adaptation of existing generative TTA ideas than a fundamentally new framework. As mentioned in the paper, authors utilize methods from Lipman et al. [13, 14] ] and Sun et al. [21]. The method uses histogram matching to place a real test scan onto a learned flow trajectory, but histogram matching aligns only the global intensity distribution, not the local OCT texture, speckle statistics, or lesion structure that actually define the domain gap. In addition, the start point s_target is a fixed global hyperparameter chosen by grid search, which further weakens the claim that the alignment is truly adaptive to each test scan. The evaluation is also still limited in scale, with 70 RETOUCH volumes and 40 paired GA patients, and only annotated B-scans used for quantitative analysis. I suggest authors should investigate bigger dataset such as AI-READI to make the evaluation more robust and reliable. In addition, the approach is computationally heavy for a TTA method, requiring a large 103M flow model, about 80 hours of training, and about 2.2 seconds per B-scan at inference. So although the method works, it is not lightweight TTA in the usual sense. It is closer to test-time generative restoration with a heavy pre-trained model. The paper writing needs to be updated. Paragraph lengths are not balanced.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The paper tackles an important real problem. Segmentation models often drop in performance when scan quality changes across scanners, especially for lower-cost devices. The most interesting part is the use of histogram alignment to match the test scan to the model’s own reference path before reconstruction. That is easy to understand and easy to implement.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The novelty is limited. Flow matching itself is standard and comes from references [13] and [14], and the choice to remove time input is already motivated by reference [21]. The added histogram step is practical, but it does not feel like a major new method on its own. Some important study details are unclear. The paper says the target reference point was picked by trying different settings, but it does not clearly explain how this was done for the target scanners. It is also not clear how much of the improvement comes from histogram matching alone versus the full method. Since the method changes medical images without a direct constraint that keeps the output close to the input, the paper should show more clearly that important structure is preserved. Also, some setup is not clear, which is understandable due to the page limit, but it should be explained more in the camera-ready version if accepted.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for their constructive feedback and are encouraged that all reviewers found our general framework to be useful and practical. We address the primary concerns below. Exclusion of data-fidelity term (R1, R3): While we agree that generative models can theoretically hallucinate structures, we did not observe this in practice. We found the bias of the starting point to be strong enough to be sufficient and data-fidelity terms very sensitive to the hyperparameters. Notably, our method outperforms multiple baselines that explicitly use data-fidelity terms (e.g., DDA and CPDM), including CPDM which utilizes a fidelity term strictly designed for OCT. Furthermore, our reported Dice scores inherently penalize such hallucinations. Suitable Baselines (R1, R2): While the classical Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) methods we compare against are older, our primary focus is on recent generative-based TTA baselines such as DDA and CPDM. Because these modern methods explicitly leverage powerful generative priors, they are theoretically expected to inherently outperform classical TTA approaches. Consequently, they serve as the most rigorous and relevant baselines to benchmark our approach against, whereas the older methods were included strictly for completeness. While our model uses 103M parameters, the diffusion baselines use the same model and same number of parameters. The runtime of the diffusion based baselines is longer as there are more neural function evaluations (100 vs 1000). Speeding up our approach is the focus of future work. Reliance on hyperparameters (R1, R2, R3): Although our system requires selecting a single hyperparameter for each target scanner, performance is highly robust to this choice (see Fig. 3). In fact, oracle selection (choosing the absolute best hyperparameter per individual patient) improves overall results by only 1 percentage point. This minimal difference represents the theoretical upper bound of what an automated tuning system could achieve, demonstrating that the manual choice is not overly sensitive to begin with. We believe that this is because the unconditional version of our approach is intrinsically robust to a variety of noise levels as can be seen in Fig. 3. Supervised performance (R1): We acknowledge the performance gap between the Topcon and Spectralis devices, however, the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) in the Topcon images is inherently much lower and the annotation was performed on each device separately. Consequently, it is unclear if the theoretical upper bound of the Spectralis device is even achievable, as certain fine structures may simply not be captured by the Topcon sensor and the annotation might be less certain. Despite this physical limitation, our approach provides a substantial performance boost compared to standard predictions directly on Topcon images. Limited novelty (R2, R3): We strongly believe that the simplicity of our approach is its greatest strength. It is highly accessible, straightforward to implement, and significantly enhances the output of generative models currently prevalent in medical imaging. Furthermore, while this approach is particularly well-suited for OCT, techniques like histogram matching have a long, proven track record of broad utility in other modalities, such as MRI. Confusing writing (R2, R3): We will utilize the additional space provided for the camera-ready version to expand and clarify the methodology section to ensure reproducibility and ease of reading. Furthermore, we have prepared a code repository to be released upon acceptance to further avoid any misconceptions.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): All three reviewers agree on acceptance, although only slightly above the bar. My own assessment goes in line with this method potentially being a meaningful contribution to the literature. The trajectory alignment is interesting to the community and the application is challenging. However, despite the overall assessment above the acceptance bar, in total there are a large number of arguments by reviewers that need clarification, especially regarding claimed novelty, lack of explicit data fidelity together with danger of hallucinations, as well as shortcomings in the evaluation regarding competing, more recent TTA methods. I invite authors to address these and other concerns in an organized manner in a rebuttal (focusing on the major issues sorted by perceived importance from the author’s point of view), to clarify the multiple mentioned issues in the reviews. | Taking into account the rebuttal in addition to the reviews, I tend to agree that this work demonstrate a good contribution which might spark some discussion at the conference. I think in case of acceptance the authors should clearly state limitations, e.g. potential hallucinations (although not appearing in their tests), and carefully clarify all points addressed in the rebuttal, e.g. the details on hyperparameters. Concerns regarding generalizability of results are noted, but I think these could be addressed in a follow up work. In case of acceptance, authors should tidy up the references, as these are not formatted in a proof-ready version yet (pages missing, inconsistent use of hyperlinks, arxiv versions of published works). Moreover, I suggest a slightly more thorough inclusion of recent works using flow matching in medical image synthetization or reconstruction. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Reviewers summarized strengths of your work, novel aspects and noted that your solution to the specific application area may be of potential interest. The rebuttal helped to clarify open issues and misunderstandings. Would the paper be accepted, authors are strongly encouraged to improve the final write-up by including recommendations by reviewers, in particular improving clarity of notations and descriptions. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): All three reviewers said the paper above the bar in the initial review and agreed the paper tackles an important OCT cross-device problem with an easy-to-implement histogram-alignment idea and a clean time-conditioning removal (R1, R3). I believe the rebuttal was most convincing on hyperparameter robustness, showing that per-patient oracle tuning buys only about a point over the single global s_target, and on why the generative-TTA baselines (DDA, CPDM) are the relevant comparisons. The residual worry (R2), is that histogram matching aligns only global intensity and the method lacks an explicit data-fidelity term, so subtle pathology preservation is argued rather than proven; I agree this is a real limitation, but note the method still beats fidelity-using baselines and that R2’s concerns were largely known at the original weak-accept stage. With R1 confirming accept, R3 unchanged and positive, and only R2 moving down on pre-existing grounds, I recommend acceptance, with the authors encouraged to revise the data-fidelity claims and expand the methodology in the camera-ready.

title: Test-time Adaptation of Pelvic Bone Segmentation Models via Dynamic Reliability-Guided
reviewer_1_strengths: Background is well formulated and the problem is of genuine interest to the community Evaluation covers important datasets in the field Visualisations for the method and results are high quality
reviewer_1_weaknesses: A few terms could benefit from an expanded explanation to make this work self-contained. One example is ‘teacher-student schemes’, which is a very wide area of research and requires a brief 1-2 sentences explanation to allow readers to fully understand the shortfalls. Several claims are unsupported by citations/evidence, please add citations to previous work to support claims: TS schemes are confined by false prediction and error accumulation at these boundaries enforcing anatomical consistency is crucial for the reliable adaptation existing methods neglect the self-supervised abilities Some maths terms are undefined at first use e. g. , \theta^t is missing a definition in the first paragraph of sec 2. reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal

reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal

reviewer_3_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: R1Q1, Q3, Q4: Terminology, Notation, and Technical Details. We have added relevant citations and refined the statements. Specifically, the teacher-student schemes refer to TTA methods where an EMA-updated teacher generates pseudo-labels for supervising the student on target domain data. We clarify that θᵗ denotes the source-trained PBS model parameters, while f(θᵗ) denotes the corresponding segmentation model. Ambiguous expressions are corrected, and θᵗ is now defined at its first occurrence in Sec. 2.During TTA, dropout is kept active, and each target sample is forwarded K times to obtain stochastic predictions P̂ᵢₖ, where k indexes the stochastic forward pass. Following [7], we analyze K=1,5,10,15 and set K=5 in all experiments. R1Q2: Evidence and Literature Support for Claims. The prior TS schemes with pseudo-label supervision have shown that unreliable predictions can be propagated and accumulated under domain shifts in the cited works [15,25]. Table 1 shows that these methods suffer from poor HD95, indicating notable boundary delineation errors. We apologize for missing citations and included works (e.g., AdaMI [Bateson et al., 2022] and EDCP [Liu et al., 2026]) showing that enforcing anatomical consistency is crucial for reliable adaptation. Cited works [14,16] and TestFit [Zhang et al., 2025] show that self-supervised learning has been widely explored in TTA, but its explicit use for enforcing target-domain anatomical consistency remains underexplored. R1Q5, Q6, Q7: Strengthening Experimental Evidence. We agree that ReGA is positioned as an application-focused TTA framework for PBS. PBS is sensitive to boundary ambiguity and anatomical inconsistency under domain shifts; ReGA is designed to suppress unreliable boundary predictions and to promote anatomical consistency across pelvic regions. Further, in a new MSD_T10 → CLINIC setting, ReGA is also superior to source-only models and other TTA baselines, i.e., TENT, InTEnt, VPTTA, CoTTA, and TEGDA. Specifically, it improves Dice by 8.8 over the source-only model while reducing HD95/ASD by 18.8/4.7 and outperforms other TTA baselines by 3.3 - 4.8 Dice, with 16.8 - 26.7/3.5 - 4.1 reductions in HD95/ASD. Paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests show that ReGA improves Dice (p≤0.008), HD95 (p≤0.001), and ASD (p≤0.002) over TTA baselines in CLINIC → KITS19, and achieves notable HD95/ASD gains (p≤0.05) with comparable Dice in CLINIC → MSD_T10. We conduct sensitivity analysis on key hyperparameters. ReGA is robust to M when M＞10, with Dice variations within 0.3.K=5 is selected as significant computation overhead would occur for K＞5 with a marginal gain of 0.1 in Dice. ReGA performs best at β=0.01 (range 0.005 - 0.020), other values degrade Dice minimally (0.6 max). Dropout rate of 0.5 (range 0.1 – 1.0) provides a balanced stochastic perturbation, yet the worst dropout rate results in only 0.6 degradation in Dice. R2Q1, Q2: Methodological Distinctions. While ReGA is partially inspired by the general adaptation philosophy of TEGDA, it targets a different task, i.e., TTA of PBS models, where boundary ambiguity and anatomical consistency are critical under domain shifts. To this end, we introduce a new metric SICE for optimization that jointly considers region overlap and boundary deviation and further uses Lrc for confidence- and SICE-weighted RCL. Thus, Lrc not only reduces computation but also promotes reliable anatomical-region feature. In Table 2, the variant w/o Lrc performs worse, especially in HD95, indicating the contribution of Lrc to preserving anatomical integrity. R3Q1: Choice of Dataset. TTA aims to adapt a source pre-trained model to the test data during inference in a source-free and online manner. Following this, the PBS model is trained on limited labeled 3D CT volumes from one institution and then adapted to unlabeled data from another institution. In the future, we aim to build a larger standardized multi-center 3D pelvic CT datasets.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The reviewers provide mixed evaluations of this paper (scores: 3, 4, 5), with strengths noted in the problem motivation, methodological formulation, and empirical evaluation, but also concerns regarding limited novelty, clarity of presentation, and depth of experimental analysis . In particular, reviewers highlight missing statistical validation, insufficient analysis of hyperparameters and sensitivity, and unclear differentiation from closely related prior work. Given these differences, I invite the authors to address these concerns in the rebuttal—especially by clarifying methodological distinctions, strengthening experimental evidence, and improving clarity where needed. A clear and comprehensive response will be important for the final decision. | After carefully reviewing the rebuttal and the post-rebuttal reviewer comments, my recommendation is to accept the paper. The paper addresses an important and clinically relevant problem in test-time adaptation for pelvic bone segmentation under domain shift. The proposed ReGA framework, including the SICE-based reliability estimation and feature refinement strategy, is well motivated and evaluated on multiple datasets. While concerns remain regarding the degree of novelty relative to existing TTA/SFDA methods such as TEGDA, the majority of reviewers considered the rebuttal sufficient and supported acceptance. The work is clearly presented, provides useful empirical validation, and offers a practical contribution for improving segmentation reliability and anatomical consistency in unseen clinical domains. Therefore, I recommend acceptance, with the expectation that the authors will further clarify the distinction from closely related methods, add missing statistical and hyperparameter analyses where possible, and temper overstated novelty claims in the final version. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The authors have addressed the reviewers’ comments well. Two reviewers acknowledged the novelty and significance of the work. Therefore acceptance of the paper is concluded. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): I recommend accept: post-rebuttal R1 raised to Accept and R3 maintained Accept (recommending Highlighted Poster), outweighing R2’s downgrade to Reject on TEGDA-similarity and workshop-venue assessments.

title: Text as a Compass: Semantic-Navigated 3D Bone Collapse Prediction via Orthogonal Micro-volume Primitives
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The paper formulates ONFH collapse prediction as a language-guided local evidence identification problem, instead of a standard global 3D classification problem. This is an interesting formulation because it is well matched to the clinical motivation that predictive signs of collapse may appear as subtle local structural changes rather than only as global volumetric patterns. 2.Another strength of the paper is the counterfactual text constraint to refine the selection of informative local tokens. Rather than relying only on positive image-text alignment, the method also uses mismatched or semantically contradictory text to suppress responses from regions that are visually salient but not supported by the queried semantics. 3.Results demonstrate that the proposed method improves performance
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The paper presents OMVP as a projection-based representation, but from the figure and formulation it seems closer to extracting three orthogonal slices from a local 3D region. The manuscript does explain whether this operation is simple slice extraction or a more general projection process. 2.The counterfactual text constraint is an important part of the proposed framework, but limited detail on the counterfactual text generation makes it difficult to understand. Its unclear if the texts are created by template replacement, manual editing, or mismatching with other samples. 3.The paper states that a sparse loss is used when fine-grained masks are unavailable, but it does not provide the explicit form of this loss or explain how the sparsity is enforced. 4.The main novelty is the use language models but at the same time, using text priors are now routinely applied, and there is no innovation in the language model.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: Evaluation of generalizability: The method is evaluated on a public dataset in addition to the internal cohort, providing some assessment of generalization beyond the training distribution. Well-justified problem formulation: The paper addresses a clearly motivated problem, particularly the challenges of detecting and localizing micro-lesions within volumetric data. Methodological novelty: The introduction of the tri-planar orthogonal micro-volume primitive (OMVP) offers an interesting topological manifold representation that aims to concentrate singularity energy along orthogonal bases, addressing issues related to volumetric smoothing. Additionally, the proposed dual-stage optimization strategy, combining semantic space alignment with textual priors to guide the transition from macro-regions of interest to micro-lesions is a novel design. Good empirical performance: The model achieves high performance, with an AUC of 97.01% on a cohort with fine-grained lesion annotations and 84.91% on a public dataset with coarse regional labels, along with reported causally verified localization.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: While the authors include text-only and vision-language baselines, in addition to label tokenization, the comparison remains limited, as other relevant multimodal fusion and geometry-aware approaches are not considered. Clinical reports are often heterogeneous and inconsistently structured; however, the paper does not discuss how variability in the clinical reports affects the robustness of the proposed approach and how they have addressed . The authors use BioBERT for textual embedding extraction. However, more recent approaches such as BioLinkBERT leverages links between documents, enabling a more comprehensive semantic finding across different reports, outperforming BERT. I recommend the authors to also consider this approach.
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.Overall, the paper is generally well-written. 2.The use of tri-planar representations to alleviate volumetric dilution is well-motivated and effective for capturing sparse lesions. 3.The semantic alignment framework with MIL-based attention for selecting relevant OMVPs is novel and technically interesting. 4.The proposed method uses text input to guide the evidence identification and adds counterfactual grounding to reduce hallucinations. The results are qualitatively evaluated in Fig. 3. 5.The ablation study confirmed the positive effects of each component proposed.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.Overstatement of OMVP novelty. OMVP is essentially a tri-planar (multi-planar) representation of a 3D volume, which has been widely used in prior works [*1, *2, *3, *4]. The novelty appears to lie more in the attention-based aggregation and top-k selection, and the use of tri-planar representation rather than the representation itself. I recommend revising the claims regarding the novelty of OMVP to better reflect this distinction. 2.Unclear use of 2D U-Net on OMVP for segmentation. The OMVP representation (H,W,3) consists of three orthogonal planes that are not spatially aligned. It is therefore unclear how a single 2D U-Net can produce a meaningful spatial output (e.g., a segmentation map) from such input. In standard practice, U-Net output channels correspond to aligned spatial features or segmentation classes, whereas in OMVP the channels represent different planes rather than consistent spatial locations. While using a 2D model may be reasonable for regression tasks (e.g., Stage I), where features are ultimately pooled into a vector, this design is questionable for segmentation. Segmentation requires pixel-wise spatial consistency, which OMVP does not provide. A more natural approach would be to process each plane independently with separate segmentation models (or at least forward passes) and aggregate the results afterward [*2, *3, *4]. The paper should clarify how the proposed U-Net handles OMVP inputs and produces spatially meaningful outputs. 3.The heuristic sparsity loss L_sarse in Eq (6) is not clearly defined, and its formulation or source is missing. 4.The parameter k used in Stage II is not specified, and the method for choosing it is unclear. title: Text as Illumination: Spatial Contrastive Retinex Learning for Language-Guided Medical Image Segmentation
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.Mapping Retinex theory to cross‑modal segmentation is creative and well‑motivated. The idea of using text as “illumination” that positively/negatively modulates features is elegant. 2.Unlike prior implicit or coarse‑grained alignment methods, the proposed RTMB produces per‑pixel similarity maps and two complementary illumination maps, enabling explicit foreground amplification and background suppression at each decoder stage.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The text encoder is a frozen CLIP model pre‑trained on general natural images and captions. Medical reports contain highly specialised terminology and different linguistic structure. No analysis or mitigation (e. g. , fine‑tuning, prompt engineering, or medical‑specific text encoder) is provided. 2.The evaluation lacks empirical efficiency profiling; while architectural complexity is quantified via parameters and FLOPs, clinically critical metrics including inference latency and memory footprint remain unreported. 3.The comparative evaluation in Table 1 exhibits methodological inconsistency in metric reporting. Specifically, some baselines (e. g. , U-Net, nnU-Net) report solely sample-level metrics (m-Dice, m-IoU), whereas certain multi-modal competitors (e. g. , TeViA) provide only global metrics (g-Dice, g-IoU). Notably, TIRNet is the sole method presenting all four metrics, precluding direct and equitable comparison across the complete metric suite. To ensure fair and transparent benchmarking, we strongly recommend that the authors compute and report the missing metrics for all comparative methods through standardized re-implementation.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.Innovative Perspective: Mapping Retinex theory from low-level vision enhancement to cross-modal feature modulation provides a novel conceptual framework for LMIS. 2.Architecture Design: The explicit decoupling of foreground enhancement (L+) and background suppression (L−) is a well-structured engineering approach to handle multi-modal interference. 3.Empirical Results: The method demonstrates competitive performance on MosMedData and QaTa-COV19 datasets compared to several recent baselines.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.Logical Conflict Between Local Receptive Fields and Global Spatial Semantics: The proposed TIRNet relies on a CNN-based U-Net architecture. While the text embeddings provide global semantic information, the visual features in the decoder stages are inherently local due to the translational invariance of convolutional kernels. The manuscript does not mention the use of explicit Positional Encodings. I am concerned about how the model manages to achieve precise spatial alignment for directional or lateral clinical instructions (e.g., “lower left lung” vs. “lower right lung” ). In the absence of a global coordinate system or positional embeddings, local features in anatomically symmetric regions may yield nearly identical similarity responses to the same global text vector, potentially leading to cross-lateral false positives. The authors should clarify how the architecture maintains global spatial consistency without explicit positional information. 2.Anomalous Performance of MSIS-Loss and Hyperparameter Sensitivity: In Table 3, the sensitivity analysis reveals a concerning trend regarding the proposed losses. The baseline model (λ_cl=0, λ_bg=0) achieves an m-Dice of 84.36.However, adding the Background Suppression Loss (BS-Loss) independently (λ_cl=0, λ_bg=0.5) results in a performance degradation to 84.20.Furthermore, when λ_cl and λ_bg are set to 0.5, the result (84.35) remains inferior to the baseline. It appears the proposed losses only provide a marginal gain at a very specific hyperparameter setting (λ_cl=1, λ_bg=0.5). This suggests that the pixel-level hard constraint of BS-Loss may conflict with the mixed-semantic nature of deep-stage features (large receptive fields), leading to optimization instability. The authors need to provide a deeper mechanistic explanation for why these losses act as negative optimizers in several parameter configurations. 3.Conceptual Overstatement of Retinex Formulation: While the “Text-as-Illumination” metaphor is inspiring, the mathematical implementation in Equation 5 is effectively a sophisticated dual-path spatial attention or feature-gating mechanism. Unlike traditional Retinex theory, which addresses an ill-posed inverse problem (decomposing unknown illumination from a single image), this framework uses feed-forward gating signals derived directly from text. Referring to this as a strict “extension of Retinex theory” feels like a conceptual overstatement. A more rigorous description would frame it as a Retinex-inspired decoupled attention mechanism.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The major strength is the Retinex-based Text Modulation Block (RTMB), which utilizes text embeddings as condition vectors to dynamically modulate visual features via a dual-path gating mechanism. This spatial weighting approach is mathematically sound and demonstrates a strong capability to selectively enhance foreground targets while suppressing complex backgrounds, offering an inspiring and practically valuable perspective for multimodal feature alignment in medical imaging.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: In Section 2.1, the Retinex formulation is introduced into a cross-modal setting, interpreting the visual decoder feature as reflectance and the text embedding as illumination. While the dual-path modulation effectively separates foreground and background, the underlying physical analogy appears conceptually forced. Retinex is inherently a low-level physical model for illumination-reflectance decomposition, whereas the proposed method operates entirely in a high-level semantic space as a form of text-guided feature modulation. In the rebuttal, I would appreciate it if the authors could clarify their justification for this strict physical analogy. Moving forward, it would be more appropriate to reframe this design as a “Retinex-inspired modulation mechanism” to improve conceptual rigor. The current ablation studies mainly demonstrate the incremental benefit of the RTMB module, which largely reflects the inherent advantage of simply incorporating cross-modal information. However, this alone does not sufficiently justify the necessity of the proposed architectural complexity. Specifically, why did the authors not explore or discuss comparisons with alternative, standard modules that serve a similar purpose, such as a standard cross-attention mechanism? Without such a de facto baseline, it is difficult to determine whether the proposed dual-path modulation offers meaningful performance or efficiency advantages over conventional cross-modal fusion methods. I look forward to the authors’ discussion and insights on this architectural choice during the rebuttal.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: To All: Q1: Retinex Rationale (MR, R2, R3) A1: In fact, our TIRNet is not a strict Retinex decomposition to solve the illumination-reflectance inverse problem. We instead use Retinex as a structural inspiration: text embeddings provide semantic illumination-like signals to modulate visual decoder features. It enhances text-relevant foregrounds and suppresses irrelevant backgrounds. In the revised version, we will clarify the above facts and provide more motivations about using the dual-path spatial gating mechanism in Eq. 5.Q2: RTMB vs. Other Fusion Methods (MR, R3): A2: To verify the effectiveness of RTMB, we replace it with two standard alternatives, i.e., concatenation fusion and cross-attention fusion. On QaTa-COV19, they achieve 82.40/73.44 and 82.88/73.90 in m-Dice/m-IoU, respectively. They are consistently lower than the ones (83.13/74.45) achieved by RTMB. These results verify that the improvement is not merely from introducing textual information, but from the proposed RTMB. Q3: Spatial Alignment w/o PE (MR, R2): A3: Indeed, explicit PE is not used in TIRNet. However, visual features of our framework are not position-agnostic. This is fully supported by three facts: (1) zero-padding can provide implicit absolute-coordinate cues (Islam et al., ICLR 2020); (2) hierarchical down-sampling and skip connections help preserve and propagate relative spatial information; and (3) deep decoder stages have a large effective receptive field, enabling them to capture holistic organ layouts rather than only local textures. In addition, TIRNet introduces explicit spatial grounding through MSIS-Loss. At each decoder stage, down-sampled masks supervise the illumination maps, thereby penalizing activations outside the text-relevant ground-truth regions. More importantly, adding normalized 2D CoordConv/PE before RTMB results in negligible gains across all metrics [84.50/76.17/91.37/84.11 (QaTa-COV19)] compared to TIRNet. It confirms that explicit PE is unnecessary here. We will add more representative visualizations to show the effect of the localization-aware text. To R1: Q1: CLIP Domain Gap A1: We further evaluate the text encoder adaptation. On QaTa-COV19, replacing frozen CLIP with BioMedCLIP and MedCLIP-ResNet50 achieves 83.57/75.00/90.58/82.79 and 83.77/75.23/90.79/83.14, respectively. They are both below the frozen CLIP setting. Besides, the prompt engineering with “A medical image showing {Text}.” yields lower results (83.82/75.25/90.80/83.15). Fine-tuning the CLIP produces comparable results (84.48/76.06/91.31/84.01). This suggests that text encoding is not the primary bottleneck in our structured-text setting. Q2: Efficiency A2: Under the same evaluation setting, TIRNet takes 115.46 ms/case with 1426 MiB peak GPU memory. While not the fastest, it remains practical and is more efficient than several LMIS baselines, e.g., LViT (378.59 ms, 17518 MiB) and LGA (117.03 ms, 4338 MiB). We will include the latency/memory and discuss the accuracy-efficiency trade-off in the revision. Q3: Metric Consistency A3: The original table followed the metrics reported in prior works. We agree that standardized evaluation is preferable. We therefore re-evaluated all compared methods under a unified protocol, which enables full comparisons, e.g., [TeViA: 84.12/75.69/90.96/83.41; U-Net: 78.46/68.59/86.66/76.47 (QaTa-COV19)]. We will update Table 1 accordingly in the revision. Note that the main conclusion remains unchanged. To R2: Q1: MSIS-Loss A1: In fact, BS-Loss is an auxiliary regularizer. With (0, 0.5), MSIS-Loss suppresses backgrounds, making the model over-conservative around small lesions, ambiguous boundaries, or deep-stage mixed-semantic features. When both weights are 0.5, the highlighted foreground remains insufficient to balance this suppression. Thus, the weights (1, 0.5) better match our design: RGC-Loss provides the main semantic alignment, while BS-Loss offers moderate background regularization. To R3: See General Response A1/A2.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This submission proposes TIRNet, a Retinex-inspired language-guided medical image segmentation framework using text-derived positive/ negative modulation maps, detail compensation, and multi-scale illumination supervision. Reviewers generally found the core idea interesting and technically promising, with competitive results on MosMedData+ and QaTa-COV19 and useful ablations supporting the RTMB/CDCB design. However, several important concerns should be addressed in rebuttal: whether the Retinex framing is conceptually justified versus a standard text-guided attention/gating mechanism; whether the method offers advantages over conventional cross-attention or alternative fusion baselines and how spatially specific text cues are handled in a CNN-based architecture without explicit positional encoding. | The rebuttal addresses reviewers’ concerns reasonably well. Overall, I recommend acceptance. The contribution is technically interesting and the rebuttal substantially reduces the main doubts about architectural necessity, spatial alignment, efficiency, and evaluation fairness. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The proposed Retinex-inspired text modulation framework is recognized as an innovative and effective approach to language-guided medical image segmentation. While initial concerns were raised regarding the forced physical Retinex analogy, spatial alignment logic in CNNs, and the optimization sensitivity of the loss functions, consensus among reviewers post-rebuttal highlights that the authors have successfully resolved these issues through comprehensive empirical clarifications. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): three accepts, i agree.

title: Text as the Sieve: Information Bottleneck Guided Prototype Sieving for Text-Guided Medical Image Segmentation
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.Accurate and Insightful Problem Formulation: The observation that existing token pruning methods target the wrong object (pruning concise text tokens instead of redundant visual ones) is valuable, with a clear motivation. The formulation of “Token Scale Mismatch” and “Interaction Paradigm” is precise. 2.Sound IB-Sieve Design: Using text as a semantic sieve to rank and hard-select visual prototypes integrates the Information Bottleneck principle with cross-modal interaction naturally. The design of aggregating residual prototypes into a background token also thoughtfully addresses information preservation. 3.Effective Axial Prototype Compression: The axial decomposition compressing H×W to H+W is a practical engineering design that balances efficiency and representational power. 4.Rationale for Asymmetric Decoder: The design of bypassing SPI to use original text embeddings directly to prevent semantic drift is logical, and ablation studies verify its superiority over symmetric designs. 5.Interpretability Analysis (Spatial Semantic Maps): The multi-scale semantic maps in Fig. 3 provide intuitive visualization of text-visual alignment, enhancing the method’s interpretability. 6.Well-Structured Ablation Studies: Table 2 covers core components such as interaction paradigms, screening mechanisms, and decoder designs, clearly showing the contribution of each module.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.Marginal Performance Gains and Lack of Statistical Significance: On QaTa-COV19-v2, TeSi (91.37%) is only 0.16% higher than FMISeg (91.21%) and 0.34% higher than ABP (91.03%). On MosMedData+, TeSi (77.96%) is notably lower than FMISeg (79.30%). Such minute differences are unconvincing without reporting standard deviations from multiple runs. The paper fails to report any statistical significance tests or variance information. 2.Narrow Dataset Coverage Limited to COVID-19 Lung Scenarios: Both datasets are COVID-19 lung images (one X-ray, one CT), making the claim of “medical image segmentation” overly broad. The lack of validation on other organs, diseases, or modalities makes it difficult to assess generalization capability. Specifically, it is unclear if the effectiveness of IB-Sieve relies on the relatively uniform background of lung images. 3.Sub-SOTA Results on MosMedData+ with Inadequate Explanation: On MosMedData+, TeSi’s Dice (77.96%) and mIoU (63.87%) are lower than FMISeg (79.30%/65.71%) and TGCAM (where mIoU is lower than TeSi). The paper attributes this to “limited training data hinders Transformer-based generalization,” yet TeSi uses a ConvNeXt backbone, not a Transformer. This explanation is self-contradictory. 4.Weak Connection to Information Bottleneck Theory: While the paper claims inspiration from the IB principle, the connection is largely intuitive. There is no formal analysis or experimental validation regarding the minimization of I(Z;X) and maximization of I(Z;Y) . IB-Sieve is essentially a similarity-based top-k selection; branding it as “Information Bottleneck” feels like over-packaging. 5.Lack of Analysis on Fixed Selection Ratio ( k=0.5 ): IB-Sieve uses a fixed 50% selection ratio, but the paper does not analyze the impact of different k values. The optimal k likely varies with lesion size and modality, making this a key hyperparameter that requires discussion. 6.Missing Computational Efficiency Comparison: The paper emphasizes reducing computational redundancy as a core motivation but fails to report efficiency metrics (FLOPs, parameter count, inference time) compared to baselines. It is impossible to judge the actual efficiency gains from axial prototype compression and IB-Sieve. 7.Negligible Contribution Differences in Ablation Studies: In Table 2, the Dice scores for Rows 2-7 range from 91.02% to 91.37%, a maximum difference of only 0.35%. This undermines the claim of “necessity” for each component—the differences may well be within the noise range. 8.Incomplete Baseline Comparisons: AT and ABP lack results on MosMedData+ (marked as “-“), weakening the completeness of cross-dataset comparisons. If this is due to unavailable code, it should be stated.
