author_feedback: We sincerely thank the reviewers for their constructive comments. Our responses are below: Q1 IB formalization (R1, R3) We appreciate this critical comment. Our method follows an IB-inspired structural bottleneck design rather than explicit variational IB optimization. Using our paper’s notation, the IB variables correspond as: X: multi-scale features {Xi} Z: sieved high-semantic prototypes Z_sem Y: segmentation mask (E_text as a semantic proxy for Y) A structural IB approximation is induced via capacity constraints on Z (see Q4), jointly promoting: Min I(Z;X): Axial compression reduces token capacity (↓H(Z)); IB-Sieve further prunes P_v to Z_sem, discarding task-irrelevant regions into the p_bg token. Max I(Z;Y): SPI aligns prototypes across modalities, ensuring Z remains predictive of Y, further reinforced by Dice/CE objectives. Our early trials with explicit IB loss led to instability with marginal gains, suggesting the structural design is sufficient in practice. Q2 Model effectiveness and module contributions (R1, R3) We respectfully clarify that the modest improvements reflect a high-performance region (>91% Dice), where only incremental gains are expected. Similar patterns also appear in prior works[16,23], including their ablations. We agree that reporting standard deviations would strengthen the results. Across 8 runs, our TeSi shows stable performance with Dice std < 0.04 pp on QaTa, while ablation gaps (0.12%–0.35%) exceed this variation range, suggesting reliable improvements. Table 2 isolates each module via targeted substitutions to disentangle specific contributions: IB-Sieve: removing sieving (Row 4) leads to the lowest performance, indicating its importance. SPI: replacing with MHCA (Row 5) results in a consistent drop, supporting the shared alignment design. Spatial map: Row 6 shows a similar decreasing trend. Decoder: Rows 2/3/7 support the asymmetric fusion design; a decoder-only variant reduces to a late-fusion scheme akin to ABP[16]. Q3 Missing Accuracy and incomplete baselines (R1, R3) We apologize for the confusion. The mention of ACC was a typo. ACC is near ceiling on this task (e.g., >97% on QaTa) and omitted in recent works[11,16,23], making it less informative for comparison. We will correct this. All baseline results are taken from original papers under their reported settings with identical dataset splits, following standard practice. ABP and AT lack MosMedData+ results due to unavailable code or missing task configurations; we avoid potentially unfair re-implementation and will clarify this in the final version. Q4 Computational efficiency (R1, R3) By compressing encoder tokens from 4165 to 147 (~28×), our design drastically cuts cross-modal encoder cost, achieving improved results with only 25.7 GFLOPs (vs. 54.2/17.7/34.3 for [9,10,23]) and ~75% of FMISeg[23]’s parameters (text encoder excluded). Q5 Sieving Ratio (R1, R2) We explored k ∈ {0.3, 0.4, 0.5, 0.6, 0.7}. Early checks suggested no clear advantage of lesion/dataset-specific tuning, so k=0.5 was chosen as a fixed midpoint to avoid overfitting. Adaptive ratios are interesting for future work. Q6 MosMedData+ results (R1) We clarify that TeSi slightly outperforms TGCAM but remains below FMISeg on MosMedData+, and our claim is therefore “competitive”, not SOTA. The confusing wording refers to the attention-based SPI module rather than the CNN backbone, and will be revised. Following prior work[10], we used mild augmentation, while FMISeg adopts heavier strategies (e.g., rotation, noise) according to its code, which may partly explain the performance gap. Q7 Dataset scope and Generalization (R1, R2) We acknowledge the current limitation to COVID-19 lung datasets, due to limited availability of public datasets with paired reports. The core design—text-driven visual sieving—does not assume lung-specific properties. The strategy can in principle be extended to 2.5D/3D prototypes, but validation on MRI and volumetric data remains future work.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper studies text-guided medical image segmentation and proposes the TeSi framework to address two limitations of existing methods: the scale mismatch between concise textual tokens and redundant visual tokens, and the delayed interaction caused by introducing textual information only at the decoding stage. Overall, the topic is relevant and meaningful, the motivation is reasonably clear, and the framework is coherently structured. However, the reviews show considerable divergence, as several central claims of the paper still require stronger experimental evidence and more rigorous theoretical justification. In the rebuttal, the authors should clearly explain the precise relationship between IB-Sieve and the Information Bottleneck principle; provide or justify the absence of standard deviations over multiple runs and statistical significance analysis; clarify the actual contribution of each proposed module; report efficiency-related metrics to verify whether axial prototype compression and visual prototype sieving indeed bring computational benefits; discuss the effect of different sieving ratios across lesion sizes and datasets; clarify whether baseline comparisons were conducted under a unified experimental setting, and explain the missing Accuracy results and incomplete baseline results; and discuss the potential applicability and limitations of the method beyond COVID-19 lung datasets, including other organs, MRI, and 3D volumetric data. | The paper addresses a meaningful problem in text-guided medical image segmentation by focusing on visual-token redundancy and the delayed use of textual guidance in existing methods. The proposed TeSi framework is coherent, with axial prototype generation, text-guided visual sieving, and an asymmetric decoder forming a clear design around early semantic filtering. The initial concerns about marginal gains, weak connection to the Information Bottleneck principle, missing efficiency evidence, fixed sieving ratio, and limited dataset scope were valid. However, the rebuttal addresses these issues in a reasonably convincing way. In particular, the authors clarify that the method is IB-inspired rather than a formal variational IB optimization, provide multi-run stability results, report computational cost showing meaningful efficiency advantages, and add analysis of the sieving ratio. Although the evaluation remains limited to COVID-19 lung datasets and the MosMedData+ results are not uniformly superior to all baselines, the method is technically sound, interpretable, and practically useful. Overall, I believe the paper makes a solid contribution to text-guided medical segmentation and would support acceptance, with the expectation that the final version clearly tempers the IB claim and discusses the dataset-scope limitation. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper proposes TeSi, a text-guided segmentation framework that performs early visual prototype sieving using textual semantics, combined with axial prototype compression and an asymmetric decoder. Reviewers agreed that the motivation is clear and that the method forms a coherent design addressing visual redundancy and late text interaction. Initial concerns included marginal gains, lack of variance/efficiency reporting, weak formal connection to Information Bottleneck theory, fixed sieving ratio, and limited validation on COVID lung datasets. Limitations remain: the MosMedData+ result is competitive but not best, and generalization beyond pulmonary datasets is unproven. Nevertheless, the method is technically sound, interpretable, and sufficiently validated for acceptance. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): The paper presents a useful framework for text-guided medical image segmentation, with meaningful early visual sieving and interpretable spatial semantic maps. However, the newly added results cannot be considered during rebuttal per MICCAI policy.

title: Text-Guided Multi-frequency Latent Diffusion for Medical Image Segmentation
reviewer_1_strengths: Clear methodological idea. The paper has a focused contribution: improving latent diffusion segmentation by enriching the conditioning signal with both semantic guidance from text and structural guidance from frequency-aware enhancement. This is more coherent than papers that combine many loosely connected modules. Well-motivated design. The paper argues that latent diffusion segmentation quality depends strongly on conditioning, and that image-only conditioning may not provide enough semantic or structural guidance in hard regions. The proposed ITCF and TGME directly target this motivation. Architectural modularity. A practical strength is that the method leaves the autoencoder and diffusion backbone frozen and only redesigns the condition encoder. This makes the contribution relatively modular and easier to integrate into existing latent diffusion segmentation pipelines. Reasonable empirical coverage. The method is tested on three public datasets spanning colonoscopy, CT, and chest X-ray segmentation, which is better than validating on only a single dataset or modality. Consistent quantitative improvements. The paper reports that TMF-Seg outperforms all listed baselines across the three datasets. Compared with SDSeg, the gains are modest but consistent: Kvasir-SEG Dice: 91.03 → 92.63 MosMedData+ Dice: 80.97 → 81.34 QaTa-COV19 Dice: 89.92 → 91.42. Ablation study supports both modules. On QaTa-COV19, adding ITCF or TGME individually improves over SDSeg, and the full model performs best, supporting complementarity between the two components. Paper organization is straightforward. The framework diagram and module descriptions are reasonably easy to follow, and the method-to-experiment flow is logical. The figures on pages 3–4 help clarify the overall pipeline and the TGME design.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Novelty appears incremental rather than strong. The paper combines known ingredients—latent diffusion segmentation, image-text fusion via cross-attention, and frequency-based feature decomposition/reweighting. The contribution is a sensible integration of these ideas, but based on the paper alone it does not yet read as a fundamentally new segmentation paradigm. The closest prior art cited by the paper already includes text-guided segmentation/diffusion and texture/semantic enhancement, so the novelty margin over existing latent diffusion conditioning approaches seems moderate. The paper should position itself more sharply against recent text-guided and semantics-enhanced segmentation works, especially SDSeg, TSLDeg, LViT, STPNet, and the cited text-guided diffusion literature. Text supervision is insufficiently specified. A central claim is that the method benefits from textual descriptions, but the paper does not clearly explain where these text descriptions come from, how they are constructed for each dataset, whether they are standardized templates, whether they are manually curated, and what information they contain relative to the mask labels. This is important because performance may depend substantially on prompt design and text quality. Without this detail, both fairness and reproducibility are weakened. The method section states that the input consists of an image and its textual description, but the dataset section does not explain the source of the text. Limited analysis of the text contribution. Although the ablation shows ITCF helps, there is no deeper study of text robustness: e. g. , different prompt templates, noisy/incorrect text, empty text, generic text, or prompt sensitivity across datasets. Because the paper’s main claim is text-guided segmentation, this missing analysis is noticeable. Ablation scope is narrow. The ablation is conducted only on QaTa-COV19.Stronger support would come from at least one additional dataset, and ideally from analysis of frequency-band weights, DCT design choices, or alternative fusion baselines. No statistical analysis or variance reporting. The reported gains on some datasets are fairly small, especially on MosMedData+. The paper does not report standard deviations, confidence intervals, or multi-seed results, so it is hard to judge whether the improvements are robust. Limited efficiency discussion. The paper states training hardware and basic settings, but does not quantify added computational overhead, parameter increase, or inference-time cost relative to SDSeg. Since the method adds text encoding and multi-frequency branches, such analysis would strengthen the practical case. Clinical impact remains indirect. The datasets are public and diverse, but there is no validation on a clinical workflow, no expert reader study, and no downstream task analysis. So the work is best viewed as a methodological paper rather than a clinically translated contribution
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.Compared to prior works, this work innovatively integrates textual semantics and multi-frequency structural modeling into the diffusion conditioning, which is well justified for medical images with ambiguous boundaries and low contrast. 2.The TGME module uses DCT-based frequency decomposition and text-guided adaptive weighting. It allows the model to dynamically emphasize high-frequency details (boundaries), mid-frequency structures, or low-frequency global context based on textual prompts. This is biologically plausible and practically beneficial for medical segmentation. 3.The experiments are complete, and the evaluated datasets are diverse. 4.The paper is well organized, with intuitive figures and reasonable explanations. The motivation, method, and logic are easy to follow.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The training loss was not descripted in the whole paper. Please add this content. 2.Can you ensure the alignment between image and text features? How to verify if text and images are aligned? Please provide corresponding attention map. 3.The novelty in core technical components is limited, for example, the ITCF module uses standard cross-attention for image-text fusion. 4.The paper does not provide examples or details of the text prompts used for each dataset. Please provide the details of the text prompts. 5.No robustness testing on noisy, low-quality, or pathological images. 6.Please provide detailed training strategy, such as loss functions.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: A major strength of the paper is the method design. The model decomposes the fused feature into different frequency components, which gives a more fine-grained way to model details, boundaries, and global structure. It then uses a weighting module to adaptively combine these frequency branches, so the text signal can provide more effective guidance during segmentation. This module provides a new angle for fusing text features and image features.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1) A major weakness is that the ablation study is limited to module-level comparisons. It only shows that the proposed module is useful as a whole, but it does not verify whether the high-, mid-, and low-frequency branches actually capture the different types of information claimed by the authors, such as fine details, boundaries, and global structure. Therefore, the current experiments do not fully support the interpretation of the proposed frequency decomposition design. 2) In addition, the paper does not provide enough analysis of the adaptive weighting process, for example how the weights are distributed across different frequency branches in practice. More experimental evidence would be helpful to clarify the contribution of the frequency decomposition design to the fusion of text and image features. 3) The related work discussion is not sufficient, author/s should discuss existing works that adopt Multi-Frequency in greater domain and differentiate the contribution against them.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for their positive feedback on the novel method design (R1, R2, R4), effective experimental results (R1, R2), clear organization (R1, R2), and ablation study (R1), and thank the AC for acknowledging these strengths. Following the rebuttal guidelines, we address remaining concerns below without new experiments. Q1: Frequency branch validation (R4) We clarify that the three frequency branches are defined by pre-defined, non-overlapping DCT coefficient index sets registered as fixed buffers (not learned): high-freq uses top-16 DCT indices (capturing fine-grained details and boundaries), mid-freq uses low-8 indices (structural transitions), and low-freq uses bottom-8 indices (global anatomical context). These index sets are mathematically disjoint by construction, guaranteeing spectral separation. The DCT filters are fixed (register_buffer), so each branch provably receives distinct frequency content. Q2: Adaptive weight distribution analysis (R4) The text-to-frequency mapping is a two-layer MLP (768→128→3) followed by Softmax, producing per-sample weights α_h+α_m+α_l=1 conditioned on each sample’s textual description via mean-pooled Bio-ClinicalBERT embeddings. For example, “Bilateral pulmonary infection, two infected areas, all left lung and all right lung.” and “one medium white round polyp, located in center of the image” encode very different semantic signals, leading to different frequency weight distributions. The Grad-CAM results in Fig. 4 further confirm that TGME shifts attention toward structure-aware regions, consistent with text-driven frequency modulation. Q3: Text prompt details (R1, R2) Text descriptions are publicly available clinical annotations. For QaTa-COV19 and MosMedData+, they are released by LViT [10] authors as structured annotations (.xlsx format) and described with specific lesion characteristics per image (e.g., for one QaTa-COV19 sample: “Bilateral pulmonary infection, three infected areas, upper middle lower left lung and upper middle lower right lung”). For Kvasir-SEG, descriptions were obtained from corresponding paper authors upon request and will be released with our code upon acceptance. All prompts are per-image clinical descriptions providing inherent semantic diversity rather than generic templates. Text robustness analysis is feasible and will be explored. Q4: Training loss and variance reporting (R2,R1) Following SDSeg [12], we adopt L = L_noise + λL_latent, where L_noise predicts Gaussian noise and L_latent minimizes latent estimation error (λ=1, both MAE). Only the condition encoder (ITCF+TGME) is trained; Diffusion backbone and autoencoder remain frozen. Variance reporting and statistical analysis will be included in the revised paper. Q5: Related work on multi-frequency methods (R4) Our TGME differs from prior multi-frequency works (e.g., [15]) in two key aspects: (1) frequency decomposition is applied in the latent conditioning space rather than image space, which is novel for diffusion-based segmentation; (2) frequency reweighting is dynamically text-guided per sample, rather than statically learned. We will expand the related work discussion to highlight these distinctions. Q6: Cross-modal fusion design and alignment (R2) Cross-attention in ITCF computes attention scores between each spatial image position (query) and text tokens (key/value), enabling image features to selectively attend to semantically relevant textual cues. Grad-CAM improvements in Fig. 4 support that meaningful semantic alignment is learned. We will include explicit cross-attention map visualizations upon acceptance. Q7: Novelty (R1, R2) The contribution lies in the principled integration of text-guided semantic conditioning and frequency-domain structural priors within latent diffusion conditioning, unexplored for medical image segmentation. Consistent gains over SDSeg, TSLDeg, and LViT (Table 1) support its practical value.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper introduces TMF-Seg, a text-guided multi-frequency latent diffusion framework that enhances medical image segmentation via image-text fusion and adaptive frequency feature reweighting. title: TG-OT: Topology-Guided CCTA-IVUS Registration via Optimal Transport Matching
reviewer_1_strengths: Using optimal transport for registration is very interesting, in particular in scenarios where little overlap is expected between two masks. The paper shows good results on challenging data. The paper is of very high quality, explains all concepts clearly and understandably, and presents a clear ablation study. Figures illustrate the method well.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: While the method is interesting, results do not entirely convincingly show superiority over alternative approaches. Authors compare their OT scheme (the main contribution) with a Dice-based optimization scheme in Table 2.Results indicate that registration with a Dice loss leads to very similar results. In fact, there’s a bit of a mismatch between the single result shown in Fig. 3 and the aggregate results shown in Table 2.In Table 2, I barely see a difference between Dice and OT (also not in terms of Sc), while in Fig. 3, Dice demonstrates an Sc of 0.12 and OT an Sc of 0.96.This example seems to be an outlier. The Discussion is a bit confusing. It says that ‘the dependency on error-prone intermediate segmentations’ is removed, but as far as I can see, the method directly depends on intermediate segmentations. The difference is not clear to me.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The primary strength of this work is the introduction of a novel approach to coronary image registration.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: However, a key limitation is the lack of clarity in the methodological description, particularly regarding notation. Many symbols used in the solution process are not explicitly defined. For instance, the parameters \theta and z, which appear in the abstract, are never introduced. Similarly, the meanings of M and F in Equation (2), presumably denoting the moving and fixed images, are left to the reader’s inference. It is also unclear what A represents in Equation (2), and the bold symbols \boldsymbol{\mu} and \boldsymbol{v} in Equation (9) are not explained.
reviewer_2_rating: (1) Strong Reject — must be rejected due to major flaws
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.Novelty in Registration Framework / Method: Novel methodology that integrates feature detection within a registration framework. Specifically, novelty is found in using an unbalanced Sinkhorn optimal transport loss to enable registration under large spatial displacement and extensive topological change between modalities. 2.Multimodal Integration: addressing the challenging task of image co-registration of CCTA and IVUS. Integrating information from both modality improves the ability to assess and diagnose coronary artery disease; and allows for a more complete analysis of both vessel morphology and plaque characteristics. 3.Robustness to Challenges: The method addresses challenges in CCTA-IVUS registration, specifically geometric deformation, calcifications, and lumen segmentation. The framework leverages topology-guided constraints and an optimal transport loss to enhance robustness in dealing with these inherently difficult aspects, which traditional registration approaches often struggle with. 4.Clinical Relevance: This improved registration accuracy and robustness has direct clinical relevance for CCTA-IVUS fusion images.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.Limited Generalizability of Dataset: Although results were quantitatively validated on 47 pairs of CCTA-IVUS images, it would be highly desirable to validate results on a much larger, more diverse dataset from various centers. The number and the dataset of the images used in the study, although sufficient for the proof-of-concept study, may not cover all possible clinical scenarios in real clinical practice. 2.Computational Complexity and Efficiency: The optimization of the algorithm for multi-RTX 2080 Ti GPU calculations resulted in the method taking approximately 90 seconds per case on a single RTX 2080 Ti GPU, which, while feasible for research purposes, does not represent real-time clinical efficiency. 3.Lack of Ablation Studies on Specific Components: Although the full pipeline is described, it would give more strength to the paper if more extensive ablation studies could be performed to quantify the contribution of individual components such as the topology-guided constraints and unbalanced Sinkhorn optimal transport loss.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and AC for their constructive feedback, and are encouraged that all reviewers recognize the novelty and clinical relevance of TG-OT. Concerns are grouped below. 1.Apparent similarity of OT and Dice in Table 2 (R1, AC) R1 correctly notes that medians appear close in Table 2, while Fig. 3 shows a large gap. Aggregated metrics mask the relevant signal as cosine similarity has a heavily skewed distribution, and OT’s benefit is concentrated in outlier cases with severe rotational drift. Once predicted plaque/bifurcation locations stop overlapping, Dice’s gradient vanishes, and alignment cannot recover. OT supplies spatially informed gradients via the cylindrical geodesic cost (Eq. 6). This is reflected in (i) Wilcoxon signed-rank significance p<0.01 (Sec. 4), (ii) the Sc Q1 shift (0.92 vs. 0.90), and (iii) Fig. 3, which is a representative drift case. 2.”Removing dependency on intermediate segmentations” (R1) We thank R1 for catching this ambiguity. We refer to volumetric lumen/wall segmentations in the 3D MPR domain, which prior methods (Kadry et al., Li et al.) rely on and which are unreliable under IVUS acoustic shadowing. Our CNN instead predicts only feature presence along radial rays on the (θ, z) cylinder, a well-posed task even under shadowing, and a strictly weaker form of supervision than full volumetric segmentation. We will clarify this in the Discussion. 3.Notation and equation clarity (R2, AC) We note that the highlighted symbols are defined in the following places in the manuscript: M_w (warped moving) and F (fixed) are introduced at the start of Sec. 2.2.(θ, z) are angular and longitudinal coordinates on the unwound cylinder (Sec. 2.1, Fig. 2 caption). A in Eq. 2 is the lumen cross-sectional area, described directly after the equation. In Eq. 8, μ and ν are the marginal probability vectors from Eq. 4, where u and v are the Sinkhorn scaling vectors described after Eq. 7.We agree that A should be labeled explicitly and the kernel iteration made fully self-contained. We thank R2 for their notes on clarity and are committed to improving these passages in a camera-ready version. 4.Reproducibility (R2, R3) Code availability is noted in Sec. 2 of the manuscript. The reference appears as plain text rather than a hyperlink, which may have caused confusion. We will highlight this. 5.Dataset, runtime, ablations (R3) Dataset: We agree that the cohort is relatively small, and we aim to evaluate performance on a larger scale in future work. Nonetheless, the dataset contained considerable variation in plaque burden, pullback length and rotational drift, which motivated our OT formulation. Runtime: Our hardware resources were unfortunately limited to an RTX 2080Ti GPU. Modern hardware would yield runtime speedups, increasing feasibility of time-critical interventions. We would also like to note that for coronary analysis, CCTA-IVUS fusion is typically diagnostic-only with a longer time horizon, allowing for more processing time. Ablations: During method development, sanity checks on synthetic data with non-overlapping and mismatched topologies motivated the unbalanced OT formulation. The 8-page limit led us to prioritize comparison against established baselines on real data. Although we agree that a comprehensive ablation on this would benefit the paper, it cannot be included per the MICCAI rebuttal guidelines. Optional concerns (R1) Frozen CNNs: CNNs are indeed pre-trained, and subsequently employed during the registration phase, which is why we note that feature detection is ‘integrated’ into the registration pipeline. We will gladly make this more explicit. Per-frame rotation correlation: This is exploited via a cumulative B-spline parameterization of θ (Sec. 2.2, Transformation model), enforcing smooth pullback twist informed by global rotational accumulation. Guidewire masking: Feature presence on (θ, z) remains detectable under shadowing, whereas NCC/NMI require pixel-level reliability.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): This paper proposes TG-OT, a topology-guided framework for CCTA–IVUS registration that formulates cross-modality alignment as an optimal transport problem, integrating feature detection and using an unbalanced Sinkhorn formulation to handle large spatial discrepancies and topological variations. Reviewers agree that the paper tackles an important and clinically relevant problem, and that the use of optimal transport for this challenging multimodal registration task is novel and technically interesting, with promising results demonstrated on a paired dataset of 47 patients. title: TGBD-Net: Tumor-Guided Bridging Distillation for Joint EGFR Mutation and Survival Prediction in Lung Cancer from CT Imaging
reviewer_1_strengths: The main contributions are summarized as follows: (1) a unified framework that incorporates patients with single-task labels into joint learning; (2) two complementary representation-level mechanisms that regularize feature formation without requiring tumor annotations for all patients, and enable knowledge transfer across patient subsets with different task labels in a shared representation space; (3) extensive experiments on 7,348 patients demonstrating the robustness of TGBD-Net across multiple tasks.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Methodology: 1、The organization and input pipeline of data for different tasks are not clearly described (i. e. , how different tasks are constructed). For each task, what do the classification and regression heads specifically output? 2、 How is qtg obtained and trained? 3、 Compared with other cross-attention mechanisms, what are the key innovations of the TGF module? 4、 How are the teacher and student models explicitly defined in the bridging distillation process? Experiments: 1、 The authors do not explain why TGBD-Net does not achieve the best performance in terms of sensitivity and specificity. 2、Although extensive comparative experiments are conducted, the paper does not present the detection performance of single-task learning under different supervision settings.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.Clinically motivated problem formulation. Heterogeneous supervision (partial labels, partial annotations) is a genuine, under-addressed challenge in real-world clinical ML. Framing MTL under this constraint is practically relevant. 2.Well-designed BD module. The anchor-based bidirectional distillation mechanism is technically interesting; using K-means prototypes with Hungarian matching to preserve identity across updates is a thoughtful design choice. The two-stage (attribute update → soft label distillation) formulation is clean and clearly explained. 3.Large-scale evaluation. 7,348 patients are a large cohort for this task domain, lending credibility to the reported performance figures. 4.Thorough ablations. The three ablation studies — module combinations, alignment strategies/feature choices, and anchor parameterization strategies — are well-structured and provide meaningful insight into each design decision.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.Single-institution data, no external validation. All 7,348 patients are from one hospital. Without external validation, it is unclear whether the learned representations generalize across scanners, protocols, or institutions. 2.Severe label imbalance in the joint set. Only 383 patients have both EGFR and PFS labels, versus 6,484 with EGFR-only. The BD module is designed to exploit partially labeled samples, but with such an extreme imbalance, the learned anchor attributes for survival may be unreliable. The paper does not analyze sensitivity to this imbalance. 3.PFS test set is very small. The test set contains 735 patients total, but only a fraction have PFS labels (roughly ~96 based on the 8:1:1 split of 481 PFS patients). KM curves show only 86 patients. 4.TGF module design has limited novelty. The tumor-guided cross-attention with conditional alignment is a reasonable engineering choice, but cross-attention with partial supervision is well-established. The claim of novelty here should be more carefully scoped relative to existing tumor-region attention methods in the CT radiogenomics literature (e.g., the MICCAI 2025 paper by Huang et al. (Feature copy paste) on EGFR prediction is cited but not compared against). 5.No comparison against the most relevant prior work on heterogeneous MTL for medical imaging. JTR-MTL (Nishi et al., CVPR 2024) is the closest baseline and was designed specifically for partially labeled MTL, yet the paper does not discuss why TGBD-Net’s BD mechanism is preferable; the analysis remains quantitative only. 6.Hyperparameter sensitivity not analyzed. K=4 anchors, τ=0.2, α=0.9, β=0.5 are set without any sensitivity analysis. Given that these govern the distillation quality, this is an important omission. 7.Model selection criterion is asymmetric. The best model is chosen based on validation AUC (EGFR), and the same checkpoint is used for PFS evaluation. This may systematically favor EGFR performance; a joint validation criterion would be more principled.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: A main strength of the paper is the BD design. I think the way the authors connect anchor-based task memory, task-specific attribute accumulation, and similarity-weighted soft label distillation is quite nice. This makes the framework more than a standard shared-backbone multi-task model, and it gives a reasonable way for partially labeled cases to still contribute across tasks through the shared anchors. Another strength is that this design may help the model capture EGFR-associated radiographic patterns in a more structured way, instead of only relying on a single global shared feature. Together with the tumor-guided feature module, the method tries to organize phenotype-related information in the shared representation while still handling missing labels and missing tumor annotations.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The survival part is still a weakness. PFS is one of the main endpoints, but the paper does not clearly explain the PFS definition, censoring details, or treatment background. Also, the number of PFS cases is much smaller than the EGFR cohort, so the survival results need stronger support. Another weakness is that some interpretation is a bit too strong. TGF alone improves EGFR prediction, but it does not improve the C-index over the baseline, and the tumor-guided feature is much worse than the final fused feature for PFS. So while the full model works better overall, the role of TGF should be discussed more carefully.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: 1.TGF novelty and methodological role Re to R1-C3, R2-C4: The key contribution of TGF is enabling tumor-guided representation regularization under partially available annotations, where attention patterns learned from annotated samples can be implicitly transferred to unannotated patients. Our work primarily focuses on joint EGFR/PFS learning with partially available labels and annotations, which differs from FCP-Net (MICCAI 2025 Huang et al.), which addresses slice-thickness variability through feature copy-paste for EGFR prediction. Re to R3-C2: TGF mainly enhances tumor-focused features, which is more beneficial for EGFR prediction due to tumor morphological patterns in CT, while PFS prediction may require broader surrounding tissue environment. Therefore, the full TGF+BD framework achieves the best overall PFS performance. 2.BD Module and difference from existing MTL methods Re to R1-C4: In BD, anchor-level attributes accumulated from labeled patients serve as teacher signals, while partially labeled patients act as students through bidirectional soft distillation (Sec. 2.2). Re to R2-C5: Compared with JTR-MTL and other optimization-level MTL approaches that mainly address task conflicts or dynamic weighting, BD performs representation-level regularization through bridging anchors in a shared semantic space. 3.Survival cohort, heterogeneous supervision and generalization Re to R2-C1/3, R3-C1: PFS was defined as the time from the initiation of treatment (EGFR-TKI) to the progression of the disease with regular follow-up; 18.5% cases were censored. External multicenter validation will be explored in future work. The PFS cohort is smaller than the EGFR cohort due to the limited availability of longitudinal follow-up data in real-world clinical settings. Nevertheless, the cohort includes heterogeneous acquisition conditions (e.g., varying CT slice thicknesses of 3–8 mm), partially mitigating overfitting to a single acquisition condition. Additionally, compared with many imaging-based survival studies, the current cohort remains relatively large-scale for PFS modeling. Re to R2-C2: To alleviate label imbalance, we adopted a weighted sampling strategy to increase the exposure of PFS samples during training (Sec.3.2). The motivation of BD is to improve PFS learning through joint supervision from the larger EGFR cohort under heterogeneous labeling. Despite limited PFS labels, TGBD-Net achieved the best survival performance among all baselines, supporting the effectiveness of the learned anchor attributes. 4.Experiments and evaluation Re to R1-Exp1/2: Regarding sensitivity/specificity, TGBD-Net achieves the best overall balance between the two metrics while also obtaining the best AUC and C-index. Table 1 includes corresponding single-task baselines (e.g., ResNet, Swin Transformer, DeepSurv), while Sup.-MTL demonstrates that simple joint learning improves over separate single-task modeling. Heterogeneous supervision is only defined in the joint multi-task setting. Re to R2-C7: Since the EGFR cohort is larger, validation AUC provides a relatively more stable selection criterion. All methods were evaluated under the same selection protocol to ensure fair comparison, and TGBD-Net still achieved the best survival performance, suggesting that the learned shared representation does not overfit to EGFR alone. 5.Additional clarifications Re to R1-C1/2: The dataset can be divided according to task labels (EGFR-only/PFS-only/both) and annotation availability, which are unified through the loss routing in Eq. (5). The EGFR head outputs classification logits, while the PFS head outputs a survival risk score. qtg is a learnable token with the same feature dimension as fg in TGF, acting as a tumor-guided prior optimized end-to-end (Sec 2.1). Re to R2-C6: Hyperparameter sensitivity experiments were conducted for K=2/3/4/6, α=0.8/0.9, β=0.5/1.0.The best-performing settings were selected. Due to page limitations, complete results were omitted.

title: The Learnability Gap in Medical Latent Diffusion
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The question of whether latent diffusion models truly preserve clinically useful class information is highly relevant, especially for long-tailed medical datasets where synthetic augmentation is often proposed as a practical solution. 2.The notion of a “learnability gap” is easy to understand and practically meaningful. The distinction between information being preserved and information being easy to learn from is an important one, and the paper makes this point effectively. 3.The analyses of reconstruction fidelity, medical-domain fine-tuning, distillation, and noise conditioning help support the claim that the issue is structural rather than simply due to poor reconstruction quality or insufficient tuning. 4.The presentation is clear, and the main message comes across well.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The diagnosis of the problem is interesting and well supported, but the proposed latent classifier only narrows the gap partially. As a result, the methodological contribution feels more incremental than the analytical one. 2.The paper argues that the problem comes from the structure of the latent space rather than information loss, which is plausible and largely supported by the experiments. However, the more specific explanation involving high-frequency patterns and inter-channel correlations remains a hypothesis rather than something directly demonstrated. 3.A major motivation of the paper is that this learnability gap may limit the usefulness of synthetic data for rare-class medical learning. However, the paper does not directly test whether a larger gap actually leads to worse downstream augmentation performance, weaker rare-class gains, or poorer class-conditional generation. 4.The paper makes a convincing case that latent-space classification is harder, but it would be more compelling to show the downstream effect on diffusion-based data generation itself. 5.Since the work is positioned in the medical imaging domain, it would be helpful to include stronger evidence that the identified issue matters for clinically meaningful pathology preservation, rather than mainly for benchmark classification performance. 6.The results strongly suggest that reconstruction fidelity alone is not the main issue, but some of the wording makes the causal interpretation sound more definitive than the current evidence fully supports.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: Major Strengths: The paper does a great job in identifying and formalizing a problem and then suggesting solutions (distillation from image space, FiLM layers). It also offers a great discussion (e.g., Why does the gap exist?). The choice of datasets for evaluation is also solid and diverse. The motivation of performing this research to explain why generative data augmentation is lacking is clear and well established. The idea is novel and interesting to the audience of MICCAI. Clever use of the Wilcoxon test to quantify the gap.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Major Weaknesses; Weak writing; equations are not clear (e.g. FiLM related equations are introduced without context), and notation is often not explained, while bold values on tables are occasionally incorrect. Figures are also not very intuitive and comprehensive. The paper is poorly organized, and there is more breadth than depth. Documenting the image space extensively is unnecessary since it is similar to the reconstruction space. Similarly, the computational efficiency advantage of latent space inference is well-established in the literature and does not require extensive investigation. This space would be better used for developing the theoretical justification for the gap. It would be interesting to mathematically explain the decomposition/compression of images in latent space and justify why discriminative information is missing. The paper has a very applied approach to a theoretical problem. Finally, I believe contrastive learning and its performance in classification tasks should also be investigated.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The approach of the paper is methodical and sound. 2.The identified learnability gap can have a major impact on using latent generative models for data generation, for the classification task. 3.The paper investigates a few approaches to mitigate the learnability gap. 4.The paper is well written and easy to follow.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.A core motivation of the paper is that synthetic data generated from latent generative models have non-discriminative features in the latent space. This leads to the learnability gap found by the paper. However, the learnability gap only shows that a classifier trained in the latent space performs poorly compared to a classifier trained in the image space. But the motivation seems to claim that this learnability gap can affect the performance of a classifier trained in pixel-space on data generated from latent generative models. This claim is not justified by the paper. 2.Limited novelty from the perspective of the concept: Prior work already suggests that standard VAE/latent-diffusion latent spaces may be poorly aligned with discriminative objectives [1, 2, 3]. This work extends this concept for the medical domain. 3.Can the authors provide evidence for their hypothesis that the reason for the learnability gap is “the pixel-wise reconstruction distributes class-discriminative features across high-frequency spatial patterns and inter-channel correlations that convolutional classifiers struggle to exploit”? [1] Kouzelis, Theodoros, et al. “Eq-vae: Equivariance regularized latent space for improved generative image modeling.” arXiv preprint arXiv:2502.09509 (2025). [2] Leng, Xingjian, et al. “Repa-e: Unlocking vae for end-to-end tuning of latent diffusion transformers.” Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF International Conference on Computer Vision. 2025. [3] Dillon, Barry M., et al. “Better latent spaces for better autoencoders.” SciPost Physics 11.3 (2021): 061.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and AC. R1, R2 and R3 all recognized the originality and clinical relevance of the learnability gap, the methodical analysis (R3), the diverse benchmarks across five autoencoder families (R2), the clear presentation (R1, R3), and the statistical rigour (R2). [A] POSITIONING: FINDING vs. METHOD (R1, R3) The paper is primarily a finding-and-analysis submission. The core contribution is revealing an intrinsic structural bottleneck in medical latent spaces. That the gap remains highly significant (p=9.5e-7 across 20 autoencoder x dataset pairs) even after extensive hyperparameter optimization (HPO), distillation, and noise conditioning is itself the key finding: misalignment between reconstruction fidelity and latent learnability is a fundamental architectural challenge that cannot be tuned away. FiLM and distillation are presented as initial mitigations and diagnostic instruments, not as the contribution. We will revise the framing to emphasize the discovery over the mitigation. [B] PROBING AS A PRINCIPLED LOWER BOUND ON GENERATIVE UTILITY (R1, R2, R3, R3.1) All three reviewers asked about downstream generative augmentation results. Our probing framework is a controlled lower-bound test for that exact question, and we argue it is the more rigorous diagnostic. A class-conditional generator p(z|y) must place mass on the class-conditional manifold in latent space. If a high-capacity HPO-tuned classifier p(y|z), tasked only with finding a decision boundary, cannot reliably extract discriminative features from the latents even with noise conditioning and image-space distillation, then no diffusion model trained with denoising losses on the same latents can be expected to allocate density to features it cannot itself separate. Probing isolates the diagnosis from the well-known confounders of generative training, such as schedule choice, classifier-free guidance scale, sample budget, and the FID vs downstream-bACC reporting mismatch. By identifying this gap at the autoencoder stage we provide a diagnostic tool, i.e., high reconstruction fidelity is a deceptive metric, and if the latent space is unlearnable, synthetic data will suffer from feature collapse regardless of diffusion training. This directly addresses R3.1. [C] CLINICAL PATHOLOGY PRESERVATION (R1.5) bACC, AUC and MCC are computed on clinical labels including pneumothorax, melanoma, AVSD and the CT-RATE findings, which are the pathologies that synthetic augmentation is intended to enrich. The gap is therefore measured on the clinical task that motivates the pipeline. R1.2, R3.3 Causal language around the decoder reassembling features. We agree this should be nuanced. We will frame the CNN-unfriendly latent format as the most plausible structural explanation consistent with our failure-to-learn results, rather than a proven cause. R2.2 Image vs Reconstruction space, purpose of the comparison. Comparing Image vs Reconstruction tests whether the autoencoder retains information; comparing Reconstruction vs Latent tests whether that information is accessible. This triangulation is essential to prove the gap is a learnability issue and not simple information loss. We will state this explicitly. R3.2 Novelty relative to cited prior work. We will cite Dillon and expand the discussion of Kouzelis and Leng, which are already cited as refs 20 and 21.Beyond demonstrating that this gap persists in medical imaging, we investigate it using probing, which unlike prior natural-image work does not rely on the confounding generative training and sampling process. The empirical finding that medical-domain autoencoder fine-tuning (MedVAE vs MedVAE-FT) does not close the gap and in fact widens it relative to RS is a direct counter to the prevailing assumption in the medical generative literature that domain-specific autoencoders solve the problem. We respectfully ask to be evaluated on the diagnosis and the framework, both of which we believe the evidence supports.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper focuses on the difficulty of downstream classification from the latent representations of autoencoders and proposes a solution to partially address this challenge. title: Through-Plane Attention for Anisotropic CT Super-Resolution Improves Quantitative Lung Cancer Analysis
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.I’m very familiar with the SR works and examined many approaches, this field in general is very challenging because the current benchmarks are extremely high and hard to beat so I welcome the authors effort to improve on top existing methods. The TAB is actual less impressive than hybrid pseudo LR aug. it’s a good approach to mitigate the data size limitation and homogeneity of real paired SR data. 2.the evaluation that improves downstream task is valuable empirical evidence on the importance of SR with a variety of task types. the paper reports consistent imporvements over original TVSRN in several settings, and the segmnetation gain on real low res CT is noticable. 3.the inclusion of extra large external validation is a strength
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.the novelty of the v2 is relatively low compare to previous work. the paper highlighted TAB as central new contribution, but TVSRN already has a TAB inside the decoder’s FIM, with two parallel branches on coronal and sagittal view. the difference is just very minor. 2.the main competition method shouldn’t be TVSRN, it should eb CTHNet which is an improved version of TVSRN and the performance is really good on the CTHNet with several substantial redesign of the architecture. 3.the empirical gains are mixed relative to the strength of the claims. reviewer_2_strengths: The problem is important, common in clinical practice, and well-motivated. The method is well-designed with a clear focus on through-plane modeling. The evaluation is comprehensive, including multi-center validation and multiple downstream tasks.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The comparisons are not fully sufficient to establish the necessity and uniqueness of the proposed design, lacking stronger 3D or inter-slice modeling baselines. The paper provides limited analysis on why downstream improvements are achieved beyond reporting performance gains.
